results.coverage:
Read every line of all 12 assigned files: engine.rs (1494 lines), serve.rs, lib.rs, time.rs, paths.rs, proc.rs, handlers/mod.rs, handlers/bus.rs, handlers/audit.rs, audit.rs, build.rs and Cargo.toml.

To check that each finding is reachable, I traced into:
- socket.rs: the bus.wait/subscribe fan-out, the inline answers_from_memory dispatch, and bind/lock.
- guardrail.rs and handlers/guardrail.rs: confirm/replay, enforce, evaluate_granted, refuse_or_user_hold.
- handlers/file.rs: root_choice / default_worktree_in.
- handlers/session.rs: the staged create/spawn/close prepares.
- handlers/task.rs (dispatch), handlers/workspace.rs (clone/remove), handlers/git.rs (commit/push/pr), worktree.rs (git()), recovery.rs (retention/VACUUM), store.rs (open/lock), sessions.rs, branch_cleanup.rs, device.rs/device_lease.rs.
- relay-bus registry/ops/schema, relay-cli main.rs (actor override, PreToolUse adapter) and mcp.rs.
- relay-native: client timeouts, the event apply path, the undo caller.

Every caller of output_with_timeout, and every `.output()`/`.status()` in relay-core, was listed and classified as locked or unlocked. The pedantic clippy file was grepped for my files; only benign casts appeared (pid u32→i32, epoch/seq u64→i64). jiff 0.2.35's Sub panic was confirmed from registry source. A read-only `ps` showed the running adb server is its own session leader, so the group kill does not reach it.

Not verified at runtime: no cargo, tests or app were run. The VACUUM cost, the schema render time, the audit growth rate and the lock-contention effects are estimates from code and file sizes. I did not confirm which real-world daemons keep inherited pipes open (the proc.rs finding is rated medium confidence for that reason). I did not run EXPLAIN on audit queries against the live store.

Two issues were dropped as too contrived: an inline keystroke write blocking a tokio worker (it needs more than ~640 KB of unread PTY input), and the post-exit group kill reaching non-setsid daemons. socket.rs issues outside event fan-out (unbounded line length, head-of-line blocking on the shared mpsc) were left to the socket/door chunk. The phone app was ignored per scope.

findings.title: guardrail.confirm replays a held agent op without the agent's session, so a confirmed agent file.write lands in the project's primary checkout
findings.evidence: `replay_registered` swaps only `actor` and `skip_policy` (`let prior_actor = std::mem::replace(&mut self.actor, actor); let prior_policy = self.skip_policy.replace(skip_policy);`). `self.session_id` stays the confirmer's, which is None for the user. `confirm` calls it at handlers/guardrail.rs:583 and only calls `ctx.set_session(hold.session_id)` afterwards, at :593. The replayed `file.write` resolves its target with `root(ctx, p.project_id, p.worktree.as_deref())` (file.rs:73), which goes through `root_choice(ctx.tx(), ctx.actor_session_id(), ..)` (file.rs:452) to `default_worktree_in`. With `session_id: None, requested: None` that returns `repo`, the primary checkout (file.rs:401-407). Agents get holds rather than refusals for `destructive_write` and `shape_gate` (guardrail.rs:1035-1036). The frozen payload has no `worktree`: fill_identity fills only required fields, and neither the MCP server nor the CLI adds it. Nested staged prepares inherit the same `session_id: self.session_id` (engine.rs:337). `evaluate_granted` also skips the agent's grants when session_id is None (guardrail.rs:484).
findings.impact: Trigger: an agent with bus writes (this user's sessions expose file_write) calls `file.write {project_id, path, text}` on a modified or untracked file, removing at least 50 lines and 40%. The write is held. The user clicks Confirm, and the text is written to `<primary checkout>/<path>` instead of the agent's worktree, with the destructive-write check skipped through skip_policy. Any uncommitted user edits to that file in the main checkout are overwritten without a check. The agent's worktree never receives the write, but the agent is told it succeeded. A second hold raised during the replay is stored with session_id NULL. The only replay test, phase8.rs `a_held_commit_still_commits_when_confirmed`, uses a user-held op, where both sessions are None.
findings.fix: Have `replay_registered` take the hold's session id (and project) and swap `self.session_id` for the duration, the same way it swaps `actor`. Have `confirm` pass `hold.session_id`. As a second guard, when a hold is created, pin the resolved worktree into the frozen payload (insert `worktree` when absent) so a replay cannot re-resolve it. Add a test: an agent file.write held by destructive_write and confirmed by the user must change the file in the agent's worktree and leave the primary checkout untouched.

v1.reason: engine.rs:364-376 `replay_registered` swaps only `actor` and `skip_policy`. `self.session_id` stays the confirmer's: None for a user, since session_id comes from resolve_actor (engine.rs:831). confirm (handlers/guardrail.rs:582-583) replays a non-gate frozen op and calls `ctx.set_session(hold.session_id)` only afterwards (:593). Bus-op holds come from `enforce` (guardrail.rs:672-704), which freezes `ctx.payload()` unchanged. fill_identity (engine.rs:1139-1170) adds only required project_id/session, never the optional `worktree`. For agents, refuse_or_user_hold (guardrail.rs:1035-1036) holds rather than refuses for destructive_write and shape_gate. On replay, file.write's `root()` (file.rs:449-456) -> root_choice -> default_worktree_in (file.rs:392-409) returns `repo`, the primary checkout, when session_id is None and requested is None. The write then proceeds there with destructive_write skipped, overwriting whatever the user has in the main checkout, and the agent's worktree never changes. The same applies to git.commit: its prepare uses resolve_root_unlocked with the Unlocked session_id copied from self.session_id (engine.rs:337, git.rs:766-773). A confirmed agent commit held by shape_gate therefore runs `git add -A` (if `all`) and commits in the user's primary checkout. The only replay tests (phase8.rs:159-175, 526-557) confirm user-originated holds, where both session ids are None.
v1.correction: Precondition: the default role allowlists (settings.rs:36-38) do not grant agents file.write/file.create/file.delete/git.commit, so this needs a customised role config. This user's sessions do expose file_write and git_commit, so it is reachable here. A confirmed user click in a normal review flow is enough to trigger it. The git.commit variant (commit or `add -A` in the primary checkout) is a second consequence worth naming. Fix as proposed: have replay_registered take and swap the hold's session_id, and pin the resolved worktree into the frozen payload when the hold is created. Add an agent-held destructive_write and confirm test that asserts the agent's worktree changed and the primary checkout did not.

v2.reason:
I traced this myself.

(a) The code does what the finding says.
- engine.rs:371-372: `replay_registered` swaps only `actor` and `skip_policy`.
- A user confirmer's `Ctx.session_id` is None: `resolve_actor` returns Ok(None) for User (engine.rs:1355), and `ConfirmIn` carries only `{hold_id, scope}`.
- `confirm` (handlers/guardrail.rs:583) replays a non-gate frozen op, and sets the session only afterwards (:593).
- The frozen payload is the request exactly as sent. `enforce` freezes `ctx.payload()` (handlers/guardrail.rs:689). The MCP `call_tool` forwards the agent's arguments unchanged (mcp.rs:139-147). `fill_identity` adds only the required `project_id`/`session`. So `worktree`, which is optional, is absent.
- On replay, `file.write` calls `root()` (file.rs:73). That goes to `root_choice(.., ctx.actor_session_id()=None, ..)` (file.rs:452) and then `default_worktree_in`, whose `None => Ok(repo)` (file.rs:404) picks the primary checkout. `worktree::contains` accepts it (worktree.rs:164, `canon(repo) == want`).
- `enforce` then runs with `skip_policy="destructive_write"`, so the size check against the primary's file is skipped. The handler writes `<primary>/<path>` through temp-and-rename. `file.write` records no undo and no trash.

(b) Reachability. It is reachable in the default configuration, not only with a customised role config.
- The native launch dialog sets "Allow agent bus writes" on by default (apps/relay-native/src/launch.rs:264-265).
- guardrail.rs:363-366 then admits every `file.*` op for any role with `bus_writes`. This session's own MCP list includes `file_write`.
- Trigger: an agent calls the bus `file.write` (MCP `file_write` or `relay q`) without `worktree` and without `expected_sha256`, on a file that is untracked or modified in its worktree (with `allow_if_recoverable`, git-restorable files are allowed, guardrail.rs:725-729). The write must remove more than 50 lines, or more than 40% of a file of at least 30 lines (guardrail.rs:720-721).
- `refuse_or_user_hold` holds agents for `destructive_write`/`shape_gate` (guardrail.rs:1035).
- The user sees "<agent> is waiting on you" and clicks "Allow once" (guardrail_pages.rs:299). That is the normal flow.
- Frequency is lower than the finding implies. Agents usually write with their native Write/Edit tools, and those go through `guardrail.gate`, whose confirm branch correctly uses the session's worktree. BUS.md §9.3 says providers do not normally call `file.write`. Still, nothing steers agents away from it.

(c) Consequence. Every time it fires:
- The agent's text is written into the user's primary checkout, with the destructive-write guard skipped.
- Any uncommitted user edits to that path are destroyed, with no undo or trash.
- Otherwise the main working tree is silently dirtied with agent content that could be committed to main.
- The agent's worktree never receives the change. The outcome shows success, so the UI raises nothing.
- The agent only sees `guardrail.resolved{state: confirmed}`. This branch returns at :596 before the mailbox message that §9.4 promises.

(d) Severity. The rubric lists data loss/corruption as critical, and this is reachable by a normal click in the default setup, so I keep critical, with the caveat that the precondition is uncommon.

(e) The fix is correct.
- Every consumer reads `self.session_id`: root resolution, grant loading (guardrail.rs:484), attribution of a nested hold, and nested staged prepares (engine.rs:337). Swapping it to `hold.session_id` and restoring it afterwards fixes all of them.
- If the session closed in the meantime, holds expire, or `default_worktree_in` errors with "bound session vanished", or `root_verify` fails. All of those are safe failures.
- Pinning `worktree` into the frozen payload passes schema validation: every caller of `enforce` (file.write, create, rename, move, delete, import, and git.commit) declares `worktree: Option<String>` under `deny_unknown_fields`. But it departs from D35's "exact original payload", so it is optional. The session swap alone is sufficient.
v2.correction:
1. The first verifier's git.commit variant is wrong. `evaluate_commit` has only the `protected_path` and `cap` policies, and `refuse_or_user_hold` refuses an agent on both rather than holding it (guardrail.rs:1035-1047). An agent's `git.commit` therefore never creates a hold, so there is no agent commit replay.
   - Agent holds raised through the bus come only from `file.write` (`destructive_write`, `shape_gate`, the 64 MiB cap) and from `file.create` (`shape_gate`, whose default list is empty).
   - `file.delete`/`rename`/`move`/`import` pass the file's own text through `guard_path_mutation`, so they never trip `destructive_write`.
   - git.rs:773 belongs in "related" only as the shared mechanism.

2. The precondition is not a customised role config. `bus_writes` is on by default in the native launch dialog (launch.rs:264-265).

3. The trigger is "more than 50 lines OR more than 40% of a file of at least 30 lines", not "50 lines and 40%". It applies only to a file git cannot restore: untracked, modified or staged in the agent's worktree.

4. Mitigations the finding omits:
   - If the agent supplied `expected_sha256`, the replay compares it against the primary's file and fails with `file.edit_conflict`, with no write (file.rs:77-90).
   - If the agent passed `worktree` explicitly, the replay hits the right tree.
   - Only the omitted-worktree, no-sha case writes to the primary checkout.
   - Actual loss of user work additionally needs uncommitted edits to that path in the primary. Otherwise it is a misplaced write plus a missing agent change.

5. "The agent is told it succeeded": more precisely, the agent sees only `guardrail.resolved{confirmed}`. The non-gate branch skips the mailbox message that §9.4 promises.

6. A secondary symptom: with `session_id` None, the agent's grants are not loaded (guardrail.rs:484). A write that relied on a `protected_path` grant is refused on replay, and the user sees "Allowed, but the action then failed".

7. Fix: swapping `session_id` in `replay_registered` is sufficient. Pinning `worktree` is optional belt-and-braces. The proposed test should omit `expected_sha256`.

findings.title: invoke_registered runs a nested staged op's prepare phase (git fetch, worktree add, hook installs) under the caller's store lock, and task.dispatch and project.remove reach it in normal flows
findings.evidence: The comment at engine.rs:325-327 says a staged op reaches this path only when `guardrail.confirm` replays a held commit ("only on this path"). In fact these calls also run `prepare(&mut stage, &payload)?` (engine.rs:342) with `held: Some(self.tx)` inside the outer transaction: `ctx.invoke_registered("session.create", ..)` (task.rs:683) and `ctx.invoke_registered(op /* session.spawn, wake or resume */, ..)` (task.rs:712) inside `task.dispatch` (plain `e.register::<Dispatch>`, task.rs:1049), and `session.close` inside project.remove (workspace.rs:328). session.create's prepare runs `refresh_new_worktree`, which calls `fetch_remote` (`git fetch --all --prune`, 20 s timeout, git.rs:969-972), then `worktree::create` (`git worktree add`, 120 s), then hook installs. The spawn and wake prepares (`stage_launch`/`prepare_launch`) install hooks (git subprocesses with 10 s timeouts), materialize skills and write brief files. The native client gives task.dispatch a 180 s timeout because of this (client.rs:69).
findings.impact: `relay cmd task.dispatch {task_id, create:{..}}`, or `fanout:true` with one create per child, holds the single store mutex for the whole fetch and checkout. Every other request blocks for seconds to minutes, including every agent's PreToolUse guardrail.gate (which blocks the agent), session.report and UI refreshes. The UI's Dispatch button on a created, parked or restorable session holds the lock through the hook and skill installs. There is also a latent deadlock: `Unlocked::engine()` lets a prepare call `engine.store.lock()` or `system_write` directly, and git.branch.cleanup's prepare does (branch_cleanup::run at branch_cleanup.rs:357 and 388). If such an op is ever nested, the dispatch thread blocks on its own non-reentrant mutex and the whole engine freezes.
findings.fix: Stop running prepare phases under the lock for composite ops. Give task.dispatch (and project.remove's close loop) their own register_staged prepare that runs the nested ops' external phases first, or split dispatch into an unlocked create/launch followed by a short locked assignment. Keep the held-connection fallback only for the confirm replay. Add a debug assertion or test that no prepare reachable through invoke_registered takes `engine.store` directly.

v1.reason: engine.rs:325-327 says a staged op reaches invoke_registered's prepare-under-lock path only through `guardrail.confirm`. That is false. task.dispatch (task.rs:1049, plain `e.register`) calls `ctx.invoke_registered("session.create", ..)` (task.rs:683) and then `ctx.invoke_registered(op, ..)` for session.spawn/wake/resume (task.rs:712). Both run their register_staged prepare with `held: Some(self.tx)` (engine.rs:328-342). session.create's prepare (session.rs:833-893) runs refresh_new_worktree -> fetch_remote, `worktree::create` and `hooks::install_git`. stage_launch/prepare_launch install git, Claude and Codex hooks, materialize skills and write brief files. project.remove with force invokes session.close (workspace.rs:328), whose prepare runs run_teardown (hook uninstalls). All of this holds the single store mutex.
v1.correction: Reachability is narrower than claimed. The native client never sends task.dispatch with `create`: launch.rs:810 creates sessions separately and dispatches with `session` and `start:false`. task_pages.rs:652 passes an existing `session`. The `fetch` plus `git worktree add` under the lock is reachable only through a manual `relay cmd`/MCP task.dispatch with `create` (or fanout), not a normal UI flow. The normal-flow cost is the UI Dispatch button on a created, parked or restorable session with start defaulting to true. That holds the lock through hook installs, skill copies and brief writes: hundreds of milliseconds, bounded by 10 s timeouts. The deadlock is not live. No prepare reachable through invoke_registered takes `engine.store` directly today (skills::apply only uses store.skills_dir(); its store.lock() calls are in tests). branch_cleanup's direct lock is only reachable if git.branch.cleanup is ever nested or held, and nothing does that now. Fix the misleading comment, and run task.dispatch's launch phase unlocked (register_staged, or launch after commit).

findings.title: Locked handlers run git clone, gh pr create and git commit with no deadline, bypassing proc::output_with_timeout
findings.evidence: `e.register::<ProjectClone>` (workspace.rs:228) runs `Command::new("git").current_dir(..).arg("clone")..output()` inside the request transaction, with no timeout and no GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0. `e.register::<PrOpen>` (git.rs:666) runs `gh pr create` via `cmd.output()` (git.rs:680). git.commit's staged finish phase, which also runs inside the transaction, calls `worktree::git_mutate(&root, &["commit", "--no-verify", ..])` (git.rs:571). That is `Command::new("git")..output()` (worktree.rs:27). proc.rs:3-6 states that every subprocess forked from inside a handler goes through output_with_timeout. project.clone's op summary says "(async; project.changed when done)" and BUS.md §5.1 says it returns a handle, but the handler is synchronous.
findings.impact: The onboarding clone (onboarding.rs:527, client timeout 1800 s) freezes the whole bus for as long as the clone runs: agents' hooks block and the UI stalls. Cloning a private HTTPS repo with GIT_ASKPASS or SSH_ASKPASS set (for example KDE's ksshaskpass) opens a password dialog, and the bus stays frozen until it is answered. `git commit` under the lock still runs the post-commit hook (--no-verify does not skip it) and gpg signing, so a pinentry prompt freezes everything. Quitting during any of these also hangs: shutdown()/mark_restorable wait for the store lock, and dropping the tokio runtime waits for the blocking task.
findings.fix: Route all three through proc::output_with_timeout, with GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0 set and GIT_ASKPASS/SSH_ASKPASS cleared. Make project.clone a real handle op: clone on a worker, then system_write project.add on completion, or use register_staged with the clone in prepare. Move `gh pr create` into a staged prepare. Give git_mutate a deadline. Add a check (a test or clippy disallowed-methods) that bans `Command::output` and `Command::status` in relay-core.

v1.reason: workspace.rs:228-237: `e.register::<ProjectClone>` runs `Command::new("git")...arg("clone")...output()` inside the locked handler transaction. It has no timeout, does not set GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0 and does not clear askpass. The op is called from onboarding.rs:527 with a client timeout of 1800 s (client.rs:67), so a large clone holds the store mutex, and with it every request, for its whole duration. That contradicts proc.rs:3-6. git.rs:666-681: `e.register::<PrOpen>` runs `gh pr create` via `cmd.output()` under the lock. That is a network call with no deadline, and the op has no actor restriction. git.rs:571: the staged finish of git.commit (which runs in the transaction) calls worktree::git_mutate -> git() (worktree.rs:24-31), a plain `.output()`. Commit is usually fast, but signing/pinentry or a slow post-commit hook would block the bus. Command::output gives the child a null stdin, but git can still prompt via /dev/tty when the engine has a controlling terminal (`relay serve` from a shell), or via GIT_ASKPASS/SSH_ASKPASS dialogs.
v1.correction: The worst case is project.clone, which turns a normal flow into a multi-minute bus freeze. git.pr.open is the next worst (network). git.commit's risk is narrower (signing/hooks). Fix: register_staged with the clone/gh in the prepare phase (as git.fetch/git.push already do, git.rs:582-600), run through proc::output_with_timeout with GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0 and askpass cleared, and give git_mutate a deadline. worktree::git() is also used by other locked handlers (e.g. CleanMerged via list_with_dirty), so a lint banning Command::output in relay-core is worthwhile.

v2.reason:
(a) The code does what the finding says.
- `project.clone` is registered with plain `e.register` (workspace.rs:228). The pipeline therefore takes `self.store.lock()` and opens the transaction before calling the handler (engine.rs:954-980). That lock is a plain std Mutex with no timed acquire (store.rs:474). It is released only after commit (engine.rs:1024-1025).
- Inside that, workspace.rs:234 runs `Command::new("git")…arg("clone")…output()` with no deadline and no `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT`.
- The same holds for `gh pr create` via `cmd.output()` in a plain `register` handler (git.rs:666-681), and for `git commit` in git.commit's staged finish (git.rs:571, reaching worktree.rs:24-31).
- Nothing upstream handles it: the socket door has no special case for these ops.
- This is an oversight, not a decision:
  - `skill.install`, which does its own GitHub `git clone`, is `register_staged` "to keep a slow clone off every other op (D144)" (provider.rs:209-211).
  - `github.connect` uses an after_commit worker.
  - device.run's `git fetch` runs in `run_worker`.
  - D149's list of converted ops (DECISIONS.md:812-814) omits project.clone and git.pr.open.
- The docs drift is real:
  - ops/workspace.rs:38 says "(async; project.changed when done)".
  - BUS.md:246-247 lists project.clone among the ops that return a handle.
  - The code, and BUS.md:657, return the project synchronously.

(b) Who can trigger it, and how often.
- `project.clone` is UserOnly. It is not only first-run onboarding: the same panel is the general "Add project" flow, opened from the Add project button (app.rs:976-978), the registry menu (shell/registry.rs:164/362/472) and the launcher (launch.rs:358).
- So a clone normally happens while agent sessions are running. Each clone stalls the store for its whole length: seconds for a small repo, minutes for a large or LFS-heavy one. The client allows 1800 s (client.rs:67).
- `git.pr.open` is reachable from the Code page (code_git.rs:662) and admits all actors. It costs a few seconds of GitHub API round-trips per PR, more on a bad network.
- `git.commit`'s finish is normally fast.

(c) What happens while the clone runs.
- Every request that touches the store waits on the mutex. Every agent socket request takes it in `check_session_token` (engine.rs:1377-1378), so every agent's PreToolUse `guardrail.gate` and every MCP call waits. Provider pre-tool hooks time out at 30 s (hooks.rs:351, :521). The PTY-exit and idle bookkeeping writes wait too.
- The UI sends `project.clone` on its shared control connection (app.rs:1111-1116). The engine serves one request per connection at a time (socket.rs:335). Every other UI data request therefore queues and fails at the 30 s client timeout ("outcome is unknown"), and a queued mutation may still apply later.
- The GTK thread is not blocked. User keystrokes, resizes and terminal output keep working through the D148 fast path, so "freezes the whole bus" is slightly overstated.
- Unbounded variants: a private HTTPS repo with no credential helper makes git prompt.
  - With SSH_ASKPASS or GIT_ASKPASS set, the prompt is a GUI dialog.
  - With the engine started by run.sh from a terminal, git reads /dev/tty. I checked this with a throwaway script: a `nohup … </dev/null &` child of a non-interactive script kept `pts/7` and could open /dev/tty.
  - In either case the store stays locked until someone answers.
- Quitting or SIGTERM also waits until the clone ends, because `shutdown()` and `mark_restorable` lock the store (engine.rs:643, 663) whenever PTYs or runs are live.

(d) High is the right severity: a bus-wide stall in a normal flow, lasting as long as the clone. It is not critical: in the common case it is bounded and sessions recover afterwards. On their own, git.pr.open would be medium and the commit low, but all three share this root cause.

(e) The fix direction is right but needs the refinements listed in the correction.
v2.correction:
1) The git.commit sub-claim is narrower than stated.
- Keeping the commit inside the transaction is documented: git.rs:531-534 says "the transaction only sees the gate and the commit itself", and D149 agrees.
- The post-commit-hook claim holds only for commits on the primary checkout. In Relay session worktrees, the worktree-scoped `core.hooksPath` points at `.relay/hooks/<session>/`, which holds only `pre-commit` (hooks.rs:68-153), and `--no-verify` skips that.
- gpg/ssh signing prompts still apply.
- Treat it as a low-impact related instance that needs a deadline, not as a co-headline.

2) Corrections to the related list.
- hooks.rs:212 (`run_user_pre_commit`) runs in git.commit's unlocked prepare (git.rs:555). It has no deadline, but it does not hold the store mutex, except when `guardrail.confirm` replays a held commit (D149).
- The first verifier's "CleanMerged via list_with_dirty" is wrong. `list_with_dirty` uses only gix (worktree.rs:135-155). CleanMerged reaches `worktree::git()` through `git_mutate("branch -d")` at git.rs:712.
- The other locked `git_mutate` callers (git.rs:374/485/503/527/712, file.rs:256) share the root cause, at low impact because they are local and fast.

3) The `register_staged` option is an incomplete fix for project.clone.
- The engine serves the UI's control connection one request at a time, so the UI would still stall for the length of the clone.
- Make it the documented handle op instead: an after_commit worker like device.run or github.connect, which emits `project.changed` and writes the `project.clone.completed` audit row (BUS.md §5.1). The onboarding panel then waits for the event.
- At minimum, also route project.clone onto its own connection in client.rs.
- A timeout alone under the lock fixes nothing, because a real clone needs a deadline of several minutes.

4) Prompt suppression needs more than clearing the variables.
- Set `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0`, and set `GIT_ASKPASS` to an empty string rather than removing it. If `GIT_ASKPASS` is unset, git falls back to `core.askPass` and then to `SSH_ASKPASS`.
- Also remove `SSH_ASKPASS`, and use `GIT_SSH_COMMAND='ssh -o BatchMode=yes'` for ssh URLs.
- For gh, set `GH_PROMPT_DISABLED=1` and move the call into a staged prepare with `output_with_timeout`.

5) Use a deadline per call site, not one across all of `git_mutate`. `git_mutate` also runs `git push` in a staged prepare (git.rs:617), where a large or LFS push legitimately takes a long time.

6) A blanket clippy disallowed-methods ban on `Command::output`/`status` would hit about 30 relay-core sites. Many are legitimate (workers, unlocked paths, tests), so each would need an explicit allow.

7) Not established: what Claude Code or Codex do when the 30 s PreToolUse hook times out. If they treat a timeout as non-blocking, guarded tools would run unchecked during a long clone. This needs a separate check.

findings.title: guardrail.gate audit rows store each agent edit's full file text (up to 64 KB), because the chatty-op cap misses the hottest op
findings.evidence: `fn store_limit(op)` caps only `"session.report" | "usage.report"` at 2 KB. Every other op keeps up to 64 KB of payload (line 88). guardrail.gate is `OpMeta::mutation(..)` with the default `Audit::Always` (relay-bus ops/guardrail.rs:16-17). The Claude PreToolUse adapter sends the whole post-edit file as `new_text` for every Edit and MultiEdit, and the full content for Write (relay-cli main.rs:415, 426-432, 455-459). The comment above CHATTY_STORE_LIMIT says 64 KB per chatty row is what grew the audit table past the rest of the store put together.
findings.impact: Every Edit by every Claude agent appends a row holding the whole file. engine.rs, for example, is 61 KB and is stored in full on every edit. A few hundred edits a day across agents is tens of MB a day, and with the 180-day retention the store grows to GBs. Once rows start ageing out, every launch prunes some and then runs a full `VACUUM` of the whole store under the lock (recovery.rs:217-221), so startup gets slower as the store grows. These rows also let any agent read other agents' file contents through audit.get and audit.list.
findings.fix: Store a digest instead of the `new_text`/`diff` bodies: keep path, kind, byte length and sha256. payload_hash is computed over the full payload before storage, so idempotency is unaffected. At minimum, add guardrail.gate to the bounded set. Also run VACUUM only above a free-page threshold (PRAGMA freelist_count), not whenever any row was pruned.

v1.reason: I checked this myself. audit.rs:22-27 `store_limit` returns 2 KB only for "session.report" | "usage.report", and every other op gets STORE_LIMIT = 64 KB (line 14, applied at 88). guardrail.gate is `OpMeta::mutation(..)` with no `.audit(..)` override (relay-bus ops/guardrail.rs:16-17), so it is Audit::Always. `should_audit` (engine.rs:1394-1400) audits it for every actor. hooks.rs:349 installs the Claude PreToolUse hook with matcher "Edit|Write|MultiEdit|Bash". The adapter (relay-cli main.rs:412-459) reads the target file, applies the edit and sends the whole post-edit file as `new_text` on every Edit and MultiEdit, and the full `content` on Write. So each agent edit to a file whose JSON-escaped text is under 64 KB stores the whole file in the audit row. The comment at audit.rs:16-19 names 64 KB of per-tool-use payload as what grew the table past the rest of the store; guardrail.gate runs at that same per-tool-use frequency but was left out of the bounded set. Default retention is 180 days (recovery.rs:18). Once rows start ageing out, every launch prunes some and runs a full `VACUUM` (recovery.rs:217-221), so startup cost grows with store size.
v1.correction: Retention bounds the growth at 180 days. It is GB-scale rather than unbounded, and a typical file is 10-30 KB rather than 61 KB. The claim about agents reading other agents' files through audit.get/list adds little, because agents can already read the same repository through file.read. Simplest fix: add "guardrail.gate" to the CHATTY_STORE_LIMIT arm, or store path, kind, length and sha256 in place of new_text/diff. payload_hash is computed before truncation, so idempotency is unaffected. Gating VACUUM on PRAGMA freelist_count is a sensible second step.

v2.reason:
(a) The mechanism is real; I checked it in the code. audit.rs:22-27 caps only "session.report" | "usage.report" at 2 KB, and every other op stores up to 64 KB (line 88). guardrail.gate is `OpMeta::mutation(..)` with no override (relay-bus ops/guardrail.rs:16-17), which defaults to Audit::Always (registry.rs:114-118). install_claude runs on every Claude launch (handlers/session.rs:483) and installs a PreToolUse hook with matcher "Edit|Write|MultiEdit|Bash" (hooks.rs:349). That hook's adapter (relay-cli main.rs:406-459) sends the whole post-edit file as `new_text` for Edit and MultiEdit, and the full `content` for Write. engine.rs:1000-1015 (allowed) and 1040-1055 (held or refused, the commit_error path) append `&req.payload` unchanged. An Edit to engine.rs produces a 63,221-byte payload, under 65,536, so it is stored whole, as the finding says.

(b) This fires on every Claude Edit, Write and MultiEdit, which is the core flow. I measured it on a scratch copy of the user's live dev store, running only aggregate queries and never opening the live file. From Sep 5 to Oct 6 there are 32,414 gate rows. Of these, 1,542 are write rows holding 24.0 MB: 15.6 KB on average, 65,418 B at most, and 22.8 MB of it is new_text. Another 116 rows were over the limit and kept only the marker. Gate rows make up 42.7 MB of the 59.8 MB of audit payload (71%). session.report, the op D151 capped, accounts for 16.7 MB. Active days add 0.2-4.2 MB of write payload, about 1.5 MB/day on average over Sep 23-Oct 6. Repeated edits pile up: scripts/combat.gd has 30 edits at about 56 KB each, 1.65 MB in total.

(c) The effect is storage growth from duplicated file text. Nothing is lost or wrong, and the bus does not freeze (the extra insert takes well under a millisecond). The audit table is already the largest object in the store: 84 MB plus about 20 MB of indexes, out of 182 MB after one month. At the measured rate, write rows level off at about 270 MB once the 180-day retention starts pruning, or about 0.5 GB counting exec rows. Upgrade backups are full copies (KEEP_BACKUPS=5), so each carries the same bloat. After day 180, every launch prunes and then VACUUMs the whole store before the doors open. That took 0.27 s for the current 190 MB copy on tmpfs; on the real btrfs disk it would take a few seconds at the steady-state size.

(d) This is not high. Growth stops at the retention window (D151), and it causes no failure, freeze or user-visible misbehaviour. It is a concrete ongoing cost (store size, backup size, launch VACUUM time) of exactly the kind D151 already judged worth fixing for session.report. That makes it medium.

(e) Bounding this payload is safe. payload_hash covers the full JSON before truncation (audit.rs:82-83). Holds freeze the envelope in holds.envelope (guardrail.rs:1223-1234, 1281-1288). Undo uses the undo_op column. The tests in tests/guardrails.rs:146 and 256 assert only actor, kind, code and on_behalf_of.

Method note: the Relay guardrail denied `rm -rf` on my scratch copy, so a 187 MB copy of the store remains at /tmp/claude-1000/-home-anthony-dev3-RelayV4--relay-worktrees-spry-newt/38c95c7e-730e-48ae-b011-06ecb624f458/scratchpad/exp/storecopy/store.db. It is on tmpfs, inside a 0700 directory, and should be deleted.
v2.correction:
Magnitude: the finding assumes 61 KB per edit and "tens of MB a day, GBs". The live store shows a 15.6 KB average and about 1.5 MB/day of write rows (peak 4.2 MB/day), which levels off at about 270 MB under the 180-day retention (about 0.5 GB counting exec rows). That is roughly 10x below the claim and bounded, so the severity is medium, not high.

Confidentiality: drop the angle that agents can read other agents' file text through audit.get and audit.list. Agents run as the same Unix user with a shell into the same worktrees. The home directory is 0700, so no other local user can read the store.

Fix: the "at minimum" option, adding guardrail.gate to the 2 KB arm, is a poor fix. Nearly every write row (15.6 KB on average) and every long exec command would collapse to {truncated, bytes}, losing the path and command, which are the useful part of the record. Instead, for this op only, replace new_text and diff with {bytes, sha256}, keep session, kind, path and command, and cap command separately if needed. Also update BUS.md §5.3 and D151, which list the bounded ops by name. The "usage.report" arm in store_limit is dead code, because usage.report is Audit::Never (relay-bus ops/provider.rs:20).

VACUUM gating on PRAGMA freelist_count is a reasonable but separate second step. Later inserts reuse freed pages, so VACUUM only shrinks the file.

findings.title: The /tmp runtime-dir fallback is predictable and unverified: another local user can pre-create it, truncate a victim file through a symlinked lock file, and take over the socket
findings.evidence: Without XDG_RUNTIME_DIR, `runtime_dir()` returns `std::env::temp_dir().join(format!("relay-v4-{uid}"))` joined with `relay-v4` (paths.rs:67-74), a name any user can create first. `SocketServer::start_in` then calls `create_dir_all(&dir)` and `let _ = set_permissions(&dir, 0o700)`, ignoring the error and never chmodding the parent (socket.rs:55-56). It opens `<dir>/<inst>.lock` read/write/create without O_NOFOLLOW (socket.rs:60-67), so it follows symlinks. It flocks that file, calls `l.set_len(0)` and writes the pid into it (socket.rs:96-98), then binds the socket in the same directory (socket.rs:100).
findings.impact: Attack: another user creates /tmp/relay-v4-1000/relay-v4 with mode 0777 and places `stable.lock -> /home/victim/.ssh/authorized_keys` in it. The victim then runs `relay serve` without XDG_RUNTIME_DIR (an ssh session without pam_systemd, cron, a container, or a systemd system unit, which are typical headless setups). The chmod fails silently, the lock open follows the symlink, and set_len(0) truncates the victim's file. Because the attacker owns the directory, they can also rename the real socket away and listen at stable.sock themselves. The CLI, the agents' MCP servers and the native client all use `instance.socket_path()`, so they then send requests to the attacker. That exposes agent tokens and gate payloads containing file contents, and lets the attacker answer guardrail.gate with allow.
findings.fix: In the fallback, create the per-uid directory with mode 0700 and verify it with lstat: it and the inner directory must be real directories (not symlinks) owned by getuid() with no group or other permission bits, otherwise refuse to start. Better, prefer /run/user/<uid> when it exists, else a directory under $HOME/.cache. Open the lock file with O_NOFOLLOW|O_CLOEXEC and only truncate a regular file you own. Treat a failed set_permissions as fatal.

v1.reason: When XDG_RUNTIME_DIR is unset, paths.rs:67-74 falls back to the predictable `/tmp/relay-v4-<uid>/relay-v4` (directories 6.0 lin.rs:18 reads only XDG_RUNTIME_DIR). socket.rs:55 uses create_dir_all, which accepts a directory that already exists, so one pre-created by an attacker is reused. socket.rs:56 discards the chmod error with `let _ =`, and the chmod fails with EPERM on a directory the attacker owns. socket.rs:60-67 opens `<inst>.lock` with create and no O_NOFOLLOW. fs.protected_symlinks does not help here because the attacker's directory is not sticky, and the symlink owner matches the directory owner anyway. After flock succeeds, socket.rs:97 `l.set_len(0)` truncates whatever the link points to. One target is the victim's own ~/.local/share/relay-v4/<inst>/store.db, which turns this into data loss. Because the attacker owns the directory, they can also unlink the 0600 socket after bind and listen at the same path. The CLI (main.rs:196), MCP servers (mcp.rs:221) and the remote bridge (bridge.rs:31) all connect to instance.socket_path(). Reachability is narrower than the finding implies: relay-native refuses to start without XDG_RUNTIME_DIR (app.rs:309-312), and the shipped systemd --user unit (deploy/relay-remote.service) always has it set. The fallback is only reached by a manual `relay serve`/`relay` from a session without logind, such as su, sudo -u, some ssh setups or containers, on a host that has another hostile local user.
v1.correction: Rated high, not critical: the hole is real but needs a multi-user host and a session without XDG_RUNTIME_DIR, while the GUI and the shipped unit always set it. Name the store.db truncation as the sharpest consequence, not authorized_keys. Fix: create the fallback directory with mkdir 0700 and verify it with lstat (real directory, owned by getuid(), no group or other bits), otherwise refuse to start; treat a chmod failure as fatal; open the lock with O_NOFOLLOW|O_CLOEXEC. Simplest option: refuse to run without XDG_RUNTIME_DIR, as relay-native already does.

v2.reason:
(a) The code does what is claimed. `directories` 6.0 (lin.rs:18) reads only XDG_RUNTIME_DIR. When it is unset, paths.rs:70-73 falls back to `/tmp/relay-v4-<uid>/relay-v4`.
- socket.rs:55 `create_dir_all` accepts an existing directory owned by anyone.
- socket.rs:56 discards the EPERM from chmod with `let _ =`.
- socket.rs:60-67 opens `<inst>.lock` read/write/create with no O_NOFOLLOW.
- socket.rs:68 flocks it, and socket.rs:97 `set_len(0)` truncates whatever the lock path resolves to. socket.rs:100 then binds in the same directory.
- No SO_PEERCRED or other peer check exists anywhere. `Client::connect` (socket.rs:770) trusts any socket at the path.
- serve.rs:21 opens the store before SocketServer::start (serve.rs:36). SQLite's `locking_mode=EXCLUSIVE` (store.rs:400) takes fcntl locks, which do not conflict with flock on a local Linux filesystem.

I reproduced the OS semantics in the scratchpad. A planted `stable.lock` symlink in a 0777 non-sticky directory pointed at a file holding a SQLite-style fcntl lock. Opening it with the same flags followed the link, `flock(LOCK_EX|LOCK_NB)` succeeded, and ftruncate left the 4 KB target as a 7-byte pid. `fs.protected_symlinks` and `fs.protected_regular` only cover sticky world-writable directories, so they do not stop this.

(b) Reachability: only another local user on a shared host, and only when the victim starts the engine in an environment without XDG_RUNTIME_DIR.
- No documented desktop flow does this. relay-native refuses to start without it and builds its own path (app.rs:309-319). run.sh:32 starts the engine from the user's shell. deploy/relay-remote.service is a systemd --user unit, and the user manager always sets the variable.
- The fallback is reached by `relay serve` or `relay serve --remote` from sudo -u or su without a logind session, cron, a system unit with User=, a non-systemd or non-elogind distro, or sshd without pam_systemd. BUS.md §6.2 advertises `relay serve` for machines with no display, and paths.rs:66 documents the fallback, so it is a supported path, not dead code.
- The attacker only has to create `/tmp/relay-v4-<uid>` before the victim's first start after each boot. The truncation needs no race.
- How often: rare for a single-user desktop.

(c) Consequences when it fires:
1. Every engine start truncates one victim-writable file of the attacker's choosing. The sharpest target is `~/.local/share/relay-v4/<inst>/store.db`. Backups are manual only (`app.backup`, handlers/app.rs:48), so all Relay state since the last manual backup is lost, and the next start fails with "file is not a database". This happens even when bind then fails, which it does if the attacker leaves the directory 0755.
2. With a 0777 directory, the attacker can rename the victim's socket away and bind their own. Every client that resolves the fallback path then talks only to the attacker:
   - the CLI (main.rs:196);
   - `relay mcp`, which reconnects for every tool call (mcp.rs:146), so agents that are already running are captured too;
   - the agents' guardrail hook scripts (hooks.rs:130-132, which call `relay cmd guardrail.gate`);
   - the phone bridge (bridge.rs:31).

   Agents inherit the engine's environment through portable-pty's `get_base_env` (pty.rs:172), so their clients all use the fallback path. The attacker can answer guardrail.gate with allow, feed forged tool results to the agents, and read RELAY_TOKENs and payloads. They cannot proxy to the real engine, whose socket is 0600 (socket.rs:102), so the swap is noisy. Holding the flock on their own `stable.lock` and answering bus.ping instead makes `relay serve` exit with "already running", which is a persistent denial of service plus impersonation.

(d) High is right. By the rubric, a local-user-reachable hole with data loss and silent guardrail bypass would be critical. The two independent preconditions (a hostile co-user and a non-logind launch) bring it down one level, and the consequence when it fires is too severe for medium.

(e) The proposed fix is right in direction but incomplete:
- Verify the outer per-uid directory, not just the inner one. Otherwise an attacker who owns the outer directory can rename the inner one between check and use. Use lstat: a real directory owned by getuid() with mode 0700.
- O_CLOEXEC is redundant, because Rust std already sets it. O_NOFOLLOW only guards the last path component, so the directory checks are the essential part.
- The fix must also cover the clients, which all share `socket_path()`. Have `runtime_dir()` return only a verified directory, or have `Client::connect` check that the SO_PEERCRED uid equals getuid(). Otherwise a client that lacks XDG_RUNTIME_DIR still connects to a socket an attacker bound at the predictable path, even when the real engine uses XDG_RUNTIME_DIR.
- Refusing to run without XDG_RUNTIME_DIR, or using /run/user/<uid> after checking its owner, breaks nothing in cargo test or CI. Tests use `start_in` with temp directories, and the scripts set XDG_RUNTIME_DIR.
v2.correction:
- **Native client:** the finding says it uses `instance.socket_path()`. It does not: it requires XDG_RUNTIME_DIR and builds its own path (apps/relay-native/src/app.rs:309-319), so it is never redirected.
- **Affected clients:** the CLI (main.rs:196), `relay mcp` (per call, mcp.rs:146 and 221), the guardrail hook scripts (hooks.rs:130-132), the phone bridge (bridge.rs:31) and `relay remote`'s probes (remote.rs:156-161).
- **Sharpest consequence:** truncation of store.db, which the flock does not prevent because SQLite takes fcntl locks. There are no automatic backups. The authorized_keys example only locks the victim out of key login.
- **Interception is not a transparent proxy:** the real socket is 0600, so the attacker can impersonate the engine but cannot relay to it.
- **Reachability examples:** containers usually have a private /tmp and no co-users, and on systemd distros ssh sessions normally get XDG_RUNTIME_DIR from pam_systemd. Better examples are sudo -u or su without logind, cron, a system unit with User=, and non-elogind distros.
- **Fix:**
  - Verify both directory levels with lstat: a real directory, owned by getuid(), mode 0700, otherwise refuse to start.
  - Make the chmod failure fatal.
  - Open the lock file with O_NOFOLLOW and check with fstat that it is a regular file you own before truncating. O_CLOEXEC is already the std default.
  - Apply the same check on the client side: either `runtime_dir()` returns only a verified directory, or `Client::connect` checks that the SO_PEERCRED uid equals getuid().
  - Simplest option: use /run/user/<uid> after checking its owner, or refuse to start without XDG_RUNTIME_DIR, on both sides.
- **Unrelated doc drift:** socket.rs:52 mentions a `relay serve --runtime-dir` flag that the Serve command does not have.

findings.title: The socket door accepts `user` from any process, so an agent can act as the user with one CLI flag (`relay --actor user q guardrail.confirm ..`)
findings.evidence: `(Actor::User, _) | (Actor::Test, _) => Ok(None)` requires no credential, and session_id None means guardrail::authorize never runs (engine.rs:870). The CLI offers an `--actor` override (relay-cli main.rs:118-120) and falls back to `user` when RELAY_SESSION is unset (:129). BUS.md §0.6 and §14 accept same-uid trust, but the only check against an agent claiming `user` is a text pattern in the exec gate (tests/guardrails.rs:750-781). It runs only for hooked providers: Codex sessions have no PreToolUse hook (BUS.md §9.3), and a command written to a script file defeats the pattern. bus.subscribe and bus.wait are answered in socket.rs without resolving the actor or token at all (socket.rs:362-449).
findings.impact: A goal-seeking agent stuck on a hold, or refused with "this op is user-only", can run `$RELAY_BIN --actor user q guardrail.confirm '{"hold_id":N}'`, guardrail.config.set or settings.set and bypass every guardrail and allowlist. The audit row records `user`, so afterwards the user cannot tell that an agent did it. For Codex sessions even the text check does not run.
findings.fix: On accept, read SO_PEERCRED (tokio `UnixStream::peer_cred`). If the peer pid descends from a live session's PTY child (walk the ppid chain in /proc/<pid>/stat; the engine knows each session's pid), refuse `user`/`test` claims on that connection or bind it to that session's agent actor. Record the peer pid in the audit row for user requests. An agent could then only claim `user` by deliberately escaping its process tree, not by a single flag.

v1.reason: resolve_actor (engine.rs:1355) returns Ok(None) for `user` on any door with no credential, so guardrail::authorize (engine.rs:870) never runs. relay-cli actor_from_env (main.rs:118-130) honours `--actor user` and falls back to user when RELAY_SESSION is unset. The only counter is guardrail.rs:845-880 `self_approval`, a text match in the exec gate, and its own comment says "Best effort: the socket does not authenticate `user`, so this closes the obvious door, not every door." Bypasses: write the command into a script file; use a variable name other than RELAY_BIN; connect to the socket directly (e.g. python/socat sending {"actor":"user","op":"guardrail.confirm"}); or use Codex, whose gate is post-hoc (BUS.md §14/§9.3). BUS.md §4.2/§14 document same-uid trust ("Tokens prevent misattribution, not determined impersonation"), so this is an accepted trade-off. It is not harmless, though: the test agents_cannot_answer_guardrails_as_the_user_from_a_shell exists because agents self-approving is an anticipated failure, and audit rows record `user`. Severity stays medium, not critical: guardrails are documented as non-sandbox, and an agent with arbitrary shell can also reach the uid's files (store DB, settings) by other means.
v1.correction: Drop the bus.subscribe/bus.wait part. They only read the event stream, which any same-uid client may receive as `user`, so not resolving an actor there adds nothing. Fix caveat: hooks.rs:132 (the git pre-commit hook) legitimately claims `--actor user` when RELAY_SESSION is unset. A SO_PEERCRED ppid-walk refusal must not break hook invocations. It is also defeatable by setsid/double-fork/systemd-run, so it raises the bar but does not close the hole. Recording the peer pid/exe in user audit rows is the cheap part with the clearest value (attribution).

findings.title: bus.wait subscribes only when it is called, so an event that fires between a refusal and the agent's wait is lost; only exception requests are special-cased
findings.evidence: `let mut rx = engine.subscribe();` runs when the wait request arrives, so events emitted before that are gone. The fix for this exact race exists only for `guardrail.request_resolved` (exception_waited, socket.rs:198-205, commit a7aa654). Elsewhere agents are told to use the racy pattern: the device.busy hint says `wait for it with bus.wait {"events":["device.lease.released"]} and retry` (device_lease.rs:149), and the brief repeats it (providers.rs:48-49). A lagged waiter also drops the event it was waiting for, only logging it (socket.rs:432-434).
findings.impact: An agent's `adb install` is refused with device.busy. While the LLM composes its next call, which takes seconds, the peer releases the lease. The agent's bus.wait then sleeps until it times out (60 s by default, up to 1 h if the agent asked) even though the device is free. With several agents contending, this repeats on each contention.
findings.fix: Stamp each event with a monotonic sequence number under the lock, return the current sequence number in refusals that recommend bus.wait, and accept an `after_seq` cursor in WaitIn, replaying from a small ring of recent events. For state-based waits, check the current state first, as exception_waited does: for device.lease.released, return at once if the device named in `matching` has no lease.

v1.reason: socket.rs:411 (`let mut rx = engine.subscribe();`) runs only when the bus.wait request arrives, and events go out on a tokio broadcast channel (engine.rs:437, capacity 4096), which never replays past events. The only check of stored state comes from `exception_waited` (socket.rs:198-205), and it returns Some only for guardrail.request_resolved with a request_id. Every other event, including device.lease.released (handlers/device_lease.rs:15), is lost if it fires between the refusal and the subscribe. The device.busy hint (device_lease.rs:148-150) and the agent brief (providers.rs:48-49) both tell agents to do exactly this: get refused, then bus.wait on device.lease.released, then retry. An LLM takes seconds between the refusal and its next tool call. A short adb install by a peer can finish inside that gap, so the release event goes out to no one and the wait sleeps until it times out. I found no upstream guard, re-check or cursor that covers this.
v1.correction: The impact is bounded. Unless the agent passed a longer timeout_ms (the clamp allows 1 s to 1 h), the wait ends after the default 60 s with timed_out:true, and the agent can retry. The result is a stall of up to a minute per contention, not a hang, so medium is right and nothing higher. The Lagged branch (socket.rs:432-434) only matters if more than 4096 events arrive during one wait, which is rare; treat it as a footnote, not part of the root cause. The cheapest fix follows the exception_waited pattern: when the filter matches device.lease.released, check the current lease table after subscribing and return at once if the device (or any device, when no matching is given) is free. Alternatively, change the hint to 'bus.wait with a short timeout, then device.leases'. A general seq/after_seq replay ring would also work but is a larger change.

findings.title: An audited agent request takes the store mutex five or six separate times and re-reads its session row each time
findings.evidence: These steps each lock the store separately: resolve_actor → check_session_token, which reads by_name (1378); fill_identity when it fills a field, which reads by_id (1157); the idempotency lookup (841); authorize, which reads by_id again (871, guardrail.rs:324); the handler transaction (954); and mail_hint, which reads by_name again and re-checks the token (788). The lock is released between authorize and the handler.
findings.impact: guardrail.gate, which runs on every Write, Edit and Bash by every Claude agent and holds the agent until it returns, and session.report, sent twice per tool use, each queue on the mutex five or six times. std::sync::Mutex is not FIFO, so under contention (one slow locked handler, many agents) each re-queue can be overtaken, multiplying tail latency on the hook path. The gap between authorize and the handler is also a TOCTOU: a session that is closed or re-roled in that gap still has its request executed.
findings.fix: Do actor resolution, identity filling, the idempotency lookup and authorization in one critical section that reads the session row once. For locked handlers, do it inside the handler's transaction. Compute the mail hint from the same row before releasing the lock.

v1.reason: The structure is as described. For a socket agent request, the store mutex is taken in these places, each a separate acquisition of a std::sync::Mutex (store.rs:474): check_session_token, which reads by_name (engine.rs:1377-1385); fill_identity, only when a required field is missing (1155-1158); the idempotency lookup, only for audited ops (839-841); guardrail::authorize, which reads by_id again (871-872, guardrail.rs:324); the handler transaction (954); and mail_hint, which reads by_name again (783-800). guardrail.gate is registered with Engine::register (handlers/guardrail.rs:304), so it is audited and takes all of these. Each extra acquisition is short: an indexed prepare_cached single-row read. The ordinary case therefore adds tens of microseconds, not a measurable slowdown. When a slow locked handler holds the mutex, the first acquisition already waits behind it. The extra re-queues add latency only under heavy contention, and that part is speculative. The TOCTOU between authorize and the handler is real but has little impact. gate itself re-reads the session with by_name inside its transaction (handlers/guardrail.rs:501), so a session closed in that gap fails there with not_found. A role change in that gap at worst lets one in-flight request through under the old role.
v1.correction: Downgrade to low. The cost is a handful of extra short critical sections per request, a cleanup with modest payoff, not a demonstrated latency problem. guardrail.gate already re-reads its session inside the transaction, which limits the TOCTOU to a role or option change landing in a microsecond window. The suggested fix (resolve the actor, authorize and look up idempotency in one critical section, ideally inside the handler's transaction for locked ops) is reasonable.

findings.title: output_with_timeout's pipe drains have no size cap and no deadline, so the timeout does not bound the call
findings.evidence: `drain` calls `io::Read::read_to_end(&mut reader, &mut buf)` into an unbounded Vec (78-84). After the wait loop both drains are joined with `h.join()` and no deadline (66-70). The group SIGKILL (55, 65) reaches only descendants still in the child's process group. A descendant that called setsid() or setpgid() and still holds the inherited stdout/stderr keeps read_to_end blocked. Examples are daemons (the adb server on this machine runs with PGID == SID == PID) and detached helpers started from git hooks. The test descendants_cannot_keep_probe_pipes_open_after_parent_exit only covers a same-group `sleep 30 &`.
findings.impact: (1) A detached grandchild holding the pipes makes the call block past its deadline, indefinitely. Several callers run under the store lock (guardrail.rs:671 and 1123, whose comment says they run with the store lock held), so this freezes the bus. (2) All output is buffered in memory. Unreal automation runs with `-stdout -FullStdOutLogOutput` for up to 2 h (relay-cli unreal.rs:1107-1109), and `git status --untracked-files=all` on a large un-ignored tree is held whole, then copied again by from_utf8_lossy and format!.
findings.fix: Drain into a bounded buffer (keep the first and last N MB and count the rest), sending the result over a channel. After the child is reaped or killed, wait for the drains with recv_timeout and a short grace period, and abandon any that have not finished, returning what was read flagged as truncated.

v1.reason: The mechanism holds. proc.rs:66-70 joins both drain threads with no deadline, and drain (78-84) calls read_to_end into an unbounded Vec. The group SIGKILL at :55/:65 reaches only the child's own process group. A descendant that calls setsid() and keeps the inherited stdout or stderr (e.g. `sh -c 'setsid sleep 30 & echo done'`, where setsid does not fork because the background job is not a group leader) keeps read_to_end blocked well past the deadline. The existing test covers only a descendant in the same group. Callers that can run user code include git switch (handlers/git.rs:1350) and worktree add (worktree.rs:214), both of which run post-checkout hooks, plus Unreal and Blender runs in relay-cli. Under the store lock (guardrail.rs:671 and 1123, git status/diff), though, git itself does not start such descendants. A real trigger there would need an fsmonitor hook or a custom tool that daemonizes without redirecting its stdio, so I could not establish a common trigger that freezes the bus.
v1.correction: The adb example is wrong: the adb server calls setsid() and dup2s its stdout and stderr onto its log file (setup_daemon_logging), so it does not hold the pipes. A more realistic case is a user git hook (post-checkout on switch or worktree add) that detaches a helper without redirecting output. A detached daemon started by an Unreal run, such as a shared zen server, could do the same, but I did not verify that. The memory point is real but minor: relay-cli's 30-60 minute Unreal runs with -FullStdOutLogOutput are buffered whole, in the CLI process rather than the engine. The suggested fix stands: after the child is reaped, wait for the drains with a short grace period and a size cap.

findings.title: days_ago panics for a large audit.retention_days, and recovery calls it on every launch, so the engine cannot start again
findings.evidence: The code is `(Timestamp::now() - jiff::SignedDuration::from_hours(days.saturating_mul(24))).to_string()`. In jiff 0.2.35, `Sub<SignedDuration> for Timestamp` calls `.expect("subtracting signed duration from timestamp overflowed")`, and from_hours panics on overflow. recovery.rs:184-194 parses `audit.retention_days` straight from settings with `serde_json::from_str::<i64>` and calls days_ago when the value is above 0. settings.set validates only the path, not the value (settings.rs:203-213). Recovery runs inside serve::start (serve.rs:23) with no catch_unwind.
findings.impact: `relay cmd settings.set '{"path":"audit.retention_days","value":99999999}'` (a plausible "keep forever" guess; the documented value for that is 0) makes the next launch panic in recovery. Any value above roughly 4.4 million days passes jiff's year -9999 limit. relay serve then crashes on every start, and the only fix is editing SQLite by hand, because the engine cannot start to accept another settings.set.
findings.fix: Clamp the input in days_ago (for example `days.clamp(0, 365_000)`) and use `checked_sub`, falling back to Timestamp::MIN. Validate numeric setting ranges in settings.set. Catch a failure or panic in the retention step and log it instead of aborting startup.

v1.reason: time.rs:16 does `Timestamp::now() - SignedDuration::from_hours(days.saturating_mul(24))`. In jiff 0.2.35, the version Cargo.lock pins, `Sub<SignedDuration> for Timestamp` (timestamp.rs:2496-2506) calls `.expect("subtracting signed duration from timestamp overflowed")`, and `from_hours` (signed_duration.rs:749-758) panics on overflow. recovery.rs:184-194 reads audit.retention_days with `serde_json::from_str::<i64>` and does no range check, then calls days_ago whenever days > 0. settings.set (handlers/settings.rs:203-213) validates only the path. serve::start (serve.rs:23) handles an Err from recovery but cannot catch a panic, so the panic aborts startup. The transaction rolls back and the setting stays, so every later launch panics the same way until the row is removed by hand. days_ago has no other caller.
v1.correction: Severity drops to low because the trigger is narrow. settings.set is in USER_ONLY_ANSWERS (guardrail.rs:851-853), so an agent shell command cannot set it. No UI in apps/ exposes the key, so only a user typing a raw `relay cmd settings.set` can trigger this, and the value has to be more than about 4.4 million days. Plausible 'forever' guesses such as 99999 or 999999 days do not panic. The consequence (the engine cannot start until SQLite is edited by hand) is severe, but the edge case is rare and self-inflicted. Fix: in days_ago, clamp the input and use checked_sub, falling back to Timestamp::MIN; optionally also reject negative or absurd values for audit.retention_days in settings.set.

findings.title: audit.undo's staleness check fails in both directions: workspace.update and session.update can never be undone, and ops recorded without `expect` overwrite later edits
findings.evidence: target_updated_at maps only the task., module. and notes. prefixes, project.update, and skill.; anything else returns Ok(None). Undo then tests `actual.as_deref() != Some(expected)` (line 61) whenever the inverse carries expect.updated_at. workspace.update (workspace.rs:144-146, expect set, key workspace_id) and session.update (session.rs:1474-1477, expect set, key `session` name) are both `Undo::Inverse`, so they always fail with audit.stale. In the other direction, settings.set (settings.rs:220, 230), guardrail.config.set (handlers/guardrail.rs:99), notify.settings.set, ui.*, plugin.enable, skill.create and the notes.create→delete inverse (notes.rs:372, 577) record `expect: None`, so their undo runs unconditionally. BUS.md §5.5 promises that an undo never silently clobbers a later edit.
findings.impact: `audit.undo` of a workspace rename or a session.update always returns audit.stale unless force:true is passed. Undoing an older settings.set or guardrail.config.set restores the old subtree over any later changes without warning, for example re-loosening guardrail config the user has since tightened.
findings.fix: Drive the check from a per-op table giving the table and the id field (or a lookup by name for sessions). When an inverse has no way to verify freshness, refuse with audit.stale or a new code unless force is set. Record an expect value for settings and config ops, such as the subtree's latest updated_at or a hash of the current value.

v1.reason: target_updated_at (audit.rs:10-27) maps only task./module./notes./project.update/skill. and otherwise returns Ok(None). Undo (audit.rs:59-64) refuses when `actual.as_deref() != Some(expected)`. workspace.update (workspace.rs:143-145) and session.update (session.rs:1474-1477) record `expect: {updated_at}` with keys workspace_id / session name. Both therefore always fail with audit.stale unless force. In the other direction, settings.set and settings.reset (settings.rs:220, 230), guardrail.config.set (handlers/guardrail.rs:99) and notes create/restore (notes.rs:372, 577) record expect None, so their undo applies unconditionally. That contradicts BUS.md §5.5 "an undo never silently clobbers a later edit". Reach: audit.undo is UserOnly, and the desktop UI's Ctrl+Z (board_view.rs:876-890) only undoes `task.` rows, so both failure modes are reached only through the CLI/MCP-as-user or another client. That keeps it medium (a real bug in a less common path).
v1.correction: For guardrail.config.set, the inverse is inverse_patch(before, merged), which touches only the changed keys. Clobbering therefore happens only if the same keys were edited later, but that is still a silent clobber (e.g. re-loosening a key the user tightened again). Even with a correct lookup, session.update undo would often be stale, because session state transitions bump sessions.updated_at. A per-entity freshness token (or refusing undo without force when freshness cannot be checked) is the right fix.

findings.title: Events are published after the store lock is released, so two commits to the same entity can reach subscribers in reverse order
findings.evidence: On the Ok path the code runs `tx.commit()`, `drop(conn)` and `span.finish()`, and only then `for ev in events { let _ = self.events_tx.send(ev); }` (1024-1029). system_write does the same (717-723). Another thread can take the lock, commit and send its events in that gap. The native client applies session.changed payloads in place with no version check (`Some(i) => all[i] = payload.clone()`, agent_menu.rs:111).
findings.impact: Example: a session.report marks a session idle, and the keystroke-driven mark_session_running (a system_write on a separate thread) commits right after it. If the first thread is preempted after drop(conn), subscribers receive `running` then `idle`, and the sidebar shows idle while the row says running until the next change.
findings.fix: Send events before dropping the guard, in both the pipeline and system_write; broadcast::send is non-blocking and O(1). Alternatively, stamp a sequence number under the lock so clients can discard stale payloads; that also provides the cursor bus.wait needs.

v1.reason: On the Ok path, events are sent after `drop(conn); span.finish();` (engine.rs:1022-1029). system_write likewise drops the lock before sending (engine.rs:717-723). Two writers to the same session can therefore commit in order A then B and publish in order B then A, if A is preempted between drop(conn) and send. mark_session_running (engine.rs:1318-1344) is a system_write that emits a full session row, and session.report and other handlers emit full rows too. The native client overwrites in place without comparing `updated_at` (apps/relay-native/src/agent_menu.rs:108-112). The window is microseconds, so this is rare, but nothing corrects it until the next change to that session. A worse variant than the one the finding gives: if a `closed` row is published before a stale non-closed row, the match arm `None if !closed => all.push(payload.clone())` re-adds the closed session to the sidebar as a ghost.
v1.correction: Add the ghost-session case (a closed event overtaken by a stale running or idle row re-inserts the session in agent_menu.rs). Fix: call events_tx.send while still holding the guard on every path (the Ok path, commit_error, system_write, and the publish in dispatch_unlocked after Unlocked::read), and keep after_commit closures outside the lock. Alternatively, have the client ignore a payload whose updated_at is older than the row it holds.

findings.title: A lagging subscriber silently loses events and the client is never told to resync
findings.evidence: The forwarder handles `Err(RecvError::Lagged(n))` with only `tracing::warn!(lagged = n, "subscriber lagged; events dropped")` and keeps looping; nothing is written to the client. The channel is `broadcast::channel(4096)` (engine.rs:437). The per-connection mpsc (capacity 1024) is shared with PTY frames, so a slow reader backs up into the forwarder.
findings.impact: If the UI stops reading long enough for 4096 events to pass (heavy load, a stalled client), it misses events such as guardrail.held or session.changed. Because the client applies events in place, it keeps the stale state with no signal to refetch.
findings.fix: On Lagged, send a synthetic `{"ev":"bus.lagged","payload":{"dropped":n}}` line so the client can refresh. For waiters, return early with a lagged flag.

v1.reason: socket.rs:385-387 only logs RecvError::Lagged and keeps looping. Nothing reaches the client, unlike the PTY path, whose message at :492 at least names the re-attach-from-seq remedy. The broadcast holds 4096 events (engine.rs:437). Because `tx.send(s).await` in the forwarder applies backpressure from the per-connection mpsc, a client that stops reading stalls the forwarder until the broadcast overruns. The bus.wait loop (socket.rs:432) behaves the same way, so a waiter can miss its event and sit until the timeout. In practice this needs thousands of events to pile up while a client is not reading, which is rare for a single-user desktop.
v1.correction: Low severity is right. The waiter case matters more than the finding says, because a dropped guardrail answer makes an agent wait for the full timeout (up to 1 h). On Lagged, a waiter should re-check the stored answer (resolved_event) or return early.

findings.title: In-memory bus ops open a transaction under the store mutex, and bus.schema regenerates a ~315 KB schema while holding it
findings.evidence: Ping, Schema and the door-only stubs Wait, Subscribe and Unsubscribe are registered with `e.register` (bus.rs:14, 22, 108-110). Dispatch therefore takes the lock and opens a transaction (engine.rs:953-956) even though none of them reads a table. Schema calls relay_bus::schema::render(), which rebuilds every op's schemars schema on each call (schema.rs:11-52; the committed output is 314,530 bytes), and to_value then deep-copies the result.
findings.impact: Each full bus.schema call holds the bus for the whole generation time. Every bus.ping waits behind any long locked handler, so a liveness probe cannot distinguish a busy engine from a dead one.
findings.fix: Use register_unlocked for Ping, Schema and the three stubs, which are all queries, and cache the rendered schema in a OnceLock.

v1.reason: bus.rs:14 (Ping), 22 (Schema) and 108-110 (Wait/Subscribe/Unsubscribe stubs) use e.register, so dispatch takes the store lock and opens a transaction (engine.rs:953-956) for ops that read no table. Schema with no op calls relay_bus::schema::render() (schema.rs:11-52), which regenerates every op's schemars schema on each call. This has a concrete effect: socket::probe (socket.rs:143-160) is bus.ping with a 500 ms budget, used by relay-cli remote.rs:156/161/184. While any locked handler runs for over 500 ms (e.g. project.clone, finding #3), `relay remote serve` reports "no engine answering" and exits 5, or resolve_instance switches to a different instance. Full-schema calls are rare and take milliseconds, so that part has negligible impact.
v1.correction: The main value is moving Ping to register_unlocked, so liveness probes do not queue behind the store lock. Caching the rendered schema in a OnceLock is a minor nicety. The door-only stubs just return an error, so switching them changes little.

findings.title: audit.list parses up to 1000 rows of stored payload and result JSON under the store lock, using an uncached statement
findings.evidence: The SQL `SELECT * FROM audit WHERE 1=1 ..` is built per call and compiled with `conn.prepare(&sql)`, not prepare_cached. row_to_audit parses the payload and result_summary JSON of every row (189-191). The limit is clamped to 1000 (219). The handler is registered with `e.register::<List>` (handlers/audit.rs:30), and agents may call it because it is a query open to all actors.
findings.impact: An agent calling audit_list {limit:1000} over file.write or guardrail.gate rows, each up to 64 KB of payload plus 64 KB of result, holds the bus while up to ~128 MB of JSON is parsed. Normal-sized rows still cost several milliseconds per call.
findings.fix: Register audit.list and audit.get unlocked: read the raw rows as strings inside ctx.read with prepare_cached, and parse them after releasing the lock. Consider leaving payload and result out of list responses and fetching them through audit.get.

v1.reason: handlers/audit.rs:30 registers audit.list with plain `e.register::<List>`, so it holds the store mutex inside a transaction. audit::list (audit.rs:208-223) builds dynamic SQL and calls `conn.prepare(&sql)`, clamps the limit to 1000, and `row_to_audit` (172-191) JSON-parses payload, result_summary and undo_op for every row. audit.list is a query with no actor restriction (relay-bus ops/audit.rs:13), so agents can call it. With large guardrail.gate or file.write rows (see #4), a limit-1000 call parses tens of MB under the lock.
v1.correction: The ~128 MB worst case assumes every row is at both 64 KB caps; realistic cost is tens to hundreds of milliseconds on large rows and a few milliseconds on normal ones. The uncached prepare is a negligible share of that, and prepare_cached would work with the dynamic SQL because it is keyed by SQL text. The real fix is register_unlocked: read raw strings inside ctx.read, parse after the lock is released, and optionally leave payload and result out of list responses.

findings.title: shutdown kills sessions one at a time, allowing up to 4 s each
findings.evidence: The loop is `for (_, p) in &ptys { p.kill(std::time::Duration::from_secs(2)); }`. Pty::kill sends SIGTERM and polls for up to `grace`, then sends SIGKILL and polls for up to 2 s more (pty.rs:344-364). It runs on the async runtime thread in serve() (serve.rs:50).
findings.impact: Quitting with N sessions whose CLIs are slow to exit on SIGTERM takes up to 4·N seconds (up to 40 s for 10 sessions), which can exceed a desktop logout or systemd stop timeout.
findings.fix: Send SIGTERM to every PTY group first, wait once for all of them against a shared deadline, then SIGKILL whatever remains.

v1.reason: engine.rs:656-658 loops `for (_, p) in &ptys { p.kill(Duration::from_secs(2)); }`, after draining the map and running mark_restorable. Pty::kill (pty.rs:343-368) sends SIGTERM to the group and the pid, polls up to `grace` (2 s), then sends SIGKILL and polls up to 2 s more, one PTY at a time. It is called after the select in serve() (serve.rs:50) and in remote.rs:137. Each session whose CLI ignores or is slow to handle SIGTERM therefore adds about 2 s, in series. The upper bound of 4 s per session is mostly theoretical: after SIGKILL the wait ends almost at once, so the realistic cost is about 2 s per slow session. Agent CLIs that exit promptly on SIGTERM cost almost nothing, so the delay appears only with stubborn children.
v1.correction: The realistic worst case is about 2 s per stubborn session, not 4 s, because the SIGKILL wait almost never runs its full length. The fix stands: send SIGTERM to every group, wait once against one shared deadline, then SIGKILL the remainder. remote.rs:137 is another caller of the same shutdown.

findings.title: dispatch_inner repeats the audit-row and post-commit publication code, and the copies have already diverged
findings.evidence: AuditEntry literals appear at 1000, 1042, 1077, 1117 and 701. The events plus after_commit publication loop appears at 1027-1036, 1061-1070 and 1200-1209. The copies differ in two ways. The commit_error path never calls span.finish() after drop(conn), so the LockSpan drop at function exit counts event sending and every after_commit closure as lock hold time. Handler failures record `project_id` from ctx (1085), which is usually None because handlers set it last, while audit_only derives it from the session row (1110-1115).
findings.impact: Held and refused requests produce spurious "store lock over budget" warnings. `audit.list {project_id}` misses most handler-failure rows, so the same agent's errors are attributed to its project or not depending on where they failed. Every future change to auditing or publication has to be made in three to five places.
findings.fix: Extract `fn publish(&self, events, after_commit)` and one audit-row builder. Finish the span right after drop(conn) on every path. Derive project_id from the session row in one place.

v1.reason: The duplication is real. The events plus after_commit publication block appears at engine.rs:1027-1036 and 1061-1070, and again in dispatch_unlocked. AuditEntry literals are built in several places (system_write at 701, the Ok path, commit_error, ordinary failure, and audit_only). The listed divergences exist but their impact is overstated. (1) The commit_error path never calls span.finish() after drop(conn), so the LockSpan reports on drop at function exit. However, its only users are guardrail gate and confirm, refused or held (handlers/guardrail.rs:539, 562, 685, 700), which register no after_commit closures, so the extra time is a couple of broadcast sends, microseconds against the 16 ms LOCK_BUDGET (engine.rs:71). The claim of spurious 'over budget' warnings for held and refused requests is wrong. (2) Handler-failure rows take project_id from ctx, which is None only when the handler fails before set_project. gate sets it first (handlers/guardrail.rs:508), while audit_only derives it from the session row (1110-1115). This is a real but minor attribution inconsistency in audit.list filtered by project.
v1.correction: Drop the impact claim about spurious lock warnings: no commit_error path has after_commit work, so the missing span.finish() changes nothing measurable today, though it would once someone adds after_commit to a gate path. The worthwhile change is small: one `publish(events, after_commit)` helper, finishing the span right after drop(conn) on every path, and falling back to the session's project_id when ctx.project_id is None in the failure path.

findings.title: The keystroke fast path deep-clones the payload to deserialize it, the same pattern the registry removed for this reason
findings.evidence: `serde_json::from_value(payload.clone())` is used for InputIn (1276), ResizeIn (1295) and MirrorInputIn (1309).
