This runs right after `(entry.validate)(&req.payload)` has already deserialized the same payload once (853). registry.rs:218-221 deliberately deserializes "through the value, not out of a clone of it" because cloning doubled the cost of large payloads. Separately, every audited success deep-clones its result for the audit entry (`outcome: &Ok(result.clone())`, 1010).
findings.impact: Every keystroke and mirror pointer event pays for an extra Value-tree clone and allocation, on the path the code measures in microseconds.
findings.fix: Use `InputIn::deserialize(payload)`, deserializing from a `&Value`, and reuse the typed value instead of validating separately for these ops. Make AuditEntry.outcome a `Result<&Value, &BusError>`.

v1.reason: pty_fast_path (engine.rs:1276 InputIn, 1295 ResizeIn) and mirror_fast_path (1309 MirrorInputIn) do `serde_json::from_value(payload.clone())`. They are reached at engine.rs:895/902, after `(entry.validate)(&req.payload)` at 853 has already deserialized the same payload. registry.rs:218-221 says it deserializes "through the value, not out of a clone" because the clone doubled the cost. The audit path at engine.rs:1010 does `outcome: &Ok(result.clone())`. The cost is real but small: session.input payloads are a session name plus a few bytes of keystroke data, so the clone is a couple of tiny allocations, next to a socket read/write and a PTY write.
v1.correction: The impact is negligible per keystroke (tens of ns for a small Value), so this is a cleanup and not a measurable latency fix. Simplest fix: `InputIn::deserialize(payload)` / `ResizeIn::deserialize(payload)` / `MirrorInputIn::deserialize(payload)` from `&Value`. Changing AuditEntry.outcome to borrow is optional and only matters for large mutation results.

findings.title: Idempotent replay cannot be reached from first-party clients, and races when it is reached
findings.evidence: The lookup takes the lock (841) and releases it at 851. The audit row is appended much later, in a separate critical section (1015), and a staged op's prepare (git push, worktree creation) runs between the two. A duplicate id arriving in that window passes the lookup, executes again, then fails the `audit.req_id UNIQUE` constraint and returns `internal` instead of the replay. Separately, `relay cmd` mints a fresh UUID for every invocation (Request::new; there is no --id option) and no client resends an id, so BUS.md §5.3's "This is what makes `relay cmd` safe to retry from a script" does not hold. Held rows also replay `held` forever, not "until the hold is resolved" as the doc says.
findings.impact: A script that retries `relay cmd task.create ..` after a timeout creates a duplicate task. A raw client that reuses an id during a slow staged op gets the external effect twice plus an internal error.
findings.fix: Reserve the id at lookup time, either with a pending audit row or an in-memory in-flight set keyed by req_id that is released on completion. Add an `--id`/RELAY_REQUEST_ID option to the CLI. Either fix the doc on held replays or implement replay after resolution.

v1.reason: The race is real. The idempotency lookup at engine.rs:839-850 takes the lock and releases it. A staged op's prepare then runs unlocked (around 905-933), and audit::append happens later, in the handler transaction (around 1012). A second request with the same id arriving in that gap passes the lookup and runs prepare again, repeating any external effects. Its own audit::append then fails on `req_id UNIQUE` (store.rs:22), and `map_err(internal)?` returns `internal` instead of the replay. The claim that no first-party client can reuse an id is wrong: `relay cmd` with a full JSON envelope keeps a caller-supplied `id` (relay-cli/src/main.rs:586-593 only mints one when it is missing). So the retry from a script that BUS.md §5.3 promises is possible, and the race is exactly what such a retry hits: a script that times out, then resends the same envelope while the first call is still in a slow staged prepare. The complaint about held replays is not a real divergence: §9.4 (BUS.md:539-540) says the original id stays audited as `held` and keeps replaying `held`, consistent with the code. Only the wording 'until the hold is resolved' in §5.3 is loose.
v1.correction: Remove the part claiming that no CLI path lets a caller set the id: the full-envelope form of `relay cmd` keeps a caller's `id`. For ordinary locked (non-staged) handlers, the duplicate's database writes are rolled back, because the audit append fails before commit. The result is only a spurious `internal` instead of a replay. External effects run twice only in staged prepare (and in any external work a locked handler does inline). The held-replay point is at most a one-line wording fix in §5.3. Fix: reserve the req_id in an in-memory in-flight set at lookup time, and have a duplicate wait for or replay the result, or map a UNIQUE conflict on req_id to a lookup and replay.

findings.title: Unused path and time helpers, and the dead Tauri door
findings.evidence: Nothing calls Instance::from_env (paths.rs:15, which also silently maps any unknown RELAY_INSTANCE to Stable), bundle_id (38), backup_dir (60; Store has its own), log_dir (63), lock_path (79) or time::now_ts (time.rs:9). Door::Tauri (engine.rs:32) is never constructed, since no Tauri crate remains and relay-native talks over the socket, yet it keeps match arms in the door check (822), mail_hint (785) and resolve_actor (1356), and no op uses Doors::TauriOnly. handlers/bus.rs:117-121 keeps `_ctx_used` and `_CALLABLE_USED` only to silence imports, and Callable is used at :82 anyway. socket.rs:57-58 formats `<inst>.lock` and `<inst>.sock` itself instead of calling lock_path()/socket_path(), which the clients use.
findings.impact: Dead surface to maintain. from_env would bring back the dev-build-on-stable-store mistake that the CLI's strict parse avoids. The server and the clients spell the socket path separately, so they can drift apart without anyone noticing.
findings.fix: Delete the unused functions, Door::Tauri and its match arms, and the dummy items. Have SocketServer::start_in get both paths from one Instance helper.

v1.reason: rg shows no callers of Instance::from_env, bundle_id, Instance::backup_dir (Store::backup_dir at store.rs:495 is the one in use), log_dir, Instance::lock_path (unreal.rs:514 is an unrelated local fn) or time::now_ts. No production code constructs Door::Tauri. It appears only in tests (tests/bus.rs:108, 114, 220), where it stands in for a non-socket door, yet it still keeps arms at engine.rs:785, 822 and 1356. Doors::TauriOnly is referenced only in the door-check match and in mcp.rs:161, and no op declares it. bus.rs:117-121 keeps `_ctx_used`/`_CALLABLE_USED` although Callable is used at :82. socket.rs:57-58 builds `<inst>.lock`/`<inst>.sock` by hand instead of calling lock_path()/socket_path(). The names agree today.
v1.correction: Door::Tauri is not entirely unused: three tests in crates/relay-core/tests/bus.rs construct it. Removing it means changing those tests to InProcess or Socket, or keeping a test-only door. The claim that from_env would 'bring back' a dev-on-stable mistake is speculation, since nothing calls it. The real reason to delete it is that it silently maps an unknown value to Stable. relay-native also builds the socket path separately (app.rs:314-318), which is a third copy.

findings.title: Stale comments and spec text in the engine core
findings.evidence: lib.rs:1-2 and serve.rs:1-2 say "the Tauri shell embeds it", but no Tauri shell exists. engine.rs:7-8 says "Doors call Engine::dispatch from spawn_blocking", but socket.rs:739 also calls it inline on runtime threads. The doc comment at engine.rs:1172 ("BUS.md §4.2. Returns the agent's session id ..") sits on dispatch_unlocked but describes resolve_actor. engine.rs:1217 calls pty_ids/mirrors "lock-free" checks, but they are std Mutexes. paths.rs:66 gives the fallback as `/tmp/relay-v4-<uid>/`; the code uses `/tmp/relay-v4-<uid>/relay-v4/`. handlers/audit.rs:1 says "`audit.undo` lands with the board (phase 7)", but it is implemented in the same file. BUS.md §5.1 describes "a single tokio::sync::Mutex .. queries may read concurrently through the WAL", but the store is one std Mutex around one connection, so reads serialize with writes. BUS.md §6.2 gives the socket as `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/relay/<instance>.sock`; the code uses `relay-v4/`.
findings.impact: Readers, including agents that read these docs, get the wrong model of locking and paths, for example assuming reads do not contend with writes.
findings.fix: Update the code comments and BUS.md §5.1 and §6.2 to match the implementation.

v1.reason: Checked every item. lib.rs:2 and serve.rs:1 still mention a Tauri shell, but the only apps are relay-native and relay-mobile. engine.rs:8 says doors call dispatch from spawn_blocking, yet socket.rs:735-739 calls `engine.dispatch(req, Door::Socket)` inline when answers_from_memory holds. engine.rs:1172 ("BUS.md §4.2. Returns the agent's session id ..") is a leftover first line sitting on top of dispatch_unlocked's real doc. handlers/audit.rs:1 says audit.undo "lands with the board (phase 7)", but the same file implements it (lines 51-55 check undo_op and undone_by). paths.rs:66 gives `/tmp/relay-v4-<uid>/`, while the code at :72-74 appends `relay-v4`. BUS.md:226-227 describes a tokio::sync::Mutex and concurrent WAL reads, and BUS.md:323/335 give `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/relay/<instance>.sock|.lock`, while paths.rs:74 uses `relay-v4`. The 'lock-free' wording at engine.rs:1217 is loose rather than strictly wrong: the checks take no store lock, but they do take small std Mutexes. CLAUDE.md already states the real locking model, which limits the harm of BUS.md §5.1 being wrong.
v1.correction: The BUS.md §5.1 and §6.2 errors carry most of the weight because agents read those docs. The comment fixes are trivial. Treat the 'lock-free' item as optional wording polish.

findings.title: self_ref is a Mutex<Option<Weak<Engine>>> that is locked on every after_commit; Arc::new_cyclic removes it
findings.evidence: `self_ref: std::sync::Mutex<Option<std::sync::Weak<Engine>>>` is set once after construction (472) and locked by every `arc()` call (585-591). arc() is called on every after_commit or deferred publication and on every idle-edge keystroke.
findings.impact: A mutex and an Option on a frequently used path guard a value that never changes after construction.
findings.fix: Build the engine with `Arc::new_cyclic(|weak| { let mut e = Engine { self_ref: weak.clone(), .. }; register_all(&mut e); e })` and make arc() `self.self_ref.upgrade()`.

v1.reason: engine.rs:410 declares `self_ref: std::sync::Mutex<Option<std::sync::Weak<Engine>>>`. It is initialised to None at 450, set once at 472 right after Arc::new, and never written again. arc() (585-591) locks it on every call. The value is immutable after construction, so the Mutex and the Option guard nothing.
v1.correction: The runtime cost is an uncontended mutex lock, a few tens of nanoseconds, so the payoff is clarity, not performance. Arc::new_cyclic works because register_all only needs &mut Engine and never upgrades during construction. A `OnceLock<Weak<Engine>>` set after Arc::new is an equally small alternative.

results.coverage:
I read every line of crates/relay-core/src/socket.rs (1055), store.rs (609) and recovery.rs (282), including their tests.

Code traced to establish reachability:
- engine.rs: parse, dispatch_inner, resolve_actor, fill_identity, answers_from_memory, pty_fast_path, shutdown/mark_restorable.
- pty.rs: Ring, the reader thread, attach, scrollback, kill, relay_children.
- handlers: session.rs (pty_by_name, spawn env), device.rs (mirror start/stop/failure, mirror_by_id/run_by_id, control socket), app.rs (backup), settings.rs, integration.rs, workspace.rs (integrations_live).
- device.rs runtimes, serve.rs, paths.rs, time.rs.
- guardrail.rs self_approval and the start of shell_commands (not the rest of the shell parser).
- relay-cli main.rs (actor_from_env, do_cmd, attach, serve) and mcp.rs; relay-remote bridge.rs and wire::gate.
- apps/relay-native client.rs and terminal.rs, for protocol expectations only.
- tests/store.rs, plus the recovery and guardrail tests in tests/sessions.rs and tests/guardrails.rs.
- Dependency sources: jiff 0.2.35 (Display precision, Sub panic), rusqlite 0.40.2 run_to_completion, and the bundled sqlite3.c (backup_step BUSY on a write transaction; VACUUM temp DB vs temp_store).
- The pedantic clippy output for the three files. Its cast warnings are the pid i64→u32→i32 casts, now part of the pid-reuse finding, and the user_version i64→usize casts, which only matter for a negative user_version in a foreign DB and are not reported.

Checked and ruled out:
- Lexicographic misordering of variable-precision jiff timestamps in the claims/audit comparisons: it needs two stamps within about 10 ns.
- Cross-test reaping through RELAY_STORE=":memory:": no test spawns PTYs on an in-memory store.

Not established (nothing was run, per the rules):
- The response/frame ordering finding depends on tokio scheduling and is a reasoned latent race.
- The detached-app reaping finding depends on launchers (xdg-open/gio, VS Code's `code`) keeping the caller's environment while detaching.
- The attach frame-loss window size was not measured.
- Whether VACUUM runs on literally every launch depends on usage density about 180 days earlier.

Out of scope and not reviewed beyond tracing needs: the rest of the guardrail shell parser, the relay-remote pairing/tunnel code, and the native UI.

findings.title: Socket door trusts the request's claimed actor: any process inside an agent session can act as `user` and approve its own guardrail holds
findings.evidence: The accept loop does `Ok((stream, _)) => { ... handle_conn(e, stream) }` and never reads peer credentials, so a connection is never bound to a session. Each line's `actor` is taken from the JSON, and engine.rs:1355 admits `(Actor::User, _) | (Actor::Test, _) => Ok(None)` with no credential. The only defence is guardrail.rs:849-881 `self_approval`, a word match over the agent's shell line; its own comment says "Best effort: the socket does not authenticate `user`". The documented full-envelope form `relay cmd '<json-envelope>'` (BUS.md §8.1; relay-cli main.rs:586-593) keeps the envelope's own actor (`if v.get("actor").is_none() { v["actor"] = ... }`). The op then sits inside one quoted word, so neither `USER_ONLY_ANSWERS.contains(word)` nor the `--actor` checks match. The tests at tests/guardrails.rs:762-768 cover `--actor`, `env -u` and `RELAY_SESSION=`, but not the envelope form or a script that writes to the socket directly.
findings.impact: Trigger: an agent whose write was held or refused runs `relay cmd '{"actor":"user","op":"guardrail.confirm","payload":{"hold_id":N}}'` from its Bash tool. The same works for `guardrail.config.set`, `settings.set guardrails.roles.builder`, or `session.input` into another agent's terminal. Consequence: the request runs as the user, and the role allowlist, guardrails and the exception/hold flow stop applying. BUS.md §0.6 scopes out hostile same-uid processes, but this is the refusal-workaround the self-approval check was written to stop, and it is one discoverable CLI call (`relay --help` shows the envelope form).
findings.fix: Bind identity at the door. On accept, read `stream.peer_cred()` to get the peer pid. Resolve the peer's session id (/proc/<pid>/stat field 6) or walk its ancestry against the live PTY child pids in `engine.ptys`; each PTY child is a session leader. If the peer is inside an agent session, refuse `user`/`test` with `bus.actor`, or bind the connection to that agent and ignore the claimed actor. The native app, the phone bridge and the user's own shell are outside session trees, so they are unaffected. Also make `relay cmd '<envelope>'` reject an explicit actor when RELAY_SESSION is set.

v1.reason: engine.rs:1347-1354 resolve_actor returns `(Actor::User, _) | (Actor::Test, _) => Ok(None)` on any door, with no credential. The socket accept loop (socket.rs:110-118) ignores peer credentials. relay-cli main.rs:583-593 handles the envelope form `relay cmd '{...}'` and keeps an explicit `actor` (`if v.get("actor").is_none()`), even when RELAY_SESSION is set. The only guard for agents, guardrail.rs:815-816 → self_approval (857-880), matches whole words: `USER_ONLY_ANSWERS.contains(word)` and `--actor`/`RELAY_SESSION=` forms. In the envelope form the op and actor sit inside one quoted JSON word, so neither matches. The test at tests/guardrails.rs:752-770 covers only the q/--actor/env -u/RELAY_SESSION= forms. So an agent whose action is held can run `relay cmd '{"actor":"user","op":"guardrail.confirm","payload":{"hold_id":N}}'` from Bash and approve its own hold, or change guardrail.config/settings. BUS.md §4.2/§14 does declare 'same uid = same trust; tokens prevent misattribution, not determined impersonation', and the code comment calls the check best effort. But the self_approval check exists specifically to stop this workaround, and this is a one-line, documented CLI form that slips past it. That makes it a safety check that can be silently bypassed (high). It is not critical, because the documented threat model excludes determined same-uid code.
v1.correction: Quick fix: in do_cmd, reject an explicit envelope actor other than the env actor when RELAY_SESSION is set. Also make self_approval inspect quoted JSON words for a user/test actor or a USER_ONLY op. The durable fix is the proposed SO_PEERCRED/session-ancestry binding at accept. Other routes, such as a script writing to the socket directly, remain open until that binding exists.

v2.reason:
(a) The mechanism is real; I traced it end to end.
- crates/relay-core/src/engine.rs:1355 accepts a claimed `user` on the socket with no credential: `(Actor::User, _) | (Actor::Test, _) => Ok(None)`. The agent's RELAY_TOKEN, which do_cmd copies in at crates/relay-cli/src/main.rs:592, is ignored for `user`.
- socket.rs:111 never reads peer credentials.
- do_cmd (main.rs:586-593) keeps an envelope's explicit `actor` even when RELAY_SESSION is set.
- self_approval (guardrail.rs:857-881) compares whole words only. shell_commands (guardrail.rs:894-955) folds quoted text into one word and splits only on whitespace and `;|&\n`. So in `relay cmd '{"actor":"user","op":"guardrail.confirm",...}'` neither `answers` nor `as_user` fires.
- confirm (handlers/guardrail.rs:570) makes no further identity check. For an exception hold, approve() (handlers/guardrail.rs:421) records a grant with `resolved_by` = "user".
- Working chain: the agent runs `guardrail.request`, then forges `guardrail.confirm`, then retries the action, which the grant now lets through.

(b) Who can trigger it, and how often.
- Any agent session with a shell can do it, but only by deliberately forging the user actor.
- That is against the role instruction (providers.rs:50, "do not work around it").
- The design rules this out of scope in four places:
  - BUS.md §0.6: "Seatbelts, not sandboxes … not a security boundary"
  - §4.2: "user needs no token (same uid, same trust)"
  - §9.5: "best effort against the obvious route, not a security boundary"
  - §14: "Tokens prevent misattribution, not determined impersonation"
- The code comment at guardrail.rs:849-850 says the same.
- Another local user cannot reach it (runtime dir 0700, socket 0600), and neither can a network peer through this path.
- An agent willing to do this already has other trivial bypasses, some by design:
  - `bash -c "rm -rf x"` (quoted words are data, D103)
  - `rm -fr`
  - writing files through Bash redirection (evaluate_exec checks no write targets)
- The self-approval check is also missed by `bash -c 'relay q guardrail.confirm …'`, by `eval`, and by `O=guardrail.confirm; relay q $O`.
- While verifying, the live Relay hook refused my own Bash heredoc of test strings as guardrail.self_approval. That shows how shallow the check is: it treats data lines as commands.
- Frequency: rare. It needs a misbehaving or prompt-injected agent.

(c) What happens when it fires.
- The agent approves its own request or hold. It can also patch guardrail config or roles for every session, and type into other sessions with `session.input`.
- The audit row and the `guardrail.resolved` event say "user", so the record shows the user approving something they never approved.
- Getting past a single rule is nothing new for a determined agent. What goes beyond the documented design is the misattribution, the persistence of config changes, and the reach into other sessions.

(d) Severity: medium, not high. The rubric's "safety check that can be silently bypassed" fits a check that fails in normal use. This one is documented as best effort and falls only to deliberate circumvention. The real defect is narrower. §9.5 promises to refuse "any relay invocation that names a user-only … answer or claims --actor user|test". The documented envelope form (`relay --help`; BUS.md §8.1) does both inside one quoted word and is not refused. That is a gap between the docs and the code in a less common path.

(e) The proposed fix is overstated.
- Peer-cred plus session/ancestry checks raise the bar, but a process can leave the PTY session and its ancestry with `setsid -f`, `systemd-run --user`, or a daemon started earlier. So this does not bind identity; §0.6 says nothing in-process can.
- It would also refuse a `user` claim from commands the person runs with Claude Code's `!` prefix inside the PTY tree.
- The pid from peer_cred can be stale by the time /proc is read.
- The CLI quick fix closes only the envelope route.
v2.correction:
Severity: high → medium.

Re-scope the title. The socket trusting `user` is a documented trade-off (BUS.md §0.6, §4.2, §9.5, §14), not the defect. The defect is that the best-effort self_approval check (crates/relay-core/src/guardrail.rs:857-881) misses the documented `relay cmd|q '<envelope>'` form, contrary to what BUS.md §9.5 promises. It also misses `bash -c`/`sh -c`/`eval` wrappers and indirection through shell variables.

Proportionate fix:
1. In do_cmd (crates/relay-cli/src/main.rs:586), refuse an envelope whose explicit `actor` differs from the environment's actor when RELAY_SESSION is set.
2. In self_approval, also inspect quoted words:
   - parse words that look like JSON for `actor` user|test or a USER_ONLY_ANSWERS op
   - re-tokenize the arguments of `-c` and `eval`
3. For user-actor socket requests, record the door and the peer pid/sid (SO_PEERCRED) in the audit row. A forged approval is then visible rather than indistinguishable from the user's.
4. Optional: refuse `user` from peers inside a PTY session. Present this as raising the bar, not as a boundary, because `setsid -f` and `systemd-run --user` still escape it, and note that it refuses `user` claims from commands typed with Claude Code's `!` prefix.

Add the envelope and `bash -c` forms to agents_cannot_answer_guardrails_as_the_user_from_a_shell (crates/relay-core/tests/guardrails.rs:753).

findings.title: Crash recovery SIGTERM/SIGKILLs whatever same-uid process now holds a session's recorded pid (pid reuse), and its whole process group
findings.evidence: Step 2 reads `pid` from `sessions` rows that a dead engine left in a live state. `Some(p) if pty::pid_alive(p as u32) => { kill_wait(p as u32); ... "pid {p} still alive from a previous engine; reaped" }`. `pid_alive` is `kill(pid, 0) == 0`, which is true for any process of the same uid. `kill_wait` (lines 20-35) does `kill(-(pid as i32), SIGTERM); kill(pid as i32, SIGTERM)`, then SIGKILL after 2 s. Nothing checks that the process is still Relay's; step 1 has already reaped, by environment, every live process that really carries this store's RELAY_SESSION. The repo's own test inserts `pid 999999` as a known-dead pid (tests/sessions.rs:576).
findings.impact: Trigger: an unclean engine exit with sessions running. Examples are a crash, an OOM kill, power loss, or `relay serve` dying with its terminal; serve() handles only SIGINT and SIGTERM, so SIGHUP kills it without shutdown(). A reboot or long downtime follows. The next launch SIGTERMs and then SIGKILLs any user process that reuses those pids, such as an editor, browser or terminal, together with its process group, losing unsaved work. `cargo test` kills any same-uid process that happens to be pid 999999 (pid_max is 4194304 on this machine class). Out-of-range stored values are worse: -1 becomes `kill(-1, SIGTERM)`, which signals every user process, and 2147483648 overflows `-(pid as i32)`, a panic with overflow checks on.
findings.fix:
Don't signal in step 2 at all. Step 1 already reaped real orphans by environment, so just mark the session restorable. If a kill is kept, verify identity first: /proc/

/environ must contain RELAY_SESSION= and RELAY_STORE=, or record the start time (/proc//stat field 22) at spawn and compare it. Reject p <= 1 and p > i32::MAX. Send all signals first and wait once, rather than 2 s per pid in sequence.

v1.reason: recovery.rs:84-93: for each sessions row still in a live state, `Some(p) if pty::pid_alive(p as u32) => kill_wait(p as u32)`. pid_alive (pty.rs:394-396) is `kill(pid,0)==0`, which is true for any same-uid process, and nothing checks the process's identity. On a clean shutdown, mark_restorable sets pid=NULL (engine.rs:676), so the rows that reach this branch come only from an unclean exit: a crash, power loss, or SIGHUP to `relay serve`, since serve.rs:45-49 handles only SIGINT and SIGTERM. Step 1 has already reaped every live process whose environ matches this store's RELAY_* values, so the step-2 kill can only hit a process that is not Relay's, such as a reused pid after a reboot, or an orphan whose environ could not be read. After a power loss and a reboot, pids are allocated again from low numbers, and a recorded agent pid can land on a user's editor or browser. That process is SIGTERMed and then SIGKILLed.
v1.correction:
Drop the out-of-range claims. The pid column is written only from a spawned u32 child pid, so -1 and values above i32::MAX need a corrupted store and are not a realistic trigger. The cargo-test pid 999999 risk is negligible. The trigger needs an unclean exit plus a pid collision, so this is medium rather than high. Fix: remove the kill in step 2 (step 1 already covers real orphans by environ) and just mark the session restorable. If a kill is kept, first check that /proc/

/environ carries RELAY_SESSION= and RELAY_STORE=.

findings.title: A large `audit.retention_days` panics recovery at every launch, so the engine can never start again
findings.evidence: `let days: i64 = ...serde_json::from_str::<i64>(&value)...unwrap_or(180); if days > 0 { let cutoff = crate::time::days_ago(days); ... }`. time.rs:16 computes `Timestamp::now() - SignedDuration::from_hours(days.saturating_mul(24))`. jiff 0.2.35 implements `Sub<SignedDuration> for Timestamp` with `.expect("subtracting signed duration from timestamp overflowed")` (timestamp.rs:2500-2506), and `from_hours` panics on overflow. Anything above about 4.39 million days (past jiff's year -9999 limit) panics. settings.set does no range check ("unknown paths are allowed", settings.rs:9-11). serve::start calls recovery with no catch_unwind (serve.rs:23), and there is none anywhere in the workspace.
findings.impact: Trigger: `relay q settings.set '{"path":"audit.retention_days","value":9999999}'`, a natural "keep forever" value (0 is the documented one). From then on every `relay serve` panics inside recovery and exits. The setting can only be changed through the engine, so the user must hand-edit store.db. Each attempt also runs steps 1-2 (process kills) before the panic rolls the transaction back, so stale pids are signalled again on every try.
findings.fix: Clamp in recovery (`days.min(36_500)`). Make days_ago use `checked_sub` and return an Option, and skip pruning on overflow. Validate `audit.retention_days` as an integer in 0..=36500 in settings.set.

v1.reason: recovery.rs:184-194 parses audit.retention_days as an i64 with no upper bound and calls crate::time::days_ago(days) when days > 0. time.rs:15-17 computes `Timestamp::now() - SignedDuration::from_hours(days.saturating_mul(24))`. In jiff 0.2.35, Sub<SignedDuration> for Timestamp does `.expect("subtracting signed duration from timestamp overflowed")` (timestamp.rs:2500-2505), and from_hours panics on overflow (signed_duration.rs:749-758). Any value above roughly 4.4M days crosses jiff's year -9999 floor and panics. settings.set does no range check ("unknown paths are allowed", settings.rs:9-10). serve::start (serve.rs:23) catches only the Err result of recovery, not a panic, and there is no catch_unwind in the workspace, so every start panics before the socket opens. Because settings live in the store, the value can't be changed without hand-editing store.db.
v1.correction: The trigger is narrower than claimed. settings.set is user-only (guardrail.rs:852 lists it among ops agents cannot call). No native UI exposes audit.retention_days, and the documented "keep forever" value is 0 (BUS.md:281, DECISIONS.md:840). The value has to be typed into the CLI and be above about 4.4 million, so this is medium rather than high: the consequence is severe but the trigger is rare. Fix as proposed: use checked_sub (or clamp days), and validate the range in settings.set.

findings.title: The /tmp fallback runtime dir is used without ownership or mode checks; the lock file is opened through symlinks and truncated
findings.evidence: When XDG_RUNTIME_DIR is unset, paths.rs:67-74 falls back to `std::env::temp_dir().join(format!("relay-v4-{uid}"))`. start_in then runs `create_dir_all(&dir)` and `let _ = std::fs::set_permissions(&dir, 0o700)`; the error is ignored and the parent directory's owner is never checked. It opens the lock with `OpenOptions::new().read(true).write(true).create(true)...open(&lock_path)`, which follows symlinks, then calls `l.set_len(0)` and writes the pid (lines 94-99), and binds the socket in the same directory.
findings.impact: Trigger: another local account, or a compromised service user, pre-creates /tmp/relay-v4-1000/relay-v4/ with a symlink `stable.lock -> ~/.bashrc` (fs.protected_symlinks does not apply because that directory is not sticky). The user then runs `relay serve` without XDG_RUNTIME_DIR (cron, su, ssh without pam_systemd, some containers). Consequence: the victim's file is truncated. If the attacker's directory is writable, the engine's socket lives there, and the attacker can unlink it and bind their own. The CLI, MCP servers and agents would then send RELAY_TOKENs and requests to the attacker and trust the forged responses.
findings.fix: Refuse to run from a runtime dir that is not owned by getuid() with `mode & 0o077 == 0`: lstat each component, reject symlinks, as tmux and ssh-agent do. Create the fallback with DirBuilder::mode(0o700). Open the lock with `custom_flags(libc::O_NOFOLLOW)`. Prefer a fallback under $HOME (e.g. ~/.cache/relay-v4/run).

v1.reason: paths.rs:67-74: when XDG_RUNTIME_DIR is unset, `directories::BaseDirs::runtime_dir()` returns None and the code falls back to `temp_dir()/relay-v4-<uid>/relay-v4`. socket.rs:55-56 does `create_dir_all(&dir)` and then `let _ = set_permissions(&dir, 0o700)`. If the directory was pre-created by another account, the chmod fails silently and ownership is never checked. create_dir_all also creates the intermediate relay-v4-<uid> with umask permissions. Lines 60-67 open the lock with create, without O_NOFOLLOW, so a planted symlink is followed. After flock succeeds, lines 94-99 call `l.set_len(0)` and write the pid into whatever file the symlink points to. That directory is not sticky, so fs.protected_symlinks does not apply. The socket is bound in that attacker-owned directory (lines 88-103), so the owner can unlink it and bind their own; the CLI and MCP clients would then send their RELAY_TOKEN and requests there. The trigger needs a second local account plus a launch without XDG_RUNTIME_DIR (cron, su, ssh without pam_systemd). A normal desktop launch has the variable set and so does every agent child, which keeps this at medium rather than critical.
v1.correction: Same lines as cited. Fix: create the fallback with DirBuilder::mode(0o700); lstat it and refuse unless it is owned by getuid() with no group/other bits; open the lock with O_NOFOLLOW. A fallback under $HOME avoids the problem entirely.

findings.title: Startup recovery kills every process that inherited a session's RELAY_* environment, including detached apps the user kept using
findings.evidence: `let orphans = pty::relay_children(instance, &store_path); for (pid, name) in &orphans { kill_wait(*pid); ... }`. relay_children (pty.rs:411-429) returns every pid whose /proc/<pid>/environ has the matching RELAY_INSTANCE and RELAY_STORE plus a RELAY_SESSION. That covers the provider process and anything that inherited its environment, regardless of process group or session. It runs on every launch, including after a clean quit. Engine::shutdown and Pty::kill signal only the PTY's process group (pty.rs:344-369), so detached descendants survive a clean quit and are hit on the next start.
findings.impact: Trigger: an agent runs `xdg-open http://localhost:3000` or `code .` (or the provider CLI opens a browser for re-login) while that app isn't already running. The browser or editor starts detached, with RELAY_SESSION/RELAY_STORE/RELAY_INSTANCE in its environment, and the user keeps working in it. Consequence: the next Relay launch SIGTERMs it and its process group, then SIGKILLs it after 2 s, losing unsaved buffers. SPEC §14 asks only to "reap orphaned claude/codex processes".
findings.fix: Restrict reaping to the provider processes Relay spawned. Record (pid, start time) at spawn; at recovery, kill only processes that still match, by session (`kill(-pid)` reaches the PTY's process group). For other processes carrying the environment, skip any whose session id (/proc/pid/stat field 6) is not a recorded session leader, or only list them in fsck_fixes.

v1.reason: pty.rs:408-429 `relay_children` returns every /proc pid whose environ carries RELAY_INSTANCE==instance, RELAY_STORE==store and any RELAY_SESSION. Its doc comment says this deliberately includes "Relay's own children (and theirs)". The env is set at spawn (handlers/session.rs:565-575) and is inherited by anything an agent launches. recovery.rs:67-69 runs `kill_wait` on each of them on every start, clean or not, and kill_wait (recovery.rs:20-35) signals -pid and then pid, with SIGKILL after 2 s. On a clean quit, Engine::shutdown (engine.rs:633-659) calls Pty::kill, which signals only the PTY child's process group (pty.rs:344-369), and closing the master sends SIGHUP only to the session leader and the foreground group. So a GUI app an agent started in another process group, or detached (xdg-open starting a browser that wasn't already running, `code .`), survives the quit and is SIGTERMed and then SIGKILLed on the next launch. D20 only scopes reaping to the store; it does not consider descendants the user has adopted. SPEC §14 says "reap orphaned claude/codex processes".
v1.correction: Reaping descendants is a deliberate choice (pty.rs doc comment), not an accident. It is useful for dev servers an agent left running, which is a reason to narrow it rather than remove it. The trigger needs an agent to launch a GUI app that wasn't already running and that the user then keeps using, so this is medium at most. Better fix: kill only the recorded provider pid and its process group (verified by start time or environ), and for other env-carrying processes outside a recorded session, only list them in fsck_fixes or limit reaping to processes whose session id (stat field 6) matches the recorded leader.

findings.title: Every `?` in handle_conn skips the cleanup block, leaving a half-open connection that keeps streaming output but never reads another request
findings.evidence: `while let Some(line) = lines.next_line().await? {` returns early on a non-UTF-8 line or a read error. `tokio::task::spawn_blocking(...).await?` (lines 361, 419, 459, 511, 524, 652, 726, 742) returns early on a handler panic, since there is no catch_unwind anywhere. The cleanup (`forwarder.abort()`, `attached.drain() ... abort()`, `attached_runs ... abort()`, lines 746-759) runs only on a clean EOF. Dropping a tokio JoinHandle detaches the task rather than aborting it. The forwarder, PTY and logcat tasks keep their `out_tx` clones, so the writer task keeps the write half open. The request that panicked gets no `internal` response.
findings.impact: Trigger: one panic in any handler reached from the native app's control or terminal connection (e.g. a poisoned std::Mutex `.unwrap()`), or a stray non-UTF-8 byte from a raw client. Consequence: the window keeps receiving events and PTY frames, but every action or keystroke on that connection times out after 30 s (client.rs:65-72). The socket never closes, so the client never reconnects.
findings.fix: Own the per-connection tasks in a struct whose Drop aborts them (or a JoinSet, or AbortOnDrop handles), so every exit path cleans up. Map a JoinError to `Response::err(req.id, BusError::internal(..))` and keep serving. Read lines as bytes (`read_until(b'\n')`) and answer invalid UTF-8 with a `bus.parse` response instead of dropping the connection.

v1.reason: socket.rs:335 `while let Some(line) = lines.next_line().await?` returns Err on a read error or invalid UTF-8. Each `spawn_blocking(..).await?` (lines 361, 419, 459, 511, 524, 652, 726, 742) returns Err on a handler panic. dispatch (engine.rs:759-772) has no catch_unwind and the workspace sets no panic=abort. On that early return the cleanup at 746-759 is skipped. The `forwarder` and the `attached`/`attached_runs` JoinHandles are dropped, which detaches their tasks rather than aborting them. Those tasks hold `out_tx` clones, so the writer task keeps `w` alive and the socket's write side never shuts down, while the read half is dropped and no further requests are served. The native control connection subscribes to events (forwarder) and terminal connections attach PTYs, so either keeps the writer alive. The client never sees EOF, so it never reconnects, and every request on that connection hits the 30 s timeout (client.rs:65-72). The panicking request also never gets a response.
v1.correction: Small correction: `attached_mirrors` holds MirrorAttachment values whose Drop aborts the task, so mirror tasks are cleaned up even on early return. Only the forwarder, PTY and run tasks (and the writer) leak. If no forwarder or attachment exists, the writer ends and the client does see EOF. The trigger needs a handler panic (e.g. a poisoned std::Mutex unwrap) or a raw client sending non-UTF-8 bytes, which keeps this at medium.

findings.title: Recovery closes interrupted device runs but not integrations; a restart mid-integration leaves it live forever and blocks project.remove
findings.evidence: Step 4 runs `UPDATE device_runs SET state='stopped',finished_at=?1 WHERE state IN ('building','running')`, and integrations get no equivalent. Integration work runs on a plain thread (handlers/integration.rs:38-40, `std::thread::spawn(move || run(engine, id, parent))`) that dies with the process, and Engine::shutdown (engine.rs:633-659) doesn't touch integrations either. handlers/workspace.rs:387-390 `integrations_live` counts `state IN ('queued','merging','building','deploying')`. Project and workspace removal refuse on that count (workspace.rs:166, 304, `project.activity_live`), even with force (tests/registry_remove.rs:150-153).
findings.impact:
Trigger: quit or crash while an integration merges or builds; builds take minutes. Consequences after restart:
- The integration shows as in progress forever, with no terminal `integration.changed` and no `.completed` audit row (BUS.md §5.1: "what happened to my request is always audit.list {parent_req}").
- Agents waiting on it time out.
- project.remove refuses until the user finds and discards it.
- The .relay/integrations/<id> worktree and the relay/integration-<id> branch linger.
findings.fix: Mirror step 4 for integrations. Set state='failed' with log_tail "interrupted by engine restart" and finished_at, append the system `integration.request.completed` audit row (the system_write path), emit `integration.changed`, and add an entry to fsck_fixes.

v1.reason: integration.request (handlers/integration.rs:30-41) inserts a 'queued' row and runs `run` on a bare std::thread::spawn, which dies with the process. Neither Engine::shutdown (engine.rs:633-659) nor recovery (recovery.rs step 4 at 112-122 handles only device_runs) touches integrations, so a row left in queued, merging, building or deploying stays that way after a restart. integrations_live (workspace.rs:387-390) counts those states, and both project.remove (workspace.rs:~304, "never interrupt it, force or not") and workspace.remove (workspace.rs:~166) refuse with project.activity_live. integration.discard (integration.rs:58-69) clears the row, but the native client only calls integration.list (code_git.rs:581), so a UI user has no way out short of the CLI.
v1.correction: The workaround is `relay q integration.discard`, which only CLI users can reach; it is not quite "forever". Fix as proposed: in recovery, set live integrations to 'failed' with a log_tail and finished_at, record the system completion audit row and emit integration.changed after startup. Leave worktree and branch cleanup to discard.

findings.title: Request lines have no size limit: one long line is buffered whole and copied several times, which can OOM the engine
findings.evidence: `let mut lines = BufReader::new(r).lines();` and `lines.next_line().await?` read until '\n' with no cap. The line is then parsed into a `Request` Value and cloned: `req.clone()` for attach, detach, mirror and runs; `req.payload.clone()` in subscribe and wait; and `serde_json::from_value(payload.clone())` in pty_fast_path. The handler then deserializes it again into the typed payload. The native client bounds incoming lines at 2 MiB before allocating (apps/relay-native/src/client.rs:48, 186-205), but the engine bounds nothing. The phone bridge forwards lines of up to tungstenite's default 64 MiB.
findings.impact: Trigger: a local client that writes without newlines (e.g. a file piped into the socket by mistake), or a huge payload such as `relay cmd file.write -` of a multi-GB file or a giant paste sent as `session.input`. Consequence: the engine holds 3-4x the line in memory. At GB scale it is OOM-killed, and every agent session dies with it.
findings.fix: Read with a bounded fill_buf/read_until loop, as the native client does (e.g. a 16-32 MiB cap). Answer an over-limit line with a typed `bus.too_large` error and discard the rest of that line. Pull the needed fields out before moving `req`, to avoid the extra clones.

v1.reason: socket.rs:323/335: `BufReader::new(r).lines()` and `next_line().await?` buffer a whole line with no cap. The line is then parsed into a Value and cloned several times (req.clone() for attach/detach/mirror/run, payload clones in subscribe/wait). The socket is chmod 0600 inside a 0700 runtime dir (socket.rs:56, 101), so only the same local user can send such a line: the user's own CLI, an agent, or a stray pipe. The phone bridge (relay-remote bridge.rs:163) forwards websocket messages, which tungstenite caps at 64 MiB by default, so a paired phone produces at most a few hundred MB transiently, not an OOM. The mechanism is real. An OOM needs a same-user client writing a multi-GB line with no newline, which is a self-inflicted, unusual trigger.
v1.correction: Downgrade to low: no other local user or network peer can reach it, and the remote path is bounded at 64 MiB by tungstenite. The fix is still reasonable: a bounded read_until loop like the native client's (client.rs:186-205), answering over-limit lines with a typed error.

findings.title: PTY attach can silently lose an output frame: `att.seq` comes from a counter that is bumped before the frame reaches the ring
findings.evidence: socket.rs:487 skips live frames with `if fr.seq <= att.seq && fr.epoch == att.epoch { continue; } // already in catch-up`. `att.seq` is the AtomicU64 read under the ring lock (pty.rs:306-317), while `catch_up` is built from ring contents. The reader thread does `let seq = sh.seq.fetch_add(1, SeqCst) + 1; let data = buf[..n].to_vec(); sh.ring.lock().unwrap().push(seq, &data); tx.send(..)` (pty.rs:215-218), so the counter advances before the ring lock is taken.
findings.impact: Trigger: an attach takes the ring lock between a reader's fetch_add and its push. That window includes a 64 KiB allocation and copy, so it is reachable on a busy agent. Consequence: catch-up ends at frame S, att.seq is S+1, and live frame S+1 is dropped as "already in catch-up". The client's sequence tracker sees S+1 followed by S+2 as contiguous, so up to 64 KiB of terminal output (often escape sequences) is missing with no gap detected. The pane is garbled on (re)attach until the next full redraw.
findings.fix: In pty.rs, take the sequence number inside the ring lock (lock the ring, fetch_add, push, unlock, send), or have attach report the ring's last pushed seq (`frames.back()`) instead of the atomic. Pty::scrollback has a wider version of this skew: it reads `self.seq()` after dropping the ring lock (pty.rs:323-339), so the `session.scrollback` → `attach {from_seq}` resume that BUS.md §7 calls exact can skip frames.

v1.reason: The race is real. In pty.rs:215-218 the reader thread runs `let seq = sh.seq.fetch_add(1, SeqCst) + 1; let data = buf[..n].to_vec(); sh.ring.lock().unwrap().push(seq, &data); tx.send(...)`, so the counter moves before the ring lock is taken. Pty::attach (pty.rs:305-317) subscribes, takes the ring lock, and reads `self.seq()` (the atomic) while holding that lock. If it lands in the reader's window between fetch_add and push, it gets seq = S+1 while the ring ends at S. socket.rs:481 then labels the catch-up line with `att.seq` (S+1) even though it only holds bytes up to S, and socket.rs:487 (`if fr.seq <= att.seq && fr.epoch == att.epoch { continue; }`) drops live frame S+1, which was already subscribed. The native client's Sequence::observe (apps/relay-native/src/terminal.rs:24-37) takes catch-up S+1 and then S+2 as contiguous, so it sees no gap and the lost bytes are never recovered. Pty::scrollback (pty.rs:323-340) reads `self.seq()` after dropping the ring lock, which leaves a wider version of the same skew.
v1.correction: There is a second consequence the finding misses. On a re-attach with from_seq == S (the native client's normal reconnect path), the same window makes `s >= seq` false while `ring.offset_after(S)` returns None, because no frame after S is in the ring yet. `.unwrap_or(0)` then sends the whole bounded 256 KiB tail again as catch-up. The native client feeds it because catch_up is set and S+1 > S, so stale output is duplicated in the terminal on top of the dropped frame. Severity is lowered to low. The window is a few microseconds per read (one `to_vec` of up to 64 KiB plus the lock), it has to coincide with an attach, which is rare, and the damage is a garbled display that the next TUI redraw usually repairs. No session data is lost. The fix stands: assign seq inside the ring lock (lock, fetch_add, push, unlock, send), or derive attach and scrollback seq from the ring's last pushed frame.

findings.title: `session.attach` takes the store mutex on a tokio worker thread, for a lookup the in-memory index already answers
findings.evidence: After `spawn_blocking(dispatch)`, the async task calls `crate::handlers::session::pty_by_name(&engine, &p.session)`. That function does `let conn = engine.store.lock(); let row = sessions::by_name(&conn, name)?` (handlers/session.rs:1732-1735), a blocking std::Mutex wait inside the runtime. The lookup is redundant: the pipeline has just validated the session, and `Engine::pty_named` (engine.rs:600-608) is the in-memory name → (id, pty) index built for this purpose (D148).
findings.impact: Trigger: the store is held for a while, by a long handler transaction, app.backup.now, or a slow `register` handler, while panes attach. Consequence: each attaching terminal pane parks a runtime worker for that long. A window restoring several panes during such a hold can occupy every worker. Inline keystrokes (answered on workers, socket.rs:735-739), PTY frames and events then stall for the duration.
findings.fix:
Use `engine.pty_named(&p.session)`, and fall back to `spawn_blocking(pty_by_name)` only to build the typed "not spawned" error. Two related paths also block a worker:
- The inline path reaches `store.lock()` when the PTY disappears between `answers_from_memory` and `pty_fast_path` (engine.rs:1271-1273 falls through to the locked handler).
- Inline `device.mirror.input` writes to a blocking TcpStream with no write timeout (device.rs:279-283). Give that stream a write timeout, or move the write off the worker thread.

v1.reason: After spawn_blocking(dispatch), the async connection task calls handlers::session::pty_by_name, which does engine.store.lock() (handlers/session.rs:1732-1735; Store::lock is a blocking std Mutex, store.rs:474) on a tokio worker. The lookup is redundant: the Attach handler (session.rs:1640-1652) has just resolved the row and checked that the PTY exists, and Engine::pty_named (engine.rs:600) answers from memory. The impact is overstated, though. The dispatch immediately before already waited for the store lock on a blocking thread, so a worker parks only if another long holder takes the lock in the microsecond gap between the dispatch returning and pty_by_name running. That can happen (backups, slow register handlers, many concurrent attaches), but it is not 'a window restoring several panes during a hold occupies every worker'. The related inline fall-through (engine.rs:1271) is a narrow race. Inline device.mirror.input does a blocking write_all on the scrcpy control TcpStream with no write timeout (device.rs:279-283). It is small control messages to a local adb forward and blocks only if the device stops draining the socket.
v1.correction: Severity is low, not medium. The trigger needs a slow lock holder to start in the gap after dispatch, because each attach has already waited out any existing hold inside spawn_blocking. The fix as proposed is good: use engine.pty_named(&p.session), and fall back to spawn_blocking(pty_by_name) only to build the typed error.

findings.title: `app.backup.now` copies the whole database inside a locked handler, and `backup_with` spins forever if called after a write
findings.evidence: handlers/app.rs:47-48 registers BackupNow with `e.register` and calls `store.backup_with(ctx.tx(), "manual")`. backup_to runs `bk.run_to_completion(256, Duration::from_millis(0), None)`. The store mutex is held for the full copy, so the 256-page steps buy nothing. SQLite's backup_step returns SQLITE_BUSY immediately while the source btree is in a write transaction (bundled sqlite3.c:85056-85063). rusqlite 0.40's run_to_completion treats Busy as sleep(0) and retry (backup.rs:301-310).
findings.impact: Trigger: the user clicks "Back up now". Consequence: every bus request except keystrokes is blocked for a full DB copy (CLAUDE.md §5.1 invariant), which takes seconds once the store holds several 8 MiB scrollback snapshots. Latent hazard: any future handler that calls backup_with after writing in its transaction (e.g. "back up before X") spins at 100% CPU while holding the store mutex, freezing the engine.
findings.fix: Register the op as staged or unlocked and copy step-wise, re-taking the store mutex for each `step(n)`. SQLite's backup follows same-connection writes made between steps. In backup_to, replace run_to_completion with an explicit loop that returns an error on repeated Busy/Locked instead of spinning. Assert that the source connection has no open write transaction.

v1.reason: handlers/app.rs:47-48 registers BackupNow with `e.register` and calls `store.backup_with(ctx.tx(), "manual")`. dispatch (engine.rs:952-980) holds `self.store.lock()` and an open transaction for the whole handler. backup_to (store.rs:555-571) calls `run_to_completion(256, Duration::from_millis(0), None)`, so the entire database is copied, and the destination committed, while the store mutex is held. That breaks the CLAUDE.md §5.1 rule. Every other bus request waits for the copy except session.input, which answers from memory. The store can hold session_scrollback rows of up to 8 MiB each (SCROLLBACK_BYTES, written by mark_restorable), so the copy grows with the number of restorable sessions. rusqlite 0.40.2's run_to_completion (backup.rs:301-310) retries Busy and Locked forever with a zero sleep, and SQLite's backup_step returns BUSY while the source btree is in a write transaction. So the latent spin described in the finding is real.
v1.correction: The spin is not reachable today. The handler transaction is a DEFERRED BEGIN (`conn.transaction()`), BackupNow writes nothing before calling backup_with, and the audit row is appended after the handler returns (engine.rs:996+). It is a hazard only for a future caller that writes first. The present cost is a stall of the bus on a rare, user-initiated action: roughly hundreds of milliseconds to a few seconds depending on store size. Unlocked registration on its own is not enough. Because the engine connection uses locking_mode=EXCLUSIVE, a second connection cannot read the store, so the backup has to stay on the engine connection and copy in steps, taking the store mutex for each step(n). Same-connection writes made between steps are carried into the backup automatically. Replace run_to_completion with an explicit loop that gives up after repeated Busy or Locked results.

findings.title: Recovery VACUUMs the entire store on practically every launch once the audit log is older than the retention window
findings.evidence: `if pruned > 0 { if let Err(error) = conn.execute_batch("VACUUM") {...} }` runs after deleting rows where `ts < now - retention`. Once the store is older than 180 days, each launch prunes the rows that crossed the cutoff since the previous launch, so `pruned > 0` on almost every start. store.rs:539 sets `temp_store=MEMORY`; VACUUM attaches an empty-name temp DB, which becomes an in-memory DB under that setting (sqlite3.c: `isTempDb && sqlite3TempInMemory(db)`). In WAL mode the rewrite goes through the WAL, and no journal_size_limit is set, so the WAL is never truncated.
findings.impact: Every engine start after the first 180 days of use rewrites the whole store while the doors are closed. That costs seconds for a few hundred MB, plus a RAM spike about the size of the store. The -wal file stays about the size of the store for the engine's lifetime. This undoes the PERF §1.5 work that deferred the dirty scan to save ~160 ms of startup.
findings.fix: VACUUM only when free pages are a large fraction of the file (`PRAGMA freelist_count` against `page_count`, e.g. above 25%). Alternatively switch to `auto_vacuum=INCREMENTAL` and run `PRAGMA incremental_vacuum(N)`. Set `journal_size_limit`, or run `wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE)` after compaction.

v1.reason: recovery.rs:186-206 deletes audit rows with `ts < days_ago(180)` (DEFAULT_AUDIT_RETENTION_DAYS=180, line 18). Lines 216-220 then run `conn.execute_batch("VACUUM")` whenever `pruned > 0`. After the first 180 days, every row's age crosses the cutoff at some point, so any launch at least a few minutes after the previous one prunes something and runs a full VACUUM. The comment "Compact only when a prune actually happened, so the usual launch pays nothing for it" assumes this is rare, and that assumption is wrong. This runs in serve::start (serve.rs:21-24) before SocketServer::start, so the door is not open yet. The store is not necessarily small: it also holds session_scrollback and file_trash (store.rs:198, 216). store.rs:539 sets temp_store=MEMORY, so the VACUUM temp copy is held in RAM. In WAL mode (store.rs:395) every page is written through the WAL, and no journal_size_limit is set, so the -wal file stays roughly the size of the store until the connection closes.
v1.correction: The cost scales with the store's size. For the tens-of-MB store that tune() assumes it is roughly 100-500 ms per launch, and seconds only for a much larger store. Calling it 'seconds' is the upper end of the range. The suggested freelist_count/page_count threshold is the right fix. A wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE) after the VACUUM fixes the WAL size.

findings.title: handle_conn is a 450-line if/else chain with hand-rolled, duplicated stream plumbing per op
findings.evidence: One function routes ten ops by string comparison. The sequence `let e = engine.clone(); let r2 = req.clone(); tokio::task::spawn_blocking(move || e.dispatch(r2, Door::Socket)).await?` is repeated at 459, 511, 524, 652, 726 and 742. The logcat `Frame { v: 1, stream: "logcat".into(), ... }` literal is duplicated verbatim (669-678 and 688-697). Mirror and logcat frames hard-code `v: 1` while PTY frames use ENVELOPE_V. Task ownership is spread over three ad-hoc maps plus a manual cleanup block (746-759).
findings.impact: The early-return leak, the unfilled-payload attach and the response/frame ordering findings all come from this shape. Every new socket-capable op adds another branch with another copy of the dispatch/attach/abort sequence.
findings.fix:
Split it up:
- A `dispatch_blocking(&engine, req) -> Response` helper that maps JoinError to `internal`.
- One `Attachments` struct (pty, runs, mirrors, forwarder) with attach/detach methods and an aborting Drop.
- A `match req.op.as_str()` that delegates to per-op functions.
- One frame helper that uses ENVELOPE_V.
This removes roughly 150 lines and the manual cleanup block.

v1.reason: handle_conn (socket.rs:281-761) is a single ~480-line if/else chain on `req.op`. The `let e = engine.clone(); let r2 = req.clone(); spawn_blocking(move || e.dispatch(r2, Door::Socket)).await?` sequence repeats for attach, detach, mirror start, run/build, run stop and the default branch. The logcat Frame literal is duplicated verbatim in the history and live loops. Mirror and logcat frames hard-code `v: 1` while pty frames use ENVELOPE_V, which is currently also 1 (envelope.rs:12), so nothing has diverged yet. The manual cleanup block at the end is what makes the early-return leak (#6) possible, so the shape has a concrete cost. That cost is the same root cause as #6, though, and fixing #6 with RAII-owned tasks removes most of it. What remains is maintainability with no current misbehavior.
v1.correction: Downgrade to low. The cost that matters (cleanup skipped on `?`) is covered by #6. The remaining payoff is a dispatch_blocking helper, one frame helper using ENVELOPE_V, and an Attachments struct with an aborting Drop. That is worthwhile, but it is not a bug and should not be a large standalone refactor.

findings.title: `bus.wait` blocks the connection's read loop for up to an hour and never notices the client leaving
findings.evidence: `let waited = tokio::time::timeout(timeout, async { loop { match rx.recv().await { ... } } }).await;` is awaited inside the request loop, with a timeout of up to 3_600_000 ms (line 409). Nothing polls the read half meanwhile, so neither EOF nor further pipelined requests are seen until the wait ends.
findings.impact: Trigger: an agent is parked or closed, or its MCP call is interrupted, in the middle of the documented exception flow ("call guardrail.request ... then bus.wait", guardrail/grants.rs:24-28). Consequence: the engine keeps the connection, its task, its fd and a broadcast receiver alive until the timeout. Any other request pipelined on that connection waits the whole time.
findings.fix: Run each wait in its own task owned by the connection, so the loop keeps reading and EOF aborts the wait. Alternatively, `select!` the wait against EOF on the reader.

v1.reason: bus.wait awaits tokio::time::timeout(timeout, ...) inline in the connection's read loop (socket.rs ~424). The timeout is clamped to 1s..3,600,000ms with a default of 60s. Nothing reads the socket during the wait, so the engine cannot see EOF and keeps the task, the fd and the broadcast receiver until the timeout. The pipelining half of the impact does not apply to real clients. The MCP server opens a fresh connection for every tool call (relay-cli/src/mcp.rs:146 call_tool -> connect) and sends one request on it, and bus.subscribe and bus.unsubscribe are not exposed over MCP. What remains is a bounded, self-healing leak: one idle task, fd and receiver per abandoned wait, for at most the requested timeout (one hour at most). The receiver is still being drained, so it adds no broadcast backpressure.
v1.correction: Drop the claim that requests pipelined on the same connection are delayed, since no in-tree client pipelines behind bus.wait. A cheap fix is to tokio::select! the wait against lines.next_line() returning None or an error (treating any other line as a protocol error or queueing it), or to cap the default lower. Effort S rather than M.

findings.title: Broadcast lag drops events silently: subscribers are never told to resync, and a waiter can miss the answer it is waiting for
findings.evidence: The forwarder handles `Err(RecvError::Lagged(n))` with only `tracing::warn!(lagged = n, "subscriber lagged; events dropped")` and continues. Events carry no sequence number, unlike PTY, logcat and mirror frames, so a client cannot detect the hole. The waiter (432-434) does the same, and the stored-answer lookup (`resolved_event`, 413-423) runs only once, before the wait starts.
findings.impact: Trigger: a window's reader stalls long enough for more than 4096 events (broadcast capacity, engine.rs:437) plus the 1024-line out queue to back up. The UI then misses state changes such as session.changed and task.* and stays stale, with no sign anything was missed. A bus.wait whose `guardrail.request_resolved` event was dropped waits until its timeout, even though the answer is already stored.
findings.fix: On Lagged, send a synthetic `bus.lagged {dropped: n}` event so clients refetch, and document it in BUS.md §6.2. In bus.wait, re-run `resolved_event` on Lagged whenever `exception_waited` returned Some.

v1.reason: The subscribe forwarder (socket.rs ~385) handles RecvError::Lagged by logging and continuing. It sends nothing to the client, and events carry no sequence number, so a dropped event is undetectable. The trigger is reachable. The native client's notice channel is async_channel::bounded(64) (apps/relay-native/src/client.rs:47,179) and is drained on the GTK main thread (app.rs ~1166). A long main-thread stall therefore backs up 64 notices, then the socket buffer, then the 1024-line out queue. After that the forwarder blocks on tx.send and stops polling the 4096-slot broadcast, so a burst (for example file.changed or git.changed) can overflow it. The window then silently stays stale until something else triggers a refresh. That needs a sustained stall plus a large burst, so it is rare.
v1.correction: The bus.wait half is close to unreachable. The waiter's receiver is polled in a tight loop with no output backpressure, so it lags only if more than 4096 events are broadcast during one scheduling gap, or during the spawn_blocking resolved_event lookup (which waits on the store lock that event-producing commits also need). Rate the wait part as theoretical. The resync-event fix for subscribers is reasonable. Re-running resolved_event on Lagged is a cheap guard, but low priority.

findings.title: Stream tasks are spawned before the response is queued, so frames can arrive ahead of it, and `Client::call` throws those frames away
findings.evidence: The attach (477), mirror (554) and run (667) branches spawn the stream task first; the response is queued later, at line 744 (`out_tx.send(serde_json::to_string(&resp)?)`). The spawned task's first action is to send its catch-up, history or status line. It wins whenever the scheduler runs it on another worker first, for example when the LIFO slot is disabled or the main task yields on its coop budget. `Client::call` ignores frames while waiting for its response (`Some(Line::Frame(_)) => {}`), and `relay attach` calls `c.call(&req, |_| {})` before it starts printing frames (relay-cli main.rs:249).
findings.impact: Intermittently, `relay attach` starts without the 256 KiB catch-up, so the existing screen is missing. The native client buffers early frames in a 64-slot notice channel, so only a large burst would affect it.
findings.fix: Queue the response first, then spawn the stream task (send `resp` inside the branch and `continue`), which makes the order deterministic. Optionally make `Client::call` buffer frames instead of dropping them.

v1.reason: Under the runtime this code actually uses (tokio 1.53.1, multi-thread scheduler), the response is always queued before the stream task's first frame. The connection task reaches the attach, mirror and run branches only after `spawn_blocking(...dispatch...).await`. The blocking-pool thread wakes it from outside any worker, so it starts a fresh run_task with a full coop budget and lifo_enabled reset. The `tokio::spawn` inside the branch goes through schedule_local into the worker's LIFO slot. That slot cannot be stolen, and when it was empty, should_notify is false (worker.rs:1376-1406), so no other worker is woken to run the task. Between the spawn and `out_tx.send(resp).await` there is one budgeted operation, so the coop-exhaustion trigger cannot fire. The LIFO slot is disabled only after 3 consecutive LIFO polls inside one chain, and this task starts its chain from the inject queue. If the 1024-slot out channel is full, tokio's bounded mpsc semaphore serves waiters FIFO, so the main task's send, queued first, still wins. Both shipped clients send session.attach as the first request on a fresh connection: relay-cli main.rs:243-249 and the native terminal.rs:475-485, which uses one Client::connect per attach. That rules out pipelined budget exhaustion too. The ordering does rest on scheduler behaviour rather than an explicit guarantee, but no reachable trigger exists in this codebase.
v1.correction: Sending the response before spawning the stream task would make the ordering explicit and costs nothing, so it is a reasonable hardening if someone touches this code. It is not a bug with a trigger today.

findings.title: The socket door stays open, and keeps dispatching, while serve() kills sessions; SocketServer cannot stop live connections
findings.evidence: Drop only aborts the accept task and unlinks the socket. Per-connection tasks are detached `tokio::spawn`s (113-117) with no shutdown signal. serve.rs:50-51 runs `served.engine.shutdown()` before `drop(served)`; shutdown() takes up to 2 s plus 2 s per live PTY, in sequence. Dispatch never checks `is_quitting()`.
findings.impact: During app.quit or SIGTERM, connected clients (native app, MCP calls, phone) keep dispatching, and new connections are still accepted. A `session.wake` or `session.spawn` in that window inserts a PTY after shutdown() has drained the map. That PTY is neither killed nor marked restorable, and its row stays 'running' for the next recovery, which is the pid-reuse path above.
findings.fix: Give SocketServer a CancellationToken or JoinSet for its connections, and close the door (stop accepting, end connections) before `engine.shutdown()`. Once `request_quit` is set, have dispatch refuse mutations with `app.quitting`.

v1.reason: serve.rs:44-51 runs `served.engine.shutdown()` (engine.rs:633-659: drains mirrors/runs/ptys, marks them restorable, then kills each PTY with a 2 s grace, one after another) before `drop(served)`. relay-cli uses #[tokio::main], which is multi-threaded, so the accept loop (socket.rs:107-126) and every detached per-connection task keep running on the other workers while shutdown() blocks one thread. Nothing on the dispatch path checks `is_quitting()`. The only checks are in branch_cleanup.rs. A session spawn/wake that commits during that window inserts into `ptys` after the drain, so it is neither marked restorable nor killed. Its row stays in a live state, and the next recovery (recovery.rs:78-100) reaps it as a crash. SocketServer::drop aborts only the accept task. The window is real but short: it lasts only until serve() returns and the runtime drops, and the spawning request has to arrive in it, which means an orchestrating agent or a client still acting after app.quit. The outcome is a session restored as 'crash' rather than 'app_restart', plus the recovery reap. Nothing is lost.
v1.correction: The window is bounded by shutdown() itself, because once serve() returns the runtime and its detached tasks are dropped. remote.rs::serve_with_door has the same sequence. The simplest fix is to make dispatch refuse lifecycle mutations once `is_quitting()` is true (SIGINT/SIGTERM must call request_quit first), and/or drop the SocketServer before calling engine.shutdown().

findings.title: MirrorAttachment::drop always announces `stopped`, relabelling a lost or failed mirror and duplicating stop events
findings.evidence: `self.runtime.finish(crate::device::MirrorState::Stopped, None, None);` ignores the return value, then `self.engine.emit_system("mirror.changed", json!({"mirror_id":self.runtime.id,"state":"stopped"}))` runs unconditionally. `finish` is first-terminal-wins (device.rs:245-258), and handlers/device.rs:736-744 emits only when finish returns true. This event also omits the `device` field that the other emitters include.
findings.impact: Trigger: the device is unplugged (`lost` is emitted) and the window then closes, or `device.mirror.stop` has already emitted `stopped`. Listeners then receive another `mirror.changed {state:"stopped"}`, and anything keyed on the last event shows "stopped" instead of "lost" or "failed". device.rs:245-246 says this relabel must not happen.
findings.fix: `if self.runtime.finish(MirrorState::Stopped, None, None) { emit_system("mirror.changed", json!({.., "device": self.runtime.device, "state": "stopped"})) }`.

v1.reason: socket.rs:229-243: MirrorAttachment::drop calls `self.runtime.finish(MirrorState::Stopped, None, None)`, discards its bool, and emits `mirror.changed {mirror_id, state:"stopped"}` unconditionally, with no `device` field. finish is first-terminal-wins (device.rs:245-258). mirror_failure (handlers/device.rs:736-745) emits only when finish returns true, and MirrorStop (handlers/device.rs:109-129) has already emitted `stopped`. The attachment stays in `attached_mirrors` after device.mirror.stop or after a lost device, so closing the connection emits a second, contradictory `stopped`. The impact is small: in this repo nothing outside the mobile app (out of scope) and the tests consumes `mirror.changed`. Only an agent's bus.wait/subscribe, or a future listener, would see the relabel.
v1.correction: Gate the emit on `finish(..)` returning true and include `"device": self.runtime.device`, as the other emitters do. Removing the entry from `attached_mirrors` once the stream reaches a terminal state would also stop the stale attachment outliving its mirror.

findings.title: bus.subscribe, bus.wait and bus.unsubscribe skip the pipeline's envelope and actor checks
findings.evidence: These branches deserialize the payload directly (`serde_json::from_value::<SubscribeIn>(req.payload.clone())`, and likewise `WaitIn`) and never call dispatch. There is no `req.v != ENVELOPE_V` check and no resolve_actor. The registered handlers only return `door_only` (handlers/bus.rs:108-110).
findings.impact: A request that claims `"actor":"system"` is accepted, although BUS.md §1.1 says "Every door rejects a request that claims it". So is `test` on a stable instance, and `agent:x` with a wrong or missing token. Each receives the global event stream, which is not scoped by project. The practical risk today is small because `user` needs no credential, but the documented contract isn't enforced, and any later per-actor event scoping would be bypassed here.
findings.fix: Add an `Engine::preflight(&req, Door::Socket)` that runs the envelope, door, actor, schema and allowlist checks without a handler, and call it before the socket-native branches.

v1.reason: socket.rs handle_conn answers bus.subscribe (line ~362), bus.wait (~400) and bus.unsubscribe (~446) directly. It parses the payload with serde_json::from_value and never calls Engine::dispatch. The checks that dispatch_inner (engine.rs:806-870) normally runs are therefore skipped: the `req.v != ENVELOPE_V` check, the door check, resolve_actor (engine.rs:1347, which rejects Actor::System, rejects Test on stable instances, and requires a valid token for agent:<name> on the socket), the op-level allowlist and guardrail::authorize. The registered handlers in handlers/bus.rs:108-110 only return door_only, so nothing else enforces those checks. As a result, a request claiming "system", or claiming agent:x with no token or a wrong one, is answered with the full unscoped event stream. Real impact is small. The socket door accepts `user` with no credential, so any process that can reach the socket can already subscribe as user. That makes this a contract gap (BUS.md:50 says every door rejects a request that claims system), not a privilege escalation today.
v1.correction: Line numbers are approximately right (subscribe branch at 362, wait at ~400, unsubscribe at ~446). There is a simpler fix than a new preflight API: in each of these branches, call engine.resolve_actor (or a small envelope+actor check) on a blocking thread and return the error first. Note that for agents this also skips layer-2 role authorization. That only matters if some role is meant to be denied bus.wait or bus.subscribe.

findings.title: Socket attach/detach re-read the caller's original payload instead of the identity-filled one, and default to an empty session name
findings.evidence: Dispatch fills a missing `session` for agents (engine.rs:1139-1170, D110). The socket then parses `req.payload.clone()`, the unfilled original, into AttachIn with `.unwrap_or(AttachIn { session: String::new(), from_seq: None, epoch: None })`. Detach reads `req.payload.get("session")` (line 513). Both ops admit agents (relay-bus ops/session.rs:153-154).
findings.impact: An agent calling `session.attach {}` gets a successful dispatch replaced by a not-found error for the session named "". `session.detach {}` returns ok but leaves the stream attached.
findings.fix: Have the attach and detach handlers return the resolved session name (and epoch/seq) and use the response, or have dispatch expose the filled request. Never default to an empty name.

v1.reason: fill_identity (engine.rs:1139-1170) inserts `session` into a copy of the request when the actor is a bound agent and the op requires that field. session.attach (AttachIn.session: String, required) and session.detach (NameIn) qualify, and as query ops both admit agents. Afterwards the socket branch (socket.rs ~461) parses the original req.payload. With `session` missing, deserializing AttachIn fails, unwrap_or substitutes an empty name, and pty_by_name(&engine, "") returns a not-found error that replaces the successful dispatch response. Detach (~513) reads req.payload.get("session"), gets None, and silently detaches nothing. Reachability is narrow. session.attach is a stream op and is not exposed over MCP (mcp.rs exposed() excludes meta.stream). Detach over MCP runs on a fresh connection, where it is meaningless anyway. So only an agent writing a raw socket client and omitting `session` hits this.
v1.correction: Fix by parsing the payload after filling, for example by having dispatch return the filled payload, or by running the agent's own-session default in the socket branch. At minimum, return a schema error instead of defaulting to an empty name.

findings.title: The lock-held path probes the socket and then returns the same error either way; the instance lock is taken only after the store is opened and recovered
findings.evidence: `if probe(&sock_path).await { return Err(BindError::AlreadyRunning{..}) } return Err(BindError::AlreadyRunning{..})` returns the same error on both paths. The probe costs up to 500 ms for nothing, and a hung engine is reported as "engine already running". BUS.md §6.2 says a dead socket means "unlink the stale socket and take over". serve.rs:21-36 opens the store exclusively and runs recovery before SocketServer::start takes the lock.
findings.impact: The behaviour and the docs disagree. A second `relay serve` on the same store fails with "database is locked" from Store::open, not the friendly AlreadyRunning message with exit code 5. With a different `--store`, it runs recovery against that store before discovering the instance is taken.
findings.fix: Drop the probe here, or return a distinct `Unresponsive { pid }` variant. In serve::start, take the instance lock first by splitting SocketServer into lock() and bind(). Update BUS.md §6.2.

v1.reason: socket.rs:68-86: when flock fails, it probes the socket (up to 500 ms) and returns the identical `BindError::AlreadyRunning` on both branches, so the probe has no effect. BUS.md §6.2 (lines 333-336) says a dead socket means 'unlink the stale socket and take over'; the code comment refuses instead. The code's choice is the safer one, but the doc has drifted. serve.rs:21-36 opens the store, which applies locking_mode=EXCLUSIVE at store.rs:398-399 and touches the database during migrate, then runs recovery, and only then calls SocketServer::start. A second `relay serve` on the same store therefore fails inside Store::open with a SQLite busy/locked error. That surfaces as BindError::Other, not the AlreadyRunning branch at relay-cli main.rs:219-222, so the user gets a generic error instead of the friendly 'engine already running' message.
v1.correction: This is mainly docs drift plus a dead probe. Severity stays low. Take the instance lock before Store::open, and fix §6.2 to match the refuse-on-held-lock behaviour.

findings.title: The migration test rebuilds old versions from today's migration text, so an edited old migration goes undetected
findings.evidence: The test builds a vK store by running `&MIGRATIONS[..k]` — the current strings — then opens it with Store::open. If the text of an old migration (say v5) changes, both the simulated old store and the upgrade path change with it, and the test still passes.
findings.impact: "Every earlier version must stay openable" (CLAUDE.md, store.rs header) relies on migrations being append-only, and nothing enforces that. An edited old migration ships green, then breaks upgrades of real stores created by the original text, for example when a later migration assumes an index or column that is now missing.
findings.fix: Pin a checksum per migration (e.g. a `const MIGRATION_SHA256: [&str; N]` asserted in the test), or commit a golden `sqlite_master` dump per version and compare against it.

v1.reason: crates/relay-core/tests/store.rs:17-30 builds each vK store by running `for m in &MIGRATIONS[..k] { c.execute_batch(m) }` over the current build's `MIGRATIONS` (crates/relay-core/src/store.rs:15), then opens it with Store::open, which applies `MIGRATIONS[v..]` (store.rs:451-453). The 'old' store and the upgrade path both come from today's text, so an edit to an old migration changes both sides and the test still passes. Nothing else in the repo pins the migration text: no checksum, no golden sqlite_master dump, no checked-in old store.db fixture (rg for sha256/checksum/golden in tests/ and store.rs finds nothing relevant).
