This only matters where the agent itself is confined (a Codex sandbox with --add-dir write roots); a Claude agent's Bash is not confined anyway. install_claude's statusline temp file has the same pattern: a write plus chmod 755 that would follow a planted symlink.
findings.fix: Write to a temp file in the same directory and rename it over the target (rename replaces a symlink instead of following it), or open with O_NOFOLLOW. Refuse to write when `.relay` or `.relay/sessions/<name>` is a symlink.

v1.reason: write_session_file (session.rs:309-323) calls fs::create_dir_all(parent) and then fs::write(path). Both follow symlinks. It writes `.relay/sessions/<name>/session-brief.md`, `.relay/session-skills.md` and `.relay/sessions/<name>/role-instructions.md` inside the worktree, which the agent can write to (session.rs:507-526). prepare_launch runs on every fresh launch, wake and resume, in the engine's unsandboxed process. DECISIONS.md:672-673 says Codex runs with `--approve-for-me` while keeping its workspace-write sandbox, so a Codex agent is confined to the worktree and its write roots, yet it can create a symlink inside the worktree. Nothing in the guardrail stops this: evaluate_exec only checks denied command patterns, and write_target is for structured writes. On the next launch Relay replaces the symlink's target outside the sandbox (for example ~/.bashrc) with brief text. That destroys the file, and an agent can control part of the content through notes.append to the standing note or through claims. Shell rc files ignore errors on the earlier lines and run a later injected command line. So a confined (for example prompt-injected) Codex agent can escape its sandbox to arbitrary file overwrite and code execution as the user. For Claude agents this is moot, as the finding says: their Bash is not path-confined. install_claude's statusline temp file (hooks.rs:388-392) has the same pattern: fs::write and set_permissions 0755 on a predictable `.relay-tmp` path follow a planted symlink before the rename. I did not verify Landlock's symlink-creation rules from the repo, but workspace-write sandboxes allow creating files of any type in the writable root.
v1.correction: Severity is high, not medium. This is a confined agent escaping its sandbox, limited by needing a relaunch and Codex as the provider, and it can destroy user files even with no malicious payload. The fix stands: write to a temp file opened with O_CREAT|O_EXCL|O_NOFOLLOW in the same directory and rename it over the target, and refuse to proceed if `.relay`, `.relay/sessions` or `.relay/sessions/<name>` is a symlink (symlink_metadata). Apply the same fix to the `.relay-tmp` files in hooks::install_claude, which already rename but first write through a predictable temp path.

v2.reason:
(a) The code does what the finding says. write_session_file (crates/relay-core/src/handlers/session.rs:309-323) calls `fs::create_dir_all(parent)` and then `fs::write(&path, text)`, and both follow symlinks. prepare_launch (session.rs:507-526) calls it for `.relay/sessions/<name>/session-brief.md`, `.relay/session-skills.md` and `.relay/sessions/<name>/role-instructions.md`. Those paths come from awareness.rs:70-74 and providers.rs:24-26, so all three sit in the worktree, which is the agent's cwd. Nothing in the launch path calls symlink_metadata or canonicalize. The engine already guards against this elsewhere: safe_join in file.rs:488-505 refuses a path that "escapes the worktree through a symlink" for file.* ops. The launch writes skip that check.

(b) Reachability. Only a deliberately hostile or prompt-injected Codex agent can trigger this. It must know Relay's layout and swap one of these files for a symlink. No ordinary agent mistake produces that. Codex starts with only `--approve-for-me` and `--add-dir` for write roots (providers.rs:213-231, session.rs:552-560). D135 (DECISIONS.md:671-674) says this keeps Codex's workspace-write sandbox and does not bypass provider boundaries. So the agent can write inside the worktree and Relay's unsandboxed engine later writes through the link. The write only happens on a later launch. Every launch goes through stage_launch -> prepare_launch, and every launch op is user-only: spawn of a non-live session, session.resume from restorable, session.wake from parked (session.rs:917-1010). These are common actions, but the user has to take one after the link is planted. Claude sessions gain nothing, because their Bash is not confined. BUS.md:29-31 says Relay's own guardrails are seatbelts against mistakes, not a boundary against hostile agents. What this bypasses is Codex's OS sandbox. Under `--approve-for-me`, Codex's escalation requests already go to an automatic reviewer rather than the user, and this path skips that reviewer silently.

(c) What happens when it fires. On the next launch, the engine truncates and rewrites one file of the agent's choosing, anywhere the user can write. The new content is brief text: Relay fixes its structure, though some sections come from agent-writable data (task body and changelog, standing notes, claims). The certain harm is a destroyed user file outside the sandbox. Anything beyond that depends on which file is targeted, and I did not establish it.

(d) Severity. High overstates it. Under the rubric's real-world-impact framing this is a rare, attacker-only path: Codex only, a deliberate and Relay-aware agent, and a user relaunch afterwards. It is not a normal-flow failure. Medium fits, with the note that it contradicts the promise in D135. It would merit high only if Codex sessions working on untrusted input are a primary use.

(e) The proposed fix is incomplete as worded. Writing to a temp file and renaming it is not enough on its own: the hooks.rs install_claude and install_codex code already renames, and it is still exposed because the temp name is predictable. Checking `.relay` and `.relay/sessions/<name>` with symlink_metadata before writing leaves a check-then-use race against an agent that is running at the same time.
v2.correction:
Severity should be medium, not high. The trigger needs a deliberately hostile, Relay-aware Codex agent and then a user-initiated spawn, wake or resume. Claude sessions are unaffected. What is bypassed is Codex's own sandbox (D135), not Relay's guardrails, which BUS.md:29-31 already describes as seatbelts rather than a security boundary.

Related locations:
- The Codex-relevant hooks.rs location is install_codex's `.codex/hooks.json.relay-tmp` (hooks.rs:544-547). It writes to a predictable temp path before renaming. Whether Codex itself stops its agent writing `.codex/` cannot be established from this repo.
- install_claude's temp files (hooks.rs:378-381, 388-393 including the 0755 chmod, 395-399, 409-411) and add_claude_mcp_servers (hooks.rs:440-442) matter only when a confined agent earlier had write access to the same worktree. Worktrees can be reused across sessions and providers (read_teardown, session.rs:333-335).
- skills::apply (skills.rs:326-346) writes into `.claude/skills` and `.agents/skills` through create_dir_all, which follows a symlinked parent. This is the same class with lower impact (fixed file names); I did not trace it fully.

Fix:
- Create any temp file with create_new (O_CREAT|O_EXCL, which refuses an existing path, including a symlink) under an unpredictable name, then rename it over the target.
- A symlink_metadata pre-check on `.relay` and `.relay/sessions/<name>` alone is racy. Either resolve every component beneath the worktree with directory fds (openat2 with RESOLVE_BENEATH|RESOLVE_NO_SYMLINKS, or an equivalent crate), or, simpler and more complete, move these engine-written launch files out of the agent's write roots (for example, into the engine's data directory) and pass absolute paths through RELAY_BRIEF and --append-system-prompt-file.
- Apply the same treatment to the hooks.rs `.relay-tmp` writes.

findings.title: BUS.md says session.done enforces the per-task file/line caps and that reviewers 'notify only'; the code does neither
findings.evidence: BUS.md §9.2 lists per-task caps (files, lines) as applying to "`gate {kind: commit}`, `git.commit`, `session.done`", with outcome `refused / guardrail.cap` (BUS.md:497). The Done handler (1140-1226) never evaluates caps, and guardrail::authorize checks only allowlists. BUS.md §10.8 (line 734) says completion "moves that task active → in_review, promotes and prompts the next queued task" and "Reviewer: notifies only". In the code, both steps wait for every builder and reviewer on the worktree, and a reviewer's done advances the group (91-132).
findings.impact: Anyone relying on the spec believes a task whose combined diff exceeds the caps cannot be reported done. It can: commit in pieces that are each under the cap, then call session.done. Agents that read BUS.md also mispredict how review groups advance.
findings.fix: Either check the task's diff against the caps in Done (as evaluate_commit does), or correct BUS.md §9.2 and §10.8 to describe the implemented behaviour.

v1.reason: BUS.md:497 lists `session.done` under the per-task caps row, and BUS.md:734 says completion moves the task to in_review, promotes the next task, and that a reviewer 'notifies only'. The code does neither. The Done handler (session.rs:1140-1226) evaluates no caps; the only cap check is evaluate_commit (guardrail.rs:757-808), which counts the staged diff of a single commit. complete_group_assignment (session.rs:91-132) waits until every builder and reviewer on the worktree has completed, and the last reviewer's done is what advances the group. The test review_group_keeps_shared_worktree... (tests/sessions.rs:1231) asserts exactly that.
v1.correction: The caps are per commit by design, not a bypass. evaluate_commit's refusal message itself says 'Commit in smaller pieces', so splitting a change into several commits is the intended route, not an exploit. The right fix is to correct the docs: BUS.md §9.2 (drop session.done and say 'per commit'), SPEC.md:138 ('per task'), and BUS.md §10.8 (describe the group barrier and that the reviewer's completion advances the group). Adding a cap check to Done is not the fix. It is docs drift with no runtime harm; agents learn op behaviour from bus.schema, not BUS.md, so this is low, not medium.

findings.title: The locked session.input/resize handlers duplicate the engine's in-memory fast path and only reach their write code in a race
findings.evidence: The engine answers every user session.input and session.resize whose PTY is registered before dispatch (engine.rs:891-897, 1269-1294), and falls through to these handlers only when `pty_named` finds nothing. Their write path (1668-1686, 1697) therefore runs only if the PTY gets registered between the fast-path miss and the locked lookup. It detects the idle edge differently (from the row's state rather than `claim_idle_edge`) and calls a potentially blocking `pty.write` while holding the store lock.
findings.impact: This code has to be kept in sync with the fast path by hand. In the race, a large paste blocks the whole bus until the child drains its input queue.
findings.fix: Reduce both handlers to returning the typed errors (not_found / not_spawned / exited). If a PTY is found, delegate to the engine's in-memory path, with no transaction.

v1.reason: session.input and session.resize are `Actors::UserOnly` with `Audit::AgentOnly` (relay-bus ops/session.rs:156-160). The engine answers both from memory whenever `!audited && session_id.is_none()` and `pty_named` finds the PTY (engine.rs:891-897, 1269-1306). No handler calls them through invoke_registered (grep finds none). pty_ids and ptys are updated together in set_pty/take_pty (engine.rs:609-622), so a name lookup miss with an id hit cannot happen in steady state. The locked handlers' write path (session.rs:1658-1686, 1689-1700) therefore runs only if a PTY is registered between the fast-path miss and the handler's lookup. That copy detects the idle edge from the row state, while the fast path uses `claim_idle_edge` plus a deferred `mark_session_running`, so it is a second implementation that has to be kept in step by hand. The 'blocks the whole bus' consequence needs a large paste exactly in that spawn race, which is negligible.
v1.correction: This is mainly duplication of a near-unreachable code path, not a live bug. The category is closer to duplication than dead-code, since the handler still provides the typed not_found/not_spawned errors. Fix as proposed: keep the handlers only for the typed errors, and on a found PTY call the same helper the fast path uses (for example a shared `Engine::write_input`) instead of a second write and idle-edge implementation.

findings.title: When a builder's process exits, its current task is marked failed even if this builder had already completed it and its partner is still working
findings.evidence: `if row.session.role == Role::Builder { if let Some(task_id) = row.session.task_id { UPDATE tasks SET state='failed' ... WHERE id=?2 AND col='active' ...` (659-668) never checks this session's task_sessions.completed_at, or whether other builders are still working on the task.
findings.impact: A builder that has already called done and is waiting for its PAIR partner exits (the user quits its CLI). The task, still active because the partner is working on it, shows as failed on the board until the partner's next tool use resets it. The same happens to a queued task the builder had just advanced to and never started.
findings.fix: Add `AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM task_sessions WHERE task_id=?2 AND session_id=?3 AND completed_at IS NOT NULL)`, and skip the update while other builders of the task are live.

v1.reason: session.rs:647-668: the exit callback flips the session to 'exited' and, for any Builder with a task_id, runs `UPDATE tasks SET state='failed' ... WHERE id=?2 AND col='active'` with no look at task_sessions.completed_at and no check for other live builders. complete_group_assignment (session.rs:91-136) leaves a finished builder's task_id on the current task while builders_left/reviewers_left != 0, so a builder that called session.done and is waiting for its partner still has task_id = the active task. If that builder exits, the task is shown as failed even though the partner is still working. The partner's next tool_use report sets it back (session.rs:1388-1398: builder state 'running' -> `UPDATE tasks SET state=?1 ... AND state!=?1`). After the group advances, a builder's task_id moves to the next queued active task (session.rs:128-131), so an exit before that task starts marks the new task failed. The board state is wrong for a while, then fixes itself.
v1.correction: The flag is display state that heals itself, so this stays low. Fix: guard with `AND NOT EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM task_sessions WHERE task_id=?2 AND session_id=?3 AND completed_at IS NOT NULL)`, and also skip the update when another non-closed builder in the same worktree still has an open task_sessions row for the task.

findings.title: session.restorable lets agents list restorable sessions from every project, contrary to D106
findings.evidence: The op is a query with the default Actors::All (relay-bus ops/session.rs:166), and the handler runs `SELECT * FROM sessions WHERE state='restorable'` with no actor or project filter (1484), then runs a git status per worktree (1491-1493). session.list and session.get, by contrast, are scoped to the caller's project.
findings.impact: Any agent can read other projects' sessions (names, worktree paths, branches, provider_ref, intent, usage), against D106's rule that an agent sees "nothing outside" its project. It can also trigger a git status of every restorable worktree on demand.
findings.fix: Mark the op UserOnly, or filter it by actor_project the way session.list does.

v1.reason: RestorableList is `OpMeta::query(Scope::Global, ...)` with the default Actors::All (relay-bus ops/session.rs:166). The handler runs `SELECT * FROM sessions WHERE state='restorable'` with no actor_project filter (session.rs:1484), while session.list and session.get are scoped per D106 (DECISIONS.md: "an agent sees the metadata of any session in its own project and nothing outside it"). The op is exposed to agents as the session_restorable MCP tool. It is registered unlocked and its git status is bounded (worktree.rs:91, 10 s timeout), so the on-demand cost is bounded. In this single-user app all projects belong to the same person, so the leak is a policy violation (cross-project metadata and worktree paths visible to an agent), not exposure to another principal.
v1.correction: Low severity is right: it breaks a documented isolation decision but exposes no other user's data. Fix: mark it Actors::UserOnly (only the launch-time resume UI needs it), or filter by actor_project the way session.list does.

findings.title: session.scrollback copies and serializes up to the full 8 MiB scrollback while holding the store lock
findings.evidence: `e.register::<Scrollback>` runs in the locked transaction. When `lines` is omitted it calls `pty.scrollback(None)`, which copies the whole ring (up to 8 MiB) and decodes it lossily, and the register wrapper serializes that string to JSON before the transaction commits. The live-PTY branch needs the store only for by_name.
findings.impact: An agent that calls session_scrollback on itself or its partner without `lines` holds the global lock for a multi-megabyte copy, decode and JSON escape.
findings.fix: Use register_unlocked: resolve the row with ctx.read, then read the PTY or the saved scrollback with no lock held; cap the default size.

v1.reason: Scrollback is registered with `e.register::<Scrollback>` (session.rs:1702), the locked transactional path, even though its OpMeta is a query (ops/session.rs:163). With `lines` omitted, `pty.scrollback(None)` copies the whole ring (`ring.bytes_from(0)`, up to SCROLLBACK_BYTES = 8 MiB, pty.rs:16, 323-339) and runs `from_utf8_lossy(...).into_owned()`. The register wrapper's `serde_json::to_value` (engine.rs:491) then clones it into a Value, all before the lock is released. The pty.rs:320-322 comment only addresses the bounded `{lines}` case. The native client never calls session.scrollback (it streams via attach), so the callers are agents through MCP (on themselves or a PAIR partner, assert_own) and the CLI. The cost is tens of milliseconds of global lock per unbounded call: real, but small and occasional.
v1.correction: Fix: register_unlocked. Resolve the row and run the ownership check with ctx.read (assert_own needs adapting to Unlocked), read the PTY or the saved scrollback outside the lock, and consider a default `lines` cap for agent callers.

findings.title: A reviewer can attach arbitrary commit SHAs to a task through session.done, although its role is not allowed task.link_commit
findings.evidence: `INSERT OR IGNORE INTO task_commits(task_id,sha,branch,linked_at)` inserts whatever `sha` the caller passed (97-99), and this runs for reviewers too (1165). The reviewer allowlist leaves out task.link_commit (settings.rs:37), and BUS.md says reviewers do "nothing that writes files, commits, or moves the task". The sha is also stored without trimming or checking that it exists, whereas task.link_commit trims it (task.rs:547).
findings.impact: A reviewer can link nonexistent or unrelated commits to the task it reviews, bypassing its role allowlist, and ' abc' and 'abc' are recorded as different commits.
findings.fix: Accept `sha` only from builders, trim it and verify it resolves in the worktree, or route it through task.rs link_commit.

v1.reason: Done runs complete_group_assignment for Role::Reviewer (session.rs:1164-1165). After the in_review check (91-94), it inserts the caller's sha untrimmed (97-99). The default reviewer allowlist (settings.rs:37) omits task.link_commit, and BUS.md:465 says reviewers do nothing that writes commits. task.link_commit trims (task.rs:547), so ' abc' and 'abc' become two separate rows through this path. The effect is limited: task_commits is display-only. It is read in task.get (task.rs:240) and shown as text in the board peek (board_view.rs:2432-2446), and nothing executes or resolves it. The 'verify it exists' part of the fix also applies to builders, because link_commit never checks existence either.
v1.correction: This is not a security hole. The bypass lets a reviewer, a cooperating local agent, add a display-only metadata row to the task it reviews. It is a role-policy inconsistency plus a missing trim, so the category is bug rather than security. Simplest fix: ignore sha for reviewers and route the builder path through task::link_commit so trimming is shared.

findings.title: Queueing a task for a session is copied in three places, and the copies already queue for different sets of sessions
findings.evidence: The `COALESCE(MAX(ord),-1)+1` / `COALESCE(MAX(queue_ord),-1)+1` / `INSERT OR IGNORE INTO task_sessions` triple appears in finish_create (821-825), Update (1468-1472) and task.rs assign_session (581-601). The task/module existence checks are also copied between validate_create (740-753) and Update (1444-1457). Update queues the task for one session, while dispatch queues it for the whole group.
findings.impact: Group members' queues diverge depending on how a task was attached. complete_group_assignment advances every member using the caller's queue (next_queued_task), so a member can be handed a task it has no task_sessions row for. It is then missing from that task's ids and completion counts and stays stuck on the task when the group advances. A fix to one copy misses the others.
findings.fix: Add one `enqueue(tx, task_id, session_ids)` helper and one task/module validation helper, used by all three call sites.

v1.reason: The ord/queue_ord/INSERT OR IGNORE triple appears word for word in finish_create (session.rs:820-824), Update (1467-1471) and task.rs assign_session (581-604). The task/module existence checks are copied between validate_create (737-753) and Update (1443-1456). The copies have already diverged. assign_session queues the task for every non-closed session in the worktree. finish_create and Update queue it only for the one session, and Update also sets sessions.task_id directly. complete_group_assignment (session.rs:122-131) takes `next` from the caller's queue only and writes it to every id in the group, so a partner can be handed a task it has no task_sessions row for. That partner is then missing from builders_left and from `ids` the next time the group advances. The next-task queries also differ: next_queued_task orders by queue_ord,t.position,t.id, while assign_session orders by queue_ord,t.id.
v1.correction: How often this bites is limited. The native UI's session.update never sends task_id (agent_menu.rs:542-547), agents have no session.update tool, and task dispatch goes through assign_session for the whole group. The divergent paths are therefore CLI session.update with task_id, or session.create with task_id plus pair_with. Low is right. One shared enqueue(tx, task_id, &[session ids]) helper and one next-task query would also remove the ordering difference.

findings.title: PAIR checks look in different directions, so a group's second builder cannot read its own reviewer's brief or scrollback
findings.evidence: assert_own allows a pair read only when the target row's pair_with names the actor (164-169), while guardrail::authorize checks the actor's own pair_with (guardrail.rs:335). In a group, R.pair_with=B1 and B2.pair_with=R. Close clears pair_with only on rows that point at the session being closed (1609), so after B1 closes, R.pair_with is NULL while B2 still points at R. validate_pair (762) then skips every group check for the next session that pairs with R.
findings.impact: The second builder in a group is refused session.brief and session.scrollback on its own reviewer (session.not_own), although D106 promises own-session-or-PAIR access. Once the first builder leaves, a new session can join R in any role (for example a second reviewer), or push the group past the two-builder limit.
findings.fix: Treat PAIR membership symmetrically (either side's pair_with, or a group id) in assert_own, authorize and validate_pair.

v1.reason: Group creation order in the native launch is B1, R(pair_with=B1), B2(pair_with=R) (launch.rs:780, 803). finish_create back-fills pair_with only when the partner's is NULL (session.rs:813-819). The result is B1.pair_with=R, R.pair_with=B1, B2.pair_with=R. assert_own admits a pair read only when the target row's pair_with names the actor (164-169). B2 reading R's brief or scrollback checks R.pair_with=B1 and gets session.not_own (Brief at 1126, Scrollback the same). That contradicts D106 ('own-session-or-PAIR'). guardrail.rs:335 checks the actor's own pair_with, but project_read (333-334) already admits same-project queries, so assert_own is the gate that decides. Close clears pair_with only on rows pointing at the closed session (1609), so after B1 closes R.pair_with is NULL. validate_pair then skips its group checks (762), and a second reviewer can join R's worktree.
v1.correction: The claim that the group can grow past two builders does not hold as written. After B1 closes and B3 joins R, the builder count is 2, R.pair_with becomes B3, and the next join is checked again. Pairing with B2 is refused because B2 is not a reviewer (766-768). What does happen is that a second reviewer, or any other role, can join R while R.pair_with is NULL. The main effect is that B2 cannot read its reviewer's brief or scrollback. Mailbox and session.get still work.

findings.title: audit.undo of a session.update always fails once the session has been spawned
findings.evidence: The undo payload always contains `"branch": s.branch` (a non-null string) plus model and effort (1474-1477). Replaying it hits `if spawned && (p.branch.is_some() || ...)`, which returns conflict session.already_spawned (1434-1437). The undo's updated_at guard is also invalidated by every tool-use report, because Report sets updated_at (1372).
findings.impact: Undoing any session.update (e.g. a bus_writes or allow_ui toggle) on a running session can never succeed. The undo would also leave behind the task_sessions row that the update inserted.
findings.fix: Put only the fields the update actually changed into the inverse payload, and never include branch/model/effort once the session has spawned.

v1.reason: Update's set_undo inverse always contains `"branch": s.branch`, a non-null String, plus model and effort (session.rs:1474-1477). audit.undo replays the inverse through `ctx.invoke_registered(&inverse.op, inverse.payload)` (audit.rs Undo handler). On a spawned session, the check `if spawned && (p.branch.is_some() || ...)` (1434-1436) fires even when the branch value is unchanged, so the undo returns session.already_spawned. session.update is a mutation with the default Audit::Always (registry.rs:117) and Undo::Inverse, so an undo row does exist. The updated_at expectation is also invalidated by every Report (1372), although `force` can skip that check. The undo also leaves behind the task_sessions row that the update INSERTed.
v1.correction: Severity stays low: the op is user-only, rarely undone, and the failure is a clean refusal, not corruption. Fix: include in the inverse only the fields the update actually changed, and omit branch, model and effort once the session has spawned (or whenever they are unchanged).

findings.title: The launch prompt is never cleared, so a fresh restart and session.bootstrap keep re-issuing an assignment that was already finished
findings.evidence: launch_nudge uses `row.launch_prompt` in preference to the current task (135-143). launch_prompt is never cleared when the work is reported done; prepare_launch keeps writing it into the brief file (500-506), and bootstrap keeps returning it as `assignment` (awareness.rs:474).
findings.impact: session.clear_restorable (a fresh launch) types "begin this assignment: <original prompt>" into a session that finished that assignment long ago and has moved through its queue. A freshly started agent's bootstrap then gives it two conflicting directives.
findings.fix: Clear launch_prompt on the first completed session.done, or use it as the nudge only on the first spawn.

v1.reason: launch_nudge prefers row.launch_prompt over the current task (session.rs:134-143). launch_prompt is written only by spawn (931-938, 627-631) and never cleared. bootstrap returns it as `assignment` for the life of the session (awareness.rs:474), and the brief file keeps it (session.rs:499-506, awareness.rs:249-256). finish_launch types the nudge for every LaunchKind::Fresh (690-700). Fresh covers session.spawn, allowed only from Created (918-919), and session.clear_restorable (960-968). After clear_restorable, a session that has moved on to Task #N is told 'begin this assignment: <original prompt>' and the nudge does not mention its current task. Bootstrap then reports both the stale assignment and the current task. No DECISIONS entry says the launch text should persist after it is done.
v1.correction: The only re-trigger of the nudge is session.clear_restorable, a rare user action; session.spawn can only run from Created. The launch text may also carry standing instructions (the native sheet's 'Additional instructions' field), so clearing it on the first done could lose those. A safer fix: on a non-first Fresh spawn, nudge with the current task and present launch_prompt as the original launch instructions, or record whether it has been delivered.

findings.title: The 'spawning' state is never written, so provider_updates' check for in-progress launches never fires; sessions::set_state is unused
findings.evidence: No code ever writes state 'spawning'. It is only read: is_live (173), provider_updates.rs:44 and notify.rs:163. A staged launch leaves the row as 'created', 'parked' or 'restorable' for the whole unlocked preparation (stage_launch, session.rs:596-611). `sessions::set_state` (164-170) has no callers; state changes are hand-written SQL in about ten places, and engine.rs mark_restorable duplicates save_scrollback's upsert.
findings.impact: provider_updates skips an update only when `pid IS NOT NULL OR state='spawning'`. During a launch's preparation pid is still NULL, so an automatic provider update can replace the binary between plan and exec (for example during resume-at-startup). The UI also cannot show that a launch is in progress, and the dead helper is misleading.
findings.fix: Mark the row 'spawning' in stage_launch's read and make finish_launch expect it, or delete the state. Either use set_state or remove it.

v1.reason: I checked this myself. No code ever writes the state 'spawning'. The only session INSERT (handlers/session.rs:804-806) writes the literal 'created'. Every `UPDATE sessions SET state=` in relay-core writes 'running', 'exited', 'parked' or 'restorable' (session.rs:75/386/653/681/991, engine.rs:676/1328, recovery.rs:97). SessionState::Spawning appears only in the string mappings at sessions.rs:24/38. `sessions::set_state` (sessions.rs:164-170) has no callers: the integration.rs `set_state` calls go to a different, local fn at integration.rs:256. In a staged launch, `stage_launch` (session.rs:596-611) reads the row in its existing state, `prepare_launch` (468ff) does the unlocked hook, skill and brief file writes, and `finish_launch` moves the row straight to 'running' with a pid (681). So the `state='spawning'` arm of the provider_updates.rs:44 guard can never match, and the `pid IS NOT NULL` arm is false during preparation. The same unreachable 'spawning' literal also appears in recovery.rs:80/149, notify.rs:163/178, engine.rs:677, session.rs:387/654 and in the native client's matches, where it is harmless. engine.rs mark_restorable (669-673) does repeat save_scrollback's upsert SQL inline, because it runs on a raw transaction outside a handler.
v1.correction: Calibrating the impact: the race window is only the unlocked preparation phase. That phase is file writes into the worktree (git hooks, provider configs, skills, brief), usually milliseconds to well under a second. The binary swap itself runs in a background thread after commit. A clash needs an automatic or manual provider update to start while a launch of the same provider is between plan and Pty::spawn, for example startup resume running alongside startup auto-update. Even then, the native self-updaters usually install a new version beside the old one and repoint a link. The likely worst case is a single launch failing or starting on the old version, not data loss. Severity stays low. The main cost is misleading dead state: BUS.md:1001 advertises 'spawning' as a reachable SessionState. Simplest fix: in stage_launch's read, run a conditional UPDATE to 'spawning'. That cannot happen inside ctx.read, so it would need a short locked write or would have to move to the start of the staged write. finish_launch would then expect 'spawning', and any failed launch would need to revert the row. Alternatively, drop the state and the dead helper, and make provider_updates hold off while a launch is in flight (e.g. an in-memory set of launching provider names on Engine). Replacing mark_restorable's inline upsert with a call to sessions::save_scrollback(&tx, ...) is a trivial cleanup.

findings.title: session.report, the busiest agent op, recompiles its SQL on every call and hashes the whole hook payload while holding the lock
findings.evidence: Report runs on every PostToolUse of every agent. It re-reads done_pending_stop with an uncached `query_row` (1354-1356) even though `sessions::by_name` already loaded the row. The state update (1371), the done_pending_stop clear (1376) and the task update (1393) use `Connection::execute`, which compiles the SQL each time. The CLI forwards the entire hook JSON, including tool_response (relay-cli main.rs:490-496), and the audit append serializes and SHA-256-hashes all of it under the lock, although it stores only 2 KB.
findings.impact: Each tool call costs several SQL compilations plus a hash of what can be hundreds of KB, all under the global store lock, multiplied by the number of agents and tool calls. CLAUDE.md asks for prepare_cached on hot paths.
findings.fix: Add done_pending_stop to Row_, switch to prepare_cached, merge the two session UPDATEs, and drop tool_response in the CLI hook adapter.

v1.reason: Report (session.rs:1349-1429) re-reads done_pending_stop with Connection::query_row (1354-1356). It then runs `ctx.tx().execute` for the state update (1371), the done_pending_stop clear (1376) and the task state update (1393); all four statements are compiled each time and none goes through prepare_cached. Claude's PostToolUse hook is installed with no matcher (hooks.rs:355-374) and Codex's likewise (hooks.rs:527), so it fires on every tool call. lifecycle_hook_report (main.rs:490-497) forwards the raw hook JSON unchanged, including tool_response. audit::append (audit.rs:81-83) serializes and SHA-256-hashes the whole payload inside the transaction before truncating what it stores.
v1.correction: The cost is small in absolute terms: a few tens of microseconds of SQL compilation per call, plus about 1 ms to hash a payload of a few hundred KB, all under the store lock. That is real but modest, so low is right. CLAUDE.md asks for prepare_cached over Connection::query_row; it does not single out hot paths, but this is one. The simplest high-payoff part of the fix is stripping tool_response (and tool_input content) in the CLI adapter, because Report only reads /tool_input/command, session_id, message and notification_type.

results.coverage:
I read every line of the three assigned files: crates/relay-core/src/guardrail.rs (1350 lines), crates/relay-core/src/guardrail/grants.rs (438) and crates/relay-core/src/handlers/guardrail.rs (778).

findings.title: guardrail.confirm replays an agent's held file.* op with no session bound, so the confirmed write lands in the project's main checkout
findings.evidence: `confirm` calls `ctx.replay_registered(&frozen.op, frozen.payload.clone(), hold.actor.clone(), hold.policy.clone())` (583) and only afterwards runs `if let Some(session_id) = hold.session_id { ctx.set_session(session_id); }` (593). `replay_registered` (engine.rs:364-377) swaps only `actor` and `skip_policy`, so the Ctx still carries the confirming user's `session_id` = None. The replayed `file.write` resolves its tree via `root(ctx, p.project_id, p.worktree)` (file.rs:73) -> `default_worktree_in(conn, None, ..)` -> `None => Ok(repo)` (file.rs:401-408), i.e. the project root. The frozen payload is the agent's own request, which omits the optional `worktree` (D111 made omission mean 'my worktree'), so nothing pins the original tree. The replayed `enforce` also judges the main checkout's file and loads no grants. Tests only replay user-actor holds (phase8.rs:159-175, 529-561), where the project root is correct.
findings.impact: A bus_writes agent's `file.write`/`file.create`/`file.rename`/`file.move` that is held (destructive_write on an untracked or modified file, or a shape gate) is confirmed by the user, and the agent's content then overwrites `<project root>/<path>` in the user's main checkout. That destroys whatever the user had there, possibly uncommitted, and the agent's worktree is left unchanged. The write that was held for being destructive is applied to a different file that nobody reviewed.
findings.fix: Bind the hold's session before replaying: `if let Some(id) = hold.session_id { ctx.set_session(id) }` before `replay_registered`, or pass the session into `replay_registered` and restore it afterwards. Better: when `enforce` freezes a hold, write the resolved absolute `worktree` into the frozen payload so a replay can never re-resolve to another tree. Add a test: bus_writes agent, destructive file.write held, user confirms; assert the session worktree changed and the main checkout did not.

v1.reason: Confirmed by reading the code. `confirm` (handlers/guardrail.rs:583) calls `ctx.replay_registered(&frozen.op, frozen.payload.clone(), hold.actor.clone(), hold.policy.clone())` for any non-gate, non-request hold. `replay_registered` (engine.rs:363-377) swaps only `actor` and `skip_policy`. `invoke_registered` keeps `self.session_id`, which is None for the confirming user (confirm is `Actors::UserOnly`). `ctx.set_session(session_id)` runs only afterwards, at line 593. The replayed `file.write` calls `root(ctx, p.project_id, p.worktree)` (file.rs:73 -> 447-455), then `root_choice` -> `default_worktree_in(conn, ctx.actor_session_id()=None, ..)`. With `requested=None` that returns `None => Ok(repo)`, the project root (file.rs:391-409). `fill_identity` (engine.rs:1139-1171) fills only `project_id`/`session`, never `worktree`, so the frozen payload of an agent that omitted `worktree` (the D111 default) does not pin the tree. On replay, `enforce` skips `destructive_write` (skip_policy). `write_target`/`write_roots` take the project root as the worktree, so the in-tree check passes, and the agent's text is written over `<project root>/<path>`. In tests, confirm replays only user holds or gate holds. No test replays an agent `file.write` (tests/guardrails.rs, phase8.rs).
v1.correction: Severity is lowered from critical to high. The trigger needs an opt-in condition: the agent session has `bus_writes` enabled (default false, providers.rs:390; guardrail.rs:365) and writes through bus `file.write`/`file.create`/`file.rename`/`file.move`, not the provider's own Write tool. That write must also be held (destructive_write on an untracked or modified file, or a shape gate) and then confirmed. When it happens, it silently overwrites the user's main checkout, possibly uncommitted work. One guard is partial: if the agent passed `expected_sha256` taken from its own worktree, the replay fails with `file.edit_conflict` instead of writing. Fix: call `ctx.set_session(hold.session_id)` before the replay, or have `replay_registered` take and restore the session id. More robust: have `enforce` freeze the resolved absolute `worktree` into the payload. Add a test where a bus_writes agent's held file.write is confirmed.

v2.reason:
(a) The code does what the finding says. I traced it myself. `guardrail.confirm` is UserOnly (relay-bus ops/guardrail.rs:38-39). `resolve_actor` gives User a session id of None (engine.rs:1355), and the Ctx starts with that None (engine.rs:972). `confirm` replays at guardrail.rs:583 through `replay_registered` (engine.rs:364-377), which swaps only `actor` and `skip_policy`. `set_session` runs only afterwards, at :593. The replayed `file.write` calls `root()` (file.rs:73, 447-455), which reaches `default_worktree_in(.., None, .., None)` and returns the project root (file.rs:401-408). `worktree::contains` accepts the repo itself (worktree.rs:164). Nothing pins the tree: `fill_identity` fills only required `project_id`/`session` (engine.rs:1139-1170), and `enforce` freezes `ctx.payload()` unchanged (guardrail.rs:691). The hook path's confirm branch is correct, because it uses `session.session.worktree` (guardrail.rs:600-617), so only bus `file.*` replays are affected. This contradicts D111 (DECISIONS.md:523-529). It is the D35 replay never updated for D111, not intended behaviour. No test replays an agent's bus-op hold: phase8.rs:159-175 and 529-561 are user holds, and guardrails.rs:207-229 is a gate hold.

(b) Who can trigger it and how often. Desktop-launched agents have `bus_writes` ON by default: launch.rs:264-265 sets `writes.set_active(true)`, and the value is sent at launch.rs:346. The MCP door then lists file.write/create/rename/move to them (mcp.rs:91-103). What limits the trigger is that agents normally edit with their provider's own tools (D5). Claude's PreToolUse hook matches only `Edit|Write|MultiEdit|Bash` (hooks.rs:350), and Codex has no MCP tools (providers.rs:84-86). So the bug fires only when an agent chooses the bus `file_write` tool, omits `worktree` (the D111 default), and rewrites a file that is untracked or modified in its worktree. The rewrite must remove more than 50 lines, or more than 40% of a file of at least 30 lines. `file.write` replaces the whole file, so any sizeable rewrite of uncommitted work qualifies. The user then clicks "Allow once" on a card that says "<session> is waiting on you" (guardrail_pages.rs:242-313). Its "Review exact action" shows `file.write {project_id, path, text}` and never names a tree. For agents, create/rename/move/delete are held only through configured shape gates or the 64 MiB cap, so `file.write` is the realistic route. The trigger is uncommon, but every time it fires it goes wrong the same way.

(c) What happens to the user. The agent's text atomically replaces `<project root>/<path>` (file.rs:104-115), with no trash and no undo. The destructive_write check is skipped, and the file actually overwritten was never evaluated. The outcome depends on the main checkout:
- Uncommitted edits at that path are lost for good.
- A clean file is silently dirtied with agent content.
- A new path creates a stray file there, or, if its parent directory is missing, fails with file.not_found.

The agent's worktree never changes. The non-gate branch sends the agent no mailbox message, only `guardrail.resolved {state: confirmed}`, so a waiting agent believes its write landed.

(d) Severity is high, not critical. This is silent corruption, with possible loss of uncommitted work and a safety check bypassed for the wrong file. But it only fires on a secondary path (bus file.write by an agent, a destructive hold, and a user approval), not frequently.

(e) The proposed fix is correct and complete. Binding `hold.session_id` before `replay_registered` (or passing the session in and restoring it afterwards) fixes `root()`, makes `enforce` load the agent's grants, and records any nested hold against the session. The staged prepare also inherits it (engine.rs:337). User holds are unaffected, and holds expire when their session closes (session.rs:1612). Pinning the absolute worktree into the frozen payload is also safe: `Hold.payload_hash` is only informational, and idempotency hashes the original request (engine.rs:843). The proposed test is right.
v2.correction:
The first verifier's limiting factor is wrong. It says `bus_writes` defaults to false and cites providers.rs:390, but that line is a unit-test fixture. The engine's `unwrap_or(false)` (session.rs:809) applies only when the caller omits the field. The desktop launch dialog always sends it, and sends true by default (launch.rs:264-265, 346), so desktop-launched agents have bus writes on. What actually limits the trigger is that agents write through their own provider tools (D5). Claude's hooks match only native tools (hooks.rs:350), and Codex gets no MCP tools.

The finding lists file.write, create, rename and move as equal routes. For agents, file.write through destructive_write is the realistic one. Create, rename, move and delete are held only by configured shape gates or the 64 MiB comparison cap.

Additional effect: the non-gate confirm branch sends the agent no mailbox message, although BUS.md §9.4 promises one. The agent therefore also misses the misfire. The fix should add that message alongside the session binding.

Severity: high (lowered from the finding's critical).

findings.title: Denied-command matching requires the pattern's exact words contiguously, so everyday spellings of the default denied commands run unchallenged
findings.evidence: `denied_matches` drops every fully quoted word (`.filter(|word| !word.quoted)`, 977) and then needs the pattern as one contiguous window: `bare.windows(wanted.len()).any(|window| window == wanted.as_slice())` (988). `shell_commands` (894-956) understands only quotes, backslash and `; \n | &`; `$(`, backticks, `(`, `sh -c '..'` and `eval` are treated as plain characters or quoted data. A Python port of these functions, which reproduces every case the repo's tests assert, shows that with the default list ["rm -rf","git reset --hard","git clean -fd","git push --force"] 26 of 29 real executions are NOT matched. Examples: `git push -f origin main`, `git push origin main --force`, `git push origin +main`, `git clean -fdx`, `git clean -xfd`, `git clean -f -d`, `git reset HEAD~1 --hard`, `git -C ../app reset --hard`, `rm -fr build`, `rm -r -f build`, `rm -rfv build`, `rm --recursive --force build`, `/bin/rm -rf build`, `"rm" -rf build`, `rm '-rf' build`, `sh -c 'rm -rf build'`, `echo $(rm -rf build)`, `(rm -rf build)`. The dry-run exemption (1012-1019) exempts a whole command, so `relay q guardrail.check $(rm -rf ~)` passes.
findings.impact: An agent that types `git push origin main --force`, `git clean -fdx` or `git reset HEAD~1 --hard` (all common LLM spellings) overwrites the remote or destroys uncommitted and untracked work with no refusal, even though the user configured exactly these rules. For shell commands from Claude's Bash tool and from Codex, this matcher is the only check.
findings.fix: Match each command on normalized argv instead of a literal window. Take the basename of argv[0]. Skip wrappers (sudo, env, command, exec, nice, time, xargs) and `VAR=val` prefixes. Keep quoted words as words, so a quoted argv[0] is still the program. Expand clustered short flags (`-fdx` contains -f and -d). Accept required flags anywhere after the subcommand, in any order, with known equivalents (-f/--force, -r/-R/--recursive), and count `+ref` refspecs as a force push. Recurse into `sh|bash|zsh -c <arg>`, `eval`, `$(..)`, backticks and subshells. Add a regression table with the variants above.

v1.reason: denied_matches (guardrail.rs ~963-997) keeps only words that are not fully quoted (`.filter(|word| !word.quoted)`), lowercases them, and matches each pattern only as a contiguous window: `bare.windows(wanted.len()).any(|window| window == wanted.as_slice())`. shell_commands (~893-956) splits only on quotes, backslash, `; \n | &` and whitespace. Tracing by hand: `git push origin main --force` gives bare [git,push,origin,main,--force], and no window equals [git,push,--force]. `rm -fr x`, `rm -r -f x`, `git clean -fdx` and `git reset HEAD~1 --hard` never produce the exact window either. `/bin/rm -rf x` gives the word `/bin/rm`, which is not `rm`. `"rm" -rf x` drops the fully quoted argv[0], so bare is [-rf,x]. `sh -c 'rm -rf x'` turns the payload into one quoted word that is dropped. `$(rm` and `(rm` stay single words that are not `rm`. BUS.md:499 and D103 promise matching on parsed argv, and the defaults in handlers/settings.rs ship exactly these four patterns. The exec gate is what the agent hook calls for shell commands (tests/guardrails.rs:343 and 590 exercise only the canonical spelling). The bypass is real, and an LLM's ordinary spellings trigger it without any adversary.
v1.correction: Severity: high rather than critical. This is a denylist tripwire that is silently bypassed by common spellings, which the rubric rates high. It is not a sandbox escape, and the provider's own permission layer sits beside it, but it can let `git push origin main --force` or `git clean -fdx` destroy work with no refusal. On the dry-run exemption: `relay q guardrail.check $(rm -rf ~)` does pass, but it would pass without the exemption too, because `$(rm` is never equal to `rm`. The root cause is the matcher, not the exemption. The proposed fix (normalize argv[0] to its basename, skip wrappers and VAR= prefixes, keep a quoted argv[0], expand flag clusters, match flags in any order, recurse into sh -c/eval/$()) is sound. The regression table is the important part.

v2.reason:
(a) The code does what is claimed. guardrail.rs:977 drops fully quoted words. Line 988 requires the pattern as one contiguous window (`bare.windows(wanted.len()).any(|window| window == wanted.as_slice())`). shell_commands (894-956) understands only quotes, backslash, `; \n | &` and whitespace. The defaults are at handlers/settings.rs:33. I ported shell_commands, is_guardrail_dry_run and denied_matches to Python, and the port reproduces all 6 assertions in tests/agent_surface.rs:238-251.

With the default list, these are refused: `git push --force origin main`, `git clean -fd`, `git reset --hard origin/main`, `rm -rf x`, `rm -Rf x` (words are lowercased), and wrapped forms such as `sudo rm -rf`, `env X=1 git push --force`, `timeout 30 rm -rf` and `find . -exec rm -rf {} +` (the window is not anchored to the first word).

These are allowed: `git push -f [origin main]`, `git push origin main --force`, `git push -u origin feat --force`, `git push origin +main`, `git clean -df`, `-fdx`, `-xfd`, `-dfx`, `-f -d`, `git reset HEAD~1 --hard`, `git -C ../app reset --hard`, `rm -fr`, `rm -r -f`, `rm -rfv`, `rm --recursive --force`, `/bin/rm -rf`, `"rm" -rf`, `rm '-rf'`, `sh -c '...'`, `echo $(...)`, `echo "$(...)"` and `(...)`. No test pins any of these variants as intended. The matcher arrived with the initial import (fcbdbce), and D103 was written about false positives, not about variant spellings.

(b) Reachability. Every agent shell command reaches this matcher. Claude's PreToolUse hook (hooks.rs:350, matcher `Edit|Write|MultiEdit|Bash`) sends the Bash command verbatim as `guardrail.gate {kind: exec}` (relay-cli main.rs:406-410). Codex does the same (main.rs:506-512). Nothing normalizes the command before evaluate_exec, which calls denied_matches. The live hook on this session also refused one of my own read-only commands: a heredoc's quotes threw off this tokenizer. That is a separate over-blocking issue, but it shows the matcher is live. No adversary is needed. Whenever an agent decides on a force push or a clean, `git push -f`, a trailing `--force` and `git clean -df` or `-fdx` are among its most common spellings. Agents choose such operations occasionally, not in every session, but each such attempt with these spellings passes.

(c) Consequence. The gate returns Decision::Allow and the hook exits 0. There is no refusal, hold or notification. Only the provider's own layer remains. Relay sets no Claude permission mode (relay.settings.json carries only a statusLine, hooks.rs:396-398), so whether Claude prompts depends on the user's own Claude settings. Codex runs with `--approve-for-me`, which hands approvals to an automatic reviewer (D135), so the user's own denied list is the only rule they set that applies there. The damage is real:
- `git clean -df` or `-fdx` deletes untracked and ignored files in the worktree (agent work in progress, `.env`, local data).
- `git reset <ref> --hard` discards uncommitted tracked changes.
- `git push -f`, `... --force` or `+main` overwrites a remote branch.
- `git -C <path>` can reach the user's main checkout.

(d) Severity is high, not critical. BUS.md §0.6 says guardrails are "seatbelts, not sandboxes" and "not a security boundary against a hostile process", so the quoting, `sh -c` and `$()` evasions are outside the stated threat model. They do not amount to an agent escaping its guardrails in the critical sense. What remains is the rubric's high case: a safety check silently bypassed by ordinary, non-adversarial spellings. The canonical spellings are caught, and any loss requires an agent to choose a destructive operation on its own.

(e) The fix points the right way, but as written it would regress cases that are caught today. Anchoring on the basename of argv[0] with a fixed wrapper list (sudo, env, command, exec, nice, time, xargs) would stop catching `timeout 30 rm -rf`, `find . -exec rm -rf {} +`, `nohup ...`, `xargs -0 rm -rf` and `sudo -u bob rm -rf`, all of which are refused now. See the correction for a design that keeps them.
v2.correction:
Severity: high, not critical (BUS.md §0.6, "seatbelts, not sandboxes"; the rubric rates a silently bypassed safety check as high).

Scope: the title says everyday spellings run unchallenged, which overstates it. The canonical spellings are refused: `git push --force <remote> <branch>`, `git reset --hard <ref>`, `git clean -fd`, `rm -rf` and `rm -Rf`. So are forms wrapped in sudo, env, timeout or find -exec, because the window is not anchored to the first word. The gap is variant spellings. Add `git clean -df` to the list of misses: it is a very common spelling and is not refused. I could not check the "26 of 29" count because the finding does not list its cases, but the result itself reproduces.

Dry-run exemption: it is not the root cause. `relay q guardrail.check $(rm -rf ~)` would pass without it, since `$(rm` never equals `rm`.

"Only check": this is the only check on the Relay side. Claude's own permission prompts may still apply, depending on the user's settings. Codex hands approvals to an automatic reviewer (D135).

Fix: do not anchor on argv[0] with a fixed wrapper list; that regresses timeout, find -exec, nohup, xargs with options and sudo with options. Instead:
- Treat any word whose basename equals the pattern's program as the start of a candidate.
- Require the pattern's subcommand words in order after it, skipping git global options (`-C <dir>`, `-c k=v`, `--git-dir=`, `--work-tree=`).
- Require the pattern's flags as a set, anywhere later in the same simple command. Expand single-dash clusters and apply equivalents per program (-f/--force; -r/-R/--recursive). Treat `+ref` refspecs as a force push.
- Keep quoted single tokens as words, so `rm '-rf'` and `"rm"` count. Quoted multi-word data must still never match, which keeps the D103 tests passing.
- Track single versus double quotes, so `$(..)` and backticks inside double quotes are inspected.
- Narrow the dry-run exemption to the relay command itself, or recursion into `$()` would be exempted wholesale.
- Keep `DeniedMatch.bare` for `grants.covers_command`.
- Update D103, BUS.md §9.2 and the "matched word by word" hint at apps/relay-native/src/guardrail_settings.rs:70. Native code cannot be compiled headless.

Cheap stopgap: add `git push -f`, `git clean -df`, `git clean -fdx`, `git clean -xfd` and `rm -fr` to the defaults. It cannot cover a trailing `--force` or `+ref` without over-blocking.

findings.title: A command grant ignores quoted words, so it covers commands with extra quoted targets (an approved `rm -rf "$TMPDIR/x"` also covers `rm -rf "/"`)
findings.evidence: `covers_command` compares `bare == words.as_slice()` (145). Both sides drop quoted words: the hit's `bare` (guardrail.rs:975-979) and the grant's `command_words` (guardrail.rs:1001-1008, `.filter(|word| !word.quoted)`). The doc comment promises "`rm -rf target` lifts `rm -rf target` and not `rm -rf target /`". Port results: a grant for `rm -rf target` covers `rm -rf target "/"` and `rm -rf target "$HOME"`, because bare is [rm,-rf,target] for both. A grant for `rm -rf "$TMPDIR/x"` reduces to [rm,-rf] and covers `rm -rf "$HOME"` and `rm -rf "/"`.
findings.impact: Quoting arguments is standard practice, so the value an agent asks for (copied from the refusal's suggestion) often contains quoted paths. The person approves one specific deletion, and the session can then run `rm -rf` on any quoted target, including "$HOME" or "/", for as long as the grant lasts. A session-scope grant lasts for the whole session.
findings.fix: Compare full argv. Keep quoted words, with their quotes removed, in both the hit and the grant, and require exact equality. In `grants::validate`, reject command values whose words still contain unexpanded `$`, backticks or globs unless the grant is an explicit prefix grant. Show the parsed argv in the approval card.

v1.reason: denied_matches builds `bare` from unquoted words only (guardrail.rs:975-979). command_words, used for the grant side, also filters `!word.quoted` (guardrail.rs:1000-1006). covers_command then compares `bare == words.as_slice()` (grants.rs:145). shell_commands marks a word quoted only when every character came from quotes (guardrail.rs:884-918), so `"/"` and `"$HOME"` are dropped. Traced cases: a grant for `rm -rf target` gives words [rm,-rf,target], which equals the bare form of `rm -rf target "/"`, so that command is lifted. A grant for `rm -rf "$TMPDIR/x"` reduces to [rm,-rf], which equals the bare form of `rm -rf "/"` and `rm -rf "$HOME"`. Those commands still hit the `rm -rf` default pattern (settings.rs:33), so only the grant lets them through. The doc comment's promise (exact command only) is broken. An agent holding such a grant can widen it simply by quoting extra targets.
v1.correction: The second case is the more serious one: any grant whose specific target was quoted collapses to the bare verb and flags. Fix: compare the full argv with quotes removed but quoted words kept, on both sides. Optionally reject unexpanded `$`, backticks or globs in command grant values.

v2.reason:
(a) The code does what the finding says. `shell_commands` marks a word quoted only when every character came from quotes (guardrail.rs:884-918). Both sides of the grant check then drop quoted words: the hit's `bare` (guardrail.rs:975-979) and the grant's `command_words` (guardrail.rs:1001-1008). `covers_command` then requires `bare == words` (grants.rs:145). I ported the parser and matcher to Python and ran it on sample commands:
- A grant for `rm -rf "$TMPDIR/x"` reduces to [rm,-rf]. It then allows `rm -rf "$HOME"`, `rm -rf "/home/anthony/dev3"` and `rm -rf "a" "b" "$HOME"`.
- A grant for `rm -rf target` allows `rm -rf target "$HOME"`, but still refuses `rm -rf target /`.
- With no grant, all of these are refused.

Nothing upstream catches it. `evaluate_granted` (guardrail.rs:478-497) loads the session's grants and re-runs the evaluation. The documented contract says the opposite: BUS.md:573 says a grant covers "that exact command", and the comment at grants.rs:137-140 says the same. The only test of this (tests/guardrails.rs:644-647) adds an unquoted word, so it passes.

(b) Who can trigger it, and how often: only the agent in the session that holds the grant. Another local user or a network peer cannot. Getting such a grant is a normal flow:
- The gate refuses every `rm -rf`, whatever the target (handlers/settings.rs:33, guardrail.rs:831).
- The refusal suggests the agent ask for its command word for word (grants.rs:344), and agents usually quote paths.
- The approval card offers "Approve for this session" with one click, next to "Approve once" (guardrail_pages.rs:445-446).
For harm, a later and different destructive command must follow in the same session, with only fully quoted targets. That is rare in any one session, but it is exactly the mistake this check exists to stop. A once grant is usually used up by the agent's immediate retry, so the real exposure is session grants.

(c) What happens when it fires: the gate allows the command with no prompt and counts it as a use of the grant the person approved. `rm -rf "$HOME"` or an absolute project path deletes data outside the worktree, and it cannot be undone.

(d) Severity: high is right. It is literally "a safety check that can be silently bypassed", within the design's stated model (BUS.md principle 6: guardrails are seatbelts that stop agents' mistakes). It is not critical: no other user or peer can reach it, and a hostile agent does not need it. The deny list already lets through `rm -fr`, `rm -r -f`, `/bin/rm -rf`, `bash -c "rm -rf …"`, `"rm" -rf` and `--recursive --force` with no grant at all (confirmed in the port). That deserves its own finding.

(e) The fix is right in direction but needs the details listed under correction. I could not establish whether the agent's own permission prompts would also stop such a command. Relay sets no bypass mode itself, so this depends on how the user configured the agent.
v2.correction:
1. The `"/"` example is weak. GNU rm refuses `/` by default (--preserve-root), so `rm -rf "/"` fails anyway. Lead with `rm -rf "$HOME"` or an absolute project path; I confirmed the widened grant allows both.

2. State exactly how far a grant stretches: it covers any number of extra targets, but only fully quoted ones. A partly quoted target (`"$VAR"/*`) or an unquoted one (`~/dev3`) is still refused. The same root cause affects the other default patterns: a grant for `git reset --hard "HEAD~1"` covers `git reset --hard "origin/main"`, and a grant for `git push --force origin "feat"` covers `git push --force origin "main"`.

The first case (an agent adding `"/"` to an approved command) is a hostile shape, which BUS.md principle 6 excludes. The default pattern is at crates/relay-core/src/handlers/settings.rs:33, not settings.rs:33.

4. Fix details:
- Keep `bare` for the pattern match (`windows`), so D103 still holds.
- Compare the grant against the hit's full argv instead. `DeniedMatch.argv` already holds every word with quotes removed.
- Make `command_words` keep quoted words. Its only caller is grants.rs:143, so the change stays local.
- Apply the same comparison to the trailing-`*` prefix branch.
- Consider comparing arguments case-sensitively. Both sides are lowercased today, so a grant for `rm -rf build` also covers `rm -rf BUILD`.
- Add regression tests next to tests/guardrails.rs:644: a grant for `rm -rf "build"` must not cover `rm -rf "src"` but must cover `rm -rf build`, and a grant for `rm -rf build` must not cover `rm -rf build "/x"`.

Without a matching hint change, an agent whose command used `$TMPDIR` would get stuck. Even exact matching compares text, not targets: variables, relative paths and a chained `cd` change what gets deleted, so the approval card should say so. The card change is in relay-native, which cannot be compiled in an agent session.

findings.title: A grant whose last word is `*` lifts every command with that prefix, so approving the suggested `cd dist && rm -rf *` grants `rm -rf /`
findings.evidence: `Some((last, head)) if last == "*" => !head.is_empty() && bare.starts_with(head)` (144) makes a trailing lone `*` Relay's wildcard. `*` is also the shell glob, and the value the refusal suggests is the raw refused line (`"denied_command" => Some((ExceptionKind::Command, details["command"]...))`, 344; hint text 357-366). Port: a grant for `cd dist && rm -rf *` covers `rm -rf /` and `rm -rf ~`.
findings.impact: `rm -rf *` (emptying a build directory) is a very common agent command. The agent is refused and asks with the suggested value. The person reads "run `cd dist && rm -rf *`" as the shell glob and approves, perhaps for the session, and has in fact granted unrestricted `rm -rf` anywhere.
findings.fix: Use a token that is not shell syntax for prefix grants, or a separate `prefix: bool` that the UI renders as 'with any arguments', and treat `*` in a grant value as a literal word. At minimum, when a requested value ends in `*`, show the widened meaning explicitly on the approval card.

v1.reason: covers_command (grants.rs:141-150) runs `super::command_words(&grant.value).iter().any(...)`, and `Some((last, head)) if last == "*" => !head.is_empty() && bare.starts_with(head)` treats a trailing lone `*` as a prefix wildcard. For the value `cd dist && rm -rf *`, command_words gives [[cd,dist],[rm,-rf,*]]. The second command matches any bare argv starting with [rm,-rf], such as `rm -rf /` or `rm -rf ~`. The suggested value is the raw refused line: refuse_or_user_hold adds details.command through grants::suggestion (grants.rs:344) and puts it in the hint and in details.exception. The approval card (guardrail_pages.rs:420-428) shows only the raw value in monospace, with nothing saying it is a prefix grant. BUS.md:573 and the doc comment document the wildcard, so the semantics are intended. But a lone `*` in a real agent command is the shell glob, and the UI never tells the two apart.
v1.correction: Also, a multi-command value is split, and each sub-command becomes its own independent grant (`.any` over the commands). So `cd dist &&` gives no confinement at all: the `rm -rf *` part alone is the grant. A `./*` or `dist/*` last word is not affected, since only a word that is exactly `*` widens. Suggested fix: use a non-shell token or an explicit prefix flag for prefix grants, treat `*` from a suggested value literally, and render the widened meaning on the card.

v2.reason:
(a) The code does what the finding claims. grants.rs:143-144 checks each sub-command of the grant value separately (`command_words(&grant.value).iter().any(...)`). A last word that is exactly `*` becomes a prefix match: `!head.is_empty() && bare.starts_with(head)`. The suggested value is the raw refused line: guardrail.rs:843 puts `command` into the details, and grants.rs:344 returns it. That line reaches the agent through the hint (grants.rs:357-366) and `details.exception` (guardrail.rs:1041-1045). I ported shell_commands, denied_matches and covers_command faithfully to Python and ran them under the scratchpad's exp/ directory. A grant of `cd dist && rm -rf *` splits into [[cd,dist],[rm,-rf,*]], and it passes `rm -rf ~`, `rm -rf /*`, `rm -rf $HOME/`, `rm -rf ../../..`, `rm -rf src` and `cd ~ && rm -rf *`. It does not pass `sudo rm -rf ~`.

(b) Reachability. This is the normal exception flow. The Claude and Codex PreToolUse hooks (relay-cli main.rs:405-410, 506-512) send the raw Bash line to guardrail.gate, and the default deny list contains `rm -rf` (settings.rs:33). The role instructions (providers.rs:50-53) tell the agent to request exactly the `value` the hint names. The approval card (guardrail_pages.rs:419-442) shows the value verbatim in monospace with "Only this rule is lifted". Nothing marks `*` as Relay's wildcard, and `guardrail.confirm` cannot narrow the value (handlers/guardrail.rs:421-433). The trigger is narrower than the finding implies, though:
- With the default list, only a denied command whose last word is a lone `*` is affected, in practice `rm -rf *` or `cd X && rm -rf *`. `dist/*` and `./*` are literal and match exactly.
- The hint's JSON carries no scope, so a request defaults to `once` (handlers/guardrail.rs:396), and "Approve once" is then the primary button (guardrail_pages.rs:445-446).
- A once grant is used up by the retry itself: on Allow, gate calls use_grants (:534), which calls grants::consume. So the widening matters in practice only when the person picks "Approve for this session". The leftover once cases are a grant that is never retried, or one line that holds several `rm -rf` (all covered by one grant, counted as one use).
So the trigger is a plausible but uncommon path.

(c) Impact. For the rest of that session, every `rm -rf <anything>` in any directory passes the exec gate without a prompt. Active Exceptions still shows only `cd dist && rm -rf *`. The worst case is an agent mistake the deny rule exists to catch, such as `rm -rf $UNSET/*`. The gate sees the unexpanded `$unset/*` and would normally refuse it, but with the grant it is allowed and the shell runs `rm -rf /*`, or the agent deletes `~` or a sibling worktree. Claude sessions get no permission mode from Relay (hooks.rs only adds the hook), so only the person's own Claude settings remain. Codex runs with a workspace-write sandbox (D135), so its blast radius is the worktree.

(d) Severity: medium, not high. The trigger needs a lone-`*` denied command and a non-default session approval. The consequence is a lost safety net, not damage on its own: harm needs a later destructive mistake by the agent. The deny rule is also only a token-window match (guardrail.rs:980-994). My port shows that `rm -fr ~` and `/bin/rm -rf ~` hit no deny pattern even without any grant. So the rule catches mistakes in the canonical spelling; it is not a containment boundary. The wildcard is deliberate and documented (BUS.md:573; doc comment at grants.rs:137-140, which says "the person approving it reads that `*`"). The defect is that it shares syntax with the shell glob in auto-suggested values and the UI never tells the two apart. That is a real, medium design flaw.

(e) The proposed fix is incomplete. Treating `*` as a literal word alone still leaves `cd ~ && rm -rf *` covered: the port shows it passes, because each sub-command of a grant is matched on its own (`.any`, grants.rs:143). So `cd dist &&` never confines anything.
v2.correction:
1. `rm -rf /` is a weak example: GNU rm refuses `/` because of --preserve-root. Use `rm -rf ~`, `rm -rf /*`, `rm -rf ../..` or `rm -rf src`. The port shows all four pass.
2. Scope the impact to session approvals. The suggested request defaults to `once` (handlers/guardrail.rs:396) and "Approve once" is the primary button. A once grant is spent by the retry (gate -> use_grants -> grants::consume at handlers/guardrail.rs:534 and 761), so "perhaps for the session" is the actual precondition, not a side note. A better title: "A session grant for a suggested command ending in a shell-glob `*` lifts the `rm -rf` deny rule for every target and directory".
3. Severity high -> medium: an uncommon path, a non-default scope, and harm still needs a later agent mistake. The deny rule is already a canonical-spelling token match (guardrail.rs:980-994) that `rm -fr` and `/bin/rm -rf` never trip.
4. Fix:
   - Make `*` a literal word. If prefix grants are kept, make them an explicit request field that the card renders as "<words> with any arguments".
   - Also match a grant against the whole line's command sequence instead of each sub-command independently (grants.rs:143, `.any`). Otherwise a literal `cd dist && rm -rf *` grant still passes `cd ~ && rm -rf *`. Failing that, the card must say the grant covers `rm -rf *` in any directory.
   - Update BUS.md §9.5 (line 573) and the doc comment at grants.rs:137-140, which document the current wildcard.
   - Add a test: tests/guardrails.rs only tests exact grants; nothing tests the wildcard.
   - Grants stored with a trailing `*` would only get narrower under the fix, which is safe.

findings.title: Glob matcher keeps one backtrack point, so `**/*.pem` matches only files exactly one directory deep and `**/x` never matches a top-level `x`
findings.evidence: `glob_match` (1171-1208) remembers only the latest star. `star = Some((p, t, crosses));` (1185) overwrites the `**` backtrack point when a later `*` is reached, and the segment-local star then fails at the first `/` (`_ => return false`, 1201) instead of letting the earlier `**` consume more. The trailing-star shortcut `return crosses || !text[t..].contains(&b'/')` (1183) has the same flaw, and `**/` requires at least one directory. A Python port that passes all 12 assertions in `glob_tests` gives: `**/*.pem` -> c.pem false, x/c.pem true, x/y/c.pem false, x/y/z/c.pem false. `src/**/*.rs` misses src/a/b/main.rs. `secrets/**/*.json` matches only secrets/x/a.json. `**/secrets.toml` misses secrets.toml, `**/.env` misses .env, and `**/secrets` does not cover a/secrets/key.txt.
findings.impact: protected_paths and shape_gates written in the most common idiom silently protect almost nothing. For example, `**/*.key` does not protect deploy/keys/prod.key and `**/.env` does not protect the root .env. Writes go through with no refusal and no warning. Path grants and the `file.search` glob (file.rs:330) use the same matcher.
findings.fix: Replace the matcher. `gix-glob` is already in Cargo.lock and implements git wildmatch semantics (`**/` matches zero or more directories, `*` stays within a segment). Alternatively, write a recursive matcher that backtracks over `**` separately from `*`. Decide and document whether a glob that names a directory covers its contents (literal patterns already do). Extend glob_tests to depths 0-3.

v1.reason: Tracing glob_match (~1170-1208) by hand for `**/*.pem` against `x/y/c.pem`: the `**` sets star=(2,0,true) and `/` matches after one backtrack. The next `*` then overwrites the star with (4,2,false), the only backtrack point left is segment-local, and on reaching `/` it hits `_ => return false`. So the earlier `**` is never retried, and only one directory depth matches. `**/` also needs at least one directory before it, so `**/.env` misses a root `.env` (the literal check in path_matches does not apply because the pattern starts with `**`). The existing glob_tests only cover one-level cases (`src/**/*.rs` on src/deep/main.rs, `**/secrets.toml` on a/b/secrets.toml, which has no second star), so they pass. protected_paths and shape_gates are user-configured, and a pattern written in the usual idiom silently protects almost nothing, with no warning. Path grants and file.search share the matcher.
v1.correction: Valid patterns that fail silently, in a safety check, are high severity. Literal directory and file patterns (`secrets`, `config/prod.json`) still work through path_matches' prefix check, which limits the blast radius. The fix should use git wildmatch semantics (gix-glob is already a dependency), make `**/` match zero or more directories, and add tests at depths 0-3.

v2.reason:
(a) The code does what the finding says. glob_match (guardrail.rs:1171-1208) keeps a single backtrack slot. When a later `*` is reached, `star = Some((p, t, crosses))` (1185) overwrites the earlier `**`. That segment-local star then fails its guard at the first `/` (1196) and hits `_ => return false` (1201), so the `**` is never retried. The trailing-star shortcut `return crosses || !text[t..].contains(&b'/')` (1183) also returns before retrying an earlier `**`. And because the `/` after `**` is a literal, `**/` needs at least one directory. I hand-traced it and also wrote a Python port that passes all 12 glob_tests assertions. Results:
- `**/*.pem`: c.pem F, x/c.pem T, x/y/c.pem F, x/y/z/c.pem F.
- `src/**/*.rs`: misses src/main.rs and src/a/b/main.rs.
- `secrets/**/*.json`: matches only secrets/x/a.json.
- `**/.env`, `**/secrets.toml`, `**/*.lock`: miss the top-level file.
- `**/*`: misses a/b/c.

Nothing upstream compensates. hook_relative_path (relay-cli main.rs:567) and write_target only turn the path into a worktree-relative one. validate_pattern only rejects empty, absolute and `..` patterns. No code rewrites patterns. Every test uses a pattern with a trailing `**` or one level of depth.

(b) Reachable by the user's own configuration, with agents as the actors who get through. protected_paths and shape_gates are empty by default (settings.rs:31-32), so nothing breaks out of the box. But the settings UI says "Worktree-relative paths or globs agents may not write" (guardrail_settings.rs:69). Since D113 made `*` segment-local (`*.env` does not match config/.env, test at line 1338), `**/*.ext`, `dir/**/*.ext` and `**/name` are exactly what a user would write to mean "anywhere". Once such a pattern is configured, the bug fires on every write at an affected depth through:
- every Claude Code Write/Edit/MultiEdit (PreToolUse hook → guardrail.gate kind=write → evaluate_write:512, 526, 548);
- every file.write/create/rename/move/delete;
- every commit through the pre-commit hook (evaluate_commit:776-778).

Literal paths, directory names and `dir/**` patterns still work.

(c) The gate returns allow. There is no refusal, hold, notification or audit refusal, and guardrail.check and explain say the same, so the user is never told. Agents can edit and commit files the user believes are protected. Shape gates silently skip validation at those depths. Data loss is concrete for a gitignored root `.env` covered by `**/.env`:
- recoverable() treats ignored files as restorable (D114), so the large-rewrite rule allows the write;
- for files under 30 lines the percentage rule is skipped and the line rule needs more than 50 removed lines;
- so protected_paths is the only guard, and it does not fire.

Path grants under-match, which fails closed (extra refusals), not open. The file.search glob under-matches results, but only through MCP or the CLI; the native editor never passes a glob (editor.rs:1109).

(d) High is right: this is "a safety check that can be silently bypassed". It is not critical:
- it needs a config the user opts into, using particular idioms;
- the defaults are unaffected;
- protected paths are not a sandbox anyway. evaluate_exec checks only denied_commands, so writes from a shell bypass them, and Codex writes are unguarded by design (BUS.md §9.3).

Calling it security is fine.

(e) The proposed recursive matcher is correct. In my Python port, a candidate where any `**` crosses `/`, `**/` at a component start may match zero directories, and `*` stays segment-local passes all 12 existing assertions plus the depth 0-3 cases, and it keeps today's meaning for `**.pem`. The gix-glob route works without a new dependency: gix 0.86 re-exports `gix_glob as glob` unconditionally (lib.rs:133). It has traps, listed in the correction.
v2.correction:
1. If gix-glob is used, call `gix::glob::wildmatch(pattern, path, gix::glob::wildmatch::Mode::NO_MATCH_SLASH_LITERAL)` directly. `Pattern::matches_repo_relative_path` applies gitignore's basename rule (NO_SUB_DIR) to patterns without a slash. That would make `*.env` match config/.env, undo D113 and fail the existing test at guardrail.rs:1338.
2. Git wildmatch treats a `**` that is not a whole path component (`**.pem`, `src/**.rs`) as a segment-local `*`. Today every `**` crosses `/`, so `**.pem` protects all depths; after a straight swap it would protect only the top level, the same kind of silent narrowing. Either reject or normalize such patterns in validate_pattern, or keep a custom matcher.
3. Wildmatch also makes `?`, `[...]` and `\` special; they are literal today. Literal patterns still hit the exact/prefix check first, but a glob such as `app/[id]/*.tsx` would change meaning.
4. The `**/secrets` vs a/secrets/key.txt sub-point is a separate design question (does a glob that names a directory cover its contents?). It is not caused by the backtracking bug, and git wildmatch does not match it either. It needs its own rule, for example also trying `pattern/**`.
