5. Update D113 and the doc comment at guardrail.rs:1158-1160 to say that `**/` matches zero or more directories.
6. Grants under-match in the fail-closed direction (extra refusals), not as a bypass.

findings.title: Confirming a held guardrail.gate never lets the held action through: the hook has already failed it, and the retry is gated fresh and held again
findings.evidence: For `frozen.op == "guardrail.gate"`, `confirm` re-evaluates with `skip_policy: Some(&hold.policy)` (598-617), returns that outcome to the confirmer and marks the hold confirmed (646-651). Nothing it records is consulted by a later gate: `evaluate_granted` loads only `op = 'guardrail.request'` grants (grants.rs:51-53). The callers cannot wait either. The Claude hook exits 2 on any non-ok response (relay-cli main.rs:472-483), and the pre-commit hook `exec`s `relay cmd guardrail.gate`, which exits non-zero on `held` (hooks.rs:130-132). BUS.md §9.3 says the hook 'blocks the tool while the verdict is hold'. Agent holds also carry no exception hint, because `refuse_or_user_hold` returns `hold(..)` for `destructive_write | shape_gate` (1035-1036) before the hint branch, which leaves `suggestion`'s "destructive_write" arm (grants.rs:345) unreachable. The test only checks that a different follow-up write is held (guardrails.rs:263-269).
findings.impact: An agent that rewrites more than 50 lines of a file it has modified or created (untracked, so not recoverable) is held. The user confirms, the agent retries as the mail 'Guardrail hold N was confirmed' invites, and it is held again, indefinitely, with a new hold row each time. A user's own over-cap commit through the pre-commit hook loops the same way until they use --no-verify. Agents then route around the rule, for example by writing through Bash, which defeats it.
findings.fix: Make a confirmed gate hold usable. On confirm, record a single-use pass on the hold (for example `details.grant = {scope:"once", match: sha256(kind|path|new_text|diff|command)}`) and have `gate()` consume a matching unused pass before evaluating. Alternatively, have both hooks wait on `bus.wait {events:["guardrail.resolved"], matching:{hold_id}}` with a timeout and exit 0 when confirmed. Either way, attach the `path` exception hint to agent holds.

v1.reason: For a `guardrail.gate` hold, `confirm` (handlers/guardrail.rs:595-660) only re-evaluates with `skip_policy` and marks the hold confirmed. Nothing a later gate reads records the confirmation. `evaluate_granted` (guardrail.rs:478-497) loads only `op = 'guardrail.request'` grants (grants.rs:50-53). The Claude hook returns exit 2 on any non-ok response, without waiting (relay-cli main.rs:472-483). The pre-commit hook `exec`s `relay cmd guardrail.gate` (hooks.rs:115-140), which fails on held. A retry is therefore evaluated fresh and held again by `destructive_decision`/`refuse_or_user_hold`, with a new hold row each time. The finding is also right that agent holds return from the `destructive_write | shape_gate` branch (guardrail.rs:1035-1036) before the hint/suggestion branch, so no `guardrail.request` hint is attached and the `destructive_write` arm of `suggestion` (grants.rs:345) cannot be reached from that path. BUS.md §9.3 says the hook 'blocks the tool while the verdict is hold', which the CLI adapter does not do.
v1.correction: The way out that exists is a `guardrail.request` path grant (`granted_path` lifts destructive_write). An agent is never told about it on a hold, and confirming the hold does not create one. The `suggestion` destructive_write arm is still reachable through `explain`, if it calls `suggestion`, so 'unreachable' applies only to the hold path. Best fix: on confirm of a gate hold, record a single-use pass keyed to the exact request, and have `gate()` consume it. The other option is to make the hooks wait on `guardrail.resolved`. Either way, also attach the path-exception hint to agent holds.

v2.reason:
(a) I traced the code myself and it does what the finding says. For a `guardrail.gate` hold, `confirm` (handlers/guardrail.rs:598-617) only runs `guardrail::evaluate` again with `skip_policy: Some(&hold.policy)`. It returns the result to the confirmer as `outcome`, marks the row confirmed (646-651) and mails "Guardrail hold N was confirmed by …" (660). Nothing a later gate reads looks at that row. `gate()` (501-526) calls `evaluate_granted`, and `Grants::load` selects only `op = 'guardrail.request' AND state = 'confirmed'` (grants.rs:51-53). A grep for "confirmed" in core finds no other consumer. The Claude adapter returns exit 2 at once on any non-ok response (relay-cli main.rs:472-483) and makes one call with a fresh uuid (`Request::new`), so there is no wait and no idempotent replay. The test confirms this. After the confirm at guardrails.rs:217-226, large.txt still has 100 lines, because the confirm wrote nothing, and the follow-up write at 263-269 is held again.

(b) Reachability. By default (settings.rs:30: more than 50 lines removed, or more than 40% of a file of at least 30 lines, `allow_if_recoverable`), any Claude builder or docs session hits this. The PreToolUse hook is installed at launch (session.rs:482-483). The trigger is a Write, Edit or MultiEdit that rewrites a file the agent has already created (untracked) or modified, since `recoverable()` returns None for any status line other than none or `!!`. Agents rewrite their own new or modified files all the time, so a heavy user will see this regularly. Shape-gate holds (`refuse_or_user_hold` returns `hold` for agents at guardrail.rs:1035-1036) loop the same way when shape gates are configured.

(c) Consequence. The native card says "<session> is waiting on you", and its "Allow once" button calls `guardrail.confirm` (guardrail_pages.rs:299). The outcome comes back ok, so the UI reports success. The write never happens, because the hook already failed it. If the agent follows the confirmation mail and retries, it gets a new hold, a new notification, a new card and a new copy of the full `new_text` in `holds.envelope`. That repeats for as long as anyone keeps retrying and confirming. The documented way out is a `guardrail.request` path grant (`granted_path` lifts destructive_write at guardrail.rs:722). The hold never points the agent to it: it carries no hint, because the `destructive_write|shape_gate` branch returns before `grants::suggestion`. `suggestion` has exactly one caller (guardrail.rs:1041), so its destructive_write arm (grants.rs:345) can never run. In practice an agent gets past the rule by splitting the rewrite into Edits under the threshold, or by writing through Bash, and both defeat it. Shape gates have no grant at all, so a confirmed shape-gate hold has no way through. There is no data loss. What breaks is a core guardrail flow, and the user sees it break. BUS.md §9.3/§9.4 promise that the hook "blocks the tool while the verdict is hold" and that a confirmed agent learns its write was confirmed. The code delivers neither.

(d) High fits the rubric: likely, user-visible wrong behavior in a normal flow, and a hold UI whose confirm does nothing. It is not critical: nothing is lost, and there are escape routes, even if they are poor ones.

(e) The direction of the fix is right. The details below need fixing.
v2.correction:
1. The first verifier's hedge is wrong. `suggestion` is not reachable through `guardrail.explain`: its only caller is guardrail.rs:1041, inside the refuse branch of `refuse_or_user_hold`. The destructive_write arm is dead on every path.

2. "Indefinitely" overstates the loop. It lasts only while the agent retries the identical write and the user keeps confirming. Agents get out through a `guardrail.request` path grant, or by working around the rule (sub-threshold Edits, Bash). Shape-gate holds are the case with no grant-based exit.

3. The pre-commit half applies only to the user's own terminal commits, through the `--actor user` branch at hooks.rs:132. Agent commits are refused, not held, because `evaluate_commit` routes protected_path and cap through `refuse_or_user_hold`. The user still has `--no-verify`, and the Git panel's `git.commit` replay works (D35/D141). That half is medium at most.

4. Fix corrections:
   - A recorded pass must not let the next gate through "before evaluating". The gate should run `evaluate` again with `skip_policy` set to the pass's policy, consume the pass only on Allow (as `use_grants` does), scope it to the same session, and let it expire with that session (D22).
   - Matching on exact content holds for a repeated Write, but not for content the model regenerates. The confirmation mail should say "retry the identical action".
   - For commit holds, `diff` is None, so a hash of kind|path|new_text|diff|command reduces to "any next commit". Key it on the staged tree (`git write-tree`) or the numstat instead.
   - If the re-evaluation produced a nested hold (confirm, 626-643), record no pass.
   - Waiting in the hook cannot stand alone. The Claude hook has a 30 s timeout (hooks.rs:351), a person who answers after that leaves the same dead end, and the hook has to check state before `bus.wait` because events are not replayed (D115).
   - A smaller variant reuses existing code. On confirming an agent's destructive_write gate hold, record a once-scoped path grant: `granted_path` already lifts destructive_write, and `consume` and the `used` event already exist. This needs `Grants::load` to see such grants, since it filters on `op = 'guardrail.request'`.
   - Either way, attach the path hint to agent destructive_write holds, and resolve the contradiction in BUS.md §9.3 between "blocks the tool while the verdict is hold" and "exits 2 on hold".

findings.title: Any agent can answer its own guardrail as `user`: the socket trusts actor:user without a token, and self_approval misses even the CLI's own envelope mode
findings.evidence: `resolve_actor` accepts `(Actor::User, _) | (Actor::Test, _) => Ok(None)` with no credential (engine.rs:1355), and BUS.md §9.5 calls `self_approval` 'best effort ... not a security boundary'. `self_approval` (857-881) needs a word whose stem starts with `relay` and either `--actor user` or a bare word equal to a user-only op. The relay CLI keeps the `actor` field of a full JSON envelope passed as the op argument (do_cmd: `if v.get("actor").is_none() {..}`, relay-cli main.rs:586-593). Port results: `relay cmd '{"actor":"user","op":"guardrail.confirm","payload":{"hold_id":5}}'` is NOT caught, and neither are `$RELAY_BIN q '{"actor":"user","op":"guardrail.config.set","payload":{"patch":{"denied_commands":[]}}}'` and `r=relay; $r q guardrail.confirm ..`. Any direct socket client (python, socat) bypasses the check entirely.
findings.impact: An agent that is refused can approve its own guardrail.request, confirm its own holds, or patch guardrail config (for example empty denied_commands or protected_paths) with one CLI call that the gate allows, and the audit log attributes the change to the user. Every policy in this chunk is therefore advisory against an agent that tries.
findings.fix: Authenticate `user` on the socket. The engine knows each session's child PID: use SO_PEERCRED on the Unix socket and refuse actor:user, or downgrade it to that session's agent, when the peer's process ancestry includes a session PTY child. Alternatively, require a user secret that is never exported into session environments, for example one handed to the GUI over an inherited fd. Until then, make `self_approval` parse JSON-envelope arguments and treat an `actor` naming user/test as self-approval.

v1.reason: resolve_actor (engine.rs ~1355) returns `(Actor::User, _) | (Actor::Test, _) => Ok(None)` with no credential, while agents need a token. do_cmd (relay-cli main.rs ~586-593) keeps the `actor` field of a full JSON envelope (`if v.get("actor").is_none()`). self_approval (guardrail.rs:857-881) matches whole words only. For `relay cmd '{"actor":"user","op":"guardrail.confirm",...}'`, the JSON is one word: no word equals a USER_ONLY_ANSWERS entry, and none is `--actor user`. The line is therefore allowed, and the engine runs guardrail.confirm or guardrail.config.set as the user, with the audit log naming the user. A second hole: `env -i relay cmd '{"op":"guardrail.confirm",...}'` with no actor in the envelope. `env -i` is not in sheds_identity, and actor_from_env then falls back to User. BUS.md §9.5 admits the check is best effort, but the CLI's own documented envelope mode is exactly the 'obvious door' it claims to close. This is a guardrail check that can be silently bypassed.
v1.correction: The threat model affects the fix. Agents run under the user's uid with a shell, so SO_PEERCRED on its own would not make guardrails a hard boundary: an agent can still edit the store or config files directly. The proportionate fix has three parts. First, in do_cmd, when RELAY_SESSION or RELAY_TOKEN is set, refuse an envelope `actor` that differs from the env-derived one. Second, have self_approval parse JSON-envelope words and treat `actor` user/test, or an `op` naming a user-only answer, as self-approval, and treat `env -i` and `env -u` as shedding identity. Third, the longer-term step: authenticate the user door with a secret that is never exported into session environments. Severity stays high as a bypassable safety check. It is not critical, because a same-uid agent with a shell is not fully containable by design.

v2.reason:
(a) The code does what the finding claims.
- `self_approval` (crates/relay-core/src/guardrail.rs:857-881) matches whole words only. `answers` (line 875) needs a word exactly equal to a USER_ONLY_ANSWERS entry. `as_user` (line 871) needs a literal `--actor user|test`.
- A JSON envelope passed to `relay cmd` or `relay q` is a single quoted word, so neither check fires.
- `do_cmd` keeps an envelope's `actor` (`if v.get("actor").is_none()`, crates/relay-cli/src/main.rs:591) and still attaches RELAY_TOKEN (main.rs:592).
- `resolve_actor` returns `(Actor::User, _) | (Actor::Test, _) => Ok(None)` (crates/relay-core/src/engine.rs:1355) and ignores the token.
- The UserOnly allowlist then admits the op. With no session id, `guardrail::authorize` is skipped.
- The hold's `resolved_by`, the `guardrail.resolved {by}` event and the audit actor all read "user".
- The example payload `{"patch":{"denied_commands":[]}}` is valid: with no workspace_id or project_id it patches the global layer.

I ported `shell_commands`, `self_approval` and `denied_matches` to pure-string Python under scratchpad/exp/port.py. The port reproduces the suite's 7 caught and 3 allowed cases (tests/guardrails.rs:628, 762-773). It confirms that four lines all pass and match no default denied command:
- `relay cmd '{"actor":"user","op":"guardrail.confirm",...}'`
- the `$RELAY_BIN q` envelope calling config.set
- `r=relay; $r q guardrail.confirm ...`
- `env -i relay cmd '{"op":"guardrail.confirm",...}'`

The suite has no envelope case. The check is one day old (6be272f).

(b) Who can trigger it, and how often:
- Only a Claude or Codex agent inside a Relay session can reach it, and only by deliberately forging `"actor":"user"`. Its instructions say "do not work around it ... only the user can approve it" (providers.rs:50). This is never a mistake path.
- The form is discoverable. Both `relay --help` (main.rs:35) and BUS.md:396 document `relay cmd '<json-envelope>'` "(id, actor, op, payload)".
- Other local users cannot reach it: socket.rs:56-102 creates a 0700 directory and a 0600 socket. Network peers cannot reach it either.
- It fires rarely, only when an agent deliberately evades.

(c) What happens when it fires:
- The agent can confirm its own exception or holds, patch guardrail config at any layer, or call `settings.set` on `guardrails.roles` to widen every session's allowlist.
- These changes persist, and the audit attributes them to "user".
- The project documents guardrails as seatbelts, not a boundary, against same-uid agents:
  - BUS.md:29-31 ("Seatbelts, not sandboxes").
  - BUS.md:208 (`user` needs no token, "same uid, same trust").
  - BUS.md:580-584 (this check is "best effort against the obvious route, not a security boundary").
  - BUS.md:1119-1120 ("Tokens prevent misattribution, not determined impersonation").
- An evading agent already has simpler routes. The same port shows the default denied list (matched on unquoted words, D103) lets `bash -c 'rm -rf build'`, `rm -fr`, `git push -f` and `git -C . reset --hard` through. Writes to protected paths made from Bash are not gated on exec at all.
- So the added harm is persistence across sessions plus misattribution. It is not data loss in itself, and config.set is undoable from the audit log.
- Side note: in this audit session, the live hook refused a heredoc that only contained the suite's sample strings, which shows the check is a heuristic over raw words.

(d) Severity:
- The gap is real against the check's own stated scope. The CLI's documented envelope form is as obvious as the `--actor user` form the check targets.
- However, "the socket trusts user without a token" is a documented non-goal, not a defect.
- The only trigger is deliberate evasion, and the underlying policies are bypassable by design. That makes it medium (a real bug in an uncommon path), not high.

(e) The proposed fix is not proportionate:
- SO_PEERCRED with a PTY-ancestry check, or a user secret passed over an inherited fd, cannot stop a same-uid agent. It can leave the process tree (setsid, a double fork, `systemd-run --user`), edit the store with sqlite3, or read any secret its uid can read.
- That fix contradicts BUS.md §14 and is L effort for little gain. A cheaper fix is in the correction.
v2.correction:
Narrow the title and evidence.
- The defect is that `self_approval` misses the CLI's own envelope mode: `relay cmd|q '<json-envelope>'` whose actor is user/test, or whose op is a user-only answer. It also misses `env -i`.
- That the socket accepts `user` without a token is documented design (BUS.md §0.6, §4.2, §14). Do not cite engine.rs:1355 as a defect.

Severity: medium, not high.
- "Every policy is advisory against an agent that tries" is true by design.
- It is already true through the word-level denied-command matcher: `bash -c 'rm -rf x'` and `git push -f` pass the default list.
- The harm this route adds is persistent config or role changes, and audit rows attributed to the user.

Fix:
1. In `self_approval`, also inspect any word that parses as a JSON object.
   - Treat `actor` ∈ {user, test}, or `op` ∈ USER_ONLY_ANSWERS, as self-approval.
   - Treat `env -i`, `env --ignore-environment` and `env -` as shedding identity.
   - Add these cases to `agents_cannot_answer_guardrails_as_the_user_from_a_shell`.
2. Optional, cheap, and independent of how the command line is spelled: on Door::Socket, refuse with `bus.actor` any request whose actor is user/test but which carries a `token`.
   - The CLI attaches RELAY_TOKEN both under the `--actor` override (main.rs:120) and in envelope mode (main.rs:592).
   - RELAY_TOKEN is exported only into Claude/Codex sessions (handlers/session.rs:566).
   - This closes `r=relay; $r ...` and scripts, unless the agent also strips the token.
   - Its only cost is the user's own `--actor user` from a shell escape inside an agent pane. It changes the documented §8.2 behavior, so update the doc.

Drop the SO_PEERCRED / process-ancestry fix and the user-secret-over-fd fix. Neither creates a boundary against a same-uid agent, and both contradict §14.

findings.title: self_approval refuses ordinary searches like `rg guardrail.confirm crates/relay-core`, and no grant can lift the refusal
findings.evidence: Any word whose file stem starts with `relay` counts as a relay invocation (`stem.to_ascii_lowercase().starts_with("relay") || word.contains("RELAY_BIN")`, 860-863). Any word equal to a user-only op (875), or starting with RELAY_SESSION=/RELAY_ACTOR= anywhere in argv (865-870), completes the match. Port: `rg guardrail.confirm crates/relay-core`, `grep -rn settings.set apps/relay-native`, `grep -rn 'RELAY_SESSION=' crates` and `cargo test -p relay-core settings.set` are all refused as `guardrail.self_approval`, which 'No grant lifts' (817-826).
findings.impact: Agents working on the Relay repository itself (this audit runs in a Relay worktree) are blocked from routine code searches and test filters, with an error accusing them of impersonating the user and no exception path.
findings.fix: Treat only argv[0], after env/sudo/assignment prefixes, as the relay binary, and look for op names only as relay's op argument. Treat RELAY_SESSION=/RELAY_ACTOR= as identity changes only in assignment position before the command word, or as operands of env/unset.

v1.reason: In self_approval (guardrail.rs:860-863), a word counts as a relay invocation when its file stem starts with `relay`. Path::new("crates/relay-core").file_stem() is "relay-core", so `rg guardrail.confirm crates/relay-core` qualifies, and the bare word `guardrail.confirm` is in USER_ONLY_ANSWERS. The check uses word.text whether or not the word was quoted, so quoting the search term does not help. Any word starting with `RELAY_SESSION=` or `RELAY_ACTOR=` triggers sheds_identity even without a relay word, so `grep -rn 'RELAY_SESSION=' crates` is refused. evaluate_exec (815-826) returns guardrail.self_approval, which no grant can lift. The user develops Relay inside Relay sessions, and the hook is live here, so this hits routine searches and test filters (`cargo test -p relay-core settings.set`) in the user's main project.
v1.correction: Workarounds exist, such as regex-escaping the term (`rg 'guardrail\.confirm'`) or using file.search, which keeps this at medium rather than high. The proposed fix is right: identify relay only as the command word, after env/sudo/assignment prefixes, check op names only in relay's op position or inside its envelope, and treat RELAY_* assignments only in prefix position or as operands of env/unset.

findings.title: A destructive rewrite of a git-ignored file is allowed as 'recoverable', but git cannot restore ignored files (.env, local config, tfstate)
findings.evidence: `Some(line) if line.starts_with("!!") => Some("ignored by git")` (687), and `destructive_decision` returns `Decision::Allow` for any `Some(reason)` (725-729). D114 justifies this with 'an ignored file is build output'. Ignored files are exactly the ones git holds no copy of: .env, *.local.*, terraform.tfstate, local SQLite databases, editor settings.
findings.impact: In a session on the primary checkout (`session.create {worktree:"primary"}`), or in a pooled worktree that has accumulated local files, an agent that rewrites an 80-line .env into a 5-line template removes 75 lines (over the 50-line limit). It is judged recoverable and the secrets are gone with no hold, since allow_if_recoverable defaults to true.
findings.fix: Return None for `!!`, since an ignored file is not recoverable, or exempt only paths under known build-output directories (crate::watch::is_generated_path). Update D114.

v1.reason: guardrail.rs recoverable: `Some(line) if line.starts_with("!!") => Some("ignored by git")`. destructive_decision returns Allow for any Some, and allow_if_recoverable defaults to true (settings.rs:30). D114 does document the intent, but its premise that "an ignored file is build output" is false: git holds no copy of an ignored file, which contradicts D114's own test ("bytes exist nowhere else"). It is intended but not harmless. Reachable: session.rs:860 supports a `primary` checkout, which carries ignored local files such as .env, local configs and SQLite databases. An agent rewriting an ignored file and removing more than 50 lines, or more than 40% of a file of 30 lines or more, gets Allow with no hold. Fresh pooled worktrees hold fewer such files, since Relay does not copy ignored files into them.
v1.correction: Treat `!!` as unrecoverable, or exempt it only under known generated or build directories (e.g. via watch::is_generated_path). Update D114 to match. The trigger needs a large removal from an ignored file, so it is less common than the finding implies, but the loss is unrecoverable when it happens.

findings.title: The commit gate parses `git diff --cached --numstat` without -z/--no-renames, so renamed and non-ASCII paths never match protected paths, and renames count as 0 lines
findings.evidence: `git_output(request.worktree, &["diff", "--cached", "--numstat"])` (760), then `splitn(3, '\t')` takes the third field as the path (766-772). Checked with git 2.55 in a scratch repo: renames print `0\t0\tconfig/{prod.env => prod.env.bak}` and `0\t0\tdocs/plain.md => secret-notes.md`, and a non-ASCII path prints `"docs/caf\303\251.md"` (C-quoted). `path_matches` compares these strings literally. The git.commit op has its own producer (`staged_numstat`, git.rs:861-871), which emits only the rename destination and ignores `renamed_from`.
findings.impact: Through the pre-commit hook, a commit passes when it renames a protected file away (config/prod.env -> config/prod.env.bak), renames a file into a protected directory, or touches a protected path with a non-ASCII name. Caps count a pure rename as 0 lines. Through git.commit, renaming a file out of a protected path also passes. The same policy has two numstat producers, and they already disagree.
findings.fix: Use `git diff --cached --numstat -z --no-renames` and split records on NUL, or keep renames and check both sides. Make `staged_numstat` emit the renamed_from side too, ideally through one helper shared by both callers.

v1.reason: evaluate_commit (guardrail.rs:757-772) runs `git diff --cached --numstat` through git_output (1122) when request.diff is None, which is the case for the pre-commit hook (hooks.rs:129-132 sends only {session,kind:"commit"}). It then takes the third tab field as the path, and path_matches (1161-1168) compares it literally or by glob. I reproduced this in a scratch repo with git 2.55: `git mv config/prod.env config/prod.env.bak` prints `0\t0\tconfig/{prod.env => prod.env.bak}`, and a modified `café.md` prints `"caf\303\251.md"`. A protected pattern `config/prod.env` never matches the brace form, and an exact or file glob pattern never matches a C-quoted path. The rename also adds 0 lines toward the caps. On the git.commit route, staged_numstat (git.rs:861-871) builds from status_files, and parse_status (worktree.rs:109-115) does capture renamed_from. staged_numstat ignores it and emits only the destination, so renaming a file out of a protected path also passes there.
v1.correction: Some cases still match. A directory pattern such as `config` matches the brace form (`config/{...}` starts with `config/`), so a rename inside a protected directory is still caught. The 0-line cap undercount applies only to the hook route: on the git.commit route, staged_numstat reads HEAD at the destination path, gets empty text, and counts the whole file as added, not 0. Fix: run `--numstat -z --no-renames` (or `-c core.quotePath=false` together with `-z`) and split on NUL. In staged_numstat, also emit a line for renamed_from. Better still, share one producer between both routes.

findings.title: Paths are matched as raw strings: `./secret/key`, `secret//key` and symlinks inside the worktree bypass protected paths and write roots
findings.evidence: `relative_path` rejects only `..`, root and prefix components (1137-1144), so `./secret/key` passes unchanged. `path_matches` compares `path.to_string_lossy()` text (1163-1164) and then the glob, so `path_matches("secret", "./secret/key")` and `path_matches("secret/key", "secret//key")` are both false (port). For absolute paths, `strip_prefix(request.worktree)` (638) keeps inner `//` and `/./` (reasoned from std's Components::as_path, which trims only the ends). Symlinks are never resolved, so a path through `link -> ~/.ssh` inside the worktree is InWorktree and never checked against write roots. Concrete route: a bus_writes agent calls `file.write {path:"./secret/key"}`; `rel()` accepts CurDir (file.rs:470-486), `safe_join` resolves it inside the worktree, and `enforce` passes "./secret/key" to the gate (file.rs:93-102).
findings.impact: A protected file is overwritten with no refusal. Through a symlink, a write leaves the worktree with no write-root check (the file.* ops canonicalize via safe_join, but the hook path does not).
findings.fix: Normalize before matching: rebuild relative paths from components(), dropping CurDir (which also collapses `//`), and do the same to absolute candidates before strip_prefix. Canonicalize the existing parent directory, as file::safe_join does, before deciding worktree vs scratch vs outside. Reject patterns that start with `./` in validate_pattern.

v1.reason: relative_path (~1123-1134) rejects only ParentDir, RootDir and Prefix, so `./secret/key` passes unchanged. path_matches compares `path.to_string_lossy()` text: `./secret/key` is neither equal to `secret` nor starts with `secret/`, and glob_match on the literal fails, so the protected path is not matched. This is reachable through file.write (handlers/file.rs Write handler): `rel()` accepts CurDir, `safe_join` resolves it inside the worktree, and `guardrail::enforce` is called with the raw `p.path`. For absolute hook paths, `strip_prefix` returns the remaining components' raw slice, which keeps interior `//` (`secret//key` misses the pattern `secret/key`, though a directory pattern `secret` still matches). write_target never canonicalizes, so `<worktree>/link/x`, where `link` is a symlink out of the worktree, is classified InWorktree and skips the write-root check. file.* ops are protected by safe_join, but the hook-driven gate is not.
v1.correction: Severity stays medium. The symlink route needs a symlink in the worktree, and an agent with shell access can write outside the roots by other means anyway, so the write-root check is not a strong boundary. The `./` route is the most concrete: an agent can rewrite a protected file through file.write or its Write tool with no refusal. Fix: normalize via components() (drop CurDir, which also collapses `//`) before matching and before strip_prefix, and canonicalize the existing parent before choosing worktree, scratch or outside.

findings.title: An old file that is not UTF-8, or cannot be read, is measured as empty, so overwriting it is never a destructive write
findings.evidence: `Ok(_) => std::fs::read_to_string(&absolute).unwrap_or_default(),` (572). `read_to_string` fails with InvalidData on any non-UTF-8 byte and on permission errors, so `old` becomes "", `changed_line_counts("", new)` yields removed = 0, and old_lines = Some(0). On the diff path, `file_lines` (695-702) returns None the same way.
findings.impact: The Write tool can replace a 500-line Latin-1, Windows-1252 or UTF-16 text file with a 3-line file and no hold is raised. The guard fails open on exactly the files that are hardest to restore by hand.
findings.fix: Read the file as bytes and count lines with String::from_utf8_lossy (or count b'\n' and hash line byte slices). On a read error other than NotFound, hold rather than allow.

v1.reason: guardrail.rs evaluate_write: `Ok(_) => std::fs::read_to_string(&absolute).unwrap_or_default()`. read_to_string returns InvalidData on any non-UTF-8 byte, so `old` becomes "". changed_line_counts("", new) then reports removed=0 and old_lines=Some(0), and destructive_decision returns Allow before recoverable() is ever consulted. Trigger: an agent's Write (gate kind=write with new_text) replaces an untracked or locally modified Windows-1252, Latin-1 or UTF-16 text file of hundreds of lines with a short one. No hold is raised and the file's unique bytes are lost. This is a silent fail-open of the guard, limited to non-UTF-8 files, which are uncommon but not rare in game and Windows-derived repos.
v1.correction: The diff-only path is only partly affected. file_lines returns None, which silences only the percentage rule. The absolute rule still uses diff_counts, so a large removal in a diff still trips it. A file the engine cannot read because of permissions is mostly moot, since the agent runs as the same user. The fix is to read bytes and use from_utf8_lossy (or count b'\n'). Hold when the read fails for a reason other than NotFound.

findings.title: guardrail.gate and guardrail.check run `git diff --cached --numstat`, `git status` and file reads of up to 64 MiB inside the store transaction, though D149 says a timeout is not enough
findings.evidence: The comment 'Both git probes here run with the store lock held, so they get a deadline (D144)' (1119-1120) cites the rule that D149 superseded ('Slow work runs outside the transaction, not merely with a timeout'). Gate and Check are registered with `engine.register` (handlers/guardrail.rs:304, 151). So `evaluate_commit` forks `git diff --cached --numstat` (760) and `recoverable` forks `git status --ignored=matching --untracked-files=all` (671-679) with the global mutex held, and `evaluate_write` reads and hashes files of up to 64 MiB in the same state (562-575). The pre-commit hook calls guardrail.gate {kind:"commit"} on every commit from every session.
findings.impact: A commit with a large staged change or many renames (rename detection is on by default) stalls every other bus request, including other agents' gates and UI queries, for up to 10 s per commit. A Write to a large generated file does the same.
findings.fix: Register guardrail.gate with register_staged: run the numstat, the git status and the file read in `prepare`, and do the evaluation, hold insert and grant consumption in `finish`. Register guardrail.check and guardrail.explain with register_unlocked. Pass the precomputed facts into evaluate, and update the comment.

v1.reason: handlers/guardrail.rs registers Check (line 151), Explain (177) and Gate (304) with plain `engine.register`, so they run inside the transaction with the store mutex held. Under that lock: evaluate_commit runs `git diff --cached --numstat` through git_output (~760), recoverable runs `git status --porcelain --ignored=matching --untracked-files=all` (~671-679), and evaluate_write does a std::fs::read_to_string of files up to 64 MiB (~562-575). write_roots also calls gix::open on every absolute write target. The comment at ~1119 cites D144 (deadline only), but D149 (DECISIONS.md:797) says slow work must run outside the transaction, not merely with a timeout, and supplies register_staged and register_unlocked for this. The timeout bounds a stall at 10 s per probe but does not release the lock.
v1.correction: Medium is right. In normal use these probes take tens of milliseconds, so this is lock contention that grows with repo size and large files, not a frequent freeze. The fix (register_staged for gate, register_unlocked for check and explain, precompute the git and file facts) is appropriate. Include write_roots' gix::open in the prepare phase too.

findings.title: Grants of closed sessions stay active forever and fill the UI's 'Active exceptions' list
findings.evidence: `active()` checks only scope, revoked_at and uses (265-271), and `exception()` adds only `hold.state == Confirmed` (277). `session.close` expires holds only `WHERE session_id = ?2 AND state = 'open'` (session.rs:1612-1616), so a confirmed session grant or an unused once grant never ends. `guardrail.requests.list {state:"active"}` selects `state = 'confirmed'` newest-first with LIMIT 500 and filters `active` afterwards (handlers/guardrail.rs:357-371). The native page renders the result under 'ACTIVE EXCEPTIONS — Approved exceptions still in force' (guardrail_pages.rs:774-786).
findings.impact: Every session exception and every unused once grant ever approved is shown as still in force, and the list grows without bound. Once more than 500 confirmed requests exist, genuinely active grants older than the newest 500 disappear from the list.
findings.fix: On session close, stamp $.grant.ended_at (or revoked_at) on the session's confirmed requests and emit guardrail.request_resolved {state:"expired"}. Filter active grants in SQL, before the LIMIT.

v1.reason: session.close expires only `state = 'open'` holds (handlers/session.rs:1611-1615), and so does the discard path near 1533. Confirmed guardrail.request holds keep state 'confirmed'. Parsed::active (grants.rs:265-271) checks only scope, revoked_at and uses, never the session's state. A closed session cannot come back (restorable is a separate state; the closed name is freed by the partial unique index at store.rs:96), so these grants are dead. guardrail.requests.list with state=active selects confirmed rows `ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 500` and filters active afterwards (handlers/guardrail.rs:354-371). The native page lists the results under 'ACTIVE EXCEPTIONS: Approved exceptions still in force' (guardrail_pages.rs:774-786). So every session-scope grant, and every unused once grant, of every closed session shows as in force forever. Past 500 confirmed rows, older live grants drop out of the list.
v1.correction: No security impact: Grants::load works by session_id, so a closed session's grants never apply to anything. The harm is a misleading, ever-growing UI list, plus the LIMIT-before-filter truncation. Fix: stamp an end on confirmed requests at session close, or filter joined against sessions.state != 'closed' in SQL before the LIMIT.

findings.title: Holds and guardrail notifications are never pruned, each write hold stores the whole new file, and every list re-parses and re-hashes every frozen envelope
findings.evidence: `gate()` freezes the full GateIn, including new_text, into holds.envelope (handlers/guardrail.rs:545-560; guardrail.rs:1223-1240), and every refusal inserts a notification (1258-1272). Nothing deletes from holds; only audit has retention (recovery.rs:179-210). `hold_row` parses the whole envelope, then re-serializes and SHA-256-hashes its payload for every row read (1291-1294). dashboard.get reads all open holds inside the transaction (notify.rs:168), and guardrail.holds.list reads up to 1000.
findings.impact: Every hold on a large file adds its full text to the store permanently, and the confirm loop described in the gate-hold finding adds it again on every retry. The dashboard and guardrail page then spend milliseconds per MB per open hold under the global lock on every refresh.
findings.fix: Compute the payload hash once at insert and store it in details or in a new column (append a migration and bump SCHEMA_VERSION). Store a hash and size instead of the full new_text for gate holds. Prune resolved and expired holds and old guardrail notifications in recovery, alongside audit retention.

v1.reason: Nothing ever deletes from holds or notifications. The only DELETEs are the project-delete cascade (handlers/workspace.rs:367, notifications only) and audit retention (recovery.rs:196). insert_hold (guardrail.rs:1212-1255) stores the whole frozen Request. In gate() (handlers/guardrail.rs:545-560) that Request is the full Gate payload, including new_text. Every refusal adds a notification row (guardrail.rs:1258-1270, called from handlers/guardrail.rs:537), and agents are refused often. hold_row (guardrail.rs:1291-1294) parses each envelope and re-hashes its payload on every read. So the retention part holds.
v1.correction: The performance half is overstated. dashboard.get reads only `state='open'` holds (notify.rs:168). guardrail.holds.list defaults to open_only=true (handlers/guardrail.rs:317), and the native page calls it with only project_id (pages.rs:45-53). session.close expires a session's open holds. So per-read hashing runs over a small, bounded set. The ongoing cost is unbounded table growth: one notification row per refusal, and a full new_text copy per destructive_write, shape_gate or user-bypass hold. Fix: prune resolved or expired holds, and read or old guardrail notifications, in recovery next to audit retention. Hashing at insert is optional.

findings.title: Shell and Codex writes never meet the protected-path or destructive-write checks, and the documented post-hoc guardrail.violation watcher does not exist
findings.evidence: `evaluate_exec` checks only self-approval and denied_commands (811-847), so a Bash `printf .. > .env`, `sed -i`, `cp`, `tee` or Python one-liner is never evaluated as a write. The Codex hook sends apply_patch, Edit and Write as kind:"exec" with the tool's `command` (relay-cli main.rs:507-512), yet `Codex::guarded()` returns true (providers.rs:212, profile at 241). BUS.md §9.3 says Codex is guarded:false and that its writes 'are detected post-hoc by the notify watcher ... raises a guardrail.violation notification' (BUS.md:524-533). Nothing in the code emits guardrail.violation: rg finds only the BUS.md text and the file.restore_head op description.
findings.impact: A protected file, or a git-ignored one where the commit-time check never fires either, can be rewritten freely through any shell command or any Codex edit. The UI labels Codex sessions guarded, and the user is promised a violation notification that never arrives.
findings.fix: Either extend evaluate_exec to judge the writes it can see (redirection targets `>`/`>>`, tee, `sed -i`, cp/mv destinations, and the `*** Update File:`/`*** Add File:` headers of apply_patch) through evaluate_write, or implement the documented watcher. Correct Codex's `guarded` flag and BUS.md §9.3 to state what is actually enforced.

v1.reason: The code matches the finding. evaluate_exec (guardrail.rs:811-847) checks only self-approval and denied_commands. codex_pre_tool (relay-cli main.rs:507-512) sends Bash, apply_patch, Edit and Write as kind "exec", and Codex::guarded() returns true (providers.rs:212, 241). Nothing emits guardrail.violation: the only reference outside the docs is the description of file.restore_head (relay-bus ops/file.rs:33). However, the gap between shell or Codex writes and protected-path checks is an intended decision. D132 (DECISIONS.md:650-655) says Codex hooks now feed guardrail.gate and 'the Git pre-commit gate remains the final write-set enforcement boundary'. So guarded:true is consistent with D132, and the post-hoc watcher was replaced, not forgotten. What is wrong is the documentation: BUS.md §9.3 (524-533) still says Codex is guarded:false and promises a guardrail.violation notification. DECISIONS.md:21 and :502 say the same, and file.restore_head describes itself as the answer to a violation that is never raised.
v1.correction: Reclassify the finding as stale docs, not a missing enforcement. Update BUS.md §9.3, DECISIONS.md:21 and :502, BUS.md:852 and the file.restore_head description in relay-bus ops/file.rs:33 so they describe D132 as built. Also document the remaining gap: write-time checks (destructive_write holds, and protected paths that are git-ignored, which the commit gate never sees) do not apply to shell or Codex writes. Extending evaluate_exec to parse redirections and apply_patch headers is an optional hardening, not a fix for a broken promise.

findings.title: Heredoc bodies, `#` comments and plain arguments are matched as commands, so harmless data is refused
findings.evidence:
A newline always ends a command (`';' | '
' | '|' | '&'`, 939-945) with no heredoc awareness, `#` is an ordinary character (946-951), and the pattern window may sit anywhere in argv (988). Port: `cat > NOTES.md <<'EOF'
Never use git push --force on main.
EOF`, `git commit -F - <<'EOF'
Document why rm -rf is denied
EOF` and `echo hi # rm -rf build` are all refused. The live hook in this session also refused a heredoc that only wrote test strings to a scratch file.
findings.impact: Writing docs, commit messages or scripts that mention a denied command is refused, and the hint invites the agent to ask the user for an exception for harmless data. That is the D103 failure mode the parser was built to prevent.
findings.fix: Skip heredoc bodies up to the delimiter line, honouring `<<-` and quoted delimiters. Treat an unquoted word starting with `#` as a comment to end of line. Anchor patterns at the command word (after wrappers) rather than anywhere in argv.

v1.reason: shell_commands (guardrail.rs ~939-951) splits commands on every newline, has no heredoc handling, and treats `#` as an ordinary character. denied_matches (~988) matches a pattern window anywhere in the unquoted words. The defaults (handlers/settings.rs:33) include "git push --force" and "rm -rf". So the heredoc line `Never use git push --force on main.` becomes its own command whose bare words contain git/push/--force, and `echo hi # rm -rf build` matches "rm -rf". Both are refused as denied commands, which is the false-positive class D103 set out to remove.
v1.correction: Two cautions on the fix. First, heredoc bodies must not simply be skipped. When the heredoc feeds an interpreter (`bash <<EOF`, `sh -s <<EOF`, `python - <<EOF`, `ssh host <<EOF`), the body is code, and skipping it would open a real bypass of denied_commands. Skip a body only when the receiving command is a known non-executing sink (cat/tee to a file, `git commit -F -`), or parse the body as commands when it feeds a shell. Second, anchoring patterns to the command word would weaken matching through wrappers such as `sudo rm -rf`, `xargs rm -rf` and `find -exec rm -rf`, which is why D103 matches anywhere in the unquoted words. Keep the any-position match, or strip known wrappers first. Handling a `#` that starts a word as a comment is safe.

findings.title: When a session holds any grant, every gate that is not allowed is evaluated twice from scratch, and each config read builds and clones every layer
findings.evidence: `evaluate_granted` re-runs `evaluate` with grants (494), which rebuilds the config and repeats `git diff --cached --numstat`, the file read and hash, and possibly `git status`. `config_for` builds every stage and raw copy through `layers()`, cloning the tree for each stage (147-153, 160), only to keep the last one (73). `authorize` (358) and each `evaluate` (467) call it, so a single agent gate builds the config 2-3 times under the lock.
findings.impact: Subprocess and I/O cost doubles on exactly the path that is already slow (refusals and holds), and every agent mutation repeats JSON tree cloning, all inside the global lock.
findings.fix: Evaluate once, returning the violations together with the facts measured (numstat, removed counts, matched patterns), then apply grants to that list. Give config() a merge path that skips the per-stage and raw bookkeeping, or cache the effective config per project, keyed on a settings generation counter.

v1.reason: The second evaluate runs only when the first is not Allow, the actor is an agent and the session holds at least one grant (guardrail.rs evaluate_granted). Grants are exceptions a person approves explicitly, so this is a rare path, and the extra git call it adds goes through output_with_timeout. The repeated config build is one cached-statement scan of the `guardrails.%` settings rows plus a handful of clones of a small JSON object, which costs microseconds next to the transaction itself. The proposed fix is effort M: it threads measured facts through every evaluator, or adds a config cache with invalidation. That is more complex than the cost it removes, so it is not worth changing.
v1.correction: If anything here matters, it is that `guardrail.gate` and `enforce` run git subprocesses (numstat, `git status` in recoverable) inside handlers registered with Engine::register under the store mutex. That is a separate root cause, not the double evaluation.

findings.title: guardrail.explain reads every listed file in full for a measurement it then discards
findings.evidence: Explain evaluates each path with `new_text: None, diff: Some("")` (207-210). That reaches `destructive_decision(.., removed=0, .., file_lines(..))` (guardrail.rs:536-541), and `file_lines` reads up to 64 MiB (695-702), but with removed = 0 neither threshold can fire.
findings.impact: A plan that lists large files reads all of them under the store lock for no result.
findings.fix: Add a path-only evaluation mode that skips the destructive-write measurement; explain cannot judge volume without text anyway.

v1.reason: The Explain handler is registered with engine.register (handlers/guardrail.rs:177), so it runs under the store lock. It evaluates each path with `new_text: None, diff: Some("")` (around lines 199-211). In evaluate_write, unless a shape gate holds first, the diff branch calls `destructive_decision(cfg, request, &path, removed, added, file_lines(request.worktree, &path))` (guardrail.rs:536-541). file_lines is evaluated eagerly and reads the whole file up to 64 MiB (guardrail.rs:697-704). diff_counts("") gives removed=0. In destructive_decision (guardrail.rs:719-722), over_lines (`0 > min_removed_lines`) and over_pct (0%) are false for any sane config, so the measurement is discarded.
v1.correction: The impact is small: explain is an occasional planning call, and most source files are small. The wasted read only matters for large listed files. Simplest fix: skip file_lines when removed == 0, for example by computing old_lines lazily inside destructive_decision only when the percentage check is needed. This avoids adding a separate evaluation mode.

findings.title: Agents can list holds and exception requests from every project, although D106 says they see nothing outside their own
findings.evidence: guardrail.holds.list and guardrail.requests.list build `SELECT * FROM holds WHERE 1=1` and `... WHERE op = 'guardrail.request'` with optional filters only (306-331, 343-373). `authorize` scopes only an explicit `session` field (guardrail.rs:328-339), and guardrail.request.get returns any id (342).
findings.impact: An agent sees other projects' session names, protected paths, refused commands and exception reasons.
findings.fix: When ctx.actor_session_id() is set, force project_id to the session's project in both lists, and check it in request.get.

v1.reason: `guardrail.holds.list` and `guardrail.requests.list` are `OpMeta::query(Scope::Global, ..)` with the default `Actors::All` (relay-bus ops/guardrail.rs:21, 126), and agents can call them (they appear in an agent session's MCP tool list). The handlers build `SELECT * FROM holds WHERE 1=1` / `WHERE op = 'guardrail.request'` with only the caller's optional filters (handlers/guardrail.rs:305-331, 342-373). `authorize` (guardrail.rs:328-339) scopes only an explicit `session` field. `guardrail.request.get` returns any id (handlers/guardrail.rs:341). An agent that omits `project_id`/`session` therefore receives every project's holds: session names, policy, and details with paths, commands and reasons. That contradicts D106 ('nothing outside it'). `guardrail.hold.get` is UserOnly, so frozen envelopes are not exposed.
v1.correction: The impact is information disclosure to an agent running as the same local user. It is not a guardrail escape, and other Global queries (e.g. project.list) already expose cross-project metadata, so the severity stays low. Fix as proposed: when `ctx.actor_session_id()` is set, force `project_id` to the session's project in both lists, and check it in `request.get`.

findings.title: Layer-3 authorization is written twice (authorize and callability), and the guardrail config handler duplicates settings::delete_under
findings.evidence: The bus_write predicate (`starts_with("file.") || matches!(.., "git.stage" | "git.unstage" | "git.commit")`) and the ui predicate, each with its message, appear in both authorize (363-383) and callability (422-436), and authorize re-inlines role_admits (359-360 vs 451-453). D104 exists precisely so that discovery and execution cannot disagree. `delete_settings_under` (handlers/guardrail.rs:30-34) copies settings::delete_under (settings.rs:193-201) and already differs from it (only one escapes `\`). ConfigSet also deletes a subtree and then calls settings::set, which deletes the same subtree again (74-76, 89-93).
findings.impact: Changing an escape hatch in one function silently puts bus.ops and the MCP tool list out of step with enforcement, and the two LIKE-escaping helpers will keep drifting apart.
findings.fix: Use one layer3(cfg, session, op) helper from both authorize and callability. Make settings::delete_under pub(crate) and drop the extra pre-delete.

v1.reason: crates/relay-core/src/guardrail.rs authorize (about 359-383) re-inlines role_admits (`allowed.iter().any(|pattern| op_matches(pattern, entry.name))`). It also repeats the bus_write predicate (`starts_with("file.") || matches!(.., "git.stage" | "git.unstage" | "git.commit")`), the ui predicate (`ui.`/`os.`) and their hint text, all of which callability has again at about 425-436. The doc comment on callability claims it is the single source (D104), so the two copies are maintained only by hand. They agree today. handlers/guardrail.rs:30-34 `delete_settings_under` is a near copy of settings.rs:193-201 `delete_under`, and only the first escapes `\`.
v1.correction: The LIKE-escape divergence is cosmetic. valid_path (settings.rs:58-66) allows only [A-Za-z0-9_-] segments, so a backslash never reaches either helper. The advice to drop the extra pre-delete is only partly right. In ConfigSet the pre-delete is redundant only when settings::set follows. When `merged` is empty (layer branch) or a key was cleared (`merged.get(&key)` is None, global branch), set is never called and the pre-delete is the only thing that removes the old rows. The fix is to make settings::delete_under pub(crate) and reuse it, keeping the delete for the clearing case. Factoring a shared layer-3 helper for authorize and callability is the worthwhile part.

findings.title: A hold created while confirming a gate hold emits no guardrail.held or notify.new, so the UI does not show it
findings.evidence: In confirm's Decision::Hold branch, `insert_hold` creates a new hold (626-644) that is returned only inside `outcome`. Unlike gate() (563-564) and enforce() (701-702), this path emits neither guardrail.held nor notify.new; the only event is guardrail.resolved for the old hold (656).
findings.impact: For example, a user bypasses a protected-path hold on a write that is also a large rewrite. The follow-up destructive_write hold exists, but every surface that follows guardrail.held stays stale until something else refreshes it.
findings.fix: Emit the same two events as gate(), carrying the new hold id.

v1.reason: In `confirm`'s `Decision::Hold` arm (handlers/guardrail.rs:622-644), `insert_hold` creates a new hold and a notifications row (guardrail.rs:1242-1253). No `guardrail.held` or `notify.new` is emitted. The only event is `guardrail.resolved` for the old hold. `gate()` (563-564) and `enforce()` (701-702) emit both. The path is reachable: a user's gate hold on a protected path is confirmed, protected_path is skipped, and destructive_write then holds again as user_bypass.
v1.correction: The real impact is smaller than claimed. The confirming client gets the new hold's `confirm` link inside `outcome`. The `guardrail.resolved` event still reaches the native client's event loop, which refreshes pages. What goes stale is the notification badge and centre (app.rs:1194-1199 refreshes only on `notify.*`), and no sound plays. Fix: emit `guardrail.held` and `notify.new` with `next_id`, as `gate()` does.

findings.title: BUS.md §9.4 says a confirmed hold is replayed as the confirmer, but the code replays it as the original agent
findings.evidence: BUS.md: 'with actor = the confirmer ... allowlist and own-task checks are the confirmer's' (BUS.md:541-545). The code calls `ctx.replay_registered(.., hold.actor.clone(), ..)` (583) and passes `actor: &hold.actor` with the comment 'Other policies still judge the original actor' (604-606).
findings.impact: Readers of the spec mispredict which policies a confirmed action still meets (agent refusals still apply after a user confirm), and the wording hides the session-binding defect in the first finding.
findings.fix: Update BUS.md §9.4 to describe the original-actor replay, and the session binding once that is fixed.

v1.reason: BUS.md §9.4 (around lines 541-545) says the held envelope is re-executed 'with actor = the confirmer, and on_behalf_of = the original actor', and that allowlist and own-task checks are the confirmer's. The code replays with `hold.actor` (handlers/guardrail.rs:583). The gate re-evaluation passes `actor: &hold.actor` with the comment 'Other policies still judge the original actor' (line 604). The audit is written via `ctx.audit_as(frozen.op, hold.actor.clone())`. The spec and the code disagree.
v1.correction: Related drift in BUS.md §9.3: it says the hook 'blocks the tool while the verdict is hold', but the CLI adapter exits 2 immediately (see #6). Update both places, and document the session binding once #1 is fixed.

findings.title: allowed_write_roots entries that are relative or start with `~` are silently ignored
findings.evidence: `.filter(|path| path.is_absolute())` (616) drops them, and validate_config (292-312) never inspects allowed_write_roots.
findings.impact: A user who sets allowed_write_roots: ["~/scratch"] gets no error, and every agent write there is still refused as write_root.
findings.fix: Validate in validate_config: reject non-absolute entries, or expand a leading `~`.

v1.reason: guardrail.rs:616 `roots.extend(cfg.allowed_write_roots.iter().map(PathBuf::from).filter(|path| path.is_absolute()))` drops relative and `~/` entries without a word, and validate_config never looks at allowed_write_roots. The schema (BUS.md:1042) and the native settings hint both say "absolute", so the intent is documented. Nothing rejects a bad entry, though, and settings.set on `guardrails.allowed_write_roots` bypasses ConfigSet entirely. The impact is mitigated: the write_root refusal lists the effective roots, so a user can see that their entry is missing.
v1.correction: Reject non-absolute entries in validate_config, which runs through typed() on every config read and so also catches a raw settings.set. Alternatively, expand a leading `~`.

findings.title: diff_counts skips removed lines that start with `--` and added lines that start with `++`
findings.evidence: `if line.starts_with("---") || line.starts_with("+++") { continue; }` (1084-1086) applies to every line, not just the file headers, and a removed `-- comment` line appears as `--- comment` in a unified diff.
findings.impact: On the diff path (guardrail.gate or guardrail.check with `diff`), removing SQL/Lua/Haskell comment blocks or YAML `---` separators is undercounted, so the destructive-write rule can stay silent.
findings.fix: Skip `---`/`+++` only in the header lines before the first `@@` of each file section.

v1.reason: diff_counts (guardrail.rs ~1080-1094) runs `if line.starts_with("---") || line.starts_with("+++") { continue; }` on every line, not only the file headers. In unified diff format, a removed line whose content begins with `--` (an SQL or Lua comment, a YAML `---` separator, a markdown rule) appears as `---…`, and an added line beginning `++` appears as `+++…`. Both are skipped. The diff is only used on the diff-only write path in evaluate_write (~536-541), so removing such lines is undercounted toward the destructive_write threshold.
v1.correction: The impact is narrow. It only matters when a large share of the removed lines start with `--`, and only on the diff-only path. The fix is right: skip `---` and `+++` only in a file's header lines, before its first `@@` hunk.

findings.title: worktree.remove recursively deletes whatever directory it is given, not just a worktree of the project
findings.evidence: Handler (handlers/git.rs:129-144) takes p.path verbatim: `std::fs::canonicalize(&p.path)...unwrap_or(p.path.clone())` (a relative path resolves against the engine's cwd). It checks only that no live session row has exactly that worktree, then calls `worktree::remove(repo, Path::new(&want), p.purge_build.unwrap_or(true))`. `remove` refuses only `repo_c == path_c`. It then runs `purge_build(path)` (deletes target/, build/, .gradle, app/build, node_modules/.cache and dist under that path) and `git(repo, &["worktree","remove","--force",&path_c]).or_else(|e| { std::fs::remove_dir_all(path)... })`, so every git failure falls through to remove_dir_all. Verified with git 2.55 in a scratch repo: git exits 128 'is not a working tree' for a plain directory and for another repository's checkout, and 'cannot remove a locked working tree' for a locked worktree; all three would hit the rm -rf fallback. Every other caller has a guard this handler lacks: session close/discard (session.rs:1521, 1577) and project removal (workspace.rs:333) only remove paths that `starts_with(worktree::pool_dir(&repo))`, and branch_cleanup (branch_cleanup.rs:295-299) refuses a checkout with uncommitted changes. The op is UserOnly, but three routes reach it: `relay mcp` started without RELAY_SESSION acts as the user and advertises every user op including this one (relay-cli main.rs:118-129, mcp.rs:76-104); the CLI sends it as-is; and the phone door forwards any op as `user` (relay-remote wire.rs:95-104).
findings.impact: A wrong path deletes that whole directory tree. Sources of a wrong path include an LLM client of the user-level MCP server hallucinating one, a CLI typo, a project_id/path mismatch, or a paired (or stolen-token) phone. What gets deleted can be another project's entire repository including .git, a home subdirectory, or a worktree the user locked to protect it. Even for a real worktree, `--force` plus the fallback throws away uncommitted work with no dirty check.
findings.fix: Canonicalize the path, then require an exact match with a linked (non-primary) entry of `worktree::list_with_dirty(repo,false)`. If only pooled worktrees should be removable, also require `starts_with(pool_dir)` on the canonical path. Refuse locked and dirty worktrees unless an explicit force flag is passed. Remove the generic remove_dir_all fallback: use it only for a registered worktree whose directory git reports missing or corrupt, then `git worktree prune`. Run the op staged (see the locked-mutations finding).

v1.reason: Confirmed by reading the code. In crates/relay-core/src/handlers/git.rs:129-144 the WorktreeRemove handler canonicalizes p.path and falls back to the raw string if that fails. Its only check is that no live session row has that exact worktree, and then it calls worktree::remove. worktree::remove (crates/relay-core/src/worktree.rs:351-367) refuses only when repo_c == path_c. When the path exists, it first runs purge_build(path) when purge is set, which is the default because purge_build.unwrap_or(true). Then it runs `git worktree remove --force <path>`, and on any git error it falls back to `std::fs::remove_dir_all(path)`. Nothing checks that the path is a registered linked worktree of this project, or that it sits under pool_dir. I checked git's behaviour in the scratchpad: `git worktree remove --force` on a plain directory exits 128 with "is not a working tree". On a locked worktree it exits 128 with "cannot remove a locked working tree" (a single -f is not enough). Both cases go to the rm -rf fallback. The op is Actors::UserOnly (crates/relay-bus/src/ops/git.rs:15-16), so agents cannot reach it. A user-actor caller can: the CLI defaults to Actor::User (relay-cli main.rs actor_from_env), `relay mcp` without RELAY_SESSION advertises it because exposed() only filters out streams and TauriOnly ops, and the phone door forwards actor `user` unchanged (relay-remote wire.rs gate). The native client never calls this op. The other remove paths have guards that this one lacks (session close/discard and workspace removal check starts_with(pool_dir)).
v1.correction: Severity: high, not critical. The trigger needs a wrong path from an actor the user has authorised: a CLI typo, an LLM driving the user-level MCP server, or a paired phone. No agent and no unauthenticated peer can reach it, and the desktop UI does not use the op. When it does trigger, though, the damage is an irreversible rm -rf of an arbitrary directory, such as another repo including its .git, or a locked worktree. An extra point the finding missed: purge_build runs before git is consulted. So even when the later steps fail (rm -rf permission error), every target/, build/, .gradle, app/build, dist and node_modules/.cache directly under the given directory is already deleted, and in some projects build/ or dist/ are source folders. A relative path resolves against the engine's cwd. Related invariant breaches in the same handler: it is registered with Engine::register, so dir_size, purge_build, the git subprocess and the rm -rf all run under the store mutex inside the transaction. The git call also goes through worktree::git (plain Command::output), not proc::output_with_timeout. Fix as proposed: require the canonical path to match a non-primary entry of worktree::list_with_dirty(repo,false) (and starts_with(pool_dir) if only pooled worktrees should be removable). Move purge_build after that validation. Keep the remove_dir_all fallback only for a registered worktree that git reports as missing or corrupt. Refuse locked or dirty worktrees unless explicitly forced. Register the op staged.

v2.reason:
(a) The code does what the finding says. handlers/git.rs:129-144 registers WorktreeRemove with Engine::register. It canonicalizes p.path and falls back to the raw string if that fails. Its only refusal is when a non-closed session of this project_id has exactly that path. It then calls worktree::remove. worktree.rs:352-369 refuses only when canon(repo)==canon(path). If the path exists, it runs purge_build (on by default), then dir_size, then `git -C repo worktree remove --force`, and on any git error it runs remove_dir_all(path) (line 365). I tested git 2.55 in a scratch repo. It exits 128 with "is not a working tree" for a plain directory, another repo, a subdirectory of a worktree, the primary's .git, the .relay pool parent and an ancestor directory. For a locked worktree it says "cannot remove a locked working tree". Every one of those cases falls through to the rm -rf. All other callers of remove pass paths the engine produced itself: session.rs:1521/1577 and workspace.rs:333 also require starts_with(pool_dir), integration uses its own row, and branch_cleanup checks status first. session.create's custom-worktree branch (session.rs:878-886) already does the exact-match validation against list_with_dirty that this handler lacks.

(b) Reachability. The op is Actors::UserOnly (relay-bus ops/git.rs:15-16), so an agent is refused before policy. No first-party client sends it: neither apps/relay-native nor the phone app contains "worktree.remove". It can be reached through `relay cmd worktree.remove`, since the CLI defaults to Actor::User (relay-cli main.rs:118). It can also be reached through a user-level `relay mcp` started without RELAY_SESSION, because exposed() (mcp.rs:159) drops only streams, TauriOnly ops and subscribe. The user has to set that server up; Relay's own per-launch MCP config inherits RELAY_SESSION, so agents never see the op. Finally, a paired phone or anyone holding its token can send it, because the wire gate checks only the actor, but that holder already has full user rights. The socket is 0600 inside a 0700 directory, so no other uid can connect. An agent claiming `user` on the socket is a separately documented design (BUS.md §4.2 and §9.5), not this root cause. How often: rarely. It needs a wrong path from the user or from an LLM driving the user-level MCP.

(c) What happens when it fires: an irreversible rm -rf, with no trash step (unlike file.delete). Concrete cases:
- path=<repo>/.relay/worktrees passes the exact-match owner check and deletes every live session's checkout, including uncommitted work, while the agents are still running in them.
- path=<repo>/.git passes the "never the primary" check and deletes the project's whole history.
- A project_id/path mismatch skips the owner check, because that check is scoped to the given project_id.
- A relative path resolves against the engine's cwd, and `relay serve` changes directory to $HOME (relay-cli main.rs:208). So "path":"." purges ~/.gradle, ~/build, ~/dist and ~/target, walks all of $HOME under the store mutex (freezing the bus), and then runs remove_dir_all($HOME).
- purge_build runs before git is consulted, so its deletions happen even when the rm -rf later fails partway.

(d) Severity: high is right. The trigger needs a mistake by an actor the user has authorised, through routes that are not the UI. No agent and no unauthenticated peer can reach it. But the loss is irreversible, and the existing safety checks (owner, never-primary) are silently bypassed, which the rubric places at high. It is not medium.

(e) The fix direction is correct, with the corrections below.
v2.correction:
Severity: high, not critical (agrees with the first verifier).

Corrections to the fix:
1. Validate before purge_build. Reject a non-absolute path. Require canonicalize to succeed whenever the path exists. Then require exact equality with a non-primary entry of list_with_dirty(repo,false). A starts_with(pool_dir) check alone is not enough. Path::starts_with is true for pool_dir itself, so `<repo>/.relay/worktrees` would pass and wipe every checkout. On a non-canonical path it also compares `..` components literally.
2. Do not simply delete the remove_dir_all fallback inside worktree::remove. Engine callers (session close and discard, project removal, integration, branch cleanup) rely on it for half-deleted pooled worktrees. The admin entry of such a worktree may already be pruned, so list_with_dirty will not list it. Keep the fallback for registered worktrees and for canonical paths strictly inside pool_dir (not equal to it), and refuse anything else there. That also gives every caller defense in depth.
3. "Refuse dirty unless forced" is a design change, not part of this defect. tests/sessions.rs:221-233 deliberately makes a worktree dirty and expects worktree.remove to succeed, and session.close also removes without a dirty check. Adding the refusal would break that test and needs a schema change. Refusing locked worktrees is reasonable, since Relay never locks worktrees itself.
4. Two more triggers worth stating:
   - "path":"." resolves to $HOME, because relay serve changes directory there (relay-cli main.rs:208).
   - The owner check is scoped to the given project_id, so passing another project's id skips it.
5. The handler being registered with Engine::register rather than staged, and worktree::git using a plain Command::output rather than proc::output_with_timeout, are separate invariant findings.

findings.title: git.diff / git.diff.file follow symlinks out of the worktree and read without bound; a symlink to /dev/zero OOMs the engine
findings.evidence: working_text is `validate_path(path)?; match std::fs::read(root.join(path))`. validate_path only rejects `..` and absolute paths. fs::read follows symlinks and reads to EOF with no cap. file.rs guards this case for file.read with safe_join (file.rs:489-505: canonicalize, then refuse 'path escapes the worktree through a symlink'); git.rs has no equivalent. `git status --porcelain=v1 -z --untracked-files=all` lists untracked symlinks (verified: links to /etc/hostname and /dev/zero appear as `?? host`, `?? zero`). The Diff handler reads every listed path (211), and DiffFileOp reads the requested path (239) and returns its full text in `new`. Who can trigger it: both ops are queries any agent may call (MCP git_diff, git_diff_file); the desktop calls git.diff.file when a changed file is clicked (code_git.rs:1338); and the phone door can call them.
findings.impact: An agent, or a checked-in fixture, creates `ln -s /dev/zero z` in a worktree. The next git.diff, or a click on `z` in the git panel, makes the engine read /dev/zero until allocation fails, which kills the engine and every session. A symlink to ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 or a credentials file returns its contents through git.diff.file, where file.read would refuse. Because the engine is not sandboxed, this works even when the agent's own sandbox denies that read. Ordinary symlinks also diff wrongly: git stores a link as its target path, so a tracked symlink always shows as modified against the target file's contents.
findings.fix: Use symlink_metadata. For a symlink, return read_link as text (this is what git compares). For anything that is not a regular file, return empty. Cap the read (e.g. 8 MiB; mark larger files binary), and reuse file.rs's canonicalize-and-contain check for regular files.

v1.reason: working_text (git.rs:842-849) is validate_path, then std::fs::read(root.join(path)). validate_path (780-800) rejects only absolute and `..` paths. fs::read follows symlinks and reads to EOF without a cap, and nothing like file.rs safe_join (488-505, canonicalize and refuse escapes) is applied. I reproduced that `git status --porcelain=v1 --untracked-files=all` lists an untracked `ln -s /dev/zero z` as `?? z`. DiffFileOp (git.rs:235-254) accepts any validated path, not just changed ones, so a tracked symlink works too, and it returns the full `new` text. git.diff reads every status path (211). Both ops are unlocked queries that agents reach as the MCP tools git_diff and git_diff_file. The desktop calls git.diff.file on click (code_git.rs:1338). A read of /dev/zero grows the Vec until allocation fails or the OOM killer acts, and either way the engine and every session die. A symlink to a file outside the worktree returns that file's contents through the engine, which file.read deliberately refuses.
v1.correction: The rating stays high rather than critical. The crash needs an agent (misbehaving or prompt-injected) or a checked-out fixture to plant a symlink to a device. Secret disclosure matters only where the agent's own shell reads are otherwise restricted, though the engine is unsandboxed and file.read shows containment is meant to be a boundary. Fix: use symlink_metadata. For a symlink, return read_link as text (git's view). For non-regular files, return empty. Cap regular-file reads (e.g. 8 MiB, flagged binary/truncated). Apply the same treatment to the directory/EISDIR case noted in core-git#6.

v2.reason:
(a) The code does what the finding says. working_text (git.rs:842-849) runs validate_path (780-800), which rejects only empty, absolute, root/prefix and `..` paths, then calls std::fs::read(root.join(path)). That read follows the final symlink and any intermediate one, checks no file type and has no size cap. Diff calls it for every git status path unless staged=true (203-212). DiffFileOp calls it for any validated path, changed or not, and returns the full text in `new` (235-254). file.read, by contrast, uses safe_join (file.rs:489-506: canonicalize, then starts_with(root)) and a 4 MiB default / 32 MiB maximum cap via take(limit+1) (file.rs:44-55).
I checked this in a scratch repo. `git status --porcelain=v1 -z --untracked-files=all` lists untracked links to /dev/zero, to /etc/hostname and to a FIFO as `??`, and a retargeted tracked link as ` M`. HEAD:tracked_link holds the link path ("real.txt"), so a changed link is diffed as its link path against the target's contents.

(b) Who can reach it, and how often:
- Agents of any role, via MCP git_diff / git_diff_file. Queries clear layers 2 and 3 (guardrail.rs:350-352, 409-411).
- The desktop, but only through git.diff.file when a git.status row is clicked (code_git.rs:896-898, 1338). It never calls git.diff.
- The phone, whose door forwards any op as `user` (relay-remote wire.rs:95-102).
- Nothing in the engine calls working_text on its own.

The crash or hang needs a symlink to an endless or blocking file (/dev/zero, /dev/urandom, a FIFO) in a dirty worktree. That does not happen in normal use; someone has to plant it. In practice that is an agent: `ln` is not gated (the default denied_commands are rm -rf, git reset --hard, git clean -fd and git push --force), and GateKind is only Write, Commit or Exec, so reads are never gated.

The documented trust model is "same uid, same trust":
- BUS.md §4.2: the `user` actor needs no token.
- BUS.md §14: tokens prevent misattribution, not determined impersonation.
- BUS.md §9.5 and guardrail.rs:849-851: the guardrail is not a security boundary.

An agent that can run `ln -s` can just as well pkill the engine or cat ~/.ssh/*. The phone already has full user power, session.input included. So neither the crash nor the read outside the worktree gives an agent, the phone or a network peer anything new. No guardrail covers reads, so none is escaped.

The realistic accidental triggers are milder:
- A changed or untracked link inside the repo, such as AGENTS.md -> CLAUDE.md, gets the wrong diff text and wrong counts.
- A large untracked or modified file, linked or not (model weights, .blend files, dumps), is read whole on every call and copied again (from_utf8_lossy, then to_string). Only a multi-GB file risks OOM.

(c) What happens when it fires. With /dev/zero, the buffer grows without bound. This machine has overcommit mode 0, 32 GB RAM plus 32 GB swap, and systemd-oomd active, and relay-remote.service sets no MemoryMax. RAM and swap run out before any allocation is refused. The OOM killer or oomd then kills the engine, the PTY masters close, and every session is hung up. A link to a FIFO instead blocks one blocking-pool thread forever: that request hangs, but the bus keeps working because the handler is unlocked.

(d) The high rating does not hold. The catastrophic outcome needs a special-file symlink planted on purpose, by a party the documented model already trusts with equal or greater power. In normal use, the consequences are wrong diffs for symlinks and memory spikes on big files. That is a real bug in an uncommon path: medium. The category is bug, not security, because no trust boundary is crossed.

(e) The proposed fix is correct in substance. The correction field gives the details and the places it does not reach.
v2.correction:
Severity medium, category bug (robustness and correctness). Under BUS.md §4.2, §9.5 and §14, neither the read outside the worktree nor an agent-triggered crash crosses a trust boundary.

Two claims are imprecise:
1. "reads /dev/zero until allocation fails, which kills the engine": the engine dies from the kernel OOM killer or systemd-oomd once RAM and swap are full; with default heuristic overcommit, no allocation is refused first. In current std, read_to_end grows its buffer with try_reserve, so a refused allocation would return an io error and the engine would survive.
2. "a tracked symlink always shows as modified" is true only for git.diff.file. git.diff lists a link only when git reports it changed, and then counts it against the target's contents.

Fix:
- Call symlink_metadata first.
- For a symlink, return the read_link bytes; that is git's blob for mode 120000.
- For a FIFO, device, socket or directory, return empty. This also removes the FIFO hang and the EISDIR failure in core-git#6.
- Read regular files with File::open(..).take(cap+1), as file.read does, and mark a truncated file as binary.
- For git.diff.file, still canonicalize and check containment, because symlink_metadata sees only the last path component (e.g. `linkdir/id_ed25519` where linkdir -> ~/.ssh).

The same special-file read exists in two more places, which should use the same helper:
- overlap.rs:246: `std::fs::read(worktree.join(path)).unwrap_or_default()` reads the whole file before the 2 MiB check in symbols(). It is reached by overlap.scan and overlap.flag for changed .rs/.ts/.tsx/.svelte/.kt files.
