Fix the race by gating a snapshot: `git write-tree` in prepare, then commit-tree plus update-ref compare-and-swap in finish, or recompute the numstat in finish and refuse if it changed.

findings.title: git.log walks breadth-first, so a parent can come before its child and the history graph grows phantom lanes
findings.evidence: `repo.rev_walk([tip.detach()]).all()` uses gix's default Sorting::BreadthFirst: a FIFO queue with a seen-set (gix-traverse 0.60 simple.rs:44, 597-602, 669-670). That is neither date order (like git log) nor topological order. Example: M merges A (main, parent X) and F2<-F1 (feature, parent X). The walk yields M, A, F2, X, F1, so X comes before its child F1. The desktop graph (code_git.rs:1822-1897) reserves a lane for each parent 'until the corresponding commit arrives'. F1 reserves a lane for X after X has already been emitted, so that lane never closes. LogIn.graph is accepted but ignored.
findings.impact: In any history where merged branches have different lengths, which is routine with agent branches, the history pane draws a lane that never ends, and commits appear in a different order from git log.
findings.fix: Use `.sorting(Sorting::ByCommitTime(CommitTimeOrder::NewestFirst))` for the list, and gix's topological walk when graph is requested.

v1.reason: crates/relay-core/src/handlers/git.rs:262-265: `repo.rev_walk([tip]).all()` without `.sorting(..)` uses gix's default `Sorting::BreadthFirst` (gix-0.86.0 revision/walk.rs `#[default] BreadthFirst`). gix-traverse 0.60 `next_by_topology` pops a FIFO VecDeque and pushes unseen parents (simple.rs:597-670). For M(A,F2), A->X, F2->F1->X, that yields M, A, F2, X, F1. I traced the native `commit_graph` (apps/relay-native/src/code_git.rs:1823-1897), which is used on git.log results at lines 580/793/2028: after X has been emitted, F1's first parent sets `active[1]=X`. X never arrives again, so lane 1 is drawn as a pass-through on every later row: a phantom lane that never closes. The list order also differs from `git log`. `LogIn.graph` (relay-bus ops/git.rs:29) is accepted and never read. Merges of agent branches with unequal lengths are routine. The damage is a cosmetic history pane, so medium fits.
v1.correction: Use `.sorting(Sorting::ByCommitTime(CommitTimeOrder::NewestFirst))` to match git log's default. Note that commit-time order alone still breaks under clock skew, so the graph view ideally needs a topological order (gix_traverse's topo walk) or a client-side topo sort before `commit_graph`.

findings.title: worktree::contains accepts any directory whose .git file names an existing slot, without checking that the slot points back
findings.evidence: contains reads <candidate>/.git and returns `canon(&gitdir).starts_with(&slots) && gitdir.join("gitdir").is_file()`. It never compares the slot's gitdir back-pointer with the candidate. The doc comment says this is 'exactly what git worktree list reads', but git actually lists a worktree from the slot's gitdir file. root_verify (file.rs:427-441) relies on contains to admit any `worktree` path a caller passes to file.* and git.* ops, agents included.
findings.impact: A `cp -r` copy of a worktree, or any directory given a forged .git pointer, is accepted as a checkout of the project. Git ops there run against the original worktree's index and HEAD: a commit from the copy moves the original's branch and leaves its index describing the copy's files.
findings.fix: Also require that the slot's gitdir file names this checkout: `canon(Path::new(read_to_string(gitdir/"gitdir").trim()).parent()) == want`.

v1.reason: worktree.rs:162-171 accepts any candidate whose `.git` file points into `<common>/worktrees/` at a slot that has a `gitdir` file. It never checks that the slot's `gitdir` back-pointer names this candidate. root_verify (file.rs:427-441) relies on this alone for file.* and git.* roots. A `cp -r` of a linked worktree therefore passes. git run in that copy uses the original's slot (index and HEAD), so a commit there moves the original branch and leaves the original's index describing the copy's files. The trigger is narrow, though. The UI only offers paths taken from `git worktree list`, and a caller has to type the copy's path deliberately. As a security issue it is weak: forging a root requires already being able to write a `.git` file into the target directory, which in practice means being able to write there anyway, and git.* and file.* already let any caller target any worktree of the project. So it is a correctness edge case, not a guardrail escape.
v1.correction: Re-categorise it as a bug, not security. One nuance for the fix: a worktree moved by hand with `mv` (without `git worktree move`) also fails the proposed back-pointer check, although git still works there. Report it as 'run git worktree repair' rather than as 'not a worktree'.

findings.title: purge_build follows symlinked parent directories, and deletes tracked build/ and dist/ before removal is known to succeed
findings.evidence: For each BUILD_DIRS entry: `let p = wt.join(d); if p.is_dir() { freed += dir_size(&p); let _ = std::fs::remove_dir_all(&p); }`. is_dir() follows symlinks, and for nested entries (node_modules/.cache, app/build) remove_dir_all resolves a symlinked parent component, so the deletion lands outside the worktree. build/ and dist/ are often tracked source. remove() purges them before `git worktree remove` runs (360-362).
findings.impact: If node_modules in a worktree is a symlink to a shared install (a common disk-saving setup with many worktrees), removing the worktree wipes the shared install's .cache, and freed reports the shared directory's size. A removal that then fails leaves the worktree missing its tracked build/ or dist/ content and any uncommitted changes in them.
findings.fix: Check every path component with symlink_metadata, or canonicalize and require the result to stay under the canonical worktree. Skip tracked directories. Purge only after git confirms the worktree can be removed.

v1.reason: purge_build (worktree.rs:339-349) does `wt.join(d).is_dir()`, which follows symlinks, then `remove_dir_all`. Rust's remove_dir_all does not follow a final-component symlink, so a symlinked `target` is only unlinked; its size is still counted through dir_size's root `is_dir` filter, so `freed` is misreported. For nested entries (`node_modules/.cache`, `app/build`), path resolution goes through a symlinked `node_modules` or `app`, so the real `.cache` inside a shared install is deleted. The confirmed damage is a rebuildable cache plus a wrong freed figure, which is low. The second claim, tracked build/ or dist/ purged before removal is known to succeed, does not hold up. remove() runs `git worktree remove --force` and on failure falls back to `remove_dir_all(path)` (worktree.rs:362-366), so the whole tree, uncommitted changes included, is deleted anyway. The early purge only matters if both of those fail.
v1.correction: Drop the tracked-build/dist part. There is a related and more serious problem in the same function. worktree.remove (git.rs:129-144) never checks that `p.path` is a worktree of the project: it only checks for an owning session, and remove() only refuses the primary. A non-worktree path makes `git worktree remove` fail, and the fallback then rm -rf's that path, after purge_build has already deleted its target/build/dist. The op is UserOnly and the desktop passes listed paths, so this needs a mistaken or crafted request. Even so, the fallback should only run for a path that `contains()` or the worktree list confirms. Separately, WorktreeRemove is registered with plain `Engine::register`, so its dir_size walk, git subprocess and rm -rf run with the store mutex held, which breaks the CLAUDE.md invariant.

findings.title: upstream_metrics resolves a branch by its short name, so a tag or top-level ref with the same name shadows it
findings.evidence: `repo.find_reference(branch)` with a short name probes refs/<name>, then refs/tags/<name>, before refs/heads/<name> (gix-ref 0.66 store/file/find.rs:110). Callers pass short branch names: Status (172), Branches (329), Push (610), briefing_state (1022-1023).
findings.impact: A branch named like an existing tag (e.g. v2), or a branch called stash (shadowed by refs/stash), shows no upstream and no ahead/behind. git.push then takes the `push -u origin <name>` path, which git refuses as an ambiguous refspec.
findings.fix: Look up refs/heads/{branch} explicitly.

v1.reason: `upstream_metrics` (git.rs:897-901) calls `repo.find_reference(branch)` with a short name. In gix-ref 0.66.0 (the locked version), store/file/find.rs probes the prefixes in the order "", "tags", "heads", "remotes". So refs/<name> and refs/tags/<name> win over refs/heads/<name>. Status (172), Branches, Push (610) and Fetch pass `head_name().shorten()` short names. A branch that shares a name with a tag (v2), or a branch named `stash`, resolves to the tag or refs/stash. It then has no remote-tracking ref, so the result is (None,None,None). Push then picks `push -u origin <name>`, which git rejects as an ambiguous refspec.
v1.correction: Look up `refs/heads/{branch}` explicitly, as `existing_worktree_branch` (963) already does. The trigger needs a tag/branch name collision, which is rare.

findings.title: git.branch.clean_merged stops at the first failed delete and does not report, audit or announce the branches it already deleted
findings.evidence: The loop `for branch in &candidates { git_mutate(.."branch","-d",branch).map_err(..)?; }` returns on the first failure. The transaction rolls back, changed() is never emitted, and the response carries only the error.
findings.impact: Branches 1..k-1 are already gone, but the caller is told the op failed. The audit trail has no record of those deletions, and the UI is not told to refresh.
findings.fix: Attempt every candidate and collect per-branch outcomes. Return them, as branch_cleanup does with its rows, and emit git.changed if anything was deleted.

v1.reason: git.rs:710-713 loops `worktree::git_mutate(.., ["branch","-d",branch]).map_err(..)?` and returns on the first failure, so changed() and the CleanMergedOut list of branches already deleted never happen. Git refs are outside the SQLite transaction, so the earlier deletions stay done while the caller sees only an error. The failure is reachable without a race. `merged` is computed against project.base_branch (branches_for, git.rs:1458-1461), but `git branch -d` checks against the branch's upstream, or HEAD when there is none. If the primary checkout is on a different branch, or a candidate's upstream is ahead, the delete fails partway through the list. The impact is small: deletions use -d, so nothing unmerged is lost; the engine audits the failed request as an error; and the op is only reachable through the bus or MCP, not the desktop.
v1.correction: Same fix as proposed: try every candidate, return deleted and failed lists, and emit changed() if anything was deleted. Alternatively use `git branch -D` only after the engine's own base-merged check, since that is the check the op is meant to apply.

findings.title: git.branch.create with checkout:false reports the checkout's HEAD instead of the new branch's tip
findings.evidence: After `git branch <name> [start]`, the handler returns `head: repo.head_id()..` of the worktree. git branch does not move HEAD, so this is the old checkout's commit.
findings.impact: A call with {name, start_point:"v1.0", checkout:false} returns the current HEAD's sha as the new branch's head.
findings.fix: Return the id of refs/heads/{name}.

v1.reason: After `git branch <name> [start]` (checkout:false), git.rs:376-377 reopens the repo and returns `repo.head_id()`. `git branch` does not move HEAD, so a call with start_point set to anything other than HEAD reports the checkout's commit as the new branch's head. The desktop client always sends checkout:true, so this affects only CLI and agent callers of the checkout:false variant.
v1.correction: Resolve `refs/heads/{name}` (repo.find_reference(full_name).peel_to_id) instead of head_id. Low severity: only the returned field is wrong, and only on the non-default path.

findings.title: list_with_owners is unused and keeps the pre-D144 'subprocess under a Transaction' shape
findings.evidence: rg finds no caller in the workspace, only the definition and a doc link at line 34. The function takes &Transaction and calls worktrees_owned_by -> worktree::list_with_dirty(repo, include_dirty). That is a git status per worktree, exactly the work D144 moved out of the lock.
findings.impact: It is a pub helper that invites the next caller to run per-worktree git status under the store mutex.
findings.fix: Delete it and the doc reference. worktree_owners plus worktrees_owned_by already cover the unlocked use.

v1.reason: rg over the workspace finds `list_with_owners` only at its definition (crates/relay-core/src/handlers/git.rs:72) and in the doc link at line 34. It takes `&Transaction` and calls `worktrees_owned_by` -> `worktree::list_with_dirty(repo, include_dirty)`, so any future caller inside an `Engine::register` handler would run per-worktree git work under the store mutex. That is the exact pattern the D144 comment at lines 51-52 warns against. The live path (WorktreeList, register_unlocked) already uses `worktree_owners` plus `worktrees_owned_by`. Because the function is `pub`, rustc's dead_code lint does not flag it.
v1.correction: Delete it and update the doc comment on `worktree_owners` (line 34), which calls it 'the store half of list_with_owners'.

findings.title: One commit with an out-of-range author date makes git.log and git.show fail
findings.evidence: `jiff::Timestamp::from_second(author.seconds()).map_err(|e| BusError::internal(..))?`. jiff can only represent years -9999 to 9999. git accepts larger values (fsck flags them as badDateOverflow, but such objects exist in imported histories).
findings.impact: Any log page or show that includes such a commit returns an internal error instead of the history.
findings.fix: When conversion fails, fall back to the raw seconds or an empty `at` instead of failing the op.

v1.reason: `commit_from_gix` (git.rs:883-885) does `jiff::Timestamp::from_second(author.seconds()).map_err(|e| BusError::internal(..))?`. jiff Timestamp only covers about years -9999 to 9999, so `from_second` returns Err for larger values. The `?` propagates out of Log's loop (256-272) and Show, so the whole page fails. A commit object with an author time past year 9999 is legal for git to store, though fsck warns about it. Such commits are rare in practice.
v1.correction: Fall back to an empty or raw-seconds `at` instead of failing the op. Severity stays low: the trigger needs a pathological commit.

findings.title: worktree.create checks branch existence three times and duplicates session.create's new-branch base sequence
findings.evidence: `if p.from.is_none() && !existing_worktree_branch(repo, Some(&p.branch))? { refresh_new_worktree(..)?; new_worktree_base(..)? }`. refresh_new_worktree calls existing_worktree_branch again (970), and worktree::create checks a third time with an untimed `git show-ref` (worktree.rs:204). session.rs:866-873 repeats the fetch -> exists -> base sequence with its own variations (no `from`).
findings.impact: Three lookups, one of them an unbounded subprocess, on every create. The two copies of the 'fresh base for a new branch' rule have to be kept in sync by hand.
findings.fix: One helper, e.g. `start_point_for_new_worktree(repo, branch, base, from) -> Result<Option<String>>`, used by both handlers. Pass its answer into create so create does not re-check.

v1.reason: crates/relay-core/src/handlers/git.rs:113 calls `existing_worktree_branch` and then `refresh_new_worktree` (lines 969-973), which calls `existing_worktree_branch` again. `worktree::create` (worktree.rs:204) then runs `git show-ref --verify` through the untimed `git()` helper (worktree.rs:26-27, plain `.output()`). session.rs:866-873 repeats the 'fetch if new -> check exists -> new_worktree_base' sequence in a different order and without `from`. The duplication and the triple check are real. The cost is small: two of the checks are in-process gix ref lookups, and show-ref is a fast local command that runs in the unlocked or staged read phase (WorktreeCreate is register_staged), so it does not block the bus.
v1.correction: The impact is mainly maintainability. The 'fresh base for a new branch' rule lives in two places with different orderings. The per-create cost is negligible: gix lookups plus one local show-ref, none of it under the store mutex. The untimed show-ref still technically breaks the 'every subprocess through proc::output_with_timeout' rule, but it is outside the lock. A shared helper that returns the start point, passed into `create` so it can skip its own show-ref, is a reasonable cleanup.

findings.title: worktree.disk walks every build directory twice
findings.evidence: `disk_mb: worktree::dir_size(path)` walks the whole checkout, including target/, build/, node_modules/.cache and the rest. `build_mb: Some(worktree::build_size(path))` then walks BUILD_DIRS again (155-156).
findings.impact: For worktrees with a multi-GB target/ (the SPEC §8 '73GB problem'), the dominant part of each worktree.disk call is done twice.
findings.fix: Do one walk that also attributes the bytes under BUILD_DIRS to build_mb.

v1.reason: crates/relay-core/src/handlers/git.rs:154-155: `disk_mb: worktree::dir_size(path)` walks the entire worktree, build directories included, and `build_mb: worktree::build_size(path)` walks the BUILD_DIRS roots again (worktree.rs:237-247, both via dir_size_all). The handler is register_unlocked, so this is latency for the caller only and never blocks the bus. No caller in apps/relay-native, relay-cli or relay-remote sends `worktree.disk`. It is reached through the generic MCP/bus surface and tests, which limits the real cost. On a second walk the dentry/inode cache is warm, so the extra cost is well under 2x.
v1.correction: Better framing: duplication plus perf. handlers/app.rs:233-258 (`dir_usage`) already does a single walk that attributes build bytes, so a one-pass implementation exists. Its definition of 'build' has drifted from BUILD_DIRS: it counts any nested `target`/`build`/`.gradle` anywhere and leaves out `node_modules/.cache` and `dist`. As a result, `app.resources` and `worktree.disk` report different build_mb for the same worktree. Fix: one shared single-pass, multi-threaded walker in worktree.rs that uses BUILD_DIRS, used by both.

findings.title: collect_skills follows a symlink in the cloned repo out of the clone, and reads SKILL.md fully before the size check
findings.evidence: safe_relative only checks that subdir components are Normal. `start = root.join(relative)`, `start.exists()` and `find_skill_files(&start, ..)` (is_file / read_dir) all follow a symlink at start itself; only entries inside are checked with file_type.is_symlink(). `fs::read_to_string(&path)` reads the whole file before the 256 KiB check (172-173).
findings.impact: A skill repo can commit `skills -> /home/<user>/.claude/skills`. Installing `../tree/main/skills` then imports SKILL.md files and their real folders (via copy_bounded) from the user's own disk under the remote source's name. The effect stays local, hence low.
findings.fix: Canonicalize start and require it to stay under the canonical clone root. Check metadata().len() before reading.

v1.reason: crates/relay-core/src/github.rs:157-160: `safe_relative` only rejects non-Normal components, then `root.join(relative)` is passed to `start.exists()` and `find_skill_files`. That function uses `path.is_file()` and `fs::read_dir(path)`, and both follow symlinks, both for `start` itself and for any intermediate component of the subdir. Only the entries found inside the directory are checked with `file_type.is_symlink()` (line 214). So a cloned repo that commits `skills -> /home/<user>/.claude/skills`, installed with `.../tree/main/skills` (provider.rs:216 -> download_skills -> collect_skills), walks the user's real directory. It reads every SKILL.md there and `copy_bounded`s each skill's real folder into staging under the remote source's name. Lines 172-173 do `fs::read_to_string` before the 256 KiB check, so the whole file is read into memory first. The effect stays local: the remote never receives the content, and the user has to paste the malicious URL themselves. Low is right.
v1.correction: The escape also works through an intermediate symlinked component (e.g. subdir `a/b` where `a` is a symlink), not only through `start`. Fix: canonicalize `start` and require `starts_with(canonicalize(root))`, or use `symlink_metadata` on every component. Check `metadata().len()` before reading. Out of scope for this finding but noticed: the `git clone` at line 109 and the `git rev-parse` at line 154 use plain `.output()`, not `proc::output_with_timeout`.

results.coverage:
I read every line of all five assigned files: pty.rs, providers.rs, provider_updates.rs, handlers/provider.rs and usage.rs. I followed callers and callees into: handlers/session.rs (launch/finish_launch, park, close, input, attach, scrollback); engine.rs (PTY registry, pty_fast_path, answers_from_memory, shutdown/mark_restorable, system_write); socket.rs (attach forwarding at line 487, inline dispatch); recovery.rs; proc.rs; skills.rs (adopt, fill, stamps, refresh_all); github.rs; awareness.rs (brief composition); hooks.rs (status-line usage writer, commit hook); store.rs (skills/provider_cache schema); the relay-bus provider ops; and the native consumers (terminal.rs Sequence, session_context.rs, tools_skills.rs, status_usage.rs, provider_updates.rs). I also checked the portable-pty 0.9.0 source: dup'ed reader/writer fds, the EOT write when the writer is dropped, the $HOME cwd fallback, and signal statuses mapping to exit code 1. signal-hook-registry uses SA_RESTART, so the reader's `Err(_) => break` is not a practical EINTR problem.

The recovery pid-reuse finding is anchored in recovery.rs, outside this chunk; I found it by tracing pty::pid_alive's callers.

Experiments, metadata only plus one byte per file, under the scratchpad: a simulation of collect_jsonl on ~/.codex/sessions (478 files, newest-32 overlap 0, 14.9-day gap), and the UTF-8 position of each large file's 1 MiB tail offset (0/181).

Pedantic cast warnings in these files were checked. The pid u32→i32 casts are safe below pid_max 4194304; millis u128→u64 is fine; the f64→u64 casts in usage saturate as intended; the ring's u64→usize casts are fine on 64-bit. None hides a bug.

Not verified:
- Codex CLI semantics of `resume --last` (whether it is scoped to the cwd) and of `--approve-for-me`.
- Whether Codex's default shell_environment_policy still strips *TOKEN* variables. If it does, RELAY_TOKEN would never reach Codex's shell tool, and both `$RELAY_BIN q` and the commit hook (hooks.rs:125) would refuse. I could not establish this, and the author reports Codex sessions working.
- Updater atomicity. Relay itself downloads and verifies nothing: it runs `<binary> update` and checks only the install location and the file owner, so trust rests on the vendor updater.
- The VecDeque growth finding relies on std's documented amortized-growth policy; there is no std source on disk.

I did not report the blocking `Pty::write` under the writer mutex on the inline runtime path: it needs roughly 64-640 KiB of queued input to a child that is not reading, so the trigger was too remote. No cargo, rustc or app runs; no repository files were modified.

findings.title: Startup recovery kills whatever process now holds a stale sessions.pid, plus its process group
findings.evidence: Step 2 does `Some(p) if pty::pid_alive(p as u32) => { kill_wait(p as u32); ...` for every row still in spawning/running/idle/blocked. `pid_alive` is only `libc::kill(pid as i32, 0) == 0` (pty.rs:394-396). `kill_wait` sends SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after 2 s, to both `-(pid)` and `pid` (recovery.rs:20-34). Nothing checks that the pid still belongs to a Relay child. Step 1 has already reaped every process carrying this instance's RELAY_SESSION/RELAY_STORE (recovery.rs:67-74, via pty::relay_children), so step 2 can only ever hit processes that are not Relay's.
findings.impact: After an unclean stop the session rows keep state `running` and their pids. Causes: power loss, kernel panic, or the engine being OOM-killed or SIGKILLed; only `Engine::shutdown` marks rows restorable. On the next start, usually after a reboot when pids are handed out from low numbers again, any same-user process that now has one of those pids gets SIGTERM and then SIGKILL, together with its whole process group: an editor, browser, terminal or desktop component. Unsaved work in it is lost, and the report calls it 'reaped'. pid reuse without a reboot is also realistic: this machine has pid_max 4194304, is already at about 4.08M after 11.5 days, and is about to wrap.
findings.fix:
Never signal by bare pid in step 2. Step 1 already reaped every env-tagged orphan, so step 2 should only mark the row restorable. If a kill is still wanted, first confirm identity: `pty::proc_env(p)` must contain RELAY_SESSION == name and RELAY_STORE == store path. Comparing /proc/

/stat starttime with spawned_at also works.

v1.reason: recovery.rs:80-93 selects every row in spawning/running/idle/blocked. If `pty::pid_alive(p)` holds (pty.rs:394-396: only `kill(pid,0)==0`, which is true for any process of the same user), it calls kill_wait(p) (recovery.rs:20-34), which sends SIGTERM and then SIGKILL to both -p and p. No identity check is made. Step 1 (recovery.rs:66-74) has already reaped every live process whose environment carries this instance's RELAY_INSTANCE and RELAY_STORE plus RELAY_SESSION, which every session child gets (handlers/session.rs:564-575). So step 2 can only reach a genuine Relay child in a narrow race (one SIGKILLed by step 1 that has not yet died), and otherwise reaches unrelated processes that reused the pid. Rows stay live with a pid only after an unclean stop: Engine::shutdown (engine.rs:633-660) marks them restorable on SIGINT/SIGTERM/app.quit (serve.rs:40-56), so power loss, a kernel panic, OOM-kill or SIGKILL leave them as they were. After a reboot, if the sessions were spawned soon after the previous boot, their pids fall in the same low range the new desktop session's processes occupy. Any match gets SIGKILLed, and so does its whole process group if it is a group leader (a terminal and its shells, a browser, an editor), and the report calls this 'reaped'. The test (tests/sessions.rs:574-576) only covers the dead-pid case (999999).
v1.correction:
Severity high, not critical: it needs an unclean stop plus a pid collision with a same-user process (other users' processes return EPERM, so pid_alive is false). The fix is right: in step 2 drop the kill and just mark the row restorable, or signal only after confirming that proc_env(p) has RELAY_SESSION == name and RELAY_STORE == store path (or comparing /proc/

/stat starttime against the row). Separately, kill_wait sends SIGKILL without waiting afterwards, so step 2 can see a step-1 victim still alive and signal it again. That is harmless only while the pid has not been reused.

v2.reason:
(a) The code does what the finding says. Step 2 (crates/relay-core/src/recovery.rs:80-93) selects every row in spawning/running/idle/blocked. If `pty::pid_alive(p)` is true (pty.rs:394-396: just `kill(p,0)==0`), it calls `kill_wait(p)`. That function (recovery.rs:20-35) sends SIGTERM to -p and p, then SIGKILL to both after 2 s. There is no identity check. This also breaks the documented decision D20 (docs/engine/DECISIONS.md:63): "Recovery reaps only its own store's orphans". The child is a setsid session leader (portable-pty 0.9.0, unix.rs:257), so for the original child -p is its own group.

(b) Reachable, but rarely. A row keeps a live state and a pid only when the engine dies without running `Engine::shutdown` (engine.rs:633-682) and before the child's exit callback runs (handlers/session.rs:653 sets pid=NULL on exit). The real launch path is run.sh:32, which starts the engine with `nohup ... serve --remote &` (this is how the engine runs on this machine: parent relay-native, no systemd unit). Because SIGHUP is ignored and SIGTERM/SIGINT/app.quit run shutdown (serve.rs:45-50, remote.rs:128-137), ordinary quits, terminal closes and system shutdowns all null the pids. Only crash-class stops leave stale rows: power loss, kernel panic or hard reset, SIGKILL/OOM, an abort. Recovery then runs once, at the next engine start (serve.rs:23). For the kill to hit a foreign process, a process of the same user must hold that exact pid at that moment. Other users' processes return EPERM, so `pid_alive` is false for them.
- Without a reboot, the pid counter must come back around to the stale pid. That is one full cycle of pid_max 4,194,304, which takes days on this machine, while the restart is normally seconds to minutes after a crash.
- After a reboot, the stale pid must be below the new boot's counter when Relay starts. That only happens for sessions spawned early in the previous boot or just after a wrap. It must then also land on a live process of the same user.

(c) When it fires, an unrelated process gets SIGTERM and then SIGKILL, along with its whole process group if it leads one: an editor, a terminal and its shells, a browser, or a desktop component. Unsaved work in it is lost, and the report calls it "reaped".

(d) High does not fit the rubric, which requires "likely ... in a normal flow". This is a real bug in a less common path that needs a pid coincidence. That is medium, at the top of medium because of what it does when it fires.

(e) Dropping the kill in step 2 (only mark the row restorable) fixes the root cause. tests/sessions.rs:563 keeps passing, because its leaked orphan carries the RELAY_* variables and step 1 reaps it. The env-check variant behaves the same way, since step 1 already killed every process that would pass that check.
v2.correction:
Severity medium, not high. The finding's "pid reuse without a reboot is realistic ... about to wrap" is wrong. A wrap restarts allocation at 300, and a given stale pid is reused only when the counter climbs back to it, about one full cycle after the session was spawned. Also, I read last pid 3,097,640 at 11.6 days uptime (/proc/loadavg), not ~4.08M. "Usually after a reboot" is also too strong: it needs the stale pid to be below the new boot's pid counter when Relay starts. And "step 2 can only ever hit processes that are not Relay's" is slightly too strong: it can also hit a step-1 victim that is not yet dead, or an orphan whose environment step 1 could not read. Fix: drop the kill in step 2. The finding's other option, "compare /proc/

/stat starttime with spawned_at", is unsound. spawned_at is only ever written as COALESCE(spawned_at, now) (handlers/session.rs:681), so it keeps the first spawn's time. A resumed session's current pid always started later: an equality check never matches, and a >= check matches any process that reused the pid. A start-time check would need a per-spawn start time (and boot id) stored with the pid, which means a new column, a migration and a SCHEMA_VERSION bump. Caveat, not verified: step 1 sees only processes whose /proc//environ it can read, so without step 2's kill a non-dumpable orphan would no longer be reaped. Such an orphan has lost its PTY and normally exits on SIGHUP. Related, same root cause: - tests/sessions.rs:576 seeds pid 999999 as a "dead" pid. Under pid_max 4194304 that is a valid pid. If a process of the same user holds it during `cargo test`, the test SIGKILLs it and its group, then fails at line 591. - crates/relay-core/examples/perf.rs:581-585 store_copy nulls every pid before running recovery on the copy, which works around this same hazard. Its comment at lines 1092-1093 credits the copy for the protection, but on a copy step 1 matches nothing; the nulled pids are what keep step 2 away from the fixture's two live sessions.

findings.title: Codex usage discovery caps the directory walk before sorting by mtime, so it reports sessions about two weeks old (confirmed on this machine)
findings.evidence: `fn collect_jsonl(..) { if depth > 4 || out.len() > 256 { return; } let Ok(entries) = fs::read_dir(dir) ...` collects in readdir order. Only afterwards does read_codex run `files.sort_by_key(|(_, modified)| Reverse(*modified))` and `.take(MAX_CODEX_FILES)` (lines 59-60). Codex writes rollouts as sessions/YYYY/MM/DD/*.jsonl, and readdir returns those directories in on-disk hash order, not date order.
findings.impact: Once there are more than 256 rollout files, the walk stops in whichever year/month/day directories readdir listed first, and the 32 'most recent' files are taken from that arbitrary subset. I ran a metadata-only simulation of this exact walk against ~/.codex/sessions here (478 files). It stops at 263 files, reaches none of the 32 newest, and the newest file it sees is 14.9 days older than the real newest. So usage.get shows Codex rate-limit windows from about two weeks ago, or none, even though fresh data is on disk.
findings.fix: Walk the date directories in descending name order (the names are zero-padded) and stop once MAX_CODEX_FILES .jsonl files are found. Alternatively, collect every path+mtime (cheap stat calls), then sort and take; drop the 256 early-return.

v1.reason: collect_jsonl (usage.rs:77-88) returns early once `out.len() > 256`, checked only when entering a directory, and collects in readdir order. read_codex (usage.rs:58-60) sorts by mtime and takes 32 only after that truncated walk. I ran my own metadata-only simulation of the same walk with Python os.scandir, which uses readdir order, against ~/.codex/sessions (btrfs, layout sessions/2026/MM/DD). It found 478 files in total, the walk stopped at 263, 0 of the 32 newest files were reached, and the newest file it saw was 14.8 days older than the real newest. This matches the finding exactly. Also, in the usage.get handler (handlers/provider.rs:60-69), the discovered item unconditionally `latest.insert`s over any hook-reported row, so the stale discovered data even replaces fresher usage.report data for Codex.
v1.correction: Additional root-cause detail: on btrfs, readdir returns entries in creation (dir-index) order, oldest first, so the truncation keeps the oldest directories by construction, not arbitrarily. Fix: walk the zero-padded YYYY/MM/DD names in descending order and stop after MAX_CODEX_FILES, or stat every file before sorting. Also have provider.rs:66 keep the newer of the reported and discovered items by taken_at instead of always overwriting.

v2.reason:
(a) Yes. At crates/relay-core/src/usage.rs:77-88, `collect_jsonl` checks `if depth > 4 || out.len() > 256 { return; }` only when it enters a directory, and it collects entries in plain `fs::read_dir` (readdir) order. `read_codex` sorts by mtime and keeps 32 only after that truncated walk (lines 58-60). The function has not changed since fcbdbce (the first commit). I ran my own metadata-only Python simulation of this walk (os.scandir keeps readdir order; no file contents were read) against ~/.codex/sessions on this btrfs /home. There are 478 rollouts across 2026/08/17 to 2026/09/16. The walk stops at 263 files after 12 day directories (08/17 to 09/01). None of the real newest 32 are in what it keeps. Its newest file is from 2026-09-01 13:35, while the real newest is 2026-09-16 09:53, a 14.8-day gap.

(b) usage.get is the only source of the meters. The native client calls it on every status refresh (status.rs:68), on the refresh key and on the optional timer. Codex meters are shown by default (`enabled` falls back to true). Nothing in the codebase sends `usage.report` (hooks.rs:577 only installs a Claude status-line script that writes a file), so discovery is Codex's only input. The trigger is a file count that only goes up. Relay starts many Codex sessions, and each one leaves a rollout file. This machine passed 256 files after about two weeks of use. Every long-term Codex user ends up in this state and stays in it.

(c) On btrfs, `ls -U` shows readdir returning creation order: months 08 then 09, days in ascending order. So the walk always keeps the OLDEST ~257 files, and the Codex meters stay frozen at the snapshot from when the count crossed 256, no matter how much Codex is used afterwards. XFS, which also returns roughly insertion order, behaves the same way. On ext4 the htree hash order makes the kept subset arbitrary, so the meters are usually wrong and occasionally right. The client does label the result honestly: `Window::stale` greys out windows whose resets_at has passed, shows "Reset since the last report" and "reported Nd ago". So the user sees old numbers marked as old, not stale numbers passed off as current. Even so, the Codex limit meter never shows current usage again. Nothing else is affected: no data loss, no lock involved (usage.get is register_unlocked, provider.rs:42-44).

(d) High fits the rubric: in a normal, default-on flow, a feature fails permanently for every Codex user once rollouts pass 256. It is at the low end of high, since the damage is a broken informational meter that is visibly marked stale.

(e) Fix option 2 (stat every file, sort, take 32, drop the 256 early return) is correct and complete. It is also safe: the handler is unlocked, and here it costs about 1k stat calls.
v2.correction:
1. "About two weeks old" is only the gap to the newest file on disk today. On btrfs/XFS (creation-order readdir) the kept subset is the oldest ~257 files by construction, so the shown snapshot is frozen and grows one day older per day: the data shown here is from Sep 1, 35 days before today. The finding's "on-disk hash order" describes ext4 only.
2. The client marks these windows stale ("Reset since the last report", "reported Nd ago"), so the impact is a Codex meter that never shows current usage. It is not stale numbers presented as current.
3. The first verifier's addition about provider.rs:66 overwriting fresher usage.report rows has no practical effect in this codebase, because nothing sends usage.report for Codex. Keeping the newer row by taken_at is a harmless extra and not part of this bug.
4. Fix: option 1 as written ("walk dates descending and stop once 32 files are found") is incomplete. A resumed Codex session appends to its original file in an older date directory (49 of 478 files here have an mtime on a later day than their directory), and finding the most recently written file is the whole reason read_codex sorts by mtime. Prefer collecting every (path, mtime), then sorting and taking 32. If a bound is wanted, walk newest-first under a generous file cap or a date horizon, not "first 32 found".
5. Separate root cause worth its own finding, not this one: usage.rs:61 `read_tail(&path, CODEX_TAIL).ok()?` drops the whole Codex result on the first unreadable tail. That includes a 1 MiB seek that lands inside a multi-byte UTF-8 character, which `read_to_string` rejects as InvalidData. 181 of the 478 rollouts here are over 1 MiB, so that seek path is common. Use `continue` and a lossy decode instead.

findings.title: PTY seq is published before its frame reaches the ring; attach can silently drop a frame or replay 256 KiB
findings.evidence: The reader does `let seq = sh.seq.fetch_add(1, Ordering::SeqCst) + 1; let data = buf[..n].to_vec(); sh.ring.lock().unwrap().push(seq, &data); let _ = sh.tx.send(...)`. Attach does `let rx = subscribe(); let ring = self.shared.ring.lock().unwrap(); let seq = self.seq();`, then `if s >= seq { Vec::new() } else { ring.bounded_bytes_from(ring.offset_after(s).unwrap_or(0)) }`. The socket door drops live frames with `if fr.seq <= att.seq && fr.epoch == att.epoch { continue; } // already in catch-up` (socket.rs:487). The native client's Sequence::observe treats the next frame as contiguous (terminal.rs:24-38).
findings.impact: Attach can land between the reader's fetch_add (seq = k) and its ring push; that window includes an allocation and a copy of up to 64 KiB. Then att.seq = k but the catch-up lacks frame k. Frame k arrives live, is discarded as 'already in catch-up', and the client sees k followed by k+1, so it cannot detect the hole. Escape sequences are lost and the pane renders wrongly until a full redraw. If the client re-attached from k-1, offset_after(k-1) is None, so `unwrap_or(0)` re-sends the last 256 KiB, which the client feeds as catch-up: duplicated output in the pane. Every pane switch re-attaches (set_active → attach_and_render) and agents emit frames continuously, so this recurs occasionally.
findings.fix: Assign seq while holding the ring lock: lock ring → fetch_add → push → unlock → send. Attach's seq then always matches the ring contents. When s is in the current epoch but no later frame is indexed, return an empty catch-up instead of `unwrap_or(0)`. scrollback() should also read seq under the lock.

v1.reason: The reader (pty.rs:215-218) does `fetch_add` (seq = k), then `buf[..n].to_vec()` (an allocation and copy of up to 64 KiB), then locks the ring and pushes. attach (pty.rs:306-312) subscribes, locks the ring, then reads `self.seq()`. If attach takes the lock in that window, it reports seq = k while the ring lacks frame k. The subscription was taken before the push, so frame k arrives live, and socket.rs:487 drops it (`fr.seq <= att.seq && fr.epoch == att.epoch`). The client's Sequence::observe (terminal.rs:24-38) then sees the catch-up at k and the next frame at k+1, which looks contiguous, so the lost bytes go undetected. Separately, when s == k-1, `offset_after(k-1)` is None (frame k is not indexed yet), and `unwrap_or(0)` sends up to 256 KiB of already-seen output as catch-up. The client feeds it because seq k > k-1. Outside this race, offset_after only returns None when s is at or past the newest frame, which the `s >= seq` branch already handles, so this window is the only way to reach the fallback.
v1.correction: The window is microseconds per frame, so this is an occasional rather than frequent glitch. It needs an attach (pane switch/reconnect) during steady output. The consequence is a silently lost frame (a corrupted pane until redraw) or a duplicated 256 KiB tail. Fix: do the fetch_add inside the ring lock (lock, fetch_add, push, unlock, then send), and make scrollback() read seq while holding the lock as well. Once seq and the ring are consistent, the unwrap_or(0) fallback for an in-epoch s should return an empty catch-up.

findings.title: Restored history on wake/resume is dropped or cut mid-sequence: it is one giant frame that the bounded catch-up cannot align to
findings.evidence: `if !spec.initial_scrollback.is_empty() { ring.push(0, &spec.initial_scrollback); }` pushes up to 8 MiB of saved history as a single frame. bounded_bytes_from aligns to the first frame whose offset is >= end-256 KiB: `let at = self.frames.partition_point(|(_, offset)| *offset < requested); let aligned = self.frames.get(at).map(|(_, offset)| *offset).unwrap_or(requested);`
findings.impact: After a wake or resume the client's epoch is stale, so attach calls bounded_bytes_from(0). If the saved scrollback is larger than 256 KiB minus the new output (any session that worked for a few minutes), the first frame boundary at or after `requested` is the first live frame. The entire restored history is omitted. The client resets the terminal on the epoch change (terminal.rs:512) and shows only the new provider output, which defeats 'prior epochs collapsed into the new terminal's initial history'. If the pane attaches before the provider's first byte, there is no later frame, and `unwrap_or(requested)` slices the history at an arbitrary byte, starting mid-UTF-8 or mid-escape-sequence. Which of the two happens depends on a race with the provider's first write.
findings.fix: Push the initial scrollback as frames of at most 64 KiB, split at '\n' boundaries (all seq 0 is fine for offset_after and the offset partition). Alternatively, when `requested` falls inside a frame, cut at the first '\n' after `requested` instead of skipping to the next frame.

v1.reason: The full scrollback is saved: mark_restorable (engine.rs:669) and session.rs:981 both call `pty.scrollback(None)`, which can be up to 8 MiB. On resume it is loaded as initial_scrollback (session.rs:454-458) and pushed as one frame at offset 0 (pty.rs:191-193). After a wake or restart the client's epoch is stale or absent, so attach takes `ring.bounded_bytes_from(0)` (pty.rs:314). bounded_bytes_from (pty.rs:96-101) sets requested = end-256 KiB and aligns to the first frame with offset >= requested. If the history is longer than 256 KiB minus the new output, that frame is the first live frame, so the whole history is skipped and only new provider output is sent. If there is no live frame yet, `unwrap_or(requested)` slices the history at an arbitrary byte, which can land inside a UTF-8 sequence or a CSI. The native client resets the terminal on the epoch change (terminal.rs:512) and feeds only that. The 256 KiB cap is intentional (pty.rs:17-19), but the intent is to show the last 256 KiB, not none of it.
v1.correction: Severity medium holds. The main visible effect is that restored history is missing or starts with a few garbage bytes after an app restart or wake of a session with more than about 256 KiB of saved output. The agent's own redraw (e.g. claude --resume) partly hides this, which is why it is not high. Fix: push initial_scrollback in chunks of at most 64 KiB split at '\n' (seq 0 for all of them is compatible with offset_after and the offset partition), or when `requested` falls inside a frame, cut at the next '\n' after `requested` instead of jumping to the next frame.

findings.title: provider.refresh runs provider subprocess probes inside the locked request transaction (D149 / CLAUDE.md invariant)
findings.evidence: `e.register::<Refresh>(|ctx: &mut Ctx, _| { let discovered = crate::providers::refresh(ctx.tx(), &ctx.now)?;`. refresh forks `<binary> --version` and `claude auth status` / `codex login status` for both providers through command_output, with PROBE_TIMEOUT = 3 s (providers.rs:320-331, 360). The comment there cites D144's timeout only. D149 says slow work runs outside the transaction, 'not merely with a timeout', and provider.list was converted to unlocked but refresh was not. provider_updates.rs:61-62 also calls `crate::providers::refresh(tx, now)` inside engine.system_write, which holds the store mutex.
findings.impact: Each 'Refresh providers' click, and every completed provider update, holds the global store mutex for as long as the slowest of four Node/Bun cold starts: typically hundreds of ms, up to 3 s at the timeout. Every other op queues behind it, including agents' PreToolUse guardrail checks and session.report hooks. Only keystrokes and resizes escape, via the fast path.
findings.fix: Register provider.refresh with register_staged. Prepare reads the cached rows and resolved paths in a short ctx.read and runs the probes unlocked; finish only upserts provider_cache and inserts the notifications. In provider_updates, probe before system_write and pass the results in. With the probes off the lock, the nested thread::scope fan-out can also go.

v1.reason: handlers/provider.rs:18-19 registers provider.refresh with plain `e.register::<Refresh>` and calls `crate::providers::refresh(ctx.tx(), &ctx.now)`. providers.rs:310-352 runs `<binary> --version` and `drv.auth(path)` for both providers inside that transaction. auth is `claude auth status` (providers.rs:201) or `codex login status` (providers.rs:245), each through command_output with PROBE_TIMEOUT 3 s (providers.rs:360). The comment at providers.rs:358-359 admits the probes 'run inside the request transaction' and cites only D144. DECISIONS.md D149 (line 797) says slow work runs outside the transaction, 'not merely with a timeout', and provides register_staged for exactly this kind of mutation. provider.list (line 13) was moved to register_unlocked; refresh was not. provider_updates.rs:61-62 also calls providers::refresh inside engine.system_write after a successful update. The trigger is reachable: the native Settings page has a 'Refresh providers' action (tools_settings.rs:396-401), and examples/perf.rs:1010 itself classes the op as Heavy. The probes run in parallel, so the lock is held about as long as the slowest Node/Bun CLI cold start, capped at 3 s. Every other bus write queues behind it for that time.
v1.correction: The worst case is bounded at about 3 s per click (the parallel probes each time out at 3 s), so this is a stall, not a hang. Medium is right. The fix is as proposed: register_staged, with prepare doing a short ctx.read of the cached rows and executable paths and then the probes, and finish doing the upserts and notifications. In provider_updates, probe before system_write.

findings.title: Codex receives the whole, uncapped brief as a single argv element; past 128 KiB every Codex launch in the project fails, and the brief is readable through ps
findings.evidence: `if let Some(brief) = brief.map(str::trim).filter(..) { text.push_str("\n\n"); text.push_str(brief); } ... format!("developer_instructions={value}")`. This is passed as one `--config` argument on Fresh (line 220) and Resume (line 227). The compact brief has no cap. It includes every assigned task's `Task body` and `Task changelog`, the full standing note, every adjacent task in the module and every plugin's instructions (awareness.rs:224-242, 285-298, 300-330, 389-392). Task bodies, changelogs and notes have no size limit, and notes.append keeps growing the standing note.
findings.impact: Linux refuses any single argv string over MAX_ARG_STRLEN (32 pages = 128 KiB) with E2BIG. Once a project's standing note, or a current task's body plus changelog, pushes the JSON-escaped brief past that (each newline becomes two bytes), Pty::spawn fails with session.spawn_failed 'Argument list too long'. That applies to every Codex spawn, resume and wake in that project. Claude is unaffected because it reads the brief from a file. Separately, task bodies, changelogs and notes become world-readable through /proc/<pid>/cmdline; awareness.rs:246-248 keeps only the launch assignment out of argv for exactly that reason.
findings.fix: For Codex, write the brief to the session file Claude already uses (.relay/sessions/<name>/...) and put only a short pointer in developer_instructions. Alternatively, cap the injected part well under 128 KiB and point to $RELAY_BRIEF for the rest.

v1.reason: codex_developer_instructions (providers.rs:81-94) appends the whole compact brief to the role text and passes it as one argv element, `developer_instructions=<json>`, on both Fresh (220) and Resume (227). The compact brief (awareness.rs ~389-392) includes every assigned task's body and changelog, the whole standing note, every adjacent task line and the plugin brief sections, none of them capped. The standing note grows through notes.append (notes.rs:413-418) with no size check. Linux execve rejects any single argument over MAX_ARG_STRLEN (128 KiB) with E2BIG. A Codex spawn, resume or wake in a project whose brief crosses that size therefore fails outright, while Claude, which reads role-instructions.md through --append-system-prompt-file, is unaffected. Reaching 128 KiB takes a large standing note or large task body plus changelog, so the path is uncommon, but the failure then covers every Codex launch in the project and the error is opaque. The /proc/<pid>/cmdline exposure is real, but awareness.rs:244-246 documents it as an accepted trade-off: only the launch assignment is kept out of argv on purpose. I count it as a design decision, not part of this bug.
v1.correction: Drop the 'readable through ps' half as a separate defect: awareness.rs:244-246 explicitly accepts that the compact brief is in argv and only protects the launch assignment. The E2BIG failure stands. Fix: put a bounded excerpt in developer_instructions and point Codex at $RELAY_BRIEF / role-instructions.md (already written at session.rs ~520-526) for the rest, or cap the inlined brief well under 128 KiB after JSON escaping.

findings.title: skill.create with a deleted skill's name revives the old GitHub row, its source fields and its asset folder; agents get the old SKILL.md and 'Update from GitHub' overwrites the user's text
findings.evidence: `Some((id, Some(_))) => { ctx.tx().execute("UPDATE skills SET name=?1,body=?2,deleted_at=NULL,updated_at=?3 WHERE id=?4", ..) }` leaves source_url, source_path and revision untouched. skill.delete only sets deleted_at, so `<store>/skills/<id>/` survives. The materializer copies library_dir(id), which includes the downloaded SKILL.md, and writes the row body only `if !instructions.is_file()` (skills.rs:328, 340-344).
findings.impact: Example: the user removes GitHub skill 'pdf', then writes their own 'pdf' in the skill editor. The new skill reuses the old id and still carries source_url. The Skills page therefore shows it as a GitHub skill with 'Update from GitHub' and no Edit button (tools_skills.rs:163-185). Every checkout's .claude/skills/pdf/ and .agents/skills/pdf/ get the old upstream SKILL.md and scripts, not the text the user just wrote. Clicking 'Update from GitHub', the only action offered besides Remove, matches the row by source (`Some(named) if Some(named.id) == source_id`) and overwrites the user's body. skill.install has no undo.
findings.fix: When skill.create revives a tombstone, clear source_url/source_path/revision and remove library_dir(id). Give skill.delete's undo its own restore path (clear deleted_at) instead of routing it through skill.create, so undo can still bring the source back.

v1.reason: skill.create (handlers/provider.rs:108-149) looks up `SELECT id,deleted_at FROM skills WHERE name=?1 COLLATE NOCASE`. On a tombstone it runs `UPDATE skills SET name=?1,body=?2,deleted_at=NULL,updated_at=?3 WHERE id=?4`, leaving source_url, source_path and revision intact. skill.delete (line 171-186) only sets deleted_at and never removes library_dir(id). The library folder holds the downloaded SKILL.md (github.rs test at 254-256 asserts SKILL.md is in the staged assets, and adopt renames it into <store>/skills/<id>). skills.rs fill (lines 325-346) copies library_dir(id) and writes row.body only `if !instructions.is_file()`, so the old upstream SKILL.md wins. The native editor creates new skills through skill.create (tools_skills.rs:473). The skill card shows 'Update from GitHub' instead of Edit whenever web_url(skill) is set (tools_skills.rs:163-185). Clicking it calls skill.install with the old source. install_downloaded_skill's source_match and name_match then resolve to the same id (line 455), and the update at line 494 overwrites the user's body. skill.install sets no undo. Trigger: remove an installed GitHub skill 'pdf', then write a new skill named 'pdf' in the editor.
v1.correction: Keeping the source on revive is what makes the undo of skill.delete (routed through skill.create at line 181) restore a GitHub skill correctly. The fix must therefore split the two paths as proposed: skill.delete's undo needs its own restore (clear deleted_at only), and a user-initiated skill.create that revives a tombstone clears source_url/source_path/revision and removes library_dir(id). The SKILL.md precedence in fill is the shared root with #24.

findings.title: skill.install moves asset folders into the library inside the transaction; a rollback leaves orphaned or replaced folders that later skills pick up
findings.evidence: `if let Some(assets) = item.assets.as_deref() { crate::skills::adopt(assets, &crate::skills::library_dir(store, id)) }` runs per item inside the finish transaction. adopt first does `fs::remove_dir_all(to)`, then renames (skills.rs:51-66). A later item can still fail, for example with skill.name_exists, and on error the finish closure only removes the staging dir (lines 232-237). skills.id is AUTOINCREMENT (store.rs:259), and a rolled-back INSERT also rolls back sqlite_sequence, so the id is handed out again.
findings.impact: Example: a repo whose skills are, in name order, 'docx' (new) then 'pdf' (conflicts). docx's folder is adopted into skills/<N>/ and the transaction rolls back. The next skill.create gets id N, and every checkout materializes that orphan folder, including docx's SKILL.md, which overrides the user's body (skills.rs:340-344). For an existing skill refreshed in a failing batch, the old folder is deleted and replaced with new upstream assets while the row's body, revision and stamp revert, so checkouts disagree about the skill's content. A refresh whose assets are None (over the copy bounds) leaves the previous folder in place, and its SKILL.md keeps overriding the new body.
findings.fix: Resolve all items, conflicts included, before adopting anything. Do the adoption in after_commit, or adopt under a temporary name and swap after commit. Remove library_dir(id) when a refresh arrives without assets.

v1.reason: In skill.install's finish closure (provider.rs:226-240), each item goes through install_downloaded_skill. That function INSERTs or UPDATEs the row and then calls skills::adopt (provider.rs:504-508), which runs `remove_dir_all(to)` and renames the staged folder into skills/<id>/ (skills.rs:51-66). All of this happens inside the request transaction. deduplicate_downloaded_skills returns items from a BTreeMap ordered by lowercase name. A later item can fail with skill.name_exists (provider.rs:455), or with valid_skill_name or valid_skill_body. The handler then returns Err, the transaction rolls back, and only the staging dir is removed, so adopted folders stay. skills.id is AUTOINCREMENT (store.rs:259); the rolled-back sqlite_sequence update hands id N out again. The next skill.create or skill.install then gets id N. fill() copies library_dir(N) and writes the row's body only when SKILL.md is absent (skills.rs:340-343), so the orphan's SKILL.md silently replaces the new skill's instructions in every checkout. For an existing row refreshed in a failing batch, the old library folder has already been replaced while the row reverts. The finding is also right that a refresh with assets=None leaves the old folder, whose SKILL.md keeps overriding the new body. A realistic trigger: a multi-skill repository where one skill's name collides with a skill the user installed from elsewhere. A successful retry with replace_skill_id overwrites id N again, but if the user abandons the install the orphan stays.
v1.correction: Category is better as bug (integrity) than data-loss: the replaced folder is upstream content that can be downloaded again. A related root cause worth its own finding: because the library SKILL.md always wins in fill() (skills.rs:340), a skill.update that edits the body of any installed skill with a library folder is never materialized; agents keep the upstream SKILL.md. Fix: resolve every item, conflicts and validation included, before touching the filesystem. Adopt in after_commit, or under a temporary name swapped in after commit. Remove library_dir(id) when a refresh has no assets, and write the row body over SKILL.md, or update the library copy, when the body changes.

findings.title: Every skill/plugin mutation spawns its own unsynchronized refresh_all, so a stale plan can win the race
findings.evidence: `ctx.after_commit(|engine| { std::thread::Builder::new().name("skill-materialize".into()).spawn(move || crate::skills::refresh_all(&engine)).ok(); });`. refresh_all reads its plan under the store lock, then prunes and writes folders with no lock held (skills.rs:267-305). Unlike prepare_launch's apply, it does not take hooks::writes(). write_skill returns early for folders whose marker already matches the stamp (skills.rs:313-315).
findings.impact: Two mutations in quick succession run two materializers at once: toggling two skills in the top-bar popover (D142), or an install followed by an enable. The newer thread skips folders the older one already stamped, so it can overtake it. If it prunes a just-disabled skill S in a checkout before the older thread reaches that checkout, the older thread then rewrites S from its stale plan. The disabled skill stays materialized and agents keep loading it until some later refresh. The reverse ordering can leave a newly enabled skill missing.
findings.fix: Funnel materialization through one worker with a dirty flag: coalesce bursts and re-plan after each pass. Alternatively, hold a dedicated mutex around plan+apply in refresh_all and around prepare_launch's apply.

v1.reason: refresh_checkouts (provider.rs:532-539) spawns a new skill-materialize thread for each skill mutation. refresh_all (skills.rs:267-305) builds its plans under store.lock() and then calls apply with no lock and no single-flight guard. Several writers can therefore run at once: two quick toggles in the popover, serve startup (serve.rs:32), workspace add (workspace.rs:215), and launches (session.rs:480; that path takes hooks::writes, but refresh_all does not take it). write_skill skips folders whose marker already matches, so a newer thread can overtake an older one that is busy copying. The older thread then acts on its stale plan. It can rewrite a skill the newer plan has just pruned, because the marker is gone, so fill() runs: a disabled skill stays materialized. It can also prune a skill the newer thread just wrote, so a newly enabled skill goes missing. Either state lasts until the next refresh or launch. Two threads can also run fill() on the same dest at the same moment (remove_dir_all and copy interleaved), which leaves mixed contents or an error that deletes the folder. A thread that sees a folder still being filled by another thread (it exists, but has no marker yet) treats it as owned by the repository and skips it (skills.rs:310-312). The window depends on how big the folders are and how many checkouts there are, but nothing serializes the writers.
v1.correction: Other unsynchronized writers: serve.rs:32, workspace.rs:215 and session.rs:480/493 (session launch takes hooks::writes; refresh_all and workspace do not). Fix: run one materializer worker behind a dirty flag (coalesce bursts and re-plan after each pass), or use a dedicated mutex that every caller of skills::apply takes around both plan and apply.

findings.title: Pty::kill signals the process group only while the leader is alive and never escalates for surviving members; the reader outlives the master
findings.evidence: `if !self.exited() { libc::kill(-(pid), SIGTERM) ...; if !self.exited() { libc::kill(-(pid), SIGKILL) ... } }`. Escalation depends only on the leader, and nothing is sent once the leader has exited. The module doc (line 3) says 'kill child → drop master → the reader ends on EIO', but the reader owns its own dup of the master (try_clone_reader, line 186). It therefore ends only when every holder of the slave has exited; dropping `master` closes just one fd.
findings.impact: On park or close, group members that survive SIGTERM after the leader exits (slow cleanup handlers, or handlers that ignore it) are never SIGKILLed. If the provider crashed or the user typed /exit, close signals nothing at all, so members that ignored the kernel's SIGHUP keep running until the next engine start reaps them by RELAY_SESSION. That can include a worktree that close has just deleted. Any such survivor still holding the slave keeps the reader thread and its 8 MiB ring alive.
findings.fix: Always signal -pid, whatever exited() says. After the grace period, SIGKILL the group if any member remains (`kill(-pid, 0) == 0`). Optionally also reap this session's env-tagged descendants with relay_children filtered to the session name, the rule recovery already applies at startup. Correct the module comment.

v1.reason: Pty::kill (pty.rs:345-366) wraps all signalling in `if !self.exited()`, and the SIGKILL escalation depends only on the leader having exited. So once the leader has exited, the process group gets nothing, and members that survive SIGTERM after the leader dies are never SIGKILLed. portable-pty 0.9.0's try_clone_reader (unix.rs:352-354) is `PtyFd(self.fd.try_clone()?)`, a dup of the master fd. The reader thread (pty.rs:186, 207-220) keeps its own master fd, so `self.master.take()` does not end it. It gets EIO only once every slave holder has closed. The module comment at line 3 ('drop master → the reader ends on EIO') is therefore inaccurate, and a surviving slave holder keeps the reader thread and the Arc<Shared> with its ring of up to 8 MiB alive. Callers: session close (handlers/session.rs:1566-1572, 150 ms grace, then the worktree is removed), park/stop (session.rs:371/374/980) and Engine::shutdown (engine.rs:657).
v1.correction: Impact is lower than the finding implies. When the session leader (the provider, which portable-pty setsid()s and gives a TIOCSCTTY) exits, the kernel already sends SIGHUP+SIGCONT to the foreground process group. Only members that ignore SIGHUP and also survive SIGTERM linger, and grandchildren that setsid() or setpgid() away escape -pid either way. The next engine start reaps env-tagged survivors (recovery.rs:67). The fix as proposed stands: always signal -pid, check kill(-pid,0) after the grace and SIGKILL the group, and correct the line-3 comment.

findings.title: Signal deaths are recorded as exit code 1, though the doc promises None
findings.evidence: `let code = child.wait().ok().map(|s| s.exit_code() as i32);`. For a signalled child, portable-pty 0.9's `From<std::process::ExitStatus>` sets `code: status.code().map(|c| c as u32).unwrap_or(1)` and keeps the signal name separately. The doc at pty.rs:165-166 says '(with its exit code, `None` if killed by signal)'.
findings.impact: An agent that is OOM-killed, segfaults or receives SIGKILL is stored as exit_code=1. The slate then says 'The process exited with code 1' (session_context.rs:196-199), indistinguishable from an ordinary error exit, so the crash cause is lost. The documented None appears only when wait() itself fails.
findings.fix: Check `s.signal()` and record None, or a distinct value such as 128+signo, for signal deaths, then update the doc. The UI can then say 'killed by signal'.

v1.reason: pty.rs:227 uses `s.exit_code() as i32`. portable-pty 0.9.0 lib.rs:214-225 maps a signalled std ExitStatus to `code: status.code().map(..).unwrap_or(1)` and keeps the signal name in a separate field. So SIGKILL/SIGSEGV/OOM deaths are stored as exit_code=1 (session.rs:653 `UPDATE sessions SET state='exited',exit_code=?1`), which contradicts the doc at pty.rs:165-166 ('None if killed by signal'). The native slate (session_context.rs:196-199) then shows 'The process exited with code 1'. Relay-initiated kills mostly go through silence_exit or mark_restorable first, so this mainly affects crashes and external kills.
v1.correction: Use `s.signal()` to record None, or 128+signo, and update the doc and the slate text. The impact is diagnostic only: the session still ends as exited and the builder task still becomes failed in either case.

findings.title: Unused PTY and driver accessors and the state behind them
findings.evidence: rg finds no callers in crates/ or apps/ for: Pty::exit_code (283-285) and the Shared.exit_code Mutex it reads (137, 203, 228); Pty::uptime (286-288) and the `started: Instant` field (153, 240); Pty::epoch (247-249); Driver::provider (providers.rs:129, 169, 210).
findings.impact: Each one suggests a feature that does not exist. exit_code costs a Mutex write on every reap that nothing reads.
findings.fix: Delete them. The exit code already reaches the session row through on_exit.

v1.reason: I searched crates/ and apps/ (tests included) and found no caller of Pty::exit_code (pty.rs:283), Pty::uptime (pty.rs:286), Pty::epoch (pty.rs:247) or Driver::provider (providers.rs:129, impls at 169/210). The only `.exit_code()` hits are the ExitStatus call inside the waiter (pty.rs:227) and an unrelated relay-cli one. Because the methods are `pub`, the compiler does not warn about them. The waiter writes Shared.exit_code (pty.rs:228) and nothing ever reads it. The `started: Instant` field (pty.rs:153, set at 240) exists only to serve uptime(). Shared.epoch itself is still used by attach/scrollback/frames; only the accessor is dead.
v1.correction: The per-reap Mutex write is trivial, so the payoff is clarity, not performance. Delete only the accessor Pty::epoch, not Shared.epoch. Removing Driver::provider means editing the trait and both impls (providers.rs:129, 169, 210).

findings.title: Pty::spawn does not check cwd; portable-pty silently falls back to $HOME, where the relative --settings/--mcp-config paths resolve
findings.evidence: `cmd.cwd(&spec.cwd);` with no check. portable-pty 0.9's CommandBuilder::as_command picks `.filter(|dir| Path::new(dir).is_dir()).unwrap_or(home.as_ref())`. prepare_launch checks `cwd.is_dir()` (session.rs:472), but it runs unlocked and the spawn happens later, in finish_launch.
findings.impact: If the worktree disappears between prepare and the locked spawn (deleted outside Relay while the launch waits for the store lock), the agent starts in the user's home. Claude's relative `--mcp-config .relay/relay.mcp.json` and `--settings .relay/relay.settings.json`, and the worktree's .claude/.codex hook files, then resolve against $HOME. The session runs without its Relay guardrail hooks, while RELAY_WORKTREE still names the missing path.
findings.fix: In Pty::spawn, refuse when `!spec.cwd.is_dir()` with a typed error (session.worktree_missing) rather than inheriting the dependency's fallback.

v1.reason: portable-pty 0.9.0 cmdbuilder.rs:506-507 does `.filter(|dir| Path::new(dir).is_dir()).unwrap_or(home.as_ref())`, so a missing cwd quietly becomes $HOME. Pty::spawn (pty.rs:174) passes spec.cwd without checking it. The only check is prepare_launch's `cwd.is_dir()` (handlers/session.rs:472), which runs in the unlocked phase. finish_launch then waits for the store lock, rechecks only the session state and epoch, and spawns. The Claude driver passes relative `--mcp-config`/`--settings`/`--append-system-prompt-file` paths (providers.rs:173-176), so those would resolve against $HOME.
v1.correction: The trigger is a narrow race. The worktree has to be deleted from outside Relay after prepare_launch has just written hook, brief and role files into it, and before finish_launch acquires the lock (normally milliseconds). Relay's own close/discard paths change the session state, and finish_launch's recheck catches that. The most likely result is that Claude fails to start because its relative settings file is missing in $HOME, not a working unguarded session. Bus ops are still token-gated. The cheap defence is still right: check `spec.cwd.is_dir()` in Pty::spawn (or re-check it in finish_launch) and return session.worktree_missing.

findings.title: A timed-out provider probe is recorded as 'not installed', clearing cached version and sign-in and raising a spurious version-changed notification
findings.evidence: On timeout, command_output returns `Some(Output { success: false, stdout: String::new() })` (lines 367-369), so version and signed_in_as become None. `let version_changed = previous_version.is_some() && previous_version != version;` is then true, the provider_cache row's version and signed_in_as are overwritten with NULL, and the handler inserts '<name> version changed' with body '<old> → not installed' (handlers/provider.rs:23-28).
findings.impact: A cold start slower than 3 s, for example with many agents building, produces a false notification and wipes the cached version and account, so the UI shows the provider as signed out until the next refresh. The recovery itself is silent because previous_version is then None.
findings.fix: Treat a failed or timed-out probe as 'unknown' and keep the cached version/signed_in_as. Report a change only when both values are known, or when the executable path disappeared.

v1.reason: command_output (providers.rs:362-369) turns a timed-out probe into Output{success:false}, so the version probe yields None (325) and drv.auth yields None (202/246). refresh then computes version_changed = previous_version.is_some() && previous_version != version (336) as true, overwrites provider_cache.version and signed_in_as with NULL (339-346), and the Refresh handler inserts a notification '<name> version changed' with body '<old> → not installed' (handlers/provider.rs:21-30). The comment at 365-366 shows the 'not installed' mapping is intended, but that does not make it harmless: it produces a false notification and wipes the cached account shown by provider.list. Refresh is user-initiated (tools_settings.rs:400) and also runs right after a successful self-update (provider_updates.rs:62). There a freshly installed binary's slow first start under the 3 s PROBE_TIMEOUT is a realistic trigger; no notification is raised on that path, but the cache is cleared.
v1.correction: An extra trigger: the post-update refresh at provider_updates.rs:62 can clear version/signed_in_as when the new binary's first run is slow. Fix: distinguish a timed-out or failed probe from a missing executable, keep the cached version/signed_in_as on an unknown result, and set version_changed only when both versions are known or the path disappeared.

findings.title: provider_updates::run is a diverged copy of proc::output_with_timeout
findings.evidence: Both functions set process_group(0), pipe stdout/stderr into drain threads, poll try_wait against a deadline, SIGKILL the group and join (proc.rs:28-73). They differ in poll cadence (a flat 10 ms here; 150 µs doubling to 5 ms in proc), output bounding (the first 64 KiB here; unbounded in proc) and drain implementation. Both join the drain threads with no deadline (provider_updates.rs:123-124, proc.rs:64-67).
findings.impact: The two copies have already diverged, and fixes do not propagate between them. In both, a descendant that calls setsid() while keeping the pipe open blocks the join forever. Here that leaves the provider stuck in engine.provider_updates ('An update is already running for this provider.') and the UI at 'Checking for an update…' until restart.
findings.fix: Give proc::output_with_timeout an output cap and a bounded join, call it from run(), and keep only the message shaping here.

v1.reason: provider_updates.rs:92-139 repeats the same steps as proc.rs:28-76: process_group(0), piped stdout/stderr drained on their own threads, a try_wait poll against a deadline, SIGKILL of the group, and an unbounded join of the drain threads. The copies already differ in poll cadence, output capping (64 KiB head here, read_to_end there) and error shape. run() executes on a detached thread after commit (line 55), not under the store mutex, so this is not an invariant break. The unbounded-join hazard is real in both copies: a descendant that leaves the process group (setsid) and keeps the pipe open blocks join, and here provider_updates.remove(name) at line 70 is never reached. That leaves the provider stuck at 'An update is already running' until restart. It needs a self-updater that daemonizes a helper holding stdout, which is rare.
v1.correction: run() can call proc::output_with_timeout(Command::new(path).arg("update"), timeout) and keep only the message shaping. If the cap matters, give the shared helper an optional cap. The unbounded join of drain threads after the group kill is a separate low-risk hazard shared by both copies (proc.rs:66-70, provider_updates.rs:123-124).

findings.title: Update result message comes from the head of the output, with stderr appended after stdout
findings.evidence: `let keep = count.min(65536usize.saturating_sub(saved.len()));` keeps the first 64 KiB of each stream. Then `output.extend(stderr.join()...)` and `output.lines().rev().find(|line| !line.trim().is_empty())` take the last line of stdout followed by stderr.
findings.impact: When an updater prints more than 64 KiB, its final status or error line is discarded and the notification shows a line from the middle. When an updater writes progress to stderr, the reported 'result' is the last stderr line rather than the outcome on stdout.
findings.fix: Keep the last 64 KiB of each stream (a ring), and report stderr's last line on failure and stdout's on success.

v1.reason: provider_updates.rs:85 keeps only the first 65536 bytes of each stream (`count.min(65536usize.saturating_sub(saved.len()))`). Lines 123-130 append the whole of stderr after stdout (`output.extend(stderr.join()...)`) and take the last non-empty line of the combined buffer. So any stderr output at all (a deprecation warning, progress text) replaces stdout's final status line as the notification body on success. That body is inserted into notifications at line 63 and emitted as provider.update.changed. The 64 KiB head truncation is real too, but `claude update` / `codex update` output is normally a few lines, so the stderr ordering is the part that will actually show up. The impact is a misleading notification string and nothing else.
v1.correction: The stderr ordering is the likely trigger. Head truncation only matters for output over 64 KiB, which is unusual for these updaters. Fix: keep each stream separate, report stdout's last line on success and stderr's (falling back to stdout's) on failure, and keep a tail rather than the head if the cap stays.

findings.title: usage.get's reported fallback selects and dates rows by sessions.updated_at and reads every session ever
findings.evidence: `SELECT provider,usage,updated_at FROM sessions WHERE usage IS NOT NULL ORDER BY updated_at DESC,id DESC` loads all rows, including closed sessions, and uses `taken_at` = updated_at (line 57). updated_at changes on every state change, not only on usage.report (line 80). Discovered usage then replaces the result regardless of age (`latest.insert(...)`, line 67).
findings.impact: A session that reported usage hours ago but changed state a minute ago wins over a fresher report from another session, and its stale windows are labelled as taken a minute ago. Every call also reads and parses the usage JSON of every session ever created, under the store lock.
findings.fix: Record the report time with the payload (a usage_at column via a migration, or embedded in the stored JSON), select the newest per provider with LIMIT 1, and compare taken_at before letting file-discovered usage override.

v1.reason: handlers/provider.rs:47 selects `provider,usage,updated_at FROM sessions WHERE usage IS NOT NULL ORDER BY updated_at DESC,id DESC` and takes the first row per provider (or_insert_with), with taken_at = updated_at (line 57). sessions.updated_at is also bumped by every state change (sessions.rs:165, `UPDATE sessions SET state = ?1, updated_at = ?2`), not only by usage.report (line 80). So session A reports, then session B reports later, then A changes state (e.g. exits), and A's older windows win, labelled with A's state-change time. The query is not limited to open sessions, so it reads every usage-bearing row ever written. In practice the effect is narrow. No hook or CLI path calls usage.report automatically (rg finds it only in role allowlists and tests), so rows come only from agents that call the MCP tool. Outside the Test instance, file-discovered usage (usage.rs read_claude/read_codex) replaces the reported entry whenever it exists (line 67), and that data comes from the provider itself.
v1.correction: The impact is lower than stated.
