The reported fallback is only seen when file discovery finds nothing, and usage rows exist only when agents choose to call usage.report, so 'every session ever' is a small set in practice. A cheap fix that needs no migration: embed the report time in the stored usage JSON (or select by a dedicated usage_at column if one is added later), and filter to the newest row per provider.

findings.title: spawn_profile is a hand-written duplicate of args() that has already drifted and is served from a stale DB cache
findings.evidence: Claude's 'resume' profile omits [--model]/[--effort], which args() appends on resume (line 188). Codex's 'resume' omits model/effort too (line 226). Neither profile lists the --add-dir, notify and plugin --config arguments that session.rs:541-559 appends. list() serves the cached copy, `cached.unwrap_or((None, None, None, None, drv.profile()))` (303-304), which refresh writes to provider_cache (338-345). No client reads spawn_profile; only a test does.
findings.impact: provider.list documents a command line Relay does not run. After a Relay upgrade it keeps showing the previous version's profile until someone clicks Refresh, and every argument change has to be made in two places.
findings.fix: Derive the profile by calling args() with a placeholder session (or drop the field), and stop storing it in provider_cache.

v1.reason: Claude::profile's 'resume' (providers.rs:196) omits the [--model]/[--effort] that args() appends on resume (line 188). Codex::profile's resume (239-240) omits the model/effort args added at line 226. Neither profile lists the notify, plugin mcp_servers or --add-dir arguments that session.rs ~541-559 appends. list() (303-304) serves the spawn_profile cached by the last refresh (338-345), so it stays stale across upgrades until provider.refresh runs. A grep finds no in-scope consumer of spawn_profile beyond the bus type and one test (tests/sessions.rs:666), so the drift costs only accuracy and double maintenance.
v1.correction: Lowest-cost fix: list() always returns drv.profile() rather than the cached column (the column is NOT NULL in store.rs:193, so refresh can keep writing it, or a migration can drop it). Better: derive the profile from args() with placeholders, or drop the field, since no in-scope client reads it.

findings.title: Ring trims after extending, so the VecDeque grows to as much as 16 MiB per PTY and copies the ring on growth
findings.evidence: `self.buf.extend(data); if self.buf.len() > SCROLLBACK_BYTES { let excess = ...; self.buf.drain(..excess); ... }`. Once len reaches a capacity near 8 MiB, the next extend triggers RawVec's amortized growth (max(2×cap, needed)), copying the whole ring under the ring lock, and the capacity never shrinks. A resumed PTY's first push is the saved history, which can exceed 8 MiB after lossy UTF-8 expansion.
findings.impact: Depending on the first frame's size, each full ring ends up with between 8 and 16+ MiB of capacity, and as the window rotates through the buffer all of it becomes resident. With 10-20 sessions that is tens to about 160 MiB of avoidable RSS, plus a one-off 8 MiB memcpy on each PTY's reader thread.
findings.fix: Create the ring with `VecDeque::with_capacity(SCROLLBACK_BYTES + 64 * 1024)` (virtual until touched), or trim before extending and push only the last SCROLLBACK_BYTES of an oversized slice.

v1.reason: pty.rs:190 creates the ring with `VecDeque::new()`. Ring::push (pty.rs:65-70) calls `self.buf.extend(data)` before trimming. Once the ring is full (len == SCROLLBACK_BYTES) every push asks for len+n > 8 MiB. VecDeque's reserve goes through RawVec's amortized growth (max(2*cap, required)), so the capacity becomes about 16 MiB, and growing copies the whole 8 MiB while the ring lock is held. Capacity never shrinks. Because drain(..excess) only moves the head, the window travels around the whole 16 MiB buffer, so over time every page gets touched and stays resident. Any session that produces more than 8 MiB of output (common for long agent runs) ends up holding about 16 MiB instead of 8.
v1.correction: The doubling does not depend on the size of the first frame. Any ring that fills settles at about 2x SCROLLBACK_BYTES, because the extend-then-trim order always asks for more than the cap once the ring is full. The cost is about 8 MiB of extra RSS per long-lived session, plus a one-time 8 MiB memcpy under the ring lock on the reader thread (attach/scrollback wait for it). Fix: trim before extending (drain max(0, len+n-cap) first, and keep only the last SCROLLBACK_BYTES of an oversized slice), or allocate with_capacity(SCROLLBACK_BYTES + 64 KiB) up front.

findings.title: Tombstoned skills keep their UNIQUE name forever; skill.update and some installs hit conflicts the user cannot see or clear
findings.evidence: skill.update's duplicate check, `SELECT id FROM skills WHERE name=?1 COLLATE NOCASE AND id!=?2`, includes soft-deleted rows and answers 'that name is used by skill {id}', a skill that skill.list hides. In install_downloaded_skill, when name_match is a tombstone different from source_match, every reclaim arm requires `source_match.is_none()`, so it falls into the conflict arm with can_replace false (455-487). The hint says 'remove one explicitly before refreshing', but both rows may already be removed. store.rs:260 declares name UNIQUE COLLATE NOCASE.
findings.impact: Renaming a skill to the name of any skill ever deleted is refused, citing an invisible id. A refresh whose upstream name now equals a deleted local skill's name becomes a permanent conflict that cannot be cleared from the UI.
findings.fix: When the conflicting row is a tombstone, free its name (rename it to a unique placeholder or hard-delete it) and proceed.

v1.reason: store.rs:260 declares `name TEXT NOT NULL COLLATE NOCASE UNIQUE`, and deletes are soft. skill.update's duplicate check (handlers/provider.rs:157-163), `SELECT id FROM skills WHERE name=?1 COLLATE NOCASE AND id!=?2`, does not filter deleted_at. Renaming a local skill in the native editor (tools_skills.rs:469-472) to the name of any removed skill is therefore refused with 'that name is used by skill N', an id skill.list hides (line 91 filters deleted_at IS NULL). In install_downloaded_skill (lines 455-487), when name_match is a tombstone whose id differs from an existing source_match, both reclaim arms require source_match.is_none(). Control falls to the conflict arm with can_replace false and the hint 'remove one explicitly before refreshing'. Removal leaves a tombstone, so the conflict persists. That install path needs an upstream rename onto a deleted local skill's name, which is rare.
v1.correction: A non-obvious workaround exists: skill.create with the tombstone's name revives it, and a skill.update rename then frees the name. The user-visible part is mostly the skill.update refusal. The minimal fix is to exclude tombstones from the duplicate check and free a tombstone's name (rename to a placeholder or hard-delete) before the UPDATE, and to do the same in the install conflict arm when name_match is a tombstone.

findings.title: enable_everywhere re-enables a skill the user switched off everywhere whenever it is refreshed or revived
findings.evidence: `if edges == 0 { conn.execute("INSERT OR IGNORE INTO skill_projects(skill_id,project_id) SELECT ?1,id FROM projects", [id]) }` runs on every install (line 509), including 'Update from GitHub', and on skill.create's revive path (line 144). Disabling a skill in every project deletes all its edges (line 199), which is indistinguishable from 'never enabled'. The function's comment claims 'An explicit per-project switch is still honoured'. D147 describes auto-enable 'on create/install' and does not single out refresh.
findings.impact: A user who turns a skill off in every project and later clicks 'Update from GitHub' finds it on again in all projects and materialized into every checkout.
findings.fix: Auto-enable only on the first insert of a row (or record an explicit-disable marker) rather than whenever the edge set is empty.

v1.reason: enable_everywhere (provider.rs:515-527) inserts edges for every project whenever COUNT(*) of the skill's edges is 0. install_downloaded_skill calls it on every install, including the refresh path where target_id is an existing row (provider.rs:509). The native 'Update from GitHub' button (tools_skills.rs:174-180) sends skill.install with the skill's own source_url and source_path. SkillEnable with enabled=false deletes the edge (provider.rs:204), so a skill the user turned off in every project has zero edges, which looks the same as 'never enabled'. Refreshing it re-enables it everywhere and materializes it into every checkout. This contradicts the function's own comment ('An explicit per-project switch is still honoured'), and D147 only describes auto-enable 'on create/install'. On the skill.create revive path (provider.rs:144), re-enabling a deleted skill whose edges are all gone is arguably the intended behaviour, so the refresh path is the real bug.
v1.correction: The decisive trigger is the refresh path at provider.rs:509 (target_id = Some(existing)); the skill.create revive path is defensible. Fix: call enable_everywhere only when a row was just INSERTed, not when an existing row is updated or revived by source match.

findings.title: skill.enable bumps skills.updated_at, which is the materialization stamp, so one toggle recopies the folder in every checkout
findings.evidence: `ctx.tx().execute("UPDATE skills SET updated_at=?1 WHERE id=?2", ..)` runs on every enable or disable. skills.rs:157 builds the stamp as `format!("{id} {updated_at} {revision}\n")`, and write_skill removes and recopies any folder whose stamp differs, up to 64 MiB / 4000 files (skills.rs:308-347).
findings.impact: Toggling a skill in one project deletes and recopies its unchanged folder in every other project root, every session worktree and both user-scope folders. While a copy is in progress, an agent loading that skill can find it missing or half-written.
findings.fix: Derive the stamp from content (body hash plus revision), or do not bump updated_at for an edge-only change.

v1.reason: provider.rs:207 runs `UPDATE skills SET updated_at=?1 WHERE id=?2` on every skill.enable, whether it turns the skill on or off. skills.rs:157 (row_of) builds the materializer stamp as `format!("{id} {updated_at} {revision}\n")`. write_skill (skills.rs:308-321) skips a folder only when its marker equals the stamp. Otherwise fill (skills.rs:324) runs `remove_dir_all(dest)` and copies the whole library folder again. So one toggle in project X rewrites the unchanged folder in every other project root, every open session worktree and both user-scope bases (enabled_anywhere) where the skill is enabled. While a folder is being rewritten, an agent that loads the skill can find it missing or partly written. The cost is low: skill folders are usually small, and the refresh runs on a background thread, not under the store lock.
v1.correction: Do not just remove the bump. updated_at is also the undo precondition (set_undo passes `{"updated_at":skill.updated_at}`) and the version carried by the skill.changed event. A better fix is to separate the materialization stamp from updated_at: derive it from the content (a hash of the body, plus revision and id), or keep a separate content-version column that only body, name and asset changes bump.

findings.title: GitHub ops registered here fork gh/git with no timeout (CLAUDE.md: every handler subprocess goes through proc::output_with_timeout)
findings.evidence: github.status calls github::status(), which runs `gh api user` with plain `.output()` (github.rs:45). github.repo.list runs `gh api --paginate` the same way (github.rs:68-70). skill.install's prepare phase calls download_skills, which runs `git clone --depth 1 ...` via `.output()` (github.rs:106-109) and `git rev-parse` (github.rs:155-156). github.connect's thread runs `gh auth login --web` via `.status()` with no bound and no single-flight guard (github.rs:56-63).
findings.impact: These run unlocked, so they do not freeze the bus. But a stalled network call, or a credential helper waiting on a dialog, leaves the request hanging indefinitely and leaks a blocking-pool thread and a child process per attempt; onboarding retries pile them up. Each click on Connect starts another concurrent browser login.
findings.fix: Route these calls through proc::output_with_timeout with network-sized deadlines (30-120 s), and keep at most one github.connect in flight.

v1.reason: github.rs:45 (`gh api user`), :68-70 (`gh api --paginate`), :106-109 (`git clone --depth 1`) and :155 (`git rev-parse`) all use plain Command::output(), not proc::output_with_timeout. Each one is forked from a bus handler (github.status and github.repo.list through register_unlocked, and skill.install's prepare). This breaks the CLAUDE.md rule that every subprocess forked from a handler goes through output_with_timeout. Git sets no default low-speed timeout. A stalled network connection, or a credential helper GUI prompting for a private or misspelt https repository, can block the child indefinitely. The impact is worse than the finding says. socket.rs:741 awaits each spawn_blocking dispatch before it reads the next line, so a connection serves its requests one at a time. The native app sends github.status and github.repo.list (onboarding.rs:422/429) and skill.install (tools_skills.rs:180/370) over its shared UI connection: app.rs:1111 `call` uses self.client, and only lifecycle ops get a connection of their own. A hung child therefore stalls every later UI request on that connection: each one times out on the client side until the child exits. That is a UI freeze, not just a leaked thread. The trigger (a network stall or a credential prompt) is uncommon, so the right severity is medium.
v1.correction: Stronger mechanism: requests on a socket connection are served serially (socket.rs:741), so a hung gh or git call blocks the native client's shared connection (app.rs:1111), not only a pool thread. The github.connect part is weak. `gh auth login --web` runs after_commit on its own thread, it is bounded by device-code expiry, and onboarding.rs:444 disables the Connect button until the flow fails. The 'concurrent browser logins pile up' claim is therefore mostly unfounded. git rev-parse is local and low risk. Fix: route `gh api` and `git clone` through proc::output_with_timeout with network-sized deadlines, and set GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0 on the clone.

findings.title: skill.update body edits never reach the materialized SKILL.md of a skill that has a library folder
findings.evidence: `UPDATE skills SET name=?1,body=?2,updated_at=?3 WHERE id=?4 AND deleted_at IS NULL` changes the row. Materialization copies library_dir(id), which contains the downloaded SKILL.md, and writes the row body only `if !instructions.is_file()` (skills.rs:340-344).
findings.impact: For a GitHub-installed skill edited over the bus (CLI/MCP), or a local skill that inherited a library folder (see the revive and rollback findings), skill.list shows the new body but every .claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md and .agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md keeps the old text. session-skills.md (the brief's full text) carries the new body, so agents see two different versions of the instructions.
findings.fix: Always write the row body as SKILL.md after copying the library folder, treating the folder only as the asset carrier. Alternatively, refuse body edits for sourced skills at the op level.

v1.reason: skill.update (handlers/provider.rs:165-166) changes only the row's name and body. skills.rs fill (lines 325-346) copies library_dir(id), which contains the downloaded SKILL.md, and writes row.body only when SKILL.md is absent. The stamp (`{id} {updated_at} {revision}`, skills.rs:157) does change, so folders are rewritten, but with the library's old SKILL.md. The native UI offers Edit only for skills without a source (tools_skills.rs:163-194), so the reachable triggers are skill.update over the CLI/MCP on a GitHub skill, and a local skill that inherited a library folder (the #7 revive).
v1.correction: This shares its root with #7: fill gives the library SKILL.md precedence over the row body. Either always write row.body as SKILL.md after the copy, or refuse body edits for sourced skills at the op level. Fixing #7 removes the main UI-reachable trigger, leaving only CLI/MCP edits of sourced skills.

findings.title: read_codex aborts the whole scan when one file's 1 MiB tail starts inside a UTF-8 character
findings.evidence: `let raw = read_tail(&path, CODEX_TAIL).ok()?;` returns None from read_codex on the first unreadable file, without moving on to the next. read_tail seeks to len-1 MiB and calls `file.read_to_string(&mut raw)?` (line 96), which fails with InvalidData if the seek lands inside a multi-byte character. The partial first line is only dropped afterwards (line 98).
findings.impact: For any rollout over 1 MiB whose byte at len-1 MiB is a UTF-8 continuation byte (common in CJK, accented or emoji-heavy sessions; 0 of 181 such files on this machine today), or any file that cannot be opened, Codex usage disappears entirely for that read, even when the next file holds valid data.
findings.fix: Read the tail into a Vec<u8>, skip past the first b'\n', then use String::from_utf8_lossy. On a per-file error, `continue` instead of using `?`.

v1.reason: usage.rs:61 `let raw = read_tail(&path, CODEX_TAIL).ok()?;` makes read_codex return None on the first file that fails, instead of moving to the next of the 32. read_tail (usage.rs:90-101) seeks to len-1 MiB and calls `read_to_string` (line 96), which returns InvalidData if the seek lands inside a multi-byte UTF-8 sequence. The same happens if the file ends in a partially flushed multi-byte character while Codex is appending to it. The partial first line is only dropped afterwards (line 98). Because files are sorted newest-first, the file most likely to be large and actively written is the one tried first, so one bad tail hides all Codex usage for that call.
v1.correction: Also covers a truncated trailing character in a file still being written, not just the seek point. The fix is right: read the bytes, skip to the first b'\n', use from_utf8_lossy, and `continue` on per-file errors.

findings.title: Single-use SaturatingSubF64 trait reimplements (a - b).max(0.0)
findings.evidence: `trait SaturatingSubF64 { fn saturating_sub(self, rhs: Self) -> Self; } impl SaturatingSubF64 for f64 { fn saturating_sub(self, rhs: Self) -> Self { (self - rhs).max(0.0) } }` is used exactly once, at line 172.
findings.impact: It is a module-level trait for one expression, and it gives f64 an integer-style method name that reads as if std provided it.
findings.fix: Inline `(seconds - now).max(0.0) as u64` at line 172 and delete the trait.

v1.reason: crates/relay-core/src/usage.rs:183-184 defines a private module-level `trait SaturatingSubF64` with a single impl for f64, `(self - rhs).max(0.0)`. An rg search for `saturating_sub` in the file finds exactly one f64 call site, line 172 in reset_label: `let remaining = seconds.saturating_sub(now) as u64;`. Line 93 also calls `saturating_sub`, but that is the std integer method on a usize length. The trait exists only to serve that one expression, and its name hides the fact that it is a local helper rather than std. Behaviour is correct, so this is cleanup only.
v1.correction: An even simpler fix is available. Since Rust 1.45, an f64-to-u64 `as` cast saturates: negative values become 0 and NaN becomes 0. So `(seconds - now) as u64` at line 172 gives exactly the same result with no `.max(0.0)`. Writing `(seconds - now).max(0.0) as u64` is also fine if the clamp should be explicit. Either way, delete lines 183-184.

results.coverage:

findings.title: avd.create and avd.boot run avdmanager/emulator/adb subprocesses while holding the store mutex, mostly with no deadline
findings.evidence: Both are registered with `e.register` (lines 321, 344), so they run inside the request transaction with the store lock held (engine.rs:953-980). AvdCreate spawns `avdmanager create avd` and blocks on `child.wait_with_output()` (line 335) with no timeout, then calls `list_avds(ctx.tx())?` (line 339). AvdBoot calls `list_avds(ctx.tx())?` (line 346). `list_avds` -> `list_avds_with` runs `Command::new(emulator).arg("-list-avds").output()` (line 478) and `running_avds_with`, which runs `adb devices -l` (2 s bound) and then `Command::new(adb).args(["-s", &device.serial, "emu", "avd", "name"]).output()` for each running emulator (line 505), with no bound. D149 (DECISIONS.md:797-814) moved avd.list and avd.catalog off the lock but missed these two.
findings.impact: Every avd.create freezes all other bus ops (UI refreshes, agent MCP calls, session ops) for the JVM start plus the creation, which is seconds. If an emulator console is wedged (`adb emu avd name` against a frozen or paused emulator) or avdmanager hangs, the whole engine freezes until it is restarted. Also, if the listing after creation fails (for example the emulator binary is missing or errors), the `?` at line 339 reports avd.create_failed even though the AVD was created, and a retry then fails with 'already exists'.
findings.fix: Register both with `register_staged`. In prepare, resolve the tool paths via `ctx.read` and run `avdmanager create` and the listing through `proc::output_with_timeout` (roughly 120 s for create, 10 s for -list-avds, 3 s per `emu avd name`). Finish only emits `avd.changed`. Make the post-create listing non-fatal by falling back to the `Avd` already built. Put `list_avds_with`/`running_avds_with` behind output_with_timeout for avd.list as well.

v1.reason: AvdCreate and AvdBoot are registered with `e.register` (handlers/device.rs:321, 344), so they run with the store mutex held. AvdCreate spawns `avdmanager create avd` and blocks on `child.wait_with_output()` with no deadline (lines 333-335). avdmanager starts a JVM, which takes seconds. AvdCreate then calls `list_avds(ctx.tx())?` (line 339). AvdBoot calls list_avds before booting (line 346). list_avds_with runs `Command::new(emulator).arg("-list-avds").output()` (line 478) with no deadline. running_avds_with runs `adb devices -l` (bounded at 2 s) and then, for each running emulator, `adb -s <serial> emu avd name` via a plain `.output()` (line 505) with no deadline. Both break the CLAUDE.md rule that every subprocess forked from a handler goes through proc::output_with_timeout, and slow work under register. D149 converted avd.list and avd.catalog to register_unlocked but left these two. The native client reaches both ops (tools_devices.rs:110, 419, 656). The finding's post-create error is also real: the `?` on line 339 turns a listing failure, such as a missing emulator binary in sdk_tool or a failing -list-avds, into an error after the AVD was already created on disk.
v1.correction: An avdmanager hang on stdin is not a risk: std's wait_with_output drops stdin before waiting, so the child sees EOF after "no\n". The routine impact is a bus stall of several seconds on every avd.create, plus up to about 2 s on avd.boot. A hang that lasts until restart needs a wedged emulator console or a stuck avdmanager, which is rare but has no bound. The related avd.catalog path (line 315) runs `avdmanager list device -c` with no timeout; it holds no lock, but it still breaks the proc::output_with_timeout rule. Fix as proposed: register_staged for both ops, every subprocess through output_with_timeout, and a non-fatal post-create listing.

v2.reason:
(a) The code does what the finding says. AvdCreate (device.rs:321) and AvdBoot (:344) use `e.register`, so dispatch_inner holds `self.store.lock()` (one Mutex<Connection>, store.rs:377/474) for the whole handler (engine.rs:953-980). AvdCreate blocks on `child.wait_with_output()` for avdmanager with no deadline (:332-335). Both then call the locked `list_avds` (:339, :346). That wrapper runs `emulator -list-avds` through a plain `.output()` (:478) and `adb -s <serial> emu avd name` through a plain `.output()` for each emulator in `device` state (:505). This breaks D144 ("every subprocess forked from a handler goes through proc::output_with_timeout") and D149, whose list of converted ops does not include avd.create or avd.boot. No DECISIONS entry exempts them. Only these two ops use the locked wrapper.

(b) Reachability. Both ops are UserOnly mutations, reached from the native Devices page (the Boot, Cold boot and Create AVD buttons at tools_devices.rs:110/117/419/656/663), from the CLI, or from a paired phone through the bridge. Agents cannot call them. The user has a real SDK and an existing AVD (~/.android/avd/Tally_API36), so this is a flow they actually use. It is infrequent, though: creating or booting an emulator.

Measured on this machine, the routine lock hold is short. avdmanager `list avd -c` takes 388-392 ms, `list device -c` 388-445 ms, `list target -c` 294 ms, and `emulator -list-avds` 13 ms. The installed android-36 image has no userdata.img to copy, and Relay never passes `-c`, so no SD card is built. avd.create should therefore hold the lock for about 0.5-2 s (a cold JVM is the high end), not "several seconds". avd.boot normally holds it for tens of ms, and at most about 2 s, because `adb devices -l` is bounded by ADB_LIST_TIMEOUT and its failure is swallowed by `.transpose().ok()`.

The unbounded case is real, and I verified it. In a scratchpad experiment, a loopback listener accepted connections and never replied. `adb -s emulator-5990 emu avd name` (adb 1.0.41 / 37.0.0) then blocked until an outer `timeout 8` killed it (exit 124). With a serial given, adb connects straight to the console port and has no deadline of its own. The trigger is a running emulator that adb still lists as `device` but whose console no longer answers (for example a frozen or SIGSTOPped emulator), at the moment the user clicks Boot or Create on a page that was already rendered. This is rare. There is a further limit: if the Devices page renders while the console is wedged, the unlocked avd.list hangs first on the same probe. socket.rs handle_conn handles each connection serially (the loop at :335 awaits each spawn_blocking dispatch), so the UI's control connection then stays stuck, and avd.create or avd.boot from the UI is never dispatched at all.

(c) Consequence. Keystrokes, resizes and mirror input are unaffected: they take the lock-free fast paths (engine.rs:891-903), each terminal pane has its own connection (terminal.rs:476), and PTY reader threads do not take the store lock. For the routine stall, the lock blocks every other connection for about 0.5-2 s. That covers agents (check_session_token locks the store; the relay-cli Client::call has no timeout, so MCP calls and session.report hooks just wait), the phone door, the CLI and background system_write. The UI's own connection waits on avd.create whatever the registration, because the per-connection loop is serial. In the wedged-console case, every store-dependent op freezes until the engine restarts. LockSpan only logs and there is no watchdog. Restarting the engine ends the running agent sessions.

(d) Severity. "High" is overstated under the rubric. The routine effect is a sub-second-to-2-second stall during a rare, user-only action, which is barely visible. The engine-wide hang is a severe outcome behind an uncommon trigger in a less common path. That is "a real bug in a less common path or edge case", so medium. It still clearly breaks a documented invariant and should be fixed.

(e) Fix. The direction is right (register_staged, bounded subprocesses, a non-fatal post-create listing), but as written it is incomplete and partly wrong. See the correction.
v2.correction:
1. Severity: medium, not high. The routine lock hold is roughly 0.5-2 s per avd.create (avdmanager measured at about 0.3-0.45 s warm on this machine) and tens of ms per avd.boot. The "several seconds of JVM start" framing overstates it. The engine-wide unbounded hang needs a running emulator whose console is wedged while adb still lists it as `device`. Keystrokes and PTY output are never affected.

2. Error code: if the post-create listing fails, the error is `avd.tool_missing` (sdk_tool) or `avd.list_failed` (list_avds_with), not `avd.create_failed`. The rest of that claim holds: the AVD already exists on disk, so a retry fails with avdmanager's "already exists" error. It is unlikely, because system-image packages depend on the emulator package.

3. The fix as written would break AVD creation. `proc::output_with_timeout` hard-codes `stdin(Stdio::null())` (proc.rs:35). In cmdline-tools 23.0 (disassembled with javap from sdklib/libavdmanager_lib.jar), `AvdManagerCli.createAvd` calls `promptForHardware()` whenever no valid `--device` is given, which is exactly the UI's "SDK default" profile, since device=None. That method calls `readLine`, which on EOF runs `new String(buf, 0, -1)` and throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException. The exception is not caught as an IOException, so avdmanager fails. A correct fix either passes avdmanager's global `-s`/`--silent` flag (then `promptForHardware` skips `readLine` and takes the "no" default) or gives output_with_timeout a variant that still writes "no\n" to stdin.

4. A simpler and safer fix for the probes: neither op uses `running_serial`. AvdBoot only checks names, and an AVD that was just created cannot be running. Calling `list_avds_with(&emulator, None)` in both therefore drops the unbounded `adb emu avd name` calls from them with no behavior change. That leaves `emulator -list-avds` to bound with output_with_timeout (it takes about 13 ms). Use register_staged for both ops. AvdCreate writes nothing to the database, so finish only emits `avd.changed` and returns the Avd.

5. The unlocked paths need bounds too. Bound `adb emu avd name` (about 2-3 s) for avd.list and `avdmanager list device -c` (avd.catalog, :315). Holding no lock does not make them safe: a hang there wedges the UI's serial control connection indefinitely, so the whole UI stops updating.

6. register_staged frees other connections (agents, phone, CLI), but not the UI's own control connection, which handle_conn processes serially. That is acceptable at about 0.5 s. If it ever matters, run the creation in an after_commit worker that emits `avd.changed` when it finishes, as avd.boot already does for the emulator launch.

findings.title: A device.run.stop that arrives before the worker registers its child is lost; the worker still builds and installs, then rewrites the stopped row
findings.evidence: RunStop (lines 263-283) calls `runtime.stop()`, releases the run's lease and writes state='stopped'. `RunRuntime::stop` (device.rs:403-408) can only kill a child that is already in the slot, and `RunRuntime::set_child` (device.rs:373-375) stores a child without checking `stopped()`. By contrast, `DeviceWatchRuntime::install` (device.rs:33-41) kills a late child. run_worker never checks `runtime.stopped()` between phases. It runs `sync_primary_checkout(&root)` (line 1665: git status, a network `git fetch`, then `merge --ff-only`). Then `stream_command` spawns the build and calls `runtime.set_child(child)` (line 1841), and its loop returns `Streamed::Stopped` on the first line (line 1844) without killing anything. After a successful build the worker runs `logcat -c`, `am start -W` and up to 10 s of pid polling, then `advance_run(..., "running", false)` (line 1734). That function's SQL is `UPDATE device_runs SET state=?1 ... WHERE id=?4` (line 2194) with no state guard, and `fail_run` (2157) and `finish_build` (2171) are just as unconditional.
findings.impact: Pressing Stop in the first seconds of a primary-checkout run (during the sync and fetch) does not stop it. The checkout is still fast-forwarded, then Gradle `installDebug` starts and nothing ever kills it. It installs onto a device whose lease RunStop already released, so another session can be installing at the same time, which is exactly the clobbering that leases exist to prevent. Pressing Stop during launch or the pid wait still launches the app and flips the row back to 'running' with no runtime behind it. The run list then shows a live run that cannot be attached (`device.run_not_live`), `project.remove` keeps refusing without force, and an `adb logcat` child is left running and unreaped.
findings.fix: Make `RunRuntime::set_child` kill the child and return false when `stopped()` is already set (as `DeviceWatchRuntime::install` does), and have callers bail out on false. Check `runtime.stopped()` before the sync, before spawning, before the launch and before each `advance_run`. Guard every worker write with `AND state IN ('building','running')` and skip the event when no row changed.

v1.reason: Checked independently. RunStop (handlers/device.rs:253-274) removes the runtime from engine.device_runs, calls runtime.stop(), releases the run's leases and writes state='stopped'. RunRuntime::stop (device.rs:403-408) sets the flag and kills only a child that is already in the slot. RunRuntime::set_child (device.rs:373-375) stores the child without checking the flag. run_worker (handlers/device.rs:1652) never checks runtime.stopped() before or after sync_primary_checkout (line 1665). sync_primary is the default for any run of the project root without an integration (line 161). It also does not check the flag before stream_command or before the launch. If Stop lands during the sync, stream_command spawns the build anyway. set_child stores it unkilled (line 1841), the loop sees stopped() on the first output line and returns Streamed::Stopped (1843-1845) without killing or waiting, and the Child is dropped. Gradle keeps running and installs onto a device whose lease RunStop already released. If Stop lands after the build, during logcat -c, resolve-activity, `am start -W` or the pidof wait of up to 10 s, the worker still launches the app and calls advance_run(...,"running",false) (line 1734). That UPDATE (around line 2194) has no state guard, so the row goes from 'stopped' back to 'running'. Then set_child(logcat) stores the logcat child unkilled, the loop returns on its first line, and the worker returns without killing or reaping it. RunStop already removed the runtime, so nothing writes the row again: it stays 'running' with no runtime behind it. fail_run and finish_build are just as unguarded, so a stopped run whose launch then fails is shown as 'failed'.
v1.correction: The relevant RunStop lines are handlers/device.rs:253-274, not 263-283. A related issue that widens the window (plausible, not fully established): stream_command spawns `fish -lc "<cmd> 2>&1"` without process_group, and stop() kills only that shell PID. A Gradle wrapper or java child launched by the shell is not signalled, so Stop in the middle of the build may also leave installDebug running. A fix should kill the whole process group, e.g. process_group(0) at spawn and kill(-pgid) in stop(). The rest of the proposed fix is right: set_child kills the child and returns false once stopped() is set, the worker checks stopped() between phases, and every worker write is guarded with `AND state IN ('building','running')`, with no event emitted when no row changed.

v2.reason:
(a) The code does what the finding says. Checked at 361c6f9:
- RunStop (handlers/device.rs:263-285) removes the runtime from the map, calls stop(), releases the run's lease (268) and writes 'stopped'.
- RunRuntime::stop (device.rs:403-408) kills only a child that is already in the slot. set_child (373-375) stores the child without checking the flag. DeviceWatchRuntime::install (33-41) does check it.
- run_worker never calls stopped() before the sync (1665), before stream_command (1674), before the launch (1690) or before advance_run (1734).
- stream_command spawns the command and calls set_child (1841). On the first line it returns Stopped (1843-1844) without killing or waiting. The Child is then dropped along with the last Arc, which does not kill it.
- The UPDATEs at 2194 (advance_run), in fail_run (2157) and at 2171 (finish_build) have no state guard. system_write (engine.rs:687) adds none either.

(b) Who can trigger it, and how often:
- Window 1 is on the default path. The Devices page's "Build from" defaults to "Primary · project branch" (tools_devices.rs:232-233), which sends worktree None, so sync_primary is true (161). The sync is a gix dirty scan plus `git fetch` with no timeout (worktree.rs:26-27) and no output. That silent phase is exactly when a user presses Stop.
- Window 2 comes after every successful build: logcat -c, resolve-activity, `am start -W`, and up to 10 s of pidof polling. Agent-menu installs pass a worktree (agent_menu.rs:742), so they skip the sync but still have window 2.
- build_worker has the same gap: load_signing_secret can wait up to 15 s (1880) before stream_command (1902), and that build may be `publish<Variant><Format>`.
- The trigger is the user's Stop button (Devices history or agent menu), or project.remove with force.

(c) What happens:
- Window 1: the fast-forward still happens, which is low-impact because D92 keeps it safe. Gradle is then spawned and never killed. A second Stop does nothing because the runtime is already gone from the map. The device lease is already free. That lease also gates agents' shell `adb install` and `gradlew installDebug` through the guardrail hook (handlers/device_lease.rs:1-2, Kind::Shell). So an agent or another run is admitted onto a device that is still being installed to.
- Caveat for window 1: with a cold Gradle daemon, the worker's early return deletes the --init-script temp file, which may make the orphaned build fail. With the usual warm daemon the script has already been read.
- Window 2: the app launches and the row goes from 'stopped' back to 'running', with a run.changed event. It stays that way until the user presses Stop again (which works, because RunStop only needs the row) or the next startup's recovery (recovery.rs:114). engine.shutdown skips its UPDATE when the map is empty (engine.rs:641).
- Meanwhile project.remove refuses (workspace.rs:315). The agent menu says "Stopped before the install finished." (agent_menu.rs:779) although the app was installed and launched. logcat is never killed or reaped. A failed launch or sync after Stop relabels the run 'failed'.

(d) Severity: each window alone lasts seconds, which on its own would be medium. High holds because:
- a lost Stop silently frees the device lease while an install is still running, which is the rubric's "safety check silently bypassed";
- window 1 is the default path and lines up with the silent fetch;
- through the shell-only kill (see correction), the same "Stop is ignored" outcome covers the entire build, including Play publishes, which D152 says cannot be recalled.

v2.correction:
1. Line numbers: RunStop is handlers/device.rs:263-285. The finding's 263-283 was right; the first verifier's 253-274 is wrong, because line 253 is the end of the SigningCreate registration.

2. Drop the claim that the run "cannot be attached (device.run_not_live)". The only attach happens inside the device.run / device.build response (socket.rs:660). No op attaches to an existing run.

3. The first verifier's process-group point is now established, not just plausible:
- A scratch experiment showed fish 4.9.3 `-c 'sleep 7.31 2>&1'` forks the command instead of exec'ing it, and the child survived a SIGKILL to the fish PID.
- fish runs no job control under -c, and stream_command (1822-1831) sets no process_group, so the whole tree shares the engine's process group.
- So stop() during a build kills only fish. The gradlew/java child keeps the pipe open, the worker returns Stopped on the next line, and Gradle very likely completes installDebug or the Play publish. The JVM ignores SIGPIPE; that the Gradle client keeps going after its stdout breaks is my inference, not tested.
- Tests cannot see any of this. Instance::Test uses sh (1821), and the tests assert only the row state. The hold test (bus.rs:614-630) even waits for the "$ ./gradlew assembleHold" line, which is pushed before the spawn (1817), so its own Stop can land in this race.

4. Add to related: handlers/device.rs:1880 (secret lookup before 1902, publish path), 1776-1777 and 1843-1844 (early returns that neither kill nor reap the child), 1821-1841 (spawn with no process group).

5. Completing the fix:
- Spawn both the run command and logcat with process_group(0), and send kill(-pid) in stop() and in set_child when stop has already been called. proc.rs:32/55/65 already uses this pattern.
- On every Stopped or early return, take_child, kill and wait.
- Check stopped() after the sync, before the spawn, before the launch, between pidof polls, and after load_signing_secret.
- Make the worker writes conditional (`AND state IN ('building','running')`) and have them report whether a row changed. When none changed, emit nothing and tear down instead of streaming logcat.

findings.title: RunRuntime::stop kills only the `fish -lc` wrapper, so Gradle keeps building and installing after Stop releases the device lease
findings.evidence: `stream_command` spawns `Command::new(shell)` with `.args(["-lc", &format!("{command} 2>&1")])`, where shell is fish in production (lines 1821-1828). The child stays in the engine's process group. `RunRuntime::stop` calls `child.kill()` on that single pid (device.rs:403-408). I tested this with fish 4.9.3: `fish -lc "sleep 7 2>&1"` forks `sleep` as a child, and SIGKILL to fish leaves `sleep` running. `./gradlew` ends in `exec java ...`, so the Gradle client is exactly such a forked child. RunStop then releases the lease straight away (line 268). On the stopped paths `stream_command` returns at lines 1844/1856 and the logcat loop at line 1777, all without `take_child()`/`wait()`, so the killed child is never reaped.
findings.impact: Stopping a device run mid-build leaves the Gradle client running. The same `stop()` is used by `project.remove --force` and by engine shutdown (engine.rs:637-640). Gradle goes on with installDebug onto a device that Relay now reports as free, and another session can take the lease and install at the same time. A chained run_cmd (`./gradlew installDebug && adb shell am start ...`) also carries on after Stop. Each Stop also leaves a zombie process until the engine exits.
findings.fix: Spawn the run shell (and the logcat child) with `CommandExt::process_group(0)`. Make `RunRuntime::stop` signal the whole group: `libc::kill(-pgid, SIGTERM)`, then SIGKILL after a short grace period, as `proc::output_with_timeout` and `provider_updates.rs` already do. Always `take_child()` and `wait()` on the stopped paths, or reap inside `stop`.

v1.reason: stream_command spawns `fish -lc "{command} 2>&1"` (device.rs:1821-1828) with no process group. RunRuntime::stop (device.rs:403-408) calls child.kill() on that single pid. The Gradle wrapper ends in `exec java`, so the Gradle client is such a grandchild and survives. Its stdout pipe closes only when the read loop next wakes (it returns Stopped at 1843-1844), and Java's PrintStream swallows EPIPE, so the client keeps driving the daemon through installDebug. RunStop (handlers/device.rs:263-269) releases the Run lease immediately, so another session can take the device while the orphaned install proceeds. A chained run_cmd keeps going too. Engine shutdown (engine.rs:637-640) uses the same stop(). The stopped paths (1844, 1856, 1777) return without wait(). After RunStop removes the runtime, the killed fish Child is dropped unreaped and stays a zombie until the engine exits. proc.rs:32/55/65 already uses process_group(0) and kill(-pid).

The bug fires every time Stop lands during the Gradle phase, which is the long phase where people actually cancel. It is deterministic, not a race. A Stop during logcat works, because that child is adb itself.

(c) The cancelled build runs to completion where the user cannot see it. installDebug still installs onto the device, replacing or killing the running app, while Relay shows the run as stopped and the device as free. Another session can then pass the lease check and install at the same time, or a new run can overlap in the same project. For release builds with publish=true, the Play upload still goes through after Stop, and D152 calls that upload irreversible. Usually one zombie fish is left per Stop.

(d) High is right. A core control silently does nothing, and the device lease, whose job is to stop concurrent installs, is voided while the install continues. There is no data loss or security hole, so it is not critical.

(e) The direction of the fix is right. Gradle 9.7.1's DaemonMain calls maybeDetachProcess (setsid), and the adb server also calls setsid, so killing the client's process group spares both. The daemon logs "client disconnection detected, canceling the build", so killing the client does cancel the build. The fix is incomplete as written, though; see the correction.
v2.correction: 1) The chained run_cmd claim is wrong as stated. Fish is the process that evaluates `&&`, so once it is killed the later links (for example `adb shell am start`) never run. Only the command already in flight, such as the Gradle client, keeps going, unless the run_cmd is a script whose interpreter is itself orphaned. 2) The zombie is left only when another line arrives after Stop, which is the usual case with Gradle. If the orphan exits without printing, the EOF path at 1854 reaps fish. 3) The logcat child is `adb` itself, so `child.kill()` already ends it. Giving it `process_group(0)` is optional; only the missing reap at 1777 matters there. 4) The fix needs two more things. (i) RunStop is registered with `Engine::register`, so the store mutex is held. `stop()` must not sleep through the SIGTERM grace period on that path, because that would freeze the bus (CLAUDE.md invariant). Send the signal to the group synchronously, and do the wait-then-SIGKILL step on a detached thread or in the worker. (ii) There is a spawn-after-stop race. If Stop arrives before the shell exists, `stop()` finds no child. That happens during `sync_primary_checkout`'s `git fetch` (line 1665), or before the worker thread starts. `stream_command` then spawns fish and returns at 1844 without killing anything, so the whole build and install run. Check `runtime.stopped()` before spawning, and make `set_child` kill the new group immediately if stop has already happened.

findings.title: device.run holds the store mutex across `adb devices -l` (up to 2 s) and other I/O instead of using register_staged
findings.evidence: RunOp is registered with `e.register` (line 140). Inside the transaction it calls `require_device(&adb, &p.device)?` (line 152), which goes to `list_with_adb` and `output_with_timeout(adb devices -l, ADB_LIST_TIMEOUT = 2s)` (lines 579-590). It also does `run_source` -> `gix::open(root)` (line 971), several canonicalize calls, a tempfile write (`gradle_init_script`) and `worktree::contains`. The same `adb devices` call was moved off the lock for device.list (comment at lines 29-31, D144) and for device.mirror.start (lines 70-72, D149). CLAUDE.md requires `register_staged` for a mutation with a slow read phase.
findings.impact: Every Run press blocks all other bus traffic for the adb round trip. That routinely exceeds the 16 ms LOCK_BUDGET even with a warm adb server, and reaches 2 s when the server is cold, which is the case the code's own comment at line 29 describes.
findings.fix: Convert to `register_staged`. In prepare, read the project and settings via `ctx.read`, do the early lease `check`, `require_device`, root resolution, wrapper and init-script creation, and `run_source`. In finish, re-read the project, acquire the lease, insert the row and schedule the worker.

v1.reason: RunOp is registered with `e.register` (handlers/device.rs:140), so it runs inside the request transaction with the store mutex held. While holding it, the handler calls `require_device(&adb, &p.device)?` (line 152), which goes to list_with_adb and runs `adb devices -l` through output_with_timeout with a 2 s deadline (lines 577-590). It also calls canonicalize, writes a tempfile (gradle_init_script, line 1480), and calls run_source, which runs gix::open (line 971). The same adb call was moved off the lock for device.list (D144, lines 29-31) and for device.mirror.start (D149, lines 70-72), but RunOp was not converted. The subprocess has a deadline, so this is a bounded stall rather than a hang: a few tens of ms with a warm adb server, up to 2 s when it is cold.
v1.correction: The worst case is bounded at about 2 s by ADB_LIST_TIMEOUT. session.input has its own lock-free fast path, so typing into terminals keeps working during the stall, but every other bus op waits. The proposed register_staged split (prepare does the adb, gix and tempfile work; finish re-reads the project, acquires the lease, inserts the row) is the right fix. The early lease check can stay in prepare as long as acquire in finish remains authoritative.

findings.title: The device watch reads `adb track-devices` line by line, but the stream is %04x-framed, so unplugging the last device emits no device.changed
findings.evidence: The worker runs `adb track-devices -l` (line 367) and emits one `device.changed` per successful `reader.read_line(&mut line)` (lines 373-378). I checked upstream adb source. `read_and_dump` copies the server stream to stdout byte for byte. The server's `device_tracker_send` writes each update as `snprintf("%04x", len)` followed by the device list, where each device line ends in '\n' and an empty list is the empty string. So 'all devices gone' arrives as a bare `0000` with no newline. `read_line` blocks until the next update and then merges the two into one line. The fake adb in tests/bus.rs:148-151 prints unframed lines, so this framing is never tested.
findings.impact: After unplugging the only (or last) phone, the status bar still says '1 device' and the Devices page still lists it until an unrelated event refreshes them; in an idle app they stay wrong. The opposite problem also occurs: an update listing N devices emits N events. The native client answers each one with `device.list` plus a page refresh (`device.list` and `avd.list`, app.rs:1190 and tools_devices.rs:11/92), so plugging in a device with 3 attached triggers about 3 times the adb and emulator subprocesses.
findings.fix: Parse the protocol: read 4 bytes, parse the hex length, `read_exact` the payload, and emit exactly one `device.changed` per frame, including `0000`. Make the fake adb emit framed output and add a test for the empty frame.

v1.reason: device.rs:365-382 runs `adb track-devices -l` and emits one device.changed per `reader.read_line`. Without --proto-text, the adb client copies the server's host:track-devices-l stream to stdout unchanged (read_and_dump). Each update is a %04x length followed by the device lines, and the empty list is the bare `0000` with no newline. So read_line blocks on 'all devices gone' until the next update arrives. Meanwhile a frame with N devices produces N events. The fake adb in tests/bus.rs:148-151 prints unframed lines, so neither case is tested. The watch is held only while the Devices page is visible (app.rs:1339-1346) or while a mirror window waits for a device (mirror.rs:1174-1202). Each device.changed causes refresh_status (app.rs:1188-1192 -> status.rs:72 device.list). As a result, unplugging the last device leaves the Devices page and status count stale in the main flow where watch is meant to work.
v1.correction: The status bar can also be corrected by unrelated usage.changed or run.changed events, so 'stays wrong' applies mainly to an idle Devices page. The extra events from multi-device frames cost a few redundant device.list calls (adb subprocesses run unlocked under D144), not a functional failure. Fix as proposed: read the 4 hex bytes, read_exact the payload, emit one event per frame, and make the fake adb emit framed output including a 0000 frame.

findings.title: The device watch stops permanently when the adb server restarts and is not respawned while clients still hold watch leases
findings.evidence: When `adb track-devices` exits (EOF or error, lines 375-376), the worker calls `runtime.finish()` and then `clear_device_watch` (lines 380-381). That drops `watch.runtime` (line 386) but leaves `watch.clients` above zero. The Watch handler only spawns a worker when a client increments the count while `runtime.is_none()` (lines 48-57). The engine also turns a repeated `{"on":true}` from a connection that is already watching into a no-op before the handler runs (engine.rs:882). Note that `read_line` returns Err, and so breaks the loop, on a non-UTF-8 byte as well.
findings.impact: `adb kill-server`, an adb crash, or the common version fight between a distro adb and Android Studio's SDK adb ('server version doesn't match this client; killing...') closes track-devices. From then on no `device.changed` events reach any window that was already watching, so the Devices page and mirror windows stop noticing plug and unplug until the user leaves the page and comes back.
findings.fix: In the worker, when the child exits and `runtime.stopped()` is false, respawn `adb track-devices` with backoff and emit one `device.changed` so clients re-list, instead of clearing the runtime. Clear it only on `stop()`.

v1.reason: When track-devices hits EOF or a read error (device.rs:375-376), the worker calls runtime.finish() and then clear_device_watch (386-388), which takes watch.runtime but leaves watch.clients unchanged. The Watch handler (44-58) starts a new worker only when `on` arrives while runtime.is_none(). A connection that already holds a lease and sends on=true again is cut short as a no-op at engine.rs:882-884. Killing or restarting the adb server (adb kill-server, or a mismatched SDK adb killing the server) closes the client's socket and the track-devices process exits. Every existing watcher then stops receiving device.changed. mirror.rs:1196-1201 waits on device.changed with no timeout, so a mirror window waiting for its device to return hangs until the window closes. Recovery requires leaving and re-entering the Devices page, or opening a new connection while runtime is None.
v1.correction: A non-UTF-8 byte from read_line would also end the loop, but adb output is ASCII, so this is mostly theoretical. Respawn with backoff while !runtime.stopped(), and emit one device.changed after each respawn so clients re-list. Clear the runtime only in stop().

findings.title: One non-UTF-8 output line ends a run's logcat stream (the run is then marked finished or hangs) and truncates build logs
findings.evidence: Both readers use `BufReader::lines()`, which yields `Err(InvalidData)` for any line that is not valid UTF-8. The logcat loop does `let Ok(line) = line else { break };` (line 1779), then `child.wait()`, and unless the run was stopped it calls `advance_run(..., "finished", true)` and `release_run` (lines 1786-1793). `stream_command` pushes `output: {error}` and breaks (lines 1848-1851), which drops the pipe while the command keeps running.
findings.impact: If an app or a native library logs a byte sequence that is not valid UTF-8 (raw bytes, Latin-1 text), its logcat stream ends. The read end closes, `adb logcat` dies on its next write, and the run is marked 'finished' with its device lease released while the app is still running. If the app goes quiet instead, the run sits in 'running' with a frozen log until someone stops it. For builds, everything after the bad line is missing from the run log, including Gradle's error messages.
findings.fix: Read raw lines with `read_until(b'\n', &mut buf)` and convert them with `String::from_utf8_lossy` (trimming `\r\n`). Never treat a decode error as end of stream; break only on real I/O errors or EOF.

v1.reason: Both readers use BufReader::lines(), which returns Err(InvalidData) for a line that is not valid UTF-8. The logcat loop does `let Ok(line) = line else { break };` (device.rs:1779), then take_child()/wait() (1787-1789). It then marks the run 'finished' and calls release_run (1790-1794) while the app is still running. stream_command pushes `output: {error}` and breaks (1848-1851). It then waits for the child, so the build log loses everything after the bad line. Realistic triggers: native/NDK logs carrying raw bytes, and logd truncating long messages (~4 KB payload limit) in the middle of a multibyte character, with no `-v printable` escaping. After the break, take_child() has already removed the child from the runtime. If adb keeps running (quiet app, or adb ignoring SIGPIPE), the worker blocks in wait() and a later Stop can no longer kill that logcat child, because RunRuntime::stop finds no child.
v1.correction: Note the extra consequence: once the child has been taken, Stop cannot kill a lingering adb logcat. Fix as proposed: read_until(b'\n') plus String::from_utf8_lossy, and break only on EOF or a real I/O error.

findings.title: Run and build workers and the AVD queries run git, adb shell and SDK tools with no deadline; a hang leaves the run in 'building' holding its device lease
findings.evidence: `sync_primary_checkout` fetches through `worktree::git_mutate`, which is a plain `Command::new("git")...output()` (worktree.rs:26-27). It has no timeout and does not set `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0`, unlike `worktree::create` (worktree.rs:213-214). `git_capture`, `git_optional` and `git_is_ancestor` (lines 1500-1543) use bare `output()`/`status()`. In the run worker, `adb ... logcat -c` (1687-1689), `cmd package resolve-activity` (2033-2049), `am start -W` (2061-2064) and every `pidof` poll (2092-2095) are bare `.output()` calls; the 10 s pid deadline is only checked between calls. `apksigner verify` and `jarsigner -verify` (1937, 1944) are the same. So are the unlocked queries: `emulator -list-avds` (478), `adb emu avd name` (505) and `avdmanager list device -c` (315). None of these children is registered with the runtime, so Stop cannot kill them.
findings.impact: `am start -W` blocks while the app waits for a debugger (the 'Wait for debugger' developer option) or never finishes launching, and a fetch can stall on the network or an askpass prompt. The run then stays in 'building' indefinitely, holding its device lease so other sessions get device.busy, and its worker thread never exits; Stop only releases the lease. A wedged emulator console makes every Devices-page refresh (`avd.list`) hang, leaving one more blocked thread and adb process per refresh.
findings.fix: Run each call through `proc::output_with_timeout` with its own budget: about 60 s for the fetch (with `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0`), 20 s for `am start -W`, 5 s for resolve-activity, pidof and `logcat -c`, 60 s for the signers, 10 s for -list-avds, 3 s for `emu avd name` and 30 s for avdmanager. Check `runtime.stopped()` between steps so Stop takes effect.

v1.reason: All the cited calls are bare `.output()`/`.status()` with no deadline. That covers `worktree::git_mutate` → `git()` at worktree.rs:26-27 (the fetch has no GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0, unlike `create` at worktree.rs:213-214) and `git_capture`, `git_optional` and `git_is_ancestor` (device.rs ≈1500-1543). It also covers `logcat -c`, resolve-activity, `am start -W` and the `pidof` polls in the run worker. In the pidof loop the 10 s deadline is checked only between calls, so a single hung `adb shell` call is never cut off. The list continues with `apksigner`/`jarsigner` in `artifact_signing`, `emulator -list-avds` (≈478), `adb emu avd name` (≈505) and `avdmanager list device -c` (≈315). The last three run inside bus handlers (`register_unlocked`), which breaks the CLAUDE.md rule that every subprocess forked from a handler goes through `proc::output_with_timeout`. They do not hold the store mutex, so they do not freeze the bus, but each hung refresh leaks a request thread and a child process. None of the run-worker children are registered with `runtime.set_child`; only logcat is (≈1771). A hang in the fetch or in `am start -W` (for example with 'wait for debugger' set) leaves the run in 'building' with its device lease held until the user acts.
v1.correction: The impact is overstated in one respect. `RunStop` (device.rs:263-284) removes the runtime, releases the run's leases and sets the state to 'stopped', so Stop does unblock other sessions and fix the run's state. What remains is that the run sits in 'building' holding the lease until someone presses Stop, and the worker thread plus its orphaned git/adb child leak after Stop. Fix as proposed: route each call through `proc::output_with_timeout` with per-step budgets, set GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0 on the fetch, and check `runtime.stopped()` between steps. The handler-side AVD queries are the clear CLAUDE.md invariant violation.

findings.title: A run's logcat is tied to the one pid found after launch: the run never ends when the app dies, and a startup crash is reported as pid_missing without its stack
findings.evidence: After launch the worker resolves a single pid with `wait_for_app_pid` (line 1724, 10 s) and streams `adb logcat ... --pid={pid}` (line 1748). The loop ends only at EOF (lines 1775-1791). `logcat --pid` keeps running after that process exits, so EOF only comes from a device disconnect or Stop. A crash only triggers `report_crash` (lines 1780-1783) and the run stays 'running'. If the app dies before `pidof` sees it, the run fails with 'device.pid_missing: the installed app did not expose a process after launch' (lines 1724-1732). The FATAL EXCEPTION in the device log is never read, even though `logcat -c` (line 1687) had just trimmed that log to this launch.
findings.impact: After the app crashes or the user closes it, the run keeps its Kind::Run lease indefinitely. Every other session's `device.run` or `adb install` gets device.busy ('holds the device until it stops'), and agents wait for a `device.lease.released` that only arrives when a person presses Stop. The most common development failure, a crash on startup, produces a generic error with no stack trace in the run log.
findings.fix: Start logcat at launch without the pid filter but with `-T <launch time>` (or `--uid` where the device supports it), and filter by pid on the client once it is known. Poll `pidof`, or watch for ActivityManager's 'Process ... has died' line, and when the process is gone end the run ('finished' or 'crashed') and release the lease. On pid_missing, dump the crash buffer (`logcat -b crash -d`) into the run log.

v1.reason: run_worker (crates/relay-core/src/handlers/device.rs:1723) resolves one pid with wait_for_app_pid (2084-2108: polls `adb shell pidof -s` every 200 ms for 10 s) and streams `adb logcat -v brief -b main,system,crash --pid={pid}` (1737-1750). The loop at 1776-1785 ends only on EOF or a read error. Android's logcat does not exit when the filtered pid dies, so a run whose app crashed or was closed stays 'running'. Its Kind::Run lease has no TTL (device_lease.rs:62, expires None) and blocks every other holder ('holds the device until it stops', device_lease.rs:143). device.lease.release refuses it (handlers/device_lease.rs:46), so only device.run.stop frees it. The crash branch at 1780-1783 only notifies and does not end the run. The launch goes through `am start -W` (2062), which waits for the launch to complete. A crash in Application/Activity onCreate therefore usually kills the process before the first pidof, and the run fails with device.pid_missing (1724-1731). The FATAL EXCEPTION sits in the crash buffer, which `logcat -c` (1687) had just cleared, and nothing reads it. D91 (DECISIONS.md:390) documents attaching to the pid. It does not address the app dying.
v1.correction: Runs are open-ended by design (they last until Stop), so this is a missed liveness check rather than a run that should 'end' at some point. The defects are two: the run does not notice the app has died, and a startup crash loses its stack. Related gaps: an app relaunched under a new pid is not followed, and wait_for_app_pid does not check runtime.stopped() during its 10 s wait. Fix: on pid_missing, dump `logcat -d -b crash` into the run log. While streaming, poll pidof (or match ActivityManager's 'Process <pkg> (pid N) has died'), and when the app is gone mark the run finished or crashed and call release_run.

findings.title: A broken or half-created Relay signing profile blocks every release build and can be neither disabled nor recreated
findings.evidence: Build calls `load_signing_profile(ctx.engine(), &project.path)?.filter(|profile| profile.enabled)` (line 210), so the `?` fails the build before `enabled` is even looked at. `load_signing_profile_disk` returns an error when profile.json is unreadable or invalid, or when `!keystore.is_file()` (lines 1226-1243). `set_signing_enabled` uses the same loader (line 1323), so disabling fails with the same error. `create_signing_profile` refuses with `device.signing_exists` whenever the directory exists (lines 1285-1291), but a directory without profile.json reads as 'not configured' (line 1223). The cleanup (lines 1316-1318) only runs when the closure returns Err, not when the engine dies during the keytool step (up to 90 s) or the Secret Service step (up to 30 s). There is no delete op (relay-bus ops/device.rs).
findings.impact: If release.p12 is moved or deleted (for example the user backs it up elsewhere, or restores the data directory only partly), every `device.build` for that project fails with device.signing_keystore_missing, even with Relay signing disabled, and the user cannot disable it from the UI. That contradicts D158, which says a disabled profile falls back to the project's normal Gradle release signing. If Relay is killed while creating a profile, signing.get says 'not configured' while signing.create answers 'already has a profile' forever. Both cases need manual deletion of a directory named by a sha256 hash.
findings.fix: Read profile.json first and validate the keystore only when the profile is enabled. Let `set_signing_enabled(false)` rewrite the JSON without requiring the keystore. Treat a profile directory with no profile.json as an incomplete creation that create may clean up, and write profile.json last (via `write_private_replace`) so it acts as the commit marker. This keeps D157's rule of no delete or replace for a real profile.

v1.reason: Build does `load_signing_profile(ctx.engine(), &project.path)?.filter(|profile| profile.enabled)` (handlers/device.rs:210). load_signing_profile_disk returns device.signing_keystore_missing whenever release.p12 is absent, and the profile_unreadable/invalid errors for a bad profile.json (lines 1226-1243), all before `enabled` is checked. So a disabled profile with a missing keystore still fails every device.build, which contradicts D158's fallback to project signing. set_signing_enabled calls the same loader (line 1323), so the user cannot disable the profile either. create_signing_profile uses fs::create_dir and returns device.signing_exists if the directory exists (lines 1285-1291). load_signing_profile_disk returns Ok(None) when profile.json is missing (line 1223). If the engine dies between create_dir and write_private_new (keytool generation runs in between), the directory is left without profile.json: signing.get reports not configured and signing.create refuses forever. Cleanup only runs on an Err return (lines 1316-1318). No delete op exists.
v1.correction: There is a third half-created state. profile.json is written before store_signing_secret runs (Secret Service), so a crash between those two steps leaves a profile that loads as configured and enabled but has no stored password. Builds then fail at secret lookup until the user disables the profile, and disabling only works while the keystore is present. The triggers are uncommon (a keystore removed by hand, the engine killed mid-create), which is why this is medium. Writing profile.json last as the commit marker, after the secret is stored, fixes both partial-create cases.

findings.title: adb is only looked up in settings and on PATH, never in the discovered Android SDK as emulator and avdmanager are
findings.evidence: `adb_path` returns the configured path or `which::which("adb")`, and otherwise fails with 'adb is not installed or not on PATH' (lines 550-572). `sdk_tool` resolves emulator and avdmanager from settings, then PATH, then `android_sdk_root` (`emulator/emulator`, cmdline-tools) (lines 397-414). `android_sdk_root` finds `$ANDROID_SDK_ROOT`, `$ANDROID_HOME` and `~/Android/Sdk` (lines 416-436), but `platform-tools/adb` is never tried. The two lookups have also drifted on an empty configured value: `sdk_tool` and `android_sdk_root` skip `""`, while `adb_path` turns it into 'configured adb does not exist: '. The Settings page promises 'Standard SDK paths are discovered automatically' (tools_settings.rs:440).
findings.impact: With Android Studio's default SDK in ~/Android/Sdk and platform-tools not on the desktop session's PATH (fish `fish_add_path` does not reach an engine launched from the desktop), device.list, device.watch, mirroring and runs all fail with device.adb_missing. Meanwhile avd.list and avd.catalog work, and Settings says discovery is automatic. A client that stores `""` for a cleared field breaks adb instead of falling back.
findings.fix: Make adb one more `sdk_tool` case (`"adb" => sdk.join("platform-tools/adb")`) and skip empty configured values. Break the `android_sdk_root -> adb_path` cycle by having the SDK-root inference use only the configured or PATH adb.

v1.reason: `adb_path` (device.rs:550-572) checks only the `device.adb_path` setting and then `which::which("adb")`, and otherwise returns device.adb_missing. `sdk_tool` (397-414) falls back to `android_sdk_root` for emulator and avdmanager. `android_sdk_root` (416-436) finds $ANDROID_SDK_ROOT, $ANDROID_HOME and ~/Android/Sdk, but nothing ever tries `<sdk>/platform-tools/adb`. Every device path depends on `adb_path`: device.list/watch (33, 46), mirroring (73), device.run (151), and running-AVD detection (303, 471). So on a stock Android Studio install with platform-tools off the engine's PATH, avd.list and avd.catalog work while device.list, run and mirror fail. That contradicts the Settings text at tools_settings.rs:440 ('Standard SDK paths are discovered automatically').
v1.correction: The empty-string drift is real in the engine: `sdk_tool` and `android_sdk_root` filter out `""` and `adb_path` does not. The native client cannot trigger it, though: tools_settings.rs:643-644 stores `Value::Null` for an empty entry. Only a CLI/MCP `settings.set` with `""` reaches it, so it is a minor side note. Fix: in `adb_path`, after PATH, try `android_sdk_root`'s env/home candidates joined with `platform-tools/adb`, and filter empty configured values. To avoid recursion, do not call `android_sdk_root` as-is, because it calls `adb_path`. Factor the env/home discovery into a helper that both functions use.

findings.title: keytool failures are reported from stderr, which holds only its progress line; the real error is on stdout
findings.evidence: On a non-zero exit the handler returns `BusError::conflict("device.keytool_failed", String::from_utf8_lossy(&output.stderr).trim().to_string())` (lines 1393-1397). I checked the local JDK keytool: a runtime failure prints `keytool error: java.io.FileNotFoundException: ...` on stdout and exits 1, while stderr contains only 'Generating 2048-bit RSA key pair and self-signed certificate (SHA384withRSA) ... for: CN=x'.
findings.impact: When signing.create fails, the user sees 'Generating 4096-bit RSA key pair and self-signed certificate (SHA384withRSA) with a validity of 10000 days ...' as the error. It reads like progress and hides the actual cause.
findings.fix: Report stdout (the `keytool error:` line) and fall back to stderr, or join both trimmed outputs.

v1.reason: On a non-zero exit, `generate_signing_keystore` returns `BusError::conflict("device.keytool_failed", stderr)` (device.rs ≈1393-1397). I reproduced the stream split with the local /usr/bin/keytool in the scratchpad, using -genkeypair into a nonexistent directory. It exited 1 with `keytool error: java.io.FileNotFoundException: ... (No such file or directory)` on stdout. stderr held only 'Generating 2048-bit RSA key pair and self-signed certificate (SHA384withRSA) with a validity of 1 days\n\tfor: CN=x'. On failure the user therefore sees the progress line and never the cause.
v1.correction: Report stdout's `keytool error:` line first, fall back to stderr, or join both.

findings.title: Native crashes never raise run.crash because only Java's 'FATAL EXCEPTION' is matched
findings.evidence: `if !crash_reported && line.contains("FATAL EXCEPTION") { ... report_crash(...) }` (lines 1780-1783). A native crash (SIGSEGV or SIGABRT in C/C++, the NDK or a game engine) logs `F libc: Fatal signal 11 (SIGSEGV) ... pid N (pkg)` from the app's own pid, so that line is in the `--pid` stream. The tombstone comes from crash_dump, which has a different pid and is filtered out.
findings.impact: Native crashes produce no run.crash event and no 'App crashed on device' notification. Combined with the pid-bound stream, the run just stays in 'running'.
findings.fix: Also match libc's `Fatal signal` and `Abort message` lines, and on any match mark the run as crashed.

v1.reason: The only crash detection is `line.contains("FATAL EXCEPTION")` (device.rs:1780), the Java AndroidRuntime marker. A native crash makes libc's debuggerd handler in the crashing process log 'F libc : Fatal signal N (SIGxxx) ... pid N (pkg)' under the app's own pid, so the line reaches the --pid stream but does not match. The tombstone/DEBUG lines come from crash_dump/tombstoned under other pids and are filtered out. So native crashes raise no run.crash event and no 'App crashed on device' notification (report_crash, 2200-2215).
v1.correction: Match 'Fatal signal' (and optionally 'Abort message') in addition to FATAL EXCEPTION. Ending the run on a crash belongs to #9's fix, not this one.

findings.title: adb shell command lines are built from an unvalidated applicationId read from the worktree's output-metadata.json
findings.evidence: `variant_application_ids` takes `applicationId` verbatim from any `build/outputs/apk/**/output-metadata.json` found under the worktree (lines 2110-2153). It is passed as an argument to `adb -s .. shell cmd package resolve-activity ... &package` (2033-2047) and `shell pidof -s package` (2092-2093), and the derived component goes to `shell am start -W -n &component` (2062). `adb shell` joins its arguments into one string that the device's `sh -c` parses, so `;`, `$()` and similar are interpreted on the device.
findings.impact: A worktree file, for example one an agent wrote in its own checkout, containing `"applicationId": "x; pm uninstall com.other"` runs that command as the device `shell` user when the user runs that worktree. This happens even with a custom run_cmd that never runs the agent's Gradle (the pidof path at 1709-1724). The impact is limited because a default run already executes the worktree's build scripts on the host, but this is exactly the `adb shell` injection pattern.
findings.fix: Before use, validate the applicationId and component against the Java package grammar (`^[A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9_]*(\.[A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9_]*)+$`, plus `/[A-Za-z0-9_.$]+` for the component), or shell-quote each argument.

v1.reason: variant_application_ids (handlers/device.rs ~2110-2123) reads applicationId verbatim from any build/outputs/apk/**/output-metadata.json under the run root. The only filter is variantName. The value is passed as a separate argv element to `adb -s <dev> shell cmd package resolve-activity ... <package>` (~2033-2047) and to `adb shell pidof -s <package>` (~2092-2093). The adb client joins the arguments of `shell` with spaces and the device's sh parses the result, so metacharacters in the value run as commands on the device. The pidof path also runs when launch_after_build is false (~1709-1724). This needs only a file in the worktree, which an agent can write in its own checkout, and it executes as the device shell user (which can, for example, pm uninstall). Low is the right rating: a default run already executes the worktree's Gradle scripts on the host, which is far more powerful. The real cost is crossing from the host worktree onto a possibly personal device in configurations that never run agent code.
v1.correction: The `am start -n <component>` sink is less direct. The component must be a line of the device's own resolve-activity output that starts with `<package>/`, so the injection happens at resolve-activity and pidof, not at am start. The fix is right: validate against the Java package grammar before any adb call.

findings.title: find_avdmanager picks the last cmdline-tools directory in string order, so 9.0 wins over 19.0
findings.evidence: When there is no `cmdline-tools/latest`, the candidates `cmdline-tools/*/bin/avdmanager` are sorted as paths and the last one is taken with `pop()` (lines 441-444). `latest_build_tool` uses the same `.max()` over paths (lines 1957-1964). cmdline-tools versions include 9.0 and 10.0 through 19.0, and '9.0' sorts after '19.0'.
findings.impact: With several versioned cmdline-tools installed and no `latest`, avd.create and avd.catalog run the oldest avdmanager, which may not recognize newer system-image packages ('Package path is not valid').
findings.fix: Compare parsed numeric version components, falling back to path order for names that are not numeric.

v1.reason: device.rs:437-447: with no cmdline-tools/latest, the candidates are sorted as PathBuf, whose components compare bytewise, and the last one is taken with pop(). Bytewise, '9.0' sorts after '19.0', so 9.0 is chosen over 16.0 or 19.0. The trigger is rare. sdk_tool first tries the configured setting, then which::which("avdmanager"), and SDK Manager normally installs into cmdline-tools/latest. So the bug needs a hand-managed SDK with several versioned directories and no 'latest', including a single-digit one.
v1.correction: The related latest_build_tool (device.rs:1957-1964) is effectively unaffected. build-tools versions all have two-digit majors (17.x-36.x), so lexical order matches numeric order within the same digit count; at most an '-rcN' suffix could misorder. Fix by comparing parsed numeric version components in find_avdmanager.

findings.title: The `forge-android/gradlew` fallback runs a nested wrapper from the repo root, where Gradle finds no settings file
findings.evidence: `gradle_wrapper` returns `./forge-android/gradlew` when the root has no wrapper (lines 1059-1064). But `stream_command` runs every command with `.current_dir(root)` (line 1824) and nothing passes `-p forge-android`. Gradle locates the build from the working directory, not from where the wrapper lives. The user's own Avex repo has a root `gradlew` shim that does `cd "$APP_HOME/forge-android" && exec ./gradlew "$@"` because tools 'look for ./gradlew at the tree root', so this fallback is never reached there.
findings.impact: Any project that relies on the fallback gets device.run/device.build failures ('does not contain a Gradle build' or task not found). The branch is a project-specific special case inside a general handler, and it is effectively dead for the project it was written for.
findings.fix: Drop the hard-coded subproject, since the configured run_cmd already covers it. Otherwise run the wrapper with `current_dir` set to its own directory (or pass `-p <subdir>`) and search generically for the nearest `settings.gradle(.kts)`.
