v1.reason: `gradle_wrapper` (device.rs:1059-1064) returns `./forge-android/gradlew` when the root has no wrapper. `stream_command` runs it with `.current_dir(root)` (≈1824) and `fish -lc "<command>"`, and nothing passes `-p forge-android` or changes directory. The standard gradlew script finds its wrapper jar and properties through APP_HOME but leaves the working directory as is. Gradle therefore searches for settings.gradle from the repo root and fails with 'does not contain a Gradle build' (Gradle 8+), or 'task installDebug not found' on older versions. The fallback is hard-coded and project-specific, and agent_menu.rs:87 advertises it to users. I could not verify the claim about the user's Avex repo shim, since that repo is outside this one, so I did not count it as evidence.
v1.correction: The fix 'drop it, the configured run_cmd already covers it' holds only for device.run. `build_command` (1082-1094) ignores run_cmd/build_cmd and also uses `gradle_wrapper`, so device.build has no override. Better fix: return the wrapper's directory and run `<wrapper> -p <subdir>`, or `cd <subdir> &&` before it. Otherwise look generically for the nearest settings.gradle(.kts) instead of the literal `forge-android`. Also see the related site at 1089.

findings.title: RunOp's session-holder branch is unreachable because device.run is UserOnly and actor_session_id() is always None
findings.evidence: The handler does `match ctx.actor_session_id() { Some(id) => sessions_holder(ctx, id)?, None => super::device_lease::worktree_holder(...)? }` (lines 146-149), backed by `fn sessions_holder` (lines 958-962). But `device.run` is `.actors(Actors::UserOnly)` (relay-bus ops/device.rs:23). `Actors::admits` rejects agents before the handler runs (registry.rs:62), and `resolve_actor` returns None for user and test actors (engine.rs:1355).
findings.impact: Dead code that suggests agents can start runs that take a lease in their own name, which misleads anyone reasoning about who owns a lease.
findings.fix: Delete `sessions_holder` and call `worktree_holder` directly. If agent-started runs are wanted, open the op to agents deliberately and test that path.

v1.reason: device.run is `.actors(Actors::UserOnly)` (ops/device.rs:23). Dispatch rejects any actor that `admits` refuses (engine.rs:855), and UserOnly admits only `is_privileged()`, meaning non-agent actors (envelope.rs:38). For User and Test actors, resolve_actor returns Ok(None) (engine.rs:1354), so `ctx.actor_session_id()` is always None in the RunOp handler. That makes the `Some(id) => sessions_holder(ctx, id)?` arm at handlers/device.rs:146-149, and `sessions_holder` at 959-962 (which has no other caller), unreachable.
v1.correction: Small cleanup. Removing it changes nothing at runtime.

findings.title: avd.boot reports 'started' for any successful spawn, discards the emulator's output and never reaps it
findings.evidence: In the after-commit closure, stdin, stdout and stderr are all `Stdio::null()` (line 357), and `let state = if command.spawn().is_ok() { "started" } else { "failed" };` (line 358) drops the `Child` immediately without waiting on it. AvdBoot also does not check `running_serial` before booting.
findings.impact: An emulator that exits immediately (AVD already running, missing system image, KVM unavailable, AVD locked) is shown as 'started', with no error anywhere. Every emulator that later exits stays a zombie until Relay quits.
findings.fix: Hand the Child to a small reaper thread that keeps the tail of stderr and emits `avd.changed {state:"failed", message}` if the emulator exits within roughly the first 10 s (and a stopped state later). Refuse when the AVD already has a running serial.

v1.reason: device.rs:344-361: the AvdBoot after_commit closure sets stdin, stdout and stderr to Stdio::null() and runs `let state = if command.spawn().is_ok() { "started" } else { "failed" };`. The Child is dropped right away and never waited on. Nothing in crates/ installs a SIGCHLD handler or calls waitpid. On Linux the emulator launcher execs qemu under the same PID, so an exited emulator stays a zombie until Relay quits. An emulator that dies at startup (missing image, no KVM, locked AVD) produces no error at all, because its stderr is discarded and spawn() already succeeded.
v1.correction: The UI never shows a 'started' label. tools_devices.rs:103-119 only shows the Boot and Cold boot buttons, or the running serial. So the visible symptom is a boot that silently does nothing: the Boot button stays and there is no error. The UI also hides Boot when running_serial is set, so the 'already running' case is mostly guarded on the client side, although the engine does not check it. A zombie costs only one PID-table entry per boot. Fix as proposed: a reaper thread that waits on the child, keeps the tail of stderr, and emits a failed avd.changed with a message on early exit.

findings.title: Four near-identical walkers over build outputs
findings.evidence: `collect_build_outputs` (lines 1982-2002) and `collect_apk_metadata` (lines 2125-2140) are the same recursive walk: cut off at depth > 5, skip `.git|.relay|node_modules|target`, and treat a `build` directory specially. `collect_files` (lines 2004-2017) and `collect_output_metadata` (lines 2142-2153) are the same inner recursion with different predicates.
findings.impact: There are two copies of the skip list and the depth limits to keep in sync. Adding `.gradle` or Unreal's `Intermediate` to one leaves the other still walking it, and these walks run over whole worktrees on every run and build.
findings.fix: Use one `for_each_build_dir(root, |build_dir| ...)` walker plus one `collect_under(dir, max_depth, predicate)`, which removes about 40 lines.

v1.reason: collect_build_outputs (~1982-2002) and collect_apk_metadata (~2125-2140) are the same outer walk. Both stop at depth > 5, both skip `.git|.relay|node_modules|target`, and both treat a `build` directory as the place to descend into outputs/apk. The only difference is the subpath and the inner collector. collect_files (depth > 3, extension predicate) and collect_output_metadata (depth > 4, filename predicate) are the same inner recursion. The skip list is duplicated verbatim, so a future edit to one copy can miss the other. The copies have not diverged in any way that matters yet: only the inner depth limits differ, and that looks deliberate.
v1.correction: The payoff is modest, closer to 20-25 lines than 40, and nothing is wrong today. The claim that the walks run over whole worktrees on every run and build is accurate (variant_application_ids runs at launch or pid time, variant_artifact at build finish), but it is a cost of the design, not of the duplication. A shared walker that takes the outputs subpath and a predicate is a reasonable cleanup.

findings.title: D157 says device.signing.create is TauriOnly, but the op has no door restriction
findings.evidence: D157 (DECISIONS.md:896) says 'this mutation is `audit: never`, `user_only`, and `TauriOnly`; agents, the socket/CLI door ... never receive the secret'. The op meta is `.audit(Audit::Never).actors(Actors::UserOnly)` with no `.doors(...)` (ops/device.rs:37-39). No op in the registry uses TauriOnly, and the GTK client talks to the engine over the socket door. The handler that receives the password is registered at handlers/device.rs:242.
findings.impact: The documented guarantee about which doors may carry the signing password is false: the request containing the password is accepted on the socket door and on anything bridged onto it. Anyone relying on D157 for the threat model is misled.
findings.fix: Update D157 to the real rule (socket door, same-uid trust per BUS.md §4.2, never audited or logged), or add a door restriction that matches how the native client connects.

v1.reason: DECISIONS.md D157 says device.signing.create is `audit: never`, `user_only`, and `TauriOnly`, and that the socket/CLI door never receives the secret. The op meta at crates/relay-bus/src/ops/device.rs:37-39 is `.audit(Audit::Never).actors(Actors::UserOnly)` and sets no `.doors(...)`, so it defaults to Doors::All (registry.rs:122/140). The door gate at engine.rs:822 therefore lets it through on the socket door. The native client connects over a UnixStream (apps/relay-native/src/client.rs:173) and sends device.signing.create from tools_devices.rs:529, so the password does cross the socket door. The only thing that honours TauriOnly is the MCP exposure filter (relay-cli/src/mcp.rs:161). The op is still UserOnly, so agents cannot call it. The gap is the documented door guarantee.
v1.correction: Agents are still refused by Actors::UserOnly, so the only thing wrong is the door claim in D157. Making the op TauriOnly would break the native client, which uses the socket door. The fix is to update D157 to describe the real rule: socket door, same-uid trust, never audited.

findings.title: Run commands get ` 2>&1` appended as text while the child's stderr goes to /dev/null, so a chained run_cmd loses Gradle's errors
findings.evidence: The spawn uses `.args(["-lc", &format!("{command} 2>&1")])` together with `.stderr(Stdio::null())` (lines 1825-1828). The redirection applies only to the last simple command. For `./gradlew installDebug && adb shell am start ...`, only `adb` gets `2>&1`; with a trailing `# comment` the redirection is swallowed entirely.
findings.impact: For a configured run_cmd that chains commands, Gradle's stderr is thrown away, and that is where 'FAILURE: Build failed...' and compiler errors go. The run log just ends with 'device.build_failed: build or install command failed'.
findings.fix: Give the child's stderr the same OS pipe as stdout (duplicate the pipe's file descriptor) and drop the text suffix, or wrap the command for fish as `begin\n{command}\nend 2>&1`.

v1.reason: stream_command appends ` 2>&1` as text and sets `.stderr(Stdio::null())` (device.rs:1825-1828). In fish, `a && b 2>&1` redirects only b, so a's stderr is discarded. A trailing `# comment` swallows the redirection entirely. The default command built by run_command (1043-1054: `{wrapper}{init} install{Variant}`) is a single command and unaffected. Only a user-configured project.run_cmd that chains or pipes commands loses Gradle's stderr ('FAILURE: Build failed...', compiler errors). The run then shows only device.build_failed.
v1.correction: Only configured run_cmd values are affected, not the default Gradle command. The simplest fix: pass the same pipe as stderr (e.g. os_pipe or dup of the stdout fd) and drop the text suffix, or wrap the command as `begin\n{command}\nend 2>&1`.

findings.title: `adb devices -l` parsing turns the 'no permissions ...' state into 'no'
findings.evidence: Each line is split with `split_whitespace`; the serial is the first token and `let Some(state) = fields.next()` takes the second (lines 599-603). For a device without udev permission adb prints `SERIAL  no permissions (user in plugdev group; are your udev rules wrong?); see [...] usb:1-1 transport_id:2`.
findings.impact: device.list reports the state as 'no', and device.run and mirroring refuse with 'SERIAL is no' instead of the actionable 'no permissions' (fix the udev rules).
findings.fix: Take the state as the text up to the first `key:value` token (or special-case `no permissions`) and report it whole.

v1.reason: `list_with_adb` splits each `adb devices -l` line with `split_whitespace` and takes the second token as the state (device.rs:599-603). For a USB device without udev permission, adb prints `SERIAL\tno permissions (...); see [...] usb:... transport_id:N`, so the state becomes `no`. No `model:` token is present, so the model falls back to the serial. device.run (152-154) then refuses with `"<serial> is no"`, and the client shows the same truncated state. The 'unauthorized' and 'offline' states are single tokens and parse correctly.
v1.correction: The state should be every token before the first `key:value` extra (usb:, product:, model:, device:, transport_id:), or `no permissions` should be special-cased and reported as such.

findings.title: Literal SQL goes through Connection::query_row instead of prepare_cached (D145), including on paths hit by many requests
findings.evidence: `adb_path` (552), `sdk_tool` (398), `android_sdk_root` (417), `resolve_run_root` (986), `finish_build`, `advance_run` and `report_crash` (2167, 2186, 2203) and `get_run` (2218) all use `conn.query_row` with literal SQL. D145 says 'Handlers now call `prepare_cached` for literal SQL'. `adb_path` runs on every device.list, and the native client issues one on every device.changed, run.changed and usage.changed event.
findings.impact: The same statements are recompiled under the store lock on fairly busy paths. Each call costs little, but this goes against a documented project rule.
findings.fix: Use `prepare_cached(...)?.query_row(...)`.

v1.reason: The cited calls exist: device.rs 398, 417, 552, 986, 2167, 2186, 2203 and 2218 all call conn.query_row with literal SQL. rusqlite's Connection::query_row prepares the statement afresh each time. This contradicts D145 ('Handlers now call prepare_cached for literal SQL') and CLAUDE.md ('Prefer prepare_cached over Connection::query_row').
v1.correction: The performance impact is negligible. Each of these is a one-row SELECT that compiles in microseconds. adb_path runs in a ctx.read before device.list forks an adb subprocess that takes milliseconds or more, so 'busy path under the store lock' overstates it. The pattern is codebase-wide, not specific to device.rs: rg counts query_row in session.rs (18), task.rs (14), notes.rs (9), workspace.rs (7), provider.rs (6), awareness.rs (6) and others. The finding is really docs drift or rule non-compliance across the codebase. Either convert mechanically everywhere, or soften D145 and CLAUDE.md to match practice. It is not a device-handler performance issue.

results.coverage:
I read every line of the four assigned files: device.rs, device_lease.rs, handlers/device_lease.rs and mirror.rs.

**Callers and callees traced to establish reachability:**
- handlers/device.rs: register (1-300), the device watch worker (365-387), the adb helpers, mirror_worker, connect/drain and send_input (525-962), run_worker, stream_command and build_worker (1640-1930), and launch, pid, advance and fail_run (2020-2200).
- socket.rs 200-760: mirror, run and watch attachments, the inline fast path, WatchLease.
- engine.rs 120-1400: Ctx/Unlocked emit and rollback semantics, shutdown, the watch short-circuit, mirror_fast_path.
- guardrail.rs gate/confirm (440-667) and shell_commands (883-998).
- session.rs report/close/exit paths; hooks.rs hook-to-kind mapping.
- integration.rs deploy; workspace.rs project.remove; proc.rs.
- tests/mirror.rs and tests/device_lease.rs.
- apps/relay-native mirror/status/app usage, read only to confirm which input types and connections are used.
- The clippy-pedantic lines for these files: the casts are bounded, and none hides a bug.

**Verification limits:**
- I ran one throwaway experiment in the scratchpad: `fish -lc "sleep 7 2>&1"`. It confirmed that fish forks the command and that the child survives SIGKILL to fish.
- I did not run adb (it would touch the user's live adb server). The forward-removal finding (high confidence), the track-devices framing finding and the watcher-death finding therefore rest on adb's protocol and source as I know them, not a live check.
- The shell-lease finding relies on Claude Code firing PostToolUse as soon as a `run_in_background` command is launched.
- I took the scrcpy v4.1 wire layouts in mirror.rs (header sizes, session flag, control message sizes) on trust from the code's own transcription and tests. They are internally consistent but not checked against upstream.

**Observed outside this chunk, not reported (for the handlers/device.rs owner):**
- AvdCreate (handlers/device.rs:321-343) runs `avdmanager create avd` with `wait_with_output()` and no timeout inside a store-locked handler. AvdCreate and AvdBoot both call `list_avds` (`emulator -list-avds`, and `adb emu avd name` via `.output()`) under the store lock with no deadline.
- RunOp runs `adb devices` (2 s bound) and `gix::open` (run_source) under the store lock.
- run_worker's `adb logcat -c`, `am start -W` and `pidof` use `.output()` with no deadline.
- The desktop status bar calls `device.list`, which spawns `adb devices -l`, on every usage.changed, device.changed and run.changed event.

findings.title: RunRuntime::stop kills only the `fish -lc` wrapper, so a stopped run or build keeps installing or publishing after its lease is released
findings.evidence: `pub fn stop(&self) { self.stop.store(true, Ordering::SeqCst); if let Some(child) = self.child.lock().unwrap().as_mut() { let _ = child.kill(); } }`. The child is the shell spawned by `stream_command`: `Command::new(shell)` with `.args(["-lc", &format!("{command} 2>&1")])` (handlers/device.rs:1822-1841), where shell is `fish` outside tests. There is no `process_group(0)`, so the SIGKILL never reaches fish's children. A throwaway experiment confirmed it: `fish -lc "sleep 7 2>&1"` forks `sleep` as a child, and the sleep was still alive after fish was SIGKILLed. RunStop (handlers/device.rs:265-270) calls `runtime.stop()`, then immediately calls `release_run(p.run_id)` and marks the row stopped. Engine::shutdown (engine.rs:637-640) stops every run the same way. On the stopped path, `stream_command` returns `Streamed::Stopped` from inside the read loop and never reaps fish. proc.rs:32/55 and pty.rs:348 already kill whole process groups; this path does not. tests/device_lease.rs uses `run_cmd: "sleep 30"` under `sh`, which execs a lone simple command, so the tests never see the orphan.
findings.impact: Trigger: the user presses Stop while a run's `./gradlew --init-script … installDebug` is building. The Gradle client keeps running and the daemon finishes the install on the phone after the device lease was already released, so another session's install that is now allowed collides with it. Stopping a `device.build` with `publish: true` still uploads to Google Play. A custom run_cmd with a long-lived child (for example a JS dev server) keeps running and holds its port for the next run. All of these orphans survive app quit, and the worker thread stays blocked on the pipe until the orphan writes again.
findings.fix: Spawn the run shell with `CommandExt::process_group(0)`. Make `RunRuntime::stop` signal the group: `libc::kill(-pid, SIGTERM)`, then SIGKILL after a short grace, as proc.rs and pty.rs do. Reap the child on the Stopped path. Optionally hold the run lease until the group is gone.

v1.reason: `RunRuntime::stop` (device.rs:403-408) only calls `child.kill()` on the shell. `stream_command` (handlers/device.rs ~1822-1841) spawns `fish -lc "{command} 2>&1"` outside tests, with no `process_group`. The only process_group users in relay-core are proc.rs:32 and provider_updates.rs:95. I reproduced it on this machine with fish 4.9.3: `fish -lc "sleep 6.41 2>&1"` forks sleep as a child, and after `kill -9` on fish, sleep was still alive, reparented. RunStop (handlers/device.rs:265-289) calls stop(), then immediately `release_run`, and marks the row stopped. Engine::shutdown (engine.rs:637-640) does the same. With the default command, `./gradlew --init-script … installDebug`, the gradlew/java client is fish's child and survives, so the Gradle daemon does not see a client disconnect and finishes the install on the phone after the lease is gone. `device.build` with publish uses the same `stream_command`, so a stopped publish keeps running too. On the Stopped path the worker stays blocked in `lines()` until the orphan writes again, then drops the pipe. fish is never reaped: no `take_child().wait()` runs, so it stays a zombie until the engine exits. Tests use `sh -lc "sleep 30"`, and sh execs a lone simple command, which hides the problem.
v1.correction: I have not verified that a Gradle client which loses its stdout pipe keeps going. Java's PrintStream swallows EPIPE, so it most likely does. Fix: call `CommandExt::process_group(0)` on the run shell. In `stop()`, signal `-pid` with SIGTERM and then SIGKILL after a short grace, as proc.rs does, and reap the shell on the Stopped path. Optionally keep the run lease until the group has exited.

v2.reason:
(a) The code does what the finding says. RunRuntime::stop (crates/relay-core/src/device.rs:403-408) sets the flag and calls `child.kill()` on the stored Child and nothing else. Outside tests that Child is the shell: stream_command (handlers/device.rs:1821-1841) builds `Command::new("fish").args(["-lc", "{command} 2>&1"])` with stdout piped and no `process_group`. The only process-group users are proc.rs:32/55, pty.rs:348 and provider_updates.rs:95.

I reproduced the exact spawn shape with fish 4.9.3. The stand-in gradlew ends in `exec`, as the real wrapper does with `exec "$JAVACMD"`. fish forks that command into its own process group, so the child shares fish's pgid. After SIGKILL to fish, the exec'd child was still alive, reparented to pid 821, and fish was left a zombie.

(b) Reachable by the user in normal use, in four ways:
- The Stop button, shown for building/running/installing/launching runs and for release builds (relay-native tools_devices.rs:205-215 and 830-850, agent_menu.rs:662).
- App quit, through Engine::shutdown (engine.rs:637-640).
- project.remove, through workspace.rs:349.

It fires on any stop during the stream_command phase: the default `./gradlew --init-script … install<Variant>` run, or any device.build. The logcat phase is not affected, because adb is spawned directly there.

(c) The Gradle client JVM stays connected to its daemon, so the build continues. Until the worker reads the next line, the pipe is still open. After that, HotSpot ignores SIGPIPE and PrintStream swallows EPIPE.
- **Run:** installDebug still installs on the phone, with `-d` (downgrade) forced by GRADLE_ALLOW_DOWNGRADE_INIT. This happens after the row says "stopped" and after RunStop has released the lease and emitted device.lease.released. That event is exactly what busy agents are told to bus.wait on, so a second install can then overlap the orphan's install or be overwritten by it.
- **Build:** publish<Variant>Bundle still uploads through Gradle Play Publisher.
- **Side effects:** each stopped run leaves a zombie fish (the in-loop Stopped return never waits), and the worker thread stays blocked until the orphan writes or exits.
- **Worse, unreported window:** a stop that lands before set_child, for example during sync_primary_checkout's `git fetch` or build_worker's secret-tool lookup, finds no child to kill. stream_command then spawns the build anyway, because it never checks stopped() first. In that case not even fish is killed.

(d) High is right. This is user-visible wrong behavior in a normal flow: Stop is the only cancel and it does not cancel. It also silently bypasses a safety mechanism, the device lease. It is not critical: there is no store corruption, no security boundary crossed, and no engine hang.

(e) process_group(0) plus a group signal does work. Non-interactive fish does no job control, and I verified that kill(-pid) reaches its child. The fix as written is incomplete and partly unsafe; see the correction.
v2.correction:
**Fix corrections:**
1. RunStop is registered with Engine::register, so it runs with the store mutex held. stop() must not sleep through a SIGTERM-then-SIGKILL grace there. Either SIGKILL the group immediately, which matches today's child.kill() semantics (a Gradle daemon cancels the build when its client dies), or send SIGTERM and let the worker thread escalate to SIGKILL and reap.
2. Add `.stdin(Stdio::null())` to the run shell, as proc.rs does. Once the shell is in its own background process group, a child that reads an inherited terminal stdin is stopped by SIGTTIN. That is the case when the engine runs from a terminal, and the Gradle client forwards stdin.
3. Close the pre-spawn window. set_child (or the code right after it in stream_command) must kill the group at once when stopped() is already true. Otherwise a stop during sync_primary_checkout or the signing-secret lookup still launches an unkillable build.
4. Keep the direct child.kill() as well. The logcat child is not a group leader.
5. Reap the shell on the in-loop Stopped return.

Holding the lease until the group is gone is worthwhile.

**Evidence corrections:**
- On this machine /bin/sh is bash, and `sh -lc "sleep 30 2>&1"` forks sleep; I verified this. So the test fixtures do orphan their sleep too. The tests miss it because they assert only the row state and lease events, never that the process exited.
- The claim that Gradle keeps running after EPIPE rests on PrintStream and HotSpot semantics. I did not run it against real Gradle. Up to the next output line, the build continuing is certain.

**Line corrections:** RunStop is at handlers/device.rs:263-289. Add crates/relay-core/src/handlers/workspace.rs:349 (project.remove) to "related".

findings.title: forward_remove_args removes the forward by its remote socket name, so every mirror leaks an adb forward
findings.evidence: `forward_remove_args` returns `["-s", serial, "forward", "--remove", socket_name(scid)]`, which is `--remove localabstract:scrcpy_<scid>`. `adb forward --remove LOCAL` matches listeners by their host-side spec only. The forward was created with `tcp:0` (forward_args), which adb records as `tcp:<resolved port>`; scrcpy removes its own forwards with `tcp:<port>`. All three teardown calls discard the result with `let _ = mirror_adb(&runtime, mirror::forward_remove_args(&runtime.device, runtime.scid), MIRROR_FORWARD_TIMEOUT);` (handlers/device.rs:782, 798, 888), even though the parsed `port` is in scope (772-773). tests/mirror.rs:71-72 pins this wrong argv, and the fake adb accepts any arguments.
findings.impact: Every mirror start leaves a listening 127.0.0.1 port and an fd in the adb server, mapped to a dead `scrcpy_<scid>` socket. That includes opening the window, Retry, reconnecting after a Lost device, and a stop during setup. The leaks accumulate in `adb forward --list` until the device disconnects or the adb server restarts. Because the error is swallowed, nothing ever reports the failed cleanup.
findings.fix: Remove by local port: change the signature to `forward_remove_args(serial, port: u16)` returning `["-s", serial, "forward", "--remove", format!("tcp:{port}")]`. Pass `port` at all three teardown sites, log a failed removal, and correct the test.

v1.reason: mirror.rs:74-82 `forward_remove_args` builds `-s <serial> forward --remove localabstract:scrcpy_<scid>`. `adb forward --remove` takes the LOCAL spec. The forward was installed as `tcp:0` (forward_args, 64-72), and adb rewrites the listener's local name to `tcp:<resolved port>` when port 0 is requested. That is also why scrcpy itself removes with `tcp:%d`. So adb finds no listener with that name and exits non-zero. `mirror_adb` (handlers/device.rs:681) turns the failure into Err, and all three teardown sites throw it away with `let _ =` (device.rs:782 stop during setup, 798 spawn failure, 888 normal and failed teardown). The parsed `port` is in scope at every one of them (772). tests/mirror.rs:71-72 pins the wrong argv. Nothing else removes forwards: there is no `--remove-all` and no kill-server. So every mirror start (open, Retry, reconnect, rung change) leaves a 127.0.0.1 listener in the adb server that points at a dead abstract socket. The listeners are cleared only when the device disconnects or the adb server restarts.
v1.correction: The consequence is limited to resources: each new mirror uses a fresh scid and port, so the stale forwards never collide with a live mirror. The leak is silent and grows slowly, and a disconnect clears it, which is why this is medium rather than high. The fix is right: pass `port` and remove `tcp:{port}` at device.rs:782, 798 and 888, log a failed removal, and fix the test.

findings.title: Shell leases shrink to the 90 s grace on the first PostToolUse, though background or parallel device commands are still running
findings.evidence: `command_finished` shortens leases when `turn_ended || command.is_some_and(|command| device_command(command).is_some())`. `shell_finished` then sets every Kind::Shell lease of the session to `min(expires, now + SHELL_GRACE)` (device_lease.rs:253-261). It is driven by `session.report kind=tool_use`, which comes from the PostToolUse hook (hooks.rs:357), and by `kind=stop` (session.rs:1379-1383). It never looks at `tool_input.run_in_background` or a trailing `&`. There is one lease per device per holder and no count of in-flight commands.
findings.impact: Trigger: an agent runs `./gradlew installDebug` with Bash `run_in_background: true`, or `adb install x.apk &`. The tool returns as soon as the command is launched, PostToolUse arrives, and the lease lapses 90 s later while the build and install run for minutes. Another session's install is then accepted onto the same phone, which is exactly the clobber the lease exists to prevent. The same happens with two parallel device commands (the first to finish shortens the shared lease) and when the turn's Stop hook fires while a background install continues.
findings.fix: Do not shorten the lease for background launches: if `data.tool_input.run_in_background` is true or the command ends in `&`, keep SHELL_RUNNING. Count in-flight device commands per (session, device) and shorten only when the count reaches zero.

v1.reason: session.rs:1378-1383 calls command_finished for every kind=tool_use (the PostToolUse hook, hooks.rs:354-358) and kind=stop report. command_finished (device_lease.rs:137-141) calls shell_finished whenever the finished command parses as a device command or the turn ended. shell_finished (device_lease.rs:253-261) caps every Kind::Shell lease of that session at now+90s. Nothing looks at tool_input.run_in_background or counts in-flight commands, and there is one lease per device key. A Bash call with run_in_background returns at once, so PostToolUse fires right after launch, and the Stop hook fires at the end of the turn while background shells still run. A long background `./gradlew installDebug` therefore loses its lease after 90 s, and another session's gate_command for the same device is then accepted. Preventing that clobber is the stated purpose of the lease (device_lease.rs:3-7). Two parallel device commands in one session have the same problem: the first PostToolUse shortens the shared lease.
v1.correction: For a background launch, keep SHELL_RUNNING; the 15-minute cap still bounds it. Parallel commands need a per-(session, device) in-flight count. A trailing `&` is already a command separator in split_commands, so detect it separately from tool_input.run_in_background.

findings.title: An expiring lease emits no `device.lease.released`, yet the device.busy hint tells agents to bus.wait for that event
findings.evidence: Expiry is only applied lazily. `expire()` runs only inside `Leases::acquire` (177) and `release_where` (234); `check`, `list` and `holder_of` merely filter lapsed leases out. No timer or sweeper exists for leases anywhere in relay-core: prune runs only from device.list, device.leases, claim, release, guardrail gate and device.run. `busy()` (148-150) hints: "wait for it with bus.wait {\"events\":[\"device.lease.released\"]} and retry". Shell leases always end by expiry (SHELL_GRACE after PostToolUse), and claims end by expiry unless released. bus.wait defaults to a 60 s timeout (socket.rs:409). Release events are not stored, so a release between the refusal and the wait call is also missed.
findings.impact: Trigger: agent B is refused because A just ran `adb install`, and B follows the hint and waits. A's lease lapses 90 s later, but no event fires unless an unrelated request happens to prune (for example the desktop's device.list). B sleeps until its own timeout (up to the 1 h maximum) before retrying a device that was already free. With a quiet UI or a headless `relay serve`, the wait never wakes on expiry.
findings.fix: Emit releases when leases lapse. Either run one timer thread that sleeps until the earliest `expires`, prunes, and calls emit_system for each release, or prune on a short tick while the map is non-empty. Add `"matching":{"device":"<serial>"}` to the hint so waiters only wake for their device.

v1.reason: Leases are only dropped lazily. expire() is called only from Leases::acquire (device_lease.rs:177) and release_where (234). check, list and holder_of only filter lapsed leases out. No timer or worker in relay-core prunes leases. The only device_leases users are the device.list, device.leases, device.claim, device.release and device.run handlers, guardrail gate_command, and session exit/close (handlers/session.rs:677, 1631). Shell leases normally end by expiry: command_finished, then shell_finished, only shortens `expires` to SHELL_GRACE (90 s) and emits nothing. Claims also end by expiry unless released. Meanwhile busy() (148-150), and the provider system prompt (providers.rs:48-49), tell agents to `bus.wait` on device.lease.released and not to poll. The bus.wait handler (socket.rs:399-440) only wakes on a broadcast event; it has no stored replay for this event (only guardrail exceptions get one). So a waiter is woken by the lapse only if some unrelated request happens to prune. A release that fires between the refusal and the bus.wait call is also missed.
v1.correction: Impact is bounded by the waiter's own timeout: the default is 60 s, and the timeout is clamped to 1 s..1 h (socket.rs:408-410). A waiter on the default retries within about a minute, so the cost is lost minutes, not a hang. The cost is unbounded only when the agent passes a long timeout_ms. The fix is as proposed: a timer that sleeps until the earliest `expires` and then calls emit_system for each lapsed lease, or prune on the session.report path. Adding `matching: {device}` to the hint is a good extra.

findings.title: Read-only adb shell commands (`wm size`, `settings get`, `cmd package list`) are classified as device writes
findings.evidence: `match command { "pm" => !PM_READS.contains(&sub), "cmd" => sub == "package" || sub == "activity", "am" => !AM_READS.contains(&sub), other => SHELL_WRITES.contains(&other) }`. SHELL_WRITES (404) contains "wm" and "settings" with no sub-verb check. `cmd package …` and `cmd activity …` count as writes whatever the next word is, although PM_READS is documented as "`pm` / `cmd package` verbs that only read" (405). Traced by hand: `adb shell wm size` → command "wm" → write; `adb shell cmd package list packages` → sub "package" → write; `adb shell settings get global x` → write. `gradle_command` (457) also treats any `install*` task, such as `installDist` in a JVM project, as a device install on `*`.
findings.impact: These are common read probes an agent runs before tapping or checking packages. Each one takes a 15-minute shell lease (90 s after PostToolUse) that refuses other sessions' installs. When another session already holds the device, the guardrail hook refuses the read itself with device.busy. `./gradlew installDist` in a non-Android project takes a `*` lease that blocks every device.
findings.fix: Classify by sub-verb. Treat `wm size` and `wm density` without a value, and `settings get` and `settings list`, as reads. For `cmd package` and `cmd activity`, look up the third word in PM_READS and AM_READS. Exclude non-Android install tasks such as `installDist` from the Gradle match.

v1.reason: I traced adb_command (device_lease.rs:415-451) by hand. `adb shell wm size`: verb 'shell', first word 'wm', so command 'wm' falls to the `other =>` arm, and SHELL_WRITES (404) contains "wm", so it counts as a write. `adb shell settings get global x` is a write the same way ("settings"). `adb shell cmd package list packages`: command 'cmd', sub 'package', and the arm `"cmd" => sub == "package" || sub == "activity"` returns true. PM_READS is documented as '`pm` / `cmd package` verbs that only read' (405) but is never consulted for `cmd`. The module docs say reads are 'free for everyone' (308-309), so this contradicts the stated intent. gate_command (handlers/device_lease.rs:121-125) then takes a Shell lease for 15 min, cut to 90 s at PostToolUse. Without -s the lease is on `*`. If another session holds the device, acquire returns device.busy and the guardrail hook refuses the read probe itself. gradle_command (457-461) also matches any `install*` task, `installDist` included, and takes a `*` lease.
v1.correction: Without -s these probes lease `*`, which conflicts with every device. So one session's `adb shell wm size` blocks every other session's installs on any phone for the 90 s grace, and is itself refused whenever anyone holds any device. The installDist case matters only when Android work is going on at the same time; it is a minor part of the finding. Fix as proposed: check the sub-verb for wm (size/density with no value), settings (get/list), and cmd package/activity (look up the third word in PM_READS/AM_READS).

findings.title: One lease per device key: a run replaces its holder's claim, and when the run ends the claim is gone
findings.evidence: `match map.get_mut(&lease.device) { Some(held) if held.kind.rank() > lease.kind.rank() => Ok(false), Some(held) if held.kind == lease.kind => {renew}, _ => { map.insert(lease.device.clone(), lease); Ok(true) } }`. A Run (rank 2) over the same holder's Claim (rank 1) overwrites it. Run(8) over Run(7) by the same holder (equal rank, different kind) also overwrites it. No release event is sent for the overwritten lease, and `release_run` (243) then removes the only entry. A user-started run on a session's worktree is held by that session (worktree_holder, handlers/device_lease.rs:79-87), so it passes `check` against that session's own claim.
findings.impact: Trigger: agent A calls device.claim on the phone for 30 minutes to run a multi-step test, then the user clicks Run on A's worktree. When the run finishes 3 minutes later, `release_run` removes the only lease, and session B's `adb install` is accepted although A's claim had 27 minutes left. In reverse, if A claims during a run, the call returns `Ok(false)` and the claim is never stored. With two runs by the same holder on one device, the second overwrites the first's lease; if the second ends first, the device is unleased while the first run is still live.
findings.fix: Keep every lease a holder has on a device, for example as `HashMap<String, Vec<Lease>>` or keyed by (device, kind). Decide conflicts across holders as now, and have release_run and expiry remove only their own entry.

v1.reason: `Leases` is a `HashMap<String, Lease>` keyed by device (device_lease.rs:168). In `acquire` (183-215), once the cross-holder check passes, a same-holder lease with a different kind and rank >= the held one goes to the `_ => map.insert(...)` arm and silently replaces the held lease. No RELEASED event is sent, because the replaced lease is not added to `pruned`. Run (rank 2) over the same holder's Claim (rank 1) replaces the claim, and `Run(8)` over `Run(7)` also replaces it, since `held.kind == lease.kind` compares run ids. `release_run` (243-245) then removes the only entry. This is reachable: RunOp's holder for a session's worktree is that session (`worktree_holder`, handlers/device_lease.rs:79-87), so `check` and `acquire` treat the user's Run click as the claiming session's own lease. The user can also start two runs on the primary checkout, both held by `Holder::User`. Going the other way, a Claim during the holder's own Run returns `Ok(false)` and is never stored. The claim handler (handlers/device_lease.rs:35-36) then returns the run lease's view, so the agent believes it holds a claim that disappears when the run ends.
v1.correction: The impact is an early end to coordination: another session's install is accepted while the first holder still believed it held the device. Nothing is corrupted, so medium is right. A fix that keeps the current per-device conflict rule: store `HashMap<String, Vec<Lease>>`, or key by (device, kind or run id). Have `release_run` and expiry remove only their own entry, and have `holder_of` and `list` report the strongest live lease.

findings.title: Mirror control writes block while holding the control mutex, which stop() also needs, so a stalled socket wedges device.mirror.stop under the store lock
findings.evidence: `send_control` does `let mut control = self.control.lock().unwrap(); if let Some(socket) = control.socket.as_mut() { socket.write_all(&bytes) }`, a blocking write with no deadline. There is no `set_write_timeout` anywhere in relay-core; the control socket is configured at handlers/device.rs:810-825 with nodelay only. `stop()` takes the same `self.control.lock()` to `socket.take()` and shut it down (326-328). `device.mirror.stop` is a locked handler that calls `runtime.stop()` (handlers/device.rs:122) while holding the store mutex. The socket door answers pointer and key input inline on its tokio task (socket.rs:735-739), and MirrorAttachment::drop calls stop() from that same task (socket.rs:238). Input sent after stop() has taken the socket is queued into `pending` and reported as Ok.
findings.impact: Trigger: the device stops draining the control socket while the TCP connection stays up (wireless adb after a Wi-Fi drop, a stalled USB transport, a server blocked in a binder call), and the user keeps dragging or pastes through setclipboard. write_all then blocks. The window's connection task and its tokio worker are stuck, every later input waits on the mutex, and closing the window cannot stop the mirror. A device.mirror.stop holds the store mutex until the kernel gives up on the connection, freezing every locked bus op for minutes.
findings.fix: Set a short write timeout on the control socket (for example 2 s) and fail the mirror when it fires. Keep a `try_clone` of the socket outside the mutex so stop() can call `shutdown(Both)` without taking the lock; the shutdown unblocks the writer. Return an error instead of Ok when input is queued after stop.

v1.reason: The mechanism is in the code. `send_control` (device.rs:279-290) calls `socket.write_all` while holding `self.control`, and no write timeout is set anywhere in relay-core: handlers/device.rs:810-825 sets only nodelay and a read timeout on the video socket. `stop()` (device.rs:321-333) takes the same `control` lock. MirrorStop (handlers/device.rs:107-127) is a plain `register` handler, so it calls `runtime.stop()` with the store mutex and transaction held. Input goes through `mirror_fast_path`, run inline on the socket door's tokio task (socket.rs:735-739). `MirrorAttachment::drop` (socket.rs:231-243) also calls stop() on a tokio thread. What I could not establish is the trigger. The control socket connects to `127.0.0.1:port`, an `adb forward` held by the local adb server, not directly to the device. `write_all` only blocks once the loopback send buffer (MB-scale with autotuning) and the adb server's buffering fill up, and the adb server must also stop reading while keeping the socket open. Touch events are 28-32 bytes each, so this needs a long stall with heavy input. Large SET_CLIPBOARD pastes (up to about 256 KiB each, mirror.rs:405) make it reachable much sooner. When the transport goes offline, adb normally closes the forwarded sockets, which turns the block into an EPIPE error.
v1.correction: The claim that input sent after stop() is queued and returns Ok is mostly moot. Both MirrorStop and the drop path remove the mirror from `engine.mirrors` first, so later input fails in `mirror_by_id`. Only an input already in flight could be queued. The impact also depends on how long adb keeps a stalled forward open, which I could not establish. The fix stands: set a write timeout on the control socket (for example 1-2 s) and fail the mirror when it fires. Also keep a `try_clone` outside the mutex so `stop()` can `shutdown(Both)` without waiting for the writer.

findings.title: Integration deploys install on a device without checking or taking its lease
findings.evidence: The deploy runs `match shell(&path, command, Some(&device))`, where `shell` is `Command::new("fish").current_dir(cwd).args(["-lc", command])` plus `cmd.env("RELAY_DEVICE", device)` and `.output()` (227-233). integration.rs never calls device_lease check or acquire. The device_lease module doc (device_lease.rs:9-14) lists the three things that take a lease, and deploys are not among them. The deploy also sets RELAY_DEVICE but not ANDROID_SERIAL, whereas device.run sets both (handlers/device.rs:1673).
findings.impact: An integration deploy replaces the app of an agent that holds a claim on the phone, or is in the middle of `adb install`, with no refusal. Agents are not refused while the deploy is installing. With several devices attached, a Gradle install in the run command installs on all of them, not just the chosen deploy device.
findings.fix: Before deploying, check and acquire a run-style lease for `device`, held by the integration's session or the user, and release it when the deploy ends. Pass ANDROID_SERIAL alongside RELAY_DEVICE.

v1.reason: In integration.rs:186-213 the deploy step runs `shell(&path, command, Some(&device))` with project.run_cmd. shell (integration.rs:227-240) only sets RELAY_DEVICE and runs `fish -lc` with output(). The integration module never calls device_lease check or acquire, and an MCP or bus call does not pass through the PreToolUse hook that takes shell leases. device.run, by contrast, checks and acquires a Run lease (device.rs:150, 177) and sets both RELAY_DEVICE and ANDROID_SERIAL (device.rs:1673). The native UI never sets deploy (code_git.rs:738 sends only build:true), so the trigger is an agent calling integration.request with deploy, an op exposed to agents, or a CLI caller. That is a less common path, but the bypass and the environment divergence are real.
v1.correction: Deploy only runs when project.run_cmd is set; there is no Gradle default here, unlike device.run. A cleaner fix than duplicating lease logic: have the integration deploy go through the device.run machinery, which already supports an integration_id, so it gets the lease, ANDROID_SERIAL, streaming and stop handling.

findings.title: device_watch_worker splits adb's length-prefixed track-devices stream on newlines, so unplugging the last device emits no device.changed
findings.evidence: `match reader.read_line(&mut line) { Ok(0) | Err(_) => break, Ok(_) => engine.emit_system("device.changed", json!({"reason":"system"})) }` over `adb track-devices -l` stdout. adb's CLI dumps the raw protocol: each update is a 4-hex-digit length followed by the device lines. An empty list is the bare `0000` with no newline, so read_line keeps waiting and that update is delivered only when it is glued to the next one. A list of N devices produces N events.
findings.impact: Trigger: the user unplugs the only phone while the Devices page is open. No device.changed fires, so the list and the status-bar count keep showing the phone until something else refreshes. Each real update with N devices sends N events, and each event makes the desktop status bar call `device.list`, which spawns `adb devices -l` again.
findings.fix: Parse the protocol: read 4 bytes of hex length, then exactly that many bytes, and emit one device.changed per block, including the empty `0000` block.

v1.reason: device_watch_worker (handlers/device.rs:365-381) runs `adb track-devices -l` and emits one device.changed for each `read_line`. The adb client prints the host service's raw protocol: for each update, a 4-hex-digit length, then that many bytes of `serial\tstate ...\n` lines. The installed /usr/bin/adb (usage 'adb track-devices [-l][--proto-text][--proto-binary]', which issues host:track-devices%s) works this way. An empty device list arrives as the bare `0000` with no trailing newline, so read_line blocks until the next update's newline. Unplugging the last device therefore emits nothing. The desktop depends on device.changed for this: app.rs:1190 refreshes on it, status.rs:72 and tools_devices call device.list, and nothing polls. The fake adb in tests/bus.rs:148-151 prints plain newline lines with no length prefix, so the tests encode the same wrong assumption. An update listing N devices also yields N events, and so N device.list calls, each running `adb devices -l`.
v1.correction: Re-plugging still emits an event, because the `0000` gets glued to the next block, which ends in a newline. So mirror.rs:1172's wait for a device to come back still works; only removal of the last device is lost. Fix: read the 4 hex digits, read exactly that many bytes, emit once per block (including `0000`), and update the fake adb to print length-prefixed output.

findings.title: The device watcher is not restarted when adb track-devices exits, and connections already watching never get device.changed again
findings.evidence: On EOF or error the worker breaks, calls `runtime.finish()`, and `clear_device_watch` drops `watch.runtime` (384-387), but `watch.clients` stays above zero. Each socket connection's WatchLease keeps `active = true` (socket.rs:246-279). A repeated `device.watch {on:true}` from such a connection is answered as a no-op before it reaches the handler (engine.rs:882-884). DeviceWatchState (device.rs:23-27) has no notion of a dead runtime.
findings.impact: Trigger: someone runs `adb kill-server` (or two adb versions fight over the server) while the Devices page is open. track-devices exits and the watch silently ends. Plugging and unplugging devices stops updating the page and the status count until the user leaves the page and comes back, or another connection starts a watch.
findings.fix: When the child exits while `!runtime.stopped()`, respawn `adb track-devices` after a short backoff instead of clearing the runtime. Clear it only on an explicit stop.

v1.reason: handlers/device.rs:376-387. device_watch_worker breaks on `Ok(0) | Err(_)` from read_line on `adb track-devices -l`, calls runtime.finish(), then clear_device_watch takes watch.runtime. It never touches watch.clients, and DeviceWatchState (device.rs:24-27) only tracks clients and runtime. The Watch handler (device.rs:44-58) starts a worker only when `watch.runtime.is_none()` on an on:true, but engine.rs:882 answers a repeated on:true from a connection whose WatchLease is already active as a no-op before the handler runs. The native client sends device.watch only when it switches into or out of the devices page (app.rs:1340-1346) or on reconnect (app.rs:1165). So after track-devices exits, no device.changed reaches the page until the user leaves it and comes back. Leaving drops clients to 0 and returning respawns the worker. Trigger: `adb kill-server`, or a second adb binary of a different version restarting the server (common when Android Studio's adb and the system adb disagree). Both end the track-devices stream. Nothing else feeds device.changed, so the page stops updating. The mirror reconnect waiter (mirror.rs:1172-1198) also relies on this watch to see a device come back.
v1.correction: Same impact for mirror.rs's wait-for-device-to-return path, which takes its own watch lease and waits on device.changed. Fix as proposed: respawn track-devices with a backoff while `!runtime.stopped()` and clients > 0, and clear the runtime only on an explicit stop. Also emit one device.changed when the stream dies or restarts, so listeners re-list.

findings.title: device_lease re-implements guardrail::shell_commands with different quote, escape and separator rules
findings.evidence: `split_commands` plus `unquote` (365-394) tokenize with `segment.split_whitespace().map(unquote)`. A quoted string therefore becomes several words and backslash escapes are ignored. guardrail.rs:894-956 (`shell_commands`) keeps a quoted string as one word, handles `\`, and tracks whether each word was quoted. device_lease additionally splits on `(`, `)`, backtick and `$(`. The comment at 431 ("`adb shell \"am start …\"` arrives as one quoted word; look inside it") describes the guardrail reader, not this one. With this tokenizer `first.split_whitespace()` never yields a second word, so the inner split at 433-435 is dead.
findings.impact: The same hook call parses the agent's command line twice: `gate` runs evaluate_granted and then gate_command. The two readers disagree on what a command and a word are, so a fix to one (escapes, subshells) does not reach the other. The lease classifier's comment already describes the wrong tokenizer.
findings.fix: Make `guardrail::shell_commands` pub(crate) and add the `(`, `)`, backtick and `$(` separators there. Build `device_command` on its `Vec<Vec<Word>>`, looking inside a quoted `adb shell` word as the comment intends. Delete split_commands and unquote.

v1.reason: device_lease.rs:365-394 (split_commands plus unquote, applied after split_whitespace) is a second shell reader beside guardrail.rs:894-956 (shell_commands). Both read the same hook command in the same guardrail.gate call (guardrail.rs:532 calls gate_command). They have diverged. The guardrail reader keeps a quoted string as one word, handles backslash escapes and treats `&&`/`||` as one separator, but does not split on `(`, `)`, backtick or `$(`. The lease reader does split on those, but turns a quoted string into several words. The comment at device_lease.rs:431 describes the guardrail behavior. Under this tokenizer `first.split_whitespace()` (433) can never produce a second word, because tokens already come from split_whitespace, so the `inner.next()` path is dead. I tried to refute this: the two readers have different needs (the guardrail one must tell data from commands; the lease one is described as conservative and 'does not try to be a shell'). Today the lease reader still gets the quoted case right by accident: `adb shell "am start -n x"` gives tokens am, start, -n, x after unquote. So there is no live wrong behavior, only a stale comment, a dead branch and two parsers to maintain.
v1.correction: Downgrade to low: the parsers have diverged, but I found no user-visible bug coming from the divergence. Unifying them would mean adding the `(`, `)`, backtick and `$(` separators to guardrail::shell_commands. That changes what the guardrail's deny matching sees, so it is not free. At minimum, fix the comment at 431 and drop the dead inner split.

findings.title: Device-to-host control messages are read and discarded; the DeviceMsg/DeviceEvent parsers, GetClipboard and clipboard acks are dead
findings.evidence: The only reader of the control socket's reverse direction is `while drain.read(&mut bytes).is_ok_and(|count| count > 0) {}` (handlers/device.rs:826-829). `DeviceMsg`, `DeviceEvent`, `device_msg_len`, `parse_device_msg` and `parse_device_event` (649-756) are referenced only from tests. Several comments describe behaviour that does not exist: the doc says "the shell's drain thread matches [`DeviceMsg`] exhaustively and allocates nothing" (711-713), the module doc claims "clipboard in both directions" (14-15), and `InputMsg::GetClipboard` says "the answer arrives as a `DeviceEvent::Clipboard`" (818-822). `SetClipboard.sequence` asks for an ack that is also discarded. The desktop never sends getclipboard; it only uses setclipboard.
findings.impact: About 110 lines of parser, plus two input variants and their tests, are maintained for a path that does nothing. A caller that sends `getclipboard` gets `{}` and never sees the device clipboard.
findings.fix: Either decode with parse_device_event in the drain thread and surface the clipboard text (for example as a `mirror` status frame), or delete DeviceMsg, DeviceEvent, the parse_* functions, GetClipboard/CopyKey and `sequence`, and correct the comments.

v1.reason: The only reader of the control socket's reverse direction is the drain thread at device.rs:826-829 (`while drain.read(&mut bytes).is_ok_and(|count| count > 0) {}`). It never calls `parse_device_msg` or `parse_device_event`. rg finds DeviceMsg, DeviceEvent, device_msg_len, parse_device_msg and parse_device_event used only inside mirror.rs and tests/mirror.rs. The comment at mirror.rs:711-713 ('the shell's drain thread matches [`DeviceMsg`] exhaustively') is false, and so is the module doc's 'clipboard in both directions' (14). `InputMsg::GetClipboard` (818-822) says the answer 'arrives as a DeviceEvent::Clipboard', but it is read and discarded. So a `device.mirror.input {type:getclipboard}` returns `{}` and the device clipboard never reaches the caller, and any `sequence` ack is discarded the same way.
v1.correction: The parse_* functions are correct and tested, so this is unwired functionality as much as dead code. Choose one: wire parse_device_event into the drain thread and surface the clipboard as a mirror status frame, or delete the parsers, GetClipboard/CopyKey and `sequence`. Either way, correct the docs at mirror.rs:14, 592-594, 711-713 and 818.

findings.title: MirrorOptions and LockOrientation are an option surface no production caller uses
findings.evidence: The only production launch is `let mut options = mirror::MirrorOptions::for_capture(runtime.max_size); options.video_bit_rate = runtime.bitrate;` (handlers/device.rs:787-791). Nothing sets `capture_orientation` (LockOrientation: 5 variants, `as_arg`, and a long v4.1 note), `power_off_on_close`, `audio`, `stay_awake`, `log_level` or `max_fps`. `server_shell_args` (227-229) is called only by tests. The struct doc calls these "The server options Relay actually varies" (118).
findings.impact: About 90 lines (enum, struct, Default, builder, wrapper, and the tests that pin them) must be kept in step with every scrcpy bump, although only two values ever vary.
findings.fix: Replace them with one `server_shell_args(serial, scid, max_size, bit_rate)` that emits the fixed keys. Delete LockOrientation, MirrorOptions and the wrapper, and add an option back when a caller needs it.

v1.reason: The only production caller is device.rs:787-791. It runs `MirrorOptions::for_capture(runtime.max_size)`, overrides `video_bit_rate` from runtime.bitrate, then calls `server_shell_args_with`. No production code sets capture_orientation (LockOrientation, mirror.rs:94-115), audio, stay_awake, power_off_on_close, log_level or max_fps. `server_shell_args` (227-229) is referenced only from tests/mirror.rs. The doc comment at 118 ('The server options Relay actually varies') is untrue for most of the fields.
v1.correction: The impact is overstated. Options left at their defaults are never emitted (the capture_orientation and power_off_on_close keys are added only when set), so a scrcpy bump does not force any change to the unused fields. The real cost is about 60 lines of speculative surface (the enum, its as_arg, the long v4.1 note and the tests pinning them) that nothing exercises in production. The cleanup is optional and the payoff is modest. Deleting LockOrientation and the unused fields and keeping a small (max_size, bit_rate) builder is enough.

findings.title: Dead device-model code: configure_mirror_server is never called; MirrorRuntime.input_width/input_height are never read
findings.evidence: `configure_mirror_server` and `MIRROR_SERVER` (14, 56-60) have no caller in the workspace, so `mirror_server_path()` always falls back to the compile-time `env!("CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR")/../../apps/relay-native/resources/scrcpy-server-v4.1`. `input_width` and `input_height` are stored (136-137, 161-162, filled at handlers/device.rs:94-95) and never read. `sessions_holder` (handlers/device.rs:958-962) duplicates `actor_holder` (handlers/device_lease.rs:67-76) and is unreachable, because device.run is UserOnly and so `actor_session_id()` is always None.
findings.impact: The API's doc ("Point the engine at a bundled scrcpy server") suggests the jar can be relocated in a packaged build, but only the build checkout's path ever works. The dead fields and branch add noise to every runtime.
findings.fix: Delete them, or wire configure_mirror_server from startup if a relocatable jar is wanted. Drop the unreachable `Some(id) => sessions_holder(...)` branch in RunOp.

v1.reason: `configure_mirror_server` (device.rs:56) has no caller anywhere in crates/ or apps/. `git log -S configure_mirror_server` shows only the commit that introduced it (fcbdbce), so a call was never added and later removed. `mirror_server_path()` (device.rs:62-67) therefore always falls back to `env!("CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR")/../../apps/relay-native/resources/scrcpy-server-v4.1`. `input_width` and `input_height` are set at handlers/device.rs:94-95 and tests/mirror.rs:692-693 and never read. The `Some(id) => sessions_holder(ctx, id)?` arm in RunOp (handlers/device.rs:147, fn at 959) cannot run. device.run is `Actors::UserOnly` (relay-bus ops/device.rs:22). `resolve_actor` (engine.rs:1355) returns `None` for User and Test. An agent is refused by the allowlist check before dispatch. `Ctx::set_session` is only called inside handlers, so `actor_session_id()` is always `None` in RunOp.
v1.correction: The mirror_server_path fallback is worth more than a dead-code note. A packaged or installed engine binary looks for the jar at a compile-time path into the build checkout, and nothing can relocate it. Once the checkout moves, `device.mirror.start` fails with `device.mirror_server_missing`. Either wire `configure_mirror_server` from engine startup (for example the native app's resource directory) or delete it. Deleting `sessions_holder` also removes the duplicate of `actor_holder`.

findings.title: MirrorBuffer's 2 MiB catch-up ring is updated on every packet but only ever read while empty
findings.evidence: `push` locks `buffer`, clones the Arc into a VecDeque and evicts down to 2 MiB on every video packet (291-315). The only `attach()` caller is the socket door, immediately after its own `device.mirror.start` returns (socket.rs:551). At that point the worker has not finished push, forward, spawn and handshake, so `history` (socket.rs:579-585) is always empty. The ring could not help a late joiner anyway: the config packet is evicted after about 2 MiB, and a packet over 2 MiB evicts itself.
findings.impact: Every frame pays for a mutex, an Arc clone and deque bookkeeping, and up to 2 MiB stays pinned per mirror, with no observable effect. It is also a second copy of RunRuntime's ring-plus-broadcast pattern.
findings.fix: Drop MirrorBuffer and have attach return only the receiver (it already subscribes before the worker starts). The ResetVideo path already handles resync.

v1.reason: The only `MirrorRuntime::attach()` caller is socket.rs:551. It runs right after `device.mirror.start` returns through spawn_blocking (socket.rs:519-523). The mirror worker is started only by `after_commit` -> `std::thread::spawn` (handlers/device.rs:100-102), and it has to finish `adb push` of the jar, `adb forward`, server spawn, both connects and the 68-byte handshake before its first `push`. That takes hundreds of ms or more. So `history` is in practice always empty and `cursor` is 0. No other door (relay-remote, the CLI) attaches mirrors: socket.rs:665, tests/bus.rs:265/617 and device.rs:421 are all `RunRuntime::attach`. Meanwhile `push` (device.rs:291-315) takes the buffer mutex, clones an Arc into the deque and evicts down to 2 MiB on every video packet. The ring could not serve a late joiner anyway, because the config/SPS packet is evicted first.
v1.correction: Keep the per-chunk `seq` counter, since windows use seq gaps to detect lag (socket.rs:607-611). Make it an AtomicU64 or keep a counter-only mutex. Drop the VecDeque and byte accounting, and have `attach` return only the receiver, or `(seq, rx)`. The 2 MiB of pinned memory is per active mirror, typically one or two.

findings.title: device.release reports other holders' lapsed leases as released by the caller
findings.evidence: `let released = leases.release_where(|lease| ...)`, and `release_where` starts with `let mut gone = expire(&mut map);` (device_lease.rs:234), which returns every lapsed lease of any holder. All of `released` then goes into `ReleaseOut { released: views }`.
findings.impact: Trigger: agent A calls device.release for its phone. The response also lists session B's lapsed claim on another device as released, which an agent reading the result can misattribute to itself.
findings.fix: Have release_where return (expired, selected) separately. Emit events for both, but return only the selected leases.

v1.reason: handlers/device_lease.rs:55-62 passes everything release_where returns into ReleaseOut.released. device_lease.rs:232-240 shows release_where starting with `let mut gone = expire(&mut map);`, which removes every lapsed lease of any holder. Those leases are then returned alongside the ones the predicate selected. The op is documented as "Release a device lease you hold" (relay-bus ops/device.rs:79-80), so other holders' lapsed leases in the result are misattributed to the caller. The emitted RELEASED events for them are correct, so only the response is wrong.
v1.correction: Have release_where return the expired and selected leases separately, or filter the response by the same predicate. Emit events for both and return only the selected leases in ReleaseOut.

findings.title: holder_of ignores a live `*` lease when the device's own entry has lapsed
findings.evidence: `map.get(device).or_else(|| map.get(ANY_DEVICE)).filter(|held| held.expires.is_none_or(|at| at > now))`. The `*` fallback is consulted only when the device key is absent, not when it is present but lapsed.
findings.impact: Trigger: a holder has a lapsed shell lease on R5 and a live `*` claim. device.list shows R5 as free, although acquire would refuse other holders on it.
findings.fix: `map.get(device).filter(live).or_else(|| map.get(ANY_DEVICE).filter(live))`.

v1.reason: The expression at device_lease.rs:226-229 does behave as described when a lapsed entry is in the map, but in practice no lapsed entry is there when holder_of runs. Both callers remove expired entries just before calling it. device.list (handlers/device.rs:36-39) first calls handlers::device_lease::prune. When the map is non-empty, prune calls Leases::prune, then release_where, then expire(&mut map), which removes every lapsed lease. holder_of is called a few lines later. device.claim (handlers/device_lease.rs:35-36) calls acquire, and acquire calls expire first. So a 'present but lapsed' device key survives only if the lease lapses in the microseconds between the prune and the holder_of call. Even then the result is a single stale device.list row that the next refresh corrects. Not worth a finding.
v1.correction: If the code is ever touched, `map.get(device).filter(live).or_else(|| map.get(ANY_DEVICE).filter(live))` is a harmless tidy-up. It is not needed for correctness today, because every caller prunes first.

findings.title: Release events for leases pruned during a refused request are discarded with the rolled-back transaction
findings.evidence: `acquire` and `check` remove pruned or expired leases from the in-memory map and queue their events on ctx (`for gone in released { ctx.emit(RELEASED, gone.event()); }`) before returning `device.busy`. On an ordinary handler error the engine rolls back and never sends ctx's queued events (engine.rs:1073-1095). guardrail `gate` returns the error without `commit_error` (guardrail.rs:531-533), and so does RunOp (handlers/device.rs:150). Conversely, a lease taken before a later failure in the same request (use_grants in gate, or the commit in RunOp) stays in memory and its ACQUIRED event is dropped.
findings.impact: Leases dropped while refusing someone else are released silently, so agents waiting on device.lease.released for those devices are not woken.
findings.fix: Emit lease releases with `engine.emit_system` at the moment of removal, as release_run and release_session already do, independent of the request's outcome.

v1.reason: handlers/device_lease.rs:112-125. acquire and check remove pruned or expired leases from the in-memory map (device_lease.rs:177, 265) and queue their RELEASED events with ctx.emit. Both then return device.busy through `?`. On an error without commit_error, engine.rs:1073-1095 rolls back and never sends the queued events. guardrail.rs:532 (`gate_command(...)?`) and device.rs:150 (`check(ctx, ...)?`) propagate without commit_error, so the in-memory removal stays and its event is lost. The reverse case is also real: in gate, a shell lease taken by gate_command stays in memory (SHELL_RUNNING, 15 min) if use_grants (guardrail.rs:533) fails afterwards, and its ACQUIRED event is dropped. Impact is small. Expiry is only ever announced when something prunes the lease, so waiters already depend on bus.wait timeouts and retries. Session-held leases are also released with events by release_session on exit.
v1.correction: Emit releases through engine.emit_system at the moment of removal, as release_run and release_session do. A related, more serious case is out of this finding's scope: in RunOp, if the transaction commit fails after acquire, the Kind::Run lease and its device_runs entry stay and never prune, because live_runs still contains the id.

findings.title: set_clipboard silently truncates text over 262,130 bytes and send_input reports success
findings.evidence: `let mut end = s.len().min(SET_CLIPBOARD_MAX_LENGTH); … let bytes = &s.as_bytes()[..end];` gives no signal to the caller, and `send_input` returns Ok. The desktop paste path sends the host clipboard as `{"type":"setclipboard","text":…,"paste":true}` (apps/relay-native/src/mirror.rs:501). The text_chunks doc in the same file calls silent truncation "exactly the failure you do not notice".
findings.impact: Pasting more than about 256 KiB into the mirror pastes a cut-off prefix on the phone, with no error.
findings.fix: In send_input, refuse with device.input when the text exceeds SET_CLIPBOARD_MAX_LENGTH (a clipboard set cannot be split), so the UI can tell the user.

v1.reason: mirror.rs:608-613 `set_clipboard` cuts the text to SET_CLIPBOARD_MAX_LENGTH ((1<<18)-14 bytes) on a char boundary and signals nothing. `send_input` (device.rs:924-956) then reports Ok. Nothing upstream stops large payloads: the socket door reads unbounded lines (socket.rs BufReader::lines), and engine.rs:1244-1251 only routes setclipboard off the inline fast path. The desktop's Ctrl+V sends the whole host clipboard as setclipboard with paste:true (apps/relay-native/src/mirror.rs:501). So a paste over about 256 KiB pastes a cut-off prefix on the device and reports no error.
v1.correction: Refusing in send_input is not enough on its own. The native client sends input fire-and-forget and logs a refusal only at debug (apps/relay-native/src/mirror.rs:1156-1158), so the UI would also need to surface the device.input error, or the client should check the length before it sends. The trigger (a paste of 256 KiB or more into a phone field) is rare, so the severity stays low.

findings.title: BUS.md still says the socket door cannot carry the mirror stream, and the device lease ops are undocumented
findings.evidence: The §7 row reads: "`mirror` | `device.mirror.start` | H.264 NAL units | Tauri `Channel<Bytes>` only; socket door returns `unavailable`". The socket door is now the mirror's only transport, using `{stream:"mirror", seq, data: base64 | status object}` frames (socket.rs:520-646). device.claim, device.release, device.leases and the device.lease.acquired/released events appear nowhere in docs/, and there is no DECISIONS entry for leases either.
findings.impact: The architecture reference contradicts the code for the mirror data plane, and the coordination protocol agents are told to follow (device.busy, then bus.wait) has no spec.
findings.fix: Update the §7 row to describe the socket framing: base64 packets plus status objects, with a terminal state ending the stream. Add the lease ops and events to the device op table.

v1.reason: The BUS.md §7 row (line 381) says the mirror stream is 'Tauri `Channel<Bytes>` only; socket door returns `unavailable`'. In fact socket.rs:520-646 serves device.mirror.start over the socket door, with `{v:1, stream:"mirror", mirror_id, seq, data}` frames, where data is a base64 packet or a status object and a terminal status ends the stream. The BUS.md device op table (859-870) leaves out device.claim, device.release and device.leases, which exist in relay-bus/src/ops/device.rs:62-73 and are granted to agent roles in settings.rs:36-38. It also leaves out the device.lease.acquired and device.lease.released events (handlers/device_lease.rs:14). rg over docs/ finds no lease spec.
v1.correction: BUS.md describes itself as 'the app's API' and says it 'wins' over SPEC, so the drift matters more than it would in an ordinary doc. The op metadata in relay-bus (reachable through bus.schema) does document the leases, which limits the practical impact. The low severity is right.

results.coverage:
I read every line of crates/relay-core/src/handlers/task.rs (1317 lines), module.rs (250) and notes.rs (705, which also contains the mailbox.* handlers), plus their op definitions in crates/relay-bus/src/ops/{task,module,notes}.rs and the related types in relay-bus/src/types.rs.

To check that each problem is reachable and not handled elsewhere, I traced into:
- engine.rs: the whole pipeline, invoke_registered and the register variants.
- guardrail.rs: authorize and callability.
- store.rs: the schema, migrations and statement-cache tuning.
- audit.rs, and handlers/audit.rs (undo and its expect guard).
- handlers/session.rs: create/spawn staging, finish_launch, complete_group_assignment, Done, announce_assignment, launch_nudge, close.
- sessions.rs: name generation.
- branch_cleanup.rs, worktree.rs (create, head_of), git.rs (fetch_remote), hooks.rs (install_git), plugins.rs (default_checkout), awareness.rs (brief), providers.rs (Codex argv), recovery.rs (audit retention), settings defaults (role allowlists).
- relay-remote wire.rs: the phone acts as the user actor.
- Native call sites: task_pages.rs, board_view.rs, launch.rs, pages.rs, client.rs, app.rs event loop.
- DECISIONS D106 and D160, BUS.md §1.3/§9.1/§10.5-10.7, and the perf baseline docs.

I checked the pedantic clippy output for these files. The usize->i64 and i64->f64 casts are all on small bounded values, so none hides a bug.

Not done:
- Nothing was executed (no cargo, per the hard rules). The task.activity and list-endpoint costs are extrapolated from the docs/perf measurements, not measured here.
- I read only the relevant regions of session.rs and of the native UI files, not all of them.
- The mobile app was not examined (out of scope).
- jiff's variable-length fractional timestamps sort out of order only for same-second prefix fractions, which is negligible, so I did not report it.

findings.title: assign_session treats every live session in the same checkout as a PAIR, so tasks fan out to unrelated agents and get stuck in Active
findings.evidence: assign_session runs `prepare_cached("SELECT id FROM sessions WHERE worktree=?1 AND state!='closed' ORDER BY id")` on the target's worktree. For every session it finds, it does `INSERT OR IGNORE INTO task_sessions(task_id,session_id,ord,queue_ord)`. If that session has no live current task, it also runs `UPDATE sessions SET task_id=...` and adds the session to newly_current. dispatch_task (714-719) then calls announce_assignment for each of those sessions that is Idle/Running/Blocked. The comment at 687-688 shows the intent was only to cover 'the second half of a PAIR'. D160, however, makes the primary checkout the default for every new session in projects with the Unreal plugin (session.rs:858 `unwrap_or(prepared.default_checkout)`, plugins.rs:210-214, plugins/unreal-engine/plugin.json `"default_checkout": "primary"`). The launch sheet also offers `primary` as a worktree. In both cases every session gets the same `primary.path` (session.rs:860-863). complete_group_assignment (session.rs:100-103) only moves a task to review when no builder sharing the worktree still has an uncompleted task_sessions row for it.
findings.impact: Example: two independent builders S1 and S2 share the primary checkout. Dispatching task A to S1 also queues A for S2, makes A S2's current task if S2 had none, writes 'Your current assignment is Task #A' into S2's PTY, and gives S2 own-task rights on A (task.update, task.move, task.link_commit). If S2 is already on its own task B, dispatching B fans B out to S1 the same way. When S1 calls session.done on A, the call returns early because S2 is an unfinished 'builder' of A; S2 hits the same wall on B. Neither task ever reaches in_review, and both agents sit idle, since the role text tells them 'do not begin queued work while peers are still building'.
findings.fix: Define group membership by explicit PAIR linkage instead of worktree equality. Options: record a group id at session.create when pair_with is set, or select `id=? OR name=row.pair_with OR pair_with=row.name`. Use the same predicate in complete_group_assignment and validate_pair (session.rs:764-766, 100-118) so co-tenants of the primary checkout stay independent.

v1.reason: assign_session (task.rs:563-613) selects every non-closed session with the same worktree and inserts a task_sessions row for each. It also makes the task current for any of them without a live current task. complete_group_assignment (session.rs:91-...) treats every non-closed builder in the same worktree that has an uncompleted row as a blocker (`builders_left != 0 -> return Ok(())`) and returns before advancing anyone. Nothing stops unrelated sessions from sharing a worktree. D160 and plugins.rs default_checkout make 'primary' the default for every session.create in a project with the Unreal plugin enabled (plugins/unreal-engine/plugin.json:18), and D160 states that 'agents sharing one checkout also share one editor'. The role defaults to Builder (session.rs:807). Take two independent Unreal builders S1 and S2 in the primary checkout. Dispatching A to S1 also queues A on S2. Dispatching B to S2 queues B on S1. When S1 reports done on A, S2's open row blocks the move to review, and S2 is in the same position on B. Neither task reaches in_review until both agents also finish the other's task. The existing tests (sessions.rs:1230ff) only cover explicit pair_with groups, where sharing by worktree is the intended meaning.
v1.correction: The trigger needs co-tenant sessions that were not created with pair_with. That is the default for Unreal-plugin projects, or happens when 'primary' or an existing path is chosen explicitly. Group membership should follow pair_with linkage, for example a group id stored at create time, rather than worktree equality. The same predicate is also used in complete_group_assignment's builders_left, reviewers_left and ids queries (session.rs ~100-115) and in validate_pair's counts (session.rs:764-766).

v2.reason:
(a) Confirmed in code. assign_session (crates/relay-core/src/handlers/task.rs:570-612) enumerates `SELECT id FROM sessions WHERE worktree=?1 AND state!='closed'`. It inserts a task_sessions row for every session found and makes the task current for any co-tenant with no live current task. complete_group_assignment (session.rs:100-103) keeps the task in Active while any non-closed builder in the same worktree has an uncompleted row. Pairing is checked only in validate_pair, and only when pair_with is set. Sessions that share a checkout without being paired are supported and tested: sessions.rs:312 and sessions.rs:1360, the latter creating three "primary" sessions.
