(b) How it is reached. D160 (plugins.rs:210-214, session.rs:858) makes "primary" the engine default for Unreal-plugin projects whenever `worktree` is omitted. That covers task.dispatch/session.create from the phone (its payloads carry no worktree), from the CLI and from MCP, and task.dispatch `create`/`fanout` templates. The plugin README describes several agents sharing the main checkout and taking turns on the editor, and D162 shows the author runs real Unreal sessions. On the desktop, the launch sheet always sends "worktree":"new" (launch.rs:260, 346), so the user has to type "primary" or a path. Unreal users need that for the live editor tools, which refuse when the agent's checkout is not the one the editor has open. Once two or more unpaired sessions share a checkout, every dispatch triggers the bug.

(c) What happens. I replayed the engine's exact SQL in sqlite (scratchpad/exp/group_sim.py, group_sim2.py):
1. Desktop batch launch of two solo agents in "primary", A for agent 1 and B for agent 2 (launch.rs:804 creates with task_id, :810 dispatches each task). Afterwards the rows (A,S1), (B,S1), (B,S2), (A,S2) all exist, with S1 current on A and S2 on B. S1's done returns early with 1 builder left, and S2's done does the same. Both tasks stay Active and both agents stay idle for good. The role text (providers.rs:55-58) tells them not to repeat session.done or start queued work, so only a manual task.move/approve clears it.
2. Phone dispatches in an Unreal project, A then B. When S1 finishes A it is moved onto B, which S2 is already doing, and is told so. Two agents then do the same task in one checkout and edit the same files. B stays Active until both report it.
3. A co-tenant that is idle with no task. Dispatching A to S1 makes A S2's current task too. Because start defaults to true (task.rs:1057, 714-717), "Your current assignment is Task #A" is typed into S2's PTY. S2 also gains own-task rights on A, because guardrail.rs:342 only checks task_sessions membership.
4. A fanout dispatch in an Unreal project hands every sub-task to every earlier session, which defeats its "one session each" purpose.
I could not establish data corruption.

(d) High fits the rubric: a hard stall or wrong assignment in a normal multi-agent flow for shared-checkout users, which is the default outside the desktop sheet for Unreal projects. It is not critical, because it needs that configuration and has a manual workaround.

(e) The group-id fix is correct and complete if it covers assign_session, the three group queries in complete_group_assignment (session.rs:101, 105, 117) and validate_pair's counts (765). It needs a migration with a backfill from the existing pair_with links. The alternative one-hop predicate is wrong for the supported three-member review group; see the correction.
v2.correction:
Mechanism. The permanent deadlock needs cross rows: each session holds an uncompleted row for the other's current task. That happens directly in the desktop launch sheet's batch launch of two or more solo agents in one checkout, each with its own task (launch.rs:804 creates with task_id, :810 dispatches each task with start:false). It does not come from "S2 already on B, then B dispatched". With one-at-a-time dispatch (the phone in an Unreal project), the result is duplicate work instead: the agent that finishes first is moved onto its peer's task, and that task stays Active until both report it.

Reachability. On the desktop, D160's default never applies, because the launch sheet always sends "worktree":"new" (launch.rs:260, 346). There the user must type "primary" or a path for several solo agents. The default does apply to the phone, CLI, MCP and task.dispatch create/fanout templates.

Fix. The proposed `id=? OR name=row.pair_with OR pair_with=row.name` predicate is incomplete. finish_create only back-fills the partner's pair_with when it is NULL (session.rs:814), so in a review group b1.pair_with=reviewer, reviewer.pair_with=b1 and b2.pair_with=reviewer. Starting from b1, the predicate finds {b1, reviewer} and misses b2. A dispatch to b1 would then leave b2 unassigned, and b1's done could move the task to review before b2 finishes. That breaks review_group_keeps_shared_worktree_until_every_participant_finishes_then_advances_fifo (sessions.rs:1231). The fix should use a stored group id, added by migration (append to store::MIGRATIONS, bump SCHEMA_VERSION, backfill from pair_with links), or a two-hop closure through the reviewer.

Also reword the role text at providers.rs:55 ("A shared-worktree group...") to describe review groups. Leave the physical-checkout queries keyed on worktree: hooks (session.rs:336), close/park (session.rs:1513, 1554), git.rs:134 and 391, and device_lease.rs:81.

findings.title: task.dispatch runs session.create/spawn's unlocked phases (git fetch, worktree add, PTY start) inside its own transaction, under the store mutex
findings.evidence: Dispatch is registered with plain `e.register::<Dispatch>`, yet dispatch_task calls `ctx.invoke_registered("session.create", ...)` (683) and `ctx.invoke_registered(op, json!({"session":name}))` for session.spawn/wake/resume (712). Engine::invoke_registered (engine.rs:325-351) runs a staged op's `prepare` with `held: Some(self.tx)`, which keeps the lock and the open transaction. Its comment claims this happens 'only on this path' (guardrail.confirm). session.create's prepare says 'Fetch, checkout... None of it belongs under the global store mutex' (session.rs:854-856). That prepare runs `git fetch --all` (git.rs:938-945, 20 s timeout) and `git worktree add` (worktree.rs:214, 120 s timeout). spawn's prepare runs git config subprocesses (hooks.rs:75) and copies skills. finish_launch then starts the PTY inside the transaction (session.rs:646). Fanout repeats all of this for every descendant (1068-1075).
findings.impact: `task.dispatch {create}` (a documented API that fanout requires) holds the global store mutex for a network fetch plus a full checkout. That can last up to about 140 s per session, multiplied by the number of fanned children. During that time every other request blocks, including every agent's guardrail.gate hook and every UI read. The native task page's Dispatch button to a Created, Parked or Restorable session also runs spawn/wake/resume's git subprocesses and file writes under the lock. The external side effects are outside the transaction. If a later step fails (for example child k's create in a fanout), the session rows roll back, but the earlier worktrees, hooks and running agent PTYs remain. Those PTYs stay in Engine::ptys with no matching row.
findings.fix: Split task.dispatch so the slow work happens outside the transaction. Options: register it as staged and create the sessions in the unlocked phase, or require existing sessions (as launch.rs already does) and start them after commit through separate session.spawn requests. Only the task and assignment writes should stay in the transaction. Correct the invoke_registered comment.

v1.reason: Dispatch is registered with plain e.register (task.rs:1049). dispatch_task calls ctx.invoke_registered("session.create", ...) (task.rs:683) and, when start is set, session.spawn/wake/resume (task.rs:712). Engine::invoke_registered (engine.rs ~309-360) runs a staged op's prepare with `held: Some(self.tx)`, so the slow phase runs under the store mutex inside the open transaction. Its comment says this is meant only for guardrail.confirm replaying git.commit. session.create's prepare (session.rs ~854-896) runs refresh_new_worktree -> fetch_remote (`git fetch --all --prune`, 20 s timeout, git.rs:938-945), worktree::create and hook installation, and its own comment says none of that belongs under the global mutex. This path is reached in normal use: the phone door's 'New request' sends exactly task.dispatch {create:{...}} (crates/relay-remote/tests/remote.rs:305-316 pins that payload). The native task page's Dispatch button (task_pages.rs:652) sends start=true by default, which runs spawn/wake/resume's staged prepare under the lock for a Created, Parked or Restorable target. While this runs, every other bus request is blocked, including guardrail gates and keystroke-adjacent ops. Fanout repeats the work per child.
v1.correction: The native multi-agent launcher (launch.rs:805-810) avoids the problem by calling session.create separately and then dispatching with start:false. The main live triggers are therefore the phone door's dispatch-with-create and the native Dispatch button. Fix: make task.dispatch staged, doing the session create/launch in the unlocked phase, or have callers create and spawn the session as separate requests and keep only the task and assignment writes in the transaction.

v2.reason:
I checked this against the code myself.

(a) The code does what the finding says. Dispatch is registered with plain `e.register::<Dispatch>` (task.rs:1049). dispatch_task calls `ctx.invoke_registered("session.create", ...)` at line 683 and `invoke_registered(op, {"session":name})` for spawn, wake or resume at line 712. In invoke_registered (engine.rs:328-349), a staged op's `prepare` runs with `held: Some(self.tx)`. Meanwhile dispatch_inner is still holding the store guard it took at engine.rs:954 and the transaction it opened at 956. `Unlocked::read` uses the held connection and does not lock again (engine.rs:177). So session.create's prepare (session.rs:833-896) runs entirely under the global mutex. That prepare calls refresh_new_worktree, then `git fetch --all --prune` (20 s timeout, git.rs:938-945), then `git worktree add` (120 s timeout, worktree.rs:214), then install_git (several git subprocesses). The default checkout is "new" (plugins.rs:210-214). When no branch is given, existing_worktree_branch(None) is false, so the fetch runs on every such create. The nested spawn then runs prepare_launch under the lock as well: hooks, adapters, the first full skills::apply copy into the new worktree, and the brief files.

(b) This is reachable in normal use. The phone door forwards any request with the user actor (wire.rs:95-103). The phone's "New request" sheet and its Board dispatch both send task.dispatch {create, start:true}, so every dispatch from the phone takes this path. On the desktop, the task page's Dispatch button sends a session with start defaulting to true (task_pages.rs:653). That runs the lighter spawn, wake or resume prepare under the lock: git config subprocesses, a skill copy on the first spawn, and file writes, roughly 0.1-0.5 s. The native multi-agent launcher is not affected (launch.rs:805-816). It calls session.create, then task.dispatch with start:false, then session.spawn, each as a separate top-level request. Fanout repeats the work for each child, but nothing in the UI sends fanout; only the CLI or socket can.

(c) For the whole fetch plus checkout, every request that needs the store waits. That includes every agent's guardrail.gate PreToolUse hook, every UI read and write, PTY exit writes and report hooks. Keystrokes still go through, because of the D148 fast path. On LFS-heavy repos the hold can pass 30 s. The native client already gives task.dispatch a 180 s budget for LFS hydration (client.rs:65-70). A 30 s hold exceeds the client's default 30 s request timeout, so UI requests time out. It also exceeds the 30 s PreToolUse hook timeout (hooks.rs:351). I could not establish from this repo whether Claude Code blocks or allows a tool call when it kills a hook. No rows are corrupted. However, external effects survive a rollback. One example is provider.not_installed raised by the nested spawn, a refusal the tests expect (board.rs:45). It leaves the new worktree, its branch and its hook config with no session row. With fanout and start, a later child's create failure leaves the earlier children's agent PTYs in Engine::ptys with no row. The rollback path drops after_commit and never touches ptys (engine.rs:1073-1095).

(d) High is right. This is a bus freeze in a normal phone flow. It is bounded by subprocess timeouts, so it is not an indefinite hang and not critical. It contradicts D144, D149 ("and only that path"), the comment at engine.rs:325-327, the BUS.md §5.1 latency budget, the comment in session.create itself (854-856), and fetch_remote's doc ("called outside the store transaction").

(e) The fix points the right way but is incomplete as written. See the correction.
v2.correction:
Corrections to the finding:
- The title lists "PTY start" as one of the unlocked phases. It is not. Pty::spawn runs in finish_launch, which holds the lock on every spawn by design (D149: "only the PTY start and the row update hold it"). What the nested path wrongly moves under the lock is the prepare work: the fetch, worktree add, install_git, the skill copy, and the adapter and brief writes.
- The live heavy trigger is the phone door: both the "New request" sheet and Board dispatch send create with start:true. Fanout has no UI caller anywhere. The native Dispatch button triggers only the lighter spawn, wake or resume prepare.
- History: session.create became staged in 6e7b044 (2026-09-09). The "only on this path" comment was written earlier, in fcbdbce (09-04). So the nested path quietly kept the old cost of running everything inside the transaction.

Caveats on the fix:
1. Do not move the spawn into a staged task.dispatch prepare. plan_launch builds the brief from the store (awareness::brief), and the brief has to see the assignment, which is written inside the transaction. Launch through a separate top-level session.spawn, wake or resume after commit, as launch.rs does. Ideally the engine runs that launch before it replies, so the phone's immediate Terminal attach does not race into session.not_spawned.
2. Keep the provider.not_installed refusal (board.rs:45) by checking providers::executable in the prepare.
3. Define what happens to checkouts already created in the prepare when a later step fails, especially for fanout's N checkouts.
4. Update D149 and the invoke_registered comment. Add a debug_assert in invoke_registered so that only the guardrail.confirm replay may run a staged prepare nested. Other nested callers exist at lower cost: project.remove{force} and workspace.remove call session.close, whose prepare runs the hook-teardown git subprocesses (workspace.rs:173 and 328).

Separate issue noticed while checking, with a different root cause: project.clone (workspace.rs:228-238) is a plain `register` handler. It runs `git clone` with `Command::output()`, which bypasses output_with_timeout and has no time limit, while holding the store mutex. The native client allows it 1800 s (client.rs:67).

findings.title: task.approve fails hard once the assigned session's branch is gone, which automatic branch cleanup causes after a merged session is closed
findings.evidence: With no sha, Approve resolves `repo.rev_parse_single(format!("refs/heads/{}", session.session.branch))` and returns `BusError::unavailable("git.head", ...)` when it fails. Its comment (1105-1108) says 'session.close deliberately keeps its branch'. That is no longer true: session.close calls `crate::branch_cleanup::after_close(engine, project_id, branch)` (session.rs:1630-1635), and branch_cleanup deletes a closed session's `relay/<name>` branch once its work is merged (branch_cleanup.rs:1-22). The sha that session.done already linked (task_commits, session.rs:97-99) is ignored. Sessions in a detached primary checkout record branch 'HEAD' (worktree.rs:122), which never resolves as refs/heads/HEAD. Neither native caller can pass a sha: board_view.rs:841 `self.act("task.approve", json!({"task_id":task["id"]}))` and task_pages.rs:625.
findings.impact: Normal flow: the agent finishes, the user merges its PR, closes the session, and the cleanup thread deletes the branch. From then on, dragging the card to Done or clicking 'Approve task' fails with unavailable/git.head, and the app gives no way to supply a sha, so the task cannot be approved from the UI. Tests never hit this because Instance::Test skips cleanup.
findings.fix: When the recorded branch does not resolve, fall back to the newest task_commits row for the task, then to the project HEAD. Fail only when nothing is known. Remove the stale comment.

v1.reason: Approve with no sha (task.rs:1094-1117) takes the newest task_sessions row and calls repo.rev_parse_single("refs/heads/<session.branch>"). If that fails it returns BusError::unavailable("git.head"). Its comment (1105-1108) says 'session.close deliberately keeps its branch'. That stopped being true in commit 2d38f75 (2026-10-05). session.close now calls branch_cleanup::after_close from after_commit (session.rs:1627-1635), and that deletes a closed session's branch once it is merged into base, matched by patch id, or covered by a merged GitHub PR (branch_cleanup.rs:1-22, with candidates at 74-80 selecting closed sessions). task.approve is the only way into Done: task.move refuses Done at task.rs:897. Neither native caller can pass a sha: board_view.rs:841 sends {task_id} from the drag-to-Done path, and task_pages.rs:625 is the Approve button. So the normal order (agent finishes, user merges the PR, closes the session, then drags the card to Done) fails with git.head unavailable, and the UI offers no way around it. The sha recorded by session.done in task_commits (session.rs:97-99) is never used as a fallback. A session in a detached primary checkout records branch 'HEAD' (worktree.rs:122), and refs/heads/HEAD never resolves either. Tests miss this because Instance::Test skips the cleanup (session.rs:1632-1633).
v1.correction: Severity stays high: a core flow (approving a finished, merged task) fails, and the user has no workaround. Fix as proposed: if refs/heads/<branch> does not resolve, fall back to the newest task_commits sha for the task, then to the project HEAD (or the base branch tip), and fail only when none exist. Update the stale comment at 1105-1108.

v2.reason:
(a) The code does what the finding says. When no sha is given, Approve (task.rs:1094-1117) reads the newest task_sessions row and runs `repo.rev_parse_single("refs/heads/<session.branch>")`. If that fails it returns `BusError::unavailable("git.head", ..)`. In gix 0.86, `find_ref` returns an error for a missing ref and has no fallback. The comment at 1105-1106 ("session.close deliberately keeps its branch") predates the branch_cleanup commit 2d38f75 (2026-10-05), and that commit did not touch task.rs. task.approve is the only path to Done: task.move refuses Done at task.rs:897, and nothing else writes col='done'. Both GUI callers send only `{task_id}`: board_view.rs:841 (drag to Done) and task_pages.rs:625 (Approve button).

(b) Who can trigger it: only the user (the op is UserOnly), through the normal board flow. It fires whenever the task's newest session is closed before approval and the cleanup has judged that session's branch merged. Three paths delete the branch:
- `after_close` runs on every close in any non-Test instance (session.rs:1630-1635).
- `after_merged_prs` runs from git.pr.list.
- The sweeper runs on every engine 90 s after start, then every 20 min (serve.rs:35). It takes every closed session (branch_cleanup.rs:74-80), so it also covers sessions ended by session.discard_restorable and sessions closed before this feature existed. On the first launch after the upgrade, every in-review task whose session had already been closed and merged becomes un-approvable.

"Merged" is broader than the finding says. I reproduced it in a scratch repo: a session branch with no commits of its own counts as an ancestor of main, `git update-ref -d` deletes it, and the ref no longer resolves. So it also fires for sessions that never committed anything. One example is phase7.rs:325 (`approve_uses_the_recorded_branch_after_the_assigned_session_is_closed`), which passes only because Instance::Test skips the cleanup. With the default close (remove_worktree false), a clean pooled worktree is removed as well. "Many agents, close finished panes, tidy the board later" is a common way to use the app, so this is not rare.

(c) The op fails with unavailable/git.head ("ref ... could not be found"). Dragging to Done first shows the toast "Approved #N into Done · Ctrl+Z undoes it" (board_view.rs:839) and then the error. The card stays in its column, so module progress and the Done-based changelog never count it. No data is lost.

(d) High fits: a hard failure in a normal flow, with no data loss. It is not critical, because approving before closing still works and there is a workaround outside the GUI.

(e) The proposed fallback is correct and safe. Existing tests are unaffected, and link_commit is INSERT OR IGNORE, so re-linking a sha that is already linked is harmless.
v2.correction:
"The user has no workaround" overstates it. The GUI has none, but `relay cmd task.approve '{"task_id":N,"sha":"<sha>"}'` works through the CLI's generic Cmd (relay-cli main.rs:36/388), and so does re-creating the branch by hand.

The trigger is wider than "a merged session": a closed session whose branch has no commits of its own is also judged "merged into main" and deleted. The periodic sweeper also reaches sessions closed by discard_restorable and sessions closed before the upgrade.

The detached-HEAD case ('HEAD' from worktree.rs:122) is a separate, rare, pre-existing cause with the same symptom. It only affects sessions in the primary checkout. The same fix covers it.

Fix order: recorded branch, then the newest task_commits sha for the task (the session.done commit), then the tip of the project's base branch (which contains the merged work) or HEAD. Fail only when the repo itself cannot be read.

Same root cause, also to update:
- the stale comment at task.rs:1105-1106;
- BUS.md:733 ("branch is kept");
- the GUI texts that promise the branch is kept: agent_menu.rs:590 and 609, and shell.rs:724 ("its worktree and branch are kept"). Cleanup can now delete both the branch and a clean pooled worktree.

Two follow-ups:
- Add a test that runs branch_cleanup::run before approving.
- Optionally, record the deleted tip in the cleanup's audit summary. It currently records branch, outcome, reason and pr, but not the sha.

findings.title: Undoing a move out of Done is always refused, which also jams the board's Ctrl+Z
findings.evidence: Move records the inverse `task.move {"column":column_str(before.column),"position":index}` (905) for every move, including Done -> In Review, a move it explicitly supports (902 sets AwaitingReview). The same handler then refuses `if p.column==Column::Done { return Err(conflict("task.column_transition","move to done through task.approve")) }` (897) with no exception for undo. audit.undo replays the inverse through invoke_registered (audit.rs:68). The native board's undo_last (board_view.rs:879-890) always undoes the newest user `task.*` row that has an undo_op and no undone_by.
findings.impact: Dragging a Done card back to In Review and pressing Ctrl+Z fails with task.column_transition. The failed row stays newest, so every later Ctrl+Z on the board picks it again and fails. Nothing older can be undone until the user makes another undoable board change.
findings.fix: When before.column is Done, record the inverse as `task.approve {task_id, sha: <latest linked sha>}`. Approve re-links the same sha (INSERT OR IGNORE) and restores Done with state none. Alternatively, let task.move accept done when it runs as an undo.

v1.reason: Move (task.rs:895-907) records the inverse as task.move with column_str(before.column) for every move. When the card came from Done, that inverse says column 'done'. The same handler refuses `p.column==Column::Done` at line 897 without exception. audit.undo (audit.rs:49-70) replays the inverse through ctx.invoke_registered, which runs the same Move handler (engine.rs:309-324), so the undo always fails with task.column_transition. The board lets a user drag a Done card to another column (board_view.rs:863-868 blocks only done->done). undo_last (board_view.rs:872-890) chooses the newest user task.* row that has an undo_op and no undone_by. A failed undo leaves undone_by NULL, so every later Ctrl+Z picks the same row and fails again until a newer undoable task change exists.
v1.correction: Moving a card out of Done to any column, not only In Review, creates a 'done' inverse that cannot be replayed. The fix should record task.approve (or a dedicated restore) as the inverse whenever before.column is Done. undo_last could also skip a row whose undo has already failed.

findings.title: Soft-deleting a parent leaves live sub-tasks attached to it; every parent.set on them then fails, and hidden subtrees escape the depth and children caps
findings.evidence: Delete (909-916) only stamps deleted_at, so children keep parent_id pointing at the deleted task. ParentSet re-emits `for parent in [before.parent_id, task.parent_id].into_iter().flatten() { let parent = get_task(ctx.tx(), parent, false)?; ...}` (1170-1172). get_task with include_deleted=false returns task.not_found for a deleted old parent, and the whole request rolls back. assert_parent's cycle walk `cursor = get_task(tx, id, false)?.parent_id` (400) fails the same way on any soft-deleted ancestor. child_ids and subtree_height (164-197) skip deleted rows, so live descendants of a deleted child are invisible to the depth check. Restore (929-951) re-attaches a task without re-running any of assert_parent's checks.
findings.impact: After deleting a parent card, its children still appear on the board with a parent badge. 'Detach from parent' (board_view.rs:2211-2214) and dropping them onto another card always fail with 'no task <deleted id>'. The only workaround is to restore the parent, re-home the children, and delete it again. Dropping any card onto a task whose grandparent is deleted fails with an id the user never chose. Moving a node whose deleted child hides live grandchildren pushes them past TASK_DEPTH_MAX (Task.depth is documented as never above 2). Restore can push a parent past TASK_CHILDREN_MAX.
findings.fix: In ParentSet, re-emit with include_deleted=true or skip parents that are not found. Walk ancestors with a cached `SELECT parent_id` as depth_of does. Then either detach live children on delete (recording them for undo) or make the depth and children checks and restore count subtrees under deleted nodes.

v1.reason: Delete (task.rs:909-916) only sets deleted_at, and nothing detaches children: the only DELETE FROM tasks is a whole-project wipe in workspace.rs:364, and there are no triggers. So live children keep parent_id pointing at the deleted row. ParentSet then re-emits both parents using get_task(..., false) (task.rs:1170-1172). get_task returns task.not_found for a deleted row (344-353), and that error rolls back the whole request. Detach from native (board_view.rs:2214, parent_id null) therefore fails for every child of a deleted parent, and so does re-parenting one by dropping it on another card (board_view.rs:859). assert_parent's ancestor walk (task.rs:400) uses get_task(tx,id,false), so choosing as the new parent any task with a soft-deleted ancestor fails with a not_found for that ancestor's id. child_ids and subtree_height (164-197) skip deleted rows, so live grandchildren under a deleted child are left out of the depth check, while depth_of (146-162) walks every row. Restore (929-951) clears deleted_at without re-checking TASK_CHILDREN_MAX or the depth cap.
v1.correction: The main user-visible effect is that the children of a deleted parent cannot be detached or re-parented until the parent is restored. Escaping the depth and children caps is a secondary, rarer effect. Minimal fix: in ParentSet, re-emit with include_deleted=true or skip a parent that is not found, and walk ancestors with a plain SELECT parent_id as depth_of does. Then pick one model, either detaching children on delete (recorded for undo) or counting subtrees under deleted nodes in the caps.

findings.title: Mailbox and task-session lookups use the session name, which is recycled after close, so a new session inherits a dead namesake's inbox and outbox
findings.evidence: Session names are drawn from 36x36=1296 adjective-animal pairs and are unique only among non-closed sessions (sessions.rs:73-89; store.rs:96 `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX sessions_live_name ... WHERE state != 'closed'`). MailboxList joins `LEFT JOIN message_recipients mr ON mr.message_id=m.id AND mr.session=?2` (672) on the name. MailboxOutbox filters `m.from_session = ?2` by name (640), as does the priority-pending check (293), and task.list's session filter uses `s.name=?` (task.rs:851). MailboxAck matches `session_id = ?3` (694).
findings.impact: Once a few hundred sessions have been closed, new sessions often get a recycled name. In the same project, the new agent's `mailbox.list {unread_only:true}` returns the old namesake's unacked mail, including system 'Your current assignment is Task #N' messages about someone else's task. Agents are told to read and ack unread mail, but every `mailbox.ack` on these fails with 'message N is not addressed to this session', so they stay unread forever. `mailbox.outbox` shows the namesake's sends, the namesake's unacked priority mail can block new priority sends, and task.list {session} plus the board's agent filter attribute the old session's cards to the new one.
findings.fix: Resolve the requested or actor session to its live id and filter `mr.session_id = ?`. Store the sender's session id on messages (migration) for the outbox and priority checks, or at minimum bound them by `sent_at >= session.created_at`. Filter task.list's session by the live session id.

v1.reason: sessions::new_name (sessions.rs:74-89) only avoids names held by non-closed sessions, from 36x36 pairs, and the unique index is partial (store.rs:96). MailboxList joins `mr.session=?2` by name (notes.rs:668) and filters `mr.acked_at IS NULL` for unread_only. Nothing deletes or acks a closed session's message_recipients rows: the only deletes are in project removal (workspace.rs:355). So a new session that reuses a name in the same project sees the dead namesake's unacked mail. mailbox.ack matches `session_id = ?3` (notes.rs:694-697), so acking those messages fails with 'not addressed to this session' and they stay unread forever. Agents are told to list unread mail and ack it (providers.rs:61-62), so they are exposed to stale assignment mail. The outbox (notes.rs:640, `m.from_session = ?2` by name) and the priority-pending check (notes.rs:289-295, sender by name) also attribute the namesake's sends to the new session. task.list's session filter joins sessions by `s.name=?` across closed sessions (task.rs:851). The engine's unread-priority count (engine.rs:1389-1391) correctly uses session_id, which confirms the name-keyed queries are the inconsistent ones.
v1.correction: How often this hits scales with N/1296 for N closed names in the same project, so it is common for long-lived projects and rare early on. The decisive harm is the un-ackable stale unread mail. The outbox and priority mix-ups are minor. The fix is as proposed: filter MailboxList by `mr.session_id` resolved from the live session (the column and index already exist), and key task.list's session filter on the live session id. For the outbox and priority checks, store the sender's session_id (migration) or bound by the session's created_at.

findings.title: Agents can read every project's tasks and modules; task.list, module.* and task.label.list ignore the actor's project
findings.symbol: List / module Get, List, Stats, ChangelogDraft / LabelList
findings.evidence: Layer-2 authorization only scopes payload `session` and `task_id` fields (guardrail.rs:328-349), and Scope::Project metadata is enforced nowhere. task.list does `if let Some(project_id) = p.project_id { get_project(...) }` and applies no project filter when project_id is absent, even with include_deleted (832-838). module.get (module.rs:125-144), module.list (145), module.stats (207), module.changelog.draft (208-215) and task.label.list (task.rs:1235-1249) never compare against the agent's project. notes.rs:47-61 assert_actor_project returns `not_own("project")` for exactly this case, session.list/get stop at the project (D106), and task.get is limited to the agent's own task.
findings.impact: Every role may call every query. An agent working an untrusted repository (and so exposed to prompt injection) can call `task.list {}` or `task.list {project_id: <other>, include_deleted: true}` and `module.get` on other projects' modules. That returns full task bodies, changelogs, attachment paths, linked commits and session names for all of the user's projects, which the agent can then exfiltrate. The boundary is also inconsistent: task.get refuses a same-project task that task.list returns, the kind of inconsistency D106 removed for sessions.
findings.fix: For agent actors, default task.list's project_id to the session's project and refuse any other. Call assert_actor_project (or session.rs's actor_project) in module.get/list/stats/changelog.draft and task.label.list.

v1.reason: The code behaves as described. guardrail::authorize (guardrail.rs:316-352) scopes only the payload's `session` and `task_id` fields and returns Ok for every Query. task.list (task.rs:832-838) applies no project filter when project_id is absent. module.get (module.rs:125), module.list (module.rs:145) and task.label.list (task.rs:1235) never compare the project against the actor's session, while notes (notes.rs:47-61), sessions (session.rs:183-202, D106) and overlap do. The security impact is much smaller than claimed, though. Agents are not confined from the user's data. file.read accepts any project_id with worktree '.', which resolves to the project root (file.rs:398-399 and 447-455) without checking the actor's project. The agent process also runs as the same OS user with a shell, so it can read the SQLite store file directly. Exfiltrating task bodies over the bus is no worse than what an injected agent can already do. This is a boundary inconsistency, the same kind D106 fixed for sessions, not an escape from guardrails.
v1.correction: Downgrade to low. The real cost is an inconsistent agent visibility boundary: task.get refuses a same-project task that task.list returns. Bus reads are not a confidentiality boundary, because file.read across projects and direct filesystem access both bypass it. The fix is still reasonable for consistency: scope task.list, module.* and task.label.list to the agent's project the way notes::assert_actor_project does. If cross-project reads are ever meant to be confidential, file.read's project_id needs the same check.

findings.title: task.activity scans and JSON-parses the project's whole audit history under the store lock every time a task is opened
findings.evidence: The WHERE clause ORs `(op LIKE 'task.%' AND json_extract(payload,'$.task_id') = ?2)`, `(op = 'task.create' AND json_extract(result_summary,'$.id') = ?2)` and `json_extract(result_summary,'$.task.id') = ?2` (763-767). The last branch applies to every op, so no audit index ((project_id, ts), (op, ts), ...) can serve it, and result_summary (up to 64 KB) is parsed for every non-matching project row. A task with fewer than limit+1 matches therefore scans back to the start of the retention window (180 days by default, settings.rs:43). That window includes every agent's audited guardrail.gate and session.report rows, which are project-tagged. The native task page runs this query on open (task_pages.rs:1134 `refresh.emit_clicked()`, call at 1056).
findings.impact: Cost grows with the project's entire audit history, not the task's, so the perf baseline note that it 'scales with the task's audit rows' is wrong. That baseline measured about 1.7 µs per row (2.6 ms at 1,500 rows). After months of hook traffic (hundreds of thousands of rows), opening a task holds the store mutex for hundreds of milliseconds to seconds, stalling the UI and every agent's guardrail gate.
findings.fix: Index the task id. Either add an `audit.task_id` column filled in audit::append from payload.task_id or the result id (migration plus index), or keep a task_audit(task_id, audit_id) link table, and page by that index.

v1.reason: task.rs:757-768 registers Activity with plain e.register, so it runs under the store mutex. Its WHERE clause ORs a branch, `json_extract(result_summary,'$.task.id') = ?2`, that applies to every op, so no audit index (store.rs:28-34 indexes ts, actor, session, op, project, parent_req, undo_of) can narrow it beyond project_id. Running EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN on the same schema shape in SQLite 3.53 gives 'SCAN audit', walking back by rowid until limit+1 matches are found. A task with fewer than 101 matching rows therefore makes the query visit every project-tagged row in the retention window (default 180 days, settings.rs:43). Those rows include every agent session.report (Audit::AgentOnly, which calls set_project at session.rs:1389) and every guardrail.gate (Audit::Always by default, set_project at guardrail.rs:509). The native task page calls this query when a task is opened (task_pages.rs:1056).
v1.correction: The finding overstates the size of the stall. In a synthetic test (300k rows) the scan cost about 0.09 µs per row with '{}' result summaries and about 0.27 µs per row with ~1 KB summaries: roughly 25-80 ms at 300k rows. Hundreds of milliseconds needs on the order of a million or more project audit rows, and 'seconds' needs several million. The 1.7 µs/row baseline includes audit::get and JSON decoding of the returned rows, not only the scan. The issue is still real: cost grows with the project's whole audit history, not with the task's, and the bus is blocked while it runs. The proposed fix is right: index a task_id column or a link table. A cheaper partial fix is to register the query with register_unlocked.

findings.title: task.attach reads and copies files of any size inside the transaction, with no size limit
findings.evidence: `e.register::<Attach>` (plain register) does `let bytes = std::fs::read(&src).bus()?;` (993) on any path that passes `is_file()`. attach_bytes then runs `std::fs::create_dir_all(&dir)` and `std::fs::write(&path, bytes)` (522-524) while the transaction and store mutex are held. task.create decodes and writes every base64 attachment the same way (746-750). There is no size cap anywhere.
findings.impact: The task page's 'Absolute image path' field accepts any path. Attaching a large file (a screen recording, a log, a disk image) loads it fully into memory and writes a copy while every other request waits: a 1 GB file freezes the bus for seconds. A file larger than available memory makes the allocation abort or the OOM killer take the engine, which ends every agent session.
findings.fix: Make task.attach staged: check the size (cap around 50 MB) and copy the file with std::fs::copy in the unlocked phase, then insert the row in finish. Apply the same cap to base64 payloads in task.create and task.attach.

v1.reason: Attach is registered with plain e.register (task.rs:985), so it runs inside the transaction with the store mutex held. The path variant runs std::fs::read(&src) on any regular file (line 993), and attach_bytes (task.rs:505-538) then runs create_dir_all and std::fs::write of the full buffer. Nothing caps the size. task.create decodes and writes base64 attachments the same way (746-750). The native task page sends whatever path the user types into the 'Absolute image path' entry (task_pages.rs:868-882). A large file therefore blocks every bus request, agent gates and keystroke-adjacent requests included, for the time a full read plus a full write takes, and allocates the whole file in engine memory.
v1.correction: The trigger is a user attaching an unusually large file, which is uncommon, so medium is right rather than high. Agents cannot reach this path: task.attach is in no role allowlist. A secondary issue is that the file is written before the transaction commits, so a rollback leaves an orphan file. The fix is to make the op staged: stat and fs::copy the file unlocked under a size cap, then insert the row in finish.

findings.title: Dispatch fanout copies the parent's whole session template (branch, worktree, pair_with, prompt) into every child
findings.evidence: `let template = p.create.clone();` (1064), then each child gets `dispatch_task(ctx, id, None, template.clone(), start)` (1073). dispatch_task overrides only task_id and module_id (681-682). CreateIn also carries branch, worktree, pair_with and prompt (ops/session.rs:7-16). worktree::create runs `git worktree add <path> <branch>` for an existing branch (worktree.rs:204-206). launch_nudge prefers launch_prompt over the task (session.rs:134-143).
findings.impact: With `branch` set, the parent's session creates the branch, then the first child's `git worktree add` fails ('already checked out'). The whole dispatch rolls back after the parent's worktree, hooks and agent were already created (see the dispatch-under-lock finding). With `prompt` set, every child agent is told 'begin this assignment: <parent's prompt>' instead of its own task. With `worktree:"primary"`, a path, or the D160 default, all children share one checkout and become a single group, contradicting 'one fresh session each'.
findings.fix: For fanned children, clear branch, prompt and pair_with, and force worktree to "new". Alternatively, refuse fanout when the template sets any of these.

v1.reason: task.rs:1064 clones p.create as the template and task.rs:1073 passes template.clone() into dispatch_task for every not-done descendant. dispatch_task (task.rs:674-683) overrides only task_id and module_id before invoking session.create. Session CreateIn (relay-bus/src/ops/session.rs:7-16) carries branch, worktree, pair_with and prompt. The create handler (session.rs:866-876) builds a 'new' worktree on p.branch. When that branch already exists, worktree::create checks it out again, and git refuses because the parent's worktree already holds it, so the whole dispatch errors. p.prompt is stored as launch_prompt (session.rs:809), and launch_nudge (session.rs:134-143) prefers it over the task id, so every child is told to start the parent's assignment. pair_with makes every child join the same review group, and validate_pair refuses once two builders are in it. Reachability is limited, though. No in-scope client ever sends fanout:true. The native client dispatches with a session name only (task_pages.rs:652, launch.rs:810), and the only callers are crates/relay-core/tests/board.rs and raw bus/CLI use (task.dispatch is UserOnly). That puts it at low, not medium.
v1.correction: Drop the D160 'primary' part of the impact. When a plugin sets default_checkout to primary, sessions are meant to share the primary checkout, so that case is intended. The real defects are branch, prompt and pair_with being copied. Severity is low because no shipped in-scope client uses fanout. Fix: for fanned children, clear branch, prompt and pair_with (or refuse fanout when the template sets them) and leave worktree as given.

findings.title: notes.append has no size cap; the standing note grows without bound and is injected into every brief, including Codex argv
findings.evidence: For an explicit note_id or the standing note, Append only checks `text.is_empty()` (466) and then writes `format!("{}{separator}{text}", before.body)` (477). The 500-character cap and the timestamp/session/task stamp apply only to the `target: suggestions` arm (438-455). `(Some(id), None, "standing") if p.target.is_none() => (id, p.text)` (415) accepts the suggestions note's id too. notes.append is in all three role allowlists (settings.rs:36-38). awareness.rs:285-297 puts the full standing body into the compact brief, and providers.rs:81-93 passes the whole brief to Codex as a single argv string `developer_instructions=<json>`.
findings.impact: Repeated agent appends grow the standing note forever, and every later dispatch carries all of it. Once the brief passes Linux's 128 KiB per-argument limit (MAX_ARG_STRLEN), every Codex spawn or resume in the project fails with E2BIG. A builder can also append unstamped, unlimited text to the suggestions note by id, forging entries that appear to come from other sessions and tasks.
findings.fix: Cap each append and the total standing-note size (or truncate it when building the brief, with a pointer to notes.get). Route any append that targets the suggestions note through the suggestions path, whichever way it was addressed.

v1.reason: Confirmed: for note_id or the standing note, Append (notes.rs:413-489) checks only that the text is non-empty. The 500-character cap and the stamp apply only to the suggestions arm. `(Some(id), None, "standing") if p.target.is_none()` accepts any note id, including the suggestions note's, so a builder or reviewer can append unstamped text there. awareness.rs:285-298 puts the whole standing body into parts.notes, and from there into `compact` (awareness.rs:389-392). providers.rs:213-227 passes compact as one `--config developer_instructions=<json>` argv element on every Codex fresh launch and resume. One argv string over MAX_ARG_STRLEN (128 KiB) makes execve fail with E2BIG. The trigger, though, is less likely than the finding says. COMMON_INSTRUCTIONS (providers.rs:40-67) tells agents to append only with `target: "suggestions"`, never to the standing note, so the standing note grows by agent appends only through misbehavior. A single huge append, or a user who writes a very long standing note, is the realistic path. The suggestions-note forgery only affects a user-review note that is never injected into agents. That makes this a rare edge, not normal-use growth.
v1.correction: The root cause is wider than notes.append: the compact brief has no size bound and goes into Codex argv. state_public also embeds every assigned task's full body and changelog (awareness.rs:224-241), and the plugins section is unbounded too. A long standing note written through notes.update, or a long task body, triggers the same E2BIG without any append. The fix belongs in the brief and Codex path: cap or truncate each section of the compact brief and point to notes.get / session.bootstrap for the full text, or pass Codex the instructions by file if it supports that. Separately, route appends to the suggestions note through the suggestions arm (or refuse note_id when the note is the suggestions note). Note also that this argv is world-readable through `ps`, which awareness.rs:246-248 acknowledges for the launch assignment but not for standing notes or task bodies.

findings.title: mailbox.list and task.list have no limit or pagination over tables that only grow
findings.evidence: MailboxList builds its SQL with no LIMIT and no cursor, plus two correlated subqueries per message (668-687). mailbox.outbox does cap with `limit.min(1000)`, and messages are never pruned. The native mailbox page calls `mailbox.list {project_id}` (pages.rs:44) and reloads it on every mailbox.new and mailbox.changed event, which every agent ack emits (app.rs:1263). task.list (task.rs:831-864) also has no limit; each row runs row_task's ~10 statements plus a subtree walk, the Done column is never archived, and the board reruns it on every task.changed.
findings.impact: The user's mailbox view returns the project's entire message history, and the board hydrates every task ever created. Both responses and their lock time grow for the life of the project and are rebuilt on every agent ack or task event. Tens of thousands of messages mean multi-MB responses rebuilt and re-rendered per ack; thousands of tasks mean tens of milliseconds of store lock per board refresh.
findings.fix: Add `limit` plus a before-id cursor to mailbox.list (default about 200, matching outbox). Give task.list an optional limit and a way to exclude old Done tasks for the board.

v1.reason: MailboxList (notes.rs:660-689) has no LIMIT or cursor. The only automatic deletion of messages is project removal (workspace.rs:355-356). The native app's pages::refresh calls `mailbox.list {project_id}` (pages.rs:44, 50-54). It then clears the body and builds a row Box, two labels and a wrapped paragraph for every message ever sent in the project (pages.rs:123-153). Every subscribed event not handled explicitly calls ui.refresh_page() (app.rs:1264), including mailbox.new, mailbox.changed, task.changed and file.changed. refresh_page coalesces to one refresh in flight plus one pending (app.rs:1662-1686), so there is no storm, but every refresh is a full rebuild. With many sessions exchanging mail, the mailbox page grows without bound and rebuilds all its widgets on the GTK main thread on nearly every engine event while it is visible. task.list (task.rs:831-864) is likewise unbounded, and row_task runs several cached statements per task under the store lock.
v1.correction: The dominant cost is the GTK rebuild of every message row on the UI thread while the page is open, not the engine lock. The correlated subqueries are cheap because they use the message_recipients primary key prefix (message_id). So the impact is UI jank and a growing response, not multi-millisecond lock stalls for other sessions, at least for the mailbox. Fix as proposed: give mailbox.list a limit (default about 200) and a before-id cursor, have the native page request the newest page, and let the board exclude or page old Done tasks.

findings.title: Undoing task.detach re-attaches a renamed, retyped copy instead of restoring the attachment
findings.evidence: Detach deletes the row and records the inverse `task.attach {"task_id":task.id,"path":attachment.path}` (1041-1045). The path variant of Attach takes the name from `src.file_name()`, which is the stored `"{id}-{name}"`, forces mime `"application/octet-stream"` (994-998), and attach_bytes inserts a new row and writes a new file `{newid}-{oldid}-{name}`.
findings.impact: Detach followed by Ctrl+Z brings the attachment back under a new id, renamed (for example '17-screenshot.png'), typed application/octet-stream, with a second copy of the file. Each detach and undo cycle prefixes another id and duplicates the file again.
findings.fix: Soft-delete attachments (a deleted_at column) and make the inverse a restore of that row, or carry name and mime in the undo payload and restore the original row.

v1.reason: Detach (task.rs:1024-1048) deletes only the attachments row and leaves the file on disk. Its recorded inverse is `task.attach {task_id, path: attachment.path}`, and attachment.path is the stored file `<root>/<task>/<id>-<name>` (attach_bytes, line 523). Replaying it through the path variant (lines 987-998) takes the name from src.file_name(), which is '<id>-<name>', sets mime to 'application/octet-stream', inserts a new row and writes a second copy named '<newid>-<id>-<name>'. Undo therefore produces a renamed, retyped duplicate rather than restoring the original row.
v1.correction: Detach also never deletes the attachment file, so files of detached attachments accumulate on disk. That is a minor leak of the same design. A soft-delete column with a restore inverse fixes both.

findings.title: Attachment files are never reclaimed: detach, rollback and delete all leave files on disk
findings.evidence: attach_bytes writes the file (`std::fs::write(&path, bytes)`, 524) before the transaction commits. If a later step in the same request fails, for example task.create's second attachment with invalid base64 (747-748), the row rolls back but the file stays. Detach only runs `DELETE FROM attachments WHERE id=?1` (1038-1040). task.delete and restore never touch files, and no code removes anything under attachments/<task>/.
findings.impact: The store's attachments directory only grows. Every detach, every detach and undo cycle (which copies the file again) and every failed create leaves files that no row references.
findings.fix: Remove files written during a failed request (a guard that deletes on Err) or write them after commit. Garbage-collect unreferenced files in recovery, keeping detached files only while their undo row is still undoable.

v1.reason: attach_bytes (task.rs:505-537) writes the file with std::fs::write inside the request, before commit. If the request fails later, the row rolls back and the file stays. One example is a later attachment in task.create (746-750) with invalid base64. Detach (task.rs:1021-1047) only deletes the row and keeps the file on purpose, because its undo is task.attach with that path. That undo copies the file again instead of reusing it. Project deletion (workspace.rs:362) deletes the attachment rows but not the files. No code anywhere removes files under attachments/. Growth depends on how many attachments users add, so the impact is modest.
v1.correction: Keeping files after detach is required for undo, so a GC must keep any file an undoable audit row still references. A further leak site is workspace.rs:362, where project delete removes attachment rows and leaves their files.

findings.title: task.relate records an undo even when nothing changed, and its duplicate_of replace misses edges to deleted tasks
findings.evidence: `let replaced = if p.relation == TaskRelation::DuplicateOf { task.duplicate_of } else { None };` (1257) reads row_task's duplicate_of, which filters `t.deleted_at IS NULL` (275). The `INSERT OR IGNORE INTO task_relations` result is discarded (1261-1266), and `set_undo("task.unrelate", ...)` is recorded whenever replaced is None (1269-1276). LabelAdd, by contrast, checks `added > 0`.
findings.impact: First, re-linking an existing blocked_by (the task page's Link combobox lists every task) changes nothing, yet Ctrl+Z on that row deletes the relation that existed before. Second, if the current duplicate_of target is soft-deleted, a new duplicate_of leaves the old edge in place, giving two duplicate_of rows. Restoring the old target can then make the stale edge win (`ORDER BY r.to_task`), and unrelating the visible one reveals the other.
findings.fix: Use the INSERT's changed count and skip set_undo when it is 0. For duplicate_of, query existing edges without the deleted filter and delete them all before inserting.

v1.reason: In Relate (task.rs:1252-1281), `replaced` comes from task.duplicate_of. row_task fills that through a query that requires t.deleted_at IS NULL on the target (around line 275). The INSERT OR IGNORE's changed count is thrown away (1261-1266), and when replaced is None, set_undo("task.unrelate", ...) is always recorded (1269-1276). Re-linking a blocked_by edge that already exists therefore leaves the store unchanged but records an undo, and Ctrl+Z deletes the edge that was there before. LabelAdd and Unrelate both check the affected-row count. For duplicate_of: if the current target is soft-deleted, replaced is None, so the DELETE is skipped and a second duplicate_of row is inserted. Once the old target is restored, row_task takes the lowest to_task, which may be the stale edge, and the user's newer choice is hidden.
v1.correction: Fix as proposed: use the INSERT's changed count to decide whether to set_undo. For duplicate_of, read the existing edges without the deleted filter, then delete them all (and record the prior target for undo) before inserting.

findings.title: task.parent.set writes its caller-supplied position into the board's column-order field without bounds or renumbering
findings.evidence: `let position = p.position.unwrap_or(before.position).max(0);` (1154) is written to tasks.position (1157). That is the field column_index, open_slot and next_position use for column order (452-479), and child_ids orders siblings by it. next_position computes `COALESCE(MAX(position),-1)+1` (453).
findings.impact: A client that passes a sibling index (for example 0 to put a child first) silently moves the card within its board column, with ties at 0 broken by id. A value at i64::MAX makes MAX(position)+1 overflow to REAL in SQLite, `r.get::<i64>` fails, and every task.create, end-of-column move, dispatch and approve into that column errors until the row is fixed.
findings.fix: Drop `position` from parent.set, or apply it through open_slot-style index semantics clamped to 0..=column length.

v1.reason: task.rs:1154 takes `p.position.unwrap_or(before.position).max(0)` and writes it straight into tasks.position (1155-1158), with no clamp and no renumbering. That same field drives column order (column_index/open_slot/next_position at 452-479) and child order (child_ids at 164-168). task.move, by contrast, goes through open_slot and clamps. The native callers (board_view.rs:859, 2214; task_pages.rs:772) never send position. However, task.parent.set is not UserOnly (relay-bus ops/task.rs:109-110), so agents can call it through MCP with any i64. If one sends a huge value, next_position's COALESCE(MAX(position),-1)+1 overflows into REAL in SQLite, r.get::<i64> fails, and task.create, task.move to the end of the column, dispatch and approve into that column all fail. A small value silently reorders the board column.
v1.correction: Only bus/MCP callers (agents included) can trigger this; native never sends position. Fix: remove position from parent.set, or route it through open_slot for the task's column so it is clamped to the column length.

findings.title: get_task recompiles its SQL on every call, and assert_parent fully hydrates the parent and each ancestor just to read three columns
findings.evidence: get_task uses `tx.query_row(sql, [id], |row| row_task(tx, row))` (350), the uncached form CLAUDE.md says to avoid. It runs per row in module.rs:115 (tasks_for), Children (1185-1187) and fanout (1069). assert_parent calls get_task on the parent (378) and on every ancestor (400) only to read project_id, depth and parent_id, yet each call runs row_task's ~10 statements and walks that node's entire subtree for its rollup.
findings.impact: Re-parenting inside a large tree hydrates the root (up to 1+100+10,000 descendants at 2 queries each) under the global lock just to read one parent_id. module.get and module.changelog.draft also recompile the SELECT for every task.
findings.fix: Use prepare_cached in get_task. In assert_parent, read `project_id, parent_id` with one cached statement and take depth from depth_of.

v1.reason: get_task (task.rs:344-354) calls tx.query_row(sql, ...), which uses the uncached prepare. assert_parent (task.rs:372-420) calls get_task on the parent and then on each ancestor in the cycle walk (cursor = get_task(tx, id, false)?.parent_id) only to read project_id, parent_id and depth. Each of those calls runs row_task (task.rs ~230-341): about 8 cached side-table queries, depth_of, and a full subtree walk for the rollup that issues 2 queries per descendant. TASK_DEPTH_MAX is 3, so the ancestor walk has at most 2 steps, but hydrating a large root still walks its whole subtree. The cost is real but small, and the trees involved are small.
v1.correction: Recompiling the trivial SELECT * is the minor part. Most of the cost is row_task's full hydration and rollup walk when only three scalar columns are needed. A lightweight cached `SELECT project_id,parent_id FROM tasks WHERE id=?1 AND deleted_at IS NULL`, plus depth_of, fixes assert_parent. Switching get_task to prepare_cached is a separate, trivial win.

findings.title: task.create accepts column=done, skipping the commit-linking that task.move enforces through approve
findings.evidence: `let column = p.column.unwrap_or(Column::Backlog);` (737) accepts Done, along with any `state`. task.move refuses Done with 'move to done through task.approve' (897), and Approve's comment calls linking a commit 'the same Done invariant' (1119-1120).
findings.impact: `task.create {column:"done"}` produces a Done task with no linked commit, which is exactly the state approve exists to prevent. module.changelog.draft, done counts and roll-ups then include it.
findings.fix: Refuse column Done in Create, or create the task in another column and then run approve.

v1.reason: Create (task.rs:737) takes `p.column.unwrap_or(Column::Backlog)` with no restriction. task.move refuses Done ('move to done through task.approve', task.rs:897), and BUS.md's transition table (BUS.md ~983-985) lists `* -> done` only via task.approve, which links a sha and is user-only, and refuses it for agents. task.create uses Actors::All (registry.rs mutation default), so an agent can create a Done task with no linked commit. It can also create an Active one, bypassing the dispatch-only `* -> active` rule. The native create form offers 'done' on purpose under an 'Advanced' expander (task_pages.rs:5, ~403), which suggests humans are meant to be able to do this, but nothing documents it.
v1.correction: For human users this seems to be a deliberate escape hatch, offered in the native Advanced create form. The real gap is the agent path: task.create lets an agent place a task in done or active, which the transition table forbids. Fix: refuse column done/active (and their states) in Create when ctx.actor.is_agent(), or document create-into-done as a user-only escape.

findings.title: module.delete and module.restore emit task.changed with a non-Task payload that does not name the affected tasks
findings.evidence: Delete emits `ctx.emit("task.changed",json!({"module_id":module.id,"unlinked":true}))` (205), and Restore emits `json!({"module_id":module.id,"restored":true})` (206). BUS.md:182 defines `noun.changed (entity upserted; payload is the full entity)`, and BUS.md §1.3 says events carry enough to update 'without a re-query'.
findings.impact: A consumer that follows the documented contract and applies task.changed payloads as Task rows gets an object with no id and cannot tell which tasks were unlinked or relinked. Only clients that ignore payloads and re-query, as the native app does, stay correct.
findings.fix: Emit one task.changed per affected task (the ids are in module_unlinked_tasks) or use a distinct event name such as `module.tasks_unlinked`.

v1.reason: module.rs:205 emits task.changed {module_id, unlinked:true} and module.rs:206 emits {module_id, restored:true}. BUS.md:182 (§3.3) says a noun.changed payload is the full entity, and BUS.md:103 says it carries enough to update without a re-query. No in-scope consumer is broken. The native app subscribes to task.changed (app.rs:1154) and handles it through the generic `ui.refresh_page()` re-query (app.rs:1264). So the problem is the gap between the documented contract and the code, not a functional bug.
v1.correction: This is not specific to module.rs. Partial or hint payloads for task.changed are already the codebase's practice: session.rs:109 {task_id,col,state}, session.rs:666 and :1182 {task_id,state}, session.rs:1398, and import_v3.rs:332-333, where a comment says it emits 'one re-query hint per entity kind' with {project_id,bulk:true}. Report it once as 'BUS.md §3.3/§1.3 promise full-entity payloads that several emitters do not deliver'. The cheaper and more honest fix is to document in §3.3 that task.changed may be a re-query hint keyed by task_id/module_id/project_id. Emitting one event per task only in module.rs would leave the other emitters still diverging.

findings.title: module.changelog.draft rejects group_by "size", which BUS.md documents as valid
findings.evidence: `if p.group_by.as_deref().is_some_and(|v| v != "priority") { return Err(invalid("module.changelog_group", "group_by must be priority")) }` (209-214). BUS.md §10.6 documents `{ module_id, group_by?: "priority"|"size" }`.
findings.impact: Clients written against the spec (CLI scripts, MCP callers) get a typed invalid error for a documented value.
findings.fix: Implement size grouping or remove "size" from BUS.md §10.6.

v1.reason: module.rs:209-214 rejects any group_by other than "priority" with invalid/module.changelog_group. BUS.md:700 documents `group_by?: "priority"|"size"`, and SPEC.md:190 mentions only priority grouping. The bus schema (relay-bus ops/module.rs:40) types group_by as Option<String> with no enum, so an MCP or CLI caller that reads BUS.md gets a typed refusal for a documented value. Impact is limited to that refusal.
v1.correction: The doc line is BUS.md:700, not 713. The simplest fix is to drop "size" from BUS.md (SPEC only promises priority grouping), or to make group_by an enum in the bus schema so the allowed value is machine-visible.

findings.title: task.copy_text is billed as the single source of the copy text, but no client calls it and the board builds a different string twice
findings.impact: The two formats have already diverged: the board puts the id last and leaves empty blank lines when the body is empty. Any change to the copy text has to be made in three places.
findings.fix: Have the board call task.copy_text, or remove the op and keep one shared formatter.

v1.correction: The op is not dead: it is exposed to agents as an MCP tool (task_copy_text), so agents and the desktop board give different text for the same task. Removing the op would break that, so the fix is not "remove the op". The better fix is to match the board's format to the op's and put the two identical board format! calls into one helper. Fetching the text from the bus asynchronously on every click is not needed. Impact is cosmetic (clipboard text layout), so low is right. The change touches apps/relay-native, which cannot be built in the headless environment.

results.coverage:
I read all four assigned files line by line (file.rs 660 lines, workspace.rs 454, overlap.rs 546, awareness.rs 520). To confirm reachability I traced callees and callers in engine.rs (dispatch, register variants, invoke_registered), guardrail.rs (evaluate_write, write_target, path_matches, relative_path, refuse_or_user_hold), handlers/guardrail.rs (enforce), worktree.rs (contains, git, ensure_excluded), watch.rs, store.rs (schema, FKs, AUTOINCREMENT), settings.rs, audit.rs, session.rs (claim, close/teardown, launch staging), task.rs (labels, assignment), socket.rs (per-connection loop), providers.rs (Codex argv), relay-bus op metadata, and the native client's editor, client and pages.

Throwaway checks run under the scratchpad: (1) a SQLite run of the projects/labels schema, which confirmed the FK failure on project.remove and project id reuse; (2) a Python port of path_matches, which confirmed that non-normalized spellings and parent directories don't match protected patterns.

Not verified by execution (no cargo per the rules):
- E2BIG for the Codex argv: inferred from the Linux 128 KiB per-argument limit.
- Real-world rev-walk cost in briefing_state.
- gix status behaviour on broken checkouts.

Clippy pedantic items for these files were checked; none of the cast warnings hides a realistic bug (the u32 line/col counters in search need a file of several GB). The overlap tree-sitter grammar node names (impl_item fields) are from knowledge of tree-sitter-rust, not read from the grammar sources. Out of scope and not reported: relay-mobile; the phone door's user-equivalent privileges (by design per wire.rs). git.rs, session.rs and guardrail.rs were read only where they bear on these handlers.

findings.title: Agents can aim file.* mutations at any project and any worktree of it; nothing confines them to their own checkout
findings.evidence: root_choice does `let project = get_project(conn, project_id)?; let chosen = default_worktree_in(conn, session_id, &project, requested)?;` with no check that `project_id` is the actor session's project, and default_worktree_in accepts `Some(PROJECT_ROOT) => Ok(repo)` and `Some(path) => Ok(PathBuf::from(path))` (L399-400). guardrail::enforce is then called with that caller-chosen `root` (L93-96), so evaluate_write treats every relative path as in-worktree. guardrail::authorize checks only `session`/`task_id` payload fields (guardrail.rs:328-349). Other handlers do enforce ownership: overlap.rs:76-77 `not_own("project")`, notes.rs assert_actor_project, session.rs assert_same_project. The hook path (handlers/guardrail.rs:516,608) always judges the session's own worktree. rel() also never refuses `.git`/`.relay` components and the default protected_paths list is empty (settings.rs:31).
findings.impact: A session with bus_writes can write, rename, move or trash files in the project's primary checkout, in peer agents' worktrees, and in any other registered project (the target project's guardrail config is the one applied). For a provider that runs sandboxed, the engine performs those writes outside the sandbox. Repository metadata and Relay-generated files under `.git/` and `.relay/` are reachable the same way, so other guardrail layers can be undermined.
findings.fix: For agent actors, require payload project_id == own session's project (one shared assert like assert_actor_project) and, for mutations, require the resolved root to be the session's own worktree unless a user grant covers it. In rel() (mutation callers) refuse any `.git` or `.relay` component.

v1.reason: root_choice (file.rs:420-428) loads any project_id and passes the caller's `worktree` to default_worktree_in, which returns `Some("@project") => repo` or `Some(path) => PathBuf::from(path)` (L399-400). root_verify (L432-447) only checks that the path is the primary checkout or a linked worktree of that same project (worktree.rs:162-171). It never checks that the project is the actor's or that the tree is the actor's own. guardrail::authorize (guardrail.rs:318-383) scopes only the `session` and `task_id` payload fields; for file.* it then admits the call when `session.bus_writes` is set (L363-366). The engine fills project_id only when it is omitted (BUS.md: 'Identity is filled in, not demanded'). guardrail::enforce then judges the caller-chosen root with the target project's config, so relative paths always count as InWorktree. The hook path, by contrast, judges the session's own worktree (handlers/guardrail.rs:501-525) and refuses absolute writes outside its write roots (write_target, guardrail.rs:623-663, D102). A bus_writes agent can therefore write, create, rename, move, delete or restore files in peer worktrees, in the primary checkout and in other registered projects, bypassing the write_root rule its own tool writes are held to. rel() (L463-478) also leaves `.git` and `.relay` components alone. With `worktree: "@project"`, `.git/` is a real directory, so `.git/hooks/*` and `.git/config` are writable. That turns into code execution the next time the user runs git in the primary checkout.
v1.correction: This requires the opt-in per-session `bus_writes` (off by default, BUS.md §9.1), which is why it is high rather than critical. file.restore (L237-251) is also unscoped: it trusts the trash row's worktree and checks only project_id. Fix: for agent actors, require payload project_id to equal the session's project. For mutations, require the resolved root to equal the session's own worktree unless a user grant covers it. Refuse `.git` and `.relay` components in rel() for mutations.

v2.reason:
(a) The code does what the finding claims. root_choice (file.rs:414-423) loads any project_id. default_worktree_in returns `Some("@project") => repo` or `Some(path) => PathBuf::from(path)` (L399-400). root_verify (L427-442) only checks that the path is the primary checkout or a linked worktree of that same repo (worktree.rs:162-171). guardrail::enforce is then called with that root (L93-96; handlers/guardrail.rs:672-680), so write_target treats every relative path as InWorktree (guardrail.rs:629-630). authorize (guardrail.rs:318-383) scopes only the `session` and `task_id` fields and admits file.* on `bus_writes`. The engine pipeline has no generic project check (engine.rs:831-879). notes.rs:47-61, overlap.rs:68-80 and session.rs:199 do enforce the agent's own project. The hook path judges the session's own worktree (handlers/guardrail.rs:516) and refuses absolute writes outside its write roots (D102). The same root cause covers git.stage, git.unstage and git.commit, which call file::root_choice (git.rs:491, 508, 543, 751-777). So an agent can, for example, `git.commit` with `worktree:"@project"` in the primary checkout.

(b) Who can trigger it, and how often. Any agent session with bus_writes, which is more of them than the first verifier said. The native launch dialog pre-checks "Allow agent bus writes" (apps/relay-native/src/launch.rs:264-265), so in practice every UI-launched agent has these ops, reviewers included. The trigger is still an explicit argument, though. An omitted worktree resolves to the agent's own tree (D111). A foreign project_id with no worktree fails root_verify, because the agent's own worktree is not a worktree of the other repo. So the agent has to deliberately name `@project`, a peer's path or the primary path. D111 documents `@project` as the "out loud" route, but it was designed for reads and tested only on a read (agent_surface.rs:177, git.status). Agents also normally write with their own tools (BUS.md §9.1). Realistically, the trigger is an agent mistake such as writing back to a peer's or the primary tree it had just read.

(c) What happens when it fires. A small edit, rename or move lands in the user's primary checkout, in a peer's worktree or in another project, with no refusal and no notification. Each such op is audited ("mutation · always"). The configured policies still apply, judged against the target tree: protected paths, shape gates, and destructive-write holds with recoverability checked on the target. Deletes go to recoverable trash. So data-loss exposure is bounded.

The escape framing does not hold. BUS.md §0.6 says guardrails are "seatbelts, not sandboxes" against agents that share the uid. §4.2 and §14, plus guardrail.rs:849-853, say the socket admits `user` with no token. Claude's Bash and every Codex edit (apply_patch, Edit, Write) are gated only as `exec`, which checks denied commands and nothing about write targets (relay-cli main.rs:406-410 and 507-512, guardrail.rs:811-847). So a hostile agent can already write `.git/config` or any peer file without the bus. Relay passes no sandbox flags to either provider (no sandbox reference anywhere in the crates), so "outside the sandbox" is hypothetical.

(d) Severity. It is not critical or high under the rubric. Nothing new is reachable for a hostile agent, and accidental cross-tree writes need an explicit wrong argument while large losses still hold. It is a real, reachable inconsistency in the agent boundary, which has diverged across handlers: the hook path and notes/overlap confine agents, file.* and git.* do not. That fits medium.

(e) The fix is right in direction but incomplete. See the correction field.
v2.correction:
Severity: medium, not high.

1. The first verifier's "off by default" is only true of the engine (store.rs:90, session.rs:809). The native launch dialog defaults bus_writes on (launch.rs:264-265).
2. Applying the target project's guardrail config is the correct config for the target files. The only check that does not run is the own-tree / write-root boundary. Protected paths, shape gates and destructive-write holds all still run.
3. The `.git` code-execution and sandbox points add nothing under BUS.md §0.6, §4.2 and §14. The agent's Bash, and every Codex edit, are already unchecked for write targets, and Relay launches no provider sandboxed. A new `.git/hooks` file written via file.write is also not executable (permissions are copied only from an existing file, L111-114), but `.git/config` is writable.
4. Related locations to add: git.rs:491, 508, 543 (git.stage, git.unstage, git.commit via resolve_root at 751-777), and file.rs:238-251 (file.restore trusts the trash row's worktree and checks only project_id).

Fix:
- Put the check on the mutation path, not in root_choice, because queries also use root_choice and agent_surface.rs:177 pins `@project` for git.status.
- For agent actors, require project_id to equal the session's project, mirroring notes.rs assert_actor_project.
- Require the canonical resolved root to equal the canonical session.worktree. This is safe for PAIR and shared-worktree groups, which reuse one worktree (session.rs:778-800), and for sessions launched on the primary checkout. Use an explicit grant for exceptions.
- Apply the same check to git.stage, git.unstage and git.commit.
- Refuse `.git` and `.relay` components for agent mutations only, so a user's edit of `.git/info/exclude` is not blocked.
- Update D111 and BUS.md:816, which advertise `@project` "throughout git.* and file.*", and the stale BUS.md:839.
- Say plainly that this restores consistency, not containment, per §0.6.

findings.title: Protected paths and shape gates are matched against the raw, un-normalized request path
findings.evidence: rel() rejects only `Component::ParentDir | Component::RootDir | Component::Prefix(_)` (L474-479) and returns `path.to_path_buf()` unchanged, so `.` components and doubled separators survive. file.write and file.create pass the raw payload string `Some(&p.path)` (L98, L143); guard_path_mutation passes `rel.to_string_lossy()` (L584). guardrail::relative_path also returns the raw path (guardrail.rs:1135-1146) and path_matches compares the raw string (guardrail.rs:1161-1168). A Python port of path_matches gives false for pattern `secrets/key.pem` vs `./secrets/key.pem`, and for `config/*.json` vs `./config/app.json`. safe_join canonicalizes and accepts these paths because the target is inside the root.
findings.impact: Any non-canonical spelling of a protected file (or a shape-gated critical file) skips the check, and the write lands on the real file. A configured safety check fails silently for every bus_writes session.
findings.fix: Normalize once in rel(): rebuild the path from Normal components only (reject CurDir and empty segments), and pass that normalized string to guardrail::enforce, to events and to the trash row. Normalize the same way in guardrail::relative_path so hook callers are covered too.

v1.reason: rel() (file.rs:463-478) rejects only ParentDir, RootDir and Prefix, and returns the raw path. file.write and file.create pass the raw payload string `Some(&p.path)` to guardrail::enforce (L93-99, L139-145). write_target sends a relative path through relative_path (guardrail.rs:1135-1146), which also returns it raw. evaluate_write then calls `path_matches(p, &path)` (guardrail.rs:512, and for shape gates 528/551). path_matches compares `path.to_string_lossy()` with only '/' trimmed (L1161-1168). So `./secrets/key.pem`, `secrets//key.pem` and `secrets/./key.pem` are neither equal to nor prefixed by `secrets/key.pem`, and glob_match does not match them either. safe_join joins and canonicalizes, so the write lands on the real file. Interior `./` also survives in the hook path, where write_target uses Path::strip_prefix on an absolute path. The protected-path and shape-gate checks on writes can be bypassed with a non-canonical spelling.
v1.correction: Downgraded from high. protected_paths and shape_gates are empty unless the user configures them (settings.rs default). An agent that wants to evade them can already write with its shell, since exec gating does not check protected paths. Agents' own Edit tools rarely produce such spellings by accident. evaluate_commit (guardrail.rs:757-790) re-checks protected paths against git's normalized numstat paths, so tracked protected files are still caught at commit time. Untracked or ignored protected files (e.g. secrets) are not. Fix as proposed: normalize once (keep only Normal components) in rel() and in guardrail::relative_path / write_target, and pass the normalized string to enforce, events and the trash row.

findings.title: project.clone runs `git clone` synchronously inside a locked handler with no timeout
