Device runs, by contrast, keep a RunRuntime and stream output (device.rs:173-177, stream_command). A hung build (e.g. waiting on a Gradle daemon or lock) leaves the row in 'building' forever, parks the thread, and — via integrations_live (workspace.rs:387-389) — blocks project.remove for that project until discarded, which the native UI cannot do.
v1.correction: Calibrate the mechanism: Command::output() gives the child a null stdin, so an interactive prompt does not hang it; hangs come from locks/daemons/network. These threads are not bus handlers and hold no store lock, so this is not the CLAUDE.md output_with_timeout invariant in the strict sense; the cost is a stuck integration, a stuck thread and a blocked project.remove. Full buffering of build output is real but rarely large in practice. The 'cargo/gradle recreates target/ after discard' consequence is plausible (both create_dir_all their output dirs) but was not verified.

findings.title: notify.settings.set stores `before` as a merge patch, so audit.undo cannot remove keys the change added
findings.evidence: `let before = settings::get(ctx.tx(), Some("notifications"))?; ... merge_value(&mut next, &payload.patch); settings::set(ctx.tx(), "notifications", &next, &ctx.now)?; ctx.set_undo("notify.settings.set", json!({"patch":before}), None);` audit.undo replays that envelope through the same handler (audit.rs:68), i.e. merge_value(current, before), which only touches keys present in the patch. guardrail.config.set computes guardrail::inverse_patch(&before, &merged) for exactly this reason (handlers/guardrail.rs:103, guardrail.rs:242). Reproduced in a Python model: after patch {categories:{integration:false}} and its undo, categories.integration is still false.
findings.impact: The native Settings save always patches notifications.categories.<cat> (tools_settings.rs:664), adding keys to the default-empty `categories`. Undoing that change via audit.undo (CLI/MCP/phone) reports success and marks the audit row undone, so it cannot be retried, while the category settings stay changed.
findings.fix: Record `json!({"patch": guardrail::inverse_patch(&before, &next)})`, or record the undo as settings.set {path:"notifications", value: before} (a full replacement).

v1.reason: handlers/notify.rs:146-150: `before = settings::get(tx, Some("notifications"))`, `merge_value(&mut next, &payload.patch)`, then `ctx.set_undo("notify.settings.set", json!({"patch":before}), None)`. audit.undo (audit.rs:68) replays it through the same handler, so the result is merge_value(current, before). merge_value (settings.rs:104-117) recurses into objects and only touches keys that are present in the patch. Take a change that adds categories.integration=false when the default `categories` is {}. The undo patch is categories:{}, which changes nothing, so the added key stays. notify.settings.set is a mutation audited with Audit::Always and Undo::Inverse (relay-bus ops/notify.rs:16-17), so an audit row with this undo exists for every native Settings save. The native client builds the patch with notifications["categories"][category] (tools_settings.rs:664, sent at :141). audit.undo then marks the row undone_by (engine.rs:1015-1020), so it cannot be retried. guardrail.config.set handles the same problem correctly with guardrail::inverse_patch (handlers/guardrail.rs:~103, guardrail.rs:242).
v1.correction: Lines are notify.rs:146-150 (set_undo at 150). The impact is narrow: only keys that were absent before are not reverted, and in practice those are notification category toggles. sound/volume do revert, because `before` carries them, defaults included. Fix: record `json!({"patch": crate::guardrail::inverse_patch(&before, &next)})`. Alternatively record the undo as `settings.set {path:"notifications", value: before}`, as settings.set itself does.

findings.title: app.reconcile and app.log.tail are success-returning stubs: the documented purge never runs, so notifications, trash and soft-deleted rows grow forever
findings.evidence: `e.register::<Reconcile>(|_ctx, _| { // ... Phase 1 has nothing to verify yet ... Ok(ReconcileOut { actions: Vec::new() }) });` BUS.md §5.4 (lines 288-291) says soft-deleted task/module/note/file rows are 'hard-deleted by the reconcile pass' after undo.grace_days, and SPEC:35 calls reconcile the only clock-driven work. No timer exists; undo.grace_days (settings.rs:42) is read nowhere; .relay/trash/<id> (file.rs:230) and the notifications table (deleted only by project.remove) are never pruned; recovery prunes only audit. app.log.tail (133-136) emits app.log.attached and attaches no `log` stream (BUS.md:383, 628), yet bus.ops reports it implemented.
findings.impact: Notifications (one per integration result, provider version change, hold...) accumulate forever, and dashboard.get / notify.list sort the whole table on each call (`ORDER BY created_at DESC,id DESC`, notify.rs:71, with no index usable without a project/category filter) under the store lock. Files deleted in a primary checkout keep their payload in .relay/trash forever; restore windows never close. log.tail callers get success and no stream.
findings.fix: Implement the pass (60 s via system_write, or at least at launch beside audit retention): hard-delete soft-deleted rows and trash older than undo.grace_days, prune read notifications past an age/count cap, add an index on notifications(created_at, id). Unregister log.tail until it exists so bus.ops reports not_implemented.

v1.reason: app.rs:137-141 registers Reconcile as `Ok(ReconcileOut { actions: Vec::new() })` with a comment saying Phase 1 has nothing to verify. Nothing calls it on a timer (it is only invoked from examples/perf.rs). `undo.grace_days` appears only in the settings defaults (settings.rs:42) and in tests. No code anywhere hard-deletes soft-deleted tasks, modules or notes, or file_trash rows and payloads, except project.remove (workspace.rs:364-369). Launch recovery (recovery.rs:179-200) prunes only audit rows. Notifications are inserted from integration, provider, session, guardrail and device-crash paths and are never pruned. BUS.md §5.4 (lines 288-292) promises a hard delete by the reconcile pass, so the documentation and the code disagree. LogTail (app.rs:133-136) only emits `app.log.attached` and attaches no `log` stream, although BUS.md:383 and :628 promise one.
v1.correction: The query-cost part is overstated. notifications has indexes (project_id, read, created_at) and (category, read, created_at) (store.rs:138-139). The unfiltered dashboard query uses LIMIT 8, so a full scan and sort of a few thousand small rows is negligible. The real ongoing cost is that `.relay/trash/<id>/payload` files in a primary checkout are never reclaimed (pooled worktrees lose theirs when the worktree is removed), plus slow row growth and docs drift. Fix: add the purge at launch beside audit retention (trash and soft-deleted rows older than undo.grace_days, read notifications past an age cap), or correct BUS.md §5.4. Either implement log.tail or leave it unregistered so it reports not_implemented.

findings.title: v3 import writes guardrail caps without validation; 0, negative or >u32 values break every agent mutation in the project
findings.evidence: `let files = s.get("max_files").and_then(Value::as_i64); ... crate::handlers::settings::set(tx, &path, &json!({ "files": files, "lines": lines }), &now)?;` with path guardrails.projects.<id>.caps, committed without re-reading the config. GuardrailCaps fields are u32 (crates/relay-bus/src/types.rs:175-176), validate_config rejects 0 (guardrail.rs:293-295), and guardrail::config -> typed() deserializes+validates on every read; authorize calls it for every agent mutation (guardrail.rs:358). guardrail.config.set validates the merged result before committing (handlers/guardrail.rs:97-98). The import also emits no settings.changed / guardrail.config_changed.
findings.impact: A v3 sessions.json entry with max_files 0 (a common 'no limit' convention), a negative number or one above u32::MAX commits a project layer that fails typed(); from then on every agent mutation in that project (session.report, task.move, guardrail.gate...) is refused with 'invalid guardrail config' until the user repairs the layer.
findings.fix: Skip non-positive/out-of-range caps with a warning, and after writing call guardrail::config_for(tx, ConfigScope::Project(project.id))? so an invalid layer rolls the import back; emit guardrail.config_changed.

v1.reason: import_v3.rs:313-317 reads max_files/max_lines with as_i64 and writes them through settings::set (settings.rs:203-213), which does no validation. Nothing re-reads the config before commit. In contrast, guardrail.config.set validates the merged result with config_for (handlers/guardrail.rs:97-98). GuardrailCaps fields are u32 (types.rs:175-176), so a negative or >u32 value fails to deserialize, and validate_config rejects 0 (guardrail.rs:293-295). typed() runs on every config read (guardrail.rs:193-197). authorize calls config(conn, Some(project_id)) for every non-query agent op that is not grants::OP (guardrail.rs:358). Once such a layer is committed, every agent mutation in the project fails with invalid guardrail config. A null value is skipped by put_raw, so a missing key is harmless. No guardrail.config_changed event is emitted either.
v1.correction: The mechanism is certain. I could not establish whether v3 ever wrote 0 or negative caps (no v3 source in the repo), so how often this triggers is unknown. The user can recover with guardrail.config.set or settings.reset on the project caps path. Fix: skip non-positive or out-of-range values with a warning, call guardrail::config_for(tx, ConfigScope::Project(id))? after writing so an invalid layer rolls the import back, and emit guardrail.config_changed.

findings.title: set_state checks 'discarded' under one lock and writes unconditionally under another, so a discard can be overwritten
findings.evidence: set_state takes the store lock three times: `if get(&conn, id)?.state == IntegrationState::Discarded { return Ok(()); }` (266-271), a separate SELECT project_id (274-282), then system_write with `UPDATE integrations SET state=?1, ... WHERE id=?7` (283-284) and no state guard. integration.discard (58-66) can commit between the first lock and the write.
findings.impact: A discard that lands while a run transitions (most likely as it finishes; discard holds the lock for the whole worktree removal, so a set_state already past its check waits and then writes) flips the row back to passed/failed with a worktree path that no longer exists, inserts a spurious 'Integration passed' notification, and device.run will accept it as a passed integration.
findings.fix: Do the check and the write in the one system_write transaction (`... WHERE id=?7 AND state!='discarded'`, skip events/notification when 0 rows changed), read project_id there too (two fewer lock round trips per transition), and return a discarded signal so run() stops.

v1.reason: set_state checks Discarded under one store lock (266-271), reads project_id under a second (274-282), then system_write takes the lock again and runs an unguarded `UPDATE integrations SET state=?1 ... WHERE id=?7` (283-284). IntegrationDiscard (58-69) holds the store mutex for its whole worktree removal; a set_state that passed its check and is waiting at 275 or in system_write will then overwrite 'discarded' with the new state, insert an 'Integration passed/failed' notification and emit events. The window is narrow (a transition coinciding with a user discard), hence low.
v1.correction: Consequence correction: device.run with that integration_id will not succeed — resolve_run_root canonicalizes the removed worktree path (device.rs:1016-1017) and fails with device.worktree; the visible effects are a resurrected passed/failed row, a spurious notification, and (if overwritten to a live state like building) integrations_live blocking project.remove. Fix as proposed: `... WHERE id=?7 AND state!='discarded'` in the single system_write, skipping events when 0 rows change.

findings.title: CPU% baseline is shared by every sampler, so a refresh right after a request reports 0% or ~1000% spikes
findings.evidence: cpu_pct reads and overwrites one per-pid baseline in engine.resource_cpu on every call: `(ticks.saturating_sub(*prior) as f64 / hz / now.duration_since(*at).as_secs_f64() * 100.0)` then `samples.insert(pid, (ticks, now))`. app.resources.get samples every pane, then spawns refresh_disk_cache whose resource_snapshot(rows, engine, true) samples the same pids milliseconds later and emits the result as resource.sample; dashboard.get (notify.rs:188) and the 2 s watch loop share the same baseline. The native panel calls watch then get back-to-back (status.rs:115-118).
findings.impact: With CLK_TCK=100 and a ~1 ms gap, a busy pane reads 0 ticks (0%) or 1 tick (1000%), so the first resource.sample after opening the panel, and samples after dashboard refreshes, plot garbage CPU. The map is never pruned: every pid ever sampled stays, and a reused pid starts from a foreign baseline.
findings.fix: Let only the periodic sampler own/advance the baseline; one-shot readers compute against it without overwriting (or require a minimum interval and reuse the last value); drop entries for pids not in the current rows.

v1.reason: cpu_pct (app.rs ~274-283) reads and overwrites a single per-pid (ticks, Instant) baseline in engine.resource_cpu on every call. The native panel (status.rs:107-118) calls app.resources.watch and then app.resources.get. The get handler samples every pane (app.rs:76) and spawns refresh_disk_cache in after_commit. Unless the 30 s cooldown is active, that call runs resource_snapshot(..., true), which samples CPU in its first loop before any disk walk, only milliseconds after the get. It then emits the result as resource.sample, which the panel renders (status.rs:131-132). With CLK_TCK=100 and a ~1 ms gap, the delta is 0 or 1 tick, so the reading is 0% or about 1000%. dashboard.get (notify.rs:188) also advances the shared baseline and can shorten the 2 s watch interval. The map is never pruned.
v1.correction: The garbage value self-corrects on the next 2 s watch tick, so the impact is a cosmetic glitch in the plotted CPU history (the first sample after opening the panel, and samples after a dashboard refresh). Growth of the map is one small entry per pid ever sampled. Fix: enforce a minimum interval, reusing the last computed value when the gap is under ~500 ms, and retain only pids present in the current rows.

findings.title: v3 import copies attachment files under the store mutex and before commit; a later failure leaves orphan files
findings.evidence: ImportV3 is registered with plain e.register (app.rs:59); import() does `std::fs::create_dir_all(&dest_dir)` / `std::fs::copy(&src, &dest)` for each attachment inside the task loop (259-263), plus notes.json/sessions.json reads and canonicalize calls, all inside the request transaction.
findings.impact: Importing a v3 store with many or large attachments (screenshots, recordings) freezes every other bus request for the copy duration (CLAUDE.md: slow work belongs in register_staged). If anything fails afterwards (a bad name, I/O error, non-UTF-8 notes.json at 280) the DB rolls back but copied files stay under attachments/<id>/, and because the rollback also rewinds AUTOINCREMENT, the next real task with that id inherits a directory of foreign files.
findings.fix: register_staged: prepare reads the v3 DB and copies into a staging dir with nothing locked; finish inserts the rows; on finish error delete the staged files.

v1.reason: app.rs:59 registers ImportV3 with plain e.register, so import() runs in the request transaction with the store mutex held. Inside the task loop, import_v3.rs:259-263 calls create_dir_all and std::fs::copy for each attachment, interleaved with tx.execute. Later steps can fail with `?`: a following task's INSERT, a later copy, read_to_string(notes.json) at line 280 on non-UTF-8 input, settings::set at 317, or the meta INSERT at 330. Any of these rolls the transaction back and leaves the files already copied. tasks.id is AUTOINCREMENT (store.rs:73), and the sqlite_sequence update is rolled back too, so the same ids are handed out again. The copy time blocks every other request. Trigger: a v3 store with large attachments. It is a one-time operation (meta key at 141-145), so low is the right severity.
v1.correction: The 'next task inherits foreign files' impact is overstated. Attachments are listed from the DB (task.rs:253-255), and task.attach writes `{id}-{name}` (task.rs:522), so the leftover files are invisible orphaned disk usage, not attachments that show up. While reading this I found a worse problem on the same lines: import_v3.rs:262 does `dest_dir.join(&name)` with the raw v3 original_name and no safe_name() check (compare task.rs:489-502). An absolute name or one containing `../` writes outside attachments/<id>/, and two attachments with the same name on one task overwrite each other. Fix: sanitise the name the way task.rs does (safe_name plus an id prefix). Copy in a staged prepare phase (register_staged), or at least delete the copied files if the handler returns an error.

findings.title: Import numbers task positions and module ord from 0 regardless of existing rows, and drops v3 note tags without a warning
findings.evidence: `let pos = positions.entry(col_s).or_insert(0);` (193-199) and module ord `i as i64` (173-174) start at 0, while task.rs:452-454 next_position appends after MAX(position). v3 notes carry `tags` (fixture tests/store.rs:113-114) that the notes loop (283-296) never reads or warns about. D14 says priorities 'carry over as-is' but map_priority (49-56) maps unknown values to medium.
findings.impact: Importing into a project that already has tasks/modules interleaves imported items with existing ones in board and module order (ties broken by id); v3 note tags are lost silently.
findings.fix: Seed each column counter from next_position and modules from MAX(ord)+1; append tags to the note body or emit a warning; correct D14.

v1.reason: import_v3.rs: module ord is `i as i64` from 0, and task positions use `positions.entry(col_s).or_insert(0)`. Neither is seeded from existing rows, while task.rs next_position appends after MAX(position). So importing into a project that already has tasks or modules interleaves them, with ties broken by id. The notes loop never reads `tags`.
v1.correction: The trigger is rare. The only UI caller (onboarding.rs:532) imports into the project that was just created by project.add or project.clone, so it is empty. Only a CLI or MCP import into a populated project hits the ordering issue (the op is UserOnly). Tag loss is not established: the only fixture has `"tags": []`, and I could not confirm that v3 ever stored non-empty tags. The D14 claim is weak: v3's priority domain is low/medium/high/urgent, which map_priority carries over as-is, and only out-of-domain values fall back to medium.

findings.title: ui.layout.save without state reads layout.current.<id>, a key nothing writes, so it saves a hard-coded grid
findings.evidence: fallback_state reads `settings::get(ctx.tx(), Some(&format!("layout.current.{project_id}")))` and otherwise returns `json!({"page":"agents","agent_layout":"grid"})`. The native client persists its arrangement under `native.layout.current.{project}` (shell.rs:308, 334). project.remove deletes only the exact path layout.current.<id> (workspace.rs:378-379), but settings::set stores an object as leaves (layout.current.7.page ...), so neither key's leaves are ever removed.
findings.impact: ui.layout.save {project_id, name} from an agent/MCP/phone (documented 'Save the current arrangement') stores the default grid, and applying it later resets the user's real layout. Since projects.id is a plain INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, a new project that reuses a removed project's id restores the dead project's layout.
findings.fix: Read the key the client writes (or have the client write the engine's key), and on project removal delete `path = ?1 OR path LIKE ?1||'.%'` for both keys.

v1.reason: ui.rs:32-40: fallback_state reads `layout.current.{project_id}`, and if that is null it returns json!({"page":"agents","agent_layout":"grid"}). Repo-wide, nothing outside tests writes layout.current.*. The native client persists to `native.layout.current.{project}` (shell.rs:308, read at :334). The native Save layout dialog always passes `state` (shell.rs:585-593), so only agents, MCP, CLI or phone callers that omit `state` hit the fallback. For them, ui.layout.save quietly stores the hard-coded grid. Applying it later emits layout.changed applied, and native apply_layout (shell.rs:350+) switches the agent layout mode to grid. project.remove (workspace.rs:378-379) deletes only the exact path `layout.current.<id>`. Since settings.set stores objects as leaf rows, that matches nothing, and the native.layout.current.<id>.* leaves are never removed. projects.id is a plain INTEGER PRIMARY KEY without AUTOINCREMENT (store.rs:51-52), so if the highest-id project is removed, the next project reuses its id and restore_layout applies the dead project's saved arrangement.
v1.correction: The impact is cosmetic: a wrong saved preset, and a stale layout restored only when the removed project had the highest id. Leftover rows grow slightly per removed project. The DECISIONS D150 text and tests/bus.rs:769 still refer to the old `layout.current.N` key, which is docs/test drift from the rename. Fix: read `native.layout.current.{id}` in fallback_state, or have the client write the engine's key; on project.remove, delete the whole subtree of both keys with the shared prefix-delete helper.

findings.title: In-memory UI model drifts: close leaves no pane flagged focused, popout leaves empty windows, move ignores edge and emits a different ui.changed shape
findings.evidence: PaneClose sets `ui.focused = ui.panes.last().map(...)` without setting that pane's `focused` flag (114-116). WindowPopout strips the pane from its old window (277-279) but never removes the now-empty popout. PaneMove does `ui.panes.remove(from); ... ui.panes.insert(to.min(len), pane)`, which lands after the target when moving forward and before it when moving backward, ignores `edge` and window membership, and emits ui.changed as `{"move":{...}}` (178-181) while every other ui op emits the full StateOut. PaneOpen ignores `at` (BUS.md:917).
findings.impact: ui.state reports `focused: pane-N` while no PaneInfo has focused=true; the native apply_ui_event keys on the per-pane flag and on page/panes (shell.rs:438-458), so it ignores the move payload and ui.pane.move is a no-op that returns success; repeated popouts accumulate empty windows in ui.window.list, and panes grow without bound if never closed.
findings.fix: Set the flag on the new focused pane; drop popout windows that become empty; compute the insert index after removal relative to the target and honour edge, or reject what is unsupported; always emit the full state.

v1.reason: ui.rs:114-116: PaneClose sets `ui.focused = ui.panes.last().map(..)` but does not set that PaneInfo's `focused` flag. Compare PaneFocus at 132-135, which sets both. So after closing the focused pane, ui.state reports a focused pane while no pane carries focused=true. WindowPopout (274-284) removes the pane from every window and pushes a new popout, but never removes a popout that is now empty. Popping out a pane that is already in a popout therefore leaves an empty window in ui.window.list. PaneMove (174-176) does remove(from) then insert(to.min(len)), so the pane lands after the target when moving forward and before it when moving backward. It ignores `edge` beyond validating it, and emits ui.changed as {"move":{..}} (178-181), while every other op emits the full StateOut. Native apply_ui_event (shell.rs:438-461) only reads `page`, `project_id` and panes[].focused/target.session, so the move payload is ignored. These ops are agent-callable (Audit::AgentOnly). The phase9 test only checks that they succeed.
v1.correction: The impact is smaller than stated. The native client does not model engine panes, ordering or popout windows at all, so pane.move and popout have no visible effect whatever their payload shape. The concrete harm is that agents reading ui.state/ui.window.list see an inconsistent model (no focused flag, empty popouts). Fix: set the flag in PaneClose, drop emptied popout windows, emit the full state from PaneMove, and either document these ops as model-only or reject `edge` values that are not implemented.

findings.title: os.reveal/os.open_url spawn xdg-open and never reap it; reveal opens path.parent() even when it is a file
findings.evidence: `ctx.after_commit(move |_| { let target = path.parent().unwrap_or(&path); let _ = std::process::Command::new("xdg-open").arg(target).spawn(); });` (343-346) and the same fire-and-forget `.spawn()` for URLs (356-360). The Child is dropped without wait and nothing in the engine reaps children (no SIGCHLD handling found). The only path check is is_absolute().
findings.impact: Every link click (tools_skills.rs:170) or reveal leaves a defunct xdg-open in the process table for the engine's lifetime. A path like `/tmp/x.jar/anything` makes reveal run `xdg-open /tmp/x.jar`, opening (for some types, executing) the file with its desktop handler instead of showing a folder; reachable by agents granted allow_ui.
findings.fix: Reap in a detached thread (`std::thread::spawn(move || { let _ = child.wait(); })`); for reveal, open `path` if it is a directory, else its parent only if that is a directory (or use the FileManager1 ShowItems D-Bus call).

v1.reason: crates/relay-core/src/handlers/ui.rs:343-346 (os.reveal) and 356-360 (os.open_url) run `std::process::Command::new("xdg-open")...spawn()` inside after_commit and drop the Child. Dropping a std Child does not wait for it. A search of relay-core turns up no SIGCHLD handler, SIG_IGN or waitpid(-1) reaper; every other wait is on a specific child (proc.rs:47/57, pty.rs:227, device.rs:50, and so on). So each xdg-open becomes a zombie once it exits and stays until the engine exits. os.open_url is reachable from the native client's link click (apps/relay-native/src/tools_skills.rs:170). os.reveal has no native caller; only perf.rs, the CLI/MCP, and agent sessions with allow_ui can reach it (the op is marked `.ui()` in relay-bus/src/ops/ui.rs:40, and guardrail.rs:369/428 gates it). The reveal handler checks only `is_absolute()` before calling `path.parent()`. A path whose parent is a regular file (e.g. `/tmp/x.jar/anything`) therefore makes xdg-open open that file with its desktop handler instead of showing a folder. The growth is one zombie per click, which costs a PID-table slot and no memory to speak of. It is bounded by how often a person clicks and is cleared when the engine restarts, so the severity stays low.
v1.correction: The reveal-opens-a-file case is not a guardrail escape. Only an agent already granted allow_ui can reach it, that grant is a deliberate escape hatch, and the same session can normally run xdg-open itself under its command guardrails. Treat it as a minor correctness bug, not a security finding. Fix: after spawning, reap the child in a detached thread (`std::thread::spawn(move || { let _ = child.wait(); })`). For reveal, open `path` itself when it is a directory, otherwise open its parent only if that is a directory, and otherwise return an error. The FileManager1 ShowItems D-Bus call is a better option if selecting the file is wanted.

findings.title: settings.set flattens object keys verbatim into dotted paths; dotted keys and root-level scalars do not read back
findings.evidence: flatten builds `format!("{prefix}.{k}")` for every object key with no validation (68-78) while valid_path checks only the request path, and set_at splits stored paths on '.' (86). A root write of a non-object or {} stores a row at path "" (flatten pushes ("", v)), which tree() applies (*root = v) but subtree() never selects (ancestors come from '.' positions and exclude "", 155-158). Python model: settings.set keybindings {"ctrl+.":{"op":"ui.toast"}} reads back as {"ctrl+":{"":{"op":"ui.toast"}}}.
findings.impact: BUS.md:909 documents keybindings as 'shortcut -> op envelope', so any shortcut containing '.' is corrupted on save; values like {"a.b":1,"a":{"b":2}} collide and fail with an internal PK error; after settings.set {path:"", value:{}} the whole-tree read returns {} while leaf reads still return defaults, breaking the D150 agreement tests/bus.rs:760 asserts.
findings.fix: In flatten, reject (BusError::invalid) object keys that are not valid path segments; require a non-empty object for settings.set at "" (or write root keys individually); if root rows must exist, include "" among subtree's ancestors.

v1.reason: settings.rs:68-78: flatten joins object keys with `format!("{prefix}.{k}")` and never validates them. valid_path (58-66) checks only the request path. set_at/get_at split on '.' (86, 124), so a key containing '.' reads back as nested objects. A root write of {} or of a scalar: flatten("", {}) reaches the `_` arm and stores a row at path "". tree() applies it with set_at(root, "", v), which sets *root = v. subtree() builds its ancestors only from '.' positions (155-158), so it never selects the "" row, and leaf reads disagree with the full tree. Only users can trigger it (Actors::UserOnly on settings.set). The shipped native client writes only fixed lowercase paths plus numeric project ids, and its keybindings map action -> shortcut string (tools_settings.rs:537-538), not the shortcut -> op form BUS.md:909 documents. So the corruption needs hand-written CLI/phone input with dotted keys, or settings.set at "" with a non-object or empty object.
v1.correction: The trigger needs user-supplied input that no shipped client produces. Impact is a corrupted or inconsistent settings row, not data loss elsewhere. Fix: validate each object key in flatten against the same segment rule as valid_path and return BusError::invalid, and reject settings.set at "" unless the value is a non-empty object. Including "" among subtree's ancestors is not needed once that write is refused.

findings.title: Settings prefix delete uses case-insensitive LIKE and exists in three already-diverged copies
findings.evidence: `DELETE FROM settings WHERE path = ?1 OR path LIKE ?2 ESCAPE ...` with the pattern built by escaping % and _ only. SQLite LIKE is ASCII case-insensitive by default; verified with sqlite3 that delete_under('theme.dark') also deletes 'theme.Dark.bg'. The same helper is re-implemented in handlers/guardrail.rs:30-34 (also escapes backslash) and workspace.rs:378-379 (no ESCAPE clause); subtree's read uses a third escape variant (159).
findings.impact: Saving or resetting a subtree silently deletes a sibling subtree that differs only in case (user-named themes/layouts); the copies already disagree on escaping, so the next fix lands in one and not the others.
findings.fix: One pub(crate) settings::delete_under used by all three, matching the prefix case-sensitively and index-friendly: `path = ?1 OR (path >= ?1||'.' AND path < ?1||'/')`.

v1.reason: The prefix-delete really exists three times: settings.rs:193-201 (delete_under, escapes % and _ but not '\'), handlers/guardrail.rs:30-34 (delete_settings_under, also escapes '\'), and workspace.rs:378-379 (no ESCAPE clause, and the layout key is matched only as an exact path). subtree's read at settings.rs:159 is a fourth variant of the escape. Nothing sets PRAGMA case_sensitive_like (no hits in crates/relay-core/src), so LIKE matching is ASCII case-insensitive. However, the claimed impact cannot happen in practice. valid_path permits only [A-Za-z0-9_-], so '%' and '\' never reach these helpers, and the escaping differences are harmless. Every settings path written by the native client, CLI or remote is a fixed lowercase identifier or a numeric project id; no user-named theme or layout subtrees exist, so no two sibling paths differ only in case.
v1.correction: Downgrade the impact. The case-insensitive deletion is latent: a user would have to hand-write mixed-case sibling paths. The real payoff is consolidation. Make one pub(crate) settings::delete_under and use it in guardrail.rs and in project.remove (workspace.rs:378). The workspace copy is the one that already diverged in a way that matters: it deletes only the exact `layout.current.<id>` row and misses its leaves (see #16). Use a case-sensitive range match (`path = ?1 OR (path > ?1||'.' AND path < ?1||'/')`) or GLOB.

findings.title: app.rs dir_usage re-implements worktree::dir_size/build_size with different build-dir rules
findings.evidence: dir_usage treats any directory named target, build or .gradle at any depth as build output (`matches!(..., "target" | "build" | ".gradle")`) and walks single-threaded; worktree.rs:12 BUILD_DIRS = [target, build, .gradle, app/build, node_modules/.cache, dist] (top level only) drives build_size (worktree.disk, git.rs:156) and purge_build, with the 4-thread dir_size_all walker.
findings.impact: The resources panel's build_mb and worktree.disk disagree for the same checkout (dist/ and node_modules/.cache counted by one; nested src/build or sub-crate target by the other), so build_mb no longer predicts what a purge frees; the periodic refresh walks each worktree on one thread.
findings.fix: Compute (disk, build) with worktree's walker against BUILD_DIRS (or a shared single-pass walker parameterised by BUILD_DIRS) and delete dir_usage.

v1.reason: dir_usage (app.rs ~249-273) is a separate single-threaded walker. It treats any directory named target, build or .gradle at any depth as build output. worktree::build_size (worktree.rs:244) walks only the top-level BUILD_DIRS (worktree.rs:12: target, build, .gradle, app/build, node_modules/.cache, dist) with the 4-thread dir_size_all walker, and worktree.disk (git.rs:145-160) and purge_build use that walker. The two have already diverged: dist/ and node_modules/.cache count only in worktree.disk, and nested */build or */target count only in app.resources. As a result, the resources panel's build_mb (status.rs:284) does not match what a purge frees.
v1.correction: dir_usage does have one advantage: it measures total and build in a single pass, where worktree.disk walks build dirs twice. The fix is a shared walker parameterised by BUILD_DIRS that returns (total, build) in one pass, used by both.

results.coverage:
I read every line of all 26 assigned files: envelope.rs, error.rs, lib.rs, registry.rs, schema.rs, types.rs, the 17 ops/*.rs files, examples/dump_schema.rs, tests/registry.rs and Cargo.toml.

To check reachability and impact I read these regions outside the chunk:
- relay-core engine.rs: parse, dispatch_inner, resolve_actor, fill_identity, register*, invoke_registered
- relay-core socket.rs: handle_conn subscribe/wait/attach/mirror, Client, probe, pty_frame_line, payload_matches
- relay-core guardrail.rs: config, layers, typed, validate_config, authorize, callability
- relay-core handlers: bus.rs, ui.rs, settings.rs, guardrail.rs (config.set, gate, check), app.rs, plus parts of workspace, session, device, device_lease, task and file
- relay-core recovery.rs and store.rs version check
- relay-remote wire.rs and bridge.rs
- relay-cli mcp.rs and parts of main.rs
- relay-native client.rs line classification, shell.rs apply_ui_event, app.rs event dispatch
- BUS.md sections 0-12 and README

I compared registry metadata to the committed schema/bus.v1.json and to BUS.md with throwaway Python scripts in the scratchpad.

Heuristics, not exhaustive proof:
- emits: global sets of emitted vs declared event names, plus spot checks for each op.
- payload fields left unused by handlers: grep for field names, so common names such as `at` were checked by hand only for the suspicious ops.
- handler coverage: type-ident mapping, ambiguous names resolved by hand.

I did not build or run anything, per the rules. The cost of render() and the duration of the workspace.discover walk are estimates. The schemars recursion behaviour behind the render_op `$ref` finding comes from reading schemars-1.2.2/src/generate.rs, not from running it.

Three findings sit in core files rather than relay-bus, and the core auditors may report them too: workspace.discover under the store lock, the missing reconcile pass, and the duplicated gating prefixes.

Noted but not reported:
- The socket door answers bus.subscribe and bus.wait before checking actor, token or v. This is in the core chunk, and same-uid `user` needs no token anyway.
- The engine's idempotency check compares only the payload hash, not the op or actor. No client reuses ids.
- The phone gate forwards non-JSON frames, so a frame containing a newline reaches the engine as several lines. No privilege beyond `user` results.
- Request derives Debug including its token. Nothing logs requests today.

findings.title: One bad `guardrails.*` key written through `settings.set` makes every guardrail config read fail, blocking all agent mutations and gated tool calls
findings.evidence: `#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)] pub struct GuardrailConfig` (types.rs:222-237). Its parts are strict too: GuardrailCaps (173), DestructiveWrite (181), ShapeGate (205), RoleAllowlist (214). Every config read lays the stored `guardrails.*` settings rows over the defaults and runs `typed()`: `serde_json::from_value::<GuardrailConfig>` followed by `validate_config` (core guardrail.rs:193-197). `settings.set` accepts any value at any dotted path, `guardrails.*` included, and never runs that check. `valid_path` only checks the characters (handlers/settings.rs:57-65, 217-224). Only `guardrail.config.set` validates, by reading the result back (handlers/guardrail.rs:100). BUS.md §10.16 lists `guardrails` as a normal settings-tree key. `authorize()` calls `let cfg = config(conn, Some(session.project_id))?;` for every agent mutation (guardrail.rs:358). bus.ops and bus.whoami call it as well (handlers/bus.rs:42,65).
findings.impact:
`relay cmd settings.set '{"path":"guardrails.caps.file","value":3}'` (a typo) or `'{"path":"guardrails.caps.files","value":"40"}'` (a string) succeeds. From then on every `typed()` returns invalid/guardrail.config ("unknown field `file`"), with these effects:
- Every agent mutation fails: session.done, mailbox.send, task.update.
- Every `guardrail.gate` errors, so the Claude PreToolUse adapter exits 2 and blocks every Write, Edit and Bash in every session.
- bus.ops, whoami and session.bootstrap fail, so MCP tools/list offers no tools.
- guardrail.config.get and config.layers fail, so the guardrail settings UI cannot load to repair it.
The same outage happens when a newer build stored a guardrail key that an older build at the same SCHEMA_VERSION does not know.
findings.fix: Send `settings.set` and `settings.reset` on `guardrails` and `guardrails.*` through the same read-back validation `guardrail.config.set` uses, or refuse them with a hint to use guardrail.config.set. Also parse persisted config leniently: drop deny_unknown_fields from the persisted shape, or deserialize into a lenient mirror and log unknown keys. A stray key then degrades to a warning instead of a global outage.

v1.reason: Every level of GuardrailConfig, and each of its parts, uses `#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]` (types.rs:172-237). config_for -> typed() runs serde_json::from_value followed by validate_config (guardrail.rs:71-75, 193-197). That is reached from authorize (guardrail.rs:358) for every non-query agent mutation, and from bus.ops and whoami (handlers/bus.rs:42, 65). settings.set (handlers/settings.rs:217-234) only runs valid_path, which checks characters, and writes leaves. Nothing special-cases `guardrails.*`. layers() reads every `guardrails.%` row into the global layer (guardrail.rs:108-138), so a typo key, a scalar written over `caps`, or `caps.files=0` makes every typed() call fail. guardrail.config.set is the only writer that validates, by reading back (handlers/guardrail.rs:96). When guardrail.gate fails, the Claude PreToolUse adapter returns 2 and blocks the tool call (relay-cli/src/main.rs:470-483). The trigger is narrower than the finding implies. settings.set is UserOnly (ops/notify.rs:23-24), and the native settings page sends guardrail values through a separate typed path rather than generic settings.set (tools_settings.rs:121, 671-679). So it takes a raw `relay cmd settings.set` on a guardrails path, or a downgrade to a build that lacks a field a newer build stored. Several fields were added with serde(default) over time (min_file_lines, allow_if_recoverable, allowed_write_roots), so that downgrade case is realistic for a developer-run engine. The failure is closed, which is safe, but it stops every agent and the guardrail UI until the user repairs it.
v1.correction: Recovery exists. `settings.reset {path:"guardrails.<key>"}` does not read the config, and neither does guardrail.config.set with a null patch, which only runs layers() before its read-back. The outage is recoverable from the CLI, but the guardrail settings UI cannot be used to repair it. Narrow the trigger description to a raw CLI settings.set, or running an older engine build over a newer store. Fix: refuse settings.set and settings.reset on `guardrails`/`guardrails.*` and point to guardrail.config.set, or apply the same read-back validation there. Also consider dropping deny_unknown_fields from the persisted shape so unknown keys are logged instead of failing.

findings.title: workspace.discover walks the filesystem inside the store transaction and any agent can call it
findings.evidence: `e.register::<WsDiscover>(|_, p| { ... discover_repositories(&path)? })` is the plain `register`, so it runs inside the transaction with the store mutex held. It is absent from the register_unlocked list. `discover_repositories` recursively calls `fs::read_dir` down to `depth >= 4` under any absolute path the caller gives (workspace.rs:393-410). The registry entry is `OpMeta::query(Scope::Global, 12, ...)` with the default Actors::All (ops/workspace.rs:12-13). `authorize` returns Ok for every query before layer 3 (guardrail.rs). This is outside the bus chunk, found while checking registry gating.
findings.impact: A call like `workspace.discover {path:"/home/<user>"}` walks four levels of ~/.cache, ~/.local/share, ~/.cargo/registry and so on while holding the one store mutex. The call can come from the onboarding UI or from any agent through MCP, because it is a callable query. Every other bus request waits for the whole walk, including guardrail.gate hook calls that every agent tool use depends on. On a cold cache that can be seconds. CLAUDE.md requires tree walks to use register_unlocked.
findings.fix: Register it with `register_unlocked`; it reads nothing from the store.

v1.reason: crates/relay-core/src/handlers/workspace.rs:114 registers WsDiscover with plain `e.register`, not `register_unlocked`. In engine.rs dispatch (~906-960), only ops in `self.unlocked` skip the lock. Every other handler runs after `self.store.lock()` and `conn.transaction()`, so `(h.call)(&mut ctx, ...)` executes with the one store mutex held. The handler never touches `ctx`; it ignores it with `|_, p|`. It calls `discover_repositories` (workspace.rs:393-413), which recursively `fs::read_dir`s to depth 4 under any absolute, existing path. It skips only .git/.relay/node_modules/target/build/.gradle and stops at repo roots. The op meta (relay-bus/src/ops/workspace.rs:12-13) is `OpMeta::query(Scope::Global, 12, ...)` with no `.actors(...)`, so sessions can call it. This session's own MCP tool list includes `mcp__relay__workspace_discover`, which confirms agents can reach it. Callers are the onboarding UI (apps/relay-native/src/onboarding.rs:336, which re-runs it each time the user changes the workspace path) and any agent. A path like $HOME or / walks tens of thousands of directories on a cold cache while every other bus request waits, guardrail.gate included. That breaks the CLAUDE.md rule on tree walks. The handler reads nothing from the store, so moving it to `register_unlocked` is a drop-in fix. Medium is right: the normal onboarding use (a ~/dev style folder) is usually fast, and the multi-second stall needs a broad path.
v1.correction: The decisive lines are workspace.rs:114-131 (registration) and 393-413 (walk). Fix: `e.register_unlocked::<WsDiscover>(|_, p| ...)`. The handler body needs no other change. Related issue in the same function: `fs::read_dir(path)?` and `entry?` propagate any I/O error, so one unreadable subdirectory makes the whole discovery fail with `workspace.discover_failed` instead of skipping it. Two examples are a root-owned or 0700 directory under $HOME, and a directory removed mid-walk. Any error in a subdirectory should be skipped, and only a failure at the root reported. Consider also capping the total number of entries visited.

findings.title: bus.wait `matching` is untyped: a non-object means "match anything" and a string id never matches
findings.evidence: `pub matching: Option<Value>`: any JSON value passes bus.schema, and the MCP inputSchema gives no type. The socket door then does `let Some(wanted) = matching.and_then(serde_json::Value::as_object) else { return true };` (socket.rs:193-196). The stored-answer shortcut uses `matching?.get("request_id")?.as_i64()` (socket.rs:200-205). BUS.md §9.5 tells agents to wait with `bus.wait {events:["guardrail.request_resolved"], matching:{request_id}}`.
findings.impact:
Two failure modes:
- A non-object `matching` (`"request_id=17"`, `[{"request_id":17}]`) is treated as no filter. The agent wakes on the first `guardrail.request_resolved` of any session and reads someone else's `state:"confirmed"` as its own approval.
- `{"request_id":"17"}` (a string id) skips the stored-answer lookup and never compares equal to the numeric id in the event. The agent blocks until the timeout (60 s by default, up to an hour) even though the answer already exists.
findings.fix: Type it as `matching: Option<serde_json::Map<String, Value>>` so a non-object is a bus.schema error. For the documented exception wait, add a typed `request_id: Option<Id>`. Alternatively reject non-object `matching` in the door.

v1.reason: WaitIn.matching is `Option<Value>` (crates/relay-bus/src/ops/bus.rs:25). socket.rs:193-196 `payload_matches` returns true when matching is not an object (`let Some(wanted) = matching.and_then(Value::as_object) else { return true }`). socket.rs:200-205 `exception_waited` uses `matching?.get("request_id")?.as_i64()`, so `{"request_id":"17"}` skips the stored-answer lookup and never equals the numeric request_id in the event payload (grants.rs:316-330). BUS.md:612 documents `matching?: object`, so the code is laxer than the contract. However, the impact is smaller than claimed. The event payload carries `request_id` and `session`, so an agent that wakes on someone else's answer gets a payload naming a different request. Enforcement is server-side: the retried guardrail.gate is judged against stored grants, so a wrong wake can never let an agent bypass a guardrail. The worst outcomes are a premature retry that is refused again, or a stall until the timeout, after which the bootstrap hint (grants.rs:24-28) tells the agent to re-check with guardrail.request.get. The trigger also needs a malformed call from the agent.
v1.correction: Downgrade to low and recategorize as error-handling/robustness rather than a correctness bug with approval consequences. A wrong wake cannot grant anything, because guardrail.gate rechecks grants. The fix stands: type `matching` as `Option<serde_json::Map<String, Value>>` so that a non-object becomes a bus.schema error. Optionally, also accept a numeric string for request_id in exception_waited.

findings.title: The ui.* contract describes a UI executor that no longer exists: core answers from an in-memory model the GTK client mostly ignores
findings.evidence:
- ui.* ops are marked `.ui()`, which sets `executor: Executor::Ui` (registry.rs:157-160). The module doc says "Executor is the main window (§6.5)". No code outside relay-bus reads `meta.executor`.
- Core registers every ui.* op as an ordinary handler over `engine.ui`. For example ui.pane.open does `ui.panes.push(PaneInfo{..})` and returns `pane-N` (handlers/ui.rs:67-100).
- The GTK client never calls ui.pane.*, ui.window.* or ui.state. Its `apply_ui_event` only applies `page` and the focused terminal pane's `target.session` (apps/relay-native/src/shell.rs:438-462), and it shows `ui.toast` through `show_error` whatever the level (app.rs:1245-1246).
- Other Tauri-era leftovers: `ui_connected: AtomicBool::new(false)` is never stored (engine.rs:446). `Doors::TauriOnly` is never assigned (registry.rs:85). `Door::Tauri` appears only in tests. Frame is documented as "mirror is Tauri-channel only" (envelope.rs:261,267), yet socket.rs:538-560 streams `mirror` frames. The README says "No Tauri or webview".
findings.impact: An agent with allow_ui calls `ui.pane.open {kind:"diff", target:{sha}}`, which is the op's own documented example. It gets `{pane:"pane-1"}` and nothing opens. ui.window.popout returns an id for a window that does not exist. `ui.state` ("What the UI has open") reports phantom panes and never the user's real ones. Headless engines answer success where §6.5 promises `unavailable`/`ui.absent`. `app.status.ui_connected` is always false while the window is open.
findings.fix: Choose a contract. Either make the GTK client the real executor: forward ui.* to it, answer from its state, and set ui_connected per connection. Or remove the fiction: drop `Executor::Ui`/`.ui()`, `Doors::TauriOnly`/`Door::Tauri` and `ui_connected`, and narrow ui.* to what the client applies (page switch, terminal focus, toast). Then fix the Frame and §6.x docs.

v1.reason: Confirmed. `.ui()` sets Executor::Ui (registry.rs:158). Nothing outside relay-bus reads meta.executor: grep finds only registry.rs and lib.rs, plus a comment in perf.rs that wrongly calls ui.* 'the refusal path'. Core handlers/ui.rs:66-99 handles ui.pane.open by pushing a PaneInfo into engine.ui and returning `pane-N`. The GTK client's apply_ui_event (shell.rs:438-462) acts only on `page` and on a focused pane's target.session. A diff/sha pane, popout windows, close, move and so on therefore have no visible effect. The handler still returns success and records phantom panes, which ui.state then reports. ui.toast is shown through show_error regardless of level (app.rs:1245-1246). engine.rs:446 sets ui_connected to false, and grep finds no store, so app.status.ui_connected (handlers/app.rs:33) is always false. Doors::TauriOnly is never assigned to any op; it is only checked (engine.rs:822, mcp.rs:161). Door::Tauri is used only in tests. BUS.md:366 promises `unavailable`/`ui.absent` when no UI is attached, and that is never produced.
v1.correction: There is a partial counterexample: ui.pane.open with kind terminal and target.session does focus that session in the client, and ui.page.switch works. The no-op applies to the non-terminal pane kinds, windows, close, move, and to ui.state's contents. The reach is limited because agents need allow_ui. Medium is right for a misleading-success path that is less common.

findings.title: The reconcile pass the bus contract relies on does not exist: deleted files stay in .relay/trash forever and app.reconcile is a no-op
findings.evidence: `e.register::<Reconcile>(|_ctx, _| { // The 60 s trust-but-verify pass. Phase 1 has nothing to verify yet ... Ok(ReconcileOut { actions: Vec::new() }) })`. No reconcile timer exists anywhere in relay-core (grep). `undo.grace_days` (settings.rs:42) is never read. `file.delete` renames the target into `<worktree>/.relay/trash/<id>/payload` (handlers/file.rs:226-233). Nothing ever purges `file_trash` rows or trash directories. Only project.remove deletes the rows, and it leaves the files (workspace.rs:369). The registry advertises `app.reconcile` as "Run the 60s trust-but-verify pass now" (ops/app.rs:58-60).
findings.impact: BUS.md §5.4 promises that soft-deleted tasks, modules, notes and files are hard-deleted after `undo.grace_days` (7). In practice nothing deleted through Relay is ever reclaimed. Deleting a large directory (build output, node_modules) from the file browser in the project root keeps it on disk indefinitely under .relay/trash. `app.reconcile` reports success with no actions.
findings.fix: Implement the pass, both on a timer and on app.reconcile. It should purge trash entries and directories older than undo.grace_days and hard-delete soft-deleted rows past the grace window. Otherwise document trash as permanent and add an explicit empty-trash op.

v1.reason: The Reconcile handler (handlers/app.rs:137-141) returns `ReconcileOut { actions: Vec::new() }` and nothing else. relay-core/src contains no other reconcile code or timer. `undo.grace_days` appears only in the defaults (settings.rs:42) and is never read. file.delete (handlers/file.rs:221-236) renames the target into `<root>/.relay/trash/<id>/payload` and inserts a file_trash row. The only removals are restore, which marks restored_at, and project.remove, which deletes rows but not the directories (workspace.rs:364-369). Soft-deleted tasks, modules and notes are likewise never hard-deleted outside project.remove. BUS.md:290-291 states they are 'hard-deleted by the reconcile pass' after undo.grace_days.
v1.correction: Calibration: trash written inside an agent worktree goes away when that worktree directory is removed, but the file_trash rows remain and point at missing paths. The trash in a project's main checkout is permanent. Growth is bounded by what the user deliberately deletes, so medium is right, not high. The category is resource-leak with docs drift from BUS.md §5.4 and the app.reconcile summary. Fix: implement the purge, either in app.reconcile on a timer or in an off-mutex task, because walking and removing large trash directories is slow and must not run under Engine::register. If that is not done, document trash as permanent and add an empty-trash op.

findings.title: device.signing.create is documented as Tauri-only and unavailable over the socket, but the registry admits it on every door
findings.evidence: BUS.md §10.14 says: "mutation · never · user · Tauri only … deliberately unaudited and unavailable over the socket so its secret never reaches audit, CLI arguments, or agents". The registry entry is `OpMeta::mutation(...).audit(Audit::Never).actors(Actors::UserOnly).emits(...)` with no `.doors(..)`, so `doors: all`. The core test dispatches it on `Door::Socket` (tests/bus.rs:430-436). The GTK client sends it over the socket (apps/relay-native/src/tools_devices.rs:529).
findings.impact: `relay cmd device.signing.create '{"project_id":1,"key_alias":"upload","password":"…"}'` is accepted. The release-keystore password then sits in the process argv, readable by other local users through /proc/<pid>/cmdline unless /proc is mounted hidepid, and in shell history. The docs say this path cannot exist. Agents are still refused by user_only.
findings.fix: The only UI now uses the socket, so state the real rule in BUS.md and the op summary. Make the CLI take this op's payload from stdin only (refuse argv), or have the engine accept it only from the GTK client's connection.

v1.reason: device.rs:37-39 registers device.signing.create with no `.doors(..)`. git show e4a60fc shows `.doors(Doors::TauriOnly)` was deliberately removed from both signing.create and mirror.start when the native GTK client (a socket client) gained these features; tools_devices.rs:529 now calls it over the socket. The docs were not updated and still claim the old rule: BUS.md:867 ("Tauri only ... unavailable over the socket so its secret never reaches audit, CLI arguments, or agents"), DECISIONS.md D157 (around line 893, "user_only, and TauriOnly"), docs/upstream-v3/DECISIONS.md D224 and docs/upstream-v3/native/SHELL-PARITY.md:49 (which says the native client cannot create a key). The secret is still kept out of agents (UserOnly) and audit (Audit::Never; engine.rs:1399). I found no payload logging in engine.rs. The relay CLI also accepts the payload on stdin (relay-cli main.rs:137), so argv is not the only route. The argv/proc exposure happens only if the user chooses to type the password on the command line themselves, which is the user's own same-uid action. This is not a hole another party can trigger.
v1.correction: Recategorize from security to docs-drift. The code change was intentional (commit e4a60fc), and only the documentation is stale: BUS.md §10.14 row, D157, D224 and SHELL-PARITY.md. Update them to say the op is allowed on the socket but user_only and never audited. Optionally have the CLI warn when this op's payload is given in argv rather than on stdin. Note that mirror.start lost TauriOnly in the same commit and its docs have the same drift.

findings.title: Actor contract disagrees with itself: the schema pattern excludes `system` that results carry, the parser accepts names the pattern rejects, and a bad actor is reported as bus.envelope
findings.evidence:
- The schema is `"pattern": "^(user|test|agent:[A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,64})$"`, described as "system is internal and rejected at every door".
- The same type is used for Event.actor (225), AuditRow.actor/on_behalf_of, Hold.actor/resolved_by and GuardrailException.resolved_by (types.rs:293,544,552,570-571).
- The engine emits events as Actor::System (engine.rs:568,720), audits async completions as system (engine.rs:705), and expires holds with `resolved_by = 'system'` (handlers/session.rs:1613).
- `Actor::parse` accepts any 1-64-byte name (envelope.rs:47: spaces, ':', '/', unicode).
- A parse failure becomes a serde custom error (78). `Engine::parse` then answers `BusError::envelope` (engine.rs:749-754), but §1.2 and §4.2 promise `bus.actor`.
findings.impact: A consumer validating against schema/bus.v1.json, which BUS.md calls the contract tools consume, rejects real events, audit rows and holds. The MCP inputSchema for `audit.list {actor}` forbids "system", so async-completion rows cannot be filtered by actor through MCP. An agent that reacts to codes gets bus.envelope for a bad actor.
findings.fix: Publish two schemas: a claimable request actor and a result actor that includes `system`. Make `Actor::parse` enforce the same character set as the pattern. Map actor parse failures to `bus.actor` by pre-reading `actor` in the Engine::parse fallback.

v1.reason: crates/relay-bus/src/envelope.rs:86-92 renders Actor with pattern ^(user|test|agent:[A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,64})$ and calls system 'rejected at every door'. The same type is used for Event.actor (envelope.rs:224) and for AuditRow.actor/on_behalf_of and Hold/Exception resolved_by (types.rs:293,544,552,570-571), and these can legitimately carry 'system'. schema/bus.v1.json:4537-4541 ships that pattern, and BUS.md §0.5 calls the file 'what tools consume'. MCP audit.list builds its inputSchema from schema['payload'] (relay-cli/src/mcp.rs:173), and audit::ListIn.actor is Option<Actor> (ops/audit.rs:8), so the published filter forbids 'system'. Actor::parse (envelope.rs:47) accepts any 1-64-byte name after 'agent:'. That is looser than the pattern but harmless, because agent identity is bound by token. Engine::parse (engine.rs:749-755) answers a bad actor string with BusError::envelope, not bus.actor. The BUS.md §1.2 table lists both codes under 'invalid', so this is a small inconsistency, not a broken contract.
v1.correction: The real effect is limited to external schema consumers and to MCP clients that enforce the pattern on audit.list {actor:'system'}. Nothing in the engine validates against the JSON schema. The simplest fix is to drop the pattern, or add 'system' to it, on result-side uses. A separate request-side actor schema is optional. Mapping parse failures to bus.actor is a nicety: kind is 'invalid' either way.

findings.title: Generated schema gets wrong envelope docs: the Response doc sits on MailHint, and the request id is said to dedupe for 24h
findings.evidence: `/// A response envelope (BUS.md §1.2). Exactly one of result / error is present.` is attached to `pub struct MailHint` (139-145). In schema/bus.v1.json, `$defs.MailHint.description` is that sentence and `$defs.Response` has no description. `Request.id` is documented as "idempotency key for 24h" (101). BUS.md §5.3 and recovery.rs instead keep ids deduplicated until audit.retention_days (180 by default). schema.rs:45 and lib.rs:5 point at docs/BUS.md, but the file is docs/engine/BUS.md.
findings.impact: Tool authors reading the generated contract get the wrong semantics. A client that trusts "24h" and reuses ids after a day gets stale `replayed` responses or bus.id_reused for months.
findings.fix: Move the comment to Response, give MailHint its own, correct the retention statement and the paths, then regenerate the schema.

v1.reason: envelope.rs:139 attaches '/// A response envelope (BUS.md §1.2). Exactly one of result / error is present.' to `pub struct MailHint`. Response (envelope.rs:147) has no doc. In schema/bus.v1.json:4663-4678, MailHint.description is that sentence. Request.id says 'idempotency key for 24h' (envelope.rs:101, and in the schema at bus.v1.json:4508). BUS.md §5.3 says ids are unique forever, bounded by audit.retention_days (default 180). schema.rs:44 and lib.rs:5 cite docs/BUS.md, but only docs/engine/BUS.md exists.
v1.correction: Downgrade the impact. Callers mint UUID v4 ids (Request::new uses Uuid::new_v4), so no real client reuses ids because of the '24h' text. This only misleads readers of the generated contract.

findings.title: Server-to-client envelope types reject unknown fields, so any additive envelope change disconnects older clients
findings.evidence: `#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]` is on Response (148), Event (218), Frame (258), MailHint (141), BusError (error.rs:48) and Confirm (error.rs:41). BUS.md §12 says additive changes do not bump `v` and that clients ignore unknown fields, and the `mail` sideband was added exactly that way. The GTK reader parses each line strictly, and any error ends the connection and fails all pending replies (apps/relay-native/src/client.rs:233-250 → Error::Protocol). `relay_core::socket::Client::next`, used by the CLI, MCP and hooks, is just as strict (socket.rs:785-797).
findings.impact: After any optional field is added to Response, Event, Frame or BusError, a client from the previous build disconnects on the first line that carries it. Mixed builds are normal in this workflow: run.sh keeps an already-running engine across rebuilds and the window can outlive an engine restart.
findings.fix: Keep deny_unknown_fields on Request and on payloads only. Remove it from the server-to-client types: Response, Event, Frame, BusError, Confirm and MailHint.

v1.reason: The mechanism is real. Response, Event, Frame and MailHint (envelope.rs:141,148,218,258) and BusError/Confirm (error.rs) are #[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]. The native reader parses each line into these types and turns any parse error into Error::Protocol, which ends the reader loop and fails every pending reply (apps/relay-native/src/client.rs:233-257). relay_core::socket::Client::next (socket.rs:785-797) is just as strict. This contradicts the crate's own rule: the result! macro (ops/mod.rs:15) is deliberately lenient because 'clients ignore unknown fields, §12', and the `mail` sideband was added to Response as an additive change. The trigger has two parts: a future additive envelope field, and an older reader talking to a newer engine. Examples of such readers: a long-lived `relay mcp` process of an agent session that started before a rebuild and engine restart, or the window reconnecting to a restarted engine. run.sh's normal path (old engine, new window) is the safe direction, so the skew needs an engine restart. Nothing breaks at this commit.
v1.correction: Latent compatibility hazard, not a current failure. The fix is as proposed: remove deny_unknown_fields from the server-to-client types (Response, Event, Frame, MailHint, BusError, Confirm) and keep it on Request and payloads. The run.sh case cited in the finding is the safe direction, because a newer client reading an older engine never sees unknown fields.

findings.title: render_op returns result schemas with a dangling `$ref` for the recursive Entry type
findings.evidence: render_op sets `inline_subschemas = true` and returns `(e.payload_schema)(&mut g).to_value()` and the result schema, then discards the generator's definitions. In schemars 1.2.2, `subschema_for` still returns a `$ref` for a type that is already being generated: `return_ref = !inline_schema && (!inline_subschemas || pending_schema_ids.contains(uid))` (generate.rs:322-323). `types::Entry` has `children: Option<Vec<Entry>>`.
findings.impact: `bus.schema {op:"file.tree"}` returns `children.items: {"$ref":"#/$defs/Entry"}` with no `$defs`, so the reference cannot be resolved. The same happens for file.create, rename, move, restore, restore_head and import, even though the doc says "self-contained (defs inlined)".
findings.fix: After generating, attach `g.take_definitions(true)` as `$defs` to the returned document whenever it is non-empty.

v1.reason: I checked this against the code. render_op (crates/relay-bus/src/schema.rs:61-75) builds a generator with inline_subschemas = true and calls payload_schema/result_schema. Both are `|g| g.subschema_for::<T>()` (registry.rs:216-217). It returns only `{op, meta, payload, result}` and never takes g.definitions(). In schemars 1.2.2 (Cargo.lock), find_ref sets `return_ref = !inline_schema && (!inline_subschemas || pending_schema_ids.contains(uid))` (generate.rs:321-322). The recursive `children: Option<Vec<Entry>>` field (types.rs:865) therefore reaches Entry while Entry is still pending. The root_schema_id_stack is empty under subschema_for, so the result is `#/$defs/Entry`, and insert_new_subschema_for puts the definition only into g.definitions, which render_op discards. The affected ops are file.tree, file.create, file.rename, file.move, file.restore, file.restore_head and file.import (ops/file.rs:7-35). The impact is small. The MCP tool list (relay-cli/src/mcp.rs:166-173) uses only schema["payload"], and no payload type is recursive, so the tool list is unaffected. Only `bus.schema {op}` and `relay schema <op>` return a result schema that cannot be resolved, which contradicts the doc comment's "self-contained (defs inlined)".
v1.correction: The affected callers are bus.schema (handlers/bus.rs:25) and the CLI (main.rs:146, 237). The MCP inputSchema is unaffected because only results contain Entry. The fix as proposed works: attach `g.take_definitions(true)` as `$defs` when it is non-empty. A test that walks render_op output for every op looking for unresolved `$ref` would stop this from recurring.

findings.title: `nullable` patch fields do not survive a typed round trip: Serialize writes "absent" as `null`, which is read back as "clear"
findings.evidence: `nullable` maps an explicit null to `Some(None)`, meaning clear. The payload! macro (ops/mod.rs:6-13) derives Serialize with no `skip_serializing_if`, so an outer `None` is also emitted as `null`. Affected fields: task UpdateIn.size/module_id (task.rs:53), task ListIn.parent_id (46), module UpdateIn.icon (module.rs:21), notes UpdateIn.title (notes.rs:16), session UpdateIn.task_id/module_id (session.rs:145), ProjectUpdateIn.build_cmd/run_cmd (workspace.rs:45). Core already serializes typed payloads to call other ops (handlers/task.rs:683 `serde_json::to_value(create)` → invoke_registered) and to freeze held envelopes (handlers/guardrail.rs:401,548).
findings.impact: Nothing triggers it today. The first time someone builds and serializes, say, `task::UpdateIn { task_id, title: Some(..), .. }` (an internal invoke, a frozen hold or a Rust client), `size` and `module_id` go out as null and the engine clears them. Likewise `task::ListIn { parent_id: None }` turns into "roots only".
findings.fix: Add `skip_serializing_if = "Option::is_none"` to every nullable field and a serialize/deserialize round-trip test.

v1.reason: The serde mechanism is real: an outer None on an Option<Option<T>> without skip_serializing_if serializes as null, and crate::nullable reads it back as Some(None). But no code path serializes any of the affected types. rg finds no construction or use of task/module/notes/session UpdateIn, task ListIn or ProjectUpdateIn outside crates/relay-bus/src/ops. The cited typed re-serializations do not involve nullable fields: handlers/task.rs:683 serializes a session.create payload, and handlers/guardrail.rs:401,548 serialize guardrail payloads. The native client and CLI build payloads as JSON. The finding itself says 'Nothing triggers it today'. Without a reachable trigger, this is a hypothetical hazard, not a bug.
v1.correction: If a typed Rust caller of these patch payloads is ever added, add skip_serializing_if = "Option::is_none" on nullable fields and a round-trip test at that point. That would be a cheap hardening, but it does not count as a finding today.

findings.title: guardrail.gate's result type advertises refuse/hold verdicts it can never return
findings.evidence: `GateOut { verdict: Verdict, error: Option<BusError>, hold_id: Option<Id> }`. The handler returns `Ok(GateOut { verdict: Verdict::Allow, error: None, hold_id: None })` and nothing else (handlers/guardrail.rs:535,622). A refusal returns `Err(error)` (544) and a hold returns `Err(held.with_confirm(..))` (556-563). BUS.md §9.3 documents `→ {verdict: allow|refuse|hold, error?, hold_id?}`, while guardrail.check really does put refuse/hold in its result (`check_out`, 772-777).
findings.impact: A hook or integration written against the schema that checks `result.verdict` never sees refuse or hold, because those arrive as ok:false. Two ops with near-identical result types report the same decision in different ways. Relay's own adapter checks `response.ok` (relay-cli main.rs:471), so it works by accident of implementation.
findings.fix: Either return `{}` and document that refuse and hold are typed errors, or return the verdict in the result the way guardrail.check does.

v1.reason: GateOut { verdict, error, hold_id } (crates/relay-bus/src/ops/guardrail.rs:15). handlers/guardrail.rs gate() returns Ok only with `Verdict::Allow, error: None, hold_id: None` (line 535). Refuse returns `Err(error)` after commit_error (line 544), and Hold returns `Err(error.with_confirm(...))` (line 563). The confirm replay at line 622 also returns only Allow in the result. BUS.md:508-512 and :793 document `{verdict: allow|refuse|hold, error?, hold_id?}`, while guardrail.check (lines 774-776) really does return refuse/hold in its result. The hooks and the pre-commit hook rely on ok:false and the non-zero exit, so Relay's own enforcement works. A third-party integration that follows the schema and reads `result.verdict` would only ever see allow (refusals arrive as errors), so it fails closed rather than open.
v1.correction: The fix is to document that refuse and hold arrive as typed errors (with the hold_id in the error's confirm), and shrink GateOut to match, or return the verdict in the result the way guardrail.check does. Because a schema-following client would see an error instead of a verdict, the result is a failure, never a bypass, so low is right.

findings.title: Registry advertises surface that does nothing: project.stats has no handler, app.log.tail attaches no stream, git.log.graph and ui.pane.open.at are ignored
findings.evidence:
- `op!(ProjectStats, "project.stats", ...)` has no handler anywhere in relay-core; the perf runs record 50/50 `bus.not_implemented`.
- `app.log.tail` declares `.stream("log")` (ops/app.rs:39), but its handler only does `emit_system("app.log.attached", ..)` and returns `{}` (handlers/app.rs:133-136), and the socket door attaches no log stream.
- `git.log {graph}` (git.rs:29) is read by no handler (grep).
- `ui.pane.open {at}` (ui.rs:12) is never used by handlers/ui.rs:67-100.
findings.impact: Callers get silent no-ops, which is what BUS.md §5.2's strict schema is meant to prevent ("silently dropped fields are how v3 shipped no-ops"). `relay cmd app.log.tail` succeeds and never streams. project.stats is published in BUS.md §10.4 and bus.v1.json.
findings.fix: Implement these or remove them from the registry. Add a relay-core test that every registered op has a handler.

v1.reason: Confirmed. project.stats is declared at ops/workspace.rs:64 and has no handler anywhere in relay-core. The app.log.tail handler (handlers/app.rs:133-136) only emits app.log.attached and returns {}. socket.rs has stream plumbing for pty, logcat and mirror, but none for `log`. LogIn.graph (ops/git.rs:29) is not read anywhere in relay-core: grep for 'graph' finds nothing relevant. PaneOpenIn.at is ignored in handlers/ui.rs.
v1.correction: project.stats is not a silent no-op. An unhandled op returns the typed `bus.not_implemented` error (engine.rs:322/912; handlers/mod.rs:2 documents this), so only app.log.tail, git.log.graph and ui.pane.open.at are silent. app.log.tail has a stream, so it is not exposed over MCP (mcp.rs exposed() filters streams). It still succeeds from the CLI/socket without streaming.

findings.title: Closed value sets are plain strings in payloads and results; docs and handlers have already diverged
findings.evidence:
Payload fields:
- `DoneIn.status: Option<String>` (completed|blocked|partial), hand-checked at handlers/session.rs:1146-1152
- `ReportIn.kind: String` (session.rs:149), hand-checked at 1359-1369
- `ChangelogDraftIn.group_by` (module.rs:40): the handler accepts only "priority" (handlers/module.rs:209), though BUS.md §10.6 documents "priority"|"size"
- task ListIn.sort (task.rs:39), PaneMoveIn.edge (ui.rs:19), ToastIn.level (ui.rs:37), AppendIn.target (notes.rs:23), file CreateIn.kind (file.rs:16), LogTailIn.level (app.rs:38), BuildIn.format (device.rs:24), ShapeGate.validator (types.rs:209)
Result fields use strings where enums already exist: `BootstrapTask.column/state` (session.rs:103) despite Column and TaskState; also DeviceLease.kind, Run.kind and Run.state.
findings.impact: The generated schema and MCP inputSchema show free strings, so agents get no list of allowed values. Validation is re-implemented per handler. The `group_by: "size"` drift is already here: the schema allows it, the docs promise it, and the handler refuses it.
findings.fix: Replace them with snake_case enums in relay-bus and delete the hand-written checks in the handlers.

v1.reason: Confirmed. DoneIn.status is Option<String> (ops/session.rs:44), and handlers/session.rs:1146-1152 hand-checks it against completed|blocked|partial. ReportIn.kind is a String (ops/session.rs:149), matched by hand in handlers/session.rs (~1359-1369) with a typed invalid error. BootstrapTask.column and .state are String (ops/session.rs:103) even though Column and TaskState enums exist. ChangelogDraftIn.group_by is Option<String> (ops/module.rs:40). handlers/module.rs:209 refuses anything other than "priority" ("group_by must be priority"), while BUS.md:700 documents `group_by?: "priority"|"size"`. So the docs and the handler have already diverged. Each handler validates, so nothing silently misbehaves. The cost is no enumerated values in the MCP/JSON schema, plus the drift.
v1.correction: The BUS.md line for the group_by drift is docs/engine/BUS.md:700. The quickest concrete fix is to make group_by an enum with only `priority` (or implement `size`) and correct BUS.md:700. Converting the other strings to enums is a modest-value cleanup, not a bug fix.

findings.title: Dead public API and placeholder items in relay-bus
findings.symbol: WireLine, OpEntry.payload_type, namespace, is_mutation, names, in_project, since/deprecated
findings.evidence:
Referenced nowhere in the workspace:
- `WireLine` (envelope.rs:279-285)
- `OpEntry.payload_type/result_type` (registry.rs:200-201, still computed for each entry)
- `OpEntry::namespace` (224), `OpMeta::is_mutation` (181), `Registry::names` (334), `Event::in_project` (250)
- `OpMeta.since` is "1.0" on all 221 ops with no way to set it, and `OpMeta::deprecated()` is never called
Items that exist only to silence unused imports: `fn _touch(_: Value)` (ops/app.rs:62-63) and `const _ACTORS_USED` (ops/bus.rs:58-59).
`Registry::payload_shapes(&self)` ignores `self` and reads `Registry::global()` (registry.rs:341-347).
findings.impact: Maintenance noise and misleading API. `WireLine` (an untagged enum) is exactly the parse-everything approach the clients deliberately avoid, and would silently misclassify lines if someone adopted it.
findings.fix: Delete the unused items and imports. Make payload_shapes an associated fn, or have it use `self`.

v1.reason: rg across crates and apps finds no use of WireLine (envelope.rs:279-285), OpEntry.payload_type/result_type (registry.rs:200-201, set at 214-215), OpEntry::namespace (224), OpMeta::is_mutation (181), Registry::names (334) or Event::in_project (250). Placeholder items exist only to silence unused imports: `fn _touch(_: Value)` (ops/app.rs:62-63), `const _ACTORS_USED` (ops/bus.rs:58-59), and in core `_ctx_used`/`_CALLABLE_USED` (handlers/bus.rs:117-121). payload_shapes(&self) (registry.rs:341) ignores self and reads Registry::global(). There is only one registry, so this is harmless, but it is misleading.
v1.correction: Remove OpMeta.since and OpMeta::deprecated() from the list. BUS.md §12 makes both part of the contract ('Every op carries since: "1.0"…', 'Deprecation is an attribute… visible in bus.ops'), and both are surfaced through OpInfo in bus.ops (registry.rs:278,281). The claim that WireLine 'would silently misclassify lines' is speculative: it is simply unused. Fix: delete the unused items and the placeholder fns/consts along with their now-unused imports.

findings.title: bus.schema re-renders the whole static schema on every call while holding the store lock
findings.evidence: `render()` builds a new SchemaGenerator and regenerates all 221 ops and 387 defs (about 315 KB pretty-printed) on every call, and clones each op object (schema.rs:36). handlers/bus.rs:22-28 registers bus.schema with plain `e.register`, so it runs inside the store transaction. The output never changes within a build.
findings.impact: Each `bus.schema {}` call, which agents can make through MCP, holds the store mutex while the schema is generated. In the opt-level-1 workspace build that plausibly exceeds the engine's 16 ms LOCK_BUDGET, and other ops wait. The response is also about 200 KB.
findings.fix: Cache `render()` (and render_op results) in a `OnceLock`, and register bus.schema as an unlocked query.

v1.reason: render() (schema.rs:11) builds a new generator and regenerates every op and def on each call. handlers/bus.rs:22-28 registers bus.schema with plain e.register, so the work runs while the store mutex is held. The output is static within a build.
v1.correction: The claim that it plausibly exceeds LOCK_BUDGET is contradicted by measurement. docs/perf/runs/2026-09-19/report.md:61 records op.bus.schema.whole at 9.72 ms p50 and 11.92 ms p99 on the dev opt-level-1 profile, below the 16 ms budget, with a ~157 KiB response. Per-op bus.schema costs 257 µs. A whole-schema call therefore stalls the bus for about 10 ms, and it is a rare call: MCP steers agents to `bus.schema {op}`. The fix is still cheap: cache render() in a OnceLock and register the op as unlocked.

findings.title: Layer-1 user-only set in code differs from module docs and BUS.md §9.1
findings.evidence:
