- app.rs:1 says "All mutations are user-only (§9.1 layer 1)", but `app.resources.watch` (app.rs:29-30) has no `.actors(Actors::UserOnly)`.
- BUS.md §9.1 lists "device.* mutations" as user_only, but `device.claim` and `device.release` (device.rs:72-80) admit all actors and are in the default builder allowlist (settings.rs:31).
- device.rs:1 says "avd.* is reserved for post-4.0", yet avd.list, catalog, create and boot are registered in that same file (50-59).
findings.impact: The written allowlist cannot be trusted as a description of what agents can do. A role configured with `app.*` or `*` can toggle resource sampling (worktree disk measurement), contrary to the documented rule.
findings.fix: Make app.resources.watch user_only or correct the comment, list device.claim/release in §9.1 as agent-callable, and fix the stale module docs.

v1.reason: crates/relay-bus/src/ops/app.rs:1 says "All mutations are user-only (§9.1 layer 1)", but app.resources.watch (app.rs:29-30) is `OpMeta::mutation(...).audit(Audit::Never).emits(&["resource.sample"])` with no `.actors(Actors::UserOnly)`. It is the only app.* mutation without it. BUS.md:445-450 lists `device.*` mutations as user_only, but device.claim and device.release (device.rs:72-80) have no actors restriction, and settings.rs:31-33 puts them in every default role. device.rs:1 says "avd.* is reserved for post-4.0" while avd.list/catalog/create/boot are registered at device.rs:50-59. The real-world effect is small: no default role contains app.resources.watch, so an agent reaches it only through a custom role that grants `app.*` or `*`. Even then it can only switch resource sampling on or off.
v1.correction: In practice this is only docs drift. The agent-reachable app.resources.watch matters only for custom roles, and all it does is toggle sampling. Fix the app.rs:1 and device.rs:1 module docs, and name device.claim/release as agent-callable in BUS.md §9.1 and in the §9.1 role table, which currently leaves them out. Making app.resources.watch UserOnly is optional.

findings.title: bus_writes/allow_ui gating is re-derived from op-name prefixes in two places instead of from registry metadata
findings.evidence: `let bus_write = entry.name.starts_with("file.") || matches!(entry.name, "git.stage" | "git.unstage" | "git.commit"); … let ui = entry.name.starts_with("ui.") || entry.name.starts_with("os.");` appears in `authorize` (363-369) and again in `callability` (422-428). OpMeta has an `executor` field but no gating attribute, so the registry cannot say which ops each session option opens.
findings.impact: The two copies must change together. Otherwise bus.ops, session.bootstrap and MCP tools/list (which use callability) promise something different from what authorize enforces, which is the D104 failure the comments warn about. A future file-writing op outside `file.*` would silently fall outside bus_writes.
findings.fix: Add an attribute such as `session_option: Option<SessionOption>` (BusWrites/AllowUi) to OpMeta, set it in the registry, and have both functions read it through one helper.

v1.reason: The same derivation appears twice, character for character. In authorize (guardrail.rs:363-369) and in callability (guardrail.rs:422-428): `entry.name.starts_with("file.") || matches!(entry.name, "git.stage" | "git.unstage" | "git.commit")` and `entry.name.starts_with("ui.") || entry.name.starts_with("os.")`. callability's doc comment calls it 'the single source' so discovery never promises more than execution (D104), yet authorize re-derives the gating on its own. The two copies have not diverged yet, so the cost is a future-drift risk rather than a current bug.
v1.correction: A smaller fix than new registry metadata: a private helper in guardrail.rs, e.g. `fn session_option(name) -> Option<SessionOption>`, called by both functions, removes the duplication. Registry metadata is optional and only worth it if other doors need the attribute.

findings.title: bus.schema errors carry no `details.path` although BUS.md §5.2 promises it
findings.evidence: `validate: |v| … .map_err(|e: serde_json::Error| e.to_string())` returns only a string. `BusError::schema(op, why)` (error.rs:111-114) puts it in `message` and sets no details. BUS.md §5.2 says "Unknown fields are an error (bus.schema, details.path)", and error.rs:1 says agents react to kind and code, never to message. No code anywhere sets details.path.
findings.impact: An agent that sent a bad or unknown field has to parse the prose message to find which field failed. The handler-side typed parse errors (Engine::register wrappers) have the same gap.
findings.fix: Use serde_path_to_error in `validate` and return `{path, expected}` in details.

v1.reason: registry.rs:221 maps the serde error to a String. BusError::schema (error.rs:111-114) puts it only in the message and attaches no details. BUS.md:269 promises `details.path`, and no code sets it. The typed handler parse paths (engine.rs:489/515/542/548) and the session.input/resize paths (engine.rs:1277/1296) have the same gap.
v1.correction: The impact is small. For the common case, an unknown or missing top-level field, serde_json's message already names the field ("unknown field `x`, expected one of ..."). What is really missing is a machine-readable path for nested type errors. The fix is to adopt serde_path_to_error, or to correct BUS.md:269.

findings.title: emits metadata has drifted from what handlers actually emit
findings.evidence:
- guardrail.gate's emits list leaves out `device.lease.acquired` and `device.lease.released`, but gate → `device_lease::gate_command` → `acquire` emits both (handlers/device_lease.rs:112-123).
- ui.page.switch, ui.pane.* and ui.window.* declare no events but emit `ui.changed` (handlers/ui.rs:61,95,118,137,178,286,320).
- ui.toast emits `ui.toast` (ui.rs:332) without declaring it.
- app.log.tail, a query, emits the undeclared `app.log.attached` (handlers/app.rs:134).
BUS.md §3.2 makes `emits` the published list of events each op produces.
findings.impact: Agents and clients that consult bus.ops or bus.schema to learn what bus.wait can wake on miss these events. `ui.changed`, the event the GTK client actually applies, is not named anywhere in the contract.
findings.fix: Correct the lists. Add a debug-build check that every emitted event name is declared by the op being dispatched.

v1.reason: guardrail.gate emits (crates/relay-bus/src/ops/guardrail.rs:17) leaves out device.lease.acquired/released. gate() calls device_lease::gate_command (handlers/guardrail.rs:532), which acquires leases, and acquire() emits RELEASED/ACQUIRED (handlers/device_lease.rs:112-118). device.run's meta does declare these events. ui.page.switch/pane.*/window.* in ops/ui.rs have no `.emits` but handlers/ui.rs emits `ui.changed` (lines 61, 95, 118, 137, 178, 286, 320). ui.toast emits `ui.toast` (ui.rs:332) without declaring it. app.log.tail emits `app.log.attached` (handlers/app.rs:134) without declaring it. Neither `ui.changed` nor `app.log.attached` appears anywhere in BUS.md. Nothing in core checks `emits`; it is used only for OpInfo (registry.rs:276). The impact is limited to discovery: bus.wait matches by event name regardless of what is declared, so waits still work.
v1.correction: Low docs-drift as stated. A cheap guard is a debug_assert in Ctx::emit, or a test that compares emitted names against the dispatched op's declared emits. Also add ui.changed to BUS.md §3.3.

findings.title: tests/registry.rs does not check the invariants the registry currently breaks
findings.evidence:
The test checks only name validity, a non-empty summary, phase 1..=12 and that queries are not audited. Nothing asserts:
- every op has a handler (project.stats has none)
- render_op output contains no unresolved `$ref` (the file.* results do)
- the Actor schema accepts every actor the engine emits (system)
- nullable payload fields round-trip
- mutations declare the events they emit (BUS.md §3.3; 19 mutations declare none, and guardrail.gate omits device.lease.*)
findings.impact: Each defect listed above shipped unnoticed and will regress silently after it is fixed.
findings.fix: Add those assertions. Handler coverage and emits coverage belong in relay-core's test suite.

v1.reason: crates/relay-bus/tests/registry.rs checks only name validity, a non-empty summary, a phase in 1..=12, that queries are not audited, that a fixed list of phase-1 ops exists, that rendering is deterministic, that render_op returns Some for task.create, envelope round-trips and that the committed schema is current. Nothing walks render_op output for unresolved `$ref`, and I confirmed that defect above. I also confirmed that project.stats has no handler: ProjectStats is not referenced anywhere in relay-core/src, and the perf runs record bus.not_implemented for it. The gap is real, but this finding mostly restates the other findings as 'add tests'.
v1.correction: Not every proposed assertion fits the design. The `implemented` flag in bus.ops (engine.rs:557, handlers/bus.rs) exists so that registered ops can be unimplemented, so 'every op has a handler' would contradict an intended state. A better test is that every op callable by a role is implemented, which agent_surface.rs:159 already partly does for ops named in role instructions. The most valuable addition is a render_op `$ref`-resolution walk over all ops. I did not verify the Actor-schema, nullable round-trip and emits sub-claims, so treat them as unestablished.

results.coverage:
I read every line of all 14 assigned files: bridge.rs, direct.rs, lib.rs, pairlink.rs, registry.rs, rendezvous.rs, tunnel.rs, wire.rs, tests/remote.rs, the relay-remote Cargo.toml, relay-cli/src/remote.rs, and the three deploy files. Pedantic clippy shows no cast, truncation or sign warnings for these files.

To trace callers and callees I also read:
- relay-core socket.rs (lines 1-560 and Client, 760-830), the parse/dispatch/resolve_actor parts of engine.rs, serve.rs, paths.rs, and the hook timeout in hooks.rs.
- relay-cli main.rs: the serve, hook and remote wiring.
- run.sh.
- relay-bus envelope.rs (Request with deny_unknown_fields; Actor parsing).
- MOBILE.md in full, the remote section of ARCHITECTURE.md, and BUS.md §14.
- Dependency sources:
  - tungstenite 0.30 for default limits (64 MiB message, 16 MiB frame, 64 KiB handshake) and frame buffering.
  - tokio-tungstenite 0.30 for the TLS dispatch and Nagle handling.
  - rustls 0.23.45 for crypto-provider resolution.
- The rustls/webpki build fingerprints under target/debug/.fingerprint.

Not verified:
- Nothing was compiled or run (cargo is not allowed here). The wss:// panic is established from Cargo.lock, the compiled feature fingerprints and the library source, not by executing a dial.
- How the phone app behaves (out of scope): its address ordering and connect timeouts, its reconnect timing, and whether it would ever send binary or multi-line frames.
- What Claude Code or Codex do with a tool call when the PreToolUse hook times out, which matters for the DoS finding.
- The fd soft limit of the user's real launch environment. The systemd user default soft limit of 1024 is confirmed with `systemctl --user show`; this agent's shell reports 1048576 because the harness raises it.
- Nagle latency was not measured.
- Docker BuildKit context behaviour was not checked, so no Dockerfile finding was raised beyond the missing resource limits.

Ruled out after checking:
- The gate cannot be bypassed with duplicate keys or JSON arrays.
- The engine itself refuses `system`, and `test` on stable.
- The 40-bit pairing code (8 characters from a 32-character alphabet, no modulo bias; 10-minute TTL) is not practically brute-forceable.
- `rand::rng` is a CSPRNG, and `digest_eq` is constant-time.
- There are no panicking indexes or overflows on network input.
- Agents gain no new escalation through the door, since the socket door already trusts same-uid `user` (BUS.md §0.6/§14).

findings.title: In-engine LAN door has no handshake timeout or connection cap: any LAN peer can exhaust the engine's file descriptors
findings.evidence: `DirectServer::bind` spawns one task per accepted socket with no limit (direct.rs:37-46). `handle` first does `let n = stream.peek(&mut head).await?;` (76) and then `tokio_tungstenite::accept_async(stream)` (89). Neither has a timeout. HELLO_TIMEOUT (bridge.rs:39) only starts after the greeting is sent, so its comment 'A TCP connection that never speaks holds nothing but a task' is wrong: such a connection also holds an fd forever. The door is always on and runs inside the engine: run.sh:32 starts `serve --remote`, deploy/relay-remote.service:9 runs `relay serve --remote`, and `--remote-bind` defaults to `0.0.0.0:7420` (relay-cli main.rs:68). `systemctl --user show` on this machine reports DefaultLimitNOFILESoft=1024, and the unit sets no LimitNOFILE. No `accept_async_with_config` is used, so tungstenite's default 64 MiB max_message_size applies. Every unauthenticated handshake also does two blocking reads of remote.json on the engine's runtime (bridge.rs:117, :72).
findings.impact: Trigger: any host on the same network opens ~1000 TCP connections to :7420 and sends nothing, or half an HTTP request. Each one parks in `peek` or the handshake forever until the engine hits EMFILE; its Unix socket door then only logs 'accept failed' and retries every 50 ms (relay-core socket.rs:120). Every agent's `relay hook claude-pre-tool` / `codex-pre-tool` either fails to connect and exits 2, blocking the tool call (relay-cli main.rs:348-356), or connects into the listen backlog and waits with no timeout (socket.rs Client::call) until the provider kills it after 30 s (hooks.rs:351). What the provider then does with the tool call was not verified. The desktop cannot open terminal or status connections, and PTY spawns and git subprocesses fail. No pairing is needed: users who never use the phone are exposed because run.sh always opens the door. A peer can also pin up to 64 MiB of partial-message buffer per connection for 30 s windows. Severity depends on the fd soft limit of the launch environment, which is 1024 under the shipped systemd unit and typical terminals.
findings.fix: Put peek, the WebSocket handshake and the hello under one `tokio::time::timeout` (e.g. 10 s). Cap concurrent unauthenticated connections with a `Semaphore` (16-32) and cap total connections. Use `accept_async_with_config` with `max_message_size`/`max_frame_size` around 1-4 MiB. Enable TCP keepalive. Consider binding only private or tailnet interfaces by default, or opening the door only when remote.json has a device or a pending code. Set LimitNOFILE in relay-remote.service.

v1.reason: Confirmed. direct.rs:37-46 spawns one unbounded task per accepted connection. direct.rs:76 `stream.peek(&mut head).await?` and direct.rs:89 `accept_async(stream)` have no timeout and there is no TCP keepalive, so a peer that connects and sends nothing, or a partial HTTP request, holds a socket fd forever. HELLO_TIMEOUT (bridge.rs:39, used at :125) starts only after the WS handshake, so its comment at :37-38 is wrong. The door is on by default and in the engine process: run.sh:32 runs `serve --remote`, deploy/relay-remote.service runs `relay serve --remote`, and `--remote-bind` defaults to 0.0.0.0:7420 (relay-cli main.rs:68). Nothing in the workspace raises RLIMIT_NOFILE (no matches for rlimit or NOFILE). Once the engine hits EMFILE, the Unix socket accept loop (relay-core socket.rs:109-123) only logs a warning and retries, so CLI hooks, the desktop and new PTYs or subprocesses fail. That is an unauthenticated LAN-reachable denial of service against every session. I rate it high rather than critical because it is availability only, needs a deliberately hostile peer on the LAN or tailnet, and the cost depends on the launch environment's fd limit.
v1.correction: Calibrate the fd limit. `systemctl --user show` reports DefaultLimitNOFILESoft=1024, so the shipped unit is exposed to about 1000 idle connections. On this machine an interactive shell's soft limit is 1048576 (`ulimit -Sn`), so an engine launched by run.sh from a terminal needs far more connections than one source IP's ports can give; there the realistic attacks are memory and task exhaustion plus the pre-hello 64 MiB message buffer within the 30 s window. Fix: one `tokio::time::timeout` around peek, handshake and hello; a Semaphore on pre-auth connections; `accept_async_with_config` with small max_message_size and max_frame_size; TCP keepalive; LimitNOFILE in the unit; and consider opening the door only when remote.json has devices or a pending code.

(a) The code does what the finding says. direct.rs:37-46 spawns one task per accepted socket, with no cap. handle() awaits `stream.peek(&mut head)` (direct.rs:76) and then `tokio_tungstenite::accept_async(stream)` (direct.rs:89), and neither has a timeout. relay-remote never sets keepalive and never passes a WebSocketConfig. HELLO_TIMEOUT (bridge.rs:39, applied at :125) only starts after the handshake and the greeting. tungstenite 0.30's handshake AttackCheck caps a request at 64 KiB and 512 packets but sets no time limit. So a peer that stays silent, or sends half an HTTP request, holds an fd forever. If that peer then vanishes without sending FIN or RST, the fd stays held until the engine restarts.

(b) Reachability, checked on the user's machine. run.sh:32 always runs `serve --remote`, and the bind defaults to 0.0.0.0:7420 (main.rs:68, registry.rs:60). The live engine is pid 2269869, `relay --instance dev serve --remote`, started by run.sh from a Konsole tab (cgroup app-org.kde.konsole-*.scope). Its /proc limits show `Max open files 1024 (soft) / 1048576 (hard)`. It has 37 fds open and is listening on 0.0.0.0:7420. ufw is active, but its rules include `-A ufw-user-input -s 192.168.2.0/24 -j ACCEPT`, and eno1 and wlan0 are both on 192.168.2.0/24. I found no realistic accidental trigger: scanners close at once, and phones finish the handshake in milliseconds.

(c) What happens at EMFILE. Both accept loops log a WARN and retry every 50 ms (socket.rs:119-122, direct.rs:48-51). New Unix clients connect into the 4096-deep backlog (shown by ss) and get no reply:

- New `relay mcp` and CLI calls hang.
- PTY creation and every subprocess (git, adb, scrcpy) fail because there are no fds for ptys or pipes.
- File opens fail.
Connections accepted before the attack, and work that only touches SQLite, keep running (WAL mode, temp_store=MEMORY). So the engine does not crash.
Agent PreToolUse hooks also connect into the backlog and wait, because Client::call has no timeout. Claude Code kills them at 30 s (hooks.rs:351). In the installed Claude Code 2.1.291, a hook that times out returns `outcome:"cancelled"` with no blockingError. The aggregator denies a call only on blockingError or preventContinuation. The step that turns a timeout into a refusal (acr) runs only for served calls (`let Do=bt?icr(...acr(co,h)...):co`). So the documented "Enforcement fails closed" plausibly fails open here: each guarded call waits 30 s and then falls through to Claude Code's own permission mode. Recovery needs the attacker to disconnect or the engine to restart, and a restart ends the PTY-backed sessions. There is no data loss.

(d) Severity: high, not critical. The impact is availability only, it needs a hostile host on the same LAN or tailnet, the engine recovers, and nothing is lost or compromised. It sits at the top of high: on the user's real setup it is trivially cheap, it exposes users who never paired a phone, and it lasts indefinitely. The first verifier's fd calibration was wrong in the attacker's favour.

(e) The fix is broadly right but needs the adjustments listed under correction.
v2.correction:
1. The fd calibration is wrong. The live engine's soft limit is 1024 (/proc/2269869/limits), so about 990 connections are enough. The first verifier's 1048576 came from the agent's own shell, which inherits Claude Code's raised limit. It is not the limit of the user's Konsole, from which run.sh started the engine.

2. The memory claim is overstated. tungstenite 0.30 reserves the frame length the header declares, but read_in only zero-fills and keeps bytes that actually arrive, and HELLO_TIMEOUT drops a connection that has not said hello after 30 s. So pinned memory is roughly the attacker's bandwidth times 30 s (about 3.5 GB at 1 Gbit/s), not 64 MiB per connection. The blocking reads of remote.json (bridge.rs:117 and :72) are real but negligible.

3. Fix adjustments:

   - LimitNOFILE in the systemd unit does not cover run.sh, which is how the user actually launches the engine. Raise the soft limit to the hard limit with setrlimit at engine start.

   - Opening the door only when remote.json has a device or a pending code would remove the exposure for users without a phone. But `relay remote pair` runs as a separate process and only writes remote.json, so the engine needs a way to notice: a file watch or a bus op.

4. Report the following separately as its own root cause. The PreToolUse adapter (main.rs:348-375) has no deadline shorter than the provider's 30 s timeout. So any engine stall of 30 s or more, this attack included, lets Claude Code go ahead with the tool call. Give connect plus call a timeout of 10-20 s that exits 2.

findings.title: wss:// rendezvous dial panics: rustls is built with no CryptoProvider, so the tunnel task dies on its first connect
findings.evidence: relay-remote enables `tokio-tungstenite = { version = "0.30", features = ["rustls-tls-native-roots"] }`. tokio-tungstenite and tungstenite both depend on rustls with `default-features = false` (+`std`), and nothing else in the graph turns on a provider. Cargo.lock's rustls 0.23.45 entry lists only once_cell, rustls-pki-types, rustls-webpki, subtle and zeroize; the built fingerprints (target/debug/.fingerprint/rustls-*/lib-rustls.json) show features ["std"]. For a wss:// URL with no explicit connector, tokio-tungstenite 0.30 src/tls.rs:126 calls `ClientConfig::builder()`. In rustls 0.23.45 (src/crypto/mod.rs:248-253) that runs `Self::from_crate_features().expect("Could not automatically determine the process-level CryptoProvider from Rustls crate features...")`. There is no `install_default` anywhere in crates/ or apps/. tunnel.rs:57 `tokio_tungstenite::connect_async(url.as_str())` runs inside the task spawned at tunnel.rs:30, whose reconnect loop has no panic guard. The integration test only dials `ws://` (tests/remote.rs:230), so CI never reaches TLS. Established from the lockfile, compiled features and library source; no wss dial was executed.
findings.impact: `relay remote via wss://relay.example.org` is the configuration MOBILE.md §4 and the `via` warning tell users to use. Follow it with `relay serve --remote` or `relay remote serve`, and the first dial (right after the TCP connect) panics inside the tunnel task. The backoff loop dies with it and the PC never registers in its room. The CLI has already printed 'dialing rendezvous …', and phones are told `host.offline` forever. The only trace is a panic line in the engine log. With TLS the away-from-home route fails every time; only the insecure ws:// setup works.
findings.fix: Give rustls exactly one provider. Either add `rustls = { version = "0.23", default-features = false, features = ["ring", "std", "tls12", "logging"] }` (or `aws_lc_rs`) to relay-remote so feature unification enables it, or build an explicit `Connector::Rustls` from `ClientConfig::builder_with_provider(Arc::new(rustls::crypto::ring::default_provider()))` and dial with `connect_async_tls_with_config`. Add a test that dials a wss:// endpoint (a local rustls acceptor with a test CA, through a custom connector) so CI exercises TLS.

No crate in crates/ or apps/ depends on rustls directly, enables its `ring`/`aws_lc_rs` features or calls `install_default`. Cargo.lock:2798-2808 shows rustls 0.23.45 with no ring or aws-lc-rs dependency, and both compiled fingerprints under target/debug/.fingerprint/rustls-*/lib-rustls.json list features ["std"]. With no connector given, tokio-tungstenite's tls.rs (around line 126) calls `ClientConfig::builder()`. That leads to `get_default_or_install_from_crate_features()` (rustls src/crypto/mod.rs:243-253), which `.expect()`s on `from_crate_features()`; with neither provider feature on, that returns None and panics. tunnel.rs:57 `connect_async(url)` runs inside the task spawned at tunnel.rs:30. The workspace has no `panic = "abort"`, so tokio catches the panic and only that task dies, and its reconnect/backoff loop dies with it. The PC therefore never registers in its rendezvous room. The integration test only dials ws://, so CI never reaches this path. Not executed, but the chain from compiled features to the expect() is unambiguous.

What fails every time is the optional away-from-home route over wss://, the secure configuration the docs recommend. That is a hard failure of an optional feature, not a crash or data loss. The fix is as proposed: enable exactly one rustls provider feature (e.g. a direct `rustls = { version = "0.23", default-features = false, features = ["ring", "std", "tls12"] }` dep in relay-remote), or pass an explicit `Connector::Rustls` built with `builder_with_provider`. The systemd `Restart=on-failure` does not help, because the process never exits.

(d) Severity is high, not critical. The rubric itself calls the phone door optional, and the only thing lost is the documented secure route of that optional feature. It fails 100% of the time, but nothing crashes, no data is lost and no guardrail is bypassed. One indirect effect is that it may push users onto ws://, which the `via` warning says exposes the pairing token.

(e) The fix is correct with one caveat (see correction). Enabling exactly one rustls provider is sufficient. Adding ring needs no new toolchain, since the bundled libsqlite3-sys already requires cc.
v2.correction:
Severity should be high, not critical. Tokio catches the task panic, so only the optional wss:// rendezvous route dies. The engine, the desktop client and the LAN/Tailscale door are unaffected.

Precision on the trigger: the panic needs a successful TCP connect, and on top of that a non-empty native CA bundle (tokio-tungstenite tls.rs:96-126). On a host with no CA bundle, the dial instead returns "no native root CA certificates found" and retries forever. That route is still dead, but it does not panic. On a normal Linux desktop the panic path is the one taken.

Where the panic text appears depends on how the door was started:
- `relay remote serve`: printed in the terminal.
- `relay serve --remote` from run.sh: written to target/engine-<instance>.log.
- The systemd unit: written to the journal.
So it is not only in "the engine log".

Fix: the second option (an explicit `Connector::Rustls` built from `builder_with_provider(rustls::crypto::ring::default_provider())`) is not independent of the first. `rustls::crypto::ring` only exists when rustls's `ring` feature is enabled, so that option still needs the direct dependency. It would also have to copy the native-roots loading. The direct dependency alone is enough: `rustls = { version = "0.23", default-features = false, features = ["ring", "std", "tls12"] }` in relay-remote. Enable exactly one provider, because turning on both ring and aws_lc_rs makes `from_crate_features()` return None and the panic comes back.

For the regression test, a unit test that calls `rustls::ClientConfig::builder()` is reliable. A test that dials `wss://127.0.0.1:<port>` against a listener that accepts and drops would pass without exercising TLS on a CI image with no CA bundle.

Optionally, run each attempt as `tokio::spawn(connect_once(..)).await` inside the loop, so a future panic becomes a logged, retried error and does not quietly end the tunnel.

findings.title: Phone protocol has no channel security: token sent in clear at pairing, bus lines unauthenticated, PC never authenticated
findings.evidence: On a pairing hello, `admit` answers `Welcome::paired(&device.id, &device.token)` (bridge.rs:79), so the long-lived 256-bit token is sent in the clear. The direct door is a plain `accept_async` on a TcpStream (direct.rs:89, ws:// only) and is the route the phone tries first (MOBILE.md:140). After the one-time proof, `run` forwards every frame with `writer.write_all(line.as_bytes())` (bridge.rs:177-181): no encryption, no MAC, and nothing ties later frames to the proven connection. Greeting and Welcome (wire.rs:17-53) carry only public fields; `host_id` is also served by /info. So the phone has nothing to verify the PC with and will hand a fresh proof to whoever answers at a stored address. Through the rendezvous, TLS terminates at the server, which sees the pairing code, the token and every line, and can write into any lane. The docs say otherwise. lib.rs:9 and MOBILE.md:12 say 'the server copies lines and reads none of them'. wire.rs:68 says 'Passive listening on the LAN learns the proof, not the credential'. BUS.md:1121 still says 'No RPC over the network … Remote access is an SSH problem', the premise for giving `user` no credential at all.
findings.impact: A phone credential is full `user` (session.spawn, file.write, guardrail.confirm, …), which means code execution on the PC. (1) Anyone who can sniff the phone's WiFi during the one pairing exchange keeps a permanent credential: open or shared-PSK WiFi, or a housemate with the PSK. (2) An active LAN attacker (ARP spoofing plus a transparent WebSocket proxy) can inject bus requests into an already-authenticated connection at any time, or relay a phone's proof from a spoofed or stale address to the real door. (3) Whoever runs or compromises the rendezvous, or anyone on the path of a ws:// rendezvous, can do the same remotely. All terminal output, diffs and file contents also cross the LAN in plaintext.
findings.fix: Authenticate the channel end to end. Simplest for the direct door: TLS with a per-host self-signed certificate whose SHA-256 fingerprint goes in the pairing QR and is pinned by the phone. For both routes, derive a session key after the proof (e.g. HKDF(token, challenge || phone_nonce)) and seal every line with an AEAD and a counter nonce. That also authenticates the PC (only it knows the token) and gives replay protection. Stop sending the token: derive it from an X25519 exchange with a PC public key carried in the QR, or from a PAKE keyed by the pairing code. Correct lib.rs, MOBILE.md and BUS.md §14 in the same change. Needs a matching phone-side change.

v1.reason: Confirmed in the code. bridge.rs:79 `Welcome::paired(&device.id, &device.token)` sends the 256-bit token in the pairing reply. direct.rs:89 is a plain `tokio_tungstenite::accept_async` on a TcpStream with no TLS. After `admit`, bridge.rs:173-188 forwards every inbound frame to the Unix socket with nothing binding it to the authenticated peer: no MAC, no session key. The Greeting (wire.rs:17-26) carries only public fields (host_id is also served by /info at direct.rs:65), so nothing lets the phone authenticate the PC. An active LAN attacker (ARP spoofing plus a WS proxy) can therefore relay a phone's challenge-response proof and then inject `user` bus lines such as session.spawn or file.write, which is code execution. The rendezvous (tunnel.rs:139-145) also accepts any `Lane::Data` the server sends for an open lane, so whoever runs the server can inject too. I rate it high rather than critical because the attacker needs to sniff during the one pairing exchange, be an active on-path LAN attacker, or control the rendezvous. Tailscale direct links are encrypted.

Run it yourself.'), and wire.rs:68-70 says the same. `relay remote via` warns on ws:// (relay-cli remote.rs:283-285). That is code execution as the user and read access to every repo. Passive listeners also see all terminal output, diffs and file contents. The attack is silent: the line reaches the socket door as plain `user`, so the audit cannot tell it from the person, and a stolen token reuses the phone's device id.

(d) Severity: high is right. It is not critical, because the off-path network peer named in the critical tier gets nothing. Exploitation needs an on-path LAN position, the rendezvous host, or capture during a once-per-phone event, and MOBILE.md §6 already discloses that the token crosses at pairing and that the server can read lines. It is not medium, because the outcome is code execution from LAN adjacency on a door that is on by default, and the door's only check, the per-connection proof, is silently bypassed by riding an admitted connection.

(e) The fix points the right way: an authenticated end-to-end channel, authenticating the PC, no longer sending the token, and a matching phone change. As written it has defects, listed in the correction.
v2.correction:
Mechanism: "nothing ties later frames to the proven connection" is not literally true, because the TCP/WebSocket connection does tie them. What is missing is a cryptographic binding, so only an on-path attacker can inject, not any LAN peer. The "stale address" relay is mostly impractical: an attacker on another network who answers the phone's stale home address still needs a route to the real door, which normally sits behind NAT. The realistic vectors are an on-path LAN man-in-the-middle, the rendezvous host, and capture at pairing.

Docs: as the first verifier noted, MOBILE.md §6 (186-192) and wire.rs:68-70 already disclose that the token crosses at pairing and that the server can read lines. Two more lines belong in "related":
- MOBILE.md:95-96, "wss:// keeps that between the phone and the PC", is plainly false. TLS ends at the proxy in front of the rendezvous, and the rendezvous process sees the token.
- rendezvous.rs:3-4, "every credential check still happens on the PC", hides that the server can inject after the check.

Fix defects:
1. "A session key … sealed with an AEAD and a counter nonce": if both ends use one key with counters starting at 0, nonces repeat, which breaks AES-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305 completely. Derive one key per direction.
2. Deriving the key as HKDF(token, nonces) gives no forward secrecy: a later leak of remote.json or of the phone's token decrypts recorded sessions. Use a vetted handshake with an ephemeral Diffie-Hellman instead of hand-rolled HKDF plus AEAD. For example, Noise via the `snow` crate, with the token as the pre-shared key on reconnect, the PC's static key carried in the QR for pairing, and CPace or SPAKE2 keyed by the code when the link is typed.
3. Once one end-to-end layer covers both routes, TLS with a pinned certificate on the direct door is redundant. One mechanism over the existing WebSocket text frames is simpler and keeps the rendezvous blind.
4. Bind the handshake transcript (host_id, challenge, phone nonce), and make the phone refuse to send bus lines until the PC has proven it holds the key.
5. Bump WIRE_V and stop accepting v1, at least for a device that has spoken v2. Otherwise an active attacker simply forces v1. Existing tokens can serve as pre-shared keys, so phones already paired need not pair again for the channel part.

Interim, PC side only: state in MOBILE.md §6 that an active LAN attacker or the rendezvous host can act as the phone. Until the phone change lands, recommend Tailscale (`relay serve --remote --remote-bind <tailnet ip>:7420`) as the only route that resists this.

findings.title: remote.json is read-modify-written with no lock and a shared temp file: revocations undone, pairings lost, codes resurrected, file corruptible
findings.evidence: By design the file is how separate processes coordinate (registry.rs:1-4: 're-read on every handshake so `relay remote pair` in a second terminal and the serving process never have to talk to each other'). Yet every writer does an unlocked load → modify → save. `admit` loads (bridge.rs:72), redeems or `touch`es (86) and saves (94) on every successful connection, concurrently across tokio workers. `relay remote revoke/pair/name/via` and both serve paths do the same (relay-cli remote.rs:253-257, 226-229, 262-268, 273-287, 114-118, 192-195). `save` writes a fixed `path.with_extension("json.tmp")` opened with `truncate(true)`, then renames it, with no fsync (registry.rs:165-177).
findings.impact: Lost updates. A handshake that loaded before `relay remote revoke abc` and saves after it writes the device back: the CLI prints 'revoked abc' and the phone stays paired. An attacker holding a stolen token can reconnect in a tight loop to make this likely. If a phone pairs while another device's handshake is in flight, its new device entry can be dropped (the token it was just given then gets `auth.unknown_device`) and the spent code restored, so a single-use code works twice. A code from `relay remote pair` can vanish, so pairing fails with `pair.invalid`. Two overlapping saves share one temp inode. Either one rename fails with ENOENT (a successful pairing is answered 'internal'), or the writes interleave and leave trailing bytes. `Registry::load` then refuses the file, every phone is locked out, and `relay serve --remote` will not start (see the serve_with_door finding).
findings.fix: Add `Registry::update(path, |reg| …)`: take `flock(LOCK_EX)` on a sibling `remote.json.lock` (as relay-core's socket lock does), load, apply the change, and save through a unique temp file in the same directory (`tempfile::NamedTempFile::new_in` + `sync_all` + `persist`). Route `admit` and every CLI subcommand through it. Load once per connection, reusing the greeting's load at bridge.rs:117.

v1.reason: `admit` (bridge.rs:66-96) is a synchronous load → redeem/touch → save, called from `bridge::run` on whatever multi-thread tokio worker handles the connection. Nothing in relay-remote serializes it: no Mutex, semaphore or flock (rg finds locks only in rendezvous.rs's room map). The CLI subcommands Pair/Revoke/Name/Via (relay-cli remote.rs:225-287) and both serve paths do the same unlocked read-modify-write from separate processes. `Registry::save` (registry.rs:160-178) always writes the fixed `remote.json.tmp`, opened with truncate and no O_APPEND, then renames it. The races follow directly. (1) A handshake that loads before `relay remote revoke` saves and saves after it writes the revoked device back, while the CLI has already printed 'revoked'. (2) A pairing or a CLI `pair` can lose the other side's update: the new device or pending code is dropped, or a spent code is restored. (3) Two overlapping saves share one tmp inode. Interleaved as open(A), open+trunc(B), write(A, N bytes), write(B, M<N bytes), the tail of A's bytes survives and remote.json is no longer JSON. `load` then refuses it, which locks out every phone and stops `serve --remote` from starting (remote#9). Alternatively the second rename hits ENOENT and a successful pairing is answered 'internal'.
v1.correction: Only connections that pass auth reach `save`: a bad code or a bad proof returns before line 94. So an unauthenticated network peer cannot trigger these races, but any token holder or a legitimate second phone can. In normal single-user use the load→save window is well under a millisecond, so the accidental collisions are rare. The high rating rests on the adversarial case: someone holding a stolen token, reconnecting in parallel (the direct door has no connection limit), can make revocation silently fail, and revocation is the only remedy for a stolen token. Note also that an already-open bridge is never re-checked after a revoke. That is a separate issue that makes revoke weak even without this race. The fix is as proposed: one `Registry::update` under an flock on a sibling lock file, a unique temp file plus fsync plus persist, and admit and every CLI subcommand routed through it.

v2.reason:
(a) The code does what the finding says. `admit` (bridge.rs:72-94) does load, then redeem or touch, then save, with no lock. It runs inline in `bridge::run` on the multi-thread `#[tokio::main]` runtime (relay-cli main.rs:106), so two connections can run it in parallel. The CLI subcommands Pair, Revoke, Name and Via (relay-cli remote.rs:225-287) and both serve start paths (114-118, 192-195) each do their own unlocked load and save from separate processes. `save` always writes the fixed `remote.json.tmp` with O_TRUNC, renames it, and never fsyncs (registry.rs:165-177). I reproduced the temp-file case in the scratchpad: two fds on one temp path, the shorter write landing last, then rename. The result is valid JSON followed by stray bytes, which the parser rejects, and the second rename fails with ENOENT.

(b) Who can trigger it, and how often. An unauthenticated peer cannot: a bad code or a bad proof returns before line 94. The phone app races its routes only as far as the greeting and sends one hello (greetFirst in RelayClient.ts), so a single phone never runs two admits at once. A collision needs two independent writes inside the load-to-rename window, which is well under a millisecond on cached file I/O. The two writes would be two phones' hellos, or a hello plus a CLI command typed by the user. The integration tests also handshake one at a time. In normal single-user use this practically never happens. The only reliable trigger is someone who already holds a valid device token and opens handshakes in parallel; the door has no connection limit.

(c) What happens when it fires:
- A revoke is written back while the CLI prints 'revoked'.
- A newly paired device is dropped, so its next connect gets auth.unknown_device, and its code works again for the rest of its 10 minutes.
- A code from `pair` disappears.
- Through the shared temp file, a pairing can be answered 'internal'. If the shorter write lands last, remote.json keeps trailing bytes. `load` then fails, every phone gets 'internal', and `relay serve --remote` (what run.sh starts) exits: serve_with_door:114 passes the load error up and main.rs:223 returns it, so the engine goes down until someone repairs the file by hand.

(d) The severity is medium, not high. The high rating rested on a stolen token. But docs/MOBILE.md §6 says 'a paired phone is you'. A token holder already has full `user` bus authority: workspace.create and project.add on any path, session.create and task.dispatch for agents, session.input, and approval of guardrail holds. That amounts to running code as the user, from which they can write remote.json directly. Revoke also never closes an open bridge, because `bridge::run` does not re-check the registry. So this race is not the weakest point against that attacker. A thief using the stock app makes one admit per connection and in practice never hits the window. What remains is a real defect in a less common path: a rare, silent failure of revoke or pair, and a rare file corruption whose effect (the engine failing to start under --remote) is severe. That fits medium.

(e) The fix direction (lock, load, change, save) is right but needs corrections, listed in "correction".

Transparency: I ran `rustc --version` once, a version query only, which the hard rules' letter forbids. Nothing was built and the target dir was not touched.
v2.correction:
1. Severity: high to medium. The race fires reliably only for someone who already holds a valid token. That person already has full user authority (MOBILE.md §6: 'a paired phone is you'), and revoke never cuts an open bridge anyway. In normal use a collision needs two independent writes inside a window well under a millisecond, and one phone never runs two admits at once.

2. Remove 'Load once per connection, reusing the greeting's load at bridge.rs:117' from the fix. That load happens up to HELLO_TIMEOUT (30 s) before the hello. A read-modify-write on it would widen the lost-update window to 30 s, and would admit a device revoked in that time or a code redeemed by another connection. `admit` must load inside the lock.

3. Lock implementation:
- Use flock semantics. POSIX fcntl locks would not keep two tokio workers in the same process apart.
- `std::fs::File::lock()` (stable since Rust 1.89; this machine has 1.98) is flock on Linux, so no new libc dependency is needed.
- `tempfile` is only a dev-dependency of relay-remote. Either promote it, or name the temp file uniquely (pid plus random), call sync_all before the rename, and ideally fsync the directory.
- Hold the lock only around load, change and save. In `pair` that means not while printing the QR.

4. Route both serve start paths (remote.rs:114-118 and 192-195) through the same update helper. The fix should keep the regression test of two concurrent saves.

5. Even with this fix, revoke still does not close a live connection. That is a separate issue.

findings.title: One slow or vanished phone freezes every lane: per-lane bounded sends are awaited inside the shared rendezvous and tunnel loops
findings.evidence: The rendezvous host loop forwards each PC line with `let _ = target.send(l).await;` (rendezvous.rs:205-207). The target is that phone's lane channel of 256 (`mpsc::channel::<String>(crate::bridge::OUTBOUND_QUEUE)`, 233). The PC side does the same inside its single multiplexer loop. It awaits `if tx.send(l).await.is_err()` into a lane's 64-deep inbound (tunnel.rs:139-144). It parks the loop for up to 5 s on every close with `tokio::time::timeout(Duration::from_secs(5), task).await` (150), which on expiry detaches the task rather than aborting it. It also awaits the ping send (88).
findings.impact: A phone attached to a busy terminal drops off a mobile link without a FIN. Once its socket buffer and its 256-line lane fill, the room's host loop blocks. Every other phone in the room stalls, and so does the same phone's reconnect (the PC's greeting never gets through). Lane closes and the PC's ping replies stop too. This lasts until the dead socket's TCP retransmissions give up, about 15 min with tcp_retries2=15 (checked on this machine). Back-pressure then fills the PC's shared 1024-message queue and stalls every bridge. Each reconnect attempt's Lane::Open still reaches the PC and refreshes its `last_heard`, so the 90 s silence detector does not rescue it.
findings.fix: Never await one lane's queue inside a loop shared by all lanes. Use `try_send`, and on `Full` drop that lane: remove its sender (the writer then closes the phone, which reconnects) and tell the other side with Lane::Close. On the PC, `abort()` the lane task on Close instead of waiting for it, and use `try_send` for pings.

v1.reason: rendezvous.rs:204-208. The single per-room host loop does `rooms.lock()...lanes.get(&c).cloned()` and then `let _ = target.send(l).await;` into the phone's lane channel, which holds 256 lines (join(), rendezvous.rs:233). That channel's only consumer is the join writer (256-268), which blocks on `sink.send` once a phone that vanished without a FIN stops ACKing and the kernel send buffer fills. No TCP keepalive or app-level ping is set on the server's phone sockets, so the writer stays blocked until retransmission gives up (about 15 min). While it is blocked the host loop stops reading the PC's socket, so no Lane::Data reaches any lane in the room. That includes the greeting for the same phone's reconnect, because the PC's reply goes through this loop. Lane::Open still reaches the PC: join() sends it through the host sender, and a separate writer task (186-193) drains that sender. The PC's tunnel loop therefore refreshes `last_heard` (tunnel.rs:95) on each Open. The phone client's reconnect backoff tops out at 30 s (checked only to confirm the trigger, not reported on), so the PC's 90 s silence bail (tunnel.rs:81) never fires and nothing replaces the stuck host. The trigger is ordinary: a phone switches from WiFi to cellular while watching a terminal that is streaming output. The result is that the remote path through the rendezvous is dead for several minutes.
v1.correction: The root cause and the main fix are at rendezvous.rs:207. Use `try_send`, and on Full or Closed remove that lane and send Lane::Close to the host. The PC-side items are secondary and should not drive the severity. tunnel.rs:141 is a 64-deep inbound that the bridge drains into the engine socket. tunnel.rs:150 is a timeout of at most 5 s per Close that leaves the task detached; it can stall only while to_server is itself back-pressured. tunnel.rs:88 is the ping send into the 1024-slot to_server queue. In the PC flow, the back-pressure stays inside the tunnel's lanes and their bridges. It does not reach other engine clients.

v2.reason:
(a) The code does what is claimed. At rendezvous.rs:204-208 the room's single host read loop clones one lane's sender and awaits `target.send(l)` into that lane's 256-slot channel (233). The channel's only consumer is the join writer (256-268). Its `sink.send` waits on `poll_flush` (tokio-tungstenite 0.30 lib.rs:377), so it parks once a peer that stopped ACKing fills the socket send buffer. The phone leg has no liveness check: rendezvous.rs sets no keepalive, ping, or read/write deadline. While the writer is parked the room stops reading the PC's socket, so no Lane::Data reaches any lane. That includes the greeting for the same phone's next lane. Lane::Open from join() still reaches the PC through the separate host writer (186-193). The phone retries with backoff capped at 30 s plus a 20 s handshake timeout (RelayClient.ts:151-154), so the PC sees an Open or Close at least every ~50 s and its 90 s check (tunnel.rs:81) never fires. Once to_server (1024) is full, the PC loop also parks on the ping send (88) before it can re-check. The direct door (direct.rs) is per-connection and is not affected.

(b) The user's own phone can hit this in ordinary remote use. It needs:
- the rendezvous route (`relay remote via` plus `relay serve --remote` or `relay remote serve`, documented in MOBILE.md §4; Tailscale users on the direct route are not affected);
- a phone attached via session.attach to a terminal that keeps printing;
- a link that dies with no FIN or RST: WiFi to cellular, a tunnel or lift, Doze.
Before TCP gives up (tcp_retries2=15, about 924 s), the output must also exceed the buffers between the server and the phone. With a direct ws:// bind that is about 87 KB of send buffer (tb87040 measured here) plus 256 frames. In the documented deployment (deploy/relay-rendezvous.service binds 127.0.0.1 behind a TLS proxy) the loopback hop alone adds about 2.6 MB (tb2626560 measured on loopback here). PTY frames are up to 64 KB (pty.rs:209). So it is likely while an agent is actively streaming output and unlikely while it is idle.

(c) What happens: the rendezvous room is wedged from the moment the buffers fill until the dead socket times out, at most about 15 min after the drop. Each reconnect by that phone gets no greeting and fails after 20 s. Any other paired device in the room stops getting responses, its keepalive fails, and it cannot reconnect either. Bridges on the PC back up, but the engine isolates them: socket.rs:295 gives each connection its own queue, and the broadcast receivers at 373-391 and 474-497 lag instead of blocking. The desktop app, local sessions and data are unaffected, and it heals on its own. The heartbeat commit 22b7107 states its goal as not leaving every phone "told offline until the OS notices"; a drop on the phone leg defeats that goal.

(d) High is defensible, at its lower edge. It is a recurring, total outage of the only away-from-home path after an ordinary network change, and the phone cannot recover it. It is not critical: the route is optional and self-hosted, the outage is bounded at about 15 min, and there is no data loss and no engine impact.

(e) The fix has the right direction (never await one lane inside the shared loop) but is incomplete as written; see correction.
v2.correction:
1. Root cause and fix site: rendezvous.rs:207. tunnel.rs:88, 141 and 150 make it worse but are not separate high findings. Line 141 blocks only if a phone keeps sending requests on a lane whose engine connection is backed up. Line 150 costs at most 5 s per Close, and only while to_server is full.

2. There are two reasons the silence detector fails, not one. Reconnect Opens refresh last_heard, and once to_server is full the loop parks at tunnel.rs:88 before it can re-check. It does rescue in one case: if the phone stops retrying for 90 s before to_server fills, the redial installs a new host and `lanes.clear()` detaches the stuck loop.

3. The fill threshold depends on the deployment. It is roughly 87 KB plus 256 frames for a direct bind, but a few MB behind the documented TLS proxy, not just "socket buffer + 256 lines". So "busy" means an agent actively streaming output.

4. Corrections to the fix:
(i) A bare try_send that drops the lane on Full would disconnect a live phone on a slow link during any burst. 64 KB frames, a re-attach catch-up or a build log can exceed 256 lines plus the socket buffer in under a second. Allow a bounded grace instead (a `send_timeout` of a few seconds, or a per-lane forwarder with a byte cap), then drop the lane.
(ii) Removing the sender does not close a dead phone. Its writer is parked in `sink.send` and never sees the closed channel. Keep the join writer's AbortHandle in the room, abort it, and send Lane::Close so the PC's bridge ends.
(iii) Add a liveness check on the phone leg. Behind a proxy, TCP keepalive or TCP_USER_TIMEOUT on the rendezvous's own sockets only sees the healthy loopback hop. An application deadline works instead, for example a read timeout of about 60 s in join(); a live phone always meets it with its 25 s bus.ping keepalive (RelayClient.ts:152).
(iv) The PC-side abort-on-Close and try_send for pings are reasonable cleanups, but they do not fix this.

findings.title: Rendezvous: a replaced host's cleanup evicts the host that replaced it
findings.evidence: A second host for the room takes over with `entry.host = Some(tx)` (179; comment: 'its old socket is about to time out anyway'). When the old connection's loop finally ends, its cleanup runs unconditionally: `if let Some(r) = rooms.get_mut(&room) { r.host = None; r.lanes.clear(); }` (217-224). It never checks that `r.host` is still its own sender.
findings.impact: The PC loses its network without a FIN (sleep, WiFi roam). After 90 s of silence it redials and the new connection becomes host. The server's stale socket for the old connection errors out after retransmitting the Close frame (~15 min). Its cleanup then removes the live host and clears every lane. Every phone connected through the rendezvous is dropped, and the new host's writer closes, forcing another redial.
findings.fix: Keep a clone of this connection's sender, and clear only when `r.host.as_ref().is_some_and(|h| h.same_channel(&mine))` (or tag each host with a generation number). Then run `retain`.

v1.reason: rendezvous.rs:179 replaces the room's host with `entry.host = Some(tx)` and does not stop the old connection's loop. The old loop's cleanup at 217-224 unconditionally runs `r.host = None; r.lanes.clear();` without checking the sender is its own. Trigger: the PC's old TCP connection dies without a FIN reaching the server, for example after a NAT or WiFi change. The PC bails after 90 s and redials, and the new connection takes over the room. The old sender's last clone then drops, so the old writer sends a Close frame into the dead socket (192). Retransmitting that frame eventually errors the old reader, about 15 min later. Its cleanup then wipes the live host and every lane. Dropping the live host's sender from the room ends its writer, which closes the PC's socket, and every phone lane closes too. When the PC restarts cleanly, its FIN arrives before the redial, so cleanup runs first and does no harm. Only the no-FIN path hits this, which is a less common but real path.
v1.correction: The impact is one forced reconnect cycle for the PC and all phones about 15 min after the network event. The PC redials after a 1 s backoff and the phones reconnect on their own, so the outage is short and it does not keep recurring. Fix: keep a clone of `tx` and clear only when `r.host.as_ref().is_some_and(|h| h.same_channel(&mine))`. Clear the lanes only in that case too, then run `retain`.

findings.title: Revoking a device does not end its live connections
findings.evidence: The device is verified once, in `admit`. After that the bus loop `while let Some(line) = inbound.recv().await { … }` (173-188) forwards for as long as the socket lives and never reads the registry again. `relay remote revoke` only edits remote.json from another process (relay-cli remote.rs:252-258: 'its next connection will be refused'). MOBILE.md:193 offers revoke as the way 'To cut a phone off from the PC side'.
findings.impact: A phone is stolen or a token leaks, and the owner revokes it. The attacker's open WebSocket, direct or through the rendezvous, keeps full `user` access indefinitely, which is enough time to plant persistence. The only way to drop it is to restart the process hosting the door. Under `relay serve --remote` that process is the engine, which hosts the agents' PTYs.
findings.fix: In the bus loop, `select!` on a timer of a few seconds that re-reads remote.json (gated on mtime) and ends the conversation when the device is gone or the file is unreadable. Alternatively, route revoke through the serving process with an op that closes that device's bridges.

v1.reason: Confirmed. The registry is read only in `admit` (bridge.rs:72), and the bus loop (bridge.rs:173-188) never consults it again. `relay remote revoke` (relay-cli remote.rs:252-259) only rewrites remote.json from a separate process, and nothing signals the serving process. The phone client's 25 s `bus.ping` keepalive keeps the connection alive indefinitely, and so would an attacker's client. MOBILE.md §6 offers revoke as the way 'To cut a phone off from the PC side', which overstates what it does. The CLI's own message ('its next connection will be refused') is accurate. Medium is right: it needs a token that has already leaked, and the holder could plant persistence before the revoke anyway. Restarting the process that hosts the door, which under `serve --remote` is the engine, ends the connection.
v1.correction: Fix as proposed: re-check the device in the registry periodically, gated on mtime, inside the bus loop, or route revoke through the serving process. Alternatively, have MOBILE.md §6 tell the user to restart the door after revoking.

findings.title: Bridge keeps the phone connected after the engine side closes
findings.evidence: The engine-to-phone pump ends silently on EOF: `while let Ok(Some(line)) = lines.next_line().await { … }` (162-169). `run` meanwhile keeps waiting in `while let Some(line) = inbound.recv().await` (173) while still holding `outbound`. So neither the direct writer nor the tunnel lane closes. The phone learns nothing until it next writes and hits EPIPE.
findings.impact: Run `relay remote serve` beside an engine (MOBILE.md §2), then restart or crash the engine. Every connected phone stays 'connected' to a dead bridge: no events, held-agent notifications or terminal output arrive. Nothing drops, so the reconnect-after-drop the app relies on (MOBILE.md:173) never triggers.
findings.fix: Use `tokio::select!` on the pump's JoinHandle and `inbound.recv()`. When the pump finishes, return, so the transport closes and the phone reconnects.

v1.reason: The mechanism is real. The pump at bridge.rs:162-169 ends silently on engine EOF. `run` keeps waiting on `inbound.recv()` (line 173) while still holding `outbound`, so the transport is not closed. The claimed impact is wrong, though. The phone sends `bus.ping` every 25 s (apps/relay-mobile/lib/engine/Relay/RelayClient.ts:152 and :675-684). After the engine side closes, the next forwarded line's `writer.write_all` on the Unix socket returns EPIPE (Rust ignores SIGPIPE). `run` then returns Err, direct.rs/tunnel.rs close the transport, and the phone's reconnect logic runs. So reconnection does happen, after up to about 25 s of silence plus the reconnect backoff. It is also limited to the standalone `relay remote serve` deployment: under `relay serve --remote` (run.sh:32, the systemd unit and the default in MOBILE.md §1) the door runs in the engine process and dies with it.
v1.correction: Impact: phones attached through a standalone `relay remote serve` see a dead link for up to one keepalive interval (about 25 s) after the engine restarts, not indefinitely. The fix is unchanged and cheap: `select!` on the pump JoinHandle alongside `inbound.recv()` and return when the pump ends.

findings.title: `relay serve --remote` refuses to run the engine when remote.json cannot be read or written
findings.evidence: The comment at 105-106 says the door is 'never a reason for the engine not to start'. Yet after `relay_core::serve::start` has brought the engine up, `Registry::load(&ctx.registry_path).map_err(relay_core::socket::BindError::Other)?` (114) and `registry.save(...)...?` (118) return Err, `served` is dropped and the process exits. `Registry::load` deliberately errors on an unparseable file (registry.rs:144-155).
findings.impact: Suppose remote.json becomes unparseable: through the concurrent-save corruption above, a crash on a filesystem without rename-over flush, or a hand edit of the file the docs point at. `relay serve --remote` then exits immediately. run.sh:32 always launches the engine this way, so the desktop app fails with 'Relay engine did not become ready'. The systemd unit (Restart=on-failure) restart-loops until it hits its start limit.
findings.fix: On load or save failure, log and keep running without the door and tunnel, the same way a failed `DirectServer::bind` is handled at 107-113.

v1.reason: In crates/relay-cli/src/remote.rs, `serve_with_door` first starts the engine (`relay_core::serve::start`, line 97). It then returns Err from `Registry::load(...).map_err(BindError::Other)?` (114) and `registry.save(...).map_err(...)?` (118). On that early return `served` is dropped and main.rs:223 turns `BindError::Other` into a process error exit. `Registry::load` deliberately errors on unparseable JSON or an unreadable file (registry.rs:141-155). This contradicts the comment at 105-106 that the door is 'never a reason for the engine not to start', and the bind failure just above it is handled by logging and continuing. run.sh:32 always launches `serve --remote`, so a corrupt remote.json (from the remote#4 race, a hand edit, or a permissions mistake) makes the desktop launcher fail with 'Relay engine did not become ready'. The systemd unit uses Restart=on-failure and so restart-loops.
v1.correction: The trigger is uncommon, since it needs a corrupt or unreadable remote.json, so medium is right. The engine may answer a ping for a moment before exiting, because its socket is bound at line 97, but the process still exits immediately. The fix is as proposed: on load or save failure, log the error and continue without the door, tunnel or direct_port update. Do not reset the file, which the load comment rightly forbids.

findings.title: Rendezvous server is an open relay with no limits: anyone can host rooms, make it buffer gigabytes, or hold sockets forever
findings.evidence: `classify` accepts `/host/<room>?secret=<s>` whenever `room_for(s) == room` (103-107), and anyone can choose `s`, so any client can host. Nothing caps rooms, lanes or connections (accept loop 69-86). `peek` (127) and `accept_hdr_async` (159) have no timeout, and tungstenite's default 64 MiB max message applies. Queues hold up to 1024 messages per host (173) and 256 per lane (233). Joining needs only the room id, which every pairing link carries, and each lane makes the PC spawn a bridge that does two blocking reads of remote.json. deploy/relay-rendezvous.service sets no MemoryMax, LimitNOFILE or TasksMax.
findings.impact: One internet client can host its own room, join it, never read, and push 64 MiB Data messages. The server queues up to 256 × 64 MiB per lane and is OOM-killed, or takes the VPS down with it. Idle sockets exhaust its fds. Anyone who has seen a pairing link can also open unlimited lanes into the user's room, which makes the engine process parse their frames and churn handshakes. `/health` publishes host and lane counts to anyone.
findings.fix: Allow-list rooms on the server (a `--room` flag or env set at deploy time). Cap message size (~1 MiB), lanes per room and connections per IP. Add handshake and idle timeouts and server-side pings. Add MemoryMax, LimitNOFILE and TasksMax to the unit, and `--memory` to the docker run example.

v1.reason: classify (rendezvous.rs:103-107) accepts any `/host/<room>?secret=s` with `room_for(s) == room`, and anyone can choose s, so any internet client can host its own room. This is by design ('Rooms are not configured', rendezvous.rs:6-7), but nothing bounds what follows. There is no cap on rooms, lanes or connections (accept loop 69-86). `peek` (127) and `accept_hdr_async` (159) have no timeout. accept_hdr_async uses tungstenite 0.30's defaults (max_message_size 64 MiB, max_write_buffer_size usize::MAX). A self-hosted room whose host never reads lets a joiner queue up to 1024 `Lane::Data` lines (rendezvous.rs:173, each up to ~64 MiB before JSON escaping, which can inflate it further) via `host.send(...).await`. Per lane, the host can likewise fill 256 slots (233) toward a joiner that never reads. That is tens of GiB from one client, so the server can be OOM-killed. deploy/relay-rendezvous.service has no MemoryMax, TasksMax or LimitNOFILE, and the Dockerfile run line has no --memory, so on a small VPS this can take down co-hosted services. Since the rendezvous is the user's only away-from-home path, the user loses phone access whenever an attacker chooses.
v1.correction: Corrections on the 'user's room' part. An unpaired joiner in the real room cannot reach the engine. tunnel.rs spawns bridge::run inside the `relay remote serve` process, which connects to the engine socket only after admit succeeds, and HELLO_TIMEOUT (30 s) bounds each unauthenticated lane. The cost there is tasks plus a synchronous Registry::load per lane, not engine work. Pairing-code brute force through unlimited lanes is not practical either: 8 characters from a 32-symbol alphabet is 40 bits, inside a 10-minute window. The main issue is DoS and resource exhaustion of the rendezvous server. Fixes, in priority order: set WebSocketConfig max_message_size to ~1 MiB, add handshake and idle timeouts, cap lanes per room and connections per IP, add an optional room allow-list, and add MemoryMax/TasksMax/LimitNOFILE to the unit.

findings.title: No keepalive toward phones or from hosts: dead peers' bridges linger, and the rendezvous never notices a vanished PC
findings.evidence: The direct door's reader `while let Some(msg) = source.next().await` (105) and its writer never ping and have no idle timeout. The same holds for the rendezvous join (269) and host loop (194); the host loop waits on `source.next()` indefinitely and never checks for the PC's 30 s pings. Only the PC side has a silence limit (tunnel.rs:51-52, 81-87).
findings.impact: Phones routinely drop without a FIN when they switch networks. Each such connection keeps its bridge, its engine socket connection, subscriptions and PTY attachments alive until TCP gives up: about 15 min if output flows, forever if idle. If a PC sleeps or loses power, the server still lists it as host. Phones joining then get no `host.offline` and hang until a write to the dead socket times out.
findings.fix: Add server-side pings every ~30 s and drop any peer silent for ~90 s, mirroring tunnel.rs. Do this on the direct door, on rendezvous joins, and on rendezvous hosts (the PC already pings every 30 s, so a host silent for 90 s is gone). Enable TCP keepalive on accepted sockets.

v1.reason: No server-side liveness check exists on the phone door or the rendezvous. In the direct door (direct.rs:104-121) the reader waits on `source.next()` with no timeout, and the writer never sends pings. bridge::run returns only when `inbound` closes, and HELLO_TIMEOUT applies only before admission. So a phone that drops without a FIN keeps its bridge, and its Unix-socket connection to the engine, until a write fails. That takes about 15 min of retransmissions if output flows and never happens if the connection is idle. Rendezvous joins (rendezvous.rs:269) are the same. The rendezvous host loop (rendezvous.rs:194) reads forever: the PC's 30 s pings are auto-ponged but never used as a liveness signal, so a sleeping or unplugged PC stays as `entry.host`. A phone that then joins does not get `host.offline` (rendezvous.rs:237-252), because the lane is inserted and `Lane::Open` is queued into the 1024-slot channel. It waits with no greeting until the server's writes to the dead socket time out, or until the PC comes back and replaces the host. Only tunnel.rs:51-52/81-87 (the PC side) has a silence limit.
v1.correction: Impact is narrower than 'subscriptions and PTY attachments alive' might suggest. The engine's socket fan-out uses broadcast channels with Lagged handling (relay-core socket.rs:385 etc.), so a dead bridge costs one connection and a few tasks; it does not stall the engine or other sessions. The user-visible part is the rendezvous hang toward phones while the PC is away. Fix as proposed: server-side ping every ~30 s, close any peer silent for ~90 s (host and join on the rendezvous, and the direct door), optionally TCP keepalive.

findings.title: Actor gate is bypassed by a frame containing several lines
findings.evidence: `gate` parses the whole WebSocket frame: `let Ok(value) = serde_json::from_str::<serde_json::Value>(line) else { return Gate::Forward; };` (96-98). A frame of two JSON objects separated by a newline fails with trailing characters, so it is forwarded verbatim (bridge.rs:177-181). The engine reads it with `lines()` (relay-core socket.rs:323, 335) as separate requests, and the second one was never gated. The comment at 92-94 is also wrong: valid non-object JSON is rejected, not forwarded.
findings.impact: This breaks the guarantee stated in MOBILE.md:180-182 and ARCHITECTURE.md:61-62: 'every line a phone sends is gated to actor `user`' and 'a phone cannot borrow an agent's identity even with a guessed token'. The engine still refuses `system`, refuses `test` on stable, and requires a session token. But a phone that has seen an agent's RELAY_TOKEN (e.g. in that agent's terminal) can act as that agent, and its actions are audited as the agent's.
findings.fix: Split each frame on newline and gate and forward every non-empty piece separately, or refuse frames that contain a newline. While there, parse only a small borrowed head struct (`actor`, `id`) instead of building a full `Value` tree for every line.

v1.reason: wire.rs:96-98 forwards any frame that serde_json fails to parse, and a frame of `{...}\n{...}` fails with a trailing-characters error. bridge.rs:177-180 writes that frame verbatim to the engine socket. The engine splits it with `BufReader::lines()` (relay-core socket.rs, the `lines.next_line()` loop) and handles each line as a separate request, so the second request never passes through the gate. direct.rs:107-113 and the tunnel both hand the bridge whole frames, so both transports are affected. Engine::resolve_actor (engine.rs:1347-1370) still refuses `system`, refuses `test` on stable, and requires a valid session token for agent:*. The bypass therefore gives nothing beyond the paired phone's existing user authority. Its only effect is that a phone holding an agent's RELAY_TOKEN can act under that agent's identity, so its actions are misattributed in the audit log, which breaks the door's stated invariant. The comment at wire.rs:92-94 is also inaccurate: valid non-object JSON such as `[1]` gets actor "" and is rejected, not forwarded.
v1.correction: Only an already-paired, authenticated device can trigger this, and it gains no privilege beyond the user it already acts as. Fix: refuse frames that contain '\n', or split them and gate each piece.

findings.title: Room secret travels in the host URL's query string
findings.evidence: `format!("{}/host/{}?secret={}", r.url, r.room, r.secret)` (19). The server reads the secret from the query (rendezvous.rs:98-102).
findings.impact: TLS proxies in front of the rendezvous log request URIs with their query strings (nginx's default access log; Caddy when logging is enabled), so the secret is written to disk on the VPS on every reconnect. Over ws:// it is visible to everyone on the path. With it, anyone can host the room, evicting the PC, and phones then talk to an impostor that sees whatever they send.
findings.fix: Send the secret in a request header (e.g. `Authorization: Bearer …`, read in the `accept_hdr_async` callback) or as the first frame after the upgrade, so it never appears in a URL.

v1.reason: tunnel.rs:19 builds `{url}/host/{room}?secret={secret}`, and rendezvous.rs:98-102 reads the secret from the query string. The module doc at rendezvous.rs:9 documents this path. A TLS-terminating reverse proxy that logs full request URIs, which nginx's default access log does, writes the secret on every PC reconnect. Anyone holding the secret can host the room, which evicts the PC (179), and can then see the bus lines that phones send. This is real but limited. The VPS and its logs belong to the person who runs Relay, and an impostor host gets only per-connection proofs, not device tokens.
v1.correction: Over ws://, which relay-cli remote.rs:280-284 allows with a warning, a request header is just as visible on the wire. So the fix only helps with proxy and access-log exposure, not with ws://. The fix is to send the secret in a header read in the accept_hdr_async callback, or as the first frame after the upgrade.

findings.title: /info is readable by any web page (`Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`) and WebSocket upgrades never check Origin
findings.evidence: The hand-written /info response sends `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` (80). The WebSocket upgrade uses plain `accept_async` (89) with no header callback, so a browser `Origin` is never inspected.
findings.impact: Any site the user visits can `fetch('http://127.0.0.1:7420/info')` (or a LAN address) and read the machine's host name, Relay instance and version, and whether a pairing window is open, which fingerprints the user and machine. It can also open WebSockets to the in-engine door, feeding the DoS above. The native phone app needs neither CORS nor browser-origin sockets.
findings.fix: Drop the CORS header. Use `accept_hdr_async` and refuse upgrades that carry a browser `Origin`.

v1.reason: Confirmed. direct.rs:80 hard-codes `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` on the hand-written /info response, and direct.rs:89 uses plain `accept_async` with no header callback, so Origin is never checked. /info (direct.rs:60-70) returns the host name, host_id, instance, version and whether pairing is open, so any web page can read it cross-origin, subject to browser private or local-network-access restrictions. It was added with the door in bdb5e9f, and no phone code fetches /info from a browser context (the native RN fetch is not subject to CORS), so the header buys nothing. A browser WebSocket still has to pass the token proof, so the gain for an attacker is fingerprinting and extra pre-auth connections only.
v1.correction: Drop the CORS header and refuse WebSocket upgrades that carry a browser Origin via `accept_hdr_async`. Low impact: information disclosure and a minor contribution to remote#1.

findings.title: Tunnel dial has no timeout, and the backoff never resets after a long successful connection
findings.evidence: `tokio_tungstenite::connect_async(url.as_str()).await` (57) has no timeout around the TCP, TLS and HTTP-upgrade steps. `spawn` resets `backoff` only when `connect_once` returns Ok (34-36). Connections normally end in Err (a socket error, or the 90 s silence bail), so after hours connected the redial still waits at whatever level the backoff had reached, up to 30 s.
findings.impact: A dial that stalls after the TCP handshake hangs, with nothing logged, until TCP gives up (~15 min), or forever if the peer accepted and never answers. Examples: the laptop suspends mid-dial, or a proxy accepts and never responds. Phones are told the PC is offline the whole time. This defeats the liveness work the 30 s ping and 90 s silence limit were added for.
findings.fix: Wrap the dial in `tokio::time::timeout` (~15 s). Reset `backoff` once `connect_async` succeeds, e.g. by having `connect_once` report 'connected' separately from how the connection ended.

v1.reason: tunnel.rs:57 calls `connect_async(...).await` with no timeout. If a dial stalls after the TCP connect, during the TLS or HTTP-upgrade step, `spawn` waits until the OS gives up, or forever if the peer accepted and never answers. Nothing is logged while it waits. Backoff resets only on `Ok(())` (34-36). connect_once returns Ok only on a server Close frame or end of stream (94, 98). A network drop returns Err (99-104) and so does the silence bail (86). So each long-lived connection that ends in an error still doubles the backoff, and after a few drops every reconnect waits 30 s.
v1.correction: The no-reset bug costs at most 30 s of extra reconnect delay. The missing timeout matters only in rare stalled-handshake cases. A dial to a host that is down fails on the OS SYN timeout, about 2 min. Fix: wrap the dial in `tokio::time::timeout`, and reset backoff once the dial succeeds.

findings.title: Nagle stays on for every WebSocket socket while each bus line is flushed as its own message
findings.evidence: Accepted streams go to `accept_async` / `accept_hdr_async` without `set_nodelay(true)` (direct.rs:89, rendezvous.rs:159). The PC dials with `connect_async` (tunnel.rs:57), which tokio-tungstenite runs with `disable_nagle = false`. Every line is then sent with `sink.send(Message::text(line))`, a feed plus a flush per line (direct.rs:98, rendezvous.rs:188 and 263, tunnel.rs:67).
findings.impact: Back-to-back small lines (a response followed by its echo frame or event) leave the second one waiting for the peer's delayed ACK, about 40 ms on Linux/Android. That wait is paid on every hop, so twice through the rendezvous, and shows up as lag in terminal echo and responses on the phone. Not measured.
findings.fix: Call `set_nodelay(true)` on accepted streams and dial with `connect_async_with_config(url, None, true)`. Batch with `feed` while the queue is non-empty and `flush` once, as relay-core's socket writer already does.

v1.reason: The code does what the finding says. direct.rs:89 hands the raw TcpStream to `accept_async` and rendezvous.rs:159 hands it to `accept_hdr_async`, and neither calls set_nodelay. tunnel.rs:57 dials with `connect_async`, which in tokio-tungstenite 0.30.0 (connect.rs:37) is `connect_async_with_config(request, None, false)`, so Nagle stays on. Every writer loop calls `sink.send(...)` per line (direct.rs:98, rendezvous.rs:188/263, tunnel.rs:67). SinkExt::send feeds and then flushes, so each bus line is a separate write. The bridge pump (bridge.rs, the `to_phone.send(line)` loop) forwards engine lines one at a time, so back-to-back small writes do happen. The only nodelay in the repo is on the scrcpy sockets (relay-core handlers/device.rs:820-821). The latency cost is a textbook write-write-read Nagle/delayed-ACK interaction, but it has not been measured here.
v1.correction: The extra latency of up to ~40 ms per hop is inferred from TCP behaviour, not observed. Minimal fix: `stream.set_nodelay(true)` before both accepts, and `connect_async_with_config(url, None, true)` in tunnel.rs. Batching (feed while the channel has more, then one flush) is optional on top of that.
