findings.title: serve_with_door leaves a stale direct_port when its door fails to bind, so `relay remote pair` links to another instance's door
findings.evidence: `if let Some(door) = &door { registry.direct_port = Some(door.local_addr.port()); }` (115-117) never clears the field when the door did not open. That happens, for example, when another instance's door already holds 7420, since every instance defaults to that port. `Pair` uses `registry.direct_port.unwrap_or(DEFAULT_PORT)` (227) and prints its 'serve has not run' note only when the field is None (231).
findings.impact: Run the dev engine with --remote while the stable engine owns 7420, then pair for dev. The link points at stable's door, the phone is greeted by the wrong instance, and pairing fails with `pair.invalid` and no hint why.
findings.fix: Set `registry.direct_port = door.as_ref().map(|d| d.local_addr.port())`, and have `pair` warn when no door is recorded for the instance.

v1.reason: remote.rs:115-118 sets `registry.direct_port` only when the door bound and never clears it otherwise. Every instance defaults to 0.0.0.0:7420 (main.rs:68), so a second instance's door fails to bind whenever another instance already holds 7420. `Pair` (remote.rs:225-233) then uses the stale port and skips its 'has not run' note. The link points at the other instance's door, whose registry does not hold the code, so the phone gets `pair.invalid`.
v1.correction: The practical difference is small. If the field were cleared to None, `pair` would still fall back to DEFAULT_PORT 7420, the same wrong door, and would print a misleading 'relay remote serve has not run' note. The useful fix is to store `door.as_ref().map(|d| d.local_addr.port())` and have `pair` say explicitly that this instance has no open door, possibly because another instance holds the port. Using a different default port per instance would remove the collision altogether.

findings.title: Phone-supplied device names keep control characters and are printed raw by `relay remote devices`
findings.evidence: `name: if name.is_empty() { … } else { name.chars().take(64).collect() }` (220) trims `hello.device_name` but keeps ESC and other control characters. relay-cli remote.rs:245 prints `d.name` straight to the terminal.
findings.impact: Whoever pairs (anyone who saw the code) can choose a name containing terminal escape sequences, such as OSC 52 clipboard writes, title changes, or cursor moves that hide or forge rows. They fire whenever the user lists devices.
findings.fix: Filter `char::is_control` (and optionally bidi override characters) when storing the name.

v1.reason: registry.rs redeem stores `name.chars().take(64).collect()` after only `trim()`, so ESC and other control characters are kept. The CLI `relay remote devices` (crates/relay-cli/src/remote.rs:245) prints `d.name` raw with `println!("{:<14} {:<24} ...")`. The name comes straight from `hello.device_name` (wire.rs:35) during pairing (bridge.rs admit). The real-world severity is minimal, though. Setting the name requires redeeming a valid 40-bit pairing code within its 10-minute window, and that already grants a full bus credential: far more power than terminal escape injection. The 64-char cap also limits the payload. Still a correct, cheap hardening.
v1.correction: The only meaningful trigger is a device that was legitimately paired, or one paired with a stolen code; the latter is already a much worse compromise. The fix is as proposed: filter `char::is_control` (and optionally bidi overrides) in redeem, or escape on output in the CLI.

findings.title: Pairing links advertise docker/libvirt/VPN addresses ahead of the real LAN address
findings.evidence: `lan_addresses` keeps every non-loopback, non-link-local IPv4 address (139-148) and sorts with `out.sort_by_key(|a| (!a.is_private(), a.octets()))` (149). Docker's 172.17.0.1 and VPN 10.x addresses therefore sort before a home 192.168.x address in the `direct=` list, which the phone tries first.
findings.impact: On a typical machine with Docker installed, the first advertised address is unreachable from the phone. If the app tries addresses in order, every connection first waits for that attempt to time out. It also widens the set of places the phone sends its proof to (see the channel-security finding). Not verified: how the app orders and times out its attempts.
findings.fix: Skip virtual interfaces by name (`docker*`, `br-*`, `virbr*`, `veth*`), or prefer the interface that holds the default route. Sort 192.168/16 ahead of the other private ranges.

v1.reason: The sort key is as described: private addresses first, then by octets, so 172.17.0.1 sorts before 192.168.x.x. But the claimed impact (each connection waits for the unreachable first address to time out) does not happen. The client races every direct route at once: RelayClient.ts routeGroups says 'every LAN address at once', and pairOnce uses `greetFirst(group, ...)`, where 'Routes race only to the greeting'. Address order in the `direct=` list therefore does not affect latency. The secondary claim about widening where the proof goes also fails. The pairing code or proof goes out only on the single socket that greeted first, and the proof is a challenge-bound digest (bridge.rs admit: `wire::proof(challenge, &device.token)`), so it is not replayable. A docker bridge address is also unreachable from the phone, so nothing listening there could receive it. What remains is a few useless entries in the link: cosmetic, not worth a finding.

findings.title: Duplicated serve, accept and transport code that has already diverged
findings.evidence: `sigterm()` (remote.rs:142-149) is a verbatim copy of relay-core serve.rs:55-62, and the quit/ctrl-c/SIGTERM select and shutdown (remote.rs:127-139) copy serve.rs:44-52. The accept loops (direct.rs:37-53 vs rendezvous.rs:69-85) and the peek-and-answer HTTP responders (direct.rs:73-87 vs rendezvous.rs:125-144) are the same code. The phone-reader loops have already diverged: direct.rs:112-116 forwards Binary frames, while rendezvous.rs:273 silently drops them, so a client that sends binary works on the LAN but not through the rendezvous. `serve_with_door` (88-126) and `RemoteCommand::Serve` (181-206) repeat the bind/registry/tunnel/print sequence with different error handling. `connect_once` repeats its lane and writer teardown three times (tunnel.rs:82-85, 100-103, 155-158).
findings.impact: Fixes such as the timeouts, limits and keepalives above must be made in two places and will drift, as the Binary handling already has. The triple teardown makes it easy for a future early return to leak lane tasks.
findings.fix: Make relay-core's `sigterm`/wait-for-quit public, or add `serve_until_quit(served, extras)`. Extract a shared `accept_loop(listener, handler)` and HTTP-probe helper, and one ws pump used by both the direct door and joins. Add one `open_door(ctx, addr, registry) -> (door, tunnel)` used by both serve paths. Move the lane teardown into a drop guard.

v1.reason: The duplication is real. `sigterm()` at relay-cli remote.rs:142-149 is identical to relay-core serve.rs:55-62, and the quit/ctrl-c/SIGTERM select plus shutdown (remote.rs:127-139) copies serve.rs:44-52. The accept loops in direct.rs:37-53 and rendezvous.rs:69-85 are the same shape. tunnel.rs repeats the lane-abort plus writer-abort teardown three times (around lines 81-85, 99-103 and 155-158). The Binary-frame divergence is real too: direct.rs forwards `Message::Binary` as lossy UTF-8, while the rendezvous join loop (rendezvous.rs around 273) drops it with `Ok(_) => continue`.
v1.correction: The payoff is modest. The two serve paths differ in error handling on purpose: `relay serve --remote` tolerates a failed door bind, while `relay remote serve` must fail. A single `open_door` helper would therefore need a policy parameter and is not a pure simplification. The two HTTP probe responders also differ in path and in CORS header. The Binary divergence has no known engine-side consequence, since the bridge protocol is line-based text. The worthwhile parts are to expose relay-core's wait-for-quit/sigterm so the shutdown code is not copied, and to put the tunnel lane teardown in a drop guard.

findings.title: Tests miss the remote door's risky paths; `a_terminal_streams_to_the_phone` streams no terminal
findings.evidence: The test named for terminal streaming only checks `session.attach` on a missing session, plus task, session and mail calls (277-330). The file header says it 'streams a terminal' (1-3), yet no pty frame ever crosses the bridge or the tunnel's Lane wrapping. The rendezvous test's host-wait loop (250-260) falls through silently if the host never registers. Every tunnel test dials `ws://` (230).
findings.impact: Every path with a defect above is untested: TLS dialing (panics), multi-line frames, host replacement, revoke with a live connection, concurrent registry writes, a slow lane, and the pty streaming the app depends on. CI is green on all of them.
findings.fix: Attach to a live session (any printing command launched through the engine's test PTY) and assert that a pty frame arrives through both doors. Assert that the host registered. Add regression tests for the findings above, including a wss:// dial through a custom connector.

v1.reason: crates/relay-remote/tests/remote.rs:277 `a_terminal_streams_to_the_phone` only calls `session.attach` on "no-such" and asserts `not_found` (lines 287-289). After that it runs workspace.create, project.add, task.create, task.dispatch with `start: false`, session.create and mailbox.send, and checks session.list counts. No session is ever started and no pty frame is ever read. The file header (lines 1-3) says the test "streams a terminal" through both doors, so the name and the header overstate what is covered: pty streaming through bridge.rs and through the tunnel's lane wrapping has no test. Every remote URL in the file is ws:// (tunnel test at about line 226), and the crate builds tokio-tungstenite with `rustls-tls-native-roots` (Cargo.toml:21), so the wss:// dial that tunnel.rs:57 makes in real use is never exercised. Calling this low is correct: it is a coverage gap, not a defect in the product.
v1.correction: One part overstates the problem. The host-wait loop (lines ~250-260) does fall through without asserting, but the test does not then pass silently. The very next `pair(&join, &code)` would get the `host.offline` frame instead of a Greeting, and the `serde_json::from_str::<Greeting>(...).unwrap()` at line 92 would panic, so the test fails with an unclear message rather than going green. The fix there is just clarity: assert `"hosts":1` after the loop. The claim that "every path with a defect above is untested" depends on the other findings and should be judged with them. The confirmed gaps here are pty frame streaming (direct and tunnel) and wss:// dialing. The fix should either launch a real session whose provider is a printing command and assert that a pty/output frame arrives through both doors, or rename the test and correct the header comment.

results.coverage:
I read every line of crates/relay-cli/src/main.rs, mcp.rs, unreal_process.rs, blender.rs and Cargo.toml. Because blender.rs embeds the Blender scripts with include_str!, I also read blender_py/common.py, run.py, info.py, export.py, render.py, mesh_check.py and rig_check.py in full. Of anim_inspect.py I read only lines 1-60, and I did not read make_fixture.py. I did not read unreal_py/* or remote.rs. Of unreal.rs I read only the parts that call into or are shared with my files: serve/handle, tool/tool_result/rpc_error, guard_project/lock, quit_editor/launch_editor, build, editor_status, remote_at, import_fbx and the test runner.

To check reachability I traced into relay-core: socket.rs (Client::call, bus.subscribe, bus.wait), engine.rs resolve_actor, guardrail.rs (write_target, evaluate_exec, self_approval), handlers/guardrail.rs gate, hooks.rs (installed matchers, timeouts, pre-commit script), proc.rs output_with_timeout, and serde_json 1.0.151 index.rs.

One suspicion turned out wrong. I suspected port_free's probe could pass while UE's own bind fails, because Rust's bind sets SO_REUSEADDR. A local TIME_WAIT experiment showed the probe and UE's bind agree in both reuse configurations, so I did not report it.

Not reported, outside my files: the Claude PreToolUse matcher "Edit|Write|MultiEdit|Bash" (hooks.rs:350) leaves NotebookEdit ungated. guardrail.gate is registered with Engine::register and can run `git status` (10 s timeout) under the store mutex, which breaks a CLAUDE.md invariant. bus.subscribe and bus.wait are served in socket.rs without resolving the actor. launch_editor reads the whole log from offset 0 straight after spawning (unreal.rs:656), so a bind failure from the previous session may be misreported (low confidence). quit_editor SIGTERMs even the correct editor after a 3 s Remote Control timeout, losing unsaved work (by its own note).

Points I could not verify: how Claude Code treats a timed-out hook, Codex's exact PreToolUse payload for apply_patch, and Claude's Edit normalisation rules. Each is flagged in the relevant finding's confidence.

findings.title: editors_for matches any editor whose argument merely ends with the same .uproject file name, so quitting or building one checkout can SIGTERM another checkout's or another project's editor
findings.evidence: `.filter(|p| p.cmdline.iter().any(|a| Path::new(a).canonicalize().map(|c| c == want).unwrap_or(false) || a.ends_with(&*uproject.file_name().unwrap_or_default().to_string_lossy())))`. The fallback accepts `/proj/Game.uproject` when the agent's project is `/proj/.relay/worktrees/w1/Game.uproject`, and `TopDownShooter.uproject` when the project is `Shooter.uproject`. A relative argument is canonicalized against the MCP server's cwd, not the editor's. If `file_name()` were None, the needle would be "" and every editor would match. `is_editor` (line 44) compares `a == "-nullrhi"` case-sensitively. quit_editor (unreal.rs:575) stores these PIDs in `before` and runs `for pid in &before { kill(*pid) }` (unreal.rs:600-603).
findings.impact: Two triggers lead to the kill. (a) Remote Control does not answer within 3 s (the editor is busy or RC is off): `notes` contains "terminate" and every matched PID gets SIGTERM at once. (b) Our editor answers and quits, but the other matched editor is still running: 20 s later all of `before` gets SIGTERM. Either way, ue_editor_quit or ue_build restart_editor=true from one checkout terminates the human's editor on another checkout, or the editor of a project whose name is a suffix match, and its unsaved work is lost. The same false positive causes three more failures. ue_build refuses with "the editor is running this project" (unreal.rs:1521-1527). ue_editor_launch returns already_running for a foreign editor (unreal.rs:624-627). engine_root takes the engine from the wrong editor (lines 119-123). The engine_root unit test also fails on a dev machine with any `*Game.uproject` editor open.
findings.fix: Match on path identity only. Resolve each argument against `/proc/<pid>/cwd`, canonicalize it, compare with `want`, and remove the `ends_with(file_name)` fallback. Compare `-nullrhi` case-insensitively. In quit_editor, only signal PIDs that still match the identity check at kill time.

v1.reason: unreal_process.rs:57 accepts any argument that canonicalizes to the project or that `ends_with` the project's file name. A worktree agent's project is <repo>/.relay/worktrees/wN/Game.uproject, and the human's editor on the main checkout has <repo>/Game.uproject, which ends with Game.uproject, so it matches. The callers act on that match. build (unreal.rs:1518-1527) refuses because 'the editor is running this project' whenever the human's main-checkout editor is open, although the worktree has its own Binaries. launch_editor (624-627) returns already_running for the foreign editor. engine_root (unreal_process.rs:119-123) takes that editor's engine. The kill path is in quit_editor (unreal.rs:572-604), called by ue_editor_quit or by ue_build with restart_editor=true (1518). If /remote/info does not answer within 3 s, notes contains 'terminate' and every PID in `before` gets kill() right away. guard_project only runs on the branch where RC answered, so it does not protect this path. If RC answers on our editor while the foreign one is also running, the loop never sees an empty list, and after 20 s all of `before`, the foreign PID included, gets SIGTERM. The code's own note says unsaved changes are lost. The engine_root test's `unwrap_err` for '4.27' would also fail on a machine with any *Game.uproject editor open.
v1.correction: Reachability is narrower than the finding implies. guard_project's message says the Unreal plugin starts new agents in the main checkout by default, so path-identical matching is the common case. The false positives need a worktree agent, or two projects whose names are suffixes of one another. When RC answers with the foreign editor's project, guard_project bails before any kill. That bail also leaks the lock taken at line 573, a separate issue. Within the worktree case, the false build refusal and false already_running are deterministic, and the SIGTERM needs a busy or unresponsive editor (>3 s). The fix is right: resolve each cmdline argument against /proc/<pid>/cwd, compare canonical paths only, drop the ends_with fallback, and re-check identity before signalling.

v2.reason:
(a) The code does what the finding claims. unreal_process.rs:57 keeps any non-commandlet UnrealEditor process with an argument that either canonicalizes to the project or plain-string `ends_with` the project's file name. "/repo/Game.uproject" therefore matches an agent whose project is /repo/.relay/worktrees/<name>/Game.uproject (worktree.rs:18 pooled_path), and "MyGame.uproject" or "TopDownShooter.uproject" matches a "Game"/"Shooter" project.

(b) Reachability is broader than the first verifier said. D160's "primary" default applies only when session.create omits `worktree` (session.rs:858). The desktop launch dialog never omits it: launch.rs:259-262 pre-fills "new", line 346 sends it, and line 784 refuses an empty value. Nothing in the native client switches it to "primary" for plugin projects; the D160 commit 7ab2769 did not touch launch.rs. So an Unreal agent launched from the app gets its own worktree unless the person types "primary" into the collapsed "Worktree and permissions" expander. On top of that, instructions.md item 5 tells every agent to run `ue_build restart_editor: true` after every C++ change, and README.md:20-21 tells worktree agents to keep to C++ work. The false match is therefore hit in the normal flow whenever the person's editor is open on the main checkout (setup.md:49 tells them to open it there).

(c) What happens:
- ue_build (unreal.rs:1518) calls quit_editor. quit_editor puts the person's editor PID in `before` (line 575) and calls remote /remote/info with a 3 s limit.
- If Remote Control answers, guard_project bails (line 579). Nothing is killed, but the worktree agent cannot rebuild with restart. Without restart, prebuild refuses with "the editor is running this project" (lines 1522-1527), although the worktree has its own Binaries. Only allow_editor_open=true, which the tool calls "usually wrong", gets past it.
- If remote() errs, `notes` contains "terminate" and line 602 SIGTERMs every PID at once. remote() errs on connection refused (web server not started; setup.md:31 offers a per-session `WebControl.StartServer`), on a non-2xx reply (passphrase mismatch), or on a 3 s read timeout (editor busy, for example with another agent's in-editor Python call). The editor lock is per checkout (`project.root/Saved`), so it does not serialize a worktree agent against a main-checkout agent.
- In UE 5.8.2, SIGTERM runs GracefulTerminationHandler, which calls RequestExitWithStatus (UnixPlatformCrashContext.cpp:155-172). The engine exits without the save prompt; the code's own note says unsaved changes are lost.
- build then relaunches an editor on the agent's worktree .uproject (unreal.rs:1572 into launch_editor), replacing the person's main-checkout editor.
- launch_editor returns a false already_running (lines 624-627).
- The engine_root unit test fails on a dev machine with any *Game.uproject editor open: by_guid returns that editor's engine.

(d) High is correct. Deterministic wrong refusals in the default C++-verification flow, plus a data-loss path (unsaved editor work) under plausible conditions. Not critical only because the kill needs Remote Control to be down, busy or misconfigured.

(e) Path identity is the right direction, but resolving against /proc/<pid>/cwd is wrong for this process. UE chdirs to the executable directory in FEngineLoop::PreInitPreStartupScreen (LaunchEngineLoop.cpp:1801-1804, UnixPlatformProcess.cpp:2113-2114 chdir(BaseDir())). A running editor's cwd is Engine/Binaries/Linux, so relative-path launches would become false negatives.
v2.correction:
1. Reachability is broader, not narrower, than the first verifier said. The desktop launch dialog always sends worktree "new" (apps/relay-native/src/launch.rs:259-262, 346, 784), so the plugin's D160 primary default (session.rs:858) never applies to agents launched from the app. Worktree Unreal agents are the default there; that is a separate bug that makes this one common. Add the README's instruction that worktree agents do C++ work, and instructions.md item 5 (restart_editor after every C++ change).

2. Trigger (a) also covers connection refused (web server not started) and non-2xx replies (passphrase mismatch). It also covers an editor busy for over 3 s with another agent's Python call; the per-checkout lock in Saved/ does not prevent that. After the kill, build relaunches the editor on the worktree copy (unreal.rs:1572).

3. Trigger (b) needs two editors running at once, with the worktree's editor holding the RC port. That is rare.

4. engine_root picking the wrong editor is harmless in the worktree case (same .uproject, same EngineAssociation). It matters only for projects whose names are suffixes of one another.

5. The file_name()==None case cannot happen: Project::find reads the path as a file first (unreal.rs:1302).

6. The case-sensitive `-nullrhi` check is a separate, low-impact issue. The tool's own headless runs pass lowercase `-nullrhi` (unreal.rs:1107).

Fix correction: do not resolve relative arguments against /proc/<pid>/cwd. UE 5.8 chdirs to Engine/Binaries/Linux at startup (LaunchEngineLoop.cpp:1801-1804), so relative launches would be missed. Instead:
- Compare absolute arguments by canonical path.
- Resolve a relative argument against PWD from /proc/<pid>/environ, or treat it as unknown.
- Pass a canonical path to launch().
- Drop the ends_with fallback.
- Before any kill, require positive identity (a canonical match, or editor_project() over Remote Control) and re-check each PID right before signalling.

Separately, even with exact matching, the terminate-when-unreachable fallback (unreal.rs:589, 600-603) still SIGTERMs the person's own main-checkout editor when a main-checkout agent restarts it while Remote Control is down or busy. The identity fix does not address that.

findings.title: Blender scripts use Action.fcurves, which Blender 5.x removed, so blender_info, skeletal export and blender_to_unreal fail on current Blender (the failing cargo test)
findings.symbol: info.py actions loop / export.py control-bone check
findings.evidence: info.py:45-46 has `groups = set(fc.data_path.split('"')[1] for fc in a.fcurves if ...)` and `"fcurves": len(a.fcurves)` for every action in bpy.data.actions. export.py:48 has `keyed = set(... for fc in act.fcurves ...)` whenever the armature has an action and kind != static. The installed Blender 5.2.1 exposes F-curves only through channelbags (`bpy_extras.anim_utils.action_get_channelbag_for_slot`, anim_utils.py:91). `cargo test` fails in blender.rs:539 (`run(PY_INFO, ...)`) with "AttributeError: 'Action' object has no attribute 'fcurves'". plugins/blender/docs/setup.md:3 promises "4.0 or newer". render.py:35 maps eevee to 'BLENDER_EEVEE', which 4.2-4.5 reject because the id there is BLENDER_EEVEE_NEXT.
findings.impact: On Blender 5.x, blender_info fails for any .blend that contains an action, and it is the documented first call. blender_export of a rig with an assigned action fails, and so does blender_to_unreal for animated characters. CLAUDE.md's `cargo test` fails on every machine with Blender 5 installed. CI runners have no Blender, so the breakage was never visible there. engine=eevee renders fail on the 4.2/4.5 LTS releases.
findings.fix: Add a `action_fcurves(action)` helper to common.py. It uses `action.fcurves` when the attribute exists and otherwise iterates `layer.strips[*].channelbags[*].fcurves`, or the assigned slot's channelbag. Use it in info.py and export.py. Pick the EEVEE id from the engine enum items. Log the Blender version in the real-Blender test, and consider a CI job with a pinned Blender.

v1.reason: info.py:45-46 iterates `a.fcurves` for every action in bpy.data.actions, and export.py:48 reads `act.fcurves` whenever the armature has an action and kind != static. I checked the installed Blender 5.2.1 LTS by running it headless with a read-only expression: `'fcurves' in bpy.types.Action.bl_rna.properties.keys()` prints False. Blender's own bundled FBX exporter and importer (io_scene_fbx/export_fbx_bin.py:2527, import_fbx.py:952) reach F-curves only through `channelbag.fcurves`. The real-Blender test (blender.rs:526ff) builds a fixture with a 'Swing' action, then calls `run(PY_INFO, ...)` and unwraps the result, so it fails wherever Blender 5 is installed. CI skips the test because its runners have no Blender. blender_info is the documented first call and fails on any .blend that has an action. blender_export with kind skeletal or animation fails on an armature that has an action, and so does blender_to_unreal, which goes through the same export.py. setup.md promises '4.0 or newer'. The EEVEE claim also fits: in 5.2 the engine enum lists 'BLENDER_EEVEE', and 4.2-4.5 use BLENDER_EEVEE_NEXT. That is a minor side issue limited to engine=eevee.
v1.correction: Only info.py:45-46 and export.py:48 use the legacy API. rig_check and anim_inspect do not use fcurves. For the helper, prefer `bpy_extras.anim_utils.action_get_channelbag_for_slot(action, slot)` (or iterate layers, strips and channelbags) and fall back to `action.fcurves` when `hasattr(action, 'fcurves')`. High rather than critical: the breakage is confined to the optional Blender plugin, not the engine.

v2.reason:
(a) The code does what the finding claims, and I reproduced it rather than inferring it. The only Blender on this machine is 5.2.1 LTS (~/.local/bin/blender, installed 2026-09-05), and find_blender() resolves it through PATH. I built the repo's own fixture (make_fixture.py) into the scratchpad. I then ran the job that run() builds: common.py, a newline, then info.py, with the same `-b <file> --factory-startup --python-exit-code 1 --python job.py -- args.json` flags. It exits 1 with no RELAY_JSON line and `AttributeError: 'Action' object has no attribute 'fcurves'` at info.py:45 (`for fc in a.fcurves`). export.py:48 (`act.fcurves`) fails the same way. That happens with the test's arguments, and also with a plain `{"objects":["Hero"]}` that asks for no action and no animations. A probe confirms that in 5.2.1 'fcurves', 'groups' and 'id_root' are absent from Action's RNA, while 'layers' and 'slots' are present. None of Blender's bundled 5.2 scripts use action.fcurves; FBX, glTF and Rigify all go through channelbag.fcurves. Nothing in Relay guards the calls: info.py:44-47 loops over every bpy.data.actions entry unconditionally, and export.py:45-48 is gated only by `act is not None and kind != "static"`.
(b) Reachable by any agent using the Blender plugin with a current Blender (5.0, 5.1 or 5.2 LTS), which is what this user has. blender_info is the documented first call (blender.rs:65 "Start with blender_info"). It fails on any .blend containing at least one action, including fake-user or stray actions. blender_export fails for any armature that has an action assigned, kind auto, skeletal or animation, even when no animation is requested. blender_to_unreal goes through the same export.py (blender.rs:399), so skeletal imports of rigs with an action fail, and kind=animation with an action always fails. Animated characters are a central use case of this plugin, which ships rigging and animation skills plus anim_inspect, so the failure is frequent. The test `the_blender_tools_work_on_a_real_rig` has no #[ignore], relay-cli is a default member, and the test finds Blender on PATH here. So CLAUDE.md's `cargo test` panics at blender.rs:539 on this machine. CI passes only because its runners have no Blender. The info.py line has existed since the plugin's first commit (d24a686, 2026-09-22) and the export.py line since b3ea46d, both after 5.2.1 was installed, so this test would have failed here from the start.
(c) Each call returns an MCP error carrying the traceback. No data is lost: info never saves, and export raises before the FBX exporter runs, so no file is written. The agent cannot inspect animated files or export rigs through Relay's tools. Its only route is raw blender_python, which loses the mesh, scale and facing checks and the Unreal measurement. Separately, the mandated `cargo test` fails on the developer machine for a reason unrelated to the change under test.
(d) High is right: this is a hard failure of the plugin's normal flow on the current Blender line. It is not critical because the plugin is optional, and there is no data loss, no security impact and no engine or bus effect.
(e) The fix works. I applied an action_fcurves helper to scratch copies only: hasattr(action,'fcurves') first, otherwise the slot channelbag via bpy_extras.anim_utils.action_get_channelbag_for_slot, otherwise all layers, strips and channelbags. With it, every step of the real-Blender test meets its assertions on 5.2.1: info finds 6 pairs with Swing showing 3 fcurves and 1 bone, rig_check passes, anim_inspect holds the sword in the right hand, the skeletal export writes the FBX without the Sword, and the render works. The test's other steps (run.py, the plate check and refused export, crate sockets) also pass unmodified. So fcurves is the only 5.x break on the test-covered paths.
v2.correction:
1) render.py:35 (eevee mapped to 'BLENDER_EEVEE') is a separate root cause and should be its own low finding. It affects only engine=eevee on 4.2-4.5; the repo's SKILL.md:241 itself documents BLENDER_EEVEE_NEXT there. Workbench, the default, is unaffected, and 5.2.1 accepts BLENDER_EEVEE. Its proposed fix, "pick the EEVEE id from the engine enum items", does not work as worded. On 5.2.1, `scene.render.bl_rna.properties['engine'].enum_items` returns only the static placeholder ['BLENDER_EEVEE'] and omits CYCLES and WORKBENCH. Use a version check (`'BLENDER_EEVEE_NEXT' if (4,2,0) <= bpy.app.version < (5,0,0) else 'BLENDER_EEVEE'`) or try/except TypeError on assignment; the TypeError lists the real ids. SKILL.md:242 gives the same misleading advice.
2) export.py should check the armature's own slot: `anim_utils.action_get_channelbag_for_slot(act, arm.animation_data.action_slot)`. This was verified on 5.2.1 (slot OBHero, 3 fcurves). Taking every channelbag would count bones from another slot when one action animates several IDs, which gives spurious "keys non-deform bones" warnings. info.py can take every channelbag, verified to give 3 fcurves. When `layers` exists (4.4+), prefer the slot or channelbag path, so that 4.4/4.5's legacy proxy, which exposes only the first slot, is not used; fall back to action.fcurves before 4.4.
3) Impact is stronger than stated. blender_export fails even with no action or animations argument whenever the armature has an action assigned (verified with {"objects":["Hero"]}). blender_to_unreal kind=animation with an action always fails. No data loss.
4) Scope: only info.py:45-46 and export.py:48 use the removed API. rig_check, anim_inspect, render (workbench), mesh_check and run.py all run correctly on 5.2.1. Not exercised: all_actions exports, fbx_options overrides, and anim_inspect partner actions.
5) setup.md:3 ("4.0 or newer") should name the tested range once fixed.

findings.title: `relay cmd '<envelope>'` sends the envelope's own actor, so an agent can act as the user and confirm its own guardrail hold without the self-approval check noticing
findings.evidence: Envelope mode only fills the actor when it is absent: `if v.get("actor").is_none() { v["actor"] = json!(actor.to_string()); }`. The engine accepts the user actor on the socket without proof: `(Actor::User, _) | (Actor::Test, _) => Ok(None)` (engine.rs:1355). BUS.md §8.2 says RELAY_ACTOR is "ignored if RELAY_SESSION is set unless --actor is passed explicitly". guardrail.rs self_approval (857-883) only flags `--actor user`/`--actor=user`, RELAY_SESSION/RELAY_ACTOR edits, or a bare word equal to a user-only op. A JSON envelope is one quoted word, so none of these match.
findings.impact: An agent whose write is held can run `relay cmd '{"op":"guardrail.confirm","actor":"user","payload":{"hold_id":7}}'`. The same works for guardrail.config.set and settings.set. The exec gate allows the command, the CLI sends it as the user, and the hold is confirmed and audited as the user's decision. This is exactly the self-approval the gate refuses for the `--actor user` spelling.
findings.fix: In do_cmd, when RELAY_SESSION is set and --actor was not given, refuse an envelope whose `actor` differs from the environment actor, or overwrite it, as §8.2 already requires for RELAY_ACTOR. Optionally make self_approval also flag `"actor":"user"` inside relay arguments.

v1.reason: do_cmd (main.rs:591-597) fills `actor` only when the envelope lacks it, so `"actor":"user"` in an envelope is sent as is, and the session's RELAY_TOKEN is still attached. engine.rs resolve_actor returns Ok(None) for Actor::User on any door without proof. self_approval (guardrail.rs:857-883) matches `--actor user`, `--actor=user`, RELAY_SESSION/RELAY_ACTOR edits, or a word exactly equal to a USER_ONLY_ANSWERS op. A JSON envelope is one word whose text is the whole object, so none of these match. The hold refusal itself gives the agent a ready envelope (`{"op":"guardrail.confirm","payload":{"hold_id":..}}`, guardrail.rs:1250 and grants.rs:409). Adding `"actor":"user"` and running `relay cmd '<that>'` passes the exec gate and confirms the hold as the user.
v1.correction: The USER_ONLY_ANSWERS comment (guardrail.rs:849-850) already says this check is best effort because the socket does not authenticate `user`. The root cause is the unauthenticated user actor at engine.rs (resolve_actor, `(Actor::User, _) => Ok(None)`): an agent can also reach the socket directly with python or socat, or pass `--actor "$U"`, which the word check does not catch either. Fixing do_cmd (overwrite or refuse the envelope actor when RELAY_SESSION is set and no --actor was given) closes this spelling, the one the hold message makes easy. A sturdier step is engine-side: reject a request that claims `user` but carries an agent session token. Even that can be dodged by sending `"token":null`, so it is still not a real fix. Medium is right: this is a bypass of a check that is documented as best effort.

findings.title: The PreToolUse adapters have no deadline of their own, so a slow engine lets Claude's 30 s hook timeout kill them instead of failing closed
findings.evidence: `let mut client = connect(instance).await?; ... let response = client.call(&request, |_| {}).await?;`. Client::call (socket.rs:801-821) loops on next_line() with no timeout. The installed hooks have `"timeout": 30` (hooks.rs:351, 521). guardrail.gate is registered with `engine.register` (handlers/guardrail.rs:304), so it runs under the store mutex and can run `git status` with a 10 s timeout (guardrail.rs GIT_TIMEOUT).
findings.impact: The engine may stay unresponsive for more than 30 s: queued gates each running git, or any handler holding the store mutex. The hook then never prints its verdict, and Claude kills it at its timeout. A killed hook is not exit 2. Claude treats non-2 hook failures as non-blocking (I could not confirm its exact handling of timeouts from this repo), so the Bash/Write/Edit runs ungated. That breaks the adapter's own rule that "Infrastructure ... must therefore fail closed too" exactly when the infrastructure is degraded. codex_pre_tool (lines 517-520) has the same gap.
findings.fix: Wrap connect + call in `tokio::time::timeout(Duration::from_secs(25), ...)`, below the 30 s hook timeout. On expiry, print "RELAY guardrail unavailable: engine did not answer within 25 s" and exit 2. Use one shared helper for both adapters.

v1.reason: claude_pre_tool (main.rs:466-472) and codex_pre_tool (main.rs:517-521) call connect() then client.call() with no deadline. Client::call (socket.rs:801-821) loops on lines.next_line() with no timeout. The installed hooks carry `"timeout": 30` (hooks.rs:351 Claude, hooks.rs:521 Codex). If the engine process is alive but wedged (a handler stuck while holding the store mutex, or a deadlock), the Unix-socket connect still succeeds through the kernel backlog. The call then never returns and the provider kills the hook at 30 s. A killed hook never prints a verdict and never exits 2. Claude Code treats only exit 2 as blocking, and the adapter comment at main.rs:352-353 says so. A timed-out hook is therefore a non-blocking failure, and the tool runs ungated. That contradicts the adapter's stated fail-closed rule. guardrail.gate is registered with plain engine.register (handlers/guardrail.rs:304), so it runs under the store mutex. Its write path can run git status with a 10 s timeout (guardrail.rs:665-680, GIT_TIMEOUT at :1120), so gates from many sessions queue behind each other. I could not confirm the provider's exact timeout semantics from the repo.
v1.correction: The most realistic trigger is a hung or deadlocked engine (or a long mutex holder), not ordinary gate queuing. A dead engine fails fast at connect and correctly exits 2. The fix is as proposed: wrap connect and call in tokio::time::timeout below 30 s (for example 25 s), and on expiry print the unavailable message and return 2. Share one helper between both adapters, since the two bodies after building the payload are near-duplicates (main.rs:463-485 vs 516-530).

findings.title: All three stdio MCP servers handle requests one at a time and ignore notifications/cancelled, so one long bus.wait, render or build blocks every later call
findings.evidence: `for line in lines { ... handle(instance, &actor, token.as_deref(), message).await ... }` processes requests strictly in sequence. `let Some(id) = message.get("id").cloned() else { return None; }` drops every notification, including cancellations. bus.wait is exposed as a tool and blocks up to `timeout_ms.clamp(1_000, 3_600_000)` (socket.rs:408-410). The guardrail hint tells agents to "wait for guardrail.request_resolved". blender.rs:37-51 and unreal.rs:57-76 use the same loop around synchronous subprocesses: renders up to 3600 s, builds up to 7200 s.
findings.impact: Suppose an agent calls bus.wait with a long timeout and is then interrupted, or issues parallel tool calls. Every later Relay tool call queues behind the wait for up to an hour. The client's cancellation is never read, so after a client-side timeout the server is still blocked and each following call times out too. A cancelled Blender render or Unreal build keeps running to its timeout and blocks that server in the same way.
findings.fix: Read stdin on its own task. Spawn each request as a task that writes through a shared `Mutex<BufWriter<Stdout>>`. Keep a map from request id to AbortHandle and abort on notifications/cancelled; dropping the socket ends the wait. For the synchronous servers, run each call on a thread and kill its child process group on cancel.

v1.reason: mcp.rs:16-33 reads stdin lines and awaits handle() for each one in turn. handle (37-41) returns None for any message without an id, so notifications/cancelled is dropped. bus.wait is exposed: exposed() at 159-163 excludes only stream ops, TauriOnly ops and bus.subscribe/unsubscribe, and bus_wait appears in the live MCP tool list. socket.rs:408-410 clamps its timeout to 1 s through 3600 s. So after a long bus.wait is interrupted or times out on the client, every later Relay tool call from that agent queues behind it until the wait ends. blender.rs:35-51 uses the same sequential loop with synchronous handling, and the unreal server is reported to do the same.
v1.correction: The impact is per agent: each agent has its own stdio server process, so only that agent's Relay tools stall, not the engine or other sessions. Medium fits. For the async relay server, a smaller fix than full multiplexing: spawn each tools/call as a task with a shared, serialized stdout writer, and abort a task on notifications/cancelled by request id. Aborting drops the socket, which ends the wait on the engine side.

findings.title: blender_python crashes the Blender MCP server when the agent's code emits a non-object (serde_json IndexMut panic)
findings.evidence: `let mut value = match result { Some(json_text) => serde_json::from_str(json_text)?, None => json!({}) }; if body == PY_RUN { value["output"] = json!(tail(...)); value["saved"] = ...; }`. run.py:186 puts `emit` into the agent's scope (`scope = {..., "emit": emit}`). serde_json 1.0.151 index.rs:96-103 shows that inserting a key into a value that is neither an object nor null does `panic!("cannot access key {:?} in JSON {}")`.
findings.impact: blender_python with `emit([o.name for o in bpy.data.objects])`, `emit(3)` or `print("RELAY_JSON:[1]")` makes the MCP server panic on the main thread and exit with code 101. Stdio MCP servers are not restarted, so every Blender tool is gone for the rest of that agent session.
findings.fix: Before inserting output/saved, wrap a non-object result: `if !value.is_object() { value = json!({"result": value}); }`. Alternatively, have run.py emit its own result object and ignore RELAY_JSON lines printed by agent code.

v1.reason: In blender.rs:362-373 the last `RELAY_JSON:` line on stdout is parsed into `value`. For PY_RUN the code then does `value["output"] = ...` and `value["saved"] = ...`. In serde_json 1.0.151 (the version in Cargo.lock), index.rs index_or_insert turns Null into an object and panics (`cannot access key ... in JSON ...`) for any other non-object value. run.py:5 puts `emit` (common.py:12, which prints `RELAY_JSON:` + json.dumps(value)) into the agent's exec scope. So `emit([..])`, `emit(3)`, `emit("x")` or a printed `RELAY_JSON:[1]` line panics on the main thread of `relay blender-mcp`. There is no catch_unwind anywhere in blender.rs or main.rs, so the process exits and every Blender tool is gone for that client until the server is restarted.
v1.correction: Downgraded to low because the trigger is rare: `emit` is not mentioned in the blender_python tool description or in any shipped skill, so an agent hits this only by guessing the helper or by printing the RELAY_JSON: prefix itself. Fix: wrap a non-object result (`if !value.is_object() { value = json!({"result": value}) }`), or have run.py ignore RELAY_JSON lines that appear between RELAY_OUT_BEGIN and RELAY_OUT_END.

findings.title: Blender job output is unbounded both in MCP-server memory and in the reply: tail() caps lines but not bytes, unlike the Unreal server's tail
findings.evidence: `relay_core::proc::output_with_timeout(&mut command, timeout)` buffers all of stdout/stderr (`read_to_end`, proc.rs:78-84). The code then copies it with `String::from_utf8_lossy` and `printed.join("\n")`. blender.rs:386-389 `tail` returns the last N lines with no byte limit. unreal.rs:1590 `tail` cuts at MAX_OUTPUT = 60_000 bytes on a char boundary, so the duplicate has already diverged.
findings.impact: Suppose agent code is stuck in a printing loop, e.g. `while f < end: print(f)` with no increment. It runs until timeout_s (300 s by default, 3600 s maximum) while the MCP server stores gigabytes and then copies them twice more, which can exhaust memory on the user's desktop. A single long print such as `print(list(me.vertices))` on a large mesh returns megabytes in `output`, twice (text content and structuredContent). That overflows the client's tool-output limit, and the result, including `saved`, is lost.
findings.fix: Cap the output at its source: in run.py, wrap sys.stdout in a writer that stops after N bytes and prints a truncation marker, or drain the pipes into a bounded buffer. Move unreal.rs's byte-capped tail into a shared module and use it for `output` and failure_text.

v1.reason: proc.rs:78-84 drain() does read_to_end with no limit, so a blender_python run keeps everything Blender writes until it exits or reaches timeout_s (default 300 s, clamped to at most 3600 s, blender.rs:249). blender.rs:356-372 then builds a Vec<&str> of every printed line and join()s it into a new String before tail() keeps 300 lines. tail() at blender.rs:386-389 limits lines but not bytes, while unreal.rs:1590-1601 cuts its tail at MAX_OUTPUT = 60_000 bytes, so the two copies have already diverged. An agent script stuck in a print loop can fill several GB in the MCP process before the timeout. A single huge print (one long line) passes through the 300-line tail intact and is serialized twice by tool_result, once as pretty text and once as structuredContent (unreal.rs:1890-1895).
v1.correction: Small correction: String::from_utf8_lossy borrows (Cow) when the output is valid UTF-8, so the extra copies come from the Vec of line slices and from join(), not from from_utf8_lossy. The fix is a bounded drain: an output_with_timeout variant with a byte cap that keeps only the tail, or a size-capped stdout wrapper in run.py. Use a shared byte-capped tail for `output` and for failure_text.

findings.title: The fail-closed hook adapters (Claude/Codex PreToolUse translation, Edit/MultiEdit reconstruction, path relativization) have no tests
findings.evidence: main.rs has no #[test] at all. relay-cli has no tests directory and nothing uses CARGO_BIN_EXE. crates/relay-core/tests/guardrails.rs only checks that the installed command strings contain "hook claude-report" / "hook codex-pre-tool" (lines 437, 507-509). Everything in main.rs:393-581 is exercised only by hand.
findings.impact: Whether every Claude/Codex write and command is gated depends on this code, and it can regress silently. Several defects in this audit sit in it untested: the missing deadline, the Codex exec mapping, and Edit semantics.
findings.fix: Factor out a pure `gate_payload(tool, tool_input, session, worktree) -> Result<Value>`. Unit-test it with real hook JSON samples: Write, Edit with replace_all, MultiEdit order, missing fields, paths inside and outside the worktree, `..`, apply_patch. Add an integration test that runs the hook binary against `relay serve --instance test` and checks exit codes 0 and 2.

v1.reason: I confirmed main.rs has no #[cfg(test)] module. The only tests in relay-cli are in unreal_process.rs and blender.rs. No tests/ directory exists and nothing uses CARGO_BIN_EXE. The only repo references to the adapters outside main.rs are the installer string checks (relay-core/tests/guardrails.rs:507 and hooks.rs constants). claude_pre_tool, codex_pre_tool, required_string and hook_relative_path (main.rs:393-581) are the fail-closed enforcement path for every Claude and Codex write and command, and they are untested. At least one real defect sits in this code: Codex apply_patch is sent as kind exec (cli-main#10). A payload-level test would have caught it.
v1.correction: The Edit-semantics defect it cites is low and only plausible (cli-main#17). The point stands because of the apply_patch mapping and the fail-open timeout. Factoring a pure `gate_payload(tool, tool_input, input, worktree)` and unit-testing it is the right shape, and it needs no engine. An integration test against `relay serve --instance test` is optional extra coverage.

findings.title: blender_rig_check re-implements the mesh check on the raw mesh with different severities, so it passes rigs that blender_export then refuses (and the reverse)
findings.evidence: rig_check.py:106-121 runs `bm.from_mesh(me)` on the un-evaluated `o.data`. Missing UVs is a `problem`, zero-area faces only a `warn` (lines 118-119), and zero-length edges are not checked. common.py:146-181 `mesh_report`, which blender_export uses (export.py:39-53), measures the evaluated mesh (modifiers applied). There, zero-area faces and zero-length edges are problems that make export refuse, and missing UVs is only a warning.
findings.impact: Take a skinned mesh whose bevel or solidify modifier collapses faces, or that has a degenerate face. blender_rig_check reports passed=true, then blender_export refuses it as "not exported, the result would be broken". A rig without UVs fails the rig check but exports. Agents told to check a rig before export get contradictory verdicts.
findings.fix: Have rig_check call `mesh_report(o)` for each skinned mesh and merge its problems and warnings, keeping only the weight/influence checks that are specific to skinning. Delete the duplicated bmesh block and decide UV severity in one place.

v1.reason: rig_check.py:72 takes `me = o.data` (the raw mesh) and runs its own bmesh pass at lines 108-121. A missing UV map is a `problem` (line 106-107), zero-area faces only a `warn` (118-119), and zero-length edges are not checked. common.py:146-181 `mesh_report`, which export.py:39 uses to decide whether to refuse, measures the evaluated mesh. There, zero-area faces (165-166) and zero-length edges (167-168) are problems, and a missing UV map is only a warning (175-176). Two triggers follow. (1) A skinned mesh whose bevel or solidify collapses faces: rig_check sees the raw mesh, warns or says nothing, and can report passed=true, then blender_export raises 'not exported, the result would be broken'. (2) A rig without UVs fails the rig check, yet exports without complaint. The duplicated logic has already diverged, which fits the rubric's medium example.
v1.correction: The cost is a wasted round trip and contradictory guidance, not broken output, because export still refuses on its own check. When unifying, keep in mind that mesh_report's evaluated mesh of a skinned object includes the Armature modifier at the current pose, while the FBX exporter writes the undeformed mesh for skeletal exports. The shared check should disable or skip the armature modifier, or pose at rest, or posed geometry will produce findings that depend on the current frame. Decide UV severity in one place.

findings.title: Codex apply_patch/Edit/Write are sent to guardrail.gate as kind "exec", so write policy (protected paths, write roots, rewrite caps) never runs for Codex file edits
findings.evidence: `let command = required_string(tool_input, "command")?; ... "Bash" | "apply_patch" | "Edit" | "Write" => json!({"session": session, "kind": "exec", "command": command})`. guardrail.rs:811-846 evaluate_exec only checks self_approval and denied_commands. evaluate_write, with write_target and protected paths, is reached only for kind "write". providers.rs:212 reports Codex as `guarded() == true`, and the Claude adapter sends Write/Edit as kind "write".
findings.impact: If Codex puts the patch text in `command`, a patch editing protected files or files outside the session's write roots passes the hook unless the text matches a denied-command pattern. Only the pre-commit gate sees in-repo changes, at commit time, and nothing sees writes outside the repository. If Codex's Edit/Write payloads carry file_path/content rather than `command`, every such call fails closed with "hook input field command is missing". Either way the mapping is wrong. I could not verify Codex's exact PreToolUse payload in this repo.
findings.fix: Send only Bash as exec. For apply_patch, parse the envelope (`*** Add File:`, `*** Update File:`, `*** Delete File:`, `*** Move to:`) and gate each path as kind "write", with new_text where it can be computed. Map Edit/Write the way the Claude adapter does.

v1.reason: codex_pre_tool (main.rs:507-514) requires tool_input.command for every tool and maps `"Bash" | "apply_patch" | "Edit" | "Write"` to `{kind: "exec", command}`. evaluate (guardrail.rs:465-471) sends Exec to evaluate_exec (guardrail.rs:811-846), which only checks self_approval and denied_commands. Protected paths, write roots, shape gates and destructive-rewrite caps live only in evaluate_write (guardrail.rs:503-570). So a Codex apply_patch is never judged as a write, while providers.rs:212 reports Codex `guarded() == true` and Claude's Write and Edit go through kind write. Codex's hook surface carries the patch body in tool_input.command (Edit and Write are matcher aliases for apply_patch), so the main branch is the one that occurs. There is also a second effect the finding missed: the patch text is fed to the shell-word parser. denied_matches (guardrail.rs:969-998) looks for any unquoted word window, so a patch whose context lines (which start with a space) contain e.g. `rm -rf build` or `git push --force` is refused as a denied command. Mitigation: D132 (DECISIONS.md:650-655) names the git pre-commit gate as the final write-set boundary, and that still catches protected in-repo paths at commit. Claude's Bash writes also skip write policy. Writes outside the worktree and destructive rewrites of uncommitted files are not caught by anything at write time.
v1.correction: Confirmed for apply_patch. The "Edit/Write fail closed for a missing command" branch probably does not occur, since those are aliases. There is also docs drift: BUS.md:524-530 still says Codex has no tool hooks and is labelled unguarded, while providers.rs:212 returns guarded() true. Fix: send only Bash as exec. Parse the apply_patch envelope (`*** Add File:`, `*** Update File:`, `*** Delete File:`, `*** Move to:`) and gate each path as kind write, with new_text for Add, the diff for Update, and a destructive check for Delete. Do not run patch bodies through the exec parser.

findings.title: launch() hands the agent's RELAY_SESSION/RELAY_TOKEN to an editor that deliberately outlives the agent
findings.evidence: `let mut command = std::process::Command::new(&binary); ... command.process_group(0);` has no env_remove, and the code comment says "the editor outlives this MCP server and the agent". The MCP server's environment carries RELAY_SESSION, RELAY_TOKEN, RELAY_WORKTREE and RELAY_PROJECT (handlers/session.rs:565-569). The generated pre-commit hook gates as the agent whenever RELAY_SESSION is set (hooks.rs:124).
findings.impact: Under D160's primary-checkout default, the editor an agent launches is the human's editor. A commit the human makes from the editor's Git integration inherits the agent's identity. While the session lives, it is judged against the agent's role caps and audited as the agent. Any `relay` call from processes the editor spawns also acts as the agent.
findings.fix: Call `command.env_remove("RELAY_SESSION").env_remove("RELAY_TOKEN")`, plus the other per-session RELAY_* variables, before spawning the editor.

v1.reason: unreal_process.rs:285-307 builds the editor Command with no env_clear or env_remove, so the editor inherits the MCP server's whole environment. That environment does hold the agent identity. handlers/session.rs puts RELAY_SESSION, RELAY_TOKEN, RELAY_PROJECT, RELAY_WORKTREE, RELAY_STORE and the others into the agent's spawn env. unreal.rs:511 (holder_id) itself reads RELAY_SESSION inside unreal-mcp, which confirms the variable reaches this process. The comment at unreal_process.rs:301 says the editor is meant to outlive the MCP server and the agent. D160 (DECISIONS.md:930) makes the primary checkout, and so the human's one shared editor, the default for Unreal projects. The pre-commit hook generated in hooks.rs (the `if [ -n "${RELAY_SESSION:-}" ]` branch) gates a commit as the agent session whenever RELAY_SESSION is set, and main.rs:122-123 makes any `relay` CLI call act as the session when RELAY_SESSION/RELAY_TOKEN are present. So a commit the human makes through the editor's Git integration, or any relay call from a process the editor spawns, is judged and audited as the agent. After the session ends, that gate is presumably refused with the stale identity.
v1.correction: Severity stays low. This does not escalate privilege: the editor already runs code the agent wrote, and it acts with the agent's own identity and caps. The real harm is misattribution and wrong gating of the human's commits made from the editor, which is an uncommon flow. A more precise category would be a correctness/attribution bug with a security flavor. Fix: env_remove RELAY_SESSION, RELAY_TOKEN, RELAY_BRIEF, RELAY_WORKTREE, RELAY_PROJECT (and, if wanted, RELAY_STORE/RELAY_BIN/RELAY_INSTANCE) on `command` before spawn.

findings.title: prebuild kills every CrashReportClient on the machine, not only those belonging to this project
findings.evidence: `crash_reporters()` selects every process whose exe name starts with "CrashReportClient". prebuild runs `for r in &reporters { if kill(r.pid) { killed.push(r.pid) } }`, and ue_build calls it with kill enabled unless keep_crash_reporters is true (unreal.rs:1521).
findings.impact: Suppose the user's other Unreal project crashed and its crash dialog is open. An agent's ue_build on a different project kills that reporter and the crash report is lost.
findings.fix: Kill only reporters whose command line references this project (its Saved/Crashes path or name) or this engine root, and report the others without killing them.

v1.reason: crash_reporters() (unreal_process.rs:61-63) returns every process whose exe name starts with CrashReportClient. prebuild (209-226) kills all of them when kill_crash_reporters is true, and build passes `args["keep_crash_reporters"] != true` (unreal.rs:1521), so killing is the default. Nothing filters by project or engine. The stated reason, that a leftover reporter makes UBT build a hot-reload module, only applies to a reporter for this project's editor, so killing reporters for other projects buys nothing and drops their crash reports.
v1.correction: The trigger needs two Unreal projects in use on one machine and a crash dialog open on the other one, so low is right. Filter on the reporter's cmdline: it normally carries the crashed app's Saved/Crashes path or project name. Report non-matching reporters without killing them.

findings.title: The launched editor's Child is dropped without being reaped, so every editor exit leaves a zombie under the MCP server
findings.evidence: `let child = command.spawn()...?; Ok(child.id())`. Dropping a `Child` does not wait on it, and process_group(0) does not change the parent process.
findings.impact: Each editor started by unreal-mcp becomes a defunct process when it quits or crashes and stays one until the MCP server exits. The documented Linux C++ loop (ue_build restart_editor=true) leaves one zombie per cycle.
findings.fix: Reap it on a detached thread: `std::thread::spawn(move || { let _ = child.wait(); });`, or double-fork/setsid so init reaps it.

v1.reason: unreal_process.rs:306-307 does `let child = command.spawn()...?; Ok(child.id())`. std::process::Child does not wait on drop, process_group(0) only sets the process group, and relay-cli never sets SIGCHLD to SIG_IGN (the only signal handling is SIGTERM in remote.rs:143). The long-lived unreal-mcp stdio server therefore stays the parent, and every editor it launched becomes a zombie when it exits, until the MCP server exits. I checked for a functional knock-on: editors_for/processes (unreal_process.rs:28-57) skip any pid whose /proc/<pid>/exe readlink fails, and that readlink fails for a zombie. So quit_editor's wait loop and the launch 'already_running' check do not see the zombie, and there is no hang.
v1.correction: The impact is only defunct process-table entries, one per editor launched by a given MCP server instance and bounded by that agent session's lifetime, so low is right. Fix: reap on a detached thread (`std::thread::spawn(move || { let _ = child.wait(); })`) or double-fork. The thread is simpler and keeps the pid valid for the return value.

findings.title: port_of parses UE_REMOTE_CONTROL_URL differently from remote_at, so launch/quit can wait on a different port than the one requests use
findings.evidence: port_of: `url.rsplit(':').next().and_then(|p| p.trim_end_matches('/').parse().ok()).unwrap_or(30010)`. remote_at (unreal.rs:1798) takes `host = rest.trim_end_matches('/').split('/').next()` and uses port 80 when the URL has none.
findings.impact: With `http://127.0.0.1:31000/remote`, port_of returns 30010 ("31000/remote" does not parse) while requests go to 31000. With `http://localhost`, port_of says 30010 while requests go to 80. wait_port_free, the launch preflight and the status advice then check the wrong port.
findings.fix: Parse the URL once with a shared `fn remote_addr(base) -> (String, u16)` and use it from both places.

v1.reason: unreal_process.rs:255-257 `port_of` takes `url.rsplit(':').next()`, trims trailing '/', parses, and falls back to 30010. remote_at (unreal.rs:1796-1799) takes the host[:port] segment before the first '/' and appends :80 when there is no port. So for `http://127.0.0.1:31000/remote`, port_of gets "31000/remote", which does not parse, and returns 30010 while requests connect to 31000. For `http://localhost`, port_of gets "//localhost" and returns 30010 while requests go to 80. port_of feeds quit_editor's wait_port_free (unreal.rs:609), launch_editor's preflight and bind message (unreal.rs:630/649, then unreal_process::launch, which waits 90 s on that port), and the status advice (unreal.rs:1652). Both values come from remote_base(), which reads UE_REMOTE_CONTROL_URL (unreal.rs:1630). The existing tests (unreal_process.rs:342-343) cover only host:port with an optional trailing slash.
v1.correction: This is a bug from two parsers that disagree, not a duplication cost. It is rare in practice. remote_at ignores any base path (the request line uses only the `path` argument), so a user has no reason to put a path in UE_REMOTE_CONTROL_URL, and an editor serving Remote Control on port 80 is unusual. The worst outcome is a 90 s wait or a misleading port in the advice text. Fix: derive the port from the same host[:port] split remote_at uses, through one shared helper.

findings.title: Every client-side error exits 5 ("engine unreachable"), including bad JSON, bus.project_required and typed bus.ops refusals
findings.evidence: `Err(e) => { eprintln!("relay: {e:#}"); ExitCode::from(EXIT_UNREACHABLE) }` turns every anyhow error from run() into exit 5. That includes "payload is not JSON", "payload must be a JSON object", the bus.project_required bail (line 185), a bad --instance, an unknown op in `relay schema`, and `bail!("bus.ops failed: {} {}")` for a typed engine refusal (line 285). BUS.md §8.2 defines 5 as "engine unreachable" and 1 as invalid.
findings.impact: Scripts and agents that branch on the exit code (Codex reaches the bus through `$RELAY_BIN q`) treat a malformed payload or a missing project as "engine down" and retry or restart the engine instead of fixing the call.
findings.fix: Return a typed error from run(). Map connect failures to 5, client-side validation errors and bus.project_required to 1, and engine errors to their kind's exit code.

v1.reason: main.rs:105-114 maps every Err from run() to `ExitCode::from(EXIT_UNREACHABLE)` (5). The errors that reach it include read_payload's "payload is not JSON" (main.rs:137), "payload must be a JSON object" (main.rs:595), the bus.project_required bail in fill_project (main.rs:185), `bad --instance` (main.rs:197), `unknown op` in `relay schema` (main.rs:228) and `bail!("bus.ops failed: {} {}")` (main.rs:285). BUS.md:421 defines 5 as "engine unreachable", 1 as invalid, and so on, and ErrorKind::exit_code (relay-bus/src/error.rs:21) already does the per-kind mapping for engine replies. So the CLI breaks its own documented contract. Impact is limited: I found no in-repo consumer that branches on exit 5 (RELAY_BIN users only read stdout and stderr), and the stderr text names the real cause. Agent sessions export RELAY_PROJECT (handlers/session.rs:568), so the project_required path is rare for agents.
v1.correction: Lines are correct: the catch-all is at main.rs:110-113. Impact is mostly docs-drift against BUS.md §8.2. No script or agent in the repo is known to retry on 5. A simple fix is a small typed error (or a downcast marker) so run() returns 1 for client-side validation and 5 only for connect() failures. The `bus.ops failed` refusal should use e.kind.exit_code().

findings.title: hook_relative_path duplicates the gate's worktree relativization with weaker root sources; the gate call is also duplicated in both adapters
findings.evidence: hook_relative_path strips RELAY_WORKTREE, falling back to the hook input's `cwd` and then to the cwd's repo root, and rejects the worktree itself. guardrail.rs write_target (623-661) already does this for absolute paths, against the session's authoritative worktree, and also rejects `..`. RELAY_WORKTREE is always set for sessions (session.rs:569), so the fallbacks never help. claude_pre_tool lines 465-483 and codex_pre_tool lines 516-530 contain the same gate call and refusal printing.
findings.impact: There are two notions of "the worktree". If they ever disagree, e.g. RELAY_WORKTREE is missing and `cwd` is a subdirectory after a `cd`, the hook sends a path relative to the wrong root and the gate judges a different file (protected `src/x` is judged as `x`). The gate logic is also maintained twice.
findings.fix: Pass `file_path` unchanged (absolute) and let the gate relativize it, then delete hook_relative_path. Factor out `async fn gate(instance, actor_override, tool, payload) -> Result<u8>` and use it from both adapters.

v1.reason: main.rs:567-582 hook_relative_path strips RELAY_WORKTREE (falling back to input cwd, then cwd_repo_root) and rejects the worktree root. guardrail.rs:623-661 write_target already strips request.worktree from absolute paths, rejects the worktree itself and rejects `..`; a relative path goes through relative_path (1135), which also rejects `..`. RELAY_WORKTREE is set from row.session.worktree (handlers/session.rs:569), the same session row the gate uses, and claude_pre_tool already requires RELAY_SESSION (main.rs:403). So the fallbacks are effectively dead, and sending the absolute path would give the same verdict. The gate call and refusal printing at main.rs:465-483 and 516-530 are line-for-line copies.
v1.correction: The impact scenario (RELAY_WORKTREE missing while cwd is a subdirectory) is practically unreachable for Relay-spawned sessions, so this is cleanup with no current misbehavior. The category is duplication rather than overengineering. The fix as proposed is sound: send file_path unchanged so write_target relativizes it, delete hook_relative_path, and factor the gate request plus refusal printing into one helper shared by both adapters.

findings.title: Edit hook translation blocks edits Claude itself would perform (new file via empty old_string, non-UTF-8 files) and reports them as infrastructure failure
findings.evidence: `let current = std::fs::read_to_string(file_path).with_context(|| format!("reading edit target {file_path}"))?; if !current.contains(old) { bail!(...) }`. Any read error or failed byte match exits 2 with "RELAY guardrail unavailable". When old_string is empty and the file exists, `replacen("", new, 1)` prepends the new text.
findings.impact: Claude's Edit can create a missing file with an empty old_string, as far as I know. It can also edit a UTF-16 or Latin-1 file, or match after its own quote and line-ending normalisation. In each case the hook blocks the edit and labels it a guardrail infrastructure failure. I could not check Claude Code's current Edit matching rules from this repo.
findings.fix: When the target is missing and old_string is empty, gate new_string as the whole new_text. On read or match failure, gate a path-only write and let the gate decide instead of reporting an infrastructure failure. Cover these cases with tests.

v1.reason: The adapter code does what is claimed. main.rs:422-426 does `std::fs::read_to_string(file_path)` then `if !current.contains(old) bail!`. Any error turns into exit 2 with "RELAY guardrail unavailable: reading edit target ..." (main.rs:348-357). A missing file, or one that is not UTF-8 (read_to_string fails on UTF-16 or Latin-1), therefore blocks the Edit as an infrastructure failure, not as a policy decision. Claude Code's Edit tool has historically created a new file when old_string is empty, and it applies its own quote normalisation when matching. Neither behaviour can be verified from this repo. The failure is closed, not open, and Claude normally recovers by using Write. The real cost is friction plus a misleading "unavailable" label. When old_string is empty and the file exists and is empty, replacen yields new_string, which is correct. When the file is non-empty, Claude itself rejects the edit, so the prepend case does not matter.
v1.correction: The decisive code is at main.rs:422-425. The gate already accepts a `diff` instead of new_text for kind write (guardrail.rs:525-541), and it holds shape-gated paths conservatively. A better fallback than a path-only write is therefore: a missing target with empty old_string becomes new_text = new_string, and a read or match failure becomes path plus diff, or path-only, and the gate decides.

findings.title: On a failed blender_python run, the agent's own printed output is dropped from the error
findings.evidence: `let all: Vec<&str> = stdout.lines().chain(stderr.lines()).collect(); let start = all.iter().position(|l| l.starts_with("Traceback")).unwrap_or(...)`. Python's traceback goes to stderr, so `start` falls inside the stderr part. Every stdout line, including the agent's prints between RELAY_OUT_BEGIN and RELAY_OUT_END, is cut.
findings.impact: An agent's script that prints intermediate values and then raises returns only the traceback. That defeats the usual print-and-retry debugging loop the tool description invites.
findings.fix: When body == PY_RUN, put the `printed` block, tailed and byte-capped, in front of the traceback in the error.

v1.reason: When the agent's code raises, run.py:7-10 prints RELAY_OUT_END in its finally block and lets the exception escape. Blender writes the traceback to stderr, and `--python-exit-code 1` makes the exit status non-zero, so blender.rs:364 bails with failure_text(). At blender.rs:381-384, `all` is the stdout lines followed by the stderr lines, and `start` is the first line beginning with "Traceback", which lies in the stderr part. Everything on stdout, including the agent's printed block, is therefore cut. The error the agent gets holds only the traceback.
v1.correction: Related gap: on timeout (`Ok(None)`, blender.rs:353-354), stdout and stderr are discarded entirely, so a hung script also returns none of its prints. For PY_RUN, put the `printed` block (tailed and byte-capped) in front of the traceback, in both the failure case and the timeout case.

findings.title: blender_export's in-checkout path rule is bypassed by fbx_options.filepath, after which the tool also reports a false failure
findings.evidence: blender.rs:236 sets `a["path"] = json!(resolve_new(&root, required(args, "path")?, "fbx")?)`, but export.py:78-79 runs `for key, value in (ARGS.get("fbx_options") or {}).items(): options[key] = ...`, so `filepath` and `use_selection` can be overridden. Line 102 then calls `os.path.getsize(path)` on the original path. resolve_new (blender.rs:266) checks components but does not resolve symlinked parents.
findings.impact: `fbx_options: {"filepath": "/elsewhere/x.fbx"}` writes outside the checkout, contradicting D161 and mcp-tools.md ("files outside it are refused"). The tool then fails with FileNotFoundError even though the file was written.
findings.fix: Strip or refuse `filepath`, `use_selection` and `check_existing` in fbx_options on the Rust side, and canonicalize the existing parent in resolve_new.

v1.reason: blender.rs:236 confines `path` with resolve_new, but export.py:78-79 copies every key of `fbx_options` over `options`, including `filepath`, `use_selection` and `check_existing`. The tool description itself says 'fbx_options overrides any exporter option'. With `fbx_options: {"filepath": "/elsewhere/x.fbx"}` the FBX is written outside the checkout, then line 80 creates the original directory and line 102 calls `os.path.getsize(path)` on the original path, which does not exist. The tool reports a failure (FileNotFoundError traceback) after it has in fact written a file. Overriding use_selection=False likewise exports the whole scene, while the report and its size_cm describe only the selected objects.
v1.correction: This is not a security finding. The same MCP server offers `blender_python` (blender.rs:202-213), which runs arbitrary agent Python in Blender and can write anywhere, so the checkout rule on export paths is a convenience, not a boundary. The symlinked-parent point in resolve_new is moot for the same reason. The real defect is the false failure, plus confusing reports when filepath or use_selection is overridden. Fix: drop or refuse filepath, use_selection and check_existing from fbx_options on the Rust side (or in export.py), and report `options['filepath']` if overriding stays allowed.

findings.title: blender_to_unreal checks destination, the editor and its lock only after a Blender export of up to 600 s
findings.evidence: `let exported = run(PY_EXPORT, ..., Duration::from_secs(600))?;` runs before `required(args, "destination")?` (line 405) and before `crate::unreal::import_fbx` (line 414), which is where Project::find, guard_project and acquire_lock run.
findings.impact: A missing destination, a closed editor, an editor open on another checkout, or a lock held by another agent is only reported after a full export. By then the export has already overwritten `Saved/Relay/Exports/<name>.fbx` (check_existing=False).
findings.fix: Validate destination and run an import preflight (Project::find, guard_project, lock check) before exporting, e.g. by exposing `crate::unreal::import_preflight()`.

v1.reason: In to_unreal (blender.rs:391-423), `run(PY_EXPORT, ..., Duration::from_secs(600))` runs before `required(args, "destination")?` and before `crate::unreal::import_fbx`. import_fbx (unreal.rs:419-422) is the first place that calls Project::find, guard_project (which needs the open editor's project) and acquire_lock. A closed editor, an editor open on another checkout, a lock held by another agent, a checkout without a .uproject, or a missing destination (the MCP server publishes `required` in the schema but does not enforce it server-side) is therefore reported only after the Blender export finishes. By then the export has overwritten Saved/Relay/Exports/<stem>.fbx (check_existing=False).
v1.correction: 600 s is the timeout, not the usual duration. A typical export takes seconds to tens of seconds, so the payoff is modest. A preflight lock check is also only advisory, since the lock can change during the export: still take the lock in import_fbx and add a cheap early check (destination, Project::find, guard_project, read_lock) before exporting.

findings.title: The round-trip height check compares a posed Blender bounding box with the reference-pose bounds of the imported skeletal mesh
findings.evidence: `let blender_height = exported["size_cm"][2].as_f64();`. export.py:85/109 computes size_cm from `world_bbox(meshes)` on evaluated, armature-deformed meshes at scene.frame_current after set_action. import_fbx.py:73-74 measures `a.get_bounds()` of the imported SkeletalMesh, which is the reference pose.
findings.impact: Take a skeletal export with an action whose current frame is a crouch, prone or jump pose. blender_to_unreal reports "X is N cm tall in Unreal but M cm in Blender ... check the object's scale", a false scale problem that sends the agent to change correct settings.
findings.fix: In export.py, measure skeletal exports at rest: temporarily set `arm.data.pose_position = 'REST'` around world_bbox, or use undeformed mesh bounds.

v1.reason: export.py:30-33 assigns the requested action (`set_action`). When no action is passed, the armature keeps any action it already has. After the FBX export, line 85 measures `world_bbox(meshes)`. world_bbox (common.py:99-108) uses `o.evaluated_get(deps).bound_box`, which includes the Armature modifier at the current frame. The FBX exporter restores the scene's current frame after baking, so the measured mesh is posed. On the Unreal side, import_fbx.py:67-74 measures `a.get_bounds().box_extent` of the imported SkeletalMesh, which reflects the bind (reference) pose. The FBX carries the undeformed skeletal mesh. compare (blender.rs:442-461) flags any ratio outside 0.9-1.1. Trigger: a skeletal blender_to_unreal of a character whose assigned action at the current frame is a crouch, prone, jump or wide-arm pose. The result is a false 'N cm tall in Unreal but M cm in Blender ... check the object's scale' problem and passed=false. kind=animation selects only the armature, so size_cm is None there and the check does not apply.
v1.correction: Fix in export.py: for skeletal exports, measure with `arm.data.pose_position = 'REST'` (and a depsgraph update) around world_bbox, or measure the bounds of the undeformed mesh. Confidence is moderate: the posed state after export depends on the exporter restoring the frame, which it does via frame_set. Upright idle poses stay within the 10% tolerance, so only strongly non-rest poses trigger it.

findings.title: The stdio JSON-RPC loop, initialize negotiation and protocol constants are copied three times (relay mcp, unreal-mcp, blender-mcp)
findings.evidence: blender.rs:34-87, unreal.rs:57-111 and mcp.rs:16-74 each implement the same line loop, protocol negotiation, ping, tools/call name check and error codes. FALLBACK_PROTOCOL and SUPPORTED_PROTOCOLS are declared three times (blender.rs:19-20, unreal.rs:22-23, mcp.rs:13-14). mcp.rs::pattern_matches is a copy of the public relay_core::guardrail::op_matches. blender and unreal rebuild the whole tools() list on every call just to check a name.
findings.impact: Every protocol change has to be made three times: a new version string, cancellation, concurrent handling (the sequential-processing finding), or the server exiting on a non-UTF-8 stdin line.
findings.fix: Write one `stdio::serve(info, list_fn, call_fn)`, with an async variant for mcp.rs, and keep the protocol constants in one place. Call relay_core::guardrail::op_matches from mcp.rs.

v1.reason: blender.rs:34-87 and unreal.rs:57-110 are line-for-line the same serve() loop and handle() dispatch (initialize negotiation, ping, tools/list, the tools/call name check that rebuilds tools() just to find a name, the same error codes). Only the serverInfo and instructions strings differ. mcp.rs:16-74 repeats the same loop and negotiation in async form. FALLBACK_PROTOCOL/SUPPORTED_PROTOCOLS are declared identically at blender.rs:19-20, unreal.rs:22-23 and mcp.rs:13-14. mcp.rs:109 pattern_matches is a body-for-body copy of the public relay_core::guardrail::op_matches (guardrail.rs:455). Some sharing exists already: blender imports rpc_error, tool and tool_result from unreal.
