In all three loops, `line.context(...)?` ends the server on a non-UTF-8 stdin line, so a fix to that would also have to be made three times.
v1.correction: Blender and Unreal can share one sync serve(info, tools_fn, call_fn) helper. mcp.rs is async and maps call results differently (a -32603 transport error), so the realistic fix there is to share the protocol constants and initialize negotiation and to call guardrail::op_matches. Merging all three into one loop is not needed. The payoff is modest.

findings.title: The 500-file cap in blender_info's art-file listing is not enforced inside a directory, and truncation is never reported
findings.evidence: `if depth > 8 || out.len() >= 500 { return; }` is checked only when walk() starts. The per-directory loop keeps pushing files, including after a recursive call has returned with the list already full. The reply has no truncated flag.
findings.impact: A folder with thousands of .fbx or .obj files is returned in full (hundreds of KB of JSON) in one blender_info reply. A listing cut off at depth 8 or at the cap looks complete.
findings.fix: Check the cap inside the loop, break when it is reached, and return `truncated: true`.

v1.reason: blender.rs:274-292: `if depth > 8 || out.len() >= 500 { return; }` runs only when walk() is entered. The per-directory `for entry in entries` loop pushes every matching file without checking the cap, and it keeps pushing after a recursive walk() call has returned with the list full. A single folder of 3,000 .fbx files (common for animation libraries) is returned whole. The reply (`{root, files, blender, blender_problem}`) has no truncation flag, so a listing cut at 500 entries or at depth 9 looks complete. The reply is also pretty-printed twice by tool_result (as text and as structuredContent).
v1.correction: Check `out.len() >= 500` inside the loop and break there. Return a `truncated` flag, and report the depth cut as well.

results.coverage: I read every line of crates/relay-cli/src/unreal.rs (2170 lines, including its tests). To trace callers and callees I also read all of crates/relay-cli/src/unreal_process.rs, the blender.rs code that shares or calls this module (lines 1-130 and 370-430, plus its helper signatures), and mcp.rs lines 1-80 and 205-225. On the engine side I read relay-core hooks.rs (the PreToolUse matchers and MCP config), plugins.rs mcp_servers and handlers/session.rs plan_launch/prepare_launch. Embedded Python I read: common.py, project_check.py, data_table.py, asset_refs.py, preview_asset.py, play.py, capture.py and anim_preview.py in full, and blueprint_info.py, anim_inspect.py (result construction) and asset_audit.py (emit) in part. I did not read import_fbx.py. Docs I read: DECISIONS D159-D162, SPEC §5, BUS.md principle 6 and §9.1-9.3, the plugin's plugin.json, docs/setup.md and docs/mcp-tools.md, and grepped the plugin's skills for RunTests/ExecCmds. Two experiments in the scratchpad confirmed (a) serde_json-escaped strings round-trip as Python literals, including U+2028, NEL, NUL escapes and emoji, so no Python injection was found in py_str, script(), search_assets_script, level_actors_script or the ue_console path; and (b) the 60 KB truncation breaks RELAY_JSON parsing at about 300 actor rows. I checked the pedantic clippy casts for this file (lines 405, 788, 933, 1010-1012); none is a real bug on 64-bit targets. Not verifiable without engine source, so these findings carry medium or low confidence: UE's SIGTERM handling (I relied on the code's own note 'unsaved changes are lost'), the -ExecCmds comma split (I relied on the plugin's own docs), Remote Control's CORS/Host/passphrase defaults, the timing of log rotation at startup, and whether the CSV profiler can emit NaN. I did not run cargo, the app, or any mcp__relay__ tool. apps/relay-mobile was out of scope.

findings.title: python_tx cuts editor output to its last 60 KB before python_json_tx looks for the RELAY_JSON line, so any tool result over ~60 KB fails
findings.evidence: python_tx stores `"output": tail(&output.join("\n"), 2000)` (1707). tail() keeps only the last MAX_OUTPUT = 60_000 bytes: `if out.len() > MAX_OUTPUT { let mut cut = out.len() - MAX_OUTPUT; ... out = out[cut..].to_string(); }` (1593-1598). python_json_tx then searches that truncated text with `.find_map(|line| line.trim().strip_prefix("RELAY_JSON:"))` (1727) and otherwise bails with 'the editor script printed no result'. Every structured tool prints its whole result as one `RELAY_JSON:` line (unreal_py/common.py:8-9). I replayed the exact algorithm (scratchpad exp/tail_check.py) with ue_level_actors-shaped rows of 204 bytes each: 200 actors parse, but at 300 actors the prefix is cut off.
findings.impact: Ordinary calls fail and return a 60 KB dump instead of a result. Affected: ue_level_actors above ~290 actors (the schema allows limit 5000); ue_search_assets above ~350 (allows 2000); ue_data_table export of any table whose CSV is over ~45-50 KB, because the text is embedded in the result and JSON escaping inflates it; ue_blueprint_info on a folder (default limit 50, and each Blueprint carries up to 300 graph-node strings); ue_asset_audit with a few hundred findings; ue_anim_inspect with many samples or problems; and import_fbx. In that last case blender_to_unreal reports a failed import after a successful one, which invites a duplicate import.
findings.fix: Find the RELAY_JSON entry in the untruncated response["LogOutput"], searching entries in reverse, and parse it before any truncation. Apply tail/MAX_OUTPUT only to the human-readable `output`. For very large payloads, have the script write JSON to a file in a capture dir and return the path. Add a test with a RELAY_JSON line over 60 KB.

v1.reason: MAX_OUTPUT is 60_000 (unreal.rs:30). python_tx (1688-1714) joins every LogOutput entry and stores `tail(&output.join("\n"), 2000)` (1707). tail() (1590-1601) keeps the last 2000 lines and then, if the result is over MAX_OUTPUT bytes, cuts from the front. python_json_tx (1721-1730) searches only that truncated `output` for a line starting with "RELAY_JSON:". Every structured script prints its whole result on one line through common.py emit(), `print("RELAY_JSON:" + json.dumps(value))`. Once that one line is longer than ~60 KB, the front cut removes the "RELAY_JSON:" prefix, and the call bails with 'the editor script printed no result' followed by a 60 KB dump. Normal inputs reach this size. ue_data_table export embeds the whole CSV/JSON text in the result (data_table.py:8), and data_table() (966-973) has no other path, so even the `file` option, which exists for large tables, fails. ue_blueprint_info on a folder emits up to 300 node strings for each Blueprint (blueprint_info.py ~87). ue_level_actors and ue_search_assets fail above a few hundred rows; their defaults (200, 100) are under the limit, but their schema maximums (5000, 2000) are well over it. Nothing upstream raises the cap or retries.
v1.correction: Lines confirmed: tail at 1590-1601, the python_tx output at 1707, the RELAY_JSON search at 1727. The fix stands: take the RELAY_JSON entry from the raw response["LogOutput"] before any truncation, searching entries from the end, and cap only the human-readable `output`. A file hand-off for very large payloads is optional. The default-limit list/search calls are fine; the failures in a normal flow are data_table export and blueprint_info on folders.

v2.reason:
(a) The code does what is claimed, and I checked it end to end. MAX_OUTPUT is 60_000 (unreal.rs:30). python_tx stores `tail(&output.join("\n"), 2000)` (1707), and tail() keeps only the last 60,000 bytes (1593-1598). python_json_tx then looks for `RELAY_JSON:` only in that truncated text (1724-1728). Every structured script prints its whole result as one line through emit() (common.py:8-9).

I confirmed the engine side in the user's own UE 5.8.2 install:
- unreal_core.py:58 makes sys.stdout a line-buffered TextIOWrapper over _Logger.
- PyCore::Log broadcasts the full FString to the capture that fills LogOutput (PyCore.cpp:1176-1188, PythonScriptPlugin.cpp:1862).
- remote_at reads the reply with read_to_end (unreal.rs:1824).

So a RELAY_JSON line over ~60 KB reaches Relay whole, and tail() is the only thing that cuts it. The sibling blender.rs:362 does this correctly: it finds RELAY_JSON in the full stdout and tails only the printed text.

My replay of tail() (scratchpad exp/skeptic_tail.py) gives these failure points:
- data_table CSV export: about 52 KB of raw CSV (350 rows of 10 quoted fields fail; 300 pass).
- ue_level_actors with World Partition-style paths: about 245 rows. The default of 200 passes at 48.7 KB.
- ue_asset_audit: about 300 findings, while the script's own cap is 400 (asset_audit.py:13).
- ue_asset_refs: about 1,400 referencers.

(b) Who and how often: any agent using the Unreal plugin against a running editor, whenever one result is over ~60 KB.
- With default arguments: ue_data_table export of any medium-sized table, which has no size option. The `file` option does not help, because the call at line 967 fails before line 970 writes the file. A whole-/Game ue_asset_audit with 300+ findings also fails.
- Other triggers need non-default arguments: higher list limits, asset_refs at depth 2+ on a widely used asset, or anim_inspect with many samples and tracked points.
- Real usage: the user's Game2/game3 transcripts hold about 24 real calls (level_actors limit 60, search_assets limits 5/10/300, blueprint_info on 1-3 explicit paths). This error never appeared. data_table and asset_audit have never been called. Game4 has a single template-sized DataTable.

(c) When it fires, the tool returns isError "the editor script printed no result:" followed by the last 60,000 bytes of the cut-off JSON, about 15K tokens of noise in the agent's context. A retry fails the same way. Nothing is corrupted, and most of these tools are read-only. For import_fbx, the import has already finished and been saved and the render check is skipped, so blender_to_unreal reports a failure after a successful import. Workarounds exist: a lower limit, a narrower path, or ue_python writing the data to a file.

(d) Medium, not high. It is a real, deterministic bug, but it sits in less common paths: the default list limits stay under the cap, the default-argument triggers are unused so far, and there is no data loss, no hang and no silent wrong result. That matches the rubric's "real bug in a less common path", not "likely failure in a normal flow".

(e) The proposed fix is correct. Find RELAY_JSON in the untruncated output before tail(), and cap only the human-readable text.
v2.correction:
1. ue_blueprint_info is overstated. On UE 5.8 it never emits graph nodes: UEdGraph::Nodes is a bare `UPROPERTY()` (EdGraph.h:78-79), and PropertyAccessUtil::CanGetPropertyValue refuses any property without CPF_Edit or CPF_BlueprintVisible (PropertyAccessUtil.cpp:425-430). So blueprint_info.py:86 raises and stores nodes=None. A folder read can only overflow through variables, functions and components across many Blueprints. That is still possible at limit 50, but it is not the "300 node strings per Blueprint" case, and it is not shown to be a normal-flow failure.

2. import_fbx does not "invite a duplicate import". run_import sets replace_existing=True (import_fbx.py:56), so a re-run replaces the assets. Reaching 60 KB also needs a very large multi-asset FBX, because "attempts" repeats "imported" and each asset counts twice.

3. Thresholds: the default ue_level_actors (200) and ue_search_assets (100) calls pass. With World Partition-style UAID paths, level_actors fails at about 245 rows, not about 290.

4. Two triggers are missing from the related list. ue_asset_audit with default arguments can fail, because its cap of 400 findings is above the roughly 300 that fit; this is a stronger default-argument case than blueprint_info. ue_asset_refs also fails at depth 2 or more on a widely used asset.

5. Fix: mirror blender.rs:362.
- Search the untruncated, joined LogOutput lines in reverse before calling tail().
- Search line by line, not only at the start of each entry: a short print arrives as "RELAY_JSON:...\n", and one entry can hold several lines.
- Apply tail and MAX_OUTPUT only to the human-readable `output` and the error text.
- Put the extraction in a pure function over the response Value, so the regression test with a LogOutput entry over 60 KB needs no UE_REMOTE_CONTROL_URL environment variable. The existing test at line 2002 covers only remote_at.

After the fix, results have no size cap: tool_result pretty-prints the whole value (line 1890), so a 5000-actor call returns over 1 MB into the agent's context. Consider lower schema maximums, or leave `text` out of the data_table export result when `file` is given.

findings.title: quit_editor sends SIGTERM without saving whenever Remote Control misses a 3 s probe, even with save=true, and the signal also hits any editor whose argv ends in the same .uproject name
findings.evidence: `match remote("GET", "/remote/info", None, Duration::from_secs(3)) { Ok(_) => { guard + save + quit } Err(_) => notes.push("the editor did not answer; asking the process to terminate instead (unsaved changes are lost)".into()) }` (577-590). The wait loop then runs `if signalled.is_none() && (notes.iter().any(|n| n.contains("terminate")) || ...) { for pid in &before { crate::unreal_process::kill(*pid); } }` (600-603). kill() runs `kill <pid>`, i.e. SIGTERM (unreal_process.rs:65-67). `before` comes from editors_for, which also matches any editor whose argument merely ends with the same file name (unreal_process.rs:57), and no guard_project runs on this path. `save` is never consulted before signalling. ue_build restart_editor=true calls quit_editor with save defaulting to true (1519). Secondary issues: the save+quit request has a 20 s reply timeout (585), yet the loop assumes 'Everything is saved by now' (598) and signals 20 s after that. The script also calls quit_editor() even when save_dirty_packages returned False (582).
findings.impact: Scenario: the human has unsaved level or asset edits, and the RC server is not answering. Causes include a failed bind after a quick relaunch (the D162 case), auto-start being off, or a game thread busy for more than 3 s loading a map or compiling. If an agent then runs ue_build {restart_editor:true} (the documented Linux C++ loop) or ue_editor_quit, the editor is terminated immediately and the edits are lost. This happens even though the tool promises 'Quit a running editor first (saving)'. If the agent works in a worktree, the editor terminated can be the human's editor on the main checkout, because it opens the same .uproject file name. A save slower than 40 s can also be signalled mid-flight.
findings.fix: When save is requested and the editor cannot be reached, refuse with instructions to start the server, or retry the probe with backoff. Only terminate when the caller passes an explicit force flag. Signal only editors whose canonical project path equals this project. In the quit script, check save_dirty_packages' result and abort the quit if it fails. Wait the full save timeout before considering a signal. Drive control flow with a bool, not `notes.contains("terminate")`.

v1.reason: crates/relay-cli/src/unreal.rs:577-590: if `remote("GET","/remote/info",None,3s)` fails, the code only pushes the note "the editor did not answer; asking the process to terminate instead (unsaved changes are lost)". `save` is never consulted on that branch. The wait loop at 600-605 then matches `n.contains("terminate")` on its first iteration and calls `unreal_process::kill(pid)` for every pid in `before`. kill() runs `kill <pid>` (SIGTERM, unreal_process.rs:65-67). ue_editor_quit (line 390) and ue_build restart_editor=true (line 1519) both pass save defaulting to true. Their tool descriptions promise "Quit the editor cleanly (saving dirty packages unless save=false)" (314) and "Quit a running editor first (saving)" (136). The 3 s probe fails whenever the editor is up but not answering. Two plausible ways this happens: the web server failed to bind, which unreal_process.rs's own module comment describes as a real occurrence after a quick relaunch; or the game thread is busy for longer than 3 s with a map load, a shader compile or a long Python call, since Remote Control requests are serviced on the game thread. In either case the human's unsaved edits are dropped on an agent's say-so. The editor-matching half also holds. `editors_for` (unreal_process.rs:57) accepts any argument that `ends_with` the .uproject file name. A worktree agent's `before` therefore contains the human's main-checkout editor, and on the unreachable branch no guard_project runs before that pid is signalled. The same over-match also makes ue_build call quit_editor for a worktree agent at all (1518). On the reachable branch guard_project (585) does bail on a mismatch, so the cross-checkout kill only happens on the unreachable path.
v1.correction: The secondary claims are weaker than stated. (1) python_tx has a 20 s read timeout. If the save takes longer, the error is recorded as a note, and the loop sends SIGTERM about 20 s after `requested`, about 40 s in. UE's Linux SIGTERM handler only requests an engine exit, so a save already running on the game thread would most likely finish before the exit is processed. Calling that "signalled mid-flight" corruption is speculative. (2) Ignoring save_dirty_packages' False return value is real but minor. The core fix stands. When save=true and the probe fails, retry with backoff, then refuse and tell the agent to ask the human, unless an explicit force flag is passed. Match editors by canonical path only, dropping the `ends_with` fallback or restricting it to a sibling of the same root. Drive the decision with a bool rather than a substring of a note.

v2.reason:
(a) The code does what the finding says. In crates/relay-cli/src/unreal.rs, a failed 3 s probe of `GET /remote/info` (577) only pushes the "terminate" note (589). `save` is never read on that branch, and `guard_project` runs only on the Ok branch (579). On its first pass the wait loop (600-603) sends SIGTERM to every pid in `before` via `kill <pid>` (unreal_process.rs:65-67). The result still reports `"saved": save`, which is true here (614). Nothing upstream steps in. `remote_at` makes one attempt with no retry (1796-1831). Relay's guardrail hooks match only Edit|Write|MultiEdit|Bash (hooks.rs:350, 517). DECISIONS.md:927 says the unreal MCP server is independent of the bus.

I checked the engine side in the installed UE 5.8.2 source. The first SIGTERM goes to GracefulTerminationHandler, which calls RequestExitWithStatus(false, 143) (UnixPlatformCrashContext.cpp:156-173). That only sets the exit flag. The main loop then ends (Launch.cpp:190) with no save prompt. UUnrealEdEngine::FinishDestroy clears the autosave restore data (UnrealEdEngine.cpp:520-524), so the next launch probably offers no recovery.

(b) Who triggers it and when: the agent, in the documented flow. instructions.md:7 tells agents to run `ue_build {restart_editor:true}` for every C++ change. ue_build without that flag refuses and tells the agent to use it (1524). The probe fails in normal use:
- The Remote Control HTTP server runs only on the core ticker on the game thread (HttpServerModule.h:24-26, LaunchEngineLoop.cpp:6103).
- The Slate modal loop does not tick the core ticker (SlateApplication.cpp:2237-2276). So the probe times out whenever the human has any modal dialog open.
- It also times out when the game thread is blocked for more than 3 s: a map load, a Blueprint compile, a large save, or the agent's own earlier ue_python call that timed out but is still running (SKILL.md:233).
- The D162 failed-bind case also applies. For that case, editor_status's own advice (1657) tells the agent to "quit the editor". The agent can only do that with ue_editor_quit, which by definition takes the terminate path there.

Auto-start is on by default in 5.8 (RemoteControlSettings.h:303), so "auto-start off" is not the main cause. Per restart call this is conditional, but it is not rare when a human and agents share one editor (default_checkout "primary", plugin.json:19).

(c) What happens: the editor exits and every dirty map and asset is discarded, the human's included. ue_build then builds and relaunches, reporting "saved": true with only a note. If a modal dialog is open, the exit happens when the human dismisses it, even after quit_editor has given up at 90 s.

The worktree over-match also holds, but only for worktree agents, which are opt-in. `ends_with` (unreal_process.rs:57) puts the human's main-checkout editor in `before`. On the unreachable path that editor gets the SIGTERM. launch_editor (1572) then relaunches the editor on the worktree's .uproject.

(d) High is correct. This is silent loss of the user's unsaved work in a documented normal flow. It depends on the probe failing at the moment of an agent restart, and no persisted data is corrupted.

(e) The core fix is right: refuse unless an explicit force flag is passed, and drive the decision with a bool. It needs the additions listed in the correction.
v2.correction:
1) The "signalled mid-flight" sub-claim is wrong. The first SIGTERM only sets the exit flag. The save paths in FileHelpers.cpp never check IsEngineExitRequested, and quit_editor sends one signal per pid. A slow save therefore finishes, and the "wait the full save timeout" item adds no safety.

2) Ignoring save_dirty_packages' result is more serious than the first verifier's "minor":
- `unreal.SystemLibrary.quit_editor()` runs QUIT_EDITOR, which calls UUnrealEdEngine::CloseEditor and then RequestEngineExit. Nothing prompts to save (KismetSystemLibrary.cpp:674-677, EditorServer.cpp:5993-5996, UnrealEdEngine.cpp:943-958).
- SaveDirtyPackages runs unattended with bUseDialog=false. It silently skips packages it cannot save (FileHelpers.cpp:5912-5958, comment at 4069), such as a never-saved Untitled map or a read-only file.
- So even on the reachable path with save=true, those packages are lost. That case is narrow and secondary.

3) The fix is incomplete in four places:
- Aborting in the script on a failed save is not enough. Any python_tx error becomes a note, and the loop still sends SIGTERM 20 s later (600). The Rust side must return an error without signalling when the script reports a save failure. Only a reply timeout after the quit was issued should lead to waiting or signalling.
- Report `saved` truthfully (614).
- Do not just drop `ends_with`. It probably exists for editors launched with a relative .uproject path, and editors_for also gates builds (1518, 1521). Resolve relative arguments against /proc/<pid>/cwd, then compare canonical paths.
- Change editor_status's failed-bind advice (1657) so it tells the agent to ask the human, not to quit an unreachable editor.

findings.title: Unreal MCP tools write files and run code with no guardrail.gate or role check, so protected paths, destructive-write holds and the reviewer role are bypassed
findings.evidence: ue_data_table export writes any relative path in the checkout. Its only check is `!f.contains("..") && !Path::new(f).is_absolute()` (962), followed by `std::fs::write(file, value["text"]...)` (970), with create_dir_all for parents (969). setup_check fix rewrites the .uproject (1459) and Config ini files (710, 743). launch_editor writes Saved/Config (645). ue_python runs arbitrary editor Python (342), and ue_build / ue_editor_launch take arbitrary UBT or editor arguments. D159 describes this server as 'independent of the bus', and none of it calls guardrail.gate. Relay's Claude PreToolUse hook matches only "Edit|Write|MultiEdit|Bash" (relay-core/src/hooks.rs:350), and Codex's matches only "Bash|apply_patch|Edit|Write" (hooks.rs:517), so mcp__unreal__* calls never reach the gate. plan_launch gives plugin MCP servers to every session regardless of role: 'A plugin that is on brings its MCP servers to every agent of the project' (handlers/session.rs:437-438). plugins::mcp_servers takes no role (plugins.rs:278).
findings.impact: A reviewer session, which BUS.md §9.1 says may do 'nothing that writes files', can change assets and files in an Unreal project through ue_python, ue_property or ue_data_table. Any agent can overwrite a protected or critical file with table text, with no destructive-write hold and no protected-path refusal. Examples: ue_data_table export with file="Source/Game/Data.h", "Config/DefaultEngine.ini", ".git/hooks/pre-commit" in the primary checkout, or ".claude/settings.local.json". An agent can also run commands the exec allowlist denies through ue_python's subprocess. Only the git pre-commit door still applies, and only at commit time. Every plugin tool silently skips the guardrails BUS.md describes as safety measures against agent mistakes (principle 6).
findings.fix: Gate plugin tools. Option one: extend the PreToolUse matcher to mcp__.* and translate the mutating plugin tools into guardrail.gate calls (ue_python/ue_console/ue_build as exec; ue_data_table export and setup_check fix as write, with path and new_text). Option two: have unreal-mcp call guardrail.gate over the bus before each file write (it inherits RELAY_SESSION) and refuse mutating tools for roles that forbid writes. Also restrict ue_data_table's `file` to a data folder and refuse dot-directories.

v1.reason: The mechanism is real. Claude's PreToolUse matcher is "Edit|Write|MultiEdit|Bash" (hooks.rs:350) and Codex's is "Bash|apply_patch|Edit|Write" (hooks.rs:517). claude_pre_tool (relay-cli main.rs:393-475) bails on any other tool. plan_launch hands plugin MCP servers to every session (session.rs:437-438), and unreal-mcp never calls guardrail.gate. So ue_data_table export (961-972, only `..` and absolute paths refused) can write table text to any relative path, protected or dot-dir included, with no gate. However, the impact is badly overstated. (1) The reviewer claim is wrong. The role allowlist (guardrail.rs:441-453, BUS.md §9.1) gates only bus ops, and evaluate_write (guardrail.rs:503ff) has no role check, so a reviewer's own Edit/Write already pass the gate. Plugin tools take away no write ban, because none exists. (2) There is no 'exec allowlist'. evaluate_exec (guardrail.rs:811-847) only checks a denied-command list, and the Bash gate never inspects redirections or interpreters. An agent can already write Config/DefaultEngine.ini or .git/hooks/pre-commit with `cat >` or `python3 -c` through gated Bash, with no protected-path refusal. ue_python therefore adds no capability beyond what Bash already grants. The guardrails guard against agent mistakes, not escapes, and plugin tools are deliberate agent capabilities per D159. What remains is a modest consistency gap: one tool whose purpose is writing a file (ue_data_table export, and setup_check's ini/.uproject rewrites) skips protected-path and destructive-write checks that Edit/Write get. A mistaken `file` argument could clobber a protected file without a hold.
v1.correction: Downgrade to low. Drop the reviewer-role and exec-allowlist claims. The real gap: ue_data_table export (unreal.rs:961-972) and setup_check fix write files without guardrail.gate. Cheap fix: have unreal-mcp call guardrail.gate kind=write with path and new_text before those writes (RELAY_SESSION is inherited), and refuse dot-directories in data_table's `file`. Extending the PreToolUse matcher to mcp__.* is not needed for parity with Bash.

findings.title: ue_editor_lock is listed in LIVE, so 'status' and 'release' need a reachable editor that has this project open
findings.evidence: The LIVE array contains "ue_editor_lock" (33-35). call() runs `let project = Project::find()?; guard_project(&project)?;` for every LIVE name (323-325) before reaching the ue_editor_lock arm (406-412). guard_project calls editor_project(), which runs Python in the editor (497). The lock itself is only the file Saved/Relay/editor-lock.json (514-516).
findings.impact: Suppose the editor crashes or is closed outside ue_editor_quit. The lock holder cannot release its lock, because the call fails with 'the Unreal editor is not answering'. Other agents' ue_editor_launch calls acquire_lock (628) and are refused for up to 15 minutes. The refusal tells them to wait for the holder to 'run ue_editor_lock with action=release' (540), which fails the same way. Agents in a checkout the editor does not have open cannot even read the lock status.
findings.fix: Remove "ue_editor_lock" from LIVE. Longer term, describe each tool once (name, schema, live flag, mutating predicate, handler) so the LIVE/MUTATING arrays, tools() and the dispatch match cannot drift apart.

v1.reason: LIVE (unreal.rs:33-35) contains "ue_editor_lock". call() (322-325) runs Project::find() and guard_project() for every LIVE name before dispatch. guard_project calls editor_project(), which runs PY_PROJECT_CHECK through python_json against Remote Control with a 20 s timeout (497) and returns Err when the editor does not answer. The ue_editor_lock arm (406-412) only reads or removes Saved/Relay/editor-lock.json, which needs no editor. So with the editor crashed or closed, both status and release fail. Meanwhile launch_editor (628) and quit_editor (582) call acquire_lock, which refuses any other holder for up to LOCK_IDLE = 15 min (40, 528). The refusal text (538-541) tells the waiting agent that the holder can run ue_editor_lock action=release, and that is the exact call that fails. The holder itself can still relaunch, because holder == me.
v1.correction: Impact is limited: the stall clears on its own within 15 minutes, the holder is not blocked, and a human can delete the file. In the 'other checkout' case the lock file is per checkout root (lock_path, 514-516), so failing to read that checkout's status costs little. The fix stands: drop "ue_editor_lock" from LIVE so it needs no editor. The 'describe each tool once' refactor is optional.

findings.title: The editor lock's idle clock advances only when a call starts, so it expires during long ue_python or in-editor test runs and is released for the whole of a ue_build restart
findings.evidence: last_used is written only in acquire_lock: `std::fs::write(&path, json!({"holder": me, "since": since, "last_used": now_secs()})...)` (550). read_lock marks the lock expired once `idle >= LOCK_IDLE.as_secs()`, 15 minutes (40, 528). ue_python accepts timeout_s up to 1800 in its schema (154), and secs() even allows 7200 (1272). run_tests in_editor acquires the lock (1082) and then polls for up to timeout_s, 1800 s by default (1085-1095), without refreshing it. quit_editor releases the lock at its end (611), so ue_build restart_editor builds for up to an hour (1547) without the lock before launch_editor takes it again (1572).
findings.impact: A 20-minute in-editor test run or batch Python script looks idle after 15 minutes. Another agent's ue_play, ue_python or ue_anim_preview then takes the lock and drives the same editor at the same time: PIE starts during the automation tests, or assets are edited mid-script. That is exactly the overlap the lock exists to prevent, and the first agent's next call is refused. During a restart build, another agent can also launch the editor while UBT is still writing binaries.
findings.fix: Refresh last_used while a locked operation runs, either by touching the file from the polling loops or with a heartbeat thread. Alternatively, record busy_until = now + timeout at acquire time and treat the lock as held until then. Keep the lock across quit, build and relaunch.

v1.reason: last_used is written only by acquire_lock (550), and read_lock marks the lock expired at 15 idle minutes (40, 528). run_tests with in_editor (1080-1095) takes the lock once and then polls the log for up to secs(timeout_s, 1800) without refreshing it. During that time the editor keeps answering Remote Control between ticks, because automation tests are latent. After 15 minutes another agent's ue_play, ue_property or similar call can take the lock and start PIE or edit assets in the middle of the test run. ue_build with restart_editor=true calls quit_editor, which releases the lock at its end (611). The build then runs for up to 3600 s (1547) unlocked, and launch_editor reacquires the lock only afterwards (1566, 628). Another agent's ue_editor_launch can start the editor during the build. When the first agent then reaches launch_editor, it sees already_running and returns, with the editor possibly running stale binaries.
v1.correction: The ue_python part of the impact is overstated. A long editor Python script blocks the game thread that serves Remote Control, so a second agent's guard_project (20 s timeout) fails rather than running scripts concurrently. There the effect is only that the lock has changed hands by the time the long call returns. The real overlaps are in-editor test runs longer than 15 minutes and the unlocked restart-build window. Fix: refresh last_used in the run_tests polling loop, or record busy_until at acquire time, and keep the lock held through quit, build and relaunch in build().

findings.title: acquire_lock is a non-atomic read-check-write, so two agents can both take the editor lock
findings.evidence: `let lock = read_lock(project); if let Some(holder) = lock["holder"].as_str() { if holder != me && lock["expired"] != true { bail!(...) } } ... std::fs::write(&path, ...)` (536-550) uses no O_EXCL, rename or flock. read_lock maps an unreadable or half-written file to Value::Null (523-524), which reads as 'free'. std::fs::write truncates the file before writing it.
findings.impact: If two agents make their first mutating call at the same moment, with no holder or an expired one, both see the lock as free, both write it, and both run scripts against the one editor. A reader that lands in the truncate-then-write window also sees 'free' and takes a lock someone holds. The window is narrow, and nothing detects the overlap afterwards.
findings.fix: Create the lock with create-new semantics: write a temp file and link or rename it into place, or hold flock on editor-lock.json during the read-modify-write. Re-read afterwards to confirm the holder.

v1.reason: acquire_lock (unreal.rs:535-551) reads with read_lock, checks the holder and writes with std::fs::write, which opens with O_TRUNC and then writes. It uses no O_EXCL, rename or flock. read_lock (522-531) maps a missing, empty or unparsable file to Value::Null, which acquire_lock treats as free. Each agent runs its own relay unreal-mcp process sharing one project root, so two processes can both see the lock as free, and both write it. A reader that hits the truncate-to-write gap also sees it as free.
v1.correction: The window is microseconds wide, and every call before acquire_lock spends tens to hundreds of ms in guard_project's Remote Control round trip, so a real collision is rare. Writing a temp file and renaming it into place closes the truncate window. Holding flock around the read-modify-write closes the check-then-write race. Low.

findings.title: log_since keeps only the last 300 lines, so ue_run_tests in_editor silently drops earlier test results and ue_play drops the first errors
findings.evidence: log_since filters and then returns `lines[lines.len().saturating_sub(300)..].to_vec()` (792). run_tests in_editor builds its whole report from that: `let lines = log_since(project, start, Some("LogAutomation")); if lines.iter().any(|l| l.contains("Automation Test Queue Empty") ...) { return Ok(test_lines(&lines)); }` (1087-1089). test_lines counts succeeded and failed only from those lines (1134-1139). ue_play's `log` and `error_lines` use the same window (938-939), as do the Blueprint compile log (396), import_fbx's import_log (425) and data_table's import errors (982).
findings.impact: Each test writes several LogAutomation lines (started, events, completed). An in-editor run of more than roughly 75-150 tests therefore reports only the last tests: an early failure is missing and the result can read failed: 0, so the agent reports a failing suite as passing. In ue_play, a session with more than 300 matching lines (the default filter includes Warning) loses its earliest errors, which are usually the root cause, and undercounts error_lines.
findings.fix: Have log_since return every matching line, or stream-parse test results over the full range. Truncate only what is returned to the agent, keep the first N errors as well as the tail, and report how many lines were omitted.

v1.reason: crates/relay-cli/src/unreal.rs:785-793: log_since filters the new log text and then returns `lines[lines.len().saturating_sub(300)..].to_vec()`. run_tests with in_editor (1078-1096) polls `log_since(project, start, Some("LogAutomation"))` and returns `test_lines(&lines)` once the window holds "Automation Test Queue Empty". test_lines (1134-1140) computes succeeded and failed only from the `Result={..} Name={..} Path={..}` lines in that window, and nothing else adds up results. The 'LogAutomation' regex matches every LogAutomationController/LogAutomationTest line: test start, completion, per-test errors and warnings. A run of a few hundred tests therefore pushes the early completion lines out of the window. A failure in that early part is silently left out, and the report can read `failed: 0`. play() at 936-938 uses the same window with DEFAULT_PLAY_LOG, which includes Warning (825), so in a warning-heavy session the first errors (usually the root cause) are dropped and error_lines is undercounted. The Blueprint compile log, import_fbx and data_table import errors use it too. The out-of-editor path does not have this problem when index.json exists (it uses the report file).
v1.correction: log_since is at 785-793 (the slice is at 792). The window also means the in-editor loop rereads the whole log file every second, which is a minor cost. Fix: collect every matching line for parsing (or count results while streaming), and cap only what is returned to the agent, keeping the head plus the tail and an omitted-count.

findings.title: Bind-failure detection scans only the last 300 unfiltered lines of whatever log is on disk, so it misses real failures and can report an earlier session's
findings.evidence: launch_editor runs `let lines = log_since(project, 0, None); let bind = crate::unreal_process::bind_failures(&lines);` (656-657). The bind regex is applied only after log_since has already cut to the last 300 lines (792). editor_status does the same with `log_since(p, log_len(p).saturating_sub(400_000), None)` (1654-1655). launch_editor polls immediately after spawning, before the new editor has rotated Saved/Logs/<Project>.log, so its first polls read the previous session's log. editor_status checks `!bind.is_empty()` first and answers 'The editor is running but its web server could not bind' without looking at `editors` (1656-1657).
findings.impact: The bind failure is logged once, at startup, and later startup logging soon pushes it out of the last 300 lines. As a result, editor_status on a running editor practically never gives the StopServer/StartServer advice it was written for: with the port held it falls through to 'Run ue_setup_check for the full picture'. ue_editor_launch can also miss a real failure and wait out its full timeout (900 s by default). In the other direction, if the previous session's last 300 lines contain a bind failure, ue_editor_launch can bail at once with 'could not bind' while the new editor is starting normally. ue_build restart_editor then reports an error for a successful build.
findings.fix: Pass the bind regex to log_since as its filter, so the 300-line cap applies to matches only. In launch_editor, record the log's inode and mtime before spawning and ignore its contents until the file belongs to the new process. In editor_status, give the bind advice only when an editor is actually running.

v1.reason: log_since (786-793) applies the optional filter and then keeps `lines[len-300..]`. launch_editor (656-657) and editor_status (1654-1655) both pass filter=None and run bind_failures on that 300-line tail, so a bind error survives only while fewer than 300 lines follow it. An editor logs thousands of lines during startup and afterwards. On a running editor, editor_status's first branch (`!bind.is_empty()`, 1656) therefore effectively never fires. With an editor running and the port held, it falls through to "Run ue_setup_check for the full picture.", so the StopServer/StartServer advice it exists to give is unreachable in practice. launch_editor polls every 2 s, so it catches a bind failure only if fewer than 300 lines follow it within one poll interval. Otherwise it waits out the full timeout (default 900 s) instead of failing fast. log_since already takes a filter parameter, so passing the bind regex as the filter fixes this.
v1.correction: The reverse case is much less likely than presented. For a stale bind failure from the previous session to trigger a false bail, it must sit in that session's last 300 lines, but the shutdown logging alone usually runs to hundreds of lines. Treat it as a minor edge case. The same goes for editor_status giving bind advice with no editor running. The main defect is the missed detection. Fix it by passing the bind regex (or a broad Http/WebControl/bind prefilter) as log_since's filter. In launch_editor, optionally ignore the log until its mtime or inode changes after the spawn.

findings.title: Early returns in ue_play and ue_profile skip stop and cleanup, leaving a SceneCapture2D in the user's level, PIE running, and the session's diagnostics discarded
findings.evidence: play() places the capture actor first (`play_step("prepare_outside", json!({}))?;`, 856). Then `let started = play_step("start", ...)?; wait_for_play(true)?;` (862-863) can return before cleanup_outside (926-928) or the stop (921-922) runs. play.py's 'start' raises 'a play session is already running' when PIE is up (play.py:32-33), by which time prepare_outside has already spawned a tagged RelayPlayCapture in the editor level (play.py:93-96). After the session, `let probes = outcome?;` (929) returns only the error, dropping shots, log lines and probes, and `_cleanup` is never set for outside_dir (857). In profile(), `throttle = play_step("start", ...)?[...]; wait_for_play(true)?;` (1031-1032) never stops PIE when the wait fails.
findings.impact: Calling ue_play with `outside` while a session is still running (for example after stop=false) leaves a SceneCapture2D in the open level and marks the level dirty. ue_editor_quit and ue_build restart, whose save defaults to true via save_dirty_packages(True, True), then write that actor into the .umap. A PIE that takes more than 30 s to start (first PIE, a large level) keeps running after the tool has reported failure. When PIE ends early, for instance because the game quits or a Blueprint error fires, the agent gets only 'no play session is running', without the log lines that explain why. The capture folder under Saved/Relay/Captures also leaks.
findings.fix: Wrap the session in a guard (Drop, or one finally block) that always stops a requested PIE, runs cleanup_outside and removes outside_dir. On error, return the partial screenshots, probes and log together with the error instead of using `?`. Prepare the outside capture only after start succeeds, or clean it up when start fails. Apply the same guard in profile().

v1.reason: In play() (unreal.rs:837-955), `play_step("prepare_outside")?` (856) spawns a tagged SceneCapture2D into the editor level (play.py:86-100). Then `play_step("start")?` (862) and `wait_for_play(true)?` (863) can return early. play.py:32-33 raises 'a play session is already running' when PIE is up (stop_existing defaults to off), and wait_for_play bails after 30 s (801-808). Neither path runs cleanup_outside (926-928) or stop. The actor is left in the level, the level is dirty, and ue_editor_quit/restart saves with save_dirty_packages(True, True) (582). Inside the session closure, a `?` on `shot` or `console` (e.g. 'no play session is running' after the game quits) aborts the closure. `outcome?` (929) then returns only the error and drops the shots, probes and log captured so far. The capture folder from capture_dir is never handed back as _cleanup. In profile() (1022-1033), a failed wait_for_play(true) returns before the stop, so a slow-starting PIE keeps running.
v1.correction: Partly self-healing: the next ue_play with `outside` destroys old tagged actors before placing a new one (play.py:88-90). The most likely retry (stop_existing=true, as the error message suggests) therefore removes the stray actor. The pollution persists only if the agent gives up, or the editor is saved or quit before a retry. Fix: run prepare_outside after start succeeds, or put stop and cleanup_outside in a guard that runs on every exit. On error, return the partial shots, probes and log together with the error.

findings.title: ue_setup_check fix commits remote Python, console commands and any-function calls, unauthenticated, into the shared Config/DefaultRemoteControl.ini
findings.evidence: RC_KEYS sets bAutoStartWebServer, bEnableRemotePythonExecution, bAllowConsoleCommandRemoteExecution and bAllowAnyRemoteFunctionCall all to "True" (675-680). They are merged into `project.root.join("Config/DefaultRemoteControl.ini")` (705-710), a project config that is normally committed, by a tool any agent can call (setup_check, 1461). launch() also always passes -RCWebControlEnable (unreal_process.rs:295). Nothing writes a passphrase, an origin restriction or a bind address. The plugin's security note says only to keep the port on localhost (plugins/unreal-engine/docs/setup.md:52-55).
findings.impact: Once an agent has run the fix and the config is committed, every teammate's editor auto-starts an HTTP endpoint on 127.0.0.1:30010 that runs arbitrary Python as that developer. The teammates never opted in. TCP localhost is reachable from every local account on a shared machine. Web pages may also reach it through DNS rebinding or permissive CORS, depending on how Remote Control handles Origin and Host headers, which cannot be checked from this repository.
findings.fix: Write these keys to the per-user Saved/Config/<Platform>Editor/RemoteControl.ini, or require explicit human confirmation before touching Default*.ini. Also turn on the engine's access restrictions (restricted origin, passphrase) and send UE_REMOTE_CONTROL_PASSPHRASE. Explain the exposure in the setup advice.

v1.reason: The facts are correct. RC_KEYS (675-680) enables auto-start, remote Python, console commands and any-function calls. write_remote_control_ini merges them into project.root/Config/DefaultRemoteControl.ini (705-710), a project config that UE projects normally commit. It is reached from ue_setup_check fix=true (1461), which an agent can call. Nothing configures origin restrictions or a passphrase. However, remote Python on localhost is the bridge's whole purpose, and setup.md documents and accepts it ("The Remote Control server can run arbitrary editor Python. Keep it bound to localhost"). The advice string at 1487 tells the agent exactly what was written. With remote Python already on, the console-command and any-function keys add no capability. What remains is the scope: writing to the shared Default*.ini turns the server on for anyone who later pulls the commit, without their opting in. The browser/DNS-rebinding route depends on Remote Control's CORS and Host handling, which cannot be established from this repository. On the single-user desktop this app targets, the exposure is the user's own documented choice.
v1.correction: UE_REMOTE_CONTROL_PASSPHRASE is already sent as a `Passphrase` header when it is set (remote_at, around line 1812, and setup.md lists it), so that part of the fix exists. A better fix is to write the keys to the per-user Saved/Config/<Platform>Editor/ ini, or to state explicitly in the advice that Config/DefaultRemoteControl.ini is shared and should not be committed without the team's agreement. Restricting origins is optional hardening. Drop the console-command and any-function keys unless a tool needs them.

findings.title: ue_play's average_fps divides by a time measured after stop and cleanup, so it under-reports and can raise the 'Under 20 fps' warning falsely
findings.evidence: `let last = play_step("status", ...)` (920) is followed by the stop, `wait_for_play(false)` and cleanup_outside (921-928). Only then is fps computed as `((b - a) as f64 / t0.elapsed().as_secs_f64() * 10.0).round() / 10.0` (933). `played_s` uses the same late `t0.elapsed()` (943).
findings.impact: The frame delta covers only the span from `first` to `last`, but the denominator also includes the stop round trips and the 250 ms polls until PIE ends, often 1-3 s. A 5 s session that really runs at 25 fps with 1.5 s of stop overhead reports about 19 fps, and the warning then blames background throttling that isn't happening.
findings.fix: Capture `let played = t0.elapsed();` immediately after taking `last`, and use it for both fps and played_s.

v1.reason: unreal.rs:919-934: `last` is read at 919. Then come the stop request, wait_for_play(false) (which polls status with 250 ms sleeps) and, with `outside`, cleanup_outside. Only after that is fps computed as `(b - a) / t0.elapsed()` (933). The numerator covers frames from `first` to `last`, but the denominator also includes the stop and cleanup round trips. With the default seconds=5.0 (838), a few hundred ms to over 1 s of overhead makes the reported fps 6-20% low. A session running at 21-24 fps can then trigger the 'Under 20 fps' warning (946), which blames background throttling. played_s (944) is inflated the same way.
v1.correction: Capture `let played = t0.elapsed();` right after taking `last` (919) and use it for both average_fps and played_s.

findings.title: ue_build with restart_editor turns a relaunch failure into an error and discards the finished build's result
findings.evidence: `let relaunched = if restart && output.status.success() { Some(launch_editor(project, &json!({"timeout_s": args["launch_timeout_s"]}))?) } else { None };` (1571-1575) runs before the result JSON is built (1576-1587).
findings.impact: If the build succeeds but the relaunch fails (port still held after 90 s, a stale bind line per the bind-detection finding, a slow first start), the agent receives only the launch error. success, errors, tail and warnings are all lost, so the agent may go looking for compile errors that do not exist.
findings.fix: Record a relaunch failure as `relaunch_error` in the result instead of propagating it with `?`.

v1.reason: In build(), the line `Some(launch_editor(project, &json!({"timeout_s": args["launch_timeout_s"]}))?)` (1571-1575) runs before the result JSON (1576-1587). launch_editor (623+) can bail in several ways: acquire_lock fails, the port bind fails (659), the editor exits during start-up (662), or the timeout runs out. Any of these makes build() return only that error, and success, errors, tail, warnings and quit_editor are all dropped after a build that succeeded. An agent can read this as a failed build and go looking for compile errors.
v1.correction: Store the launch failure in the result, e.g. `relaunch_error`, instead of propagating it with `?`. The build outcome is then always returned.

findings.title: ue_build reads `save` and `launch_timeout_s`, but its schema (additionalProperties: false) does not declare them
findings.evidence: build() reads `args["save"].as_bool().unwrap_or(true)` (1519) and `args["launch_timeout_s"]` (1572). The ue_build schema (129-139) declares only target, platform, configuration, timeout_s, restart_editor, allow_editor_open and keep_crash_reporters, and tool() emits "additionalProperties": false (116). plugins/unreal-engine/docs/mcp-tools.md:32 matches the schema.
findings.impact: A restart build always saves dirty packages, with no way to discard them, and the relaunch always uses the 900 s default timeout. Clients that validate against the schema reject both keys.
findings.fix: Declare both parameters in the schema and docs, or remove them from the code.

v1.reason: build() reads `args["save"].as_bool().unwrap_or(true)` (1519) and `args["launch_timeout_s"]` (1572). The ue_build schema (129-139) declares neither, and tool() sets additionalProperties:false (116). An agent that follows the schema cannot discover or send either parameter. The defaults (save, then a 900 s launch timeout through launch_editor's unwrap_or(900) at 650) match the restart_editor description, "Quit a running editor first (saving)", so the observable behavior is the documented one. The only losses are the option to discard unsaved packages and a longer relaunch timeout for slow cold starts. The MCP server does not validate arguments itself.
v1.correction: Impact is minor: hidden options, not wrong behavior. Either declare `save` and `launch_timeout_s` in the schema and in mcp-tools.md, or drop them from the code.

findings.title: ue_run_tests' filter check misses ',' (which -ExecCmds splits on) and the headless run passes no -TestExit, so it can hang until the timeout and lose all output
findings.evidence: The check is `anyhow::ensure!(!filter.contains(';') && !filter.contains('"'), ...)` (1079), and the command is built as `.arg(format!("-ExecCmds=Automation RunTests {filter};Quit"))` (1105). The plugin's own reference documents -ExecCmds as comma-separated (`-ExecCmds="cmd1,cmd2"`, plugins/unreal-engine/skills/unreal-performance/reference/console-commands.md:4,68) and recommends -TestExit (skills/unreal-build-packaging/reference/uat-commands.md:123). On timeout, output_with_timeout returns Ok(None), so `.ok_or_else(...)?` (1109-1110) throws stdout away, and the report dir created at 1100-1101 is removed only on the success path (1129).
findings.impact: A filter such as "MyGame.A,MyGame.B" becomes two commands, "Automation RunTests MyGame.A" and "MyGame.B;Quit", so the Quit never reaches the automation handler. The editor process then idles until timeout_s (1800 s by default), and the agent gets 'did not finish within its timeout' with no test output. Each timeout also leaves a Saved/Relay/TestReport/<uuid> folder behind.
findings.fix: Reject ',' or translate it to '+', the RunTests separator. Add -TestExit="Automation Test Queue Empty". Remove the report dir on every path, and return the partial stdout on timeout (this needs output_with_timeout to hand it back).

v1.reason: The guard at 1079 rejects only ';' and '"'. The headless command is `-ExecCmds=Automation RunTests {filter};Quit` (1105) and adds no -TestExit, although the repo's own skill references add -TestExit (uat-commands.md:123, unreal-testing-debugging/SKILL.md:100). The same references describe -ExecCmds as comma-separated (console-commands.md:4,68). If UE splits ExecCmds on ',', which matches its documented behavior but I could not check against engine source here, a filter like "A,B" leaves "B;Quit" as an unknown command, so Quit never runs. The headless editor then idles until timeout_s (1800 s by default). On timeout, output_with_timeout returns Ok(None), and `.ok_or_else(...)?` (1109-1110) drops all stdout. The early return also skips the report-dir cleanup at 1129, which leaves Saved/Relay/TestReport/<uuid> behind. The trigger requires an agent to pass a comma in a field the schema describes as a single 'test path prefix', so it is uncommon.
v1.correction: The leaked report dir on any error or timeout path is certain. The comma split depends on UE's ExecCmds parsing. Cheapest fix: reject ',' in the guard (or map it to '+'), add -TestExit="Automation Test Queue Empty" as a backstop, and remove the report dir on every exit path.

findings.title: Log reads load the whole log on every call and poll: log_since reads from byte 0 and allocates every line, and ue_log joins all matches only to split them again
findings.evidence: log_since runs `let Ok(bytes) = std::fs::read(project.log_path())`, slices `&bytes[start..]`, and calls `.map(str::to_string).collect()` for every line (787-791). It is polled every second in run_tests in_editor (1087, 1094) for up to 30 minutes and every 2 s in launch_editor with start=0 (656, 667). editor_status reads the whole file only to keep the last 400 KB (1654). log() runs `kept.join("\n")` over every matching line, and tail() then splits that string back into lines (1618-1623). unreal_process::engine_root also reads the whole log just to scan its first 400 lines (unreal_process.rs:126).
findings.impact: With a multi-hundred-MB editor log (verbose categories, long sessions), every poll re-reads and re-allocates the whole file. ue_log on a 1 GB log peaks at several GB: the bytes, a Vec<&str>, the joined string and a second Vec.
findings.fix: Open the file, seek to `start` and read only the new bytes. In log(), take `kept[kept.len().saturating_sub(lines)..]` before joining.

v1.reason: log_since (787) does `std::fs::read(project.log_path())` for the whole file on every call. run_tests in_editor calls it every 1 s for up to 1800 s (1083-1094), and launch_editor every 2 s with start=0 (656). editor_status reads the whole file only to slice off the last 400 KB (1654). log() (1611-1623) builds Vec<&str>, then `kept.join("\n")`, and tail() splits that string again. engine_root reads the whole log to scan 400 lines (unreal_process.rs:126). This all runs in the relay-cli MCP server process, not in the engine's bus handlers, so no store mutex or bus latency is involved. With typical editor logs of tens of MB, the cost is wasted I/O and memcpy each second rather than a user-visible stall. Only very large logs make it material.
v1.correction: Only launch_editor (start=0) allocates every line. The other callers slice from `start` and allocate only the new bytes, but still read the whole file. Fix by seeking to `start` (File::seek plus read_to_end), slicing `kept` to its last `lines` entries before joining in log(), and reading only the head of the file in engine_root.

findings.title: The MCP stdio server and its helpers are copied between unreal.rs and blender.rs (and partly mcp.rs), and the copies have diverged
findings.evidence: serve() (57-76) and handle() (78-110) are line-for-line copies of blender.rs:34-87. FALLBACK_PROTOCOL and SUPPORTED_PROTOCOLS are defined in unreal.rs:22-23, blender.rs:19-20 and mcp.rs:13-14. rpc_error exists in unreal.rs:1899 and mcp.rs:214. required, secs and tail exist in both unreal.rs and blender.rs with different behaviour: unreal's tail caps output at MAX_OUTPUT (1590-1601) while blender's (blender.rs:386-389) has no byte cap, and secs clamps to 5..7200 here but 10..3600 there (1271-1273 vs blender.rs:248-250).
findings.impact: Every MCP protocol bump or transport fix (argument validation, cancellation, answering ping during long calls) has to be made two or three times. The copies already disagree: blender_python's 300 output lines have no byte cap, while ue_python's output does.
findings.fix: Move serve/handle (parameterized by server info, tools() and call()), the protocol constants, rpc_error and the argument helpers into one shared mcp_stdio module used by all three servers. Keep a single tail with an explicit byte cap.

v1.reason: serve() and handle() in unreal.rs:57-110 and blender.rs:34-87 are copies that differ only in serverInfo and instructions. FALLBACK_PROTOCOL and SUPPORTED_PROTOCOLS are defined three times (unreal.rs:22-23, blender.rs:19-20, mcp.rs:13-14). rpc_error is defined in both unreal.rs:1899 and mcp.rs:214. The two tail() functions really have diverged. unreal.rs:1590-1601 caps output at MAX_OUTPUT bytes, while blender.rs:386-389 does not, so blender_python output (blender.rs:372, tail(...,300)) has no byte cap. A script that prints very long lines can therefore put an unbounded amount of text into the agent's context.
v1.correction: Some sharing already exists: blender.rs imports rpc_error, tool and tool_result from unreal.rs (blender.rs:10), so rpc_error is duplicated only between unreal.rs and mcp.rs. The different secs() clamps (5..7200 vs 10..3600) are per-plugin tool policy, not drift, and the two required() functions differ deliberately in return type. mcp.rs's handle is async and bus-backed, so it cannot share serve/handle as it stands. The only divergence that matters is the missing byte cap in blender's tail. Fix that and share the protocol constants and the stdio loop between unreal and blender. The cost is modest, so this rates low.

findings.title: remote_at buffers the editor's reply with no size limit, and ue_call/ue_property return it untruncated
findings.evidence: The reply goes through `stream.read_to_end(&mut raw)` (1824), then `raw[split + 4..].to_vec()` or dechunk (1837, 1849), then `String::from_utf8_lossy(&body).into_owned()` (1826), then a serde_json Value (1827). python_tx keeps only 60 KB of that (1707), so the rest is parsed and dropped. ue_call and ue_property return the raw Value as the tool result (353, 365).
findings.impact: An agent's ue_python that prints in a loop over every asset, producing hundreds of MB of LogOutput, makes the MCP server hold several copies in memory before it throws away all but 60 KB. A ue_property read of a large array or map property floods the agent's context with an unbounded JSON result.
findings.fix: Bound the read, for example Read::take(64 MB) with a clear error. Pass ue_call and ue_property results through the same output cap, summarizing when larger.

v1.reason: The claimed mechanism is real. `remote_at` (crates/relay-cli/src/unreal.rs:1823-1827) reads the whole reply with `stream.read_to_end(&mut raw)` and no size limit. `parse_response` copies the body with `raw[split + 4..].to_vec()` (1836), and `dechunk` copies it again for a chunked reply (1849, 1857-1868). The body then becomes a String through `String::from_utf8_lossy(..).into_owned()` and is parsed into a serde_json Value. That means several full copies are in memory at once. For ue_python, `python_tx` cuts the joined LogOutput down with `tail(.., 2000)`: the last 2000 lines, then at most MAX_OUTPUT = 60_000 bytes (lines 30, 1590-1601). Everything else is parsed and then dropped. `ue_call` (353) and `ue_property` (365) return the `remote(...)` Value directly. `tool_result` (around 1878-1896) serialises it whole, twice: once as pretty text and once as structuredContent. So a READ_ACCESS of a big array or map property, or a function call that returns a lot of data, reaches the agent with no cap. The impact is limited, though. The peer is the user's own Unreal editor on a localhost Remote Control port, which is not an attacker. The MCP server is a separate per-agent CLI process, so a memory spike there cannot hang the engine or the bus. The editor itself has to build that huge JSON first. Real but rare, with modest consequences, so low is the right rating.
v1.correction: One detail in the finding is off. ue_python output is cut by `tail(&output.join("\n"), 2000)` at 1707: the last 2000 lines, then 60_000 bytes (MAX_OUTPUT, line 30). It is not simply a 60 KB cut. Also, `python_tx` passes `response["CommandResult"]` through untouched. Fix: wrap the stream in `Read::take(N)` before `read_to_end`, with a clear error when the reply is bigger than N. In `tool_result`, cap the serialised text the same way for every tool (ue_call, ue_property, CommandResult), using the existing MAX_OUTPUT, so each call site does not need its own cap.

findings.title: remote_at tries only the first resolved address, so UE_REMOTE_CONTROL_URL=http://localhost:... can fail
findings.evidence: `address.to_socket_addrs().with_context(...)?.next().ok_or_else(...)?` (1800-1804) keeps one address, followed by a single `TcpStream::connect_timeout(&socket, Duration::from_secs(3))` (1805). port_free() checks only 127.0.0.1 (unreal_process.rs:261), consistent with an IPv4 listener.
findings.impact: Where `localhost` resolves to ::1 first (the usual glibc ordering) and the editor's web server listens on 127.0.0.1, every live tool reports 'the Unreal editor is not answering' even though the editor is up.
findings.fix: Iterate over all resolved addresses and try connect_timeout on each until one connects.

v1.reason: remote_at (1796-1806) calls `.to_socket_addrs()...next()` and makes a single connect_timeout to that one address. Rust resolves through getaddrinfo with AF_UNSPEC, which usually puts ::1 before 127.0.0.1 for 'localhost'. port_free in unreal_process checks only 127.0.0.1, so the code itself assumes an IPv4 listener. Against an IPv4-only listener, the ::1 attempt is refused and the tool reports 'the Unreal editor is not answering'. The trigger is opt-in, though: DEFAULT_REMOTE and setup.md:63 use http://127.0.0.1:30010, so the bug appears only when the user sets UE_REMOTE_CONTROL_URL with a hostname such as localhost. The default configuration is unaffected.
v1.correction: This affects only a non-default UE_REMOTE_CONTROL_URL that names a host. The fix is to try each resolved address in turn until one connects.

findings.title: A comment in launch_editor says the next call will re-ask the editor's project, but nothing invalidates editor_project()'s cache
findings.evidence: `// The editor now owns the project; tell the next status call to ask again.` (653) is followed only by `return Ok(json!(...))`. The cache is a function-local `static CACHE` inside editor_project() (491) with a 30 s TTL (493), and nothing outside that function can clear it. Per git log -S, the comment has had no matching code since it was introduced in b3ea46d.
findings.impact: The comment misleads readers. If a guard check cached another project in the last 30 s (the editor was swapped quickly), the first live calls after a launch are judged on stale data. This is rare, because launches usually take longer than 30 s.
findings.fix: Hoist the cache to a module-level static with an invalidate() and call it from launch_editor and quit_editor, or delete the comment.

v1.reason: unreal.rs:653 reads `// The editor now owns the project; tell the next status call to ask again.` and is followed only by `return Ok(json!(...))`. The cache is a function-local `static CACHE` inside editor_project() (490-501) with a 30 s TTL, and no code outside that function can reset it. git log -S shows the comment was added in b3ea46d. The behavioral impact is negligible. launch_editor waits up to 90 s for the port and then for the editor to start, so the 30 s entry has almost always expired. The cache is also per MCP-server process. In practice this is a misleading comment.
v1.correction: Delete the comment, or make the cache module-level with an invalidate() called from quit_editor and launch_editor. Deleting it is the proportionate fix.

findings.title: summarize_csv sorts with partial_cmp().unwrap(), so a 'nan' cell in a timing column panics and kills the MCP server
findings.evidence: Cells are parsed with `cells[*i].trim().parse().ok()` (1003), and Rust's f64 parser accepts "nan", "NaN", "-nan" and "inf". The values are then sorted with `v.sort_by(|a, b| a.partial_cmp(b).unwrap())` (1011) and `worst.sort_by(|a, b| b.1.partial_cmp(&a.1).unwrap())` (1017). serve() has no catch_unwind.
findings.impact: If the CSV profiler ever writes a NaN for a FrameTime, thread or GPU stat, ue_profile panics and the unreal MCP server exits for the rest of the agent's session. I could not establish whether UE ever writes NaN in these columns.
findings.fix: Sort with f64::total_cmp, or skip non-finite values when parsing.

v1.reason: The code pattern exists: summarize_csv sorts with `partial_cmp().unwrap()` (unreal.rs ~1011 and ~1017), and serve() (57-76) has no catch_unwind, so a NaN would panic the server. But no trigger is established. The values come from Unreal's own CSV profiler output, and neither the auditor nor I could show that it ever writes `nan`/`inf` into the FrameTime, thread-time or GPU columns. A Windows-style `-nan(ind)` would not parse, and that row would simply be skipped. With no reachable trigger, this is defensive hardening, not a demonstrated bug. The consequence, an MCP server restart for that agent, is minor as well.
v1.correction: Optional hardening only: use f64::total_cmp, or filter out non-finite values at parse time.

findings.title: ue_blueprint_info is annotated read-only although compile=true changes Blueprints and takes the editor lock
findings.evidence: tools() declares ue_blueprint_info with read_only=true (273), which tool() turns into `readOnlyHint: true, destructiveHint: false` (117). Yet call() treats it as mutating when compiling, via `(name != "ue_blueprint_info" || args["compile"] == true)` (329; MUTATING at 37-38), and the script does compile (unreal_py/blueprint_info.py:96-98).
findings.impact: Clients that treat read-only tools as safe, for example by allowing them in plan or read-only modes, let an agent compile Blueprints without the mutating-tool treatment. Compiling regenerates classes and marks packages dirty, and a later quit with save persists those changes.
findings.fix: Mark the tool read_only=false, or split compiling into its own tool.

v1.reason: tools() declares ue_blueprint_info with read_only=true (unreal.rs:266-273), and tool() turns that into readOnlyHint:true, destructiveHint:false (117). call() itself treats compile=true as mutating and takes the editor lock (329-333), and blueprint_info.py:96-98 calls BlueprintEditorLibrary.compile_blueprint. The annotation is therefore wrong for one mode of the tool.
v1.correction: Within this server the lock is already applied correctly. The only effect is on MCP clients that act on readOnlyHint, and the finding does not show any client here that auto-approves based on it. Compiling a Blueprint is also not destructive in the usual sense. Mark the tool read_only=false, or split compile into its own tool. Low severity.

results.coverage:
I read every line of all 23 assigned files. I also read the Rust code that feeds and parses them: all of blender.rs (run, resolve, to_unreal, compare, tests) and the relevant parts of unreal.rs (script/py_str, python_tx and python_json, import_fbx, play/play_step, anim_preview, capture_dir/with_images, data_table, quit_editor, the call dispatch, and the tests that run run_inspect.py). I also checked the PreToolUse matcher in relay-core/src/hooks.rs, D5/D161/D162, and the plugin docs (blender mcp-tools.md, unreal mcp-tools.md).

What I ran: on the installed Blender 5.2.1 I built the fixture (into scratch) and ran every Blender script through a harness that mirrors blender.rs::run(). I probed the slotted-action API, slot auto-assignment, the render engine enum and the FBX operator properties. I tested excluded and eye-hidden collections, re-importing the exported FBX to see what it contained, quaternion and glTF rotation, framing of a tall subject (and viewed the image), the fbx_options filepath override, a ':tail' grip, a run.py save (.blend1), add-on failure reporting, and stdout interleaving (no line splitting found, so not reported). Under python3 -I -B on scratch copies I ran run_inspect.py against the stand-in unreal module (it passes), plus probes for the vacuous assertion and contact suppression, and plain-Python checks of twin(), the null materials default and exec's __name__.

Not verifiable here, with no Unreal editor and no Blender 4.x: the Unreal enum str() format (asset_audit:63), whether spawn_actor_from_class(transient=True) avoids dirtying the level, whether get_bone_poses_for_time exists, the delete_asset failure in import cleanup, sky-gradient coverage in a real level, whether save_config is exposed on EditorPerformanceSettings, and the BLENDER_EEVEE_NEXT identifier on 4.2-4.5. Those findings carry medium or low confidence.

Injection: arguments reach Blender as a JSON file and Unreal as a JSON string literal (py_str), and both are safe. The only fixed-script inputs that reach a console command are integers. The real exposure is agent-supplied code and paths, reported as the guardrail-bypass and fbx_options findings.

clippy-pedantic.txt has no entries for the .py files. Its cast warnings in blender.rs and unreal.rs belong to other chunks.

findings.title: Blender 5.x removed Action.fcurves: blender_info and blender_export crash on any animated file
findings.evidence: info.py:45-46 `groups = set(fc.data_path.split('"')[1] for fc in a.fcurves if ...)` and `"fcurves": len(a.fcurves)`; export.py:48 has the identical expression `for fc in act.fcurves`. On the installed Blender 5.2.1, info.py run on the test fixture fails with `AttributeError: 'Action' object has no attribute 'fcurves'`, and export.py fails the same way at line 48. A probe shows the action is layered (`is_action_layered True`): its F-curves live in `action.layers[0].strips[0].channelbags[<slot>].fcurves`, and `bpy_extras.anim_utils.action_get_channelbag_for_slot` exists. With a channelbag shim, both scripts ran to completion, so this is the only crash in them. export.py:48 runs whenever the armature has an active action and kind != static, even when animations are off.
findings.impact: On Blender 5.0 and later, three flows fail: blender_info, the documented first call, on every .blend that contains an action; blender_export for skeletal or animation kinds on any rig with an assigned action; and therefore blender_to_unreal. The Rust real-rig test fails for the same reason.
findings.fix: Add one helper to common.py, e.g. `action_fcurves(action, slot=None)`. It returns `action.fcurves` when that attribute exists (before 4.4); otherwise it returns the channelbag F-curves for the given slot (via `anim_utils.action_get_channelbag_for_slot`), or for all channelbags. Use it in info.py and export.py, together with a shared `keyed_bones()` so the duplicated `data_path.split` expression lives in one place. Report counts per slot in info.

v1.reason: I checked this myself on the installed Blender (blender -b --factory-startup, scratchpad only). On 5.2.1 LTS, `hasattr(bpy.types.Action,'fcurves')` and `hasattr(bpy.data.actions.new('A'),'fcurves')` are both False. info.py:45-46 iterates `a.fcurves` for every action in bpy.data.actions, so blender_info raises AttributeError on any .blend that contains an action of any kind. export.py:45-48 reads `act.fcurves` whenever the armature has an active action and kind != 'static', even when animations are off. That path is reached by blender_export and by blender_to_unreal (blender.rs:399), which runs PY_EXPORT. find_blender picks the newest install, and the user's machine has 5.2.1, so this is a hard failure of the documented first call and of the export flow for any animated rig. Blender's own FBX exporter in the same install reads channelbag.fcurves instead (export_fbx_bin.py:2527-2530), and bpy_extras.anim_utils.action_get_channelbag_for_slot exists (anim_utils.py:91). The project's skill files have the same problem (blender-animation/reference/animation-recipes.md:13/26/72/82/109, rig-recipes.md:83, rigify-game-skeleton.md:131, rigging-recipes.md:212): they teach agents `act.fcurves`, which also fails on 5.x.
v1.correction: Also update the plugin skill recipes that use act.fcurves (plugins/blender/skills/blender-animation/reference/animation-recipes.md, blender-fundamentals/reference/rig-recipes.md:83, blender-rigging/reference/*.md). For an action, iterate `for layer in a.layers for strip in layer.strips for cb in strip.channelbags for fc in cb.fcurves`. For the active action, use action_get_channelbag_for_slot(act, arm.animation_data.action_slot).

v2.reason:
(a) I reproduced the crash on the installed Blender, which reports 5.2.1 LTS. Runs used `blender -b --factory-startup` on scratchpad copies only. In this version `hasattr(bpy.types.Action,'fcurves')` is False. The Action type has `layers` and `slots`, but no `fcurves` and no `groups`.

I built the fixture with tests/make_fixture.py. It builds fine on 5.2.1. I then ran common.py+info.py exactly as run() does it (blender.rs:330-350). The run exits 1 with `AttributeError: 'Action' object has no attribute 'fcurves'` at info.py:45.

common.py+export.py with only `{"objects":["Hero"]}` (animations off) fails the same way at export.py:48. That line runs before os.makedirs and before the exporter, so no FBX is written.

I added a test-only shim that gives Action an `fcurves` property listing all channelbag F-curves:
- info.py then completed and reported Swing correctly: 3 F-curves, 1 bone.
- The animated export completed: a 162 KB FBX, kind skeletal.
- Without the shim, rig_check, anim_inspect and a kind=static export also run.

So this is the only crash in the two scripts. Blender's own bundled FBX exporter reads `strip.channelbags` -> `channelbag.fcurves` (export_fbx_bin.py:2526-2530). No bundled 5.2 script uses `action.fcurves`.

(b) Reachability. blender.rs:195 (blender_info with a file), :237 (blender_export) and :399 (blender_to_unreal) all run these scripts through run(). Nothing catches or retries the error; run() fails and returns the traceback.

The trigger is Blender 5.0 or later together with either:
- any .blend that contains an action, for blender_info;
- a rig with an assigned action exported as skeletal, animation, or auto (which resolves to skeletal), for blender_export and blender_to_unreal. This includes every call that passes `action`, because set_action assigns it.

The project's own skill, blender-animation/SKILL.md:44-45, says `action.fcurves` "is removed in 5.0". plugins/blender/docs/setup.md:3 tells users to install "4.0 or newer; LTS releases are the safest" from blender.org, and the current LTS there is the 5.x line. The only Blender on this machine is ~/.local/bin/blender -> blender-5.2.1. Commit b3ea46d says the scripts only "ran against Blender 4.0".

So every agent doing character or animation work with the plugin hits this, every time. Static meshes and rigs with no assigned action are not affected.

(c) What happens. The tool returns an error containing the traceback:
- blender_info returns nothing for animated files, and it is the plugin's documented first call.
- blender_export writes no FBX.
- blender_to_unreal never reaches the Unreal import.

No data is lost: nothing is saved, and the crash comes before any write. The agent's only workaround is to write its own export in blender_python, which skips the plugin's checks that refuse broken meshes and wrong scale.

There is also a second consequence:
- The test `the_blender_tools_work_on_a_real_rig` is at blender.rs:526. It is not #[ignore] and is skipped only when no Blender is found. CI has no Blender.
- On any machine with Blender 5.x on PATH, this test panics at blender.rs:539, the `.unwrap()` on `run(PY_INFO, ...)`.
- relay-cli is a default member, so plain `cargo test`, the verification command in CLAUDE.md, fails on this machine for agents verifying unrelated changes.

I worked this out from the code; I did not run cargo, as the rules require.

(d) High is right. This is a deterministic hard failure of the plugin's normal flows on the current LTS. It is not critical: the plugin is optional, the failure is loud rather than silent, and no data is lost.

(e) The proposed fix is right in substance: one channelbag-aware helper in common.py, used by info.py and export.py. It needs the version correction below.
v2.correction:
1. Fix the version boundary in the proposed helper. `Action.fcurves` still exists in 4.4 and 4.5, as a legacy view of the first slot. It was removed in 5.0, so "(before 4.4)" is wrong.
   - Use the layered API whenever `action.layers` exists (4.4 and later). Fall back to `action.fcurves` only on 4.0-4.3. Otherwise a multi-slot action on 4.4/4.5 would show only its first slot.
