   - In export.py, read the armature's assigned slot with `bpy_extras.anim_utils.action_get_channelbag_for_slot(act, arm.animation_data.action_slot)`. Guard the import, because that function only exists from 4.4. If no slot is assigned, fall back to all channelbags.
   - In info.py, go through layers -> strips -> channelbags -> fcurves.

2. Correct the first verifier on find_blender. It picks the newest install only in the Windows Program Files scan. On Linux it takes the first `blender` on PATH. Here that is 5.2.1, the only install, so the conclusion does not change.

3. Add the impact on `cargo test`. The real-rig test (blender.rs:526) panics at blender.rs:539 whenever Blender 5.x is on PATH. CI does not catch this because it has no Blender.

4. Related lower-severity docs drift with the same root cause. These skill recipes still teach `act.fcurves`, although SKILL.md:44-48 does warn about 5.0:
   - plugins/blender/skills/blender-animation/reference/animation-recipes.md:13, 26, 72, 82-83, 109, 182
   - plugins/blender/skills/blender-animation/SKILL.md:59
   - blender-fundamentals/reference/rig-recipes.md:83
   - blender-rigging/reference/rigging-recipes.md:212
   - blender-rigging/reference/rigify-game-skeleton.md:131

   Until the fix lands, setup.md:3 ("4.0 or newer") should name the range the scripts were actually tested on.

findings.title: set_action never assigns an action slot: on Blender 4.4+/5.x another rig's action silently leaves the pose at rest
findings.evidence: `arm.animation_data.action = action` / `return action`, with no slot handling. On 5.2.1 with the fixture, assigning 'Swing' (slot OBHero) to Partner left `animation_data.action_slot` as None and upper_arm.R at (0,0,0) at frame 20. anim_inspect with armature=Partner and action=Swing returned `"action": "Swing", "passed": true`, with hand.R at [0,70,135] in every frame. The same call on Hero moves the hand from [0,70,135] to [0,20,185].
findings.impact: Some actions do not auto-assign a slot: clips imported from FBX or Mixamo, actions appended from a library, actions made on a duplicate rig, and the `partner` armature. For those, the action is attached but animates nothing. blender_anim_inspect then measures the rest pose and passes, blender_render shows the rest pose, and blender_export bakes a motionless animation, all while reporting the action's name.
findings.fix: After assigning the action, if `hasattr(ad, 'action_slot')` and `ad.action_slot is None`, choose a slot: an explicit `slot` argument, else the single slot whose `target_id_type` is OBJECT or UNSPECIFIED; otherwise raise and list `action.slots`. Set `ad.action_slot` to it, raise if the action has no slots, and report the slot used.

v1.reason: common.py:118-127 set_action only does `arm.animation_data.action = action`. I reproduced this in Blender 5.2.1 (background, factory startup, scratchpad script). The action 'Swing' was keyed on Hero, which gave it slot 'OBHero'. Assigning it to Partner left `action_slot` None and Partner's bone at rest at frame 20 while Hero's bone was rotated. A clip whose original armature was deleted (the import/Mixamo case), assigned to Hero, also got `action_slot` None. The tools then report the action name: anim_inspect.py:175 and export.py:108 read `animation_data.action.name`. So blender_anim_inspect measures the rest pose and can return passed=true, blender_render shows the rest pose, and blender_export bakes a motionless clip, all with no error. Callers: anim_inspect.py:9 and :19 (partner), render.py:20, export.py:32.
v1.correction: After assignment, if `hasattr(ad,'action_slot') and ad.action_slot is None` and `action.slots` exist, pick a slot: an explicit argument; otherwise the only slot, or the slots whose target_id_type is OBJECT/UNSPECIFIED when exactly one fits. If none or several fit, raise and list `action.slots`. Report the slot used. Severity is high because a verification tool silently passes on the rest pose in the documented retarget and partner workflows.

v2.reason:
(a) Yes. common.py:118-127 `set_action` only does `arm.animation_data.action = action` (line 126). Blender 4.4 and later auto-assign a slot only when the action has a slot named like the object's last-used slot or like the object itself (or an untyped single slot). I tested this myself on the installed Blender 5.2.1, running the real script (common.py plus anim_inspect.py, invoked as blender.rs:336-347 does) on the fixture from make_fixture.py:
- An action appended from a .blend whose rig was named "Rig" (slot OBRig), inspected on Hero: `action_slot` stays None. Output is `"action":"A_Lib_Wave","passed":true` with hand.R at [0,70,135] at frames 1, 10 and 20.
- Hero's Swing on Partner: same result.
- With a patched set_action that assigns the single OBJECT slot, both cases move hand.R to [0,57.5,168.1] and then [0,20,185], matching Hero.

So the slot is the cause, and anim_inspect.py:175 still reports the action name.

(b) The caller is an agent passing `action` or `partner.action` that was keyed on a different object. Cases I verified that trigger it:
- another character's action;
- an action appended from a file whose rig had another name;
- FBX-imported clips (the 5.2.1 importer names every slot "Slot", import_fbx.py:1109) applied to a rig that has never played an imported clip.

Cases I verified that do NOT trigger it:
- a rig's own actions, even after renaming the rig (new slots reuse the last identifier OBHero);
- actions keyed on a duplicated rig (they inherit OBHero and auto-assign back to Hero);
- the partner's own action (skill section 6, recipe 7);
- recipe-9 retargeting (the source stays on its own rig, and nla.bake creates the target's action).

So the first verifier's claim about the "documented retarget and partner workflows" is wrong. I also checked copies of the user's real Game4 files (DuelFighter, Traveler, GateWarden, GreatswordAnimated). Every authored action's slot matches its rig, and the legacy third-party clips stored there do not fit CombatRig's bones anyway (3 of about 200 paths resolve). This is a less common path, not the normal flow.

(c) No file is modified and no data is lost. anim_inspect returns a false pass on the rest pose, and blender_render shows the rest pose at every frame. The skill requires the agent to look at those renders, and identical tracked points across samples are visible in the output. A static FBX export happens only on Blender 4.4/4.5. On 5.x, export.py:48 (`act.fcurves`, removed in 5.0) raises AttributeError before anything is written: I reproduced this for both Hero and Partner. That is a separate bug.

(d) Under the rubric, a real bug in a less common path with no data loss is medium, not high.

(e) The fix is correct in direction; my minimal version of it works.
v2.correction:
Severity medium, not high. The trigger is applying an action keyed on another object (another character's action, an action appended from a file whose rig had a different name, or an FBX-imported clip whose slot is "OBSlot" applied to a native rig).

Corrections to the finding's impact list:
- "Actions made on a duplicate rig" is wrong. Duplicates inherit last_slot_identifier OBHero, and their new actions get slot OBHero, which auto-assigns back to Hero.
- "The partner armature" applies only when the partner is given another rig's action. A partner's own action works.
- The export consequence (a motionless bake) applies only to Blender 4.4/4.5. On 5.x, export.py:48 crashes first on `act.fcurves`. info.py:45-46 has the same separate bug.
- The fixture repro is confounded. Partner's upper_arm.R uses QUATERNION rotation while Swing keys rotation_euler, so Partner stays at rest even with the slot assigned. Clean repros: set Partner's bone to XYZ, or append an action keyed on a rig named "Rig" and inspect it on Hero.

Fix:
- After assignment, if `hasattr(ad, 'action_slot') and ad.action_slot is None`, pick a slot whose F-curve paths all resolve on the armature (the same rule as Blender's FBX exporter `find_validate_action_slot`, export_fbx_bin.py:2523). Fall back to the single OBJECT or UNSPECIFIED slot.
- If no slot fits, or several do, raise and list `action.slots`.
- Report the slot used. Also flag when no keyed path resolves on the armature.
- An explicit `slot` argument needs plumbing in the blender.rs schemas (anim_inspect and partner, render, export, to_unreal).
- Read F-curves through `bpy_extras.anim_utils.action_get_channelbag_for_slot`, not `Action.fcurves`.

findings.title: blender_export ignores view-layer visibility: excluded collections crash it, eye-hidden collections are silently left out of the FBX
findings.evidence: Lines 57-60 clear only object-level flags (`o.hide_set(False)`, `o.hide_viewport = False`), then call `o.select_set(True)` and export with `use_selection=True`. The default object list (line 7) comes from `scene.objects`, which includes objects in excluded collections. Both cases reproduced on 5.2.1. (a) With a mesh in an excluded 'Reference' collection, the default export fails with `RuntimeError: Object 'RefBox' cannot be selected because it is not in View Layer`. (b) With a mesh in a collection hidden by its eye icon (`LayerCollection.hide_viewport`), export exits 0 and reports `"objects": ["SM_Crate"], "size_cm": [100,100,100], "bytes": 4220`, but re-importing the FBX finds no objects. Control: with the collection visible, the file is 13100 bytes and contains SM_Crate.
findings.impact: An agent exports a prop, or a character whose body sits in a hidden collection, and gets a success result with an empty or incomplete FBX. blender_to_unreal then imports nothing, or a skeleton without its mesh. The mesh checks and the size were reported for objects that were never written.
findings.fix: Build the candidate set from `bpy.context.view_layer.objects`, and skip or report excluded objects explicitly. Make the chosen objects visible: un-hide their LayerCollection chain, or link them temporarily into `scene.collection`. Before exporting, assert `set(bpy.context.selected_objects) == selected` and fail with the names that could not be selected.

v1.reason: export.py:7 builds the default candidates from `scene.objects` (filtered only by type, hide_render and parent), which includes objects in excluded collections. Lines 55-60 clear only object-level hide flags before `select_set(True)` and `use_selection=True`. I reproduced both cases in Blender 5.2.1. (a) `select_set` on an object in an excluded collection raises 'Object ... cannot be selected because it is not in View Layer', so the default export crashes. (b) In a collection hidden with LayerCollection.hide_viewport, after `hide_set(False)`/`hide_viewport=False`/`select_set(True)`, `selected_objects` is [] and visible_get() is False. The FBX is written with no objects (about 4 KB), the script still emits success, and `objects`/`size_cm`/mesh_checks are computed from the Python `selected` set rather than from what was written. blender_to_unreal then imports nothing, or an armature without its mesh.
v1.correction: Take candidates from `bpy.context.view_layer.objects` and report excluded objects. Make the chosen objects selectable (un-hide their LayerCollection chain, or temporarily link them into scene.collection), and before exporting assert `set(bpy.context.selected_objects) == selected`, failing with the names that are missing. Explicitly named objects (`ARGS['objects']`) have the same problem.

v2.reason:
(a) Reproduced on the user's own Blender 5.2.1 (~/.local/bin/blender). The job was built exactly as blender.rs:336-347 builds it: common.py + "\n" + export.py, the same flags, and cwd set to the file's folder. Case (a): with a root mesh in an excluded collection, the default export exits 1 with "RuntimeError: Error: Object 'RefBox' cannot be selected because it is not in View Layer 'ViewLayer'!". Case (b): objects=["SM_Crate"] in an eye-hidden collection exits 0 and writes 4236 bytes. Re-importing that FBX finds 0 objects, yet the report says objects [SM_Crate, SOCKET_Top], sockets [SOCKET_Top], size_cm [100,100,100], problems []. The visible control writes 14156 bytes and re-imports both objects. No DECISIONS entry covers this. Lines 58-59 try to force visibility, so the gap is an oversight.

(b) Reachability: this is the pipeline's export path, and commit b3ea46d shows it is used in real game sessions. The silent case fires when any exported object sits in a collection that is eye-hidden, monitor-disabled or not selectable, or has object hide_select. That covers a named root, a SOCKET_/UCX_/_LOD child, or a mesh skinned to the armature. All of these states persist in the saved .blend. They are normal in files a person has edited (hidden collision/LOD collections, character parts) and rare in files agents build from the skill recipes. Case (a) needs only the default path (no objects) plus any root mesh or armature in an excluded collection. That includes every Rigify file: in 5.2.1 the WGTS_rig collection is excluded and holds 220 root WGT meshes with object-level hide_render False, and the default export failed on 'WGT-rig_tweak_spine.002'.

(c) Consequence: blender_export reports success with an empty or partial FBX, plus objects/sockets/collision/size_cm/mesh_checks for objects that were never written. I reproduced two partial cases. A skinned body in a hidden collection gives an Armature-only FBX. A UCX_ child in a hidden collection is dropped while the report still lists it under collision. In blender_to_unreal, a fully empty FBX does end as passed:false (import_fbx.py:183 sets failed, which blender.rs:428 turns into a problem), but the message blames the importer. A partial FBX passes the size and render checks unless the height drifts by more than 10%. Because replace_existing=True, it also overwrites the existing Unreal asset with the degraded one. The .blend file is never modified. Case (a) is a loud error the agent can recover from by passing objects, not a crash.

(d) High is justified by the silent half: wrong output reported as verified success in the main export flow, triggered by common Blender file states. Case (a) on its own would be medium.

(e) The proposed fix is only partly right; see the correction. Experiment scripts are in scratchpad/exp/final-cli-python-3/.
v2.correction:
1. The root cause is wider than claimed. On 5.2.1, three more states also silently produce the 4236-byte empty FBX with exit 0: Collection.hide_viewport (monitor icon), Collection.hide_select, and Object.hide_select. The script never clears o.hide_select.

2. "Crash" overstates case (a). Blender exits 1 and the tool returns the traceback. It also hits every Rigify file on the default path, because WGTS_rig is excluded. The Rigify recipe passes objects, which avoids it.

3. blender_to_unreal is not silent for a fully empty FBX: it returns passed:false, but blames the importer. Partial FBXs pass. The claim that it imports "a skeleton without its mesh" is unverified (no Unreal was available here); the import more likely fails.

4. The fix has three problems.
   - Un-hiding the LayerCollection chain fixes only the eye case. It did not fix the monitor icon, collection hide_select or object hide_select.
   - Linking each chosen object into scene.collection fixed the excluded, eye, monitor and collection hide_select cases. It still needs `o.hide_select = False`. Keep the assert that `set(bpy.context.selected_objects) == selected`.
   - Do not force in derived objects found through scene.objects (line 20) or children_recursive when they sit in excluded collections; report them instead. An example is an archived body that is still skinned to the rig.

5. The default filter at line 7 checks only object-level hide_render. Rigify sets hide_render on the collection, which the filter misses.

6. Update the docs that promise "every visible root": plugins/blender/skills/blender-to-unreal/SKILL.md:58-59, plugins/blender/skills/blender-to-unreal/reference/troubleshooting.md:87, and plugins/blender/skills/blender-fundamentals/reference/bpy-recipes.md:194-199.

7. On the related locations: render.py:8 shares the default-candidate cause, but the effect is only camera framing. mesh_check.py:3 neither selects nor exports anything, so this failure does not apply to it.

findings.title: Plugin MCP tools run agent-supplied code outside Relay's guardrails
findings.evidence: run.py:8 `exec(compile(ARGS["code"], "script", "exec"), scope)` runs arbitrary Python as the user (os, subprocess, shutil). play.py:79 runs arbitrary console commands, including `py`. ue_python and the ue_play probe (unreal.rs:348, :878) run arbitrary editor Python. Relay's enforcement doors are the PreToolUse hooks (D5). Their matcher is `"Edit|Write|MultiEdit|Bash"` (relay-core/src/hooks.rs:350; Codex `Bash|apply_patch|Edit|Write` at :517). These servers 'never touch the Relay bus' (unreal.rs header), and Relay does not pre-approve them, so no guardrail sees mcp__blender__* or mcp__unreal__* calls. In this audit session Relay refused a Bash `rm -rf`; the same deletion via blender_python `shutil.rmtree(...)` is never checked.
findings.impact: With the Blender or Unreal plugin on, any agent can delete or overwrite protected paths, run denied commands, or write outside its checkout by wrapping them in blender_python, ue_python, ue_console or a ue_play probe. The only remaining gate is the agent CLI's own MCP permission prompt. Users of these tool-heavy plugins are likely to allow them wholesale, but I could not establish their settings.
findings.fix: Route these tools through guardrail.gate. Either add the plugin tool names to the PreToolUse matcher and map them to gate kinds (code-running tools to an 'exec' or new 'script' kind carrying the code, which policy can deny or hold), or have the plugin MCP servers call guardrail.gate before executing. At minimum, document that enabling these plugins bypasses command and path guardrails.

v1.reason: The mechanism is real. The PreToolUse matcher is `Edit|Write|MultiEdit|Bash` (hooks.rs:350) for Claude and `Bash|apply_patch|Edit|Write` (hooks.rs:517) for Codex. Plugin MCP servers are merged into .relay/relay.mcp.json and into Codex `--config` (hooks.rs add_claude_mcp_servers, D159), and blender_python, ue_python and the console tools run arbitrary code without any guardrail.gate call. The impact claim is overstated, though. Relay's exec guardrail (guardrail.rs:811-846) is a denylist matched against Bash argv: the defaults are `rm -rf`, `git reset --hard`, `git clean -fd` and `git push --force` (handlers/settings.rs:33). Protected and write-root paths are checked only for the Edit/Write/MultiEdit tools (main.rs:405-440). A Claude agent can already do every example in the finding through Bash, for instance `python3 -c "import shutil; shutil.rmtree(...)"`, `find -delete` or `sed -i` on a protected file, with no guardrail objection. The plugin tools therefore add little new reach for Claude agents, and the pre-commit hook still applies to anything committed. Two things are real. First, these calls are invisible to Relay's gate and audit. Second, for Codex (workspace-write sandbox, D135), MCP servers are spawned by Codex outside its exec sandbox, so plugin tools likely let code write outside the workspace, which shell commands cannot. That second point is plausible but I did not verify it against Codex itself.
v1.correction: Downgrade to medium. The proposed fix is mostly ineffective. Sending blender_python or ue_python code through the exec gate would match it against argv denylist patterns like `rm -rf`, which never match Python such as `shutil.rmtree`. The honest fixes are: document that Relay's command and path guardrails are a best-effort denylist for Bash and Edit/Write tools only and do not cover plugin MCP tools; route plugin tool calls through a PreToolUse matcher (`mcp__blender__.*|mcp__unreal__.*`) so they are at least audited and can be held for user confirmation per tool; and for Codex, note that plugin MCP servers run outside its sandbox.

findings.title: fbx_options can override the export filepath, bypassing the checkout and .fbx checks
findings.evidence: `for key, value in (ARGS.get("fbx_options") or {}).items(): options[key] = ...` runs after `filepath=path`. Rust validated only `path` (blender.rs:236 `resolve_new`: inside the checkout, .fbx extension). Test: `fbx_options: {"filepath": ".../elsewhere_target/not_an_fbx.txt"}` wrote the 13 KB FBX there. The script then failed at `os.path.getsize(path)` with FileNotFoundError, after the write. The `batch_mode` and `use_batch_own_dir` options can likewise write files elsewhere.
findings.impact: blender_export is documented as refusing files outside the checkout, yet it can overwrite any user-writable file (e.g. ~/.bashrc) with FBX bytes. The agent sees only an unrelated error, so the overwrite goes unnoticed.
findings.fix: Reject `filepath`, `check_existing`, `batch_mode` and `use_batch_own_dir` in fbx_options, or better, allowlist the exporter options an agent may override.

v1.reason: The mechanism is real. export.py:78-79 merges fbx_options after `filepath=path`, and resolve_new (blender.rs:266) checks only `path`. But the claimed security bypass does not exist. The same MCP server exposes blender_python (blender.rs:104-114 and 198-208; run.py:8 is `exec(compile(ARGS["code"], ...))`), which runs arbitrary Python with the agent's privileges and can write any file. Nothing in relay-core gates individual blender tools: an rg for blender/mcp__ in crates/relay-core/src finds only the plugin manifest test. So the resolve_new check on export is a convenience path check, not a security boundary, and an agent gains nothing through fbx_options that it does not already have. The tool description also says outright that 'fbx_options overrides any exporter option'. What is left is a confusing FileNotFoundError at export.py:102 `os.path.getsize(path)` if an agent passes filepath by mistake. That is too minor to report.
v1.correction: If kept at all, this is a low code-quality item: drop `filepath` from fbx_options (or report the path actually written) so the result is not a misleading error. It is not a security finding, because blender_python in the same server already allows arbitrary file writes.

findings.title: Blender anim_inspect: a grip bone written as 'bone:tail' (the documented form) does not exempt the gripping hand, giving false clipping
findings.evidence: `allowed |= near_chain(g.get("bone"))`. near_chain calls `arm.data.bones.get(bone)`, which returns None for 'hand.L:tail', so the chain is empty; resolve() understands ':tail' but near_chain does not. The tool schema (blender.rs:99) recommends 'bone:tail' because 'a hand bone's tail is usually the palm end'. Repro on 5.2.1: a bar carried by the spine and gripped with {point: item:Bar:center, bone: hand.L:tail} produced 27 'clipping' problems ('end_a of 'Bar' is 5.0 cm inside the body near hand.L'). The same grip written as 'hand.L' produced no clipping.
findings.impact: Two-handed weapons and off-hand grips fail blender_anim_inspect with clipping into the very hand that holds them. The main hand is only spared because the holder bone's chain is exempt.
findings.fix: Normalize the reference before walking the chain, e.g. `near_chain(g.get('bone', '').split(':')[0])`, and normalize the contact names used by the partner exemption the same way.

v1.reason: anim_inspect.py:112 does `allowed |= near_chain(g.get("bone"))`, and near_chain (line 81-82) calls `arm.data.bones.get(bone)`. That returns None for 'hand.L:tail', so nothing is exempted. resolve() (lines 74-75) does handle the ':tail' suffix. The schema at blender.rs:99 documents 'bone:tail' for grips, and the tool's own example at blender.rs:549 uses 'hand.R:tail'. Hand, forearm and upper-arm bones are deform bones with parents and do not match SKIP, so they are in arm_segments. When an item is held by one hand and gripped by the other through 'X:tail', the item's ends fall within body_radius of the gripping hand's segments and are flagged as clipping. When the grip bone is also the holder, that hand is already exempt, so only off-hand and two-handed grips are affected.
v1.correction: Normalise before walking the chain, e.g. `near_chain(g.get('bone','').rsplit(':tail',1)[0])`. The same mismatch exists in the partner exemption (line 153): probe names are bare bone names, so a contact written as 'hand.L:tail' never matches 'hand.L' and does not suppress partner_clipping.

findings.title: Ground checks compare the ankle with the lowest rest point, so a foot must sink by its whole ankle height before 'ground' fires
findings.evidence: Blender: `ground = frame["center"].z` is the minimum z over all bone heads and tails at rest (common.py:79-80, toe tails included), and `heights = head(arm, n).z - ground` is taken at the foot bone's head (the ankle). A problem is flagged only below -2.0; the fixture reports feet_height 8.0 cm at rest. Unreal: ground is the minimum z of any bone named foot, ball or toe (common.py:259-260, which includes ik_foot_root at 0 on the UE mannequin), while heights come from foot_* (the ankle) at about 10 cm; flagged when `low < -2.0` (anim_inspect.py:185-189).
findings.impact: A planted foot sinking 5-10 cm into the floor, which is clearly visible, passes both blender_anim_inspect and ue_anim_inspect. 'ground' fires only once the ankle itself is 2 cm below toe level.
findings.fix: Measure each foot against its own rest height (store each foot bone's rest z and flag `pose_z - rest_z < -2`), or measure the lowest point of each foot chain (ball and toe tails) against the ground.

v1.reason: Blender: ground is the minimum z over every bone head and tail at rest (common.py:79-80, toe tails included), and anim_inspect.py:157 measures `head(arm, n).z - ground` for foot bones. That is the ankle, not the sole. It flags only below -2.0 (line 159), so a foot has to sink by its full ankle height plus 2 cm before 'ground' fires. Unreal: ground is the minimum z of any foot/ball/toe bone (unreal_py/common.py:259-260), and the heights are foot bone positions (unreal_py/anim_inspect.py:90, 185-189). The result is the same: the ankle sits about 8-13 cm above ground, so a visibly sunk foot passes. The emitted message ('a foot is X cm below the rest-pose ground') hides that it measures the ankle. A per-frame feet_height is reported, but nothing flags the sink.
v1.correction: The simplest fix is to compare each foot bone with its own rest height (`pose_z - rest_z < -2`). Another is to measure the lowest point of each foot chain (the toe/ball tail) against ground. This is an insensitive check (false negatives) in a dev verification tool, not a crash, so medium is the ceiling.

findings.title: An expected 'touch' contact disables that bone's partner-clipping check at every time and against every partner bone
findings.evidence: `allowed = any(c.get("expect", "touch") == "touch" and name in (c["a"], c["b"]) for c in ARGS.get("contacts", []))` ignores both the contact's window and its other end. Run against the stand-in editor module: adding {a: hand_r, b: partner:head, window: [0,0]} reduced partner_clipping problems from 12 to 11. The one suppressed was 'hand_r is 8.0 cm inside the partner near upperarm_r' at t=1.0, which is outside the window and against a different bone than the head. The Blender twin (anim_inspect.py:153-154) is identical.
findings.impact: Consider a punch authored to touch the partner's head on its impact frames. If the same hand passes through the partner's torso or arm anywhere else in the clip, that clipping is hidden and the broken interaction passes.
findings.fix: Exempt a probe only inside the contact's window, and only against the segments of the contacted partner bone. Resolve `partner:<bone>` and skip just those segments rather than the whole check.

v1.reason: unreal_py/anim_inspect.py:180: `allowed = any(c.get("expect", "touch") == "touch" and name in (c["a"], c["b"]) for c in ARGS.get("contacts", []))`. It ignores `c["window"]`, which the contact check just above does honour (`in_window`, line ~158), and it ignores which partner bone the contact names. The exemption covers the probe against every partner segment at every sampled time. Any declared touch contact on hand_r (e.g. b = partner:head with a window) therefore suppresses all partner_clipping problems for hand_r over the whole clip, and `passed` can come back true. `keep_min` still records the clearance in closest_approach before the exemption, so the number is visible there, but problems and passed hide it, and those are what the tool tells agents to rely on ('Returns problems[] and passed'). The Blender twin at blender_py/anim_inspect.py:153-155 (`intended = ...`) has the same logic.
v1.correction: Exempt only inside the contact's window. Exempt only when the nearest partner segment (best[1]) belongs to the contacted partner bone, or skip just that bone's segments: resolve `partner:<bone>` to that bone and compare it with the segment endpoints. Fix both files together, since they are twins.

findings.title: blender_to_unreal never imports materials by default: Rust sends materials=null, which the script reads as false
findings.evidence: `ui.set_editor_property("import_materials", bool(ARGS.get("materials", kind != "animation")))` (import_textures on line 32 is the same). blender.rs:404-407 builds `"materials": args["materials"]`, which is JSON null when the agent omits it. `ARGS.get('materials', default)` then returns None because the key is present, and bool(None) is False. Checked in plain Python: null gives False, an absent key gives True.
findings.impact: The intended default, importing materials and textures for static and skeletal meshes, never applies. Meshes arrive with default materials unless the agent passes materials=true, and the transient-material checks never see a material in the default flow.
findings.fix: In Rust, insert only keys that are present and non-null. Alternatively, in Python treat None as absent: `m = ARGS.get('materials'); m = (kind != 'animation') if m is None else bool(m)`.

v1.reason: blender.rs:404-407 builds the import args with `"materials": args["materials"]`, which is Value::Null when the agent omits the optional boolean (schema at blender.rs:181). script() (unreal.rs:466-467) serialises args to JSON unchanged, so the Python ARGS dict has 'materials': None. import_fbx.py:31-32 `bool(ARGS.get("materials", kind != "animation"))` returns None because the key is present, and bool(None) is False. The default of importing materials and textures for static and skeletal meshes never applies. blender_to_unreal is the only caller of import_fbx (unreal.rs:419, blender.rs:414). Every default import arrives with default materials unless the agent passes materials=true. The same null-key pattern affects 'animations' at import_fbx.py:30, but that one is harmless because bool(None) or kind==animation keeps the intended default.
v1.correction: The best fix is in Rust: insert materials (and skeleton/name/animations) only when the value is non-null, as the loop at blender.rs:409-413 already does for importer/normals/socket_rotation. Alternatively, treat None as absent in Python.

findings.title: Import render check counts sky gradients as the subject, and failed pixel reads count as visible
findings.evidence: coverage() takes pixel (1,1) as the background and counts samples whose summed RGB difference from it exceeds 24. The import preview is spawned 500 m above the editor camera, in the level's sky (preview_asset.py:13). The 'front' view is horizontal (pitch 0), so its upper rows are sky and its lower half is horizon, ground or atmosphere, all of which differ from the corner. On any error, `except Exception: return None`. Rust then computes `visible = coverage.is_empty() || coverage.iter().any(|c| *c > 0.002)` (unreal.rs:446), and 0.002 of the 529 samples is just 2 pixels. Each of the ~530 samples is a separate `read_render_target_pixel` GPU readback.
findings.impact: In any level with a sky, an invisible imported mesh (the D162 'only its shadow rendered' failure) still reports renders=true, and blender_to_unreal passes the broken asset. If the pixel reads fail, the check also passes silently.
findings.fix: Capture each view twice, once with the subject in `hidden_actors` and once without, and count the pixels that differ. Read each render target once with `RenderingLibrary.read_render_target`. Return an explicit error rather than None, and have Rust treat missing coverage as 'not verified'.

v1.reason: capture.py:38-52: coverage() uses pixel (1,1) as the background and counts samples whose summed RGB difference from it exceeds 24, out of a 23x23 grid. On any exception it returns None. unreal.rs:450-451 drops non-numeric coverage with filter_map, then sets `visible = coverage.is_empty() || coverage.iter().any(|c| *c > 0.002)`. A failed read therefore yields renders=true: the check passes silently, and the cause is directly visible in the code. The import check (unreal.rs:438-446) places the mesh 500 m above the viewport camera (preview_asset.py:13). It then captures 'front' with forward (0,1,0), a horizontal view because look_rotation gives pitch 0 for a horizontal offset, and 'three_quarter', with no isolation and SCS_FINAL_COLOR_LDR. In a level with SkyAtmosphere or a sky sphere, the zenith-to-horizon gradient and the ground or haze below the horizon will very likely differ from the top-left corner by more than 24 in at least 2 of the 529 samples, the bar needed to exceed 0.002. An invisible mesh would then still read as rendering. I could not run the editor, so the sky false positive rests on reasoning, but the None path is certain.
v1.correction: The Rust lines are unreal.rs:450-451, not 446. A more robust check is to capture each view with the subject hidden (hidden_actors=[subject]) and visible, and count the pixels that differ. Treat missing or None coverage as 'not verified', not as renders=true. The ~530 per-pixel GPU readbacks per view are slow but secondary; they fit inside the 120 s timeout.

findings.title: Preview and capture actors dirty the user's level, and the bridge's own quit/restart then saves the .umap
findings.evidence: capture.py:57/80, preview_asset.py:15/19 (the import render check), anim_preview.py:25/69 and play.py:93 spawn, label and destroy ordinary actors in the editor level. The docs acknowledge 'the level stays marked modified, so do not save it for this' (plugins/unreal-engine/docs/mcp-tools.md:190, also :121). quit_editor runs `unreal.EditorLoadingAndSavingUtils.save_dirty_packages(True, True)` by default (unreal.rs:582). `ue_build restart_editor`, the Linux C++ loop, quits with save=true (unreal.rs:1519).
findings.impact: After any ue_screenshot, ue_anim_preview, ue_play outside capture or blender_to_unreal, the next ue_build restart_editor or ue_editor_quit rewrites the open .umap even though nothing in it was meant to change. That .umap is binary and often LFS-locked, so the result is git churn and conflicts with whoever owns the map.
findings.fix: Before Relay's helper tools run, record whether the map package is already dirty (`EditorLoadingAndSavingUtils.get_dirty_map_packages`). If only Relay dirtied it, have quit and restart save content packages only (`save_dirty_packages(False, True)`), or say what they skipped. Where the engine supports it, also spawn helpers with `transient=True`.

v1.reason: capture.py:57 and :80, preview_asset.py:15/19, and the anim_preview and play helpers spawn and destroy ordinary editor actors through EditorActorSubsystem.spawn_actor_from_class without bTransient. The tool's own description (unreal.rs:231) and plugins/unreal-engine/docs/mcp-tools.md:122 and :190 say the level is left marked modified and should not be saved for this. Yet quit_editor (unreal.rs:572-583) runs `unreal.EditorLoadingAndSavingUtils.save_dirty_packages(True, True)` whenever save is true, and the first argument is bSaveMapPackages (FileHelpers.h:108). Both ue_editor_quit (unreal.rs:390) and ue_build restart_editor (unreal.rs:1519) default save to true. On Linux there is no Live Coding, so restart_editor is the normal build loop, and a screenshot followed by a build, or an import followed by its render check (blender_to_unreal), saves the map nobody meant to change.
v1.correction: Impact depends on the map. A classic single-file .umap is rewritten, which is git and LFS churn, or a write to a file someone else has locked. With World Partition or one-file-per-actor maps, the spawned actor's own external package is dirtied rather than the .umap, so the effect is smaller. Whether a resave of an unchanged map yields different bytes was not established. Fixes: UE 5.8's SpawnActorFromClass takes bTransient (EditorActorSubsystem.h:228), which sets RF_Transient; pass transient=True for the helper actors, and/or record get_dirty_map_packages before the helpers run and save content packages only when Relay alone dirtied the map.

findings.title: Default renders crop tall subjects: framing uses the horizontal FOV for a landscape image
findings.evidence: `dist = radius / math.tan(fov / 2) * 1.15`, with `cam_data.angle = fov` (line 58). Blender applies that angle to the wider image side under AUTO sensor fit. At the defaults (640x480, 40 degrees) the vertical half-FOV is 15.3 degrees, but the bounding sphere needs about 17.6 degrees. Repro on 5.2.1: a 0.6 x 0.25 x 1.8 m box (standing A-pose proportions) rendered front at default size covers pixel rows 0-479; I viewed the image and its top and bottom are cut off. capture.py:22 uses the same formula (Unreal's FOVAngle is also horizontal), so ue_screenshot at 640x480 and fov 50 crops the same subject.
findings.impact: blender_render's default views of a standing character in A-pose, or in arms-down animation frames, and ue_screenshot of a tall actor lose the head and feet, which are the parts the agent usually needs to check.
findings.fix: Frame against the narrower field: `half = atan(tan(fov/2) * min(w, h) / max(w, h))`, then `dist = radius / sin(half) * margin`.

v1.reason: render.py:58 sets cam_data.angle = fov, and with the default AUTO sensor fit that angle applies to the wider side of the image (640 wide at the 640x480 default). Line 74 then computes dist = radius / tan(fov/2) * 1.15, so the bounding sphere is fitted to the horizontal half-angle only. I checked the arithmetic. For the 0.6 x 0.25 x 1.8 m box at 40 degrees: radius 0.957 m, dist 3.02 m, and the visible half-height at the front face is (3.02 - 0.125) * tan(20deg) * 0.75 = 0.79 m, against the 0.9 m the box needs. The head and feet are cut off, and the narrower side views are closer and crop more. unreal_py/capture.py:22 uses the same formula, and UE's SceneCapture fov_angle is horizontal. A 180 x 50 x 30 cm actor at the default 50 degrees and 640x480 has 76 cm of visible half-height against the 90 cm it needs, so it is cropped too. A wide T- or A-pose (arms span of 1.2 m or more) only just fits, but arms-down poses and slim props do not. This hits the default views of the main 'see a model/pose' tool.
v1.correction: Related sites: capture.py:22 (where the radius is floored at 20) and render.py:58. Fix: compute half = atan(tan(fov/2) * min(w,h) / max(w,h)), then dist = radius / sin(half) * margin. sin is the exact sphere fit; it is slightly larger than tan, which matters at wide angles. Apply the same change in capture.py using width and height.

findings.title: Unapplied-rotation checks read only rotation_euler, missing quaternion-mode objects such as every glTF import
findings.evidence: `any(abs(r) > 1e-4 for r in o.rotation_euler)`; rig_check.py:24 (the armature) and :75 (skinned meshes) do the same. On 5.2.1 a QUATERNION-mode object rotated 90 degrees about Z reported `flags: []`. A .glb round trip showed that Blender's glTF importer sets rotation_mode QUATERNION on every object, leaving rotation_euler at (0,0,0) while the object stays rotated.
findings.impact: Rotated meshes and rigs from glTF/glb files, which blender_info lists as art files, and any quaternion or axis-angle object pass blender_info and blender_rig_check, then export rotated.
findings.fix: Check the rotation the object actually uses: `o.matrix_basis.to_quaternion().angle > 1e-4`, or the right property for `o.rotation_mode`. Include delta rotations.

v1.reason: info.py:9-10, rig_check.py:24 and rig_check.py:75 check only `rotation_euler`. A repo-wide rg finds no read of rotation_quaternion, rotation_axis_angle, rotation_mode or matrix_basis in blender_py. In Blender, rotation_euler is ignored when rotation_mode is QUATERNION or AXIS_ANGLE. The installed 5.2.1 glTF importer (io_scene_gltf2/blender/imp/node.py:100-101) sets `obj.rotation_mode = 'QUATERNION'; obj.rotation_quaternion = rot` on every imported object. A .glb cannot be passed to blender_info directly, because blender -b opens .blend files. But the usual flow imports it through blender_python and saves it as a .blend, and the quaternion mode survives that. A rotated object then passes info and rig_check with no flag and exports rotated. blender_to_unreal's facing check catches some skeletal cases afterwards, but not static meshes.
v1.correction: Delta rotations (`delta_rotation_*`) are also unchecked. A mode-independent check is `o.matrix_basis.to_quaternion().angle > 1e-4`, or decompose matrix_basis, which also covers delta transforms. Severity stays medium: these are lint checks in an art pipeline, and the rotation shows up in Unreal.

findings.title: ue_anim_inspect silently measures the reference pose when the animation cannot be sampled
findings.evidence: `try: pose[n] = from_ue(unreal.AnimationLibrary.get_bone_pose_for_time(anim, n, time, False)) except Exception: pose[n] = self.ref_local[n]`. anim_length (lines 222-228) swallows both getters and returns 0.0. `load(ARGS["animation"])` (anim_inspect.py:6) accepts any asset class. When get_ref_pose_transform is missing, the Skeleton fallback (lines 178-182) drops every reference-pose rotation without a warning.
findings.impact: If the agent passes a BlendSpace, an AnimBlueprint, a mesh, or any asset the library rejects, every bone sits at the reference pose and sampling covers zero length. The report still says `passed: true` under the animation's name, and nothing indicates the animation never played.
findings.fix: Check `isinstance(anim, unreal.AnimSequenceBase)` up front. Count per-bone failures and raise, or add a problem, if any bone fails. Have anim_length raise instead of returning 0.0, and raise when get_ref_pose_transform is unavailable.

v1.reason: The code matches the claim. common.py:189-192 replaces every bone's pose with ref_local when get_bone_pose_for_time raises. anim_length (common.py:222-228) returns 0.0 when both getters fail, so sample_times gives all-zero times. anim_inspect.py:6 loads any asset class. The emit (anim_inspect.py:203-216) still returns `passed: not problems`. A BlendSpace is not an AnimSequenceBase, so the Python binding should raise TypeError on every bone and the tool would silently measure the reference pose. I could not confirm the engine's behaviour from here: whether UE raises or just logs for a montage, an AnimSequence from another skeleton, or a missing bone track. Without that, the only trigger I can stand behind is an agent passing the wrong asset type. That is a misuse of a parameter documented as 'Animation sequence path'.
v1.correction: The claim that nothing shows the animation never played is overstated: the output reports `length_s: 0.0` (anim_inspect.py:206) and all sample times as 0. The get_ref_pose_transform fallback (common.py:181-182) only matters on engine versions without that UFUNCTION, which recent UE versions have, so it is a minor aside. Severity is low because the cause is a misused parameter and a hint is visible. Fix: check `isinstance(anim, unreal.AnimSequenceBase)` up front (or reject length 0), and count the bones that fell back and add a problem when any did.

findings.title: Broken imports are deleted with a path function the code documents as failing after a failed import, and Rust then says they were deleted
findings.evidence: `ok = unreal.EditorAssetLibrary.delete_asset(package)`, with exceptions swallowed. common.py:28-30 and D162 note that EditorAssetLibrary's path functions (does_asset_exist, save_asset, delete_asset) 'were seen returning False for every asset for the rest of a session after a failed import'. The import task has already saved the assets (line 55, `save=True`). blender.rs:428-432 tells the agent 'the broken assets were deleted again' whenever the import failed, without reading the per-path `deleted` flags.
findings.impact: In exactly the failure this cleanup exists for, broken assets (empty meshes, transient materials) can stay saved in Content/ while the agent is told they were deleted.
findings.fix: Delete by object (`EditorAssetLibrary.delete_loaded_asset(unreal.load_asset(p))`, or AssetTools/ObjectTools), confirm the deletion through the registry (`asset_exists`), and have Rust report every path whose `deleted` is false.

v1.reason: remove() (import_fbx.py:105-115) calls EditorAssetLibrary.delete_asset and swallows exceptions. common.py:28-30 and D162 (DECISIONS.md:962-963) record that this library's path functions, delete_asset by name, returned False for a whole session after a failed import, and asset_exists() was added to work around it. The import task saves with save=True (line 55), so a delete that silently fails leaves the broken assets on disk. compare() at blender.rs:428-432 always says 'the broken assets were deleted again' when failed is true. However, that message also embeds the full attempts JSON, which includes each path's `deleted: false`, so the agent is not left with only the false claim. A retry with replace_existing also overwrites a leftover from the first attempt. Leftovers therefore stay only when every importer fails and delete_asset also misbehaves. I could not establish that the empty-mesh or transient-material outcome counts as the 'failed import' that triggered the documented EditorAssetLibrary breakage.
v1.correction: Leftover broken assets need both importers to fail and delete_asset to misbehave, and the deleted:false flags are already in the returned text. Fix: have compare() read attempts[-1].cleaned_up and name the paths whose deleted is false. Optionally confirm each delete with asset_exists() (registry-based), or delete by loaded object.

findings.title: Blender scripts re-implement the mesh and skinning checks per script, and the copies already disagree
findings.evidence: rig_check.py:106-121 repeats mesh_report's bmesh checks (common.py:146-181), on the original rather than evaluated mesh, with opposite severities. A missing UV map is a problem in rig_check (line 107) but a warning in mesh_report (175-176). Zero-area faces are a warning in rig_check (118-119) but a problem in mesh_report, which makes blender_export refuse (165-166). 'Meshes skinned to the armature' is defined three different ways: export.py:20-22 (Armature modifier only), rig_check.py:64 (modifier or parent_type ARMATURE) and render.py:15 (any child, including bone-parented props, or the modifier). rig_check.py:28 computes `deform_roots` and never uses it.
findings.impact: A mesh can pass blender_rig_check and then be refused by blender_export for degenerate faces, or fail the rig check for a missing UV map that export accepts. A body parented with the legacy ARMATURE parent type passes the rig check but is left out of the skeletal FBX.
findings.fix: Have rig_check call mesh_report(o) and add only the skin-specific checks on top. Add one `skinned_meshes(arm)` helper in common.py and use it in export, rig_check and render.

v1.reason: I verified each divergence. rig_check.py:106-121 runs its own bmesh pass on the un-evaluated o.data, while mesh_report (common.py:146-181) runs on the evaluated mesh. A missing UV map is a problem in rig_check (line 107), which fails 'passed', but only a warning in mesh_report (175-176). Zero-area faces are only a warning in rig_check (118-119) but a problem in mesh_report (165-166), and export.py:52-53 refuses to export when a problem is present. So a rig can pass blender_rig_check and then be refused by blender_export, or fail the rig check for a missing UV that export accepts. The skinned-mesh definitions differ too. export.py:20-22 counts only an Armature modifier. rig_check.py:64 adds parent_type == 'ARMATURE'. render.py:15 counts any child of the armature. A legacy armature-parented body with no modifier is not a root (its parent is the armature), so export.py:7 does not choose it, and line 16 skips children of an armature, which leaves it out of the skeletal FBX even though rig_check accepts it. rig_check.py:28 computes deform_roots, and grep shows nothing uses it.
v1.correction: Two qualifications. First, render.py:15 including bone-parented props is arguably intended, since a render should show held items. export.py:13-15 deliberately excludes such props with a comment. So the shared skinned_meshes(arm) helper should cover the modifier and parent_type ARMATURE cases for export and rig_check, and render can add children on top. Second, if rig_check reuses mesh_report, the evaluated mesh carries the current pose's deformation. That is acceptable for these checks, but the call has to keep rig_check's weight and influence checks on o.data. The legacy-parent export omission is a real but rare case, since modern Ctrl+P creates a modifier.

findings.title: The Blender and Unreal animation checks are parallel copies that have diverged
findings.symbol: mirror_name / twin, SKIP lists, probes, ground
findings.evidence: Left/right naming: blender_py/common.py:42 PAIRS includes '-L'/'-R' and tries prefixes only after every suffix; unreal_py/common.py:143 LEFT_RIGHT has no '-L'/'-R' and interleaves the prefix checks. Segment filters: Blender's SKIP (anim_inspect.py:21-22) has 'ik', 'pole', 'ctrl', 'mch', 'org'; Unreal's SKIP_SEGMENT (common.py:280-281) has 'ik_', 'attach', 'socket', 'camera', 'correct', '_end', 'tip'. Partner probes: Blender adds 'forearm' and 'shin'. Ground: Blender uses the minimum over all bone heads and tails; Unreal uses only foot, ball and toe bones. D161 says both sides use 'the same character frame', so that a problem 'is caught before export and measured again after import'.
findings.impact: The same rig and clip can pass in one tool and fail in the other. For example, a rig named with -L/-R gets pairs and a facing in Blender but falls back to the default frame in Unreal. So the before/after comparison D161 promises is not like-for-like, and every fix has to be made twice: the grip, ground and contact bugs above all exist in both copies.
findings.fix: Move the host-independent logic (pair naming, segment and probe filters, contact, partner and ground checks on plain tuples) into one shared Python file that both blender.rs and unreal.rs include ahead of the host script. Keep only pose sampling host-specific.

v1.reason: The two copies have measurably diverged. blender_py/common.py:42 PAIRS includes ('-L','-R'), but unreal_py/common.py:143 LEFT_RIGHT does not. A rig named with -L/-R therefore gets left/right pairs and a facing in Blender, while Unreal falls back to right=(0,1,0) (common.py:252-253). The precedence also differs: Unreal checks the l_/L_ prefixes inside the loop before the later 'Left'/'left' entries, whereas Blender checks them only after every suffix. The segment filters differ: Blender's SKIP (anim_inspect.py:21-22) has 'ik', 'pole', 'ctrl', 'mch', 'org', and Unreal's SKIP_SEGMENT (common.py:279-280) has 'ik_', 'attach', 'socket', 'camera', 'correct', '_end', 'tip'. The partner probes differ: Blender adds forearm and shin (anim_inspect.py:145). Ground differs: Blender takes the minimum over all bone heads and tails (common.py:78), Unreal the minimum over foot/ball/toe joint positions only (common.py:255). Both tools then report feet_height relative to their own ground, so the same clip measures differently before export and after import. D161 (docs/engine/DECISIONS.md, lines ~952-954) promises 'the same character frame ... as the Unreal checks, so a problem is caught before export and measured again after import'.
v1.correction: Sharing is feasible: Blender uses mathutils Vectors and Unreal uses tuples, so the shared module has to run on plain tuples. A pragmatic first step that removes most of the drift is to share only the name tables and the twin/mirror function, the SKIP and probe lists, and the ground rule, as one Python snippet that both blender.rs and unreal.rs prepend (both already concatenate a common script).

findings.title: Data-table import reports saved=true without checking the save
findings.evidence: The result of `save_asset(table)` is discarded, then `emit({..., "saved": True})`. save_asset (common.py:39-47) swallows the first exception and returns the bool of a fallback save. import_fbx.py:154 also ignores the result after editing sockets.
findings.impact: When the save fails (a read-only or source-controlled file, or the path-function failure described in common.py), the agent is told the table or the socket fixes were saved.
findings.fix: Use `saved = save_asset(table)` and emit or raise on False. Do the same in fix_sockets.

v1.reason: data_table.py:14-15 ignores the result of `save_asset(table)` and emits `"saved": True`. save_asset (common.py:39-47) swallows the exception from save_loaded_asset and returns the bool from save_packages, so it can return False. The Rust caller (unreal.rs:979-983) passes the Ok value through without checking. When the save fails (read-only or checked-out file, or the path-function failure described in common.py:28-30), the agent is told the table was saved. The table is still filled in memory and dirty in the editor, so data is lost only if the editor closes without a save.
v1.correction: The import_fbx.py:154 location is weaker: fix_sockets never claims a save, it only lists the fixes it made. Its result is still ignored, so that is the same root cause. Fix: `saved = save_asset(table)`, then emit `saved` or raise on False.

findings.title: rig_check reports a missing right twin but never a missing left twin
findings.evidence: `side_named = [n for n in names if twin(n) and twin(n) not in names]`, but twin() (common.py:45-54) only maps left-side names to right. Checked in Python: for names [root, hand.R, forearm.R, upper_arm.R, hand.L] the result is [], so forearm.R and upper_arm.R are not reported; for [hand.L, forearm.L, hand.R] it is ['forearm.L']. The Left/left substring rule also maps 'cleft_chin' to 'cright_chin', which produces a false report.
findings.impact: Half of the naming errors this warning exists for are never reported.
findings.fix: Add the reverse mapping (right to left) and check both directions. Match Left/left only as a whole name token.

v1.reason: twin() at common.py:45-54 maps only left-hand forms to their right counterparts: suffixes .L/.l/_L/_l/-L, the substrings Left/left, and the prefixes l_/L_. It returns None for any right-side name. rig_check.py:51 keeps only names where twin(n) is truthy, so a right bone without a left twin is never reported. I ran the copied function: ['root','hand.R','forearm.R','upper_arm.R','hand.L'] gives [], ['hand.L','forearm.L','hand.R'] gives ['forearm.L'], and ['cleft_chin'] gives ['cleft_chin'] because 'left' in 'cleft_chin' maps it to 'cright_chin'. The output is only a warning, which keeps the severity low, but half of the naming mistakes the check exists for go unreported, and substring matches produce false positives.
v1.correction: The same unanchored substring rule also affects left_right_pairs and body_frame, but a false pair forms only if the substituted name exists as well, so the impact there is small. Fix: add a right_to_left mapping, check both directions, and match Left/left only as a whole token at a name boundary.

findings.title: Unreal body-frame fallback uses actor axes in mesh space, and neither side recognises Biped L/R names
findings.evidence: With no pairs, `right = (0.0, 1.0, 0.0)`, which makes forward +X. The rest of the code and its tests treat skeletal meshes as facing +Y in mesh space (tests/unreal.py:21; the blender.rs round-trip test expects forward [0,1,0]). Blender's own fallback uses its own front (-Y). Neither twin() nor mirror_name() matches 3ds Max Biped or CAT names such as 'Bip01 L Hand' / 'Bip01 R Hand'.
findings.impact: For a Biped-named skeleton, ue_anim_inspect's 'right' axis is the character's forward. Sides and [forward, right, up] coordinates come out rotated 90 degrees, so checks like 'which hand holds the sword' are wrong; the only hint is left_right_pairs_found: 0.
findings.fix: Fall back to right = (-1, 0, 0), i.e. mesh-space +Y forward, and say in the output that the fallback was used. Add ' L ' / ' R ' infix pairs to the shared naming rules.

v1.reason: common.py:256-258: with no left/right pairs, `right = (0.0, 1.0, 0.0)`, so forward = cross(right, up) = (1, 0, 0). The rest of the code assumes +Y forward and -X right in mesh space. The test stand-in says so (tests/unreal.py:1-3, 'right side is -X'), capture uses forward [0,1,0] (unreal.rs:443), and blender.rs compare maps Blender's (x,y,z) to (x,-y,z). Blender's fallback (blender_py/common.py:75-78) uses right=(-1,0,0) and forward=(0,-1,0), which maps to UE forward (0,1,0). Neither LEFT_RIGHT (common.py:143) nor PAIRS/twin (blender_py/common.py:42-54) matches 'Bip01 L Hand' / 'Bip01 R Hand'. Concrete trigger: blender_to_unreal on a skeleton with Biped or other unrecognised side names. Both sides fall back, Rust expects [0,1,0], UE reports [1,0,0], dot = 0 < 0.9, and compare (blender.rs:470-479) pushes a false 'it is rotated' problem. In ue_anim_inspect, sides and [forward, right, up] are 90 degrees off.
v1.correction: A second consequence the finding left out: blender_to_unreal reports a false facing problem. Fix the UE fallback to right = (-1, 0, 0) so it matches the Blender fallback and the documented convention, and flag in the output that the fallback was used. Adding an ' L '/' R ' infix rule to both name tables is optional. Low severity, because it needs an unpaired naming scheme.

findings.title: blender_python's exec scope: a non-object emit() crashes the MCP server, and main-guarded scripts silently do nothing
findings.evidence: `scope = {"bpy": ..., "emit": emit}` exposes emit but sets no `__name__`. blender.rs:366-373 parses the last RELAY_JSON line and then does `value["output"] = ...`. serde_json's IndexMut panics when the Value is not an object or null, and nothing catches the panic (main.rs:231). Also, `exec(code, {...})` resolves `__name__` to 'builtins' (verified), so an `if __name__ == "__main__":` block never runs.
findings.impact: `emit("done")`, `emit([...])` or `emit(3)` in blender_python panics `relay blender-mcp`, and the Blender tools are gone for the rest of the agent session. A script written with a main guard returns empty output and no error.
findings.fix: In Rust, wrap non-object results (`if !value.is_object() { value = json!({"value": value}) }`). Add `"__name__": "__main__"` to the scope.

v1.reason: `emit` (blender_py/common.py:12) is `print("RELAY_JSON:" + json.dumps(value))`, and run.py:5 puts it into the agent's exec scope. blender.rs:362-374 takes the last RELAY_JSON line, parses it into `value`, and when body == PY_RUN does `value["output"] = ...` and `value["saved"] = ...`. serde_json's IndexMut<&str> panics when the Value is a string, number, bool or array. Null is turned into an object, so it is safe. `serve()` (blender.rs:34) is a plain loop with no catch_unwind, and it runs directly from main (main.rs:230). A panic therefore ends the `relay blender-mcp` process, and the agent loses the Blender tools until it relaunches. The `__name__` half also holds: run.py:8 passes a globals dict with no `__name__`, so the lookup falls through to builtins and gets 'builtins', and an `if __name__ == "__main__":` block silently does not run. The trigger is uncommon. `emit` appears in no tool description or plugin doc (the description says 'Print what you need to see'), so an agent would only call it after finding it in the scope, and main guards are rare in these snippets.
v1.correction: The panicking assignments are at blender.rs:372-373 (`value["output"]`, `value["saved"]`). A simpler and more robust fix: for PY_RUN, ignore anything other than an object (`if !value.is_object() { value = json!({"value": value}) }`), or leave `emit` out of the run.py scope, since it is undocumented for blender_python. Add `"__name__": "__main__"` to the scope.

findings.title: blender_python hides add-on enable failures
findings.evidence: `addon_utils.enable(module, default_set=True)` returns None on failure and prints 'Add-on not loaded: ..., cause: ...' before `print("RELAY_OUT_BEGIN")`. blender.rs:358-361 returns only the lines between the markers. Test with addons ['rigify_typo']: exit code 0, and the cause line is outside the returned output.
findings.impact: A typo or a missing add-on shows up later as an unrelated AttributeError in the agent's code, with its real cause filtered out.
findings.fix: `if addon_utils.enable(module, default_set=True) is None: raise RuntimeError('add-on %r did not load' % module)`.

v1.reason: run.py:3-4 calls addon_utils.enable(module, default_set=True) and ignores the return value. In the installed Blender 5.2.1 addon_utils.py (lines 473-511), a failed import sets ex.msg to 'Add-on not loaded: "...", cause: ...'. The default handle_error then print()s it to stdout, or prints a traceback for other errors, and enable returns None without raising. That line comes before print('RELAY_OUT_BEGIN') at run.py:6, so blender.rs:358-361 drops it from the returned output, and the exit status is 0. If the agent's code later fails, failure_text (blender.rs:378-382) starts at the first line beginning with 'Traceback'. A missing module prints a message and no traceback, so the cause still lands before that cut and is dropped. The agent sees only the later, unrelated error.
v1.correction: Fix as proposed: if addon_utils.enable(module, default_set=True) is None, raise RuntimeError('add-on %r did not load' % module). The run then fails through the failure_text path, which shows the agent the cause.

findings.title: save=true leaves a .blend1 backup in the checkout
findings.evidence: `bpy.ops.wm.save_mainfile()` runs under factory settings, where save_version is 1. Test: saving savecheck/hero.blend left both hero.blend and hero.blend1 on disk.
findings.impact: Every blender_python save leaves a full-size binary copy next to the asset. It shows up as an untracked file and gets committed by a blanket `git add`.
findings.fix: Set `bpy.context.preferences.filepaths.save_version = 0` before both save and save_as.

v1.reason: blender.rs:344 launches Blender with `--factory-startup`, and factory preferences keep one save version (Save Versions = 1). run.py:20 `bpy.ops.wm.save_mainfile()` overwrites the opened file, which rotates the old copy into `<name>.blend1`. A search of the repo found nothing (no `save_version`, no `.blend1` cleanup or ignore) that suppresses or removes it. This also contradicts D161's claim that calls 'cannot leave state behind'. The result is an untracked binary the size of the asset next to it in the agent's checkout. It is easy to commit with `git add -A`, though a user can delete or ignore it.
v1.correction: save_as_mainfile at run.py:15 creates a backup too, but only when save_as overwrites an existing file. Set `bpy.context.preferences.filepaths.save_version = 0` once before either save. The same applies to any other blender_py script that saves the mainfile.

findings.title: The eevee engine identifier is valid only on Blender <=4.1 and >=5.0
findings.evidence: `"eevee": "BLENDER_EEVEE"`. On 5.2.1 the engine enum accepts BLENDER_EEVEE and rejects BLENDER_EEVEE_NEXT (probed). Blender 4.2-4.5 call EEVEE Next 'BLENDER_EEVEE_NEXT'; no 4.x build was available to run here. find_blender() uses whichever Blender is installed.
findings.impact: engine=eevee fails with an enum TypeError on 4.2 LTS through 4.5 LTS. Combined with the .fcurves crash on 5.x, no Blender release from 4.2 on can run every tool.
findings.fix: Pick the identifier from `scene.render.bl_rna.properties['engine'].enum_items`, preferring BLENDER_EEVEE_NEXT when present and falling back to BLENDER_EEVEE.

v1.reason: render.py:35 maps engine 'eevee' to the fixed identifier 'BLENDER_EEVEE', and line 36 assigns it straight to scene.render.engine with no fallback. Blender 4.2 through 4.5 expose EEVEE Next as 'BLENDER_EEVEE_NEXT', and 5.0 renamed it back to 'BLENDER_EEVEE'. Assigning an identifier that is not in the enum raises TypeError, and the run then fails through blender.rs:363. blender.rs:127 advertises 'eevee' in the tool schema. find_blender takes whatever Blender is on PATH (the newest folder on Windows), and nothing in the repo pins a version: the skills cite 4.0.2, and the local install is 5.2.1. So a user running a 4.2 to 4.5 LTS build gets a hard failure on engine=eevee. Workbench, the default, and cycles are unaffected.
v1.correction: This is limited to the optional eevee engine; the default path works. The proposed fix is right: read scene.render.bl_rna.properties['engine'].enum_items and use BLENDER_EEVEE_NEXT when it is present, otherwise BLENDER_EEVEE. The finding's side remark that no release from 4.2 on can run every tool relies on a separate act.fcurves issue (export.py:48, info.py:45-46). That is not established here and should be judged as its own finding.

findings.title: import_fbx still returns tautological hand_sides, and the docs still promise a hand-side check
findings.evidence: Lines 97-99 compute the sides of hand_l and hand_r in a frame built from those same name pairs, so the answer is always left and right. Commit 42b325d stopped compare() from using it for exactly that reason. blender.rs:170 still advertises 'which hand ends up on which side', and D161 says the handoff 'compares height, root bone scale and hand sides'.
findings.impact: Agents may read `hand_sides: {hand_l: left, hand_r: right}` as confirmation, although it can never reveal a mirrored rig; only the facing comparison can.
findings.fix: Remove hand_sides (the facing comparison already covers mirroring) and update the tool description and D161.

v1.reason: import_fbx.py:97-99 picks a hand bone and its mirror_name twin, and side() (common.py:275) projects each onto body_frame's `right` axis. body_frame (common.py:241-258) builds that axis by summing (right twin - left) over every name pair, so hand_r is on the +right side by construction unless a rig's hand pair runs against all its other pairs. The output is name-derived, as the finding says. The code already admits this in blender.rs:423-425 ('Sides are worked out from bone names on both sides, so a mirrored rig would still look right-handed') and in plugins/blender/skills/blender-to-unreal/SKILL.md:171 ('hand_sides: informational only'). Commit 42b325d moved the mirroring check to the facing comparison. But the blender_to_unreal tool description (blender.rs:170, 'which hand ends up on which side') and D161 (DECISIONS.md:955, 'compares height, root bone scale and hand sides') still promise the check.
v1.correction: The D161 text is at docs/engine/DECISIONS.md:955, not :944. The skill doc already marks hand_sides as informational, so the drift is limited to the tool description and D161. Either drop hand_sides or label it name-derived in the output, and fix those two texts.

findings.title: play.py 'run' action is dead code
findings.evidence: No call site uses play_step('run'); ue_play probes run through their own preamble (unreal.rs:878). The branch also has an unused `emit_value` and would throw away the probe's output (`emit({"ok": True})`).
findings.impact: A second, divergent probe path to maintain, which would lose output if anyone wired it up.
findings.fix: Delete it, or make unreal.rs run probes through it so there is one path.

v1.reason: play_step (unreal.rs:795) is the only caller of PY_PLAY, and every call passes a literal action: stop, prepare_outside, start, status, console, shot, outside_capture or cleanup_outside (lines 849-1045). No call passes 'run'. ue_play probes run through their own inline preamble via python_tx at unreal.rs:878. The 'run' branch at play.py:81-85 is therefore unreachable. It also carries an unused emit_value key and emits only {ok: true}.
v1.correction: Delete the branch and drop 'run' from the action list in the header comment on line 1.

findings.title: ue_play turns off the user's background CPU throttle permanently
findings.evidence: On every start it sets `throttle_cpu_when_not_foreground` to False, then `if ARGS.get("persist", True) and hasattr(settings, "save_config"): settings.save_config(); throttled = False`. Rust never sends `persist` (unreal.rs:862, :1031), so the change is saved and never restored. The ue_play docs do not mention it. D162 says the throttle is off 'during play', and ue_editor_launch documents the throttle as off 'for this session'. I could not confirm that `save_config` is exposed to Python.
findings.impact: Every ue_play or ue_profile run changes a user preference for good, and the editor keeps burning CPU in the background, unlike the documented per-session behaviour.
findings.fix: Default persist to False so stop restores the old value, and leave permanent changes to `ue_setup_check fix=true`.

v1.reason: Persisting the throttle setting is deliberate. Commit e33daf2's message says 'play sessions save it off where the engine allows, so it no longer comes back on every relaunch', and the code comment at play.py:41-42 says the same. The editor-launch path persists it too: unreal.rs:634-647 writes bThrottleCPUWhenNotForeground=False into Saved/Config/<Platform>Editor/EditorPerProjectUserSettings.ini by default, with a comment explaining the setting otherwise 'comes back on every start'. ue_setup_check fix=true also writes it permanently. A permanent change is the project's intended behaviour, not an accidental leak from ue_play, so making ue_play restore the old value would contradict the launch path's design.
v1.correction: The only real issue is wording. ue_editor_launch's keep_background_throttle description (unreal.rs:312, 'default: off for this session') and D162 ('turns the background throttle off during play') understate that the setting is saved permanently to the per-project user config. This is a low-severity docs-drift, not a bug in play.py.

findings.title: run_inspect's 'item extends outward' assertion is vacuous, and the fake Rotator has UE's pitch sign reversed
findings.evidence: The assertion compares end_b_at_start, which is the item's origin end ((0,0,0) in item space), with fwd_right_up, the attach point; the two are equal by construction. Running against the stand-in module, the wrong-way blade (end_a at right = -30) satisfies it as well. tests/unreal.py:16 builds pitch as `(0, sin(hp), 0, cos(hp))`, whereas FRotator::Quaternion gives Y = -sin(pitch/2).
findings.impact: The orientation the test describes is not actually checked, and any future pitch test would validate the opposite of Unreal's convention.
findings.fix: Assert on end_a, e.g. `end_a[1] > attach[1] + 50`, and negate the fake's pitch component.

v1.reason: In the fake, the sword's bounds have origin (50,0,0) and extent (50,3,1), so end_b = origin - 50*X = (0,0,0) in item space, which is the attach point (anim_inspect.py:39). end_b_at_start therefore always equals fwd_right_up, and the check at run_inspect.py:48 (end_b[1] > attach[1] - 1) is always true. I ran the stand-in in a scratch copy: with rotation [0,0,0] (the wrong-way blade) and with [0,180,0] alike, fwd_right_up and end_b_at_start were both [0,70,135]. end_a was [0,-30,135] for the wrong blade and [0,170,135] for the correct one. The pitch claim is also correct: FRotator::Quaternion has Y = -CR*SP*CY - SR*CP*SY, which is -sin(pitch/2) when roll and yaw are 0, while the fake at tests/unreal.py:16 uses +sin(hp). It is latent, though: offset_transform maps rotation [pitch,yaw,roll], and no test uses a non-zero pitch.
v1.correction: Assert on end_a, e.g. end_a_at_start[1] > fwd_right_up[1] + 50. The pitch sign in the fake is latent (no test exercises pitch) and is worth fixing only alongside a future pitch test.

findings.title: Materials outside /Game and /Engine count as transient, so imports into plugin content always fail
findings.evidence: `[m for m in mats if m and ("/Transient" in m or not m.startswith(("/Game", "/Engine")))]` treats any material under a plugin or Game Feature mount (/MyFeature/...) as broken. The mesh is then deleted, the other importer is tried, and the final result is failed.
findings.impact: blender_to_unreal with materials into a Game Feature or plugin content folder fails, and deletes its result, every time.
findings.fix: Flag only transient packages (paths under /Engine/Transient), or check that the material asset exists in the registry.

v1.reason: import_fbx.py:86 flags any material path not starting with /Game or /Engine as transient. import_fbx.py:168 then counts the mesh as broken, line 173 deletes it, and the retry and the final result fail (blender.rs:49-53 reports a failed import). The destination is not restricted to /Game: the schema at blender.rs:177 only gives it as an example. The legacy importer creates materials next to the mesh, so with materials imported into a plugin or Game Feature mount (/MyFeature/...), the materials are under /MyFeature and the import always fails and deletes itself. Rust (blender.rs:462-463) also tells the user the materials 'are not saved assets', which is wrong.
v1.correction: Because of cli-python#9, this only happens today when the agent passes materials=true explicitly; with materials off, the slots get /Engine default materials. Fix: test only for '/Transient' (or `/Engine/Transient`), or check that the material's package exists with asset_exists().

findings.title: Export height is measured on the posed character but compared with Unreal's bind-pose bounds
findings.evidence: `world_bbox(meshes)` reads the evaluated meshes after set_action, at the scene's current frame. blender.rs:442-461 compares `size_cm[2]` with the bounds of the imported skeletal mesh, which come from its bind pose, and flags any ratio outside 0.9-1.1 as a unit or scale problem. rig_check.py:123-127 also measures height in the current pose.
findings.impact: Exporting a rig whose file was saved on a crouch, jump or attack frame produces false 'x0.8 ... check the object's scale' problems in blender_to_unreal.
findings.fix: Measure with `arm.data.pose_position = 'REST'` and restore it afterwards.

v1.reason: export.py:85 calls `world_bbox(meshes)`, and common.py:99-108 evaluates the depsgraph at the scene's current frame with the assigned (or set_action'd) action, so the armature modifier deforms the mesh into the current pose. Blender's FBX exporter writes the skinned mesh in the rest pose: installed 5.2.1 export_fbx_bin.py:2708-2722 sets `armature.pose_position = 'REST'` while it evaluates meshes. Unreal's import_fbx.py:73-74 measures `get_bounds()` of the imported SkeletalMesh, which is the reference pose. blender.rs:442-461 compares the two and flags any ratio outside 0.9-1.1. A rig whose file was saved on a crouch or wide-stance frame therefore gets a false 'check the object's scale' problem in blender_to_unreal, which also sets passed=false. The rig_check.py:127 related location does measure posed height too, but its thresholds (<10 or >500 cm) make a pose irrelevant there, so that part does not hold.
v1.correction: Remove rig_check.py:127 from related: its 10-500 cm bounds cannot be tripped by a pose. Fix: set `arm.data.pose_position = 'REST'`, call `bpy.context.view_layer.update()`, measure, then restore, as the FBX exporter itself does. A pose_position change has no effect without a depsgraph update.

findings.title: Unreal pose sampling calls the anim library once per bone per sample on the editor's game thread
findings.evidence: `for n in self.names: get_bone_pose_for_time(anim, n, time, False)`, and each call evaluates the whole pose. anim_inspect.py:198 recomputes the first pose once per item. anim_preview's check rebuilds the Skeleton and the pose up to 8x8 times. An explicit `times` list (common.py:232-233) is uncapped, while samples is capped at 60. The script keeps running in the editor after the Rust HTTP timeout.
findings.impact: Large skeletons (MetaHuman-scale) or long time lists freeze the shared editor for minutes, past the tool's own timeout.
findings.fix: Where available, use `get_bone_poses_for_time(anim, names, t, False)` once per sample time. Compute the first pose once, outside the item loop, and cap `times` the way samples is capped.

v1.reason: Skeleton.local_pose (unreal_py/common.py:184-193) calls unreal.AnimationLibrary.get_bone_pose_for_time once per bone per sample time. In UE 5.8 (AnimationBlueprintLibrary.cpp:2904-2912 -> GetBonePosesForTimeInternal at :75-96), each call fetches the bone track names and runs UAnimPoseExtensions::GetAnimPoseAtTime, a full-pose evaluation, just to read one bone. Sampling is therefore O(bones^2) per time. anim_inspect.py:198 recomputes the pose at times[0] inside the per-item loop. sample_times (common.py:231-233) returns ARGS['times'] uncapped, while samples is capped at 60. ue_anim_inspect runs with a 300 s timeout (unreal.rs:386) and ue_anim_preview with 120 s (unreal.rs:1219), and the editor-side script keeps running after Rust gives up. Ordinary game skeletons of about 70-100 bones are fine; MetaHuman-scale rigs or long time lists can stall the editor.
v1.correction: The proposed fix does not work. get_bone_poses_for_time is deprecated since 5.2, and in 5.8 it calls the same internal function, which still evaluates the full pose once per bone inside its loop (AnimationBlueprintLibrary.cpp:87-96), so it is just as quadratic. The right fix: call unreal.AnimPoseExtensions.get_anim_pose_at_time(anim, t, options) once per sample time, then AnimPoseExtensions.get_bone_pose(pose, name, AnimPoseSpaces.LOCAL) for each bone. Also hoist the first-pose computation out of the item loop and cap ARGS['times'].

findings.title: Long editor loops show no progress dialog and cannot be cancelled
findings.evidence: `with unreal.ScopedSlowTask(...)` never calls `task.make_dialog(True)` or checks `should_cancel()`; the same applies at :74 and blueprint_info.py:116. The file header claims the audit 'shows progress in the editor'. ue_asset_audit can run for up to 1800 s (unreal.rs:400).
findings.impact: During an audit the editor looks hung for minutes, with no way to stop it.
findings.fix: Call `task.make_dialog(True)` and break out of the loop when `task.should_cancel()` is true.

v1.reason: asset_audit.py:39 and :74 and blueprint_info.py:116 open `unreal.ScopedSlowTask` and call only `enter_progress_frame`. They never call `task.make_dialog(True)` or check `task.should_cancel()`. Without make_dialog, no progress dialog appears unless an outer slow task created one, so the file header's claim (asset_audit.py:2 'shows progress in the editor') is inaccurate. The plugin's own skill (plugins/unreal-engine/skills/unreal-editor-automation/SKILL.md:136-139, :192-195) teaches exactly make_dialog plus should_cancel, so the bundled scripts have drifted from the guidance they ship. Impact is modest: these are read-only audits bounded by `limit` (default 400 assets, 50 blueprints), and the editor is busy on the game thread either way.
