v1.correction: Call `task.make_dialog(True)` after entering each scope, and break when `task.should_cancel()` is true, so the partial results are still emitted. Alternatively, correct the header comment.

findings.title: The no-mipmaps check matches on the enum's string form
findings.evidence: `str(mips).endswith("NO_MIPMAPS")`. If Unreal's enum str() returns the repr form '<TextureMipGenSettings.TMGS_NO_MIPMAPS: 13>', this never matches. Without an editor I could not confirm which str format Unreal uses.
findings.impact: World textures without mipmaps may never be reported.
findings.fix: `mips == unreal.TextureMipGenSettings.TMGS_NO_MIPMAPS`.

v1.reason: The auditor could not confirm the enum's str() format, so I checked it in the installed engine source. /home/anthony/Applications/UE_5.8.2/.../PythonScriptPlugin/Private/PyWrapperEnum.cpp:385 has Str returning PyUnicode_FromFormat("<%s.%s: %d>", ...), and lines 484-485 assign it to both tp_str and tp_repr. So str(mips) is '<TextureMipGenSettings.TMGS_NO_MIPMAPS: 13>', which ends with ': 13>'. The test at asset_audit.py:63, `str(mips).endswith("NO_MIPMAPS")`, can therefore never be true, and the 'no mipmaps on a world texture' finding never fires. The same file compares enums correctly at line 57 (`comp != unreal.TextureCompressionSettings.TC_NORMALMAP`). Line 96 uses an `in` substring test, which happens to work with this format.
v1.correction: The auditor's confidence was low; the engine source now settles the format. Fix: `mips == unreal.TextureMipGenSettings.TMGS_NO_MIPMAPS`, or test `mips.name`. A second problem on the same line: `"ui" not in path.lower()` also skips any path that merely contains the letters 'ui', for example /Game/Buildings/... or /Game/Equipment/..., so even after the fix many world textures would be silently exempt. Match a path segment or a prefix such as '/ui/' or 'T_UI_' instead.

findings.title: UCP_ capsule collision is not recognised
findings.evidence: Only UCX_, UBX_ and USP_ are recognised, in info.py:29 and export.py:39, :84 and :107. Unreal's FBX static mesh import also accepts UCP_ (capsule).
findings.impact: UCP_ meshes are mesh-checked like render meshes, so their problems can block an export. They are also counted in size_cm and missing from the collision list.
findings.fix: Use one COLLISION_PREFIXES tuple in common.py that includes UCP_.

v1.reason: Collision prefixes are hard-coded as ('UCX_','UBX_','USP_') at info.py:29, export.py:39, export.py:84 and export.py:107 (repeated literals, with no shared constant). The project's own skills tell agents that UCP_ is a valid capsule collision prefix: plugins/blender/skills/blender-to-unreal/SKILL.md:37 and blender-modeling/SKILL.md:193. Unreal's FBX static-mesh import does accept UCP_. A UCP_ capsule is therefore mesh-checked as a render mesh at export.py:39, so a problem in it can block the export without allow_problems. It also counts towards size_cm at export.py:84-85, missing from the collision list at :107, and is not labelled collision by blender_info. The impact is small: capsule proxies are usually clean, closed geometry inside the render bounds.
v1.correction: Add one COLLISION_PREFIXES = ('UCX_','UBX_','USP_','UCP_') to common.py and use it at all four sites, and add UCP_ to the blender_export tool description (blender.rs:157).

findings.title: Attachment length uses local max scale instead of world length
findings.evidence: `round(it["points"]["_length"] * TO_CM * max(o.scale), 1)` ignores the parent's scale, e.g. an armature at 0.01, which is common after FBX import. It also assumes the long axis carries the largest scale.
findings.impact: length_cm is 100x off for props on FBX-imported rigs, and wrong for non-uniformly scaled items.
findings.fix: `(o.matrix_world @ end_a - o.matrix_world @ end_b).length * TO_CM`.

v1.reason: anim_inspect.py:169 reports `it['points']['_length'] * TO_CM * max(o.scale)`. o.scale is the object's local scale: it ignores parent and armature scale and the parent-inverse matrix, and it applies the largest scale component even when the long axis has a different one. With scale (1,3,1) and local X extent 2, the world X length is 2 but the report says 6. The clearance and grip maths all use matrix_world correctly, so only this informational length_cm field is wrong.
v1.correction: Use `((o.matrix_world @ end_a) - (o.matrix_world @ end_b)).length * TO_CM`. The '100x on FBX-imported rigs' claim only holds when the prop was parented without a compensating parent-inverse (keep-transform parenting cancels the 0.01). The non-uniform-scale case holds in general.

The JSON-escaping expansion of a lossy-decoded binary (×2.37) was measured with a Python experiment in the scratchpad.

findings.title: project.clone runs an unbounded `git clone` inside a store-locked handler, freezing the whole engine for the clone (out of chunk, reached from native onboarding)
findings.evidence: `e.register::<ProjectClone>(|ctx: &mut Ctx, p| { … let output = Command::new("git").current_dir(&workspace.path).arg("clone").arg("--").arg(&p.url).arg(&destination).output()` (workspace.rs:228-235). `Engine::register` runs the handler inside the SQLite transaction with the store mutex held; `register_unlocked`/`register_staged` exist to avoid exactly this. There is no `proc::output_with_timeout`, no `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0` and no bound of any kind. The op metadata says "Clone a repo into the workspace and register it (async; project.changed when done)" (relay-bus ops/workspace.rs:38), but the handler is synchronous. Native onboarding calls it with `setup.ui.call(if gh {"project.clone"} else {"project.add"},payload)` (onboarding.rs:527), and the client works around it with an 1800 s timeout (client.rs:67). The same `output_with_timeout` bypass appears elsewhere. `worktree::git`/`git_mutate` (worktree.rs:26-36) uses a bare `.output()` with no `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT` and serves git.push (git.rs:617) and the device primary-sync `git fetch` (device.rs:1575). `run_user_pre_commit` runs the user's hook with a bare `.output()` (hooks.rs:210-213) from git.commit's prepare phase (git.rs:555). By contrast, git.fetch (git.rs:938-952) and worktree add (worktree.rs:212-215) are bounded.
findings.impact: Cloning a sizeable repo through Open repository → GitHub holds the store mutex for the whole download. Every agent's bus call (including the exec/write guardrail gates), every other UI request and the phone door block until it ends. The hang becomes indefinite on a stalled network, or when an HTTPS credential or SSH host-key prompt goes to the engine's controlling terminal (run.sh starts the engine with nohup from the launching shell). A hung git.push or pre-commit hook wedges the connection that sent it, which for the native app is its single control connection.
findings.fix: Register project.clone with register_staged: clone in the unlocked prepare phase via proc::output_with_timeout (stdin null, GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0, generous bound) and only insert the project in the short finish phase. Alternatively make it actually async, as its description claims. Route worktree::git through output_with_timeout with GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0 (longer bound for network ops), and bound run_user_pre_commit.

v1.reason: workspace.rs:228-248 registers ProjectClone with Engine::register, which runs the handler inside the transaction with the store mutex held. The handler runs `Command::new("git")...arg("clone")...output()` with no proc::output_with_timeout, no GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0 and no low-speed limit. The op metadata says 'async; project.changed when done' (relay-bus ops/workspace.rs:38), but the handler is synchronous. Native onboarding calls it (onboarding.rs:527) over the control connection, under the 1800 s client timeout (client.rs:67). Every locked handler blocks while the clone runs: guardrail gates, other UI requests, the phone door. For a large Unreal repo, including LFS smudge during the clone, that is minutes in normal use. It becomes indefinite on a stalled network, or when git or ssh prompts on /dev/tty while the engine has a controlling terminal. The other locations are real violations of the output_with_timeout rule, but they run in the unlocked prepare phase of register_staged: worktree::git/git_mutate (worktree.rs:26-36) used by git.push (git.rs:617), and run_user_pre_commit (hooks.rs:210-213) from git.commit prepare. They block only the issuing connection, because socket.rs handle_conn awaits each dispatch in turn, not the store.
v1.correction: Rated high rather than critical: this is a user-initiated bus freeze, bounded by the clone's duration in the normal case, and the indefinite hang needs a stalled network or a tty prompt. Correction on prompts: Command::output() gives the child a null stdin, so plain stdin prompts fail fast. Only /dev/tty prompts (git credential prompt, ssh host-key or passphrase) hang, and only when the engine has a controlling terminal. The device.rs:1575 primary-sync git fetch also goes through git_mutate and is unbounded; whether a store lock is held there was not checked. Fix as proposed: register_staged, with the clone in the prepare phase through proc::output_with_timeout (GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0, a generous bound) and only project.add in the finish phase. Route worktree::git through output_with_timeout with a longer bound for network ops, and bound run_user_pre_commit.

v2.reason:
(a) The code does what the finding says. workspace.rs:228 registers ProjectClone with plain `Engine::register`. Line 234 runs `Command::new("git")...arg("clone")...output()` with no timeout and no GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT. The pipeline takes `self.store.lock()` and opens the transaction before calling the handler (engine.rs:953-980), so the mutex stays held until git exits. There is no prepare stage for this op; the only registration is at workspace.rs:228. This breaks D144 and D149 (DECISIONS.md:729-738, 797-815). project.clone is missing from D149's converted list, although nearby code already sets GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0 (worktree.rs:213, git.rs:943).

(b) Who can trigger it: the user, any time. "Add project…" and "Open repository" (registry.rs:472, app.rs:978/1413, launch.rs:358) call onboarding::open. Choosing GitHub then sends project.clone with the API clone_url (onboarding.rs:527) over the native control connection, because it is not in is_lifecycle_request. It can also be run with `relay cmd`. It is UserOnly, so agents cannot start it. It happens occasionally. A small repo takes seconds. A large or LFS game repo takes minutes, because git-lfs smudge runs inside the clone. The author's 1800 s client timeout (client.rs:67) expects this.

(c) What happens while the clone runs:
- Everything that needs the mutex waits. Every agent request first locks the store for its token check (check_session_token, engine.rs:1377-1378). That covers MCP tools, session.report hooks and the guardrail.gate PreToolUse hook. Session attach and lifecycle connections, other UI connections, the phone bridge (it is just a socket client, bridge.rs:156) and system_write background work also wait.
- handle_conn awaits each dispatch on a connection in turn (socket.rs:335-744). Every native UI request queued behind the clone therefore fails after 30 s with "Request timed out. Its outcome is unknown", and still runs once git exits.
- Not affected: PTY output on terminals that are already attached, and user keystrokes and resizes. These use the D148 fast path (answers_from_memory and pty_fast_path, engine.rs:1222-1303; mail_hint returns early for the user actor).
- No data is lost, and everything resumes when git exits.
- The hang becomes indefinite only in edge cases. One is an engine started from a terminal with ./run.sh: nohup keeps the controlling tty, `.output()` leaves git in the same foreground process group, and a credential or ssh prompt then waits in that terminal. A desktop-launched engine has no tty, so the prompt fails fast. The other is a connection that stalls without dropping; git's low-speed limit is off by default.
- Aggravating, separate root cause (not fully established): Relay installs Claude's PreToolUse hook with "timeout": 30 (hooks.rs:351), and claude_pre_tool's Client::call has no deadline (socket.rs:801-818). A gate stuck behind a lock held longer than 30 s therefore ends in Claude Code's hook timeout, not in Relay's exit-2 fail-closed path (main.rs:348-357). Strings in the locally installed Claude Code 2.1.291 record a timed-out command hook as outcome "cancelled", not "blocking". The tool very likely proceeds without the guardrail, but this was not established from the minified code.

(d) High, per the rubric ("a freeze of the bus"). It is user-initiated, bounded by the clone in the normal case, loses no data, and sessions and PTYs survive. Critical would need the uncommon indefinite case.

(e) The staged conversion is right but incomplete. handle_conn serializes each connection, so even with the clone out of the lock, the native control connection still sits behind a long clone.
v2.correction:
Severity is high, not critical.

The related items are a different, lower-severity root cause and should be a separate finding, rated medium:
- git.push (git.rs:600-617) and run_user_pre_commit (hooks.rs:210-213, called from git.rs:555) run in register_staged prepare phases, which hold no store lock.
- The device.rs:1575 primary-sync fetch runs on the run_worker thread (device.rs:1652-1671), not in a handler.
- Unbounded, these block only the connection that sent them (for the native app, its control connection) or that one device run. They do not freeze the bus.

Corrections to the impact:
- PTY output and user keystrokes keep working (D148). The stale "including PTY keystrokes" line in proc.rs:3-4 dates from before D148.
- A credential or ssh prompt can hang only when the engine has a controlling tty (started from a terminal with ./run.sh). Started from the desktop entry, it fails fast, because Command::output gives git a null stdin and there is no tty.
- Docs drift: OpMeta (relay-bus workspace.rs:38) says "async; project.changed when done", and BUS.md:246-247 promises a returned handle and a project.clone.completed audit row. The handler is synchronous and writes no such row.

Fix:
1. Register project.clone with register_staged.
   - prepare: read the workspace with ctx.read, check the destination, then run git clone through proc::output_with_timeout. Set GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0, and for SSH URLs set GIT_SSH_COMMAND="ssh -o BatchMode=yes". Prefer http.lowSpeedLimit/lowSpeedTime over a tight wall-clock limit, keeping an outer limit of at least 1800 s so a legitimate LFS clone is not killed.
   - finish: invoke_registered("project.add"). On failure, remove the directory after the transaction rather than under the lock.
2. Native client: send project.clone on its own connection, the way Client::lifecycle_request does (client.rs:133). Otherwise the control connection stays blocked behind a long clone. The alternative is to make the op truly async, as the docs describe, but that changes the result that onboarding.rs:528 reads.
3. File the PreToolUse fail-open on hook timeout as its own finding. Fix: give claude_pre_tool and codex_pre_tool a socket deadline shorter than 30 s that exits 2.

findings.title: Any single response line over 2 MiB tears down the whole UI control connection (git.diff.file of a large or binary file; notes.list of a large notes corpus)
findings.evidence: The reader does `if line.len() + n > max_line { return Err(Error::Protocol(format!("frame exceeds {} MiB", …))) }` (client.rs:200-205), which ends the reader task. `outcome.unwrap_err()` then fails every pending request and sends Notice::Disconnected (259-265). app.rs:1267-1275 drops the client, shows "Engine disconnected" and requires Reconnect, and reconnecting stops and recreates every terminal pane (app.rs:1139-1144). MAX_LINE is 2 MiB (client.rs:48). Two engine responses exceed it in normal use. (1) git.diff.file returns `old`, `new` and the full unified diff in one response with no cap (git.rs:235-254), reading whole files and lossy-decoding binaries (git.rs:802-848). The Git panel requests it for any changed non-image file (code_git.rs:896-898 → 1338) and only checks `old.len() + new.len() > 1048576` after the response has arrived (code_git.rs:1350). A lossy-decoded random binary grows ×2.37 when JSON-escaped (measured in the scratchpad), so a substantially changed ~250 KB .uasset/.fbx/.wav (about four copies: old, new and both sides of the diff) or a ~1 MB text file (lockfile, generated code) exceeds 2 MiB. (2) notes.list returns every note with its full body and no limit (notes.rs:339-349), and agent-callable notes.append grows notes without a cap. The client calls notes.list on every Ui::refresh (app.rs:1440 → notes_window.rs:208), including the first refresh after each connect.
findings.impact: Clicking a large changed file in the Git panel disconnects the whole UI. In-flight requests such as a save fail with "Invalid engine response: frame exceeds 2 MiB" even though the engine may have applied them. Reconnecting re-attaches every terminal, and reopening the diff repeats the failure. Once a project's notes exceed about 2 MiB, every connect is followed by a notes.list that kills it again, so the client can no longer stay connected.
findings.fix: Make an oversized line a per-request failure. Skip to the next newline without buffering, take the id from the `{"v":1,"id":"…"` prefix, fail only that pending request with a typed too-large error, and keep the connection open; add a test for this path. Also cap on the engine side: git.diff.file should refuse or truncate above the editor's 1 MiB limit and skip binaries, and notes.list should return summaries with bodies fetched through notes.get.

v1.reason: The reader in client.rs (around lines 196-205) returns Err(Protocol("frame exceeds 2 MiB")) as soon as one line passes max_line (MAX_LINE = 2 MiB at client.rs:48). That ends the reader task, which then drains every pending request with that error and sends Notice::Disconnected. app.rs:1267-1275 then drops the client and shows 'Engine disconnected'. Nothing reconnects automatically: reconnecting is the button at app.rs:972 → connect(), which stops and clears every pane (app.rs:1137-1141). git.diff.file is register_unlocked (git.rs:235-254) and returns full `old`, full `new` and a full unified diff in one response with no size cap. revision_text and working_text read whole blobs and files and lossy-decode binaries (git.rs:802-848). The engine socket has no outbound cap. code_git.rs open_diff only skips images (code_git.rs:1325) and checks `old.len() + new.len() > 1048576` only after the response has arrived (code_git.rs:1350), and by then the connection is already dead. A changed text file of about 600 KB or more (old + new + a diff of comparable size) is enough, and so is a changed binary of a few hundred KB, which grows when lossy-decoded and JSON-escaped (U+FFFD is 3 bytes, control bytes become \u00XX). That is routine for .uasset files in this app's Unreal use case. The notes.list path is also real but less likely: notes.list (notes.rs:339-349) returns every body with no limit, the standing-note append by project_id has no length cap, and refresh calls pages::refresh_notes → notes_window.rs:208 after every connect.
v1.correction: The notes.list trigger needs about 2 MiB of note bodies in one project, which is unusual. The git.diff.file trigger is the one that matters. Fix both sides. On the client, fail only the oversized request: skip to the next newline and recover the id from the prefix. On the engine, give git.diff.file a size limit and binary detection that refuses before building the response.

v2.reason:
(a) The code does what the finding says. The reader returns Err(Protocol("frame exceeds 2 MiB")) on the first line over max_line (client.rs:200; MAX_LINE = 2 MiB at :48). It then drains every pending request with that error (:259-262) and sends Notice::Disconnected (:264). The UI loop takes the client and shows "Engine disconnected" (app.rs:1267-1275). ARCHITECTURE.md says "Disconnect recovery is explicit", so the user has to press Reconnect (app.rs:970-972). connect() then stops and clears every pane (app.rs:1137-1141).

The engine never bounds this response:
- git.diff.file (git.rs:235-254, register_unlocked) returns the whole `old` and `new` plus a full unified diff.
- revision_text and working_text read whole blobs and files and lossy-decode them (git.rs:802-848).
- The socket writer sends serde_json::to_string(&resp) of any size (socket.rs:744).

The only caller is a click on a Git panel row (code_git.rs:898 -> 1338). That panel lists every changed and untracked file (`git status --untracked-files=all`, worktree.rs:89) and skips only images (:1325). Its 1 MiB check (:1350) runs only after the response arrives. By contrast, the editor bounds file.read with max_bytes 1048576 (editor.rs:636), so the diff path is the outlier.

(b) Who can trigger it and how often: the user, through a normal click. I measured real files, modelling from_utf8_lossy and serde_json escaping in Python:
- A 328 KB UE Blueprint (installed UE 5.8's BP_Sky_Sphere.uasset) escapes 4.48x because of its many zero bytes. As an untracked or LFS-modified asset it produces a ~2.8 MiB line. With LFS, the HEAD blob is the ~130 B pointer and every new line appears in the diff. The client-side old+new is only 373 KB, so it would have passed the 1 MiB check.
- This repo's own 733 KB scrcpy-server binary, added as a new version, gives ~3.3 MiB.
- docs/perf profiles.json (556 KB), fully regenerated, gives ~2.46 MiB.

Changed .uasset files are routine for this app's Unreal use. Large lockfiles and generated files are common in code projects too.

(c) What the user sees when it fires:
- The diff never opens, and a misleading error appears: "Invalid engine response: frame exceeds 2 MiB".
- The whole control plane goes down: every UI call fails, and events stop arriving (guardrail.held prompts, notifications, session updates) until the user presses Reconnect.
- Reconnect stops every pane and re-attaches it with catch-up.
- Clicking the same file again repeats the failure every time.

No data is lost. Engine sessions keep running, and terminals keep their own sockets until Reconnect.

(d) Severity: high is right. A core panel action in a normal flow fails, the UI is cut off from the engine until manual recovery, and it reproduces every time. It is not critical: nothing is lost, the engine is unaffected, and one click recovers.

(e) The proposed fix is sound and feasible. Response serializes `v` then `id` first (envelope.rs:149-152), so the id can be read from the line prefix. The engine-side cap is also needed.
v2.correction:
Thresholds, using measured factors: lossy-decoded and escaped binary grows 2.35-2.5x for mesh-like data and up to 4.5x for zero-heavy Blueprint data. Text grows about 1.1x. The line exceeds 2 MiB for:
- an untracked or LFS-modified binary of about 230-450 KB;
- a fully changed non-LFS binary of about 120-210 KB;
- a small edit to a text file of about 1 MB or more, or a full rewrite of about 500 KB or more.

The "in-flight save" example is weak, because open_diff refuses when the editor is dirty (code_git.rs:1320). The real collateral damage is lost event delivery (guardrail.held prompts included) until a manual Reconnect, plus any unrelated concurrent request.

The notes trigger is rarer (about 2 MiB of note text in one project), but it is worse than stated. notes.changed events carry the full note body (notes.rs:63-66). The notes window exists from startup (notes_window.rs:153-166), so notes.list runs after every connect. One oversized note therefore kills every subscribed client on each save, and keeps killing it on every reconnect.

Additional related locations: crates/relay-core/src/handlers/notes.rs:65 (event payload) and crates/relay-core/src/socket.rs:744 (unbounded writer).

Fix refinements:
1. Client: also skip oversized Event lines and trigger a refresh instead of disconnecting.
2. Engine: in git.diff.file, check the blob or file size before reading. Detect binaries and LFS pointers, reusing git.diff's `binary` heuristic at git.rs:224. Return a typed BusError rather than changing DiffFileOut, which lives in schema/bus.v1.json.
3. Optionally, have socket.rs replace any response over the wire limit with a typed bus error, which fixes every op at once.
4. If notes.list moves to summaries, the native notes page must fetch bodies through notes.get.

findings.title: Every UI request shares one control socket that the engine serves one request at a time, so any slow op stalls the whole UI
findings.evidence: Ui::call sends every op except the nine `is_lifecycle_request` ops through the single control client: `client.request(&self.rt, op, payload).await` (app.rs:1111-1116). The engine's per-connection loop awaits each request's dispatch before reading the next line: socket.rs:335 `while let Some(line) = lines.next_line().await?` … 740-744 `tokio::task::spawn_blocking(move || e.dispatch(req, Door::Socket)).await?` followed by `out_tx.send`. The client's out-of-order correlation (client.rs:1, "Bounded, concurrent socket transport") therefore gives no concurrency. The crate's own test `lifecycle_actions_bypass_a_stalled_status_request` (client.rs:345-430) demonstrates the stall and works around it only for lifecycle ops. Slow ops the UI sends on this socket: git.pr.list (`gh api --paginate`, up to 10 s; code_git.rs:582, git.rs:83), git.commit (runs the user's pre-commit hook, unbounded; git.rs:555), git.push (unbounded; git.rs:617), file.tree (runs git status for badges; file.rs:30-31), git.status on large repos, and project.clone. The editor's save sends `expected_sha256` of the pre-save text (editor.rs:700-704) and leaves `original` unchanged on error.
findings.impact: While a pre-commit hook runs or gh waits on the network, page loads, saves, navigation sync, settings writes and refreshes all queue behind it. Each request's 30 s timer runs while it is queued, so a long request at the head makes everything behind it fail with "Request timed out. Its outcome is unknown", and those requests still execute afterwards. A file.write that times out this way still lands, and the user's retry is refused as file.edit_conflict because its expected hash is the old content.
findings.fix: Have handle_conn run each request on its own task and write responses as they complete; the client already correlates out-of-order replies and has a test for it. Alternatively, send known-slow ops (git.commit/push/pr.list, file.tree/search, project.clone) over a separate connection, as lifecycle ops already are. Either way, timeouts should not count time spent queued behind other requests.

v1.reason: The engine's handle_conn (crates/relay-core/src/socket.rs:335 to 744) reads one line, awaits that request's dispatch (spawn_blocking(...).await?), sends the response and only then reads the next line, so each connection is served strictly in order. Ui::call (apps/relay-native/src/app.rs:1111-1116) sends everything except is_lifecycle_request ops (client.rs:50-62) over the one control client. guarded() (code_git.rs:1722) also goes through ui.call. Slow ops do reach that path. git.commit runs run_user_pre_commit (hooks.rs:210, a bare Command::output with no timeout) in its staged read phase. git.push runs worktree::git_mutate, which is a bare `Command::new("git")...output()` (worktree.rs:26-36) with no timeout. git.pr.list is bounded at 10 s (git.rs:83). Staging releases the store mutex but not the UI connection's request queue. The client's timer covers queueing as well as execution (client.rs:325-331: tokio::time::timeout wraps tx.send plus reply.await, 30 s by default), so a pre-commit hook that runs for tens of seconds makes every request behind it fail with "Request timed out. Its outcome is unknown", even though the engine later executes those requests. editor.rs:700-704 sends expected_sha256 of `original` and keeps `original` unchanged on error, so a timed-out file.write that later lands makes the retry fail with a conflict. The test lifecycle_actions_bypass_a_stalled_status_request shows the authors know about the head-of-line stall and worked around it only for lifecycle ops.
v1.correction: Events are not stalled. The engine's forwarder writes them to out_tx independently, so only request/response traffic queues. Per-request concurrency in handle_conn has to keep ordering where it matters: session.input keystrokes on terminal connections, attach/detach and the watch toggles that change per-connection state. So either make only the control connection concurrent, or route known-slow ops (git.commit, git.push, git.fetch, git.pr.list, project.clone, file.search/tree) over a separate connection the way lifecycle ops already are. Separately, git.commit's pre-commit hook and git.push run with no timeout (hooks.rs:210, worktree.rs:27), which breaks the CLAUDE.md rule that subprocesses go through proc::output_with_timeout. That is worth its own engine finding.

v2.reason:
(a) I checked the code myself and it does what the finding says. handle_conn (socket.rs:281) serves every socket connection (socket.rs:114). Its loop reads a line at :335 and then waits for that request's dispatch (`spawn_blocking(...).await?` at :742, or the special-op branches) before `out_tx.send` at :744 and before it reads the next line. So each connection is served strictly in order. Ui::call (app.rs:1111-1116) sends everything except the 9 is_lifecycle_request ops (client.rs:50-62) over the one control client. That includes guarded() (code_git.rs:1722), Ui::mutate, guardrail.confirm (guardrail_pages.rs:299/477), file.write (editor.rs:704) and all page loads. client.rs:325-331 wraps `tx.send` + `reply.await` in one tokio timeout, 30 s by default, so time spent queued counts against it. A timed-out request is already on the socket and still runs later, and its reply is dropped.

(b) Reachable in normal use, by the user alone. Slow ops that release the store lock but still hold the connection:
- git.commit runs the user's pre-commit hook with no time limit (git.rs:555 -> hooks.rs:210 bare `.output()`).
- git.push has no time limit either (git.rs:617 -> worktree.rs:27).
- git.fetch is capped at 20 s.
- git.pr.list is capped at 10 s. It fetches every PR page and runs on every git-panel refresh (code_git.rs:578-582).
- git.status and the file.tree badges run git status, capped at 10 s each.

Each refresh_git is triggered by page opens, saves, git actions, and file.changed/git.changed events on the code/agents page (app.rs:1232-1239 -> editor.rs:508). The author has already hit this: commit d849b98 "Stop Git refresh storms and keep session controls responsive" added the lifecycle bypass and its test, which reproduces exactly this stall. It also defeats D149's stated goal (DECISIONS.md:815, "those queries now genuinely run in parallel"). That holds for other doors, but not for requests on one socket connection, which is the native UI's only door.

(c) Terminal keystrokes, terminal output and events are not affected:
- Each terminal has its own connection (terminal.rs:476).
- session.input is answered inline.
- Events go through the forwarder task.

What does stall is the UI's whole request/response path: page loads, git panel, settings, task actions and guardrail approvals that unblock agents. Most of the time the stall is 1-3 s behind refresh traffic. During a long pre-commit hook or push (an LFS push can take minutes) it lasts the whole run. Once past 30 s, every queued action fails with "Request timed out. Its outcome is unknown" but still runs afterwards. The commit or push request at the head also times out at 30 s while it is still running.

(d) High fits the rubric: in normal flows the UI's request/response path freezes, at worst for the full length of the hook or push, and is plainly user-visible.

(e) The fix direction is right but needs the caveats listed in the correction.
v2.correction:
1) Drop project.clone from the examples. It is registered with plain Engine::register (workspace.rs:228) and runs `git clone` (workspace.rs:234) with the store mutex held and no timeout. It stalls every connection and every request that touches the store, and a separate connection would not help. The same holds for git.pr.open (git.rs:666-679: `gh pr create` via bare `.output()` in a locked handler). Both belong in their own invariant findings. So do the untimed hooks.rs:210 and worktree.rs:27.

2) The save-then-conflict consequence is an edge case. save_file returns early while its own editor's git action is in flight (editor.rs:681, git_busy). A save therefore only queues behind background refresh ops, each capped at 10 s, or behind a git action that has already timed out on the client side. The result is a misleading "file.edit_conflict … Your draft has not been written" message on retry. The first write did land, so no data is lost.

3) Fix caveats:
- Fully concurrent handle_conn: these ops must stay sequential because they change per-connection state: bus.subscribe/unsubscribe, session.attach/detach, device.watch/app.resources.watch, device.mirror.start, device.run/build/run.stop and bus.wait.
- session.input must stay in order.
- Pipelined mutations from one client must stay in order. The store's std Mutex is not FIFO, so concurrent navigation or settings writes could commit out of order.
- Safer alternatives:
  - Run only register_unlocked queries and register_staged ops concurrently.
  - Or give the UI a second slow-lane connection, or a per-request one like lifecycle_request, for git.commit/push/fetch/pr.list/status, file.tree/search, worktree.list, skill.install and device/avd ops.
- git.commit and git.push also need longer client timeouts than the 30 s default (client.rs:64-71).
- "Timeouts should not count queued time" cannot be done on the client without protocol support. Removing the queue is what fixes it.

4) Docs drift: D149 (DECISIONS.md:815) says unlocked queries now run in parallel. That is not true for requests on one socket connection.

findings.title: The client's timeout table gives 30 s to ops whose handlers do long synchronous work before replying (session.close teardown, git.commit hook, git.push)
findings.evidence: `match op { "project.clone" => 1800 s, "session.create" | "git.worktree.create" | "task.dispatch" => 180 s, _ => 30 s }` (client.rs:65-71). session.close's prepare phase kills and silences the PTY, then runs teardown and `worktree::remove(&repo, wt, p.purge_build.unwrap_or(true))` before replying (session.rs:1566-1582). remove runs purge_build (dir_size plus remove_dir_all of the build dirs), dir_size of the whole worktree, then `git worktree remove --force` (worktree.rs:352-369). The native close menu offers both remove-worktree and purge-build (agent_menu.rs:612). git.commit runs the user's pre-commit hook unbounded (git.rs:555), and git.push is a network operation (git.rs:617).
findings.impact: Closing an agent with remove-worktree on a large Unreal/Android checkout reports "Could not close X: Request timed out…". close_agent's error path (agent_menu.rs:166-168) then refreshes the wall, and the pane comes back LIVE although its process was already killed and silenced, until the close commits and the pane disappears. A second Close in the meantime runs another teardown and rm -rf concurrently on the same tree. A commit whose hook takes longer than 30 s is reported as timed out and then succeeds.
findings.fix: Give session.close, git.commit and git.push the long timeout. Better, derive timeouts from op metadata in relay-bus so this table cannot drift from the handlers. For close, consider reporting progress through events instead of holding the reply.

v1.reason: request_timeout (client.rs:65-71) gives every op other than project.clone, session.create, git.worktree.create and task.dispatch 30 s. session.close is a lifecycle request (client.rs:50-61), so it goes on its own connection through Client::lifecycle_request, but it still uses request() with the 30 s timeout. The Close handler is register_staged (session.rs:1546). Before replying, its prepare phase kills and silences the PTY (take_pty, silence_exit, kill), runs run_teardown, then worktree::remove (worktree.rs:351-368): purge_build does dir_size and remove_dir_all on BUILD_DIRS, then dir_size of the whole tree, then `git worktree remove --force`. On a large Unreal or Android checkout this can take more than 30 s. When it does, close_agent (agent_menu.rs:148-170) removes the name from `closing`, shows 'Could not close X: Request timed out…' and calls ui.refresh(). The session row is still non-closed until finish commits, so reconcile puts the pane back although its process is already gone. A second Close then finds take_pty None and runs teardown and remove again, at the same time as the first, on the same tree. git.commit (git.rs:535, prepare runs run_user_pre_commit with no bound) and git.push (git.rs:600, a network push, often with LFS in Unreal repos) go on the control connection with the same 30 s timeout: they report a timeout and then succeed in the background.
v1.correction: The engine is not blocked by any of these: all three are register_staged and the slow work is in the unlocked prepare phase. The harm is client-side: a false 'timed out' error and the close pane being resurrected. Fix as proposed: a long timeout for session.close (at least when remove_worktree is set), git.commit and git.push. Better, derive timeouts from op metadata in relay-bus.

findings.title: Reconnecting throws away the wall's pane order and focused pane, and the next save persists the reset
findings.evidence: connect() runs `self.ordered.borrow_mut().clear(); self.layout();` (app.rs:1143-1144). With no names, layout() sets `*self.focused.borrow_mut() = names.first().cloned()`, which is None (shell.rs:148-155). The saved arrangement is only re-applied by restore_layout, which returns early when `self.restored_project.get() == project` (shell.rs:323-325). Only open_project resets restored_project (shell.rs:33); connect() does not. reconcile() then rebuilds `ordered` in session.list order (app.rs:1459-1465). The next save_layout (any navigation, mode change or sidebar toggle; it only requires restored_project == project, shell.rs:290) writes that order to native.layout.current.{project}.
findings.impact: After an engine restart, or a click on the Reconnect key that appears beside any notice, agent tiles come back in creation order, and in focus mode the first agent replaces the one the user had focused. The drag-arranged order is then overwritten permanently on the next navigation.
findings.fix: Don't clear `ordered` in connect(); reconcile() already prunes names that no longer have sessions. Or reset `restored_project` to 0 in connect() so the next refresh re-applies the saved layout.

v1.reason: connect() (app.rs:1143-1144) clears `ordered` and calls layout(). With no names, layout() sets focused to names.first(), which is None (shell.rs:148-155). restore_layout returns early when restored_project == project (shell.rs:323-325), and only open_project resets restored_project (shell.rs:33). connect() does not, and grep shows no other reset. The refresh after reconnect calls reconcile() (app.rs:1448-1465), which appends sessions in session.list order to the now-empty `ordered`. restore_layout (app.rs:1439) is then a no-op. Reconnect is reachable whenever the notice is visible (app.rs:963-974 ties the Reconnect key's visibility to the notice), so clicking Reconnect beside any error, or after an engine restart, triggers it. The next save_layout (set_mode, navigation and so on; its guard at shell.rs:290 passes because restored_project == project) writes the reset order and focus to native.layout.current.{project}.
v1.correction: The simplest fix is `self.restored_project.set(0)` in connect(), which matches what open_project already does. That re-applies the saved order and focus on the first refresh after reconnecting.

findings.title: refresh() clears registry_dirty before fetching and never restores it on failure, leaving a stale or empty project list (and possibly opening onboarding)
findings.evidence: `if ui.registry_dirty.replace(false) { let (projects, workspaces) = tokio::join!(ui.call("project.list",…), ui.call("workspace.list",…)); … (Err(e), _) | (_, Err(e)) => { ui.show_error(&e.to_string()); break; } }` (app.rs:1372-1388). Nothing sets the flag back. Later passes skip the registry fetch and use `ui.projects` as it is. With an empty list the next pass sets the project to 0 and runs `if !ui.setup_checked.replace(true) && ui.projects.borrow().is_empty() { ui.open_repository(); }` (app.rs:1412-1414). Realistic failures: a 30 s timeout while the control socket is stalled behind a slow op, or a refresh() triggered by open_project/mutate while connecting (client None → Disconnected). restore_layout has the same consume-before-fetch pattern: it sets restored_project before its settings.get (shell.rs:326-341), so a failed read means that project's saved layout is never applied and the next save_layout overwrites it.
findings.impact: If project.list fails on the first connection, the next refresh shows "No project" and an empty sidebar and opens the add-repository onboarding even though projects exist. On later connections the sidebar stays stale (removed projects listed, new ones missing) until some project.* or workspace.* event arrives.
findings.fix: Set registry_dirty back to true on the error path, or clear it only after a successful fetch. Likewise, set restored_project only after settings.get succeeds.

v1.reason: app.rs:1372 does `if ui.registry_dirty.replace(false)`. On the `(Err(e), _) | (_, Err(e))` arm (1384-1387) it shows the error and breaks without setting the flag back, so later passes use the stale ui.projects. Realistic trigger: connect() sets registry_dirty=true (app.rs:1133) before the client exists. If any open_project or mutate calls refresh() during "Connecting…", ui.call fails at once with Error::Disconnected (app.rs:1112) and the flag is gone. When the connection succeeds, its refresh() (app.rs:1162) skips the registry fetch, so the sidebar stays stale until a project.* or workspace.* event arrives. restore_layout (shell.rs:323-341) has the same consume-before-fetch pattern: restored_project is set before settings.get. If that read fails, the saved layout is never applied, and save_layout (shell.rs:290) then overwrites it.
v1.correction: The onboarding scenario needs project.list to fail on the first connection, right after bus.subscribe succeeded on the same client (a 30 s timeout, client.rs:65-70). That is rare. The more likely case is a reconnect where the user clicks during "Connecting…", which leaves a stale list rather than opening onboarding, because setup_checked is already true. The generation-mismatch `continue` at 1377 is safe, since connect() sets the flag again. Fix as proposed: restore the flag on error, or clear it only after success. Do the same for restored_project.

findings.title: The reader drains pending replies before closing the notice channel, so a request issued in between waits its full timeout; the comment says the opposite
findings.evidence: On exit the reader runs `for (_, reply) in waiting.lock().unwrap().drain() {…}`, then `// Close before notifying so request callers and drains cannot wait forever.` followed by `let _ = reader_notices.send(Notice::Disconnected(error)).await; reader_notices.close();` (client.rs:259-265). The code notifies first, with an await that blocks while the 64-slot queue is full, and closes afterwards. request_with_id's only guard is `if self.0.notices.is_closed()` before inserting into `pending` (client.rs:309-315). A request made in that window is inserted after the drain. If the reader died of a protocol error (such as the 2 MiB cap), the writer and socket are still alive: the request is written, its reply is never read, and because the caller's Client clone keeps the Connection alive, Connection::drop never clears it.
findings.impact: Such a request hangs for its whole timeout (30 s; 180 s for session.create/task.dispatch; 30 min for project.clone) instead of failing immediately.
findings.fix: Track the closed state inside the pending mutex (for example Option<HashMap>) and set it in the same critical section as the drain, so request_with_id refuses atomically. Correct the comment.

v1.reason: At client.rs:258-265 the reader drains `waiting`, then awaits reader_notices.send(Notice::Disconnected) on a bounded(64) async_channel, and only then calls close(). The comment says 'Close before notifying', the reverse of what the code does. request_with_id checks notices.is_closed() and then inserts into pending in a separate step (client.rs:309-315). A GTK-thread request that lands after the drain and before close() is inserted into a map nothing will drain again. After a protocol-error exit (for example the 2 MiB cap) the writer task is still alive, so tx.send succeeds and the request waits out its full timeout. The window is microseconds unless the notice queue is full, in which case it lasts until the UI drains it. The UI handles Disconnected by dropping its client, which narrows the window further.
v1.correction: Simply reordering to close-then-send would lose the Disconnected notice (async_channel rejects send after close), and is_closed-then-insert would still be a TOCTOU. Use the proposed fix: keep closed state inside the pending mutex (Option<HashMap>) and set it in the same critical section as the drain. Also fix the comment. Impact is limited to a rare stray 30 s wait.

findings.title: connect() does not re-check the generation after awaiting bus.subscribe, so a superseded attempt marks the UI connected
findings.evidence: The generation is checked only before `*ui.client.borrow_mut() = Some(client)` (app.rs:1150-1153). After `ui.call("bus.subscribe",…).await` the code unconditionally runs `ui.connected.set(true)`, `ui.status.set_text("")`, `ui.notice.set_visible(false)`, `ui.refresh()`, `load_appearance()` and so on (app.rs:1154-1164). The Reconnect key is visible while "Connecting to the Relay engine…" is shown (app.rs:963-969), so a second click during a slow subscribe starts generation N+1 while N is still waiting.
findings.impact: The stale continuation hides the new attempt's "Connecting…" banner, clears the status bar and fires refreshes with no client (spurious "Connection closed" errors). If the newer attempt then fails, `connected` stays true: its error auto-dismisses (show_error only times out notices while connected, app.rs:1086-1091) and the status bar stays blank although nothing is connected.
findings.fix: After every await in the connect future, run `if generation != ui.generation.get() { return; }` before touching shared state, including before the device.watch call and on the error paths.

v1.reason: In connect()'s future the generation is checked only once, after Client::connect (app.rs:1150). After `ui.call("bus.subscribe", ...).await` (app.rs:1154) the code sets connected=true, clears the status, hides the notice, and calls refresh(), load_appearance() and device.watch, all with no generation check. The Reconnect key is visible while "Connecting to the Relay engine…" is shown, so a second connect() can start while the first is awaiting subscribe. The stale continuation then overwrites state the newer attempt set. The drain loop itself does check generation (app.rs:1174).
v1.correction: Rare in practice. Both connects go to a local Unix socket and bus.subscribe is answered inline (socket.rs:362), so the window is milliseconds. The bad end state, connected stuck at true while nothing is connected, also needs the newer attempt to fail right after the older one succeeded, which is unlikely against the same engine. The usual result is a few spurious "Connection closed" notices from refreshes fired while ui.client is None. Fix: re-check `generation == ui.generation.get()` after each await.

findings.title: On connect, device.watch is awaited before the notice loop starts draining, so 64 queued events block its reply
findings.evidence: `if *ui.page.borrow() == "devices" { let _ = ui.call("device.watch", json!({"on":true})).await; }` runs after bus.subscribe has succeeded but before `while let Ok(notice) = notices.recv().await` (app.rs:1165-1170). The reader pushes events with `reader_notices.send(Notice::Event(event)).await` into a 64-slot channel (client.rs:179, 235-238) and reads no further lines while that send waits. The device.watch response behind the 65th event is therefore never read.
findings.impact: Reconnecting while on the Devices page during an event burst (for example several agents editing files; file.changed is debounced only per worktree, watch.rs:120) stalls every request on the control connection until device.watch times out after 30 s.
findings.fix: Spawn the device.watch call as its own future, as navigate() already does (app.rs:1339-1347), and enter the drain loop immediately.

v1.reason: The mechanism is real. On reconnect while the Devices page is open, `ui.call("device.watch", ...).await` (app.rs:1165-1167) runs before the `notices.recv()` drain loop starts. The client's reader task sends each Event into a 64-slot bounded channel with `.send(...).await` (client.rs:181, 235-238) and reads no further socket lines while that send is pending. If more than 64 events arrive before the device.watch response, the response is never read, the call times out after 30 s, and every other response on that connection, including the refresh() calls just fired, is stuck behind it. navigate() already spawns device.watch as a separate future (app.rs:1339-1347).
v1.correction: I could not show that more than 64 subscribed events realistically arrive in the few milliseconds between the subscribe reply and the device.watch reply. That needs a heavy event burst at the moment of a manual reconnect while the Devices page is shown (at startup the page is not Devices, so it applies only to Reconnect). It recovers after the 30 s timeout. Fix as proposed: spawn the device.watch call instead of awaiting it before the drain loop.

findings.title: The "Reconnect to engine" key follows the notice's visibility, so it appears beside every message while connected
findings.evidence: `ui.notice.connect_label_notify(move |notice| { recovery_label_key.set_visible(!notice.text().is_empty()); })` and `ui.notice.connect_visible_notify(move |notice| recovery_key.set_visible(notice.is_visible()))` (app.rs:963-969). show_error is the single banner for errors, info and toasts (for example "Wait for agent launch to finish before closing.", provider update messages and ui.toast text). Clicking the key runs connect(), which drops the healthy client and stops and recreates every terminal pane (app.rs:1137-1144), with no launch_busy or dirty check.
findings.impact: Users are offered an engine reconnect next to unrelated messages. Using it needlessly re-attaches every terminal, drops keystrokes still queued in each pane's input channel (Pane::stop aborts the input task), loses the wall order (see the reconnect finding) and, mid-launch, removes the launch's placeholder panes.
findings.fix: Show the key only while `!ui.connected.get()`, toggling it wherever `connected` changes, and refuse connect() while launch_busy.

v1.reason: The reconnect key is `icon_button("view-refresh-symbolic", "Reconnect to engine")` in top_actions (app.rs:432-434). Its visibility follows the notice: `connect_label_notify` -> `set_visible(!notice.text().is_empty())` and `connect_visible_notify` -> `set_visible(notice.is_visible())` (app.rs:962-969). show_error (app.rs:1079-1081) is the one banner for everything, including toasts (`ui.toast` -> show_error at app.rs:1245-1246), the close guards ("Wait for agent launch to finish before closing.", app.rs:1034) and success/info text. While connected, the key therefore appears beside every message. Clicking it runs connect() (app.rs:1131-1145) with no busy check. connect() drops the client, calls `p.stop()` on every pane (terminal.rs:576-585 aborts the stream and the input tasks, which discards queued input), clears `panes` and `ordered`, and reconnects.
v1.correction: Harm only comes from a deliberate click on a key labelled "Reconnect", so the impact is a confusing affordance plus a disruptive re-attach, not silent damage. Low is right. Fix: make the key's visibility depend on `!ui.connected.get()` (toggle it where `connected` is set in connect() and in the close handler), and refuse connect() while launch_busy.

findings.title: The event subscription is a hand-maintained allow-list that omits workspace.deleted, although the router handles every workspace.* event
findings.evidence: The bus.subscribe list (app.rs:1154) includes "workspace.changed" but not "workspace.deleted", which the engine emits on workspace.remove (workspace.rs:179). The router treats `e.ev.starts_with("project.") || e.ev.starts_with("workspace.")` as a registry change (app.rs:1223-1225). The engine's filter supports `prefix.*` subscriptions (socket.rs:212-221).
findings.impact: Removing an empty workspace from the CLI, the phone or another window leaves it in the native sidebar, because no project.deleted accompanies it, until some other registry event arrives. "Add a project…" under it then fails.
findings.fix: Subscribe by prefix for the families the router handles by prefix ("project.*", "workspace.*", "session.*", "notify.*", "guardrail.*", …), and keep the list as one const next to the router.

v1.reason: The bus.subscribe list at app.rs:1154 includes workspace.changed but not workspace.deleted. WsRemove emits workspace.deleted (handlers/workspace.rs:179), and for an empty workspace (n == 0) it emits no project.deleted, because the project.remove loop never runs. The engine filters events by subscription (socket.rs:207-221), so the native window never receives it. The router's prefix branch (app.rs:1223) would otherwise set registry_dirty and refresh. A removal from the CLI or another client therefore leaves the workspace showing in this window's sidebar until some other registry event arrives.
v1.correction: Narrow trigger: only an empty workspace removed by another client. Removing a non-empty one also emits project.deleted, which is subscribed. Adding "workspace.deleted" (or "workspace.*") to the list fixes it.

findings.title: Coarse event routing re-fetches whole pages, the full appearance and the Notes rail for unrelated changes
findings.evidence: Every event without a dedicated branch, including usage.changed, notify.*, guardrail.*, run.changed and device.* after their own handling, reaches `} else { ui.refresh_page(); }` (app.rs:1263-1265). On the Board that means task.list, module.list and board_view::show (pages.rs:41-88). Each settings.changed under appearance.* or terminal.font_size calls load_appearance() (app.rs:1257-1262). That issues six settings.get calls, decodes the base64 wallpaper JPEG on the GTK thread, reloads a display-wide CssProvider and restyles every terminal (shell.rs:1116-1245). The Settings page saves one settings.set per changed field (tools_settings.rs:147-151), so one Save triggers the full reload once per appearance field, with no coalescing. Every Ui::refresh() also calls refresh_notes (app.rs:1440): a notes.list plus a full rebuild of the Notes rail and picker (notes_window.rs:206-210, note_pages.rs:1121-1131), although notes changes arrive as their own events (app.rs:1209-1212).
findings.impact: Background agent activity keeps re-querying and re-rendering whichever page is open, adding requests to the single serialized control connection. Saving appearance settings stutters the UI through several main-thread JPEG decodes and CSS recomputes.
findings.fix: Map events to the pages they affect (task.*/module.* → board/modules, mailbox.* → mailbox, guardrail.* → guardrails) and ignore the rest. Coalesce load_appearance with pending/dirty flags as refresh() does, and re-decode the wallpaper only when appearance.wallpaper changed. Drop refresh_notes from refresh() except while the Notes window has no project yet.

v1.reason: The coarse fall-through to `ui.refresh_page()` at app.rs:1263-1265 is real. Every settings.changed under appearance.* or terminal.font_size calls load_appearance (app.rs:1257-1262). That runs six settings.get calls and decodes the base64 wallpaper into a gdk::Texture on the main thread every time (shell.rs:1116-1245). Settings Save sends its settings.set calls one after another (tools_settings.rs:147-151), so each changed appearance field triggers its own full reload and decode.
v1.correction: Part of the claim is overstated. refresh_page is coalesced (page_dirty/page_pending, app.rs:1662-1686) and does nothing on the agents/code pages (app.rs:1672), which is where the user usually is while agents work. So the extra page re-queries only happen when Board, Mailbox or similar is open. refresh_notes returns at once unless the Notes window exists (notes_window.rs:168-177), so it does not rebuild the rail on every refresh(). The cost that remains: several wallpaper decodes and CSS reloads per Save, and Board re-fetches (task.list plus module.list) on unrelated events. Fix: decode the wallpaper only when appearance.wallpaper changed, coalesce load_appearance with a dirty/pending flag, and route events to the pages they affect.

findings.title: ui.toast text is shown unattributed in the system error banner
findings.evidence: `} else if e.ev == "ui.toast" { ui.show_error(text(&e.payload, "text")); }` (app.rs:1245-1246) ignores `e.actor` and the payload's `level` and `ttl_ms` (handlers/ui.rs:331-333). Agents that were granted allow_ui can call ui.toast (ops/ui.rs:1, 38; guardrail.rs:369-381).
findings.impact: An agent with UI control can place arbitrary text, such as instructions to run a command, in the same banner that carries Relay's own engine errors (with the Reconnect key beside it), and the user cannot tell them apart. Info-level toasts also read as errors.
findings.fix: Prefix the actor ("agent:foo: …"), style by level, honour ttl_ms, and keep the reconnect key off toasts.

v1.reason: app.rs:1245-1246 does `else if e.ev == "ui.toast" { ui.show_error(text(&e.payload, "text")); }`. The engine handler (handlers/ui.rs:331-333) emits text, level (default "info") and ttl_ms (default 4000), and the client throws away level, ttl_ms and the event's actor. show_error (app.rs:1079-1109) puts the text in the same notice label used for engine errors. It sets the auto-dismiss time from the message length, not from ttl_ms. The recovery/reconnect key is shown whenever the notice is visible (app.rs:964-969). An agent can reach this with allow_ui: guardrail.rs:369-371 lets any ui.*/os.* op through when session.allow_ui is set.
v1.correction: I rated this a functional bug, not a security issue. allow_ui is a deliberate per-session grant, and it already gives os.open_url, ui.page.switch and pane control (ops/ui.rs). So a spoofed banner adds very little to what such an agent can already do, and the call is audited (Audit::AgentOnly). What is really wrong: level is ignored, so info toasts look like errors; ttl_ms is ignored; nothing shows who sent the toast; and the reconnect key appears next to it. The fix stands: show the toast in its own style, or at least prefix the actor, style it by level, honour ttl_ms, and keep the recovery key off toasts.

findings.title: refresh() replaces the wall's session rows wholesale, dropping launch placeholders mid-launch
findings.evidence: `*ui.sessions.borrow_mut() = all.iter().filter(|s| s["project_id"].as_i64() == Some(project)).cloned().collect();` (app.rs:1427-1431) discards the synthetic `"placeholder": true` rows that launch_placeholders pushed (agent_menu.rs:219-223). It also admits the launch's own `created` rows, which apply_session_event deliberately withholds while launch_busy (agent_menu.rs:123-127). launch_adopt then cannot find the placeholder's slot in `ordered` (agent_menu.rs:255-259).
findings.impact: A refresh during a launch (session.create can run for 180 s), triggered by any project.* or workspace.* event such as an edit from the phone or CLI, makes the "new agent N" panes vanish. launch_progress updates then go nowhere, and adopted agents land at the end of the wall instead of in their slot.
findings.fix: While launch_busy, keep placeholder rows and apply the same created-row filter as apply_session_event when replacing ui.sessions.

v1.reason: launch_placeholders pushes rows with `"placeholder": true` into ui.sessions (agent_menu.rs:211-226). refresh() then replaces ui.sessions wholesale with the filtered session.list (app.rs:1427-1431) and calls reconcile. reconcile prunes `ordered` to the names that exist (app.rs:1449-1455), so the placeholder panes disappear. That refresh also adds the launch's own `created` rows, which apply_session_event deliberately holds back while launch_busy (agent_menu.rs:123-127). After that, launch_adopt finds no placeholder slot in `ordered` (agent_menu.rs:255-259), so the adopted session is not put in its slot, and launch_progress on a placeholder finds no pane (agent_menu.rs:232). Neither refresh() nor reconcile looks at launch_busy.
v1.correction: The launch does not trigger this itself. launch_busy is set (launch.rs:779) before open_project (launch.rs:791), so open_project never refreshes there. session.create and session.spawn emit row-bearing session.changed events, which are applied in place. Only an outside refresh() during the launch window causes it: a project.* or workspace.* event from another client, a non-row session event, or another UI action that ends in mutate()/refresh(). The result is cosmetic and temporary: launch_abort and the final refresh() (launch.rs:823-825) restore a consistent wall. Fix as proposed: while launch_busy, keep placeholder rows and filter out `created` rows when refresh() replaces ui.sessions.

findings.title: "The active project disappeared" is handled in two places that have diverged
findings.evidence: refresh() moves to the first project and only resets the editor (app.rs:1391-1410). registry_removed picks the nearest neighbour in sidebar order and goes through open_project (shell/registry.rs:676-690). open_project also dismisses panels, refuses during a launch, hides the launch sheet, re-filters sessions and resets ordered and restored_project (shell.rs:10-37).
findings.impact: When a project is removed from another client, the UI lands on a different project than a local removal would choose. It also leaves panels or the launch sheet for the removed project open (their later calls fail with not-found), even mid-launch.
findings.fix: Route both paths through one helper that picks the neighbour and calls open_project.

v1.reason: A project deleted from another client (phone, CLI) arrives as a project.* event. That event only sets registry_dirty and calls refresh() (app.rs:1223-1225). The removed-project branch in refresh() (app.rs:1389-1410) sets the first project and resets the editor. It does not call dismiss_panels, check launch_busy, hide the launch sheet, re-filter sessions or clear `ordered` as open_project does (shell.rs:10-37). A local deletion goes through registry_removed (shell/registry.rs:663-694), which picks the nearest neighbour in sidebar order and calls open_project. The two paths have diverged in which project they choose and in what they clean up.
v1.correction: The real impact is small. In the refresh path, session.list re-filters sessions for the new project and reconcile drops stale names from `ordered`, so the wall ends up correct. What differs is which project is chosen, and that panels or the launch sheet for the deleted project stay open. Fix as proposed: one helper that picks the neighbour and calls open_project, used by both paths.

findings.title: NON_UNIQUE application: the present-existing-window branch is dead, and a second launch starts a second full client
findings.evidence: `.flags(gtk::gio::ApplicationFlags::NON_UNIQUE)` (app.rs:322). activate begins with `if let Some(window) = app.active_window() { window.present(); return; }` (app.rs:325-328), but a NON_UNIQUE app never forwards a second launch to the running process, and nothing in the crate re-emits activate. The installed desktop entry runs run.sh, which ends with `exec "$PWD/target/debug/relay-native"` (run.sh:46).
findings.impact: Launching Relay again (for example from the app menu while its window is on another workspace) opens a second independent client. Both play every notification sound, both write native.layout.current.{project} (shell.rs:305-309), and each follows the other's page switches through ui.changed (app.rs:1247-1248).
findings.fix: Drop NON_UNIQUE and use an instance-specific application id (for example com.quietsoftware.Relay4.dev) so dev and stable can still run side by side; the existing activate branch will then present the running window.

v1.reason: app.rs:320-322 builds the application with `.application_id("com.quietsoftware.Relay4").flags(gtk::gio::ApplicationFlags::NON_UNIQUE)`. With NON_UNIQUE, GIO does no single-instance negotiation, so a second launch never forwards activate to the running process. Nothing in the crate calls `app.activate()` (the only `.activate()` is a list row at note_pages.rs:649). So the `if let Some(window) = app.active_window() { window.present(); return; }` branch at app.rs:325-328 cannot run, and a second launch builds a whole second Ui and connects a second client. The installed desktop entry runs run.sh (scripts/install-native-desktop.py:8,22), and run.sh ends with `exec "$PWD/target/debug/relay-native"`, so every menu launch starts a new client process. docs/VERIFICATION.md's "second launch reuses the same process" means the engine, not the client: scripts/test-launcher-real.py:39 asserts that the engine pid is reused.
v1.correction: NON_UNIQUE probably exists so that clients for different instances can run side by side: scripts/native-smoke.py:114 starts a client with RELAY_INSTANCE=test next to a real one, and dev/stable are separate instances. The fix therefore needs an instance-specific application id (for example com.quietsoftware.Relay4.<instance>, with StartupWMClass and the .desktop file updated to match), as proposed. The trigger is less common than it sounds: GNOME's dash usually focuses an already-running app instead of launching a new one. That is why this is low.

findings.title: Closing the main window leaves detached mirror windows, and with them the process, running
findings.evidence: The close handler closes panels and drafts and explicitly destroys the Notes window with `if let Some(notes) = owned.notes_window.borrow_mut().take() { notes.window.destroy(); }` (app.rs:1055-1064), then drops the client and panes. A detached device mirror is a separate application window: `gtk::Window::builder().application(&ui.window.application().unwrap()).transient_for(&ui.window)`, with no destroy_with_parent (mirror.rs:587-593). GtkApplication keeps running while any of its windows exist.
findings.impact: After the user closes Relay, the process keeps running with the mirror window still streaming the device; the mirror's socket attachment keeps capture alive on the engine. Controls that need the main UI (device list, re-dock: mirror.rs:584, 726, 956) stop working.
findings.fix: In the close handler, close every other application window (app.windows()), or create mirror windows with destroy_with_parent(true).

v1.reason: mirror.rs:586-593 creates the detached mirror as `gtk::Window::builder().application(&ui.window.application().unwrap()).transient_for(&ui.window)` with no destroy_with_parent. In GTK4 a transient child is destroyed with its parent only when destroy_with_parent is set; otherwise only the transient link is cleared. The main close-request handler (app.rs:1032-1072) closes panels and drafts, destroys the notes window, drops the client and stops panes, but never touches mirror views (the VIEWS thread-local in mirror.rs). Nothing in the crate connects shutdown or window-removed, calls quit or iterates app.windows(). So the mirror window stays registered with the GtkApplication, the process keeps running, and the mirror's own connection (`Client::connect_with_limit`, mirror.rs:1083) keeps device.mirror.start capture alive on the engine.
v1.correction: The window stays on screen, so this is not a hidden leak. The user sees the mirror and can close it, which runs close() (mirror.rs:668) and ends capture. That makes it a bug (unexpected lifetime after closing the main window) rather than resource-leak. Controls that need the main Ui (ui.upgrade() in start/dock/detach) do nothing once Ui is dropped. Fix: in the main close handler, close every VIEWS mirror (or app.windows() other than the main one), or set destroy_with_parent(true) in detach().

findings.title: relay-native declares serde and anyhow but never uses them
findings.evidence: `serde = { workspace = true }` (Cargo.toml:11) and `anyhow = { workspace = true }` (Cargo.toml:19). An rg search finds no `serde::` path, no Serialize/Deserialize derive and no `anyhow` anywhere under apps/relay-native/src.
findings.impact: Extra compile work and a misleading dependency list on a crate that can only be built on a GTK 4.22 machine.
findings.fix: Remove both lines.

v1.reason: apps/relay-native/Cargo.toml:11 declares `serde = { workspace = true }` and :19 declares `anyhow = { workspace = true }`. Searching the whole apps/relay-native tree for `serde\b`, `serde::`, `Serialize`, `Deserialize` and `anyhow` finds only those two Cargo.toml lines. All JSON work goes through `serde_json` (client.rs:5, pages.rs:4 and others), and errors use `thiserror` (client.rs:74). There are no derive macros or `#[serde]` attributes, so neither crate is referenced. The other declared dependencies (uuid, base64, sha2, tokio, tracing_subscriber, async_channel, pango) are all used.
v1.correction: The payoff is only a cleaner manifest. Both crates are already compiled for other workspace members, so the build saving is close to zero. Removing them is a change under apps/relay-native/ that cannot be compiled in the agent image (CLAUDE.md), so the PR must say it was not built.

findings.title: Ui::build is a ~700-line constructor mixing widget construction, signal wiring and close policy, and it already hides dead state
findings.evidence: build spans app.rs:374-1075 (688 lines, per clippy::too_many_lines). Inside it, `settings_return` is a `(String, bool)` whose bool is written by `*return_state.borrow_mut() = (mut_previous.borrow().clone(), ui.sidebar.is_visible())` (app.rs:871-872) but never read: only `.0` is used (app.rs:897), while `ui.settings_sidebar` (app.rs:870) holds the same value. `track_navigation`'s `if name == "agents"` branch (app.rs:205-207) can never match any of the five names passed to it (app.rs:815-821).
findings.impact: The wiring that decides window, settings back-key and close behaviour is hard to review in one 700-line function, which is how duplicated and dead state like the above survives.
findings.fix: Split it into builders that return small structs (top bar, sidebar, wall, status bar, launch sheet) plus an install_handlers(&Rc<Ui>) step. Replace settings_return with a plain String and read settings_sidebar instead.

v1.reason: Ui::build runs from app.rs:374 to 1075, about 700 lines. The dead state is real. `settings_return` (app.rs:858) is a `(String, bool)`. Its bool is written at app.rs:871-872 (`(mut_previous.borrow().clone(), ui.sidebar.is_visible())`) but never read: the only read is `.0` at app.rs:897. The sidebar visibility is already kept in `ui.settings_sidebar` (set at :870, read at :875 and shell.rs:319, restored at shell.rs:393). `track_navigation` (app.rs:204-207) checks `if name == "agents"`, but its only caller (app.rs:829) passes dashboard/skills/plugins/board/notes. That branch can never run.
v1.correction: The concrete, low-cost payoff is removing the dead pieces: make settings_return a plain String (it also duplicates the mut_previous value captured when settings opens) and drop the unreachable "agents" branch. Splitting build into builders is a reasonable refactor but optional. Its value is reviewability, and no bug has been shown to come from the length itself.

findings.title: Smoke-test assertions live in the production Ui impl
findings.evidence: verify_shell, verify_launch, verify_terminal_input, terminal_contents_contain and verify_burst (app.rs:1585-1661) are called only from smoke.rs and roadmap_smoke.rs. They assert fixture specifics (`assert_eq!(self.panes.borrow().len(), 11)`, `self.launch.width() == 780`), index `panes[text(session, "name")]` (which panics on a missing pane) and paste text into every live terminal. ARCHITECTURE.md describes smoke.rs as "excluded from normal runtime behavior".
findings.impact: About 80 lines of fixture-only code sit in the core shell module and ship in every build, and they would panic or type into agents' terminals if ever reached outside the fixture.
findings.fix: Move them into a #[cfg(feature = "smoke")] child module of app (like shell.rs) so they keep field access, or gate them behind the smoke env check.

v1.reason: The methods do exist at app.rs:1585-1661 and are called only from smoke.rs and roadmap_smoke.rs. But nothing outside the opt-in smoke harness reaches them, so the 'would panic or type into agents' terminals' impact has no trigger. The proposed fix also rests on something that does not exist: Cargo.toml has no `smoke` feature, and main.rs compiles smoke.rs, roadmap_smoke.rs, smoke_registry.rs and smoke_project_files.rs into every build anyway. Moving about 80 lines that need private field access from one always-compiled module into another changes neither behaviour nor binary contents. The payoff is cosmetic, so this is not worth changing.
v1.correction: If anything is done, the real cleanup is gating all the smoke modules (smoke.rs, roadmap_smoke.rs, smoke_registry.rs, smoke_project_files.rs and these verifiers) behind a new cargo feature. That is a build-config decision, not a defect.

results.coverage:
I read every line of apps/relay-native/src/shell.rs (1-1247) and apps/relay-native/src/shell/registry.rs (1-1012). To trace callers and callees I also read: app.rs (Ui struct, call/mutate/connect event loop/navigate/refresh/reconcile/update_attachments/refresh_page), panel.rs, client.rs, terminal.rs, agent_menu.rs 1-360, project_files.rs 1-120, tools_plugins.rs 1-200, tools_market.rs 700-760, tools_settings.rs (sync_wallpaper, Save handler, collect_settings, wallpaper import/decode), wallpaper_rotation.rs, icons.rs, shortcuts.rs, pages.rs (open_task, project menu), task_pages.rs open(), and roadmap_smoke.rs 170-260. On the engine side I read handlers ui.rs, workspace.rs 120-380, provider.rs skill.enable, settings.rs set/reset, the session.rs report handler, the engine.rs audit paths, the relay-bus Page enum, the Project/Workspace/Notification types, OpMeta::mutation defaults, and the store.rs schema.

Two hypotheses were checked empirically, outside the repo. A scratch PyGObject script against the installed GTK 4.22.5 confirmed that gtk_widget_set_name permanently interns the name as a GQuark. Symbol inspection of libvte-2.91-gtk4 0.84.1 showed it has no drop target, so dragging a pane header cannot paste text into a PTY; not a finding.

Not verified at runtime (the native app cannot be built or run here): the size of the popover-cycle leak (the cycle itself follows from gtk-rs strong refs and GtkMenuButton's dispose only unparenting its popover; the MB/hour figure is an estimate), and the keyboard-focus loss on sidebar rebuild.

The pedantic clippy cast warnings for these files (pane counts, durations, layout widths, split ratio) were all checked and none hides a real bug.

Considered and not reported as harmless or trivia: apply_layout's order.dedup() only removing adjacent duplicates (ordered never holds duplicates locally); registry_menu's no-op sort_by_key; open_project dismissing panels before refusing a switch; the unreachable Escape-closes-launch branch in app.rs's bubble controller (shadowed by install_shortcuts); the fixed 100 px drop threshold in install_pane_controls; navigation_echoes growth (the engine always emits ui.changed for ui.page.switch); and RefCell borrows across GTK calls (no re-entrant double borrow found).

findings.title: Every sidebar row's ⋯ menu leaks: its buttons hold the popover strongly, and the whole tree is rebuilt on every agent state change
findings.evidence: registry.rs:505-512: `let pop = popover.clone(); key.connect_clicked(move |_| { pop.popdown(); if let Some(ui) = weak.upgrade() { action(&ui); } });`. `key` is a child of `body` (504), and `body` is the popover's child (514). That makes a cycle: popover → body → key → clicked closure → popover. When a row is removed, GtkMenuButton's dispose only unparents its popover. The popover then stays referenced by its own buttons' closures, so it is never disposed. The leak includes the popover, body, title/path labels, separators, 4-5 buttons (each a Box, Image and Label), and the Action closures holding three clones of the project/workspace JSON (470, 478). One menu is built per workspace header (366) and per visible project row (439). render_projects rebuilds every row whenever its signature changes (133-137), and the signature includes every session's state in every project. Each running/idle/blocked transition emits session.changed (crates/relay-core/src/handlers/session.rs:1424-1426), which calls render_projects through apply_session_event (agent_menu.rs:131). The codebase already uses the safe pattern elsewhere (pages.rs:229 `let pop = popover.downgrade();`). registry_editor repeats the mistake: `check` holds `save` strongly (828), save's clicked closure holds name/branch/build/run/pinned strongly (912), and their changed/notify handlers hold `check` (871-888). So save and the inputs form a cycle that survives Panel::close's clear(body).
findings.impact: Memory grows for as long as the app runs, in proportion to agent activity times the number of sidebar rows. Every agent turn boundary in any project rebuilds the tree and leaks one popover subtree per visible row. For example, 20 rows and a few hundred agent state transitions an hour leak thousands of widget subtrees per hour (rough estimate, not measured). Each open/close of Project or Workspace settings leaks about 10 more widgets.
findings.fix: Capture the popover weakly (`let pop = popover.downgrade();` and upgrade it inside the handler, as pages.rs:229 does), or use `glib::clone!(#[weak] popover, ...)`. Better still, build the menu lazily with MenuButton::set_create_popup_func, so rows that are never opened allocate nothing. In registry_editor, capture `save` and the labels weakly inside `check` (the inputs are already weak there), or capture the inputs weakly in the save closure.

v1.reason: The cycle is real. In registry.rs:505-512 every menu entry's clicked closure captures `pop = popover.clone()`, a strong GObject ref. `key` is a child of `body`, and `body` is the popover's child (`popover.set_child(Some(&body))`). Once the row is removed, GtkMenuButton's dispose only unparents its popover, which drops the parent's reference. The N strong refs held by the buttons' own signal closures keep the popover's refcount above zero, so dispose never runs and the handlers are never torn down. Nothing breaks the cycle: `clear()` in app.rs:64-68 just calls `container.remove(&w)`, and no code calls run_dispose or disconnects these handlers.
