- the plugin stays under the 'Suggested' filter, and its count doesn't change;
- project_switches shows a 'Suggested' chip next to a switch that is on (:863).
This lasts until the next full reload.
findings.fix: In set_enabled, when the response shows the project as enabled, also remove that project id from item["suggested_for"].

v1.reason: On success, toggle (tools_market.rs:731) calls set_enabled, and set_enabled (:477-486) patches only `item["enabled_in"]`. The engine computes suggested_for only in plugin.list (provider.rs ~287-293, which filters out enabled projects). plugin.enable returns `to_bus(plugin, enabled_in, Vec::new())` (provider.rs ~335), so the client never gets a corrected suggested_for. The plugin.changed event has its project set via ctx.set_project. app.rs:1213-1222 drops it when project_id != ui.project (unless the page is dashboard or notifications), so no refresh_page/plugin.list follows for a non-active project. The Suggested filter (tools_plugins.rs:47 `3 => suggested(plugin, project)`) and the chip in project_switches (tools_market.rs:863) both test suggested_for without checking enabled. The card at tools_plugins.rs:193 does guard with `&& !enabled`. After you switch a suggested plugin on for a non-active project, that project stays in the Suggested filter and its count, and keeps its chip next to an 'on' switch. For the active project the event triggers refresh_page and a re-list, which corrects it.
v1.correction: The staleness lasts only until the next plugin.list. Any later engine event for the active project that reaches refresh_page triggers one, so it is not strictly 'until the next full reload'. Switching a plugin off has the mirror problem: it does not reappear as suggested. Fix: in set_enabled, remove the project from suggested_for when it is enabled. Or make the Suggested predicate `suggested && !enabled` in tools_plugins.rs:47 and in the chip test, as the card already does.

findings.title: A failed read of the usage display preferences is never retried, and the options panel is built from preferences that may not be loaded and is never resynced
findings.evidence: Discovery runs only when `installed.is_none_or(|(seen, _)| *seen != generation)` (:320-321). `installed` is stamped as soon as provider.list succeeds (:348-355), but prefs are replaced only `if let Some(Ok(v)) = prefs` (:356-358). usage_options builds its switches and chips once from `self.usage.prefs.borrow().clone()` (:671, :680, :693). For Value::Null, enabled() defaults to true and interval() to 0. After a refused settings.set, reload_usage_prefs (:423) re-renders only the strip.
findings.impact: If the settings.get inside discovery fails (for example a timeout behind the connect burst) while provider.list succeeds, later automatic refreshes never read the preferences again. Hidden meters reappear in the strip, and a configured auto-refresh interval is ignored until the user presses refresh or a settings event arrives. If the popup opens before the preferences load, or after a refused write, the switches show defaults or the rejected value. For example, with Codex hidden its switch shows on, so the first click changes nothing.
findings.fix: Track whether the preferences have loaded separately from `installed`, and keep discovering until both reads succeed. Update the option widgets from render_usage_popup, blocking their handlers while doing so, instead of building them only once.

v1.reason: status_usage.rs:319-321: discovery is forced only while `installed` is None or from another generation. :348-355 stamps `installed` whenever provider.list succeeds, and :356-358 replace prefs only on `Some(Ok(v))`. So if settings.get fails while provider.list succeeds, prefs stay at their initial Value::Null (:252), where enabled() falls back to true and interval() to 0. Timer and popup refreshes call refresh_usage(false) (:405, :666, status.rs:68) and never re-read them. Only the refresh button/key (refresh_usage(true) at :295/:634) or a settings.changed event (app.rs:1255) recovers. usage_options (:670-748) reads prefs once and is never resynced: render_usage_popup does not touch the switches. After a refused settings.set, reload_usage_prefs (:377-388) re-renders only the strip, so the switch keeps the rejected position. Every trigger is rare: settings.get has to fail while provider.list succeeds, the popup has to open in the milliseconds before the startup discovery returns, or a settings.set has to be refused. The impact is cosmetic or a missed auto-refresh.
v1.correction: Prefs survive a reconnect (they are never reset per generation), so only the very first load can leave Null. The simplest fix is to stamp `installed` only when both reads succeed, or to track prefs-loaded separately. Resyncing the switches in render_usage_popup needs signal blocking, because the handlers write settings.

findings.title: A hand-written (provider, meter) → settings-path table has a catch-all arm that silently writes the wrong key
findings.evidence: `let path: &'static str = match (provider, meter) { ("claude", Meter::FiveHour) => "claude.five_hour", ... (_, Meter::FiveHour) => "codex.five_hour", _ => "codex.weekly" };` and `let path = if provider == "claude" { "claude.enabled" } else { "codex.enabled" };` (:712). Both restate PROVIDERS and Meter::key, while the strip reads `prefs[provider][meter.key()]` (:164-165).
findings.impact: Add a meter to meters("codex") (for example Fable) or add a third provider, and its chip silently toggles codex.weekly or codex.enabled. The strip then ignores the chip.
findings.fix: Build the path from data with `format!("{provider}.{}", meter.key())` and `format!("{provider}.enabled")`. Let set_usage_pref take a String, which the closure can own. This removes both tables.

v1.reason: status_usage.rs:696-702 maps (provider, meter) to a static path with the catch-alls `(_, Meter::FiveHour) => "codex.five_hour"` and `_ => "codex.weekly"`, and :712 uses `if provider == "claude" { "claude.enabled" } else { "codex.enabled" }`. The strip and the popup read `prefs[provider][meter.key()]` (:164-165, :461, :599). Every pair is correct today, because meters("codex") (:44-50) has only FiveHour and Weekly and PROVIDERS has two entries. The divergence only appears when a meter or a provider is added. It is a latent trap with a simpler data-driven replacement, not a current bug.
v1.correction: Nothing is wrong today; this is a latent issue only. Fix it with `format!("{provider}.{}", meter.key())` and change set_usage_pref to take String or Cow. The `path == "refresh_minutes"` comparison at :415 still works with that change.

findings.title: The once-per-launch startup update is marked done before the settings read succeeds
findings.evidence: `if ui.provider_updates_checked.replace(true) { return; }` runs before `let Ok(config) = ui.call("settings.get", json!({"path":"providers"})).await else { return; };` (:12-14). startup is called only from the connect path (app.rs:1156).
findings.impact: If that first settings.get fails, the update the user opted into is skipped for the rest of the app session, with no message. It can fail by timing out behind the connect burst on the sequential control connection, or because the engine drops right after connect.
findings.fix: Set the flag only after the settings read succeeds (or reset it on error), so the next connect retries.

v1.reason: provider_updates.rs:7 sets `provider_updates_checked.replace(true)` before the `settings.get` at :12. The `let Ok(config) = ... else { return; }` returns without resetting the flag. startup is called only from connect() (app.rs:1156), which runs again on every reconnect, so the flag is the only thing that limits the attempt to once per launch. A failed read therefore means no attempt at all for the rest of the launch, and no message is shown. The trigger is rare: bus.subscribe has just succeeded on the same connection, and ui.call's default timeout is 30 s (client.rs:65-71), so a timeout is unlikely. The realistic trigger is the engine dropping or restarting right after connect.
v1.correction: The realistic trigger is a disconnect right after bus.subscribe, not a timeout: the request timeout is 30 s, not short. The fix stands: set the flag only after settings.get returns Ok, or reset it in the Err branch.

findings.title: Provider-update messages overwrite each other in the single notice, and each finished update triggers a full shell refresh
findings.evidence: startup and event() report through `ui.show_error` (:25, :27, :49-53), which writes one shared label, so the next provider's message or a later event replaces the previous one. For every state other than 'updating', event() calls `ui.refresh()` (:54-56). That runs session.list, layout restore and a notes refresh (app.rs:1362-1446), none of which shows provider versions. The Settings page is already repainted by the notify.new event the engine emits alongside (provider_updates.rs engine side, :67).
findings.impact: With auto-update on for both providers and live sessions, 'claude: Update skipped…' is immediately replaced by 'codex: Update skipped…', so the Claude outcome is never visible. Each completed update also costs a session.list round trip and a layout restore for nothing.
findings.fix: Join the per-provider startup results into one message, or rely on the provider notifications the engine already writes. Drop the ui.refresh() call in event().

v1.reason: show_error (app.rs:1079) sets the text of one shared `notice` label, so each later call replaces the earlier one. startup (provider_updates.rs:15-31) loops claude then codex and calls show_error for every result that did not start. The engine returns 'Update skipped while this provider has a live session' (core provider_updates.rs:48) when sessions are live, which happens when the UI is launched against an engine that already owns sessions. In that case the claude message is replaced as soon as codex's provider.update returns. 'complete' and 'failed' outcomes are also written as notifications (core :63-67), so only the not-started messages are truly lost. In event() (:54-56), ui.refresh() re-lists projects and sessions and restores the layout (app.rs:1362-1446), and none of that shows provider versions. The notify.new emitted alongside falls through to `ui.refresh_page()` in the event dispatcher (app.rs:1263), which repaints the current page, including Settings.
v1.correction: The cost of the extra refresh is small: refresh() is coalesced through refresh_pending/refresh_dirty, and it runs about once per finished update, so it amounts to roughly one session.list per launch. The lost message is limited to started:false results (skipped, managed, disabled, already running). Completed and failed updates stay in the notification center.

results.coverage:
I read every line of all eight assigned files (2,827 lines): guardrail_pages.rs, guardrail_settings.rs, pages.rs, panel.rs, sounds.rs, wallpaper_rotation.rs, fonts.rs and shortcuts.rs.

**Traced outside the chunk:**
- app.rs: the Ui struct, the event loop and its refresh_page fan-out, show_error, call, connect and navigate.
- client.rs: the 2 MiB line cap, the reader and writer tasks, and request_with_id.
- shell.rs: install_shortcuts (capture phase) and load_appearance (main-thread texture decode).
- tools_settings.rs: settings-page retention, keybinding validation and the 1.5 MB wallpaper cap.
- tools.rs: the dashboard hold queue. Also note_pages.rs (module_composer, modules), task_pages.rs (Draft cleanup) and tools_skills.rs (panel TextView).
- Engine and CLI paths that decide outcomes for these files: handlers/guardrail.rs (request, approve, confirm, reject, list ops), guardrail.rs (refuse_or_user_hold, destructive_decision), guardrail/grants.rs (validate, covers_command), session close expiry, notify.rs (dashboard holds_open), relay-cli's Claude/Codex hooks, BUS.md §9.3–9.5 and D35/D112–D114/D141/D150.
- Crate sources in ~/.cargo/registry: glib 0.22.9 (spawn_future_local catches panics inside the task; SourceId::remove unwraps) and gtk4 0.11.4 (clicked_trampoline is a bare extern "C" fn, so a panic in a click handler aborts).

**Not established:**
- Nothing was compiled or run. That is per the rules, and relay-native cannot be built in CI or agent images anyway. The RefCell panic rests on Rust's temporary-scope rules for edition 2021, not on a reproduction.
- How long the UI freezes for a 0.1–2 MiB label is an estimate. The forced disconnect above 2 MiB is certain from the code.
- The "Allow once" finding is inferred from the code paths. I did not run an agent through hold → confirm → retry.
- Which terminal TUIs bind Ctrl+K and Ctrl+N is assumed from readline and Emacs conventions.

**Pedantic clippy:** I grepped clippy-pedantic.txt for these files. The only casts are on detail-row indices and dropdown positions, which are small and harmless, plus the sounds.rs sample math; none hides a real bug.

**Considered and dropped:**
- fonts.rs: non-atomic writes into the cache directory that dev, test and stable instances share. The race window only exists when two instances start at once, so the impact is near zero.
- DISMISSED grows without bound, but only by 8 bytes per answered prompt.
- The Panel::close RefMut is held across closed callbacks, but no current callback re-enters it.
- The wallpaper timer's SourceId removal cannot double-remove in practice.
- sounds.rs reaping is sound: kill_on_drop plus tokio's orphan reaper, and overlapping sounds are blocked by sound_busy.
- The guardrail editor's widget references: no Rc cycles (all handlers hold weak references, and the root's destroy handler owns the editor).

findings.title: close_prompt panics on a RefCell double borrow whenever a waiting prompt should be promoted (crash or dead event loop with 4+ open requests)
findings.evidence: `if let Some(next) = WAITING.with(|w| (!w.borrow().is_empty()).then(|| w.borrow_mut().remove(0))) {`. The workspace is edition 2021 (Cargo.toml:9). The `Ref` temporary from `w.borrow()` is not in any shorter temporary scope, so it lives until the closure body ends. It is therefore still held when `bool::then` runs `w.borrow_mut()`, which panics with `already borrowed: BorrowMutError`. WAITING is non-empty as soon as more than TRAY_LIMIT (3) requests are open: show_prompt pushes the 4th and later ones there (573-579). `removed` is true whenever the closed id is one of the visible prompts. Consequences, verified in the crate sources: (a) gtk4-0.11.4 `clicked_trampoline` is a plain `unsafe extern "C" fn`, so a panic in a click handler aborts the process. (b) glib-0.22.9 `TaskSource::poll` wraps `spawn_future_local` futures in `catch_unwind` and then ends the task.
findings.impact: With 4 or more open exception requests, closing any visible prompt panics. (1) The "Answer later" X (459) runs close_prompt inside a click handler, which aborts the whole desktop client. (2) An answer from the Guardrails page, the phone, the CLI, or session expiry arrives as `guardrail.resolved`. guardrail_event (691) then runs close_prompt inside the long-lived event-loop task (app.rs:1147-1202). That task dies, so the client silently stops applying engine events (sessions, notifications, prompts, page updates). Its dropped receiver then makes the reader task close the connection without a Disconnected notice: the status bar still looks connected while later calls fail with "Connection closed". (3) Approve or Deny in the prompt kills either that action's task or the event loop, whichever reaches close_prompt first. (4) restore_prompts (711) on reconnect or session-close expiry dies the same way. The queue the tray exists to drain can never drain.
findings.fix: Use one mutable borrow: `let next = WAITING.with(|w| { let mut w = w.borrow_mut(); (!w.is_empty()).then(|| w.remove(0)) }); if let Some(next) = next { show_prompt(ui, &next); }`. Move the WAITING/DISMISSED/tray-count bookkeeping into a small GTK-free struct, with a unit test for "4 requests, close one, the 4th is promoted".

v1.reason: guardrail_pages.rs:666 reads `WAITING.with(|w| (!w.borrow().is_empty()).then(|| w.borrow_mut().remove(0)))`. The closure body is one expression, so it is the temporary scope: the `Ref` from `w.borrow()` (the receiver of `is_empty` under `!`) lives until the whole body has finished, including the eager `bool::then` call that runs `w.borrow_mut()`. That borrow_mut panics with BorrowMutError. Cargo.toml:9 is edition 2021, and the edition-2024 tail-expression change would not help either, because the Ref is still alive while `.then` runs. The path is reachable: TRAY_LIMIT is 3 (line 17), show_prompt pushes the 4th and later requests into WAITING (573-579), and `removed` is true when the closed id is a visible slot. I checked both panic consequences in the crate sources. gtk4-0.11.4 button.rs:514 `clicked_trampoline` is an `unsafe extern "C" fn`, so the "Answer later" X (459) aborts the process. glib-0.22.9 main_context_futures.rs:262 wraps local futures in catch_unwind, so a panic in the long-lived connect task (app.rs:1147-1202, which calls guardrail_event at 1201) ends that task. The client then stops processing events. The same applies to the Approve/Deny futures (382, 479) and to restore_prompts (711).
v1.correction: The proposed fix is right: take a single `borrow_mut` and bind the result before calling show_prompt. Severity stays high, not critical, because this is a client crash or freeze, not an engine failure, and it needs 4 or more open exception requests at once.

v2.reason:
(a) The code does what the finding says. guardrail_pages.rs:666 is `WAITING.with(|w| (!w.borrow().is_empty()).then(|| w.borrow_mut().remove(0)))`. The closure body is a bare expression, so its temporary scope is the whole closure body. The `Ref` that `w.borrow()` creates as the autoref'd receiver of `is_empty` is therefore still alive when `bool::then` (`if self { Some(f()) }`) runs `w.borrow_mut()`. That call panics with BorrowMutError. RefCell guards are dropped at the end of their scope, not at last use, so NLL does not help. Edition 2024 would not help either. I could not compile a sample, because the rules forbid rustc. This is standard temporary-scope behaviour, and only line 666 in the workspace repeats it on a single RefCell. The other same-line borrow/borrow_mut pairs (shell.rs:27, mirror.rs:676) use two different cells.

(b) Reachability:
- TRAY_LIMIT is 3 (line 17). show_prompt queues the 4th and later requests in WAITING (573-579).
- `removed` is true whenever the closed id belongs to a visible slot (659-661).
- The engine creates a separate open request for each distinct (session, kind, value) (handlers/guardrail.rs:392-394). There is no cap, and requests stay open until answered or until the session closes.
- guardrail.held/resolved reach guardrail_event for every project (app.rs:1201, which runs before the project filter).

So about 4 agents blocked on guardrail.request at once, or agents whose waits timed out and then asked for something else, arm the bug. After that, the user's natural next action fires it: answering a visible prompt. This is not every session, but it fits the multi-agent use the app targets, and the queue code exists for exactly this case. The code landed on 2026-10-05 (4f62e33), and no smoke test exercises promotion.

(c) What happens:
- "Answer later" X (459) runs inside gtk4-0.11.4's `unsafe extern "C" fn clicked_trampoline` (button.rs:514). With the system rustc 1.98.1, no rustup and no panic=abort profile, unwinding out of it aborts the client. Engine sessions survive (run.sh: "The engine outlives the window"), but unsaved editor buffers (editor.rs is_dirty) are lost.
- A phone or CLI answer arrives only as guardrail.resolved with hold_id, so close_prompt runs inside the connect task (app.rs:1147-1202). glib-0.22.9 TaskSource::poll (main_context_futures.rs:262) catches the panic and returns Ready. The task's future is then dropped, which drops the notices Receiver and closes the channel (async-channel-2.5.0 lib.rs:609-611).
- From then on the client applies no events, and every ui.call fails at once with "Connection closed" (client.rs:309). `connected` stays true, and the status bar never says "Engine disconnected". The Reconnect button only appears once some error toast sets the notice text.
- An in-prompt Approve/Deny (479/382), or an answer from the Guardrails page, races its own future against the event loop. Whichever runs first dies.
- Because promotion never happens, WAITING keeps its entry. Every later close of a visible prompt panics again until that waiting request is itself resolved.

(d) High is right. This is a client crash or a silently dead control plane in a normal flow. It is not critical: the engine and agent sessions are unaffected, and the trigger needs 4 or more concurrent requests.

(e) The fix is correct. Take one `borrow_mut`, bind the Option, and call show_prompt after the borrow is released. It also handles a request that sits in both the tray and WAITING, because show_prompt returns early when the id is already shown.
v2.correction: Impact (2) is slightly wrong about session expiry. The session-close expiry event carries no hold_id (handlers/session.rs:1620-1624), so guardrail_event calls restore_prompts (a separate spawned future) instead of close_prompt. In that case only the restore task dies, as item (4) already says, not the event loop. The phone and CLI answers are the paths that kill the event loop for certain. The Guardrails-page answers race like (3). A further consequence the finding understates: after the first panic, WAITING is never drained by promotion. A reconnect's restore_prompts can then put the queued request into the tray while it also stays in WAITING, so every later close of a visible prompt panics again until that request is resolved. The fix needs one caveat, per CLAUDE.md: relay-native cannot be compiled in CI or in an agent session. The suggested GTK-free unit test would therefore run only on a GTK 4.22 developer machine (`cargo test -p relay-native`), and the change must be described as not compiled.

findings.title: Guardrail surfaces fetch and render unbounded agent and payload text: a big reason or a held large-file write freezes the UI or forces a disconnect loop
findings.evidence: The prompt pops up by itself on `guardrail.held` and renders the agent's text in full, in wrapping selectable labels: `let why = paragraph(&format!("“{reason}”"), "body");` (431) and `card.append(&mono(value));` (427). Nothing bounds that text: `grants::validate` (crates/relay-core/src/guardrail/grants.rs:195-216) only checks emptiness and `..`, and `guardrail.request` is AgentOnly, "every agent may call it" (relay-bus ops/guardrail.rs:103). "Review exact action" pretty-prints the whole frozen payload: `shown.push_str(&serde_json::to_string_pretty(&request["payload"])...)` (333). The Claude hook sends the entire resulting file as `new_text` for every Write and Edit (crates/relay-cli/src/main.rs:415, 432), and an agent's destructive_write hold keeps that envelope. The control socket caps a line at 2 MiB, and an over-long line tears the whole connection down (client.rs:48, 200-205 `Err(Error::Protocol("frame exceeds ..."))`). Several calls return these texts on that socket: restore_prompts calls `guardrail.requests.list {state: open}` (706) on every connect (app.rs:1160), the Guardrails page calls `guardrail.holds.list` (pages.rs:45), and the dashboard's `holds_open` has no LIMIT (handlers/notify.rs:168).
findings.impact: An agent that pastes a build log into `reason` (or a prompt-injected one, on purpose) pops a label of that size onto the main thread: a long freeze, repeated on every relayout. Past about 2 MiB, `guardrail.request.get`, the open-request list sent on connect, the Guardrails page and the dashboard all exceed the frame cap. The desktop client then disconnects right after every reconnect, until the request is answered from another client or its session closes. Reviewing an agent's held rewrite of a large file (for example a regenerated lockfile) has the same effect: above 2 MiB it disconnects. Because "Allow once" is only enabled after a successful review, such a hold can never be allowed from the desktop.
findings.fix: Put no unbounded text in labels. Cap value and reason at a few KB, with a "Show all (N KB)" expander that opens a TextView. For the exact action, show op, path, sizes and a capped preview or diff stat instead of the raw new_text. Cap value and reason length in `grants::validate`. Have `guardrail.hold.get` elide large string fields unless explicitly asked. Bound the list ops (and dashboard `holds_open`).

v1.reason: The engine's socket reader (crates/relay-core/src/socket.rs:323-335, `BufReader::lines()`) puts no limit on the size of a request. `grants::validate` puts no limit on value or reason, and `guardrail.request` can be called by any agent. The native client caps each received line at MAX_LINE = 2 MiB (apps/relay-native/src/client.rs:47). When a line is longer, the reader returns `Error::Protocol("frame exceeds ...")` (client.rs:200-205) and the connection dies. On every connect, app.rs:1160 calls `crate::pages::restore_prompts`, which calls `guardrail.requests.list {state: open}` (guardrail_pages.rs:706), and that response includes reason and value. An open request with a reason over 2 MiB therefore drops the connection right after each reconnect. This lasts until the request is answered from the CLI or its session closes. The Guardrails page and the dashboard list the same rows. Below the cap, text of 100 KB or more goes in full into a wrapping, selectable GtkLabel (431, 427) on the main thread, which is slow to lay out. For held writes, "Review exact action" fetches `guardrail.hold.get` and pretty-prints the full frozen payload, new_text included (333). For a large file, that is a multi-MB label, or a disconnect above 2 MiB.
v1.correction: Rated medium rather than high because every trigger is abnormal. It needs an agent that is confused or prompt-injected into writing a multi-MB reason or value, or a held rewrite of a file over 2 MiB. A held destructive_write does not cause the reconnect loop: holds.list details carry only numbers and the path, and new_text appears only in hold.get, so that case gives one failed review and one reconnect, not a loop. The loop comes only from exception requests. Fix: cap reason and value length in grants::validate, cap engine request line size, show new_text as a capped preview or summary in the exact-action view, and truncate long labels behind an expander.

findings.title: Every engine event clears and rebuilds the Guardrails page: review state and half-typed denial reasons are lost, and Approve keys shift under the pointer
findings.evidence: For "guardrails", refresh runs `let body = page.last_child()...; clear(&body);` and then rebuilds every card through `guardrail_pages::page(...)` (157). refresh_page fires from app.rs:1263-1264 (`} else { ui.refresh_page(); }`) for every current-project event that is not project, session, file, layout, ui or settings: task.*, mailbox.*, guardrail.*, notify.*, overlap.changed, module.*, run.*, usage.changed. The "Keep forms mounted" owner check (91-93) only protects what sits above the list, but on this page the interactive state lives inside the list: the denial Entry (guardrail_pages.rs:288, 351-403), the exact-action pane that gates "Allow once" (276-278, 316-346), and the Details expanders. The rebuild also awaits twice mid-way (guardrail_pages.rs:774, pages.rs:161), so partial content is drawn and the scroll position clamps. Holds are listed newest first (`ORDER BY id DESC`, handlers/guardrail.rs:320), and exception cards' Approve keys are enabled immediately.
findings.impact: While agents are active, the user's typed denial reason vanishes, and the reviewed payload collapses with "Allow once" going insensitive again before it can be clicked. Expanders close and the scroll jumps. Answering one card emits guardrail.resolved and mailbox.new for the same project, which resets every other card. A new request is inserted at the top and pushes the others down by about one card height. That can put a different agent's always-enabled "Approve once" or "Approve for this session" key under the pointer at click time. With many open holds (up to 1000 listed), each event also recreates thousands of widgets on the main thread.
findings.fix: Reconcile instead of rebuilding. Key cards by hold id (the widget name already carries it), insert new cards, remove resolved ones, and update the "ago" labels in place, leaving existing cards and their form state untouched. Refresh this page only for guardrail.* and overlap.* events. List open requests oldest first (append at the bottom) so that arrivals never move existing keys.

v1.reason: pages::refresh for 'guardrails' always runs `clear(&body)` (pages.rs:123-124) and rebuilds every card through guardrail_pages::page. The mount check at 91-93 only keeps the header. refresh_page (app.rs:1662-1686) coalesces calls, but each pass still rebuilds. In the event loop (app.rs:1263-1264) refresh_page is the fall-through for task.*, mailbox.*, guardrail.*, notify.*, overlap.changed, module.*, run.*, device.changed and usage.changed. usage.changed is emitted by usage.report (provider.rs:75-83) after ctx.set_project(the session's project), so it passes the project filter. audit.rs:16-17 documents that the provider hooks call usage.report 'on every window refresh', so the page rebuilds continually while agents in that project are running. Each rebuild discards the denial Entry (guardrail_pages.rs:351-403). It also hides the exact-action pane again and resets 'Allow once' to insensitive (276-278, 316-346), so a review must be redone, and it collapses the Details expanders (207-220). guardrail.holds.list orders by `id DESC` (handlers/guardrail.rs:319), so new holds are prepended and push existing cards down, and exception-card Approve keys are enabled from the start. The page also awaits mid-rebuild (guardrail_pages.rs:774, pages.rs:161), so it is drawn partially.
v1.correction: The most frequent trigger is usage.changed from the statusline hook, not only task and mailbox events. The approve-under-pointer harm depends on timing; the certain harm is losing typed reasons and completed reviews during a normal flow. The fix is right: reconcile cards by hold id, and limit this page's refreshes to guardrail.* and overlap.* events, or at least drop usage.changed, run.* and device.changed.

v2.reason:
(a) The code does what the finding says. For the guardrails page, pages::refresh always runs `clear(&body)` (pages.rs:123-124), and app.rs:64-68 removes every child. It then rebuilds every card through guardrail_pages::page. The owner check at pages.rs:91-93 keeps only the title and the intro paragraph; the actions row is inside body and is rebuilt too. A rebuilt hold_row starts with the exact pane hidden and "Allow once" insensitive (guardrail_pages.rs:269-278). Its denial form is hidden with a new, empty Entry (351-361), and the Details expander starts collapsed (220). Nothing in refresh_page (app.rs:1662-1686) or refresh skips the rebuild while a form is open. No decision record says this is intended.

(b) It is reachable in normal use. The Guardrails page is the only desktop place to answer held actions: the dashboard queue (tools.rs:365-373) and notifications only link to it. The event loop sends every non-session, non-file, non-ui event for the current project, and every event with no project, to refresh_page (app.rs:1213-1264). I checked that these emitters set the session's project:
- Each new hold emits guardrail.held and notify.new (guardrail.rs:413-416, 563-564, 701-702).
- Each answer emits guardrail.resolved and mailbox.new (436-458, 744-747), and the button's own handler also calls refresh_page.
- When an agent's turn ends, session.report "stop" produces notify.new and mailbox.new, or notify.changed (session.rs:261-299).
- An idle_prompt or permission notification moves the session to blocked, which emits task.changed, notify.new and mailbox.new (session.rs:1390-1413). The next tool use moves it back to running and emits task.changed again.
- Agent mailbox, task and overlap traffic, and system device-lease releases that carry no project (device_lease.rs:146,153), also trigger it.

The held agent itself usually produces one of these within about a minute: a turn end, then an idle_prompt. With several agents active, a 10–60 s review or a typed reason is likely to be wiped.

(c) The typed denial reason is lost, and focus goes with the destroyed Entry. The review must be redone before "Allow once" works again, and expanders close. No stored data is lost. Holds are listed `ORDER BY id DESC` (guardrail.rs:320), with exception requests partitioned first (guardrail_pages.rs:761). So a new request is inserted above all existing cards. Its "Approve once" and "Approve for this session" keys are enabled from the start (445-446). A click that lands just after a request arrives can approve a different agent's exception, and the toast does not name the session. This is real but depends on timing.

(d) High fits the rubric: a likely, user-visible wrong behavior in a normal flow on the safety-decision page. It is not critical because nothing persistent is lost and the misclick is a rare tail risk.

(e) The fix direction is right (reconcile by hold id, narrow the refresh triggers, stop arrivals from moving keys), with the completeness notes in the correction.
v2.correction:
The first verifier's "most frequent trigger is usage.changed from the statusline hook" is wrong. At HEAD the Claude statusline script (crates/relay-core/src/hooks.rs:576-578) only writes ~/.claude/relay-usage.json, and no hook or CLI path calls usage.report: D64 makes stored usage.report rows only a fallback, and the comments at audit.rs:16-17 and in D151 are stale. usage.changed fires only if an agent calls the usage.report tool itself. device.changed from the adb watcher runs only while the Devices page is open (app.rs:1338-1346), so it does not reach this page. The real frequent triggers are the session.report lifecycle events (notify.new/changed, mailbox.new, task.changed when a session goes running↔blocked), guardrail.held/resolved together with their notify.new and mailbox.new, and agent mailbox, task and overlap traffic.

Smaller corrections:
- Only exception cards carry the hold id in their widget name (guardrail_pages.rs:417). hold_row cards have no name, so they need one for reconciling.
- The awaits at guardrail_pages.rs:774 and pages.rs:161 run after all request and hold cards are appended. Only the ACTIVE EXCEPTIONS and overlap tail is briefly missing, and scroll clamps only when the viewport reaches it.
- "Up to 1000 holds" is not a realistic case, because open holds expire when their session closes (session.rs:1612-1625).

Fix completeness:
- If refresh is limited to guardrail.* and overlap.*, also subscribe to guardrail.grant_used (emitted at guardrail.rs:763, not in app.rs:1154). Otherwise the grant's "used N times" count, which today updates only as a side effect of other events, goes stale.
- Sort oldest first on the client. Do not change `ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 1000`, which would change which 1000 rows come back and the order every other consumer sees.
- Keep each card's review state and open denial form, keyed by hold id.
- Oldest first stops new arrivals from moving keys, but a resolution above (answered from the tray prompt, from the phone, or expired) still shifts cards up. To close the misclick risk, briefly desensitize Approve keys after the layout moves.

findings.title: "Allow once" on an agent's held write releases nothing: the hook has already exited and the retry is held again
findings.evidence: The card sends `guardrail.confirm {hold_id}`, and the section says "Paused until you decide" (769). Agents get holds, not refusals, for destructive_write and shape_gate (crates/relay-core/src/guardrail.rs:1035-1036). The Claude adapter returns `Ok(2)` immediately on any non-ok gate response (crates/relay-cli/src/main.rs:471-483), so the tool call has already been refused when the card appears. `confirm` on a frozen `guardrail.gate` re-evaluates it with `skip_policy` and returns the verdict as `outcome` (handlers/guardrail.rs:598-667), which nothing consumes, and records no grant. The agent's retry then goes through `gate(ctx, payload, None)` (handlers/guardrail.rs:304) and is evaluated from scratch, with only exception grants (`granted_path`) consulted. The agent is meanwhile mailed "Guardrail hold N was confirmed". BUS.md:511 says the hook "blocks the tool while the verdict is hold", but the adapter does not wait.
findings.impact: The user reviews and allows a large rewrite of a modified or untracked file. The agent is told it was confirmed and retries, and the identical write is held again as a new hold, in a loop. The only real way through is an exception request, which holds do not hint at. I did not run this end to end; the conclusion rests on the code paths above, and I found no path that lets the retry through.
findings.fix: Engine: when a gate hold is confirmed, record a one-use grant keyed by session and path (plus payload hash) that the identical retry consumes, as exception grants do, and say "retry now" in the mailbox message. UI: until then, label the button for what it does, or route agent gate holds through "Approve as exception" (a path grant).

v1.reason: I traced the whole path. refuse_or_user_hold (crates/relay-core/src/guardrail.rs:1035-1036) gives agents a Hold, not a Refuse, for destructive_write and shape_gate. The hold freezes a `guardrail.gate` request (handlers/guardrail.rs:546-551). claude_pre_tool (crates/relay-cli/src/main.rs:469-483) makes a single `client.call` and returns `Ok(2)` on any non-ok response, so the Write/Edit has already failed and nothing waits for the verdict. confirm (handlers/guardrail.rs:599-667) re-evaluates the frozen gate with `skip_policy: Some(&hold.policy)`. It puts the verdict in `outcome`, marks the hold confirmed and mails "Guardrail hold N was confirmed". It writes no grant and nothing else that a later request could find. The agent's retry runs `gate(ctx, payload, None)` (line 304). That calls evaluate_granted (guardrail.rs:478-497), which consults only `Grants::load`, and those come only from confirmed `guardrail.request` rows (grants.rs:52). destructive_decision checks only `skip_policy` and `granted_path`, so the identical retry is held again. BUS.md §9.3 says "the hook blocks the tool while the verdict is hold", but the adapter does not block. DECISIONS D22/D35 describe confirmation as a replay. That holds for bus ops (file.write and others replay through `replay_registered`), but for `guardrail.gate` nothing happens. Normal use triggers it: any agent Write/Edit that removes more than 50 lines of an untracked or modified file (for example, rewriting a file the agent just created) produces such a hold, and "Allow once" then does nothing useful.
v1.correction: This affects only holds whose frozen op is `guardrail.gate`, which is the provider-hook path (Claude, and Codex if its adapter is the same). Holds raised through `enforce` (file.write, git.commit over the bus) are replayed and do take effect on confirm. Fix in the engine: on confirming a gate hold, record a one-use grant keyed by session, path and kind (ideally with a hash of new_text/command) that evaluate_granted consumes. Alternatively, convert the hold into a path exception. Also change the mailbox text to "retry now". The UI wording is a symptom of the engine problem, not the root cause.

v2.reason:
I re-traced every step myself at 361c6f9.

(a) The code does what the finding says.
- crates/relay-core/src/guardrail.rs:1035 gives an agent a hold, not a refusal, for destructive_write and shape_gate.
- gate() (handlers/guardrail.rs:538-558) freezes a `guardrail.gate` envelope and returns Err(held). That error has no hint: hints are added only on the refusal branch of refuse_or_user_hold.
- claude_pre_tool (crates/relay-cli/src/main.rs:469-483) makes one `client.call` and returns Ok(2) on any non-ok response. It does not wait, and it never prints the hold id. Claude Code's PreToolUse exit 2 denies the tool call on the spot.
- confirm() (handlers/guardrail.rs:597-667) handles `frozen.op == "guardrail.gate"` by re-running evaluate() with skip_policy, putting the verdict in `outcome`, marking the hold confirmed and mailing "Guardrail hold N was confirmed by user." It writes nothing a later gate reads.
- The retry goes through `gate(ctx, payload, None)` (line 304) and then evaluate_granted. That function loads only `op = 'guardrail.request'` rows (grants.rs:52). Nothing reads confirmed gate holds; `rg confirmed` finds no consumer.
- A new hook request gets a new Uuid (Request::new), so the idempotent-replay path does not apply either.
- tests/guardrails.rs:263-268 shows the engine re-holding a later write to the same path right after a confirm.

(b) Who triggers it, and how often. Any default Claude agent session can. Its Write, Edit or MultiEdit removes more than 50 lines, or more than 40% of a file of at least 30 lines (handlers/settings.rs:30), on a file that is untracked, modified or staged. recoverable() lets only committed-and-clean or ignored files through. That describes most files an agent is actively working on before it commits, so this happens routinely. A configured shape gate that fails validation also triggers it.

Sessions default to bus_writes=false (handlers/session.rs:809), so they cannot call file.write or git.commit. Those are the only agent hold paths that confirm actually replays. As a result, every agent hold a default session can raise is a gate hold, and "Allow once" never works for any of them.

(c) What happens to the user. It fails closed, so there is no data loss. But the user's explicit decision is discarded:
- The card vanishes as if the action succeeded (outcome ok, no error shown, guardrail_pages.rs:299-305), under a section that says "Paused until you decide" (line 769).
- The agent is told the hold was confirmed. It retries, and the identical write becomes a new hold, round after round.
- The loop ends only when the agent splits the write into sub-threshold Edits, asks for a path exception, or writes through Bash, which the exec gate checks only against denied commands. Nothing points it to the exception route: held errors carry no hint, and the role instruction (providers.rs:50-53) covers only refusals.
- For shape_gate holds no exception can help, because shape gates are not grantable.

(d) High is right. This is user-visible wrong behaviour in the normal flow of the guardrail's main agent interaction. It is not critical, because the guard stays closed and workarounds exist.

(e) The engine direction in the finding is right; the details need the corrections below. The UI relabel is only a stopgap.
v2.correction:
Scope:
- For agents this affects Claude only. codex_pre_tool (main.rs:504-512) sends only kind=exec, and agent exec violations are refused, never held.
- The same root cause also hits the user's own terminal `git commit` in a Relay worktree. The generated pre-commit hook (crates/relay-core/src/hooks.rs:132) calls `--actor user cmd guardrail.gate {"kind":"commit"}`, and a cap or protected-path breach becomes a user_bypass gate hold. Confirming it does nothing, and the retry holds again, so only --no-verify gets through.
- BUS.md contradicts itself here: line 511 says "blocks the tool while the verdict is hold", while line 517 says the adapter "exits 2 on hold".

Fix corrections:
1. The path-grant alternative is incomplete. Shape gates are not grantable: see BOOTSTRAP_HINT, and the new_text shape check in evaluate_write has no granted_path. A once path grant would also let any content through, which is broader than the "exact action" the card makes the user review.
2. Prefer a one-use allowance recorded at confirm time:
   - Key it on session_id plus a hash of the frozen gate payload (kind, path, new_text/diff/command).
   - Consume it in gate() by evaluating with skip_policy = hold.policy, so other policies still judge it, and mark it used only on Allow.
   - Expire it when the session closes.
   - For Write, also bind the hash of the file on disk at hold time, or require removed lines to be at most the approved count, so a file changed in between is not rewritten under the old approval. Edit-derived new_text already encodes the old content.
   - For commit holds the payload `{session, kind}` is the same for every commit, so key on the staged diff or tree instead.
3. Give held errors a hint naming the hold id ("wait for guardrail.resolved, then retry the identical call"), have the adapter print it, and put the path plus "retry now" in the confirm mail.
4. Optionally, have the adapter bus.wait on guardrail.resolved for a bounded time, exiting on its own before the 30 s hook timeout rather than relying on that timeout. That would give the "paused" behaviour the card promises.

findings.title: Approval prompts show agent-chosen commands and paths without neutralising bidi or invisible characters
findings.evidence: `card.append(&mono(value))` goes through `paragraph()` to `gtk::Label::new(Some(text))`. Pango applies the Unicode bidi algorithm to label text, honouring U+202A–U+202E and U+2066–U+2069, and renders zero-width and format characters (U+200B–U+200D, U+2060, U+FEFF) as nothing. Nothing rejects or escapes them: `grants::validate` checks only emptiness and `..`. The exact-action view uses `serde_json::to_string_pretty` (333), which escapes only `"`, `\` and C0 controls, so U+202E passes through raw there as well. The engine relies on the person reading the value exactly: `covers_command` matches the grant's words literally, and "a grant ending in a lone `*` covers everything that starts with the words before it, and the person approving it reads that `*`" (grants.rs:137-149).
findings.impact: A prompt-injected agent can request an exception whose displayed command or path reads differently from the bytes that will be granted (Trojan-Source-style reordering, or look-alike values containing invisible characters). The user approves what they see, and the grant lets the logical command past the denied-commands rule.
findings.fix: Route every agent-supplied string through one display helper. It should replace bidi controls, zero-width and format characters, and non-newline controls with visible, highlighted escapes, and flag the card "contains hidden characters". Also reject such characters for `command` values in `grants::validate`.

v1.reason: The missing neutralisation is real. Values reach `gtk::Label` through paragraph/mono (guardrail_pages.rs:24-36, 427), `grants::validate` (grants.rs:195-216) checks only emptiness, `..` and cap syntax, and Pango applies bidi to label text. The claimed exploit is much weaker than stated, though. Bidi controls cannot hide characters; they only reorder them. Any control character placed in a command becomes literal bytes in a shell word: `command_words` (guardrail.rs:1001-1008) splits on shell syntax, so `‮target` is a different filename, not `target`. A display that looks harmless while the bytes are harmful therefore needs the controls to stand as separate words that reorder whole arguments, which only matters for order-sensitive commands such as cp, mv or ln. Zero-width characters change bytes but do not make a command more dangerous. I could not build a convincing case where the approved display reads benign and the granted command is destructive. The agent can also simply ask for a dangerous command openly. What remains is defense-in-depth hardening.
v1.correction: Downgrade to low and treat it as hardening: escape or flag bidi, format and zero-width characters in agent-supplied values before display, and reject them in grants::validate for command values. A related and more consequential problem showed up while verifying this, and should be checked separately: command_words drops quoted words (`filter(|word| !word.quoted)`) on both the grant and the run command. A command grant therefore does not bind its quoted arguments, which the person approving it does read.

findings.title: "N more waiting · open Guardrails" opens the current project's page, which cannot show other projects' waiting requests
findings.evidence: Prompts come from every project: guardrail_event runs before the project filter (app.rs:1201-1203), and restore_prompts lists open requests with no project_id. The overflow key, however, does `ui.navigate("guardrails")`, and that page lists `guardrail.holds.list {"project_id": project}` for `ui.project` only (pages.rs:45, 53).
findings.impact: When the hidden requests belong to another project, the user lands on a page saying "Nothing is waiting for you: no exception requests and no held actions." (pages.rs:129) while the tray says N are waiting. Those agents stay blocked, and the WAITING queue is the one that currently cannot drain (see the close_prompt panic).
findings.fix: Point the overflow key at the dashboard, whose `holds_open` is already cross-project and opens the right project per row, or switch to the project of the oldest waiting request. Show the project name on each prompt.

v1.reason: WAITING is filled across projects. guardrail_event runs before the project filter (app.rs:1201, ahead of the project_id check at ~1210), and restore_prompts calls `guardrail.requests.list {state: open}` with no project_id (guardrail_pages.rs:706). The ExceptionsList handler (handlers/guardrail.rs:343) filters by project only when one is given. The overflow key does `ui.navigate("guardrails")` (551). That page fetches `guardrail.holds.list {project_id: ui.project}` (pages.rs:45/50-53), plus active requests for the same project (guardrail_pages.rs:774). When the hidden requests belong to another project, the page shows the empty-state text at pages.rs:129, while the tray says N are waiting.
v1.correction: How often this hurts depends on native-misc#1. While that panic exists, WAITING can never be promoted, so the misdirection is the only route the tray offers to those requests. Showing the project name on each prompt is a cheap partial fix. The dashboard fix is only valid if its holds_open list is cross-project, and I did not verify that.

findings.title: Default shortcuts Ctrl+K and Ctrl+N are taken from focused terminals; chords are not checked for duplicates or reserved terminal keys
findings.evidence: DEFAULTS binds `("palette", .., "Ctrl+K")` and `("new_session", .., "Ctrl+N")` (line 8). shell.rs:1065-1098 installs the matcher on the window with `PropagationPhase::Capture` and returns `Propagation::Stop` on a match, without looking at the focused widget, so a VTE pane never receives the key. `valid()` (29-35) only requires a modifier. It therefore accepts Ctrl+C, Ctrl+D, Ctrl+Z and Ctrl+Shift+C/V, which the settings page itself documents as terminal copy and paste (tools_settings.rs:543). Each field is validated on its own (tools_settings.rs:636), so two actions can share a chord, and the first one in DEFAULTS silently wins.
findings.impact: In every agent terminal, Ctrl+K (readline/Emacs kill-to-end-of-line) opens the command palette, and Ctrl+N (next history line) opens the new-session sheet, instead of editing the line. A user who binds an action to Ctrl+C can no longer interrupt an agent from its pane.
findings.fix: Skip window shortcuts while focus is inside a terminal unless the chord includes Shift, or switch to Ctrl+Shift defaults. In validation, reject Ctrl+C/D/Z, Ctrl+Shift+C/V and duplicate chords, with a message naming the conflict.

v1.reason: shell.rs:1065-1101 adds a capture-phase key controller to ui.window. It bails out only when a panel is open (`!ui.panels.borrow().is_empty()`) and never looks at the focused widget. On a match it returns Propagation::Stop, so the capture phase consumes the key before a VTE pane in that window gets it. DEFAULTS (shortcuts.rs:4,8) bind Ctrl+K and Ctrl+N, which are readline/Emacs kill-to-end-of-line and next-history, and are also used in agent TUIs. In a focused terminal they open the command palette or the launch sheet instead. valid() (shortcuts.rs:29-35) only requires Ctrl, Meta or Alt, so Ctrl+C, Ctrl+D and Ctrl+Z are accepted. tools_settings.rs:633-641 checks each entry on its own, so duplicate chords are not caught, and the DEFAULTS loop order decides which action wins. The Notes window is a separate window with its own Ctrl+N/Ctrl+K handler, so it does not collide.
v1.correction: Other lines: the window handler is at shell.rs:1066-1093, the per-field validation at tools_settings.rs:636. The main impact is Ctrl+K and Ctrl+N being stolen from every focused terminal with the default settings. Rebinding to Ctrl+C is a self-inflicted edge case. Fix: skip the window shortcuts (or the ones without Shift) when the focus widget is a vte::Terminal or inside one, and reject duplicate and reserved chords in settings validation.

findings.title: The prompt tray is stacked below every panel opened after the first prompt
findings.evidence: The tray is created once with `ui.overlay.add_overlay(&tray)` and never re-added. `Panel::present` later adds each panel's layer to the same overlay (`self.host.add_overlay(&self.layer)`, panel.rs:249; the host is `ui.overlay` for `Panel::new`, panel.rs:24). Overlay children stack in insertion order, and each layer's main child is a full-size scrim button: 35% black for modal panels, transparent for utility panels (theme.css:114, 147).
findings.impact: While the guardrail settings panel, a confirmation dialog, onboarding, or the bottom-right Usage, Resources or Device panel is open, new prompts sit hidden behind the frame or dimmed under the scrim. A click on one hits the scrim and closes the panel, or does nothing if the panel is guarded. The guarantee at 674-675 ("has to reach the user wherever they are") does not hold there.
findings.fix: Keep the tray on top: re-append it after a panel is presented (`remove_overlay` then `add_overlay`), or host it on a dedicated overlay above `ui.overlay`.

v1.reason: tray() adds the tray to `ui.overlay` once (guardrail_pages.rs:518). It is created on every connect, because restore_prompts calls tray(&ui) (708) from Ui::connect. Panel::new hosts panels on `ui.overlay` (panel.rs:24), and Panel::present calls `self.host.add_overlay(&self.layer)` (panel.rs:249) each time a panel opens. Every later panel layer therefore stacks above the tray. Each layer's main child is a full-size scrim button (panel.rs:41-45): 35% black (theme.css:114), or transparent for utility layers (147). Picking hits the topmost overlay first, so a prompt under an open panel is dimmed or covered by the right-aligned frame, and a click on it lands on the scrim. Nothing raises the tray afterwards.
v1.correction: Panels are transient, so the prompt is reachable again as soon as the panel closes. Page panels (Panel::page) use ui.page_overlay and are not affected. Low is the right rating.

findings.title: A prompt can outlive its request: shown after a stale read, stale waiting entries promoted, and error paths leave it up
findings.evidence: guardrail_event awaits `guardrail.request.get`, then shows the prompt if `request["state"] == "open"` (682-684). It does not re-check whether a `guardrail.resolved` for that id was processed during the await. restore_prompts closes stale tray prompts (709-713) before it filters WAITING against `open` (714), so close_prompt can promote a waiting entry that is itself stale. When confirm or reject fails because the hold is already resolved (`guardrail.hold_resolved`), the approve path only re-enables the keys (483-488).
findings.impact: A request answered from the phone or CLI, or expired, while its prompt is being fetched stays on screen. Pressing Approve then shows "hold N is Confirmed", and the prompt remains until the user finds the X.
findings.fix: Track resolved ids (or reuse DISMISSED) and skip show_prompt for them after the await. In restore_prompts, filter WAITING first. On a `guardrail.hold_resolved` or `not_found` error, call `close_prompt(id)` instead of re-enabling the keys.

v1.reason: Part 2 is deterministic. In restore_prompts (guardrail_pages.rs:703-719), the loop at 709-713 calls close_prompt for each tray id that is no longer open. close_prompt (652-672) retires the card, then at 666-667 pops WAITING[0] and calls show_prompt on it, which has no staleness check. The filter of WAITING against `open` only runs afterwards, at 714. restore_prompts runs when guardrail.resolved arrives without a hold_id, which session.rs:1620 emits when a closing session expires its open holds, and also on reconnect. Example: the tray holds A (session X), B and C, and WAITING holds D (session X) and E. Closing X retires A and promotes D, which is already expired. TRAY_LIMIT is 3 (line 17), so D takes a slot and E goes back to waiting. Part 3 is also real. On a confirm error the approve handler (483-488) only shows the error and turns the keys back on. A dead prompt therefore stays until the user clicks the X. Part 1 is real in the code: close_prompt marks an id DISMISSED only if a card was actually removed (664-665), so a guardrail.resolved that lands during the guardrail.request.get await leaves nothing to stop show_prompt. The window is one local round trip, though, and the reply would have to report 'open' while the resolve event is handled first.
v1.correction: Part 2 (a stale waiting entry promoted) is the reliable trigger. It needs more than TRAY_LIMIT=3 open requests and a session that has requests both in the tray and in WAITING when it closes. Part 1 (the stale-read race) is a narrow window of one local round trip. Part 3 is what makes either case linger. The fix is right: filter WAITING before the close loop, record ids resolved while a fetch is in flight, and close the prompt on a hold-resolved or not-found error instead of turning the keys back on.

findings.title: Approval keys are live the moment a prompt slides in under the pointer
findings.evidence: show_prompt appends the slot without any gating, and its tick callback reveals it on the next frame (605-614). The card's "Approve once" and "Approve for this session" keys (445-446) are sensitive and targetable from that first frame. The tray sits over the bottom-right of the terminal wall (halign/valign End, 511-514). The success notice (480) says "Exception approved once" without naming the request.
findings.impact: A click aimed at the bottom-right terminal can land just as a prompt arrives and approve an exception the user never read. The confirmation does not say which request was approved.
findings.fix: Keep the keys insensitive until the slot has been revealed for about 500 ms (arm a timeout on child-revealed), as browser permission prompts do. Name the session and value in the success notice.

v1.reason: The mechanism is accurate. show_prompt appends the slot (582), and the tick callback reveals it on the next frame (605-614), with no arming delay. The Approve keys (445-446) are sensitive and targetable once they are drawn, and the tray sits bottom-right over the terminal wall (511-514). The notice at 480 says only "Exception approved once/for this session" and does not name the request. A mis-click approval needs a click at the bottom-right of the right-most pane, within a frame or two of an unpredictable async arrival (held event, then request.get). The key row sits at the bottom of a 420px card, and during SlideUp only part of the card is visible. An agent cannot aim this at the user's pointer, and the keyboard cannot approve because the prompt takes no focus. The risk is real but small, and this is defense-in-depth hardening rather than a demonstrated bypass.
v1.correction: Arming the keys about 300-500 ms after child-revealed, and naming the session and value in the confirmation notice, are reasonable cheap hardening. This is not a guardrail bypass, and it should not rate above low.

findings.title: The guardrail editor's "Saved" confirmation is erased by its own reload
findings.evidence: On success, save() calls `editor.load()` (371) and then sets "Saved for this project." (373-377). load() spawns its own request, and when it completes it runs `editor.status.set_text("")` (321), which always lands after the save message.
findings.impact: The confirmation is visible only for one local round trip, so a user who saved a safety setting never sees that it took effect.
findings.fix: Have load() take an optional status to show on success (or skip clearing when the status is a save confirmation), and show "Saved…" there.

v1.reason: save() (guardrail_settings.rs:354-385) calls editor.load() synchronously when the scope is unchanged, which sets the status to 'Loading…' and spawns the request. It then sets 'Saved for this project.' When the load future completes, it runs editor.fill() and then `editor.status.set_text("")` (around 316-321). That always comes after the save message, so the confirmation shows for only one local round trip. The only other feedback is that the row captions change and Save turns insensitive.
v1.correction: Let load() take an optional message to set on success in place of "" (or set the saved message after the reload resolves). The fault is in the success branch of load() that clears the status, not the line that sets the save message.

findings.title: Reset and Save stay live while another scope's layers load, so a reset can clear a field at the wrong scope
findings.evidence: load() switches to the new `scope` but disables only the inputs (`row.input_widget_sensitive(false)`, 305-307). It keeps `layers` from the previous scope, and the Reset buttons stay visible and clickable. The reset handler compares the old layers' source with the new scope's layer name (590-592) and sets `cleared`, which makes patch() send `null` for that path (334-336). If the load fails (323-325), this state persists indefinitely.
findings.impact: After switching from project A to project B while the load is slow or failed, pressing a Reset left over from A's view and then Save clears B's override for that field. The user never saw that change.
findings.fix: At the start of load, set `layers` to Null so that dirty() is 0, hide the Reset keys, and disable Save and Discard until the new answer arrives. Keep the form disabled if the load fails.

v1.reason: The mechanism is real. load() (guardrail_settings.rs:297-327) disables only the inputs and keeps the previous scope's `layers`. The reset handler (around 587-597) compares `layers["sources"]` with the new scope's layer name, and project A and project B share the same name ('project'), so it sets `cleared`. patch() (330-352) then sends null for that path to the new scope. However, a successful load runs fill(), which resets every `cleared` flag and refills the inputs (237-246), so in the normal case a stray Reset is wiped out. The bad outcome needs one of two things. Either the user clicks Reset and then Save within the in-flight window of one local guardrail.config.layers call, or that one read fails while the engine still accepts guardrail.config.set. The 'old engine' error at 323-325 does not produce it, because then layers was never loaded and stays Null, so `here` is false. A transient failure on the switch, or a store mutex held by slow handlers that stretches the window, is needed, and I could not establish how likely that is.
v1.correction: Nearly all the risk is in a failed load after a successful one; the in-flight race is milliseconds. A minimal fix: at the start of load(), set layers to Null and call refresh(), which hides the Reset keys and disables Save and Discard. Leave them that way if the load fails.

findings.title: Shortcut matching compares the layout-translated character: no shortcuts on non-Latin layouts, and shifted punctuation never matches
findings.evidence: `key.to_unicode().and_then(|c| c.to_lowercase().next()) == Some(letter)`. Under a Cyrillic or Greek layout, Ctrl+K produces the Cyrillic keyval, so no chord matches. For a chord such as "Ctrl+Shift+,", holding Shift produces the keyval `less` ('<') rather than ',', yet `valid()` accepts the chord.
findings.impact: Users with a non-Latin layout active get no shortcuts at all, and some chords the settings page accepts can never fire.
findings.fix: Use GTK's trigger matching (`gtk::ShortcutTrigger::parse_string` with `gdk::KeyEvent::matches`, which falls back across layout groups), or compare the hardware keycode translated in group 0. Reject shifted punctuation in `valid()`.

v1.reason: shortcuts.rs:37-46 matches with `key.to_unicode().and_then(|c| c.to_lowercase().next()) == Some(letter)`. The keyval from EventControllerKey::key-pressed is translated for the active layout group, so under a Cyrillic or Greek layout Ctrl+K yields a Cyrillic keyval and no default chord fires. There is no fallback to the hardware keycode or to group 0. With Shift held, punctuation and digits translate to the shifted symbol (Ctrl+Shift+, gives `less`, Ctrl+Shift+1 gives `exclam`). parse/valid accept such chords, but they can never match. Letters are fine, because the code lowercases them.
v1.correction: Shifted digits are affected as well as punctuation. A simple fix: when to_unicode does not match, compare against the keyval translated from the keycode in group 0 (the display's map_keycode or translate_key), or use gtk::ShortcutTrigger matching.

findings.title: The panel focus trap swallows Tab in multi-line editors hosted in panels
findings.evidence: A capture-phase controller on every panel layer intercepts `Key::Tab | ISO_Left_Tab` with any modifiers, moves focus, and returns `Propagation::Stop` (102-122). TextViews hosted in panels never receive Tab: the skill instructions (tools_skills.rs:413) and task text (task_pages::multiline, inside Panel::page). Because Ctrl is not excluded, Ctrl+Tab cannot type a tab either.
findings.impact: A tab can never be typed into skill instructions, task descriptions or other panel text areas; Tab silently jumps focus instead.
findings.fix: Return Proceed when the focus widget is a TextView with `accepts_tab()` (and let Ctrl+Tab move focus out), and trap Tab only when focus would leave the frame.

v1.reason: panel.rs:102-122 adds a capture-phase EventControllerKey to the panel `layer` (an ancestor of every widget in the panel). On Tab or ISO_Left_Tab with any modifiers it calls frame.child_focus and returns Propagation::Stop. Capture runs from the root down, so a TextView inside the panel never sees the key. tools_skills.rs:398-413 builds the skill editor with Panel::new and puts a monospace gtk::TextView ("Instructions") in it. task_pages.rs:26 `multiline` builds TextViews used in Panel::page (task_pages.rs:76, 336). Both have accepts_tab at its GTK default (true), and Tab still moves focus instead of inserting a tab.
v1.correction: The trap is at panel.rs:106 (match) and panel.rs:117 (Stop). The Ctrl+Tab point is wrong: in GtkTextView, Ctrl+Tab moves focus by design and never inserts a tab, so only plain Tab is lost. Fix: return Proceed when the focus widget is a TextView with accepts_tab() and no Ctrl is held, and keep the cycling for everything else.

findings.title: pages::refresh carries unreachable notes and board branches (including all of note_composer), and the empty Modules page shows the notes text
findings.evidence: `ui.page` is written only by navigate (app.rs:1348), which returns early for "notes" (1303-1305), so refresh never runs for notes; "board" returns at 86-89. That leaves these parts unreachable: the notes op (46), the notes branch (82-85), the `"board" => "Board"` and `_ => "Notes"` title arms (99-110), `"notes" => note_composer(...)` (113) and therefore all of note_composer (401-451), the `"board" => "No tasks yet..."` text (127), and the notes loop (178-182). The live fallout: an empty Modules page falls through to `_ => "No project notes yet."` (130), and note_pages::modules has no empty state of its own.
findings.impact: An empty Modules page tells the user there are no notes. About 70 dead lines, including a whole composer, look live and invite edits that do nothing.
findings.fix: Delete the notes and board arms and note_composer, and give Modules its own empty text ("No modules yet. Create one above.").

v1.reason: ui.page is only assigned at app.rs:1348 inside navigate, and navigate returns early for 'notes' (app.rs:1303-1305). The initial value is 'agents' (app.rs:747), and refresh_page (app.rs:1681) is the only caller of pages::refresh. So refresh never runs with 'notes'. 'board' returns at pages.rs:86-89 before the shared section. That makes the following dead: the notes op (46), the notes branch (82-85), the board and notes title arms (99-110; `if name != "board"` is always true at that point), `"notes" => note_composer` (113) and with it note_composer (401+, whose only reference is line 113), the board empty text (127), and the notes loop (178-182). The live bug is real too: note_pages::modules (note_pages.rs:1259) has no empty state, so an empty Modules list falls through to `_ => "No project notes yet."` (pages.rs:130).

findings.title: Wallpaper rotation re-downloads and re-hashes the whole library on every appearance change, so each tick loads everything twice
findings.evidence: refresh() fetches `appearance.wallpaper_rotation` and the whole `appearance.wallpapers` library, which can be up to 1.5 MB of base64 (tools_settings.rs:1012). signature() serialises the full library to a String in order to hash it (61-62). refresh() runs from load_appearance (shell.rs:1117) on every `settings.changed` under `appearance.`, for `terminal.font_size`, or for the root (app.rs:1257-1262). That includes the `appearance.wallpaper` change each rotation makes itself. So one tick fetches the library twice (151-158, then refresh) and the current image twice, and load_appearance decodes the image on the GTK thread (shell.rs:1230 `Texture::from_bytes`).
findings.impact: Every rotation, and every font-size or opacity change, moves several MB over the single control socket and through the engine's store lock. It also re-serialises and hashes up to 1.5 MB and decodes a full image on the GTK thread, causing a frame hitch.
findings.fix: Call refresh only for `appearance.wallpaper_rotation`, `appearance.wallpapers` or root changes. Build the signature from the config plus image count and ids instead of the whole library. Decode the texture off the main thread and hand the result back.

v1.reason: Confirmed by reading the code. app.rs:1257-1262 calls ui.load_appearance() for any settings.changed whose path starts with `appearance.`, equals `terminal.font_size`, or is empty. shell.rs:1117 load_appearance always calls wallpaper_rotation::refresh. refresh (wallpaper_rotation.rs:92-98) fetches both `appearance.wallpaper_rotation` and the full `appearance.wallpapers` library. configure then hashes `config.to_string()` and `library.to_string()` (lines 59-63). rotate_once (151-158) already fetches config, library and current, and its settings.set of `appearance.wallpaper` (175-178) emits a settings.changed. That event runs load_appearance again, which fetches the library a second time through refresh, fetches the current image again (shell.rs:1129), and base64-decodes it into a gdk Texture on the GTK main thread (shell.rs:1222-1231). The signature check only stops the timer from being re-armed; it does not stop the fetch or the serialisation. The library cap is enforced in tools_settings.rs:1012: serde_json::to_vec(&library).len() > 1500000. Each entry stores `image` and `preview` as the same string, so the payload really is about 1.5 MB.
v1.correction: The impact is smaller than claimed. Rotation runs at most once a minute (default every 15 minutes, interval clamped to 1-1440 min), so the redundant transfer is roughly 1.5 MB of library plus one image per tick, not 'several MB'. The appearance sliders (tools_settings.rs:291-325) do not write live; they are saved on Save, so the redundant work happens once per saved appearance field, not per slider movement. The cost per event is one extra round trip of up to 1.5 MB over the local socket, a 1.5 MB to_string plus hash, and one JPEG decode (at most 1280x900, about 10 ms) on the GTK thread. That is a minor hitch, not a recurring freeze. The most useful fix is to run refresh only when the path is `appearance.wallpaper_rotation`, `appearance.wallpapers` or empty, and to leave it out of the general load_appearance path. Moving the texture decode to ui.rt.spawn_blocking, as the add-wallpaper flow already does, is a secondary improvement. The relay-native crate cannot be compiled in this environment.

findings.title: Background sound and rotation failures go to the single notice banner, cryptically, overwriting more important messages
findings.evidence: `ui.show_error(&format!("Notification sound: {e}"))` runs for every failed notification sound. With ffplay missing, the spawn error reads "No such file or directory (os error 2)" and never names ffplay, unlike the mirror's FFMPEG_MISSING (mirror/decode.rs:243). The rotation timer keeps firing while disconnected and reports `Wallpaper rotation failed: Connection closed…` (wallpaper_rotation.rs:138-139). While disconnected, show_error never auto-hides (app.rs:1086-1088).
findings.impact: Without ffplay, every notification replaces whatever the banner said (an approval result, an error) with an unexplained message. During an engine outage, the "Start relay serve… then reconnect" guidance is replaced by a wallpaper error every interval.
findings.fix: Map NotFound to a one-time actionable message ("Notification sounds need ffplay; install FFmpeg or set Sound to Off") and stop retrying for the session. Skip rotation ticks while `!ui.connected`, and do not surface Disconnected errors from background timers.

v1.reason: sounds.rs:6-24: every failed play calls `ui.show_error(&format!("Notification sound: {e}"))`. sounds::notify (sounds.rs:89-106, called for every notify event from app.rs:1195) plays the engine's default sound "chime" (handlers/settings.rs:18). Without ffplay, spawn fails with ENOENT, so each notification replaces the single banner with "Notification sound: No such file or directory (os error 2)", which never names ffplay. wallpaper_rotation.rs:126-142: the timer is not removed on disconnect. When it fires, ui.call returns Error::Disconnected (app.rs:1112) and the timer shows "Wallpaper rotation failed: Connection closed. Reconnect to the engine." show_error does not auto-hide while disconnected (app.rs:1086-1088).
v1.correction: The disconnect part is weaker than the finding says. The "Start relay serve…" text appears only on a failed initial connect (app.rs:1281-1283). After a disconnect, the banner already says connection closed, and the rotation message still says to reconnect. It also needs rotation enabled with at least 2 images. The main cost is the ffplay case: a cryptic message on every notification, overwriting more important messages.

findings.title: Four relative-time formatters with diverged output, and a byte-identical paragraph() in pages.rs and tools.rs
findings.evidence: guardrail_pages::ago rounds (`(seconds + 30) / 60` minutes, then "N days ago"). session_context::relative_time truncates and switches to "yesterday" or a date. board_view::ago_between prints "5m", "3h", "2w". status_usage::ago prints "5m ago". pages.rs:34-39 and tools.rs:19-24 `paragraph` are identical, and guardrail_pages.rs:24 and shell/registry.rs:1007 are near copies.
findings.impact: The same timestamp reads differently on the Guardrails page, in the session context and on the board: an item 90 seconds old is "2 min ago" on the Guardrails page and "1 min ago" in the session context. Every fix has to be made four times.
findings.fix: Keep one relative_time in app.rs (session_context's is the most complete), with an optional compact form. Delete pages::paragraph in favour of tools::paragraph, or move one copy next to label and button in app.rs.

v1.reason: The code matches the finding. guardrail_pages.rs:38-49 `ago` rounds: `(seconds + 30) / 60` min, `(seconds + 1800) / 3600` h, then "N days ago". session_context.rs:26-52 `relative_time` truncates with `as_minutes()` and moves on to "yesterday" or a date. So a timestamp 90 s old reads "2 min ago" on a guardrail card and "1 min ago" in the session context. They also handle a timestamp that will not parse differently: one returns an empty string, the other returns the raw ts. pages.rs:34-39 and tools.rs:19-24 `paragraph(value)` are byte-identical (label "body", wrap, selectable). The impact is cosmetic and the fix is small.
v1.correction: Only one divergence is a real inconsistency: guardrail_pages::ago against session_context::relative_time. Both produce the long "N min ago" form for the same kind of surface. board_view::ago_between ("5m", "2w") and status_usage::ago ("5m ago", which takes seconds rather than a timestamp) are deliberately compact forms for dense rows, and are not the same function repeated. shell/registry.rs:1007 `paragraph` uses a different CSS class and is not selectable, so it is not a copy. Fix: replace guardrail_pages::ago with session_context::relative_time (moved to app.rs), and drop pages::paragraph in favour of tools::paragraph.

findings.title: Toolchain drift: native clippy fails on Rust 1.98 at sounds.rs:150, while CI pins 1.94 and never lints relay-native
findings.evidence: `bytes.chunks_exact(4).all(...)` trips clippy's chunks_exact_to_as_chunks lint on 1.98, the local rustc 1.98.1. As a result, the README step `cargo clippy -p relay-native --all-targets -- -D warnings -A deprecated` fails. CI pins `toolchain: "1.94"` (ci.yml:30) and leaves relay-native out entirely (ci.yml:70-85).
findings.impact: The only lint gate for the native client is a developer machine, and it is red today for reasons unrelated to any change.
findings.fix: Use `bytes.as_chunks::<4>().0.iter()` (stable since 1.88, so fine on 1.94). Add a rust-toolchain.toml matching CI so local and CI lints agree.

v1.reason: sounds.rs:150 is `bytes.chunks_exact(4).all(...)` in a test. The local toolchain is rust 1.98.1 (pacman), and its clippy-driver contains the lint clippy::CHUNKS_EXACT_TO_AS_CHUNKS ("using `chunks_exact` with constant when `as_chunks` is more ergonomic"). There is no clippy.toml or rust-version msrv to suppress it, and it is the only chunks_exact call in the repo. Running clippy is forbidden here, so I could not confirm that the lint is warn-by-default and makes the README's `cargo clippy -p relay-native --all-targets -- -D warnings -A deprecated` fail. CI pinning 1.94 and leaving relay-native out are both deliberate and documented (ci.yml:25-27 and ci.yml:65-80, README Verify section), so those parts are not defects.
v1.correction: Reduce this to: on the 1.98 toolchain the developer has locally, the native lint step likely fails on sounds.rs:150. The fix is `bytes.as_chunks::<4>().0.iter().all(|b| { let v = f32::from_le_bytes(*b); ... })`, valid on 1.94. A rust-toolchain.toml pinned to 1.94 is optional and is a policy choice. The CI exclusion should not be counted as part of this finding.

findings.title: The large-rewrite explanation always says git cannot restore the file, even when recoverability was never checked
findings.evidence: The destructive_write sentence ends "…and git cannot restore what is there now." The engine only asks git when `allow_if_recoverable` is on (crates/relay-core/src/guardrail.rs:725-730).
