Suppose a Relay `git.commit` (the UI commit or an agent's MCP git_commit) runs in that checkout after the bad close and before the last close. refresh_git (git.rs:548, hooks.rs:160-185) recreates the dead session's directory. Its previous-path lookup falls back to `rev-parse --git-path hooks` (hooks.rs:98), which returns the Relay directory itself, so `.relay-previous-hooks-path` is written pointing at its own directory. This has four effects:
   - The user's chained pre-commit hook is dropped.
   - run_user_pre_commit runs Relay's own gate script as if it were the user's hook.
   - At the last close, uninstall_git_any (hooks.rs:239-262) re-sets the same path on every pass and exits with core.hooksPath still pointing at `.relay/hooks/<dead>`.
   - After the next engine start, the sweep (recovery.rs:138) deletes that directory and the path dangles. A worktree-level hooksPath overrides local and global config, so all of the user's hooks in that checkout (often the primary checkout) stay off until another Relay session runs a full cycle there. The model reproduced every step.

3. A more precise trigger: the active owner is the session that last ran install_git (create, spawn, resume, wake or clear_restorable), not only the last one launched. The siblings that keep teardown from running include parked, restorable and created rows (`state!='closed'`).

4. The PAIR side path (session.rs:900) is a rare race: it needs two concurrent creates, or a partner that changes between the two phases. If it happens, its name has no session row, so it is never in the teardown list. The last close's uninstall_git_any then treats the path as not owned and leaves it pointing at a directory the sweep deletes, permanently.

5. The fix is sound in direction. The simplest complete version: when `others > 0`, either keep the closing session's directory if it is the active hooksPath, or re-point the checkout at a live sibling first, running install_git under hooks::writes() while the old directory and its previous-path file still exist. At teardown (`others == 0`), remove every listed name's directory after uninstall. Also make install_git never record a previous path inside `.relay/hooks`: skip the rev-parse result when it resolves to a Relay directory. Without that, the self-reference from correction 2 survives. Apply the same re-pointing at session.rs:900 instead of skipping the undo.

6. The suggested test should also cover a user path in local config, plus a git.commit between closing the newest session first and the last close. It should assert that no worktree-level `.relay/hooks` path remains at the end.

findings.title: Crash recovery kills every process carrying a session's RELAY_* env, including an Unreal Editor an agent launched on purpose to outlive the session
findings.evidence: At every engine start (serve.rs:22), step 1 does `let orphans = pty::relay_children(instance, &store_path); for (pid, name) in &orphans { kill_wait(*pid); ...` (recovery.rs:67-73). relay_children matches any process whose /proc environ has RELAY_INSTANCE, RELAY_STORE and RELAY_SESSION, whatever its process group (pty.rs:411-429). kill_wait sends SIGTERM and then SIGKILL to `-(pid)` and `pid` (recovery.rs:20-35). Session children get those variables (session.rs:564-576), and MCP servers inherit them by design (hooks.rs:401-402: 'it inherits the session/token/project environment from the Claude process'). I verified this here: the running `relay --instance dev mcp` processes carry RELAY_SESSION, RELAY_STORE, RELAY_INSTANCE and RELAY_TOKEN. ue_editor_launch (unreal.rs:389, 649) spawns UnrealEditor with that inherited environment, in its own group so it survives: `// Its own process group: the editor outlives this MCP server and the agent.` / `command.process_group(0);` (unreal_process.rs:302-304). Session close and Engine::shutdown only signal the provider's group (pty.rs:348), so the editor survives them, and the next start reaps it. The tests pin the env-wide sweep (sessions.rs:554, 583-589) and never cover a process that left the provider's group.
findings.impact: An agent opens the Unreal Editor with ue_editor_launch and the user keeps working in it. Then Relay is restarted for any reason: quit and relaunch, an update, or a crash. Recovery finds the editor by its environment, SIGTERMs its whole process group (editor and shader workers) and SIGKILLs it 2 s later, so unsaved level and asset work is lost. The same happens to anything an agent started that detached into its own group or session, such as an adb server or a Gradle daemon. The surviving editor also keeps the agent's RELAY_TOKEN in its environment.
findings.fix: Reap only what a previous engine owned: processes whose process-group id equals a recorded session pid, or descendants still in that group. Skip processes that are their own group or session leader. Separately, have unreal_process::launch (and any tool meant to outlive the agent) call env_remove for RELAY_SESSION, RELAY_TOKEN and RELAY_STORE. Add a recovery test with a setsid'd child that must survive.

v1.reason: recovery.rs:62-73 reaps every pid returned by pty::relay_children. That function (pty.rs:411-429) matches any process whose /proc environ carries RELAY_INSTANCE and RELAY_STORE equal to this engine's plus any RELAY_SESSION, regardless of process group or ancestry. kill_wait (recovery.rs:20-35) sends SIGTERM and then, 2 s later, SIGKILL to both -(pid) and pid. Session children get all three variables (session.rs:564-575), and Claude's MCP servers inherit them (hooks.rs:401-402). unreal_process::launch (relay-cli unreal_process.rs:284-307) spawns UnrealEditor with the inherited environment (no env_remove anywhere in unreal.rs or unreal_process.rs) and puts it in its own process group precisely so it outlives the agent. SPEC.md:354 describes recovery as reaping 'orphaned claude/codex processes', not every descendant, so killing a deliberately detached editor on the next engine start is not documented intent. The editor's pid is its group leader, so -(pid) kills the editor and its worker processes, and unsaved work is lost.
v1.correction: Also a credential exposure: the detached editor and any Python it runs keep RELAY_TOKEN and RELAY_SESSION. Cheapest fix: call env_remove for RELAY_SESSION, RELAY_TOKEN and RELAY_STORE in unreal_process::launch and any other launcher meant to outlive the agent. Then restrict the recovery sweep to the process groups of recorded session pids (or skip processes that lead their own group or session). Note that kill_wait runs serially, up to 2 s per orphan, before the store opens.

v2.reason:
(a) The code does what the finding says. Every engine start (serve.rs:23) runs recovery::run_with. Step 1 (recovery.rs:66-74) calls kill_wait on every pid that pty::relay_children returns. relay_children (pty.rs:411-429) matches any /proc entry whose environ has this engine's RELAY_INSTANCE and RELAY_STORE plus any RELAY_SESSION. It does not look at process group, ancestry or exe. kill_wait (recovery.rs:20-35) sends SIGTERM to -(pid) and to pid, polls for 2 s, then sends SIGKILL to both.

The env reaches the editor this way:
- Session children get all three variables (handlers/session.rs:564-576).
- The unreal server is `<relay binary> unreal-mcp` (plugins.rs:290-295), written into .relay/relay.mcp.json with no env field (hooks.rs:430-438). Claude spawns it with its own environment. I checked this on the live machine, looking only at variable names: every `relay --instance dev mcp` process carries RELAY_SESSION, RELAY_STORE, RELAY_INSTANCE and RELAY_TOKEN, and its pgid and sid are those of the claude process.
- `relay unreal-mcp` never strips env (main.rs:230; no env_remove or env_clear anywhere in relay-cli).
- unreal_process::launch (unreal_process.rs:285-307) starts UnrealEditor with that inherited env and calls `process_group(0)` "so the editor outlives this MCP server and the agent".
- Session close and Engine::shutdown signal only the provider's group (pty.rs:348; engine.rs:657), so the editor survives both. The next engine start then matches it and kills it.

Nothing upstream prevents this. SPEC §14 says recovery reaps "orphaned claude/codex processes", and nothing documents killing a deliberately detached editor.

(b) Who and how often: a project with the Unreal plugin on and a Claude agent. Relaunching the editor is the plugin's standard loop: instructions.md:7 says to verify every C++ change with `ue_build restart_editor: true`, and that path calls launch_editor (unreal.rs:1572 -> 649). After an agent's first C++ change, the editor the human uses is agent-launched. Any engine restart while it is open then fires the bug:
- app.quit followed by ./run.sh, which the app itself tells the user to do when the engine is stale (tools_plugins.rs:14);
- a crash, which systemd restarts automatically (relay-remote.service has Restart=on-failure);
- an update.
For the author, who develops Relay and uses it on a UE 5.8 game (D162), this is a realistic recurring event. I did not establish whether Codex passes RELAY_* to MCP servers; the Claude path is verified.

(c) What the user loses: on SIGTERM, UE's GracefulTerminationHandler (UE_5.8.2 UnixPlatformCrashContext.cpp:156-170) asks the engine to exit with no save prompt. kill_wait's second SIGTERM can force `_exit(1)`, and SIGKILL follows after 2 s. Every dirty package is lost; the repo already says so at unreal.rs:589 ("asking the process to terminate instead (unsaved changes are lost)"). The kill also takes down the editor's group (shader workers), gives no warning before the doors open, and delays engine start by up to 2 s. UE's autosave (every 10 min by default) can restore some work after an unclean exit, which bounds the loss.

(d) High is right. This is a silent kill of the user's working app with loss of unsaved work, in the plugin's normal loop. It is not critical: it needs the plugin, an agent-launched editor and an engine restart, the loss is limited to unsaved editor edits, and autosave partly mitigates it.

(e) The env_remove half of the fix is correct and complete. unreal_process::launch is the only long-lived detached spawn in relay-cli; blender and UBT runs are transient under output_with_timeout. The sweep-narrowing half is wrong; see the correction.
v2.correction:
Citation fixes: the env is set in crates/relay-core/src/handlers/session.rs:564-576 (crates/relay-core/src/session.rs does not exist), and recovery is called at serve.rs:23.

Fix correction: do NOT narrow the sweep to the process groups of recorded session pids, and do NOT skip group or session leaders. Claude Code runs every Bash-tool command in a new session. I observed this here: the Bash tool's shell has PID = PGID = SID and no tty, while the `relay mcp` servers sit in claude's group. Session close and Engine::shutdown signal only the provider's group (pty.rs:348), so the env-wide sweep is the only thing that ever reaps processes an agent leaves behind: setsid'd background commands, nohup'd or daemonized children. The zero-orphans contract pins it: SPEC §14, SPEC.md:394, CONTRACTS.md:93, and tests/sessions.rs:554.

Keep the sweep and make the deliberate detach opt out. In unreal_process::launch, call `command.env_remove("RELAY_SESSION").env_remove("RELAY_TOKEN").env_remove("RELAY_STORE")`. Removing RELAY_SESSION alone already defeats the relay_children match; removing RELAY_TOKEN also stops the agent's credential from riding along. Add a test that a live process without RELAY_SESSION survives recovery, or assert the launch Command's env.

Impact refinements:
- The adb server and Gradle daemon cases fit the zero-orphan design and are mostly harmless; the real harm is the user-facing editor.
- The RELAY_TOKEN carry-over is minor. The token stays valid while the session is not closed (engine.rs:1376-1382), but Remote Control remote Python on localhost already gives code execution inside the editor.

findings.title: worktree::git, the helper behind every git mutation, has no timeout and runs with the store mutex held in git.stage/unstage/commit, branch create/delete, file.restore_head and session.update
findings.evidence: `let out = Command::new("git").arg("-C").arg(repo).args(args).output()` (worktree.rs:27). It does not use proc::output_with_timeout, does not set GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0, and inherits stdin. Locked callers (plain `register` handlers, or the in-transaction finish of a staged one): git.stage runs `git add --` (git.rs:490/503); git.unstage (527); git.commit runs `commit --no-verify` inside the transaction (finish, git.rs:560-571); git.branch.create and git.branch.delete (374, 485); file.restore_head runs `checkout --` (file.rs:253/256); session.update calls rename_branch, which runs `check-ref-format` and `branch -m` (session.rs:1431/1460, worktree.rs:377-378). The phase-six session test exercises the session.update path (sessions.rs:980). By contrast fetch_remote (git.rs:938-946) uses output_with_timeout with GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0 and null stdin. hooks::run_user_pre_commit (hooks.rs:210) repeats the omission with a bare `.output()`.
findings.impact: Each of these holds the one store mutex for as long as git runs, and every bus request except keystrokes waits: UI reads, agents' tool calls and guardrail hooks, which then hit their own timeouts. Concrete triggers: `git add` of LFS-tracked Unreal assets runs the LFS clean filter for seconds or minutes; `git commit` with commit.gpgsign=true and an uncached passphrase waits on pinentry until the user answers; a hanging prepare-commit-msg or post-commit hook in a checkout without Relay's hooksPath never returns. With no deadline, a wedged git freezes the bus until someone kills it. Unlocked callers (git.push prepare, git.rs:617) can hang forever on a terminal credential prompt when `relay serve` was started from a shell.
findings.fix: Route worktree::git through proc::output_with_timeout with GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0 and null stdin, and map a timeout to a typed refusal. Move `git add`, `checkout --` and `branch -m` into register_staged prepare phases. For git.commit, keep the gate in finish but bound the commit with a deadline. Give run_user_pre_commit the same timeout.

v1.reason: worktree.rs:26-33: `Command::new("git").arg("-C").arg(repo).args(args).output()` has no timeout and no GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT, and stdin is inherited. git_mutate (worktree.rs:36) is a bare wrapper around it. These callers are plain `e.register` handlers, so they run inside the store transaction with the mutex held: Stage (git.rs:490, git add at 503), Unstage (507/527), BranchCreate (345/374), BranchDelete (445/486), file RestoreHead (file.rs:253-256, `checkout --`) and session Update (session.rs:1431, rename_branch at 1460 -> worktree.rs:376-378). CommitOp is staged, but its finish closure runs `commit --no-verify` under the lock (git.rs:571-572). --no-verify skips pre-commit and commit-msg only: prepare-commit-msg, post-commit, gpg signing and LFS filters still run. By contrast fetch_remote and branch switch (git.rs:1351) use output_with_timeout, so the omission is an inconsistency, not a design choice. This breaks the CLAUDE.md rule that every handler subprocess goes through proc::output_with_timeout, and a wedged git (LFS clean or smudge on large Unreal assets, a pinentry prompt for commit.gpgsign, a hanging hook) holds the mutex and stalls every other bus request except memory-path keystrokes.
v1.correction: hooks.rs:210 (run_user_pre_commit, bare `.output()`) and git.push (git.rs:617) run in the unlocked prepare phase. They hang only their own request, not the whole bus, so they are related but lower impact. The same is true of `git add -A` in the commit prepare (git.rs:545). Fix: route worktree::git through proc::output_with_timeout with GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0 (that call already nulls stdin and kills the process group on timeout). Move add, reset, checkout and branch -m into staged prepare phases where possible.

v2.reason:
(a) Confirmed at 361c6f9. worktree.rs:26-33 runs `Command::new("git")...output()` with no deadline, and git_mutate (worktree.rs:36) only wraps it. dispatch_inner takes `self.store.lock()`, opens the transaction and calls the handler (engine.rs ~953-956). Stage (git.rs:490/503), Unstage (507/527), BranchCreate (345/374), BranchDelete (445/485), file RestoreHead (file.rs:253/256) and session Update -> rename_branch (session.rs:1431/1460, worktree.rs:377-378) are all plain `e.register` handlers. CommitOp's finish runs `git commit --no-verify` under the lock (git.rs:571). This breaks D144 as written in DECISIONS.md: "Every subprocess forked from a handler goes through proc::output_with_timeout". D149's list of handlers converted to staged leaves these out. The same file and its siblings already use the timed form: status_files (10 s, worktree.rs:91), worktree::create (120 s, :214), hooks.rs's own git helper (10 s, :583), run_switch (120 s, git.rs:1350) and fetch_remote (20 s, git.rs:945). So this is an oversight, not a design choice.

(b) Who can trigger it, and how often. Everyday Git-panel buttons reach these handlers: "Stage all changes" sends every changed path in one git.stage (code_git.rs:467-484), plus commit, create branch, delete branch and restore file. Agents reach them through the git_stage, git_unstage and git_commit tools. Most git calls take milliseconds and nobody notices. The realistic slow triggers are:
- Clean filters on `git add`. LFS is a real use case here: worktree.rs:82-84 and the test at :398-430 cite "an editor touching an identical LFS-managed asset".
- `git commit` refreshing the index and re-running filters, or signing through pinentry.
- prepare-commit-msg, post-commit or reference-transaction hooks in the primary checkout. Session worktrees get a hooksPath that holds only Relay's pre-commit, so those hooks do not run there.
- `switch -c <name> <start>` in branch.create, which defaults to checkout, and `checkout --` in restore_head. Both run smudge filters, which can download LFS objects. The sibling git.branch.switch was moved to staged with a 120 s timeout precisely because `git switch` walks the checkout (comment at git.rs:384).

There is also a common flow that is worse than the finding says. A UI commit over the default caps (40 files or 2000 lines, settings.rs:29) or one touching a protected path is held as guardrail.user_bypass (guardrail.rs:1021-1033). The UI's `guarded` helper then asks "Allow this held action once?" and calls guardrail.confirm (code_git.rs:1722-1750). guardrail.confirm is a plain register handler (guardrail.rs:339) that replays the commit via invoke_registered, and that function runs the staged prepare against the open transaction (engine.rs:325-342). The result is that `git add -A`, the user's own pre-commit hook (bare `.output()`, hooks.rs:210) and `git commit` all run with the store mutex held and no deadline.

(c) What happens when it fires. While git runs, every request that needs the store waits: UI panel reads, agents' tool calls, mail hints and guardrail.gate calls from agents' PreToolUse hooks. Only UI keystrokes, resizes and mirror input (the D148 fast path) keep flowing. Nothing watches the lock: LockSpan only logs. A wedged child (an unanswered pinentry dialog, a hung hook or filter, LFS over a stalled network) therefore freezes the bus until someone kills the child.

(d) High is right. The rubric lists "a freeze of the bus" as high, and this one is reachable from normal flows in this user's setup (Unreal plus LFS, large UI commits). I would not call it critical: the indefinite hang needs an unusual environment, and keystrokes still work.

(e) The fix direction is right but incomplete. Details are in the correction.
v2.correction:
1. Stdin is not inherited. `Command::output()` gives the child a null stdin by default, per its documented std contract. Prompts reach the user through /dev/tty (credential and ssh passphrase prompts, only when the engine has a controlling terminal) or through a GUI pinentry. So GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0 still matters, but "null stdin" in the fix is redundant; output_with_timeout already sets it.

2. The first verifier's correction is wrong for one path. run_user_pre_commit (hooks.rs:210) and `add -A` (git.rs:545) do run locked whenever a held git.commit is confirmed: guardrail.confirm -> replay_registered -> invoke_registered runs the prepare with `held: Some(self.tx)` (engine.rs:328-342). That makes hooks.rs:210 a locked location, and it is reached through an ordinary UI flow.

3. The listed callers differ in impact.
- Millisecond ref/index operations with no filters or network: unstage, `branch -d`, check-ref-format and `branch -m`. These break the invariant but are not realistic freeze triggers.
- Real freeze risks: git.stage, the git.commit finish, git.branch.create with checkout and a start point, file.restore_head, and the guardrail.confirm replay.

4. Callers the finding missed:
- Locked, via git_mutate:
  - CleanMerged (git.rs:686-712) runs a `branch -d` loop and list_with_dirty.
  - IntegrationDiscard (integration.rs:58-64) runs worktree::remove (purge and dir_size walks, then `worktree remove --force`) followed by `branch -D`.
- Same invariant, different code path: PrOpen (git.rs:666-684) runs `gh pr create`, a network call, with a bare `.output()` in a plain register handler. It may deserve its own finding.
- Worker thread only, untimed: device.rs:1575 runs `fetch` through git_mutate on run_worker (device.rs:1665), and the helpers at device.rs:1500-1534 are also untimed. These can hang a device run but not the bus.

5. Fix caveats.
- A single deadline inside worktree::git would also hit unlocked callers that are legitimately slow: `git push` of LFS objects (git.rs:617), the integration `merge` (integration.rs:128) and `worktree remove`. Deadlines need to be per call site and generous; run_switch's 120 s is a reasonable reference.
- output_with_timeout SIGKILLs the process group, so git cannot remove `.git/index.lock` or ref `.lock` files. A killed add, commit or checkout can leave a stale lock that blocks every later git command in that checkout, including agents' commands.
- So the primary fix is to move stage, unstage, restore_head, branch.create and clean_merged into register_staged prepares. Keep the deadline as a backstop: send SIGTERM before SIGKILL, and make the refusal name the lock file.
- invoke_registered must stop running prepares under the lock, or the confirm path stays exposed.

6. Not verified: Relay sets a 30 s timeout on Claude's PreToolUse hook (hooks.rs:351, :521), and the hook client waits with no deadline of its own (socket.rs:801-821). A bus stall longer than 30 s therefore gets the hook killed. Whether Claude Code then runs the tool (the guardrail failing open) depends on Claude Code and cannot be established from this repo.

findings.title: worktree.remove deletes any directory it is given: there is no worktree check, a remove_dir_all fallback, and relative paths resolve against the engine's cwd ($HOME)
findings.evidence: The handler canonicalizes the raw payload path and only refuses one that a live session owns: `let want = std::fs::canonicalize(&p.path)...unwrap_or(p.path.clone());` ... `worktree::remove(repo, Path::new(&want), p.purge_build.unwrap_or(true))` (git.rs:132-139). worktree::remove refuses only the repo root. Otherwise it runs purge_build(path), which deletes target, build, .gradle, app/build, node_modules/.cache and dist under that path, then dir_size(path), then `git worktree remove --force` with `.or_else(|e| { std::fs::remove_dir_all(path)...` (worktree.rs:352-366). I checked in a scratch repo that `git worktree remove --force <a directory that is not a worktree>` exits 128 ('is not a working tree'), which is exactly the case that takes the remove_dir_all fallback. The validator worktree::contains exists and file.rs:433 and device.rs:1026 use it, but this handler does not. `relay serve` sets the engine cwd to $HOME (relay-cli main.rs:208). The handler is a plain `register`, so the walk and the deletion happen with the store mutex held. The phone door forwards any `user` op (relay-remote wire.rs:95-103). The only test removes a valid pooled worktree (sessions.rs:231).
findings.impact: Say a user inside a worktree types `relay q worktree.remove '{"project_id":1,"path":"."}'` meaning 'remove this one'. The path canonicalizes to $HOME, and the engine deletes ~/.gradle and ~/target, walks the whole home directory under the store lock, then runs remove_dir_all on $HOME. A workspace-root path deletes every project in it. The same request can come from a buggy or compromised paired phone, or from an agent using the documented best-effort user-actor route. No shipped UI sends this op, but its contract ('Remove a worktree') makes the outcome surprising and irreversible.
findings.fix: Reject relative paths. Require worktree::contains(repo, path) and a linked worktree, preferably under worktree::pool_dir(repo) or listed by worktree::list. Allow the remove_dir_all fallback only inside the pool. Make the handler register_staged so the purge, walk and delete run unlocked. Add tests that '.', the workspace root and a plain directory are refused and left intact.

v1.reason: git.rs:129-143: the WorktreeRemove handler is a plain `e.register`. It canonicalizes the raw `p.path`, which resolves relative paths against the engine cwd; relay-cli main.rs:208 sets that cwd to $HOME. The only check is the session-owner lookup. worktree::remove (worktree.rs:351-367) refuses only `repo_c == path_c`. After that it runs purge_build(path), which deletes target/build/.gradle/app/build/node_modules/.cache/dist under the path, then dir_size(path), then `git worktree remove --force`, and on any error it falls back to `std::fs::remove_dir_all(path)`. A directory that is not a worktree makes git fail, so it hits the rm -rf fallback. Nothing in the path checks that the target is a worktree of the project. worktree::contains and the pool_dir check that session.close uses (`wt.starts_with(worktree::pool_dir(&repo))`, session.rs:1576) are not applied here. The op is UserOnly (relay-bus ops/git.rs:15), and BUS.md §9.5 states that the socket does not authenticate the user actor. The phone door forwards every `actor:user` line (relay-remote wire.rs:95-103). No native UI caller exists, so the realistic triggers are the CLI, the phone, or an agent spoofing the user actor. That keeps it at high, not critical.
v1.correction: Primary mechanism: any path (absolute, or relative to $HOME) that is not a registered worktree goes to purge_build and then the remove_dir_all fallback at worktree.rs:362. Besides the fix proposed, the cheapest guard is to require that the canonical path appears in worktree::list(repo) and is not the primary checkout, mirroring session.rs:883-886, and to keep the remove_dir_all fallback for paths under pool_dir only. Moving the work to register_staged is a separate invariant point: the purge and the walk currently run under the store mutex.

v2.reason:
(a) The code does what the finding claims. git.rs:129 is a plain `e.register::<WorktreeRemove>`, so it runs with `&mut Ctx` inside the locked transaction. git.rs:132 canonicalizes the raw `p.path` against the process cwd. relay-cli main.rs:207-208 sets that cwd to $HOME for `relay serve`, the engine the native client expects (app.rs:1282). The only guard is an exact-path owner lookup (git.rs:133-138). In worktree::remove, worktree.rs:355 refuses only `repo_c == path_c`. Then it runs, in order:
- `purge_build(path)` (360), which deletes target, build, .gradle, app/build, node_modules/.cache and dist under the path before anything is validated;
- `dir_size(path)` (361);
- `git worktree remove --force`, falling back on ANY error to `std::fs::remove_dir_all(path)` (362-366).

I reproduced the git side with git 2.55.0 in a scratch repo. All four of these exit 128 with 'is not a working tree', so each reaches the rm -rf fallback: a foreign directory, a subdirectory of the primary checkout, the pool dir `.relay/worktrees`, and a parent of the repo. Every other path-taking project op validates membership: file.rs:433 and device.rs:1026 via worktree::contains, and session.create at session.rs:880-886 via absolute path plus `.git` plus listed in worktree::list. This op does not. The only tests (sessions.rs:231, 310) use a valid pooled path.

(b) Reachability. No shipped client sends this op: rg finds no reference in apps/relay-native or apps/relay-mobile. The UI removes worktrees through session.close and discard_restorable, and both guard with `wt.starts_with(pool_dir)` (session.rs:1521, 1577). The real triggers are narrower:
- A person using the documented CLI. `relay q`/`relay cmd` defaults to the user actor and passes `path` through unchanged (main.rs:118-142).
- User scripts.
- A user-actor `relay mcp`. mcp.rs:91-103 lists every op the actor may call, but Relay's own sessions run as agents, so this needs a manual setup.
- The phone door. It forwards user lines (wire.rs:95-103), but the phone app never sends this op, and a paired phone is the user by design.
- An agent spoofing the user actor on the raw socket. BUS.md §9.5 says that route is 'not a security boundary', and it gives nothing a shell does not.

So the trigger is rare: user error on a raw op. The mistakes are natural ones, though: '.' or '..' (resolved against $HOME, not the caller's cwd), the pool dir ('clean up worktrees'), a subdirectory, or a workspace root.

(c) What happens when it fires. The deletion is irreversible and the op reports success with freed_mb.
- '.' deletes ~/.gradle, ~/build, ~/dist and ~/target, walks all of $HOME while holding the store mutex (freezing other bus requests meanwhile), then runs remove_dir_all($HOME) until the first error.
- The pool dir deletes every agent worktree, including live sessions' uncommitted work. The exact-path owner check is bypassed.
- A workspace root deletes every project, .git included, so unpushed commits are lost.
- A subdirectory of the primary deletes that subtree, including its uncommitted work.

(d) Severity: high is correct. The impact is catastrophic and irreversible. The op's documented safety contract ('conflict if a session owns it', 'never the primary') is silently bypassed by any parent or child path, which matches the rubric's 'safety check that can be silently bypassed'. It is not critical: no shipped flow sends the op, no unauthenticated network or other-local-user route exists, and the agent route is a documented non-boundary.

(e) The fix is right in direction but needs the ordering and placement corrections below.
v2.correction:
1. The membership check must run BEFORE purge_build. Restricting only the remove_dir_all fallback still lets purge_build (worktree.rs:339-349, called at 360) delete target, build, .gradle, dist and the rest under any path; '.' would still wipe ~/.gradle. Put the guard in worktree::remove itself, so every caller is covered, not only the handler.

2. Model the guard on session.rs:880-886. Reject a relative path. Require that the canonical path appears in `worktree::list_with_dirty(repo, false)`; use that, not `list()`, because list() spawns a `git status` per worktree. Require that it is not the primary. Allow the remove_dir_all fallback only when the canonical path is strictly under canon(pool_dir(repo)). worktree::contains alone trusts a `.git` pointer file, so it is weaker than git's own list.

3. When moving to register_staged, do the owner check and the validation in the prepare phase. session.create can attach a session to an existing worktree path (session.rs:878-887), so re-check ownership in the finish phase or accept the same window session.close already has.

4. A separate root cause on the same path: worktree.rs:26-33 `git()` uses `Command::output()` without proc::output_with_timeout, for both `worktree remove` and `worktree prune`, today under the store lock. That breaks a CLAUDE.md invariant. Report it separately, not as part of this finding.

5. Add tests that '.', the pool dir, a subdirectory of the primary and a parent directory are each refused and left intact. Today the only tests are sessions.rs:231 and 310, which use a valid pooled path.

6. Related lines: worktree.rs:360 (purge before any validation) and worktree.rs:362-366 (any git error leads to remove_dir_all).

findings.title: Crash recovery SIGTERM/SIGKILLs whatever process now holds a stale session PID, with no identity check
findings.evidence: For every row still in spawning, running, idle or blocked: `Some(p) if pty::pid_alive(p as u32) => { // alive but not ours (we just started) — reap unless it was already` / `kill_wait(p as u32);` (recovery.rs:86-88). pid_alive is only `libc::kill(pid as i32, 0) == 0` (pty.rs:394-396), which is true for any process of this user. kill_wait signals `-(pid)` and `pid` with SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after 2 s (recovery.rs:20-35). Step 1 has already reaped every genuine Relay child by its environment, so step 2 can only hit a non-Relay process that reused the PID. The test seeds exactly such a row with a hard-coded PID, `VALUES ('ghost-heron', ... 'running', 999999, ...)` (sessions.rs:575-576), and asserts it reads as dead (591). kernel.pid_max is 4194304 on this machine, so 999999 is a valid PID. The alive-but-not-ours branch is never tested.
findings.impact: After an unclean engine exit (crash, OOM kill, power loss or reboot), session rows keep their old PIDs. On the next start, any of the user's processes that has since taken one of those PIDs (a browser, an editor, a terminal shell, plus its whole process group if it leads one) gets SIGTERM and then SIGKILL, possibly losing unsaved work. Running `cargo test` does the same to PID 999999 if the developer happens to own a process with that PID.
findings.fix: Verify identity before signalling: proc_env(pid) must contain RELAY_SESSION equal to the row's name and RELAY_STORE equal to this store, or /proc/<pid>/stat starttime must match the spawn time. Otherwise only mark the row restorable. In the test, use a PID above PID_MAX_LIMIT (e.g. 2_000_000_000) or one taken from an already-reaped child, and add a case where an unrelated live process must survive.

v1.reason: recovery.rs:84-93: for every row in spawning/running/idle/blocked with `Some(p) if pty::pid_alive(p as u32)` it calls kill_wait(p), and kill_wait (recovery.rs:20-35) sends SIGTERM to -(pid) and pid, then SIGKILL after 2 s. pid_alive (pty.rs:394-396) is only `kill(pid, 0) == 0`. Step 1 (recovery.rs:65-73) has already reaped every process whose /proc environ carries this RELAY_INSTANCE+RELAY_STORE (pty.rs:411-429), so any process that is still alive at a stored PID in step 2 is, in practice, not a Relay child: it is an unrelated process that reused the PID. Nothing checks identity (no environ, no starttime). Trigger: an unclean exit (crash, OOM kill, power loss) followed by a restart or reboot. PIDs are reassigned and every stale row is a lottery ticket, more so with many concurrent sessions. The test (sessions.rs:574-576, 591) seeds PID 999999 and only covers the dead branch. The live-but-foreign branch has no test.
v1.correction: There is one more victim the finding misses. Step 2 does not skip std::process::id(), which step 1 does at pty.rs:417. After a reboot, the new engine (or the process that hosts it) can itself hold a PID recorded in a stale row, since processes started early at login get similar low PIDs. The engine would then SIGTERM and SIGKILL itself, and its process group too if it leads one. The fix stays the same: before signalling, require /proc/<pid>/environ to carry this row's RELAY_SESSION and this store's RELAY_STORE, or require a matching starttime. Otherwise just mark the row restorable. Also never signal std::process::id() or pids <= 1.

v2.reason:
(a) The code does what the finding says. For every row in spawning, running, idle or blocked, recovery.rs:84-93 calls kill_wait(p) when `pty::pid_alive(p as u32)`. pid_alive is only `libc::kill(pid, 0) == 0` (pty.rs:394-396). kill_wait (recovery.rs:20-35) sends SIGTERM to -(pid) and to pid, then SIGKILL after 2 s. Nothing checks environ, start time or boot. The only caller is serve::start (serve.rs:23), which runs before the socket opens. DECISIONS D20 says "Recovery reaps only its own store's orphans ... two instances never cross". Step 2 breaks that, so this is not intended behavior.

(b) How it is reached. No attacker is involved: the engine does this to itself at start. Two conditions are needed.
1. The engine exited uncleanly while sessions were live. A clean exit clears every pid: shutdown() → mark_restorable sets pid=NULL (engine.rs:676), and an exit callback sets pid=NULL (session.rs:653). So only SIGKILL, OOM, power loss, a kernel panic or a hard reset leave pids behind.
2. At the next start, a stale pid now belongs to a live process or thread of the same user.

Without a reboot, condition 2 almost never holds. pid_max is 4194304. This machine allocates about 282k PIDs a day (last PID 3.29M after 11.7 days up). Today's live claude session leaders are at 2.27M-2.41M, so a pid is reused only once the counter wraps, about 11 days of downtime from now. After an unclean reboot, PIDs restart at 300. A row's pid then lands in the range the new boot fills at login if its session was spawned early in the previous boot, or soon after a counter wrap. Sessions resumed right after launch are exactly that case.

Thread IDs count as well. On this kernel (7.2.7) I checked with a throwaway process that kill(TID, 0) succeeds and kill(TID, SIGTERM) kills the whole process. The relevant density is therefore the user's live thread IDs: 1281 here, 189 of them at or below 2000. When run.sh starts the engine after other apps, those apps are exposed. When the systemd unit starts it at login, the counter is near the engine's own pid, which leaves mainly the engine's own main thread and 16 tokio workers exposed.

(c) What happens when it fires. An unrelated process of the user gets SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after 2 s if it is still alive. If it leads a process group, the whole group is signalled. Unsaved work in it can be lost. The only record is a line in app.recovery.last. If the stale pid hits the engine's own pid or a thread, the engine dies at once from SIGTERM: no handler is installed until serve()'s select! runs after start() returns. Under the shipped unit (Restart=on-failure), systemd counts death by SIGTERM as a clean exit and does not restart it.

(d) Severity. The consequence is destructive, but it needs an unclean exit followed by a PID collision, which is realistic mainly after a power loss or hard reset. That is a real bug in a less common path, which is medium in the rubric, not "likely in a normal flow". The cargo test hazard is tiny: PID 999999 is live only briefly as the counter passes it, and it was not live when checked.

(e) The fix. The environ check is correct and consistent with D20. It makes step 2's kill nearly redundant with step 1, which is acceptable: orphans have already had SIGHUP from the closed PTY master. The start-time alternative does not work as written (see correction). The test changes are right.
v2.correction:
1. Lower severity to medium. In practice the trigger is an unclean reboot, not any crash. A restart without a reboot does not reuse pids for days, because pid_max is 4194304 and the counter only wraps after about 15 days on this machine.

2. Thread IDs widen the target set. kill(TID) signals the whole process; I checked this on the 7.2.7 kernel. So a stale pid can hit any thread of any of the user's processes, and also the engine's own main thread and 16 tokio workers. The first verifier's "skip std::process::id()" is therefore incomplete. A self-hit kills the engine immediately through SIGTERM's default action, not "SIGTERM and SIGKILL". Under run.sh the engine is not a process-group leader, so kill(-pid) fails with ESRCH.

3. "Step 2 can only hit a non-Relay process" overstates it. Step 2 still reaps real orphans that step 1 cannot see: their environ is unreadable (non-dumpable) or rewritten, or their RELAY_STORE string differs.

4. The start-time branch of the fix fails with the data that exists today. spawned_at is `COALESCE(spawned_at, now)` (session.rs:681), so it is the first spawn, not the current process. It is also wall-clock text at one-second resolution, while /proc/<pid>/stat starttime counts ticks since boot. It would need a new per-epoch start-ticks column plus the boot id, which means a migration and a SCHEMA_VERSION bump.

5. A cheaper fix for the main case: store /proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id in meta (no migration needed) and never signal in step 2 when it differs. Otherwise, require RELAY_STORE to equal this store and RELAY_SESSION to equal the row's name, or simply stop signalling in step 2.

6. Also reject p <= 1 before signalling. A tampered row with -1 becomes kill(-1, SIGTERM), which signals every process the user owns; 0 signals the engine's own process group. Only store tampering reaches this.

7. Same root cause in another form: one Relay instance's recovery can kill another instance's live session that reused the pid, against D20.

8. Test: use a pid above PID_MAX_LIMIT (for example 2_000_000_000), and add a live unrelated child, such as `sleep`, that must survive recovery.

findings.title: The D148 test (input_bypasses_the_store_...) cannot fail if session.input goes back through the store
findings.evidence: The test sends input to an idle session and waits for `state() == "running"` (503-504), then checks the echo and the state (507-515). The registered slow-path handler produces the same observable results: `if row.session.state == SessionState::Idle && !p.data.is_empty() { ... UPDATE sessions SET state='running' ...` (handlers/session.rs:1676-1686), and user input is never audited (AgentOnly). So if the fast path at engine.rs:891-898 were removed or bypassed, every assertion would still pass. The comment 'Every keystroke after the edge is pure memory: no further writes' (506) is asserted nowhere. No other test dispatches session.input against a held lock; engine.rs's inline_path_tests (1436) only check answers_from_memory.
findings.impact: CLAUDE.md lists 'session.input must not touch SQLite (D148)' as an easy-to-break invariant. A regression would pass CI, and typing would queue behind slow handlers again (the lag D148 fixed). Examples: a new lookup that takes self.store.lock() before the fast path, or a change to its `!audited && session_id.is_none()` guard.
findings.fix: Hold `e.store.lock()` on the test thread, send session.input from another thread, and assert it returns within a bound (recv_timeout) and the echo reaches the scrollback while the guard is held. Then drop the guard and assert the idle-to-running write lands.

v1.reason: The test (sessions.rs:466-516) only observes that input wakes an idle session to running and that the echo lands. The locked Input handler (handlers/session.rs:1661-1687) gives exactly the same results: it writes the PTY, does UPDATE state='running' on Idle and emits session.changed. User input is not audited, so no audit-row difference exists either. Removing the fast path at engine.rs:891-898, or breaking its `!audited && session_id.is_none()` guard, leaves every assertion green. The comment at 506 ('no further writes') is never asserted. engine.rs's inline test (around 1436-1490) checks only answers_from_memory routing, not that dispatch avoids the store lock. So the D148 invariant, which CLAUDE.md explicitly flags as easy to break, has no regression test that can fail.
v1.correction: Proposed fix: on the test thread, hold `e.store.lock()` and dispatch session.input from another thread. Assert it returns within a short bound and the echo reaches the PTY's scrollback (read it from the Pty in memory, not through session.scrollback, which may need the store) while the guard is still held.

findings.title: The write-roots launch test computes its expected roots with the code under test and never checks the configured root
findings.evidence: The test sets `guardrails.allowed_write_roots = [extra]` (251). It then derives the expected list from the same production function the launch uses: `let roots = relay_core::guardrail::write_roots(&cfg, &worktree);` (259-260; the launch calls it at handlers/session.rs:453). It asserts each element appears as `--add-dir` and gets an allow verdict (263-269). `extra` is never named in an assertion. `extra` is f.root.join("agent notes"), which is under the system temp dir, and write_roots always ends with `roots.push(std::env::temp_dir());` (guardrail.rs:617). write_target treats anything under a non-worktree root as Scratch (guardrail.rs:645), so extra/note.md is allowed whether or not the setting is honoured. No other test exercises allowed_write_roots.
findings.impact: If cfg.allowed_write_roots stopped reaching write_roots (guardrail.rs:616), through a settings-path rename or a serde default for example, the expected list would shrink in step and the /tmp root would still satisfy the verdict check, so the test would stay green. Users' configured roots would silently stop reaching the providers' `--add-dir` and the guardrail.
findings.fix: Assert explicitly that args contain ["--add-dir", extra] and that an unlisted sibling directory is refused. Place `extra` outside the temp dir, e.g. under env!("CARGO_TARGET_TMPDIR"), so the always-present temp root cannot satisfy the verdict.

v1.reason: sessions.rs:259-260 builds the expected list with `relay_core::guardrail::write_roots(&cfg, &worktree)`, the same function the launch uses (handlers/session.rs:453). `extra` (sessions.rs:249) is under f.root, a canonicalized tempfile::tempdir(), and write_roots always appends std::env::temp_dir() (guardrail.rs:617). write_target accepts anything under a non-worktree root as Scratch (guardrail.rs:644-646). If allowed_write_roots stopped reaching write_roots, the expected list would shrink with it, and the verdict check on extra/note.md would still pass through the /tmp root. No other test sets guardrails.allowed_write_roots (grep shows only sessions.rs:251). guardrails.rs:849 covers path grants, not this setting.
v1.correction: Severity lowered to low. A regression would fail closed: configured roots get refused, which a user notices, and no guardrail is bypassed. The test still provides real coverage of the memory roots and of --add-dir plumbing. Fix as proposed: assert ["--add-dir", extra] explicitly, put extra outside temp_dir, and add a refused-sibling case. The reverse direction is untested too: a relative entry must be dropped (guardrail.rs:616 filters is_absolute).

findings.title: The migration test builds old stores from today's migration text, with empty tables, so it cannot catch an edited shipped migration or a data-dependent failure
findings.evidence: Each 'prior version' is built with `for m in &MIGRATIONS[..k] { c.execute_batch(m).unwrap(); }` (24-26), i.e. today's text of every migration, and the only row inserted is meta.created_at (28). The doc says 'the way a build of that era would have', but an in-place edit to MIGRATIONS[i] changes the simulated old store and the upgrade in the same way. The only append guard is `assert_eq!(MIGRATIONS.len() as i64, SCHEMA_VERSION)` (18). Data-transforming steps such as v14's `UPDATE task_sessions SET queue_ord=task_id;` (src/store.rs:292-293) only ever run on empty tables.
findings.impact: CLAUDE.md says a new column means appending a migration, and every earlier version must stay openable. Suppose a contributor or agent adds a column by editing v20 instead of appending v21. SCHEMA_VERSION still equals the count, fresh and simulated-old stores both get the column, and this test passes. Every real store already at v20 never gets the column and fails with 'no such column' at runtime. A future UNIQUE index, CHECK or table rebuild that fails or drops rows on populated tables would also pass.
findings.fix: Pin each shipped migration (a constant SHA-256 list or golden .sql fixtures) and assert the list is append-only. Before reopening a version-k store, seed one representative row in every table that exists at k, and assert the rows survive with the expected defaults.

v1.reason: tests/store.rs:24-26 builds each prior-version store by running today's MIGRATIONS[..k] text, and the only data it inserts is meta.created_at (28). Store::open (src/store.rs:430-456) migrates by running MIGRATIONS[v..] from the stored user_version. So a column added by editing a shipped migration in place (e.g. v20) reaches both the simulated old store and fresh stores, and the test passes, while real stores already at that version never get the column. No golden fixture or hash of shipped migrations exists anywhere in crates/relay-core (rg finds none). The only append guard is MIGRATIONS.len() == SCHEMA_VERSION (18). Data-transforming steps like v14's `UPDATE task_sessions SET queue_ord=task_id;` (store.rs:292-293) only ever run on empty tables. CLAUDE.md names this exact invariant as easy to break, and agents edit this file, so the test does not protect the rule it appears to cover.
v1.correction: git history (9b4a327 for v20, 54e6bbc for v19) shows migrations have been appended correctly so far, so no edit-in-place has happened yet. The cost is a missing safety net, not something that has already diverged. Pinning shipped migration text (a hash list or golden .sql fixtures checked append-only) is the high-value part of the fix. Seeding representative rows before upgrading is a secondary improvement.

findings.title: Wall-clock lock tests use 60 ms and 100 ms bounds against a 150 ms grace, so they flake under the parallel runner and can pass vacuously
findings.evidence: `std::thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(60)); ... ok(&f.engine, "session.list", ...); ... assert!(waited < Duration::from_millis(60), ...)` (1321-1326). For close, the failure being guarded against is a lock held through `pty.kill(Duration::from_millis(150))` (handlers/session.rs:1571), only about 90 ms past the bound. `assert!(start.elapsed() < Duration::from_millis(100), "close took {:?}", ...)` (286) times a close whose prepare runs git subprocesses under the process-wide `hooks::writes()` mutex (hooks.rs:61-64, taken in run_teardown at handlers/session.rs:353). Every other test's launch holds that same mutex across install_git, install_claude and the skill-folder copy (handlers/session.rs:480-560; the Unreal plugin is 20 skills and 57 files, copied twice). The 60 ms sleep only guesses that the stopping thread has reached its kill; if it has not, session.list runs first and passes even with the bug. A similar `elapsed < 500ms` bound is at 1298.
findings.impact: `cargo test` runs these alongside about 20 other tests in the binary that spawn sessions and git. A scheduling stall, or a wait on hooks::writes(), longer than 60 or 100 ms fails a correct build. A slow thread start lets a lock-holding regression pass. Flaky CI trains people to just rerun it.
findings.fix: Synchronize instead of guessing. For close with remove_worktree:false, assert alive(pid) immediately after close returns: the TERM-ignoring child can only already be dead if close waited out the grace. For park and close, poll until e.pty(id).is_none() (take_pty done) while the child is still alive, then time session.list against a generous bound (e.g. 1 s against the 3 s park grace).

v1.reason: The bounds are as quoted. sessions.rs:286 asserts the remove_worktree:false close returns in under 100 ms. That close's prepare (handlers/session.rs:1547-1597) calls run_teardown (353), which takes the process-wide static hooks::writes() mutex (hooks.rs:61-64) and forks up to two git processes through uninstall_git_any (hooks.rs:233-280). It also does the uninstall_claude file rewrites before the commit. hooks::writes() is shared by every test thread in the binary, and stage_launch (session.rs:480) and session.create (891, 905) hold it across install_git and its git subprocesses. sessions.rs has 22 session.spawn calls running in parallel under plain `cargo test --locked` (ci.yml:38). So a wait on that mutex plus two forks on a loaded 2-core runner can plausibly exceed 100 ms, and 100 ms is the only thing that separates a correct close from a regression that holds the 150 ms grace. The 60 ms check in park_and_close (1321-1326) is less exposed. Each test has its own Store, so session.list (register::<List>, session.rs:1023) only competes with this test's own stopping thread. That thread is in kill(3 s) for park and kill(150 ms) for close at that point, so a false failure needs session.list itself to take over 60 ms. The vacuous-pass half is real but only happens under heavy scheduling delay, and the 3 s park grace makes it unlikely there. git history has no flake fixes or bound bumps for these tests, so I could not show that any flake has actually happened.
v1.correction: The real exposure is mainly sessions.rs:286, the 100 ms close bound. The 60 ms check at 1326 is lower risk because the store mutex is per test. The claim that every other test's launch copies the Unreal plugin's 20 skills / 57 files twice is wrong. Skills are copied only where a plugin is enabled (the plugin test at sessions.rs:782); the shared cost is the hooks::writes() mutex held across install_git/install_claude git subprocesses in launches and creates. The 500 ms bound at 1298 is generous and not a meaningful flake source. Severity is low: it is a possibly flaky test with no evidence of flakes, and no product impact. The suggested fix is sound: for close(false), assert alive(pid) right after close returns instead of timing it, and for park/close, poll until e.pty(id) is gone before timing session.list against a generous bound.

findings.title: provider.refresh runs both provider CLIs inside the transaction, holding the store mutex for up to 3 s
findings.evidence: `e.register::<Refresh>(|ctx: &mut Ctx, _| { let discovered = crate::providers::refresh(ctx.tx(), &ctx.now)?;` (handlers/provider.rs:18-19). refresh forks `<binary> --version` plus `auth status` / `login status` for both providers inside that transaction (providers.rs:320-331). The code relies on a deadline: '/// Provider probes ... run inside the request transaction, so the deadline is what keeps a wedged binary from holding the store mutex indefinitely (D144).' `const PROBE_TIMEOUT: Duration = Duration::from_secs(3);` (providers.rs:358-360). D149 later says slow work runs outside the transaction 'not merely with a timeout'; provider.list was converted, refresh was not. It is called from the native 'Refresh providers' button (relay-native tools_settings.rs:396-402) and in tests at sessions.rs:660/669.
findings.impact: Each click holds the global lock while real CLIs start: node startup for claude --version, and `claude auth status` may hit the network. Every other request (UI reads, agent tool calls, guardrail hooks) waits for roughly 0.5 to 3 s. That is the stall D144/D149 set out to remove; the timeout only bounds it.
findings.fix: Use register_staged: probe in prepare (read configured paths with a short ctx.read, run the probes unlocked), then write provider_cache and the notifications in finish.

v1.reason: handlers/provider.rs:18-19 registers Refresh with plain `e.register` and calls providers::refresh(ctx.tx(), ...). providers.rs:309-331 then runs `<binary> --version` and the auth probe for both providers on scoped threads, inside the transaction, each bounded by PROBE_TIMEOUT = 3 s (358-360). D149 (DECISIONS.md:797) says slow work runs outside the transaction, 'not merely with a timeout'. It converted provider.list but not provider.refresh. The caller is the native 'Refresh providers' button (tools_settings.rs:400). The probes run in parallel, so the lock is held for at most about 3 s, typically the startup time of node/claude.
v1.correction: Related: provider_updates.rs:62 also calls providers::refresh inside engine.system_write, under the store lock, after a provider update. Fix both with register_staged: probe in prepare, upsert provider_cache in finish. For the update path, probe before system_write. This is a user-initiated, infrequent and bounded stall, so medium is appropriate.

findings.title: The v3 importer copies attachments to a path built from the untrusted v3 original_name, so an import can write outside the store
findings.evidence: `let dest_dir = attach_root.join(new_id.to_string()); std::fs::create_dir_all(&dest_dir).bus()?; let dest = dest_dir.join(&name); std::fs::copy(&src, &dest).bus()?;` (import_v3.rs:260-263). `name` is attachments.original_name read from the source relay.db (239-243), and `src` may be any absolute `path` in the same row (246-247). PathBuf::join replaces the base for an absolute argument and keeps `..` components. The op is UserOnly but takes an arbitrary `source` (onboarding text field, relay-native onboarding.rs:531-532; the CLI; the phone door). The test only covers benign names (store.rs:108).
findings.impact: A user imports v3 data from a repository containing a crafted .relay/relay.db. If an attachment row has original_name '../../../../../../.bashrc' (counted from <data>/relay-v4/stable/attachments/<id>/) or an absolute path, and `path` points at a payload file in that repo, the import overwrites ~/.bashrc (or any user-writable file), which runs code at the next shell. Separately, two attachments with the same name on one task overwrite each other's file.
findings.fix: Keep only the final normal component (Path::new(&name).file_name()), reject empty, '.' and '..', and de-duplicate per task. Require the resolved src to be under the v3 dir or repo. Assert dest.starts_with(&dest_dir) before copying. Add a traversal case to v3_import_dry_run_then_real.

v1.reason: import_v3.rs:259-264: `let dest = dest_dir.join(&name); std::fs::copy(&src, &dest)`, where `name` is attachments.original_name read straight from the source relay.db (239-243) and never sanitized. PathBuf::join keeps `..` components and replaces the base for an absolute name, so a crafted row writes any user-writable file. `src` can be any absolute path (246-247). The `source` comes from the onboarding text field (relay-native onboarding.rs:531-532) or the CLI. Separately, two attachments with the same original_name on one task copy to the same dest, so one file silently overwrites the other while both DB rows point at it.
v1.correction: The trigger needs the user to import an attacker-supplied v3 .relay/relay.db, a one-time and deliberate action, so the traversal is medium rather than higher. The same-name collision is the more likely real-world loss. Fix: keep only the file_name() component, de-duplicate per task, and assert dest.starts_with(dest_dir).

findings.title: The backup-retention test's 'newest first' check is guaranteed by the sort it tests and cannot tell which five backups were kept
findings.evidence: `assert!(b[0]["created_at"].as_str().unwrap() >= b[4]["created_at"].as_str().unwrap(), "newest first");` (74). list_backups already sorts on that field: `v.sort_by(|a, b| b.created_at.cmp(&a.created_at));` (src/store.rs:607). `b[0]["reason"] == "manual"` (75) holds for all seven backups. The `path` returned by each app.backup.now is never compared with the list.
findings.impact: If the prune in backup_to pruned from the wrong end (`all.remove(0)` instead of `all.pop()`, src/store.rs:569), every manual or pre-upgrade backup would be deleted as soon as it was made, and this test would still see five sorted entries and pass.
findings.fix: Collect the path from each app.backup.now. Assert the listed paths equal the last five returned and that the first two no longer exist on disk.

v1.reason: list_backups sorts newest first (src/store.rs:607: `v.sort_by(|a, b| b.created_at.cmp(&a.created_at))`), so the test's `b[0].created_at >= b[4].created_at` check (tests/store.rs:74) always holds. `reason == "manual"` (75) holds for all seven backups, and the paths returned by app.backup.now are never compared. backup_to's prune (store.rs:567-572) pops from the end of that newest-first list, which removes the oldest backup. If it were changed to remove index 0, each new backup would be deleted as soon as it was written once five exist, and the test would still see five sorted manual entries and pass. No other test covers pruning; rg finds list_backups used only at tests/store.rs:54 for the upgrade-backup count.
v1.correction: The prune is at store.rs:567-572. The proposed fix is right and cheap: collect each returned `path`, assert the listed paths equal the last five returned, and assert the first two no longer exist on disk. A secondary weakness: the 2 ms sleeps rely on millisecond timestamp resolution to give each file a distinct name.

findings.title: Three session-test assertions claim behaviour the test cannot observe: mid-turn injection, survival of a partial launch, and detach
findings.evidence: (a) `assert!(!...scrollback...contains(&next_prompt), "Done must not inject into its own unfinished provider turn")` (914-915) runs immediately after session.done returns. An injected prompt only shows up once the fake provider reads and echoes it, so a regression usually lands after the check. Later, `contains` (924-930) cannot distinguish one injection from two. (b) The 'partial launch' is a session.create of a different session with `"worktree":"invalid-relative-worktree"` (1127-1134), refused in prepare before anything is allocated (handlers/session.rs:878-882). Only `!...ok` is asserted, so any error passes, and the session under test is never partially launched. (c) `// detach stops frames on term2` is followed by an unchecked `term2.call(... "session.detach" ...)` (431-432). Nothing verifies that frames stop, although the socket door implements it (socket.rs:514).
findings.impact: Regressions in Done-turn assignment injection, in launch-prompt preservation across a failed spawn, and in socket detach all pass, while the test names and comments say they are covered.
findings.fix: (a) After the trailing Stop, wait and assert the next-task echo appears exactly once, and keep the negative check only after a bounded wait. (b) Make the same session's spawn fail (point providers.claude.path at a missing file), restore it, respawn, and assert the stored assignment and the provider.not_installed code. (c) After detach, send input and assert term2 receives no frame within ~500 ms while `term` does.

v1.reason: (c) sessions.rs:431-432 sends session.detach and only unwraps the transport result. It never asserts resp.ok and never checks that term2 stops getting frames, even though socket.rs:507-517 implements exactly that, aborting the attach task when the response is ok. (b) In allocated_assignments_survive_partial_launch_and_omitted_spawn_prompt (sessions.rs:1091+), the 'later allocation can fail' step is a session.create of another session with worktree 'invalid-relative-worktree'. Prepare refuses it at handlers/session.rs:877-879 (`!path.is_absolute()`) before anything is written, and only `!ok` is asserted. The session under test never goes through a failed launch. (a) The negative check at sessions.rs:914-915 runs right after session.done returns. An injection done straight into the PTY would show up only after the fake provider echoes it, so the check usually races ahead of a regression.
v1.correction: For (a), the finding overstates it. Duplicate deferred assignment is partly covered: mail_count == 1 (sessions.rs:931-934) catches duplicated assignment mail, and the agent_done count and state checks (sessions.rs:919-922) cover the trailing-Stop marker logic. What stays uncovered is a double PTY injection, or an injection into the unfinished turn. These are weak assertions that don't match their comments, not missing coverage of whole features. Severity stays low.
