findings.title: Confirming a hook-raised guardrail hold grants nothing, so the agent's (or your own) retry is held again
findings.evidence: For a held `guardrail.gate`, `confirm` only re-runs `guardrail::evaluate(... skip_policy: Some(&hold.policy), grants: None)` (598-617). It returns a synthetic `GateOut { verdict: Allow }` as `outcome` (619-624), marks the hold confirmed (646-651) and mails "Guardrail hold {} was confirmed by {}." (657-665). Nothing is persisted that a later gate reads. `Grants::load` selects only `op = 'guardrail.request' AND state = 'confirmed'` (guardrail/grants.rs:51-53), and `gate()` (501-568) never looks at earlier holds. The hook that raised the hold has already exited: `claude_pre_tool` returns `Ok(2)` for any non-ok response (relay-cli/src/main.rs:471-483), and `codex_pre_tool` does the same (520-530). tests/guardrails.rs:219-229 and 170-177 assert only `outcome.ok == true` and never re-run the gate. At 263-269 the next gate on the same file is simply held again.
findings.impact: Trigger: a Claude or Codex agent's Write/Edit removes more than 50 lines of an untracked or modified file (destructive_write), or fails a shape gate. The edit is held. The user clicks "Allow once" (apps/relay-native/src/guardrail_pages.rs:276, on a card reading "{who} is waiting on you", :254). The agent is told the hold was confirmed and retries. Each retry creates a new hold and notification, and the edit never goes through. The same loop hits the user's own terminal `git commit` through Relay's pre-commit hook (`--actor user` gives a user_bypass hold). Only bus-op writes (file.write, git.commit) work, because confirm replays those (582-596). Docs promise otherwise: BUS.md:500 says "you confirm, it proceeds".
findings.fix: When confirming a hold whose frozen op is guardrail.gate, record a one-use permission for exactly that action (session, kind, path, hash of new_text/diff/command). `gate` should check it before evaluating and consume it on use. Alternatively, convert the hold into a once-scoped grant through the existing grants machinery (path for destructive_write, command or cap for the others), and extend it to user actors for the pre-commit case. Add a test: hold → confirm → identical gate allows once → a second identical gate holds again.

v1.reason: I traced this independently. guardrail.rs:574-668 `confirm`: when the frozen op is "guardrail.gate", it only re-runs `guardrail::evaluate` with `skip_policy: Some(&hold.policy)`. It returns a synthetic GateOut Allow, marks the hold confirmed and mails the session. It writes no row or grant that a later gate consults. `gate()` (501-568) calls `evaluate_granted`, and that function loads only `Grants::load`. Grants::load selects `op = 'guardrail.request' AND state = 'confirmed'` (grants.rs:51-53), so a confirmed guardrail.gate hold is never read again. The PreToolUse adapters do not wait for a resolution: `claude_pre_tool` and `codex_pre_tool` (relay-cli/src/main.rs:466-483, 521-530) print the error and return exit 2. The provider tool call is therefore already blocked by the time the user confirms. The agent's only route is to retry, and the retry is evaluated from scratch. For an agent, `destructive_decision` (guardrail.rs:722-752) holds through `refuse_or_user_hold`, then `hold()`, whenever the file is not recoverable from git (allow_if_recoverable). Shape gates hold the same way, so the retry is held again. A user actor (pre-commit hook) gets a user_bypass hold every time. The test at tests/guardrails.rs:213-229 asserts only `outcome.ok`. At 263-269 it shows that the next gate is held again. The behaviour contradicts BUS.md:500 ("you confirm, it proceeds") and the "Allow once" button in guardrail_pages.rs:276. D22 covers what confirmation skips, not this gap. The workaround is the agent asking for a path exception through guardrail.request, but the hold error carries no hint pointing there, because `hold()` adds no hint.
v1.correction: The confirm logic for gate holds is at handlers/guardrail.rs:597-668. The original's 598 is the start of the gate-payload branch. The test showing a re-hold (guardrails.rs:263) uses a different new_text ("tiny\n"), not an identical retry, so it is weaker evidence than claimed. The mechanism still stands from the code. The fix as proposed is sound: on confirm, record a one-use permission keyed on session, kind, path and a hash of the payload, and have gate consume it. The simplest variant inserts a once-scoped exception through the existing grants machinery. That machinery is agent-only (`evaluate_granted` returns early for non-agent actors), so the user pre-commit case needs its own handling.

v2.reason:
(a) I confirmed this from the code myself. For a frozen op of "guardrail.gate", `confirm` (handlers/guardrail.rs:598-666) only re-runs `guardrail::evaluate` with `skip_policy: Some(&hold.policy)`. It returns a synthetic `GateOut{Allow}`, marks the hold confirmed and mails "Guardrail hold N was confirmed". Nothing it writes is read by a later gate. `gate()` (501-568) calls `evaluate_granted`. That function reads only `Grants::load`, whose query is `op = 'guardrail.request' AND state='confirmed'` (grants.rs:51-53). The engine never writes the frozen new_text. Contrast the bus-op path (582-596), which really replays file.write/git.commit. The Claude adapter returns exit 2 on any non-ok response without waiting (relay-cli/src/main.rs:471-483), and its hook has a 30s timeout (hooks.rs:351). So the tool call is already dead when the user confirms. BUS.md:550 says the mail exists "so a waiting agent learns the answer". The agent's only move is to retry, and the retry is judged from scratch against an unchanged file, so it is held again with a new hold and a new notification (insert_hold at guardrail.rs:1242-1254). D35 shows the author believed hook holds get the same "frozen hold replay" as bus edits.

(b) Reachability. With default config (settings.rs:29-32: shape_gates and protected_paths empty), the agent trigger is destructive_write: more than 50 lines removed, or more than 40% of a file of at least 30 lines. Because allow_if_recoverable passes committed-unmodified and ignored files (guardrail.rs:725-729), it fires only on untracked or modified files. That is exactly an agent's own work in progress, for example rewriting a 60-line file it created earlier with 25 of its lines changed. So it happens in normal Claude sessions, not just rare ones. The user trigger is a terminal `git commit` in a Relay worktree (no RELAY_SESSION, hooks.rs:132 `--actor user`) over 40 files or 2000 lines. That gives a user_bypass hold whose message says "confirm to bypass this policy" (1032). Confirming it does nothing for the next commit.

(c) Consequence. The "Allow once" button (guardrail_pages.rs:276) reports success, since outcome.ok is true. The agent stays blocked, and every retry adds a hold and a notification. There is no data loss, because the write is blocked, which is the safe direction. Partial escapes exist:
- For destructive_write, the agent can ask for a path grant with guardrail.request (granted_path at guardrail.rs:722). The hold error carries no hint pointing there, because `refuse_or_user_hold` adds hints only on the refuse branch (1035-1036).
- A stuck agent can write through Bash (`cat > f`), since exec gates do not measure writes. Then the guardrail is sidestepped rather than honoured.
- The user can commit with `--no-verify`, or from the Git panel, where git.commit replays properly (D141).
- A configured shape-gate hold is a pure dead end: shape gates are not grantable (grants.rs:28, no grant check at guardrail.rs:526-534 and 548-560).

(d) High fits the rubric: a failure in a normal flow, where the user's approval of a held agent write never takes effect. It is not critical: there is no data loss, no security hole and no hang, and workarounds exist.

(e) The one-use, per-action permission is the right fix, with the adjustments listed in the correction field.
v2.correction:
1. Codex is not affected. `codex_pre_tool` sends every tool, including Write, Edit and apply_patch, as `kind: exec` (relay-cli/src/main.rs:507-512). For an agent, the exec policies only refuse (guardrail.rs:815-846; `refuse_or_user_hold` holds agents only for destructive_write and shape_gate, 1035-1036). The trigger is Claude Write/Edit/MultiEdit, plus user-actor commit gates from the pre-commit hook.
2. "The edit never goes through" overstates it. For destructive_write, a guardrail.request path grant does lift the retry (guardrail.rs:722), but nothing on the hold tells the agent so. An agent can also sidestep the rule through a Bash write. Only configured shape gates are a hard dead end.
3. Fix refinements:
   - (a) On a matching permission, evaluate with `skip_policy = hold.policy` instead of skipping evaluation. D22 says confirmation skips exactly one policy, and protected paths and caps must still be re-checked against current files.
   - (b) For commit gates the frozen payload is just `{session, kind}`. A payload hash would then admit whatever is staged next, so the key must include the staged numstat or the hold's details.
   - (c) Converting the hold to a grant cannot cover shape_gate, which is not grantable. `evaluate_granted` also ignores grants for non-agents (guardrail.rs:484), and a path grant is broader than the confirmed action.
   - (d) Give agent hold errors a hint: wait for the confirmation mail, then retry the identical action.
   - (e) Expire the permission with the session, the same way holds expire.
4. Minor: the re-hold test at tests/guardrails.rs:263-269 uses a different new_text ("tiny\n"), so it is consistent with the claim but does not prove it on its own.

findings.title: Default denied commands only match their canonical spelling: `git push origin main --force`, `git push -f`, `rm -fr`, `git clean -fdx` all pass the gate
findings.evidence: `denied_matches` lowercases the unquoted words of each command and requires the pattern's words as one contiguous window: `bare.windows(wanted.len()).any(|window| window == wanted.as_slice())` (975-988). The defaults are `["rm -rf", "git reset --hard", "git clean -fd", "git push --force"]` (handlers/settings.rs:33). I ran a faithful Python port of shell_commands/denied_matches. Only `git push --force origin main` and `git reset --hard HEAD` were denied. These were all allowed: `git push origin main --force`, `git push -f origin main`, `git push --force-with-lease`, `git push origin +main`, `git -C . push --force`, `rm -fr build`, `rm -r -f build`, `rm --recursive --force build`, `git clean -fdx`, `git clean -df`, `git reset HEAD~1 --hard`. The tests that claim to resist bypass use only the canonical spelling (tests/guardrails.rs:339-346, 590-597, 645-652; the test fn is named `..._resist_bypass`).
findings.impact: Agents routinely put the force flag last, or write `-f`, `rm -fr` or `git clean -fdx`. Each of these runs with no refusal, no notification and no `refused` audit row, so the protection silently does not apply to the commands it exists to stop.
findings.fix: Normalize each command before matching. Skip git global options before the subcommand (`-C <dir>`, `-c k=v`, `--git-dir=`). Split combined short flags (`-fr` → `-f -r`). Treat a pattern as program + subcommand + a set of required flags matched in any order. Add flag aliases: `-f`/`--force`/`--force-with-lease`/`+refspec` for push; `-r`/`-R`/`--recursive` with `-f`/`--force` for rm; any flag cluster containing f and d for clean. Table-test every spelling above.

v1.reason: `denied_matches` (guardrail.rs:971-992) lowercases a command's unquoted words and requires the pattern's words as one contiguous window: `bare.windows(wanted.len()).any(|window| window == wanted.as_slice())`. The defaults at handlers/settings.rs:33 are `rm -rf`, `git reset --hard`, `git clean -fd` and `git push --force`. By direct reading, `git push origin main --force` (bare=[git,push,origin,main,--force]) has no window [git,push,--force]. `git push -f`, `rm -fr`, `rm -r -f`, `git clean -fdx`, `git clean -df`, `git -C . push --force` and `git reset HEAD~1 --hard` all fail to match too. Nothing in D103 or BUS.md (line 1041 says only 'matched against parsed argv') describes the patterns as exact contiguous spellings. Each of these runs with no refusal, which fits the rubric's 'safety check that can be silently bypassed'.
v1.correction: `--force-with-lease` is arguably a deliberately safe variant and need not be denied, so leave it out of the alias set. The pre-commit/write gates do not cover destructive shell commands, so nothing else catches these. Fix as proposed: normalize git global options, split combined short flags, and match program + subcommand + required flag set in any order. Table-test each spelling.

v2.reason:
(a) Confirmed two ways: by reading the code, and with a faithful Python port of shell_commands, is_guardrail_dry_run and denied_matches (guardrail.rs:894-998). denied_matches lowercases a command's unquoted words. It accepts a default pattern only if the pattern's words appear as one contiguous window (line 988). None of the 12 claimed spellings matches. The controls are all denied: `git push --force origin main`, `git reset --hard HEAD~1`, `sudo rm -rf /`, `rm -Rf x` and `cd repo && git push --force origin main`.

(b) It is reachable on every agent Bash call. install_claude registers `relay hook claude-pre-tool` for `Edit|Write|MultiEdit|Bash` (hooks.rs:350). claude_pre_tool sends each Bash command as `guardrail.gate {kind: exec}` and blocks only when the gate refuses (relay-cli/src/main.rs:393-466). The gate path is gate -> evaluate_granted -> evaluate_exec -> denied_matches, with no normalization at any step. On Allow it adds only the device-lease check (handlers/guardrail.rs:532). Write roots apply only to Write and Edit. Relay's generated Claude settings hold only statusLine, with no permission deny rules (hooks.rs:397). guardrail.check and guardrail.explain use the same matcher, so an agent that asks first is told `git push -f` is allowed. Who triggers it: a well-meaning agent using a common spelling, such as `git push -f`, `git push origin <branch> --force`, `git clean -fdx` or `rm -fr`. This is not every session, but it is routine whenever an agent cleans a tree or re-pushes after a rebase.

(c) The command runs with no refusal, no hold, no notification and no refusal audit row. Meanwhile the native settings page describes the list as 'Commands agents may not run' (apps/relay-native/src/guardrail_settings.rs:70). A force push overwrites remote history, and commits that exist only on the remote are lost. `git clean -fdx`, `git reset HEAD~1 --hard` and `rm -fr` destroy uncommitted or untracked work in the session's checkout. A session created with worktree `primary` runs in the user's own checkout (handlers/session.rs:860).

(d) High fits the rubric: 'a safety check that can be silently bypassed'. It is not critical. The list was never a boundary against an agent deliberately evading it: quoted `bash -c` bodies, scripts and interpreters pass regardless. Harm also requires an agent to choose a destructive command in the first place. It is not medium either, because the shipped defaults miss the most common spellings of exactly the commands they name. The tests use only canonical spellings: guardrails.rs:279 (the `_resist_bypass` test), 339-346, 590-597 and 645-652, and also agent_surface.rs:229-239.

(e) The proposed fix is right in direction; caveats are under correction.

Side note for the user: while I was verifying this, the user's live Relay hook refused one of my Bash commands. The command only wrote this test data into a scratchpad heredoc. Relay's reader has no heredoc support, so it read the data as commands. A guardrail refusal for this audit session will therefore appear in Relay's notifications. I did not try to bypass it or ask for an exception. Nothing destructive was run.
v2.correction:
The lines and mechanism are accurate.

Same root cause, not in the finding:
- A path-qualified program also passes: `/bin/rm -rf x`, `/usr/bin/git push --force`.
- So does any option placed between the subcommand and the force flag: `git push -u origin main --force`, `git push origin HEAD --force`.

Caveats on the fix:
1. Keep searching for the program word anywhere in the command, compared by basename. Do not anchor it at argv[0]. `sudo rm -rf`, `xargs rm -rf`, `env X=1 git push --force` and `find . -exec rm -rf {} +` are denied today only because matching is unanchored, and a naive argv[0] normalization would let them through. Requiring the program word to start a word also removes today's false positive, `echo git push --force`, which is refused.
2. Splitting short-flag clusters and matching flags in any order can be generic, so user-configured patterns benefit too. Long/short aliases cannot: `-f`/`--force` for push and `-r`/`-R`/`--recursive` for rm are specific to each program. They need an explicit alias table for the shipped defaults.
3. A `+refspec` is a real force push and belongs in the alias set. Whether to deny `--force-with-lease` is a policy choice; agree it is optional.
4. Grants are unaffected, because covers_command compares exact bare words.
5. Two related gaps are separate root causes, and flag normalization does not close them. Parentheses are not separators, so `(rm -rf build)` passes. `bash -c '...'`, `sh -c` and `eval` bodies are treated as quoted data under D103.

Even after the fix, the list guards against accidental spellings, not against an agent deliberately evading it. Add the table test to agent_surface.rs as well as guardrails.rs.

Separately, as observed live: the reader has no heredoc support, so heredoc data containing a pattern is refused. This fails closed (a false positive), so its severity is low.

findings.title: Heredoc bodies (and Codex patch lines) are parsed as shell commands, so writing text that mentions a denied command is refused
findings.evidence:
`shell_commands` ends a command on every newline (`';' | '
' | '|' | '&' => { ... end_command!(); }`, 939-945) and does not recognize `<<TAG`. On the Python port, `cat > NOTES.md <<'EOF'
Never run rm -rf on the build host.
EOF` splits into commands `[cat > NOTES.md <<EOF] [Never run rm -rf on the build host.] [EOF]` and gives `denied_by=['rm -rf']`. The same splitter feeds `self_approval` (858). In this audit session the live Relay PreToolUse hook refused one of my Bash commands with guardrail.self_approval; the command only wrote a Python analysis script through a heredoc. Codex edits go through the same path: `codex_pre_tool` sends `apply_patch`/`Edit`/`Write` as `kind: exec` with `tool_input.command` (relay-cli/src/main.rs:506-512; D132), so every patch line becomes a "command".
findings.impact: D103's promise that data naming a pattern is not a match does not hold for heredocs, or for any Codex patch. An agent writing a README, Makefile or CI script with an unquoted `rm -rf` or `git push --force` line is refused with guardrail.command. Text that looks like a Relay CLI call is refused as self-approval, which no grant can lift.
findings.fix: Teach the splitter heredocs: on `<<`/`<<-` followed by a (possibly quoted) delimiter, consume the body through the terminator line and record it as quoted data. Gate a Codex apply_patch as writes (paths plus content), not as an exec command line. Add tests next to guardrails.rs:772.

v1.reason:
`shell_commands` (guardrail.rs:892-958) ends a command on every '
', ';', '|' and '&' (lines 939-945) and has no heredoc handling. In `cat > F <<'EOF'
Never run rm -rf here
EOF`, the body line becomes its own command with unquoted words [never, run, rm, -rf, ...]. `denied_matches` (guardrail.rs:971-992) then finds the window `rm -rf` and refuses it. `self_approval` uses the same splitter, so a body line such as `relay q guardrail.confirm` is refused as self-approval, which no grant can lift (guardrail.rs:816-826). For Codex, `codex_pre_tool` (relay-cli/src/main.rs:507-512) sends `apply_patch`, `Edit` and `Write` as `kind: exec` with `tool_input.command`, which is the whole patch text. Every added line of a patch is therefore parsed as a shell command. D132 says patch invocations take the same gate path but does not address this. D103's intent, that data merely naming a pattern is not a match, is broken here.
v1.correction: Prose in a patch adds a second failure mode: an unmatched apostrophe (`don't`) opens a quote that swallows text up to the next `'`. That can hide a line or expose one, so matching on patch text is unreliable in both directions. Fix: skip heredoc bodies in the splitter. Gate Codex apply_patch, Edit and Write as file writes (the target paths), not as exec, since the pre-commit gate is the write-set boundary under D132.

findings.title: Agents can still answer their own guardrails as `user`: the CLI honours `--actor user` inside a session, and the gate only string-matches the command
findings.evidence: `actor_from_env` returns the override before it looks at the session: `if let Some(a) = override_ { return Ok((Actor::parse(a)..., std::env::var("RELAY_TOKEN").ok())); }` (118-121). The socket accepts `user` with no credential: `(Actor::User, _) | (Actor::Test, _) => Ok(None)` (engine.rs:1355). The only barrier is `self_approval` (guardrail.rs:857-881). It flags a command only when some word's file stem starts with "relay" or the word contains "RELAY_BIN" (860-863). By code reading only (I deliberately did not run this against the live engine): in `R=relay; $R --actor user q guardrail.confirm '{"hold_id":N}'` the second command has no qualifying word, so it is allowed. Any non-relay socket client (python, `nc -U`) is never inspected at all. BUS.md:580-584 and §14 document this as best effort, but the test at guardrails.rs:753 is named `agents_cannot_answer_guardrails_as_the_user_from_a_shell` and checks only literal spellings.
findings.impact: One level of indirection is enough. An agent (for example one steered by injected repo or web content) can confirm its own exception requests, revoke grants, or call `guardrail.config.set`/`settings.set` to remove denied commands and protected paths. Every guardrail can be switched off by the agent it is meant to constrain.
findings.fix: Cheap hardening: the CLI refuses `--actor user|test` and `RELAY_ACTOR` whenever `RELAY_SESSION` or `RELAY_TOKEN` is in its environment. On the socket, read SO_PEERCRED at accept and refuse `user`/`test` claims from a peer whose /proc environ holds a live session token, or whose parent chain reaches a live session PTY (pty::relay_children already scans /proc environ). Rename the test, or add the indirect spellings as documented known gaps.

v1.reason: `actor_from_env` (crates/relay-cli/src/main.rs:118-121) checks the `--actor` override before it looks at RELAY_SESSION. `resolve_actor` (crates/relay-core/src/engine.rs:1355) accepts `Actor::User` on any door with no credential. The only agent-side barrier is `self_approval` (guardrail.rs:857-881), called from `evaluate_exec` at guardrail.rs:816. It needs a word whose file stem starts with "relay" or that contains RELAY_BIN, plus an `--actor user|test` word or an answer op name. In `R=relay; $R --actor user q guardrail.confirm ...` the second command has neither a relay stem nor RELAY_BIN, so it is allowed. `env -i $R q guardrail.confirm` also gets through, because `-i` is not one of the identity-shedding forms it checks. Any non-CLI socket client is never inspected at all. BUS.md:580-584 and BUS.md:30 say this is best effort and not a security boundary against a same-uid process, so the gap is documented. It is not harmless: the agents being constrained can still turn off every guardrail. The test at tests/guardrails.rs:753 checks only literal spellings while its name claims the general property.
v1.correction: This is a documented design limitation, not an accident. Guardrails are already bypassable by same-uid code in other ways, for example by writing a script file and running it, so medium is the right ceiling rather than critical. The concrete, cheap fix is in the CLI: refuse an explicit `--actor user|test` or RELAY_ACTOR when RELAY_SESSION or RELAY_TOKEN is set. Peer-credential or /proc checks on the socket would be a larger design change. Also rename the test, or document the known gaps in it.

findings.title: device.run.stop and build stop kill only the wrapper shell; the Gradle process, and the test's held build, keep running
findings.evidence: The command is spawned as `Command::new(shell).args(["-lc", &format!("{command} 2>&1")])` with no process group (1821-1828); there is no `process_group`/`setsid` anywhere in the device code. `RunRuntime::stop` SIGKILLs only the direct child (`child.kill()`, crates/relay-core/src/device.rs:403-408). A /proc probe on this machine shows the command is a grandchild: for `sh -lc "sleep 1.5 2>&1"` the direct child is `sh` with `sleep` under it, and for `fish -lc "sleep 1.5 2>&1"` it is `fish` with `sleep` under it. `set_child` (device.rs:373-375) ignores an earlier stop, unlike `DeviceWatchRuntime::install` (33-41). The read loop returns `Streamed::Stopped` without waiting for the child (1842-1845). The test at bus.rs:614-640 waits for the `$ ./gradlew assembleHold` line, which is pushed at 1817 before the spawn. It then stops the run and asserts only `state == "stopped"`.
findings.impact: Stopping a device run or release build leaves Gradle running, and the worker thread stays blocked on the open pipe. An install the user cancelled can still land on the phone after RunStop has already released the device lease to other sessions (268-270). A stop that lands in the spawn window kills nothing, and a killed shell can be left as a zombie. In the test, the 10 s hold loop survives every run unnoticed.
findings.fix: Spawn the shell with `CommandExt::process_group(0)`. Have `RunRuntime::stop` signal the whole group (`libc::kill(-pid, SIGTERM)`, then SIGKILL after a grace, as recovery::kill_wait does). Make `set_child` kill at once if the run is already stopped. Always take and wait the child on the Stopped path. In the test, have the fake gradlew write `$$` to a file and assert that pid is gone after device.run.stop.

v1.reason: handlers/device.rs:1821-1828 spawns `fish -lc "<command> 2>&1"` (sh on the test instance). It sets no process_group, setsid or pre_exec; grep finds none in device code. `RunRuntime::stop` (device.rs:403-408) calls only `child.kill()` on the direct child. fish does not exec its last command. The command is `./gradlew ... install<Variant>` (run_command, 1037-1055), a script that execs java, and that java process is a grandchild that survives SIGKILL of fish. After stop, the read loop (1842-1845) returns Stopped on the next line without taking or waiting the child. That drops the pipe reader, and Gradle's PrintStream swallows write errors, so the build and install continue. The killed fish stays a zombie in runtime.child, and the runtime has already been removed from engine.device_runs. RunStop (handlers/device.rs:263-284) releases the device lease immediately, so an install the user cancelled can still land on a device that is now leased to another session. `set_child` (device.rs:373-375) does not check `stopped()`, unlike `DeviceWatchRuntime::install` (33-41). A stop issued between spawn and set_child therefore kills nothing. The bus test (bus.rs:614-640) asserts only the row state.
v1.correction: The worker thread does not stay blocked indefinitely. It exits on the first line Gradle prints after the stop, but the Gradle process keeps running. Fix: spawn with `process_group(0)` and have stop signal `-pid` (TERM, then KILL, as recovery.rs:20 kill_wait does). Killing the Gradle client also cancels the daemon's build. Also make set_child honour an earlier stop, and reap the child on the Stopped path.

findings.title: Run commands use a login shell, so the device bus tests depend on the developer's /etc/profile and ~/.profile
findings.evidence: The comment at 1818-1820 promises to "Keep bus tests independent of the developer's interactive shell", yet the test instance runs `sh -lc "{command} 2>&1"` (1821-1825). `/bin/sh` is bash here (readlink: /usr/bin/bash). For `sh -l`, bash reads /etc/profile (and through it /etc/profile.d/*.sh) and ~/.profile. Relay's `.env("ANDROID_HOME", sdk_root)` (1830) is set before those scripts run, so a profile export wins. bus.rs:271, 420-424, 472-478 and 517-524 assert the wrapper saw the fixture SDK. The bundle signing check also runs the real `jarsigner` found via JAVA_HOME or PATH (1939-1944). I checked this machine's profiles: none set ANDROID_*, so nothing triggers here.
findings.impact: On a machine whose profile exports ANDROID_HOME (the AUR android-sdk /etc/profile.d script, or `export ANDROID_HOME=` in ~/.profile), the device tests fail with a foreign SDK path. A profile that execs another shell breaks them entirely. In production, fish always reads config.fish, so `set -gx ANDROID_HOME` there silently overrides the configured device.sdk_path for Gradle, while adb and apksigner keep using the configured SDK.
findings.fix: Drop `-l` for the test instance (plain `sh -c`). In production, set ANDROID_HOME/ANDROID_SDK_ROOT inside the command string after shell start-up (for example a `set -gx ANDROID_HOME ...;` prefix), so the configured path wins.

v1.reason: `stream_command` (handlers/device.rs:1817-1831) runs `sh -lc` on the test instance and `fish -lc` in production, then sets ANDROID_HOME/ANDROID_SDK_ROOT on the process environment. A login `sh` (bash in sh mode, or dash) reads /etc/profile, which sources /etc/profile.d/*.sh, and ~/.profile. An export there replaces the fixture SDK path before the command runs. The comment at 1818-1820 claims the tests are independent of the developer's shell. Tests such as bus.rs:271 and bus.rs:420-424 assert that the fixture SDK path was seen, so they fail on a machine whose profile exports ANDROID_HOME. On Arch-family systems the android-sdk package ships such a /etc/profile.d script. In production, fish reads config.fish even for `-c`, so a `set -gx ANDROID_HOME` there overrides the configured device.sdk_path for the Gradle command only.
v1.correction: This is purely environmental: nothing triggers on this machine or, as far as can be shown, in CI, so low is right. Fix: drop `-l` for the test instance. In production, prepend the SDK exports to the command string (or pass `--no-config`), so the configured SDK path wins over shell start-up files.

findings.title: Socket-door test relies on 100 ms sleeps for a bus.wait to subscribe before the event it waits for
findings.evidence: `tokio::time::sleep(std::time::Duration::from_millis(100)).await;` with the comment "Give the waiter time to subscribe" (1049-1050, and again at 1070). The server subscribes only when it processes the request (`let mut rx = engine.subscribe();`, socket.rs:411). If the settings.set is dispatched first, the waiter sleeps its full 5 s and the test fails. Related ad-hoc timing in the same file: a hand-rolled 3 s deadline for the run to reach running (253-261, while wait_until uses 10 s). The fake logcat's `sleep 5` (186) is an unstated deadline too: if device.run.stop (281) arrives more than 5 s after running, the row reads "finished" and line 283 fails.
findings.impact: Intermittent failures on a loaded CI runner or developer machine, where many parallel tests are spawning shells. They are hard to reproduce.
findings.fix: Wait on a deterministic signal before mutating. For example, expose the broadcast receiver count (`Engine::subscriber_count()`) and poll until it rises. Use wait_until for the run state. Make the fake logcat block on a sentinel file the test removes, instead of `sleep 5`.

v1.reason: The 100 ms sleeps (bus.rs:1049-1050, 1070) are the only synchronisation between the waiter subscribing (`engine.subscribe()` inside the server's bus.wait handling, socket.rs:411) and the settings.set that should wake it. If the event is broadcast first, the waiter misses it and times out at 5 s, and the outer 5 s timeout or the `timed_out == false` assertion fails. However, this is a default `#[tokio::test]`, i.e. a current_thread runtime. During the sleep, the spawned waiter, the server's accept loop and the connection task all run on the same thread and need only microseconds of work. A loss needs the runtime thread starved for the whole window, with an unlucky poll order afterwards. The device-run 3 s deadline (bus.rs:253-261) and the fake logcat `sleep 5` (186) are similar unstated deadlines, but the steps between them are fast local waits. The race is real in principle; I could not establish that it ever fires.
v1.correction: The probability is lower than implied because the socket test runs on a current_thread runtime. A deterministic fix such as polling a subscriber count, or a wait_until on the run state instead of the hand-rolled 3 s loop, is cheap and removes the timing assumption. Of the three, the logcat `sleep 5` is the least likely to matter.

findings.title: Several bus.rs and guardrails.rs assertions cannot fail for the behaviour their comments claim
findings.evidence: (a) Subscription filter: settings.set (1026) is sent before workspace.create (1028), so the single `sub.next()` (1029) always sees settings.changed first. An unfiltered workspace.changed would come next and be swallowed by `sub.call(&...unsubscribe..., |_| {})` (1034), because Client::call hands events to on_event (socket.rs:810). The comment "the workspace event was filtered out" is never checked, and no unit test covers socket.rs's Filter. (b) "the signing password must not enter build output" (479-482) searches tasks.log. The fixture writes that file itself from `$1|$ANDROID_HOME|$RELAY_SIGNING_KEY_ALIAS|$secret|$2`, where `$secret` is only "set" or "bad". The run log, run.changed events and audit rows are never checked. (c) `assert!(!agent.ok, "a release build is user-only")` (663) and guardrails.rs:168 accept any error. (d) The comment at 928 says the failed mutation "was audited as error", but the test only checks project.get.
findings.impact: These regressions would all pass CI: broken event filtering (agents flooded with events), the password leaking into run logs, or a refusal raised for the wrong reason.
findings.fix: (a) Read events until the settings event and assert no workspace.changed arrives; or create the workspace first and assert the first event is settings.changed. (b) Assert the run buffer, event payloads and audit rows do not contain the password. (c) Assert the code `actor.allowlist`. (d) Assert the audit row, or fix the comment.

v1.reason: (a) bus.rs:1026 sends settings.set before workspace.create (1028), and connection tasks forward events in broadcast order, so the single `sub.next()` (1029) always gets settings.changed first. Any unfiltered workspace.changed would arrive next and be passed to the no-op on_event in `sub.call(...bus.unsubscribe...)`, because Client::call hands events to on_event (socket.rs:810). So 'the workspace event was filtered out' is never checked. socket.rs has no unit test of Filter::matches (211-221). The remote test (remote.rs:130) only checks that a matching event arrives. (b) The gradle fixture (bus.rs:349-356) writes only `$1|$ANDROID_HOME|$alias|$secret|$2` to tasks.log, where `$secret` is 'set' or 'bad'. `!tasks.contains("test-secret-123")` (479-482) can never fail: a password leaked into argv beyond $2, the run buffer, run events or audit rows would not be caught. (c) bus.rs:663 and guardrails.rs:168 assert only `!ok`, so any error code passes. (d) The comment at bus.rs:927 says 'was audited as error', but the code only checks project.get → not_found.
v1.correction: In (c), the in-process `Actor::Agent("merry-badger")` has no session. resolve_actor (engine.rs:1359-1363) accepts it with session id None, so the refusal is expected to come from the op's actor allowlist. Asserting that specific code would make the test meaningful. (b) is the most valuable fix: also assert that the run's attach() buffer and the run.changed and audit payloads lack the password.

findings.title: Hook-install test calls install_claude itself after session.spawn, so it cannot detect spawn no longer installing the Claude guardrail hook
findings.evidence: After `session.spawn` (420-425) the test runs `relay_core::hooks::install_claude(&worktree, Instance::Test, Path::new("relay")).unwrap();` (426). Only then does it assert the PreToolUse group count, the lifecycle hooks and `.relay/relay.mcp.json` (427-440). install_claude is idempotent (hooks.rs:333-353, 364-375), so those assertions hold whether or not prepare_launch (handlers/session.rs:482-484) installed anything.
findings.impact: A regression in which Claude sessions launch without Relay's PreToolUse hook would still pass. Such agents would run completely unguarded.
findings.fix: Assert the hooks and MCP config right after session.spawn. Keep the explicit second install only as an idempotency check, comparing against counts taken before it.

v1.reason: guardrails.rs:420-425 calls session.spawn. Line 426 then calls `relay_core::hooks::install_claude(&worktree, Instance::Test, Path::new("relay"))` before every assertion on settings.local.json: the PreToolUse group count of 2, the `Edit|Write|MultiEdit|Bash` matcher, the lifecycle hooks, and relay.mcp.json. install_claude is idempotent and merges, so those assertions hold even if prepare_launch (handlers/session.rs:482-484) stopped calling install_claude. No other test in crates/relay-core/tests checks that spawn installs the PreToolUse or claude-report hooks; a grep for MultiEdit and claude-report finds only this test.
v1.correction: Only part of this is uncovered. sessions.rs:805 and :832 independently check that session.spawn writes `.relay/relay.mcp.json`, so the MCP-config part is covered elsewhere. The gap is the PreToolUse guardrail hook and the lifecycle hooks. Fix: assert those right after session.spawn, then keep the explicit install_claude call only as an idempotency check, comparing group counts before and after.

findings.title: bus.rs fake adb carries dead `exec-out` and `cmd input` branches and leaves `sleep 5` grandchildren behind
findings.evidence: No production code runs `adb exec-out` or `adb shell cmd input`; `exec-out` appears only in device_lease.rs's command classifier. On the test instance, device.mirror.start never starts the worker (handlers/device.rs:103-105). device.mirror.input goes to `MirrorRuntime::send_control`, which queues into `pending` when no control socket exists (device.rs:279-289). The fixture's `$0.input` file (167) is never read, and bus.rs:224-225 assert only Ok. The track-devices, exec-out and logcat branches print and then `sleep 5` (150, 163, 186). Killing the `sh` that runs the script leaves `sleep` alive, so the device-watch and logcat worker threads stay blocked on the pipe for up to 5 s after a stop.
findings.impact: The test reads as if mirror input were verified end to end here; in fact the encoding is covered byte-exactly in tests/mirror.rs. Stray processes and threads outlive each run.
findings.fix: Delete the exec-out and cmd input branches, or assert the queued control bytes through a test accessor. Use `exec sleep 5` so a kill reaches the sleeping process.

v1.reason: In bus.rs:145-195 the fake adb has an `exec-out` branch (161-165) and a `shell cmd input` branch writing `$0.input` (166-169). Production code issues neither command. In crates/relay-core/src, `exec-out` appears only in device_lease.rs's classifier, and the only adb "cmd" use (handlers/device.rs:2038) is not `cmd input`. The `$0.input` file is never read. On the test instance, device.mirror.start never spawns mirror_worker (handlers/device.rs:103-105). device.mirror.input therefore only queues bytes into `pending` (device.rs:279-289), and bus.rs:224-225 assert only Ok, despite the test's name "..._mirror_input_...". In the track-devices, exec-out and logcat branches, `sleep 5` is not the script's last command (an `exit 0` follows). sh therefore forks it rather than exec'ing it, and killing sh leaves sleep holding the pipe for up to 5 s.
v1.correction: The impact is limited to test hygiene: misleading coverage and stray `sleep` processes for a few seconds. Fix as proposed: delete the dead branches (or assert the queued control bytes), and use `exec sleep 5`.

findings.title: Signing test leaves a plaintext test password and stub keystore in /tmp
findings.evidence: With an in-memory store, `signing_root` falls back to `std::env::temp_dir().join(format!("relay-signing-test-{}", std::process::id()))` (handlers/device.rs:1197-1205). The test instance writes the password in plaintext to `.test-secret` (1410-1413) and writes a stub keystore (1362-1365). The test removes only the per-project subdirectory, as its very last step (`std::fs::remove_dir_all(signing_dir)`, 665-668). The `relay-signing-test-<pid>` root is never removed, and any failed assertion before 668 leaves the whole profile behind.
findings.impact: Every cargo test run leaves a directory under /tmp. A failing run also leaves a file there containing `test-secret-123`.
findings.fix: Point the in-memory engine's signing root at a TempDir the test owns (for example via a configurable data dir), or create a drop guard for cleanup before calling device.signing.create.

v1.reason: The tests build the engine with `Store::open_memory()` (tests/bus.rs:13), whose path is `":memory:"` (store.rs:418). Its parent is the empty string, which `signing_root` filters out, so the root falls back to `temp_dir()/relay-signing-test-<pid>` (handlers/device.rs:1197-1205). With Instance::Test, `generate_signing_keystore` writes a stub keystore (1361-1365) and `store_signing_secret` writes the password to TEST_SIGNING_SECRET_FILE (1410-1413). The test only runs `remove_dir_all(signing_dir)` on the per-project subdirectory, as its last statement (bus.rs:665-668). So on success the empty `relay-signing-test-<pid>` directory is left behind. On any earlier assertion failure the profile, including the plaintext fixture password, is left too.
v1.correction: The impact is smaller than stated. The leftover secret file is created 0600 (`write_private_new`, device.rs:1338) and holds only the fixture string `test-secret-123`, not a user secret. On a passing run the leak is one empty directory per test process. This is test hygiene (test-quality) rather than a real resource leak. Fix: let the in-memory engine take a signing or data root (for example a TempDir owned by the test), or put the cleanup in a drop guard created before device.signing.create.

findings.title: Test-only behaviour is switched on `Instance::Test` inside production handlers, so the bus tests skip the real paths and the app's test instance fakes them
findings.evidence: Examples: `let shell = if engine.instance == Instance::Test { "sh" } else { "fish" };` (1821). The mirror worker is never started on the test instance (103-105). Signing writes a stub keystore and a plaintext password (1362-1365, 1410-1413, 1440-1442). session.rs:553 skips creating provider write roots. session.rs:1633 and git.rs:638 skip branch cleanup. provider.rs:60 skips the usage files. skills.rs:188 empties the user skill bases. `test` is a user-selectable instance (`RELAY_INSTANCE=test` or `--instance test`), and the native smoke harness runs on it (smoke_notes.rs:39-43).
findings.impact: The production branches never run in the bus suite: the fish invocation, the mirror worker started from the handler, keytool/secret-tool signing, and post-close branch cleanup. The process-tree bug in the stop finding is exactly the kind of production-path behaviour that ships untested this way. Running the real app as the test instance gives mirrors stuck at "starting" and a fake signing keystore.
findings.fix: Replace the instance checks with explicit engine options set by tests (shell program, whether to spawn the mirror worker, signing backend, inline branch cleanup, provider-home writes). Default every option to production behaviour on every instance.

v1.reason: The Instance::Test branches exist as cited. They are a deliberate hermetic seam for an instance that exists only for tests and the fixture smoke harness: smoke_notes.rs:39-43 requires RELAY_NATIVE_FIXTURE=1 together with RELAY_INSTANCE=test. The production branches they replace (fish, keytool, secret-tool, the scrcpy mirror worker, writes under the provider home) need external tools or a desktop keyring. CI and the bus suite do not have these. Replacing the instance checks with per-engine options would leave the same fakes in the tests, and no production path would gain coverage. The cited process-group bug is not masked by the seam either: `sh -lc` on the test instance has the same grandchild behaviour, and the test fails to catch it only because it asserts nothing about the process. A fake keystore on an instance named "test" is the intended behaviour, not a user-facing defect. The refactor costs effort and buys nothing concrete.

findings.title: `Door::Tauri` and `Doors::TauriOnly` are never used in production; bus.rs door tests exercise a door no client takes
findings.evidence: Outside tests, `Door::Tauri` is only ever matched, never constructed (engine.rs:785, 822, 1356). No op declares `Doors::TauriOnly` (relay-bus/src/registry.rs:85). The native client, CLI, MCP server and phone bridge all connect to the Unix socket (apps/relay-native/src/client.rs:173, relay-cli/src/main.rs:196-197, mcp.rs:221-222, relay-remote/src/bridge.rs:156). bus.rs:107-115 test "Tauri door carries only the user actor", and bus.rs:220 starts a mirror through that door.

findings.fix: Remove the Tauri door variant and `Doors::TauriOnly`, and point the door tests at Door::Socket.

v1.reason: Outside tests, `Door::Tauri` is never constructed. Every production dispatch uses Door::Socket (socket.rs:459, 511, 524, 652, 726, 739, 742) or Door::InProcess (socket.rs:927, provider_updates.rs:221). v1.correction: The impact is mostly cleanup: dead match arms and one misleading test assertion. That the real door accepts an unauthenticated `user` is the subject of finding #4, so it should not count again here. Fix: remove `Door::Tauri` and `Doors::TauriOnly`, including the mcp.rs:161 filter. Point bus.rs:220 at Door::Socket or InProcess, and drop the Tauri-door assertions.

findings.title: Every relay-core integration test file re-implements call/ok/wait_until and its fixtures
findings.evidence: 17 of the 18 files in crates/relay-core/tests define their own `fn call(`, and 13 define `fn ok(`. bus.rs, registry_remove.rs and sessions.rs each define `wait_until`. bus.rs and mirror.rs each define a `fake_adb`. guardrails.rs's Fixture (git init/config/commit, Store::open, workspace.create, project.add; 24-41) is repeated in agent_features.rs, agent_surface.rs and sessions.rs. There is no tests/common module. Within bus.rs alone, the chmod-755 block appears four times (191-193, 242-244, 293-295, 373-375) and the repo+workspace+project setup twice (228-234, 305-331).
findings.impact: Fixture-wide fixes must be repeated file by file. Examples: isolating the developer's git config (Fixture::new runs `git commit` under the global config, so commit.gpgsign=true would prompt or fail), or deterministic waits. The copies already differ.
findings.fix: Add crates/relay-core/tests/common/mod.rs with call/ok/err/wait_until/write_executable and a project fixture (setting GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL=/dev/null and GIT_CONFIG_NOSYSTEM=1 for fixture git calls), then `mod common;` in each file.

v1.reason: 17 of the 18 files in crates/relay-core/tests define `fn call(` (mirror.rs does not), about 12 define `fn ok(`, and bus.rs, registry_remove.rs and sessions.rs each define `wait_until`. There is no tests/common module. About ten files repeat the git init, config user.email/name and commit fixture. None of them isolates the global or system git config: only phase12.rs sets GIT_CONFIG_* env, and only for protocol.ext. A developer with commit.gpgsign=true or a global commit hook would see fixture commits prompt or fail in many files at once.
v1.correction: The divergence between copies is mostly in signature (with or without an actor argument, e vs engine), not behaviour, and `call` is a two-line wrapper. The real payoff is a shared repo fixture with git config isolation (GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL=/dev/null, GIT_CONFIG_NOSYSTEM=1), not deduplicating `call`. Low, modest payoff.

findings.title: task.dispatch runs session.create/spawn's slow prepare phases (git fetch, worktree add, hook install, skills copy) inside its locked transaction
findings.evidence: `task.dispatch` is a plain `e.register::<Dispatch>` handler (task.rs:1049), so its whole body runs with the store mutex held (engine.rs:954 `let mut conn = self.store.lock();` … 980 `(h.call)(&mut ctx, …)`). `dispatch_task` calls `ctx.invoke_registered("session.create", …)` (task.rs:683) and `ctx.invoke_registered(op, json!({"session":name}))` for session.spawn/wake/resume (task.rs:712). With `fanout` it repeats this for every not-done descendant (task.rs:1067-1075). `invoke_registered` runs a staged op's prepare 'against the transaction already open' (engine.rs:325-342). session.create's prepare is exactly the work its own comment says must stay unlocked: 'Fetch, checkout, `git worktree list` and the hook install all shell out … None of it belongs under the global store mutex' (session.rs:854-856). That work is `refresh_new_worktree` → `git fetch --all --prune` with a 20 s timeout (git.rs:938-945), `worktree::create` → `git worktree add` with 120 s (worktree.rs:214), and `install_git` (session.rs:892). The launch prepare (session.rs:468-593) runs `git config` hook installs, copies skill folders and writes brief files before finish_launch forks the PTY (session.rs:646). D149 says this nested path is taken 'only' by guardrail.confirm replaying git.commit. The native client already gives task.dispatch a 180 s timeout (client.rs:69). board.rs:528-532 exercises the create+fanout path.
findings.impact: Trigger: `task.dispatch {task_id, create:{…}, fanout:true}` (CLI or any bus client) on a project with a remote, or the task page's Dispatch button (task_pages.rs:652) aimed at a Created/Parked/Restorable session. Consequence: the one store mutex is held through every fetch (≤20 s), checkout (≤120 s) and hook `git config` call, per dispatched task. Every other request stalls for seconds to minutes: UI refreshes, every agent's MCP calls, every PreToolUse `guardrail.gate`. The side effects also happen inside a transaction that can still roll back (engine.rs:1074). So a fanout that fails on a later child (e.g. a fetch timeout) leaves earlier children's worktrees, branches, hook dirs and running agent PTYs behind, while their session rows vanish.
findings.fix: Stop reaching staged ops through invoke_registered from a locked handler. Split dispatch into three steps: (1) create the sessions through their own staged `session.create` requests, with an unlocked prepare; (2) one short locked transaction for the task/queue assignment; (3) launch each session through its own staged `session.spawn`/`wake`/`resume`. Add a test in the style of mirror.rs's `mirror_input_is_answered_without_the_store` that proves another request is served while a dispatch's checkout runs. Correct the invoke_registered comment and D149.

v1.reason: Task.dispatch is a plain `e.register::<Dispatch>` (task.rs:1049), so it runs with the store mutex and transaction held (engine.rs:952-980). `dispatch_task` calls `ctx.invoke_registered("session.create", …)` (task.rs:683) and `ctx.invoke_registered(op, …)` for spawn, wake or resume (712). It repeats both for each descendant under fanout (1067-1075). For a staged op, `invoke_registered` (engine.rs:308-360) runs its prepare inside an `Unlocked` with `held: Some(self.tx)`, i.e. under the lock. The prepare of session.create (session.rs:833-895) is the work its own comment (854-856) says must not run under the mutex: `refresh_new_worktree` (a fetch when the branch does not exist, git.rs:969-973), `worktree::create`, and `hooks::install_git`. Launch prepare (`prepare_launch`, session.rs:~468) installs git, Claude and Codex hooks and copies skills. D149 (DECISIONS.md:816-818) says this nested-prepare path is used 'only' for guardrail.confirm replaying git.commit, so dispatch is an undocumented second user and the doc has drifted. The flow is reachable in normal use. The op is UserOnly, but the phone door calls `task.dispatch` with `create` (relay-remote/tests/remote.rs:311-315, start:false still runs session.create's fetch and worktree add). The native task page's Dispatch button sends an existing `session` with start defaulting to true (task_pages.rs:646-654), which runs the launch prepare under the lock. The rollback concern also holds: `finish_launch` forks the PTY inside the transaction (session.rs:646). If a later fanout child fails, the rollback removes the earlier session rows but leaves their worktrees, hook config and running PTYs behind.
v1.correction: Calibration: the native UI's Dispatch button uses an existing session, so it pays only the launch prepare (git config hook installs and skill copies, usually well under a second). The long freezes (a fetch up to its timeout, a `git worktree add` with LFS filters) come from the create path, used by the phone door's dispatch, the CLI and fanout. A single fanout pays this once per child, serially under one lock. Also correct D149 and the comment on `invoke_registered`, which claim the nested prepare is used only by guardrail.confirm.

v2.reason:
(a) The code does what the finding says. `task.dispatch` is a plain `e.register::<Dispatch>` (task.rs:1049) and is registered nowhere else, so its body runs under `self.store.lock()` and inside the transaction (engine.rs:954-980). `dispatch_task` calls `ctx.invoke_registered("session.create", …)` (task.rs:683), then spawn, wake or resume (task.rs:712). For a staged op, `invoke_registered` runs its prepare with `held: Some(self.tx)` (engine.rs:328-342). `Unlocked::read` then reuses the held connection (engine.rs:177-179), so the whole prepare runs under the global mutex. That prepare is the work its own comment says must not be locked (session.rs:854-856). With no `branch` in the payload, `existing_worktree_branch(root, None)` returns false, so every create runs `git fetch --all --prune` (20 s bound, git.rs:938-973). It then runs `git worktree add` (120 s bound, worktree.rs:214) and `install_git`, which makes about four `git` calls with a 10 s bound each (hooks.rs:75-154). The launch prepare (session.rs:468-593) adds the hook and adapter installs, skill copies and brief writes. Then `Pty::spawn` forks the agent inside the transaction (session.rs:646). This breaks CLAUDE.md's first invariant and BUS.md §5.1 ('p99 < 5 ms … anything that takes longer (git, spawn, build) returns a handle'). No comment or decision exempts it: D149 (DECISIONS.md:815-819) and engine.rs:145-148 and 325-327 accept the nested cost 'only' for guardrail.confirm replaying git.commit.

(b) Who triggers it. The main trigger is the phone, not fanout. The phone app's default "New request" (`onBoard` defaults to true) and its Board dispatch action both send `task.dispatch {create:{project_id,provider,role}, start:true}`. relay-remote/tests/remote.rs:311 pins that payload, and the phone door admits the user actor (wire.rs:100). So every phone-initiated dispatch takes this path. On the desktop, the main launch flow avoids it on purpose (launch.rs:798-819 runs session.create, then dispatch with a session and start:false, then session.spawn). The desktop's task-page Dispatch button (task_pages.rs:647-654, start defaults to true) pays only the launch prepare, and only when the chosen session is Created, Parked or Restorable. That is tens to hundreds of ms. No first-party client sends `fanout:true`; only a hand-written `relay cmd` or a custom client does.

(c) What happens. While a dispatch holds the lock, every request that needs the store waits. That includes every agent's Edit/Write/Bash PreToolUse `guardrail.gate` (a plain register at guardrail.rs:304, with a 30 s hook timeout at hooks.rs:350-351), every agent socket call (the token check locks the store, engine.rs:1378), lifecycle reports and all desktop data requests. Desktop requests have a 30 s client timeout (client.rs:70), so an LFS-heavy checkout makes them fail with "Request timed out". Keystrokes still work (D148). How long the stall lasts:
- A project with no remote: `git fetch --all --prune` exits 0 at once (I checked this in a scratch repo), so the stall is the checkout plus hook installs, roughly seconds.
- A project with a remote: one network fetch (up to 20 s) is added.
- A large or LFS-backed checkout can take up to 120 s. The native client's 180 s timeout and its LFS comment (client.rs:68-69) show the author expects creates to be that slow.

The rollback concern is real but secondary. In the phone's single dispatch, a failure in the spawn phase (for example `provider.not_installed` from providers::executable) rolls back the session row and task move. The worktree, the branch and the worktree's core.hooksPath stay behind. Recovery sweeps the hook directory at the next start (recovery.rs:123-143). Running agent processes are orphaned only when a later step fails after a spawn, which in practice means fanout. Recovery reaps those only on the next engine start (recovery.rs:64-74).

(d) High is right: the bus freezes in a normal flow (every phone dispatch), for seconds up to minutes, across all agents. It is not critical: every step has a time limit, nothing is lost, and the engine recovers.

(e) The fix's direction is correct, and effort L is fair. The launch must stay after the assignment is committed, because the launch reads the brief, which includes the assignment (plan_launch → awareness::brief). So each sub-step needs its own short transaction, in the order create → assign → launch. Inline composition cannot do this.
v2.correction:
1. Restate the trigger. The common path is the phone's default "New request" and its Board dispatch, both sending `task.dispatch {create, start:true}` with no fanout. That runs one fetch, one `git worktree add`, the hook installs and the launch prepare under the lock. Fanout reaches this only through hand-written bus calls, so the per-child repetition and the rollback that orphans running agents apply only to that path. The desktop Dispatch button pays only the launch prepare, under a second.

2. The fetch only costs time when the project has a remote; with none, `git fetch --all` returns immediately.

3. Add the missing references: BUS.md §5.1 (p99 < 5 ms; anything slower returns a handle), engine.rs:145-148 (a stale doc comment on `Unlocked.held`), guardrail.rs:304, engine.rs:1378 and hooks.rs:351 for which requests stall, and DECISIONS.md:815-819 for the exact D149 sentence (line 797 is only where D149 starts).

4. The same nested-prepare-under-lock also happens in project.remove → session.close (workspace.rs:328). It costs much less there (hook teardown `git config` calls) and the op is rare, but it is another reason D149's "only that path" is stale.

5. Fix:
   - Make `invoke_registered` refuse staged ops except an explicit allowlist (guardrail.confirm's replay), so no composite can quietly regain this cost.
   - Implement dispatch as a staged op whose prepare issues session.create, then the assignment with `start:false` (as it is done today), then spawn/wake/resume, each as its own in-process request. Alternatively, have the phone compose those three calls the way launch.rs does.
   - Keep the order create → assign (committed) → launch.
   - Return per-child outcomes, because fanout becomes partial-commit rather than all-or-nothing. Today's all-or-nothing is already not real: worktrees, hooks and processes are not rolled back.
   - Add the concurrency test and correct D149 and both engine.rs comments.

findings.title: denied_commands matcher misses ordinary spellings of the default patterns (flag position, git -C, -fdx, /bin/rm, sh -c, $(…))
findings.evidence: `denied_matches` keeps only wholly-unquoted words (`.filter(|word| !word.quoted)`, guardrail.rs:975-979). It then requires the pattern as one contiguous, exact, lower-cased window: `bare.windows(wanted.len()).any(|window| window == wanted.as_slice())` (988). `shell_commands` (894-956) splits only on `; \n | &`. It never descends into a `sh -c`/`bash -c` argument, `$(…)`, backticks or `( … )`, and keeps the command word as written, with no basename. The defaults are `["rm -rf", "git reset --hard", "git clean -fd", "git push --force"]` (handlers/settings.rs:33). I ported the reader and matcher line by line to a pure string-processing script in the scratchpad. It returns allow for: `git push origin main --force`, `git push -f origin main`, `git -C . reset --hard`, `git clean -fdx`, `git clean -xfd`, `rm -fr build`, `rm -r -f build`, `/bin/rm -rf ~/project`, `'rm' -rf ~/project`, `sh -c 'rm -rf build'`, `bash -c "git reset --hard"`, `echo $(rm -rf ~/x)` and `relay q guardrail.check $(rm -rf ~/x)`. The last one passes because the dry-run exemption at 1012-1019 skips the whole command. The only test, agent_surface.rs:229-252, checks canonical spellings only. The same naive reader also produces false positives on heredoc data: in this audit session, the live hook refused a `cat > file <<'EOF'` whose body contained `&& rm -rf /tmp/x`.
findings.impact: Trigger: an agent, with no malice needed, runs `git clean -fdx`, `git -C <worktree> reset --hard`, `git push origin <branch> --force`, `rm -fr`, or wraps a command in `sh -c '…'` / `timeout 60 bash -c "…"`. Consequence: the PreToolUse gate answers allow and the destructive command runs. The seatbelt BUS.md §0 point 6 promises against agent mistakes does not engage on the commonest spellings of those mistakes. The same root cause lets `sh -c 'relay --actor user q guardrail.confirm {…}'` pass `self_approval` (857-881): the payload is one quoted word, so the `--actor`/`user` and `guardrail.confirm` word checks never see it.
findings.fix:
Normalise argv before matching:
- Basename the command word, and treat a quoted command word as bare.
- Recursively parse the string argument of `sh|bash|zsh|dash -c`, `eval`, `env`, `timeout`, `nice`, `sudo` and `xargs`, plus the bodies of `$(…)`, backticks and subshells; exclude heredoc bodies.
- For git, skip global options (`-C <dir>`, `-c k=v`, `--git-dir`) and match subcommand plus flag set in any position. Expand bundled short flags (`-fdx` ⊇ `-f -d`, `-fr` ≡ `-rf`, `-f` ≡ `--force` for push).
Back it with a table-driven adversarial test, as SPEC §16 asks for the other guardrail paths.

v1.reason:
I read denied_matches (guardrail.rs ~969-1000) and shell_commands (~894-956) myself. Quoted words are dropped from `bare`, and the pattern must match exactly as one contiguous window (`bare.windows(wanted.len()).any(|w| w == wanted)`). The command word is never basenamed, bundled short flags are never expanded, and nothing descends into `sh -c` strings or `$(...)`. Traced by hand against the defaults `["rm -rf","git reset --hard","git clean -fd","git push --force"]`, these all yield no match:
- `git push origin main --force` and `git push -f`: the flag is not contiguous, or is spelled differently.
- `git -C . reset --hard`: `-C .` sits between `git` and `reset`.
- `git clean -fdx`: the bundled flags differ from `-fd`.
- `rm -fr`: the flags are in the other order.
- `/bin/rm -rf`: `/bin/rm` != `rm`.
- `'rm' -rf` and `sh -c 'rm -rf x'`: the quoted words are filtered out.
- `echo $(rm -rf x)`: the word is `$(rm`.
The dry-run exemption (`is_guardrail_dry_run`) skips the whole command, so `relay q guardrail.check $(rm -rf ~)` passes. D103 deliberately made quoted words inert to stop false positives on data, but it does not justify missing reordered or bundled flags, global git options or path-qualified binaries. Those are ordinary spellings an agent produces without any malice. This is a safety check that is silently bypassed, which the rubric rates high.
v1.correction: There is a nuance in the self_approval sub-claim. self_approval (guardrail.rs ~857-881) does not filter quoted words. With `sh -c 'relay --actor user q guardrail.confirm …'` it still sets `relay` true, through file_stem of the whole quoted word. It misses `--actor user` and `guardrail.confirm` because they sit inside one word, not because quoted words are filtered. Lines 849-850 also say outright that self_approval is best effort ('closes the obvious door, not every door'), so treat that part as secondary. The heredoc false-positive aside is anecdotal. The main finding stands as stated.

v2.reason:
(a) The code does what the finding says. I read it myself at 361c6f9.
- `denied_matches` (guardrail.rs:969) drops wholly-quoted words (975-979) and needs the pattern as one exact contiguous window (988).
- `shell_commands` (894-956) splits only on `; \n | &`. It does not basename words, expand bundled flags, or descend into `-c` strings, `$(…)`, backticks or `( … )`.
- `is_guardrail_dry_run` (1012-1019) skips any command whose first word is `relay` and that has a `guardrail.check` word.

I ported the reader line by line to a string-only script. It reproduces all six verdicts of agent_surface.rs:229-252. It returns allow for: `git push origin main --force`, `git push -f origin main`, `git push origin main -f`, `git -C . reset --hard`, `git -c k=v push --force`, `git clean -fdx`/`-xfd`/`-f -d`/`-df`, `rm -fr`, `rm -r -f`, `rm --recursive --force`, `/bin/rm -rf`, `'rm' -rf`, `sh -c '…'`, `bash -c "…"`, `eval "rm -rf build"`, `echo $(rm -rf ~/x)`, `echo "$(rm -rf ~/x)"`, `(rm -rf build)` and `relay q guardrail.check $(rm -rf ~/x)`.

(b) It is reachable on every agent shell call. Claude's PreToolUse matcher `Edit|Write|MultiEdit|Bash` (hooks.rs:349-352) and Codex's `Bash|apply_patch|Edit|Write` (hooks.rs:516) both run the CLI adapter. The adapter sends the raw `command` to `guardrail.gate` (relay-cli main.rs:405-410, 506-512). The handler passes it unmodified to `evaluate_exec` (handlers/guardrail.rs:521). No malice is needed. It fires only when an agent decides to run a destructive command, but then `git clean -fdx`, `git push -f` and a trailing `--force` are at least as likely as the canonical spellings. `git -C <dir>` and `sh -c` are less common.

(c) The gate allows and the hook exits 0, which is "no decision". The command then depends only on the provider's own permission mode. Relay sets none for Claude (its settings file carries only hooks and a statusLine), and Codex runs with `--approve-for-me` (D135). What can happen:
- `reset --hard` throws away uncommitted work.
- `clean -fdx` deletes untracked and ignored files (.env, local config).
- A force push overwrites remote history.
- `rm -fr` deletes directories.

The watcher keeps no snapshots, so Relay cannot restore any of it. Write roots apply only to kind=write, so `git -C /main/checkout reset --hard` run from a worktree is not stopped either. Several gaps cannot be closed by configuration. Patterns are literal contiguous words, so `git -C <any dir> …`, `git push <remote> <branch> --force` and quoted `-c` payloads cannot be listed. `-fdx`/`-xfd`/`-dfx` would each need its own pattern.

(d) The rubric names "a safety check that can be silently bypassed" as high, and this is that. It is not critical:
- BUS.md §0.6 scopes guardrails as seatbelts against mistakes.
- The agent must first choose a destructive command.
- The provider's own permission layer may still stop it.

The `self_approval` part needs deliberate intent and is documented as best effort (guardrail.rs:849-850, BUS.md §9.5; the socket accepts `Actor::User` without authentication, engine.rs:1354). It adds no severity.

(e) The fix points the right way but is over-specified in one place and wrong in another; see the correction.
v2.correction:
1. Wrappers are not a gap. The window slides over every bare word, so `timeout 60 rm -rf build`, `sudo rm -rf /opt/x`, `env FOO=1 rm -rf build`, `xargs rm -rf` and `find . -exec rm -rf {} +` are all refused today. Only these evade:
- quoted payloads: `sh|bash|zsh|dash -c '…'`, `eval "…"`, and probably `su -c` and `ssh host '…'`;
- `$(…)`, backticks and `( … )`;
- `$(…)` and backticks inside double quotes. `echo "$(rm -rf ~/x)"` is allowed because the whole word is quoted, yet bash runs it. D103's "quoted words are inert" is true only for single quotes.

Cut the fix's wrapper list down to these.

2. Do not "exclude heredoc bodies" wholesale. `bash <<'EOF'` / `rm -rf build` / `EOF` is refused today, because the body line is read as a command. Excluding every body would let it through. Skip a body only when the command that reads it is not a shell or `eval`.

3. Qualify the impact. When the matcher misses, the hook makes no decision; it does not approve the command. The command runs unless the provider's own permission mode stops it. Relay sets no mode for Claude, and Codex runs with `--approve-for-me`.

4. Keep grants matching. `covers_command` compares a grant to `hit.bare` exactly (grants.rs:141-148). Either keep the raw bare words for grant comparison, or normalise grant values the same way. Otherwise a grant like `git push --force origin main` stops covering the command it was issued for.

5. Flag equivalence depends on the command:
- push: `-f` ≡ `--force`;
- rm: `-r` ≡ `-R` ≡ `--recursive`.

A force push can also be written `git push origin +main`, which needs refspec handling. Whether `--force-with-lease` should be denied is a policy choice.

6. Reuse the existing reader. device_lease.rs:318-380 already has a second command reader that splits on `( )`, backticks and `$(`, skips `env`/`sudo`/`timeout`, and basenames the program. The two readers have diverged; build on one rather than growing both.

7. "The only test" is slightly wrong. guardrails.rs:343 and 590-657 also test the exec gate, but likewise only with canonical, contiguous spellings.

8. On self_approval I agree with the first verifier. It sees `relay` through file_stem of the whole quoted word, and misses `--actor user` / `guardrail.confirm` because they sit inside one word, not because quoted words are filtered. It is documented best effort, so treat it as secondary.

9. The heredoc false positive is confirmed first-hand. During this verification, the live hook refused my own Bash call because a heredoc's data contained a line starting `rm -rf /tmp/whatever`.

findings.title: agent_surface: the 'escape can be switched off' assertion cannot fail because tracked.rs is still modified when it runs
findings.evidence: Line 462 rewrites tracked.rs to `{long}extra\n`, and line 463 asserts hold because the file is modified. Nothing restores it. So at 471-473 (`guardrail.config.set … allow_if_recoverable: false`, then `check("tracked.rs")` == "hold") the file is still modified. `recoverable()` returns None for any status line other than `!!` (guardrail.rs:684-690), so the verdict is hold whether or not the switch is honoured (guardrail.rs:725-729). `allow_if_recoverable` appears in no other test (rg). The same mistake is at line 398: `!compact.contains("Launch assignment")` cannot fail because the fixture's sessions have no launch prompt. sessions.rs:1007-1012 covers the real case.
findings.impact: Trigger: a regression that stops honouring `destructive_write.allow_if_recoverable` (e.g. a config-layer merge bug). Consequence: a user who turned the escape off still has committed files gutted without a hold, and the suite stays green. The only test of the switch's off state asserts nothing.
findings.fix: Before flipping the switch, `git checkout -- tracked.rs` (or commit a fresh clean file) and assert `allow`. Flip the switch and assert `hold`. Also assert that the ignored `generated.rs` flips to hold. For line 398, create the builder with a launch prompt or drop the assertion.

v1.reason: agent_surface.rs:462 writes `{long}extra\n` to tracked.rs and nothing restores it. So at 471-473 the file is still modified. `recoverable()` (guardrail.rs:670-690) returns None for any porcelain line that is not `!!`, so destructive_decision (guardrail.rs:725-729) falls through to hold whether or not `limits.allow_if_recoverable` is honoured. rg finds `allow_if_recoverable` only in types.rs, settings.rs defaults, guardrail.rs:725 and this test, so the off state of the switch has no effective test. Line 398 has the same problem. The Fixture's session.create calls (lines 66-71) pass no launch prompt, and awareness.rs:249-256 appends 'Launch assignment' only when `launch_prompt` is non-empty, so `!compact.contains("Launch assignment")` cannot fail. sessions.rs:986-1010 spawns with a prompt and checks the role file and provider args. It never checks session.brief's `compact` field, so the compact-brief exclusion is not directly covered anywhere.
v1.correction: Counts and lines are accurate. Fix: restore tracked.rs (`git checkout -- tracked.rs`) and assert `allow` before flipping the switch. Then assert `hold` for both tracked.rs and the ignored generated.rs, because the ignored case is the one that changes most visibly. For line 398, spawn or create the builder with a launch prompt so the assertion can fail. sessions.rs covers the role file and argv, not the `compact` string.

findings.title: Destructive-write rule treats any gitignored file (.env, local configs) as 'recoverable', though git cannot restore it
findings.evidence: `Some(line) if line.starts_with("!!") => Some("ignored by git")` (guardrail.rs:687). Any Some(reason) turns an over-threshold rewrite into `Decision::Allow` (725-729). D114 justifies this as 'an ignored file is build output'. But the rule's stated premise is 'whether the content can come back', and git keeps no copy of an ignored file. The settings UI tells the user the opposite: 'Committed, unmodified or ignored files can always come back.' (apps/relay-native/src/guardrail_settings.rs:66). agent_surface.rs:465-468 pins the allow.
findings.impact: Trigger: an agent regenerates `.env` from `.env.example`, or rewrites a gitignored `config.local.json`, `secrets.toml` or notes file, removing more than 50 lines (or more than 40% of a 30+ line file). Consequence: the write is allowed with no hold, and the original contents, often credentials, are gone for good. That is exactly the loss D114 says this rule exists to stop.
findings.fix: Count only 'committed and unmodified' as recoverable and hold on ignored files like untracked ones. If build output needs a pass, allow-list known output directories explicitly. Correct the UI hint and D114, and flip agent_surface.rs:465-468.

v1.reason: guardrail.rs:671-691 `recoverable` returns Some("ignored by git") for any `!!` status line. destructive_decision (723-729) then returns Decision::Allow before any hold whenever allow_if_recoverable is set, and the default is true (handlers/settings.rs:30). The doc comment at 667-670 and D114 (DECISIONS.md:546-552) both say the rule exists because 'the question that matters is whether the content can come back', yet they class every ignored file as build output. git keeps no copy of an ignored file, so a gitignored .env, *.local.json or secrets file is in the same position as an untracked one, which the rule does hold. The settings hint at apps/relay-native/src/guardrail_settings.rs:66 ('Committed, unmodified or ignored files can always come back.') is factually wrong. The decision is intended, but it is not harmless. That rules out the 'documented and harmless' exemption.
v1.correction: The trigger needs a gitignored file in the session's worktree that the agent rewrites past the defaults: more than 50 lines removed, or more than 40% of a file of at least 30 lines. That is a narrower case than 'any .env', so medium is the upper bound. Fix: treat `!!` like untracked (hold), or allow it only under an explicit build-output allow-list. Then correct D114, the doc comment at guardrail.rs:667-670 and the UI hint.

findings.title: guardrail.check / guardrail.gate run git subprocesses while holding the store mutex
findings.evidence:
Both are plain `engine.register` handlers (handlers/guardrail.rs:151 `register::<Check>`, 304 `register::<Gate>`), so they run in the request transaction with the store lock held. The shared evaluator shells out in two places:
- `recoverable()` runs `git status --porcelain --ignored=matching --untracked-files=all -- <path>` (guardrail.rs:671-679) on every over-threshold write.
- `evaluate_commit` runs `git diff --cached --numstat` whenever no diff is supplied (guardrail.rs:760). Relay's own pre-commit hook never supplies one: its payload is `{"session":…,"kind":"commit"}` (hooks.rs:129-132).
Both are bounded only by GIT_TIMEOUT = 10 s (guardrail.rs:1120). D149 lists the git ops it moved out of transactions, and guardrail.* is not among them. agent_surface.rs:404-474 drives the `recoverable` path.
findings.impact: Trigger: an agent's Write/Edit that removes more than 50 lines (PreToolUse → guardrail.gate), or any agent `git commit` (pre-commit hook → guardrail.gate kind=commit), in a large repository or on a slow filesystem. Consequence: every other bus request waits behind that git subprocess for up to 10 s. With several agents committing or rewriting at once, the stalls chain.
findings.fix: Register guardrail.check with `register_unlocked` and guardrail.gate with `register_staged`. Read config and grants in a short `Unlocked::read`, run `recoverable`/numstat with nothing locked, and persist the hold and notification in the short finish phase.

v1.reason:
handlers/guardrail.rs registers both Check (~151) and Gate (~304, `engine.register::<Gate>(|ctx, payload| gate(ctx, payload, None))`) with plain `engine.register`. Neither uses register_unlocked or register_staged, so both run inside the request transaction with the store mutex held. `gate` (~501-526) calls guardrail::evaluate_granted(ctx.tx(), …) directly. From there:
- destructive_decision runs `recoverable`, a `git status` subprocess (guardrail.rs:671-679), on an over-threshold write.
- evaluate_commit runs `git diff --cached --numstat` through git_output (guardrail.rs ~760, 1122) whenever no diff is supplied.
Relay's own pre-commit hook (hooks.rs ~128-130) sends only `{"session":…,"kind":"commit"}`, so every agent commit forks git under the lock. Both calls go through proc::output_with_timeout with GIT_TIMEOUT = 10s, so the stall is bounded, not a hang. D149 introduced the split shapes for exactly this case (git under the global lock), and guardrail.* was never moved.
v1.correction: Usually numstat and status take tens of milliseconds. The cost becomes noticeable in big repositories, on slow filesystems or with several agents committing at once, so medium fits. Related: `file_lines` (guardrail.rs ~695-702) reads a file of up to 64 MB under the same lock on the write path. Fix as proposed: register_unlocked for Check, and register_staged for Gate, which persists holds, notifications and grant use in finish.

findings.title: task.activity scans the project's whole audit history with json_extract under the store lock on every page
findings.evidence: The query is `SELECT id FROM audit WHERE project_id = ?1 AND (?3 IS NULL OR id < ?3) AND ((op LIKE 'task.%' AND json_extract(payload, '$.task_id') = ?2) OR (op = 'task.create' AND json_extract(result_summary, '$.id') = ?2) OR json_extract(result_summary, '$.task.id') = ?2) ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT ?4` (task.rs:763-767). No index covers the task id: audit indexes are on ts, actor, session, op and project only (store.rs:28-34). The third disjunct has no op filter.
