report.py:163 tells the reader 'a ratio near 10 is linear ... well below is a fixed cost'. FIXES-2026-09-20.md:20 had to correct a row by hand ('fewer audit rows in this shorter run').
findings.impact: Scaling conclusions are wrong for every query over a table that accumulates: notify.list reads as a fixed cost when it is linear. Per-op numbers shift with --only selection and case order, so compare.py diffs between differently-selected runs do not compare like with like.
findings.fix: Back up the store after populate and restore it, or rebuild the engine on a fresh copy, before each case. At least do this before the SCALE_OPS cases in the native pass, or run the x1 list cases in their own pass that mirrors the x10 pass. Record row counts before the loop and print them beside the ratio.

v1.reason: perf.rs:1566 builds one Fixture for every selected case. The cleanup doc comment at 142-145 claims each case sees the clean fixture, but cleanup only undoes rows that a measured region registered. The committed native.jsonl `rows` fields show the store growing across cases: audit rows go from 137 to 25,844, messages from 10 to 500, notifications from 2 to 405, and closed sessions from 0 to 145. The scale10 pass runs on a fresh fixture with 1,127 audit rows, 2 notifications and 0 closed sessions. Measured ratios: op.notify.list is 779 us at x1 against 28 us at x10 (ratio 0.04), op.session.list.all is 1.27 ms against 31 us, and op.task.activity is 2.63 ms against 1.37 ms. These ratios are inverted or meaningless, yet report.py:163 tells the reader that 'well below [10] is a fixed cost'. FIXES-2026-09-20.md:20 already needed a hand-written caveat for task.activity. The results also depend on --only selection and case order.
v1.correction: Medium is kept only as a measurement-tooling defect with an ongoing cost: the scaling table actively misleads perf decisions, as the inverted notify.list and session.list.all ratios show. It has no user-facing impact. Simplest fix: copy the populated store file once after Fixture::build and restore it, or rebuild the engine on a copy, before each SCALE_OPS case in the x1 pass. Alternatively, run the x1 scale cases in their own fresh-fixture pass that mirrors the x10 pass. Note that `rows` is captured after the loop (perf.rs:1444), not before it.

findings.title: 'during' cases wait a fixed 5 ms and never check the other op is still running; FIXES records a 470x win measured with no overlap at all
findings.evidence: The other op starts on a thread, then `std::thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(5))` (1250), then the measured request runs. There is no barrier, no start/end timestamps and no overlap check (1242-1257; during_session sleeps 2 ms at 1278). FIXES-2026-09-20.md:14 reports 'session.scrollback tail while a device.build runs 22.7 ms -> 48 us (470x)', while :27 shows device.build itself now takes 76 us. The build therefore finished about 5 ms before the measured read, and 48 us is an uncontended read. session_list.during_task_list (1266) cannot overlap either: task.list is 0.76 ms after the fixes. On a loaded machine the thread may not start within 5 ms at all.
findings.impact: The cases meant to make the store-mutex invariant 'a number' can report no contention when none was measured. That would hide a regression that puts slow work back under the lock, and the docs already contain an artefactual result.
findings.fix: Have the other op signal once it is inside its handler, or record its start and end Instants. Mark iterations whose measured request began after the other op finished, and report the overlap fraction. Drop or lengthen the task.list and device.build variants.

v1.reason: perf.rs:1242-1257: `during` spawns the other op on a thread, then `std::thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(5))` (1250), then issues the measured request. There is no barrier, no start/end timestamps and no overlap check. `during_session` does the same with a 2 ms sleep (1278). FIXES-2026-09-20.md line 14 records 'session.scrollback tail while a device.build runs 22.7 ms -> 48 us (470x)', and line 27 of the same table shows device.build (no Gradle wrapper, the fixture's case) now takes 76 us. So in the 'after' measurement the build had finished almost 5 ms before the tail was issued. The 'while a device.build runs' label is false and the 48 us is an uncontended read. session_list.during_task_list (1266) cannot overlap either, because task.list is 0.76 ms after the fixes. The doc text at FIXES line 37 ('the mutex invariant is a number from now on') relies on this harness. Impact is limited to perf tooling and documentation: no user-facing behaviour is affected. A regression that made the other op slow under the lock would usually still show up, because the op would then outlast the 5 ms sleep. The real blind spots are short ops and a thread that is scheduled late.
v1.correction: Severity lowered to low: this is a perf-harness accuracy problem with no effect on the app, and slow-under-lock regressions (the case that matters) would mostly still be caught. The fix is still sound: signal from inside the other op, or record its start and end Instants and report the fraction of iterations that overlapped. Drop or re-label the device.build and task.list variants.

findings.title: baseline.py burst phase measures its own byte-at-a-time Python reader, and any 1 s gap before BURST-END crashes the run
findings.evidence: `stream = sub.makefile("rwb", buffering=0)` (520), then `stream.readline()` (531). readline on a raw SocketIO does one recv per byte. A scratch test here measured 2.2 MiB/s unbuffered against 820 MiB/s buffered. The engine drops frames for a lagging subscriber (socket.rs:491-493). The committed process.json shows 1,194,990 payload bytes received of about 5.0 MB, 1.78 MB on the wire and mib_per_s_to_client 0.4. BASELINE-2026-09-19.md:488-496 reads this as what 'an attached reader that cannot keep up sees' and concludes that bursts leave terminal gaps. Second problem: `sub.settimeout(1.0)` (523). After the first timeout, SocketIO refuses further reads with OSError('cannot read from timed out object') (verified in a scratch test on Python 3.14), and `except socket.timeout` (532) does not catch that. The 'keep waiting' path after a failed scrollback check (546-549) therefore raises out of run_process, process.json (594) is never written, and main() aborts before the callgrind pass and report.py.
findings.impact: seconds_until_stream_quiet, mib_per_s_to_client, frames and payload_bytes_received describe the harness, not the engine, and they drove a product conclusion. On a loaded machine, a stall of 1 s or more before BURST-END reaches the scrollback kills the whole baseline run.
findings.fix: Read with select/selectors plus `sub.recv(1 << 16)` into a bytearray and split lines yourself, with no socket timeout under a makefile. Count dropped frames from seq gaps explicitly. Use a buffered reader in Engine.call (347) as well.

v1.reason: baseline.py:520 `stream = sub.makefile("rwb", buffering=0)` returns a raw SocketIO. IOBase.readline on it has no peek, so it reads one byte at a time. socket.rs:491-493 drops frames for a lagging subscriber, so the measured frames and payload_bytes_received (1.19 of 4.9 MB) are bounded by this reader's speed. That makes them a property of the harness more than of the engine. A scratch test (Python 3, socketpair, makefile buffering=0, settimeout 0.2) printed 'timeout caught', then 'OSError cannot read from timed out object' on the next readline. So once the 1 s timeout at baseline.py:523 fires, the loop can continue only by breaking. If BURST-END is not yet in the scrollback, the next readline raises an OSError that `except socket.timeout` does not catch, run_process aborts, and process.json is never written (line 594).
v1.correction: Lowered to low: this is a dev-only perf harness, and the BASELINE doc already frames the result as what 'an attached reader that cannot keep up sees'. The doc's point about the native client's 256 KiB catch-up does not depend on this measurement. The crash needs a stall of 1 s or more before the burst ends. Fix: read with select plus recv into a buffer, split lines yourself, and count dropped frames from seq gaps.

findings.title: path.engine.startup and path.recovery.run leave one recovery-dirty-scan thread per iteration running `git status` over every worktree during later measurements
findings.evidence: Since f2789df both cases call `recovery::run_with(&engine, DirtyScan::Deferred)` (1098, 1108). For an Arc'd engine, recovery.rs:223-243 spawns a detached 'recovery-dirty-scan' thread that holds an engine clone and runs dirty_worktrees -> worktree::list -> is_dirty. That is `git status --porcelain -z --untracked-files=all` with GIT_OPTIONAL_LOCKS=1 (worktree.rs:86-92) on the primary checkout and on every linked worktree of the 1,500-file fixture: builder, reviewer, clean, kept-worktree sessions. Nothing joins these threads; drain_cleanup joins only handles pushed through join_later. ALLOCS/ALLOC_BYTES and getrusage(RUSAGE_SELF) are process-wide (1417-1430), and so is callgrind instrumentation.
findings.impact: About 64 background scans (30+2 iterations of each case) overlap the following iterations and the cases after them (skills.refresh_all, request.parse_8k, socket.*). They inflate those cases' CPU, allocations, Ir and wall time with work from earlier scenarios. They also take index.lock in worktrees that later cases operate on. The FIXES figure '161 ms -> 4.4 ms' and every number measured after it come from this contaminated window.
findings.fix: Outside the timed region, wait until the copy engine's background work is done before the next iteration, for example by polling Arc::strong_count(&engine) == 1. Or measure the dirty scan in its own explicitly named inline case.

v1.reason: Both path.engine.startup (perf.rs:~1090-1103) and path.recovery.run (perf.rs:~1105-1111) call `recovery::run_with(&engine, DirtyScan::Deferred)` on an Arc'd engine (Engine::new returns Arc<Engine>, and engine.arc() upgrades self_ref). recovery.rs:223-243 then spawns a detached 'recovery-dirty-scan' thread. The thread holds an engine clone and calls dirty_worktrees -> worktree::list -> is_dirty -> status_files, which runs `git status --porcelain=v1 -z --untracked-files=all` with GIT_OPTIONAL_LOCKS=1 (worktree.rs:86-92). It does this for the primary checkout and every linked worktree of each project repo. Nothing joins these threads. Neither engine.shutdown() nor dropping the local Arc stops them. The harness's ALLOCS/ALLOC_BYTES and RUSAGE_SELF counters are process-wide, so later iterations and later cases (skills.refresh_all, request.parse_8k, response.serialize.*, socket.*) absorb the background scans' CPU and allocations.
v1.correction: The mechanism is confirmed but the magnitude was not established. The threads run at background_priority. The cases right after are few, and most are cheap in-memory or socket rows, so the contamination mainly affects CPU and alloc counts, not core results. The FIXES '4.4 ms' figure is the intended deferred-scan cost. Only later iterations' contention inflates it, and the claim that it is invalid goes too far. Severity is low. Fix: outside the timed region, wait for the copy engine's background work to finish, for example by polling Arc::strong_count or having run_with return a JoinHandle in test builds. Alternatively, add an explicit inline-scan case.

findings.title: native-baseline.py takes its 'steady' counters after the perf window, overlapping the client's scheduled exit
findings.evidence: RELAY_NATIVE_SMOKE_SECONDS is set to seconds+2 (211-212). The client arms that timer in smoke::install at activation (app.rs:368; smoke.rs:512-516, 724), then captures and closes. When perf is available, the script first runs `perf record ... -- sleep seconds` (93) starting at t≈2 s; that returns only after perf has written and post-processed the data. Only then does it call `window(native.pid, 1.0)` (228). The comment at 227 says 'The perf window and the counter window are the same seconds', but the two windows are sequential. The 1 s window therefore starts near or after the client's exit at about seconds+2 s plus activation time. Until native.wait() (231) the process is a zombie, whose /proc stat shows rss 0, one task and no CPU.
findings.impact: With perf installed (the default path), steady CPU %, wakeups/s, RSS and thread counts per page are near zero or measure shutdown, which makes the client look idle. If the process is reaped first, the page becomes an error row and its startup and profile data are lost.
findings.fix: Read counters() just before starting perf and again right after `sleep` ends, so the counter window is the perf window. Give the smoke run margin, e.g. SMOKE_SECONDS = seconds + 2 + 5, and only then wait for the client.

v1.reason: The windows run one after another, and the counter window lands after the client has quit. open_page sets RELAY_NATIVE_SMOKE_SECONDS=seconds+2 (native-baseline.py:212). smoke::install arms that timer at activation (app.rs:368, smoke.rs:512-516, 724). When it fires, it captures a screenshot within 50 ms-2 s and calls ui.window.close() (smoke.rs:801), which ends the app. The script sleeps 2 s, then calls perf_profile (line 226). That function runs `perf record -p pid -- sleep seconds` (line 93), so recording ends about seconds+2 s after spawn. It then also runs `perf report` twice with -g call graphs (lines 97-110) before returning, which can take seconds on a GTK profile. Only after that does window(native.pid, 1.0) start (line 228). By then the client, which exits around spawn+activation+seconds+2 plus capture, has usually closed. It stays a zombie until native.wait() at line 231, because Popen does not reap it. A zombie's /proc/pid/stat shows rss 0, frozen CPU ticks and one task, so steady CPU % and wakeups/s come out 0, RSS 0 and threads 1. The comment at line 227 says the windows are 'the same seconds', which contradicts the code. This is the default path whenever perf is installed.
v1.correction: The mechanism is worse than stated: perf_profile also runs both `perf report` passes before returning, so the counter window starts even later and almost certainly after the client exits. Fix: take counters() just before perf record and again right after it returns, before running perf report. Move the report folding after native.wait(), and give the smoke timer a margin over the perf window.

findings.title: native-baseline.py points the GTK client's XDG_RUNTIME_DIR at a temp dir, so on Wayland GDK cannot reach the compositor and silently falls back to XWayland
findings.evidence: desktop_env sets `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR=str(runtime)` for the client (203-204). The client only needs that variable to exist, because RELAY_NATIVE_SOCKET is given (app.rs:309-319). libwayland resolves a relative WAYLAND_DISPLAY (here 'wayland-0') under $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR, so GDK's Wayland backend fails and GDK falls back to X11 through DISPLAY=:0 (XWayland); without DISPLAY the client cannot start. Sibling scripts that override XDG_RUNTIME_DIR set GDK_BACKEND=x11 explicitly (scripts/test-launcher-real.py:21-23, scripts/native-setup-smoke.py:79). run.sh launches the real client without the override. This was not run, because relay-native cannot be built here.
findings.impact: On the user's Wayland session the baseline profiles the XWayland path, with a different frame clock, presentation and GL path, and with XWayland's own CPU not counted. That is not the native Wayland client the user actually runs. On a Wayland-only session every page fails.
findings.fix: Leave XDG_RUNTIME_DIR alone for the client, since RELAY_NATIVE_SOCKET already selects the fixture engine. Or set WAYLAND_DISPLAY to the absolute path under the original runtime dir. Record the GDK backend in native.json.

v1.reason: native-baseline.py:203-204 builds desktop_env with XDG_RUNTIME_DIR=str(runtime), a fresh temp dir, for the GTK client. The client needs XDG_RUNTIME_DIR to exist (app.rs:309-312), but RELAY_NATIVE_SOCKET (app.rs:313) already points it at the fixture socket, so the override serves no purpose. libwayland-client looks up a relative WAYLAND_DISPLAY (normally 'wayland-0') under $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR, and the temp dir has no compositor socket. So GDK's Wayland backend cannot connect, and GDK either falls back to X11 through DISPLAY (XWayland) or fails if no DISPLAY is set. The sibling it was derived from, scripts/native-smoke.py:114, builds its client env from os.environ and keeps the real runtime dir. The user runs CachyOS, likely on a Wayland session, so the baseline would profile the XWayland path rather than the client as actually run. No native run exists in docs/perf/runs yet, so no published numbers are affected so far.
v1.correction: Part of the evidence is wrong. scripts/native-setup-smoke.py does not override XDG_RUNTIME_DIR for the client: its runenv (line 77) is built from os.environ, and GDK_BACKEND=x11 at line 79 applies only to the pointer-driver mode. The right precedent is native-smoke.py:114, which leaves XDG_RUNTIME_DIR alone for the client. Fix: drop XDG_RUNTIME_DIR from desktop_env, since RELAY_NATIVE_SOCKET already selects the engine, and record GDK_BACKEND or the display type in native.json. Rated low, not medium: this dev-only harness has never been run and still produces numbers, just for a different display path.

findings.title: Crash recovery SIGTERMs, then SIGKILLs, any live process whose pid matches a stale session row, plus its process group (the harness works around this)
findings.evidence: Step 2 (84-97) does `Some(p) if pty::pid_alive(p as u32) => { kill_wait(p as u32); ... "still alive from a previous engine; reaped" }`. pid_alive is only `kill(pid, 0) == 0` (pty.rs:394-396). kill_wait (20-35) sends SIGTERM to `-(pid)` and to `pid`, waits 2 s, then sends SIGKILL to both. Step 1 (66-74) has already reaped every process carrying this instance's RELAY_SESSION and RELAY_STORE. A pid still alive at step 2 is therefore one recovery could not identify as Relay's: a recycled pid or a zombie. Stale pids only exist after an unclean exit, since Engine::shutdown clears them (engine.rs:676). perf.rs:579-586 nulls pids in its store copies because 'crash recovery reaps any live pid it finds in the store'. The committed process.json shows step 2 reaping pid 17325, which step 1 had not matched. tests/sessions.rs:574-576 seeds a ghost row with the fixed pid 999999; on this machine (pid_max 4194304, last pid 2,683,297) that is a valid pid that could belong to the developer.
findings.impact: Trigger: an engine crash, OOM kill or power loss, followed by a reboot or pid wrap. The next Relay start can then kill an unrelated program owned by the same user, and its whole process group if it is a group leader (a terminal job, an editor, a desktop component), losing unsaved work. `cargo test` can do the same through the 999999 row.
findings.fix: In step 2, signal only if proc_env(pid) shows RELAY_SESSION equal to the row's name and RELAY_STORE equal to this store; alternatively, record the process start time from /proc/<pid>/stat at spawn and compare it. Otherwise treat the pid as gone. Never signal a process group that has not been verified. In the test, use a pid above pid_max.

v1.reason: recovery.rs:84-93: for every session row in a live state with a recorded pid, `Some(p) if pty::pid_alive(p as u32) => { kill_wait(p as u32); ...`. pid_alive is only `kill(pid,0)==0` (pty.rs:394-396). kill_wait (recovery.rs:20-35) sends SIGTERM and then SIGKILL to both `-(pid)` and `pid`, with no check of who owns the pid. Step 1 (relay_children, matched on RELAY_SESSION/RELAY_STORE in /proc environ) has already handled every process it could identify as Relay's. So step 2 signals a process exactly when it could not identify it, apart from the harmless case of an orphan step 1 just SIGKILLed that has not exited yet. Clean shutdown nulls pids (engine.rs:676-679), so stale pids exist only after a crash, kill -9, OOM or power loss. After a reboot, or after pid reuse, a recorded pid can belong to an unrelated process of the same user, and if that process leads a group the whole group is killed. perf.rs:579-586 nulls pids for this very reason. The sessions.rs test seeds pid 999999, which is a valid pid with pid_max 4194304.
v1.correction: The realistic trigger is crash, then reboot, then Relay autostarts. Pid reuse without a reboot is unlikely with pid_max 4M, and after an engine crash the PTY hangup usually kills the old provider anyway. The chance is low per crash, but the consequence (SIGKILL of an unrelated process group, unsaved work lost) is real, so medium holds. Fix: in step 2, signal only when proc_env(pid) carries RELAY_SESSION equal to the row's name and RELAY_STORE equal to this store, or when the start time from /proc/<pid>/stat matches one recorded at spawn. Never signal a process group that has not been verified. The test should use a pid above pid_max, or no pid.

findings.title: Notifications and mailbox messages are never pruned, and the shell's global notify.list does a full scan plus sort under the store mutex
findings.evidence: perf.rs:844-845 says 'A refusal leaves a notification and a hold leaves a row; neither can be deleted', and :755 says 'Messages have no delete'. The only DELETEs are on project removal (workspace.rs:356, 367); recovery prunes only the audit table. notify.list is registered with engine.register (86) and builds `SELECT * FROM notifications WHERE 1=1 [AND read=0] ORDER BY created_at DESC,id DESC LIMIT ?` (58-71). Both indexes lead with project_id or category (store.rs:138-139). EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN on that schema (scratch test, SQLite 3.53) gives 'SCAN notifications' plus 'USE TEMP B-TREE FOR ORDER BY' for the shell's `{"unread_only":true,"limit":100}` (shell.rs:756, re-run on every notify.* event per app.rs:1197-1199) and for the notification center's `{"limit":100}` (notification_center.rs:134). The committed baseline measured 780 us with 203 rows against 28 us with 2.
findings.impact: Every guardrail refusal or hold, provider update and session report adds a row that is kept forever. The unread-count refresh that follows each notification scans and sorts the whole table while holding the mutex. Its cost, and the stall it puts on every other locked request, grows linearly over the life of the install.
findings.fix: Append a migration that adds an index on (read, created_at) and one on created_at, and bump SCHEMA_VERSION. Add a retention pass next to the audit retention in recovery, for example deleting read notifications and read mail older than N days.

v1.reason: notify.rs:51-82 builds `SELECT * FROM notifications WHERE 1=1 [AND read=0] ... ORDER BY created_at DESC,id DESC LIMIT ?` and is registered with engine.register (line 86), so it runs under the store mutex. The only indexes are notifications_project(project_id, read, created_at) and notifications_category(category, read, created_at) (store.rs:138-139). Neither can serve a query with no project or category filter, so the shell's `{"unread_only":true,"limit":100}` (shell.rs:756) scans the table and sorts in a temp B-tree. app.rs:1197-1199 re-runs that query on every notify.* event. The table only has rows inserted, from guardrail.rs:1243/1266, grants.rs:404, session.rs:274, provider.rs:26, provider_updates.rs:63, integration.rs:285 and device.rs:2212. The only DELETEs on notifications and messages are in project removal (workspace.rs:355-367). Recovery prunes only audit (recovery.rs:196) and claims (recovery.rs:156). So the growth is unbounded and the cost of the refresh grows with it.
v1.correction: The impact is slower than the finding implies. Rows are small and grow at roughly tens per day, and session.input does not touch SQLite (D148), so keystrokes do not stall. What slows is every other locked request during the refresh, by a few milliseconds per tens of thousands of rows. That is medium, not high. A single index on (read, created_at) serves both the unread_only and the plain listing, because SQLite can walk created_at in order with read=0 as a prefix, or skip-scan it. Retention for read notifications and acknowledged messages fits beside the audit retention in recovery.rs. I did not check the messages/mailbox query plan separately.

findings.title: Several path.* cases report ok:true even when the measured call fails
findings.evidence: recovery.run returns `Outcome::plain(r.is_ok() as usize)` (1110), and plain() always sets ok:true. engine.startup discards the recovery result with `let _ =` (1098). guardrail.config_load returns `Outcome::plain(config(..).is_ok() as usize)` (1320). worktree.status_files uses `.map(|s| s.len()).unwrap_or(0)` (1314). request.parse_8k (1122) and response.serialize.session_list (1126) use `.unwrap_or(0)`.
findings.impact: If one of these paths starts failing (for example git status hitting its 10 s timeout, or a recovery SQL error), the report shows 'ok' with a faster time, and compare.py marks it as an improvement.
findings.fix: Return `Outcome { ok: r.is_ok(), code: r.err().map(|e| e.to_string()), bytes }` for fallible paths.

v1.reason: Outcome::plain (perf.rs:97-99) always sets `ok: true, code: None`. path.recovery.run returns `Outcome::plain(r.is_ok() as usize)` (~1110), and path.guardrail.config_load returns `Outcome::plain(config(..).is_ok() as usize)` (~1320). engine.startup discards the recovery Result with `let _ =` (~1098). worktree.status_files uses `.map(|s| s.len()).unwrap_or(0)` (~1314). request.parse_8k and response.serialize.session_list also use unwrap_or(0) (~1122, ~1126). A failure in any of them is therefore counted as ok.
v1.correction: There is partial mitigation: a failure shows up as result_bytes 0 instead of 1 or N, so it is detectable by eye but not flagged. It is a minor harness accuracy issue, so low is right. Fix: build `Outcome { ok: r.is_ok(), code: r.err().map(|e| e.to_string()), bytes }` for the fallible paths.

findings.title: compare.py diffs runs without checking they are comparable; different iteration counts mark every row 'outcome changed'
findings.evidence: Line 44 checks `a.get("codes") == b.get("codes") and a["ok"] == b["ok"]`, which compares absolute counts. A --quick run (iters-div 4) against a full run differs on every row: {'github.gh_missing': 30} vs 7, ok 200 vs 50. compare.py never reads environment.json (machine, sha, profile, load), iteration counts or scale, yet still flags wall p50 changes. report.py:194 likewise hard-codes '20 000 mixed operations' even when --quick runs 4,000.
findings.impact: The documented regression workflow produces noise or meaningless output unless both runs used identical options on the same machine, and it gives no warning.
findings.fix: Compare ok/iters ratios and code sets rather than counts. Load both environment.json files and warn on a different machine, profile or quick mode. Print iters per row. In report.py, use soak['ops'].

v1.reason: compare.py:44 sets the outcome as changed unless `a.get("codes") == b.get("codes") and a["ok"] == b["ok"]`. native.jsonl rows carry absolute counts (`"iters":200,"ok":200,"codes":{}`), and --quick passes --iters-div 4 (baseline.py:625). So comparing a quick run against a full run flags every row as 'outcome changed'. compare.py never reads environment.json, iters or scale. report.py:194 hard-codes 'Memory over 20 000 mixed operations', while quick mode runs `--ops 4000` (baseline.py:639).
v1.correction: Low impact: the documented workflow (docs/perf/README.md:14) compares two full runs, which works. Compare ok/iters ratios and code sets, warn when the environment or quick mode differs, and print soak['ops'] in report.py.

findings.title: Engine-fixture helpers are copy-pasted across the perf scripts and have already diverged
findings.evidence: baseline.py has Engine.start/call/fixture (315-404); native-baseline.py has inline copies (143-199), and scripts/native-smoke.py has another. baseline.py opens a new socket for each connect retry and waits for bus.ping ('Ready means answering, not just accepting', 348-349). native-baseline.py reuses one socket across failed connects, sends ops as soon as connect succeeds, and its call() runs json.loads(b"") on EOF (161) instead of raising a clear error. There are also two fake providers (PROVIDER_PY, PROVIDER) and two /proc counter readers (proc_counters, counters) that handle threads differently.
findings.impact: Fixes reach only one copy, as the readiness check already shows. Every protocol or fixture change has to be made in three places.
findings.fix: Move engine start, call, fixture, provider and /proc counters into a shared scripts/perf/_fixture.py and import it from both scripts.

v1.reason: The duplication is real. scripts/perf/baseline.py:315-404 (class Engine: start/call/stop/fixture), scripts/perf/native-baseline.py:142-199 (an inline engine start, a call closure and a fixture) and scripts/native-smoke.py:29-116 all repeat the same engine fixture: env/XDG setup, `relay --instance test serve`, a connect retry loop, a newline-JSON call that skips ev/stream frames, a git repo, workspace.create/project.add, provider settings and session.create+spawn+scrollback polling. Each also carries its own fake provider (PROVIDER_PY, PROVIDER, an inline one) and /proc counter reader (proc_counters vs counters). The claimed divergences are mostly harmless, though. On Linux, retrying connect() on the same AF_UNIX socket after ENOENT/ECONNREFUSED works. Skipping bus.ping is harmless because the first real call (workspace.create) blocks on readline until the engine answers. Some differences are deliberate: the native fixture adds 200 source files for the Code page and waits for a different marker. The one concrete divergence is the error message: native-baseline's call() runs json.loads on b"" at EOF and raises JSONDecodeError instead of a clear 'engine closed the connection'.
v1.correction: Lower the impact. The copies have not diverged in a way that breaks anything. Only the EOF error at native-baseline.py:161 is worse, and the socket-reuse and readiness-check differences are not bugs. A shared helper module is a modest cleanup. Keep the per-script fixture contents (file tree, provider script) as parameters, because they differ on purpose.

findings.title: Fixture repos inherit the developer's global git config; signing is disabled for one repo but not the others
findings.evidence: build_repo sets `commit.gpgsign false` (173). skill_repo (244-249, inside Fixture::build) and small_repo (646-656) commit without it. The fixtures in baseline.py:379-386 and native-baseline.py:171-182 do the same. HOME is not isolated, so ~/.gitconfig applies to all of them, including gpgsign, core.hooksPath and templates. None of these is set on this machine.
findings.impact: With a global commit.gpgsign=true and a passphrase-protected key, every `perf run` panics in Fixture::build at the skill repo commit (the git() helper asserts success) or blocks on pinentry. A global hooksPath runs the user's hooks on fixture commits.
findings.fix: Run fixture git with `-c commit.gpgsign=false -c core.hooksPath=/dev/null`, or set GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL=/dev/null and GIT_CONFIG_NOSYSTEM=1, in git(), small_repo and the Python fixtures.

v1.reason: git() (perf.rs:150-153) runs plain `Command::new("git")` with the inherited environment. build_repo sets `commit.gpgsign false` (perf.rs:173). The skill_repo commit in Fixture::build (perf.rs ~244-249) and small_repo (perf.rs ~646-655) do not. git() asserts success, so if a global commit.gpgsign=true signing fails or blocks, Fixture::build panics or hangs on pinentry. The Python fixtures have the same gap. baseline.py:379-386 and native-baseline.py:171-182 run git without env=, so XDG_CONFIG_HOME isolation reaches only the engine, and ~/.gitconfig still applies. Neither gpgsign nor hooksPath is set globally on this machine today.
v1.correction: This is a latent robustness gap that only bites with a global signing or hooks config. Low severity is right. The simplest fix is to set GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL=/dev/null and GIT_CONFIG_NOSYSTEM=1 (or `-c commit.gpgsign=false -c core.hooksPath=/dev/null`) inside git()/git_out() and in the Python git() helpers.

findings.title: BUS.md says ui-executor ops are forwarded to the UI (refused when headless) and that pty streams never drop; the engine does neither, and the harness relies on the doc
findings.evidence: BUS.md:361-366 says ui.* ops are 'forwarded to the UI client ... If no UI is connected (headless), they return unavailable / ui.absent', and :177 says the same. No code in relay-core reads OpMeta.executor, and `ui.absent` appears nowhere in the code. ui.* handlers change engine-side state, and os.reveal/os.open_url spawn xdg-open in the engine itself (ui.rs:335-361). BUS.md:380 says the pty stream's 'Backpressure: coalesce, never drop', but socket.rs:491-493 drops frames for a lagging subscriber. perf.rs:1044 and report.py:73 repeat the §6.5 claim.
findings.impact: Readers, including the harness author, believe headless or in-process ui and os calls are inert refusals, which led directly to the xdg-open storm finding. A headless `relay serve` on another host runs xdg-open for os.open_url. Client authors are told the stream never drops.
findings.fix: Rewrite §6.5, §10.17 and §7 for the current design: UI state held by the engine plus events, os.* executed by the engine, and lagging pty subscribers dropping frames and re-attaching from their seq. Alternatively, implement the documented forwarding.

v1.reason: BUS.md:177 and §6.5 (around lines 365-369) say executor=ui ops are forwarded to the UI client over bus:ui-op and return unavailable/ui.absent when headless. No code reads executor outside registry.rs metadata (registry.rs:95/158/273). `ui.absent` and `bus:ui-op` appear nowhere in the code. ui.rs handlers act inside the engine, and os.reveal/os.open_url run `std::process::Command::new("xdg-open")` in after_commit (ui.rs:335-361). The §7 table says pty 'Backpressure: coalesce, never drop', but socket.rs:491-493 handles RecvError::Lagged by logging 'frames dropped' and carrying on.
v1.correction: The line numbers drift slightly: §6.5 text is at about BUS.md:365-369 and the §7 pty row at about 380. The drift is real and the fix is a doc rewrite. The claim that the doc 'led to' a separate xdg-open finding is the auditor's own history, not a property of the code.

The live store files are created with the default umask: ~/.local/share/relay-v4/dev/store.db, -wal and backups/*.db are 0644 and the directories 0755 (Store::open, store.rs:384-400). remote.json is correctly 0600.
