Every spawn, resume, wake and clear_restorable pays this, and so does every agent's session.brief.
findings.fix: Read only row data under the lock and compute briefing_state after releasing it. Register session.brief as unlocked: read the rows in ctx.read, then call briefing_state. In stage_launch, return worktree/branch/base out of ctx.read and compute the git section (and write_roots) outside it. Optionally cap the divergence walks (e.g. report "1000+").

v1.reason: session.rs:1124-1129 registers Brief with plain `e.register`, and it calls `crate::awareness::brief(ctx.tx(), ...)`. awareness.rs:211-215 calls `handlers::git::briefing_state`, which does `gix::open(root)` (git.rs:1019) and then upstream_metrics for the branch and for the base, plus a branch-vs-base `divergence`. Each of those is an unbounded `rev_walk([from]).with_hidden([hidden]).all()...try_fold` count (git.rs:922-935, 1029-1033). On the launch path, stage_launch (session.rs:604-609) runs plan_launch inside `ctx.read(|conn| ...)`. plan_launch calls awareness::brief (session.rs:451) and guardrail::write_roots (session.rs:453), and write_roots does another gix::open (guardrail.rs:607). engine.rs:171-172 says Unlocked::read's closure is "back on the one global lock". D149 names `gix` among the work that must run outside the transaction. Every spawn, resume and wake (session.rs:918/944/960/1000) and every session.brief therefore holds the store mutex for a repo open and up to three history walks. I found no cache and no cap.
v1.correction: Walk cost is per commit decoded, so most repos pay single-digit to tens of ms. A local base branch that has fallen far behind its upstream pays proportionally more. That is real but not a multi-second freeze in typical use, so medium is right. Fix as proposed: in stage_launch, return worktree, branch and base from ctx.read and build the git section (and write_roots) after the lock is released. Register session.brief as unlocked and read its rows via ctx.read. Capping the walk (e.g. reporting "1000+") is a cheap extra safeguard.

findings.title: avd.create and avd.boot run avdmanager/emulator/adb with no timeout inside the transaction
findings.evidence: avd.create is a plain `register` (device.rs:321). It runs `command.stdin(Stdio::piped())…spawn()` and then `child.wait_with_output()` (device.rs:332-335): the JVM-based avdmanager creating an AVD, with no deadline. It then calls `list_avds(ctx.tx())` (device.rs:339). avd.boot (plain, device.rs:344-346) also calls list_avds(ctx.tx()). list_avds → list_avds_with runs `Command::new(emulator).arg("-list-avds").output()` (device.rs:478). For each running emulator it also runs `Command::new(adb).args(["-s", serial, "emu", "avd", "name"]).output()` (device.rs:505). Both are unbounded, and there is an `adb devices -l` (2 s) on top. The read-only avd.list and avd.catalog were converted to unlocked; these two mutations were not.
findings.impact: Creating an AVD from the Devices page (tools_devices.rs) holds the global lock for avdmanager's JVM start and image setup, which takes seconds. If an emulator console is wedged, `adb emu avd name` never returns, and avd.boot then freezes the bus indefinitely.
findings.fix: Register avd.create and avd.boot as staged. Read the tool paths in prepare via ctx.read, run avdmanager and list_avds_with there through proc::output_with_timeout, and keep only event emission in finish. avd.boot already spawns the emulator after commit.

v1.reason: AvdCreate is a plain register (device.rs:321). It spawns avdmanager with piped stdio and calls `child.wait_with_output()` (device.rs:332-335) with no deadline. It then calls `list_avds(ctx.tx())` (device.rs:339). AvdBoot (device.rs:344-346, plain) also calls list_avds before the emulator spawn, which is correctly deferred to after_commit. list_avds_with runs `Command::new(emulator).arg("-list-avds").output()` (device.rs:478) with no timeout. running_avds_with runs `Command::new(adb).args(["-s", serial, "emu", "avd", "name"]).output()` per running emulator (device.rs:505), also with no timeout. Both run on top of the 2 s `adb devices -l`. That breaks both CLAUDE.md rules: a subprocess not run through proc::output_with_timeout, and slow work under the store mutex. The comment above list_avds_with ("so the emulator and adb calls happen with nothing locked (D144)") is true only for the unlocked avd.list caller. avdmanager is a JVM tool, so every AVD creation freezes the whole bus, keystrokes excepted (D148), for its full multi-second run. A wedged emulator console (`adb emu` waits on the emulator's telnet console) or a hung `emulator -list-avds` would hold the lock indefinitely.
v1.correction: Raised to high: the rubric counts a bus freeze as high, and this one is unbounded and guaranteed to last seconds on every create. The trigger is a rarer user action (Devices page), which keeps it below critical. Related: avd.catalog (device.rs:314) runs `avdmanager list device -c` via `.output()` with no timeout. It is unlocked, so it does not hold the mutex, but it still breaks the output_with_timeout rule and can hang its caller. Fix as proposed: make avd.create and avd.boot staged. In prepare, read the tool paths via ctx.read, then run avdmanager and list_avds_with through proc::output_with_timeout, and give the `emu avd name` probes a deadline too.

v2.reason:
(a) The code does what is claimed. AvdCreate and AvdBoot use plain `e.register` (crates/relay-core/src/handlers/device.rs:321, :344). Engine::dispatch_inner takes `self.store.lock()`, opens a transaction and runs the handler while holding it (crates/relay-core/src/engine.rs:953-980).
- avd.create spawns avdmanager and blocks in `child.wait_with_output()` (device.rs:332-335). There is no deadline and it does not go through proc::output_with_timeout. It then calls `list_avds(ctx.tx())` (:339).
- avd.boot calls `list_avds(ctx.tx())` (:346) before it defers the emulator spawn to after_commit (:353).
- list_avds_with runs `Command::new(emulator).arg("-list-avds").output()` (:478), and for each running emulator `adb -s <serial> emu avd name` via `.output()` (:505). Both are unbounded. Only `adb devices -l` has a bound: 2 s (:577-590).
- D144 (DECISIONS.md:729) and D149 (:797) require the opposite. D149 converted avd.list and avd.catalog to unlocked but left these two out, and nothing documents an exception. The doc comment at device.rs:475-476 ("nothing locked") holds only for the avd.list caller.

(b) Reachability. Both ops are Actors::UserOnly (relay-bus ops/device.rs:55-59), so agents cannot trigger them. The user can: through the "Create AVD" form and the Boot / Cold boot buttons on the native Devices page (tools_devices.rs:106-119, 400-424, 652-665), and through a paired phone, since the phone door forwards any `user`-actor request (relay-remote wire.rs gate). This user has a real toolchain: ~/Android/Sdk/cmdline-tools/latest/bin/avdmanager is a JVM launcher, and there is one AVD and one API 36 image. The path is real, but AVD creation is rare and boot is occasional.

(c) What happens when it fires. For the whole avdmanager run (JVM start, SDK scan, AVD write), every request that needs the store waits. Typically that run takes a few seconds; this user's image ships no userdata.img to copy. The requests that wait:
- every agent request, because socket auth in check_session_token takes the lock (engine.rs:1377). That includes the PreToolUse `guardrail.gate` hook each agent runs before Bash/Edit/Write, and MCP calls;
- UI requests on other connections;
- phone requests;
- system writes such as session exit and idle-to-running.

Keystrokes and terminal output are not affected. A user `session.input` takes pty_fast_path before any lock (engine.rs:891-898), each pane has its own socket (terminal.rs:476), and the PTY reader never takes the store. Everything resumes when avdmanager exits, and no data is lost.

avd.boot normally holds the lock for `emulator -list-avds`, plus at most 2 s for `adb devices`, plus milliseconds for each emulator probe: usually well under a second. The indefinite freeze needs a running emulator that adb still reports as `device` but whose console does not answer `adb emu`, or a hung avdmanager or emulator binary. I could not establish from the repo whether the adb client has its own deadline for `emu`.

(d) Severity should be medium, not high. The usual case is a bounded stall of a few seconds in a rarely used user action, keystrokes and terminals keep working, and the user is unlikely to notice. Only the unbounded edge case matches the rubric's "freeze of the bus", so overall this is "a real bug in a less common path or edge case".

(e) The fix points the right way (register_staged; read tool paths via ctx.read; run the subprocesses with deadlines in prepare; finish emits avd.changed and queues the spawn). As written it would break avd.create; see correction.
v2.correction:
Severity goes back to medium. avd.boot normally holds the lock for well under a second; only a wedged emulator console makes it unbounded, and whether `adb emu` has its own deadline is not established.

Fix correction: proc::output_with_timeout forces `stdin(Stdio::null())` (crates/relay-core/src/proc.rs:35). avd.create depends on answering avdmanager's custom-hardware-profile prompt with "no\n" on a piped stdin (device.rs:332-334). Routing avdmanager through the helper unchanged would give that prompt EOF and would probably make AVD creation fail. Add a variant that takes stdin bytes: spawn with stdin piped, write "no\n", drop the pipe, then use the same deadline loop, drain threads and process-group kill.

The fix also needs:
- A short deadline on each `adb emu avd name` probe, with a timeout treated as "serial unknown" rather than an error.
- An avdmanager deadline chosen with the UI in mind. The native client gives avd.create a 30 s request timeout (apps/relay-native/src/client.rs:65-71). The socket door serves one request at a time per connection (crates/relay-core/src/socket.rs:335-744), so after the fix the main window's other calls still queue behind avd.create. Either keep the deadline under 30 s, raise the client timeout for avd.create, or send it on its own connection the way lifecycle ops are sent (client.rs:131-141).

More related locations:
- device.rs:315: avd.catalog runs `avdmanager list device -c` with no timeout. It is unlocked, so it does not hold the mutex, but it breaks the output_with_timeout rule.
- avd.list (unlocked; called on every Devices page render, tools_devices.rs:92 and :643) runs the same unbounded list_avds_with. If an emulator console is wedged, it stalls the UI's main connection without holding the store. Putting the deadlines inside list_avds_with fixes this too.

findings.title: file.write reads the whole old file and runs an unbounded Myers line diff inside the transaction
findings.evidence: file.write is a plain `register` (file.rs:72). It reads the current file with no size cap: `let old = fs::read_to_string(&path);` (file.rs:76). It then computes `let (removed, added) = line_counts(&old, &p.text);` (file.rs:103). line_counts is `TextDiff::from_lines(old, new).iter_all_changes()` (file.rs:599-610). In similar 2.7, TextDiff::from_lines uses the default TextDiffConfig: Myers with `deadline: None` (similar-2.7.0 src/text/mod.rs:42-46, types.rs:24-27). Its time is O((N+M)·D). The guardrail check that runs just before deliberately avoids this: "Linear multiset line comparison… This deliberately avoids quadratic LCS work on large generated files" (guardrail.rs:1096-1099). The socket door reads request lines with no length limit.
findings.impact: Saving, or an agent writing, a large regenerated file with many changed lines (a lockfile, generated JSON, a minified bundle) makes the diff quadratic: seconds to minutes. Every other request waits on the store mutex for that time. The counts are only informational (WriteOut.removed_lines/added_lines).
findings.fix: Use the guardrail's linear changed_line_counts, or TextDiff with a short `timeout`. Cap the old-file read; the guardrail already caps its comparison at 64 MiB. Alternatively compute the counts outside the lock, since they do not affect the write.

v1.reason: file.write is a plain register (file.rs:72). It reads the old file in full with `fs::read_to_string(&path)` (file.rs:76) and computes `line_counts(&old, &p.text)` (file.rs:103). line_counts (file.rs:599-610) is `TextDiff::from_lines(old, new).iter_all_changes()`. I checked similar 2.7.0 in the registry: TextDiffConfig derives Default with `deadline: None` and the Myers algorithm, and the docs say "By default a diff will take as long as it takes". Myers costs O((N+M)·D) after prefix/suffix trimming. A write that replaces most lines of a large file therefore does quadratic work while the store mutex is held. Just above, guardrail::enforce deliberately uses the linear changed_line_counts and says it "deliberately avoids quadratic LCS work on large generated files" (guardrail.rs:1096-1099). The result is used only for the informational WriteOut.removed_lines/added_lines.
v1.correction: The trigger needs a large file with many changed lines: about 10k fully changed lines costs on the order of a second, and less changes cost far less. That is a less common path (the editor's save, or an agent's file.write via MCP), so it stays medium rather than high. Simplest fix: reuse guardrail's linear changed_line_counts, or set a short `.timeout()` on the TextDiff config. Either keeps the write itself unchanged.

findings.title: task.attach, file.import and file.rename/move do unbounded file reads and copies inside the transaction
findings.evidence:
- task.attach with a path (plain register, task.rs:982) runs `let bytes = std::fs::read(&src).bus()?;` with no size check. attach_bytes then writes the bytes back with `std::fs::write(&path, bytes)` (task.rs:505-538). All of it happens in the transaction.
- file.import (plain, file.rs:262-298) recursively copies arbitrary absolute source trees with `copy(source, &dest)` (file.rs:293, 612-627).
- file.rename and file.move call guard_path_mutation. It reads the entire source file into memory with `fs::read_to_string(content).unwrap_or_default()` (file.rs:578), before enforce, which itself caps reads at 64 MiB.
Related one-shot cases:
- app.backup.now copies the whole database inside the transaction (app.rs:48, store.rs:556-564).
- skill.install's finish may copy up to 64 MiB in skills::adopt's copy fallback (provider.rs:505, skills.rs:51-66).
- app.import.v3 copies attachments (import_v3.rs:263).
findings.impact: Three user actions hold the global lock for a full read or copy and load the whole file into memory: attaching a large file to a task ("Attach image" takes a typed path, task_pages.rs:880), importing a directory, and renaming a multi-GB asset. Every agent hook and UI request waits meanwhile.
findings.fix:
- Attachments: cap the size and stream the copy (fs::copy) outside the lock. As a staged op, copy to a temp name in prepare, then insert the row and rename in finish.
- file.import: stage it the same way.
- guard_path_mutation: use a capped read (the gate's 64 MiB rule) instead of read_to_string of the whole file.

v1.reason: task.attach is a plain register (task.rs:982). The path branch does `std::fs::read(&src)` with no size cap (task.rs:993), and attach_bytes then runs `std::fs::write(&path, bytes)` (task.rs:524), all under the transaction. file.import (file.rs:262) is plain and recursively copies arbitrary absolute sources with fs::copy (file.rs:293, 612-627). guard_path_mutation (file.rs:571-585) reads the whole source with `fs::read_to_string(content).unwrap_or_default()`. std's read_to_string reads every byte before it validates UTF-8, so a multi-GB binary is loaded in full before it fails to "". file.rename and file.move call it twice per request (file.rs:180-181, 209-210), so a large asset is read twice under the lock. task.attach and file.rename/move are not UserOnly, so agent sessions can trigger this as well.
v1.correction: Also file.delete (file.rs:224) calls guard_path_mutation and reads the whole file. A side observation worth its own look: for a directory source, guard_path_mutation's read_to_string fails to "", so file.import gates only the top-level dest path and never the files copied beneath it. The app.backup.now case is arguably intentional, because a consistent snapshot needs the lock. Fix: before enforce, use a metadata-capped read (the gate's 64 MiB rule) or skip content for binaries; cap attachment size; stage the copies.

findings.title: The socket door takes the store mutex on a Tokio worker thread for session.attach
findings.evidence: In handle_conn's session.attach branch, after the spawn_blocking dispatch returns, `match crate::handlers::session::pty_by_name(&engine, &p.session)` runs directly in the async task (socket.rs:469). pty_by_name does `let conn = engine.store.lock(); let row = sessions::by_name(&conn, name)?;` (session.rs:1732-1735). That is a blocking std::sync::Mutex acquisition on a runtime worker. Every other store access in the door goes through spawn_blocking. Keystrokes are deliberately answered inline on these same workers (socket.rs:735-739), on the premise that nothing there blocks. The engine already keeps an in-memory name→PTY index (Engine::pty_named, engine.rs:600-608).
findings.impact: Each terminal pane opens its own connection and attaches at startup and again whenever its stream ends (terminal.rs:474-485). While a slow handler holds the store mutex (any of the long holds above), each of those attaches parks a Tokio worker. Once as many panes attach as there are workers (`#[tokio::main]` defaults to one per core), the runtime stops. Keystrokes, PTY output forwarding and the phone door all stall until the mutex frees.
findings.fix: Resolve the PTY with `engine.pty_named(&p.session)`, which needs no store access. Alternatively wrap pty_by_name in spawn_blocking like the rest of the door.

v1.reason: In handle_conn's session.attach branch, socket.rs:469 calls `crate::handlers::session::pty_by_name(&engine, &p.session)` directly in the async task. pty_by_name does `engine.store.lock()` (session.rs:1733), a blocking std Mutex (store.rs:474-476), on a Tokio worker. Every other store access in the door is wrapped in spawn_blocking. Engine::pty_named (engine.rs:600-608) resolves name to PTY with no store access, and the preceding session.attach dispatch has already validated the session.
v1.correction: The trigger is narrower than claimed. The attach's own dispatch has already waited for and released the lock in spawn_blocking, so the worker parks only if another slow lock holder grabs the mutex in the gap before pty_by_name. Stopping the whole runtime would need that to happen for as many concurrent attaches as there are workers. In practice this is an occasional stall of one connection, not a likely runtime freeze, so low rather than medium. The fix stands: use engine.pty_named, or wrap the call in spawn_blocking.

findings.title: A task.dispatch that fails after a nested launch rolls back the session row but leaves the spawned agent process registered under an id that will be reused
findings.evidence: When task.dispatch invokes session.create and session.spawn nested (task.rs:683, 712), finish_launch starts the child and registers it in memory: `let pty = Pty::spawn(spec, …)` and `ctx.engine().set_pty(sid, &name, pty)` (session.rs:646, 685). A later step of the same dispatch can still fail, for example the next fanout child's `dispatch_task(ctx, id, None, template.clone(), start)?` hitting git.fetch_failed (task.rs:1073). dispatch_inner then rolls the transaction back (engine.rs:1074), but nothing undoes set_pty or kills the child. The worktree, branch and hooks created by the nested session.create prepare (session.rs:874, 892) also stay on disk. sessions.id is AUTOINCREMENT (store.rs:86), and a rolled-back insert's id is handed out again. I checked this with sqlite3: the rolled-back insert got id 2 and the next insert also got id 2.
findings.impact: The orphaned claude/codex process keeps running with no session row; its own bus calls fail authentication. The next session.create receives the same id, so `engine.pty(id)` returns the orphan for the new session. Attaching shows the orphan's output, and the session.input fallback handler (session.rs:1660-1675) writes the user's keystrokes into the orphaned agent. At shutdown, mark_restorable writes the orphan's scrollback and state over the new session's row (engine.rs:661-679).
findings.fix: Do not start PTYs inside a transaction that can still fail. Either have finish_launch queue the spawn/set_pty in after_commit, or record PTYs spawned in the request on Ctx and take/kill them on rollback in dispatch_inner. Alternatively, make task.dispatch commit each child dispatch separately.

v1.reason: finish_launch calls Pty::spawn and then `engine.set_pty(sid, &name, pty)` (session.rs:646, 685). Both are in-memory side effects inside the request's transaction. dispatch_inner's failure branch only does `tx.rollback()` (engine.rs:1074), and nothing kills or takes the PTY. sessions.id is AUTOINCREMENT (store.rs:86). sqlite_sequence is updated inside the same transaction, so the rolled-back id is handed out again. The failure is reachable with fanout. task.dispatch (task.rs:1066-1075) creates and launches the parent first and then each child in the same transaction. A template carrying an explicit `branch` fails on the first child every time: the parent's worktree already holds that branch, so `git worktree add <path> <branch>` fails (worktree.rs:204-217) with worktree.create_failed. A transient fetch failure or timeout in a later child does the same. The orphaned agent keeps running, and the worktree, branch and hook directory are left on disk with no row. The next session.create gets the same id, so `engine.pty(id)` returns the orphan until that session is spawned.
v1.correction: The finding misses a worse consequence when the reused id is later spawned. set_pty returns the orphan and finish_launch calls kill_detached(old) (session.rs:685-686), which does not silence_exit. The orphan's exit callback then runs `UPDATE sessions SET state='exited' WHERE id=N AND epoch=1 AND state IN live` (session.rs:651-655). The new session's first launch also uses epoch 1 (row.epoch+1, session.rs:580), so the freshly started session is marked exited, and its task is marked failed if it is a builder. Reachability is narrower than the finding implies. task.dispatch is UserOnly, and no client (native, CLI or remote) sends `fanout`, so the trigger needs a raw bus/CLI call. Without fanout, the steps after the launch almost never fail. Fix: on failure, record PTYs spawned during the request on Ctx and kill them with silence_exit in the rollback branch, or defer spawn/set_pty to after_commit.

findings.title: task.activity scans the project's whole audit history with json_extract inside the transaction
findings.evidence: The query filters `project_id = ?1`, then `(op LIKE 'task.%' AND json_extract(payload, '$.task_id') = ?2) OR (op = 'task.create' AND …) OR json_extract(result_summary, '$.task.id') = ?2 … ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT ?4` (task.rs:763-767). The last OR arm applies to every op, so every audit row of the project is parsed. Those rows are dominated by guardrail.gate and session.report rows, written on each agent tool use and kept 180 days (D151, recovery.rs:18). EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN on the real schema gives `SEARCH audit USING INDEX audit_project_ts (project_id=?)` plus `USE TEMP B-TREE FOR ORDER BY`. A synthetic in-memory run over 300 000 rows with ~2 KB payloads took 71 ms to return 48 rows.
findings.impact: Opening or refreshing a task's activity costs time proportional to the project's total audit volume, not the task's. A busy multi-agent project with millions of retained rows holds the global lock for a large fraction of a second per click, longer with a cold page cache.
findings.fix: Restrict the result_summary arm to the task ops that return a task (op IN (…)). Better, store task_id in its own indexed audit column at append time and query by that.

v1.reason: task.activity is a plain register (task.rs:757). Its query (task.rs:763-767) filters only on project_id. Its last OR arm, `json_extract(result_summary, '$.task.id') = ?2`, applies to every op, so for a task with fewer than limit+1 matches every audit row of the project is visited and its result_summary parsed. In the schema (store.rs:21-26), result_summary comes after payload, so each row read also walks the payload. Payload and result_summary are capped at append (audit.rs:88-97), which bounds the per-row cost; the total is still proportional to the project's whole audit volume under 180-day retention (recovery.rs:18). The query runs on opening and paging task activity (task_pages.rs:1056).
v1.correction: The payload-side json_extract is short-circuited by `op LIKE 'task.%'`, so only result_summary is parsed for non-task rows. Payload caps limit the per-row cost. The impact is a sub-second lock hold per click on large histories, so low is right. Fix: restrict the third arm to the ops that return {task:...}, or add an indexed task_id column.

findings.title: overlap.scan/flag finish re-activates overlaps for a session that closed while the scan ran
findings.evidence: collect_changes runs in prepare, from scan_targets read earlier (overlap.rs:455-464, 531-535). apply_scan, in finish, builds File/Symbol findings purely from that snapshot (overlap.rs:320-347). It runs `UPDATE overlaps SET active=0 WHERE project_id=?1` and re-inserts the findings with `ON CONFLICT(fingerprint) DO UPDATE … active=1` (overlap.rs:424-437). Only claims are re-read joined against live sessions (overlap.rs:350-356). The doc comment claims "A session that closed while the scan ran simply has no row to collide with" (overlap.rs:315-316). session.close's release_claims deactivates that session's overlaps (session.rs:250-254), and a scan prepared before the close turns them back on.
findings.impact: If a session closes while a scan or flag is running, the overlap list shows active file/symbol collisions naming the closed session until the next scan.
findings.fix: In apply_scan, drop `changes` entries whose session is no longer live, by re-reading the live session names inside the transaction. Correct the comment.

v1.reason: collect_changes runs in prepare over a snapshot of targets (overlap.rs:301-313). apply_scan builds File/Symbol findings from that `changes` map alone (overlap.rs:320-347). Only claims are re-read against live sessions (`s.state!='closed'`, overlap.rs:350-356). The claim-vs-changes loop (overlap.rs:376-392) also pairs live claims with changes from closed sessions. Apply_scan deactivates every overlap in the project and then upserts the findings with `active=1` (overlap.rs:424-437). So when a session closes during the unlocked scan, release_claims's deactivation (session.rs:248-254) is undone, and overlaps naming the closed session show again until the next scan. The doc comment at overlap.rs:315-316 claims otherwise and is wrong for File/Symbol findings.
v1.correction: In apply_scan, filter `changes` to session names that are still non-closed in the transaction before building any findings, and fix the comment. The impact is a stale overlap entry that the next scan clears.

findings.title: workspace.discover walks the directory tree inside a transaction although it is a query that never touches the store
findings.evidence: WsDiscover is declared OpMeta::query (ops/workspace.rs:12-13), but it is registered with plain `e.register::<WsDiscover>(|_, p| …)` (workspace.rs:114). The closure never uses the context. discover_repositories recurses up to depth 4 over every directory it does not exclude (workspace.rs:393-413).
findings.impact: Pointing onboarding (onboarding.rs:336) at a large directory, such as a home directory or a monorepo parent, holds the global lock for the whole walk.
findings.fix: Register it with register_unlocked; it needs no store access at all.

v1.reason: WsDiscover is OpMeta::query (ops/workspace.rs:12-13) but is registered with plain `e.register::<WsDiscover>(|_, p| ...)` (workspace.rs:114). The closure never touches ctx, yet dispatch opens a transaction and holds the store mutex for the call. discover_repositories (workspace.rs:393-413) walks up to depth 4, skipping only .git/.relay/node_modules/target/build/.gradle, and does not skip hidden dirs such as ~/.cache or ~/.local. With no path given, it walks the parent of the engine's cwd repo, or the cwd itself. The op is not UserOnly, so an agent can also point it at `/`.
v1.correction: Separately, `entry?` / `read_dir(path)?` propagate the first permission error, so one unreadable subdirectory fails the whole discovery. Fix: register_unlocked, and skip unreadable entries rather than aborting.

findings.title: Unlocked and prepare-phase subprocesses still bypass proc::output_with_timeout
findings.symbol: Push prepare / github::status / github::repositories / download_skills / avd catalog
findings.evidence:
- git.push's prepare runs `worktree::git_mutate(&root, &args)` (git.rs:617), which is a plain `.output()` (worktree.rs:27). It also lacks GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0, which fetch_remote does set (git.rs:943).
- github.status runs `Command::new(gh).args(["api","user",…]).output()` (github.rs:45).
- github.repo.list runs `gh api --paginate …` with `.output()` (github.rs:68-70).
- skill.install's prepare runs `git clone --depth 1` with `.output()` (github.rs:106-109).
- avd.catalog runs `avdmanager list device -c` with `.output()` (device.rs:315).
- avd.list runs `emulator -list-avds` (device.rs:478).
- The normal (unlocked) git.commit prepare runs the user's pre-commit hook via run_user_pre_commit, `.output()` with no deadline (hooks.rs:210-213).
None of these hold the store lock on their normal path. CLAUDE.md still requires every handler subprocess to go through output_with_timeout.
findings.impact: Some of these calls can block forever: a push waiting for credentials (git prompts on the engine's controlling terminal when relay serve was started from a shell), or a gh/git call on a stalled network. When that happens, the blocking-pool thread is leaked and the client waits until its own timeout, while the push may still complete later without anyone seeing it. If any of these ops is ever invoked nested via invoke_registered, the hang moves under the lock.
findings.fix: Run all of them through proc::output_with_timeout with suitable deadlines, and set GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0 / GH_PROMPT_DISABLED=1.

v1.reason:
I checked each call site:
- git.push prepare calls `worktree::git_mutate` (git.rs:617), which is a plain `.output()` (worktree.rs:27-28) and does not set GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0. fetch_remote does set it (git.rs:943-947).
- github::status (github.rs:45) and github::repositories (github.rs:68-70) use `.output()`. They are registered unlocked (provider.rs:247, 264).
- download_skills runs `git clone` with `.output()` (github.rs:106-109); it is called from skill.install's prepare (provider.rs:216).
- avd.catalog runs `avdmanager` (device.rs:315) and list_avds_with runs `emulator -list-avds` (device.rs:478), both with `.output()`.
- run_user_pre_commit uses `Command::new(&hook)...output()` (hooks.rs:210-213).
None of these goes through proc::output_with_timeout, which breaks the CLAUDE.md rule. On their normal path none of them holds the store lock, so a hang leaks a blocking-pool thread and the client times out, but the bus is not frozen. The exception is run_user_pre_commit when guardrail.confirm replays a held commit, which runs under the lock; #2 covers that.
v1.correction: A push prompt can hang only when the engine has a controlling tty. `.output()` already gives the child a null stdin, but git opens /dev/tty for credentials unless GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0 is set. Note also that github::connect (`gh auth login --web`, `.status()`) blocks without a deadline, apparently on purpose; at least give it a generous one.

findings.title: BUS.md §5.1 and D149 describe a store-locking model the code does not implement
findings.evidence: BUS.md:225-229 says: "a single `tokio::sync::Mutex` around the engine's write side; queries may read concurrently through the WAL… Anything that takes longer (git, spawn, build) is a handler that returns quickly with a handle". In the code, the store is one rusqlite Connection behind a std::sync::Mutex (store.rs:474-476, `self.conn.lock()`). Every query, locked or unlocked, serializes on it, and project.clone, worktree.remove, avd.create and others run synchronously. DECISIONS.md:816-819 says the nested-prepare cost is paid on guardrail.confirm's replay "and only that path". In fact task.dispatch, project.remove and workspace.remove also nest staged ops (task.rs:683, 712; workspace.rs:173, 328).
findings.impact: Readers, including agents that read BUS.md, assume reads run concurrently and long ops are asynchronous. That assumption is how the slow handlers above ended up registered as plain handlers without anyone noticing.
findings.fix: Update §5.1 to the actual model: one connection behind a std Mutex, reads serialize, three handler shapes. List every nested invoke_registered path in D149.

v1.reason: Both claims hold. BUS.md:225-229 (the first §5.1 bullet) still says "a single `tokio::sync::Mutex` around the engine's write side; queries may read concurrently through the WAL" and that git, spawn and build work "is a handler that returns quickly with a handle". The code has one `Mutex<Connection>` (std::sync, store.rs:9, 377, 474-475), and every read takes it. The third bullet of the same section (D144/D149, three handler shapes) already contradicts the first, so the section is internally inconsistent rather than simply out of date. DECISIONS.md D149 says nested prepare runs on guardrail.confirm's replay "and only that path". invoke_registered (engine.rs:309-345) runs the prepare of any staged op it reaches. Its callers include task.rs:683 (`session.create`, staged at session.rs:833), task.rs:712 (launch_op, i.e. session spawn/resume, both staged), workspace.rs:328 (`session.close`, staged at session.rs:1547) inside project.remove, and workspace.rs:173 (workspace.remove -> project.remove -> session.close). So the nested-prepare cost is paid on several more paths. Impact is limited to misleading readers, hence low.
v1.correction: The extra nested-staged paths go through session.create/spawn/resume (task.dispatch) and session.close (project.remove, and workspace.remove via project.remove), not through those composite ops being staged themselves. Fix: rewrite the first §5.1 bullet to match the actual model (one connection behind a std Mutex, reads serialize, three handler shapes), and list every invoke_registered caller that reaches a staged op in D149.

results.coverage:
Scope: cross-cutting "lens-subprocess" sweep over relay-core, relay-cli, relay-remote, relay-native (relay-mobile excluded). Patterns used (rg): `Command::new`, `std::process::Command`, `tokio::process::Command`, `CommandBuilder`, `spawn_command`, `portable_pty|native_pty_system`, `glib::spawn|spawn_async|gio::Subprocess|SubprocessLauncher`, `output_with_timeout`, `process_group|pre_exec|setsid|kill_on_drop|libc::kill|\.kill\(\)|\.wait(`, `git_mutate|status_files|list_with_dirty|gix::open`, `set_var|remove_var|env_clear`, and env-var reads. Enumerated every spawn site outside tests and traced callers to see which run under the store mutex (`Engine::register` = locked) vs `register_unlocked`/`register_staged`/worker threads/`after_commit`.

Verified good (not reported): `proc::output_with_timeout` kills the whole process group with SIGKILL and reaps (child.wait) on timeout, drains stdout+stderr on separate threads (no pipe-buffer deadlock); `pty::Pty::kill`/`Drop` SIGTERM→SIGKILL the group then reap; `provider_updates::run` bounds via try_wait+group-SIGKILL+wait; mirror_worker drains both pipes and reaps; `provider::refresh`, `device.list/size`, `branch_cleanup`, `guardrail recoverable/git_output`, `hooks::git`, Unreal `run_tests`/`build`, Blender runner, and `worktree::create`/`fetch_remote` all use `output_with_timeout`. ffplay/ffmpeg in relay-native use tokio `kill_on_drop(true)` + explicit kill/wait.

Judged non-findings: shell interpolation — `fish -lc`/`sh -c` command strings come from the user's own project `run_cmd`/`build_cmd` or Relay-built strings; secrets (keystore password) are passed via env, not argv/shell (device.rs store_signing_secret). Dash/option injection — git refs reaching `git branch/switch/merge` are validated by `validate_branch_name` (check-ref-format rejects leading `-`) or by gix `rev_parse_single`, and file paths use `--` separators + `validate_path`; no exploitable trigger found. Env leakage — the engine process does not hold RELAY_TOKEN (only per-PTY), so git/adb/gh children do not inherit it; PTY children inherit the engine's full env via portable-pty's base env, which is expected for a dev tool. portable-pty dup'd fds are F_DUPFD_CLOEXEC and it calls close_random_fds before exec.

Not fully checked: apps/relay-native cannot be compiled in this environment (GTK/VTE version pin per CLAUDE.md), so native findings are from source reading only; its many `glib::spawn_future_local` sites are async tasks, not subprocesses, and were not each traced. relay-remote (the phone door) spawns no subprocesses. I did not exhaustively audit every `.output()` in test/example/smoke code (out of scope). The claim that LFS smudge under the store lock reaches the network is inferred from standard git-lfs behavior + this repo's LFS use (worktree.rs:84, bundled jar); I verified locally that a configured clean/textconv filter blocks `git add`/`git status -- <path>` for the filter's full duration, but did not reproduce an LFS network fetch specifically.

findings.title: project.clone runs `git clone` synchronously inside the store-locked transaction
findings.evidence: `e.register::<ProjectClone>` (workspace.rs:228) is a plain locked handler — `register`, not `register_staged` — so its whole closure runs inside the request's SQLite transaction with the store mutex held (engine.rs dispatch_inner opens `conn`+`tx` then calls `(h.call)`). Inside it, line 234 does `Command::new("git").current_dir(&workspace.path).arg("clone").arg("--").arg(&p.url).arg(&destination).output()` — a plain `std::process::Command::output()` with no timeout and not through `proc::output_with_timeout`. The op's own metadata (ops/workspace.rs:38) advertises it as "Clone a repo into the workspace and register it (async; project.changed when done)", but the implementation is fully synchronous.
findings.impact: Cloning any non-trivial repo (seconds to many minutes over the network) holds the single store mutex for the entire clone. Every other bus request serializes behind it: file reads, task/board updates, session.list, and crucially every other agent's `guardrail.gate` (its Bash/Edit hook blocks, freezing that agent). This is the exact case CLAUDE.md/D144 forbids ("a network call … blocks every other request"). A clone that stalls on auth/network holds the lock until the OS gives up.
findings.fix: Convert to `register_staged`: do the `git clone` (and the nested project.add) in the unlocked `prepare` phase under `proc::output_with_timeout` (or an explicit long deadline), and only record the new project row in `finish`. Set `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0` and `stdin(null)` so a credential prompt cannot hang it. This also makes the "async" the op description already promises true.

v1.reason: ProjectClone is registered with plain e.register (crates/relay-core/src/handlers/workspace.rs:228), not register_staged. At :234 it runs `git clone -- <url> <dest>` with Command::output() inside the request transaction with the store mutex held. There is no timeout, GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT is not set (other git call sites set it: worktree.rs:213, git.rs:943/1349, branch_cleanup.rs:114), and stdin is inherited. The developers know the op takes a long time: the native client gives project.clone a 1800s timeout (apps/relay-native/src/client.rs:67). The op metadata calls it async (crates/relay-bus/src/ops/workspace.rs:38: "(async; project.changed when done)"), but the handler is fully synchronous. It is reached in a normal flow: onboarding's clone-from-GitHub (apps/relay-native/onboarding.rs:527). While a network clone runs, every bus request queues behind the mutex for its whole duration, including running agents' guardrail.gate hook calls, file/task/session ops and git status. This is exactly the D144/D149 case.
v1.correction: The finding's citation ops/workspace.rs:38 is actually crates/relay-bus/src/ops/workspace.rs:38. The call also goes over the UI's shared main connection, which the engine serves serially (socket.rs:741), so the desktop UI stalls even apart from the mutex. Fix as proposed: register_staged with the clone in prepare, bounded by a long deadline through output_with_timeout (process-group kill), GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0, stdin null, and project.add's row insert in finish. Alternatively, make it truly async with after_commit plus a worker emitting project.changed, as the op description promises.

v2.reason:
(a) The code does what the finding says. workspace.rs:228 uses plain `e.register::<ProjectClone>`. dispatch_inner (engine.rs:954-956) takes `self.store.lock()`, opens the transaction and then calls `(h.call)`. Line 234 runs `Command::new("git")...arg("clone").arg("--").arg(&p.url).arg(&destination).output()` inside that call, with no deadline, no `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0` and stdin inherited. This breaks D144: every subprocess forked from a handler must go through `proc::output_with_timeout`. It also breaks D149, which converted the other slow git ops but left project.clone out. git blame shows the code dates from the initial commit, before D144 and D149, so it was missed rather than chosen. No DECISIONS entry excuses it. The op metadata (crates/relay-bus/src/ops/workspace.rs:38) calls the op "async". BUS.md:246-247 says it writes a `project.clone.completed` audit row, but no code does that.

(b) Reachable in normal use. project.clone is user-only. The "Add project…" item, offered on every workspace (shell/registry.rs:472 and :164), leads through app.rs:1690 to onboarding::open. Its clone-from-GitHub path calls project.clone at onboarding.rs:527. This works at any time, not only on first run, so a user can clone a project while agents are working in other projects. `relay cmd project.clone` reaches the same handler. How long it takes depends on repo size and network. The perf baseline already measured 263 ms p50 and 694 ms p95 on a local 1,500-file fixture. A real GitHub clone takes seconds to minutes. A stalled transfer has no upper bound, and the UI cannot cancel it.

(c) While git runs, every request that needs the store mutex waits:
- Every agent socket request, because check_session_token takes the lock (engine.rs:1378).
- guardrail.gate, which is a locked handler (handlers/guardrail.rs:304). Claude and Codex PreToolUse hooks for Edit, Write and Bash call it with a 30 s hook timeout (hooks.rs:351, :521).
- Relay MCP tool calls.
- The claude-report lifecycle hooks. They have a 10 s timeout and fail open, so session-state reports are lost.
- Lifecycle ops and every UI query, including unlocked ones, which take the lock briefly through Unlocked::read.

The desktop UI's shared main connection is also blocked by the clone itself, because socket.rs:335-742 serves one connection's requests one at a time. UI requests hit their 30 s client timeout and show "Request timed out". The client's 1800 s timeout for project.clone only stops the client waiting; the engine keeps the lock until git exits. Keystrokes and PTY output are not affected: they use the D148 in-memory path, and each pane has its own connection (terminal.rs:476). No data is lost or corrupted. The effect is a temporary global bus freeze.

(d) High is right. The rubric lists "a freeze of the bus" in a normal flow under high. It is not critical: the user starts it, it normally ends when the clone ends, terminals stay live and no data is lost.

(e) The fix direction is right, with the corrections below.
v2.correction:
1. Citation: the op metadata is at crates/relay-bus/src/ops/workspace.rs:37-38, not ops/workspace.rs:38. Related docs drift: BUS.md:246-247 says the op completes asynchronously and writes a `project.clone.completed` audit row, but no code does this.

2. The fix must not run "the nested project.add" in prepare. project.add is a mutation and needs the transaction.
   - In prepare: read the workspace through ctx.read, compute clone_destination, check that it exists, then run the clone. Run it through output_with_timeout (process group, stdin null) with a long deadline, about 1800 s to match the client, and with GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0.
   - In finish: call `ctx.invoke_registered("project.add", ...)`. Keep `remove_dir_all` on its failure. project.add already re-validates the workspace, which matters because it may be removed while the lock is released.
   - Once the clone runs unlocked, two concurrent clones to the same destination can both pass the exists() check. git's refusal of a non-empty directory covers most of this. Reserving the destination in memory would close the gap.

3. register_staged alone does not unfreeze the desktop UI. Ui::call (apps/relay-native/src/app.rs:1111) sends project.clone on the shared main connection, which the engine serves one request at a time. The client should send it on its own connection, as it already does for is_lifecycle_request (client.rs:50). Per CLAUDE.md, that change cannot be compiled in an agent session and must be described as not verified. The alternative is the truly async design the docs promise: return a handle, clone on a worker, emit project.changed and write the `.completed` audit row. That needs onboarding.rs:527 to change too.

4. Impact wording: keystrokes and PTY output are not frozen (D148). Everything else that takes the store lock waits.

5. Not established: what Claude Code does when a PreToolUse hook is killed at its 30 s timeout. If it lets the tool proceed, a clone longer than 30 s would also let agents' Edit, Write and Bash calls run without the gate. That would be a separate finding about the hook failing open, and nothing in this repo settles it.

findings.title: worktree::git_mutate runs system git unbounded, and locked handlers call it — LFS smudge/clean runs under the store mutex
findings.evidence: `git()` (worktree.rs:27) is `Command::new("git").arg("-C").arg(repo).args(args).output()` — no timeout, not `proc::output_with_timeout`, and no `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0`. `git_mutate` (line 36) is just `git`. It is called from plain `register` (store-locked) handlers: `git.stage` → `git add --` (git.rs:503), `file.restore_head` → `git checkout -- <path>` (file.rs:256), `git.branch.create` → `git switch -c` (git.rs:374), `git.unstage` (git.rs:527), `git.branch.delete` (git.rs:485), `git.branch.clean_merged` (git.rs:712), and `git.commit` finish → `git commit` (git.rs:571). `git add` runs the `clean` filter and `git checkout --` runs the `smudge` filter; this repo uses Git LFS (worktree.rs:84 comment; bundled scrcpy jar), and LFS smudge fetches missing objects from the LFS server — a network operation executed while the store mutex is held.
findings.impact: A slow or hung content filter (LFS smudge fetching an uncached object from an unreachable/slow server, or any `.gitattributes` filter) makes `git.stage`/`file.restore_head`/`git.branch.*` hold the store mutex for the whole filter run, freezing every other bus request (other agents' guardrail gates, UI reads, task updates) until it returns — with no deadline to end the wait. Measured locally: a tracked file with a configured clean/textconv filter makes `git status -- <path>` and `git add` block for the filter's full duration.
findings.fix: Route every `git_mutate`/`git()` call through `proc::output_with_timeout` with a bounded deadline, and move the filter-running mutations (stage, restore_head, branch switch/create) into `register_staged` prepare phases so they run with the store unlocked (as `git.commit`'s staging/hook phase already does). Add `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0` and `stdin(null)` as `worktree::create`/`fetch_remote` already do.

v1.reason: worktree.rs:26-33 `git()` is a bare `Command::new("git").arg("-C").arg(repo).args(args).output()` with no deadline, and `git_mutate` (line 36) only forwards to it. That breaks the CLAUDE.md rule that every subprocess forked from a handler goes through `proc::output_with_timeout`. The same file already applies the rule elsewhere: `status_files` (lines 86-96) uses `output_with_timeout` with a 10 s limit, and its comment says the reason is repository filters. I checked engine.rs:478 to confirm these handlers use plain `Engine::register`, which runs inside the transaction with the store mutex held. The handlers are `git.stage` (git.rs:490-505, `git add -- <paths>`, which runs the clean filter and hashes every staged blob), `git.unstage` (git.rs:506-530), `git.branch.create` (git.rs:345-382; `git switch -c <name> <start>` checks out the start point's tree, which runs smudge filters), `git.branch.delete` (git.rs:459-489), `git.clean_merged` (git.rs:690-720) and `file.restore_head` (file.rs:253-261, `git checkout -- <path>`, which runs smudge; for an LFS pointer whose object is missing locally, git-lfs fetches it over the network). Neighbouring ops follow the documented D144/D149 design: `BranchSwitch`, `Commit`, `Fetch` and `Push` are `register_staged` and do their git work in the unlocked prepare phase. So these locked ones are inconsistent with that design, not an intended exception. Trigger: an agent or the UI stages large LFS/binary assets (e.g. Unreal .uasset files), or restores a file whose LFS object is not cached while the LFS server is slow or unreachable. Consequence: the store mutex is held for the whole git run with no upper bound, so every other bus request (guardrail gates of other agents, UI reads, task updates) waits. session.input does not use SQLite (D148), so keystrokes themselves are not blocked.
v1.correction: Line numbers are close: `git()` is at worktree.rs:26 and the git.stage call is at git.rs:503. Two parts of the finding need correcting. (1) The `git.commit` entry (git.rs:571) is in the locked finish phase, but `git commit` with an already-built index does not run clean or smudge filters, and its staging (`add -A`) already happens in the unlocked prepare phase. Its only remaining exposure under the lock is hooks that `--no-verify` does not skip, such as post-commit (git-lfs installs one). It belongs in 'related' as a minor case, not as one of the main examples. (2) The other `git_mutate` callers are not affected: device.rs:1575-1618 (`fetch`/`merge`) runs on the run_worker thread without the lock, and integration.rs:121/128 runs on the spawned integration thread. integration.rs:64 (`IntegrationDiscard`, `branch -D`) is locked but fast. Fix: give `git()` a deadline through `proc::output_with_timeout`, with `stdin(null)` and `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0`. Then convert `Stage`, `Unstage`, `BranchCreate` and `RestoreHead` to `register_staged`, doing the subprocess in prepare and only `changed()` in finish, as `BranchSwitch` already does. `branch -d` in `BranchDelete`/`CleanMerged` only needs the timeout. Also related: `git.pr_open` (git.rs:666-689) runs `gh pr create`, a network call, with bare `.output()` inside a locked `register` handler. That is the same invariant broken in a worse way.

v2.reason:
(a) The code does what the finding says. worktree.rs:26-33 `git()` is a bare `Command::new("git").arg("-C").arg(repo).args(args).output()`: no deadline and no GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT. `git_mutate` (line 36) only forwards to it. A plain `Engine::register` handler runs after `self.store.lock()` and `conn.transaction()` (engine.rs:954-956). These locked handlers call it:
- git.branch.create (git.rs:345, call at 374)
- git.branch.delete (git.rs:445, call at 485)
- git.stage (git.rs:490, call at 503)
- git.unstage (git.rs:507, call at 527)
- git.branch.clean_merged (git.rs:693, call at 712)
- file.restore_head (file.rs:253, call at 256)
This breaks the CLAUDE.md rule, D144 (every subprocess through output_with_timeout) and D149 ("not merely with a timeout"). The code's own comment at git.rs:384 says `git switch` does not need the store, yet BranchCreate runs `git switch -c` under it.

(b) Who triggers it, and how often. All of these are normal desktop UI flows in the Source Control panel:
- Stage, Stage all, Mark as resolved (code_git.rs:470-474 and 904-908)
- Unstage and Unstage all
- branch Create (code_git.rs:1035; always sends checkout:true, with an optional start point)
- branch Delete
- Restore from HEAD
Agents can also reach git.stage and git.unstage over MCP. On an ordinary source repo each call takes tens of ms, so nobody notices. The hold becomes seconds to minutes when git has real work to do:
- staging or unstaging large binary or LFS assets (the clean filter hashes them; non-LFS binaries are zlib-compressed)
- restoring a large LFS file from HEAD
- creating a branch from a start point whose tree differs, where smudge runs and git-lfs downloads objects not yet local
That is the author's target setup. Three places say LFS asset repos are expected: the comment at worktree.rs:83-85, the filter fixture test at worktree.rs:398-430 (commit d849b98 "Stop Git refresh storms"), and client.rs:68 ("A new checkout may hydrate large LFS assets"). I could not confirm that the user's own game repos use LFS: the ~/dev3 game folders are not git repos in this sandbox. A filter-timing experiment in the scratchpad was blocked by a shell safety check, so the filter behaviour rests on standard git semantics and the repo's own fixture test.

(c) What happens when it fires. The store mutex is held for the whole git run. Every other request that needs the store waits:
- other agents' PreToolUse gate on each Bash/Write/Edit
- actor resolution and guardrail::authorize for every agent call
- the short `Unlocked::read` bursts of "unlocked" queries (engine.rs:181)
The user's own keystrokes are not blocked (the D148 fast path). Relay's PreToolUse hook has a 30 s timeout (hooks.rs:351) and the native client gives up after 30 s by default (client.rs:65-70). A hold past 30 s therefore becomes failed or blocked agent tool calls in every session, plus errors and stale panes in the UI. Relay imposes no deadline, so the hold ends only when git does; a slow LFS server or a credential helper waiting on the user stretches it. No data is lost.

(d) Severity: high is right. It is a bus-wide freeze in a normal flow for asset-heavy repos, which is the stated domain. It is not critical: it is transient in the common case, loses no data, and is negligible on plain source repos.

(e) The fix direction is correct and matches the existing BranchSwitch, CommitOp and Push design. The refinements are in the correction.
v2.correction:
1. Wrong evidence: RelayV4 itself does not use Git LFS. .gitattributes has no filter=lfs, and apps/relay-native/resources/scrcpy-server-v4.1 is an ordinary 733,706-byte blob (`git check-attr filter` reports unspecified). The LFS exposure is in the user projects Relay manages (worktree.rs:83-85, client.rs:68).

2. Scope of the listed handlers:
- `git.commit` finish (git.rs:571) is a minor related case, as the first verifier said. The staging already runs unlocked; under the lock `git commit` only has an index refresh and post-commit hooks left.
- `git.branch.create` rewrites files only when start_point names a different tree. `switch -c` from HEAD is cheap.
- `branch -d` (BranchDelete, CleanMerged) runs no filters. It only breaks the timeout rule.
- `git.unstage`'s cost comes from the index refresh after `reset`, which re-reads the reset entries through the clean filter. That is from git's refresh semantics; I could not measure it.

3. Missed instance of the same root cause: `worktree::remove` uses the same bare `git()` (worktree.rs:362 `worktree remove --force`, worktree.rs:368 `worktree prune`) after tree walks (`purge_build` and `dir_size`). It is called from two locked `register` handlers: `worktree.remove` (git.rs:129-144) and `integration.discard` (integration.rs:62). An integration worktree is a full project checkout, so discarding one deletes it under the store, a longer hold than any `git add`. The first verifier's "integration.rs:64 is locked but fast" misses line 62 in the same handler. Reach is low: neither op is called by the native UI or exposed in the agents' MCP tool list.

4. More related locations:
- `git.pr.open` (git.rs:666-692): `gh pr create` is a network call with bare `.output()` in a locked handler, triggered from a UI button (code_git.rs:662).
- git.rs:1269-1273: `check-ref-format` with bare `.output()`. Harmless.

5. Fix refinements:
- `stdin(null)` adds nothing. It is already the default for `Command::output()` and is set by output_with_timeout (proc.rs:35). Only GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0 is new.
- The primary fix is `register_staged`: run the git subprocess in an unlocked prepare via `resolve_root_unlocked`, and only call `changed()` in finish. Do this for Stage, Unstage, BranchCreate, RestoreHead and PrOpen. Guardrail authorization runs in dispatch before prepare, so no check is lost.
- Caveat on adding a deadline: output_with_timeout SIGKILLs the whole process group (proc.rs:53-58). Killing a mutating git (add, reset, checkout, switch, branch) skips git's lockfile cleanup. It leaves `index.lock` or a ref `.lock` behind, and every later git command in that checkout then fails with "Unable to create .../index.lock: File exists" until the file is removed by hand. A killed checkout or switch can also leave a half-updated tree.
- So use a generous deadline (the 120 s that run_switch and worktree::create use), not a short one. Preferably send SIGTERM before SIGKILL, since git removes its lockfiles on SIGTERM. Report a timeout as a typed refusal that says what may be left behind.

findings.title: blender_python / ue_python MCP tools execute agent-supplied code with no guardrail gate
findings.evidence: `blender_python` (blender.rs:197) takes the agent's `code` and runs it via `run(PY_RUN, &a, …)` (blender.rs:207) which writes the agent script into `job.py` (blender.rs:336) and executes `blender -b … --factory-startup --python job.py`. PY_RUN executes the agent's code with full `bpy`, and nothing stops `import os, subprocess`. The subprocess itself is bounded by `output_with_timeout`, but its *contents* are ungated. Relay's guardrails are enforced only through the provider PreToolUse hook, whose matcher is `Edit|Write|MultiEdit|Bash` (hooks.rs:350) / `Bash|apply_patch|Edit|Write` (hooks.rs:517) and whose adapter only understands those tools (main.rs:405-462). An MCP tool call named `mcp__blender__blender_python` is not matched by that regex, so no `guardrail.gate` fires. There is no `guardrail` call anywhere in blender.rs/unreal.rs.
findings.impact: An agent that is otherwise guardrailed (denied commands like `rm -rf`/`curl | sh`, write-root limits, destructive-write caps) escapes all of it in any project with the blender or unreal plugin enabled: `blender_python` with `code="import shutil; shutil.rmtree('/home/<user>/…')"` or `import os; os.system(...)` runs unmediated with the engine user's privileges. `ue_python`/`ue_console`/`ue_call` give the same arbitrary-code capability inside the Relay-launched editor process.
findings.fix: Route plugin MCP tool invocations that can execute code or write files through the same `guardrail.gate` path (treat blender_python/ue_python/ue_console as `kind:exec`), or gate the MCP server behind an explicit per-session capability the user grants, so these tools cannot silently bypass the command/write guardrails. At minimum, document that enabling these plugins disables guardrails for the session.

v1.reason: The code paths are as described: blender_python (crates/relay-cli/src/blender.rs:197-207) runs agent code through run(PY_RUN, ...), which calls proc::output_with_timeout at :351. The PreToolUse matchers at crates/relay-core/src/hooks.rs:350 and :517 do not match MCP tool names. But the finding's premise that this lets an otherwise-guardrailed agent escape is wrong. Relay's exec guardrail is not a sandbox. evaluate_exec (crates/relay-core/src/guardrail.rs:811-847) only checks the command line against denied_commands, and the default list is ['rm -rf','git reset --hard','git clean -fd','git push --force'] (handlers/settings.rs:33). Matching is on parsed argv (D103) and does not look inside interpreter arguments. So the same agent can already run `python3 -c "import shutil; shutil.rmtree(...)"` or `python3 script.py` through the gated Bash tool, and that bypasses the command denylist and the Edit/Write path policies alike. The code says as much at guardrail.rs:849-850: "closes the obvious door, not every door". blender_python and ue_python give the agent no capability it lacks through Bash. They run as the same user, only in a project where the user explicitly turned the plugin on (plugins.rs header, D159). Claude sessions launch without any skip-permissions flag (providers.rs:195), so MCP tool calls still go through the provider's own approval prompts. No reachable escalation beyond the existing design was established.
v1.correction: If anything, this is a docs note: guardrails are a denylist against agent slips, not a containment boundary. Bash with an interpreter and plugin MCP code tools both sit outside it. Gating MCP tools would not change the threat model unless interpreter use through Bash were also contained.

findings.title: device.run.stop kills only the fish wrapper, not the gradle process group
findings.evidence: `stream_command` spawns the build with `Command::new(shell).args(["-lc", …])` (device.rs:1822) and never calls `process_group(0)`, so the child leads no separate group. `RunRuntime::stop` (device.rs:403) does only `child.kill()` — a single SIGKILL to the direct `fish -lc` PID, with no process-group kill and no `wait()`. On `device.run.stop` the worker may observe `runtime.stopped()` at the top of the read loop and `return Streamed::Stopped` (device.rs:1844) before reaching the `take_child().and_then(|c| c.wait())` reap at device.rs:1854.
findings.impact: Stopping a run kills the shell wrapper but leaves the gradle client (java) it spawned running/orphaned, so `device.run.stop` does not actually stop the build; and on the early-return race the wrapper child is left unreaped (a zombie) until the engine exits. Repeated start/stop accumulates orphaned builds competing for the device and CPU.
findings.fix: Spawn run/build children with `process_group(0)` and, on stop, SIGKILL the whole group (`libc::kill(-pid, SIGKILL)`) then `wait()` the child — the pattern `proc::output_with_timeout` and `provider_updates::run` already use. Ensure the stopped path reaps the child before returning.

v1.reason: stream_command (crates/relay-core/src/handlers/device.rs:1806-1863) spawns `fish -lc '<command> 2>&1'` (or sh under the test instance) without process_group(0). It stores the Child in the runtime (:1838). RunStop (:263-266) calls RunRuntime::stop (crates/relay-core/src/device.rs:403-408), which does only child.kill() on the direct shell PID. Fish does not tail-exec the command, so the gradle wrapper/java client is a grandchild. It survives the SIGKILL and keeps the stdout pipe open, so the build continues after the user pressed Stop. The engine already uses process-group kills elsewhere (proc.rs:32/55, provider_updates.rs:95/120, pty.rs:348), so the omission here is inconsistent. Reaping: if a line arrives after stop, the loop returns Streamed::Stopped at :1840-1842 before take_child().wait() at :1854. The killed shell stays in the runtime unreaped and becomes a zombie once the runtime is dropped. The logcat loop in run_worker (:1773-1776) has the same early return without reaping its adb child. Whether the orphaned gradle client exits on EPIPE once the reader is dropped was not established; Java's PrintStream usually swallows write errors, so it most likely runs to completion.
v1.correction: Also related: device.rs:1773-1776 (logcat early return, adb child left unreaped). Fix: process_group(0) on run/build spawns, killpg(SIGKILL) in RunRuntime::stop, and always take_child().wait() on the Stopped path. Impact is a build that keeps running after Stop and a zombie per stop; the Gradle daemon then stays busy, so the next run may start a second daemon.

findings.title: GitHub `gh`/`git clone` subprocesses have no timeout
findings.evidence: `status()` runs `gh api user` via `Command::output()` with no timeout (github.rs:45); `repositories()` runs `gh api --paginate user/repos` the same way (github.rs:68); `download_skills()` runs `git clone --depth 1 <url>` with `Command::output()` and no timeout (github.rs:109). These are network operations. They are reached from `github.status`/`github.repo.list` (register_unlocked, provider.rs:247/262) and `skill.install` prepare (provider.rs:216) — unlocked, so no store-mutex freeze, but there is no deadline at all.
findings.impact: A hung or very slow network (proxy, captive portal, stalled TLS) makes the GitHub-status/repo-list/skill-install request hang indefinitely, tying up a blocking-pool thread and leaving the UI call that issued it waiting forever with no refusal. Unlike the adb/provider probes (D144), these `gh`/clone calls were never given the `output_with_timeout` treatment.
findings.fix: Run all `gh`/`git clone` calls through `proc::output_with_timeout` with a network-scale deadline (as `branch_cleanup::merged_prs` and `git.pr.list` already do), returning a typed `unavailable` on timeout.

v1.reason: crates/relay-core/src/github.rs runs `gh api user` (:45), `gh api --paginate user/repos` (:68-70) and `git clone --depth 1` (:106-109) with plain Command::output(). There is no deadline and GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT is not set for the clone. Callers: GitHubStatusOp and GitHubRepoList use register_unlocked (handlers/provider.rs:247, :262), and skill.install runs the clone in a register_staged prepare (provider.rs:211-216). So the store mutex is not held, as the finding says. The finding gets the UI impact wrong in both directions. The UI does not wait forever: the native client gives every op except project.clone and a few session ops a 30s request timeout (apps/relay-native/src/client.rs:65-71). But the real impact is worse than a stuck pool thread. The engine handles one socket connection's requests serially: socket.rs:741 awaits spawn_blocking(dispatch) before it reads the next line. Ui::call sends every non-lifecycle request over one shared connection (apps/relay-native/src/app.rs:1111-1116). github.status and github.repo.list are called on that connection from onboarding (onboarding.rs:422, :429), and skill.install from tools_skills.rs:180/370. If gh or git stalls (dead TCP, captive portal, stalled TLS; git has no low-speed limit by default), every later UI request on that connection queues behind it and each one times out client-side until the child exits.
v1.correction: Impact: a stalled gh/git child blocks the desktop UI's main bus connection for as long as it runs, because socket.rs:741 serializes requests per connection. It is not merely an orphaned blocking thread, and the UI call itself errors after 30s rather than waiting forever. Fix as proposed: put proc::output_with_timeout around gh api and git clone, and set GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0 with stdin null. github::connect (:56-63) also uses an unbounded .status(), but it runs on an after_commit worker thread with --web login, so a long wait there is expected.

findings.title: avd.create spawns avdmanager and waits unbounded inside a locked handler
findings.evidence: `e.register::<AvdCreate>` (device.rs:321) is a plain locked handler. It builds `Command::new(avdmanager) create avd …`, `spawn()`s it (device.rs:332) and then `child.wait_with_output()` (device.rs:335) with no timeout and not through `proc::output_with_timeout`, all while the store mutex and transaction are held. `avd.catalog`/`avd.list` run their avdmanager/emulator/adb probes with unbounded `.output()` too (device.rs:315, 478, 505), though those are `register_unlocked`.
findings.impact: `avdmanager create avd` is a JVM tool that can stall (slow disk, waiting on input, sdkmanager locks). While it runs, the store mutex is held, freezing every other bus request — the D144 violation. The unlocked avd.list/catalog probes can instead hang their request thread forever with no deadline.
findings.fix: Move AvdCreate's subprocess into a `register_staged` prepare phase bounded by `proc::output_with_timeout`, and route the avd.list/avd.catalog probes through `output_with_timeout` as well.

v1.reason: AvdCreate is registered with plain e.register (crates/relay-core/src/handlers/device.rs:321), so it runs inside the request transaction with the store mutex held. At :332-335 it spawns avdmanager and calls child.wait_with_output() with no timeout, which breaks D144 (every subprocess forked from a handler goes through output_with_timeout) and D149. Then at :339, still under the lock, list_avds(ctx.tx()) runs `emulator -list-avds` with an unbounded .output() (:478). Through running_avds_with it also runs `adb -s <serial> emu avd name` for each running emulator, unbounded (:505). AvdBoot (:344-346) calls list_avds under the lock the same way. The finding's claim that avdmanager might stall waiting on input is weak. The handler writes "no\n", and std's wait_with_output drops stdin before waiting, so the child gets EOF. The realistic cost is the bus freezing for the JVM tool's whole run (seconds, longer on a cold or slow disk), plus the emulator/adb probes. Every request stalls during that time, including agents' guardrail.gate calls. Both ops are user-only and infrequent, which keeps this at medium.
v1.correction: Add AvdBoot (device.rs:346, list_avds under the lock) as a related location. The input-stall mechanism is unlikely, because stdin is closed after "no\n". The concrete harm is the mutex held for avdmanager's runtime plus unbounded emulator/adb probes under the lock. AvdList and AvdCatalog (:301-319) are unlocked, so there the problem is only a missing deadline (lower impact). Fix: register_staged with the avdmanager run and list_avds_with in prepare under output_with_timeout.

results.coverage:
I read all of relay-core's SQLite-touching code: store.rs (migrations v1–v20, tune, backups), engine.rs (pipeline, fast paths, system_write), audit.rs, recovery.rs, sessions.rs, awareness.rs, guardrail.rs plus grants.rs, and these handlers: session, task, notes, overlap, guardrail, workspace, module, integration, notify, settings, app, audit, bus, provider (partial), import_v3, ui (layouts), device_lease, plus device.rs and git.rs (SQL sites and the subprocess calls they reach), skills, plugins, providers, provider_updates and branch_cleanup. relay-bus, relay-cli, relay-remote and relay-native contain no SQL (checked by grep); I traced only their call sites for the heavy ops: task_pages.rs, board_view.rs, pages.rs, app.rs event loop, shell/registry.rs and launch.rs.

Grep patterns used: query_row\(, \.prepare\(, prepare_cached\(, \.execute\(, execute_batch, query_map, \.transaction\(, with_tx, store\.lock\(\), pragma_, DELETE FROM, LIKE|GLOB, json_extract|json_each|json_set, set_undo, system_write, datetime\(|strftime|julianday, get::<_,\s*(u32|i32…)>, git_mutate|worktree::remove|rename_branch, Command::new/.output() in locked handlers (partial).

Experiments, all under scratchpad/exp/sqlite-lens; the large databases were deleted afterwards:
- built the v20 schema from MIGRATIONS
- EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN for the audit, mailbox, notification, session, holds, settings and branch-cleanup queries
- replayed project.remove's DELETE list against a labelled project (FK failure confirmed)
- benchmarked task.activity and audit.list (60k and 300k rows), mailbox.list (20k messages), the unread-notification badge (100k rows, 2 ms, not reported), the overlaps UPDATE (20k rows) and task.list hydration (2000 tasks)
- measured VACUUM peak RSS with temp_store=MEMORY versus default, and the WAL size left behind

Checked and found OK, not reported:
- Migrations: append-only, SCHEMA_VERSION == MIGRATIONS.len() is asserted in tests, one transaction per step, ALTER defaults satisfy CHECK constraints, and the upgrade backup is taken first.
- D148 holds: the session.input/resize/mirror fast paths and mail_hint never lock the store for user actors.
- LIKE patterns are escaped or constant, and no SQL is built from user input; JSON TEXT columns are parsed leniently; timestamps all come from jiff RFC3339 UTC, and dashboard datetime() handles fractional seconds and Z; no integer-width bugs found; hot pipeline lookups are prepare_cached and indexed.

Not reported:
- Free-form `since`/`until` strings (Ts = String) are compared lexicographically against stored timestamps.
- The non-constant-time token compare.
- store.db and backups get default 0644 permissions, so the home directory's permissions are the only protection.
- Idempotency race: the same request id sent twice concurrently gets an internal error rather than a replay.
- In-memory device-lease and provider_updates state is not rolled back with the transaction.
- Not finished: the non-SQL logic of device.rs workers (lines 600–2150), hooks.rs, the GTK UI beyond the traced calls, and Rust-side timings (cargo not run; costs were measured on equivalent SQL in Python's SQLite 3.53).

findings.title: project.remove / workspace.remove always fail with FOREIGN KEY error once a project has a task label, after already SIGKILLing the project's agents
findings.evidence: The delete list at workspace.rs:354-374 covers message_recipients … plugin_projects but never `labels`. Migration v16 defines `labels(... project_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES projects(id) ...)` with no ON DELETE CASCADE (store.rs:315-319), foreign_keys=ON (store.rs:397), and nothing in the crate ever deletes a label row (`label_id()` task.rs:124-142 only inserts; no `DELETE FROM labels` anywhere). So `DELETE FROM projects WHERE id = ?1` (workspace.rs:380) raises `FOREIGN KEY constraint failed`. I reproduced this by building the v20 schema from MIGRATIONS and replaying the handler's exact DELETE list against a project with one label. Before that statement runs, with `force` (the native dialog always sets `payload["force"] = json!(true)`, shell/registry.rs:626), the handler invokes `session.close {remove_worktree:false}` for every open session (workspace.rs:327-329). Close's prepare phase runs the hook teardown on the filesystem (core.hooksPath restored, adapters removed, hook dir deleted), and its finish phase calls `take_pty` and leaves the kill in `after_commit` (session.rs:1602-1607). When the request fails, the transaction rolls back and the after_commit closures are dropped. Each closure held the last `Arc<Pty>`: socket attach streams hold only a broadcast receiver, and reader and waiter threads hold `Arc<Shared>`. So `Drop for Pty` SIGKILLs the agent's process group (pty.rs:381-390), and the un-silenced exit callback then marks the session `exited` and its builder task `failed`.
findings.impact: Trigger: tag any task (task.label.add, or the board's labels field on create), then later remove the project, or the workspace that contains it. Consequence: removal always fails with an internal FOREIGN KEY error, and the project can never be removed. Each attempt also SIGKILLs every running agent of that project. Those sessions end `exited`, not `restorable`, so the conversations are lost. Their Relay commit hooks are uninstalled and their builder tasks are marked failed, while the project stays.
findings.fix: Add `"DELETE FROM labels WHERE project_id=?1"` after the task deletes (task_labels cascades), and add a project.remove regression test that uses a labelled task. Also stop nested session.close from detaching PTYs before commit: move `take_pty` into the after_commit closure, so a rolled-back request leaves the PTY registered.

v1.reason:
I confirmed each step myself. Migration v16 creates `labels(project_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES projects(id))` with no ON DELETE CASCADE (store.rs:315-319), and foreign_keys is ON (store.rs:397/414). Of the 15 tables that reference projects(id), `labels` is the only one missing from the dependency-ordered DELETE list in ProjectRemove (workspace.rs:354-374). No code anywhere runs `DELETE FROM labels`: task.rs only inserts labels (137) or removes task_labels rows (431, 1219). So `DELETE FROM projects WHERE id=?1` (workspace.rs:380) fails the FK check whenever the project has ever had a label. That breaks workspace.remove too, because it calls project.remove through invoke_registered (workspace.rs:173). No test covers project.remove with a labelled task.

The collateral damage is also real. With force set (the native dialog always sets it, registry.rs:626), each open session goes through session.close {remove_worktree:false} first (workspace.rs:327-329). When invoke_registered is used, the staged prepare runs against the held tx (engine.rs:326-347), so run_teardown and remove_hook_dir touch the filesystem with nothing to roll them back (session.rs:1572-1596). The finish phase calls `take_pty` and leaves the kill in after_commit (session.rs:1602-1607). On an ordinary error the dispatcher calls tx.rollback() and drops the after_commit closures without running them (engine.rs ~1075). The PTY is already out of engine.ptys, so the closure held the last Arc<Pty>, and `Drop for Pty` SIGKILLs the process group (pty.rs:381-390). The rolled-back rows still say running, so the agents' exit callbacks record them as exited.
v1.correction:
Fix: add `DELETE FROM labels WHERE project_id=?1` after the tasks delete (task_labels cascades), and add a regression test that removes a project with a labelled task. Separately, keep a nested close from detaching the PTY before commit: call take_pty inside the after_commit closure, or restore it on rollback. The hook teardown done in prepare also cannot be rolled back.

One caveat on impact: the claim that the conversations are "lost" depends on the provider. Many CLIs keep their own transcripts on disk. What is lost for certain is Relay's restorable state.

v2.reason:
I confirmed this myself from the code and with a replay against the real v20 schema.

(a) The code does what is claimed.
- `labels.project_id REFERENCES projects(id)` has no ON DELETE clause (store.rs:317), and `foreign_keys=ON` (store.rs:397). Nothing later turns it off.
- No code ever runs `DELETE FROM labels`. `label_id()` only inserts (task.rs:137). `task.label.remove` and `set_labels` delete only `task_labels` rows (task.rs:431, 1219).
- The ProjectRemove delete list (workspace.rs:354-374) covers 14 of the 15 tables that reference projects; `labels` is the one missing. So `DELETE FROM projects` (workspace.rs:380) fails with "FOREIGN KEY constraint failed".
- The script `exp/skeptic-final-labels/replay.py` builds the schema from the MIGRATIONS text and runs the handler's exact DELETE list. Without a label it succeeds. With one label it fails. Un-labelling the task first still fails, because the `labels` row survives.
- `.bus()` maps the error to `BusError::internal` (engine.rs:1414). The dispatcher then calls `tx.rollback()` (engine.rs:1074) and drops the destructured `after_commit` closures without running them.

(b) Reachability. Any user who ever labels a task in a project triggers it.
