It fails closed (exit 2) only when the function returns an Err (main.rs:348-357, whose comment says "Claude Code only treats exit 2 as blocking"). guardrail.gate is a locked handler (`engine.register::<Gate>`, handlers/guardrail.rs:304), so it queues on the store mutex behind any long holder (see the dispatch, clone and worktree-removal findings). std::sync::Mutex also lets new arrivals barge ahead of waiters. When the provider kills the hook at 30 s, the exit-2 path is never reached. Not verifiable in this repo: that Claude Code treats a timed-out hook as non-blocking. The engine still runs the queued gate later, because a spawn_blocking dispatch cannot be cancelled. That late gate can insert holds or refusal notifications, or take a 15-minute device shell lease, for a call that already ran or was abandoned.
findings.impact: While the bus is stalled for more than 30 s (the user clones a project, or confirms a commit whose pre-commit hook runs tests), every agent's Bash, Edit and Write proceeds without guardrail evaluation. Afterwards stale holds and leases appear for actions that already happened.
findings.fix: Wrap the gate call in tokio::time::timeout (for example 20 s, under the provider's limit) and exit 2 with "guardrail unavailable" when it expires. Have the engine skip gate requests whose connection has already closed. Remove the long lock holds.

v1.reason: Both PreToolUse hooks are installed with "timeout": 30: Claude at crates/relay-core/src/hooks.rs:351 and Codex at hooks.rs:521. claude_pre_tool (crates/relay-cli/src/main.rs:471) and codex_pre_tool (main.rs:520) await `client.call(&request, |_| {}).await?` with no deadline. They fail closed with exit 2 only when the function returns Err (main.rs:348-357), so a hook the provider kills at 30 s never reaches exit 2. guardrail.gate is a locked handler (`engine.register::<Gate>`, handlers/guardrail.rs:304), so it queues behind any long store-lock holder. Such a holder exists today: ProjectClone (handlers/workspace.rs:228-234) runs `git clone` with plain `.output()` and no timeout inside a locked handler, so cloning a large repo holds the store lock for well over 30 s in a normal flow. The queued gate still runs after the hook is gone. On Allow it calls device_lease::gate_command, which can take a 15-minute SHELL_RUNNING lease (handlers/device_lease.rs:126-130). On Refuse it inserts a refusal notification. Both can happen for a tool call that already ran or was abandoned. One part cannot be checked from the repo: that Claude Code and Codex treat a timed-out hook as non-blocking. Claude Code's documented contract treats only exit 2 as blocking, so the tool very likely runs unchecked.
v1.correction: The other long lock holds are the root cause of the stall, and the ProjectClone `git clone` under the lock is one concrete instance. This finding is the fail-open that lets such a stall bypass the guardrail, and it should be fixed on its own as defense in depth. Wrap the connect and call in claude_pre_tool and codex_pre_tool in tokio::time::timeout of about 20-25 s, and return Err so the existing exit-2 path fires. The stdlib-mutex barging point is incidental and not needed for the finding.

v2.reason:
(a) The code does what the finding says. Both hooks are installed with "timeout": 30 (hooks.rs:351 and :521). The live settings.local.json in this very worktree carries the same value. claude_pre_tool (main.rs:471) and codex_pre_tool (main.rs:520) await Client::call, which loops on next_line with no deadline (socket.rs:800-818). They exit 2 only through the Err arm (main.rs:348-357), so a hook the provider kills never gets there. guardrail.gate is a locked handler (guardrail.rs:304). resolve_actor/check_session_token and the handler both block on the std Mutex, which has no timeout (store.rs:474). This contradicts D23 directly: "adapter/infrastructure failures block instead of failing open".

The premise the finding marked unverifiable now holds for Claude Code. I read the installed binary (~/.local/share/claude/versions/2.1.291). When a command hook is aborted by its own timeout, it yields only {type:"hook_cancelled", timedOut:true, outcome:"cancelled"}. That result has no blockingError and no permissionBehavior. The PreToolUse aggregator denies only on blockingError or permissionBehavior "deny". The stop branch fires only on the parent abort signal, i.e. the user interrupting. Command hooks have no fail-closed-on-timeout option: timeoutFailsClosed exists only for cloud "device hooks". The UI renderer returns null for hook_cancelled unless the event is UserPromptSubmit, so the bypass leaves nothing in the transcript. So the tool falls through to Claude's own permission mode. For Codex (0.154.0), the binary contains "hook timed out after", a "timeout" error class, and blocking tied only to exit 2 or deny. That is consistent with failing open, but the control flow was not confirmed.

(b) Reachable through normal user flows, not by an agent at will. Every slow locked op is UserOnly, and self_approval refuses `relay --actor user`. Locked holders that can exceed 30 s:
- project.clone runs `git clone` via plain .output() inside e.register (workspace.rs:228-234). It is reachable from Add project/onboarding, and the native client gives it 1800 s.
- Confirming a held git.commit from the Code page (code_git.rs:1722-1750) replays the staged prepare under the lock (engine.rs:325-342). That includes run_user_pre_commit with an unbounded .output() (hooks.rs:210-213), so a pre-commit that runs tests holds the bus for the whole run.
- worktree.remove of a large worktree runs purge, dir_size and `git worktree remove` without a bound (git.rs:129, worktree.rs:352-368).
These are occasional, but with many concurrent agents every Bash/Edit/Write in every session is affected while the stall lasts.

(c) Each tool call waits 30 s and then runs without Relay's checks, silently. Bypassed: denied_commands, the self-approval refusal, protected and critical paths, write roots, destructive caps and device leases. Only the provider's own mode still applies: Claude prompts in default mode but not in auto, acceptEdits or bypass mode; Codex keeps its sandbox and auto-reviewer. The pre-commit gate still catches in-worktree writes at commit time, but not exec actions or writes outside the worktree. Because the socket door does not authenticate `user` (resolve_actor, engine.rs:1355), an agent's `relay --actor user cmd guardrail.confirm` also gets past the hook during a stall and runs once the lock frees. The queued gate still runs later. Refuse persists a refusal notification (commit_error), telling the user an action was refused when it actually ran. Hold persists a hold, so rejecting it gives false assurance. Allow takes a 15-minute shell lease (device_lease.rs:126-130) and consumes once-grants.

(d) The rubric's high tier covers "a safety check that can be silently bypassed", which fits exactly. It is not critical: an agent cannot trigger the stall on demand, and the trigger is occasional.

(e) A client-side deadline is the right fix. tokio "time" is enabled in the workspace and main uses #[tokio::main]. It is a CLI-only change, so it covers existing worktrees at once. Raising the provider "timeout" instead would not fix this. Any finite value still fails open, and install_claude/install_codex skip worktrees whose command is already installed (hooks.rs:333-341, 513-515), so a new value never reaches existing installs.
v2.correction:
Upgrade the evidence. The behaviour the finding marked "not verifiable" is confirmed for the installed Claude Code 2.1.291. A command hook killed by its own timeout yields hook_cancelled/outcome "cancelled", which is non-blocking. Claude does not show it for PreToolUse, so the bypass is silent. Codex 0.154.0 most likely behaves the same; its strings fit, but the control flow was not confirmed. Cite D23, which this violates.

Stall sources: replace the vague "dispatch" holder with three concrete ones.
- project.clone (workspace.rs:234).
- guardrail.confirm of a held git.commit, which runs the user's pre-commit under the lock (engine.rs:325-342 with hooks.rs:210-213).
- worktree.remove (worktree.rs:352-368).
task.dispatch{create} is UserOnly, and the native client dispatches to existing sessions, so it is a minor path. The stdlib-mutex barging point is incidental.

Add these consequences: a late Refuse leaves a refusal notification for an action that actually ran, and a late Allow consumes once-grants.

Fix:
(1) In claude_pre_tool and codex_pre_tool, wrap connect plus call in tokio::time::timeout of about 20 s. Return Err so the existing exit-2 path fires.
(2) The engine cannot notice that a connection closed while it is awaiting dispatch, because the per-connection loop does not read during that wait. Carry a deadline in the gate request instead. After acquiring the lock, gate should return an error with no side effects (no hold, notification, lease or grant use) once the deadline has passed.
(3) Separately, remove the long lock holds.
Do not rely on raising the hook "timeout": it still fails open and does not reach existing installs.

findings.title: Worktree file watchers are never removed: each watched root keeps an inotify instance, a thread and a recursive watch set for the engine's lifetime, and a recreated path keeps a dead watcher
findings.evidence: `Engine.watchers: Mutex<HashMap<String, RecommendedWatcher>>` (engine.rs:420) gains an entry at watch.rs:134-139 and nothing ever removes one (grep finds no other writer). ensure_after_commit returns early once the key exists: `if engine.watchers.lock().unwrap().contains_key(&key) { return; }` (watch.rs:53). Every file.tree, file.read, file.search and git.status call registers its root (file.rs:21, 41, 301; git.rs:164). In notify 8.2, each INotifyWatcher spawns a "notify-rs inotify loop" thread and holds an inotify fd, an epoll fd and an eventfd. `RecursiveMode::Recursive` (watch.rs:133) adds an inotify watch for every directory via WalkDir, including target/ and node_modules; is_generated_path only filters events, not watches. Session names come from a 36×36 vocabulary and a closed session's name can be reused (`state != 'closed'`, sessions.rs:80). A new session can therefore land on a deleted session's `.relay/worktrees/<name>` path, and the stale key suppresses registration.
findings.impact: In a long-running engine, every worktree an agent or the UI ever touched keeps about 3 fds and a thread, plus its watches while the directory exists. With the usual 1024 soft fd limit, a few hundred sessions exhaust the engine's fds: accept, openpty and git spawns then fail engine-wide. The watchers also consume the user's per-user inotify instances, which other applications need. A session that reuses a closed session's name gets no file.changed events at all, so its Code view never auto-refreshes.
findings.fix: Drop the watcher when its root disappears (handle the root's remove event) and on session close or worktree removal. Key the dedupe by (path, inode), or re-register when the stored watcher is dead. Do not recurse into generated trees: add per-directory non-recursive watches that skip target/ and node_modules.

v1.reason: `Engine.watchers` (engine.rs:420) is written only at watch.rs:138, and nothing in the crate ever removes an entry. `ensure_after_commit` returns early when the canonical path is already a key (watch.rs:53), and `ensure` refuses to insert a duplicate (watch.rs:135). Four handlers register a root: file.rs:21/41/301 and git.rs:164 (git.status, which the native Code view calls from code_git.rs:159). Agents reach the same handlers through MCP, so in practice every session worktree that gets touched picks up a watcher. In notify 8.2.0 each INotifyWatcher holds an inotify instance (Inotify::init, inotify.rs:539), a mio Poll and a Waker, plus a spawned event-loop thread (inotify.rs:96-125), and all of it lives as long as the engine. No setrlimit/RLIMIT_NOFILE call exists anywhere in the repo. Session names are reused once a session closes: `new_name` checks only `state != 'closed'` (sessions.rs:80) and draws from a finite adjective x animal vocabulary. When a worktree directory is deleted, the kernel drops its inotify watches, but the map key stays. A new worktree at the same path is then skipped at watch.rs:53 and never emits file.changed.
v1.correction: The limit that is hit first is probably not the 1024 file-descriptor limit. It is the per-user inotify instance limit, fs.inotify.max_user_instances, which is 128 by default on many kernels. Every leaked watcher uses one instance for the life of the engine, so after enough sessions `notify::recommended_watcher` fails. New worktrees then silently get no auto-refresh (watch.rs:132 falls to `false`), and other applications run by the same user can no longer create inotify instances. Running out of file descriptors needs a few hundred distinct worktrees and is the less likely outcome. Recursive watches on deleted directories are freed by the kernel, so the lasting leak is the instance, its fds and its thread, not the watch set. Fix: remove the map entry when a session closes or its worktree is removed (session.close, worktree.remove and project removal), and also when the watcher sees a remove event on its root. Watching target/node_modules recursively is a separate cost (max_user_watches) that is worth noting but is not part of this root cause.

v2.reason:
(a) The code does what the finding says. `Engine.watchers` (engine.rs:420) is written only at watch.rs:138. rg over crates/ and apps/relay-native finds no remove, retain or clear. `ensure_after_commit` returns early when the key exists (watch.rs:53). The only release is notify's `Drop for INotifyWatcher` (notify-8.2.0/src/inotify.rs:606, which sends Shutdown), and Drop never runs. Each watcher holds an inotify fd (inotify.rs:539), a mio epoll (96), an eventfd waker (98) and a "notify-rs inotify loop" thread (124). I checked the live engine (`relay --instance dev serve --remote`, up 6h06m) read-only through /proc: it holds 3 inotify fds and 3 notify threads.

(b) How it is reached and how often. The four unlocked handlers register the canonical, verified worktree root (file.rs:21/41/301, git.rs:164).
- The native Code view leaves out `worktree` by default. The UI has no actor session, so `root_choice` falls back to the project root, and the usual result is one watcher per project.
- A session worktree gets a watcher only in two cases. One is the user picking that checkout: project_files.rs:170/231 and code_git.rs:1097 call `select_checkout`. `open_path`'s Some(worktree) branch is never used, because editor.rs:880 passes None. The other is an agent calling relay's file.tree/read/search or git.status, which default to its own worktree (D111). The role instructions do not steer agents toward those tools.
- Live evidence: after 6 hours with 4 live sessions, the 3 watcher roots are the primary checkouts of RelayV4, Avex and Tally (matched by inode). No session worktree has a watcher.
- Limits: the live engine's soft RLIMIT_NOFILE really is 1024, so fds run out only after about 320 leaked watchers. fs.inotify.max_user_instances is 1024 here, with 81 in use across the whole desktop. Exhaustion therefore needs hundreds of distinct worktrees opened in a single engine run, which is not normal use. On distros that keep the kernel default of 128, it would take roughly 40-50.
- Dead watcher: session.create skips any name whose pooled path still exists (handlers/session.rs:839-841). A path can only be recreated if all of these hold: the earlier worktree was watched, it was then removed (close defaults to remove_worktree:true at :1548; also DiscardRestorable at :1522 and worktree.remove), the same name was drawn again (about 1 in 1296 per create), and all of it happened in one engine run.

(c) What the user sees. Each watched root keeps 3 fds, one parked thread and one per-user inotify instance until the engine restarts. If a limit is eventually hit, later watchers fail silently: watch.rs:132-146 just leaves `registered` false, so there is no auto-refresh. Other apps then cannot create inotify instances. Engine-wide failures (accept, openpty, git spawn) start only at about 320 watchers. The dead-watcher result is milder than "never auto-refreshes": app.rs:1233-1240 calls `editor.invalidate` (editor.rs:508) on any file.changed, git.changed or worktree.changed from any root. The stale view therefore refreshes whenever another event arrives, and only edits confined to that one worktree go unnoticed until then.

(d) Severity should be medium, not high. This is a real leak that only grows, in a path used constantly, and it has an ongoing cost. But it grows slowly, is bounded by the distinct worktrees someone explicitly opens, resets on restart, and has caused no observed harm. The dead-watcher half is a rare edge case with low impact.

(e) Fix assessment. Removing the entry on session.close (when it removes the worktree), DiscardRestorable, worktree.remove and project removal is correct. Removing it on the root's Remove event needs a generation or inode guard, so that a late event cannot drop a newer watcher for a recreated path. notify does not report whether a watcher is still alive, so "re-register when dead" needs a flag that the callback sets. The "don't recurse into generated trees" part is a separate root cause, and its skip list leaves out `.relay`, which is the dominant cost (see correction).
v2.correction:
1. Change severity from high to medium.

2. The fd-exhaustion trigger needs about 320 explicitly viewed worktrees in a single engine run, so it is far from normal use. In the live engine (6 hours, 4 sessions) the only watchers were the three project primary checkouts. Session worktrees get watchers only when the user picks that checkout or an agent calls relay's file or git tools.

3. Preconditions for the dead watcher:
- The earlier worktree had a watcher, was removed, and its name was reused, all in one engine run. session.create (handlers/session.rs:840) skips any name whose path still exists.
- The effect is a stale view, not one that never refreshes: app.rs:1233-1240 refreshes the Code view on file.changed, git.changed or worktree.changed from any root.

4. Fix completeness. Removal points are session.close with remove_worktree, DiscardRestorable, worktree.remove and project removal. Removal on the root's Remove event needs a generation or inode guard.

5. Split into a separate finding: the recursive watch scope. `.relay/worktrees` sits inside the project root, so the project-root watcher also watches every session checkout and its target/. Live data for the RelayV4 root watcher:
- It holds 24,540 inotify watches. Of 24,634 directories in that checkout, 19,915 are under .relay and 2,356 under target/.
- is_generated_path discards the events for all of them, which is about 90% of the watches.
- Any skip list therefore has to include `.relay`, which the proposed fix leaves out.

6. Also separate: notify 8.2.0 leaks entries for deleted directories. `remove_watch` returns through `?` when inotify_rm_watch fails (inotify.rs:483), before `self.paths.remove(&w)` (484).
- For a directory deleted under a recursive watch, the kernel has already dropped the watch, so rm_watch fails with EINVAL. A scratch test confirmed this.
- The wd-to-path entry therefore stays, so build churn under watched trees grows notify's map in normal use. On the live watcher the highest watch descriptor is 55,784, against 24,540 live watches.

findings.title: remote.json is read-modify-written by concurrent phone handshakes and CLI commands with no lock and a shared temp file: revocations can be undone and the file corrupted
findings.evidence: For every handshake, admit() loads the registry (`Registry::load`, bridge.rs:72), applies redeem or touch, then calls `registry.save(...)` (bridge.rs:94). It runs concurrently from every direct and tunnel connection task. `relay remote revoke`, `pair`, `name` and `via` do load→modify→save from a separate process (remote.rs:226-229, 252-258, 261-268, 272-287). serve_with_door also saves at startup after the door is already accepting connections (remote.rs:107-118). save() always writes the fixed path `path.with_extension("json.tmp")`, opened with truncate(true), then renames it over remote.json (registry.rs:165-177). Nothing serializes any of these writers.
findings.impact: If a handshake loads the file before `relay remote revoke` and saves after it, the revoked device and its token are written back. The CLI has printed "its next connection will be refused", yet a stolen phone that keeps reconnecting can race the revoke and keep access. Two saves that both open the shared temp file before either writes can interleave (a shorter JSON written over a longer one) and rename a corrupt file into place. Registry::load then errors on every handshake, deliberately with no silent reset, so every phone is locked out. A handshake racing `pair` loses the new code (pair.invalid). Two concurrent redeems of one code admit both phones but persist only one credential.
findings.fix: Serialize registry mutations with an flock on a sidecar lock file, held across load→save in both processes. Write through a unique temp file (tempfile::NamedTempFile in the same directory, then persist). Apply only the delta (touch or redeem) to freshly loaded state while holding the lock.

v1.reason: `admit` (bridge.rs:68-96) does Registry::load, then redeem or touch, then save. It runs synchronously inside per-connection tokio tasks for both the direct door and the tunnel, so two handshakes can execute it in parallel on the multi-thread runtime. The CLI's pair, revoke, name and via commands (remote.rs:226-229, 252-258, 261-268, 272-287) do the same load/modify/save from a separate process, and serve_with_door saves again after the door is already bound (remote.rs:107-118). `save` always writes the fixed `remote.json.tmp`, opened with truncate and no O_EXCL, and then renames it (registry.rs:165-177). Nothing locks across load and save. The races are real: (1) a handshake whose load comes before a revoke and whose save comes after it writes the revoked device back; (2) two saves that interleave on the shared temp file can leave a longer document's tail behind a shorter one, and the rename then installs invalid JSON, after which Registry::load fails on every handshake because parse errors are deliberately not reset (registry.rs:144-150); (3) a handshake can drop a code that a concurrent `pair` just added.
v1.correction: I am lowering this to medium. Each load-to-save window is a file read, a JSON parse and a small write, so roughly a millisecond. A revoked phone undoes the revoke only if its handshake lands inside the CLI's equally short window. That is possible for an attacker who reconnects in a tight loop, but it is not reliable, and `relay remote devices` would show the device still present. Corrupting the file needs two saves to overlap on the temp file within microseconds, for example two phones, or one phone on both the direct and tunnel paths, connecting at the same moment. The finding is right that the consequence is severe (every phone locked out until remote.json is fixed by hand), but the trigger is rare. The suggested fix is correct: an flock on a sidecar file held from load to save in both processes, a unique temp file via tempfile::NamedTempFile::persist, and re-applying only the delta under the lock.

findings.title: Rendezvous: when a replaced host connection finally ends, its cleanup deregisters the new host and drops its lanes
findings.evidence: A second host replaces the first: `entry.host = Some(tx);` (rendezvous.rs:179). When the old host's read loop later ends, its cleanup runs unconditionally: `if let Some(r) = rooms.get_mut(&room) { r.host = None; r.lanes.clear(); }` (rendezvous.rs:218-222). It never checks that r.host is still its own sender. The comment at 177-178 expects exactly this overlap: "its old socket is about to time out anyway".
findings.impact: After a laptop sleep or network change, the PC's tunnel reconnects (tunnel.rs SILENCE_LIMIT) while the server still holds the old, silently dead TCP connection. When that old socket finally errors, minutes later, the room's host is cleared even though the new connection is healthy. Every phone then gets host.offline until the PC's connection happens to drop again. The PC keeps believing it is reachable because its pings are still answered.
findings.fix: Clear the room only if the stored sender is this task's own (`r.host.as_ref().is_some_and(|h| h.same_channel(&tx))`), and only clear lanes this host opened. Alternatively, tag each host connection with a generation number.

v1.reason: `host()` replaces the room's sender (rendezvous.rs:179). Its cleanup (217-223) clears `r.host` and `r.lanes` without checking that the stored sender is its own, and `rooms.retain` then removes the room entirely. The trigger is reachable: the server never pings a host, so a silently dead host socket (NAT mapping expired, laptop changed network) leaves the old task stuck in `source.next()`. The PC's tunnel reconnects after SILENCE_LIMIT (tunnel.rs:52, 81-86). The old task's writer exits once its senders are gone and calls `sink.close()`. Writing that Close frame to the dead peer eventually fails, the old read loop ends, and its cleanup wipes the new host's registration and lanes.
v1.correction: The impact is smaller than claimed, because the system heals itself. Once the stale cleanup drops the new host's `tx` (r.host = None, then the room is removed) and clears the lanes, the join tasks close their phones and drop their `host` clones. With no senders left, the new host's writer sees `rx.recv()` return None and calls `sink.close()` (rendezvous.rs:186-193). The PC tunnel receives Message::Close, breaks out (tunnel.rs:98), and reconnects about 1 s later (tunnel.rs:34-43). The real effect is a spurious disconnect of every tunneled phone, plus about a second of host.offline, some minutes after a network change. It does not mean 'offline until the PC's connection drops again'. That is medium, not high. The suggested fix is right: clear the room only if `r.host.as_ref().is_some_and(|h| h.same_channel(&tx))`, or use a generation counter.

findings.title: The phone door (inside the engine process) and the rendezvous accept unlimited connections with no timeout before the hello, so a LAN peer can exhaust the engine's file descriptors
findings.evidence: Every accepted TCP connection gets its own task with no cap (direct.rs:37-46). handle awaits `stream.peek(&mut head).await?` (direct.rs:76) and then `tokio_tungstenite::accept_async(stream).await` (direct.rs:89), with no timeout on either. HELLO_TIMEOUT (bridge.rs:39) only starts after the WebSocket handshake. `relay serve --remote`, which run.sh:31 launches, runs this door inside the engine process (remote.rs:107), bound to 0.0.0.0:7420 by default (main.rs:68). The rendezvous server, meant to face the internet, has the same pattern (rendezvous.rs:127, 159).
findings.impact:
Any host on the LAN can open ~1000 idle TCP connections (sending nothing, or a partial HTTP request) and hold them forever. Once the engine reaches its fd limit (typically 1024 soft):
- the Unix socket door cannot accept, so UI reconnects, MCP calls and every agent hook fail (the hooks fail closed, so every agent tool call is blocked)
- PTYs cannot be opened
- git subprocesses cannot be spawned
The result is an engine-wide outage triggered by an unauthenticated network peer.
findings.fix: Bound peek, the WebSocket handshake and the hello with tokio::time::timeout (a few seconds). Cap concurrent unauthenticated connections with a semaphore, also per IP. Consider raising RLIMIT_NOFILE at engine start.

v1.reason: DirectServer::bind starts a task for every accepted TCP connection with no cap (direct.rs:37-46). `handle` waits on `stream.peek(&mut head).await?` (direct.rs:76) and then `tokio_tungstenite::accept_async(stream)` (direct.rs:89), neither under a timeout. HELLO_TIMEOUT (bridge.rs:39) only starts after the WebSocket upgrade has finished. `relay serve --remote` runs the door inside the engine process (remote.rs:97-118), and run.sh launches the engine that way by default. The default bind address is 0.0.0.0:7420 (main.rs:68). The repo never raises RLIMIT_NOFILE. An unauthenticated LAN peer can therefore open idle connections until the engine runs out of file descriptors. After that, accept on the engine's Unix socket fails (new UI, MCP and hook connections), as do openpty and spawning subprocesses. The rendezvous server (rendezvous.rs:125-161) has the same pattern, but it runs as its own process, so there it only takes down the relay.
v1.correction: Timeouts on peek and the WebSocket handshake are not enough on their own. A peer that finishes the upgrade still holds a socket for up to HELLO_TIMEOUT (30 s) and can simply reconnect, so it can keep about 1000 sockets open at a steady rate. The essential fix is a semaphore capping concurrent unauthenticated connections, preferably also per IP, which also limits connections from tailnet addresses. It should be paired with short timeouts on the pre-hello phase, and optionally with raising the soft RLIMIT_NOFILE at engine start. Sessions that are already running and their existing UI connection keep working. What fails is every new connection and every new fd, and agent hooks open new connections.

v2.reason:
(a) The code does what the finding says. `DirectServer::bind` starts a task for every accepted connection with no cap (direct.rs:37-46). `handle` then waits on `stream.peek(&mut head).await?` (direct.rs:76) and on `tokio_tungstenite::accept_async(stream)` (direct.rs:89), with no timeout on either. tungstenite 0.30's handshake has no timeout of its own. Nothing in relay-remote sets TCP keepalive or uses a semaphore. The only time bound is HELLO_TIMEOUT (bridge.rs:39, applied at :125), and it starts only after the WebSocket upgrade. Its doc comment says "A TCP connection that never speaks holds nothing but a task". That is wrong for the phase before the upgrade, where a silent connection holds a socket fd indefinitely.

`relay serve --remote` runs the door inside the engine process (main.rs:203-213 → remote.rs:97,107). It binds the door whether or not any phone is paired, by default on 0.0.0.0:7420 (main.rs:68). run.sh:32 always passes --remote, the desktop entry runs run.sh (install-native-desktop.py:22), and deploy/relay-remote.service runs the same command without a LimitNOFILE setting. No code anywhere raises RLIMIT_NOFILE.

(b) Who can trigger it: any host that can reach port 7420 (the LAN, the tailnet, or another local user). It needs no credentials, only enough idle TCP connects to fill the fd table. On this machine right now:
- the live engine is `relay --instance dev serve --remote`
- it listens on 0.0.0.0:7420
- its fd limit is soft 1024 / hard 1048576, with 37 fds in use
- ufw is active, but its user rules accept all traffic from 192.168.2.0/24

So about 990 idle connects from any LAN device are enough. Benign traffic does not trigger it: scanners close their connections and phones upgrade within milliseconds. It needs a hostile or compromised device on the network.

(c) What happens: once the engine reaches the limit, every new fd fails with EMFILE:
- the Unix door's accept (socket.rs:108-123 logs a warning and retries every 50 ms)
- openpty for a new session (pty.rs:170)
- every subprocess
- file operations

A throwaway experiment with a 64-fd process reproduced this. Idle TCP connections used up the fds. accept on the Unix listener and a subprocess spawn both failed with EMFILE. A separate client process could still connect and write, then got no reply. Once fds were freed, the queued connection was accepted with its request still buffered. In Relay terms, these all hang: new UI panes (terminal.rs:476 opens one connection per pane), new CLI and MCP connections, and agent hooks.

Already-open connections and running PTYs keep working. SQLite runs in WAL mode with temp_store=MEMORY, so the store keeps its fds and no data is lost. The engine recovers when the attacker closes the sockets. If the attacker simply disappears, the sockets never die: the engine sends nothing while in peek and there is no keepalive. The engine then stays broken until it is restarted, and systemd's Restart=on-failure does not fire because nothing crashes.

(d) High is the right severity. This is a default-on, unauthenticated, cheap denial of service against every new connection and new fd in the engine. It affects availability only, needs a hostile device on the network, and running sessions survive. It would be critical only if the hook path described in the correction turns out to fail open.

(e) The verifier's correction stands. Timeouts alone do not stop the exhaustion: a peer that keeps reconnecting holds (connect rate × timeout) sockets at any moment. The essential part of the fix is a cap on concurrent connections that have not yet been admitted, global and per IP, applied at accept with any excess dropped immediately. It should be paired with short timeouts on peek and on the upgrade. The proposed fix is correct with that change.
v2.correction:
The impact on hooks is misstated. Agent hooks do not fail closed promptly. The Unix listener's backlog is somaxconn (4096 here, because mio passes -1 on Linux), so a hook's connect and write succeed even though the engine cannot accept. `Client::call` (socket.rs:801-819) has no timeout. The hook therefore hangs until the provider kills it at the configured 30 s (hooks.rs:351 for Claude, :521 for Codex). Every agent tool call stalls for 30 s, and when the attack ends the engine runs the stale requests left in the queue. Whether Claude Code or Codex then block the tool or run it is outside this repo and was not established. If a timed-out PreToolUse hook does not block, the guardrails are bypassed for as long as the attack lasts. That is worth its own check, and a client-side timeout under 30 s that exits 2 would rule it out.

Minor corrections: the launch line is run.sh:32, not :31. Besides LAN peers, tailnet peers and local users can also trigger this.

Fix additions:
- If RLIMIT_NOFILE is raised at engine start, restore the original soft limit for spawned children, which inherit it.
- Add TCP keepalive or WebSocket pings so that connections from peers that have vanished are reaped.
- Also cap admitted connections. Under `serve --remote` each one costs the engine three fds: the TCP socket, the bridge's UnixStream at bridge.rs:156, and the end the engine accepts. Reaching that limit does require a paired device.

The rendezvous (rendezvous.rs:127, 159) has the same pattern. It runs as its own process and is meant to face the internet, so there the impact is limited to that relay route, and it needs the same fix.

findings.title: PTY attach can replay 256 KiB of old output or drop a frame because the reader bumps seq before the frame is in the ring
findings.evidence: The reader runs `let seq = sh.seq.fetch_add(1, SeqCst) + 1; let data = buf[..n].to_vec(); sh.ring.lock().unwrap().push(seq, &data);` (pty.rs:215-217): the counter moves before the ring lock is taken. attach reads `let seq = self.seq();` while holding the ring lock (pty.rs:308-309), so it can see N+1 while the ring still ends at frame N. For a client cursor from_seq = N, `ring.offset_after(N)` finds nothing and `unwrap_or(0)` (pty.rs:312) makes the catch-up the whole last 256 KiB. That catch-up is sent with `seq: att.seq` (socket.rs:480-481), and the native client feeds it because catch_up yields Feed (terminal.rs:31). The forwarder then skips live frame N+1 because `fr.seq <= att.seq` (socket.rs:487). A fresh attach hitting the same window simply loses frame N+1.
findings.impact: The race window is the copy between fetch_add and the ring lock, so it is likely while an agent prints heavily. That is also when lag makes the native client reconnect after a Gap (terminal.rs:511). The terminal is then fed up to 256 KiB of output it already showed, which garbles a TUI and duplicates scrollback. It also silently loses one chunk of new output, and the client detects no gap.
findings.fix: In the reader, allocate seq inside the ring lock: lock, fetch_add, push, unlock, then send. Alternatively, have attach derive seq from ring.frames.back(). In both cases, treat `offset_after(s) == None` with s at the ring's last frame as nothing to catch up.

v1.reason: In the reader (pty.rs:215-218), `seq = sh.seq.fetch_add(1)+1` runs before `sh.ring.lock().unwrap().push(seq, &data)`, with the `buf[..n].to_vec()` copy in between. attach (pty.rs:305-316) subscribes to rx, locks the ring and reads `self.seq()`. If it runs in that window, it sees N+1 while the ring's last frame is N. With a client cursor from_seq=N, `s < seq`, `offset_after(N)` returns None, and `unwrap_or(0)` turns the catch-up into bounded_bytes_from(0), the last 256 KiB (ATTACH_CATCHUP_BYTES). The catch-up is sent tagged with att.seq=N+1 (socket.rs:480-481). The client's Sequence::observe returns Feed while catch_up is set (terminal.rs:31), so already-displayed output is fed again. In every case the forwarder skips `fr.seq <= att.seq` (socket.rs:487), so live frame N+1, which the ring did not yet hold when the catch-up was cut, is dropped. The next frame is N+2 == s+1, so the client sees no Gap. The window is a 64 KiB memcpy per read, so it is narrow, but a busy agent's reader loop spends a real share of its time there, and re-attaches cluster at heavy output.
v1.correction: The lost frame happens for any attach that lands in the window, not only from_seq=N: a cursor below N gets frames up to N and still loses N+1. Allocating seq inside the ring lock (lock, fetch_add, push, unlock, send) closes both symptoms. offset_after(s)==None with s at or after the ring's last frame should then mean an empty catch-up.

findings.title: DeviceWatchRuntime::finish waits on the adb child while holding the child mutex, so stop() can block forever (under the store lock when device.watch turns off)
findings.evidence: finish is `if let Some(mut child) = self.child.lock().unwrap().take() { let _ = child.wait(); }` (device.rs:49-51). In edition 2021 the MutexGuard temporary lives through the if-let body, so wait() runs with the child mutex locked. The worker reaches finish() with `adb track-devices` still alive in two cases. One: read_line returns Err, for example on a non-UTF-8 byte in the -l output (handlers/device.rs:375-377). Two: it sees the stop flag set by stop() before stop() has taken the lock (device.rs:43-44). stop() needs the same lock to kill the child (device.rs:44). It is called from the device.watch {on:false} handler, which is a locked handler (handlers/device.rs:59-65), and from WatchLease::drop on a tokio worker (socket.rs:275-277).
findings.impact: The child is never killed and never exits, so finish waits forever while holding the lock. The next device.watch off then blocks inside the store transaction and permanently freezes every non-keystroke bus request. When the watching window disconnects instead, a tokio worker is lost for good.
findings.fix: Take the child out of the mutex before waiting, and kill it first: `let child = self.child.lock().unwrap().take(); if let Some(mut c) = child { let _ = c.kill(); let _ = c.wait(); }`. Move stop() out of the Watch handler into after_commit.

v1.reason: The workspace uses edition 2021 (Cargo.toml:9). In `if let Some(mut child) = self.child.lock().unwrap().take() { let _ = child.wait(); }` (crates/relay-core/src/device.rs:49-51), the guard temporary in the scrutinee therefore lives through the body, and wait() runs with the child mutex held. stop() (device.rs:42-47) needs the same mutex before it can kill. The worker (handlers/device.rs:367-380) reaches finish() with `adb track-devices -l` still alive in two cases. (a) read_line returns Err, such as InvalidData on non-UTF-8 output. finish then hangs forever, the device watch silently dies, and the runtime stays in engine.device_watch because clear_device_watch runs only after finish. (b) stop() sets the flag just after read_line returned a line, the worker sees stopped() and enters finish before stop() takes the lock. In both cases, when the last client turns the watch off, stop() blocks forever. That happens either from the locked `register::<Watch>` handler (handlers/device.rs:43, stop at :65), inside the store transaction, which freezes every locked bus request, or from WatchLease::drop (socket.rs:275-277), which loses a tokio worker. Both triggers are rare: a narrow race, or non-UTF-8 adb output. The consequence is a permanent freeze of the bus.
v1.correction: Severity is medium because the trigger is rare, even though the consequence is a whole-bus freeze. Fix: `let child = self.child.lock().unwrap().take(); if let Some(mut c) = child { let _ = c.kill(); let _ = c.wait(); }`. Also call stop() from after_commit rather than inside the Watch transaction.

findings.title: Mirror control writes block while holding the control mutex, and every stop() path needs that mutex (including device.mirror.stop under the store lock)
findings.evidence:
send_control locks `control` and does a blocking `socket.write_all(&bytes)` (device.rs:279-283). The control TcpStream has no write timeout: handlers/device.rs:810-825 set read timeouts only, on the video socket. stop() locks `control` to shut the socket down (device.rs:326-328), so it cannot interrupt a blocked writer. Callers of stop():
- device.mirror.stop, a locked handler (handlers/device.rs:109-123)
- MirrorAttachment::drop, on a tokio worker (socket.rs:231-238)
- Engine::shutdown, while holding the mirrors map lock (engine.rs:634-636)
Pointer and key device.mirror.input events are written inline on a tokio worker (engine.rs:901-902, 1244-1251).
findings.impact: Suppose the device-side scrcpy server stops draining control messages (a wedged device whose USB link is still up). Input writes fill the socket buffer and block while holding the lock. The user's Stop then blocks inside the store transaction, freezing the whole bus, and closing the mirror window wedges a tokio worker. Both last until adb drops the forward.
findings.fix: Keep a try_clone() of the control socket outside the mutex so stop() can call shutdown(Both) on it. Set a write timeout on the control socket. Move runtime.stop() out of the MirrorStop transaction into after_commit.

v1.reason: The mechanism is real. send_control (crates/relay-core/src/device.rs:279-283) does a blocking `socket.write_all` while holding the control mutex. The control TcpStream never gets a write timeout: the only set_*_timeout calls are read timeouts on the video socket (handlers/device.rs:812, 833, 855). stop() (device.rs:322-333) shuts the video socket first and then blocks on the control mutex, so it can neither shut the control socket nor reach child.kill(). After the video shutdown, mirror_worker itself calls runtime.stop() (handlers/device.rs:882) and blocks on the same mutex. The drain thread's try_clone (handlers/device.rs:823) is never used to shut the socket down. Callers of stop() include the locked MirrorStop handler (handlers/device.rs:109-122, inside the store transaction), MirrorAttachment::drop on a tokio worker (socket.rs:231-238), and Engine::shutdown while holding the mirrors map lock (engine.rs:634-636). The engine code itself admits that writes can block: "Text and clipboard payloads can be large enough to block on a full socket" (engine.rs:1244-1245). Pointer events still run inline. I could not establish how likely the trigger is. It needs a peer that stays connected but stops draining: a wedged adb server, or a scrcpy controller that stops reading. Small pointer messages would also have to fill a localhost send buffer of several hundred KB to MB. If USB drops or the server dies, the socket errors and the writer unblocks.
v1.correction: The writer can block in two places: on the inline fast path in a tokio worker for pointer and key events, and in a normal dispatch for text and setclipboard. Fix: keep a try_clone of the control socket outside the mutex so stop() can shutdown(Both) without the lock, set a write timeout on the control socket, and move runtime.stop() in MirrorStop to after_commit.

findings.title: The socket door blocks tokio worker threads on the store mutex and on fd writes
findings.evidence:
Several blocking calls run directly on runtime worker threads:
- After a successful session.attach, the async task calls `crate::handlers::session::pty_by_name(&engine, &p.session)` (socket.rs:469), which does `let conn = engine.store.lock();` (session.rs:1733) on the runtime thread.
- The app.resources.watch tick task does `let conn = engine.store.lock();` inside `handle.spawn(async …)` every 2 s (handlers/app.rs:121-124).
- Keystrokes that pass answers_from_memory are dispatched inline (socket.rs:735-739) and call pty.write (engine.rs:1284). That takes the PTY writer mutex, which a paste over 1 KiB holds on the blocking pool across a blocking write_all (pty.rs:290-295).
- If the PTY vanishes between the check and the dispatch, the request falls through to the locked session.input handler, still inline.
- Drop impls call stop() methods that can block (socket.rs:238, 276).
findings.impact: Whenever a locked handler runs long (a clone, a dispatch, a worktree removal), each attach and each resource tick parks a whole tokio worker on the mutex. With several panes re-attaching, all of the runtime's workers can be parked. That stalls every connection, including the D148 keystroke fast path, which exists so typing never waits on the store.
findings.fix: Resolve the PTY from memory (engine.pty_named) or inside the spawn_blocking closure. Read resource rows through spawn_blocking. Run Drop-time stop() calls through spawn_blocking. Only inline a keystroke after a try_lock of the PTY writer succeeds.

v1.reason: The blocking calls on runtime threads are real. socket.rs:469 calls session::pty_by_name, which does `engine.store.lock()` (session.rs:1733) inside the async task. The app.resources.watch loop does `engine.store.lock()` inside a spawned async task every 2 s (app.rs:121-124). Small session.input requests run inline (socket.rs:735-739) and take the PTY writer mutex in Pty::write (pty.rs:290-295), which a paste over INLINE_INPUT_BYTES holds on the blocking pool for as long as the child does not drain input. The impact is overstated, though. The attach request is dispatched through spawn_blocking first, so it already waits off-runtime for a long locked handler, and pty_by_name only parks a worker if another long handler grabs the lock in the microseconds between. The resource tick is a single engine-wide loop, so it parks at most one worker. A stuck keystroke parks one worker per connection, and that connection was already serialized behind its own paste. The Drop-time stop() calls only set flags, kill children and shut down sockets (device.rs:42-47, 321-332, 403-408), so they do not block meaningfully. Parking all workers on a multi-core default runtime is not credible in normal use.
v1.correction: The realistic cost is that one tokio worker is lost for the duration of a long locked handler (resource tick), plus a narrow attach window. Drop the Drop-impl part of the claim. Fix by resolving the PTY with engine.pty_named (memory) in the attach path, reading resource rows inside spawn_blocking, and inlining keystrokes only when try_lock on the writer succeeds.

findings.title: `relay mcp` handles one JSON-RPC message at a time: a bus.wait blocks every other tool call from that agent, and cancellation is never read
findings.evidence: `for line in lines { … handle(instance, &actor, token.as_deref(), message).await … }` (mcp.rs:20-31) runs each message to completion before reading the next. bus.wait holds its socket connection for timeout_ms (default 60 s, clamped up to 3_600_000 ms, socket.rs:408-409), and agents are told to rely on it instead of polling (providers.rs:45-52). A notifications/cancelled message is only read after the current call returns. The Unreal and Blender MCP servers use the same serial loop (unreal.rs:57-60, blender.rs:34-37), with builds that run up to an hour (unreal.rs:1547).
findings.impact: Parallel tool calls from one agent queue behind a wait. If the user interrupts an agent during a wait, every Relay tool call it makes next (session.done, mailbox.send, guardrail.request…) hangs until the old wait expires, which can be up to an hour.
findings.fix: Spawn each tools/call as its own task and write responses through a single stdout writer. Map notifications/cancelled (by requestId) to aborting that task; dropping its socket also ends the engine-side wait.

v1.reason: serve (crates/relay-cli/src/mcp.rs:16-34) iterates `stdin.lock().lines()` and awaits `handle(...)` to completion for each message before reading the next line. The stdin read is blocking and synchronous, inside an async fn. handle returns None for notifications (mcp.rs:38-41), so notifications/cancelled is ignored even once it is read. bus.wait holds its connection for the requested timeout, defaulting to 60 s and clamped to 1 s..3_600_000 ms (crates/relay-core/src/socket.rs:408-410). The provider prompt tells agents to use bus.wait instead of polling (providers.rs:45-52). So once an agent's wait is interrupted, its next Relay MCP calls queue behind the remaining wait, which can last up to an hour if the agent chose a long timeout. Parallel tool calls also serialize.
v1.correction: Fix: spawn each tools/call as its own task and send all output through one stdout writer, read stdin asynchronously, and abort the matching task on notifications/cancelled. Dropping the task's socket ends the engine-side wait. I did not re-verify the Unreal and Blender loops line by line; they are listed as related.

findings.title: Waiting on device.lease.released is lossy: most leases end by silent expiry, and the release can fire before the wait subscribes
findings.evidence: The device.busy refusal tells agents to "wait for it with bus.wait {\"events\":[\"device.lease.released\"]} and retry" (device_lease.rs:148-149; providers.rs:47-50). Shell leases end by expiry, 90 s after the command (SHELL_GRACE, device_lease.rs:35, 253-261), and claims end by their TTL. Expiry is lazy: expire() (device_lease.rs:274-278) runs only inside acquire and release_where. check, list and holder_of just filter out expired leases without emitting anything (device_lease.rs:202-229). So device.lease.released for an expired lease is emitted only when some later lease operation happens to prune it. bus.wait subscribes when it is called (socket.rs:411); only guardrail.request_resolved gets the stored-answer check (socket.rs:200-205, 413-423).
findings.impact: An agent refused with device.busy waits its full bus.wait timeout even though the device has freed up. That is 60 s by default, or up to an hour if it picked a long timeout. The same happens when the holder's run ends during the agent's thinking time between the refusal and the wait.
findings.fix: Treat lease waits like exception requests. When bus.wait filters on device.lease.released with matching.device, check the lease map at subscribe time and answer at once if the device is free. Cap the wait at the lease's expiry and re-check, or emit release events from a deadline-driven wake.

v1.reason: The device.busy hint says "wait for it with bus.wait {\"events\":[\"device.lease.released\"]} and retry" (crates/relay-core/src/device_lease.rs:147-149), and the provider prompt repeats it. Shell leases end through shell_finished, which sets a 90 s expiry without emitting anything (device_lease.rs:244-252). Claims end at their TTL. expire() is called only from acquire and release_where (device_lease.rs:186, 233). check, list and holder_of only filter out expired leases. A release event for an expired lease is emitted only when a later device.list, device.leases, acquire or check prunes the map. Nothing does that on a timer: the native client calls device.list only on connect and on device.changed, usage.changed or run.changed events (apps/relay-native/src/app.rs:1158, 1186-1192). bus.wait subscribes when it is called, and only guardrail exception waits check stored state (socket.rs:411-423). A release that happens between the refusal and the wait is therefore also missed. So a refused agent sleeps its full bus.wait timeout, 60 s by default or up to an hour if it chose a long one, after the device is actually free.
v1.correction: The category is a functional bug rather than a data race. Impact is extra latency, not a failure, because the agent retries after the timeout. Fix: when bus.wait filters on device.lease.released, prune and check the lease map at subscribe time and answer at once if the matching device is free. Also cap the wait at the blocking lease's expiry, or emit release events from a deadline-driven wake.

findings.title: device.run.stop races the run worker: the worker rewrites 'stopped' to 'running' and leaks the logcat child
findings.evidence: RunStop removes the runtime, calls runtime.stop() (which kills only a child currently in the slot), releases the lease and sets the row to 'stopped' (handlers/device.rs:263-285). After the build, run_worker never checks runtime.stopped() before wait_for_app_pid and `advance_run(…, "running", false)` (1724-1734). advance_run updates unconditionally: `UPDATE device_runs SET state=?1 … WHERE id=?4` (2193-2194). The worker then spawns logcat. On the first line, `if runtime.stopped() { return; }` (1775-1778) returns without killing or reaping the child and skips the cleanup at 1786-1793. In stream_command, a stop between spawn() and set_child() (1832-1841) finds no child to kill; the loop then returns Stopped and the build keeps running.
findings.impact: Pressing Stop during install or launch, a few seconds after the build finishes, leaves the run shown as 'running' until the engine restarts and leaks one orphan `adb logcat` per such run. The device lease is already released, so another session can install over a run the UI still shows as live.
findings.fix: Check stopped() before each phase transition and before spawning a child. Make advance_run, fail_run and finish_build conditional (`AND state IN ('building','running')`). On the stopped early return, kill and wait the child. After set_child, re-check stopped() and kill if set.

v1.reason: RunStop (device.rs:263-285) removes the runtime from device_runs, calls runtime.stop(), releases the lease and sets the row to 'stopped'. RunRuntime::stop (device.rs core, device.rs:401-406) sets the flag and kills only the child currently in the slot. After the build, stream_command has already taken and waited the child, so for a stop during `logcat -c`, launch_installed_app or wait_for_app_pid (up to 10 s), there is nothing to kill. run_worker never checks stopped() before `advance_run(..., "running", false)` (device.rs:1734). advance_run's UPDATE is unconditional: `UPDATE device_runs SET state=?1 ... WHERE id=?4` (device.rs:2194). So the row goes from 'stopped' back to 'running'. The worker then spawns `adb logcat --pid=`, stores it with set_child, and on the first line `if runtime.stopped() { return; }` (device.rs:1775-1778) returns without killing or waiting the child, skipping the device_runs/lease cleanup. The Child is dropped, not killed, so adb logcat keeps running. If the app logs nothing, the worker thread blocks on read indefinitely. fail_run and finish_build are also unconditional, so they can overwrite 'stopped' as well. The stream_command window between spawn() and set_child() (device.rs:1832-1841) is real but only microseconds wide.
v1.correction: The main trigger is pressing Stop in the seconds between the build finishing and logcat attaching, and the app is still launched after the stop. Fix: check stopped() before launch, before advance_run and after set_child; make advance_run, fail_run and finish_build conditional with `AND state IN ('building','running')`; on the stopped early return, take_child and kill/wait it.

findings.title: A panic in any dispatched handler makes handle_conn return early and detach its subscription and attach tasks, leaving a half-alive connection
findings.evidence: Every dispatch is `tokio::task::spawn_blocking(move || e.dispatch(..)).await?` (socket.rs:361, 419, 459, 511, 524, 652, 726, 742). A handler panic becomes a JoinError, and `?` returns from handle_conn, skipping the cleanup at 746-759. The forwarder (373), the PTY attach tasks (477) and the run streams (667) are plain JoinHandles, which detach rather than abort on drop. They hold clones of out_tx, so the writer task (296) keeps the socket's write half open. Mutexes other than the store use .lock().unwrap(), so a panic while holding one makes later requests panic too.
findings.impact: On the UI's main connection (subscribed to events) or a terminal pane connection, events or terminal output keep streaming but no further request is ever read. Every call times out after 30 s, and the client never gets a Disconnected notice; the user has to find the Reconnect button.
findings.fix: Turn a JoinError into an internal-error response instead of using `?`. Hold the per-connection tasks in an abort-on-drop guard so any exit path aborts them.

v1.reason: Neither engine.rs nor socket.rs has a catch_unwind, and the release profile does not set panic=abort, so a handler panic inside `spawn_blocking(...).await?` comes back as a JoinError. The `?` then returns from handle_conn (socket.rs:281) before the cleanup at 746-759. The forwarder, the `attached` and `attached_runs` JoinHandles drop without abort, so those tasks detach. They hold out_tx clones, so the writer task keeps the write half open and streams events and PTY frames, but no further request line is read. The accept loop only logs the error at debug level (socket.rs:114-116). MirrorAttachment's Drop still runs and the WatchLeases are released, so the half-alive state is limited to the detached streams. Handler panics are uncommon (the store mutex is poison-tolerant), so low is right.
v1.correction: A second trigger needs no panic: `lines.next_line().await?` (socket.rs ~335) returns Err when a client sends a line that is not valid UTF-8. The same early `?` return then leaves the subscription and attach tasks detached. Fix both paths at once: put the per-connection JoinHandles in an abort-on-drop guard, and turn a JoinError into an internal-error response.

findings.title: Events are published after the store lock is released, so session.changed can arrive out of commit order and the UI keeps the stale row
findings.evidence: After tx.commit() the store guard is dropped (`drop(conn)`, engine.rs:1024-1026) and only then do the events go out: `for ev in events { self.events_tx.send(ev) }` (1027-1029). system_write does the same (717-723). Another writer can commit and publish in between. The deferred idle→running write runs on a thread spawned per idle-edge keystroke (engine.rs:1288-1291), so it can commit after a later `session.report stop`. The native UI applies session.changed payloads in place, with no version check (agent_menu.rs:111, 122).
findings.impact: Rarely (a preemption at exactly that point, or a keystroke just as the agent stops), the UI shows a session as running, idle or a closed ghost contrary to the database. It stays wrong until another change for that session arrives.
findings.fix: Send events before dropping the store guard (broadcast::send never blocks). Stamp session.changed with a monotonic per-row version that the UI compares. Make mark_session_running conditional on the idle generation it observed.

v1.reason: dispatch_inner commits, runs `drop(conn)`, then loops `self.events_tx.send(ev)` (engine.rs:1023-1029). system_write does the same (engine.rs:716-722). events_tx is a tokio broadcast::Sender (engine.rs:404), whose send does not block, so sending before the drop is cheap. Between the drop and the send, another thread can take the lock, commit and publish first, so events for the same row can arrive in reverse commit order. The native client replaces the row wholesale from each session.changed payload, with no version check (agent_menu.rs:98-122), so the stale row stays until the next change or a full session.list.
v1.correction: The window is the few microseconds between drop(conn) and the send loop, so this needs two writers to the same session at almost the same instant (for example the PTY exit callback and session.report). mark_session_running is not a strong example: its UPDATE is guarded by `AND state='idle'` (engine.rs:1328), so it can only flip idle→running, and only when the spawned thread loses a millisecond race against a stop that lands just after the keystroke. The simplest fix is to publish before dropping the guard in both dispatch_inner and system_write. The per-row version and idle-generation changes are optional.

findings.title: integration.discard is undone by the integration worker (check-then-write across two lock acquisitions)
findings.evidence: set_state checks `if get(&conn, id)?.state == IntegrationState::Discarded { return Ok(()) }` under one lock acquisition (266-271). Later it writes `UPDATE integrations SET state=?1 … WHERE id=?7` in a separate system_write (283-284), with no state guard. A discard (58-69) can commit in between. The worker's build and run commands go through shell() and `cmd.output()` (228-242) and cannot be cancelled.
findings.impact: A discarded integration flips back to building, passed or failed, and its build keeps running in the worktree that discard removed.
findings.fix: Put the discarded check into the UPDATE itself (`AND state != 'discarded'`), in the same transaction. Give the worker a cancel flag or child handle that discard can kill.

v1.reason: set_state checks `get(&conn,id)?.state == Discarded` under one lock acquisition (integration.rs:266-271). It then reads project_id under a second acquisition and writes `UPDATE integrations SET state=?1 ... WHERE id=?7` in a third, system_write (integration.rs:283-284), with no state guard. IntegrationDiscard (integration.rs:58-69) can commit between the check and the write, and then the worker's write flips the row back from 'discarded'. The worker's shell() (integration.rs:228-242) uses a bare `cmd.output()` that discard cannot cancel, so the build or run command keeps executing in the force-removed worktree.
v1.correction: In practice the flip-back almost never happens. If discard commits before the worker's next transition, which is the normal case (discard during a multi-minute build), the existing check sees Discarded and the write is skipped. Only a discard landing in the sub-millisecond gap between the check and system_write reverts it. The observable harm is the uncancellable build or deploy still running after discard, and with deploy set it can still install to a device. Put the guard into the UPDATE (`AND state != 'discarded'`), and give discard a child handle or flag to kill the worker's command. Separately, IntegrationDiscard runs worktree::remove and `git branch -D` inside a plain `register` handler, so under the store mutex. That is a CLAUDE.md invariant issue worth tracking on its own.

findings.title: One tunnel loop serves all phones, so a slow lane or a closing lane stalls every lane and the keepalive
findings.evidence: Lane data is delivered with `tx.send(l).await` into a 64-slot channel (tunnel.rs:139-145). A Close waits with `tokio::time::timeout(Duration::from_secs(5), task).await` (146-152). Both happen inside the single select loop that also sends pings and reads the socket. The rendezvous host loop likewise awaits `target.send(l).await` per lane (rendezvous.rs:204-209).
findings.impact: A bridge that stops consuming blocks the whole tunnel indefinitely, other phones' traffic and the 30 s ping included. That happens when its engine connection is busy in a long request, so its write_all blocks. Each lane close also pauses every lane for up to 5 s.
findings.fix: Use try_send and close lanes whose channel is full. Move the 5 s close wait into its own task.

v1.reason: The mechanism is in the code. `tx.send(l).await` into a lane's 64-slot inbound channel (tunnel.rs:139-145) and the up-to-5 s `timeout(..., task).await` on Close (146-152) both run inside the single select loop that also reads the socket and sends pings. The rendezvous host loop likewise awaits `target.send(l).await` for each lane (rendezvous.rs:204-209). The triggers are much narrower than the finding says, though. The bridge drains inbound continuously and only blocks in `writer.write_all` when the engine stops reading that Unix socket while its kernel buffer, roughly 200 KB, is full. On top of that, the 64 channel slots must fill, which a phone sending small requests will not do in practice. On Close, dropping `tx` makes the bridge's `inbound.recv()` return None at once, and forward/Close then complete in milliseconds, so the 5 s ceiling is almost never reached.
v1.correction: The more realistic head-of-line case is on the rendezvous side, not the PC's tunnel. With a phone on a poor link, terminal output fills the join lane's 256-line channel, and `target.send(l).await` (rendezvous.rs:207) then stops the host read loop for every lane in the room. While stopped it also sends no pongs, so a stall longer than 90 s makes the PC tunnel reconnect (tunnel.rs:81-86) and drop every phone. In a single-user app with usually one phone, the cross-phone stall rarely matters. Fix: use try_send and close a lane whose queue is full, on both the server and the tunnel, and move the Close wait into a spawned task.

findings.title: Skill folder materialization is unserialized: concurrent refresh_all threads and launches rewrite the same folders, and an older plan can win
findings.evidence: Every skill mutation spawns a new skills::refresh_all thread (provider.rs:533-538); project.add and engine startup spawn one too (workspace.rs:213-222, serve.rs:29-33). Only launches hold hooks::writes() while applying (session.rs:480-496). fill() calls remove_dir_all(dest), then rewrites the files and the marker (skills.rs:325-347), and prune removes folders of disabled skills.
findings.impact: Toggling skills quickly, or launching a session during a refresh, can leave a disabled skill materialized, or an old version marked current, until the next refresh. When an overlapping write fails, it deletes the folder.
findings.fix: Serialize apply and refresh behind one lock (or a single coalescing worker) and re-plan while holding it.

v1.reason: provider.rs:532-538 refresh_checkouts spawns a fresh `skill-materialize` thread running skills::refresh_all after every skill mutation commits. workspace.rs:213-223 (project.add) and serve.rs:29-33 (startup) spawn similar threads. refresh_all (skills.rs:267-306) snapshots its plans under the store lock, then applies them with no lock held. apply (skills.rs:230-251) runs prune(), which deletes marker-owned folders not in plan.rows, then write_skill/fill. fill begins with remove_dir_all(dest) (skills.rs:326). Only the launch path takes crate::hooks::writes() around apply (session.rs:480-496), and refresh_all never takes it, so nothing serializes the threads. Trigger: toggle skill X off and on in quick succession, or off while an earlier refresh is still applying. If thread A planned with X enabled and thread B planned with X disabled, B can prune X and A can then rewrite it. The disabled skill then stays materialized until the next refresh. Two threads filling the same dest can also interleave remove_dir_all and writes; the loser's error path runs remove_dir_all(dest) (skills.rs:319) and leaves the folder missing. Both states heal at the next refresh or launch, and the effect is only on provider skill folders, so low is right.
v1.correction: refresh_all does not take hooks::writes(), so even the launch lock does not order a launch against a refresh. The lock would serialize them only if it were taken around the whole apply loop in refresh_all and in the project.add thread. The simplest fix is that plus re-planning while the lock is held, or a single coalescing materialize worker.

findings.title: In-memory engine state is mutated inside handlers and not rolled back when the transaction fails, so device.run's phantom run can hold the device forever
findings.evidence: RunOp inserts the runtime into device_runs and acquires a Kind::Run(id) lease (handlers/device.rs:176-177) before the pipeline appends the audit row and commits (engine.rs:999-1024). If that fails, the row is rolled back and the worker (an after_commit action) never starts, but the map entry and the lease stay. prune treats any id still in device_runs as live (handlers/device_lease.rs:94-96). device.release refuses Run leases, and device.run.stop fails with run_not_found. The same pattern appears in the gate's shell lease (handlers/guardrail.rs:532) and in set_pty during finish_launch (session.rs:685).
findings.impact: After a commit failure (for example disk full), the device stays "in use by device run N" until the engine restarts.
findings.fix: Register these in-memory side effects as after_commit actions, or record compensations that run on rollback.

v1.reason: RunOp inserts into `device_runs` and acquires a Kind::Run lease inside the handler (device.rs:176-180) and only defers the worker to after_commit. prune keeps any Run lease whose id is still in device_runs (device_lease.rs:94-98). If the transaction rolls back after the handler returns, the map entry and the lease survive and nothing removes them. The finding's trigger, a commit failure, is very rare: one connection, no SQLITE_BUSY. But the same root cause has a much more reachable trigger in a related site the finding lists. finish_launch calls `Pty::spawn` and `ctx.engine().set_pty(...)` inside the handler (session.rs:646-686), and task.dispatch nests it with invoke_registered. With `fanout`, dispatch_task first creates and spawns the parent's session, then does the same for each child (task.rs:1067-1075). If a later child's nested session.create fails, the `?` rolls back the whole transaction, including the parent's session row. For example, the template carries an explicit `branch` that is already checked out in the parent's new worktree, so `git worktree add` fails, or a name reservation fails. The agent process is still running and registered in the PTY map, under a session name that no longer exists in the store. Its new worktree and git hooks also stay on disk.
v1.correction: Re-anchor the finding on the composite-rollback trigger (session.rs:685 under task.rs:712 + task.rs:1073), not on a commit failure. The consequence there is an orphaned live agent PTY, its worktree and its hooks, with no session row. For device.run the impact is as described but needs a commit failure. guardrail.rs:532 (gate_command lease) has the same shape. Fix: move in-memory registrations (set_pty, device_runs insert, lease acquire) into after_commit, or record rollback compensations that kill the PTY or release the lease when the pipeline's Err branch runs.

results.coverage:
Scope: the sec-local-ipc sweep, followed across relay-core (socket.rs, engine.rs pipeline, guardrail.rs, guardrail/grants.rs, hooks.rs, sessions.rs, paths.rs, store.rs open/backup, handlers: guardrail, file, git commit, session spawn/attach/report/done, notes/mailbox, audit, integration, ui os.*, device_lease, settings defaults), relay-bus (envelope Actor/Request, registry Actors, every op! declaration's kind/actors), relay-cli (main.rs actor_from_env/do_cmd/hook adapters, mcp.rs; unreal/blender MCP only scanned for listeners and process spawning), relay-remote (bridge.rs, wire.rs gate, registry save mode), and apps/relay-native (client.rs actor, guardrail_pages confirm call, a grep for Pango markup — none found).

Search patterns used: `Door::|Actor::User|resolve_actor|check_session_token|token`; `set_permissions|mode(0o|create_dir_all|runtime_dir|XDG_RUNTIME_DIR|temp_dir`; `actor_session_id|assert_own|assert_actor_project|actor_project|not_own|project_id !=`; an extraction of every `op!(..)` with its `Actors::`/`Audit::`/`Doors::` metadata; `RELAY_[A-Z_]+`; `Command::new` with and without `output_with_timeout`; `hooksPath|no-verify|settings.local|install_claude|install_codex|already_installed`; `replay_registered|invoke_registered|default_worktree|root_verify`; `path_matches|relative_path|fn rel|safe_join|covers_path`; `set_markup|use_markup`; `subscribe|bus.wait|exposed`.

Verification method: the path_matches/glob_match and shell_commands/self_approval/denied_matches results come from Python transliterations run as string-only simulations in the scratchpad (exp/pm.py, exp/sa.py), not from executing Rust. This session is itself gated by the Relay dev-instance hook, and it refused one of my Bash heredocs because its quoted body contained test strings; that refusal is the live evidence cited in the self_approval finding. I did not try to get around it and did not run relay.

Not finished or not verifiable:
- Claude Code and Codex runtime behaviour: whether settings edits hot-reload, how disableAllHooks and --settings precedence apply, the exact Codex PreToolUse tool_input shape for apply_patch, and whether Claude Code prompts before editing its own settings file (hence medium confidence on the hook-tamper finding).
- Per-handler authorization inside task.* and module.* beyond the task_id check in authorize.
- Phone-door network and crypto: pairing, rendezvous, tunnel, direct.rs frame handling. That belongs to another sweep; I confirmed only that the gate admits user/test and that the registry is 0600.
- Native-client UI flows beyond actor use, the confirm call and markup.
- Skills materialization into ~/.codex.
- The integration build shell hard-codes `fish -lc` with no timeout; this is outside the IPC concern and was not filed.

Observed but not filed:
- os.reveal/os.open_url spawn xdg-open without waiting on it, which likely leaves zombie processes.
- The dev store.db on this machine is about 180 MB, which may matter to whoever audits retention.

findings.title: Socket door accepts a client-claimed `actor: "user"` with no credential, so any agent process can act as the user
findings.evidence: resolve_actor: `(Actor::User, _) | (Actor::Test, _) => Ok(None),`. Only `agent:<name>` needs a token (check_session_token, 1377). The accept loop (socket.rs:110 `listener.accept()`) never reads peer credentials. The native UI is itself just a socket client sending `Request::new(Actor::User, op, payload)` with no token (apps/relay-native/src/client.rs:312). The CLI forwards whatever actor it is given: `--actor user` (relay-cli main.rs:118-121), or a full JSON envelope whose `actor` it uses verbatim (main.rs:586-593, advertised in `relay cmd --help`, main.rs:35). Agents run as the same uid with `RELAY_BIN` in their environment (handlers/session.rs:571). BUS.md:29 (§0.6), :207-208 and :583 acknowledge 'The socket does not authenticate the user actor'.
findings.impact: From any agent session, or anything it spawns, one line approves the agent's own exception or held write: `$RELAY_BIN cmd '{"actor":"user","op":"guardrail.confirm","payload":{"hold_id":N}}'`. The same route reaches guardrail.config.set (clear protected_paths, denied_commands or role allowlists), settings.set, session.input into another session's terminal, session.spawn, task.dispatch and worktree.remove. Each of these is audited as `actor: user`, so the audit log ('source of truth', §0.4) records the agent's act as yours. A prompt-injected agent needs no exploit, and both providers are still labelled guarded: true. Agent-to-agent impersonation works the same way: a session's RELAY_TOKEN is a bearer secret in its environment, readable through /proc/<pid>/environ by any same-uid process, and session.list/get give same-project peers its pid.
findings.fix: Authenticate at the door instead of by command-line pattern. On accept, read UnixStream::peer_cred() and require uid == the engine's uid. Then walk /proc/<pid>/status PPid up to the engine: if a live session's PTY child is an ancestor, treat the connection as that session. Refuse user/test (typed bus.actor) and accept agent:<name> only for that session's own subtree, which also stops cross-session token reuse. Make the engine a child subreaper (prctl PR_SET_CHILD_SUBREAPER) so daemonized agent descendants re-parent to it and remain classifiable. This covers every route (python, scripts, the envelope form, MCP) uniformly. Cheap belt: when RELAY_SESSION is set, the CLI should refuse --actor or an envelope actor other than the session's own. If this stays out of scope by design, say in the UI that guardrails are advisory and that audit rows showing actor:user may be an agent.

v1.reason: resolve_actor (engine.rs:~1355) returns Ok(None) for User/Test on every door, and only agent:<name> on the socket checks a token. The CLI lets --actor override RELAY_SESSION (actor_from_env, main.rs:118-128), and the envelope's actor wins outright. Agents receive RELAY_BIN and RELAY_TOKEN in their environment (handlers/session.rs:566-575). So an agent can call guardrail.confirm, guardrail.config.set or settings.set as the user, and the call is audited as user. The mechanics are as described.
v1.correction: This is an explicitly documented design decision, not an oversight: BUS.md §0.6 ('Seatbelts, not sandboxes … not a security boundary against a hostile process on your own machine'), §4.2 ('user needs no token (same uid, same trust)'), §9.5 and §… 1119. It is not harmless: a prompt-injected agent can self-approve, and the audit log misattributes the act. So it stays a finding, rated below high. The proposed peer-cred and ancestry check would not create a boundary either. Agents also get RELAY_STORE, the SQLite path (session.rs:~575), plus full same-uid filesystem access, so they can edit the store or the settings directly. Its real payoff is correct audit attribution and making self-approval non-trivial. If that is not pursued, the honest minimum is to state in the UI that guardrails are advisory.

findings.title: Confirming an agent's held bus write replays it against the project root (your main checkout) instead of the agent's worktree
findings.evidence: For a non-gate hold, confirm calls `ctx.replay_registered(&frozen.op, frozen.payload.clone(), hold.actor.clone(), hold.policy.clone())`. replay_registered (engine.rs:364-377) swaps only `actor` and `skip_policy`, so ctx.session_id stays the confirmer's, which is None for the user. file.write resolves its tree via `root(ctx, p.project_id, p.worktree.as_deref())` -> `default_worktree_in(conn, ctx.actor_session_id(), ..)`, which returns `None => Ok(repo)` (file.rs:398-408). The frozen envelope never carries a worktree: enforce freezes `ctx.payload()` (handlers/guardrail.rs:691), and D111 tells agents to omit `worktree`. root_verify accepts the root (worktree::contains: `if canon(repo) == want { return Ok(true) }`), and with skip_policy = destructive_write the replayed enforce allows the write. The existing confirm tests (tests/phase8.rs:159-175 and 541-556) confirm only user-originated holds, for which the root is the correct tree.
findings.impact: Trigger: a session with bus_writes enabled rewrites more than 50 lines of a file it had already modified (`file.write {path:"src/x.rs", text}`). This user's sessions do use bus_writes: the relay MCP tool list offers file_write and git_commit. The write is held as guardrail.destructive_write. You click Allow on the guardrail page, which sends `{hold_id}` (apps/relay-native/src/guardrail_pages.rs:299).
