What the provider does with a timed-out hook is decided outside this repo. If it treats a timeout as non-blocking, gated tools run unchecked during the attack. Only Edit, Write, MultiEdit and Bash go through this hook, not every tool call.

2. The remote.json reads at bridge.rs:117 and :72 happen only after the upgrade. Idle sockets that have not upgraded cause no file IO, so "every attempt" overstates it. This point is minor.

3. Memory. The first verifier is right that reserve() by itself only reserves address space. The hold is not limited to the 30 s hello window, though. After HelloTimeout, handle waits on `writer.await` (direct.rs:126) with no bound. `sink.close()` stays pending forever if the peer sent pings and never read the automatic pongs, because its receive window is then zero and the server's send buffer fills. tungstenite flushes pongs from the read path (protocol/mod.rs:457-465), and tokio-tungstenite's poll_close returns Pending on WouldBlock (lib.rs:388-404). The TCP fd stays held, and so do up to 64 MiB of incomplete fragments (`incomplete`, max_message_size) per connection, with no time limit. Across about 990 connections that is far more than RAM, so the kernel could plausibly OOM-kill the engine. I reasoned this from the tungstenite 0.30 source and did not run it.

4. Fix gaps.
- Bound the drain: wrap `writer.await` in a short timeout and then abort it, as tunnel.rs:150 already does.
- Put peek, upgrade, hello and admit under one deadline, not just peek and upgrade.
- A global Semaphore on connections that have not been admitted is what actually bounds fds and memory. Hold the permit until admission or until the task ends, including the drain. A per-IP cap helps, but it is not enough on its own.
- "Few KiB before admission, few MiB after" cannot be done on one stream. tokio-tungstenite 0.30's WebSocketStream has get_config but no set_config, and the stream is split before the hello. Use one connection-wide max_message_size and max_frame_size, sized for the largest real phone payload, and reject an oversized first message.
- Add TCP keepalive, or application-level pings after admission.
- Raising NOFILE only moves the threshold.
- Consider not opening the door on every run.sh launch when no phone is paired.

Line note: the EMFILE retry is at socket.rs:119-122, and the door's own accept loop at direct.rs:48-51 also spins.

findings.title: `relay remote revoke` does not disconnect a phone that is already connected: admission is never re-checked
findings.evidence: Admission is decided once (bridge.rs:137). After that, bridge.rs:173-188 (`while let Some(line) = inbound.recv().await { ... writer.write_all(line.as_bytes()) ... }`) forwards to the engine until the transport closes. The pump (bridge.rs:162-169) keeps streaming events and PTY frames. Nothing reloads or watches remote.json, and nothing listens for a revoke. `RemoteCommand::Revoke` (remote.rs:252-259) only edits the file from another process and prints 'revoked {id}; its next connection will be refused'. MOBILE.md:193-194 presents this as how 'to cut a phone off from the PC side'. The direct door has no idle timeout or ping. The rendezvous path behaves the same way: tunnel.rs:118-137 keeps the lane's bridge until the server closes the lane.
findings.impact: Take a lost or stolen phone that is connected when its owner revokes it. The app keeps the link open in the foreground and reconnects on its own (MOBILE.md:172-174). Whoever holds the phone keeps full `user` control for as long as the socket stays open: dispatching agents, approving guardrail holds, and reading every event and terminal. The only real cut-off is restarting the door, and with `relay serve --remote` that means restarting the engine.
findings.fix: Have each bridge re-check its device on a timer: every 5-10 s, compare remote.json's mtime and confirm the device id still exists. Alternatively, have the door watch remote.json with inotify and close bridges whose device has gone. Make `revoke` report whether a live connection was cut. Consider token expiry or rotation.

v1.reason: Admission is checked once (bridge.rs:137). The loop at bridge.rs:173-188 and the pump at :162-169 then run until the transport closes, with no re-check, file watch or timer. The direct door (direct.rs:96-127) has no idle timeout. On the tunnel, a lane lasts until the server closes it (tunnel.rs:118-137). RemoteCommand::Revoke (remote.rs:252-258) only edits the file, and the integration test (tests/remote.rs:190s) only checks that a new connection is refused. MOBILE.md:177 says the link stays open with the app in the background, so a lost phone is almost always connected when it is revoked, and it keeps full `user` access until the door or engine restarts. MOBILE.md:193-194 presents revoke as the way 'to cut a phone off'. I rate it medium rather than high. The CLI output is honest ('its next connection will be refused'), so the bypass is not silent. Exploiting it needs an attacker who already holds a device or token, and restarting the door ends it.
v1.correction: The background persistence comes from MOBILE.md around line 160 ('With the app in the background ... it comes from the PC link'), which strengthens the trigger more than the foreground reconnect at :172-174 does. Fix options: have each bridge re-check its device id periodically (cheap: stat the mtime of remote.json and reload only when it changes), or add a revoke signal the door can act on. Update MOBILE.md:193 and the revoke message to say whether a live connection was cut.

findings.title: remote.json is read-modify-written with no lock and through one shared tmp path: a handshake in flight undoes a revoke, and concurrent saves can corrupt the file
findings.evidence: Every successful proof rewrites the whole registry from the copy it loaded: bridge.rs:72 `let mut registry = Registry::load(&ctx.registry_path)`, bridge.rs:86 `registry.touch(id)`, bridge.rs:94 `registry.save(&ctx.registry_path)`. Other processes do the same load, modify and save: `relay remote revoke` (remote.rs:252-258), `pair` (remote.rs:225-229), `via` (remote.rs:272-287), `name` (remote.rs:261-268), `serve` (remote.rs:192-195) and `serve --remote` (remote.rs:114-118). Admits also run in parallel on the multi-thread runtime (main.rs:106). Registry::save (registry.rs:165-177) opens the fixed path `remote.json.tmp` with create and truncate, writes, and renames it. It takes no flock.
findings.impact: (1) If a revoke's save lands between an admit's load and its save, the admit writes the revoked device back, after the CLI has already printed 'revoked'. Someone holding a stolen token can keep handshakes in flight all the time and make every revoke lose. (2) A phone paired while another phone reconnects can be dropped from the file even though it holds a token; it is then refused as auth.unknown_device. (3) Two saves that both open the tmp file before either renames it overwrite each other from offset 0. If the second is shorter, the file keeps the first one's tail. I reproduced this with two O_TRUNC fds on one path: the result is unparseable ('Extra data') and the second rename fails with ENOENT. Registry::load refuses a file it cannot parse (registry.rs:146-150). After that, every connection is dropped before the greeting (bridge.rs:117) and every `relay remote` subcommand fails until the file is fixed by hand.
findings.fix: Hold an exclusive flock on a sidecar file (remote.json.lock) around every load, modify and save. Write to a unique tmp name (pid plus random) and fsync before the rename. Stop rewriting the file on every connection: keep last_seen in memory, or persist it at most every few minutes under the lock.

v1.reason: admit (bridge.rs:72-94) runs on every connection and does Registry::load, then touch or redeem, then save of the whole file. It holds no lock and runs synchronously on tokio workers, so several can run in parallel. Registry::save (registry.rs:165-177) always writes the fixed `remote.json.tmp` with create+truncate and then renames it. CLI commands from another process do the same read-modify-write: revoke remote.rs:253-257, pair :226-229, name :262-268, via :273-287, serve :192-195, and serve_with_door :114-118. registry.rs:3-4 states the design deliberately has processes not talk to each other. The effects are real. A revoke saved inside an admit's load/save window is undone after the CLI has already printed 'revoked'. A `pair` code or a just-redeemed device can be lost when another phone reconnects concurrently. Two overlapping saves on the shared tmp inode can leave trailing bytes, and then load() at registry.rs:149 refuses the file and every connection and CLI command fails until the file is repaired by hand. Each window is microseconds to milliseconds, and a single user with one or two phones rarely hits it. The deliberate version (a token holder flooding handshakes to beat a revoke) needs a stolen token. So medium rather than high.
v1.correction: Both the lost update and the corruption rest on the same missing serialization. Take an flock on a sidecar file around load-modify-save, use a unique tmp name, and fsync before the rename. Stop rewriting the file on every handshake: last_seen can live in memory or be written rarely. Related: admit also does blocking file I/O on an async worker (bridge.rs:137), which is minor.

findings.title: A phone credential carries the whole `user` bus (every op in the 220-op catalogue) instead of the roughly 30 ops the phone uses
findings.evidence: The door's only filter is the actor check at wire.rs:99-100: `let allowed = actor == "user" || (actor == "test" && instance.accepts_test_actor());`. lib.rs:13-14 says the bridge 'forwards bus lines to the socket door as actor `user`'. On the socket door `user` has no scope: engine.rs:1355 `(Actor::User, _) | (Actor::Test, _) => Ok(None)` means the role and scope guardrail layer (engine.rs:870 `if let Some(sid) = session_id`) never runs, and every UserOnly op is admitted (relay-bus registry.rs:59-63, envelope.rs:37-40). That trust model was written for local callers with the same uid: BUS.md:1119-1121 says 'Same uid = same trust (§0.6) ... No RPC over the network. Unix socket only.' A phone can therefore call settings.set, including `providers.claude.path` and `device.adb_path`, which choose the executables the engine runs (providers.rs:271-280, handlers/device.rs:550-560). It can also call guardrail.config.set, guardrail.grant.revoke, file.write/delete, project.add/remove, worktree.remove, git.push, app.quit, skill.install, plugin.enable and github.connect. MOBILE.md:144-169 lists what the app actually uses: session.*, task.*, mailbox.send, guardrail.confirm/reject, git.status/diff and notify.*.
findings.impact: Each other weakness in the door turns straight into arbitrary code execution as the user: a token sniffed at pairing, MITM or rendezvous injection, a revoke that leaves the live link up, or a code redeemed by someone who saw the QR. For example, an attacker can point `providers.claude.path` at another binary, or relax the guardrail config, then start a session. Audit rows also cannot tell phone actions from keyboard actions. MOBILE.md:195 accepts that 'a paired phone is you', but nothing the phone does needs to reconfigure executables or guardrails.
findings.fix: Filter by op as well as by actor. Add an explicit allow-list in wire::gate of the ops the app sends, after fixing the newline-framing bypass. Refuse settings, guardrail.config, provider, plugin, skill, file, worktree, app.quit and similar ops. Better: give remote connections their own actor (for example `remote:<device>`) with an engine-side allowlist layer and their own audit attribution.

v1.reason: The facts check out. gate() filters only on the actor (wire.rs:99-100), and on the socket door `user` resolves to no session (engine.rs:1355), so a paired phone can call any user op. That includes settings.set, guardrail.config.set, file.*, app.quit and the rest. The behavior is intended, though: MOBILE.md:144 says "Everything is an existing bus op, so the list is the bus's", and MOBILE.md:195 says "a paired phone is you". The claimed amplification ("each other weakness turns straight into arbitrary code execution") does not depend on the missing allow-list. Ops the app genuinely needs and that would stay on any allow-list already give a stolen credential code execution. session.create plus session.spawn start an agent with an arbitrary prompt, guardrail.confirm approves whatever it gets held on, and session.input types straight into an agent's terminal. So the allow-list is defense in depth, not the boundary the finding presents it as.
v1.correction: Severity drops from medium to low. An allow-list would not prevent code execution from a compromised phone credential. What it would buy is narrower: (1) the phone could not make persistent reconfigurations that outlive a `relay remote revoke`, such as providers.*.path, device.adb_path, guardrail.config.set or plugin/skill install; (2) phone actions could be told apart in the audit, given a distinct actor such as remote:<device>. Implement it only after the newline-framing bypass (#11) is fixed, and update MOBILE.md §5/§6, which currently promise the full user bus.

findings.title: Every desktop launch opens the phone door on every interface (0.0.0.0:7420), even if no phone has ever been paired
findings.evidence: run.sh:32 always starts the engine with `serve --remote`. The desktop entry that scripts/install-native-desktop.py installs runs run.sh. main.rs:68 defaults `--remote-bind` to `0.0.0.0:7420`, remote.rs:22 does the same for `relay remote serve`, and deploy/relay-remote.service:9 runs it at login. serve_with_door (remote.rs:107) binds whether or not remote.json has any device or pending code. MOBILE.md:49 documents the 0.0.0.0 bind.
findings.impact: Every desktop-app user, with or without a phone, takes an unauthenticated TCP listener onto every network the machine joins: café or hotel Wi-Fi, an office LAN, docker bridges, the tailnet, any public address. By default this exposes the following to those networks: the pre-auth descriptor-exhaustion DoS, the /info disclosure, pairing-code guessing while a window is open, and on-path interception. It also contradicts BUS.md:1121 'No RPC over the network'.
findings.fix: Make the door opt-in (a setting, or for example `RELAY_REMOTE=1` in run.sh). Bind only while remote.json has at least one device or an open pairing window. Default the bind to the private and tailnet interface addresses, which `lan_addresses()` already computes, instead of 0.0.0.0.

v1.reason: run.sh:32 always starts the engine with `serve --remote`, and the installed desktop entry launches run.sh (scripts/install-native-desktop.py:8,22). `--remote-bind` defaults to 0.0.0.0:7420 (main.rs:68). serve_with_door (remote.rs:107) binds whether or not remote.json holds any device or pending code. The listener runs in the engine process itself, and its pre-auth handling has no bounds: direct.rs:39-46 spawns a task for every accepted connection, with no limit, and `stream.peek` (direct.rs:76) and `accept_async` (direct.rs:89) have no timeout. HELLO_TIMEOUT (bridge.rs:39) only starts after the WebSocket upgrade. So any peer on any network the laptop joins can hold open as many idle TCP connections as it likes and exhaust the engine process's file descriptors, which breaks SQLite, PTY spawns and the Unix socket for every session. /info (direct.rs:77-86) also tells any peer the host name, host_id, instance, version and whether a pairing window is open, with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`. Guessing the pairing code is not a practical attack: it is 8 characters from an alphabet of about 32 (registry.rs:103-104), roughly 40 bits, single-use and open for 10 minutes. The core issue stands, though: users who never paired a phone get a network listener anyway.
v1.correction: The main concrete risks are the unbounded pre-auth connections in the engine process, where descriptor exhaustion takes down every session, and the /info disclosure. Pairing-code guessing is negligible. Fix as proposed: make the door opt-in, or bind it only once remote.json has a device or an open pairing window; default to the lan_addresses()/tailnet addresses rather than 0.0.0.0; and add a handshake timeout and a connection cap to direct.rs whatever the bind.

findings.title: Pairing is first-come and silent: whoever presents the code first gets a permanent full-access token, with no confirmation or notice on the PC
findings.evidence: bridge.rs:73-80 issues the token to the first Hello whose code matches (`registry.redeem(code, ...)` then `Welcome::paired(&device.id, &device.token)`). The only trace is `tracing::info!(... "remote device admitted")` at bridge.rs:153. `relay remote pair` (remote.rs:225-235) prints the code and QR and exits. Nothing waits for, confirms or announces the pairing, and no bus event or notification is sent. The link carries every route, including the rendezvous join URL (pairlink.rs:36-37, 53-56), so the code can be redeemed from anywhere. registry.rs:204-216 spends the code on first use, so the real phone just sees pair.invalid.
findings.impact: Suppose the QR or the `relay://pair?...` line is seen by anyone within 10 minutes: through a screen share, a stream, a screenshot, a terminal recording, or scrollback in a shared tmux. They can pair first over the internet using `via=` and keep the token indefinitely. The owner's phone fails, the owner runs `relay remote pair` again and succeeds, and nothing on the desktop ever shows the extra device. It appears only in `relay remote devices`, and a device can hide its own row there (see the device-name finding).
findings.fix: Require confirmation on the PC before issuing the token: keep `relay remote pair` running and ask `Pair "Pixel 8"? [y/N]`, or raise a desktop notification through the bus. Show a short verification code derived from the handshake on both screens. Cancel older pending codes when a new one is issued, and send a notification for every new device.

v1.reason: bridge.rs:73-80 gives the token to the first Hello whose code matches, and registry.rs:212-216 spends the code on that first use. The only trace is the tracing::info at bridge.rs:153. `relay remote pair` (remote.rs:225-235) saves a pending code, prints the QR and link, and exits. Nothing confirms, waits or notifies; there is no bus event and nothing in the desktop client. The link carries `via=` (pairlink.rs:37, 53-56), so anyone who sees the QR or link within 10 minutes, for example on a screen share or stream, can redeem it over the internet. They then get a permanent `user` token, which can dispatch agents with arbitrary prompts. The owner's phone only gets `pair.invalid`, with no attribution. Medium fits: exploiting it needs a leaked code within a 10-minute window, and the consequence is full engine control.
v1.correction: Note that every `relay remote pair` adds another pending code (begin_pair pushes and never clears older ones), so several codes can be live at once. That widens exposure a little. The fix as proposed is sound. At minimum, emit a notification or bus event when a device is added, and require confirmation on the PC before issuing the token.

findings.title: Rendezvous has no consistent size, count or idle limits: an unpaired joiner can tear down the PC's tunnel with one 16 MiB frame, and anyone can exhaust the server
findings.evidence: rendezvous.rs:159 `accept_hdr_async` uses tungstenite's defaults (64 MiB messages, 16 MiB frames), and neither it nor `stream.peek` (rendezvous.rs:127) has a timeout. The accept loop (rendezvous.rs:69-86) has no cap. Any client can create a room by choosing its own secret, because classify (rendezvous.rs:103-107) only checks `room_for(secret) == room`. Queues are bounded by message count, not bytes: 1024 per host (rendezvous.rs:173) and 256 per lane (rendezvous.rs:233). A joiner's text is re-encoded into one Lane line (rendezvous.rs:275), and JSON escaping can grow it up to 6x for control characters. tungstenite sends each message as a single unfragmented frame (protocol/mod.rs:503-504). The PC's client keeps the default 16 MiB frame limit, and any read error drops every lane (tunnel.rs:99-104). The host and join loops have no server-side ping or idle timeout. deploy/relay-rendezvous.service sets no MemoryMax, LimitNOFILE or TasksMax.
findings.impact: (1) Anyone who knows the room id can join and send one text frame of about 16 MiB, or about 3 MiB of control characters. No pairing is needed. The id is in every pairing link and QR and never rotates, so a revoked phone also knows it. The re-wrapped line exceeds the PC's frame limit, so the PC's tunnel errors out, drops every connected phone and redials with growing backoff, and the attacker can repeat this indefinitely. A legitimate engine reply over 16 MiB going the other way kills the host connection in the same way. (2) Anyone on the internet can host a room with a secret they made up, join it, and stream 64 MiB frames without ever reading the host socket. The server queues up to 1024 such lines per room, with no limit on rooms, until the VPS runs out of memory. About 1000 idle connections would instead exhaust the service's descriptors.
findings.fix: Cap the message size at the server well below the PC's frame limit (bus lines need 1-4 MiB), and make the tunnel close only the offending lane instead of the whole socket. Bound queues by bytes. Add handshake and idle timeouts and server-side pings, and cap connections per IP, rooms, and lanes per room. Optionally let the operator restrict the server to known room ids. Allow rotating the room secret without re-pairing. Add MemoryMax=, LimitNOFILE= and TasksMax= to the unit.

v1.reason: rendezvous.rs:159 calls accept_hdr_async with the default config (64 MiB messages, 16 MiB frames). Neither peek (rendezvous.rs:127) nor the handshake has a timeout, and the accept loop (rendezvous.rs:69-86) has no connection cap. classify (rendezvous.rs:103-107) only checks `room_for(secret) == room`, so anyone can create a room with a secret they made up. The join path (rendezvous.rs:230-278) forwards a joiner's text before any authentication: auth happens only on the PC, in bridge.rs. Each message is wrapped in one Lane::Data line (rendezvous.rs:275) and written to the host as a single unfragmented frame. The PC dials with connect_async defaults (tunnel.rs:57), so its frame limit is 16 MiB. A joiner message whose wrapped form exceeds 16 MiB therefore makes the PC's read fail: tunnel.rs:99-104 aborts every lane and returns Err. spawn() does not reset backoff on Err, so repeated attacks push the redial delay to 30 s each time. Queues are bounded by count only: 1024 per host (rendezvous.rs:173) and 256 per lane (rendezvous.rs:233). With self-made rooms, a client can fill a 1024-entry queue with multi-MiB lines toward a host socket it never reads, with no limit on rooms. The unit (deploy/relay-rendezvous.service) sets no MemoryMax, LimitNOFILE or TasksMax.
v1.correction: Part (1) requires the room id (not the secret). The id is a 128-bit digest, so it cannot be guessed. It is known to paired phones, including revoked ones, to anyone who saw the pairing link or QR, and to the server operator, so the attacker set is narrow. A joiner does not need the 16 MiB single-frame or control-character escaping trick: tungstenite reassembles fragmented messages up to 64 MiB, so any text message over about 16 MiB is enough. The reverse direction, an engine line over 16 MiB going PC to server, breaks the server's host read in the same way and drops every lane. Part (2) only takes down the user's own self-hosted rendezvous, not the engine, and a TLS reverse proxy in front may impose some limits of its own. Medium is right.

findings.title: One slow or frozen phone stalls every phone on the rendezvous and blocks the PC's tunnel loop, because per-lane sends are awaited inside shared loops
findings.evidence: In the server's host loop, rendezvous.rs:205-207 `if let Some(target) = target { let _ = target.send(l).await; }` awaits one lane's 256-slot channel (rendezvous.rs:233). While it waits, the server stops reading the host socket for every lane. On the PC, the tunnel's single select loop awaits `tx.send(l).await` into one lane (tunnel.rs:141), awaits `to_server.send(Message::Ping(...)).await` (tunnel.rs:88) into the shared 1024-slot channel (tunnel.rs:64) that every lane's forwarder also fills (tunnel.rs:123-127), and waits up to 5 s for each closed lane (tunnel.rs:150).
findings.impact: Take a phone attached to a busy terminal that stops reading, because its app is suspended in the background or it loses coverage without a FIN. Its lane fills, and the server stops reading the PC. The PC's writer and shared channel then fill, and the tunnel loop blocks in the ping branch, so the 90 s silence check (tunnel.rs:81) can never run. Every other phone and every new join gets nothing until the stalled TCP connection times out, which is about 15 minutes with Linux defaults. Even a merely slow mobile link holds every lane to its speed.
findings.fix: Never await a per-lane send inside a shared loop. Use try_send, and close the lane whose queue is full, on both the server and the PC. Send pings with try_send and run the silence check independently of the channel. Bound per-lane buffering in bytes.

v1.reason: Server: the host loop (rendezvous.rs:204-208) awaits `target.send(l).await` on one lane's 256-slot channel (rendezvous.rs:233). That lane's writer (rendezvous.rs:256-268) blocks in sink.send once a non-reading phone's TCP buffers fill. The host loop then stops reading the host socket for every lane and every new Open. PC: forwarders and pings share one 1024-slot channel (tunnel.rs:64, 88, 123-127). When the server stops reading, the PC writer blocks, that channel fills, and the select loop blocks inside the ping branch at `to_server.send(...).await` (tunnel.rs:88). The SILENCE_LIMIT check (tunnel.rs:81) can then no longer run, and the PC stops reading server messages, including Opens for new joins. Everything recovers only when the stalled phone's server-side socket errors. For a dead peer that is the TCP retransmission timeout, about 15 minutes. A suspended app that still advertises a zero window can stall it longer. A busy terminal stream fills 256 lines easily, and a phone going to the background mid-stream is a normal flow.
v1.correction: The tunnel.rs:141 `tx.send(l).await` into a lane's inbound channel (64) is less relevant: that channel drains into the engine socket and only blocks if the engine stops reading that connection. The main chain is the server's rendezvous.rs:207, plus the PC's to_server await at tunnel.rs:88. The 5 s wait at tunnel.rs:150 is a minor, separate stall. Fix as proposed: use try_send and drop the lane when its queue is full, on both ends, and send pings with try_send.

findings.title: Rendezvous: when a replaced host's connection finally ends, its cleanup evicts the host that replaced it
findings.evidence: host() replaces the room's host when the PC reconnects. rendezvous.rs:176-183 calls this 'the common case, and its old socket is about to time out anyway'. But when the old connection finally ends, its cleanup clears the room unconditionally: rendezvous.rs:219-223 `if let Some(r) = rooms.get_mut(&room) { r.host = None; r.lanes.clear(); } rooms.retain(...)`. It never checks that `r.host` still holds this connection's sender.
findings.impact: This happens when the PC reconnects while its previous connection is still half-open on the server: after sleep and resume, a Wi-Fi switch, or the silence-limit redial. When the old socket times out, it unregisters the live host and drops its phones' lanes, and new joins get host.offline. The PC is told to redial only once the last joiner holding the evicted host's sender leaves. A phone whose connection died silently can therefore keep the room dark indefinitely, while the PC's pings still succeed.
findings.fix: In cleanup, clear the host only if the stored sender is this connection's own (compare with `Sender::same_channel`), and leave a newer host's lanes alone.

v1.reason: host() at rendezvous.rs:174-184 replaces entry.host with the new connection's sender. When any host connection's read loop ends, its cleanup (rendezvous.rs:217-224) unconditionally sets `r.host = None; r.lanes.clear()` without checking that r.host is still its own sender. The trigger is reachable. The PC redials after a network change or the 90 s silence limit (tunnel.rs:81) while the server still holds the old half-open socket. The server has no pings or keepalive, so the old socket ends only when a write to it fails. That happens after all old txA clones drop: the writer then calls sink.close(), and the TCP retransmission timeout (about 15 minutes) also fails the pending read. When it ends, it evicts the live host B and drops all of B's phone lanes, and new joins get host.offline. B's writer ends only when every clone of txB is gone. tungstenite flushes pongs on read, so the PC's pings keep succeeding and it does not notice.
v1.correction: Usually the outage is brief, not indefinite. If no phone lane holds a txB clone, dropping the room's sender ends B's writer at once. It sends Close, the PC's connect_once returns Ok and it redials within about 1 s. The cost is that every connected phone is disconnected roughly 15 minutes after a PC network change. The room stays dark longer only while a joiner on B is itself half-open, and that is bounded by that socket's own retransmission timeout (also about 15 minutes), not indefinite. Fix: in cleanup, clear host and lanes only if `r.host.as_ref().is_some_and(|h| h.same_channel(&tx))`. That requires keeping a clone of tx, or comparing against the writer's channel.

findings.title: The actor gate can be bypassed by putting a newline inside one WebSocket frame
findings.evidence: wire.rs:96-98 forwards any frame that does not parse as a single JSON value: `let Ok(value) = serde_json::from_str::<serde_json::Value>(line) else { return Gate::Forward; };`. bridge.rs:177-181 then writes the frame verbatim, plus a newline, to the socket door, which splits its input on newlines (socket.rs:323 `BufReader::new(r).lines()`, socket.rs:335). A frame made of a user request, a newline, and a second request with actor `agent:<name>` and a token fails the whole-frame parse (trailing characters). Its second line then reaches the engine as an agent request. The rendezvous path behaves the same way (tunnel.rs:139-141).
findings.impact: The door's stated guarantee does not hold. ARCHITECTURE.md:61-62, MOBILE.md:180-182 and wire.rs:91-94 all say every line a phone sends is gated to actor user. Today the gain is small: user already outranks agents, the engine refuses `system` and refuses `test` on stable, and session tokens are 192-bit. But any restriction added to gate() later would be bypassed the same way, including the op allow-list recommended above.
findings.fix: Reject frames that contain a newline or carriage return, or split them and gate each line. Answer frames that do not parse with a local bus.parse error instead of forwarding them.

v1.reason: wire.rs:96-98 forwards any frame that does not parse as a single JSON value (`let Ok(value) = serde_json::from_str(line) else { return Gate::Forward; }`). A frame of the form `{user req}\n{agent req}` fails serde_json with "trailing characters". bridge.rs:177-181 writes it verbatim plus "\n" to the Unix socket, and socket.rs:323/335 splits that input with BufReader::lines(). The second line therefore reaches Engine::parse and resolve_actor (engine.rs:1365-1371) as `agent:<name>` with whatever token the frame carries. The LAN door (direct.rs:107-116, Binary frames included) and the rendezvous (tunnel.rs:139-141) both feed bridge::run, so both are affected. The documented guarantee is broken: MOBILE.md:180-182 says the door refuses any non-user actor before the engine sees it. The real gain is small. `system` is refused at engine.rs:1349, `test` is refused on stable at engine.rs:1352, an agent actor needs a valid session token, and user already outranks agents. The main effect is that an action can be logged as an agent's.
v1.correction: Fix as proposed: in bridge::run, split each inbound frame on \n/\r (or reject frames containing them) and gate every line separately. Do this before adding any further restriction to gate(), since it would be bypassed the same way.

findings.title: `GET /info` answers any website (Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *) with the host name, a stable host_id and whether a pairing window is open
findings.evidence: direct.rs:79-83 adds `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` to the unauthenticated /info response. Its body (direct.rs:60-70) contains `host` (from /etc/hostname), `host_id`, `instance`, `version` and `pairing_open`. The WebSocket upgrade (direct.rs:89) does not check Origin either, and the greeting repeats the same fields (bridge.rs:98-108).
findings.impact: Any page open in the user's browser can fetch http://127.0.0.1:7420/info, or probe LAN addresses, and read the machine's hostname (often the user's name), a stable identifier usable for tracking, the Relay version, and whether `relay remote pair` is open right now.
findings.fix: Drop the CORS header, since the native app does not need it. Reject upgrades that carry a browser Origin. Leave host_id and pairing_open out of the unauthenticated response.

v1.reason: direct.rs:79-80 writes `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` on the unauthenticated /info response. info_json (direct.rs:60-70) returns host_name (from /etc/hostname, registry.rs:94-101), host_id, instance, version and pairing_open. accept_async at direct.rs:89 does no Origin check, and the greeting (bridge.rs:98-108) repeats host, host_id, instance and version, so a browser page can read the same data over a WebSocket, which CORS does not cover. The mobile client is React Native, which has no CORS, so nothing needs the header. The impact is only information disclosure. The pairing code is 8 characters from a 32-letter alphabet (about 2^40) and expires after 10 minutes, so pairing_open does not make a brute force practical.
v1.correction: Recent Chromium versions put public-site requests to loopback or private addresses behind Local Network Access or Private Network Access checks, so 'any website' is narrower in Chrome than the finding implies. Other browsers and LAN pages are still exposed. Dropping the CORS header alone is not enough: the WebSocket greeting leaks the same fields, so also reject upgrades that carry a browser Origin header.

findings.title: The rendezvous host secret is sent as a URL query parameter, and the default and documented bind serves it as plain ws on every interface
findings.evidence: tunnel.rs:18-19 `format!("{}/host/{}?secret={}", r.url, r.room, r.secret)`, and rendezvous.rs:98-102 reads the secret from the query string. `relay remote rendezvous` defaults to `0.0.0.0:7430` (remote.rs:43), and MOBILE.md:87 tells the user to run exactly that, while MOBILE.md:90-91 says the deployments bind to loopback. `relay remote via` accepts ws://, with a warning that mentions only the token (remote.rs:283-285).
findings.impact: Request lines containing the secret end up in reverse-proxy access logs (nginx's default combined log format records the full URI). Over ws:// they also cross the network in clear. Anyone holding the secret can host the room, because a second host replaces the first (rendezvous.rs:177-183). They can then impersonate the PC to every phone that uses the rendezvous: capture pairing codes sent to it and feed phones false state.
findings.fix: Send the secret in a header (for example `Authorization: Bearer`) or as the first WebSocket message. Default `relay remote rendezvous` to 127.0.0.1 and fix MOBILE.md:87. Refuse ws:// for a rendezvous that is not on loopback unless the user forces it.

v1.reason: tunnel.rs:18-19 builds `{url}/host/{room}?secret={secret}`, and rendezvous.rs:97-107 (classify) reads the secret from the query string and checks `room_for(secret) == room`. `relay remote rendezvous` defaults to 0.0.0.0:7430 (remote.rs:43), and MOBILE.md:87 tells the user to run exactly that, even though MOBILE.md:90-91 says the shipped deployments bind loopback behind TLS. `via` accepts ws:// with a warning that mentions only the token (remote.rs:283-285). Whoever holds the secret can take the room: host() at rendezvous.rs:176-183 replaces the existing host and closes every lane. The impact is low for three reasons. The secret normally travels inside wss://. The proxy log that would record it belongs to the user, since the docs say to run the server yourself. And on ws:// the phone's token is already exposed in clear, which is the worse leak.
v1.correction: The impact is mostly denial of service, not full impersonation. A fake host cannot relay a phone's challenge proof to the real PC, because the real PC has been displaced from the room. It can capture pairing codes sent during an open window and show a phone a fake greeting, since the phone does not authenticate the PC. Worse, the displaced PC's server-side handler keeps reading its socket, so tungstenite keeps answering the PC's pings. last_heard keeps updating (tunnel.rs:95), so the PC never hits SILENCE_LIMIT and never redials. Once the attacker leaves, the room has no host until the PC's engine restarts. The proposed fix still holds: send the secret in a header or as the first frame, and default the bind to 127.0.0.1 or fix MOBILE.md:87. Also have the server close a replaced host's socket rather than leaving it orphaned.

findings.title: The tunnel's dial has no timeout: a rendezvous that accepts TCP but never answers leaves the PC's tunnel stuck until the engine restarts
findings.evidence: tunnel.rs:57 awaits `tokio_tungstenite::connect_async(url.as_str())`, which covers TCP, TLS and the HTTP upgrade, with no timeout. The retry and backoff loop (tunnel.rs:29-45) runs only after this call returns, and the 90 s silence check (tunnel.rs:81) exists only once the connection is up.
findings.impact: The server, or the TLS proxy in front of it, may accept the connection and then stall: when overloaded, when out of descriptors (see the rendezvous DoS finding), when the proxy waits on a dead upstream, or because of a middlebox. The dial then never finishes and is never retried. Phones are told host.offline indefinitely, even after the server recovers.
findings.fix: Wrap the dial in tokio::time::timeout (for example 20 s) and treat expiry as an error, so the backoff loop retries.

v1.reason: tunnel.rs:57 awaits `tokio_tungstenite::connect_async(url)` with no timeout. The backoff loop (tunnel.rs:32-44) only runs after that call returns, and the 90 s silence check (tunnel.rs:80-87) exists only after the upgrade. A peer that has acknowledged the request bytes but never answers, such as a server or VM that dies hard after accepting, or a middlebox that black-holes the flow, leaves the PC reading forever: no TCP keepalive is set, and the PC has nothing more to send that could time out on retransmission. The tunnel then stays down until the engine restarts.
v1.correction: The trigger is narrower than claimed. The TCP connect itself is bounded by the kernel's SYN retries. Descriptor exhaustion on the server usually recovers on its own: the connection waits in the kernel's accept queue and is handled once accept() succeeds again. A proxy whose upstream is dead normally answers 502 quickly, which makes the dial return an error that is then retried. What remains is a rare hard stall after the server has acknowledged the request. The fix is still a one-liner: wrap the dial in tokio::time::timeout (for example 20 s).

findings.title: A pairing phone's device_name is stored and printed raw, so terminal escape sequences reach `relay remote devices`
findings.evidence: registry.rs:217-220 keeps the name the phone supplies after only `trim()` and `chars().take(64)`, so control characters survive. remote.rs:245 prints it straight to the terminal: `println!("{:<14} {:<24} {:<26} {}", d.id, d.name, d.created_at, ...)`.
findings.impact: Whoever redeems a code, for example someone who saw the QR, can name the device with ANSI sequences such as cursor-up and erase-line. Its row then disappears from `relay remote devices`, the one place the owner can see paired phones, or shows misleading text.
findings.fix: Strip control characters when redeeming (`c.is_control()`), and escape non-printable characters when printing.

v1.reason: registry.rs:217-220 keeps the phone-supplied name after only `trim()` and `chars().take(64)`, and wire.rs:35 accepts `device_name` as an arbitrary string. remote.rs:245 prints it with `println!("{:<14} {:<24} ...", d.id, d.name, ...)` and no escaping. ESC/CSI sequences therefore reach the owner's terminal and can erase or overwrite that row. The precondition is a redeemed pairing code, which already means full `user` access to the engine. So the only extra harm is hiding the device from the one listing that shows paired phones (it pairs with #7). Low is right.
v1.correction: Escape or replace control characters both at redeem (registry.rs:217) and when printing (remote.rs:245, for files already on disk). The `{:<24}` padding also misaligns with multi-byte or wide names, which is cosmetic.

results.coverage: Traced guardrail enforcement end to end: provider hook adapters (crates/relay-cli/src/main.rs claude_pre_tool/codex_pre_tool), the installed hooks (crates/relay-core/src/hooks.rs install_claude/install_codex/install_git, PreToolUse matchers and the git pre-commit script), the engine gate (handlers/guardrail.rs gate/confirm/approve/enforce), pure policy (guardrail.rs evaluate_write/evaluate_commit/evaluate_exec, write_target, denied_matches, shell_commands, self_approval, path_matches/glob_match), grants (guardrail/grants.rs load/consume/covers_*), file ops (handlers/file.rs rel/safe_join/guard_path_mutation), defaults (handlers/settings.rs line ~29-34), providers.rs guarded(), and the phone door actor mapping (relay-remote/src/wire.rs:99 — paired devices act as `user` by design; pairing strength is another auditor's concern). Validated the denied-command and self_approval bypasses with faithful Python reimplementations under scratchpad/exp (python -I); results quoted in the findings. Search patterns (rg/grep): guardrail, denied_commands, allowed_write_roots, protected_paths, destructive, shape_gate, min_removed, self_approval, shell_commands, GateKind::Write|Exec, evaluate_, enforce, gate, violation, post-hoc, no-verify|core.hooksPath, PreToolUse, guarded|unguarded, Actor::User|user_only|UserOnly, holds|expired, Resume|INSERT INTO sessions. Not done / caveats: (1) strictly static review — I did not run cargo, rustc, or the live engine (the environment's own Relay engine gates my Bash tool, which I avoided triggering; one accidental heredoc trigger occurred and was worked around via the Write tool); (2) did not exhaustively audit every CLI/MCP subprocess spawn in relay-cli unreal/blender for reuse of evaluate_exec, but those paths share the same exec gate so the argv/wrapper findings apply; (3) session-scoped grants are NOT expired on session.close (session.rs:1612 expires only state='open'), but closed session ids are never reactivated (resume requires parked/exited/restorable, reusing the same row id), so I found no cross-session privilege leak and did not raise it; (4) did not evaluate whether the device-lease call on exec-allow (handlers/device_lease::gate_command) does slow work under the store lock — out of scope for this concern.

findings.title: Shell file-writes (Bash tool) bypass every write-path guardrail; only Write/Edit/MultiEdit and file.* are gated
findings.evidence: The PreToolUse adapter maps the Bash tool to `kind:"exec"` (main.rs:406-410 for Claude; main.rs:508-512 maps Codex Bash|apply_patch|Edit|Write ALL to exec). evaluate_exec (guardrail.rs:811-847) checks only self_approval + denied_commands (+ a device lease on allow). It never evaluates protected_paths, allowed_write_roots, destructive_write or shape_gates — those live only in evaluate_write (guardrail.rs:503), reachable solely from the Write/Edit/MultiEdit tools and the file.* bus ops (file.rs:72,127 call guardrail::enforce with GateKind::Write). There is no post-hoc write detector: watch.rs emits only reconciliation events, and the `guardrail.violation` watcher described in BUS.md §9.3 is unimplemented (no `violation` emitter exists in crates/).
findings.impact: A builder session whose project sets protected_paths (e.g. `**/*.env`, `**/secrets.*`) or shape gates can modify or destroy those files with an ordinary shell command the gate waves through: `printf 'KEY=leak\n' >> config/.env`, `sed -i 's/.*/x/' src/critical.rs`, `: > important.rs`, `truncate -s0 f`, `tee`, `cp`, `python -c 'open("x","w")...'`. protected_paths / destructive_write / shape_gates / write_roots are all skipped; nothing is held, refused, or detected afterward. These are routine (non-adversarial) agent actions, so the seatbelt misses the mistakes it exists to catch. Only a later commit through the hooked git (and only if the agent does not add --no-verify, see separate finding) would catch a protected path — caps/destructive/shape are never re-checked.
findings.fix: Gate writes regardless of the tool used: in the exec gate, detect obvious file-mutating commands (redirections `>`/`>>`, sed -i, tee, cp/mv/dd/truncate/install, interpreter one-liners) and run their target paths through the write policy; and/or implement the documented post-hoc violation watcher for Claude too (re-run write policy on watched file.changed, raise guardrail.violation + file.restore_head). At minimum stop advertising write guardrails as binding when the agent holds the Bash tool.

v1.reason: Confirmed at crates/relay-cli/src/main.rs:405-409. The Claude adapter sends Bash as `kind:"exec"` with only `command`. evaluate_exec (crates/relay-core/src/guardrail.rs:811-847) checks self_approval and denied_commands and nothing else. protected_paths, write_roots, destructive_write and shape_gates are only checked in evaluate_write (guardrail.rs:503), and that is reached only from the Write, Edit and MultiEdit tools and from file.*. So `cat > f <<EOF`, `sed -i`, `>`, `tee` and `cp` skip every write rule, inside or outside the worktree. Agents do these things in ordinary work, not only when misbehaving. Some of these rules apply even with default settings: destructive_write and write_roots are on by default, while protected_paths and shape_gates start empty (crates/relay-core/src/handlers/settings.rs:29-34). Nothing catches the write afterwards. BUS.md:530-531 promises a post-hoc `guardrail.violation` notification, but `rg violation crates/` finds only the file.restore_head description and no code that raises it.
v1.correction: The problem is wider than shell writes. The Codex adapter (main.rs:506-512, matcher `Bash|apply_patch|Edit|Write` in hooks.rs:517) sends every Codex tool, including its own file-editing tools (apply_patch, Edit, Write), as `kind:"exec"`. So for Codex the write rules are never checked at all. Yet providers.rs:212 now reports Codex as `guarded() = true`, and D107 and BUS §9.3 still describe a watcher that was never built (docs drift). Better fix: catch writes after they happen rather than parsing commands for redirections. A PostToolUse hook already exists for Bash and apply_patch (it feeds session.report). It could run the write policy on the paths that changed, raise a notification and offer file.restore_head. Matching redirections in the exec gate is fragile and easy to get around. At minimum, ProviderInfo.guarded and the docs should say that write rules do not bind shell writes or Codex.

v2.reason:
(a) The code does what the finding says. For Claude, main.rs:406-410 sends Bash as {kind:"exec", command}. For Codex, main.rs:506-512 sends Bash, apply_patch, Edit and Write all as exec. gate() (handlers/guardrail.rs:501) calls evaluate_granted and then evaluate_exec (guardrail.rs:811-847). That function checks only self_approval and denied_commands; the only other step for exec is device_lease::gate_command, which matters for adb and gradle commands. evaluate_write (guardrail.rs:503-584) holds every write rule: write_roots, protected_paths, shape_gates and destructive_write. It runs only for kind:write, meaning Claude's Write/Edit/MultiEdit and the file.* ops. Nothing checks a write after it lands. watch.rs contains no policy code. "violation" appears only in the description of file.restore_head (relay-bus ops/file.rs:33). PostToolUse calls session.report, which updates session state and the device lease and nothing else. evaluate_commit (guardrail.rs:757-809) checks only staged protected paths and caps. It never checks destructive_write or shape gates, and it never sees a gitignored protected file such as .env.

(b) Any builder or docs session can trigger this without meaning to. Reviewers cannot: they are refused guardrail.gate, so their Bash calls are blocked outright. For Codex, every normal edit is an apply_patch, so the write rules never run on any Codex edit. For Claude, it happens whenever the agent writes through Bash: sed -i renames, heredoc file creation, codegen, `git checkout -- f`, cp or mv. Claude Code's auto-mode system prompt tells the model it may edit files with sed or heredocs. Relay sets no Claude permission mode, so whether a person ever sees the command depends on the user's own Claude config. Codex runs with --approve-for-me (D135), so for Codex no person sees the write.

(c) What the user loses:
- A configured protected path is changed with no refusal. A tracked one is caught only at commit, if the hook runs; an ignored one is never caught.
- A shape-gated file can be emptied or broken and then committed.
- A large rewrite of modified or untracked work can be lost with no hold. Under the default allow_if_recoverable, that is the only content destructive_write still protects. It includes a peer's work in a shared-worktree group (D131) and the user's own uncommitted edits.
- Claude's shell writes outside the worktree are not refused. Codex's own workspace-write sandbox largely covers this case for Codex.

The product tells the user otherwise. The settings UI says "Worktree-relative paths or globs agents may not write" (guardrail_settings.rs:69) and "A write that removes more lines than this is held for you" (:63). SPEC §5 says "any file write ... made impossible to do silently". providers.rs:171 and :212 report guarded()=true for both providers. The documentation does not excuse the gap. BUS.md §0.6 ("Seatbelts, not sandboxes") rules out hostile agents only, and these are routine actions. D132 calls the pre-commit hook "the final write-set enforcement boundary", but that hook checks neither destructive_write nor shape gates. BUS §9.3 and D5 rely on a post-hoc watcher that was never built.

(d) High is the right severity: in a normal flow, a safety check is silently skipped. It is not critical, because the documented threat model leaves out hostile agents, and real loss needs both an agent mistake and content that git cannot restore.

(e) The proposed fixes are incomplete; see the correction.
v2.correction:
Put the Codex half first. For Codex, no write rule runs on any edit, not only on shell writes. The apply_patch envelope is structured (`*** Add File:`, `*** Update File:`, `*** Delete File:`, `*** Move to:`). The Codex adapter can parse it and send one kind:write gate per file. It can pass the hunks as `diff`, which diff_counts already counts by '+' and '-', or apply the hunks in memory to produce new_text, the way the Claude Edit adapter does. That gives Codex the same protection as Claude's Write and Edit at low cost.

I inferred that Codex's apply_patch hook input carries a `command` field from strings in the installed Codex binary, not from its documentation. If the field is missing, the adapter fails closed and blocks every patch, which would be a different bug.

The first verifier's suggestion, a PostToolUse check that offers file.restore_head, does not work as written. restore_head runs `git checkout -- path`, which restores HEAD. That cannot bring back modified or untracked content, and that content is the only thing destructive_write still guards under the default allow_if_recoverable (D114). A post-hoc check needs a snapshot taken before the command runs, to diff against and restore from. The PreToolUse adapter could take one: point GIT_INDEX_FILE at a temporary index, run `git add -A` and `git write-tree`, and copy any ignored protected files separately.

That snapshot and diff must run in the CLI hook process, not inside guardrail.gate. guardrail.gate is registered with Engine::register (handlers/guardrail.rs:304) and holds the store mutex, so a tree walk there would stall every session (CLAUDE.md invariant). In a shared-worktree group (D131), the diff cannot tell which session made a change.

Checking redirections before the command runs can only cover protected_paths and write_roots for obvious targets. It cannot measure destructive_write or shape gates. The existing shell_commands reader also treats `>` as an ordinary word character and splits commands on `&`, so `2>&1` breaks into two commands; it would need a real redirection parser.

Docs drift to fix:
- BUS.md §9.3 (lines 524-533) still says Codex is unguarded and its writes are caught post-hoc.
- D5 says the same.
- guarded() returns true for Codex.
- The UI hints promise more than the code does.

findings.title: denied_commands defeated by argv variants: exact, contiguous, whole-word matching
findings.evidence: denied_matches (guardrail.rs:969-998) lowercases a command's unquoted words into `bare`, splits each pattern on whitespace into `wanted`, and matches only when some contiguous window `bare[i..i+len] == wanted` exactly (guardrail.rs:988). Word comparison is literal equality, program names are not basename-normalized, and short-flag clusters are not decomposed. I reproduced the matcher faithfully and tested the 4 default patterns (handlers/settings.rs:33 = ["rm -rf","git reset --hard","git clean -fd","git push --force"]): ALLOWED (bypass): `rm -fr`, `rm -r -f`, `/bin/rm -rf`, `git clean -xdf`, `git clean -df`, `git push -f`, `git push --force-with-lease`, `git push origin main --force`, `git -C . push --force`, `git reset HEAD~1 --hard`. BLOCKED only the exact spellings (`rm -rf`, `rm  -rf`, `env rm -rf`, `command rm -rf`, `xargs rm -rf`).
findings.impact: The denylist fails on the synonyms a well-intentioned agent naturally emits: `rm -fr` and `git push -f` are everyday spellings, and any global git option (`git -C .`, `git -c k=v`) or an argument between the subcommand and the flag (`git push origin main --force`) slides straight through. An agent is one flag reorder away from the destructive command the rule names. (Note: BUS.md §0.6 frames guardrails as seatbelts vs mistakes, not a sandbox vs hostile code — but missing `rm -fr`/`git push -f` is a failure at the seatbelt's own stated job.)
findings.fix: Match semantically, not positionally: compare program by basename (so /bin/rm == rm), decompose clustered short flags (-fr == -f -r), and treat a pattern as `program + subcommand + a required set of flags` present in the command (subsequence/flag-set), not a contiguous literal window. Equivalent long/short flags (`-f`==`--force`) need canonicalization or explicit listing. Consider an allowlist for the few commands agents truly need.

v1.reason: denied_matches (guardrail.rs:969-998) lowercases the command's unquoted words and matches a pattern only as an exact, contiguous run of those words (`bare.windows(len) == wanted`, line 988). Program names are compared as written (no basename), clustered short flags are not split, and flag order and position count. With the defaults ["rm -rf","git reset --hard","git clean -fd","git push --force"] (handlers/settings.rs:33), all of these pass by inspection: `rm -fr`, `rm -r -f`, `/bin/rm -rf`, `git push -f`, `git push origin main --force`, `git -C . reset --hard`, `git clean -fdx`/`-xdf`. Nothing upstream normalizes the command; the gate gets the raw string. D103 only fixed quoted-data false positives and did not attempt to handle variants. These are everyday spellings in non-adversarial agent output, so the default seatbelt misses the mistakes it is there to stop. That is the rubric's 'safety check that can be silently bypassed'. (Side observation: the same parser treats the body of a heredoc as commands, so unquoted text inside a heredoc is a false positive. This verifier was blocked writing a test script whose heredoc contained the pattern as data.)
v1.correction: Fix: match on meaning rather than position. Compare the program by basename. Skip git global options (-C, -c, --git-dir). Split clustered short flags. Treat a pattern as program plus subcommand plus a set of required flags that may appear anywhere among the arguments, with known aliases (-f/--force, --force-with-lease) listed or canonicalized. Also skip heredoc bodies in shell_commands so data stops being read as commands.

v2.reason:
(a) The code does what is claimed. `denied_matches` (crates/relay-core/src/guardrail.rs:969) lowercases a command's unquoted words into `bare` and matches a pattern only when an exact, contiguous run of those words equals it: `bare.windows(wanted.len()).any(|window| window == wanted.as_slice())` (line 988). `shell_commands` (line 894) starts a new command only at `; \n | &` (line 939). It does not reduce a program to its basename, split short-flag clusters or skip git's global options. I ported both functions to Python faithfully and ran them against the defaults (handlers/settings.rs:33).
- Allowed (not caught): `rm -fr`, `rm -r -f`, `rm -rfv`, `/bin/rm -rf`, `git push -f`, `git push origin main --force`, `git push -u origin HEAD --force`, `git -C /abs/wt reset --hard HEAD`, `git --no-pager reset --hard`, `git reset HEAD~1 --hard`, `git clean -df`, `git clean -xdf`, `git clean -fdx`, `git clean -f -d`.
- Blocked (caught): `rm -rf`, `rm -Rf` (because of the lowercasing), `sudo`/`env`/`xargs`/`timeout`/`find -exec rm -rf`, `git reset --hard HEAD~1`, `git push --force origin main`.

(b) Reachability. Claude's Bash command goes to `guardrail.gate` as the raw string (relay-cli/src/main.rs:406). Codex's does too (main.rs:508). Nothing normalizes it, either in handlers/guardrail.rs or in `evaluate_exec` (guardrail.rs:831). The defaults are the base config layer (guardrail.rs:142), so the four patterns are live out of the box. Nothing else in Relay catches these commands:
- Relay installs only a pre-commit hook, no pre-push hook.
- Relay sets no Claude permission mode (providers.rs:171-190), so this gate is Relay's only check on Bash.

Ordinary, non-hostile agent output triggers it. Claude Code steers agents away from `cd` and toward absolute paths, which produces `git -C <path> …`. `git push -f`, `push -u origin HEAD --force` and `clean -fdx` are everyday spellings. An agent refused on `rm -rf` is one reorder away from `rm -r -f`; the role instructions (providers.rs:37) tell it not to work around a refusal, but nothing enforces that. Destructive commands come up occasionally rather than in every session. When they do come up for the git patterns, the uncaught spellings are common.

(c) What happens when it fires. The gate returns allow, so there is no refusal, hold or notification: it fails silently. `reset --hard` or `clean -fdx` wipes uncommitted work, and `-x` also deletes ignored files such as `.env` and Relay's own `.relay/`. PAIR and review groups share one worktree (D32, D153), so one agent's mistake destroys a peer's uncommitted work. A force push rewrites remote history using the user's credentials. These are exactly the losses the default list names. The UI promises "Commands agents may not run" (apps/relay-native/src/guardrail_settings.rs:70).

(d) Severity: high. This matches the rubric's "a safety check that can be silently bypassed". It is not critical:
- BUS.md §0.6 limits guardrails to catching mistakes, not stopping hostile agents.
- The user's own Claude permission mode may still prompt.
- Codex's workspace-write sandbox blocks network by default, so its force push fails anyway.
- The damage stays within one worktree or one remote branch.

(e) The proposed fix points the right way but is incomplete as written (see correction).
v2.correction:
Evidence:
- Drop `git push --force-with-lease` as a "bypass". It is the safe alternative, and folding it into `--force` would block the behaviour worth encouraging.
- `rm -Rf` is caught by the lowercasing.
- Add these verified misses: `rm -rfv`, `git push -u origin HEAD --force`, `git --no-pager reset --hard`, `git clean -f -d`, `(rm -rf x)` and `$(rm -rf x)`.
- The subshell forms get past even the exact pattern, because `shell_commands` does not end a command at `(`, `)`, `$(` or a backtick. `device_lease::split_commands` (device_lease.rs:375) does.
- The `related` entry grants.rs:141 (`covers_command`) is a different matter. Grants should stay exact matches.

Fix requirements:
1. Keep catching wrapped commands. Today the match window can start anywhere, which is why sudo/env/xargs/timeout/`find -exec rm -rf` are caught. Pinning the program to argv[0] would lose that. Instead, find the program by basename anywhere in the command.
2. Skip git's global options. `-C` and `-c` take a value; also skip `--git-dir=`, `--work-tree=` and `--no-pager`.
3. Split only `-[A-Za-z]+` flag clusters.
4. Require the pattern's subcommand and flag set to appear after the program, in any order.
5. Handle aliases with a small table or extra defaults. `-f`/`--force` and a `+refspec` push are tool-specific; the simplest step is to also ship `git push -f`.
6. End commands at `(`, `)`, `$(` and backticks.

A looser matcher will add to an existing false positive. Heredoc bodies are already parsed as commands: `cat <<EOF` followed by the line `Never run rm -rf` is refused today. Skipping heredoc bodies is needed, but it is a separate false-positive issue.

Add bypass tests next to agent_surface.rs:229 and guardrails.rs:339; both test only the exact spellings.

findings.title: Shell wrappers (bash -c / sh -c / python -c / script file) evade denied_commands and self_approval
findings.evidence: shell_commands (guardrail.rs:894-956) tokenizes one level and treats a quoted word as inert data (D103, guardrail.rs:884-892). It never descends into the string argument of `bash -c`, `sh -c`, `python -c`, `eval`, etc. Both denied_matches (guardrail.rs:969) and self_approval (guardrail.rs:857-881) see only top-level words. Reproduced: `bash -c 'rm -rf /x'` → ALLOWED by the denylist; `bash -c 'relay --actor user cmd guardrail.confirm {}'`, `sh -c "..."`, `echo ... > /tmp/x.sh; sh /tmp/x.sh`, and `python3 -c "subprocess.run([...])"` → NOT caught by self_approval (the direct `relay --actor user ...` and `env relay ...` forms ARE caught).
findings.impact: Wrapping any denied command in `bash -c '...'` runs it unflagged. More seriously, self_approval is the only barrier (BUS.md §9.5) stopping an agent from acting as `user` on the socket, which is unauthenticated for `user` (BUS.md §4.2). Via `bash -c 'relay --actor user cmd guardrail.confirm {hold_id}'` (or a script file, or python subprocess) an agent approves its OWN exception requests, or runs guardrail.config.set / settings.set to rewrite or disable guardrails for its project. The authors concede this net is best-effort, but it is defeated by the most common wrapper an agent uses.
findings.fix: When the first word is a known shell/interpreter with `-c`/`eval`, re-parse the following string argument as a command line and apply denied_matches + self_approval to it recursively; apply the same to obvious `<<EOF`/script-then-run patterns where feasible. Longer term, authenticate the `user` actor on the socket so self-approval is impossible rather than merely discouraged.

v1.reason: shell_commands (guardrail.rs:885-956) reads a quoted string as one opaque word. denied_matches (guardrail.rs:969-998) also drops quoted words from its comparison. So `bash -c 'rm -rf x'` leaves only [bash, -c] to match, and nothing matches. self_approval (guardrail.rs:857-881) does look at quoted words, but only as whole words. For `bash -c 'relay --actor user cmd guardrail.confirm {}'` the `relay` test passes, because the file_stem of the quoted string starts with "relay". But `as_user` needs a standalone `--actor` word and `answers` needs an exact standalone op name, so the line is not flagged. (A wrapped `RELAY_SESSION=` prefix happens to be caught by starts_with.) Calibration: BUS.md §0.6 and §9.5 say outright that self_approval is best effort and not a security boundary. The socket does not authenticate `user` and agents run as the same uid, so a determined agent can also just open the socket directly. That leaves the denylist evasion through `sh -c` or `find -exec sh -c` as the part that fails at the stated mistake-catching job, and that is uncommon in honest agent output.
v1.correction: Rated medium, not higher, because the self-approval half is a documented best-effort check and needs an agent that is deliberately evading. Fix: when the program's basename is sh, bash, zsh, dash or eval and it is given `-c`, parse the next argument with shell_commands again and apply denied_matches and self_approval to it, limiting how deep the nesting goes. Do not present authenticating `user` as possible while agents share the uid. §0.6 already concedes that nothing in-process can stop a hostile process running as the same user.

findings.title: Commit guardrails (caps, protected-path-at-commit) skippable with `git commit --no-verify`
findings.evidence: For an agent's own `git commit`, the sole binding is the generated pre-commit hook that calls `guardrail.gate {kind:commit}` (hooks.rs:116-137; BUS.md §9.3 'this binds both providers' commits'). git's `--no-verify`/`-n` skips all pre-commit hooks, and `git -c core.hooksPath=/dev/null commit` repoints them. Neither `git commit --no-verify` nor `git -c core.hooksPath=... commit` is in denied_commands, and the exec gate does not flag them (verified: `git commit --no-verify -m x` → ALLOWED). The in-process enforcement in git.commit (evaluate_commit, guardrail.rs:757) only applies to the file.*/git.commit bus ops, which agents do not use for their own commits.
findings.impact: An agent trivially bypasses the per-task caps (default 40 files / 2000 lines) and the commit-time protected-path check by appending `--no-verify` — a known agent habit when a hook blocks it. A large or protected-file commit lands with no hold and no refusal. Caps are the backstop for the many-small-writes path, so losing them removes the only size guard on a commit.
findings.fix: In the exec gate, refuse `git commit` carrying `--no-verify`/`-n`, and refuse `git -c core.hooksPath=...`/`-c core.hooksPath` overrides, with a grantable hint. Optionally detect commits post-hoc and re-check caps.

v1.reason: An agent's own `git commit` is gated only by the generated pre-commit hook (crates/relay-core/src/hooks.rs:116-137), installed through a worktree-local core.hooksPath (D23). git skips pre-commit hooks under `--no-verify`/`-n`, and `git -c core.hooksPath=/dev/null commit` points git at an empty hooks directory. None of these match the default denylist, and evaluate_exec has no commit-specific check. The in-process evaluate_commit (guardrail.rs:757) runs only for the git.commit bus op, which itself commits with `--no-verify` after checking (handlers/git.rs:571). I found no later check of caps or protected paths after the commit lands. Calibration: Claude Code's own instructions discourage --no-verify, but agents do reach for it after a hook refuses, and Codex has no such rule. The trigger is an agent reacting to a cap refusal, which is plausible in normal use. The damage is a commit that went past the caps and can be reverted, so medium is right.
v1.correction: Also close `-n` and the `-c core.hooksPath=` and GIT_CONFIG_* routes. A commit-specific rule in the exec gate is cheap. Make it a grantable refusal that explains why, since a user may want to allow it. A sturdier backstop is to re-check caps and protected paths after the commit, using the PostToolUse hook or the worktree reconciliation watcher.

findings.title: gate write-path resolves no symlinks: a symlink made in the worktree escapes write_roots / protected_paths
findings.evidence: write_target (guardrail.rs:623-664) rejects `..` and, for an absolute path, string-prefix-strips the worktree, but never canonicalizes symlinks; a relative path with no `..` is accepted as InWorktree (guardrail.rs:628-630) and protected_paths/destructive are then matched against the literal relative string (guardrail.rs:512,548). The file.* bus ops are protected because file.rs::safe_join canonicalizes and rejects escapes (file.rs:489-506), but the PreToolUse gate that binds the providers' own Write/Edit tools has no equivalent.
findings.impact: An agent runs `ln -s ~/.ssh link` (a Bash exec, not denied), then uses the Write tool on `link/authorized_keys`: the gate sees relative `link/authorized_keys`, treats it as in-worktree, allows it, and the provider writes through the symlink to a path outside the worktree and outside every allowed_write_root. The same trick defeats protected_paths (symlink named differently from the protected pattern). write_roots is a stated policy (D102); this silently voids it.
findings.fix: Canonicalize the write target (or its nearest existing ancestor) in write_target before the worktree/root/protected checks, exactly as file.rs::safe_join already does, and refuse paths whose real location leaves every write root.

v1.reason: write_target (guardrail.rs:623-664) never resolves symlinks. A relative path with no `..` is accepted as in-worktree by relative_path (guardrail.rs:1135). An absolute path is handled by a plain text `strip_prefix(request.worktree)` (guardrail.rs:635). After that, protected_paths and the destructive check look at the literal path string. So a write to `link/x`, where `link` is a symlink pointing outside the worktree, is judged as an in-worktree file. file.rs::safe_join canonicalizes; the gate does not. The incremental impact is small, though. To exploit it an agent must first create the symlink with Bash, and per #1 that same Bash access can already write anywhere without any write check. The only innocent trigger is a symlink already committed in the repository that points outside it, followed by a Write or Edit through it.
v1.correction: Treat this as a small extra on top of #1, not a separate medium-severity hole. The fix is cheap and still worth doing: canonicalize the nearest existing ancestor of the target, as file.rs::safe_join does, before the worktree, root and protected checks. Compare the real path against canonicalized roots, so a worktree path that itself goes through a symlink does not get misclassified as outside.

findings.title: Codex sessions report guarded=true while Codex writes are gated only as exec; documented post-hoc watcher absent
findings.evidence: providers.rs:212 returns guarded()=true for Codex (test at providers.rs:447 asserts it), but BUS.md §9.3/§11.4 (lines 524,1057) state Codex's guarded is false and its writes are caught post-hoc by a notify watcher. That watcher does not exist in the code (no `guardrail.violation` emitter anywhere under crates/), and the Codex PreToolUse adapter maps apply_patch/Edit/Write to kind:exec (main.rs:508-512), so Codex file writes never reach the write policy (same root cause as the Bash-write finding).
findings.impact: The settings/UI surface labels Codex sessions as guarded, implying write enforcement that is not actually applied to Codex's file edits, and promises a post-hoc safety net that is not implemented. A user trusting the 'guarded' badge may run unsupervised Codex work against protected paths believing writes are checked.
findings.fix: Either implement the post-hoc violation watcher (and keep guarded=true honest) or set Codex guarded to reflect that its writes are not gated, and reconcile BUS.md §9.3/§11.4 with the shipped behavior.

v1.reason: providers.rs:212 `fn guarded(&self) -> bool { true }` for Codex, asserted at providers.rs:447. This is deliberate: DECISIONS D132 (DECISIONS.md:650-655) supersedes D107. Codex now gets a provider-native PreToolUse hook that hooks.rs:494-548 (install_codex) merges into `.codex/hooks.json` with matcher `Bash|apply_patch|Edit|Write`, so 'guarded' is not simply false. The docs are stale, though. BUS.md:524-530 (§9.3) still says Codex has 'no tool hooks', `guarded` is `false`, sessions are labelled unguarded, and writes are caught post-hoc by a `notify` watcher. D107 (DECISIONS.md:498-504) says the same without being marked superseded. No such watcher exists: no `guardrail.violation` emitter appears anywhere under crates/. The only Codex notify is `codex_notify` (main.rs:533), which turns agent-turn-complete into a lifecycle `stop` report and does no write detection. The substantive part also holds: codex_pre_tool (main.rs:508-512) sends apply_patch/Edit/Write as `kind: exec` with the patch text as `command`. evaluate_exec (guardrail.rs:811-847) checks only self-approval and denied_commands and never calls evaluate_write, so protected-path and write policy never run on Codex file edits. D132 itself says only the git pre-commit gate is 'the final write-set enforcement boundary', which is an admission, not a documented harmless choice. Still, the enforcement gap is the root cause of the sibling Bash/exec-write finding. Rated as docs drift, this finding is low: the label is mostly honest, since commands are gated, and the stale text is the documentation.
v1.correction: Do not 'set guarded=false': D132 set guarded=true on purpose. The fix is to: update BUS.md §9.3 (lines 524-530) to describe the D132 hook path and delete the nonexistent post-hoc notify watcher; mark D107 as superseded by D132; and, under the sibling write-bypass finding, either gate Codex apply_patch/Edit/Write through kind=write (parse the patch's file headers into paths) or state plainly in the ProviderInfo.guarded doc (BUS.md:1057) that Codex is guarded for commands only, not for writes. Another caveat belongs there too: per D132 the Codex hook runs only after the user trusts it once through `/hooks`. Until then nothing is gated, yet guarded still reports true.

results.coverage: Scope: cross-cutting sec-fs-injection over all crates except apps/relay-mobile. Read in full: crates/relay-core/src/handlers/file.rs, guardrail.rs (+grants.rs), hooks.rs, handlers/git.rs, worktree.rs, branch_cleanup.rs, handlers/integration.rs, handlers/device.rs (signing+build+adb), providers.rs, plugins.rs, skills.rs, github.rs, store.rs (open/backup), socket.rs (bind/perms), paths.rs, handlers/session.rs, handlers/workspace.rs, handlers/settings.rs, handlers/audit.rs, sessions.rs, handlers/ui.rs (xdg-open/markup), all of crates/relay-remote (wire.rs, bridge.rs, rendezvous.rs, tunnel.rs, direct.rs, registry.rs, pairlink.rs), crates/relay-cli/src/main.rs (hook path handling), blender.rs, and the Python-building portions of unreal.rs. Native client (apps/relay-native) checked by grep for set_markup/markup, UriLauncher, Command::new, std::fs writes, /tmp — only fixed-content writes under the user cache dir and a scheme-checked UriLauncher were found; its ~16k lines (board_view.rs, code_git.rs, editor.rs) were not read line-by-line and cannot be compiled here (GTK 4.22). Grep patterns used: set_markup|markup_escape|use_markup; Command::new/sh -c/fish -lc/\"-c\"|\"-lc\"; format!(\"SELECT|UPDATE|INSERT|DELETE|...)/execute(&format!/prepare(&format!; MATCH|LIKE ?; temp_dir()|/tmp|tempfile|NamedTempFile|uuid; set_permissions|from_mode|umask|0o700|0o600; remove_dir_all|worktree::remove|purge_build; py_str|format!(r#|repr|json.loads; \"--\"|literal-pathspecs; token|secret|password|keystore; canonicalize|starts_with|ParentDir|symlink. Verified against gating metadata (Actors::UserOnly, role allowlists, bus_writes) and the stated threat model (BUS.md §0.6/§9 seatbelts-not-sandboxes, MOBILE.md 'a paired phone is you'). Checks performed and found NOT to be defects: git arg-lists guard leading-dash via `--`/check-ref-format and gix rev-parse for revisions; shell interpolation into fish/sh uses only user-configured build/run cmds (UserOnly) and shell_quote() for hook scripts; Blender/Unreal embedded Python interpolates only via py_str()/serde_json JSON-string literals and args-as-JSON-file; SQL is parameterized with the one dynamic table name drawn from a fixed list; file.*/git.* path args reject absolute/.. and safe_join canonicalizes against the canonical worktree root to block symlink escape; worktree/trash/cleanup removals are confined to the pooled checkout and refuse the primary; pairing secrets/tokens are never logged (tunnel logs only base URL) and are stripped from frozen hold envelopes. Could not establish on a live engine: real-world reachability of finding 1 depends on the host's home-dir permissions and presence of other local accounts (not inspectable from the repo); finding 2's trigger ($XDG_RUNTIME_DIR unset) was not exercised.

findings.title: store.db, its WAL, and backups are created world-readable, unlike the deliberately 0600 remote.json/signing files
findings.evidence: Store::open does std::fs::create_dir_all(dir) (line 386, default 0777&~umask => 0755) then Connection::open_with_flags(path, ...CREATE...) (line 388) with no mode — SQLite creates store.db (and store.db-wal/-shm) at 0644&~umask. backup_to() (line 557-560) is the same: create_dir_all(dir) then Connection::open(&dest) at 0644. Nothing in store.rs/serve.rs/paths.rs/recovery.rs ever chmods the data dir or the DB (grep for set_permissions/from_mode/umask over the engine shows hits only in socket.rs, registry.rs, device.rs, hooks.rs). By contrast the same author hardens every other sensitive artifact: remote.json is opened .mode(0o600) (registry.rs:165-173), the signing dir/keystore/secret are 0700/0600 (device.rs:1282-1399), and the socket+runtime dir are 0600/0700 (socket.rs:56,102). The store holds plaintext session tokens (store.rs:92 `token TEXT`, read/inserted verbatim in sessions.rs), full per-session terminal scrollback (session_scrollback table, store.rs:198; save_scrollback in sessions.rs:184), and audit payloads up to 64 KiB that include file.write new_text and every executed command (audit.rs:88-121).
findings.impact: On a multi-user host where $HOME/.local/.local/share are traversable (commonly 0755), another local user can read ~/.local/share/relay-v4/<instance>/store.db and backups/ and recover agents' full scrollback, audited file contents and commands, and session tokens — a confidentiality breach of project data. (Session tokens alone are low-value since the socket is 0600 inside a 0700 $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR, so they cannot be replayed by that user; the exposed transcripts/payloads are the real loss.) On a single-user desktop there is no exposure, which is why this is medium, not high; impact depends on the machine actually having other local accounts and on the home-dir perms.
findings.fix: Create the instance data dir with 0700 and chmod store.db (+ -wal/-shm) and each backup file to 0600 right after creation, mirroring Registry::save and the signing code. Simplest: in Store::open, after create_dir_all, set_permissions(dir, 0o700) and after the DB exists set_permissions on store.db to 0o600; do the same for dest in backup_to.
