A process-wide umask(0o077) at engine startup would also cover the WAL/SHM side-files that SQLite creates itself.

v1.reason: Store::open (store.rs:384-393) runs create_dir_all on the data dir and then Connection::open_with_flags with no mode. backup_to (store.rs:557-560) also uses create_dir_all and then Connection::open(&dest). A grep finds no set_permissions or umask call on the data dir, store.db, the WAL/SHM files or backups/. The only hardening is remote.json (registry.rs:171) and the signing files (device.rs), so under the usual 022 umask these files come out 0644 and their directories 0755. They do hold sensitive data: session tokens (store.rs:92), session_scrollback (store.rs:198) and audit payloads. The exposure, though, depends entirely on the user's home directory being traversable by other local users. Arch-family distros (this user runs CachyOS), Fedora, and Ubuntu since 21.04 create homes as 0700 or 0750. It also needs a multi-user host. On the single-user desktop this app targets, nothing is exposed, so this is defense-in-depth hardening and does not reach medium.
v1.correction: Lower severity to low: it only matters when $HOME is world-traversable on a shared machine. The logs/ dir (paths.rs:63) is affected in the same way and belongs under 'related'. Simplest fix: create the instance data_dir with mode 0700, through DirBuilder::mode(0o700) plus a chmod of an existing dir, once at engine startup. That covers store.db, -wal/-shm, backups/ and logs/ together, so the individual files need no per-file chmod.

findings.title: runtime-dir fallback /tmp/relay-v4-<uid> is attacker-pre-creatable: the 0700 chmod is best-effort and the lock file is opened without O_EXCL
findings.evidence: When $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR is unset, runtime_dir() falls back to std::env::temp_dir().join(format!("relay-v4-{uid}")) (paths.rs:71-72) — a fixed, world-known path in the sticky /tmp. start_in() then does create_dir_all(&dir) and `let _ = std::fs::set_permissions(&dir, 0o700)` (socket.rs:55-56): if another local user has already created /tmp/relay-v4-<uid> as a directory they own, create_dir_all succeeds, the chmod fails with EPERM and the error is discarded, and the engine proceeds to use an attacker-controlled directory. The lock file is then opened with OpenOptions::new().read().write().create(true).mode(0o600) (socket.rs:60-67) — create(true) without create_new, so if `stable.lock` is a symlink the open follows it and the subsequent set_len(0)+write(pid) (socket.rs:96-98) truncates and writes into the symlink target as the engine's user.
findings.impact: A second local user, only when $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR is unset (uncommon on the systemd desktop this targets, but possible for a bare `relay serve` under su/cron/minimal env), can pre-own the runtime dir and either deny the engine its socket (bind fails on a squatted path) or, via a planted `stable.lock` symlink, cause a truncate+PID write to an arbitrary file the engine's user can write. Narrow trigger, hence low/low.
findings.fix: Treat a pre-existing fallback dir defensively: fail if set_permissions does not succeed (don't discard the error) or if the dir is not owned by the current uid with mode 0700, and open the lock with create_new / O_NOFOLLOW semantics (or O_EXCL on first create) so a symlract cannot be followed. Preferably refuse to run at all when $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR is unset rather than silently using /tmp.

v1.reason: paths.rs:67-75: when directories::BaseDirs gives no runtime_dir ($XDG_RUNTIME_DIR unset), the base is std::env::temp_dir().join("relay-v4-{uid}"), and runtime_dir() then appends "relay-v4". socket.rs:55-56 runs create_dir_all(&dir), then `let _ = std::fs::set_permissions(&dir, 0o700)`, which throws away the error. If another local user has already created /tmp/relay-v4-<uid>/relay-v4 and owns it, create_dir_all succeeds, the chmod fails with EPERM, and the engine carries on inside the attacker's directory. The lock is opened at socket.rs:60-67 with create(true).truncate(false).mode(0o600) and no O_NOFOLLOW or create_new, so it follows a planted <instance>.lock symlink. Once flock succeeds, socket.rs:96-98 runs set_len(0) and writes the PID into the symlink target. fs.protected_symlinks does not stop this, because it only applies to sticky world-writable directories and the attacker's own subdirectory is neither. The trigger needs $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR to be unset, which is uncommon on a systemd/pam_systemd desktop, so low severity is right.
v1.correction: Path fix: the fallback dir is /tmp/relay-v4-<uid>/relay-v4/, not /tmp/relay-v4-<uid>, and the lock is named <instance>.lock, e.g. stable.lock. The finding misses a larger impact: the attacker owns the directory, so they can unlink or replace <instance>.sock after the bind and put their own listener there. CLI and MCP clients that resolve the same socket_path would then talk to the attacker and send it session tokens and requests. That is a man-in-the-middle, beyond the denial of service and the file truncation. Fix: if $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR is unset, either refuse to start or create the fallback with mkdir 0700 and then lstat it, requiring that the owner is the current uid, the mode is 0700 and it is not a symlink. Treat a set_permissions failure as fatal. Open the lock with O_NOFOLLOW.

results.coverage:
Read in full: Cargo.toml (workspace and all 5 crates), Cargo.lock (all 383 packages extracted and reverse-deps mapped), both workflows, run.sh, scripts/install-native-desktop.py, crates/relay-core/build.rs, deploy/* (2 systemd units, Dockerfile), plugins/*/plugin.json, relay-core hooks.rs, plugins.rs, skills.rs, providers.rs, provider_updates.rs, github.rs, handlers/provider.rs (to line 360 plus install/enable_everywhere), relay-remote wire.rs, bridge.rs, registry.rs (to line 200), direct.rs (to line 90), relay-cli blender.rs (to line 420). Read in part: main.rs (hooks, actor_from_env, serve), unreal.rs (constants, setup_check, RC ini, launch), unreal_process.rs launch, handlers/session.rs (launch, resume/wake, report), integration.rs, workspace.rs (clone), git.rs (registrations, commit, push), file.rs (registrations), guardrail.rs (header, write_roots, recoverable, git probes), socket.rs (bind, Client), paths.rs, store.rs (open), device.rs (mirror path, signing secrets), mirror.rs (push and launch args), BUS.md §0, §4, §9, D23/D132/D135/D147/D158-D160, MOBILE.md §1-2 and §6.

Search patterns: Command::new|output_with_timeout|\.output\(\); hasTrustDialog|dangerously|bypassPermissions|approve-for-me|sandbox|approval; curl|wget|https?://|download|clone; scrcpy-server|include_bytes|MIRROR_SERVER|configure_mirror_server; provider.update|auto_update; install_git|install_claude|install_codex|core.hooksPath|matcher|timeout; read_to_string|from_reader (repo-sourced config); provider_ref; register(_staged|_unlocked)?::<; protected_paths defaults; set_permissions|mode(0o; token in log macros; guardrail.violation|restore_head; autoexec|exec(|addon_utils (embedded Python).

External checks, read-only via WebFetch: rustsec.org advisory index (all of 2026 plus older pages, filtered to locked crates; only faster-hex 0.10.0 is flagged); Claude Code hooks reference (exact-list matcher semantics, timed-out hooks do not block); upstream scrcpy v4.1 doc/build.md (vendored jar SHA-256 matches); Epic URemoteControlSettings docs.

Checked and found no problem: the provider auto-update runs only `<installed binary> update`, and only for canonical, user-owned paths under ~/.local/share/claude/versions or ~/.codex/packages/standalone/releases; it is opt-in and Relay downloads nothing itself, leaving verification to the vendor's updater. build.rs bundles only the repo's own plugins/ into the binary; its digest is a freshness stamp, not integrity. install-native-desktop.py: Exec quoting is fine, and desktop launchers do not use a shell. Blender runs `-b <file> --factory-startup`, so auto-run of scripts embedded in .blend files stays off, and Blender's Python is isolated. Plugins come only from the build, never from a project repo. Relay reads no engine config from repositories. Codex MCP config keys are validated. Signing secrets go through environment variables and secret-tool.

Not verified: Codex CLI internals (hook timeout semantics, whether its sandbox lets sandboxed commands connect to the Relay socket, exact clap handling of an injected `resume` argument). The Claude CLI behaviour for an injected `--resume` value is inferred from commander's documented handling of optional option arguments. Yanked status of locked crates was not checked (no network cargo). relay-native was not compiled. tunnel.rs, rendezvous.rs and pairlink.rs were only skimmed, and the native client's rendering of untrusted content was not reviewed. apps/relay-mobile is out of scope and was not examined.

findings.title: Agent-reported provider_ref goes unvalidated into the provider CLI's argv on resume, letting an agent inject CLI flags
findings.evidence: `let provider_ref = data.get("session_id").or_else(|| data.get("provider_ref")).and_then(Value::as_str);` is stored by `UPDATE sessions SET ... provider_ref=COALESCE(?2, provider_ref)` (1371-1373). There is no format check. `session.report` is AgentOnly with `data: Option<Value>` (relay-bus ops/session.rs:149-151). It is in the default builder, reviewer and docs allowlists (handlers/settings.rs:36-38) and only needs the caller's own session (`assert_own`, 1351). Agents also get it as the `session_report` MCP tool. On resume or wake the stored string becomes an argv element: Claude gets `args.extend(["--resume".into(), reference.to_string()])` (providers.rs:185), and Codex gets `args.push(reference.to_string())` as the trailing positional after `--config developer_instructions=…` (providers.rs:229). The PTY spawn uses no shell, so a value starting with `--` is parsed by the provider CLI as an option. Resume and wake happen in normal use: `session.resume` and `session.wake` (session.rs:944, 1000), and `task.dispatch` starts `session.wake`/`session.resume` on its own for a parked or restorable session (task.rs:695-696).
findings.impact: A prompt-injected agent calls `session.report {kind:"session_start", data:{provider_ref:"--config=sandbox_mode=\"danger-full-access\""}}`. Relay already passes `--config` to `codex resume`, so clap accepts the `--config=` form. Other values work too, such as `--dangerously-skip-permissions`, or Claude's `--settings=/tmp/x.json` pointing at a file with `{"disableAllHooks":true}` (/tmp is always an allowed write root, guardrail.rs:617). The next resume, wake or dispatch then starts the provider without Codex's workspace-write sandbox (which D135 relies on), or without Relay's PreToolUse guardrail and Claude's permission prompts. A confused-deputy variant sets another session's id, so the resume opens that session's conversation.
findings.fix: Validate provider_ref when it is written. Provider session ids are UUID-like, so accept only `[0-9A-Za-z-]` with no leading `-`, and refuse anything else in session.report. Pass the value in a form that cannot be read as an option (`--resume=<id>`; put `--` before Codex's positional). Prefer taking provider_ref only from the provider-hook payload shape (claude-report/codex-report), not from arbitrary `data.provider_ref`.

v1.reason: Verified. session.report reads `data.session_id` or `data.provider_ref` with no format check (handlers/session.rs:1358) and stores it via `provider_ref=COALESCE(?2, provider_ref)` (1371-1373). The only check is assert_own (1351), and session.report is in the default builder, reviewer and docs allowlists (settings.rs:36-38). On resume or wake, stage_launch passes row.session.provider_ref (session.rs:533-538) into Driver::args. Claude gets `["--resume", reference]` (providers.rs:185); Codex gets the reference as a bare trailing positional (providers.rs:228-230). There is no `--` separator and no `--resume=` form, and the PTY spawn uses no shell. Claude's `--resume` takes an optional value, so the CLI parser (commander) reads a following `--flag` as an option rather than the value. Codex's clap parses a leading `--` token as a flag. Wake and resume happen in normal use: idle parking (parking.idle_minutes 30) followed by session.wake (session.rs:1000), session.resume (944), and task.dispatch. So a prompt-injected agent can plant flags such as a second `--settings=/tmp/x.json` (last one wins, which drops Relay's hook settings), `--dangerously-skip-permissions`, or Codex's `--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox` / `--config=sandbox_mode=...`. They take effect on its next launch.
v1.correction: Severity is high rather than critical. It needs an already compromised agent and waits for a park/wake or resume, and the system already accepts that same-uid agents have other imperfect escape routes (BUS.md §14; guardrail.rs:849). Still, this is a clean argv injection through a typed op, and it defeats the provider sandbox and Relay's hooks for that session, so it should be fixed. I could not run the provider CLIs to confirm how each flag is parsed; that relies on commander's and clap's documented behaviour. Fix as proposed: reject provider_ref values that are not `[0-9A-Za-z_-]` or that start with '-' in session.report, emit `--resume=<id>` for Claude, and put `--` before Codex's positional.

v2.reason:
(a) The code does what the finding says. session.report reads data.session_id or data.provider_ref with no format check (crates/relay-core/src/handlers/session.rs:1358) and stores it with `provider_ref=COALESCE(?2, provider_ref)` (1371-1373). The only gate is assert_own (159-180), which limits the call to the caller's own row. The op is AgentOnly and in all three default role allowlists (handlers/settings.rs:36-38). The relay MCP server forwards any tool arguments unchanged (crates/relay-cli/src/mcp.rs:147). On a LaunchKind::Resume launch, prepare_launch hands the stored value to Driver::args (session.rs:527-539). Claude gets it as the element after `--resume` (providers.rs:185); Codex gets it as a bare positional (providers.rs:228-230). There is no `--` and no `=` form. Pty::spawn passes the args with no shell (pty.rs:172-173), so this is option injection, not shell injection. Relay itself depends on both CLIs reading options after this slot: Claude's `--model`/`--effort` follow the value, and for Codex prepare_launch appends `--config` notify, plugin MCP configs and `--add-dir` after the positional (session.rs:541-558). So for Codex, a value starting with '-' is read as an option rather than an id; Relay's own working argv shows this. For Claude it depends on commander's optional-value rules, which I could not run.

(b) Reachability. Only the agent can trigger this, and only on purpose (prompt-injected or hostile). Benign values come from provider hooks. Two facts narrow it, and both earlier reviews missed them. First, nothing parks sessions automatically: `parking.idle_minutes` is never read by the engine; it appears only in settings.rs:44 and the native settings page. The real Resume launches are an app restart (Engine::shutdown marks live sessions restorable, engine.rs:632-679) followed by session.resume or task.dispatch, and a manual Park followed by Wake. Both are common. Second, the provider's own hooks keep overwriting the value. install_claude registers PostToolUse with no matcher, so it fires for MCP tools too, plus Stop (hooks.rs:352-373). install_codex does the same (hooks.rs:525-541). Both forward the hook JSON unchanged (relay-cli main.rs:490-497), and its `session_id` replaces the stored value. A value planted through an ordinary tool call is therefore reset by that call's own PostToolUse report or by the turn's Stop. It survives only if it is written after the last hook, or if the process is killed before the next report (for example, the app is quit mid-turn). For Codex I could not confirm from the repo that its hooks fire on MCP calls or carry session_id on every event.

(c) Effect when it fires. The next resumed launch silently runs with options the agent chose: no hold is raised, and the value shows only as provider_ref in session.get. For Codex this can remove the workspace-write sandbox that D135 says every resumed session keeps. That sandbox is a real OS boundary, and the agent reaches it through the MCP server process, which runs outside the sandbox. For Claude, Relay already leaves the provider's in-worktree hook/settings file writable (protected_paths defaults to []; install_claude merges and keeps other keys). BUS.md §0.6, §9.5 and §14 also say guardrails are seatbelts, not a boundary against a hostile same-uid process. So the new exposure is mainly the Codex sandbox. The confused-deputy variant (pointing at another conversation's id) matters little given same-user trust.

(d) Severity is high, not critical. It needs a deliberate, Relay-aware agent and careful timing. It is still a silent bypass of a provider sandbox that the design promises on resume, through an op every role is granted.

(e) Fix: see correction.
v2.correction:
Severity: high, not critical. Trigger: there is no automatic idle parking, because parking.idle_minutes is never read by the engine. Resume happens after an app restart (Resume or task.dispatch) or after a manual Park and Wake. Exploitation is harder than described: every later Claude PostToolUse/Stop hook report (and probably Codex's) overwrites provider_ref with the real session_id. A planted value only lasts if it is written after the last hook or if the session is killed before the next one. The impact is mostly the Codex sandbox, since Relay already leaves the Claude settings/hook file in the worktree unprotected and documents guardrails as seatbelts (BUS.md §0.6).

Fix corrections:
(1) Validate in two places. Reject in session.report anything empty, overlong, starting with '-', or outside a conservative id charset. Also check again at launch, in prepare_launch or Driver::args, because rows written before the fix may already hold a bad value. When the value is bad, fall back to --continue / --last, or refuse.
(2) For Claude, emit `--resume=<id>`.
(3) For Codex, putting `--` before the positional inside Driver::args, as proposed, would break every Codex resume. prepare_launch appends `--config` notify, plugin MCP `--config`s and `--add-dir` after Driver::args returns (session.rs:541-558), and after a `--` clap would read those as extra positionals. The `--` and the id must come last, after all options, or rely on strict validation alone.
(4) Taking provider_ref only from the hook payload shape does not help. At the bus, hook calls and agent calls look the same: same session token, the hook forwards stdin JSON unchanged, and the MCP server forwards any arguments.
(5) Update the argv tests in providers.rs:402-410.

findings.title: integration.request lets any builder agent have the engine run its branch's build outside any sandbox, with user-level bus rights
findings.evidence: `integration.request` is in the default builder allowlist (handlers/settings.rs:36; BUS.md:464). It accepts any two refs the agent names (lines 18-30) and `build` defaults to true (`p.build.unwrap_or(true)`, line 32). After commit, `run()` merges the branches into `.relay/integrations/<id>` and executes `shell(&path, command, None)` (165), which is `Command::new("fish")…args(["-lc", command])` … `cmd.output()` (229-234). That process inherits the engine's environment, with no RELAY_SESSION or RELAY_TOKEN and no timeout. `deploy` (207) runs the user's `run_cmd` with an agent-chosen `RELAY_DEVICE`, without the device lease that the user-only `device.*` ops take. The CLI falls back to actor `user` when RELAY_SESSION is absent (crates/relay-cli/src/main.rs:129), and BUS.md §4.2 says `user` needs no token.
findings.impact: An agent (prompt-injected, or a Codex agent inside its workspace-write sandbox) commits a malicious build step on its branch, such as Cargo build.rs, an npm prebuild or a Gradle task. It then calls `integration.request {branches:["main","relay/<self>"]}`. Relay runs that code as the user, with network and full filesystem, outside the provider sandbox and without any Claude permission prompt or exec gate. Any `relay cmd …` the build runs is actor `user`, so it can approve its own guardrail requests, change settings, or type into other sessions. A build that hangs pins the thread forever, and the hard-coded `fish` fails on machines without it.
findings.fix: Require user confirmation (a hold) before building or deploying an agent-requested integration, or make build and deploy user-only. Run the build with the requesting session's RELAY_SESSION/RELAY_TOKEN so its bus calls stay agent-scoped. Use proc::output_with_timeout and `sh -c` (or $SHELL) instead of `fish -lc`. Take the device lease for deploy.

v1.reason: The code matches. integration.request is in the default builder allowlist (settings.rs:36; BUS.md table at ~464 lists it for builder from SPEC's agent action list). The handler takes agent-named branches or sessions, `build` defaults to true (integration.rs:32), and `deploy` is an agent-chosen Option<String> (relay-bus ops/git.rs:137). run() merges the branches and executes project.build_cmd through shell() = Command::new("fish").args(["-lc", command]) ... cmd.output() (integration.rs:165, 228-234). That inherits the engine's environment, has no timeout and runs in no sandbox. Deploy sets RELAY_DEVICE to the agent's string and runs run_cmd (integration.rs:207) without taking a device lease. So for a Codex agent, code committed on its branch (build.rs, an npm/gradle task) runs outside Codex's workspace-write sandbox, which D135 says is kept.
v1.correction: Severity is medium, not high. Building agent code is the op's documented purpose (BUS.md builder row; D38), and the command is the user's own build_cmd. For Claude agents there is little extra power: they can already run `cargo build` themselves, and Relay's guardrail only inspects command lines, not what build.rs does. The real extra power is escaping the Codex OS sandbox and the agent-chosen deploy device with no lease. The claim that 'bus calls run as user' is the documented same-uid trade-off (BUS.md §4.2, §14: 'Tokens prevent misattribution, not determined impersonation'; guardrail.rs:849-850 calls the identity-shedding check best effort), so it adds no new capability. The missing timeout runs on a detached thread, not under the store lock: a hung build leaves the integration stuck in Building and leaks the process, but the bus stays responsive. Fix: put the agent-requested build/deploy behind a user hold (or make build/deploy user-confirmed), export the requester's RELAY_SESSION/RELAY_TOKEN, use proc::output_with_timeout, take the device lease for deploy, and do not hard-code fish.

findings.title: PreToolUse matchers list tool names exactly, so plugin MCP tools (blender_python, ue_python, …) and NotebookEdit never reach guardrail.gate
findings.evidence: Claude gets `"matcher": "Edit|Write|MultiEdit|Bash"` (350) and Codex gets `"Bash|apply_patch|Edit|Write"` (517). The Claude Code hooks docs say a matcher made only of letters and `|` is evaluated as a list of exact tool names. So `NotebookEdit` and every `mcp__<server>__<tool>` call never run `relay hook claude-pre-tool`. Plugins add exactly such tools: `plugins::mcp_servers` (plugins.rs:278-299) is merged into `.relay/relay.mcp.json` (hooks.rs:417-444) and into Codex `--config mcp_servers.*` (session.rs:546-548). `blender_python` runs arbitrary bpy/Python and can `save` or `save_as` .blend files (relay-cli/src/blender.rs:109-118, 197-208). `blender_export` writes an FBX path (233-238). `ue_python`, `ue_console` and `ue_call` run arbitrary editor Python and commands (relay-cli/src/unreal.rs:33-38, 340-389). These servers run independently of the bus (D159) and never call guardrail.gate.
findings.impact: With the Unreal or Blender plugin on, protected paths, write roots, destructive-write holds and denied commands silently stop applying to those tools. For example, with `Content/**` or `*.blend` protected, `blender_python {file:"Hero.blend", save:true}` or an asset save through `ue_python` overwrites the file with no hold, and Python's os/subprocess runs any command without the exec gate. The plugin's own standing rule tells agents that Relay's guardrail holds large rewrites (plugins/unreal-engine/instructions.md:16), which is not true for these tools. NotebookEdit writes to .ipynb files are ungated the same way.
findings.fix: Use a match-all matcher (`"*"`) and let the adapter allow read-only tools and fail closed on unknown ones (`claude_pre_tool` already exits 2 on an unsupported tool). Alternatively, add `NotebookEdit` and a regex such as `mcp__(blender|unreal)__.*` with a mapping to gate kinds. Or have the plugin MCP servers call guardrail.gate themselves, using the RELAY_SESSION/RELAY_TOKEN they inherit, before mutating tools.

v1.reason: hooks.rs:350 installs matcher "Edit|Write|MultiEdit|Bash" and hooks.rs:517 installs "Bash|apply_patch|Edit|Write". The current Claude Code hooks reference says a matcher containing only letters, digits, _, -, space, comma and | is compared as a list of exact names, and gives `mcp__memory` matching no tool as its example. So NotebookEdit and every mcp__<plugin>__* tool never run `hook claude-pre-tool`. Neither blender.rs nor unreal.rs contains the word guardrail, so these servers never gate themselves either. The adapter would fail closed if it ever saw such a tool: claude_pre_tool bails on an unsupported tool and the dispatcher at main.rs:349-357 turns any error into exit 2. That confirms a match-all matcher is a safe fix. The plugin's standing rule (instructions.md:14) tells agents that Relay's guardrail holds large rewrites, which is untrue for ue_python and blender_python.
v1.correction: Lower the severity to medium. BUS.md:29-31 says guardrails are "seatbelts, not sandboxes": they stop agent mistakes and are not a security boundary. The Bash gate is already only a denylist (evaluate_exec, guardrail.rs:811), so `python3 -c`, `cp` or `sed -i` can write a protected path through Bash anyway. Two things limit the impact. Claude still asks for permission on MCP tools unless the user has allowed them. And the destructive-write line counting has no meaning for binary .uasset or .blend files. The real cost: a protected_paths entry, write roots and the self-approval check do not cover the normal channel for editing binary assets or notebooks, so an honest mistake there is not caught. Fix: use matcher "*" (or a regex such as `^(Edit|Write|MultiEdit|Bash|NotebookEdit)$|^mcp__`) and have the adapter allow read-only or known-safe tools explicitly and fail closed on anything else. Mutating plugin tools could also call guardrail.gate themselves.

findings.title: The 30-second PreToolUse hook timeout lets the tool call proceed, and the adapter has no deadline of its own while guardrail.gate waits for the store mutex
findings.evidence: The hook is `{"type": "command", "command": command, "timeout": 30}` (351; Codex at 521). Claude Code's hooks reference says a timed-out command hook "doesn't block the tool call". `claude_pre_tool` connects and calls `client.call(&request, …)` with no timeout (relay-cli/src/main.rs:465-471), and `Client::call` loops on `next()` without one (socket.rs:801-818). `guardrail.gate` is a locked handler (handlers/guardrail.rs:304), so it waits behind any open transaction. Long transactions occur in normal flows. `project.clone` runs a network `git clone` inside its transaction (handlers/workspace.rs:228-235). `git.stage` and `file.restore_head` run git add/checkout (with LFS filters) under the lock with no deadline (git.rs:490-503, file.rs:253-256). `git.commit`'s finish phase runs `git commit` under the lock (git.rs:571), which waits on GPG pinentry when signing is on. Each gate can also spend up to 10 s per git probe (guardrail.rs:670-680, 1120). D23 (DECISIONS.md:75-79) states that adapter or infrastructure failures block instead of failing open.
findings.impact: Whenever any such operation holds the store for more than 30 s, Claude kills each agent's Bash/Write/Edit hook at 30 s and runs the tool anyway. Denied commands (`rm -rf`, `git reset --hard`, `git push --force`), protected paths and destructive-write holds are skipped without any message for as long as the bus is busy. Many agents queueing behind one slow gate in a large LFS repo is enough to trigger it.
findings.fix: Wrap connect and call in an internal deadline below the hook timeout (for example, tokio::time::timeout of 20 s) that prints 'RELAY guardrail unavailable' and exits 2. Raise the configured hook timeout (Claude's default is 600 s) so Relay's own deadline decides, not Claude's kill. Keep slow subprocesses out of locked handlers (see the git-subprocess finding).

v1.reason: hooks.rs:351 and hooks.rs:521 set `"timeout": 30`. The Claude Code hooks reference states that a timed-out command hook on PreToolUse "doesn't block the tool call. The call continues through the normal permission flow". The default timeout is 600 s. The adapter has no deadline of its own: claude_pre_tool connects and calls client.call with no timeout (main.rs:465-471), and Client::call loops on next() indefinitely (socket.rs:801-818). So a guardrail.gate stuck behind the store mutex for more than 30 s fails open, contradicting D23 ("adapter/infrastructure failures block instead of failing open"). Long locked holders exist. project.clone is registered with e.register and runs `git clone` with plain .output() and no timeout inside the transaction (workspace.rs:228-235). git.stage runs worktree::git_mutate (plain Command::output, worktree.rs:26-33) under the lock. git.commit's locked finish phase runs `git commit` with no deadline (git.rs:571), which waits on pinentry if signing is on. Each queued gate can also spend up to 10 s per git probe (guardrail.rs:1120), so several agents queuing behind each other can add up.
v1.correction: Lower the severity to medium. The trigger needs the store to be held for more than 30 s, which is itself a separate bus-freeze bug and uncommon in normal use. The tool also falls through to Claude's own permission flow rather than running completely unchecked; it is only auto-allowed where the user's Claude permissions already allow it. Fix as proposed: wrap connect and call in an internal tokio timeout well below the hook timeout that prints 'RELAY guardrail unavailable' and exits 2, and raise the configured hook timeout (or omit it to get 600 s) so Relay's own deadline decides. Codex has the same issue at hooks.rs:521.

findings.title: Files that Relay generates and the provider executes or trusts sit unprotected in the agent-writable worktree: the statusline script, and settings.local.json hooks checked by substring
findings.evidence: `install_claude` writes `<worktree>/.relay/agent-statusline.sh` with mode 0755 and points `.relay/relay.settings.json` `statusLine.command` at that absolute path (384-399). Claude runs that command on every status-line refresh. Guardrail hooks go into `<worktree>/.claude/settings.local.json`. On every launch Relay treats them as installed if any PreToolUse handler's command merely `contains(CLAUDE_PRE_TOOL)` (333-341). The matcher is never compared, and keys such as `disableAllHooks` are left untouched. Codex uses the same substring check (512-514). Default guardrail `protected_paths` is `[]` (handlers/settings.rs:31), and `relative_path`/`write_target` (guardrail.rs:623, 1135) accept `.relay/…` and `.claude/…`, so the agent's own Write/Edit of these files is allowed.
findings.impact: An agent whose file edits are auto-approved (Claude's acceptEdits mode) can rewrite `.relay/agent-statusline.sh`, and Claude then runs that code on the next refresh: arbitrary commands with no Bash permission prompt and no exec gate. Editing `.claude/settings.local.json` (setting the guardrail matcher to something that never matches, or adding `"disableAllHooks": true`) takes effect at the next resume or wake. Relay's reinstall check keeps the tampered entry, so that session runs without guardrails from then on.
findings.fix: Generate per-session provider config outside the worktree, for example `<data dir>/sessions/<name>/{settings.json,mcp.json,statusline.sh}` passed by absolute path. Claude's `--settings` can carry the hooks as well as the statusLine, and the write-root check already refuses writes there. If anything must stay in the worktree, protect `.relay/**`, `.claude/settings*.json` and `.codex/hooks.json` by default, and on each launch rewrite Relay's entries exactly (matcher and command) and remove `disableAllHooks`.

v1.reason: Each claim matches the code. install_claude writes .relay/agent-statusline.sh with mode 0755 inside the worktree and points statusLine.command at it (hooks.rs:384-399), so Claude runs it automatically. already_installed checks only `command.contains(CLAUDE_PRE_TOOL)` (hooks.rs:333-341) and never compares the matcher or removes a `disableAllHooks` key; Codex does the same at 512-514. Default protected_paths is [] (settings.rs:31), and guardrail.rs has no hard-coded protection for .relay/ or .claude/, so an agent's Write to these files passes the gate as an InWorktree path. Claude's hooks docs say edits to hooks in settings files are picked up by the file watcher, so tampering with settings.local.json can take effect immediately, not only at the next launch. In acceptEdits mode, an edit to the statusline script turns into command execution with no Bash prompt.
v1.correction: This only matters for a hostile or prompt-injected agent. BUS.md:29-31 says guardrails are seatbelts against mistakes and not a boundary against a hostile same-uid process. The statusline route mainly weakens Claude's own edit-versus-exec permission split rather than Relay's guardrail, and acceptEdits already opens many indirect execution routes (build scripts, tests). I could not establish whether current Claude Code itself requires approval for writes to .claude/settings*.json even in acceptEdits, which would close that half. The statusline script and relay.mcp.json are rewritten on every launch, so tampering with them lasts only for the live session, while a tampered settings.local.json matcher persists because of the substring check. Rated medium. Best fix: keep the generated statusline script and settings outside the worktree (data dir) and pass them by absolute path through --settings. On each launch, rewrite Relay's PreToolUse entry exactly (matcher and command) and strip disableAllHooks.

findings.title: Network git clone and other git subprocesses run with no deadline inside store-locked handlers; project.clone holds the mutex for the whole clone
findings.evidence: `e.register::<ProjectClone>` (228) runs `Command::new("git").current_dir(&workspace.path).arg("clone").arg("--").arg(&p.url).arg(&destination).output()` (234). That is a network clone inside the transaction, with no timeout. The native client gives this op 1800 s (apps/relay-native/src/client.rs:67), and onboarding uses it for GitHub repos (onboarding.rs:527). `worktree::git` (worktree.rs:26-32) calls `.output()` with no deadline and backs `git_mutate`, which locked handlers use: `git.stage`'s `git add` (git.rs:490-503), `git.unstage` (507-527), `file.restore_head`'s `git checkout --` (file.rs:253-256), branch create/delete (git.rs:374, 485), and `git.commit`'s finish-phase `git commit` (git.rs:571). Other calls are unlocked but unbounded: the skill clone (github.rs:105-110), `gh api` (github.rs:45, 68-70) and `git push` (git.rs:617). CLAUDE.md requires every subprocess forked from a handler to go through proc::output_with_timeout, and slow work must stay off the store mutex.
findings.impact: Cloning a large or LFS-heavy repository, staging large LFS assets (the clean filter hashes them), restoring an LFS file (smudge downloads it), or committing with GPG signing (pinentry waits for the passphrase) freezes every other bus request for as long as git runs. That includes the UI, MCP calls and agents' guardrail gates, which then fail open (see the hook-timeout finding). A stalled network or an askpass dialog freezes it indefinitely. The client gives up after 30 minutes, but the engine keeps holding the lock.
findings.fix: Make project.clone a register_staged op: clone in prepare with proc::output_with_timeout and GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0, then run project.add in finish. Route worktree::git through output_with_timeout. Move git add, checkout and commit into staged prepare phases. Give skill clones and gh calls a deadline.

v1.reason: ProjectClone is registered with plain `e.register` (handlers/workspace.rs:228), so it runs inside the transaction with the store mutex held. It runs `Command::new("git")...arg("clone")...output()` (workspace.rs:234), a network clone of any size with no deadline and no GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0, then project.add. Every other bus request, including PTY-adjacent and guardrail ops, waits for the whole clone. That breaks both CLAUDE.md rules: slow work belongs in register_staged/register_unlocked, and handler subprocesses go through proc::output_with_timeout. worktree::git (worktree.rs:26-32) also uses bare .output(). It backs git_mutate in locked handlers: git.stage `git add` (git.rs:490-503), git.unstage (507-527), BranchCreate/BranchDelete (345, 445), file.restore_head, and CommitOp's finish phase `git commit --no-verify` (git.rs:571), which still runs under the lock and can block on GPG/pinentry signing.
v1.correction: The decisive part is project.clone, which is an unbounded network operation under the lock and is used in onboarding for GitHub repos. The locked git add/checkout/commit calls are usually fast and only become slow with LFS filters or commit signing, which is a secondary concern. CommitOp is already staged; only its `git commit` step remains locked, and the hooks run in prepare. The skill clone (github.rs:109) runs in a staged prepare phase and the gh calls are unlocked, so they only stall their own request; list them as missing timeouts, not lock holders. Fix: make project.clone register_staged, cloning in prepare via proc::output_with_timeout with GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0, and route worktree::git through output_with_timeout.

v2.reason:
(a) The code does what the finding says. `e.register::<ProjectClone>` (crates/relay-core/src/handlers/workspace.rs:228) is a plain locked handler: dispatch_inner takes `self.store.lock()` and opens the transaction (engine.rs:954-956) before calling it. Line 234 then runs `Command::new("git")...arg("clone").arg("--").arg(&p.url).arg(&destination).output()`, which has no deadline, does not set GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT and has no askpass control, then runs project.add through invoke_registered. This is not intended. The op's own metadata says "Clone a repo into the workspace and register it (async; project.changed when done)" (crates/relay-bus/src/ops/workspace.rs:38). BUS.md:247 lists project.clone among the ops that return a handle and complete asynchronously, like integration.request, which does run on an after_commit worker. D144 and D149 say slow work never runs under the mutex. The perf baseline calls the 263 ms local clone just "the work".

(b) The user reaches it in a normal flow. The sidebar "Add project…" item (apps/relay-native/src/shell/registry.rs:472) opens onboarding, and choosing a GitHub repo sends project.clone with its clone_url (onboarding.rs:527) over the shared UI connection. `relay cmd` can also send it. The op is UserOnly, so agents cannot trigger it. It runs once per project added from GitHub, and how long it takes depends on the repo. If git-lfs is installed, the checkout's smudge step downloads every LFS object inside the same `.output()` call, which takes minutes for an Unreal-style repo.

(c) For the whole clone, everything that needs the store lock waits:
- every locked handler and every `Unlocked::read` (engine.rs:173-187);
- every agent socket request, because `check_session_token` locks the store (engine.rs:1378). That covers MCP calls, `guardrail.gate` (a plain register, guardrail.rs:304) from each PreToolUse hook, and the pre-commit gate;
- session.create and the other lifecycle ops on their dedicated connection, and the phone door.

The native UI's main connection stalls completely, because socket.rs handle_conn awaits each `spawn_blocking(dispatch)` before reading the next line (socket.rs:334, 742). Every other UI call fails after 30 s with "Request timed out. Its outcome is unknown", and the queued requests all run when git exits.

Some things keep working: keystrokes, resize and mirror input use lock-free fast paths on per-terminal connections, and PTY output flows from a ring buffer. Nothing cancels the clone. The client's 1800 s timeout does not stop git, and LockSpan only logs.

The hold can become indefinite. With no prompt control, a credential request can wait forever: run.sh starts the engine with `nohup … &`, which keeps the launching terminal as its controlling tty, and a desktop SSH_ASKPASS dialog has the same effect. A stalled HTTPS transfer has no speed limit to end it.

The git_mutate sub-claims also hold. Stage (git.rs:490-503), Unstage (507-527), BranchCreate (345/374), BranchDelete (445/485) and RestoreHead (file.rs:252-256) are plain register handlers that call worktree::git's bare `.output()`. CommitOp's finish runs `git commit` under the lock (git.rs:571). These calls are fast in the common case and only slow with LFS clean/smudge filters, GPG pinentry, or a branch create whose start_point forces a checkout. That makes them secondary. The skill clone (staged prepare, provider.rs:211), the gh calls (register_unlocked) and git push (staged prepare) do not hold the lock. They only lack deadlines, so each stalls just its own request.

(d) High is correct. The rubric names "a freeze of the bus", and here it happens in a normal flow. It is not critical: git's own duration bounds the freeze, except in prompt or stall cases that depend on the environment, and terminals stay usable.

(e) The fix points the right way but is incomplete, and one part of it is wrong (see the correction).
v2.correction:
Claim corrections:
1. "Freezes every other bus request" overstates it. session.input and session.resize, device.mirror.input, PTY output, and queries that never take the lock (github.status, github.repo.list) keep working.
2. "Guardrail gates then fail open" cannot be established from this repo. The Relay hook fails closed (exits 2) on errors, but it has no deadline of its own. What happens is decided by how Claude Code and Codex handle their own 30 s hook timeout.

Fix corrections:
1. register_staged alone frees the store mutex but not the native UI. The prepare phase still runs inline in socket.rs's one-request-at-a-time connection loop, so the shared UI connection stays stalled for the whole clone. Also add project.clone to `is_lifecycle_request` so it gets its own connection, or make it the async op its metadata and BUS.md §5.1 describe: return at once, clone on an after_commit worker, emit project.changed, and write the `.completed` audit row.
2. Use a generous or stall-based deadline. The client already allows 1800 s, so a short output_with_timeout would kill large clones that are working fine. Combine a long deadline with `-c http.lowSpeedLimit=… -c http.lowSpeedTime=…`.
3. GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0 is not enough, because git tries GIT_ASKPASS and SSH_ASKPASS before it looks at that variable. Also neutralize askpass and use GIT_SSH_COMMAND='ssh -o BatchMode=yes'.
4. Remove the partial destination after a timeout kill. Otherwise every retry fails with project.clone_destination.
5. Do not move `git commit` into prepare. It must stay after `guardrail::enforce` in finish, which can create a hold that guardrail.confirm later replays through invoke_registered. Give it a deadline instead.
6. A blanket timeout inside worktree::git needs a deadline set per call. That helper also runs git push (LFS pre-push uploads), the integration merge and the device-sync fetch, which can rightly take minutes.

Related location to add: BranchCreate with a start_point runs a full `git switch -c` checkout under the lock (git.rs:345/374). It has the same root cause.

findings.title: run.sh opens the phone door on 0.0.0.0 at every launch; it is plain ws://, and after the one-time challenge any line is accepted as `user`
findings.evidence: run.sh:32 runs `nohup "$relay" --instance "$RELAY_INSTANCE" serve --remote` on every launch. `--remote-bind` defaults to `format!("0.0.0.0:{}", relay_remote::DEFAULT_PORT)` (relay-cli/src/main.rs:68), and deploy/relay-remote.service:9 does the same. The direct door upgrades raw TCP with `tokio_tungstenite::accept_async(stream)` (relay-remote/src/direct.rs:89), with no TLS. `bridge::run` authenticates once (`admit`; proof = sha256(challenge:token), wire.rs:71-73), then writes every later inbound line to the engine socket after checking only its `actor` field (bridge.rs:335-343, wire.rs:95-103). The pairing reply carries the 256-bit device token in clear (wire.rs:67-70). `GET /info` answers with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` (direct.rs:80). MOBILE.md §6 (lines 180-192) only considers passive proof replay.
findings.impact: An on-path attacker on the same Wi-Fi or LAN (ARP spoofing, rogue AP) can inject bus lines as `user` while the paired phone is connected. Examples are `session.input` keystrokes into an agent terminal, `settings.set` or `guardrail.confirm`, which give command execution on the PC. Passive capture reads all terminal output and file contents that reach the phone. Capturing one pairing yields the permanent device token. The listener is open on every desktop launch, including for people who never pair a phone, and any web page can read host, instance and `pairing_open` from /info.
findings.fix: Start the door from run.sh only when remote.json lists paired devices, or make it opt-in, and bind to the chosen interface. Add transport integrity: TLS with a self-signed certificate whose fingerprint is carried in the pairing QR, or a session key derived from the challenge and token with a MAC and counter on every line. Drop the wildcard CORS header.

v1.reason: I verified each part. run.sh:32 starts `serve --remote` on every launch where no engine is running. relay-cli main.rs:68 defaults `remote_bind` to `0.0.0.0:<DEFAULT_PORT>`, and `serve_with_door` (relay-cli remote.rs:88-113) binds it unconditionally, whether or not any device is paired. direct.rs:89 runs `tokio_tungstenite::accept_async` on raw TCP, so there is no TLS. bridge.rs:112-153 authenticates once through `admit` (proof = sha256(challenge:token), wire.rs:71-73). After that, bridge.rs:173-187 forwards every inbound line to the engine socket, and the only check is `wire::gate` (wire.rs:95-116), which looks at nothing but the `actor` string. No per-message integrity or session key is derived. `Welcome::paired` (wire.rs:56-58, bridge.rs:79) sends the permanent 256-bit token in clear. direct.rs:80 sends `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` on /info. MOBILE.md §6 (lines 180-187) addresses passive proof replay and accepts the cleartext pairing reply on a LAN, but does not address active injection or hijacking after authentication. Exploitation needs a paired phone and either an on-path attacker during a live session or a passive capture of the pairing exchange; with that, the attacker can send `user` envelopes (settings, guardrail.confirm, session.input), which amounts to code execution as the user. The pairing code (32^8, 10-minute single window, registry.rs:105-116,193-198) is not practical to brute-force, so an unpaired install exposes only /info. That precondition keeps this at high rather than critical.
v1.correction: The bridge line numbers are wrong: bridge.rs has 246 lines, and the post-admit forwarding loop is at bridge.rs:173-187 (gate call at :177), not :335-343. The /info CORS leak is minor: it exposes host name, host_id, instance, version and pairing_open. Highest-value fixes, in order: (1) do not open the door from run.sh/`serve --remote` unless remote.json has paired devices or the user opted in, and bind to a chosen interface; (2) protect the transport by deriving a per-connection key from challenge+token and MACing each line with a counter, or use TLS pinned through the pairing QR; (3) drop the wildcard CORS.

v2.reason:
(a) The code does what the finding claims. I checked it myself.
- **Launch.** run.sh:28-32 starts `relay serve --remote` whenever no engine answers ping. The desktop entry also goes through run.sh (scripts/install-native-desktop.py:22), so every launch that starts an engine opens the door. The engine outlives the window, so the door stays open while it runs.
- **Bind.** main.rs:68 defaults --remote-bind to 0.0.0.0:7420. serve_with_door (relay-cli/src/remote.rs:107) binds it whether or not remote.json lists any device.
- **No TLS.** direct.rs:89 runs accept_async on a raw TcpStream, and pairlink.rs:36 puts plain `ws://ip:port` URLs in the QR.
- **No integrity after login.** After `admit`, bridge.rs:173-187 writes every inbound line to the engine socket. The only check is wire::gate (wire.rs:95-116), which looks only at the `actor` string. There is no session key, MAC or counter tying later lines to the token.
- **What `user` can do.** The engine accepts `user` with no token (engine.rs:1355, BUS.md §4.2). `user` may call guardrail.config.set, guardrail.confirm, session.create/spawn with any prompt, and session.input (ops/guardrail.rs:38,58; ops/session.rs:17,25,156). For `user`, refuse_or_user_hold (guardrail.rs:1028) turns a guardrail refusal into a hold that `user` can confirm.
- **Token in clear.** Welcome::paired (wire.rs:56, bridge.rs:79) sends the 256-bit token in clear.
- **Not a documented, harmless choice.** No DECISIONS entry covers this. MOBILE.md §6 calls the LAN route private and says passive listening "yields proofs that are only good for that connection" (lines 186-187). In fact every later line, terminal (PTY) output included, crosses the network in cleartext.

(b) Who can trigger it, and how often:
- **Attacker.** Someone on the same local network who can listen to or sit in the path of traffic: ARP spoofing, a rogue access point, a compromised router, open WiFi, or another member of a WPA2-PSK network. Off-the-shelf tools do this.
- **Timing.** The attacker needs either a live phone connection over the LAN route or one pairing exchange. The app keeps the link open and reconnects whenever it comes to the foreground (MOBILE.md:160-162, 173-174).
- **Not just any peer.** A peer that can only connect gets nothing. A pairing code is one of 32^8 values and lives 10 minutes (registry.rs:104-117, 193-202), and tokens are 256-bit. An install that was never paired exposes only the greeting and /info.
- **This user is exposed.** The author pairs a phone (MOBILE.md §1). The pairing link lists LAN addresses before the Tailscale one (direct.rs:149), so pairing at home normally uses the plaintext route.

(c) What happens when it fires:
- **Active.** The attacker relays the challenge and the proof, then injects `user` lines and filters the replies. That is code execution as the user: spawn an agent with any prompt, relax guardrails, confirm holds, and type into agent terminals, including the providers' own y/n prompts.
- **Indistinguishable.** The engine cannot tell these lines from the user's, so the audit log blames the user.
- **Passive.** A listener reads all terminal output and diffs.
- **Persistent.** One captured pairing gives a credential that works from the LAN until someone revokes it by hand.

(d) High is the right severity. The impact is code execution, and the challenge-response is a safety check an on-path attacker silently bypasses. It is not critical: it needs a privileged network position plus a connected or pairing phone, and a peer with ordinary connectivity cannot get in.

(e) The fix is partly incomplete; see correction.
v2.correction:
**Locations.**
- The post-login forwarding loop is bridge.rs:172-188 (gate call at :177, write at :179-180), not :335-343.
- MOBILE.md §6 is lines 178-195.
- "At every launch" should read "at every launch that starts the engine (run.sh:28); the door then stays open while the engine runs". This also covers menu launches (scripts/install-native-desktop.py:22).
- Related locations to add: `relay remote serve` defaults to 0.0.0.0 (relay-cli/src/remote.rs:22), and pairlink.rs:36 hard-codes ws://.

**The proposed fix, part by part.**
1. *Start the door only when remote.json lists devices, or make it opt-in.* This protects only users who never paired, and the paired user is the one exposed. It also breaks the documented first-pairing flow (MOBILE.md §1: run.sh, then `relay remote pair`), because nothing would be listening. That flow would have to become `relay remote serve --pair`, and MOBILE.md §1 and §2 would need updating.
2. *TLS with a self-signed certificate whose fingerprint is in the QR.* This is the complete option: it protects the pairing token, keeps traffic private and stops injection. But the phone uses React Native's built-in WebSocket (apps/relay-mobile/lib/engine/Relay/RelayClient.ts:207), which cannot pin a self-signed certificate without a native module. Agent sessions cannot build or run Android (CLAUDE.md).
3. *A key derived from challenge and token, with a MAC and counter per line.* This stops injection only.
   - It leaves the token in cleartext in the pairing reply, so whoever sniffs the pairing can derive every later key.
   - It leaves all content readable.
   - To be complete it needs a high-entropy secret carried in the QR (or a PAKE) to protect the pairing reply, encryption (AEAD) rather than a MAC alone, MACs in both directions, and a phone-chosen nonce in the key derivation.
4. *Drop the wildcard CORS header.* This is safe. Only relay-remote/tests/remote.rs:205 reads /info, and it does not check the header; the phone app never fetches /info. But the WebSocket greeting (bridge.rs:98-108) gives the same host, host_id, instance and version to any web page that opens ws://127.0.0.1:7420, because accept_async does not check the Origin header. An Origin check on the WebSocket upgrade closes both leaks. The data leaked is low-value.

The fix should also correct the docs that describe the LAN route as private: MOBILE.md:186-187, direct.rs:2, relay-remote/src/lib.rs:7, and BUS.md §14 ("No RPC over the network").

**A separate problem that deserves its own entry.** It has a different cause from this finding.
- direct.rs:76 (`stream.peek`) and direct.rs:89 (`accept_async`) have no timeout; HELLO_TIMEOUT (bridge.rs:39) only starts after the WebSocket upgrade.
- The accept loop (direct.rs:37-54) has no connection cap.
- A grep found no raise of the open-file limit (RLIMIT_NOFILE) anywhere.
- Under `serve --remote` the door runs inside the engine process.
- So an unpaired LAN peer that holds about 1,000 idle TCP connections can plausibly use up the engine's file descriptors. The local socket would then refuse new connections, breaking the desktop app, the CLI and the agent hooks; the hooks fail closed, so agents' tool calls would be blocked.
- I did not check the session's actual file-descriptor limit.

findings.title: The fallback runtime dir under /tmp has a predictable name and its owner is never checked; the lock file is opened through symlinks and then truncated
findings.evidence: Without XDG_RUNTIME_DIR, `runtime_dir()` is `std::env::temp_dir().join(format!("relay-v4-{uid}"))`/relay-v4 (paths.rs:67-75). `start_in` calls `create_dir_all(&dir)`, then `let _ = std::fs::set_permissions(&dir, 0o700)` with the error ignored (socket.rs:55-56). It opens `<dir>/<instance>.lock` with `read(true).write(true).create(true)` and no O_NOFOLLOW (60-66). After taking the flock it runs `l.set_len(0)` and writes its PID (93-98). Clients connect to `<dir>/<instance>.sock` without checking who owns it (relay-cli/src/main.rs:195-198).
findings.impact: On a multi-user host where Relay runs without XDG_RUNTIME_DIR (su or sudo shells, cron, some SSH or container setups), another local user pre-creates `/tmp/relay-v4-<uid>/relay-v4/` and plants `dev.lock -> ~/.bashrc` (or the store). The victim's `relay serve` then truncates that file and overwrites it with a PID. Alternatively the attacker swaps in their own `dev.sock`, so the CLI, hooks and agents talk to an impostor engine that answers every guardrail.gate with ok and collects session tokens.
findings.fix: Create the fallback directory with DirBuilder mode 0700, then lstat it and refuse to continue unless it is owned by the current uid, is not a symlink and has mode 0700. Open the lock with O_NOFOLLOW. Have clients check the socket owner's uid (or SO_PEERCRED) before connecting.

v1.reason: Without XDG_RUNTIME_DIR, runtime_dir() is temp_dir()/relay-v4-<uid>/relay-v4 (paths.rs:67-75). start_in calls create_dir_all, which succeeds when another user already created the directories, and then ignores the result of set_permissions(0o700) (socket.rs:55-56). That chmod fails when the attacker owns the directory. The lock file is opened read/write/create with no O_NOFOLLOW (socket.rs:60-66). After flock it is truncated with set_len(0) and the PID is written (socket.rs:93-98). The planted symlink sits in the attacker-owned, non-sticky subdirectory, not directly in sticky /tmp, so fs.protected_symlinks does not stop the victim from following it. A symlinked dev.lock therefore truncates the target file (data loss). Because the attacker owns the directory, they can also swap dev.sock after the bind. Clients connect by path with no owner or peer-credential check (main.rs:195-198), so they would talk to an impostor engine.
v1.correction: Keep the severity at medium. It is a local-user attack, but it only applies on a multi-user host where Relay's engine starts without XDG_RUNTIME_DIR. That is unusual for a desktop GTK app launched from a logged-in session. Fix as proposed: create the directory with DirBuilder mode 0700, then lstat both levels and refuse unless they are owned by the current uid, are not symlinks and have mode 0700. Open the lock with O_NOFOLLOW, and have clients check the socket owner's uid or SO_PEERCRED.

findings.title: ue_setup_check fix=true commits remote-code-execution settings into the project's tracked Config/DefaultRemoteControl.ini with no access restriction
findings.evidence: `RC_KEYS` sets bAutoStartWebServer=True, bEnableRemotePythonExecution=True, bAllowConsoleCommandRemoteExecution=True and bAllowAnyRemoteFunctionCall=True (675-680). `write_remote_control_ini` merges them into `Config/DefaultRemoteControl.ini` (702-711) whenever `fix` is true (1461). Nothing sets bRestrictServerAccess, AllowedOrigin or a passphrase, and Epic enforces the passphrase only for clients outside localhost. The skill tells agents to run `ue_setup_check {"fix": true}` (plugins/unreal-engine/skills/unreal-editor-automation/SKILL.md:26, 266-268). Config/ is tracked, since the plugin's gitignore template ignores only Binaries, Intermediate, Saved and DerivedDataCache. Epic's URemoteControlSettings docs say of bEnableRemotePythonExecution and bAllowAnyRemoteFunctionCall that "enabling this could open you up to vulnerabilities if an outside actor has access to your server".
findings.impact: Once an agent commits the file, every editor launch of the project, on the user's machine and on every teammate's, starts an unauthenticated HTTP endpoint on 127.0.0.1:30010 that runs arbitrary Python and console commands. Any local process or user can drive it. Localhost HTTP services without Host or Origin checks are a known DNS-rebinding target from web pages. The plugin's setup doc (docs/setup.md:52-55) only advises keeping it on localhost.
findings.fix: Do not write these keys into tracked Default*.ini. Pass them per launch (launch already adds -RCWebControlEnable; add -ini: overrides) or write them to the untracked Saved/Config per-user ini. If they must persist, also set bRestrictServerAccess with an AllowedOrigin and a passphrase, and have the human confirm.

v1.reason: The code matches the claim. RC_KEYS (unreal.rs:675-680) enables auto-start, remote Python, console commands and any remote function call. `write_remote_control_ini` (702-711) merges them into the project's tracked `Config/DefaultRemoteControl.ini` whenever `setup_check` runs with fix=true (unreal.rs:1461). No access-restriction or passphrase keys are written. This is the documented purpose of the bridge, though. The advice text (1487) and plugins/unreal-engine/docs/mcp-tools.md:19 both say what gets written. The bridge exists to run Python in the editor, and launch adds -RCWebControlEnable anyway. What is new is persistence in a committed Default*.ini, so every editor start of that project, including teammates' starts, auto-starts the unauthenticated endpoint. I could not establish the exploitation path. I did not verify the RC server's default bind address, or whether it checks Host or Origin, which DNS rebinding depends on. A local attacker already running as the user gains nothing new.
v1.correction: A better fix is to write these keys to the per-user `Saved/Config/<Platform>Editor/RemoteControl.ini` (untracked), the way write_editor_settings_ini already handles Saved/Config, or to pass them per launch. That keeps the bridge working without committing the settings for the whole team.

findings.title: The per-worktree core.hooksPath override silently turns off every git hook except pre-commit, including in the main checkout during primary-checkout sessions
findings.evidence: `install_git` creates `<repo>/.relay/hooks/<session>/` containing only `pre-commit` (100-148) and runs `git config --worktree core.hooksPath <that dir>` (150-154). Git then looks for every hook only in that directory. Only the previous pre-commit is chained (D23, DECISIONS.md:75-77). It is installed on every launch (session.rs:481), including sessions in the primary checkout. That is the Unreal plugin's default (`default_checkout: "primary"`, plugins/unreal-engine/plugin.json:55), and there the setting lands in `.git/config.worktree` for the user's own main checkout. Relay's `git.push` runs a plain `git push` in the checkout (git.rs:612-617).
findings.impact: In every Relay worktree, and in the main checkout while a primary-checkout session is alive, pre-push, commit-msg, prepare-commit-msg, post-checkout and post-merge hooks never run. That covers secret scanners, Gerrit Change-Id, commitlint, push test gates and Git LFS's hooks. In an LFS repository, unless git-lfs reinstalls its hooks into the Relay directory, a push can publish commits whose LFS objects were never uploaded, and teammates get missing-object errors.
findings.fix: Fill the Relay hook directory with forwarding stubs for every hook name, each exec'ing the same-named script in the previous hooks directory (already recorded in .relay-previous-hooks-path) when it is executable. At minimum, chain pre-push, commit-msg, prepare-commit-msg and the post-* hooks.

v1.reason: install_git creates `<repo>/.relay/hooks/<session>/` containing only `pre-commit`, which chains the previous pre-commit (hooks.rs:100-148). It then sets `git config --worktree core.hooksPath <dir>` (hooks.rs:150-154). With core.hooksPath pointing there, git finds no pre-push, commit-msg, prepare-commit-msg, post-checkout, post-merge or post-commit hooks. D23 (DECISIONS.md:75-80) documents chaining only the prior pre-commit and does not address the other hooks, so the gap is not a recorded, accepted decision. install_git runs on every launch (session.rs:481), and plugin default_checkout 'primary' (plugins/unreal-engine/plugin.json:18; plugins.rs:210-213) puts sessions in the main checkout, where `--worktree` lands in .git/config.worktree for the user's own checkout. git-lfs installs pre-push, post-checkout, post-commit and post-merge into .git/hooks, so pushes from these checkouts skip the LFS upload. Unreal repos commonly use LFS.
v1.correction: The plugin.json line is 18, not 55. The effect lasts until the session closes and uninstall_git restores the old setting, or longer if the engine dies first. The fix as proposed is right: write forwarding stubs for every standard hook name that exec the same-named script in the recorded previous hooks dir (.relay-previous-hooks-path) when it is executable.

findings.title: skill.install installs a GitHub repo's HEAD wholesale and publishes every SKILL.md folder, scripts included, machine-wide with no preview or pin; the subdir path follows repo symlinks
findings.evidence: `git clone --depth 1` of the default branch (or the URL's branch) runs with no commit pin and no timeout (github.rs:105-110). Every SKILL.md under the root or subdir is collected (158-170) and its whole folder staged, scripts included (177-189). `install_downloaded_skill` then calls `enable_everywhere`, which turns it on in every project when nobody had it (provider.rs:517-528, D147). `refresh_checkouts` writes it into every project root, every live worktree, and the user-level `~/.claude/skills` and `$CODEX_HOME/skills` (skills.rs:175-197, 267-305), so Claude and Codex sessions outside Relay get it too. The UI installs on one click without listing what will be installed (apps/relay-native/src/tools_skills.rs:357-367). `safe_relative` checks only path syntax, while `root.join(subdir)`, `start.exists()` and `read_dir` follow a symlink committed in the repo (github.rs:158-166, 202-213).
findings.impact: Pasting one URL, or pressing 'Replace' later for a repo that has since been compromised, silently changes the instructions and scripts that every agent on the machine loads, in every project and in non-Relay sessions. No review of bundled scripts is offered, and only `revision` records what was taken. A URL whose folder is a symlink such as `pack -> ../../..` makes Relay walk from / to depth 8 and import every local folder that contains a SKILL.md.
findings.fix: Before installing, show the skills and files to be added and flag executables. Pin to the cloned commit and make refresh an explicit, diffed action. Consider enabling a new skill only for the current project rather than machine-wide. Canonicalize `start` and require it to stay under the clone root, clone with `-c core.symlinks=false`, and give the clone a deadline and size limit.

v1.reason: Partly right, mostly by design. skill.install is Actors::UserOnly (relay-bus ops/provider.rs:45-46), so an agent cannot trigger it; the user pastes the URL. Enabling a new skill in every project is D147, documented in the enable_everywhere comment (handlers/provider.rs:513-528). 'Replace' is also a user action. That leaves the lack of preview and pinning as UX/policy choices about a source the user picked on purpose, not a hole. The part that holds is the subdir symlink escape. safe_relative (github.rs:192-198) checks only path syntax. root.join(relative), start.exists(), path.is_file() and fs::read_dir(path) (github.rs:158-166, 200-206) all follow a symlink committed in the repo at the start path or any intermediate component. Only symlinks inside the walk are skipped (github.rs:209). git clone checks symlinks out by default on Linux.
v1.correction: Severity drops to low. The download runs in the unlocked prepare phase of register_staged (provider.rs:211-216), so the clone with no deadline stalls only that request, not the bus. The symlink impact is overstated. A link to / or to another user's home makes `fs::read_dir(path)?` hit an unreadable directory and abort the whole install with skill.read_failed. A link to the user's own home imports local SKILL.md folders (for example ~/.claude/skills/*) back into Relay's library. That is local-to-local copying: nothing leaves the machine, and materialized folders are git-excluded. Fix: canonicalize `start` and require it to stay under the clone root (or reject a symlink in any subdir component), and give the clone a deadline through proc::output_with_timeout. A preview or pin is an optional UX improvement, not a security fix.

findings.title: The scrcpy server jar is read from the build checkout at runtime and pushed to and run on devices without checking its pinned SHA-256; configure_mirror_server is never called
findings.evidence: `mirror_server_path()` returns `MIRROR_SERVER`, which is set only by `configure_mirror_server` and that function has no caller. Otherwise it returns `Path::new(env!("CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR")).join("../../apps/relay-native/resources/scrcpy-server-v4.1")` (55-68), an absolute source-tree path fixed at compile time. `mirror_worker` pushes whatever file is there with `adb push --sync` (handlers/device.rs:763-768, mirror.rs:37-56) and runs it as the shell user through `CLASSPATH=… app_process` (mirror.rs:236-245). The README pins SHA-256 `deacb991…8850cae` (apps/relay-native/resources/README.md:7). That matches the vendored file and upstream scrcpy v4.1's doc/build.md, but no code checks it. Error text calls it 'the bundled scrcpy server' (handlers/device.rs:87).
findings.impact: Any change to that file in the checkout the binary was built from (a branch switch or merge carrying a binary diff no one can review, or an agent session working in that primary checkout) is pushed silently to every mirrored Android device. It then runs with shell privileges, which can install apps, grant permissions, read storage and inject input. Separately, a binary built elsewhere (cargo install, Docker, a moved checkout) has no mirror at all.
findings.fix: Embed the jar with include_bytes! and write it to the data dir on first use, or call configure_mirror_server with a packaged resource. Check its SHA-256 against a constant next to SCRCPY_VERSION before every push, so that changing the jar requires a visible code change.

v1.reason: Verified. `configure_mirror_server` (device.rs:56-60) has no caller anywhere in crates/ or apps/, so MIRROR_SERVER is never set. `mirror_server_path` (62-68) therefore always falls back to `env!("CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR")/../../apps/relay-native/resources/scrcpy-server-v4.1`, a source-tree path fixed at compile time. mirror_worker (handlers/device.rs:763-768) pushes whatever file sits there, with no hash check. The vendored file matches the README's SHA-256 (deacb991...8850cae). The security framing is overstated. Whoever can change files in the build checkout can already change Relay's source and the scripts the user runs. Agent sessions work in separate worktrees, and a change to the jar would arrive as a visible binary diff in a merge. What is concrete: a dead configuration hook, a runtime dependency on the build tree, so a moved or installed binary has no mirror (handlers/device.rs:86 refuses), and no integrity check against the documented pin.
v1.correction: Re-categorized from security/medium to code-quality/low, with a hardening note. Embed the jar with include_bytes! (about 90 KB) and write it to the data dir, or wire configure_mirror_server from relay-native's resource lookup. Either way, check a SHA-256 constant next to the version.

findings.title: CI actions are pinned to mutable tags or a branch, and the mobile-apk job exposes a write token and the signing secrets to every step and third-party action
findings.evidence: `permissions: contents: write` is set for the whole workflow (37-38). `actions/checkout@v4` (68) keeps the token in .git/config by default. `npm ci` (111-112), which runs dependency install scripts, `npx expo prebuild` and the Gradle/CMake build (166-173) all run while it is readable. The keystore and passwords are written to `android/app/release.keystore` and `android/gradle.properties` (117-131) and stay there for later steps and for the post-job hooks of `gradle/actions/setup-gradle@v4` (101) and `hendrikmuhs/ccache-action@v1.2` (106). The release upload uses `softprops/action-gh-release@v2` (198). Every action is referenced by tag. ci.yml uses `dtolnay/rust-toolchain@master`, a branch (28), and `Swatinem/rust-cache@v2` (33), and has no `permissions:` block. deploy/rendezvous.Dockerfile uses unpinned `rust:1.94-bookworm` and `debian:bookworm-slim` (46, 54).
findings.impact: A compromised npm or Gradle dependency, or a re-pointed action tag (as in the tj-actions/changed-files incident of March 2025), running in mobile-apk could push commits, tags and releases with the write token. It could also take the Android release keystore and passwords, enabling signed malicious updates of the phone app that controls the PC. Any push to dtolnay/rust-toolchain's master branch runs in every engine CI job.
findings.fix: Set `permissions: contents: read` at workflow level and grant `contents: write` only to a separate release job that downloads the built artifact. Set `persist-credentials: false` on checkout. Pin every action to a full commit SHA (Dependabot can keep them current). Materialize signing files only in the Gradle step and delete them afterwards. Pin Docker base images by digest.

v1.reason: Verified. mobile-apk.yml:37-38 sets `permissions: contents: write` for the whole workflow. `actions/checkout@v4` (68) runs with the default persist-credentials. `npm ci` (112), `expo prebuild` (115) and the Gradle build (170) run with that token readable. The signing step writes the keystore and passwords into android/app/release.keystore and gradle.properties (125-131). Every action is pinned by tag. ci.yml:28 uses `dtolnay/rust-toolchain@master` and has no `permissions:` block. Impact is limited, though. The workflow has no `pull_request` trigger, so fork contributors cannot run it, and exploiting it needs an upstream compromise of an npm/Gradle dependency or an action tag. GITHUB_TOKEN also cannot modify workflow files. This is standard CI hardening, not a hole reachable by a local user or a network peer, so medium overstates it.
v1.correction: The Dockerfile lines are deploy/rendezvous.Dockerfile:9 and :17, not 46/54. 'Materialize signing files only in the Gradle step' does little against a compromised Gradle or npm-native dependency, because signing needs the key inside that same Gradle process. The parts that help: least privilege (a read-only token by default, with `contents: write` only in a separate release job that uploads the downloaded artifact), `persist-credentials: false`, and SHA-pinned actions. This workflow builds the out-of-scope phone app, but the finding concerns repository token scope, so it stays.

findings.title: Nothing scans dependencies for advisories, and Cargo.lock currently carries a RustSec-flagged crate
findings.evidence: CI runs only `cargo test --locked` and clippy (37-41). There is no cargo-audit or cargo-deny job, no deny.toml and no Dependabot config. Cargo.lock pins `faster-hex` 0.10.0 (Cargo.lock:577-578), which RUSTSEC-2026-0306 flags (AVX2 read past the source buffer in `hex_decode_unchecked`, patched in ≥0.10.1). gix reaches it only through the checked `hex_decode`, which requires `src.len() >= 2*dst.len()`, so it is not exploitable here, but nothing reported it. I checked every 2026 RustSec advisory: the locked versions of rustls (0.23.45), rustls-webpki (0.103.15), event-listener, memmap2, anyhow, rand and bytes are already patched. All dependencies come from crates.io, with no git or wildcard sources.
findings.impact: The next advisory against a crate on the network-facing phone door (tungstenite, rustls) or the repository-parsing path (gix, tree-sitter) will go unnoticed. `--locked` keeps the vulnerable version until someone bumps it by hand.
findings.fix: Add a PR and scheduled `cargo deny check advisories bans sources` job (or `cargo audit`), with a deny.toml that refuses git and unknown registries. Enable Dependabot for cargo and github-actions. Run `cargo update -p faster-hex`.

v1.reason: ci.yml:37-41 runs only `cargo test --locked` and clippy. There is no deny.toml, no .github/dependabot.yml and no audit job. Cargo.lock:577-578 pins faster-hex 0.10.0. RustSec lists RUSTSEC-2026-0306 (2026-09-23, an AVX2 out-of-bounds read in `hex_decode_unchecked`) against faster-hex. Two crates depend on it (Cargo.lock:1223, 1397), via gix. As the finding says, gix reaches it only through checked decoding, so it is not exploitable today. The real gap is that nothing would report the next advisory. That makes it a hardening item, low severity.
v1.correction: I did not verify the exact patched version (>=0.10.1) or the claim that gix uses only the checked path; I checked only that the advisory exists. Fix as proposed: a scheduled `cargo deny check advisories` or `cargo audit` job, plus Dependabot.

findings.title: CI's push trigger covers only `main`, but the repository's default branch is `relay/proud-otter`, so merged states are never tested
findings.evidence: The trigger is `on: push: branches: [main]` plus `pull_request` (6-9). `origin/HEAD` points to `origin/relay/proud-otter`. PRs #28 and #29, both based on e1024ca, were merged into that branch as 22d8cd7 and 361c6f9 with no push-triggered run. CLAUDE.md:10 says 'Both run in CI on every push and pull request'.
findings.impact: The default branch is never tested after a merge. Two PRs that were each green against their old base (as #28 and #29 were here) can combine into a broken default branch without CI noticing.
findings.fix: Add the default branch to `push.branches`, or use a merge queue with a `merge_group` trigger. Correct the claim in CLAUDE.md.

v1.reason: The premise is wrong. The local `refs/remotes/origin/HEAD -> origin/relay/proud-otter` is a stale local ref. `git ls-remote --symref origin HEAD` returns `ref: refs/heads/main`, so the repository's real default branch is `main`. Commit 361c6f9 (the merges of #28 and #29) is an ancestor of origin/main (d04b526, which also carries the later merges #30 and #31). origin/relay/proud-otter is far behind at 61a6a1b (PR #8). So the merges landed on `main`, and `on: push: branches: [main]` (ci.yml:7-8) does run CI on them. CLAUDE.md:10 is accurate for the default branch.
v1.correction: If anything, the local clone's origin/HEAD is stale; `git remote set-head origin -a` fixes that. It is not a CI problem.

findings.title: The dev and stable instances share the machine-wide skill folders, and each one prunes the other's skills
findings.evidence: `user_bases` returns `~/.claude/skills` and `$CODEX_HOME/skills` for every instance except Test (179-197). `apply` calls `prune(base, rows)`, which deletes every folder carrying the `.relay-skill` marker that is not in this instance's rows (230-236, 350-361). Each launch plans the user folders (handlers/session.rs:445), and engine start refreshes them (267-305). Dev and stable have separate stores (paths.rs:51-56).
findings.impact: With both `stable` (the CLI default) and `dev` (run.sh's default) in use, each dev launch removes skills that only stable has enabled from `~/.codex/skills`, the only place Codex reads skills, and the reverse. Same-named skills with different stamps are deleted and rewritten on every launch, possibly while an agent is reading them.
findings.fix: Record the instance in the marker and prune only folders owned by the current instance, or materialize user-level skills from one instance only.

v1.reason: skills.rs:179-197 `user_bases` returns `~/.claude/skills` and `$CODEX_HOME/skills` for Stable and Dev alike (only Test is excluded). `apply` (skills.rs:230-236) calls `prune(base, &plan.rows)` for every base. `prune` (skills.rs:350-361) deletes any folder that has the `.relay-skill` marker and is not in this instance's rows. The marker (skills.rs:345) holds only `row.stamp` and says nothing about which instance wrote the folder. `plan_user` runs on session launch (handlers/session.rs:445/493) and in `refresh_all` (skills.rs:280).
