The stores are separate per instance (paths.rs:51-56 `data_dir` = relay-v4/<instance>), so the two `enabled_anywhere` sets differ. Running both instances is the author's normal setup: run.sh defaults to dev, while `Instance::from_env` and the CLI default to stable. Each instance therefore removes the other's skills from the shared folders, and when the stamps differ it rewrites the same-named folders (fill does remove_dir_all and then copies).
v1.correction: The same clash also hits project checkouts: if both instances register the same project path, `plan(conn, root, ..)` prunes `<root>/.claude/skills` etc. by the same marker rule. The fix should cover both cases: record the instance in the marker and prune only folders owned by the current instance (or have one instance own user-scope materialization).

findings.title: BUS.md §9.3 says Codex is unguarded and has a post-hoc guardrail.violation watcher; the code does the opposite and has no such watcher
findings.evidence: BUS.md:524-533 says "Codex (no tool hooks): ProviderInfo.guarded is false … writes are detected post-hoc by the notify watcher — a destructive write that already landed raises a guardrail.violation notification", and line 852 describes file.restore_head as the answer to that notification. In the code, Codex has `fn guarded(&self) -> bool { true }` (providers.rs:212), Codex PreToolUse hooks are installed (hooks.rs:492-548, D132), and nothing emits `guardrail.violation` (rg finds it only in docs). D132 adds that patches reach the gate only as `exec` and the git pre-commit gate is the boundary for the write set.
findings.impact: Anyone using the security-model document to judge write protection for Codex sessions will trust a detection-and-restore path that does not exist, and will misread which provider is guarded.
findings.fix: Rewrite the §9.3 Codex bullet to match D132/D135 (hook-based exec gating, patches gated only as exec, commit gate as the write-set boundary), and drop or mark as not implemented the post-hoc watcher, including at line 852.

v1.reason: BUS.md:524-533 says Codex has `ProviderInfo.guarded` false, has no tool hooks, and gets a post-hoc `notify` watcher that raises `guardrail.violation`. The code says otherwise: providers.rs:212 `fn guarded(&self) -> bool { true }` for Codex, and D132 (DECISIONS.md:650-655) documents Codex PreToolUse hooks routed through guardrail.gate, with patches gated as shell and the git pre-commit gate as the write-set boundary. A search for `guardrail.violation` outside docs finds nothing, so the watcher does not exist. BUS.md:852 describes file.restore_head as the answer to that notification. The op itself does exist (relay-bus ops/file.rs:32, handlers/file.rs:257), but nothing ever triggers it that way.
v1.correction: Only the violation watcher and notification are missing; `file.restore_head` is implemented. Line 852 only needs its 'answer to a post-hoc guardrail.violation' clause changed, not the op removed.

findings.title: Relay rewrites a repository-tracked .codex/hooks.json with machine-specific commands, and git-ignores the path for new files
findings.evidence: `install_codex` merges Relay's handlers, which hold the absolute path to the user's relay binary and `--instance`, into `<worktree>/.codex/hooks.json` and rewrites the file pretty-printed (494-548). `ensure_excluded` adds `.codex/hooks.json` to `.git/info/exclude` (worktree.rs:39-41), which does nothing for a tracked file. `git.commit {all:true}` runs `git add -A` (git.rs:545).
findings.impact: In a repository that commits its Codex project hooks, the file shows as modified throughout every Codex session. An `add -A` commit by an agent or by Relay pushes `'/home/<user>/…/relay' --instance 'dev' hook codex-pre-tool` to teammates, whose Codex then calls a binary that does not exist on every tool use. Teardown leaves formatting churn. Conversely, a `.codex/hooks.json` the user creates for their project is silently ignored by git.
findings.fix: Check whether the file is tracked (`git ls-files --error-unmatch`). If it is, deliver Relay's hooks through a layer that is not shared (a per-launch config override or a user-level, cwd-scoped hooks file), or refuse clearly. Exclude the path only when Relay created it.

v1.reason: install_codex unconditionally merges handlers containing the absolute relay binary path and --instance into <worktree>/.codex/hooks.json and rewrites it (hooks.rs:494-548). It never checks whether the file is tracked. ensure_excluded adds `.codex/hooks.json` to info/exclude (worktree.rs:40), which git_dir_of resolves to the repository's common dir (worktree.rs:71-73). An exclude entry has no effect on a tracked file, and git.commit {all:true} runs `git add -A` (git.rs:545) with nothing filtering the file out, so Relay's machine-specific handlers can be committed. uninstall_codex reserialises the whole file pretty-printed (hooks.rs:560-574), so a hand-formatted tracked file shows whitespace churn after teardown. Key order is kept because serde_json has preserve_order (Cargo.toml:18).
v1.correction: One addition: the exclude entry is written to the common dir's info/exclude, so it applies to the main checkout and every worktree. A .codex/hooks.json the user creates anywhere in the repository is silently ignored by git. Repositories that commit .codex/hooks.json are uncommon, so severity stays low. Fix as proposed: detect a tracked file with `git ls-files --error-unmatch` and either use a non-shared hook layer or refuse clearly. Exclude the path only when Relay created the file.

findings.title: The store, its WAL and the backups are created world-readable, though they hold terminal scrollback and bus payloads
findings.evidence: `Store::open` creates the parent with `create_dir_all` and opens SQLite with default modes (384-394). On the author's machine `~/.local/share/relay-v4/dev` is drwxr-xr-x, store.db, -wal and -shm are -rw-r--r--, and backups/ is drwxr-xr-x (permissions only, contents not read). The store holds session scrollback (`session_scrollback`, store.rs:198), audit payloads including file.write text, notes, and live session tokens. By contrast remote.json is written 0600 (relay-remote registry.rs:171) and signing directories 0700 (handlers/device.rs:1282).
findings.impact: On a multi-user host with traversable home directories (0755 or 0711, the old Ubuntu/Debian default), any local user can read every agent's terminal output, including secrets it printed, plus notes and file contents written through the bus. The author's home is 0700, so this machine is not exposed.
findings.fix: Create the data dir with mode 0700 and set 0600 on store.db, -wal, -shm and the backup files.

v1.reason: `Store::open` (store.rs:383-394) calls `create_dir_all` and then `Connection::open_with_flags` with no chmod or umask handling. Nothing in relay-core sets modes on the data dir, the store or the backups: the set_permissions/mode calls cover only the socket dir (socket.rs:56/65/102), the signing dirs (device.rs) and remote.json (registry.rs:171). On this machine the files are as described: relay-v4/dev is drwxr-xr-x, store.db/-wal/-shm are -rw-r--r--, backups/ is drwxr-xr-x, and remote.json is -rw-------. The home directory is drwx------, so this machine is not exposed. That bounds the impact to multi-user hosts with traversable homes, which fits low.
v1.correction: The fix belongs in `Instance::data_dir` creation (0700) as well as in Store::open, so it also covers logs/ and skills/. Tightening the directory alone is enough to protect the files, since they cannot be reached through a 0700 directory.

Nothing was built or run except one throwaway git experiment in the scratchpad. It confirmed that `git worktree remove --force` exits 128 for a path that is not a worktree and for a locked worktree, which is what triggers the rm -rf fallback.

Invariant issues seen but left to other lenses: file.import, app.backup.now, app.import.v3, worktree.remove and integration.discard all do slow filesystem work under Engine::register, and worktree::git and integration::shell run without proc::output_with_timeout.

findings.title: worktree.remove can rm -rf any directory: the op takes an unvalidated (even relative) path, and worktree::remove falls back to remove_dir_all whenever git refuses
findings.evidence: handlers/git.rs:132-139: `let want = std::fs::canonicalize(&p.path).map(...).unwrap_or(p.path.clone())`. The only check before `worktree::remove(repo, Path::new(&want), p.purge_build.unwrap_or(true))` is that no live session owns exactly that path. worktree.rs:355-366 refuses only the primary checkout, then runs `if purge { freed += purge_build(path); } freed += dir_size(path); git(repo, &['worktree','remove','--force',&path_c]).or_else(|e| std::fs::remove_dir_all(path)...)`. In a scratch repo, `git worktree remove --force` exits 128 both for a path that is not a working tree ('is not a working tree') and for a locked worktree ('cannot remove a locked working tree'). So the rm -rf fallback runs for exactly the paths git refused. `relay serve` changes directory to $HOME (relay-cli/src/main.rs:208), so a relative path resolves under the home directory. The handler is registered with Engine::register, so all of this runs while holding the store mutex.
findings.impact: A single user-actor request deletes an arbitrary directory. Examples: `relay q worktree.remove '{"project_id":1,"path":"."}'`, a mistyped path, `<repo>/.relay/worktrees`, a sibling repo, or the same op from a paired phone through the remote door. The op first purges target/build/.gradle/dist under the path. It then walks the whole tree with the bus frozen, then calls remove_dir_all on it. This can wipe the user's home directory, every pooled worktree (including live agents' uncommitted work), or a worktree the user deliberately locked.
findings.fix: In WorktreeRemove, require an absolute path, and accept it only if `worktree::contains(repo, path)` confirms it is a linked worktree of this project (and inside pool_dir unless explicitly allowed). In worktree::remove, delete the remove_dir_all fallback. Alternatively, confine it to a pooled path whose `.git` file points into this repo's `worktrees/` dir and that git lists as prunable. Never fall back after a 'locked' or 'not a working tree' refusal. Purge build dirs only after git has accepted the removal.

v1.reason: git.rs:129-143 registers WorktreeRemove with Engine::register. Its only checks are canonicalize(&p.path) with a fallback to the raw string, and a lookup for a non-closed session whose worktree equals exactly that path. It then calls worktree::remove(repo, want, purge_build.unwrap_or(true)). worktree.rs:351-369 refuses only when canon(path) equals canon(repo). It then purges the BUILD_DIRS under the path, runs dir_size over the whole tree, and calls `git worktree remove --force`. On any git error it falls back to `std::fs::remove_dir_all(path)`. I checked in a scratch repo that `git worktree remove --force <plain dir>` exits 128 with 'is not a working tree', so the rm -rf fallback runs for exactly the paths git refuses. `relay serve` sets the process cwd to $HOME (relay-cli main.rs:208), so `"."` canonicalizes to the home directory. A parent such as `<repo>/.relay/worktrees` also passes the owner check, because that compares exact paths only. The op is Actors::UserOnly, so agents cannot call it (BUS.md:582 also stops agents from claiming --actor user). It is still reachable from raw `relay q` and from the phone door, which forwards any op as actor `user` (relay-remote wire.rs:99-101). The two internal callers (session.rs:1521 and 1578) are already guarded by `wt.starts_with(worktree::pool_dir(&repo))`; only the bus op has no guard.
v1.correction: Severity is high, not critical. Neither the native client nor any CLI subcommand calls worktree.remove (rg finds no caller outside tests and perf.rs). A trigger therefore needs a user-trust actor sending a wrong path through raw `relay q` or a paired phone. It is not reachable by an agent or an unpaired network peer. The consequence is still catastrophic (the home directory or the whole worktree pool deleted) after one typo, with the bus frozen during the dir_size walk. Fix it the way the internal callers already do: require the canonical path to be a linked worktree of this project, for example listed by `git worktree list --porcelain` or `worktree::contains`, and inside pool_dir unless explicitly allowed. Only fall back to remove_dir_all for a pool path whose `.git` file points into this repo's worktrees dir. Also move the purge, the walk and the git subprocess out of the locked phase with register_staged, as session.close does.

v2.reason:
(a) The code does what the finding claims. handlers/git.rs:129-143 registers WorktreeRemove with `e.register` and runs it under the store transaction. It sets `want = std::fs::canonicalize(&p.path)...unwrap_or(p.path.clone())`. Its only check is an exact-equality owner query (`worktree = ?2 AND state != 'closed'`). It then calls `worktree::remove(repo, Path::new(&want), p.purge_build.unwrap_or(true))`. worktree.rs:351-369 refuses only `canon(repo) == canon(path)`. It then runs `purge_build(path)` (deleting target/build/.gradle/app/build/node_modules/.cache/dist) and `dir_size(path)`, and only then calls `git worktree remove --force`. The `.or_else(|e| std::fs::remove_dir_all(path)...)` at 362-365 runs on any git error without looking at it. I checked this with git 2.55.0 in a scratch repo: `git -C repo worktree remove --force` exits 128 with "is not a working tree" for a plain dir, for `<repo>/.relay/worktrees`, for a subdirectory of the primary checkout and for an ancestor of the repo. It exits 128 with "cannot remove a locked working tree" for a locked worktree. So rm -rf runs on exactly the paths git refused. `relay serve` does `set_current_dir(&home)` (relay-cli main.rs:207-208), and both run.sh and deploy/relay-remote.service start the engine that way, so `"."` resolves to $HOME.

(b) Only user-trust callers can trigger it, and only by passing a wrong path:
- raw `relay q`/`relay cmd` (no CLI subcommand wraps the op);
- `relay mcp` run outside a session, where actor_from_env falls back to Actor::User and the tools filter advertises worktree.remove, so an LLM harness picks the path;
- a paired phone (wire.rs `gate` forwards any op from actor user).

The native client never sends it (rg finds only worktree.list), and the phone app does not send it either. Agents are refused by Actors::UserOnly at engine.rs:855. That the socket does not authenticate `user` is documented (BUS.md §9.5, "not a security boundary") and is a separate root cause. Frequency is rare: no normal UI flow reaches it. Relative paths resolving against $HOME instead of the caller's cwd make the "." mistake easy, though. The internal callers (session.rs:1521/1578, workspace.rs:333) are already limited to pool paths. session.create (session.rs:878-886) validates a user-given worktree against `git worktree list`, but worktree.remove does not.

(c) "." wipes these first: ~/.gradle (caches plus gradle.properties, which often holds signing secrets), ~/target, ~/build and ~/dist. It then walks all of $HOME with the store mutex held, so every locked op stalls. Finally remove_dir_all($HOME) deletes until the first non-ENOENT error. Nothing goes to a trash, and the Relay store itself may be among the deleted files. Passing `<repo>/.relay/worktrees` passes the exact-path owner check, deletes every pooled worktree including live agents' uncommitted work, and is followed by `git worktree prune`. A locked worktree is deleted despite its lock.

(d) Severity is high, not critical. The damage is catastrophic but needs a mistaken path from a user-trust caller in a raw bus or MCP call. It is not reachable by an unpaired network peer, by another local user, or through the intended agent route. It fits "a safety check that can be silently bypassed": git's not-a-worktree and locked refusals, and the owner check, are all silently overridden.

(e) The fix direction is right, but as written it is incomplete or partly wrong; see correction.
v2.correction:
The locations are handlers/git.rs:129-143 and worktree.rs:351-369, with the fallback at 362-365. Severity should be high, not critical (I agree with the first verifier). Add `relay mcp` outside a session (actor User) as a reachable route: it advertises worktree.remove to whatever LLM harness the user connects.

Corrections to the fix:
1. `worktree::contains` (worktree.rs:162) returns true for the primary checkout, and it requires the `.git` pointer file. So it must be combined with the existing primary refusal. It is also a poor fit for half-deleted worktrees. Simpler: in the handler, reject non-absolute paths, canonicalize, and require that the path is a strict child of canon(pool_dir(repo)) (or a non-primary entry of `git worktree list --porcelain`). Refuse it if git lists it as locked.
2. Do not delete the remove_dir_all fallback outright. session.close, session.restorable.discard and project.remove rely on it to clean up half-deleted pool worktrees. Confine it to strict children of pool_dir, and never run it after a "locked" refusal.
3. "Purge build dirs only after git accepted the removal" does not work as written, because `git worktree remove --force` deletes the tree. Validate the path before purging.
4. Make the owner check prefix-based: refuse when any live session's worktree is equal to or under the target.
5. Tighten the internal `wt.starts_with(pool_dir)` guards to exclude pool_dir itself.

Separately, as an invariant issue: move the op to register_staged as session.close does, and run git through proc::output_with_timeout.

findings.title: project.remove / workspace.remove permanently delete the project's board, notes and modules with no warning, undo or backup, and moving a repo leaves no other option
findings.evidence: workspace.rs:354-380 runs `DELETE FROM messages ... tasks ... modules ... notes ... notifications ... file_trash ... integrations ... WHERE project_id=?1`, then deletes the project row. These are hard deletes, with no set_undo and no store.backup_with. The native confirmation (shell/registry.rs:539-581) reads 'Remove “X” from Relay?', 'N agents will be stopped and closed.' and 'Repository files are never touched.'. It never mentions tasks or notes. ProjectUpdateIn (relay-bus ops/workspace.rs:44-48) has no `path` field, so a project whose folder was moved or renamed can only be repointed by remove + add. workspace.remove with force runs the same cascade for every project (workspace.rs:172-175). D56 calls this 'forgets Relay metadata', but tasks and notes are user-authored content that exists nowhere else.
findings.impact: A user who removes and re-adds a project after moving its repository, or who tidies the sidebar, permanently loses that project's data: every task (with sub-tasks, labels and commit links), every note (including the standing note injected into agents), modules, mailbox history and file-trash records. Ctrl+Z cannot undo it. Only restoring a whole-store backup (manual, or the last pre-upgrade copy) recovers it, and that also loses everything done since.
findings.fix: Make removal a soft delete (an archived_at column; rows kept; restorable from the sidebar). At minimum, take `store.backup_with(ctx.tx(), "project-remove")` in the handler and report its path. Show the counts that will be deleted (tasks, notes, modules) in the dialog. Add a relocate op (project.update {path}, validated as the same repository, e.g. same root commit) so moving a repo never requires removal.

v1.reason: workspace.rs:354-381 hard-deletes the project's messages, tasks (with commits, attachments and unlinked-module rows), modules, notes, notifications, file_trash, integrations, layouts and device_runs, then the project row. There is no set_undo and no backup_with. The only automatic backup is the pre-upgrade one (store.rs:442); the only other is the manual app.backup (app.rs:48). The native dialog (registry.rs:539-583) says 'Remove “X” from Relay?', lists agents and says 'Repository files are never touched.' It never says that tasks, notes and modules are permanently deleted. ProjectUpdateIn (relay-bus ops/workspace.rs:44-48) has no path field, so a moved repository can only be repointed by remove and re-add, which loses the board. WsRemove with force calls project.remove per project (workspace.rs:171-176). D56 documents clearing project-owned rows as intended, but it does not make the loss harmless: tasks and notes are user-authored and exist only in the store.
v1.correction: Severity is medium rather than high. It is a deliberate, confirmed, user-only action, and D56 makes the deletion a documented design choice. The concrete defects are that the dialog does not disclose the loss, that there is no undo or snapshot, and that there is no relocate path. The cheapest fix is `store.backup_with(ctx.tx(), "project-remove")` before the cascade, plus task/note counts in the confirmation. A project.update path, validated as the same repository, removes the need for remove-and-re-add after a move.

findings.title: Approving a task fails once branch cleanup has deleted its closed session's branch: task.approve resolves refs/heads/<branch> with no fallback
findings.evidence: task.rs:1109-1116, for the task's last session: `repo.rev_parse_single(format!("refs/heads/{}", session.session.branch)...).map_err(|e| BusError::unavailable("git.head", ...))?`. The comment above it (1105-1108) still assumes 'session.close deliberately keeps its branch'. But Close's after_commit calls branch_cleanup::after_close (session.rs:1630-1635). Together with the 20-minute sweeper and after_merged_prs (git.rs:631-641), it deletes the branch with `update-ref -d` (branch_cleanup.rs:314). This happens as soon as the tip is in the base branch or a merged PR covers it, which is immediate for an agent that made no commits. The board approves with `{task_id}` only (board_view.rs:841), and Done can only be reached by approve (task.rs:897). The test phase7.rs:325 'approve_uses_the_recorded_branch_after_the_assigned_session_is_closed' runs in Instance::Test, where after_close is skipped (session.rs:1633), so the production path is untested.
findings.impact: In the normal flow an agent finishes, its PR is merged (or it committed nothing), and the user closes the session. When the user then drags the task to Done, the board shows 'Approved #N into Done', but the call fails with git.head 'reference not found'. The task can no longer be completed from the UI.
findings.fix: When the branch is gone, have task.approve fall back to the newest task_commits sha (session.done links one) or to the tip that branch_cleanup records in its audit summary. Better, have branch_cleanup link the deleted tip to the session's tasks before deleting the branch. Fix the stale comment, and make the test run branch_cleanup::run before approving.

v1.reason: task.rs Approve (~1109-1116) resolves `refs/heads/{session.branch}` for the task's last session and maps a failure to `BusError::unavailable("git.head")`. There is no fallback to task_commits or to anything else. The comment at ~1105-1107 ('session.close deliberately keeps its branch') is stale. Close's after_commit calls branch_cleanup::after_close for non-Test instances (session.rs ~1630-1635). For closed sessions, branch_cleanup deletes the branch with `update-ref -d` (~314) when its tip is an ancestor of the base branch, which includes a session with no commits, or when a merged PR covers it. The board's drag to Done shows 'Approved #N into Done' and then calls task.approve with only task_id (board_view.rs:839-841). The task page's Approve button does the same (task_pages.rs:625). Done is reachable only through approve (Move refuses Done). The test phase7.rs:325, titled 'Approve after cleanup', closes the session in Instance::Test, where after_close is skipped, and never runs branch_cleanup::run, so the production path is untested.
v1.correction: It fails only after the session is closed and cleanup has decided the work is merged. That is the normal finish of a PR-merged flow, so high is justified. Fallback order: the newest task_commits sha for the task, then the deleted tip recorded in branch_cleanup's audit row, then refuse with a clear message. Better still, have branch_cleanup link the tip to the session's tasks (task_commits) before it deletes the branch. Update the test to call branch_cleanup::run before approving.

v2.reason:
(a) The code does what the finding says. task.rs:1097-1101 picks the task's last task_sessions row. task_sessions rows survive a close, and are deleted only when a project is removed (workspace.rs:359). sessions::by_id returns closed rows. Lines 1112-1114 then call `repo.rev_parse_single("refs/heads/<branch>")` with no fallback and map any error to `BusError::unavailable("git.head")`. In gix 0.86, find_ref on a missing ref fails (gix-0.86.0/src/revision/spec/parse/delegate/revision.rs:18-32), so the call errors. The comment at 1105-1106 ("session.close deliberately keeps its branch") was written in fcbdbce (2026-09-04). It went stale with 2d38f75 (2026-10-05), which added branch_cleanup and did not touch task.rs. Close's after_commit calls branch_cleanup::after_close for every non-Test instance (session.rs:1630-1635). The sweeper starts from serve.rs:35 and runs every 20 minutes, and git.pr.list also starts a cleanup (git.rs:631-641). evaluate() deletes the branch with `update-ref -d` (branch_cleanup.rs:314) in any of three cases: its tip is an ancestor of local or origin base, which covers a session with no commits; every commit is upstream by patch id; or gh reports a merged PR that contains the tip. Nothing in candidates() (lines 74-104) checks whether the session's task is Done. tests/branch_cleanup.rs:103-117 shows a merged, closed session's branch being deleted.
(b) Reachable by the user in a normal flow. Approve-after-close is a designed path: the comment, and the test at phase7.rs:325, which runs in Instance::Test where after_close is skipped. Both UI entry points send only task_id: board_view.rs:841 (drag to Done) and task_pages.rs:625-626 (Approve button). The close dialog even promises "Stop this agent and close its pane? The branch is kept." (agent_menu.rs:609). So the bug fires every time someone closes a session whose work has merged (PR merged, local merge, or no commits) and approves its task afterwards. If the PR merges after the close, it fires within 20 minutes.
(c) The board first shows "Approved #N into Done", then shows the git.head error, and the task stays in In Review. Move refuses Done (task.rs:897) and every UI approve fails the same way, so the task cannot be completed from the UI. It also stays out of module progress and changelog roll-ups. No data is lost, because cleanup deletes only merged work. The only workaround is the CLI (`relay cmd task.approve '{"task_id":N,"sha":"..."}'` runs as User), which nothing in the UI points to.
(d) High fits: a user-visible hard failure in a normal flow, introduced one day before this audit. It is not critical, because the CLI workaround exists and no data is lost.
(e) The proposed fix is partly wrong; see the correction.
v2.correction:
Fix corrections:
(1) branch_cleanup's audit row does not record the tip. record() (branch_cleanup.rs:373-376) writes only branch, session, outcome, reason, pr, removed_worktree and deleted_remote, so "fall back to the tip recorded in the audit summary" does not work unless record() starts storing it.
(2) "The newest task_commits sha" is often missing. session.done links a sha only when the agent passes the optional `sha` (session.rs:97-98), and the role instructions (providers.rs COMMON_INSTRUCTIONS) never ask for it, so on its own this fallback does not fix the common case.
Complete fix, either of two:
(a) The simplest: have candidates() skip any closed session that task_sessions still links to a task that is neither Done nor deleted. The branch then survives until approval, approve links its tip, and the next sweep deletes it.
(b) Have cleanup link the tip into task_commits for the session's open tasks (in the system_write it already makes, before or alongside the delete). Then have approve, when the ref is missing, fall back to the latest task_commits row, then to the base-branch head (cleanup only deletes merged or commit-less branches), and otherwise refuse with an actionable message.
Also: make phase7.rs:325 merge the branch, close the session, call branch_cleanup::run, and only then approve.
Related drift that the same fix should cover: the close-dialog text "The branch is kept" (agent_menu.rs:590, 609) and the Discard tooltip "its worktree and branch are kept" (shell.rs:724) are now false. after_close also removes a clean pooled worktree whose work is merged, even with remove_worktree:false. Line references in the finding are accurate (task.rs:1112, comment at 1105-1108).

findings.title: Integration worktrees and relay/integration-N branches are never discarded: every 'Test together' leaves a full checkout plus build output
findings.evidence: integration.rs:86-101 creates `<repo>/.relay/integrations/<id>` on branch `relay/integration-<id>` and runs build_cmd in it. Every terminal state keeps the worktree: Passed (216-225), and Failed/Conflict via fail() (`worktree=COALESCE(?2,worktree)`). Only integration.discard removes it (58-69). That op is UserOnly (relay-bus ops/git.rs:145-146), and the native app never calls it: code_git.rs:738 requests integrations and lists the last three, nothing more. Nothing else sweeps them. branch_cleanup and recovery's dirty scan only look under `.relay/worktrees`. project.remove deletes the integrations rows (workspace.rs:370) but leaves the worktrees registered in git and the branches in place. The default builder role allowlist includes integration.request (settings.rs:36).
findings.impact: Each 'Test together' click, and each agent-requested integration, permanently adds a full checkout and its build directory under the repo's .relay/ (Gradle or Cargo output is routinely several GB). It also adds a branch and a `git worktree list` entry. This is unbounded disk growth in normal use, and nothing in the app removes it.
findings.fix: Discard automatically once the result is recorded (keep log_tail), or keep only the latest N per project and remove older ones in recovery. Expose Discard in the Code panel. Remove integration worktrees and branches in project.remove.

v1.reason: integration.rs run() creates `<repo>/.relay/integrations/<id>` on branch `relay/integration-<id>` (lines ~87-101), runs the build in it, and keeps it on Passed, Failed and Conflict. Only IntegrationDiscard (58-69) removes it. Discard is UserOnly (relay-bus ops/git.rs:145-146), and no caller exists in apps/relay-native: code_git.rs:581 lists integrations and 738 requests them, nothing else. The only other caller is the test phase8.rs:519. Nothing sweeps `.relay/integrations`; worktree.rs pool_dir is `.relay/worktrees`. project.remove deletes the integrations rows (workspace.rs:370) but not the checkouts or branches. Builder agents may call integration.request (settings.rs:36). Each Test together therefore leaves a full checkout plus build output (Gradle or Cargo) and a branch, with no way to reclaim them from the UI.
v1.correction: Do not discard right after Passed: device.rs:~987 deploys from an integration's worktree by integration_id, so the latest passed checkout is used later. Keep the newest N per project (or those newer than a TTL), prune older ones in recovery or the branch-cleanup sweep, and add a Discard action in the Code panel. Separately, IntegrationDiscard is registered with Engine::register and calls worktree::remove(…, purge=true): a build-dir purge, a dir_size walk and git subprocesses while holding the store mutex. That breaks the CLAUDE.md slow-work invariant and should be register_staged, like session.close.

v2.reason:
(a) Verified at 361c6f9.
- integration.rs:86-101 creates `<repo>/.relay/integrations/<id>` on a new branch `relay/integration-<id>` and records the path at Merging (line 96). The build runs inside that checkout: `shell(&path, command, None)` at line 165.
- Passed keeps the path (line 221). Failed and Conflict keep it through `worktree=COALESCE(?2,worktree)` (line 284).
- Only integration.discard (lines 58-69) removes it. That op is UserOnly (relay-bus ops/git.rs:145-146), and `git grep integration.discard HEAD -- apps/` finds nothing. The desktop client only lists integrations (code_git.rs:581, three plain labels at 753) and requests them (738).
- Nothing else reaches the directory:
  - branch_cleanup only takes closed-session branches and refuses any checkout outside `.relay/worktrees` (branch_cleanup.rs:221 onward).
  - recovery.rs never mentions integrations.
  - project.remove deletes the rows (workspace.rs:370). Its remove_worktrees option covers only pooled session checkouts (332-334).
  - git.branch.delete refuses these branches as unmerged and checked out (git.rs:471, 481).
  - worktree.remove could delete them, but no desktop code calls it.
- The discard step is designed but never performed. D38 says the worktree "survives for inspection until explicit discard". SPEC §7:212-215 ends the flow with "→ discard". phase8.rs:519 tests it.

(b) Reachable from the Code panel's MERGE TEST button ("Test merge + build"), a first-class SPEC flow shown whenever two or more sessions are open. Builder agents can trigger it too, since the default allowlist includes integration.request (settings.rs:36). Every use leaks. On this machine no `.relay/integrations` directory exists anywhere under ~ (depth 6), and the RelayV4 repo has no `relay/integration-*` branches. The leak is therefore certain on use, but not yet observed here.

(c) Each run leaves a full checkout, a branch and a `git worktree` entry. A RelayV4 checkout is 24 MB; LFS or Unreal repos are far larger. When the project has a build_cmd, the build output stays too. Existing RelayV4 worktree target dirs on this machine measure 6.4 GB and 21 GB.
- The growth is silent. The resource panel measures only open sessions' worktrees (app.rs:184), there is no disk-threshold alert, and `.relay/` is in info/exclude.
- It also adds clutter and cost:
  - worktree.list has no pool filter (worktree.rs:135), so the editor scope picker and the Devices picker list every leaked checkout.
  - The Devices page (default include_dirty) and the startup dirty scan each run one `git status` per leaked checkout.
  - Branches the user cannot delete pile up in the branch picker.
- No data is lost.

(d) High fits "unbounded growth in normal use". The growth is per explicit use rather than passive, and the GB-scale cost needs a build_cmd. That is still the configured "Test merge + build" case, and SPEC §8 records that the author was already hit by a 73 GB build-output leak.

(e) The proposed fix is partly wrong; see the correction.
v2.correction:
Overstated: "nothing in the app removes it".
- The generic CLI runs as the user by default (relay-cli main.rs:118-129), so `relay cmd integration.discard '{"integration_id":N}'` removes one integration at a time.
- What is missing is any desktop UI path, any retention policy and any visibility.
- After project.remove deletes the rows (workspace.rs:370), Relay cannot discard them at all; only manual git cleanup works.
- Build output only builds up when build_cmd is set; it is NULL by default (store.rs:54). Without it, each run still leaks a checkout, a branch and a worktree entry.

Fix corrections:
1. Do not discard on Passed. device.run and device.build with integration_id require state "passed" and the worktree on disk (device.rs:983-1015, BUS.md:864-865, SPEC §9). D38 keeps Failed and Conflict checkouts for inspection.
2. Instead:
   - Add a Discard button per row in the Code panel's MERGE TEST list.
   - Add a retention policy: keep the newest N finished integrations per project, or use a TTL.
   - Prune outside the store lock, either in the integration worker once it finishes or in the 20-minute branch_cleanup sweep.
   - Skip integrations in live states and any checkout an active device run is building from.
3. Prerequisite before adding any UI button: IntegrationDiscard is registered with Engine::register (integration.rs:58), so it holds the store mutex. Under that lock it runs:
   - purge_build: a dir_size walk plus remove_dir_all over a multi-GB target/.
   - Subprocesses with no timeout, through worktree::git and Command::output: `git worktree remove --force`, `git worktree prune` and `git branch -D`.

   Exposed as-is, each click would freeze the bus for seconds. Make it register_staged with the removal in the unlocked phase, as session.close does (session.rs:1547/1577). The lock problem is a separate root cause (invariant) and should be its own finding.
4. Make project.remove's remove_worktrees also remove `.relay/integrations/*` and the `relay/integration-*` branches, after commit.
5. Show integration checkouts in the resource panel.

Extra related locations: crates/relay-core/src/handlers/app.rs:184, crates/relay-core/src/worktree.rs:135, crates/relay-core/src/handlers/git.rs:471, docs/engine/DECISIONS.md:138, docs/engine/SPEC.md:212.

findings.title: Trashed files and soft-deleted notes cannot be restored from the app: no op lists them and the Undo button is transient, yet the delete dialog promises 'restored from Relay trash'
findings.evidence: editor.rs:1225 tells the user 'The file can be restored from Relay trash.' The only restore path is the 'Undo trash' button appended to file_undo (1300-1334). reset() clears it on any project switch (476), and it does not survive a restart. The bus has file.restore {trash_id} but no op that lists trash (relay-bus ops/file.rs). notes.list always filters `deleted_at IS NULL` and has no include_deleted (handlers/notes.rs:341-345, ops/notes.rs:6). The board's Ctrl+Z only searches `op_prefix: task.` (board_view.rs:882). Trash payloads are stored inside the worktree (file.rs:230), so they vanish when a pooled worktree is removed while the file_trash row stays open. BUS.md §5.4 promises these items are 'restorable by *.restore for the grace window'.
findings.impact: A file deleted by mistake from the Code tree, or a note deleted in the Notes window, cannot be recovered from the UI after a project switch or restart, although the bytes and rows are still kept. Recovery means digging the trash_id or note_id out of audit.list through the CLI. Files trashed inside an agent worktree are lost outright when that worktree is removed.
findings.fix: Add file.trash.list (open rows per project/worktree) and a Trash view in Code. Add include_deleted to notes.list and a 'Recently deleted' section with Restore, plus an undo toast after notes.delete. Keep trash under the project's primary `.relay/trash` (or the store dir) rather than a worktree that may be removed.

v1.reason: editor.rs:1225 shows the dialog copy 'The file can be restored from Relay trash.' The only restore path in the native client is the transient 'Undo trash' button at editor.rs:1299-1334, which calls file.restore with the trash_id held in the closure. Editor::reset (editor.rs:473-476) runs clear(&self.file_undo), and reset is called on every project switch (shell.rs:32) and on app.rs:1408. Nothing persists the button across a restart. relay-bus ops/file.rs has Delete and Restore but no op that lists trash. No other native code calls file.restore; project_files.rs:301 reuses the same Editor::file_action. notes.list (ops/notes.rs:6) takes only project_id and pinned_only, and handlers/notes.rs:342/344 always filter on deleted_at IS NULL. notes.restore exists (ops/notes.rs:31), but note_pages.rs:1086 confirm_delete offers no undo, and the board's audit-based undo filters on op_prefix 'task.' (board_view.rs:882). BUS.md §5.4 says soft-deleted items are listed with include_deleted:true and restorable. Trash sits at <worktree>/.relay/trash/<id>/payload (file.rs:230). `.relay/` is git-excluded (worktree.rs:40), and worktree::remove deletes the whole directory (worktree.rs:362), so payloads under a pooled worktree disappear while the file_trash row stays open.
v1.correction: Part of this is also docs drift: BUS.md §5.4 promises include_deleted on list ops, but notes.list does not implement it. Note also that nothing ever hard-deletes file_trash rows or payloads: the only DELETE is on project removal (workspace.rs:369), so the 'grace window' in §5.4 is not enforced for files. The fix should add the listing ops, a trash and recently-deleted UI, and trash storage that outlives the worktree.

findings.title: Per-repo .relay/ state is shared by the stable and dev instances, but each instance's cleanup treats it as its own: hook dirs get swept and trash slots overwritten
findings.symbol: recovery step 5; hooks::sweep_hook_dirs; file.delete trash slot
findings.evidence: paths.rs:2 promises 'one set per instance so dev and stable never cross-corrupt'. But several things live in the repository, not the instance dir: hook dirs (`<repo>/.relay/hooks/<session>`), trash (`<root>/.relay/trash/<id>/payload`, file.rs:230), the worktree pool and relay/<name> branches. recovery.rs:125-138 builds `live` from this store's sessions only, and hooks.rs:291-308 calls remove_dir_all on every other `.relay/hooks/*`. install_git runs on every launch (session.rs:481). When the active hook dir is missing, it finds no PREVIOUS_HOOKS_PATH and records the Relay dir itself as 'previous' (hooks.rs:82-98, 140-145). file_trash ids are a per-store AUTOINCREMENT, and file.rs:231-232 does `create_dir_all(trash.parent())` then `fs::rename(&path, &trash)` with no existence check. rename(2) silently replaces an existing file. The same id reuse happens after restoring an older store backup, or when a delete's commit fails after the rename.
findings.impact: Assume the same repo is registered in both instances (the user's live engine is the dev instance; run.sh also launches stable). (a) Starting one engine deletes the other engine's live sessions' hook directories. Those agents' commits then run neither Relay's commit guardrail nor the user's chained pre-commit hook. The next launch rewrites the chain to point at itself, so after close a primary checkout's core.hooksPath points at a deleted dir and the user's own hooks stop running. (b) The next file trashed in one instance silently replaces a file trashed with the same id in the other, and 'Undo trash' restores the wrong content under the original name. Branch sweeps likewise judge which worktrees are live from one store only.
findings.fix: Namespace everything Relay writes into a repository by instance (e.g. `.relay/<instance>/hooks`, `.relay/<instance>/trash`, pool names prefixed by instance), or have sweeps honour a per-instance ownership marker. Make trash slots collision-proof: a uuid directory, create_dir rather than create_dir_all, and refuse if the payload already exists.

v1.reason: Several kinds of state live inside the repository rather than the instance data dir, so the per-instance store isolation promised in paths.rs:1-2 does not cover them. (a) recovery.rs:120-138 builds the live set from this store's non-closed sessions only, and hooks.rs:291-308 calls remove_dir_all on every other `<repo>/.relay/hooks/*` directory. If the same repository is registered in dev and stable and one engine starts while the other has live sessions, the second engine's active hook dirs are deleted. Git then finds no pre-commit hook at the configured core.hooksPath, so the commit guardrail and the chained user hook both stop running. install_git (hooks.rs:82-98) then reads no PREVIOUS file. I confirmed that its fallback `git rev-parse --git-path hooks` returns the configured core.hooksPath, so the Relay dir itself is recorded as 'previous'. uninstall_git_any (hooks.rs:255-260) later restores that deleted path. (b) file.rs:225-232 uses the store's AUTOINCREMENT id (store.rs:217) as the trash slot `<root>/.relay/trash/<id>/payload`. It runs create_dir_all, then fs::rename with no existence check. For a file, rename silently replaces an earlier payload with the same id from the other instance, or from a pre-restore store. Restoring that id then brings back the wrong content.
v1.correction: The mechanism is established in code. The trigger needs the same repository to be used from two instances, or a store restored from a backup (that path covers the trash collision only). It is a valid configuration, since run.sh accepts dev, stable and test, but probably not the common one, so medium is right. The trash collision also occurs within a single instance after restoring an older backup. Rename over a non-empty directory fails with ENOTEMPTY rather than overwriting, so only file payloads are silently lost. Fixes: namespace `.relay/hooks` and `.relay/trash` by instance, and make the trash slot exclusive (create_dir rather than create_dir_all, and refuse if the payload exists).

findings.title: A close that keeps the worktree still lets after_close branch cleanup force-remove that worktree and delete the branch, destroying git-ignored files
findings.evidence: The UI promises the branch and worktree survive: agent_menu.rs:590 ('the worktree and branch are kept unless you choose otherwise'), 609 ('The branch is kept.') and shell.rs:724 ('its worktree and branch are kept'). Yet Close's after_commit runs branch_cleanup::after_close (session.rs:1630-1635). evaluate() treats the branch as merged when `merge-base --is-ancestor tip base` holds (246), which is true for any agent that made no commits. If `worktree::status_files(path)` is empty (295-301), it runs `worktree::remove(&candidate.repo, path, true)` (307), meaning purge plus `git worktree remove --force`, and then `update-ref -d` (314). status_files runs `git status --porcelain=v1 -z --untracked-files=all` without --ignored (worktree.rs:89), so ignored content never counts as dirty.
findings.impact: Seconds after a close where the user explicitly kept the worktree, the pooled checkout is deleted. Build outputs, ignored config the agent or user created (.env, local.properties) and the worktree's own .relay/trash are all lost, and the trash's file_trash rows become unrestorable. The branch the UI said is kept no longer exists, which also breaks task.approve.
findings.fix: Never auto-remove a worktree the user chose to keep. In after_close, delete only the ref, and only when no checkout holds it. If removal stays, include --ignored in the dirtiness check and treat a non-empty .relay/trash as dirty. Update the UI copy to say merged branches are cleaned up.

v1.reason: Close (session.rs:1547 onward) honours remove_worktree:false by skipping worktree::remove. Its after_commit then unconditionally calls branch_cleanup::after_close(engine, project_id, branch) (session.rs:1630-1636) for the just-closed branch, and the 20-minute sweeper (branch_cleanup.rs:429) reaches it later anyway. In evaluate, a pooled checkout of the branch that no open session owns becomes `removable` (234). For an agent with no commits, `merge-base --is-ancestor tip base` holds (246), so the branch counts as merged. status_files (worktree.rs:86-89) runs `git status --porcelain=v1 -z --untracked-files=all` without --ignored, and `.relay/` is in info/exclude (worktree.rs:40), so ignored content and the worktree's .relay/trash never count as dirty. evaluate then calls worktree::remove(repo, path, true) (307): purge_build followed by `git worktree remove --force`, then update-ref -d. The UI promises the opposite. agent_menu.rs:590 says 'the worktree and branch are kept unless you choose otherwise' and :609 says 'The branch is kept.'. shell.rs:724's 'Discard session' tooltip says 'its worktree and branch are kept' and sends remove_worktree:false. The module doc (branch_cleanup.rs:13-15) states that pooled-checkout removal is intended, but the user's explicit keep choice and the UI copy contradict it, and the dirtiness check misses ignored files.
v1.correction: It fires only when the branch is 'merged', but a session with zero commits always qualifies. This is the common case of a closed or discarded idle agent, as well as genuinely merged work. Lost data is limited to git-ignored or excluded content: build outputs, .env and local.properties, and .relay/trash payloads, whose file_trash rows become unrestorable. Medium is appropriate. The minimal fix is to skip worktree removal in the after_close path when the close passed remove_worktree:false, and to include --ignored (minus build dirs) or a non-empty .relay/trash in the dirtiness check.

findings.title: Worktree removal on session.close / project.remove / discard_restorable force-deletes uncommitted work with no dirty check, and session.close removes by default
findings.evidence: session.rs:1548 sets `let remove = p.remove_worktree.unwrap_or(true);`, and 1577-1579 call `worktree::remove(&repo, wt, p.purge_build.unwrap_or(true))` (git worktree remove --force) with no status check. DiscardRestorable does the same (1519-1523). project.remove with remove_worktrees queues the same removal after commit (workspace.rs:330-345). In the UI, the 'Also remove the worktree' checkbox (agent_menu.rs:594) sits under 'Stop this agent and close its pane? The branch is kept.' and gives no hint of uncommitted changes. By contrast, git.branch.switch (git.rs:411-432), the device primary sync (device.rs:1566-1571) and branch_cleanup (branch_cleanup.rs:295-301) all refuse a dirty checkout. BUS.md:733 documents the remove-by-default.
findings.impact: An agent that has not committed yet (crashed, interrupted or mid-task) loses all its edits and new files in three cases: the user ticks 'Also remove the worktree'; the user removes a project with 'Also delete agent worktrees'; or any bus client calls `session.close {session}` relying on the documented default.
findings.fix: In the prepare phases, run worktree::status_files on the checkout. Refuse with conflict `worktree.dirty` (details: count and sample paths) unless the caller passes an explicit `discard_changes: true`. Show the count in the confirm strip and dialog. Change remove_worktree's API default to false to match the UI.

v1.reason: session.rs Close prepare (1548, 1577-1579) and DiscardRestorable (1519-1523) call worktree::remove, which runs `git worktree remove --force` and falls back to remove_dir_all (worktree.rs:362-366), with no status_files check. branch_cleanup does refuse a dirty checkout (branch_cleanup.rs ~295-301). So the safety check exists elsewhere but is missing here, and uncommitted agent edits can be destroyed.
v1.correction: The trigger is narrower than claimed. session.close and discard_restorable are Actors::UserOnly (ops/session.rs:38-39), so agents cannot call them. The native client closes with remove_worktree false by default: the checkbox starts unticked (agent_menu.rs:594/612) and shell.rs:734 sends false. Native never calls session.discard_restorable. project.remove removes worktrees only when its dialog checkbox is ticked (registry.rs:627). Every removal therefore needs an explicit user opt-in. What is missing is a warning that the checkout holds N uncommitted changes, plus an API default (remove_worktree=true, BUS.md:733) that is riskier than the UI's. Low severity: add a dirty check that refuses with worktree.dirty unless discard_changes is set, and flip the API default.

findings.title: file.write replaces a symlink with a regular file; file.create and file.import follow a dangling symlink out of the worktree
findings.evidence: safe_join (file.rs:489-506) validates `fs::canonicalize(path)` but returns the unresolved `root.join(rel)`. Write reads through the link with `fs::read_to_string(&path)` (so expected_sha256 matches), then calls `fs::rename(&temp, &path)` (115), which replaces the link itself. For a dangling link, `path.exists()` is false, so safe_join only canonicalizes the parent. Create's `fs::write(&path, text)` (154) and Import's `fs::copy` (624) then open the link target wherever it points. The guardrail's write_target treats any relative path as InWorktree without resolving links (guardrail.rs:628-630). The Code tree treats symlinks as files and opens them in the editor (editor.rs:748).
findings.impact: Editing a symlinked file such as CLAUDE.md -> AGENTS.md in the editor and saving turns CLAUDE.md into an independent copy. AGENTS.md keeps the old text, so Codex agents read stale instructions, and git shows a typechange the user may commit. Separately, an agent (file.create is on its MCP surface) can plant a dangling link and make Relay write a file outside every write root.
findings.fix: Use symlink_metadata in safe_join. Either refuse symlinks for write/create/import, or operate on the canonical target (temp file in the target's directory, renamed onto the target). Open new files with create_new(true) and O_NOFOLLOW.

v1.reason: safe_join (file.rs:489-505) canonicalizes to check containment but returns the unresolved root.join(rel). Write (file.rs:72-115) reads the old text through the link with fs::read_to_string(&path), so expected_sha256 matches, then calls fs::rename(&temp, &path). rename replaces the symlink itself, so saving a symlinked file (CLAUDE.md -> AGENTS.md) in the editor turns it into an independent regular file and leaves the target stale. entry() reports symlinks as EntryKind::Symlink (file.rs:539), and the editor treats any non-'dir' kind as a file it can open (editor.rs:748-753). For a dangling link, path.exists() is false, so safe_join canonicalizes only the parent, which passes. Create (file.rs:128-154) then runs fs::write(&path, text), which follows the link and creates the target outside the worktree. Import's copy (file.rs:284-293, then fs::copy at ~624) follows a dangling dest the same way. guardrail write_target (guardrail.rs:628-630) maps any relative path to InWorktree without resolving links.
v1.correction: The escape only creates new files: an existing outside target canonicalizes outside root and is rejected, and Create refuses existing paths. Import is Actors::UserOnly, so only file.create is agent-reachable. An agent that can run `ln -s` can usually write outside the worktree through its shell directly, and the same unresolved-symlink gap applies to the provider's native Write tool through the hook guardrail. The escape is therefore a secondary guardrail weakness, and the symlink-clobber on save is the main user-visible bug. Medium is correct.

findings.title: The v3 import copies attachments to attachments/<task>/<original_name>, so same-named attachments overwrite each other; note tags are silently dropped
findings.evidence: import_v3.rs:260-265 does `let dest = dest_dir.join(&name); std::fs::copy(&src, &dest).bus()?;` and then inserts a row pointing at `dest`. v3 allowed several attachments with the same original_name on one task. Its store prefixes each stored file with a counter (`.relay/attachments/<slug>/<n>-<name>`, add_attachment_bytes), its own test attaches the same file twice, and pasted images arrive under the webview's name (typically image.png). v4's attach_bytes avoids the collision with `{id}-{name}` (task.rs:523). v3 notes.json entries carry `tags`, but the importer reads only title/body/pinned/created_at/updated_at (283-289) and does not warn about the rest.
findings.impact: Importing a v3 task with two pasted screenshots that share a name leaves two v4 attachment rows pointing at one file that holds only the second image. The first image is lost once the v3 .relay/ folder is cleaned up. Every note's tags disappear without a warning. The import is one-time (import.already_done), so it cannot simply be redone.
findings.fix: Insert the attachment row first and copy to `{row_id}-{sanitized name}`, as attach_bytes does, or disambiguate when dest already exists. Fold tags into the note body (e.g. a 'Tags:' line), or emit a warning for each note that has tags.

v1.reason: import_v3.rs:259-264: `let dest_dir = attach_root.join(new_id.to_string()); ... let dest = dest_dir.join(&name); std::fs::copy(&src, &dest)` with `name` = the v3 `original_name` column (query at 239). Nothing makes dest unique, so two v3 attachment rows on one task with the same original_name end up as two v4 rows pointing at one file that holds only the last copy. v3 stores `path` and `original_name` as separate columns (schema in tests/store.rs:98), so it clearly allowed duplicate display names. The import is one-time (import.already_done, 143), so the result cannot be redone in place. Notes: lines 283-289 read only id/title/body/pinned/created_at/updated_at and emit no warning for any other field.
v1.correction: The v3 source is not in this repository, so I could not check the claims about v3's `<n>-<name>` storage scheme or that notes.json carries `tags`. The overwrite follows from the v4 code alone. Treat the tags loss as unverified. The v3 source files survive until the user deletes the old .relay/, which limits the impact. A related problem: `name` comes from the v3 DB and is joined without sanitising, so a name containing '/' or an absolute path is written outside dest_dir. The fix should both disambiguate (`{row_id}-{sanitized basename}`) and sanitise the name.

findings.title: Crash recovery kills whatever process now holds a stored session PID, and its process group, without checking it is a Relay child
findings.evidence: recovery.rs:84-93 handles every session row still in spawning/running/idle/blocked with `Some(p) if pty::pid_alive(p as u32) => { kill_wait(p as u32); ... }`. pid_alive is only `kill(pid, 0) == 0` (pty.rs:394-396), and kill_wait (20-35) sends SIGTERM and then SIGKILL to both `-(pid)` and `pid`. Step 1 already reaps real orphans, identified by /proc environ (RELAY_INSTANCE, RELAY_STORE, RELAY_SESSION; pty.rs:411-428). So any process step 2 still finds alive is not identified as a Relay child.
findings.impact: Rows stay 'running' only after an unclean stop (power loss, kernel panic, OOM-kill, kill -9). On the next start, often right after login when PIDs again fall in the range the previous boot's agents used, any unrelated process that received one of those PIDs is terminated. That could be an editor, a browser, a game, or a group leader such as a shell together with its jobs, and its unsaved work is lost.
findings.fix: Before killing, verify identity the way step 1 does (environ carries this RELAY_SESSION/RELAY_INSTANCE/RELAY_STORE), or compare /proc/<pid>/stat start time with the row's spawned_at. Otherwise only mark the row restorable.

v1.reason: recovery.rs:76-99, step 2, kills every stored session pid that `pty::pid_alive` reports alive. That check is only `kill(pid,0)==0` (pty.rs:394). kill_wait (recovery.rs:20-35) sends SIGTERM and then SIGKILL to both `-pid` (the process group) and `pid`. Step 1 (recovery.rs:66-74) has already reaped every process whose /proc environ carries this instance's RELAY_INSTANCE, RELAY_STORE and RELAY_SESSION (pty.rs:411-428). So whatever step 2 still finds alive is, by construction, not identified as a Relay child. A clean shutdown marks sessions restorable with pid=NULL (engine.rs:676), so step 2 only matters after an unclean stop: a crash, SIGKILL, OOM-kill or power loss. After that, a same-uid process that has reused one of those PIDs is terminated, together with its process group if it is a group leader. kill(pid,0) fails with EPERM for processes owned by another uid, so only the user's own processes are at risk.
v1.correction: The trigger needs an unclean engine stop followed by a PID collision with a same-uid process. That is uncommon but realistic after a reboot, when processes started at login reuse similar PID ranges. The fix is to drop the kill in step 2, or to gate it on the same environ identity check step 1 uses, or on a /proc/<pid>/stat start time compared with the row. Then the row is just marked restorable.

findings.title: BUS.md promises soft-deleted rows and trash are purged after undo.grace_days; nothing implements it, so .relay/trash and deleted rows grow forever
findings.evidence: BUS.md:288-291 says soft-deleted items are 'restorable by *.restore for the grace window (settings: undo.grace_days, default 7), then hard-deleted by the reconcile pass'. app.reconcile is a no-op (handlers/app.rs:137-141: 'Phase 1 has nothing to verify yet'). recovery.rs prunes only audit rows. `undo.grace_days` appears in the settings defaults (settings.rs:42) and is read nowhere.
findings.impact: Every file deleted through Relay keeps its full bytes in .relay/trash indefinitely, so trashing a large asset folder never frees disk. The setting the user can change does nothing. Anyone relying on the doc expects deleted data to disappear after 7 days.
findings.fix: Either implement the purge (in recovery, remove file_trash payloads and hard-delete soft-deleted task/note/module rows older than grace_days, keeping undo pairs consistent), or change §5.4 to say trash is kept until removed and drop the dead setting.

v1.reason: BUS.md:286-291 (§5.4) says soft-deleted task/module/note/file/session rows are restorable for `undo.grace_days` (default 7) and then hard-deleted by the reconcile pass. app.reconcile (handlers/app.rs:137-141) returns an empty action list, with the comment 'Phase 1 has nothing to verify yet'. `undo.grace_days` appears only in the settings defaults (settings.rs:42) and in two tests (tests/bus.rs:729, 786). No engine code reads it. Recovery prunes only audit rows (recovery.rs:196) and closed sessions' claims (156). Every file_trash write is in handlers/file.rs. file.delete (226-236) moves the file to `<root>/.relay/trash/<id>/payload`, and file.restore (241-249) has no age check. The only thing that deletes trash is workspace removal, which deletes file_trash rows (workspace.rs:369) and nothing else. The native client and the CLI never purge it either. So trashed bytes and soft-deleted rows are kept forever, and the documented setting does nothing.
v1.correction: The real effect is the reverse of data loss: deleted data is kept longer than the doc says. Restore works with no time limit, and disk use from .relay/trash only grows. For worktree sessions the trash lives under the worktree root, so removing the worktree removes it; growth is confined to project roots that are kept. Also note that workspace.rs:369 deletes file_trash rows but leaves the `.relay/trash` payload directories on disk, which are then orphaned. Fix: either add a grace-window purge (for example in recovery or reconcile, outside the store mutex for the filesystem removal), or rewrite §5.4 to say trash is kept until removed and drop `undo.grace_days`.

findings.title: Unreal ini merges treat any read error as an empty file and then overwrite the whole ini
findings.evidence: unreal.rs:706-711 does `let text = std::fs::read_to_string(&path).unwrap_or_default(); let merged = merge_ini(&text, ...); if merged != text { ... std::fs::write(&path, &merged)?; }`. The same pattern appears at 739-743 for Config/DefaultEditorPerProjectUserSettings.ini (always in the list), and at 641-645 for Saved/Config/<Platform>Editor/EditorPerProjectUserSettings.ini on every editor launch. read_to_string fails on non-UTF-8 content (an ini saved as Latin-1 or UTF-16 by another tool) and on permission errors, and the write is non-atomic. The local UE 5.8 build writes UTF-8, so the trigger is a file edited or produced elsewhere.
findings.impact: Running setup_check with fix, or launching the editor, on a project whose ini is not valid UTF-8 replaces that file with a single Relay section. That wipes the project's committed config or the user's per-project editor settings. A crash mid-write truncates the file.
findings.fix: Treat only ErrorKind::NotFound as empty, and propagate (or skip the file on) any other error. Write via a temp file plus rename.

v1.reason: All three locations use read_to_string(...).unwrap_or_default(): unreal.rs:641 (launch, Saved/Config/<Platform>Editor/EditorPerProjectUserSettings.ini), 706 (Config/DefaultRemoteControl.ini) and 739 (the write_editor_settings_ini loop). Each then merges and writes the result with a plain fs::write whenever it differs. A non-UTF-8 file reads as empty, merge_ini returns only the Relay section, and that overwrites the file. The trigger is more realistic than the finding suggests. Unreal's FFileHelper::SaveStringToFile in AutoDetect mode writes UTF-16LE with a BOM whenever the text contains non-ANSI characters, so a per-user Saved ini holding a non-ASCII path or string is exactly the file that gets replaced on the next ue launch. The write_editor_settings_ini loop is partly guarded, because it only adds Saved files that read successfully. Config/Default*.ini is normally committed and ASCII, which leaves the launch path at 641 as the main exposure.
v1.correction: The main risk is unreal.rs:641 in the editor-launch path. The Saved per-user settings it can wipe are not under git, unlike Config/Default*.ini. A fuller fix also decodes UTF-16 BOM files and writes back in the original encoding, rather than only skipping on error.

findings.title: remote.json is read-modify-written by concurrent bridges and CLI commands through one fixed temp name with no lock
findings.evidence: registry.rs:165-177 writes through `let tmp = path.with_extension("json.tmp")`, opened with truncate(true), then renames it over remote.json. bridge.rs:72-94 does load → redeem/touch → save for every connection, on whichever tokio worker runs it. `relay remote pair` and `relay remote revoke` (remote.rs:226-229, 253-257) do the same from another process. Nothing serialises these cycles.
findings.impact: Two admissions at once (e.g. two lanes opening together), or an admission racing `relay remote revoke`, can drop an update. A newly paired device's token can be lost, or a revocation undone so the revoked phone keeps working. The two writers can also interleave in the shared temp file, leaving remote.json unparsable so the door refuses every phone.
findings.fix: Write through a unique temp file in the same directory, and hold an flock on a sidecar lock file across load-modify-save. Alternatively, route CLI mutations through the serving process.

v1.reason: registry.rs:159-177 `save` always writes through the fixed `path.with_extension("json.tmp")`, opened with create+truncate, then renames it over remote.json. bridge.rs:68-95 `admit` does Registry::load (72), redeem or touch, then save (94). It is called from `run` (bridge.rs:137) for every connection, both direct and tunnel lanes (tunnel.rs:137 spawns a task per lane), with no mutex around it. relay-cli/src/remote.rs does the same load/modify/save from a separate process for pair (226-229), revoke (253-257), name and rendezvous config (262-287). Nothing in relay-remote or the CLI takes a lock: rg finds no flock and no registry mutex. So the lost-update and torn-temp-file interleavings are real. The window is narrow, though. Each cycle is synchronous with no await between load and save, so it lasts well under a millisecond, and the trigger needs two admissions, or an admission and a CLI mutation, in that same instant. Most such overlaps are two `touch` calls, where only last_seen is lost and nothing breaks. The harmful cases are rarer: a just-redeemed pairing dropped, a revoke undone, or remote.json torn so that Registry::load fails and the door refuses every phone until the file is fixed. The bad outcomes are real, which puts it at low rather than lower.
v1.correction: Mechanism as stated. The realistic consequence is mostly a lost last_seen. A revoked device being re-added needs the revoke to land inside one admission's sub-millisecond load-save window. If the file is torn, load returns an error (registry.rs:146-151 refuses to reset), so the door stays down until someone fixes the file by hand. Fix: write each save through a unique temp file in the same directory (e.g. tempfile::NamedTempFile::persist), and hold an flock on a sidecar `remote.json.lock` around each load-modify-save, in both bridge::admit and the CLI commands. Separately, admit does blocking file I/O on a tokio worker, which is minor.

findings.title: install_codex rewrites the repository's .codex/hooks.json even when it is tracked, so agents can commit machine-specific Relay hooks
findings.evidence: hooks.rs:494-548 parses `<worktree>/.codex/hooks.json`, appends handlers whose command is the absolute local relay path with `--instance <name>`, and renames a re-serialised copy over the file. uninstall_codex (553-573) re-serialises it again. ensure_excluded adds `.codex/hooks.json` to info/exclude (worktree.rs:40), which has no effect on a tracked file. Confidence is low because it depends on whether the user's repositories commit a project-level hooks file.
findings.impact: In a repository that commits a project-level .codex/hooks.json, every Codex session leaves the file modified. An agent's `git add -A` then commits Relay's absolute paths and instance name into the shared hooks file, and the hook fails closed for teammates. Even after uninstall, the file differs from HEAD in key order and formatting.
findings.fix: Skip the project layer when the file is tracked (git ls-files --error-unmatch), and inject Relay's hooks through an untracked or per-launch layer. Restore the original bytes when nothing Relay-owned remains.

v1.reason: hooks.rs:494-548 reads `<worktree>/.codex/hooks.json` if it exists, appends Relay handlers containing the absolute relay binary path and `--instance <name>`, and renames a re-serialized copy over it. uninstall_codex (hooks.rs:553-573) re-serializes again and leaves behind any arrays or keys Relay created. ensure_excluded adds `.codex/hooks.json` to info/exclude (worktree.rs:40), but exclude has no effect on a tracked file. So in a repository that commits a project-level `.codex/hooks.json`, every Codex session leaves it modified. An agent's `git add -A` then commits machine-specific Relay commands.
v1.correction: The workspace enables serde_json `preserve_order` (Cargo.toml:18), so key order is preserved. After uninstall, only whitespace or formatting and any empty containers Relay added differ from HEAD. The trigger needs a tracked `.codex/hooks.json`, which is rare, so the rating stays low. Fix: skip the project layer, or restore the original bytes, when `git ls-files --error-unmatch .codex/hooks.json` succeeds.

findings.title: Branch cleanup fails open when `git worktree list` fails and can delete a branch that is checked out
findings.evidence: branch_cleanup.rs:140 has `let Ok(ran) = git.run(&["worktree","list","--porcelain"], GIT_TIMEOUT) else { return Vec::new() };`, and `ran.ok` is never checked. A timeout or git error therefore reads as 'checked out nowhere', and evaluate skips the primary, outside-pool and live-session checks (222-235). It then runs `update-ref -d refs/heads/<branch> <tip>` (314), which, unlike `git branch -d`, does not refuse a checked-out branch.
findings.impact: On a slow or locked repository, the sweep can delete the branch currently checked out in the primary checkout or in one of the user's own linked worktrees. HEAD then points at a missing ref, and git shows every file as newly staged until the branch is recreated.
findings.fix: Return a Result from checkouts, and keep the branch ('could not list worktrees') on any failure or non-zero exit.

v1.reason: branch_cleanup.rs:140 is `let Ok(ran) = git.run(&["worktree","list","--porcelain"], GIT_TIMEOUT) else { return Vec::new() };`, and ran.ok is never checked. A timeout, spawn failure or non-zero exit therefore yields no checkouts. evaluate (223-235) then skips the primary, live-session and outside-pool refusals, leaves removable as None, and goes on to `update-ref -d refs/heads/<branch> <tip>` (314), which git performs even for a branch checked out in a worktree. Candidates are closed sessions' branches. A user who checked one out in the primary checkout, or who has a live checkout outside the pool, is protected only by this list. The trigger needs worktree list to fail while the rev-parse, merge-base and update-ref calls around it succeed, which is rare: a transient 20 s timeout on a busy repo, or a lock.
v1.correction: Low severity is right because the trigger is rare. Fix it by returning Result from checkouts and treating Err, or !ran.ok, as 'kept: could not list worktrees'.

findings.title: Agent task and note writes have no optimistic check, so an agent silently overwrites a newer user edit
findings.evidence: task.update applies `expected` only when the caller supplies it (task.rs:871-881), and agents may write body/changelog (868-870). task.changelog.write has no expected at all (965-981). notes.update is the same (notes.rs:379-389), and the default 'docs' role may call it (settings.rs:38). The UI always sends `expected` (task_pages.rs:219, note_pages/doc.rs:1133), so it never clobbers an agent's edit. The reverse is unchecked, and the board's undo lists only the user's own rows (board_view.rs:882).
findings.impact: Suppose an agent reads a task body or note, the user then saves an edit, and the agent writes afterwards. The user's text is replaced with no conflict. The user's version survives only in the audit row's undo_op, reachable through audit.undo from the CLI.
findings.fix: Require `expected` (or an expected updated_at) for agent writes of task body/changelog and notes, and return task.edit_conflict otherwise. Add `expected` to task.changelog.write.

v1.reason: task.rs Update (~867-890) checks `expected` only when the caller supplies it. Agents may update body and changelog, since the guard only forbids title, priority and the other fields. ChangelogWrite (~965-981) overwrites the changelog with no expected-value check at all. notes.rs Update (376-389) is the same, and the docs role may call notes.update (settings.rs:38). If an agent reads, the user saves, and the agent then writes, the user's edit is replaced with no conflict. The old value survives only in the audit undo payload (set_undo).
v1.correction: The impact is limited: the previous text is recoverable through audit.undo, and only a race between a user edit and an agent write triggers it. A cheaper fix than requiring `expected` on every agent write: have agent task.update and changelog.write refuse when the row's updated_at is newer than the agent's last read, or accept an `expected` on changelog.write and have the MCP tool descriptions ask agents to send it.

results.coverage:
Search patterns (rg over apps/relay-native/src): block_on|recv_blocking|send_blocking|thread::sleep|spawn_blocking|Command::new|.output()|.status()|.spawn(); std::fs::*|from_file|Texture::from_bytes|Pixbuf::from|Svg::from_bytes|save_to_png; timeout_add*|idle_add*|timeout_future|SourceId|.remove()|add_tick_callback|ControlFlow; thread::spawn|spawn_future_local|rt.spawn; borrow()/borrow_mut() together with .await; overlapping borrow and borrow_mut in one expression; for/if-let/match scrutinees that hold RefCell borrows across their bodies; connect_* on self./ui./struct-field receivers (for handlers re-connected on refresh); strong `.clone()` of popover/panel/form/revealer/container widgets moved into signal closures; set_create_popup_func; unwrap/expect outside #[cfg(test)]. I checked the toolkit behavior that the severities rely on in the registry sources. gtk4 0.11.4 signal trampolines are `extern \"C\"` with no catch_unwind (panic = abort), glib 0.22.9 TaskSource::poll catches panics in spawned futures, and glib SourceId::remove unwraps g_source_remove. Every stored-SourceId site (wallpaper rotation, notes persist, doc autosave/count, usage timer, image hover) clears its id before the source finishes, so none can double-remove.

No synchronous bus request exists: every ui.call/Client::request is awaited inside glib futures on the tokio runtime. Background tokio/blocking tasks (mirror decode, sounds, image decode, wallpaper import) touch only gdk-pixbuf/bytes, not widgets. The terminal feed loop yields every 64 KiB, and attach catch-up is bounded at 256 KiB by the engine.

Read fully or substantially: client.rs, terminal.rs, app.rs, panel.rs, editor.rs, project_files.rs, image_preview.rs, code_git.rs (1-1666), shell.rs, shell/registry.rs 1-560, agent_menu.rs, guardrail_pages.rs, notification_center.rs, session_context.rs, status.rs, status_usage.rs 220-849, wallpaper_rotation.rs, notes_window.rs, pages.rs, tools.rs, mirror.rs 1-60 and 460-1245, mirror/decode.rs, sounds.rs, provider_updates.rs, launch.rs 340-836, board_view.rs 470-810 and 1181-2300, tools_market.rs 400-700, tools_settings.rs 1-560 and 770-1031, onboarding.rs 60-330, guardrail_settings.rs 280-420 and 590-673, icons.rs, fonts.rs. So I cannot rule out more sibling-capture cycles in the unread or partly read parts. Smoke files (smoke*.rs, roadmap_smoke.rs) run blocking std::process/std::fs on the GTK thread, but they are opt-in test harnesses gated on RELAY_NATIVE_SCREENSHOT, so they are not reported. The GTK C behavior I relied on (MenuButton dispose only unparents its popover; unparent does not dispose) comes from GTK4 semantics and was not checked against C sources.
