Findings 4 and part of 3 reach into engine code because the UI-triggered path ends there; the user asked for a full audit. Outside this lens, I noticed that device.run (crates/relay-core/src/handlers/device.rs:140) is registered with Engine::register and calls require_device → `adb devices -l` (list_with_adb, ADB_LIST_TIMEOUT 2 s) while holding the store mutex. That looks like a breach of the CLAUDE.md register_staged rule; engine auditors should confirm it.

findings.title: Exception-prompt queue panics with BorrowMutError when a prompt closes while a 4th request waits; this aborts the client or kills its event loop
findings.evidence: `if let Some(next) = WAITING.with(|w| (!w.borrow().is_empty()).then(|| w.borrow_mut().remove(0))) {`. The `Ref` from `w.borrow()` is a temporary in the closure's tail expression. It lives until the closure returns, so the `w.borrow_mut()` inside `then` runs while that shared borrow is still live. It panics whenever WAITING is non-empty. WAITING fills once the tray holds TRAY_LIMIT = 3 prompts (line 17; show_prompt pushes extra requests at 573-579). Callers: (1) the 'Answer later' key calls it directly in a clicked handler (457-461). gtk4 0.11.4's `clicked_trampoline` is `unsafe extern "C"` with no catch_unwind, so the panic aborts the process. (2) guardrail_event → close_prompt (689-691) runs synchronously inside the Ui::connect notice loop (app.rs:1201-1203). glib 0.22.9 TaskSource::poll wraps the future in catch_unwind, so that future silently ends. (3) The approve, deny and restore futures (479, 382, 711).
findings.impact: Needs 4 or more open exception requests at once (likely with many agents). Then: clicking X on a prompt crashes the whole desktop client. If a request is answered elsewhere (phone, CLI) or expires, the `guardrail.resolved` event panics the main notice-loop future. Its notices Receiver is dropped, so the reader task sees a closed channel. Every pending and later `ui.call` then fails with 'Connection closed' while `connected` stays true. The wall, prompts and notifications stop updating until a manual reconnect. Approving or denying from a prompt panics that future instead: the waiting request is never shown and the confirmation/refresh are skipped. After a reconnect, restore_prompts can panic the same way before re-showing prompts.
findings.fix: Take the value in one mutable borrow: `let next = WAITING.with(|w| { let mut w = w.borrow_mut(); (!w.is_empty()).then(|| w.remove(0)) }); if let Some(next) = next { show_prompt(ui, &next); }`

v1.reason: guardrail_pages.rs:666 `WAITING.with(|w| (!w.borrow().is_empty()).then(|| w.borrow_mut().remove(0)))`. The `Ref` from `w.borrow()` is a temporary in the receiver of `.then(...)`. A unary `!` does not end a temporary scope, so the Ref lives for the whole full expression, including the `then` closure. Its `borrow_mut()` therefore panics whenever WAITING is non-empty. The workspace is on edition 2021 (Cargo.toml:9), and edition 2024 would not change this. The line runs only when `removed` is true, meaning a tray prompt was taken down, and WAITING fills once the tray holds TRAY_LIMIT=3 (lines 16, 573-579). So with 4 or more open requests, closing any tray prompt panics. Reachable callers: (a) the 'Answer later' clicked handler (457-461), a GTK signal trampoline (extern "C"), so the panic aborts the client; (b) guardrail_event's `guardrail.resolved` arm (689-691), called synchronously from the notice loop (app.rs:1201-1203). glib 0.22.9 TaskSource::poll (main_context_futures.rs:262-276) catches the panic and ends that future, so the notice loop dies and its Receiver drops; (c) the confirm, reject and restore futures (479, 382, 711). The engine emits `guardrail.resolved` with hold_id on every confirm or reject (handlers/guardrail.rs:595, 656, 747). So simply approving a prompt in the UI while a 4th request waits panics whichever of the reply future or the event loop reaches close_prompt first.
v1.correction: Worse than stated: an ordinary Approve/Deny from a prompt is enough to trigger it once 4+ requests are open, because the engine's own guardrail.resolved event re-enters close_prompt. If the event arrives first, the main notice loop is killed (the UI stops receiving events and later calls fail, while `connected` stays true). The proposed fix, a single borrow_mut, is correct.

v2.reason:
(a) Confirmed. guardrail_pages.rs:666 is `WAITING.with(|w| (!w.borrow().is_empty()).then(|| w.borrow_mut().remove(0)))`. The closure body is an expression, not a block, so the temporary `Ref` from `w.borrow()` lives until the whole closure body ends. `!`, the parentheses and a method receiver do not end a temporary scope. So the `borrow_mut()` inside `then` runs while the Ref is still live and panics with "already borrowed". This holds in edition 2021 (Cargo.toml:9) and in 2024. RefCell does not poison, so the unwind just drops the Ref. The line came in with 4f62e33 one day ago, and no smoke test touches the tray.

(b) Reachable. close_prompt reaches 666 only when a live `guardrail-request-{id}` slot was retired. WAITING is non-empty once a request arrives while 3 prompts show (TRAY_LIMIT at line 17; show_prompt 573-579). Requests come from agents. By default each refused agent is told to call guardrail.request (providers.rs:51, grants.rs:24 and :360), and one session may hold several open requests (grants::existing is keyed on session, kind and value). So 4 or more undismissed open requests is a normal state with many agents, for example when the user steps away. Line 666 is the only way a waiting prompt reaches the tray, and it always panics. So once WAITING is non-empty, every later close of a tray prompt panics, even after fewer than 4 remain open. DISMISSED is in-memory, so after a relaunch all open requests are shown again and the state comes back.

(c) What happens when it fires:
- The X button ("Answer later") is a gtk::Button (app.rs:46). gtk4 0.11.4's clicked_trampoline is `unsafe extern "C"` (button.rs:514), and the toolchain is rustc 1.98.1 with panic=unwind. So the panic aborts the desktop client, and unsaved in-app editor buffers and task drafts are lost (in-memory only). The engine and agents survive (run.sh:45).
- Approve, Deny, or resolution from the phone or CLI, whether answered from the prompt or the Guardrails page (same handlers): engine confirm and reject emit guardrail.resolved with hold_id (guardrail.rs:439, 747). That event is broadcast inside dispatch (engine.rs:1027-1029), before handle_conn queues the response, which waits on spawn_blocking (socket.rs:741-743). So the notice loop usually reaches close_prompt first (app.rs:1201-1203). glib 0.22.9 catches the panic (main_context_futures.rs:262-276) and drops the future. The async-channel Receiver drops and the channel closes (lib.rs:609-610). Every later ui.call then fails at client.rs:309 with "Connection closed. Reconnect to the engine." while `connected` stays true. The wall, notifications and prompts stop updating until the user clicks Reconnect. If the response wins the race, the reply future panics instead: no confirmation, no refresh, and nothing is promoted from the queue.
- Session close emits an expired event with no hold_id (session.rs:1620). The restore_prompts future then panics at 711 and leaves stale prompts up.
- The approval itself is committed in the engine first, so engine data is not affected.

(d) High fits: a client crash and a dead event loop in a normal flow. It is not critical: the engine and sessions survive and engine data is intact.

(e) The fix is correct and complete. One borrow_mut takes the value, and the RefMut is dropped before show_prompt re-borrows WAITING (574, 584). It compiles under 2021: no temporary with a Drop impl borrows the local. No other double borrow exists in this module.
v2.correction: TRAY_LIMIT is defined at line 17 (line 16 is its doc comment). Precondition: 4 or more undismissed open requests are needed only to fill WAITING the first time. After that, any close of a tray prompt panics until the waiting request is answered elsewhere or pruned by restore_prompts. A relaunch shows every open request again, because DISMISSED is in-memory. The approve/deny path most often kills the notice loop rather than the reply future, because the engine broadcasts guardrail.resolved before it queues the response. That outcome is recoverable with the Reconnect button (app.rs:970-974). Terminal panes keep working because each has its own connection (terminal.rs:476). An in-flight call whose response arrives before the next event still succeeds; only later calls fail at client.rs:309. The X-button abort also loses unsaved editor buffers and task drafts. findings.title: Signal closures hold strong refs into their own widget trees, so each Git refresh and sidebar rebuild leaks the old branch picker, merge-test rows and project/workspace menus
findings.evidence: render_branch_picker builds a cycle between two widgets. 997 `let query = search.clone();` feeds 999 `create_key.connect_clicked(move |_| { ... reveal(form) ... query ... })`. 1195 `let create = create_key.clone();` feeds 1196 `search.connect_activate(move |_| { first(entries)... create.emit_clicked() })`. So search ↔ create_key reference each other, and `entries` keeps every branch row and key alive. The merge-test section has a second cycle: each `pick.connect_toggled` holds `test` (700-701), and `test.connect_clicked` owns `picks` (719). refresh_git runs `clear(&e.git)` (170) and builds a fresh picker (779) on every call. GTK only unparents removed children and never disposes an object whose refcount stays above zero, so the closures are never freed. The same mistake appears in shell/registry.rs:506: each menu key captures `popover.clone()`, and the MenuButton's dispose only unparents its popover. The sidebar is cleared and rebuilt (registry.rs:133-137) whenever its signature changes; the signature includes every session's state (127-132) and the filter text. Other sites: agent_menu.rs 451, 541, 578 and 608 (the popover is captured by its own keys and is only unparented on close, 371-374); agent_menu.rs:835 (revealer ↔ cancel); task_pages.rs:490-497 (`create` owns its ancestor `form` and the Rc<Panel>, whose guard holds more of the form).
findings.impact: refresh_git runs on every navigation to Agents (app.rs:1350-1351 → project_files.rs:63-67), after every save or git action, and up to once a second from Editor::invalidate while agents change files. Each run strands one search entry, the create form, one row per local and remote branch (about 8-10 widgets each; about 200+ widgets for this repo's 21 local branches), and one CheckButton group per live session. Each sidebar rebuild (every agent running↔idle↔blocked flip, every filter keystroke) strands one popover of about 15 widgets per workspace header and visible project row. Agent-settings and New-task panels leak once per open. Memory grows without bound for the life of the window (sizes estimated, not measured).
findings.fix: Capture weak references, as the same files already do elsewhere (code_git.rs:1021 `popover.downgrade()`, project_files.rs:135). Use `search.downgrade()` (or `create_key.downgrade()`) in one of the two handlers, `test.downgrade()` in the pick toggles, `popover.downgrade()` in registry_menu and agent_settings_body, `revealer.downgrade()` in confirm_strip, and `form.downgrade()` / `Rc::downgrade(&panel)` in the task composer. glib::clone!(#[weak] ...) makes this systematic.

findings.title: Every file/git/worktree event re-fetches and rebuilds the hidden Files tree and Git panel, including a paginated `gh api` call, up to once a second while agents work
findings.evidence: `if matches!(ui.page.borrow().as_str(), "code" | "agents") && !self.invalidate_pending.replace(true)` arms a 1000 ms timer (514). The timer runs load_tree or run_search, then refresh_git and refresh_scopes (519-525), with no check of `file_sidebar.is_visible()` or `git.is_visible()`, although both start hidden (299-300). navigate() never stores "code" (app.rs:1314-1315), so the gate reduces to 'the default Agents page'. Routing is at app.rs:1232-1240. Each refresh_git sends git.status (code_git.rs:159), then git.branches, git.log, integration.list and git.pr.list together (578-583). The engine serves git.pr.list with `gh api --paginate --slurp repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls?state=all&per_page=100` and no cache (crates/relay-core/src/handlers/git.rs:625-628, 1083-1094). load_tree re-requests file.tree for the current directory and for every expanded folder (editor.rs:575-582, 866-867 → 841-842). Each of those runs `git status --porcelain=v1 -z --untracked-files=all` (file.rs:30-31 → worktree.rs:86-89). The watcher emits file.changed for a watched root at most every 125 ms while files change (watch.rs:113-129).
findings.impact: With panels hidden, sustained activity in a watched root of the current project (main checkout, the user's own saves, any worktree once listed/read through the bus, git.changed/worktree.changed) triggers about one refresh per 1-2 s. Each refresh costs: (a) 2+N full git status scans in the engine; (b) one GitHub REST call per page of PRs, roughly 1,800-3,600 calls/hour/page against the 5,000/hour token budget that agents' own `gh` use shares; (c) a main-thread rebuild of the whole tree (about 8 widgets + 3-5 controllers per entry; list_dir is uncapped) and the Git panel (one change_row per file at code_git.rs:488; untracked=all lists every untracked file). That is hundreds of ms per refresh for a few thousand entries, plus a finding-2 leak each time. With the Git panel open, each refresh destroys it (clear at 170): scroll resets, an open branch picker or commit menu closes, and the commit-message TextView is unparented and re-parented (297-311) without grab_focus. A user typing a commit message while agents work loses keyboard focus.
findings.fix: Refresh only what is shown. Reload the tree only if `file_sidebar.is_visible()` and git only if `git.is_visible()`; otherwise set dirty flags that toggle_files/toggle_git/show_files consume. Ignore events whose `payload.worktree` is not the editor's scope. Take git.pr.list out of the automatic refresh (fetch it on panel open or explicit Refresh, or add an engine-side TTL cache). Cap rendered rows (e.g. the first 500 plus 'N more') or use a virtualized ListView. Keep the panel's persistent widgets (scroller, commit box, pickers) across refreshes, or restore focus and scroll.

v1.reason: Editor::invalidate (editor.rs:508-529) arms a 1 s timer whenever the page is 'agents' (navigate maps 'code' to 'agents', app.rs:1314-1315). The notice loop routes file.changed, git.changed, worktree.changed, integration.changed and integration.result for the current project to invalidate (app.rs:1213-1240). refresh_git (code_git.rs:142-170) has no visibility check. It sends git.status, then git.branches, git.log, integration.list and git.pr.list together (578-583). The engine's PrList (handlers/git.rs:625-628) runs `gh api --paginate --slurp .../pulls?state=all` (1083-1095) on every call, with no cache. Watchers are registered for any root, including worktrees, touched by git/file handlers (git.rs:164, file.rs:21/41/301) and emit file.changed at most every 125 ms (watch.rs:113-129). So sustained agent activity drives roughly one full tree, Git and GitHub refresh every 1-2 s on the default page. With the Git panel open, clear(&e.git) plus detach(&message) (code_git.rs:170, 297) unparents the focused commit TextView's ancestors, and nothing restores focus (no grab_focus on that path apart from line 387). So the cursor is lost while typing a commit message.
v1.correction: The GitHub rate-limit figures assume continuous activity and are upper-bound estimates. Every one of these refreshes also adds to the #2 leak, which compounds both. - Each refresh runs 2+N git status scans and one GitHub REST call per page of PRs, against D130.

- Give watcher events a project, either by emitting them with in_project or by filtering on payload.project_id.

- Keep refreshing on primary-root ref events and on worktree.changed, because the branch and PR labels depend on them.

v2.correction:

About one refresh a second needs a watched root that keeps changing. Examples: a worktree the user has browsed, one the phone has read, or one an agent has queried through relay tools; a "primary" session; or untracked churn such as __pycache__ or .venv. The GitHub rate-limit figures are upper bounds. Running out needs sustained churn and a repo with more than about 150 PRs, since state=all pages through every PR the repo has ever had.

Each refresh's git.pr.list and status scans block every other UI request on the single, strictly in-order UI socket (crates/relay-core/src/socket.rs:334; apps/relay-native/src/app.rs:1111-1116; apps/relay-native/src/client.rs:136). The result is app-wide sluggishness while agents work; terminals are not affected.

5. Related symptom: the "Files changed on disk" error (editor.rs:530-532) appears on every such event while an open document is modified, including events from unrelated projects or worktrees.

Additional references:
- docs/engine/DECISIONS.md:427-434 (D97) and :635-640 (D130).
- The expanded-folder re-fetch is at editor.rs:826-842.

findings.title: Any bus response over 2 MiB tears down the UI's whole control connection; opening the diff of a modified binary or ~1 MiB file in the Git panel triggers it
findings.evidence: `if line.len() + n > max_line { return Err(Error::Protocol(format!("frame exceeds {} MiB", ...))); }` exits the reader loop. Lines 259-265 then fail every pending request with that error, send Notice::Disconnected and close. app.rs:1267-1275 marks the engine disconnected and drops the client. code_git.rs:1338 sends `git.diff.file` on this 2 MiB connection and only checks `old.len() + new.len() > 1048576` (1350) after a successful reply. The engine returns full `old`, `new` and a whole-file unified diff with no size cap or binary detection (crates/relay-core/src/handlers/git.rs:236-254), built with `String::from_utf8_lossy` over the entire blob or file (826, 845). Only image reads use the bounded 24 MiB side connection (client.rs:122-130).
findings.impact: Clicking a changed non-image binary in the Git panel can produce a line over 2 MiB. Examples: .uasset/.umap/.blend/.fbx files; with Git LFS the HEAD side is a pointer and the working side the full binary; invalid bytes become 3-byte U+FFFD and control bytes 6-byte \u00XX escapes. Roughly a few hundred KB of binary, or a text file near 1 MiB (old + new + diff, e.g. a lockfile), is enough. Every in-flight UI request then fails, the banner says the engine disconnected, and all actions fail until Reconnect. Clicking the same file again repeats it. git.status with very many untracked files, or file.tree on a huge directory, can do the same during automatic refreshes. Terminals survive because they use their own connections.
findings.fix: In the reader, when a line exceeds max_line, discard to the newline and take the id from the `{"v":1,"id":"..."` prefix (shape() already relies on that field order). Fail only that request with a typed error and keep the connection. In the engine, give git.diff.file a byte cap and binary detection (return a truncated/binary marker, as file.read does with max_bytes), and cap git.status and file.tree entries. Until then, route git.diff.file through a bounded side connection like Client::image_read.

v1.reason: client.rs:48 sets MAX_LINE = 2 MiB. Lines 200-205 return Err(Protocol) from the reader loop when a line exceeds it. Lines 259-265 then fail every pending request and send Notice::Disconnected, and app.rs:1267-1275 sets connected=false, drops the client and breaks the notice loop. Ui::call (app.rs:1111-1117) sends git.diff.file on this main connection; only file.read images use the 24 MiB side connection (client.rs:122-130). open_diff (code_git.rs:1319-1350) special-cases only images, and checks the 1 MiB editor limit after a successful reply. The engine's DiffFileOp (handlers/git.rs:235-254) returns the full `old`, the full `new` and a whole-file unified diff, with no size cap or binary detection. Both sides use from_utf8_lossy (git.rs:826, 845). In an Unreal/Blender project, clicking a modified .uasset/.umap/.blend in the Git panel (open_diff from code_git.rs:898) easily produces a JSON line over 2 MiB and drops the UI's control connection until Reconnect.
v1.correction: No change to mechanism. The git.status and file.tree overflow claims are plausible but were not separately verified. The main fix is engine-side: give git.diff.file a byte cap and a binary marker. Recovering per request in the client reader is a good complement.

At app.rs:1267-1275 the UI sets connected=false, drops the client, shows "Engine disconnected" and breaks the event loop. Ui::call (app.rs:1111-1117) sends every op except lifecycle ops on this one connection. Only file.read for images uses the 24 MiB side connection (client.rs:124-130).

Clicking any row in the Git panel calls open_diff (code_git.rs:896-899). Those rows come from git.status (code_git.rs:159), with no binary marker. open_diff diverts only images (image_preview.rs:7-17: png/jpg/.../svg). It checks the 1 MiB limit (code_git.rs:1350) only after a successful reply.

Both sides go through from_utf8_lossy (git.rs:826, 845). serde_json 1.0.151 escapes bytes 0x00-0x1F as 6-byte \u00XX (ser.rs ESCAPE table). The engine writer (socket.rs:299-322) sends lines of any size. ARCHITECTURE.md:22 documents the 2 MiB bound, but nothing documents tearing down the whole control connection as intended.

I modelled lossy decoding plus serde escaping in a Python script:
- a real 497 KB .blend as a new file, or as an LFS pointer→binary pair: 2.30 MiB line;
- the repo's own 733 KB scrcpy-server binary as a new file: 3.34 MiB;
- the trigger point is about 440 KB for compressed binaries. A modified non-LFS binary includes both sides in full, so about 440 KB per side is enough even with an empty diff;
- lockfile-like text edited in place: over 2 MiB once each side is about 930 KB or more.

(b) Who and how often: the user clicks a changed file in the code page's Git panel, the panel's main interaction. The app targets Unreal and Blender work (relay-cli unreal and blender tooling, LFS hydration noted at client.rs:68), so .uasset, .umap, .blend and .fbx changes over a few hundred KB are routine. It fires every time, on every such click, and again on a repeat click. It needs no attacker.

(c) What happens: every in-flight UI request fails with the misleading "Invalid engine response: frame exceeds 2 MiB". Live events stop: session, task and notify updates, and guardrail.held, so new exception prompts do not appear until reconnect. Every UI action then fails with Disconnected until the user clicks Reconnect. Reconnect calls Ui::connect (app.rs:1131-1144), which stops and clears every terminal pane and rebuilds it. restore_prompts (guardrail_pages.rs:703) recovers open guardrail requests afterwards. No data is lost: open_diff refuses to run with a dirty buffer, and the engine and agent sessions are unaffected.

(d) Severity: high fits the rubric. It is a deterministic, user-visible failure in a normal flow that takes down the whole UI control plane. It is not critical: there is no data loss, no engine or session impact, and one click recovers.

(e) The fix is sound. The best order is to make the engine fix first: a byte cap on git.diff.file plus a binary flag (NUL sniff, as git.diff already does at git.rs:224), shown in the UI as "binary file not shown". Then make the client fail only the oversized request, taking the id from the `{"v":1,"id":` prefix and discarding bytes up to the newline.

   - Prefer the engine-side cap and binary flag. It is in relay-core, so `cargo test` can verify it.
   - Make DiffFileOut fields additive and regenerate schema/bus.v1.json.
   - The client-reader change is under apps/relay-native, which CLAUDE.md says cannot be compiled on Ubuntu 24.04 runners, and must be reported as unverified.
   - The side-connection stopgap does isolate the failure. It still ships up to 24 MiB that the UI then rejects at 1 MiB, so a request-side max_bytes is better.

findings.title: Wallpaper images are decoded synchronously on the GTK thread: N+1 full-size decodes per gallery render, plus one more on every appearance reload
findings.evidence: Lines 838-853 base64-decode each card's `preview` and call `gtk::gdk::Texture::from_bytes` on the main thread. The preview is the full 1280×900 JPEG (1011 stores `"preview":image`). wallpaper_texture decodes the current image again (903, 1023-1030). render_wallpapers reruns on every pick, remove or clear click (868-891, 974-980) and from sync_wallpaper on each appearance change. shell.rs:1222-1231 decodes the wallpaper again in load_appearance on every `appearance.*` or terminal.font_size settings change, including each rotation. mirror.rs:943 encodes screenshots to PNG on the GTK thread. image_preview.rs, by contrast, decodes in `rt.spawn_blocking`.
findings.impact: Each ≤1280×900 JPEG decode takes on the order of 5-15 ms. With a full library (about 5-7 images under the 1.5 MB cap), each gallery click stalls the UI for roughly 50-120 ms, and each wallpaper rotation re-decodes on the main thread. These are estimates; nothing was measured.
findings.fix: Decode in `ui.rt.spawn_blocking` into pixel bytes and build a MemoryTexture on the main thread, as image_preview.rs does. Store a small preview (e.g. 256 px) separately from the full image. Cache the decoded current-wallpaper texture by content hash.

v1.reason: render_wallpapers base64-decodes and calls gdk::Texture::from_bytes on the GTK thread for every card (tools_settings.rs:838-853), plus once more for the current image through wallpaper_texture (903, 1023-1030). It reruns on every pick or remove click and from sync_wallpaper. The stored `preview` is identical to the full 1280x900 JPEG (1011: `"preview":image`). shell.rs:1222-1231 decodes the wallpaper again on the main thread in load_appearance. All of this is real but small: the 1.5 MB library cap (1012) allows only a few images, so a stall is tens of ms per click.
v1.correction: mirror.rs:943 (save_to_png) runs once per explicit screenshot save and is not worth listing. Side observation: because `preview` duplicates `image`, every wallpaper is stored twice in the library JSON, which roughly halves how many images fit under the 1.5 MB cap. Storing a small thumbnail as the preview fixes both.

results.coverage: Method: per-file enumeration of non-test regions (cut at first #[cfg(test)]) with rg/grep for: .unwrap()/.expect( (all ~200 sites inspected), .lock().unwrap / poisoning (catch_unwind, into_inner, set_hook), range slicing `[a..b]` on str/slices, binary subtraction on unsigned, .clamp( with non-constant bounds, % / rem_euclid divisors, serde_json IndexMut `x["k"] =`, with_capacity/vec![..; n]/repeat, truncate/split_at/remove/insert/swap, `let _ =`, `.ok()?`/`.ok();`/unwrap_or_default, BufRead::lines/read_to_string on external streams, jiff/Duration arithmetic, partial_cmp().unwrap(), `if let/match ... .borrow()` RefCell re-entrancy (sampled), and (kind, code) pairs across all BusError constructors plus the io_err/gix_err/git_mutation helpers. Panic architecture verified: Store::lock tolerates poisoning, Transaction rolls back on unwind, engine survives handler panics via spawn_blocking; other engine mutexes (ptys, mirrors, ui, device_watch…) use .lock().unwrap() but no code path that can panic while holding them was found. Read fully: engine.rs, socket.rs, handlers/{session,file,git,guardrail,integration,workspace,settings,ui,app,audit,overlap,import_v3}.rs, guardrail.rs (most), guardrail/grants.rs, store.rs (open/migrate/backup), audit.rs, pty.rs, proc.rs, device.rs, device_lease.rs, usage.rs, hooks.rs, recovery.rs, branch_cleanup.rs, providers.rs (probe half), provider_updates.rs, watch.rs, github.rs, sessions.rs, paths.rs, relay-remote (rendezvous, tunnel, bridge, wire, direct, registry), relay-cli main.rs, mcp.rs, remote.rs (serve path) and the dispatch/IO parts of unreal.rs and blender.rs. Partially read: handlers/device.rs (~65%: watch, mirror, run/build workers, AVD), handlers/task.rs (dispatch/activity), mirror.rs (parsers). Not read beyond grep: handlers/{notes,module,notify,bus,device_lease,provider rest}.rs, awareness.rs, skills.rs, plugins.rs, pairlink.rs, most of unreal.rs/unreal_process.rs, and apps/relay-native (grep-targeted only; GTK RefCell double-borrow analysis was sampled, not exhaustive — no confirmed GUI panic found). Several findings (unbounded subprocesses under the store lock, rendezvous host clobber, recovery pid kill) are outside the strict panic/error lens but were verified and included because they are the triggers or consequences of lens findings. Claude Code's treatment of a timed-out hook as non-blocking (finding 1) and Android's modified-UTF-8 log encoding (finding 7) are external behaviours not verifiable from this repo, hence medium confidence.

findings.title: Claude PreToolUse guardrail adapter has no deadline: a slow engine makes Claude Code time the hook out and run the tool unguarded
findings.evidence: claude_pre_tool does `let mut client = connect(instance).await?;` (466) then `let response = client.call(&request, |_| {}).await?;` (471) with no tokio::time::timeout; socket::Client::call loops on next_line forever. The hook is installed with `"timeout": 30` (hooks.rs:351). main.rs:352-353 itself notes `Claude Code only treats exit 2 as blocking`. guardrail.gate is `engine.register::<Gate>` (handlers/guardrail.rs:304), i.e. it must acquire the single store mutex, and several register handlers hold that mutex for unbounded time (see the unbounded-subprocess finding: project.clone `git clone`, git.pr.open `gh pr create`, git.commit's in-transaction `git commit`, worktree.remove, avd.create).
findings.impact: While any long handler holds the store (cloning a large repo from onboarding — the client allows 1800 s, client.rs:67; `gh pr create` on a stalled network; a signed commit waiting on pinentry; a slow post-commit hook; removing a multi-GB worktree), every agent's Bash/Write/Edit hook queues behind it. After 30 s Claude Code kills the hook, which is not an exit 2, so the tool runs: protected paths, denied commands and destructive-write holds are skipped for every running agent for the duration, with no record. An engine deadlock has the same effect for all tool calls.
findings.fix: Bound the gate call inside the adapter below the provider timeout (e.g. `tokio::time::timeout(Duration::from_secs(25), ...)` around connect+call) and return exit 2 with `RELAY guardrail timed out` on expiry; do the same in codex_pre_tool. Longer term take slow handlers off the store lock so gate never waits behind them.

v1.reason: claude_pre_tool (main.rs:466-471) and codex_pre_tool (517-521) call `connect(instance)` and then `client.call(...)`. socket::Client::call (socket.rs:801-823) loops on next_line and has no timeout. guardrail.gate is `engine.register::<Gate>` (handlers/guardrail.rs:304), so it waits for the single store mutex (store.rs:474, a plain Mutex::lock). Several `register` handlers hold that mutex while a subprocess runs with no deadline: project.clone runs `Command::new("git").arg("clone")...output()` (workspace.rs:234), git.pr.open runs `gh pr create` via `.output()` (git.rs:666-682), git.commit's locked phase runs `git commit` through git_mutate (git.rs:571), and worktree.remove deletes directories (git.rs:129-143). The hooks are installed with `"timeout": 30` (hooks.rs:351, 521). The adapter fails closed only when it exits 2 itself (comment at main.rs:352-353). A Claude Code hook that is killed on timeout is a non-blocking error, so the tool runs ungated. Example: the user clones a large repository from onboarding while agents are working, and every Bash/Write/Edit from any agent in that window skips protected paths and command and destructive-write checks, with nothing recorded. An engine deadlock has the same effect.
v1.correction: project.clone is UserOnly, so an agent cannot open this window on purpose. It needs a slow user-initiated or network-bound operation (or an engine deadlock) to hold the lock for more than 30 s. The code side is fully established. That a killed hook lets the tool proceed comes from Claude Code's documented behaviour, not from this repository, and Codex's timeout semantics were not checked. Fix as proposed: wrap connect+call in `tokio::time::timeout` at about 25 s, below the 30 s hook timeout, and exit 2 with `RELAY guardrail timed out` in both adapters. Longer term, move clone, `gh pr create` and the commit subprocess off the store lock (register_staged/unlocked), which is also a CLAUDE.md invariant (no proc::output_with_timeout).

v2.reason:
(a) The code does what the finding says. claude_pre_tool connects at main.rs:466 and awaits `client.call` at main.rs:471. codex_pre_tool does the same at 517/520. Neither has a deadline: socket.rs:801-823 loops on `next_line` until a response arrives. The hooks are installed with `"timeout": 30` (hooks.rs:351 for Claude, hooks.rs:521 for Codex). guardrail.gate is a plain `register` (handlers/guardrail.rs:304). An agent's socket request also takes the store lock in check_session_token (engine.rs:1378) before the handler runs inside the locked transaction. store.rs:474 is an unbounded Mutex::lock, and LockSpan only logs.

I checked Claude Code's side in the installed 2.1.291 binary. When a command hook overruns its timeout, Claude Code logs "timed out after" and yields `outcome:"cancelled"` with a `hook_cancelled` message. That result carries no blockingError and no permissionBehavior. The only code that turns a cancelled PreToolUse hook into a refusal is `acr` ("gave no verdict in time; refusing the call"), and it runs only when `bt=w?.remoteCall!==void 0`, meaning a call served to a cloud session. Relay spawns `claude` locally in a PTY (providers.rs:169-191), so the tool goes on to Claude Code's ordinary permission flow. This contradicts D23 ("adapter/infrastructure failures block instead of failing open") and the comment at main.rs:352-353, so the behaviour is not intended.

(b) Reachability. The trigger is any locked handler that holds the store for more than 30 s, or an engine hang.
- project.clone runs `git clone` with `.output()` and no deadline inside `register` (workspace.rs:234). It is reachable at any time from the "Add project…" GitHub flow (registry.rs:472, onboarding.rs:527), and the native client allows it 1800 s (client.rs:67). Cloning a large or LFS repository while agents work in another project is a plausible normal flow.
- Agents can call git.pr.open, which runs `gh pr create` with `.output()` under the lock (git.rs:666-682), so a stalled network can open the window.
- Agents can call git.commit, whose locked phase runs `git commit --no-verify` through an untimed `git()` (worktree.rs:26-36). Signing and post-commit hooks still run there.
- worktree.remove (a tree walk plus deleting build dirs) and avd.create also hold the lock without a deadline.

This is occasional, not constant. An agent cannot open the window on purpose through project.clone (UserOnly), and a deliberate agent-made window was not established.

(c) Consequence. During the window every agent's Bash/Write/Edit waits 30 s and then runs without Relay's checks: the default denied commands (settings.rs:33: rm -rf, git reset --hard, git clean -fd, git push --force), protected paths, shape gates, destructive-write holds, device leases (gate_command) and the self-approval check. Whether the call actually runs depends on the agent's Claude permission mode. Relay passes no mode flag and ~/.claude/settings.json sets no defaultMode, so in default mode Claude Code still prompts for unapproved commands and edits; in auto, acceptEdits or bypass mode, or with "don't ask again" rules, it runs.

(d) High fits the rubric's "a safety check that can be silently bypassed". The control is the product's core safety layer, it is documented as fail-closed, and slow lock holds keep recurring in this codebase (D144/D149).

(e) The fix is correct: bound connect+call below the hook timeout and exit 2. See the correction for what remains open.
v2.correction:
1. "With no record" is wrong. send_raw delivers the request before Claude Code kills the hook, and the engine finishes the spawn_blocking dispatch once the lock frees. The gate then commits its refusal notification, hold or audit row (D22) and emits guardrail.refused or guardrail.held after the tool has already run. Relay therefore records a refusal, or asks the user to confirm a hold, for an action that already happened, and nothing records that the action ran ungated. That is misleading rather than silent.

2. Claude Code's behaviour is now verified against the installed 2.1.291 binary, not just its documentation: a timed-out hook is "cancelled", and only cloud-served calls fail closed. Codex's timeout semantics are still unverified. Its binary contains "hook timed out after", but I could not establish whether that blocks.

3. The impact depends on the permission mode. In Claude's default mode the user still sees Claude Code's own prompt and would approve without knowing Relay would have refused.

4. Fix. Wrapping connect+call in `tokio::time::timeout` at about 25 s and exiting 2 with `RELAY guardrail timed out` is right for both adapters. Derive that deadline from the same constant as the installer's `"timeout": 30` so the two cannot drift apart. The abandoned gate still runs later and creates holds and refusals, or consumes grants, for a call that never ran. To make the fix complete, have the request carry a deadline, or have the engine drop a gate whose client has disconnected. The real cure is to take project.clone, git.pr.open, the locked `git commit`, worktree.remove and avd.create off the store lock using register_staged or proc::output_with_timeout.

findings.title: Crash recovery SIGTERM/SIGKILLs whatever process now holds a stale session pid, with its whole process group (contradicts D20)
findings.evidence: Step 2 reads `SELECT id, name, state, pid FROM sessions WHERE state IN ('spawning','running','idle','blocked')` and for each row `Some(p) if pty::pid_alive(p as u32) => { // alive but not ours ... kill_wait(p as u32);` (86-88). pid_alive is just `kill(pid,0)==0` (pty.rs:394-396) and kill_wait sends SIGTERM to `-(pid)` and `pid`, then SIGKILL after 2 s (20-35). There is no identity check, unlike step 1 (`relay_children`, pty.rs:411-429) which requires RELAY_INSTANCE/RELAY_STORE/RELAY_SESSION in /proc/<pid>/environ. DECISIONS D20: `Recovery reaps only its own store's orphans`.
findings.impact: Live states and pids stay in the table whenever the engine dies without shutdown() (power loss, OOM kill, kernel crash, kill -9, battery death). Genuine orphans are already reaped by step 1, so step 2's kill branch effectively only fires for a pid that is NOT a Relay child: after a reboot, any of the user's own processes that reused the pid (editor, browser, terminal, desktop component) is SIGTERMed then SIGKILLed — and its process group if it leads one — the next time the engine starts. Unsaved work in that application is lost.
findings.fix: Only signal the pid when pty::proc_env(pid) shows this store's RELAY_STORE/RELAY_INSTANCE and RELAY_SESSION == name (the D20 check step 1 already uses); otherwise just mark the row restorable with `pid gone`.

v1.reason: recovery.rs:84-93: for every sessions row in spawning/running/idle/blocked with a pid where `pty::pid_alive` (just kill(pid,0)==0, pty.rs:394-396) is true, it calls kill_wait. kill_wait (20-35) sends SIGTERM and then SIGKILL to both -(pid) and pid. There is no proc_env/RELAY_STORE check, unlike step 1's relay_children (pty.rs:411-429). Step 1 has already reaped every live process that carries this store's RELAY_SESSION, and the stored pid is the PTY child, which carries that env. So the step 2 kill branch effectively fires only when the pid now belongs to an unrelated same-user process; other users' processes return EPERM and count as dead. Rows stay live only after an unclean engine exit (shutdown runs mark_restorable, engine.rs:655). After a power loss or crash reboot, the pid counter restarts. If Relay and its sessions start at a similar point in the boot each time, desktop processes in the same pid range can occupy stored pids, and one of them, with its whole group if it leads one, gets killed when the engine starts. This contradicts D20 ('Recovery reaps only its own store's orphans').
v1.correction: In practice this needs an unclean shutdown plus pid reuse, so it is occasional rather than routine, but when it happens it silently kills an arbitrary user application. Fix as proposed: signal only when proc_env(pid) shows this store's RELAY_STORE/RELAY_INSTANCE (and RELAY_SESSION == name); otherwise record 'pid reused' and just mark the row restorable.

v2.reason:
(a) The code does what is claimed. recovery.rs:80-93: for every row in spawning/running/idle/blocked whose pid passes `pty::pid_alive` (just `kill(pid,0)==0`, pty.rs:394-396), it calls `kill_wait` (20-35). That sends SIGTERM to `-(pid)` and `pid`, polls for 2 s, then sends SIGKILL to both. There is no identity check, unlike step 1's `relay_children` (pty.rs:411-429), which requires RELAY_INSTANCE, RELAY_STORE and RELAY_SESSION in /proc/<pid>/environ. D20 (DECISIONS.md:63-65) says "Recovery reaps only its own store's orphans … two instances never cross."

The stored pid is the PTY child (session.rs:681-683). That child gets the RELAY_* env (session.rs:564-576; portable-pty 0.9 `as_command` does env_clear and then applies the builder's env) and calls setsid (portable-pty unix.rs:257), so its pgid equals its pid. Step 1 therefore always finds and kills a genuine survivor. Step 2's kill branch only acts on (i) a process step 1 already signalled that is still a zombie, which is a harmless re-signal, or (ii) a pid that now belongs to some other process.

The author has met this: examples/perf.rs:584 nulls every pid in its store copy (`UPDATE sessions SET pid=NULL`), and the comment at :1093 says recovery "would reap the fixture's own sessions".

(b) Reachability. Rows keep a live state and a pid only when the engine dies without `shutdown()`.
- SIGINT and SIGTERM run `shutdown` (serve.rs:45-50), which nulls the pids before killing anything (engine.rs:651-680).
- run.sh:32 starts the engine under `nohup`, so closing the terminal does not trigger this.
- What does trigger it: power loss, a kernel panic or hard freeze, an OOM kill or SIGKILL of the engine, or a crash of the engine itself.

Without a reboot, the stale pids are simply dead ("pid is dead"). The next start comes minutes later, pid_max here is 4194304, and the counter advances about 290k a day (3.4M after 11.7 days of uptime), so the pids have not wrapped around to be reused.

A real collision needs a reboot, because the pid counter restarts and low pids are full of long-lived desktop processes. Even then, a stored pid must already be allocated in the new boot when run.sh starts the engine, and must belong to a live process of the same user. Other users' processes return EPERM and are treated as dead. On this machine today the live session pids are 2.27M to 2.41M, so a crash and reboot now would hit nothing. The risk is real mainly when the previous boot's sessions were spawned early (low pids, for example resumed right after an earlier crash) and the engine starts later in the new boot. That makes it occasional at most, counted per crash-and-reboot, not per day.

There is a second trigger that the finding does not mention, and it backs the D20 claim. If an engine is opened on a copy or backup of a live store (`relay serve --instance test --store <copy>`; Store::open's exclusive lock only covers its own file), its step 1 matches nothing, but step 2 deterministically SIGTERMs and then SIGKILLs every agent of the real engine that is still live in the copy, with no pid reuse needed. This is a developer-only path and not a documented workflow.

(c) When it fires, the unrelated process gets SIGTERM and, if still alive 2 s later, SIGKILL. If it leads a process group (shells, setsid'd services, many apps), the whole group is killed too. Nothing tells the user: app.recovery.last only says "pid P still alive from a previous engine; reaped". Unsaved work in that application can be lost. Relay's own data is not affected.

(d) Severity. High in this rubric means likely wrong behaviour in a normal flow. This needs an unclean death plus a reboot plus a pid collision, or a developer opening a copy of the store. The first verifier itself calls it "occasional rather than routine". It is a real bug on a less common path, with a serious outcome when it fires, which is medium. The category is better called bug (the wrong process is killed); data loss is a possible knock-on effect in another app, not in Relay.

(e) The fix is correct. Signal only when proc_env(pid) shows this store's RELAY_STORE and RELAY_INSTANCE and RELAY_SESSION == name; otherwise mark the row restorable with "pid gone or not ours". Step 1 already kills every process carrying this store's markers, so the simplest complete version drops the kill from step 2 entirely. The test `recovery_reaps_orphans_and_fscks` would still pass, because step 1 reaps its orphan and the row still becomes restorable.
v2.correction:
Severity: high to medium. Category: data-loss to bug.

Corrections and additions:
- Mechanism detail: the stored pid is reliably recognised by step 1. The PTY child carries this store's RELAY_* env (session.rs:564-576) and is a setsid session leader (portable-pty unix.rs:257). So the kill branch in recovery.rs:86-92 only matters for a zombie step 1 already signalled, or for a pid that now belongs to another process.
- Trigger (impact): unclean engine death alone is not enough. Without a reboot, pid_max is 4194304 and the pids are simply dead. A collision effectively needs a reboot, and the stored pid must already be allocated and owned by a live same-user process when run.sh starts the engine. Today's session pids on this machine are about 2.3M, so a crash and reboot now would hit nothing.
- Second trigger not in the finding: an engine opened on a copy or backup of a live store (for example `relay serve --instance test --store <copy>`) deterministically kills the running engine's live agents through step 2. The author worked around exactly this in examples/perf.rs:584 (`UPDATE sessions SET pid=NULL`) and :1093, instead of fixing recovery.
- Related location to add: crates/relay-core/tests/sessions.rs:576 inserts a live row with hard-coded pid 999999 and expects "dead". With pid_max 4194304, that pid can belong to a live process of the user, and `cargo test` would SIGTERM and SIGKILL it and its process group before failing.
- Fix: gate any signal on the proc_env identity check, or simply drop the kill from step 2, because step 1 already reaps everything carrying the markers.
- Optional hardening for the fix: require p > 0 before kill_wait. kill_wait(0) would signal the engine's own process group, and a negative pid would become kill(-1)-style signals to every process the user owns. This is not reachable today, because pids only come from pty.pid().

findings.title: Destructive-write guard reads a non-UTF-8 or unreadable file as empty, so any rewrite of it is allowed silently
findings.evidence: `Ok(_) => std::fs::read_to_string(&absolute).unwrap_or_default(),` (572) turns InvalidData/permission errors into ""; `changed_line_counts(&old, new_text)` then reports removed=0 and old_lines=Some(0) (575-583), so destructive_decision returns Allow (over_lines false; removed_pct None because 0 < min_file_lines). The Claude Write hook sends kind=write with the full new_text (main.rs:411-416). file.rs:578 guard_path_mutation and file.rs:92 use the same `unwrap_or_default` pattern. The commit gate's numstat parser maps binary `-\t-` rows to 0/0 lines (guardrail.rs:767-768), so caps don't catch it either.
findings.impact: An agent's Write over a Latin-1/Windows-1252 source file, a UTF-16 file (e.g. Unreal localization .archive/.manifest, Windows .rc), or any file with a single invalid byte — replacing thousands of lines with a stub — passes guardrail.gate as Allow with no hold, notification or audit warning. The policy whose purpose is catching accidental wipes is bypassed exactly for files that cannot be regenerated from text.
findings.fix: Read bytes (`std::fs::read`) and compare `String::from_utf8_lossy` lines (or count b'\n' lines) instead of defaulting to ""; if the old content cannot be read at all, hold with reason `cannot measure` rather than allow.

v1.reason: guardrail.rs:572 `Ok(_) => std::fs::read_to_string(&absolute).unwrap_or_default()` turns an InvalidData error (any non-UTF-8 byte) into "". changed_line_counts("", new) at 1099-1117 then returns removed=0, and old_lines=Some(0), so destructive_decision (704+) has over_lines=false and removed_pct=None (0 < min_file_lines), and returns Allow. The Claude Write hook (relay-cli main.rs ~411-416) sends kind=write with new_text, so this is the path an agent's full-file rewrite takes. file.rs Write (old = fs::read_to_string(&path) ... unwrap_or_default) feeds guardrail::enforce the same way, and guard_path_mutation (file.rs ~578) reads the moved content with unwrap_or_default. file_lines (701) returns None for such a file, which only disables the percentage rule on the diff path.
v1.correction: Narrower than claimed. When the rule trips and allow_if_recoverable is set, recoverable() (670-691) already allows any file that is committed and unmodified or ignored by git, so the bypass only matters for a non-UTF-8 file that is untracked or has uncommitted changes. Within that set it is silent: no hold and no audit warning. Most source trees are UTF-8, so the trigger is uncommon, and a permission-denied file usually cannot be written by the agent anyway. That puts it at medium rather than high. Fix as proposed: read the bytes and count lines with from_utf8_lossy or by counting b'\n'. If metadata succeeds but the read fails, return a hold such as 'cannot measure' instead of treating the file as empty.

findings.title: Rendezvous: when a replaced host connection finally drops it clears the room's new host, leaving phones on host.offline
findings.evidence: host() registers `entry.host = Some(tx);` replacing any previous host (174-184; comment: `A second host for the same room replaces the first ... its old socket is about to time out anyway`). On exit it unconditionally does `if let Some(r) = rooms.get_mut(&room) { r.host = None; r.lanes.clear(); }` (217-224) without checking that r.host is still this connection's sender.
findings.impact: A laptop that sleeps or switches network: the PC tunnel declares the socket dead after 90 s of silence (tunnel.rs:81-87) and reconnects as host B; the server's socket for old host A is half-open and only errors after TCP retransmission timeout (its writer sends a Close frame once its sender is dropped). A's cleanup then sets host=None for the room. B stays connected and keeps receiving Pongs, so the PC never re-registers; every phone that joins gets `host.offline` until the engine is restarted.
findings.fix: Keep a clone of the sender and only clear when `r.host.as_ref().is_some_and(|h| h.same_channel(&mine))`; only drop lanes opened under this host.

v1.reason: rendezvous.rs:174-184: host() replaces `entry.host = Some(tx)` and clears the lanes. On exit (217-224) it runs `r.host = None; r.lanes.clear();` without checking that the room's host is still its own sender. Trace for a replaced host A: once B replaces it, A's room sender is dropped, and the join tasks that held clones exit because their lanes were cleared. A's writer then sees rx None and sends a Close frame. A's `source.next()` returns Err only when the peer's FIN/RST arrives or TCP retransmission gives up (about 15 min on Linux). The rendezvous server sets no keepalive, timeout or server-side ping (grep finds none). In the normal PC-restart case the old FIN arrives first and nothing goes wrong. In the sleep/NAT-expiry or network-switch case, the PC tunnel (tunnel.rs, SILENCE_LIMIT 90 s or a socket error) reconnects as B while the server still holds a half-open A. When A's socket finally errors, its cleanup sets host=None and clears B's lanes, which also closes any phone connected through B. B's socket stays healthy: the server's tungstenite answers B's pings with pongs, so the PC never re-registers. Every later join then gets `host.offline` at line 244 until the PC's tunnel reconnects for some other reason or the engine restarts. A laptop that sleeps or roams is a normal flow, and this leaves the rendezvous phone path silently dead.
v1.correction: There is a second effect: A's cleanup also clears B's lanes, which disconnects phones attached to the new host, not only future joins. Fix: keep `let mine = tx.clone()` before registering, and at exit clear `r.host` and the lanes only if `r.host.as_ref().is_some_and(|h| h.same_channel(&mine))` (tokio mpsc::Sender::same_channel). Lanes are already cleared on replacement, so lanes left at exit belong to the current host and must not be cleared by a stale host. Also consider TCP keepalive or a server-side read timeout so half-open host sockets end sooner.

v2.reason:
(a) The mechanism is real. host() swaps in the new sender at rendezvous.rs:179 (`entry.host = Some(tx);`). On exit it runs `r.host = None; r.lanes.clear();` (217-224) whether or not a newer host has replaced it.

(b) Reachable, but only on the opt-in path: the user must run `relay remote via` and self-host the server, which docs/MOBILE.md puts behind Caddy. The trigger is a silent break in the PC's path to the server: a network switch, a router IP change, or NAT expiry during sleep. The tunnel then redials as B, either on an RST or after SILENCE_LIMIT (90-120 s), while the server or proxy still holds A. B's registration drops tx_A, so A's writer sends a Close frame into the dead path. The kernel gives up after about 15 min (tcp_retries2), or sooner on an RST, and A's cleanup then runs after B is registered.

(c) This is where the claimed impact breaks. Line 220 drops tx_B and line 221 drops B's lanes, so phones attached through B are disconnected. That part is real and visible. But host() keeps no clone of its own sender; the only clones are taken by join() at line 239. Those join tasks exit promptly: their lanes are gone, so their writers close the phone sockets, and the phones answer the Close. Once they exit, B's writer gets None from `rx.recv()` and calls `sink.close()` at line 192. In tokio-tungstenite 0.30, poll_close (lib.rs:388-410) calls tungstenite close(), which writes a Close frame (protocol/mod.rs:597-607). The PC reads it as Message::Close (mod.rs:664, do_close). tunnel.rs:98 then breaks the loop, returns Ok(()), resets the backoff to 1 s and redials, and the room is re-created.

So the claim "B keeps receiving Pongs, so the PC never re-registers ... until the engine is restarted" is false. The gap is about 1-2 s. tunnel.rs:150 can add up to 5 s for each lane being closed. The gap is longer only if a phone attached through B is itself half-open at that moment, and even then it ends when that socket's TCP retransmission times out (about 15 min). In practice: minutes after a PC network change, rendezvous phones are dropped once, and a join that lands in that window gets host.offline. A later join succeeds.

(d) High is not supported. This is a transient, self-healing glitch on an opt-in path, so low (arguably medium). There is no persistent outage, no data loss and no hang.

(e) The proposed fix is right in intent but flawed as written. Holding a strong `mine = tx.clone()` for host()'s whole lifetime keeps a replaced host's channel open, so its writer never sends Close. A live replaced host is then never told to leave. A half-open one never has anything written to it, and the server sets no keepalive and sends no pings. With nothing in front of the server, that host's task and socket would leak until restart; behind Caddy or nginx, the proxy's own timeout would probably still close it.
v2.correction:
Impact: this is not a persistent outage. After a stale host clobbers the room, the current host's server-side writer (rendezvous.rs:186-193) sees all senders dropped and sends a Close frame at line 192. The PC tunnel treats that as a clean close (tunnel.rs:98, then lines 34-37 and 42) and redials after 1 s. The real effect is a one-time drop of the phones attached through the new host. Joins fail with host.offline only for about 1-2 s, and up to one TCP retransmission timeout if a phone attached through B is itself half-open. Severity high becomes low.

Fix: do not keep a strong sender clone for the lifetime of host(). Use an identity that does not own the channel:
- Store a per-connection generation id alongside the sender (e.g. `host: Option<(u64, Sender)>`) and at exit clear host and lanes only if the id still matches.
- Or keep `tx.downgrade()` and clear only if `weak.upgrade().is_some_and(|me| r.host.as_ref().is_some_and(|h| h.same_channel(&me)))`.

Either way, a replaced host keeps getting its Close frame, and a half-open one is not kept alive. Lanes left at exit belong to the current host, so clear them only when this connection is still the host. A server-side ping or read deadline on host sockets is a sensible addition, so a stale socket ends sooner than TCP's roughly 15 min.

findings.title: Handlers registered with Engine::register run unbounded git/gh/avdmanager/adb subprocesses while holding the store mutex
findings.evidence: ProjectClone (register, 228) runs `Command::new("git")...arg("clone")...output()` (234). PrOpen (register, git.rs:666) runs `gh pr create` via `cmd.output()` (679). worktree::git (worktree.rs:26-33) uses plain `Command::output()` and backs `git_mutate`, called from register handlers git.stage (git.rs:503), git.unstage (527), git.branch.create (374), git.branch.delete (485), git.clean_merged (712), git.commit's finish phase inside the transaction (571), file.restore_head (file.rs:256), integration.discard (integration.rs:62-64) and worktree.remove (git.rs:139 → purge_build + dir_size + `git worktree remove`). avd.create/avd.boot (device.rs:332-345) use `wait_with_output` and list_avds, whose `adb -s <emu> emu avd name` is plain `.output()` (device.rs:505). CLAUDE.md: every subprocess forked from a handler goes through proc::output_with_timeout and slow work must not hold the store.
findings.impact: A network clone (client allows 30 min), `gh` on a stalled network, a commit waiting on GPG pinentry or a slow post-commit hook, `git add` of large LFS assets, deleting a multi-GB worktree, or `adb emu` against a frozen emulator blocks every other request — UI refreshes, agents' MCP calls, guardrail.gate — for its whole duration, forever if the child hangs (git clone without GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0 can prompt on the engine's controlling tty). Combined with the adapter-deadline finding, agents' tools run unguarded meanwhile.
findings.fix: Move these into register_staged prepare phases or after_commit workers, run every child through proc::output_with_timeout with GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0 / GH_PROMPT_DISABLED=1, and give worktree::git a deadline.

v1.reason: Engine::register (engine.rs:478-495) runs the closure inside the request transaction with the store held. ProjectClone is registered that way (workspace.rs:228) and runs `Command::new("git")...arg("clone")...output()` (234) with no deadline and no GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0. The native client allows it 1800 s (client.rs request_timeout), so the authors expect it to be slow. PrOpen (git.rs:666) runs `gh pr create` via `.output()` (680). worktree::git (worktree.rs:26-33) is plain `Command::output()` and sits behind git_mutate, which register handlers call: BranchCreate 374, BranchDelete 485, Stage 503, Unstage 527, CleanMerged 712. It also runs in CommitOp's finish phase (571), which executes inside the transaction. WorktreeRemove (git.rs:129) is register and calls worktree::remove (worktree.rs:352-370), which does purge_build, dir_size (a tree walk) and `git worktree remove` all while the lock is held. IntegrationDiscard (integration.rs:58-64) does the same. AvdCreate (device.rs:321) is register and uses spawn + wait_with_output with no deadline, then list_avds, which runs `adb -s <emu> emu avd name` with plain `.output()` (device.rs:505). By contrast, worktree::create (214), Fetch, Push and BranchCleanup already use register_staged or output_with_timeout, so these call sites are leftovers, not a design choice.
v1.correction: AvdBoot is not a valid example. It only calls list_avds under the lock (one bounded `adb devices` plus the unbounded `emu avd name` per running emulator) and spawns the emulator in after_commit. AvdCatalog's unbounded `avdmanager list device` (device.rs:314) is register_unlocked, so it does not hold the store. The commit in finish passes --no-verify, so it is a commit.gpgsign pinentry, not a hook, that can stall it. The fix is right: move the slow work into register_staged prepare phases, put deadlines on worktree::git/gh/clone, and set GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0 / GH_PROMPT_DISABLED=1.

v2.reason:
(a) The code does what the finding says. dispatch_inner (engine.rs:952-978) takes `self.store.lock()`, opens a transaction and only then calls a `register` handler. Four calls run inside that window:
- ProjectClone (workspace.rs:228-234) runs `git clone` through plain `.output()`.
- PrOpen (git.rs:666-681) runs `gh pr create` through `.output()`.
- Stage, Unstage, BranchCreate, BranchDelete, CleanMerged and RestoreHead (git.rs:503/527/374/485/712, file.rs:256) call git_mutate, which reaches worktree::git (worktree.rs:26-33), a plain `Command::output()`.
- WorktreeRemove (git.rs:129-139) and IntegrationDiscard (integration.rs:58-64) run purge_build, dir_size and `git worktree remove`. AvdCreate (device.rs:321-335) runs avdmanager via wait_with_output and then list_avds. CommitOp's finish (git.rs:571) runs `git commit` inside the transaction.

Nothing exempts these:
- D144 and D149 say slow work never holds the store and that every subprocess forked from a handler goes through output_with_timeout. D149's list of converted ops leaves all of these out.
- BUS.md §5.1 says git work "returns quickly with a handle".
- project.clone's own op summary reads "async; project.changed when done".
- list_avds_with's doc comment claims its calls run "with nothing locked". AvdCreate and AvdBoot still use the locked list_avds.

(b) Who can trigger it, and how often:
- The user adds a project by cloning from GitHub (onboarding.rs:527). The native client allows that call 1800 s (client.rs:67).
- The Code page: stage and unstage, open a pull request, create and delete branches (code_git.rs). Agents can also call git.stage, git.unstage and git.pr.open.
- The Devices tool: avd.create and avd.boot.
- git.commit's finish, used by both the user and agents.

Durations:
- A clone takes seconds to many minutes, longer with LFS.
- `git add` of large or LFS assets takes seconds or more, because the clean filters run.
- `gh` and avdmanager take seconds.
- The remaining calls are usually milliseconds.
- worktree.remove, integration.discard, file.restore_head and clean_merged are not wired into the native client; only the CLI or the phone can reach them.
- A hang with no end needs a prompt. Examples: git's askpass dialog or a /dev/tty prompt (the engine started by ./run.sh from a terminal keeps that terminal), a GPG pinentry, or a wedged emulator console.

(c) What happens: while the child runs, every request that needs the store waits behind it.
- Every agent request blocks, because check_session_token takes the lock before anything else (engine.rs:1378). That includes guardrail.gate from the PreToolUse hooks, which Claude Code times out after 30 s (hooks.rs:351), and every MCP call.
- Requests from the phone door, and the UI's lifecycle connection, also block.
- UI requests fail after 30 s with "outcome unknown".
- Keystrokes and PTY output are not affected: the D148 fast path runs on per-pane connections, and the PTY reader never takes the store.
- No data is lost.

(d) "A freeze of the bus" in normal flows is exactly what the rubric calls high. It is not critical: in the common case the freeze ends on its own, terminals keep working, and no data is lost.

(e) The direction of the fix is right, with the gaps listed under corrections.
v2.correction:
1. Corrections to the first verifier:
- AvdBoot is a valid instance, though a minor one. Under the lock, its list_avds runs `emulator -list-avds` through plain `.output()` (device.rs:478), as well as `adb emu avd name` (505).
- The finding's statement that avd.boot uses wait_with_output is wrong: only avd.create does.
- `--no-verify` skips only the pre-commit and commit-msg hooks. prepare-commit-msg and post-commit still run wherever the user's hooks directory is active, which is the primary checkout. Relay-hooked session worktrees have only pre-commit, so this does not apply there. GPG pinentry can also stall the commit.

2. Related sites to add:
- task.dispatch with `create` (task.rs:1049, a `register` handler) calls invoke_registered("session.create") (task.rs:683). That path runs session.create's prepare inside the transaction (engine.rs:326-348): a `git fetch --all` capped at 20 s, a `git worktree add` capped at 120 s (with LFS), and the hook install. With fanout this repeats once per sub-task. This is the payload the phone sends (relay-remote/tests/remote.rs:311-313).
- guardrail.confirm replaying a held git.commit runs the commit's prepare under the lock. That includes the user's pre-commit hook via unbounded `Command::output()` (hooks.rs:209-212). D149 acknowledges this cost.

3. Corrections to the fix:
- project.clone should return a handle and do the clone on an after_commit worker, as BUS.md §5.1 and its own op summary say. The engine's socket loop handles one request at a time per connection (socket.rs:335-745). A clone that is only staged, but still sent on the UI's main socket, would therefore still stall every other UI request on that socket. Either make it async or send it on its own connection, as the client already does for lifecycle ops.
- A clone killed at its deadline leaves a partial destination directory, which must be removed.
- Do not give worktree::git one short blanket deadline. The same helper also runs long operations that are already unlocked: `git push` (Push prepare), `git add -A` (commit prepare) and `git worktree remove`. Size deadlines per call.
- `git commit` must stay after guardrail::enforce inside finish, both for gate atomicity and for the confirm replay. Bound it with a deadline; do not move it.
- GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0 does not stop GIT_ASKPASS or SSH_ASKPASS dialogs. Moving the work out of the lock and adding a deadline is what bounds those.

findings.title: Integrations interrupted by a restart or a hung build stay 'building' forever and then block project/workspace removal with a misleading hint
findings.evidence: Recovery step 4 closes device_runs in building/running (107-118) but nothing ever touches `integrations`. Only the per-integration thread writes terminal states (integration.rs:72-226); its `shell()` uses `cmd.output()` with no deadline (228-242), and intermediate/final writes are `let _ = set_state(...)` (91, 155, 197, 216, 252). project.remove refuses `force or not` while any integration is queued/merging/building/deploying (workspace.rs:304-307; workspace.remove 165-169) with hint `wait for the integration to finish before removing the project`. The native UI never calls integration.discard (only integration.list/request, code_git.rs:581,738).
findings.impact: An engine restart (reboot, crash, app.quit) during a merge/build, or a build/run command that never exits (a dev server, an interactive prompt), leaves the integration 'building' forever: the Code page shows it running, the project and its workspace can never be removed from the UI, and the error tells the user to wait for something that cannot finish (only `relay cmd integration.discard` gets out).
findings.fix: In recovery mark queued/merging/building/deploying integrations failed (`interrupted by restart`) like device_runs; run build/deploy through proc with a deadline and kill the child from integration.discard; expose discard in the UI and name it in project.remove's hint.

v1.reason: Only the per-integration thread spawned in after_commit (integration.rs:39-41, run at 72-226) ever moves an integration to a terminal state. Recovery closes device_runs (recovery.rs:107-118), and no file other than integration.rs/workspace.rs/store.rs touches integrations, so nothing resumes or closes a queued/merging/building/deploying row after a restart. shell() (228-242) runs `fish -lc <build/run cmd>` with a plain `.output()` and no deadline. A run_cmd that does not exit (such as a dev server) leaves the row in 'deploying' forever, and a hung build leaves it in 'building'. integrations_live (workspace.rs:387-391) counts exactly those states, and project.remove refuses with no force override (workspace.rs:304-307, 'never interrupt it, force or not'), as does workspace.remove (165-169), with the hint 'wait for the integration to finish'. The native client calls only integration.list/request, never integration.discard, so the user has no in-app way out.
v1.correction: A run_cmd that never exits is arguably the most likely trigger, since a deploy/run command is often long-lived. Also, integration.discard does not kill the running child, so after a discard the orphaned shell keeps running.

findings.title: Device run/build log streaming stops at the first non-UTF-8 line and the worker then blocks forever in child.wait()
findings.evidence: run_worker: `for line in BufReader::new(stdout).lines() { ... let Ok(line) = line else { break }; ... }` (1775-1785) then `if let Some(mut child) = runtime.take_child() { let _ = child.wait(); }` (1786-1788). stream_command: `Err(error) => { runtime.push(format!("output: {error}")); break; }` (1848-1851) then `child.wait()` (1854). BufRead::lines yields Err(InvalidData) for any line that is not valid UTF-8; after the break nothing drains the pipe, and logcat `--pid` keeps running while the app lives.
findings.impact: One non-UTF-8 line from logcat (raw bytes from NDK logging, or Java log text such as emoji passed through modified UTF-8) or from a Gradle/adb build (e.g. a compiler echoing a Latin-1 source line): logs silently freeze (run_worker records no reason), the worker blocks in wait() as the child fills the pipe, the run stays 'running'/'building', the RunRuntime stays in device_runs and its Run lease (device_lease Kind::Run) keeps the phone `device.busy` for every agent until someone presses Stop.
findings.fix: Read with `read_until(b'\n')` and `String::from_utf8_lossy`, never break on decode errors; if the loop must end early, kill the child before waiting. Apply the same to drain_server_lines, whose `map_while(Result::ok)` stops draining the scrcpy server's pipes.

v1.reason: The loops do stop at the first decode error. run_worker (device.rs ~1775-1785) has `let Ok(line) = line else { break }` with no message, and stream_command (~1846-1852) pushes `output: {error}` and breaks. BufRead::lines yields InvalidData on a non-UTF-8 line. drain_server_lines (~715) uses map_while(Result::ok) and ends its thread the same way. However, the claimed hang does not follow. The lines() iterator owns the BufReader and therefore the stdout pipe, and it is dropped when the for loop ends, before child.wait(). Rust's Command resets SIGPIPE to the default in the child, so adb logcat's next write kills it with SIGPIPE or fails with EPIPE, and wait() returns. Nothing is left undrained and blocking.
v1.correction: Real consequence: on the first non-UTF-8 logcat line, log streaming stops silently and logcat dies on the broken pipe. run_worker then marks the run 'finished' and releases the Run lease while the app is still running, and FATAL EXCEPTION detection is lost for the rest of the run. For stream_command, the build's output is cut off and the build (fish/gradle) may then fail on EPIPE. For drain_server_lines, the closed pipe can kill the scrcpy server process. I could not establish how often logcat actually emits invalid UTF-8; the JNI modified-UTF-8 encoding of emoji and raw NDK bytes are the plausible sources. There is no freeze and no permanent device.busy, so the severity is low. Fix as proposed: use read_until(b'\n') with String::from_utf8_lossy.

findings.title: Codex usage vanishes whenever the 1 MiB log tail starts inside a multi-byte character
findings.evidence: read_tail seeks to byte `len - 1 MiB` and calls `file.read_to_string(&mut raw)?` (93-96); read_to_string fails with InvalidData when the first bytes are a UTF-8 continuation, before the `split_once('\n')` that would drop the partial line (97-99) runs. read_codex then does `let raw = read_tail(&path, CODEX_TAIL).ok()?;` (61), returning None for the whole provider instead of trying the next file.
findings.impact: Codex writes raw UTF-8 JSONL; once the newest session log exceeds 1 MiB and contains non-ASCII text (curly quotes, dashes, arrows, emoji, box-drawing output), usage.get for Codex intermittently (growing file) or permanently (finished file) returns nothing and the status-bar meter goes blank.
findings.fix: Read the tail as bytes, skip to after the first b'\n', decode with from_utf8_lossy; `continue` to the next file on error instead of `?`.

v1.reason: usage.rs:90-101 `read_tail` seeks to `len - 1 MiB` and calls `file.read_to_string(&mut raw)?`. std's read_to_string returns InvalidData when the bytes are not valid UTF-8. A leading continuation byte makes them invalid, and so does a character cut short at EOF in a file still being written. Both are checked before the `split_once('\n')` that would drop the partial first line. read_codex (line 61) does `read_tail(...).ok()?`, which returns None from the whole function instead of moving on to the next file. In handlers/provider.rs UsageGet, a None from discovery falls back to a Codex usage row reported by a session, if there is one. Otherwise the Codex entry is missing. The bug is real, but it needs the newest Codex log to be over 1 MiB and the cut point to land inside a multi-byte character. In mostly-ASCII logs that is a small fraction of positions. The only effect is a blank or stale status-bar meter, with no data loss and no wider failure.
v1.correction: Category is bug rather than error-handling. The cause covers both ends of the slice: the start offset and a partial write at EOF. Fix: read the tail as bytes (`read_to_end`), drop everything up to the first b'\n' when start > 0, decode with `String::from_utf8_lossy` (or drop the last incomplete line), and `continue` to the next file on an I/O error instead of `?`. Severity is low: a cosmetic meter in an edge case.

findings.title: file.create / file.write cannot create a file or folder whose parent does not exist yet, and say the file is missing
findings.evidence: safe_join with may_not_exist canonicalizes `path.parent()` (494) and maps failure to `io_err("file.not_found", rel, e)` (498), so the handlers' `fs::create_dir_all(parent)` (Write 104-106, Create 150-153) is unreachable for a missing parent. crates/relay-core/tests/phase8.rs:64-72 creates `src` before `src/main.rs`.
findings.impact: The editor's Create dialog (placeholder `relative/path.rs`, editor.rs:1202-1260) fails for `docs/new/guide.md` or a nested folder with `docs/new/guide.md: No such file or directory (os error 2)` (kind unavailable): the user is told the file is missing while creating it, and must create each folder level by hand; same for agents with bus_writes using file.write.
findings.fix: Canonicalize the nearest existing ancestor, check it is under root, then let the handler create the missing directories.

v1.reason: safe_join (file.rs ~488-505) handles a nonexistent path with may_not_exist by calling `fs::canonicalize(path.parent().unwrap_or(root))`. When the parent is also missing, canonicalize fails and the error is mapped to `io_err("file.not_found", rel, e)`, which is kind unavailable. As a result, the `fs::create_dir_all(parent)` calls in Write (~104) and Create (~150) can never create more than zero missing directory levels. The native editor's create dialog (editor.rs 1185-1260) takes a free relative path with the placeholder 'relative/path.rs', so typing `docs/new/guide.md` with docs/new absent fails with 'No such file or directory'. phase8.rs:64-72 creates `src` before `src/main.rs`, which works around the limitation instead of testing it. The same applies to file.write from agents.
v1.correction: Fix: canonicalize the nearest existing ancestor, check that it starts_with(root) so the symlink-escape guard is kept, and then let the handlers' create_dir_all build the rest. Medium is appropriate: it fails a normal action, but only with nested new paths, and creating each level by hand works around it.

findings.title: Socket door's early `?` returns skip task cleanup, so a handler panic turns the UI connection into a zombie
findings.evidence: Every dispatch is `tokio::task::spawn_blocking(...).await?` (742; also 361, 419, 459, 511, 524, 652, 726). A panicking handler makes the await an Err and handle_conn returns early, skipping the cleanup that aborts forwarder/attached/attached_runs (746-759). Dropping a tokio JoinHandle detaches, so the bus.subscribe forwarder (373-391) keeps its out_tx clone, the writer task keeps the write half, and nobody reads the socket any more. (Store-mutex poisoning itself is tolerated, store.rs:475, and the transaction rolls back on unwind.)
findings.impact: The native app uses one connection for bus.subscribe and every non-lifecycle request (app.rs:1148-1154). After any handler panic on it, events keep arriving so the window looks connected, but every later request is never read and fails after 30 s with `Request timed out` (client.rs:65-72); no Disconnected notice fires, so nothing recovers until the window is restarted. Detached PTY forwarders also outlive the connection.
findings.fix: Run the request loop in an inner function and always run the cleanup (or keep the tasks in a JoinSet/abort-on-drop guard); turn a JoinError into a per-request `internal` response instead of ending the connection.

v1.reason: handle_conn (socket.rs:281-761) awaits spawn_blocking with `?` (e.g. 726, 742, 361), and there is no catch_unwind anywhere and no panic=abort profile. A handler panic therefore returns early, skipping the cleanup at 746-759. Dropping the forwarder JoinHandle detaches it; it keeps an out_tx clone, so the writer task (296-319, which owns the write half) keeps sending events. The read half is dropped, but a Unix socket is not closed while the write half lives, so the client gets no EOF. The native app sends bus.subscribe and its requests on one connection (app.rs:1148-1154). After the panic, its events still arrive, but every request times out after 30 s (client.rs request_timeout/Timeout), and no Disconnected notice fires. Attached PTY and device-run forwarder tasks leak in the same way.
v1.correction: The `?` on lines.next_line() (335) is a second path to the same zombie: a non-UTF-8 line returns InvalidData and leaves the same way. The trigger depends on some handler panicking (or a poisoned `lease.active.lock().unwrap()` after one), so this is an amplifier of other bugs, which keeps it at medium.
