Fix: put the cleanup in a drop guard or an inner function and map a JoinError to an `internal` response instead of ending the loop.

findings.title: A scalar stored at guardrails.projects.<id> (or .workspaces.<id>) makes every guardrail config read for that project panic
findings.evidence: settings.set accepts any value at any valid path (settings.rs:217-224). In layers(), put_raw(own, "", 5) calls merge_value, which replaces the {} with the scalar (207-209; settings.rs:115); `merge_value(&mut next, &own)` (161) makes `next` a number; `next["protected_paths"] = json!(protected_paths);` (174) is serde_json IndexMut on a non-object, which panics.
findings.impact: After e.g. `settings.set {path:'guardrails.projects.3', value:false}`, authorize() for every agent mutation in project 3, every guardrail.gate (hooks see a dropped connection and block all tools), session.spawn/resume (plan_launch reads the config) and guardrail.config.get/set/layers panic; config.set cannot repair it because it calls layers() first, and doing it from the UI zombifies its connection (previous finding). Recovery needs settings.reset from the CLI.
findings.fix: Only merge layer values that are objects (flag others as invalid config), and replace the IndexMut with `if let Some(map) = next.as_object_mut()`; optionally validate guardrails.* subtrees in settings.set.

v1.reason: settings.set accepts any value at any valid dotted path (settings.rs:58-66, 203-213); `guardrails.projects.3` with value `false` is stored as one leaf row. In layers() (guardrail.rs:117-139) that row maps to `own` with an empty `at`. put_raw with an empty path calls merge_value(root, false), whose fallback arm `*dst = patch.clone()` (settings.rs:115) turns `own` into `false`. Then `merge_value(&mut next, &own)` (161) makes `next` false, and `next["protected_paths"] = json!(...)` (174) is IndexMut on a Bool, which panics. The same happens with a scalar or array at guardrails.workspaces.<id> for any project in that workspace. Nothing calls catch_unwind. The socket door's spawn_blocking(...).await? (socket.rs:459 etc.) ends that connection, and the store lock recovers from poisoning, so the engine survives but every project-scoped guardrail read panics.
v1.correction: settings.set is Actors::UserOnly (relay-bus ops/notify.rs:23-24), so only the user, typing a bad CLI or API call, can trigger this. Agents cannot. Hooks see 'connection closed' and exit 2, so tools are blocked (fail closed), not bypassed. A workspace-only scope does not panic: typed() returns an error. settings.reset repairs it. Fix as proposed: merge only object-valued layers, and use `as_object_mut()` instead of IndexMut.

findings.title: audit.retention_days above ~4.4 million days panics crash recovery on every engine start
findings.evidence: `(Timestamp::now() - jiff::SignedDuration::from_hours(days.saturating_mul(24))).to_string()`; jiff's `impl Sub<SignedDuration> for Timestamp` does `.expect("subtracting signed duration from timestamp overflowed")` once the result is before year -9999 (jiff-0.2.35 timestamp.rs:2500-2506). recovery.rs:184-194 reads the setting unvalidated (only `days > 0`) and calls days_ago; serve.rs:23 handles only Err, so the panic unwinds out of serve::start.
findings.impact: Setting retention to `forever` with a big number (e.g. 9999999; settings.set accepts any number) makes `relay serve` panic at every launch: run.sh reports the engine never became ready, and since settings can only be changed through a running engine, the user needs a manual sqlite edit to get Relay back.
findings.fix: Clamp days (e.g. to 100 years) or use checked arithmetic and treat overflow as `keep everything`; validate the setting when it is set.

v1.reason: time.rs:16 does `Timestamp::now() - SignedDuration::from_hours(days.saturating_mul(24))`. In jiff (0.2.35 in Cargo.lock; same code in 0.2.28) `Sub<SignedDuration> for Timestamp` calls `.expect("subtracting signed duration from timestamp overflowed")`, and `from_hours` panics once hours*3600 overflows i64. recovery.rs:184-194 reads `audit.retention_days` and checks only `days > 0` before calling days_ago. settings.rs:203 `set` checks the path but not the value. serve.rs:23 handles only the Err from run_with, so the panic unwinds out of serve::start at every launch. days_ago has no other caller. The mechanism is real, but the trigger is unlikely. The docs (BUS.md:281, DECISIONS.md:840) say `0` keeps everything. No native UI writes this setting. settings.set is on the user-only list (guardrail.rs:852), so an agent cannot set it. Only a user who deliberately types a value above about 4.4 million days hits it. The consequence is still severe: the engine will not start, and the store has to be edited by hand.
v1.correction: The panic can come from two places: `SignedDuration::from_hours` (when days*24*3600 overflows i64) or the `Timestamp - SignedDuration` expect (when the result is before year -9999). Both fire inside the recovery transaction during serve::start. Fix: use `Timestamp::now().checked_sub(SignedDuration::try_from_hours(..)?)` and skip pruning when either fails (overflow means keep everything). Optionally clamp or validate the setting in settings.set. Severity is low because the documented way to keep everything is 0, and the setting has no UI and cannot be set by agents.

findings.title: A malformed or unsavable remote.json stops `relay serve --remote` from running the engine at all
findings.evidence: Comment at 105-106: `The door is a convenience on top of the engine, never a reason for the engine not to start`, yet `let mut registry = Registry::load(&ctx.registry_path).map_err(...)?;` (114) and `registry.save(...)...?` (118) return before the run loop, dropping the just-started engine. Registry::load deliberately errors on a parse failure (registry.rs:146-157).
findings.impact: run.sh always launches `serve --remote`; a hand-edited, truncated or schema-incompatible remote.json, or a save failure, prevents the engine from starting — no sessions at all — instead of just disabling the phone door.
findings.fix: On load/save error, log it and continue without the door and tunnel, as the failed-bind branch (107-113) already does.

v1.reason: serve_with_door (remote.rs:88-141) starts the engine at line 97. Then `Registry::load(...).map_err(...)?` (114) and `registry.save(...)...?` (118) return Err before the run loop, so `served` is dropped and the process exits, even though the comment at 105-106 promises the door is never a reason for the engine not to start. Registry::load deliberately fails when it cannot parse the file (relay-remote registry.rs: 'A registry that cannot be parsed is an error, not a silent reset'), and save can fail on disk-full or permission errors. run.sh:32 and deploy/relay-remote.service:9 both launch `serve --remote`, so a corrupt remote.json means no engine at all, with the error only in a background log.
v1.correction: The trigger is rare: save is atomic (tmp + rename), fields use serde(default), and unknown fields are ignored, so it takes a hand edit or a filesystem failure. The fix should also drop or avoid the already-bound DirectServer and skip the tunnel. Do not reset the file, since it holds phone credentials. Log the error and run the engine without the door, as the bind-failure branch does.

findings.title: Claude hook install never refreshes a stale Relay command, and a hook that cannot start exits 127, which Claude treats as non-blocking
findings.evidence: `let already_installed = pre.iter().any(|group| ... command.contains(CLAUDE_PRE_TOOL))` (333-341) skips writing whenever any Relay pre-tool handler exists, even one whose baked-in binary path (`shell_quote_path(relay)`, 343-348) no longer exists; the git hook, by contrast, is rewritten by refresh_git (160-185). main.rs:352-353 notes only exit 2 blocks in Claude Code.
findings.impact: Worktrees whose .claude/settings.local.json was written by an engine binary that has since moved (another checkout's target/, a removed Relay worktree) keep calling the dead path: the shell exits 127, Claude proceeds, and every Bash/Write/Edit in sessions launched or resumed there runs without guardrails. The same happens for every hooked session while target/debug/relay is absent (e.g. after cargo clean, before the rebuild).
findings.fix: Rewrite any Relay-owned handler whose command differs from the current one (match on the marker, replace the command); make the command fail closed when it cannot execute, e.g. append `|| exit 2`.

v1.reason: install_claude (hooks.rs:333-353) only checks whether any PreToolUse handler's command contains CLAUDE_PRE_TOOL. If one does, it never rewrites that handler, so the binary path and --instance baked into it stay whatever they were when first written. The MCP config, by contrast, is rewritten with the current relay path on every launch (lines 425-434). relay_bin() resolves to current_exe's sibling, e.g. <worktree>/target/debug/relay. This user develops Relay inside Relay worktrees that get removed, so a baked path pointing into a removed checkout is a realistic case. When that happens the shell exits 127. relay-cli main.rs:352-353 itself says Claude only treats exit 2 as blocking, so a 127 is a non-blocking error and the tool call goes ahead with no guardrail. Clean close calls uninstall_claude (session.rs:356), which limits the stale case to worktrees that were never cleanly torn down: engine crash, restorable sessions resumed later, or a worktree shared by several sessions. install_codex (hooks.rs:512) has the same skip-if-present logic.
v1.correction: The cargo-clean case (the binary missing temporarily) is not specific to this code: any external hook command fails open the same way. That case is fixed only by making the command fail closed (e.g. `|| exit 2`), not by refreshing the path. The stale-instance case (a hook installed for another instance is kept) comes from the same root cause. Fix: replace any handler carrying CLAUDE_HOOK_MARKER whose command differs from the current one, in both install_claude and install_codex.

findings.title: blender_python panics the Blender MCP server when the script's emit() result is not a JSON object
findings.evidence: run() parses the last `RELAY_JSON:` line as the result (362-369); blender_py/run.py puts `emit` in the agent script's scope and common.py:12-13 prints `RELAY_JSON:` + json.dumps(value) for any value. For PY_RUN, `value["output"] = json!(...)` (372) and `value["saved"] = ...` (373) are serde_json IndexMut, which panics on an array/string/number. serve() (34-52) has no catch_unwind.
findings.impact: `emit([1, 2])` or `emit('done')` in an agent's blender_python code kills the `relay blender-mcp` stdio process; the agent loses every Blender tool for the rest of the session.
findings.fix: Wrap non-object results (`json!({"result": value})`) before adding fields, or insert via `as_object_mut()`.

v1.reason: blender.rs:362 takes the last stdout line starting with `RELAY_JSON:` and parses it as `Value` (366-369). For PY_RUN, 371-374 then does `value["output"] = ...` and `value["saved"] = ...`. serde_json's IndexMut turns Null into an object but panics on bool, number, string or array. run.py puts common.py's `emit` (which prints `RELAY_JSON:` + json.dumps(value) for any value) into the agent script's scope, and the script can also just print such a line itself. The call chain is serve() (34-52) -> handle -> tool dispatch (207) -> run(), and nothing on it calls catch_unwind. So `emit([1,2])`, `emit('done')` or `print('RELAY_JSON:5')` panics the main thread, and the `relay blender-mcp` stdio process exits.
v1.correction: Lines 371-374 (IndexMut on `value`). Besides `emit`, a plain `print("RELAY_JSON:...")` in the agent's code triggers it too. Fix: when the result is not an object, wrap it as `json!({"result": value})` before adding the `output`/`saved` keys.

findings.title: Edit/MultiEdit hook reports an ordinary non-matching edit as `RELAY guardrail unavailable`
findings.evidence: claude_pre_tool bails with `Edit old_string does not occur in {file_path}` / `reading edit target` (422-426; MultiEdit 438-448), and run() turns every Err into `eprintln!("RELAY guardrail unavailable: {error:#}")` with exit 2 (348-356).
findings.impact: Claude receives a blocking message saying Relay's guardrail is down when the cause is its own stale old_string (or an Edit on a file that does not exist yet); agents misread an infrastructure failure and may retry blindly or route around it with Bash.
findings.fix: Distinguish input/content problems (exit 2 with `RELAY: old_string not found in X; re-read the file`) from engine/infrastructure failures.

v1.reason: main.rs:421-426 (Edit) and 438-449 (MultiEdit) bail with `reading edit target ...` or `Edit old_string does not occur in ...`. The HookCommand::ClaudePreTool arm (348-357) prints every Err as `RELAY guardrail unavailable: {error:#}` and exits 2. The mislabeling is real. The impact is smaller than claimed: `{error:#}` includes the real cause (`... old_string does not occur in X`), so the agent does see what went wrong.
v1.correction: Claude Code most likely runs its own Edit validation (file exists, old_string matches) before PreToolUse, so a stale old_string usually never reaches this hook. The case that matters more is where the hook's re-implementation of Edit disagrees with Claude Code: the hook requires an exact `contains` match and an existing file, so an edit Claude Code would accept (for example one it matches after normalizing quotes, or an empty-old_string Edit that creates a new file) is blocked outright, and the block is reported as an infrastructure outage. Fix: report content and input failures in their own words (`RELAY: cannot preview this edit: ...`), separately from engine failures.

findings.title: Inconsistent error kinds: io_err maps every filesystem error to `unavailable`, gix_err maps bad revisions to `unavailable`
findings.evidence: io_err always returns `BusError::unavailable(code, ...)` regardless of io::ErrorKind (658-660), so file.read/move/rename/delete of a missing path return kind=unavailable code=file.not_found (via safe_join 498), while file.tree returns kind=not_found for the same code (25-28). gix_err (git.rs:1441-1443) maps every gix error to unavailable, so git.log {branch:'nope'} / git.show {sha:'bad'} give unavailable `git.revision` (258-261, 278-280), while git.branch.create's unknown start point is invalid (362-364) and branch.switch's is not_found (1342).
findings.impact: error.rs:1 tells agents to react to kind and code; a typo'd path or revision reads as an infrastructure outage (CLI exit 4, retry later) instead of a caller mistake (exit 1), so MCP agents retry instead of fixing the argument.
findings.fix: Map io::ErrorKind::NotFound to not_found, AlreadyExists to conflict, PermissionDenied to refused; map gix rev-parse failures to not_found/invalid.

v1.reason: io_err (file.rs ~658-660) always returns BusError::unavailable whatever the io::ErrorKind. A missing path in file.read/move/rename/delete therefore comes back via safe_join as unavailable/file.not_found, while file.tree returns not_found/file.not_found for a non-directory. gix_err (git.rs 1441-1443) maps every gix error to unavailable, so a bad revision in git.log or git.show is unavailable/git.revision. By contrast, git.branch.create maps an unknown start point to invalid (~362). error.rs:1 says agents react to kind and code, and ErrorKind::exit_code maps unavailable to CLI exit 4 but not_found/invalid to 1. BUS.md:90 defines unavailable as 'a dependency is missing or down'.
v1.correction: No in-repo client (native, CLI, remote) branches on these kinds, so the impact is limited to inconsistent contract signals and exit codes for agents, not a concrete malfunction. The claim that MCP agents retry is speculative. Fix as proposed: match on io::ErrorKind in io_err, and map rev_parse failures to not_found or invalid.

findings.title: file.search fails entirely on the first unreadable or vanished directory
findings.evidence: Inside the walk: `fs::read_dir(&dir).map_err(|e| io_err("file.search_failed", &dir, e))?` (317-318), whereas unreadable files are skipped (`if read.is_err() { continue; }`, 334-339); skip_dir excludes only .git/.relay/node_modules/target.
findings.impact: A root-owned docker volume directory, a permission-restricted folder, or a build/ or dist/ directory deleted mid-walk by a concurrent build makes every project search from the editor return `file.search_failed` instead of results.
findings.fix: Skip directories whose read_dir fails (optionally report how many were skipped).

v1.reason: Search is registered unlocked. Inside the walk, `fs::read_dir(&dir).map_err(|e| io_err("file.search_failed", &dir, e))?` (file.rs ~317-318) aborts the whole op with no partial hits. Unreadable files, by contrast, are skipped (`if read.is_err() { continue; }`). skip_dir only excludes a fixed set of directories, so a mode-700 root-owned subdirectory (for example a docker volume) or a directory deleted between being pushed and being popped makes every project search fail.
v1.correction: The error kind is unavailable, so the editor shows a failure rather than an empty result. Fix: on a read_dir error, `continue` and optionally count the skipped directories in the result.

results.coverage:
Method (all read-only; experiments under scratchpad/exp/lensdd):
(1) Ops vs handlers: extracted every `op!(Type, "name"` in crates/relay-bus/src/ops/*.rs (221 ops) and matched each to `register(_unlocked|_staged)?::<Type` in relay-core, using the ops module each handler file imports.
(2) Ops vs clients: scanned for string literals of op names in apps/relay-native, relay-cli, relay-remote, relay-core, tests, scripts and plugins. The mobile app was grepped only to learn whether an op has a caller; nothing is reported about it. Then cross-checked each op's actors against the role allowlists.
(3) Events: multi-line `emit(_system)?("…")`, tuple and const event names, compared with `.emits(&[…])` declarations, the native `bus.subscribe` list and `e.ev ==` matches.
(4) Dead items: every `fn`, `struct`, `enum` and `const` whose name occurs nowhere else in the workspace, with comments stripped; `allow(dead_code|unused)`; and same-name `fn` definitions across files as duplicate candidates (ago, canon, hex, git, git_optional, relative_path, frontmatter, named, rpc_error, column_str, …), each inspected by hand.
(5) CSS: selectors in theme.css and css/*.css compared with every token in native Rust, including format-prefix handling.
(6) Settings: defaults in settings.rs compared with readers (settings::get, raw `SELECT … FROM settings`), native settings.get/set paths and `setting:` widget names.
(7) Subprocesses: every `Command::new`, `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT`, `output_with_timeout`, `git_mutate` and `worktree::remove` call site, each with its registration kind (locked, staged or unlocked).
(8) Schema ownership: the CREATE TABLE list compared with project.remove's delete list, reproduced in sqlite3 with the real 20 migrations; SQLite id reuse confirmed.
(9) Error codes the native client matches on, compared with codes the engine produces.

Not finished or limits:
- relay-native cannot be compiled here and CI does not lint it. Dead private code there was found only by unique-name heuristics; methods that share a common name (refresh, open, section, …) could hide unused copies.
- Four icon geometries (clear, folder-plus, graph, resume) are never requested by a literal name; not checked against dynamically built names.
- Field-level use of relay-bus types was not checked.
- blender_py and unreal_py common.py were not compared for duplication.
- Finding 5 depends on whether Claude Code passes tool_input.file_path unnormalized; not verified. The engine-side file.write route does not depend on it.
- The shell-tokenizer results come from a faithful Python port run on neutral placeholder words, not from running Rust.
- I saw but did not follow up several problems outside this lens; other auditors should cover them: the notify.settings.set undo merge does not revert added keys; quoted first words are treated as data by the denied-command matcher (noted in finding 2); responses over 2 MiB on native's main socket, which could include wallpaper-library reads.

findings.title: project.remove (and workspace.remove) fails with a FOREIGN KEY error once any task in the project has a label
findings.evidence: The delete list at workspace.rs:354-375 removes rows from 17 project-owned tables (message_recipients, messages, claims, task_sessions, sessions, tasks, modules, notes, overlaps, file_trash, integrations, ui_layouts, device_runs, skill_projects, plugin_projects, …) and then runs `DELETE FROM projects WHERE id = ?1` (380). `labels` is not in the list. Migration v16 created `labels (… project_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES projects(id) …)` with no ON DELETE CASCADE (store.rs:315-319), and the store runs with `foreign_keys = ON` (store.rs:397). Label rows are inserted by task.rs label_id (`INSERT INTO labels(project_id,name,created_at)`, task.rs:136-139) from task.label.add and task.create {labels}, and nothing anywhere deletes from labels. I applied all 20 real migrations in sqlite3, inserted a project, a task and a label, then ran project.remove's statements: `DELETE FROM projects WHERE id = 1` failed with `FOREIGN KEY constraint failed`.
findings.impact: Trigger: the user labels any task (native task_pages.rs:707 calls task.label.add), then uses "Remove project…" or removes the workspace (shell/registry.rs:621-627). Result: the transaction rolls back with an internal storage error, and the project or workspace can never be removed from the UI or the CLI. workspace.remove fails the same way because it calls project.remove for each project (workspace.rs:172-177). No test removes a project that has labels (registry_remove.rs has none).
findings.fix: Add `DELETE FROM labels WHERE project_id=?1` after the task deletes (task_labels rows cascade). Alternatively, add ON DELETE CASCADE through a new migration. Add a registry_remove test that removes a project with a labelled task. Also consider a test that compares the delete list with `PRAGMA foreign_key_list` for every table, so the next project-owned table cannot be missed again.

v1.reason: project.remove's delete list (crates/relay-core/src/handlers/workspace.rs:354-375) covers every table with a project_id foreign key except `labels`. Migration v16 declares `labels.project_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES projects(id)` with no ON DELETE CASCADE (store.rs:315-319), and foreign_keys is ON (store.rs:397, 414). Labels are created by task.rs:136-139 (task.label.add, task.create/update {labels}), and nothing ever deletes them. I reproduced the failure in sqlite3: tasks deleted, then `DELETE FROM projects WHERE id=1` returns `FOREIGN KEY constraint failed` while a label row exists. workspace.remove calls project.remove through invoke_registered (workspace.rs:172-177), so it fails the same way. The whole transaction rolls back, so nothing is half-deleted, but the removal can never succeed.
v1.correction: Only `labels` is missing; every other project_id table is covered. Fix: add `DELETE FROM labels WHERE project_id=?1` after the task deletes (task_labels cascades from either side), and add a test that removes a project with a labelled task.

v2.reason:
(a) Confirmed at 361c6f9. The delete list in project.remove (workspace.rs:354-375) has no `labels` entry, and the handler then runs `DELETE FROM projects WHERE id = ?1` (workspace.rs:380). Migration v16 creates `labels.project_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES projects(id)` with no ON DELETE action (store.rs:315-319). No later migration touches that table. Every connection sets foreign_keys=ON (store.rs:397, 414). Label rows are inserted by label_id (task.rs:136-139), which is reached from task.create and task.update {labels} through set_labels (task.rs:429-441, 745) and from task.label.add (task.rs:1190-1199). No code anywhere runs `DELETE FROM labels`: label.remove and set_labels only delete task_labels edges.

I reproduced it myself. I pulled all 20 MIGRATIONS out of store.rs and the 20 delete statements out of workspace.rs with a script, and ran them in SQLite with foreign_keys=ON. A project with one labelled task fails on DELETE FROM projects with "FOREIGN KEY constraint failed" and rolls back. It fails the same way after the label has been taken off the task, because the label row stays behind. A PRAGMA foreign_key_list sweep shows labels.project_id is the only foreign key into any table the handler deletes from that is neither on the list nor ON DELETE CASCADE/SET NULL. No test covers this: the removal test in bus.rs:958 creates its task without labels, and registry_remove.rs has none.

(b) The user triggers it in normal use. Labels come from the native "Labels · optional" field when creating a task (task_pages.rs:495) or the "Add label" button (task_pages.rs:701-709), and also from any CLI or agent call to task.create/update with labels. After that, "Remove project…" or removing the workspace (registry.rs:621-626, which always sends force=true), or project.remove / workspace.remove on the bus, fails every time. Once one label has ever existed in the project, removal fails forever: no operation deletes a label, and removing it from every task does not help. Project removal is an occasional flow, not a frequent one.

(c) `.bus()` maps the error to an internal BusError. Dispatch rolls back the transaction (engine.rs ~1076) and the dialog shows the SQLite text. The project and the workspace cannot be removed without hand-editing SQL.

There is a worse effect that neither the finding nor the first verifier mentions. With force=true, workspace.rs:328 first calls session.close for each open session through invoke_registered, and session.close has side effects outside SQLite that a rollback cannot undo:
- Its prepare phase runs run_teardown, which uninstalls the git, Claude and Codex hooks from the worktree, and remove_hook_dir (session.rs:1575, 1596).
- Its commit phase calls take_pty (session.rs:1602), which takes the PTY out of the engine registry and queues the kill as an after_commit callback.
- On rollback, dispatch drops that callback. That releases the last Arc<Pty>, and Pty::drop SIGKILLs the agent's process group (pty.rs:381-389).
- The exit callback was not silenced (remove_worktree is false), so it marks each session 'exited' and marks a builder's active task 'failed' (session.rs:646-668).

So a failed forced removal kills the project's agents without a graceful stop, removes their hooks, and flips builder tasks to failed, and the project is still there. With workspace.remove, agents in projects processed before the failing one are killed too. Worktrees are not deleted (that after_commit callback is dropped as well), so checkout data is not lost.

(d) High fits the rubric: a deterministic, permanent failure of a normal flow with no workaround in the app, plus wrong side effects on live agents. It is not critical: no data is lost or corrupted, the store stays consistent, and removal is not a frequent core flow.

(e) The fix is correct and complete for this root cause. In the same SQLite experiment, adding `DELETE FROM labels WHERE project_id=?1` after the task deletes lets the removal commit and leaves no task_labels rows, since task_labels cascades from both of its foreign keys. The alternative, ON DELETE CASCADE through a migration, would need a full SQLite table rebuild and gains nothing. Both proposed tests are sound: removing a project that has a labelled task, and a schema check that every foreign key into projects either cascades or is on the delete list.
v2.correction:
The first verifier wrote that "the whole transaction rolls back, so nothing is half-deleted". That holds only for SQLite. On the forced path, which the native dialog and workspace.remove always take, each open session's session.close has already run its non-transactional side effects before the FK failure:
- run_teardown and remove_hook_dir strip the session's hooks (session.rs:1575, 1596).
- take_pty removes the PTY from the registry (session.rs:1602). The queued kill callback is then dropped on rollback, so Pty::drop SIGKILLs the agent (pty.rs:381-389).
- The unsilenced exit callback marks the session 'exited' and a builder's active task 'failed' (session.rs:646-668).

The project itself survives. The impact should therefore read: removal fails permanently, and every live agent in the project (and, for workspace.remove, in the earlier projects too) is killed and its hooks removed as a side effect. Severity stays high, since no data is lost.

The fix as proposed is right: add `DELETE FROM labels WHERE project_id=?1` (task_labels cascades). Prefer it over a cascade migration, which needs a table rebuild in SQLite.

A separate issue, outside this finding's root cause: project.remove does irreversible teardown before its final DELETE. Fixing labels removes this deterministic trigger, but any later failure in that handler would still kill agents while the database rolls back.

findings.title: Guardrail denied-command matching misses commands in ( ), $( ) and backticks, which the device-lease parser in the same gate call already splits on
findings.evidence: guardrail::shell_commands splits commands only on `';' | '\n' | '|' | '&' =>` (939). Every other character falls to the default arm, so `(`, `)`, `` ` `` and `$(` stick to words. For `(git reset --hard)` the bare words are ["(git","reset","--hard)"], and the word-window match in denied_matches (969-1001) never hits. device_lease::split_commands (device_lease.rs:365-389) is a second shell splitter in the same crate. It splits on `(None, ';' | '\n' | '|' | '&' | '(' | ')' | '`')` and on `$(`, and it unquotes tokens. guardrail.gate runs both on the same command: evaluate_granted first, then device_lease::gate_command (handlers/guardrail.rs:510-532). I ported shell_commands and denied_matches to Python and used a neutral pattern. `zap --all` matched. `(zap --all)`, `cd src && (zap --all)`, `echo $(zap --all)`, `` `zap --all` ``, `"zap" --all` and `echo "\"" ; zap --all ; echo "\""` were all NOT matched (the last one because a backslash-escaped quote inside double quotes flips the quote state).
findings.impact: An agent whose Bash call runs `(cd sub && git reset --hard)` or `git clean -fd` inside a subshell or command substitution executes a denied command without any hold or refusal. This is a common, non-adversarial shell idiom. self_approval (857) uses the same tokenizer: `(relay --actor user …)` produces the word "(relay", which fails the `starts_with("relay")` stem check. D103 covers quoted data, not subshells.
findings.fix: Give relay-core one shell tokenizer. It should split on `(`, `)`, backtick, `$(`, `{` and `}`, honour backslash escapes inside double quotes, and treat a quoted first word as the program. Use it in both guardrail and device_lease, and add tests for subshell and command-substitution forms.

v1.reason: guardrail.rs:937-941 splits commands only on `';' | '\n' | '|' | '&'`. Every other character goes to the default arm (942-946), so `(`, `)` and backtick stick to the words and `$(` is never split off. denied_matches (969-998) compares lowercased bare-word windows against the pattern words. For `(cd sub && git reset --hard)` the second command is ["git","reset","--hard)"], which does not equal ["git","reset","--hard"]. The defaults in settings.rs:33 are "rm -rf", "git reset --hard", "git clean -fd" and "git push --force", so the miss applies to the shipped configuration. Inside a quote (918-925) a backslash is not treated as an escape, so `\"` closes the double quote early and flips the quote state. evaluate_exec (811-846) checks only self_approval and denied_matches, and both use this tokenizer, so nothing else catches these forms. device_lease::split_commands (device_lease.rs:365-389) does split on ( ) ` and $(. The gate handler runs it after evaluate_granted has already allowed the command (handlers/guardrail.rs:510-532). That is a second, already-diverged shell splitter. D103 only settles that quoted data is not matched; it says nothing about subshells. `(cd dir && cmd)` is an idiom agents use routinely, so this is a safety check that is silently bypassed in normal use.
v1.correction: Line refs are accurate: tokenizer at guardrail.rs:894-952, separator arm at 937, matcher at 969-998, self_approval at 857. The denied list was never a hard boundary even against a deliberately evasive agent: `bash -c 'git reset --hard'` is a quoted word and goes unmatched by design (D103). High is still right because the subshell and `$( )` misses occur in non-adversarial use. Besides sharing one tokenizer, strip leading `(`/`{` and trailing `)`/`}` from words when they are not quoted.

v2.reason:
(a) The code does what the finding says, at 361c6f9.
- `shell_commands` (guardrail.rs:894-956) splits only at the `';' | '\n' | '|' | '&'` arm (939). `(`, `)`, `` ` `` and `$(` stay attached to words.
- The quote arm (922-931) reads up to the next matching quote and does not treat a backslash as an escape.
- `denied_matches` (969-998) compares contiguous windows of lowercased unquoted words (988).
- `device_lease::split_commands` (device_lease.rs:365-390) splits on `( ) `` ` `` and `$(`. The gate handler runs it on the same command after `evaluate_granted` returns Allow (handlers/guardrail.rs:511-533).

To check behaviour I ported `shell_commands`, `denied_matches`, `is_guardrail_dry_run` and `self_approval` to Python. The port agrees with every assertion in tests/agent_surface.rs:238-251 and tests/guardrails.rs:645-657 and 761-774. With the shipped defaults (settings.rs:33), these are NOT matched:
- `(cd sub && git reset --hard)`
- `(cd sub && git clean -fd)`
- `(cd sub && git push --force)`
- `(git reset --hard)` and `(rm -rf build)`
- `out=$(git reset --hard HEAD~1)`
- `` `git reset --hard HEAD` ``
- `"git" reset --hard`
- `git commit -m "fix \"foo\" bug" && git push --force`. The escaped quote flips the quote state, so the rest of the line is read as quoted data.

`self_approval` also misses `(relay --actor user q guardrail.confirm x)` and `$(relay ...)`.

(b) Reach. Every agent Bash or exec call goes through this check:
- Claude: the PreToolUse hook passes `tool_input.command` verbatim as `{kind: exec}` (relay-cli main.rs:405-410).
- Codex: the same, at main.rs:506-512.

BUS.md principle 6 ("Seatbelts, not sandboxes") puts mistakes by non-hostile agents in scope. These forms are what a non-hostile agent can produce by accident, so they are not adversarial evasion like `bash -c '...'`, which D103 leaves unmatched on purpose.

Frequency is occasional, not "common". A trailing `)` defeats the match only when the pattern's last word is the last word inside the parentheses. A leading `(`, `$(` or backtick defeats it only when attached to the program name. The escaped-quote case needs a `\"` earlier in the same line, which is a frequent shape in agent commands (commit messages, JSON payloads, grep patterns).

(c) When it fires, the gate returns Allow:
- No hold, refusal, notification or refusal audit row is created.
- The command runs and can discard uncommitted work (`reset --hard`), delete untracked files (`clean -fd`), rewrite a remote branch (`push --force`) or delete files (`rm -rf`).
- Relay sets no Claude permission mode: relay.settings.json carries only `statusLine` (hooks.rs:396-398). So Claude's own prompt is a second layer only if the user has not already allowed Bash broadly.
- Codex is launched with `--approve-for-me` (providers.rs:218).

(d) High matches the rubric item "a safety check that can be silently bypassed". The trigger is a normal shell form, and the consequence can be data loss. It is not critical: the bypass is occasional, and the docs disclaim guardrails as a boundary against hostile agents.

(e) The fix is right for this root cause, but incomplete for the purpose of the check (see the correction).
v2.correction:
1. The impact is overstated. A trailing `)` does not defeat the match when an argument follows the pattern. These are still DENIED:
- `(cd frontend && rm -rf node_modules)`
- `(cd sub && git reset --hard origin/main)`
- `(cd sub && git clean -fd .)`

The reliable misses are:
- the program glued to `(`, `$(` or a backtick;
- the pattern's last word followed directly by `)`;
- an escaped `\"` inside double quotes earlier in the line, which can hide every later command on that line.

The escaped-quote case should be stated as a co-equal trigger, not an aside.

2. The fix is necessary but not sufficient. The contiguous-window matcher (guardrail.rs:985-988) separately lets all of these through today:
- `git -C <dir> reset --hard` and `git -C sub clean -fd`
- `git push origin main --force` and `git push -f`
- `git clean -fdx` and `git clean -df`
- `rm -fr`, `rm -r -f` and `rm --recursive --force`

`git -C` is arguably the most frequent miss, because Claude Code agents are told to avoid `cd`. That is a separate root cause: the matcher compares a contiguous run of words, where it should match the program plus its required subcommand and flags in any position, with flag bundling allowed. If no other finding reports it, it should be its own finding. A tokenizer-only fix will leave the denied list unreliable.

3. Implementation notes for the fix:
- Inside double quotes, apply the POSIX rule: a backslash escapes only `$`, backtick, `"`, `\` and newline. Inside single quotes it escapes nothing.
- Splitting on `{` and `}` is harmless for matching. `find -exec rm -rf {} \;` still matches before the `{`.
- Grant values are re-tokenized at check time by the same function (guardrail/grants.rs:143), so grant comparison stays consistent after the change.
- The device_lease splitter special-cases `&>` (device_lease.rs:376) and re-splits quoted text on whitespace with `unquote` (321, 392-394). Moving it to the shared tokenizer actually fits the "one quoted word" comment at 431. Its tests need re-running.
- Prefer splitting over the first verifier's idea of stripping `(` and `)` from words. Stripping misses `$(` and backticks unless those are also stripped.
- The `self_approval` sub-point is low impact on its own: its comment at guardrail.rs:849-850 says it "closes the obvious door, not every door", and invoking relay as the user is a deliberate act.
- There are no tests for subshells, command substitution or escaped quotes. Add them together with the fix.

findings.title: project.clone runs an unbounded `git clone` inside the store transaction
findings.evidence: `e.register::<ProjectClone>` (228) runs `Command::new("git").current_dir(&workspace.path).arg("clone").arg("--").arg(&p.url).arg(&destination).output()` (234) while the handler's transaction (`ctx.tx()`) is open. It does not go through proc::output_with_timeout and does not set GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0. The native client allows this op 1800 s (`"project.clone" => Duration::from_secs(1800)`, client.rs:67), so clones are expected to take minutes. The other `git clone` in the engine, for skill.install, was moved to the staged phase precisely so that "a slow clone [stays] off every other op (D144)" (provider.rs:209-216).
findings.impact: While a repository clones from the onboarding or registry UI, the single store mutex stays held. Every audited request waits for the whole clone: each agent's guardrail.gate hook (so every agent tool call), task and session updates, and UI refreshes. For a private https URL with no credential helper, git prompts for a username on the terminal the engine inherited (run.sh starts it with nohup from the user's shell) and waits there, so the lock can stay held indefinitely.
findings.fix: Use register_staged. In prepare, clone with output_with_timeout, GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0 and stdin null, and remove the destination on failure. In finish, run project.add.

v1.reason: ProjectClone is registered with `e.register` (workspace.rs:228), so its body runs inside the locked transaction. It runs `Command::new("git")...arg("clone")...output()` (workspace.rs:234) with no timeout, no GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0 and stdin inherited. The native onboarding calls project.clone (onboarding.rs:527) and allows it 1800 s (client.rs:67), which shows multi-minute clones are expected. skill.install's clone was deliberately staged for D144 (provider.rs:209-211). For the whole clone the store mutex is held, which freezes every audited op, guardrail gates included.
v1.correction: Whether git actually waits on a credential prompt depends on how the engine was launched (a controlling tty or a GUI credential helper). The bus freeze for the full length of a normal large clone needs no prompt. Fix as proposed: register_staged, with the clone in prepare through output_with_timeout and GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0, and project.add in finish.

v2.reason:
(a) The code does what the finding says. `e.register::<ProjectClone>` (workspace.rs:228) is a plain locked handler. dispatch_inner takes `self.store.lock()` and opens `conn.transaction()` (engine.rs:954-956) before it calls the handler. Inside, `Command::new("git")...arg("clone").arg("--").arg(&p.url).arg(&destination).output()` (workspace.rs:234) runs with no deadline and no GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0. The other git callers do set that variable: worktree.rs:213, git.rs:943 and 1349, branch_cleanup.rs:114. Nothing in the docs makes this intended. D144 and D149 (DECISIONS.md:729 and 797) forbid slow subprocesses under the store mutex, and project.clone is missing from D149's list of converted ops. BUS.md:246-248 and the op's own description ("async; project.changed when done") call it async, but it runs synchronously.

(b) How it is reached: in the native app, the sidebar's "Add project…" (shell/registry.rs:472) or first-run setup opens the GitHub tab, which calls project.clone (onboarding.rs:527). Any user-door client can also call it: the CLI, or a paired phone through bridge.rs. It runs about once per project added from GitHub, so it is rare but part of a normal flow. The freeze lasts as long as the clone: a few seconds for a small repository (this one's pack is about 8 MiB), and minutes for a large or LFS-heavy one. The client allows 1800 s for this op (client.rs:67), and its 180 s worktree timeouts cite LFS hydration, so long clones are expected.

(c) What happens while it runs: every request that touches the store waits. Every agent socket request blocks first in check_session_token, which takes the lock (engine.rs:1378), so every MCP call and every Claude PreToolUse guardrail.gate hook stalls. That hook has a 30 s budget (hooks.rs:351). What Claude Code does when the hook times out cannot be established from this repo. Session exit and state writes through system_write (engine.rs:697), other connections and the phone door also wait. Keystrokes and resizes are not affected: they use the D148 fast path, and each pane has its own connection (terminal.rs:476).

There is also a worse case. run.sh puts the engine in the launching terminal's foreground process group (nohup + &, no setsid), so /dev/tty can be opened. Cloning a private https repository with no credential helper then makes git wait on a username prompt in that terminal, and the lock stays held until someone answers. When Relay is launched from the .desktop entry (Terminal=false), git fails at once instead, unless an askpass helper is set; in that case the lock is held while the dialog is open.

(d) High is correct. The rubric names "a freeze of the bus" as high. It is not critical, because the freeze is bounded by the clone's duration except in the terminal-launch, missing-credential case.

(e) register_staged is the right shape (as for skill.install and worktree.create) and removes the engine-wide freeze, but the fix is incomplete as written; see the correction.
v2.correction:
1. The first verifier's "stdin inherited" is wrong. `Command::output()` sets stdin to null by default. git prompts through /dev/tty, not stdin, so the indefinite wait needs the engine to have a controlling terminal.

2. Staging the clone does not stop the desktop UI from stalling. The socket door handles one request at a time per connection: the loop at socket.rs:335 awaits each dispatch (line 742) before it reads the next line. `ui.call` sends project.clone on the main UI connection (app.rs:1111-1116), because it is not in is_lifecycle_request (client.rs:50-62). So every UI refresh still queues behind the clone and times out after 30 s. Send project.clone on its own connection, the way lifecycle requests already are, or make it truly async as BUS.md describes.

3. Changes needed to the cleanup:
   - git already removes a partial checkout on most failures. It leaves the repository behind when only the checkout fails ("Clone succeeded, but checkout failed", for example an LFS smudge error), and it cannot clean up after the SIGKILL at the deadline.
   - Delete only a directory this request created. Once the clone runs unlocked, two clones to the same destination can race, and a blind remove would delete the other one's checkout. Cloning into a unique temporary sibling and renaming it into place on success solves both problems.
   - In finish, keep calling project.add, which re-checks the workspace. During the unlocked clone, workspace.remove can run, and the clone must then be deleted.

4. Two smaller points:
   - GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0 does not stop ssh host-key or passphrase prompts. The deadline bounds those, or set `GIT_SSH_COMMAND` to `ssh -o BatchMode=yes`.
   - Set the engine deadline below the client's 1800 s so that the typed timeout reaches the UI.

Related: the skill clone in github.rs:109 also skips output_with_timeout and GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0. It runs in the staged prepare, so it ties up one request, not the store.

findings.title: The shared mutating-git runner worktree::git/git_mutate has no deadline and no prompt suppression, unlike the six other git runners
findings.evidence: `let out = Command::new("git").arg("-C").arg(repo).args(args).output()` (27), wrapped by `pub fn git_mutate` (36), sets no timeout and no GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT. Six bounded copies already exist: worktree::create (211-216: GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0 and 120 s), git.rs fetch_remote (938-959: GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0 and 20 s), run_switch (1347-1352), branch_cleanup::Git::run (111-122), hooks::git (583-597) and guardrail::git_output (1122-1133). Callers of the unbounded runner include network operations: git.push prepare (git.rs:617) and the device primary-sync fetch/merge on the run worker (device.rs:1575, 1618). They also include handlers holding the store lock: git.branch.create (374), git.branch.delete (485), git.stage/unstage (503/527), the git.commit finish phase inside the transaction (571), git.branch.clean_merged (712), file.restore_head (file.rs:256) and integration.discard (integration.rs:64). More hand-rolled unbounded runners: validate_branch_name (git.rs:1269), device git_capture/git_optional/git_is_ancestor (device.rs:1500-1545), and github::download_skills `git clone` (github.rs:109) and rev-parse (155). The same split exists for gh: git.pr.open runs `gh pr create` with `cmd.output()` under the lock (git.rs:666-680), while git.pr.list bounds gh at 10 s (1094) and branch_cleanup sets GH_PROMPT_DISABLED.
findings.impact: Violates CLAUDE.md: "Every subprocess forked from a handler goes through proc::output_with_timeout". git.push to a remote that needs credentials can block its request indefinitely, while git.fetch on the same remote fails fast because fetch_remote sets GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0. A primary-sync fetch that hangs leaves the device.run 'building' and holding its device lease (other sessions get device.busy) until it is stopped by hand. device.run.stop cannot kill that git child (RunRuntime.stop only kills the installed child), so the child and its worker thread leak. In the locked handlers, any git that blocks freezes the whole bus: a gpg pinentry on `git commit` with commit.gpgsign, or LFS clean filters on `git add`.
findings.fix: Make worktree::git the single runner: output_with_timeout with a per-call timeout, GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0 and stdin null. Route the hand-rolled copies and the gh calls through equivalent bounded helpers. Move push, commit and stage work off the lock where possible.

v1.reason: worktree::git (worktree.rs:26-33) calls `.output()` with no deadline, no GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT and stdin inherited. git_mutate (line 36) exposes it, and its callers include locked handlers: git.branch.create (git.rs:374), branch delete (485), stage/unstage (503/527), the commit finish phase inside the transaction (git.rs:571; register_staged's finish holds the lock), and file.restore_head (file.rs:256). The device primary-sync runs an unbounded `git fetch` (device.rs:1575) plus hand-rolled unbounded git_capture/git_optional/git_is_ancestor (device.rs:1500-1545). git.fetch, by contrast, uses the bounded, prompt-suppressed fetch_remote. The worst case is git.pr.open: it is registered with plain `e.register` and runs the network call `gh pr create` via `cmd.output()` under the store lock (git.rs:666-680).
v1.correction: git.push is register_staged with the push in prepare (git.rs:598-617), so a hanging push blocks only its own request, not the bus. The finding's "locked handlers" list should not imply otherwise. The most severe concrete break is gh pr create under the lock (network latency on every PR open) and git commit in the locked finish phase (gpg signing or pinentry). Fix: make the shared runner use proc::output_with_timeout with GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0 (and GH_PROMPT_DISABLED for gh), and move PrOpen to register_staged.

v2.reason:
(a) The code checks out at 361c6f9.
- worktree::git (worktree.rs:26-33) calls `Command::new("git")...output()` with no deadline and no GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT. git_mutate (line 36) passes straight through to it.
- D144 (DECISIONS.md:729-738) and CLAUDE.md both require every subprocess a handler forks to go through proc::output_with_timeout.
- The six bounded runners are where the finding says.
- Plain `e.register` handlers that call the unbounded runner, so with the store mutex held: BranchCreate (git.rs:345/374), BranchDelete (445/485), Stage (490/503), Unstage (507/527), CleanMerged (693/712), file RestoreHead (file.rs:253/256) and IntegrationDiscard (integration.rs:64).
- CommitOp runs its `git commit` in the staged finish (571), and finish runs under the lock (engine.rs:953-977).
- PrOpen (git.rs:666) is a plain register handler that runs `gh pr create` via `cmd.output()` (679-680) with the mutex held.

(b) Reachable, in normal flows:
- The native Git panel's Open PR button sends git.pr.open (code_git.rs:662). Every PR open holds the store mutex across gh's GitHub API round trips: about 1-3 s normally, and with no limit on a stalled network. The code's own comment at git.rs:1090-1092 says this exact unbounded gh wait "used to be an unbounded wait for every other bus op behind it".
- Agents can call git.commit and git.stage over MCP, since neither op is UserOnly. With commit.gpgsign and a cold gpg-agent cache, `git commit` waits on pinentry with the lock held. That can happen from an agent's commit while nobody is watching. This user's own git config does not sign commits.
- git.branch.create, from the UI with a start point (code_git.rs:1035), runs `git switch -c name start`. That is a full checkout, under the lock and unbounded, and LFS smudge may download from the network. Its sibling git.branch.switch was deliberately moved off the lock and bounded at 120 s for this reason (git.rs:384).
- Staging LFS assets runs the clean filter under the lock. That costs seconds, but it is slow rather than hung.

(c) What happens while the lock is held:
- Every op except keystrokes waits; D148 exempts only session.input and session.resize.
- That includes guardrail.gate, a plain register handler (guardrail.rs:304). Each agent's PreToolUse hook calls it before every Edit, Write or Bash (hooks.rs:349-351, 30 s hook timeout), so all sessions stall.
- UI requests time out at 30 s (client.rs:65-71).
- Unverified: if Claude Code lets a tool call proceed when its hook times out, a freeze longer than 30 s would also skip the gate.
- Callers that run off the lock hang only their own request or run: the push prepare, the skill-install clone, and the device primary-sync on the run worker. A stuck sync keeps the run "building" and keeps its device lease until someone stops it. RunStop cannot kill the git child (device.rs:403-408).

(d) High fits the rubric's "a freeze of the bus":
- git.pr.open causes a guaranteed bus-wide stall in a normal UI flow.
- The pinentry case and a stalled network can make that stall indefinite.
- It is not critical: an indefinite freeze needs signing, a stalled network or an engine attached to a terminal, and most git_mutate calls take milliseconds.

(e) The fix points the right way but is incomplete and has a side effect; see correction.
v2.correction:
1. stdin is not inherited, so the first verifier is wrong on that point. `Command::output()` already gives the child /dev/null as stdin, which makes the fix's "stdin null" a no-op. Only git_is_ancestor's `.status()` call (device.rs:1528) inherits stdio.

2. The push-hangs-while-fetch-fails-fast contrast only holds when the engine has a controlling terminal, for example `relay serve` started from a shell (nothing calls setsid). Under deploy/relay-remote.service, git cannot open /dev/tty and the push fails at once with ENXIO. GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0 also does not stop ssh passphrase or host-key prompts, nor an askpass helper. git.push runs in an unlocked prepare (git.rs:598-617), so it never holds the lock. LFS clean filters are slow, not blocking.

3. The clearest bus freeze, git.pr.open, does not go through the shared runner. It is a plain register handler doing network I/O under the lock, which breaks D149, so a deadline alone only caps the freeze. Fix: make it register_staged and run gh in prepare, using output_with_timeout and GH_PROMPT_DISABLED=1. Do the same for:
   - BranchCreate (reuse run_switch)
   - Stage, Unstage and RestoreHead
   - CleanMerged

4. Two related sites are missing from the finding. worktree.remove (git.rs:129-141) and integration.discard (integration.rs:62) run worktree::remove under the lock. That means purge_build and dir_size walks plus an unbounded `git worktree remove --force` (worktree.rs:362). session.close and session.discard_restorable do the same work in an unlocked prepare (session.rs:1505-1524 and 1547-1579).

5. Side effect of the fix: output_with_timeout kills with SIGKILL. If the deadline fires on a git command that writes (commit, add, checkout, switch, merge --ff-only), it can leave .git/index.lock or ref locks behind, and every later git write in that checkout fails until someone deletes them. Use generous per-command deadlines, or send SIGTERM before SIGKILL, because git removes its lockfiles on SIGTERM. run_switch and worktree::create already carry this risk at 120 s.

6. `git commit` sits in the finish on purpose, straight after guardrail::enforce (git.rs:557-572). Moving it off the lock must keep the gate-then-commit order, and its deadline must leave time to type a passphrase into pinentry.

7. A separate bug that a deadline would not fix: device.run.stop during the sync phase does not cancel the worker. When the fetch returns, the worker still fast-forwards the primary checkout and starts the run command. stream_command checks stopped() only after the first output line, then returns without killing that child.

findings.title: Protected paths and shape gates match unnormalized path strings, so a write to `a/./b` gets past a rule for `a/b`
findings.evidence: There are four near-identical relative-path validators: guardrail::relative_path (1135-1146), file::rel (file.rs:470-487), git::validate_path (git.rs:780-800) and overlap::relative_path (overlap.rs:82-96). Each checks `path.components()`, which skips interior `.` and empty segments, and none returns a normalized path: guardrail's returns `Ok(path.to_path_buf())` with the raw text. path_matches (1161-1168) then compares `path.to_string_lossy()` as text: `pattern == path || path.starts_with(&format!("{pattern}/")) || glob_match(…)`. file.write and file.create pass the raw `p.path` to guardrail::enforce (file.rs:93-102, 138-147), and rename/move pass `rel.to_string_lossy()` (file.rs:584). The CLI hook's `path.strip_prefix(&root)` (relay-cli main.rs:574) keeps interior `/./` as well.
findings.impact: Example: protected_paths contains "config/prod.env", a multi-segment directory such as "config/secrets", or a shape gate on a critical file. An agent session with bus_writes calls file.write {path:"config/./prod.env"}. The rule does not match, the write is allowed, and the protected file is overwritten. A Claude Write to "/wt/config/./prod.env" is gated as "config/./prod.env" with the same result, assuming Claude Code passes tool_input.file_path through unnormalized, which I did not verify. Single-segment directory patterns ("secrets") still match through the "dir/" prefix test. Grants (grants.rs:105) use the same matcher.
findings.fix: Add one shared normalizer: reject or collapse `.` and empty segments and return the joined Normal components as a '/'-separated string. Call it from every validator, and run path_matches only on its output. Add tests for "a/./b" and "a//b".

v1.reason: For a relative path, write_target (guardrail.rs:628-630) returns relative_path(raw) unchanged. relative_path (1135-1146) rejects only ParentDir, RootDir and Prefix, and returns `path.to_path_buf()` with the raw text. path_matches (1161-1168) compares the raw string: `pattern == path || path.starts_with("{pattern}/") || glob_match`. "config/./prod.env" therefore misses the protected pattern "config/prod.env", and evaluate_write (512) and the shape-gate lookups (526 onward) allow it. file.write passes the raw `p.path` to enforce (file.rs:93-102), and the file is then written at root.join(rel), which the OS resolves to config/prod.env. file::rel (470-487) and git::validate_path (git.rs:780-800) are the same non-normalizing validators. overlap::relative_path (overlap.rs:82-96) differs: it rejects every non-Normal component. In the absolute branch (638-642), Path::strip_prefix keeps an interior `/./` in the remaining slice, and so does the CLI hook_relative_path (main.rs:567-580). grants.covers_path (grants.rs:99-110) uses the same matcher.
v1.correction: The hole is wider than stated: a leading `./` also defeats single-segment directory patterns, because "./secrets/x" does not start with "secrets/". Severity is medium, not high. evaluate_exec (811-846) does no path checking for Bash at all, so any agent can already overwrite a protected path with `cat > config/prod.env`. Protected paths and shape gates only ever guarded the Write/Edit tools and the file.* ops. Also, Claude Code normally sends normalized absolute paths, so a non-adversarial agent rarely hits this. Fix: give one helper that rejects or collapses `.` and empty components and returns a '/'-joined string. overlap.rs already rejects them, so its rule is the one to share.

findings.title: worktree.remove and integration.discard still purge build dirs and run `git worktree remove` with the store lock held
findings.evidence: `e.register::<WorktreeRemove>` (129) calls `worktree::remove(repo, Path::new(&want), p.purge_build.unwrap_or(true))` (139). That function runs purge_build (remove_dir_all of target/build/.gradle…), a dir_size tree walk and an unbounded `git worktree remove --force` (worktree.rs:352-370), all inside the transaction. integration.discard does the same (integration.rs:58-64). The other three callers were deliberately moved off the lock. session.close and discard_restorable are register_staged ("git subprocesses and a tree walk. That half runs before the transaction opens", session.rs:1503-1504). project.remove defers removal to after_commit "instead of holding the bus through all of it" (workspace.rs:320-347).
findings.impact: Running `relay cmd worktree.remove` on an agent checkout with a large target/ (SPEC §8's 73 GB case), or discarding an integration, freezes every bus request, including every agent's guardrail gate, for the duration of the delete. Neither op has a UI caller, so these leftover copies are the ones nobody exercises.
findings.fix: Register both ops staged: check ownership in a short read, remove the worktree unlocked, and record the result in finish. Alternatively queue the removal with after_commit as project.remove does.

v1.reason: git.rs:129 registers WorktreeRemove with plain `e.register`. It calls worktree::remove (worktree.rs:352-370), which runs purge_build (dir_size plus remove_dir_all of every BUILD_DIRS entry), a full dir_size walk, and `git worktree remove --force` and `git worktree prune`, all inside the store transaction. integration.rs:58-69 IntegrationDiscard does the same and then runs `git branch -D`. Also, worktree.rs:26-33 `git()` uses `Command::new("git")...output()` directly, not proc::output_with_timeout, so these subprocesses have no timeout either, which breaks a second CLAUDE.md invariant. session.close/discard_restorable (staged) and project.remove (after_commit) were moved off the lock, which confirms these two are leftovers. Both ops are UserOnly (ops/git.rs:15-16, 145-146), and no caller exists in native, remote or CLI code other than generic `relay cmd`.
v1.correction: The trigger is limited to a user running `relay cmd worktree.remove` or `relay cmd integration.discard`, since no UI path or agent can reach them. That keeps severity at medium rather than high, even though the effect, a bus freeze for the whole delete of a large target/, is severe. The fix should also route worktree.rs `git()` (and with it `git_mutate`) through proc::output_with_timeout, or keep these calls outside the transaction. That `git()` helper is shared by many callers, so check which of them run under the lock.

findings.title: ui.pane.*, ui.window.* and ui.state answer from a shadow UI model the GTK client never fills; the BUS.md §6.5 forwarding was never built
findings.evidence: BUS.md:362-367 says ui.* ops are forwarded to the UI client over bus:ui-op and return `ui.absent` when no UI is connected. Instead, handlers/ui.rs mutates the engine-side UiRuntime and always succeeds. UiRuntime is seeded with a hard-coded "main" window (engine.rs:48-63); window.popout pushes a fake "popout-N" (262-290); pane.move emits `json!({"move":{…}})` (178-181). The native client never calls ui.state, ui.pane.* or ui.window.*. Its apply_ui_event (shell.rs:438-462) reads only page/project_id and the session of a focused pane, never `windows`, so the move payload is ignored. `Engine.ui_connected` (engine.rs:406) is never stored anywhere, so app.status reports `ui_connected: false` permanently (handlers/app.rs:33). Executor::Ui (registry.rs:158) is metadata nothing acts on.
findings.impact: An agent with allow_ui calls ui.window.popout and gets {window_id:"popout-1"}, but no window appears. ui.pane.move and ui.pane.close report success and change nothing on screen. ui.state and ui.window.list are queries exposed over MCP to every agent; they describe panes and windows that do not exist (one empty "main" window whatever is open). app.status says no UI is connected while the GTK client is attached.
findings.fix: Either build the registration and forwarding path (the native door sets ui_connected and executes ui ops), or remove ui.pane.move/close, ui.window.* and the pane/window fields of ui.state from the registry and BUS.md. Keep page.switch, pane.open/focus, layouts, toast and os.*, which the client does honour.

v1.reason: BUS.md:362-367 says ui.* ops are forwarded to a registered UI executor and return `ui.absent` when none is connected. Instead, handlers/ui.rs mutates an engine-side UiRuntime and always succeeds: WindowPopout invents `popout-N` (ui.rs:262-290), and PaneMove reorders an in-memory vec and emits a `move` payload (ui.rs:143-181). `Engine.ui_connected` is initialised false (engine.rs:446) and never stored anywhere, so app.status always reports ui_connected:false (app.rs:33). The native client never calls ui.state, ui.pane.* or ui.window.* (no matches in apps/relay-native/src). Its apply_ui_event (shell.rs:438-462) reads only page, project_id and the focused pane's session, so popout, move and close have no visible effect. ui.state's panes and windows reflect only panes opened through ui.pane.open, not what is on screen.
v1.correction: ui.pane.open/focus partly work: the client reacts to the focused pane's session. The clearer category is bug/docs-drift, since agents receive false success and false state, not merely unused code. Medium is right: it misleads agents but corrupts nothing.

findings.title: The documented grace-window purge never runs: app.reconcile is a no-op and undo.grace_days is read by nothing
findings.evidence: `e.register::<Reconcile>(|_ctx, _| { … Ok(ReconcileOut { actions: Vec::new() }) })` (137-141). Nothing calls app.reconcile and there is no 60 s timer. `"undo": { "grace_days": 7 }` exists only in defaults (settings.rs:42). BUS.md:288-292 promises soft-deleted task, module, note and file rows are "restorable … for the grace window (settings: undo.grace_days, default 7), then hard-deleted by the reconcile pass". The task, notes and module restore handlers check only `deleted_at.is_none()` (task.rs:931, notes.rs:544, module.rs:206). file.delete moves the file to `<worktree>/.relay/trash/<id>/payload` (file.rs:221-236), and nothing ever removes those payloads; launch recovery prunes only audit rows (recovery.rs:179-205).
findings.impact: Every file trashed from the Code view (editor.rs:968, project_files.rs:301) stays on disk in the project checkout's .relay/trash for good. Soft-deleted rows accumulate in the one store forever and remain restorable indefinitely, which contradicts the documented contract and the setting.
findings.fix: Implement the purge in launch recovery next to audit retention, driven by undo.grace_days. Hard-delete rows whose deleted_at is past the window, remove their trash payloads, and record the actions. Otherwise, delete the setting and the stub op and correct BUS.md §5.4.

v1.reason: handlers/app.rs:137-141 registers Reconcile as `Ok(ReconcileOut { actions: Vec::new() })` with the comment 'Phase 1 has nothing to verify yet'. Nothing in native, CLI or remote calls app.reconcile; it appears only in the registry test and in examples/perf.rs. undo.grace_days appears only in the defaults (settings.rs:42) and in tests (bus.rs:729, 786). No code hard-deletes soft-deleted tasks, notes or modules, and none removes .relay/trash payloads. The only DELETEs are the whole-project removal in workspace.rs:364-369, and even that does not remove the files on disk. file.delete writes `<root>/.relay/trash/<id>/payload` (file.rs:226-236). BUS.md §5.4 promises a hard delete after the grace window, so the docs and the code disagree.
v1.correction: The growth is proportional to the user's own deletions, so it is slow, and keeping something restorable forever does not lose data. That makes medium the ceiling. It is part resource-leak (trash payloads on disk and soft-deleted rows) and part docs-drift (BUS.md §5.4 and the dead setting). The fix as proposed is sound. Note that workspace.rs:369 also leaves the trash payload files behind when a project is removed.

findings.title: Settings → "Park idle sessions after (minutes)" saves parking.idle_minutes, which nothing reads
findings.evidence: `setting_number(ui, &agents, "Park idle sessions after (minutes)", "parking.idle_minutes", …)` (428-436) is saved through collect_settings, with a default at settings.rs:44. A search for `idle_minutes` and `parking` finds no reader in relay-core or the native client; session.park is only ever manual. SPEC.md:264-265 specifies "Parking: idle > T minutes → offer to kill the CLI process". Other defaults that nothing reads: top-level "layout": {} and "theme": {} (settings.rs:45-46), top-level "roles": {} (51; the real allowlists live under guardrails.roles), and appearance.wallpaper_preview (17), which the native client itself calls legacy (tools_settings.rs:817).
findings.impact: The user sets 10 minutes and expects idle agents to be parked. Idle sessions keep their CLI processes and RAM for good, with no sign that the setting does nothing.
findings.fix: Implement idle detection (last_output_at is already tracked) that offers or performs session.park after the configured time. Otherwise remove the control and the dead default keys.

v1.reason: tools_settings.rs:428-436 shows a 'Park idle sessions after (minutes)' spin control bound to parking.idle_minutes (default 30 at settings.rs:44). Outside those two places, a repo-wide search finds no reader of idle_minutes or settings["parking"]. session.park is invoked only by the manual Park button (shell.rs:690) and by tests. SPEC.md:264-265 describes idle > T → offer to park, and that is not implemented. So the visible setting has no effect, and idle agents keep their CLI processes. I also confirmed that top-level layout {}, theme {}, roles {} and appearance.wallpaper_preview have no readers: guardrail roles come from guardrails.roles via cfg.roles, and tools_settings.rs:817 calls wallpaper preview legacy.
v1.correction: This is a misleading user-facing control, not just dead code, so the category is bug. Medium fits: it gives no wrong data, but a setting the user changes silently does nothing. The leftover default keys (layout, theme, top-level roles, wallpaper_preview) are a separate low-severity dead-code cleanup.

findings.title: A removed workspace's guardrail overrides survive, and the next workspace that reuses its id inherits them
findings.evidence: workspace.remove (150-180) removes the projects and runs `DELETE FROM workspaces WHERE id = ?1` (178), but it never deletes the settings under `guardrails.workspaces.{id}` that guardrail.config.set writes (handlers/guardrail.rs:69). project.remove does clean `guardrails.projects.{id}.%` (workspace.rs:378-379). workspaces and projects use `id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY` without AUTOINCREMENT (store.rs:46-55), even though the v2 comment (store.rs:62-64) explains AUTOINCREMENT was adopted elsewhere because a bare rowid recycles deleted ids. I confirmed with sqlite3 that deleting the highest id and inserting again reuses it. guardrail::layers applies `workspaces.{workspace_id}` to every project in that workspace (guardrail.rs:107-131).
findings.impact: Example: the user's only workspace (id 1) had loosened guardrails, such as denied_commands cleared, caps raised or roles.builder widened. The user removes it and adds a workspace again; the new one gets id 1 and silently applies those overrides to every agent in it. project.remove's LIKE also misses an exact `guardrails.projects.{id}` row, and the native keys native.layout.current.{id} and native.sidebar.collapsed_workspaces carry over the same way.
findings.fix: In workspace.remove, delete `guardrails.workspaces.{id}` and everything under it. In project.remove, also delete the exact `guardrails.projects.{id}` row. Consider migrating workspaces and projects to AUTOINCREMENT.

v1.reason: guardrail.config.set with workspace_id writes `guardrails.workspaces.{id}` through settings::set, which flattens it into leaf rows `guardrails.workspaces.{id}.<key>...` (handlers/guardrail.rs:69-76, settings.rs:203-212). workspace.remove (workspace.rs:150-180) deletes the projects and the workspace row but no settings rows, and nothing else in the code deletes `guardrails.workspaces.*`. workspaces.id is `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY` without AUTOINCREMENT (store.rs:46-49), so deleting the highest-id workspace lets the next insert reuse its id. guardrail::layers then applies the leftover `workspaces.{id}` layer to every project of the new workspace (guardrail.rs:107-131). The trigger is a narrow but ordinary flow: loosen a workspace's guardrails, remove that workspace, then add a workspace again.
v1.correction: The secondary claim is wrong: project.remove's LIKE `guardrails.projects.{id}.%` does clean project overrides, because settings::set stores only leaf rows and prune_empty means no row exists at the exact `guardrails.projects.{id}` path. Only the workspace layer leaks. Fix: in workspace.remove, call delete_settings_under(tx, "guardrails.workspaces.{id}"), and optionally move workspaces to AUTOINCREMENT in a new migration.

findings.title: Native saves its layout under native.layout.current.{id}; the engine reads and cleans layout.current.{id}, which nothing writes
findings.evidence: shell.rs:306-309 and 332-335 write and read `format!("native.layout.current.{project}")`. ui.rs fallback_state (32-39) reads `layout.current.{project_id}` and, when that is null, returns `{"page":"agents","agent_layout":"grid"}`. project.remove deletes `layout.current.{id}` (workspace.rs:378-379) but not the native key. DECISIONS D150 (docs/engine/DECISIONS.md:826) still says a page switch persists `layout.current.<id>`.
findings.impact: ui.layout.save without `state` is allowed by the schema and is how an agent or `relay cmd` saves "the current arrangement"; it always stores the hard-coded default. Removing a project leaves its native layout row behind, and a later project that reuses the id restores it.
findings.fix: Use one key on both sides and have project.remove clean it. Alternatively, make `state` required and delete fallback_state.

v1.reason: The native client writes and reads `native.layout.current.{project}` (shell.rs:306-309, 332-335). The engine's fallback_state (ui.rs:32-39) reads `layout.current.{project_id}`, which nothing writes in production; only the bus.rs:769 settings test sets it. ui.page.switch (ui.rs:43-65) persists nothing to settings, so D150's 'a page switch persists layout.current.<id>' is stale. ui.layout.save has `state: Option<Value>` (ops/ui.rs:24), carries no actors restriction, and calls fallback_state when state is None (ui.rs:200-203). An agent or `relay cmd` saving 'the current arrangement' without state therefore always stores the hard-coded {page:agents, agent_layout:grid}. project.remove (workspace.rs:378-379) deletes `layout.current.{id}` but not `native.layout.current.{id}`. The projects table uses `id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY` without AUTOINCREMENT (store.rs:51-52), so removing the project with the highest id lets the next project reuse that id and inherit the old native layout.
v1.correction: Also count it as docs drift for DECISIONS.md:826. The native UI itself always passes state (shell.rs:592-593), so the wrong default only reaches stateless callers. Simplest fix: have project.remove also delete `native.layout.current.{id}` (or `LIKE '%layout.current.{id}'`), and either make `state` required or have fallback_state read the native key.

findings.title: Two diverged definitions of "build output": worktree::BUILD_DIRS and app.rs dir_usage
findings.evidence: worktree::BUILD_DIRS lists `["target", "build", ".gradle", "app/build", "node_modules/.cache", "dist"]` at the worktree root (worktree.rs:12). It drives purge_build on removal and worktree.disk's build_mb (git.rs:145-160). app.resources' dir_usage instead counts any directory named `"target" | "build" | ".gradle"` at any depth and ignores node_modules/.cache and dist (app.rs:235-259). The native status panel shows that second number as "N build" for each worktree (status.rs:283-287).
findings.impact: In a Gradle multi-module or JS monorepo checkout, the panel's build figure differs from worktree.disk for the same path and from what a worktree removal actually purges. For example, core/build is counted but never purged, and node_modules/.cache and dist are purged but never shown. A source directory named build/ is reported as build output.
findings.fix: Define one predicate in worktree.rs and use it in both walks.

v1.reason: worktree.rs:12 BUILD_DIRS = ["target","build",".gradle","app/build","node_modules/.cache","dist"], rooted at the worktree. It drives build_size (worktree.rs:244-247) and therefore worktree.disk's build_mb (git.rs:145-160), plus the purge (worktree.rs:341). app.rs dir_usage (235-259) instead marks any directory named target, build or .gradle at any depth, and leaves out node_modules/.cache and dist. The two definitions have already diverged. The native status panel shows the app.resources figure as "N build" (status.rs:283-287).
v1.correction: Impact is cosmetic. The native client never calls worktree.disk, so the user only ever sees one of the two numbers and is never shown them side by side. Nothing is mis-purged or lost; the only effect is that the panel's "build" figure is not what a worktree removal would free. Low rather than medium. There are also two separate directory walkers (dir_usage and the parallel dir_size_all). Sharing a predicate would close the divergence, but reusing dir_size_all for the resources sample is optional.

findings.title: Ops in the catalogue that were never implemented: project.stats has no handler, and app.log.tail attaches no stream
findings.evidence: `op!(ProjectStats, "project.stats", …)` (64) is in the registry and in BUS.md:662, but there is no register::<ProjectStats> anywhere, so every call answers bus.not_implemented (the 2026-09-19 perf runs record 100% bus.not_implemented). app.log.tail is declared as a stream op with `.stream("log")` (ops/app.rs:39; BUS.md:383, 628), but its handler only emits an `app.log.attached` event that nothing consumes and returns {} (handlers/app.rs:133-136). No client attaches it, and Instance::log_dir (paths.rs:63) is unused.
findings.impact: The schema, `relay ops` and BUS.md advertise capabilities that fail or silently do nothing.
findings.fix: Implement both or remove them from the registry, the schema and BUS.md.

v1.reason: `op!(ProjectStats, "project.stats", …)` is at crates/relay-bus/src/ops/workspace.rs:64 and is listed in `entries!` (line 66). A repo-wide grep finds no `register::<ProjectStats>`, and engine.rs:322/912 answer `bus.not_implemented` for registry ops that have no handler. docs/perf/runs/2026-09-19/strace.jsonl:31 records 50 of 50 calls returning bus.not_implemented. app.log.tail is declared `.stream("log")` (ops/app.rs:39), but its handler (handlers/app.rs:133-136) only emits `app.log.attached` and returns Empty. Nothing in crates/ or apps/relay-native consumes that event, and no log stream is ever attached. `Instance::log_dir` (paths.rs:63) has no callers. BUS.md:383, 628 and 662 advertise both ops.
v1.correction: The impact is that clients are misled, with no runtime harm: no in-scope client calls either op. app.log.tail returns success, so a caller cannot tell that nothing is attached. That silent no-op is worse than the explicit not_implemented from project.stats. Fix: delete both ops (and log_dir) from the registry and BUS.md, or have app.log.tail return not_implemented until it is built.

findings.title: Unused public helpers, including a lock-holding subprocess trap and a configuration hook nobody calls
findings.evidence: list_with_owners (git.rs:72-81) takes a `&Transaction` and runs `git worktree list` through worktrees_owned_by, which is exactly what D144 forbids; it has no callers. configure_mirror_server (device.rs:55-60) has no caller, so MIRROR_SERVER is never set and mirror_server_path() always falls back to the compile-time `env!("CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR")/../../apps/relay-native/resources/scrcpy-server-v4.1` (63-66).
