IDEs and other tools then fail to watch files, and Relay's own later registrations fail silently (registered = false at watch.rs:132-146).
findings.fix: Release watchers when their worktree stops mattering. Remove the map entry in session.close and discard (when no other open session uses that checkout), worktree.remove, integration.discard and project.remove. Also schedule removal when the watched root itself is deleted (a remove or IN_IGNORED event for the root). Optionally cap the map with an LRU, or use one shared watcher with per-root watch/unwatch instead of one inotify instance per root. To match D57, stop recursing into generated directories: watch non-recursively and add subdirectories yourself, skipping target/, node_modules/, .relay/ and .git/objects.

v1.reason: Engine::watchers (engine.rs:420) is only ever checked with contains_key and insert (watch.rs:53, 133-138), and grep finds no remove anywhere in relay-core. ensure_after_commit is called by file.tree, file.read and file.search (handlers/file.rs:21, 41, 301) and by git.status (git.rs:164). The root comes from root_unlocked/root_choice, which uses the actor session's own worktree. Every session worktree that an agent or the Code view touches therefore gets a permanent RecommendedWatcher (an inotify fd, an epoll fd, an eventfd and a thread), plus a recursive watch on every directory, target/ and .git/objects included. is_generated_path filters only events, not watches. The shell closes sessions with remove_worktree:false (session.rs:1543-1548 comment), so the checkouts stay and their watch sets keep counting against max_user_watches. A removed checkout frees its watches, but the instance and thread remain. The engine is built to outlive the UI (run.sh comment), so this growth has no limit in normal use. On this machine max_user_instances is 1024 rather than 128 and max_user_watches is 524288, so the realistic failure is the watch count from kept Rust/Node worktrees, not the instance count.
v1.correction: On this host max_user_instances is 1024, so instance exhaustion takes far longer than the finding's 128 suggests. The practical limit is max_user_watches (524288), consumed by recursive watches on kept worktrees with build trees, which also starves other tools. The fix is as proposed: remove the map entry in session.close/discard, git.worktree.remove, integration.discard and project.remove, and stop recursing into generated directories.

v2.reason:
(a) The mechanism is real. Engine::watchers (engine.rs:420) is only ever read with contains_key and written with insert (watch.rs:53, 135-138). Nothing removes an entry anywhere. The notify 8.2.0 source confirms that each INotifyWatcher has its own inotify fd, a mio epoll fd, an eventfd waker and a "notify-rs inotify loop" thread, all stopped only by Drop (inotify.rs:121-150, 175-182, 606-611). Recursive add_watch walks every directory with WalkDir and no filter, and it adds new subdirectories on CREATE|ISDIR. An agent's read defaults to its own worktree (file.rs default_worktree_in). The Code view switches to an agent checkout through the scope picker or "open that checkout" (project_files.rs:170,231; code_git.rs:1097).

(b) The leak is reachable, but its trigger is narrower than the finding implies. Nothing steers agents to the relay file/git MCP tools: the role instructions and settings do not mention them, and Claude Code uses its native tools. The Code view's default scope is the project root. I checked the user's live dev engine read-only through /proc (relay serve, up about 20 h, 4 live agent sessions across 3 projects). It has exactly 3 watchers and 3 notify threads, one for each project root (RelayV4, Avex, Tally), and no watcher on any session worktree. The engine log shows 15 starts in 31 days, with lifetimes from a few hours to about 7 days, so the leak resets often.

(c) Each leaked root holds one idle thread, 3 fds (soft NOFILE is 1024 with 40 in use) and one inotify instance (the limit here is 1024, and the whole user session uses 84). When a checkout is deleted, the kernel frees its watches and only the empty instance and thread remain. Deletion happens on close with remove, on git.worktree.remove, and also through branch_cleanup's automatic removal of merged checkouts (branch_cleanup.rs:307, 405-415), which the finding does not mention. So only unmerged kept checkouts keep their watch sets. Most checkouts here have 800 to 1,600 directories. Only one heavy checkout (13,635 directories in apps/relay-mobile/node_modules) is anywhere near the finding's figure. Reaching the 524,288-watch limit through leaked per-worktree watchers would take about 35 such checkouts browsed in one engine lifetime. Running out of instances is plausible only on a kernel with the 128 default, after heavy reviewing over a long engine lifetime.

The finding also misses a real functional consequence. The stale key blocks re-registration when a deleted root's path comes back. Closed-session names are reused (sessions.rs:74-89, 1,296 names), and session.create skips only paths that exist. That new checkout then never refreshes live in the Code view until the engine restarts. Once the watch limit is reached, a failed registration is retried on every file or git read, because the key is removed from watcher_registrations at watch.rs:147, and each retry walks the tree until ENOSPC.

(d) This is not high. No user-visible failure in a normal flow is shown, and the live engine has no leaked watchers. It is medium: a real, monotonic leak in a normal path with modest cost, plus a rare refresh bug from the stale key.

(e) The fix points the right way but is incomplete. Its list of removal points leaves out branch_cleanup and deletions made outside Relay. Dropping the watcher when its root is deleted (DELETE_SELF on the root) covers all of these and should be the core of the fix. Removal must match the canonical key: canonicalize fails once the directory is gone and falls back to the raw path, so compute the key before deletion or drop every key under the removed path. Dropping the watcher on close with the checkout kept is safe. session.close emits worktree.changed, and a client showing that checkout then re-reads it after a second, which registers the watcher again (editor.rs:508-528). An LRU cap could silently stop refresh for a checkout that is still on screen. Stopping recursion into generated directories is a separate root cause.
v2.correction:
Severity is medium, not high. The impact is overstated. The live engine (about 20 h, 4 sessions) holds 3 watchers, all on project roots, and none on a session worktree. branch_cleanup removes merged checkouts, so kept watch sets do not grow without limit. "Kept watchers go on emitting file.changed for dead sessions" happens only if something writes into a closed checkout. The 128 instance limit and the 1 KiB-per-watch starvation figures do not apply to this host (1024 instances, 84 in use across the whole user session).

What the finding missed: (1) a stale map key blocks re-registration when a removed root's path is reused, through a reused session name or a project directory re-cloned in place, so that checkout gets no live refresh until the engine restarts; (2) branch_cleanup.rs:307 worktree::remove is another removal path the fix list omits.

Report separately: the project-root watcher's recursion into nested .relay/worktrees and build directories is a different root cause and the main watch cost. The RelayV4 root watcher alone holds 24,540 watches, about 19.9k of them under .relay/worktrees, which is 98% of the user's 39,165 inotify watches. Dropping per-worktree watchers does not change it. In pooled worktrees .git is a file, and the main .git/objects has only 4 directories, so .git/objects is negligible.

Fix: drop the watcher when its root is deleted (DELETE_SELF or IN_IGNORED on the root). Also drop it explicitly in session.close when no other session uses the checkout, and in git.worktree.remove, branch_cleanup, integration.discard and project.remove. Match keys by the canonical path computed before deletion, or by prefix. Avoid an LRU cap, which could stop refresh for a checkout that is on screen.

findings.title: Crash recovery SIGTERMs, then SIGKILLs, any process that inherited RELAY_* environment variables at every engine start, including the Unreal Editor that relay-cli deliberately detaches
findings.evidence: Recovery step 1 does `let orphans = pty::relay_children(instance, &store_path); for (pid, name) in &orphans { kill_wait(*pid); ... }` (recovery.rs:67-70). relay_children (pty.rs:411-429) selects every live process whose /proc/<pid>/environ has RELAY_SESSION plus a matching RELAY_INSTANCE and RELAY_STORE. That is an inherited-variable test, not a parent/child relation. kill_wait sends SIGTERM to -(pid) and pid, waits 2 s, then sends SIGKILL to both (recovery.rs:20-35). Agents receive these variables at spawn (session.rs:564-576) and pass them to everything they start. relay-cli's Unreal tooling launches the editor with the inherited environment and `command.process_group(0)`, commented 'Its own process group: the editor outlives this MCP server and the agent' (unreal_process.rs:291-306). SPEC §14 scopes the reaper to 'orphaned claude/codex processes'.
findings.impact: Recovery runs before the doors open, whenever the engine starts while such a program is still running: an app restart or update, or a crash followed by a systemd restart (Restart=on-failure). An Unreal Editor started through the ue_* tools is killed together with its whole process group after a 2 s grace, losing unsaved level and asset edits. The same happens to Android emulators, Gradle/Kotlin daemons, an adb server, or a browser or IDE that an agent opened (`xdg-open`, `code .`). The only trace is a line in app.recovery.last.
findings.fix: Reap only what Relay can prove is its own orphan. Record each PTY child's pid, start time (/proc/<pid>/stat field 22) and process-group id in the session row, and at recovery kill only those processes and members of those groups. For launches that are meant to outlive the agent (unreal_process::launch), remove RELAY_SESSION, RELAY_TOKEN, RELAY_STORE and RELAY_INSTANCE from the child's environment with env_remove. The session token should not leak into a long-lived editor anyway.

v1.reason: recovery.rs:65-74 calls kill_wait on every pid that pty::relay_children (pty.rs:411-429) returns. That selection is purely by inherited environment (RELAY_SESSION plus a matching RELAY_INSTANCE/RELAY_STORE), and kill_wait (recovery.rs:20-35) sends SIGTERM and then SIGKILL to both -(pid) and pid. Engine::shutdown (engine.rs:633-659) already kills each PTY's group on a clean stop, so what survives to the next start is exactly the processes that left the PTY's process group. unreal_process::launch (unreal_process.rs:291-307) puts the editor in its own process group 'so it outlives this MCP server and the agent', and does no env_remove. The relay-cli MCP server inherits RELAY_* from the agent (session.rs:565-576), and relay-cli reads RELAY_SESSION itself (main.rs:122, unreal.rs:511). On the next engine start after any restart (update, crash, manual restart), recovery therefore SIGTERMs the editor and, after 2 s, SIGKILLs its whole group, and unsaved editor work is lost. D20 only addresses cross-store scoping, and SPEC §14 says to reap 'orphaned claude/codex processes', so killing arbitrary descendants is not a documented decision.
v1.correction: Other detached descendants that carry the variables (adb server, Gradle daemons, emulators started by an agent) are also killed, but they are mostly restartable. The Unreal editor and any user-facing app an agent opened are the data-loss cases. Fixes: (1) in unreal_process::launch, env_remove RELAY_SESSION, RELAY_TOKEN, RELAY_STORE and RELAY_INSTANCE (this also stops the token leaking into a long-lived process); (2) have recovery reap only recorded PTY child pids/pgids, checked against their start time, instead of every process carrying the inherited variables.

v2.reason:
(a) The code does what the finding says. recovery.rs:67-69 calls kill_wait on every pid that pty::relay_children returns. relay_children (pty.rs:411-429) selects a process only by its environment: RELAY_INSTANCE and RELAY_STORE must match, and RELAY_SESSION must be present. It does not check parentage, exe or pgid. kill_wait (recovery.rs:20-35) sends SIGTERM to -(pid) and to pid, and SIGKILL to both after 2 s.

(b) Reachable, by the user of the Unreal plugin with Claude agents:
- Agents get RELAY_* at spawn (session.rs:564-576).
- Claude Code passes its environment to stdio MCP servers. hooks.rs:401-402 relies on this for `relay mcp`, and the installed Claude Code 2.1.292 bundle builds a stdio server's env from `ss()`, which is process.env, plus the config's env. So `relay unreal-mcp` carries RELAY_SESSION, RELAY_INSTANCE and RELAY_STORE.
- unreal_process::launch (unreal_process.rs:291-307) spawns the editor with the inherited environment, no env_remove, and process_group(0). It therefore survives Pty::kill and Engine::shutdown, which only signal -(pty pid).
- The plugin's standing rule (plugins/unreal-engine/instructions.md:7) tells agents to verify every C++ change with `ue_build restart_editor:true`. That path runs quit_editor and then launch_editor (unreal.rs:1519, 1572), which calls unreal_process::launch. So after the first C++ build an agent makes, the user's working editor in the primary checkout is normally a Relay-launched one.
- The next engine start runs recovery before the socket opens (serve.rs:23). An engine start happens on the documented update path (`app.quit` with force, then ./run.sh; tools_plugins.rs:14), or on the next launch through run.sh or the .desktop entry after a crash or kill. On that start recovery reaps the editor and its process group. Frequency: every engine restart while such an editor is open.

(c) Consequence. In the user's installed UE 5.8.2, GracefulTerminationHandler (UnixPlatformCrashContext.cpp:156-171) turns SIGTERM into a non-forced RequestExit, so the save-dirty-packages prompt never appears. A second signal forces the exit, and kill_wait sends two SIGTERMs (to the group, then to the pid) and SIGKILL after 2 s. Unsaved level and asset edits are lost.
- If the shutdown finishes, UnrealEdEngine.cpp:521-524 turns off the autosave restore file, so no restore is offered next time.
- If SIGKILL arrives first, at best the last autosave is offered. Autosave runs every 10 min by default (BaseEditorPerProjectUserSettings.ini).
- The only trace is a "reaped orphan pid" line in app.recovery.last.

(d) High is right. This is a real, silent loss of the user's work in a normal workflow. It is not critical: it needs an engine restart while a Relay-launched editor is open, it is bounded to unsaved edits, and it does not touch the store or the repository.

(e) Fix 1 is correct and enough for the reaper. Stripping RELAY_SESSION alone already excludes the editor, because relay_children requires that variable. Nothing under plugins/ or in the editor reads RELAY_*. Stripping also keeps RELAY_TOKEN out of a long-lived process, and stops the commit hook (hooks.rs:124) from attributing git commits made from the editor to the agent.

Fix 2 as written would be a regression. The Claude Code bundle's bash shell provider spawns with detached:true, which calls setsid. Agent tool processes therefore run in their own session and group, not in the PTY pid's group. A reaper limited to recorded PTY pids and pgids would no longer reap them after a crash, which is exactly what the env scan exists to do.
v2.correction:
1. Reopening the app is not enough to trigger this. run.sh reuses a running engine ("The engine outlives the window"). The trigger is an engine restart: `app.quit` with force followed by ./run.sh (the documented update path), killing the engine, or a crash followed by the next launch.

2. The systemd scenario is misattributed. Under deploy/relay-remote.service (default KillMode=control-group), the editor runs in the service's cgroup, so systemd kills it on any engine stop or restart before recovery ever runs. Recovery is what kills it in the run.sh deployment (`nohup relay serve --remote &`), which is also what the .desktop launcher uses. For the same reason, the env_remove fix alone does not protect the editor under the systemd unit. That case needs the editor launched outside the unit's cgroup (for example `systemd-run --user --scope`) or KillMode=mixed/process, which is a separate root cause.

3. Provider scope: confirmed for Claude agents. Codex's MCP client is believed to pass only a whitelisted environment; I did not verify that here. If so, editors launched by Codex agents are not affected.

4. The other victims (adb server, Gradle daemons, a browser or IDE an agent started fresh) are mostly restartable. The Unreal editor is the data-loss case.

5. Fix: keep fix 1 (env_remove of RELAY_SESSION, RELAY_TOKEN, RELAY_STORE and RELAY_INSTANCE in unreal_process::launch). Drop fix 2 as written. Keep the env scan, and exclude deliberate long-lived launches by stripping these variables or with an explicit opt-out marker.

6. Separate root cause, not part of this finding: recovery step 2 (recovery.rs:84-93) calls kill_wait on a recorded session pid with no start-time check. After a power loss or reboot, that pid can belong to an unrelated process, and the -(pid) signal would also reach that process's group.

findings.title: The phone door keeps unauthenticated LAN connections open forever, inside the engine process: no handshake timeout, no keepalive, and 64 MiB messages accepted before authentication
findings.evidence: handle() does `let n = stream.peek(&mut head).await?;` (direct.rs:76) and then `tokio_tungstenite::accept_async(stream).await` (89-91), neither with a timeout. HELLO_TIMEOUT (bridge.rs:39, applied at bridge.rs:125) starts only after the WebSocket handshake. accept_async uses tungstenite 0.30's default WebSocketConfig: max_message_size 64 MiB and max_frame_size 16 MiB (tungstenite protocol/mod.rs:101-102). The reader task copies the whole first message (`text.to_string()`, direct.rs:108) before bridge::run parses the Hello. Neither the reader loop (104-121) nor the bridge sends pings or enables TCP keepalive. `relay serve --remote` runs this door inside the engine process (remote.rs:88-113), bound to 0.0.0.0:7420 by default (main.rs:68), and run.sh starts the engine exactly that way (run.sh:32). The rendezvous server has the same shape: peek at rendezvous.rs:127, accept_hdr_async at 159-161, and a join loop with no pings.
findings.impact: Any peer on the same network can open connections to port 7420 and send nothing, or a slow HTTP upgrade. Each connection pins a task and an fd forever. With the common RLIMIT_NOFILE soft limit of 1024 (this session's limit is 1,048,576), about 1,000 idle sockets leave the engine unable to accept on its Unix socket, open PTYs or create pipes for git. Every agent hook and the GUI then fail, and the accept loops log 'accept failed' every 50 ms. Under a high fd limit the same works as memory exhaustion: a few dozen connections each sending a frame of about 64 MiB before authentication cost 64-128 MiB apiece and can get the engine OOM-killed, taking every PTY with it. In normal use, an admitted phone that drops off WiFi without a FIN can keep its bridge, its engine socket connection and any device.watch lease (an `adb track-devices` child) alive indefinitely when nothing is written to it.
findings.fix: Wrap the peek and the handshake in tokio::time::timeout (for example 10 s). Use a WebSocketConfig with small max_message_size and max_frame_size until the Hello is verified, then raise them. Cap concurrent unauthenticated connections with a semaphore. Enable TCP keepalive on accepted sockets and send WebSocket pings with a silence limit, as tunnel.rs already does, on both the direct and rendezvous paths. Consider not binding 0.0.0.0 by default from run.sh.

v1.reason: direct.rs:74-91: handle() runs `stream.peek(&mut head).await?` and then `tokio_tungstenite::accept_async(stream).await`, neither with a timeout. HELLO_TIMEOUT (bridge.rs:39), whose comment claims a silent connection 'holds nothing but a task', is applied only inside bridge::run (bridge.rs:125), after the WebSocket handshake has finished. accept_async uses the default WebSocketConfig, so the reader (direct.rs:104-121) accepts messages of up to 64 MiB before the Hello is checked, and in_tx has capacity 64. Nothing sends pings or sets TCP keepalive. `relay serve --remote` runs this door inside the engine process (remote.rs:88-113) on 0.0.0.0:7420 by default (main.rs:68), and run.sh:32 starts the engine that way. Any LAN peer can therefore pin tasks and fds forever with connections that never finish the upgrade, which exhausts the engine's fds wherever the soft RLIMIT_NOFILE is 1024 (Rust and tokio do not raise it). Within the 30 s Hello window, many connections each streaming a large message can also run the engine out of memory, which takes every PTY down with it.
v1.correction: The rendezvous paths cited in related run in a separate server process, not the engine, so they do not threaten the engine. This host's fd limit is 1,048,576, so here memory pressure is the more practical attack. On a default 1024 limit, fd exhaustion is a cheap pre-auth DoS of the whole engine. The fix is as proposed: put a timeout on the peek and the handshake, use a small max_message_size/max_frame_size until the Hello is admitted, cap concurrent unauthenticated connections, and add keepalive or pings after admission.

v2.reason:
(a) The code does what the finding says. In direct.rs:73-91, handle() calls `stream.peek(&mut head).await?` and then `tokio_tungstenite::accept_async(stream).await`, and neither has a timeout. accept_async goes to accept_hdr_async_with_config(.., None), so it uses WebSocketConfig::default(): 64 MiB messages and 16 MiB frames (tungstenite-0.30.0 protocol/mod.rs:101-102). HELLO_TIMEOUT (bridge.rs:39) is applied only at bridge.rs:125, after the handshake. tungstenite's handshake AttackCheck (handshake/machine.rs:163-189) limits header size and packet count but not time. relay-remote has no keepalive, no Ping, no semaphore and no WebSocketConfig anywhere (rg). The door runs inside the engine process (remote.rs:88-113). It binds 0.0.0.0:7420 by default (main.rs:68, registry.rs:60), and run.sh:32 always passes --remote.

(b) Reachability. Any host that can reach port 7420 can do this, before any authentication and with no skill: open about 1,000 TCP connections and send nothing. On the author's own machine:
- The live engine (pid 2269869, `relay --instance dev serve --remote`) listens on 0.0.0.0:7420.
- Its /proc limits show a soft RLIMIT_NOFILE of 1024 and a hard limit of 1048576, with 40 fds open.
- ufw accepts everything from 192.168.2.0/24 (/etc/ufw/user.rules), so every device on the home WiFi can reach the door.

Accidental scanners do not trigger it: a connect-then-close makes peek return EOF or an error, and the handler exits. A slow genuine leak exists too (a phone that loses its link after connecting, or an admitted phone that dies while no traffic flows), but that is minor. The real trigger is a hostile or compromised LAN or tailnet device: rare at home, trivial to carry out.

(c) What happens. Once about 980 sockets are pinned, the engine hits EMFILE:
- Its Unix-socket accept loop (socket.rs:110-122) and the door's loop (direct.rs:48-51) each fail and log 'accept failed' every 50 ms.
- New bus clients sit unaccepted and hang. That includes every `relay hook claude-pre-tool` call (one per agent tool call, which fails closed with exit 2 or hangs until the hook times out), new GUI connections (terminal.rs:476, agent_menu.rs:731 and others), the CLI and phone bridges.
- New PTYs and subprocess pipes (git) cannot be created.
- Existing connections, running PTYs and the WAL-mode store keep working.
- No keepalive and no writes means the sockets are never reclaimed if the attacking host vanishes without a FIN or RST. Recovery then needs an engine restart, which kills the live agent PTYs.

(d) Severity: high is right. This is a pre-auth bus freeze, reachable over the network, in the default launch configuration. It is not critical: it affects availability only, needs a hostile peer, does not crash the engine, and loses no data.

(e) The fix is correct in direction but incomplete as written (see correction).
v2.correction:
1) Fd limit. The '1,048,576' aside in the finding and the first verifier's 'memory pressure is the more practical attack here' are both wrong for the engine. 1,048,576 is the agent shell's limit. The running engine has a soft RLIMIT_NOFILE of 1024, and the shipped systemd --user unit would also get a soft limit of 1024 (/usr/lib/systemd/user.conf.d/10-limits.conf: DefaultLimitNOFILE=1024:1048576). Fd exhaustion is therefore the practical attack on this machine.

2) The memory claim is overstated.
- The maximum frame is 16 MiB, so a 64 MiB message needs at least 4 frames.
- Pre-auth state after the handshake is freed when HELLO_TIMEOUT fires: the bridge returns, the reader is aborted and the writer closes. Pinned memory is therefore about attacker bandwidth × 30 s, roughly 3.75 GB at full gigabit and far less over WiFi, so OOM is conditional, not expected.
- Before the handshake, AttackCheck limits each connection to 64 KiB, but with no time limit.

3) The rendezvous runs only in its own process (`relay remote rendezvous`, remote.rs:293-296), so its pre-auth issues do not touch the engine. Its join loop (rendezvous.rs:269-278) has no pings, though. A phone that vanishes keeps the engine-side tunnel lane's bridge, and its engine socket connection, alive until something is written. When there is traffic, the TCP retransmission timeout clears it in about 15 minutes.

4) Fix corrections.
- Timeouts alone do not stop an active attacker, who can reconnect every 10 s. The essential part is the pre-auth cap: accept, then `try_acquire_owned` on a small semaphore, drop the stream immediately when no permit is free, and release the permit on admission.
- tokio-tungstenite 0.30's WebSocketStream has get_config but no set_config. Raising the limits after the Hello therefore needs `into_inner()` plus a re-wrap with `from_raw_socket`, or one modest cap passed through `accept_async_with_config`.
- tokio 1.53's TcpStream has no set_keepalive. Use socket2::SockRef; socket2 0.6.5 is already in Cargo.lock but would need to become a direct dependency.
- Pings need the reader to count Pong frames and any other frame as 'heard'; today they fall into `Ok(_) => {}`.
- Do not drop the 0.0.0.0 default. It is the documented feature (docs/MOBILE.md §2), and removing it breaks WiFi pairing. As cheap defense in depth, raise the soft RLIMIT_NOFILE to the hard limit at engine start, or set LimitNOFILE= in deploy/relay-remote.service.

findings.title: Subprocesses still run with no deadline while the store mutex is held; project.clone runs a whole `git clone` inside the transaction
findings.evidence: `e.register::<ProjectClone>` (workspace.rs:228) runs `Command::new("git").current_dir(&workspace.path).arg("clone").arg("--").arg(&p.url).arg(&destination).output()` (234) inside the handler transaction. It sets no timeout and no GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0 (branch_cleanup.rs:114 does set it). The native onboarding calls it on the control connection (onboarding.rs:527) with a 1800 s request timeout (client.rs:67). BUS.md §5.1 lists project.clone among the ops that return a handle and finish asynchronously. The same pattern appears in other handlers registered with Engine::register, which hold the store mutex: git.pr.open runs `gh pr create` through `.output()` (git.rs:666-680). git.worktree.remove runs purge_build, dir_size tree walks and `git worktree remove` (git.rs:129-140 into worktree.rs:352-369). git.stage, git.unstage, git.branch.create, git.branch.delete, git.clean_merged and file.restore_head use worktree::git(), which is a bare `.output()` (worktree.rs:26-33; git.rs:374,485,503,527,712; file.rs:256). session.update calls rename_branch (session.rs:1460). device.avd.create waits on avdmanager with wait_with_output (device.rs:332-335). device.avd.create and device.avd.boot both call list_avds, which runs `emulator -list-avds` and `adb emu avd name` through `.output()` (device.rs:478,505). integration.discard runs worktree::remove (integration.rs:58-62).
findings.impact: While any of these runs, every other bus request queues on the one connection: agents' PreToolUse hooks (guardrail.gate), session.report and the GUI. Cloning a large repository freezes all sessions for minutes. A clone that hits a credential or host-key prompt never returns, and neither does one on a stalled network; an engine started from a terminal by run.sh keeps that terminal as its controlling tty, so git can prompt there. The engine is then stuck until it is killed. `gh pr create` on a slow network, or removing a multi-GB worktree or integration checkout, freezes the bus for its duration. This breaks the CLAUDE.md invariant that every subprocess forked from a handler goes through proc::output_with_timeout and that slow work goes through register_unlocked or register_staged.
findings.fix: Make project.clone asynchronous like integration.request: commit a row, clone on a worker with a deadline, GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0 and a non-interactive SSH command (BatchMode=yes), and emit a completion event. At minimum use register_staged with the clone in the prepare phase. Move pr.open, worktree.remove, integration.discard, avd.create, avd.boot and the git_mutate callers into staged prepare phases, and route worktree::git() through proc::output_with_timeout. The unlocked sites listed under related also need deadlines.

v1.reason: workspace.rs:228-238: ProjectClone is registered with e.register and runs `Command::new("git")...clone...output()` with no deadline inside the locked handler, so the store mutex is held for the whole clone. BUS.md:246-247 lists project.clone among the handle-returning async ops, but the implementation is synchronous. The native client allows 1800 s for it (client.rs:67), which shows long runs are expected. In the same file, git.rs:129-140 (WorktreeRemove: worktree::remove with purge_build and a tree walk) and git.rs:666-680 (PrOpen: gh pr create via .output()) are both e.register, while their siblings in that file use register_staged/register_unlocked. worktree::git (worktree.rs:26-33) is a bare .output() used by git_mutate, and Stage/Unstage/BranchCreate/BranchDelete/CleanMerged are e.register handlers. proc::output_with_timeout exists (proc.rs:28) but is not used at any of these sites. Every other request queues behind the mutex, including guardrail.gate from agent hooks.
v1.correction: Rust's Command::output() sets the child's stdin to null, so git cannot read a prompt from stdin. A credential or host-key prompt can still block only by opening /dev/tty (git and ssh both do this) when the engine has a controlling terminal. Without one, they fail quickly. A stalled network hangs regardless. The stage/unstage/branch git_mutate calls are usually fast; the material bus freezes come from project.clone, pr.open, worktree.remove and integration.discard. A further fix: make project.clone actually asynchronous, as BUS.md documents, with GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0 and GIT_SSH_COMMAND='ssh -oBatchMode=yes', and route worktree::git through output_with_timeout.

v2.reason:
(a) The code does what the finding says. workspace.rs:228 registers ProjectClone with plain `e.register`. engine.rs dispatch_inner takes `self.store.lock()` (a std Mutex, store.rs:474), opens the transaction and only then calls the handler. So the `git clone` at workspace.rs:234 (`Command::new("git")...clone...output()`) runs with the global lock held, with no deadline and no GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT. That breaks D144/D149 (DECISIONS.md:729-809) and the CLAUDE.md rules. The code's own sibling paths do the right thing: git.fetch is staged, uses output_with_timeout(20 s) and sets GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0 (git.rs:938-952), and skill.install moves its network clone into a staged prepare "so a slow clone stays off every other op" (provider.rs:209-216). BUS.md:247 and the op's metadata ("async; project.changed when done", relay-bus ops/workspace.rs:37-38) both describe an async op that returns a handle, but the implementation is synchronous. No DECISIONS entry exempts it.

Also verified under the lock: PrOpen (git.rs:666-680, `gh pr create` via .output()), WorktreeRemove (git.rs:129-139 into worktree.rs:352-369: purge_build, dir_size, remove_dir_all, then `git worktree remove`), IntegrationDiscard (integration.rs:58-62), AvdCreate (device.rs:321-338: avdmanager plus list_avds) and AvdBoot (device.rs:344-346: `emulator -list-avds` and `adb emu avd name` with no deadline). worktree::git is a bare .output() (worktree.rs:26-27) and is used by the e.register handlers Stage, Unstage, BranchCreate, BranchDelete, CleanMerged, RestoreHead (file.rs:253-256) and session.update (session.rs:1431/1460).

(b) Reachability. The trigger is the user's own action through "Add project…" in the registry (registry.rs:472) or the first-run panel. Both open onboarding.rs, which sends project.clone with the GitHub `clone_url` on the shared UI connection (app.rs:1111-1116); the client allows it 1800 s (client.rs:67). Users add projects occasionally, and in a multi-agent app agents are usually running when they do. git.pr.open uses the default `Actors::All`, so any agent can trigger the same kind of freeze, though only for one gh network round trip.

(c) Consequence while the lock is held:
- Every agent socket request blocks before dispatch, because check_session_token locks the store (engine.rs:1377-1378). That covers every MCP tool call and every PreToolUse hook. The hook CLI waits on the engine with no timeout (relay-cli main.rs:393-475), and the host kills it after 30 s (hooks.rs:351).
- GUI requests and phone requests also wait.
- On top of that, socket.rs:335 handles each connection's requests strictly one after another, so every other GUI request on the UI connection queues behind the clone and times out at 30 s.
- Keystrokes and PTY output keep working: each pane has its own connection (terminal.rs:476), session.input uses the lock-free fast path, and pty.rs never takes the store lock.
- The freeze lasts as long as the clone: seconds for small repos, many minutes for large or LFS-heavy repos (the client's 1800 s allowance shows long clones are expected).
- Permanent hang is possible but needs specific conditions. run.sh starts the engine with `nohup ... &` and no setsid, and then execs relay-native in the foreground. The engine therefore keeps the launching terminal as its controlling tty and stays in its foreground process group, so git's /dev/tty credential prompt appears in that terminal and blocks until someone answers it.

(d) Severity: high is correct. The rubric names "a freeze of the bus" in a normal flow as high. Critical would need the permanent-hang variant, which requires a terminal-launched engine with an unanswered prompt, or a dead network with an SSH URL.

(e) The fix direction is right but incomplete; details are in the correction field.
v2.correction:
Op names: the ops are `worktree.remove` (not git.worktree.remove), `avd.create`/`avd.boot` (not device.avd.*) and `git.branch.clean_merged`.

Hang claims need narrowing:
- Command::output() sets stdin to null, so git and ssh can only prompt through /dev/tty, which needs a controlling terminal.
- A launch from the desktop entry has no tty, so prompts fail fast. The exception is a configured GIT_ASKPASS/SSH_ASKPASS GUI helper: its dialog then waits for the user while the bus stays frozen.
- The GUI clones the HTTPS clone_url, so SSH host-key prompts only arise from SSH URLs supplied through the CLI or the phone.
- A dead HTTPS peer is eventually dropped by curl's TCP keepalive (minutes). A slow trickle has no limit, because http.lowSpeedLimit is unset.
- The common case is a bounded freeze for the length of the clone, not a permanent hang.

Which sites matter:
- Material lock holders: project.clone, git.pr.open, worktree.remove, integration.discard (multi-GB target/ removals) and avd.create/avd.boot.
- Real invariant breaches with low practical impact, since they are local and usually fast: the git_mutate callers and session.update's rename_branch.
- Not lock holders: integration.rs:234 and device.rs:1575 run on worker threads; github.rs:70 runs in an unlocked handler; github.rs:109 and hooks.rs:212 run in staged prepare phases. They lack deadlines, but they cannot freeze the bus, so they do not support the headline claim.

Fix:
1. register_staged alone is not enough. It releases the store lock, but socket.rs:335 handles each connection's requests one at a time, and the native client sends project.clone on its shared UI connection. The GUI's other requests would still queue behind the clone. Either make it truly async (return a handle, finish on a worker, emit project.changed or project.clone.completed; this changes ProjectCloneOut and onboarding.rs:527-528, which reads value["project"]), or send it on a dedicated connection the way lifecycle_request does.
2. A fixed overall deadline would kill legitimate long LFS clones. Prefer stall detection (`-c http.lowSpeedLimit=... -c http.lowSpeedTime=60`) plus a generous cap, run through proc::output_with_timeout. Its process_group(0) also turns a /dev/tty read into SIGTTIN instead of a prompt in the launching terminal.
3. Setting GIT_SSH_COMMAND overrides the user's core.sshCommand and could break custom key setups. Set BatchMode only when core.sshCommand is unset, or detach the child from the tty instead.
4. Fold the docs drift (BUS.md:247 and the op description say it is async) into the same fix.

Separate follow-up worth checking: during any bus freeze longer than 30 s, the PreToolUse hook is killed by its host-side timeout. The CLI comment at main.rs:352 says only exit 2 blocks. If the host treats a timed-out hook as non-blocking, guardrail checks are skipped for the duration of the freeze. This could not be confirmed from the repository.

findings.title: mailbox.list returns a project's entire message history, which is never pruned; the GUI re-fetches it on every event and drops its whole control connection once the reply passes 2 MiB
findings.evidence: MailboxList (notes.rs:660-689) builds `SELECT m.*, CASE ... (correlated NOT EXISTS / MAX subqueries per row) FROM messages m LEFT JOIN message_recipients ... WHERE m.project_id=?1 ... ORDER BY m.sent_at, m.id` with no LIMIT. For the user (session None) there is no recipient filter, so it returns every message ever sent in the project. It runs inside the locked transaction (`e.register`). Messages are deleted only by project.remove (workspace.rs:355-356). The engine itself appends broadcast ('*') messages to every live peer: when an agent turn ends without session.done and the previous notification was read (notify_completion, session.rs:285-292, with the text set to the agent's last assistant message), on every session.done (1212-1219) and on every blocked report (1408-1411). The GUI's Mailbox page calls `mailbox.list {project_id}` (pages.rs:44, 51-58). Every event without special handling falls through to ui.refresh_page() (app.rs:1263-1264), so the query re-runs on task.changed, mailbox.new, notify.*, overlap.changed and others. The control connection rejects any line longer than MAX_LINE = 2 MiB (client.rs:48, 200-205); that error ends the connection, and app.rs:1267-1275 then shows 'Engine disconnected'.
findings.impact: Lock hold time and reply size grow linearly with history. With agent summaries of several hundred bytes to a few KB, roughly 1,000-2,000 messages exceed 2 MiB. From then on, opening the Mailbox page disconnects the whole GUI: the terminals' control plane, events and every request. Each reconnect while that page is open fails the same way. task.list has the same shape: full body and changelog plus about 9 queries per task (task.rs:236-337) for every non-deleted task, re-fetched by the board on every event (pages.rs:43). A long-lived board reaches the same limit.
findings.fix: Paginate. Give mailbox.list and task.list a limit/before cursor with a default (for example 200), have the GUI request pages, and refresh the mailbox page only on mailbox events. Prune or archive acknowledged system broadcasts after N days. Cap the stored text of system broadcasts, since the full summary already lives in the notification. Separately, the client should fail only the oversized request instead of dropping the whole connection.

v1.reason: notes.rs:660-689: MailboxList is registered with e.register (locked transaction) and has no LIMIT. With no session filter (the user), it returns every message in the project, plus correlated subqueries for each row. Messages are deleted only by project.remove (workspace.rs:355-356). send() (notes.rs:209+) stores a '*' broadcast whenever at least one live peer exists. notify_completion (session.rs:280-292) runs on every turn that ends without session.done (session.rs:1415-1422), using the agent's unbounded last-assistant-message as the text. It is gated only by record_agent_notification returning true, which happens whenever the previous card was read. session.done (1212-1219) and blocked reports (1405-1411) also broadcast. pages.rs:41-58 calls mailbox.list {project_id} with no limit. app.rs:1263 sends unhandled events to refresh_page, which re-runs pages::refresh for the current page. client.rs:48/200-205 returns Error::Protocol('frame exceeds 2 MiB') from the reader loop. That ends the connection, and app.rs:1267-1275 marks the GUI disconnected and breaks out of its loop, so reconnecting is manual. With several sessions per project, and agent-to-agent mailbox traffic on top of the system broadcasts, about 1-2k messages of a few KB each is realistic over weeks.
v1.correction: Only the Mailbox page (and the Board, through task.list) triggers this. Other pages do not call mailbox.list. The mirror connection uses a 32 MiB limit (mirror.rs:41); the control connection uses 2 MiB. Fixes, in priority order: (1) bound the reply with a default limit and a before/since cursor, like mailbox.outbox, which already takes a LIMIT (notes.rs:641); (2) cap the stored text of system broadcasts, since the notification already carries the full summary; (3) make an oversized response fail only that request instead of tearing down the control connection.

v2.reason:
(a) The code does what the finding says.
- notes.rs:660-689 registers MailboxList with e.register and builds SQL ending in "ORDER BY m.sent_at, m.id" (684) with no LIMIT. For the user, session is None, so every message in the project comes back. MailboxListIn (relay-bus ops/notes.rs:55) has no limit field.
- Messages are deleted only by project.remove (workspace.rs:355-356). recovery.rs prunes the audit log only. SPEC "Mailbox ... persistent" and D26 ("preserves history") make keeping history intentional. Nothing documents fetching all of it in one reply.
- The GUI calls mailbox.list {project_id} (pages.rs:44, 53) when the page opens (navigate -> refresh_page, app.rs:1360). It also calls it on every event that reaches the final else at app.rs:1263-1264: task.changed, mailbox.*, notify.*, overlap.changed, usage/device/run.changed and others. Each time it clears and rebuilds one GTK row per message (pages.rs:124-154).
- The engine writes each response as one unbounded line (socket.rs:296-321).
- The control client returns Err(Protocol("frame exceeds 2 MiB")) from its reader loop when a line passes 2 MiB (client.rs:48, 200-205). That ends the connection. app.rs:1267-1275 then shows "Engine disconnected" and leaves the loop. Reconnecting is manual (app.rs:970-973).

(b) Who triggers it, and how often: the user's own normal use, with no attacker needed.
- Mail sources:
  - '*' broadcasts. Because from="system", the reporting session is itself a recipient, so these are always stored. They come from turn ends (session.rs:285-292, 1415-1422), done (1212-1219) and blocked reports (1403-1411).
  - Assignment notices (session.rs:56).
  - Guardrail decision mail (guardrail.rs:450/487/658/743).
  - Agent-to-agent mail, which COMMS_HINT and the reviewer prompt at session.rs:150 actively encourage.
- Broadcast rate is capped by the record_agent_notification dedupe: one per unread card per session/task link (test repeated_reports_coalesce_unread_cards_and_do_not_replay_alerts). So that rate follows how often the user reads cards, plus new tasks and sessions.
- Message size: the installed Claude Code 2.1.292 sends the full last_assistant_message in Stop-hook input. Neither mailbox.send nor done summaries have a length cap.
- Size model: each row costs about 183 bytes of JSON plus its text. 2 MiB is reached at about 1,750 messages averaging 1 KB, about 3,000 at 500 B, and about 5,400 at 200 B. For a project run with several concurrent agents, that is weeks to months, not days.
- Once past the threshold, every Mailbox visit fails, every time.

(c) What happens to the user.
- The GUI's control/event connection drops. Events, notification updates and guardrail prompts stop arriving. Every Ui::call fails, including lifecycle ops, because app.rs:1112 checks self.client first. That blocks launches, board edits and guardrail approvals until a manual Reconnect.
- After a reconnect while still on Mailbox, the next unhandled event re-runs the fetch and drops the connection again. The only way out is to navigate away first.
- The page stays broken for that project permanently. The only in-product remedy is removing the project.
- No data is lost.

(d) Severity: high fits "unbounded growth in normal use" ending in a hard, deterministic failure. It is not critical: Mailbox is a secondary page, the state is recoverable, and terminals survive.

(e) The proposed fix is in the right direction but needs the corrections below.
v2.correction:
Corrections to the impact:
- Terminals are not disconnected. Each pane opens its own socket (terminal.rs:476 Client::connect in attach_and_render). Panes are torn down and re-attached only when the user clicks Reconnect (app.rs connect(), 1139-1142).
- The lock-hold growth is minor. message_recipients has PRIMARY KEY (message_id, session_id), so the correlated subqueries are index lookups, and at the 2-5k rows where 2 MiB bites the query takes milliseconds. The real costs are the reply size and the full GTK rebuild per event.
- "1,000-2,000 messages" assumes a 1-2 KB average text. A mixed average gives about 2,500-5,000 messages.

Extra trigger: mailbox.new events carry the full message text (notes.rs:625, session.rs:293, 1217, 1411) on the same 2 MiB connection. A single message over about 2 MiB would drop the GUI on any page. There is no text cap (notes.rs:220-226). This is rare, since model output limits make such a message unlikely.

task.list (related): it is unbounded (task.rs:836-863, every non-deleted task including done ones, with body and changelog). The Board also refreshes after every refresh() (app.rs:1441), so past 2 MiB it would drop the GUI right after each reconnect. Reaching that takes about 800 or more tasks with multi-KB bodies and changelogs, so it is less likely.

Fix refinements:
1. A plain LIMIT on the current ascending order would show the oldest 200 messages and hide new mail. Return the newest N for the user view (ORDER BY sent_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT n+1, then reverse) with a before cursor and a next value, as task.activity already does (task.rs:788-827). Keep agents' oldest-first unread_only behavior. Update MailboxListIn and BUS.md §10.7.
2. In the GUI, request one page at a time, refresh only on mailbox.new and mailbox.changed, and append rows instead of rebuilding.
3. In client.rs, recover the response id from the line prefix (Response serializes v and then id first, which shape() at client.rs:34-45 already relies on). Discard the rest of an oversized line and fail only that request, instead of returning Err from the reader loop.
4. Capping stored broadcast text (the notification keeps the full summary) and mailbox.send text is sound. Pruning conflicts with D26 and with task.activity's task-linked messages, so it is a product decision, not part of the fix.

findings.title: Each integration run leaves a full checkout, its build output and a relay/integration-<id> branch on disk forever, and the GUI offers no way to discard them
findings.evidence: run() creates <repo>/.relay/integrations/<id> on branch `relay/integration-{id}` (integration.rs:86-104). It merges, runs project.build_cmd inside that checkout (152-165) and finishes as passed, failed or conflict with both left in place (214-224, fail()). Only integration.discard removes them (58-68), and it is Actors::UserOnly (ops/git.rs:145-146). The native client requests integrations with build:true (code_git.rs:738-741), lists them showing `.take(3)` (code_git.rs:581) and never calls integration.discard. integration.list stops at `LIMIT 100` (integration.rs:49), so older runs drop out of every listing. project.remove deletes the integrations rows but removes only pool worktrees of open sessions (workspace.rs:326-343, 370). Recovery's dirty-worktree scan and branch_cleanup look only at .relay/worktrees and session branches. D38: the worktree 'survives for inspection until explicit discard'.
findings.impact: Every 'test together' click, and every agent integration.request (builders may call it), costs a full checkout plus a full build: several GB for a Rust or Gradle project. That space is never reclaimed, and the runs soon drop out of every listing. Branches pile up in `git branch`, and the project-root watcher also walks the nested checkouts.
findings.fix: Discard automatically. When a run reaches a terminal state, remove its worktree (purging build output) and delete its branch; keep only a conflict checkout, and only for a bounded time (until the next integration or N days). Alternatively, expose Discard in the Code view and add a retention sweep for old integrations on the existing branch-cleanup thread. Have project.remove remove .relay/integrations/* as well.

v1.reason: In crates/relay-core/src/handlers/integration.rs:85-104, run() creates <repo>/.relay/integrations/<id> on branch relay/integration-<id>, merges, and runs build_cmd inside it (152-172). Every terminal state (passed, failed, conflict) leaves the worktree; set_state uses COALESCE(?2, worktree), so the path stays recorded. Only integration.discard (58-68) removes it and deletes the branch, and that op is Actors::UserOnly (crates/relay-bus/src/ops/git.rs:145-146). The native client calls integration.request with build:true (code_git.rs about 738-741) and integration.list (about 581), shows only .take(3) runs, and never calls integration.discard; rg finds no other reference in apps/relay-native. integration.request has no actor restriction, so agents can trigger runs too. integration.list is capped at LIMIT 100 (49). project.remove deletes the integrations rows (workspace.rs:370) and removes only open sessions' pool worktrees, leaving .relay/integrations/* and the branches orphaned with no record at all. D38 says the worktree 'survives for inspection until explicit discard', but the GUI provides no explicit discard, so each 'test together' run costs a permanent checkout plus build output.
v1.correction: D38 makes keeping the worktree for inspection intentional. The defect is the missing discard path in the GUI and the absence of any retention policy, not the retention itself. High holds under 'unbounded growth in normal use' when the Code view's test-together action is used: several GB per run for Rust or Gradle builds. If that feature is rarely used, medium would also be defensible.

v2.reason:
(a) The code does what the finding says.
- crates/relay-core/src/handlers/integration.rs:85-104 creates `<repo>/.relay/integrations/<id>` on branch `relay/integration-<id>`. It merges at 124-143, builds at 153-176 (only when `project.build_cmd` is set), and can deploy.
- Every terminal state keeps the checkout and the branch: Passed at 216-225, and Failed or Conflict through fail() (244-253, which passes path None). Because of `worktree=COALESCE(?2,worktree)` at 284, the path recorded at 91-100 stays.
- Only two paths remove a checkout: integration.discard (58-69, `Actors::UserOnly` at crates/relay-bus/src/ops/git.rs:145-146), or a discard that lands while the worktree is being created (113-123).
- Nothing else sweeps them:
  - `branch_cleanup::candidates` (branch_cleanup.rs:74-80) looks only at closed-session branches.
  - Recovery's dirty scan (recovery.rs:261-268) looks only at `pool_dir`.
  - `git.clean_merged` (handlers/git.rs:693-705) skips branches checked out in a worktree.
  - `project.remove` deletes the rows (workspace.rs:370) but removes only open sessions' pool checkouts (326-343).
  - `app.resources` measures only open sessions' worktrees (app.rs:182-196), so the space never appears in the GUI.

(b) Who can trigger it, and how often.
- The user, from the Code view → Git → MERGE TEST panel (apps/relay-native/src/code_git.rs:673-750). Its copy reads "Safely test agent branches together in a disposable worktree", and it sends `build:true`.
- Nothing in apps/relay-native calls integration.discard, worktree.remove or worktree.disk.
- The branch picker's delete button requires the branch to be merged and not checked out in any worktree (code_git.rs:1114-1122), so it never applies to these branches.
- Builder agents have integration.request by default (handlers/settings.rs:36; BUS.md:464), with no rate limit, and they cannot discard.
- The only ways out are `relay cmd integration.discard` from a terminal (relay-cli main.rs:36) or manual git.
- Every run leaks, without exception. On this machine, though, none of about 10 Relay-managed repos has a `.relay/integrations` directory or a `relay/integration-*` branch. The feature has not been used yet, so the leak is latent.

(c) What happens when it fires. No data is lost. Each run leaves:
- a checkout of the tracked files: about 18 MB for this repo, and much more for LFS-heavy Unreal repos, whose working copy is smudged;
- if a build command is configured, the full build output (this repo's own `target/` is 16 GB);
- a git worktree entry and a branch.

The checkouts pile up as "relay/integration-N · Checkout" in the Code view's CHECKOUTS & BRANCHES picker (project_files.rs:147-158) and in the Devices page's worktree list, with no remove action. The Devices page's `worktree.list` call (tools_devices.rs:630, include_dirty defaulting to true) also dirty-scans each one. After project.remove, the checkouts are orphaned with no record.

(d) Severity. High fits "unbounded growth in normal use". This is a first-class flow: SPEC §8 (SPEC.md:212-216) ends it with "→ discard", and the UI promises a disposable worktree. It leaves GBs per use once a build command is set, with no way to reclaim the space from the GUI and nothing in the resources view. Medium would also be defensible, because growth needs repeated deliberate use and this user has not used the feature yet.

(e) The proposed fix is incomplete. See the correction.
v2.correction:
1. Build output is left only when `project.build_cmd` is set. It is NULL by default: project.add does not set it (workspace.rs:202). Without it, each run leaves only a checkout of tracked files. "A full checkout plus a full build: several GB" holds only once a build command is configured.

2. "The runs soon drop out of every listing" is wrong. `worktree.list` enumerates git worktrees, so the checkouts stay listed in the Code view's CHECKOUTS & BRANCHES picker and on the Devices page, and the branches stay in the branch list. None of those offers a remove or delete action. What drops out is `integration.list`: the GUI shows 3 rows and the API returns 100. The checkouts are missing only from the resources/disk view.

3. The watcher point is mechanically true: notify 8.2's recursive inotify walks `.relay`, and events there are filtered by `is_generated_path` (watch.rs:157-187). The cost is negligible, though: a 16 GB Rust `target/` has about 2,400 directories against a 524,288 watch limit. Drop it from the impact.

4. Fix caveats:
   - Auto-discarding every terminal run would break `device.run` and `device.build` with `integration_id`, which require state `passed` and the recorded worktree (device.rs:982-1016). It would also defeat D38's "survives for inspection". Instead, purge build output when a run finishes, and keep a bounded number of checkouts (for example the latest passed or conflict run per project, or N days), removed by a sweep that runs off the store lock and skips live states.
   - Do not expose the current `integration.discard` in the GUI as it stands. It is registered with `Engine::register` and runs `worktree::remove(.., purge=true)` inside the store transaction. That means `purge_build` (a directory walk plus `remove_dir_all` of multi-GB output), `dir_size`, and `git worktree remove`, `git worktree prune` and `git branch -D` through plain `Command::output`, not `proc::output_with_timeout` (worktree.rs:26-34, 339-371). Exposing it would freeze the bus for seconds per discard. Move the disk work to `register_staged` or `after_commit` first.

5. A separate, related issue worth its own finding: nothing resets an integration left in queued, merging, building or deploying when the engine exits mid-run. Recovery has no handling for integrations, and the only UPDATEs are in integration.rs. Such a row makes `project.remove` and `workspace.remove` refuse permanently, even with force (workspace.rs:303-307, 164-169). With no discard in the GUI, the user cannot clear it there.

findings.title: Crash recovery kills whatever process now owns a session's recorded pid, without checking that it is still the session's process
findings.evidence: For every session still marked spawning, running, idle or blocked, recovery runs `Some(p) if pty::pid_alive(p as u32) => { // alive but not ours (we just started) — reap unless it was already` followed by `kill_wait(p as u32);` (recovery.rs:84-93). pid_alive is only `kill(pid, 0) == 0` (pty.rs:394-396). kill_wait signals -(pid) and pid with SIGTERM, then SIGKILL (recovery.rs:20-35). Step 1 has already killed every real orphan identified by its environment, so a pid that is still alive here is in practice a different process that reused the number.
findings.impact: After any unclean end of the engine (power loss, kernel panic, OOM kill or SIGKILL, which is exactly when recovery matters), the session rows keep their pids. On the next start, possibly after a reboot when pids restart low, any same-user process that now has one of those pids is terminated. If it leads a process group (a shell, a browser, a desktop component), the whole group goes with it.
findings.fix: Check identity before signalling. Store the child's start time (/proc/<pid>/stat field 22) or the boot id with the pid and compare them, or check /proc/<pid>/environ for this session's RELAY_SESSION and RELAY_STORE as step 1 does. Otherwise just mark the row restorable without killing anything, and never signal -pid unless that process group was recorded as Relay's.

v1.reason: recovery.rs:84-93: for every session row in spawning/running/idle/blocked, `Some(p) if pty::pid_alive(p as u32)` calls kill_wait(p), and kill_wait (recovery.rs:20-35) sends SIGTERM and then SIGKILL to both -(pid) and pid. pid_alive is only `kill(pid,0)==0` (pty.rs:394-396), so it checks nothing about who owns the pid. Step 1 (relay_children, pty.rs:411-429) has already reaped every process whose /proc environ carries this instance's RELAY_INSTANCE, RELAY_STORE and RELAY_SESSION. Whatever still answers at a recorded pid is therefore almost always a different process that reused the number. A clean shutdown is not affected: engine.rs:632-676 marks sessions restorable with pid=NULL. The rows keep their pids only after an unclean end (SIGKILL, OOM, power loss). After a reboot, desktop processes get pids from a similar low range on every boot, so a match with a stale session pid is realistic. When it happens, a same-user process is killed, along with its whole group if it leads one. Other users' processes are safe because kill returns EPERM, so pid_alive is false.
v1.correction: The decisive lines are recovery.rs:84-93, with kill_wait at recovery.rs:20-35. The simplest fix is to drop the kill from step 2 entirely: step 1 already reaps by identity, so step 2 should only mark rows restorable. If a fallback is wanted, check /proc/<pid>/environ for this session's RELAY_SESSION/RELAY_STORE before signalling, as step 1 does.

findings.title: Stopping a device run or build, or discarding an integration, does not stop the processes it started
findings.evidence: stream_command spawns `Command::new(shell).args(["-lc", &format!("{command} 2>&1")])`, with fish in production (device.rs:1821-1828). It sets no process group and stores only that child (1841). RunRuntime::stop calls `child.kill()` on that pid (crates/relay-core/src/device.rs:403-408): SIGKILL to the fish wrapper, not to Gradle, adb or whatever the shell forked. After a stop, the worker returns Streamed::Stopped (1843-1845) or leaves the logcat loop (1776-1777) without waiting on the killed child. device.run.stop releases the device lease immediately (handlers/device.rs:268-270). Integration builds: shell() runs `fish -lc build_cmd` through `.output()` with no deadline and keeps no handle (integration.rs:228-241). integration.discard only deletes the row and the worktree (58-68), and Engine::shutdown has no record of integrations at all (engine.rs:633-659).
findings.impact: Stop leaves `./gradlew installDebug`, or a compound run_cmd, running. It can still install onto the phone after its lease was released, which is the clobber that device leases exist to prevent, and it keeps CPU and disk busy. Each stop also leaves a zombie shell under the engine. A hung integration build (a watch-mode build_cmd, or a test waiting on a lock) pins its worker thread and stays in 'building' forever, which also blocks project.remove (workspace.rs:303-306). Discarding such an integration deletes the worktree out from under a build that is still running.
findings.fix: Spawn run, build and integration commands with process_group(0), and on stop, discard and shutdown signal the whole group: kill(-pid, SIGTERM), a grace period, then SIGKILL. Always wait() on the child after killing it. Give integrations a RunRuntime-like handle registered in the engine, with a deadline, so that discard and shutdown can stop them.

v1.reason: In crates/relay-core/src/handlers/device.rs, stream_command (about 1806-1850) spawns `fish -lc "{command} 2>&1"` with no process_group and stores only that child. RunRuntime::stop (crates/relay-core/src/device.rs, about 403-408) calls child.kill() on that single pid. Fish does not exec its -c command, so gradlew/java, adb and other descendants keep running. Their stdout pipe is closed once the worker returns, but the JVM ignores SIGPIPE, so Gradle carries on. After a stop the worker returns Streamed::Stopped at the stopped() check inside the read loop, or before take_child, without waiting on the killed child, which leaves a zombie. The logcat loop also returns early without waiting. The RunStop handler releases the run's device leases immediately (handlers/device.rs about 263-270), so an orphaned `installDebug` can still install after another run has taken the lease. Integration builds: handlers/integration.rs shell() (228-242) runs `fish -lc` with a plain .output(), with no deadline and no handle kept. integration.discard (58-68) removes the worktree without stopping anything. project.remove refuses while integrations_live > 0 (workspace.rs about 303-306), so a hung build blocks project removal indefinitely.
v1.correction: Contrast with proc::output_with_timeout, which already uses process_group(0) and kill(-pid). The same pattern applies here: spawn with process_group(0), have stop() signal -pgid, then wait(). Separately, integration.discard calls worktree::remove synchronously inside an Engine::register handler, which is slow disk work under the store mutex; that is a distinct invariant issue. Integration deploy also runs run_cmd on a device without taking a device lease.

findings.title: remote.json is read, modified and saved with no lock and a single shared tmp file: concurrent handshakes lose updates or corrupt it, and a corrupt file stops `relay serve --remote` from starting
findings.evidence: save() writes `path.with_extension("json.tmp")`, opened with create and truncate, then renames it over remote.json (registry.rs:159-179). admit() does Registry::load, then touch or redeem, then save on every handshake (bridge.rs:72-94). It runs on whichever tokio worker handles that connection (#[tokio::main] is multi-threaded), with no mutex or file lock. `relay remote pair`, `revoke`, `name` and `via` do the same from another process (remote.rs:226-287). A scratchpad experiment (exp/race.py) reproduced the interleaving open(trunc) A, open(trunc) B, write A, write B, rename, rename: the second rename fails with ENOENT and remote.json ends with trailing bytes from the longer write, which fails to parse ('Extra data'). The last_seen timestamps written by jiff vary in length, so two writers' documents differ in size. load() treats an unparseable registry as an error (registry.rs:146-157), and serve_with_door propagates it with `Registry::load(...)?` (remote.rs:114).
findings.impact: A phone that opens several connections at once, or reconnects while `relay remote pair` is running, can cause three failures. A freshly issued pairing code or device credential can be lost. A device that was just revoked can come back. Or remote.json can be corrupted. Once it is corrupt, every phone is refused, and the next run.sh launch (`serve --remote`) exits before the engine is ready.
findings.fix: Serialize registry changes with a process-wide Mutex plus an flock on remote.json.lock around each load-modify-save. Write to a unique tmp name in the same directory (tempfile), fsync, then rename. Make serve_with_door log the error and continue without the door rather than abort the engine on a bad registry.

v1.reason: The mechanism is real. Registry::save (crates/relay-remote/src/registry.rs:159-179) always writes to the fixed path `path.with_extension("json.tmp")`, opened with create+truncate, and then renames it over remote.json. Nothing serializes this. bridge::admit (bridge.rs:68-96) does a synchronous load, then redeem/touch, then save. It runs inside a task spawned per connection on the multi-threaded #[tokio::main] runtime (direct.rs:37-47, tunnel.rs:118-122). The CLI subcommands pair, revoke, name and via do their own load-modify-save from a separate process (relay-cli/src/remote.rs:192-287), so two writers can overlap. Two overlapping saves can lose an update: a touch written after a pair or revoke can drop the new pending code or bring back a revoked device. Two saves that interleave inside the open/write window can leave trailing bytes, and the second rename then fails with ENOENT. A corrupt file is fatal at the next start: serve_with_door does `Registry::load(...).map_err(...)?` (remote.rs:114). That contradicts the comment just above it, which says the door should "never [be] a reason for the engine not to start". The trigger, though, is much rarer than the finding implies. (1) Only authenticated handshakes reach save(). Unknown device, bad proof and an invalid pair code all return before it, so a LAN peer cannot drive writes. (2) The phone does not open several handshakes at once. RelayClient.greetFirst races its routes only up to the greeting, keeps the first and closes the rest, and sends hello on the winner only. (3) In admit the window between load and save is a few file syscalls, microseconds to about a millisecond. So it takes two phones admitted in the same instant, or a CLI pair/revoke landing inside that sub-millisecond window. The race exists but almost never fires in a single-user app.
v1.correction: Severity is low, not medium. Its realistic triggers are a phone reconnect that lands in the same sub-millisecond as `relay remote pair`/`revoke`, or two different phones admitted at once. One phone opening several connections is not a trigger, because the phone only sends hello on one socket. A secondary point is the more useful fix and holds regardless of the race. A remote.json that will not parse, for any reason including a hand edit, aborts `serve --remote` at remote.rs:114 after the engine has already started, despite the comment that the door must never stop the engine. That line should log the error and run without the door. For the race, use a process-wide Mutex around admit's load-modify-save plus an flock on a sidecar lock file shared with the CLI, and a unique tmp name (or tempfile::NamedTempFile in the same directory) for the write.

findings.title: The branch sweep re-examines every closed session's branch every 20 minutes, forever, so its cost and log volume grow with history
findings.evidence: candidates() selects every closed session with a non-base branch (branch_cleanup.rs:76-79), and session rows are never deleted. run() evaluates each one (361-368). A branch that no longer exists comes back 'gone' after one `git rev-parse` subprocess and is skipped without recording that result (213-217, 365), so the next sweep checks it again. Each unmerged branch costs about 8 git subprocesses: worktree list, config, three rev-parse calls, merge-base, cherry and rev-list. A merged branch whose checkout was kept also gets a `git status` of that checkout (296). Every subprocess goes through output_with_timeout, which starts 2 pipe-drain threads. record() logs `tracing::info!(... "kept session branch")` for every kept branch on every sweep, even when it is not audited (377-381). The sweeper runs every 20 minutes (42, 429-456).
findings.impact: Background work and log volume scale with the total number of sessions ever closed. At tens of sessions a day, a sweep spawns thousands of git processes within months, against SPEC §15's idle budget, and appends thousands of identical log lines a day to the engine log.
findings.fix: Persist the result. Mark the session's branch as cleaned (a column or a branch_cleanup table) when it is gone or deleted. Skip unmerged branches whose tip has not changed since the last verdict by storing the tip with the verdict. Run `git worktree list` once per repository per sweep. Log a kept branch only when its verdict changes.

v1.reason: In crates/relay-core/src/branch_cleanup.rs:74-80, candidates() selects every closed session with a non-base branch. Session rows are only deleted by project.remove (workspace.rs:360). evaluate() resolves the branch with a git rev-parse subprocess (213). run() skips 'gone' rows without persisting anything (365), so every sweep repeats that subprocess for every branch already deleted. A kept, unmerged branch runs about 8-10 git subprocesses each time: worktree list, config, rev-parse for the remote tip, config merge, two base resolves, merge-base and cherry per base, and rev-list (237-290). A pushed branch also re-asks gh once an hour (GH_RECHECK). record() logs tracing::info!("kept session branch") for every kept branch on every sweep, whether or not the outcome is audited (379). spawn_sweeper runs every 20 minutes (42, 429-455). Each subprocess goes through output_with_timeout, which spawns 2 drain threads and polls.
v1.correction: The cost is real but runs at background priority on its own thread and never holds the store, so it is ongoing waste rather than a freeze. Medium is the ceiling. A minimal fix is to remember 'gone' and unchanged-tip 'kept' verdicts (in memory keyed by (repo, branch, tip) like GH_CACHE, or in a column), and to log kept branches only when their verdict changes.

findings.title: Once the store is older than the audit retention window, almost every launch VACUUMs the whole database before the socket opens, with the copy held in RAM because temp_store=MEMORY
findings.evidence: Launch recovery deletes audit rows older than audit.retention_days (default 180; recovery.rs:183-206), then runs `if pruned > 0 { conn.execute_batch("VACUUM") }` (217-221) on the engine connection. tune() sets that connection to `temp_store = MEMORY` (store.rs:539). Recovery runs in serve::start before SocketServer::start (serve.rs:23, 36). Once the store is older than the window and Relay is used daily, each launch finds rows that crossed the cutoff since the previous launch, so pruned > 0 almost every time. D151 notes that the audit table is most of the database.
findings.impact: After about six months of use, each start rewrites the entire database. Because temp_store is MEMORY, SQLite builds VACUUM's temporary copy in memory, so peak RSS is roughly the store size. Every page is then written through the WAL, and the WAL file keeps that size because no journal_size_limit is set. Start-up time grows with the store, and run.sh waits only 15 s (run.sh:34) before reporting 'Relay engine did not become ready'. Conversely, an engine that is never restarted never prunes at all.
findings.fix: Prune in bounded batches on a background thread, and periodically rather than only at launch. Use auto_vacuum=INCREMENTAL with PRAGMA incremental_vacuum, or VACUUM only when the free-page count is a large fraction of the file (freelist_count against page_count). Run that statement with temp_store=FILE, and set journal_size_limit.

v1.reason: recovery.rs:182-221: the prune deletes audit rows with ts < days_ago(retention) (default 180), and `if pruned > 0 { conn.execute_batch("VACUUM") }` follows. Once the oldest rows cross the cutoff, any launch after a day of use deletes something, so the whole file is VACUUMed. That runs in serve::start (serve.rs:23) before SocketServer::start (serve.rs:36), so the bus is unavailable for the whole time. tune() sets temp_store=MEMORY on that connection (store.rs:539), so VACUUM's temporary copy lives in RAM. In WAL mode the rewritten pages go through the WAL, and nothing sets journal_size_limit (grep finds none). Real data backs up the scale: the user's live store (~/.local/share/relay-v4/dev/store.db) is already 192 MB after about a month, so at the 180-day window it would be several hundred MB to GB-scale. Each restart would then pay seconds of rewrite against run.sh's 15 s readiness deadline (run.sh:33-37, which starts target/debug/relay). The claim that an engine left running never prunes is also correct: the prune exists only in launch recovery.
v1.correction: The VACUUM is at recovery.rs:217-221 and the prune at recovery.rs:182-206. A threshold on freelist_count/page_count, or auto_vacuum=INCREMENTAL with incremental_vacuum, removes the cost on every launch. Pruning can also run periodically on a worker, with the work split into bounded batches.

findings.title: Nothing ever empties Relay's trash, deletes detached task attachments or hard-deletes soft-deleted rows; the reconcile pass promised in BUS.md §5.4 does not exist
findings.evidence: file.delete moves the entry to <worktree>/.relay/trash/<id>/payload (file.rs:226-233), and only file.restore moves it back (238-249). Task attachments are written to <data dir>/attachments/<task>/<id>-<name> (task.rs:481-488, 519-526). task.detach deletes the row but keeps the file so undo can re-attach it (1021-1047). project.remove deletes the attachments and file_trash rows without touching the files (workspace.rs:362, 369). BUS.md §5.4 says soft-deleted tasks, modules, notes and files are hard-deleted 'by the reconcile pass' after undo.grace_days. undo.grace_days exists only as a default value (settings.rs:42), and app.reconcile returns an empty action list (handlers/app.rs:137-141). .relay/ is listed in .git/info/exclude, so the trash does not show up in git status.
findings.impact: Every file or folder deleted from Relay's file tree in the primary checkout keeps its bytes forever; deleting a build folder from the UI frees nothing. Every attachment that was ever detached, or that belonged to a removed project, stays in the data directory. There is no UI to empty either one.
findings.fix: Implement the documented pass, either on the existing branch-sweep thread or at launch. It should hard-delete trash entries, file_trash rows and attachment files whose rows are gone or whose undo window (grace_days or audit retention) has passed, and project.remove should delete the project's attachment files. Alternatively, change BUS.md to say the trash is kept until emptied and add an 'empty trash' op.

v1.reason: In crates/relay-core/src/handlers/file.rs (Delete handler, about 221-237), file.delete renames the entry into <root>/.relay/trash/<id>/payload. The only code that moves it back out is file.restore, and no code anywhere deletes trash payloads. The native client offers 'Move to trash' and 'Undo trash' but has no empty-trash action. The app.reconcile handler (handlers/app.rs about 137-141) returns an empty action list. BUS.md §5.4 (about 288-292) promises a hard delete 'by the reconcile pass' after undo.grace_days, but grace_days exists only as a settings default (settings.rs:42) and is read nowhere in crates/. task.detach (task.rs about 1021-1047) deletes the row and keeps the file for undo, and nothing ever deletes it. project.remove deletes the attachments and file_trash rows (workspace.rs about 362, 369) and leaves the files. Soft-deleted tasks, modules and notes are likewise never hard-deleted.
v1.correction: For a pool worktree, the trash goes away when the worktree is removed, so the permanent leak applies to the primary checkout (and to attachment files in the data directory). Severity medium is right: disk use grows silently, with no correctness impact. This is also docs drift: BUS.md §5.4 describes a pass that does not exist.

findings.title: `relay mcp` handles one tool call at a time, so an agent's bus.wait (up to 1 h) blocks all its other Relay tools and ignores cancellation
findings.evidence: serve() reads stdin one line at a time and awaits `handle(...)` before reading the next line (mcp.rs:20-31). Notifications, including notifications/cancelled, are not acted on (38-41). call_tool opens a connection and awaits client.call with no timeout (138-149). In the engine, bus.wait blocks that connection's loop for timeout_ms, clamped to 1 s-3,600,000 ms, and never watches the socket for the client going away (socket.rs:400-449). The bootstrap hint tells agents to bus.wait on guardrail.request_resolved after a guardrail.request (grants.rs:24-28).
findings.impact: While an agent waits for an approval, any other Relay MCP call it makes sits unread in the pipe until the wait times out, which can be up to an hour; this covers parallel tool calls and the next turn after the user interrupts the agent. MCP pings go unanswered meanwhile. In the engine, the waiter, its broadcast receiver and its socket stay alive until the timeout even after the MCP process has exited.
findings.fix: Handle each tools/call on its own task (for example a JoinSet keyed by request id) and write responses through a single stdout writer. Honour notifications/cancelled by aborting that task, which drops its socket. In the engine, race the bus.wait future against the connection's read half with select, so a closed client ends the wait.
